https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.23759.Summary: Fudan University researchers developed Selfment, a fully self-supervised framework for accurate object segmentation that operates without manual annotations, pre-trained models, or post-processing. The method achieves new state-of-the-art performance in unsupervised saliency detection and demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization for camouflaged object detection, often rivaling supervised approaches.
Problem: Traditional object segmentation relies on costly, time-consuming pixel-level human annotations, limiting scalability and adaptation to new domains.
Prior "unsupervised" or "weakly supervised" segmentation methods often still depend on human-provided signals, pre-trained supervised components, or post-processing.
Existing attempts to derive segmentation directly from self-supervised features frequently resulted in coarse or unstable masks requiring heavy post-processing.
Method: Utilizes a frozen DINOv3 backbone to extract dense, object-centric patch features, followed by Normalized Cut (NCut) for an initial coarse foreground-background bipartition.
Introduces an Iterative Patch Optimization (IPO) module to iteratively refine these initial coarse masks into highly accurate, spatially coherent pseudo-labels.
Employs a lightweight segmentation head trained in a self-supervised manner using IPO-generated pseudo-labels, leveraging a combination of contrastive, Dice, and BCE losses.
Results: Achieves new state-of-the-art results in unsupervised saliency detection with Fmax gains of +4.0% on ECSSD and +7.0% on DUTS, benefiting from higher inference resolutions.
Demonstrates remarkable zero-shot generalization for camouflaged object detection, outperforming all prior unsupervised methods and often rivaling supervised models (e.g., 0.910 S_m on CHAMELEON).
Ablation studies confirm the critical role of Iterative Patch Optimization (IPO), which alone yields significant performance gains (e.g., +4.8% Fmax on ECSSD).
Takeaways: Dense, object-centric features from self-supervised vision transformers like DINOv3 are robust enough for high-quality dense prediction tasks without any human labels.
Iterative refinement of graph-based segmentations (IPO) effectively transforms noisy initial masks into clean, semantically consistent pseudo-labels.
A lightweight network can be reliably trained with self-generated labels using specific loss functions to learn stable and transferable object representations.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.06569.Title: Penguin-VL: Exploring the Efficiency Limits of VLM with LLM-based Vision Encoders
https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.06569.Summary: The Tencent AI Lab's Penguin-VL framework constructs compact Vision-Language Models (2B and 8B parameters) by initializing the vision encoder directly from a text-only Large Language Model, rather than traditional contrastive vision models. This approach achieves leading performance across diverse image and video understanding benchmarks, including document, chart, and temporal video reasoning, while using significantly less pre-training data.
Problem: State-of-the-art Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are often very large, hindering deployment on resource-constrained mobile and edge devices.
Traditional VLM vision encoders, pre-trained with contrastive learning, suppress fine-grained visual cues critical for complex generative VLM tasks.
Many existing VLMs struggle with consistent performance across both image and video understanding tasks, particularly temporal reasoning.
Method: A Penguin-Encoder is introduced, initialized directly from a text-only Large Language Model (Qwen3-0.6B) and trained with generative-aligned objectives, including a reconstruction-based relation loss.
A Temporal Redundancy-Aware (TRA) token compression mechanism is developed for efficient video encoding, dynamically allocating token budgets based on frame characteristics.

A comprehensive, multi-stage training pipeline utilizes high-quality, large-scale multimodal recaption and QA datasets for image and video understanding, incorporating image region grounding and multi-granularity video annotations.
Results: Penguin-VL 2B and 8B models achieve leading performance on numerous image benchmarks, including DocVQA (96.2 for 8B), ChartQA (90.5 for 8B), InfoVQA, and MathVista, often surpassing larger baseline models.

The models demonstrate robust video understanding, excelling in long-form video comprehension (LongVideoBench 67.0 for 8B) and precise temporal reasoning (Charades-STA 61.4 for 8B), significantly outperforming competitors.

Ablation studies confirm that LLM-initialized vision encoders and the relation loss are critical for performance gains, with the Penguin-Encoder outperforming traditional contrastive encoders using substantially less pre-training data (~240M vs. >40B samples).
Takeaways: Initializing vision encoders from text-only Large Language Models offers a more synergistic and efficient approach to multimodal learning than using contrastively pre-trained vision models.

Incorporating a relation loss in the vision encoder training is crucial for preserving fine-grained visual details and effectively modeling inter-patch relationships, improving generative task performance.

Achieving state-of-the-art performance in VLMs is possible with compact model sizes (2B and 8B parameters) by focusing on improved visual representation and aligned training, rather than solely on increasing model scale.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.04333.Title: What Does Flow Matching Bring To TD Learning?
https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.04333.Summary: Researchers from Carnegie Mellon University explain the empirical success of flow-matching critics in Temporal Difference (TD) learning, attributing their benefits to Test-Time Recovery and Plastic Feature Learning rather than distributional modeling. This approach significantly enhances performance and stability in high update-to-data online reinforcement learning, yielding up to 2x higher final performance and 5x better sample efficiency.
Problem: The underlying mechanisms driving the observed empirical gains and robustness of flow-matching critics in RL remained largely unexplained.
Prevailing hypotheses attributed flow-matching success to implicit modeling of return distributions, similar to distributional RL, requiring rigorous testing.
Standard TD learning algorithms suffer from pathologies like plasticity loss and sensitivity to non-stationary targets, which existing methods often address with explicit regularization.
Method: The `floq` architecture, which uses flow matching solely for expected Q-value parameterization, was utilized to disentangle its benefits from distributional RL.
A rigorous combination of theoretical analysis and empirical validation was applied to formalize and test two proposed mechanisms: Test-Time Recovery (TTR) and Plastic Feature Learning.
Controlled experiments, including injecting staleness, adding noise, and freezing features, were designed to validate these mechanisms and compare flow-matching critics against monolithic baselines.
Results: Flow-matching critics demonstrate approximately 2x higher final performance and 5x better sample efficiency in high update-to-data online RL on OGBench tasks compared to monolithic baselines.

They exhibit strong Test-Time Recovery, maintaining comparable performance even when 25-50% of initial integration steps use stale parameters, and show significantly higher robustness to noisy TD targets.

The learned features in flow-matching critics display improved plasticity, allowing adaptation to non-stationary TD targets through feature reweighting, while monolithic critics suffer severe performance collapse when features are frozen.
Takeaways: The success of flow-matching critics is not due to their ability to model return distributions; an expected-value flow-matching critic performs comparably to or better than distributional variants.

Test-Time Recovery (TTR), enabled by iterative integration, allows flow-matching critics to correct imperfect intermediate estimates and dampen errors, with error effects decaying polynomially with integration steps.

Dense velocity supervision during training induces Plastic Feature Learning, allowing flow-matching critics to adapt to non-stationary TD targets by reweighting existing features rather than modifying them directly.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.03944.Title: Spatial Causal Prediction in Video
https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.03944.Summary: Researchers from the National University of Singapore and collaborators introduce Spatial Causal Prediction (SCP), a novel task and benchmark, SCP-Bench, designed to evaluate AI models' ability to infer unseen past or predict future spatial states and their causal relationships from video. Evaluations reveal a substantial gap between state-of-the-art multimodal large language models and human performance, highlighting causal reasoning as a primary limitation and showing that model scaling and providing textual causal scaffolds enhance capabilities.
Problem: Existing spatial intelligence research predominantly focuses on the perceptual understanding of *observed* static or dynamic scenes.

Current AI systems lack the ability to infer *unseen* past or anticipate *future* spatial states, and to understand the underlying causal relationships driving these dynamics beyond immediate observations.
There was no comprehensive benchmark to systematically evaluate models on dynamic, causal, and predictive spatial understanding.
Method: Formalized Spatial Causal Prediction (SCP) as a multi-choice question-answering task that requires models to reason beyond directly visible video content.

Constructed SCP-Bench, a benchmark comprising 2,500 QA pairs across 1,181 video clips, designed with 8 question types, 2 causal directions (backward/forward), 4 perspective settings (single/multi-view), and diverse scene categories.

Developed a semi-automatic pipeline leveraging GPT-5 for initial content generation (dense captions, QA candidates) followed by rigorous, multi-round human verification and refinement to ensure high-quality and consistent annotations.
Results: The top-performing MLLM, GPT-5, achieved 66.24% accuracy on SCP-Bench, significantly trailing human performance of 89.61%, demonstrating a considerable 23.37% gap in unseen spatio-temporal causal prediction.

Open-source models, such as Qwen3-VL-235B (61.04%), exhibited performance comparable to, and occasionally surpassed, proprietary models, while spatially specialized models often underperformed general-purpose MLLMs.

Models struggled particularly with multi-view prediction and forward prediction tasks, and showed limited temporal extrapolation benefits across short, mid, and long prediction horizons, maintaining an average accuracy of 46.8%.
Takeaways: Spatial causal reasoning, rather than pure visual perception, is the primary bottleneck preventing current MLLMs from accurately predicting unseen spatial changes.

MLLMs show limited ability to leverage temporal continuity or inherently understand causal dynamics, as indicated by minimal performance changes when processing single frames versus multi-frame video or when input videos are temporally inverted.

Model scaling consistently yields performance improvements, and providing 'causal scaffolds'—specifically textual descriptions of future spatial states—offers the most substantial gains for enhancing causal prediction capabilities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.03857.Title: DeepScan: A Training-Free Framework for Visually Grounded Reasoning in Large Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.03857.Summary: DeepScan is a training-free framework that equips large vision-language models (LVLMs) with robust visually grounded reasoning by mimicking human bottom-up scanning processes. It achieved a 16.3% accuracy improvement over vanilla Qwen2.5-VL-7B on the V* benchmark, outperforming existing training-free and several 70B general LVLMs.
Problem: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) struggle with visually grounded reasoning, especially in complex or noisy scenes.
LVLMs suffer from "attention sink" and "attention drift," leading to hallucinations and suboptimal performance in fine-grained understanding.
Existing training-free grounding methods primarily use a top-down localization strategy that is susceptible to noisy contexts and similar objects.
Method: A **Hierarchical Scanning** component employs a bottom-up visual grounding paradigm to robustly localize visual evidence using local cues and multi-scale extraction.
A **Refocusing** component optimizes the evidence view by collaboratively searching for an evidence-centric crop with an optimal surrounding context.
An **Evidence-Enhanced Reasoning** component integrates both fine-grained localized evidence and the optimized coarse-grained view into a multi-image prompt for the LVLM's final answer generation.
Results: DeepScan achieved 90.6% overall accuracy on V* with Qwen2.5-VL-7B, demonstrating a 16.3% improvement over the vanilla model and outperforming other training-free baselines by up to 6.3%.
It attained state-of-the-art performance on perception tasks like V* Attribute (93.0-93.9%), surpassing several 70B general LVLMs and competing favorably with RL-based methods.

The framework scaled effectively across diverse LVLMs (7B to 72B parameters), improving Qwen2.5-VL-72B by 9.4% on V* while achieving a favorable performance-latency trade-off (3.1s vs. 6.9s for DeepEyes).
Takeaways: Mimicking human bottom-up scanning provides a more robust mechanism for visually grounded reasoning, especially for fine-grained details, compared to traditional top-down methods.
Point-based proxies, which fuse geometric and semantic information, combined with morphological post-processing, are effective for extracting integral and precise visual evidence from local cues.

Optimizing the contextual view around localized evidence, through both zoom-in and zoom-out actions, significantly enhances reasoning performance by balancing necessary information with distracting context.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.03818.Title: Pretrained Vision-Language-Action Models are Surprisingly Resistant to Forgetting in Continual Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.03818.Summary: Large pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models show surprising resistance to catastrophic forgetting in continual robot learning, maintaining performance on past tasks with minimal Experience Replay. The research from The University of Texas at Austin and Microsoft demonstrates that pretraining fundamentally alters continual learning dynamics, enabling rapid recovery of seemingly forgotten knowledge.
Problem: Robots must continually acquire new skills without catastrophically forgetting previously learned abilities, a challenge exacerbated by the stability-plasticity dilemma.

Traditional continual learning approaches for smaller, non-pretrained policy models have relied on complex algorithms (e.g., large replay buffers, regularization, architectural isolation) to mitigate forgetting.
The behavior of large-scale pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models regarding catastrophic forgetting was largely unexplored, especially in robot policy learning.
Method: Empirically investigated the continual learning dynamics of pretrained VLAs (Pi0, GR00T N1.5) on sequential robot manipulation tasks using the LIBERO benchmark.
Utilized Experience Replay (ER) as the primary continual learning mechanism, evaluating its effectiveness with varying and often small replay buffer sizes.
Conducted ablations to isolate the role of pretraining, analyzed knowledge retention through component swapping, and measured the efficiency of recovering 'forgotten' skills via finetuning.
Results: Pretrained VLAs achieved near-zero to positive Negative Backward Transfer (NBT) across multiple LIBERO benchmarks, outperforming non-pretrained models by 2-4x, even with only 2% of data in the replay buffer.
The vision-language backbone was identified as the dominant source of apparent forgetting when swapping components, correlating with task diversity.
Seemingly forgotten skills in VLAs were rapidly recovered, with models like Pi0 regaining peak performance in less than 10% of the original training steps, indicating knowledge retention.
Takeaways: Pretrained VLAs exhibit remarkable inherent resistance to catastrophic forgetting, achieving near-zero or even positive backward transfer with simple Experience Replay.
Large-scale pretraining is integral to mitigating forgetting, particularly in low-data replay regimes, enabling high forward transfer while preserving old skills.
Apparent performance degradation on previous tasks in VLAs often signifies inaccessible rather than entirely lost knowledge, allowing for rapid recovery with minimal finetuning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.03276.Title: Beyond Language Modeling: An Exploration of Multimodal Pretraining
https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.03276.Summary: Researchers from FAIR, Meta, and NYU developed a unified autoregressive Transformer framework, Transfusion, to explore native multimodal pretraining from scratch. This approach reveals that Representation Autoencoders (RAEs) effectively unify visual understanding and generation, enables the emergence of world modeling from general data, and scales efficiently with Mixture-of-Experts architectures.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) are limited by their sole reliance on text, often described as a 'lossy compression of reality,' which hinders true world understanding.
The design space for natively multimodal models trained from scratch is opaque, with existing approaches often adapting language models or using separate visual representations for different tasks.

There is a lack of systematic, controlled experiments to isolate factors influencing multimodal capabilities and scaling properties without confounding effects from prior language-centric pretraining.
Method: Develops Transfusion, a single, autoregressive, decoder-only Transformer backbone, pretrained from scratch with a unified objective for both language and vision.
Explores Representation Autoencoders (RAEs) combined with frozen semantic visual encoders to create a unified visual representation suitable for both understanding and generation tasks.
Systematically investigates the impact of diverse data sources, architectural choices (such as Mixture-of-Experts), and scaling properties through controlled experiments on multimodal performance.
Results: RAE-based visual representations leveraging semantic encoders consistently surpass VAE-based encoders across both visual understanding (VQA) and generation benchmarks.

Multimodal co-training with diverse visual and language data yields synergistic improvements, with general pretraining outperforming scaling task-specific data for VQA, and raw video driving world modeling capabilities that transfer with minimal in-domain alignment.

Mixture-of-Experts architectures demonstrate superior performance and efficiency in multimodal scaling compared to dense models, fostering natural modality specialization and harmonizing the identified scaling asymmetry where vision is more data-hungry than language.
Takeaways: Representation Autoencoders (RAE) using semantic encoders provide an optimal unified visual representation, excelling in both visual understanding and generation, simplifying multimodal architectures.
Diverse visual and language data are complementary, with multimodal co-training yielding synergy that enhances downstream capabilities like VQA and naturally leads to world modeling.
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures enable efficient and effective multimodal scaling, naturally inducing modality specialization and harmonizing the scaling asymmetry between vision and language.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.03241.Title: UniG2U-Bench: Do Unified Models Advance Multimodal Understanding?
https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.03241.Summary: UniG2U-Bench provides a diagnostic testbed for evaluating whether generative capabilities in multimodal AI models genuinely advance their understanding. The research, benchmarking over 30 models, reveals that unified models often incur an "alignment tax" on general understanding, but explicit generation (GtA) can improve performance in transformation-intensive tasks like spatial reasoning, with gains primarily driven by the underlying VLM's foundational representations.
Problem: It was unclear whether generative capabilities in unified multimodal models truly enhance understanding or if there's an inherent "alignment tax" from joint training.
Existing multimodal benchmarks lacked the diagnostic rigor and task variety to systematically evaluate the "Generation-to-Understanding" (G2U) synergy.

Many current understanding benchmarks could be solved by converting visual inputs into text, obscuring scenarios where visual transformations or externalized reasoning are crucial for true visual comprehension.
Method: Introduced UniG2U-Bench, a large-scale diagnostic testbed comprising 3,000 instances across 7 high-level categories and 30 fine-grained subtasks, specifically designed to probe G2U interactions.
Developed a dual-protocol prompting system (Direct vs. Generate-then-Answer - GtA) to rigorously compare how explicit visual externalization impacts understanding against direct inference.

Benchmarked 35 diverse models (base VLMs, native unified models, agentic unified models) under controlled conditions, using metrics like G2U Gain (Δ) and diagnostic scores for GtA intermediate fidelity.
Results: Unified models showed an overall performance degradation compared to base VLMs on general understanding tasks, with consistent gains observed only in specific Spatial Intelligence and Visual Illusion tasks.

GtA typically degraded performance across most logic-intensive tasks but yielded noticeable gains in transformation-intensive regimes such as Maze navigation, Sliding puzzles, and Multi-Step Spatial Reasoning.

The utility of intermediate visual generations depends on their fidelity and structural necessity; high fidelity does not guarantee performance gains in perception tasks, while low fidelity causes severe harm in logic-intensive tasks.
Takeaways: Unified models generally exhibited an "alignment tax," underperforming their purely discriminative VLM counterparts on standard understanding tasks, suggesting objective interference from joint generative and discriminative training.

The GtA paradigm risks "visual error propagation" from inaccurate intermediate generations, often degrading performance in logic-intensive tasks, but acts as a beneficial "Visual Chain-of-Thought" for transformation-intensive tasks.

G2U gains are predominantly determined by the inherited foundational representations from the base VLM rather than the specific generative architecture, indicating the importance of core understanding capabilities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.03026.Title: Any Resolution Any Geometry: From Multi-View To Multi-Patch
https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.03026.Summary: Researchers at KAUST developed the Ultra Resolution Geometry Transformer (URGT) for joint depth and surface normal estimation from a single image at arbitrary resolutions. This method reinterprets a high-resolution image as a set of patches for a multi-view transformer, significantly enhancing detail and global consistency at resolutions up to 8K, achieving a 49% reduction in AbsRel for depth and lower mean angular error for normals on UnrealStereo4K.
Problem: Existing joint depth-normal estimation models operate at low resolutions due to computational constraints, leading to a loss of fine detail in high-resolution imagery.
Patch-based refinement methods improve local detail but often introduce discontinuities or inconsistencies at patch boundaries due to a lack of global reasoning.
Multi-view transformer architectures offer global reasoning but are primarily designed for multi-view scenarios at moderate resolutions, not high-resolution monocular inputs.
Method: The Ultra Resolution Geometry Transformer (URGT) re-imagines a high-resolution single image as a 'set of patches' processed by a multi-view transformer architecture.
It employs a specialized attention mechanism, combining intra-patch attention for local detail with cross-patch attention using global positional encoding (RoPE) to ensure global coherence.
A GridMix patch sampling strategy is introduced during training to improve spatial robustness and generalization by probabilistically using various grid configurations.
Results: URGT reduced the AbsRel for depth by 49% (from 0.0582 to 0.0291) and RMSE by 35% (from 2.17 to 1.31) on UnrealStereo4K compared to prior state-of-the-art.
For surface normal estimation, the joint model reduced the mean angular error from 23.36° to 18.51° on UnrealStereo4K, outperforming Metric3D v2.

The method demonstrates strong zero-shot and cross-domain generalization, preserving sharp boundaries, fine details, and smooth transitions across resolutions up to 8K in real-world images with an inference time of approximately 0.97 seconds for a 4K image.
Takeaways: Treating a single high-resolution image as a collection of interacting patches processed by a transformer allows for simultaneous high-detail local refinement and global consistency.
Global positional encoding (RoPE) effectively maintains spatial relationships across patches, crucial for seamless geometric transitions and preventing boundary artifacts.
Probabilistic patch sampling (GridMix) acts as a data augmentation strategy, enhancing the model's ability to generalize across different image compositions and improve inter-patch coherence.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.02556.Title: Through the Lens of Contrast: Self-Improving Visual Reasoning in VLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.02556.Summary: A framework called Visual Contrastive Self-Taught Reasoner (VC-STaR) improves Vision-Language Model visual reasoning by using visual contrast to reduce hallucinations in model-generated rationales. This approach yields an average performance increase of 2.6% across various benchmarks, notably achieving a 5.7% improvement on MMVP and 3.2% on the Hallusion Benchmark for hallucination mitigation.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are highly susceptible to generating visual hallucinations within their reasoning paths.

Existing self-improving methods, successful in Large Language Models (LLMs), fail to effectively verify or rectify visual inaccuracies in VLM rationales, often prioritizing textual priors over actual visual evidence.
This limitation leads to unreliable and misleading explanations, hindering the development of robust visual reasoning in VLMs.
Method: The Visual Contrastive Self-Taught Reasoner (VC-STaR) framework is introduced, leveraging the observed phenomenon that VLMs perform better visual discrimination when contrasting information.

A scalable and task-agnostic pipeline was developed to automatically curate high-quality contrastive VQA pairs from 21 diverse datasets, resulting in the VisCoR-55K dataset of median-difficulty samples.

A three-step 'Thinking-Contrasting-Rethinking' process refines initial VLM rationales: a coarse rationale is generated, then a contrastive analysis with a counterpart is performed, and finally an LLM rectifies the rationale using the visual insights from the contrastive step.
Results: VC-STaR consistently outperforms the base Qwen2.5VL-7B model with an average performance improvement of 2.6% across all evaluated benchmarks.
The framework effectively mitigates visual hallucinations, showing improvements of +5.7% on MMVP and +3.2% on the Hallusion Benchmark.

VC-STaR surpasses existing self-improving baselines and models trained on state-of-the-art visual reasoning datasets, while also proving model-agnostic, providing consistent gains across Qwen2.5VL-3B and InternVL2.5-8B architectures.
Takeaways: VLMs demonstrate enhanced visual perception and accuracy when tasked with contrasting visually similar images or synonymous questions, suggesting 'VLMs can see better during contrasting'.
Curating contrastive VQA pairs based on an optimal difficulty level (median-difficult) significantly benefits reasoning, preventing 'overthinking' easy problems and focusing on solvable challenges.

The combination of initial VLM rationale generation, VLM-driven contrastive analysis, and subsequent LLM-based rethinking effectively rectifies visual hallucinations by grounding rationales in clearer visual evidence.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.02188.Title: Multi-Head Low-Rank Attention
https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.02188.Summary: Multi-Head Low-Rank Attention (MLRA) enhances large language model inference efficiency and scalability for long contexts in distributed environments. It achieves state-of-the-art perplexity and zero-shot reasoning accuracy while demonstrating substantial decoding speedups and reduced Key-Value (KV) cache loading compared to previous methods.
Problem: Long-context inference in large language models (LLMs) is bottlenecked by Key-Value (KV) cache loading, leading to memory-bound operations and high latency during decoding.

Existing efficient attention mechanisms, such as Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA), use a single, non-partitionable latent head, which creates a sharding bottleneck for Tensor Parallelism (TP) in distributed decoding.
This sharding limitation forces each GPU in a TP configuration to redundantly load the entire KV cache, negating the benefits of TP for weight sharding and increasing memory traffic.
Method: MLRA decomposes the latent attention computation into independent, partitionable low-rank branches by shifting the summation from the KV computation to the attention output.

MLRA-4 explicitly splits the latent head into four distinct latent heads, where attention is computed independently for each branch using the full set of query heads, and the resulting outputs are summed. This design inherently supports efficient 4-way Tensor Parallelism.

Variance calibration is integrated through scaling factors for query and KV latent states and attention outputs to ensure variance alignment between RoPE and NoPE components and maintain stable training.
Results: MLRA-4 achieved the lowest average perplexity (13.672) and highest average zero-shot accuracy (58.84%) across tested benchmarks using a 2.9B parameter Llama-3 model.
It delivered a 2.8x speedup over MLA and up to 1.26x speedups over GQA for long-context decoding (up to 2M tokens) on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU.
MLRA-4 reduced per-device KV cache loading to 1.5d_h with 4-way Tensor Parallelism, significantly outperforming MLA (4.5d_h) and GLA-2 (2.5d_h) and matching GTA with fewer TP devices.
Takeaways: Shifting the summation of block-wise projections from the KV computation to the attention output enables the creation of independent, low-rank attention branches that can be efficiently sharded.

Decomposing the latent attention mechanism into multiple distinct heads (e.g., four in MLRA-4) directly resolves the sharding bottleneck observed in single-head latent attention approaches under Tensor Parallelism.

Applying variance-calibrating scaling factors to latent states and attention outputs is crucial for stable convergence and improved perplexity when combining multiple attention components and branches.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.01097.Title: Understanding LoRA as Knowledge Memory: An Empirical Analysis
https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.01097.Summary: Researchers from KAIST, Samsung SDS, and NYU systematically audited Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) as a parametric knowledge memory for large language models, mapping its intrinsic capacity, optimization strategies, and scalability in multi-LoRA systems. They found LoRA to be a controllable memory unit with finite capacity, benefiting from high-density synthetic data, and performing best in hybrid systems with in-context learning, offering computational advantages for repeated knowledge access.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) possess a static knowledge base fixed during pretraining, making continuous updating with new facts or domain-specific information costly and prone to catastrophic forgetting.

Existing inference-time methods like In-Context Learning (ICL) and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) face limitations such as context window constraints, high computational costs, and retrieval fragmentation.
A systematic understanding of LoRA's fundamental memory properties, capacity, composability, and limitations for knowledge storage, beyond its conventional use for task adaptation, was lacking.
Method: Conducted the first systematic empirical analysis of LoRA as a knowledge memory, utilizing custom benchmarks (PhoneBook, PaperQA) and existing ones (CounterFact, NarrativeQA, QuALITY) for fine-grained investigation.

Explored LoRA's behavior across four dimensions: its intrinsic memory properties, optimization strategies for a single LoRA, scaling to multi-LoRA systems, and its performance in long-context and hybrid memory scenarios.
Experiments involved Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B base models, varying LoRA rank, knowledge size, synthetic data formats, routing mechanisms, merging strategies, and combining LoRA with ICL or RAG.
Results: LoRA's memory capacity scales with rank but shows diminishing parameter efficiency at higher ranks, with peak efficiency often found at lower ranks (e.g., r=4).
Synthetic data (QA format from GPT-4.1) substantially improved memorization over raw text, achieving stronger gains and better token-efficiency.

Under ideal (oracle) routing, multiple small LoRAs outperformed a single large LoRA, but practical embedding-based routing incurred significant performance drops, necessitating merging strategies like TIES-merging to partially recover performance.

LoRA-based methods demonstrated computational advantages with shorter pure inference times for repeated queries, particularly when preloaded, and achieved stronger performance when combined with ICL compared to standalone LoRA, RAG, or ICL.
Takeaways: LoRA modules function as finite, rank-dependent memory units where increasing rank enhances capacity but with diminishing returns in parameter efficiency.
High-density, task-aligned synthetic data (especially QA pairs) significantly boosts LoRA's memorization and token-efficiency, with diverse data combinations offering complementary benefits.

While multi-LoRA systems theoretically scale capacity, practical challenges like routing accuracy and interference during merging are critical bottlenecks, requiring robust strategies like TIES-merging for partial mitigation.
LoRA acts as a powerful complementary memory axis, performing strongest when integrated with external context methods like ICL, which helps restore narrative cohesion for complex reasoning tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00905.Title: pySpatial: Generating 3D Visual Programs for Zero-Shot Spatial Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00905.Summary: The pySpatial framework equips Multi-modal Large Language Models with explicit and robust 3D spatial reasoning by generating executable Python programs that orchestrate specialized 3D vision tools. This approach achieved 58.56% accuracy on the MINDCUBE benchmark, outperforming GPT-4.1-mini by 12.94%, and successfully guided real-world robot navigation.
Problem: Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) consistently struggle with robust 3D spatial reasoning, especially in multi-view settings, limiting their application in robotics and embodied AI.
Current MLLM approaches often rely on implicit 'imagination' or 2D cognitive maps, which lack explicit geometric grounding and robustness for complex 3D tasks.
Sparse and costly explicit 3D supervision in MLLM training data hinders the development of reliable language-to-3D correspondences.
Method: Developed `pySpatial`, a visual programming framework that enables MLLMs to generate executable Python programs, orchestrating a defined API of specialized spatial tools.
The API includes functions for 3D scene reconstruction from 2D image sequences, natural language descriptions of camera motion, novel view synthesis, and camera manipulation (e.g., rotate, move).

Implemented a multi-stage process where an MLLM generates a program, an interpreter executes it to produce explicit intermediate outputs (text or images), and the MLLM then integrates these outputs with the original query to form the final response.
Results: Achieved an overall accuracy of 58.56% on the MINDCUBE benchmark, outperforming the strongest proprietary model (GPT-4.1-mini) by 12.94% and specialized spatial models by 16.5%.

Successfully demonstrated zero-shot real-world robot navigation, guiding a quadrupedal robot through complex indoor environments with geometrically consistent motion plans, where MLLM baselines struggled.

Showed robustness to different MLLM code agents and 3D reconstruction backbones, with performance improvements consistently attributed to the 3D visual programming paradigm rather than the specific underlying MLLM.
Takeaways: Grounding MLLMs' spatial reasoning in explicit 3D geometry via reconstructive vision tools and visual programming yields superior performance compared to implicit or 2D cognitive map methods.
A modular API for 3D spatial operations allows MLLMs to generate interpretable, compositional programs for multi-step, multi-view spatial queries, enhancing transparency and verifiability.

The zero-shot visual programming paradigm effectively leverages advanced 3D computer vision techniques without gradient-based fine-tuning, demonstrating strong generalizability across various MLLMs and reconstruction backbones.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00515.Title: MLLM-4D: Towards Visual-based Spatial-Temporal Intelligence
https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00515.Summary: MLLM-4D equips Multimodal Large Language Models with 4D spatial-temporal intelligence, enabling them to perceive and reason about dynamic 3D environments from 2D video inputs. It establishes new state-of-the-art performance on the MLLM4D-Bench benchmark with an average score of 72.7%, substantially surpassing proprietary models like Gemini 2.5 Pro.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) lack robust capabilities for 4D spatial-temporal intelligence, specifically perceiving and reasoning about the evolution of 3D space over time from purely visual inputs.
A critical bottleneck is the scarcity of high-quality, large-scale 4D instructional data, as manual annotation is costly and unscalable.

Existing MLLMs, even those with 3D understanding, are constrained to static scenes or rely on auxiliary 3D geometric inputs, struggling with dynamic environments without complex architectural changes.
Method: A cost-efficient, automated data curation pipeline converts existing stereoscopic video datasets into large-scale, high-quality 4D instructional data, including MLLM4D-2M (SFT), MLLM4D-R1-30k (RFT), and MLLM4D-Bench (evaluation).
A two-stage post-training framework is applied to standard MLLM architectures, avoiding architectural modifications.

Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) builds foundational 4D understanding, followed by Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RFT) that incorporates a Spatiotemporal Chain-of-Thought (ST-CoT) prompting strategy and physics-grounded Spatiotemporal reward functions.
Results: MLLM-4D achieves state-of-the-art performance on the MLLM4D-Bench benchmark with an average score of 72.7%, significantly outperforming proprietary models like Gemini 2.5 Pro (46.6%) and other open-source MLLMs.

The framework demonstrates strong generalizability and robustness on the out-of-distribution VLM4D benchmark, maintaining superior performance over base models and specialized 3D spatial reasoning models.

Ablation studies confirm that the scalable data curation and the hierarchical post-training strategy, particularly the physics-grounded Spatiotemporal Reward, are crucial for building robust 4D understanding and reasoning, with performance scaling observed with increased data.
Takeaways: Leveraging existing stereoscopic video datasets with an automated pipeline is a scalable and cost-effective method to generate large volumes of high-quality 4D instructional data.

Standard MLLM architectures can acquire sophisticated 4D spatial-temporal reasoning capabilities through a hierarchical post-training strategy, negating the need for complex architectural modifications.

Integrating a Spatiotemporal Chain-of-Thought and physics-grounded rewards effectively grounds the model's reasoning in visual physics, leading to more interpretable and physically plausible 4D understanding.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00207.Title: VisRef: Visual Refocusing while Thinking Improves Test-Time Scaling in Multi-Modal Large Reasoning Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00207.Summary: VisRef introduces a training-free framework that dynamically re-injects relevant visual tokens into Multi-modal Large Reasoning Models during inference, effectively countering visual token dilution and boosting reasoning accuracy. The approach leverages Determinantal Point Processes for visual token selection and an adaptive stopping criterion, yielding consistent performance improvements across various benchmarks.
Problem: Multi-modal Large Reasoning Models (MLRMs) experience "visual token dilution," where the influence of visual input diminishes during extended textual reasoning.
This dilution causes MLRMs to increasingly rely on textual priors rather than visual grounding, leading to potential performance degradation and visual hallucinations.
Prior test-time scaling methods for MLRMs extend textual reasoning but do not actively maintain visual grounding, failing to address the fading visual information problem.
Method: VisRef proposes a training-free framework that iteratively selects and re-injects a coreset of relevant visual tokens at each step of an MLRM's reasoning process.
It utilizes Determinantal Point Processes (DPPs) to select visual tokens that optimally balance relevance to the current textual reasoning state with visual diversity.
An adaptive stopping criterion, based on the entropy of the model's predicted answer distribution, efficiently determines when to terminate reasoning and provide a final answer.
Results: VisRef consistently achieved substantial accuracy improvements, for example, boosting InternVL-3.5-8B's performance on MathVista by 5.4% absolutely over standard thinking and 4.5% over textual self-reflection.
The framework demonstrated superior test-time scaling, delivering higher accuracy for equivalent computational budgets compared to parallel text-only reasoning across all evaluated benchmarks.
When combined with training-based methods like "Look-Back," VisRef produced the best overall performance, achieving 83.1% on MathVista, highlighting its additive value.
Takeaways: Dynamically refocusing visual attention at test time can significantly improve MLRM performance on visual reasoning tasks without requiring additional model training.
The use of Determinantal Point Processes provides a principled method for selecting visual tokens that are both relevant to the ongoing reasoning and diverse in their visual coverage.
VisRef offers complementary gains and can be combined with existing training-based methods, indicating its potential as an orthogonal enhancement for improving MLRMs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00142.Title: Evaluating Theory of Mind and Internal Beliefs in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00142.Summary: An evaluation of multi-agent systems augmented with Theory of Mind and internal beliefs, verified by symbolic logic, reveals that the efficacy of these cognitive enhancements is highly conditional on the underlying LLM's capacity. Top-performing LLMs like ChatGPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet maintain robust performance, while less capable models may benefit or be hindered by the added cognitive load.
Problem: Large Language Model (LLM) agents often exhibit inconsistent and variable performance in complex multi-agent systems, particularly when dealing with partial or conflicting information.
Existing multi-agent systems frequently rely on rigid rules, limiting their adaptability and scalability in dynamic, real-world environments.
A lack of comprehensive, synergistically integrated architectures that combine Theory of Mind (ToM), internal belief systems, and logical verification within LLM-based multi-agent systems.
Method: A novel agent architecture was proposed, integrating Theory of Mind (ToM) capabilities, internal belief states (IB), and logical verification using an Answer Set Programming (ASP) solver.
The agents were deployed in an interactive city resource allocation simulation, designed to be dynamic and require effective coordination under resource consumption scenarios.

A modular agent design allowed for systematic evaluation of four configurations (Base, ToM Only, IB Only, ToM + IB) across diverse LLMs, with iterative logical consistency checking for internal beliefs.
Results: ChatGPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet consistently achieved the highest median final health scores (e.g., around 70% for ChatGPT-4o), showing high reliability in collaborative resource management.

Less capable LLMs, such as Meta Llama 3.1 8B, showed varied impacts, with performance sometimes improving (e.g., ToM Only at 38.33% vs. Base 35.00%) and sometimes declining (e.g., ToM+IB at 30.02%) when cognitive mechanisms were added.

For models with restricted reasoning abilities, the additional cognitive load from simultaneously processing ToM and internal beliefs, coupled with iterative logical verification, could lead to miscoordination or decreased overall performance.
Takeaways: The choice of the underlying LLM is a dominant factor, with models like ChatGPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet demonstrating superior and more consistent performance regardless of added cognitive mechanisms.

The effectiveness of integrating explicit cognitive mechanisms (ToM, internal beliefs with ASP verification) is not universally beneficial and depends critically on the LLM's inherent capacity to process complex information and manage cognitive load.

While logical verification of internal beliefs can promote more organized thinking and prevent errors, its ultimate utility is contingent on the LLM's ability to produce consistent and interpretable natural language inputs for the solver.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.24041.Title: Look Carefully: Adaptive Visual Reinforcements in Multimodal Large Language Models for Hallucination Mitigation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.24041.Summary: Researchers from the University of Science and Technology of China and Nanyang Technological University developed the Adaptive vIsual Reinforcement (AIR) framework to mitigate hallucinations in multimodal large language models. The training-free, inference-time method selectively reinforces salient visual information using prototype-based token reduction and Optimal Transport-guided patch selection, achieving reduced hallucination rates across various MLLMs while maintaining general performance.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) frequently generate content that deviates from or contradicts visual input (hallucination), hindering their reliability for real-world applications.
Existing hallucination mitigation strategies are often computationally intensive, require costly human annotations (training-time), or can compromise stability/efficiency (inference-time).
Current vision-enhancement methods for MLLMs indiscriminately inject all visual tokens, including irrelevant background information, which can distract the model and exacerbate hallucinations.
Method: Introduced Adaptive vIsual Reinforcement (AIR), a training-free, inference-time framework that selectively amplifies critical visual evidence and suppresses redundancy within MLLMs' feed-forward networks.

Employed prototype-based token reduction, which condenses the numerous visual tokens into a compact subset by selecting the Top-Q most distinctive tokens based on their Euclidean distance to a global prototype.

Utilized Entropically Regularized Optimal Transport (OT) to quantify the fine-grained semantic alignment between the model's hidden states and cropped image patches, selecting and reinforcing only the most relevant visual patches.
Results: AIR consistently reduced hallucination rates across LLaVA-1.5-7B, Qwen-VL-Chat, and GLM-4V-9B on the CHAIR (e.g., LLaVA-1.5-7B CHAIR_S reduced from 22.0 to 18.4) and POPE benchmarks, demonstrating improved robustness without degrading general reasoning.
The framework operates with only a marginal increase in average latency (e.g., 2.07s for AIR vs. 1.68s for vanilla LLaVA-1.5-7B) and GPU memory, making it practical for real-world deployment.

Ablation studies confirmed that both prototype-based token reduction and OT-guided patch reinforcement contribute to hallucination mitigation, with optimal performance achieved when applying reinforcement in mid-to-deep Transformer layers (e.g., layers 24-32).
Takeaways: Indiscriminate re-injection of all visual tokens, including irrelevant noise, can be detrimental to MLLM performance by distracting the model from critical visual cues and potentially increasing hallucination.

Salient visual patches consistently exhibit higher semantic alignment with MLLM decoder hidden states than irrelevant background regions, suggesting that selective reinforcement of these areas is more effective.

Optimal Transport offers a more sensitive and principled measure for assessing the fine-grained semantic alignment between multimodal representations (hidden states and visual patches) compared to simpler distance metrics.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.23959.Title: Thinking with Images as Continuous Actions: Numerical Visual Chain-of-Thought
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.23959.Summary: The Numerical Visual Chain-of-Thought (NV-CoT) framework allows Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to generate continuous numerical bounding box coordinates for region-grounded reasoning. This approach achieves 59.5% Bounding-box IoU on the Vis-CoT-363K dataset with an ℓ1 loss and improves overall reasoning accuracy by up to 3.7% on the V*Bench benchmark.
Problem: Existing text-based Visual Chain-of-Thought (CoT) methods suffer from modality mismatch (continuous visual coordinates represented as discrete text tokens) and semantic fragmentation due to numerical tokenization.
Patch-based Visual CoT methods are constrained by fixed spatial granularity from vision backbones and often require extensive architectural changes, limiting flexible and precise region selection.
These limitations lead to imprecise localization, brittle numerical reasoning, and inefficient learning for MLLMs in complex visual reasoning tasks.
Method: NV-CoT augments the MLLM output head with lightweight linear layers to directly predict continuous numerical bounding box coordinates and a shared dispersion parameter, expanding the action space beyond discrete tokens.
The framework is compatible with Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) using regression losses (e.g., ℓ1 loss) for coordinates and also extends to Reinforcement Learning (RL) with GRPO-style algorithms.

For RL, it employs stochastic Gaussian or Laplace policies with reparameterized sampling, analytically tractable importance ratios, and KL divergence penalties for stable and efficient continuous policy updates.
Results: NV-CoT consistently outperforms its backbone models and larger MLLMs across V*Bench, HR-Bench 4K, and HR-Bench 8K, with up to a 3.7% overall accuracy improvement on V*Bench for SFT and 2.6% for RL.

The approach substantially improves localization precision, achieving 59.5% Bounding-box IoU on the Vis-CoT-363K dataset with ℓ1 loss, a gain of over 12 percentage points compared to the 47.3% of the text-based Vis-CoT.

Ablation studies confirm the superiority of the Laplace policy, the effectiveness of the shared uncertainty parameter, and demonstrate the robustness of the framework across hyperparameter variations.
Takeaways: Directly modeling bounding box coordinates as continuous actions resolves the modality mismatch and semantic fragmentation issues inherent in text-based Visual CoT, leading to more precise visual grounding.
Integrating probabilistic policies with reparameterization enables effective and stable application of Reinforcement Learning for continuous action spaces within existing MLLM architectures.
The Laplace policy (and ℓ1 regression loss) proves more robust and effective for bounding box localization tasks compared to the Gaussian policy (ℓ2^2 loss), yielding higher precision.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.23320.Title: ParamMem: Augmenting Language Agents with Parametric Reflective Memory
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.23320.Summary: Researchers from MBZUAI and Carnegie Mellon developed ParamMem, a parametric memory module that enhances language agents by encoding cross-sample reflection patterns directly into model parameters. This system consistently achieves substantial performance improvements across programming, mathematical reasoning, and multi-hop QA tasks while enabling self-improvement without reliance on stronger external models.
Problem: Existing self-reflection mechanisms in language agents often produce repetitive, inaccurate, or unhelpful outputs, hindering their ability to explore diverse solutions and diagnose errors.

Previous retrieval-based approaches to improve reflection diversity (e.g., DoT-bank) have limitations in capturing compositional patterns and are susceptible to embedding collapse, reducing retrieval effectiveness.
Empirical evidence shows a strong positive correlation (average Pearson coefficient of 0.76) between reflective diversity and task success in language agents.
Method: ParamMem builds a parametric memory module (`M_g`) by fine-tuning a lightweight LLM (e.g., LLaMA-3.1-8B with LoRA) on an auxiliary dataset of input samples paired with expert-generated 'global reflections'.
The fine-tuned ParamMem module generates diverse reflections via temperature-controlled sampling, encoding cross-sample patterns directly into its parameters.

ParamMem is integrated into agent frameworks (ParamAgent and ParamAgent-plus), unifying this parametric memory with existing episodic memory and, in the case of ParamAgent-plus, cross-sample memory (like DoT-bank) to condition the actor LLM.
Results: ParamAgent and ParamAgent-plus achieve consistent and substantial performance gains over state-of-the-art baselines across programming (HumanEval, MBPP, LiveCodeBench), mathematical reasoning (MATH), and multi-hop QA (HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA) tasks.

ParamMem significantly increases reflective diversity, evidenced by higher average pairwise cosine distances between reflections (0.351 vs. 0.200 for frozen LLM) and a larger optimal number of reflection clusters (K*=39 for ParamAgent vs. K*=11-33 for baselines).

The method demonstrates high sample efficiency, maintaining strong performance even when trained on a small dataset (e.g., 500 samples), and iterative self-teaching further improves performance without external supervision.
Takeaways: Introducing a parametric memory module for reflection generation provides an orthogonal and complementary source of diversity to episodic and cross-sample memories, enabling generalization of reflection patterns.
ParamMem allows for effective self-improvement of language agents using only the base model itself for data generation, without requiring stronger external models or explicit reward signals.
The approach facilitates weak-to-strong transfer, where a ParamMem module built on a weaker LLM can still effectively augment the reasoning capabilities of a stronger agent.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.22859.Title: From Blind Spots to Gains: Diagnostic-Driven Iterative Training for Large Multimodal Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.22859.Summary: Researchers from Peking University and Shandong University developed Diagnostic-driven Progressive Evolution (DPE), an iterative framework that diagnoses and corrects specific weaknesses in Large Multimodal Models (LMMs). DPE enables stable, continual performance gains, achieving state-of-the-art results in visual math (e.g., MathVista 76.2) and hallucination mitigation (e.g., HallusionBench 74.13) with significantly less data than traditional methods.
Problem: Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) struggle with identifying and correcting 'capability blind spots' due to reliance on static training data and fixed recipes, leading to inefficient learning on long-tail weaknesses.
There is a scarcity of high-quality, human-annotated multimodal reasoning data, which hinders the scalable and continuous improvement of LMMs.

Existing self-evolving LMM frameworks often lack interpretable diagnostics, leading to 'blind' evolution and potential distribution drift, and are limited by static image sets that restrict visual diversity and cause performance plateaus.
Method: Introducing the Diagnostic-driven Progressive Evolution (DPE) framework, an iterative 'diagnose-and-correct' loop that explicitly controls the category composition and question emphasis of training data based on identified model weaknesses.

Implementing an Adaptive Diagnosis Mechanism that provides interpretable failure attribution and capability decomposition across 12 dimensions, generating a structured report to guide subsequent data generation.

Developing a Multiple Agents Questioner System equipped with tool-use capabilities (e.g., web search, image editing) to dynamically source, filter, edit, and compose diverse, high-quality, and weakness-focused visual content and questions.
Results: DPE consistently achieved stable and continual performance improvements, setting new state-of-the-art records in visual math on MathVista (76.2) and MathVision (53.88), and leading HallusionBench with 74.13, surpassing larger models like GPT-4o (56.1 overall average) with an 8B parameter backbone (64.39 overall average).

The framework demonstrated exceptional data efficiency, achieving superior performance across key benchmarks (e.g., MMMU 56.44 vs 54.8, MathVista 69.5 vs 68.8) using only 3,000 iteratively generated samples, roughly 1/15th of a comparative static dataset.

Ablation studies confirmed that the diagnostic module is indispensable for maintaining stable evolution and preventing performance stagnation or regression, while image retrieval and editing tools are critical for expanding visual diversity and avoiding early performance plateaus on tasks like OCR and chart understanding.
Takeaways: Explicitly diagnosing a model's specific weaknesses and then generating targeted training data is crucial for stable and continuous improvement, mirroring efficient human learning processes.

Dynamically expanding visual context through image retrieval and editing tools, coupled with weakness-focused data generation, is essential for addressing long-tail reasoning challenges and preventing overfitting to narrow visual distributions.

Focusing on generating high-quality, moderately difficult samples for identified blind spots can achieve superior LMM performance with substantially less data compared to using large, untargeted static datasets.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.22766.Title: Imagination Helps Visual Reasoning, But Not Yet in Latent Space
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.22766.Summary: Researchers from Beijing Jiaotong University and Tsinghua University critically investigated the efficacy of latent visual reasoning (LVR) in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) and found that latent tokens exhibit limited causal influence on reasoning outcomes. They propose CapImagine, an explicit text-space imagination method, which demonstrated superior performance, including average improvements of 3.44% on HR-Bench and 2.6% on V* over existing LVR approaches.
Problem: The underlying mechanisms driving the effectiveness of Latent Visual Reasoning (LVR) in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) remained poorly understood.
It was unclear whether MLLMs truly performed deliberative visual reasoning within their latent space or if latent tokens served a more superficial role.
A lack of rigorous investigation into the causal validity and functional role of latent tokens in existing LVR methods existed.
Method: A Causal Mediation Analysis was conducted, modeling the LVR process as an Input → Latent Tokens → Final Answer causal chain, with targeted interventions on both input and latent tokens.
CapImagine was proposed, a text-space imagination method that converts semantic changes from intermediate visual manipulations into explicit textual captions for MLLMs.
A high-quality dataset was constructed by extensively rewriting and filtering existing MLLM training data, formalizing visual imagination directly in text space.
Results: Causal analysis confirmed latent tokens' high inter/intra-instance cosine similarity and their negligible impact on answer accuracy even after significant corruption, indicating limited causal activity.
CapImagine consistently outperformed latent-space baselines (e.g., Monet, LVR), achieving average improvements of 3.44% on HR-Bench and 2.6% on V*, and over 10 points on BLINK tasks.

Dependency analysis on CapImagine showed strong causal influence from its explicit text-form imagination variable, and the method achieved inference speeds comparable to latent-space alternatives while being twice as fast as some tool-augmented methods.
Takeaways: Latent tokens in current LVR methods are largely homogeneous, insensitive to input variations, and progressively collapse into highly identical states, indicating an 'Input-Latent Disconnect'.

Drastic alterations to latent tokens resulted in only marginal changes to model accuracy, demonstrating a 'Latent-Answer Disconnect' and suggesting they exert minimal causal influence on the final output.
Explicit, text-based imagination maintains diverse, causally active intermediate representations, supporting more faithful and effective visual reasoning than opaque latent-space operations.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.22703.Title: Enhancing Geometric Perception in VLMs via Translator-Guided Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.22703.Summary: Researchers at Tsinghua University and Guangdong Laboratory of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Economy developed GEOPERCEIVE, a benchmark for geometric perception, and GEODPO, a translator-guided reinforcement learning framework. This approach enhanced Vision-Language Models' ability to interpret geometric diagrams, boosting downstream reasoning accuracy by up to 39% on MathVista and substantially reducing geometric hallucinations.
Problem: Vision-language models (VLMs) demonstrate limitations in geometric perception, often misinterpreting fundamental geometric primitives and their relationships (e.g., confusing an intersection with a tangency).
Existing end-to-end benchmarks for geometric problem solving conflate visual misinterpretation with symbolic reasoning failures, making it difficult to precisely diagnose VLM limitations.
Current domain-specific languages (DSLs) for geometric problems suffer from ambiguity or verbose syntax, which hinders rigorous evaluation and stable model training.
Method: Introduced GEOPERCEIVE, an automatically generated benchmark featuring pixel-level geometric diagrams paired with unambiguous, canonical GEODSL programs, designed for isolated geometric perception evaluation.
Developed GEODPO (Translator-Guided Direct Preference Optimization), a reinforcement learning framework that uses an NL-to-GEODSL translator to provide fine-grained, DSL-level reward signals.

GEODPO fine-tunes VLMs to generate improved natural language descriptions by leveraging Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), which addresses permutation-equivalence and maintains alignment with the VLM's natural language pretraining.
Results: GEODPO consistently improved geometric perception scores (in-domain) by +14.2% to +26.46% across various VLM backbones compared to raw models.

The framework demonstrated superior generalization, improving out-of-domain perception by +3.68% to +8.0% and achieving substantial gains of up to 39.0% on the MathVista geometry subset for downstream reasoning.
Qualitative analysis showed a substantial reduction in geometric hallucinations, with GEODPO-trained models more accurately grounding visual elements and their relationships in diagrams.
Takeaways: A canonical and unambiguous Domain-Specific Language (GEODSL) is critical for precise, program-level evaluation and scalable, automated data generation in geometric perception tasks.

Employing a pre-trained NL-to-DSL translator effectively bridges the VLM's natural language output space to the formal geometric representation, enabling fine-grained supervision via reinforcement learning.

Trajectory-level reinforcement learning (DPO) applied to NL outputs provides superior generalization and robustness to distribution shifts compared to token-level supervised fine-tuning in improving VLM geometric perception.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21992.Title: PanoEnv: Exploring 3D Spatial Intelligence in Panoramic Environments with Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21992.Summary: Researchers introduce PanoEnv, a framework featuring a synthetic, geometry-grounded benchmark and a reinforcement learning method, which substantially improves Vision-Language Models' 3D spatial reasoning in panoramic images. The PanoEnv-RL model achieves a 132% relative gain in open-ended 3D reasoning, outperforming larger baselines and showing strong sim-to-real transferability.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) struggle with 3D spatial reasoning in 360° panoramic (ERP) images due to severe geometric distortions and misaligned 2D learning priors.
Existing VQA datasets for panoramic images lack precise, objective 3D geometric ground truth, hindering the development and evaluation of true 3D spatial intelligence.
Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) alone is insufficient for fostering complex, generative reasoning and robust 3D understanding in VLMs.
Method: Development of PanoEnv-QA, a large-scale VQA benchmark with over 14.8K geometry-grounded QA pairs programmatically generated from synthetic 3D environments (TartanAir), providing objective ground truth for depth, segmentation, and 3D bounding boxes.

Introduction of PanoEnv-RL, a 3D-aware reinforcement learning post-training framework using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on a VLM (Qwen2.5-VL-7B), equipped with a multi-faceted, geometry-aware reward system leveraging PanoEnv-QA's ground truth.

Implementation of a two-stage curriculum strategy for stable RL training, starting with structured questions and progressing to a balanced mixture of structured and open-ended questions to mitigate catastrophic forgetting and enhance generative spatial reasoning.
Results: Benchmarking reveals that state-of-the-art VLMs achieve low performance on PanoEnv-QA, with the best baseline (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) reaching only 49.34% overall accuracy and a mere 6.39% on open-ended questions.
PanoEnv-RL (GRPO-Balanced) on Qwen2.5-VL-7B improves overall accuracy to 52.93% and dramatically boosts open-ended question accuracy to 14.83%, representing a +132% relative gain over the baseline.

The PanoEnv-RL model demonstrates robust zero-shot transferability to real-world datasets like OSR-Bench, outperforming larger baselines (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL-72B) on tasks such as Object Counting and Relative Distance.
Takeaways: Current state-of-the-art VLMs are largely incapable of robust 3D spatial reasoning in panoramic environments, particularly for open-ended questions requiring precise metric or compositional relations.

Leveraging precise 3D geometric ground truth from synthetic environments for reinforcement learning reward signals, combined with a progressive curriculum, enables VLMs to acquire complex 3D spatial intelligence stably and effectively.
Training on high-fidelity synthetic data with physically-grounded rewards can instill transferable geometric logic, allowing models to generalize zero-shot to real-world panoramic reasoning tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21628.Title: RuCL: Stratified Rubric-Based Curriculum Learning for Multimodal Large Language Model Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21628.Summary: The RuCL framework enhances Multimodal Large Language Model reasoning by applying a stratified rubric-based curriculum learning approach that reorients curriculum from data selection to dynamic reward design. This method yielded an average accuracy of 60.06% across seven visual reasoning benchmarks, improving the base model's performance by 7.83% and setting a new state-of-the-art for 7B-scale open-source models while mitigating reward hacking.
Problem: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) for MLLMs suffers from "reward hacking," leading to unreliable reasoning processes despite correct final answers.
Existing fine-grained, rubric-based supervision methods are computationally costly due to instance-specific rubric generation.
These methods also exhibit inefficient training dynamics by treating all reasoning skills (rubrics) as equally challenging, generating noisy gradients.
Method: The RuCL framework constructs generalized rubrics, filtering and stratifying them into foundational and advanced levels based on empirical model pass rates.
A dynamic, stability-aware curriculum mechanism progressively weights foundational and advanced rubric rewards during reinforcement learning.
It employs Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to optimize a hybrid reward function combining rule-based outcome and curriculum-modulated rubric supervision.
Results: Attained state-of-the-art average accuracy of 60.06% across seven visual reasoning benchmarks, representing a +7.83% improvement over the baseline 7B-scale model.
Showed significant performance enhancements in multimodal mathematical reasoning (+12.97% on WeMATH) and complex logical deduction (+10.40% on LogicVista).
Ablation studies confirmed the efficacy of stratified rubrics and dynamic, sigmoid-based curriculum scheduling in improving training stability and overall reasoning performance.
Takeaways: Curriculum learning can be effectively applied to the reward function itself, dynamically adjusting supervision complexity based on model proficiency.
Stratifying reasoning skills (rubrics) by empirically determined difficulty levels improves training stability and mitigates gradient noise from premature penalization.
Generalized rubric construction offers a computationally efficient method for providing fine-grained process supervision, crucial for addressing reward hacking.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21619.Title: When More Is Less: A Systematic Analysis of Spatial and Commonsense Information for Visual Spatial Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21619.Summary: Researchers at The University of Melbourne systematically analyzed how injecting external spatial contexts, commonsense knowledge, and reasoning instructions impacts visual spatial reasoning in vision-language models, revealing that excessive or irrelevant information often degrades performance rather than improving it. The study provides evidence that a targeted, concise approach to information injection is more effective than indiscriminate aggregation.
Problem: Vision-language models (VLMs) frequently struggle with ambiguous, frame-dependent, or imprecise visual spatial reasoning (VSR) despite general image-text task proficiency.

Existing inference-time information injection techniques, used to augment VLM inputs with external cues, show inconsistent benefits and lack a systematic understanding of when they genuinely improve or degrade performance.
There is an unexamined assumption that providing more input information inherently leads to better reasoning, which has not been consistently supported by empirical evidence.
Method: Conducted a hypothesis-driven empirical analysis, treating three representative VLMs (Qwen, LLaVA, BLIP-3) as fixed black-box systems.

Systematically varied the type and quantity of external information injected into prompts: nine types of spatial contexts (verbalized vs. numerical), commonsense knowledge (varying relevance and quantity), and spatial reasoning instructions (Chain-of-Thought).
Evaluated the impact of these interventions on VSR performance using two public benchmarks: the VSR dataset (fine-grained relations) and the EmbSpatial dataset (cluttered scenes).
Results: Targeted spatial context injection yielded the most consistent improvements, with accuracy gains up to 9.6% across models, consistently outperforming a generic spatial grounding baseline.
Aggregating multiple spatial contexts generally led to diminishing returns and performance degradation, with models performing best with the injection of a single spatial context.

Verbalized spatial contexts consistently outperformed their numerical counterparts, with numerical inputs often degrading performance by up to 9.2% by introducing complexity; CoT prompting improved performance up to +12.2% on EmbSpatial but degraded it up to -2.0% on VSR, depending on the clarity of spatial grounding.
Takeaways: Injecting more information does not inherently lead to better visual spatial reasoning; excessive or irrelevant inputs can degrade VLM performance due to integration burden and cognitive overload.
Effective spatial grounding requires careful selection of a single, task-relevant spatial cue, which is often more beneficial in a verbalized format than as precise numerical values.
Commonsense knowledge and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting improve reasoning only when strictly relevant and when spatial grounding is already sufficiently precise and unambiguous, respectively.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21497.Title: See It, Say It, Sorted: An Iterative Training-Free Framework for Visually-Grounded Multimodal Reasoning in LVLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21497.Summary: The "See It, Say It, Sorted" (ECRD) framework improves visually-grounded multimodal reasoning in Large Vision-Language Models by iteratively supervising each reasoning step with dynamically generated textual visual evidence. This training-free approach effectively reduces visual hallucination propagation, achieving up to 29.5% relative gains on reasoning benchmarks without costly retraining.
Problem: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) frequently suffer from visual hallucination propagation, especially during extended Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, leading to incorrect final answers despite logical coherence.

Current methods to mitigate hallucination are primarily training-based, demanding significant computational resources, extensive curated data, and complex reward designs, making them costly and model-specific.
A lightweight, generalizable, and training-free approach is lacking to effectively enhance visual grounding at test time across diverse LVLM architectures.
Method: An iterative, training-free, and plug-and-play framework, Evidence-Constrained Reweighting Decoding (ECRD), is introduced to enhance visual grounding at test time without modifying base LVLMs.
A Distribution Supervisor adaptively reweights the base model's next-token probabilities using an "Evidence Pool" of dynamically growing textual visual observations.

An Uncertainty-Triggered Visual Decider, a lightweight VLM, is invoked on-demand when the base model's confidence is low, providing specific textual "micro-observations" to ground subsequent reasoning steps.
Results: ECRD consistently improved reasoning accuracy on the TreeBench benchmark, achieving relative gains of 16.5% to 29.5% across various open-source LVLM backbones (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL, LLaVA-OneVision).
It surpassed the performance of several closed-source models (e.g., Gemini-2.5-Flash, GPT-4o) and training-based visual-grounded reasoning models on TreeBench, all without additional training.

The framework enhanced the reasoning-perception balance on RH-Bench, increasing the RH-AUC from 0.51 to 0.58, and showed generalizable improvements across five diverse multimodal benchmarks like OCRBench and HallusionBench.
Takeaways: Visual hallucination in LVLMs can be effectively mitigated at test time by dynamically integrating semantic textual evidence into the decoding process without costly retraining.
An adaptive negotiation mechanism, where the visual evidence's influence scales with the base model's uncertainty, is crucial for balancing the LVLM's fluent generation with robust visual grounding.

Employing a lightweight, specialized visual decider only when the model exhibits low confidence allows for targeted visual clarification, preventing error propagation with minimal computational overhead.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21198.Title: Learning from Trials and Errors: Reflective Test-Time Planning for Embodied LLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21198.Summary: This research introduces Reflective Test-Time Planning, a framework that allows embodied Large Language Models to learn from their mistakes and adapt during deployment by converting verbal reflections into self-supervised training signals for model parameter updates. The system achieved a 33.65% average success rate on the Long-Horizon Household benchmark, outperforming baselines like 3DLLM-Mem (11.13%), and demonstrated robust adaptation in fitting tasks and generalization to new environments.
Problem: Existing embodied LLMs are "brittle static oracles" that struggle to adapt to unforeseen circumstances and cannot learn from execution failures during deployment.
Current AI reflection mechanisms often store critiques as context, influencing future actions indirectly without updating underlying model parameters, leading to repeated mistakes.
Addressing long-horizon temporal credit assignment is challenging, where immediate successful actions might lead to long-term task failures.
Method: A Reflective Test-Time Planning framework integrates three interacting multimodal LLMs (action generation, internal evaluator, external evaluator) to unify reflection-in-action and reflection-on-action.
Reflection-in-action uses an internal evaluator to score and select the best action from multiple candidates before execution, simulating outcomes.

Reflection-on-action employs an external evaluator to provide immediate feedback, and crucially, retrospective reflection to re-evaluate past actions with hindsight, generating self-supervised training signals for parameter updates via LoRA.
Results: The full Reflective Test-Time Planning framework achieved an average 33.65% success rate on the Long-Horizon Household benchmark, significantly outperforming the strongest baseline (3DLLM-Mem) at 11.13%.

Ablation studies confirmed that both reflection-in-action and reflection-on-action components are mutually dependent and essential for performance, with removing either leading to significant degradation.

The framework demonstrated robust generalization to photorealistic Habitat-Matterport 3D (HM3D) scenes, achieving 19.5% success on preparation tasks despite being trained only on synthetic data, showcasing transferability under domain shift.
Takeaways: Unifying 'reflection-in-action' (pre-execution mental simulation) and 'reflection-on-action' (post-execution learning from outcomes) creates a robust, adaptive learning cycle for embodied agents.

Converting verbal reflections into self-supervised parameter updates enables "double-loop learning," where agents correct not just actions but also the underlying assumptions and policies guiding those actions.
