Retrospective reflection, by re-evaluating past decisions with full hindsight, effectively solves the challenging problem of temporal credit assignment in long-horizon tasks, distilling long-term foresight into actionable learning signals.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21186.Title: Spa3R: Predictive Spatial Field Modeling for 3D Visual Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21186.Summary: Spa3R introduces Predictive Spatial Field Modeling (PSFM), a self-supervised deep learning framework that enables Vision-Language Models to learn holistic, view-invariant 3D spatial representations directly from unposed multi-view 2D images. This approach achieved a state-of-the-art average accuracy of 58.6% on the VSI-Bench, outperforming previous spatially-grounded baselines by 1.3 percentage points, and showed strong generalization across various spatial reasoning benchmarks.
Problem: Current Vision-Language Models (VLMs) exhibit superficial comprehension and reasoning abilities in 3D space despite their strengths in 2D visual tasks.

Existing methods for imparting 3D spatial awareness often rely on expensive explicit 3D data or provide only partial, view-conditioned geometric priors, which leads to inefficient and suboptimal spatial reasoning.

Scaling VLMs with extensive multi-view data paired with spatial Question-Answer (QA) annotations is data-intensive and forces the language model to inefficiently learn fundamental spatial understanding from scratch.
Method: Introduces Predictive Spatial Field Modeling (PSFM), a self-supervised framework that learns a unified, view-invariant spatial representation from unposed multi-view 2D images by synthesizing feature fields for arbitrary, unseen views.

Develops a specialized Spa3R encoder-decoder architecture featuring an Asymmetric View Aggregator, a Transformer-based Spa3R Encoder, and a Spa3R Decoder that utilizes Relative 3D Positional Encoding (PRoPE) for target view feature synthesis.

Integrates the pre-trained Spa3R Encoder into a base VLM (Qwen2.5-VL) via a lightweight Residual Cross-Attention Adapter, enabling the VLM to query the holistic spatial latent representation without compromising its original capabilities.
Results: Achieved state-of-the-art average accuracy of 58.6% on the VSI-Bench, surpassing the previous best (Cambrian-S-3B) by 1.3 percentage points, demonstrating superior visual-spatial intelligence from video inputs.
Exhibited strong cross-domain generalization, outperforming baselines on diverse spatial reasoning benchmarks such as SPAR-Bench, where Spa3-VLM scored 58.4% compared to SpaceR-7B's 37.6%.

Ablation studies confirmed the effectiveness of Spa3R's unified spatial representation (+3.5% over partial priors), the synergy of geometric and semantic reconstruction targets, and the crucial role of the Residual Cross-Attention Adapter (+7.5% over naive token appending).
Takeaways: Holistic, view-invariant 3D scene understanding can emerge inherently through a predictive modeling paradigm from 2D multi-view data, offering a scalable alternative to explicit 3D data or fragmented priors.
Decoupling the learning of robust 3D spatial representations from the subsequent language reasoning task provides a more effective and scalable foundation for 3D grounding in VLMs.
The combination of both geometric and semantic feature reconstruction targets during pre-training is crucial for developing comprehensive and robust spatial representations within the model.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21158.Title: SELAUR: Self Evolving LLM Agent via Uncertainty-aware Rewards
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21158.Summary: SELAUR introduces a reinforcement learning framework that integrates multi-type intrinsic uncertainty signals into reward shaping for large language model (LLM) agents, achieving superior task success rates on interactive benchmarks like ALFWorld and WebShop. This approach enables agents to learn more effectively from both successful and failed reasoning trajectories by providing dense, confidence-aligned supervision.
Problem: Existing reinforcement learning approaches for LLM agents often rely on sparse, outcome-based rewards, offering limited guidance for complex, multi-step reasoning processes.
Traditional reward signals typically indicate correctness but do not account for the LLM's confidence, overlooking valuable intrinsic uncertainty signals.
Effectively extracting learning signals from failed trajectories is challenging, as conventional binary rewards often discard valuable gradient information when an agent fails to achieve a goal.
Method: A multi-metric uncertainty estimation module quantifies token-level uncertainty using a weighted combination of entropy, least confidence, and margin.
Hierarchical aggregation mechanisms transform token-level uncertainties into step-level and exponentially discounted trajectory-level uncertainty scores.

A novel failure-aware reward shaping mechanism augments step rewards and replaces trajectory rewards with uncertainty signals in failed cases, converting failures into positive learning opportunities.
Results: SELAUR consistently outperformed strong reinforcement learning baselines (PPO, RLOO, GRPO, GiGPO) on ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks, achieving up to 0.8906% success rate on ALFWorld (Qwen2.5-1.5B) and 0.8935 task score on WebShop (Qwen2.5-7B).
Ablation studies confirmed that the full integration of all three uncertainty measures and the proposed failure-aware reward shaping mechanism were crucial for achieving optimal performance.

Qualitative case studies demonstrated SELAUR's ability to avoid repetitive, suboptimal loops and adapt exploration dynamically based on confidence levels, leading to more coherent and efficient decision trajectories.
Takeaways: Intrinsic uncertainty, derived directly from an LLM's probability distributions, serves as a dense and valuable learning signal for reinforcement learning agents.
By explicitly learning from failed trajectories through uncertainty-aware rewards, agents can achieve more robust policy improvements and overcome limitations of sparse reward systems.

Combining diverse uncertainty metrics (entropy, least confidence, margin) provides a more comprehensive characterization of model confidence, leading to more stable and effective exploration strategies.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21054.Title: VAUQ: Vision-Aware Uncertainty Quantification for LVLM Self-Evaluation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21054.Summary: VAUQ introduces a training-free self-evaluation framework for Large Vision-Language Models that quantifies reliance on visual evidence to mitigate hallucinations. It achieved a +13.3% improvement in self-evaluation AUROC on counterfactual images while reducing inference time by 94.6% compared to prior methods.
Problem: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) frequently generate 'hallucinations' or outputs ungrounded in visual evidence, limiting their safe deployment in real-world applications.
Existing LLM self-evaluation methods, primarily language-centric, fail in multimodal contexts due to LVLM's 'language-prior dominance,' leading to confident but visually incorrect answers.
Current external evaluation (human annotation, LLM-as-a-judge) and some LVLM-specific hallucination detection methods are often costly, time-consuming, or computationally expensive.
Method: VAUQ develops an Image-Information Score (IS) that quantifies the reduction in predictive uncertainty when an image is present versus absent, indicating the model's utilization of visual information.

It employs an unsupervised core-region masking strategy, leveraging the LVLM's internal visual attention weights (from middle-to-later transformer layers) to identify and effectively remove semantically relevant visual evidence.
The final VAUQ score combines the model's predictive entropy with a 'core-masked' IS, explicitly discounting uncertainty by the model's reliance on identified core visual evidence.
Results: VAUQ consistently achieved state-of-the-art self-evaluation performance (AUROC) across various benchmarks (ViLP, MMVet, VisualCoT, CVBench) and three major LVLM architectures.

On the challenging ViLP dataset with counterfactual images, VAUQ demonstrated a +13.3% improvement in self-evaluation AUROC compared to existing methods, effectively mitigating language-prior dominance.
The framework reduced per-sample inference time by 94.6% compared to multi-sampling-based baselines while delivering superior accuracy, making it highly efficient for practical deployment.
Takeaways: Informative visual evidence, when properly utilized by an LVLM, should lead to a measurable reduction in its predictive uncertainty, which can be quantified as an Image-Information Score.

An LVLM's internal visual attention weights, particularly from mid to later layers, can effectively pinpoint task-relevant visual regions for unsupervised masking without requiring ground-truth annotations.

Combining a standard predictive entropy with a vision-aware uncertainty signal (IS_core) provides complementary insights, improving self-evaluation accuracy, especially in scenarios where visual grounding is critical over language priors.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.20980.Title: CrystaL: Spontaneous Emergence of Visual Latents in MLLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.20980.Summary: CrystaL is a self-supervised, single-stage framework for Multimodal Large Language Models that cultivates robust latent reasoning by enforcing consistency across dual processing paths, leading to the spontaneous emergence of task-relevant visual semantics. The framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on perception-intensive benchmarks with a significant reduction in training data.
Problem: Existing latent Chain-of-Thought (CoT) methods for MLLMs suffer from insufficient supervision signals for intermediate latent states, hindering genuine visual reasoning.
Prior approaches often depend on external modules, auxiliary human annotations, or complex multi-stage training, increasing complexity and cost.
The reliance on indirect supervision can lead to MLLMs performing superficial reasoning or struggling with fine-grained visual information in complex perception tasks.
Method: A single-stage, self-supervised framework employs a dual-path architecture to process high-fidelity and stochastically corrupted visual inputs concurrently.
Visual latent tokens from the intact path are copied to the corrupted path, creating an information bottleneck that compels these latents to encode essential visual semantics.
Alignment objectives, including predictive distribution consistency and mechanistic consistency, enforce similarity between the two paths' outputs and internal reasoning patterns.
Results: CrystaL achieved a state-of-the-art average score of 75.4% across diverse perception-intensive benchmarks, surpassing strong baselines.
The framework demonstrated enhanced performance in high-resolution perception, improving scores on HRBench 4K by 4.8% and HRBench 8K by 6.2% over Qwen2.5-VL-7B.
It exhibited high data efficiency, achieving top accuracy with only 16,000 training samples, a more than 6x reduction compared to some previous methods.
Takeaways: Self-supervised consistency training can compel MLLMs to spontaneously distill task-relevant visual semantics into their internal latent representations.
Stochastic image corruption acts as an effective information bottleneck, forcing the model to rely on visual latent tokens and ensuring their functional indispensability.
Aligning both the output predictive distributions and the internal attention mechanisms provides strong supervisory signals for effective latent visual reasoning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.20901.Title: SpatiaLQA: A Benchmark for Evaluating Spatial Logical Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.20901.Summary: Researchers from Zhejiang University introduce SpatiaLQA, a benchmark demonstrating current Vision-Language Models struggle with spatial logical reasoning, particularly in complex multi-step planning and inferring action preconditions. Their proposed Recursive Scene Graph Assisted Reasoning (RSGAR) technique helps models better integrate visual-spatial information for improved performance.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) reportedly lack "spatial logical reasoning"—the ability to understand spatial relationships and infer logical dependencies for multi-step tasks in complex, real-world environments.
Existing benchmarks (VQA, logical reasoning, embodied QA) do not adequately or systematically assess this integrated spatial and logical reasoning capability.

State-of-the-art VLMs struggle with making sound decisions in scenarios requiring complex interdependencies in physical space, such as needing to remove obstructions before manipulating a target object.
Method: Developed SpatiaLQA, a large-scale benchmark comprising 9,605 image–text QA pairs from 241 real indoor scenes, requiring multi-step, open-vocabulary answers with explicit precondition annotations.

Implemented a three-stage data augmentation process (manual annotation, subgraph extraction, graph expansion) to create diverse and complex reasoning scenarios, enhancing dataset scale and difficulty.

Proposed Recursive Scene Graph Assisted Reasoning (RSGAR), an iterative method that uses visual foundation models (Depth Anything V2, SAM) to generate task-relevant scene graphs, guiding VLMs in multi-step reasoning.
Results: Evaluated 41 VLMs on SpatiaLQA, revealing a substantial performance gap: the best VLM (GPT-5) achieved F1 scores of 76.0 (content) and 47.0 (preconditions), while humans achieved 97.6 (content) and 92.5 (preconditions).

VLMs demonstrated a notable deficiency in causal reasoning, with precondition prediction (F_p) consistently much lower than step content prediction (F_c), highlighting struggles in inferring logical dependencies.

The proposed RSGAR method, using GPT-4o, improved performance to F_c 69.8 and F_p 28.1, outperforming baselines and showing particular benefits for complex tasks with more answer steps. Ablation studies confirmed the importance of both recursive scene graph generation and perception maps.
Takeaways: Spatial logical reasoning is a distinct and crucial cognitive capability for VLMs, bridging spatial perception and multi-step logical inference, which is foundational for embodied AI tasks.
Automated evaluation of open-vocabulary, multi-step answers with preconditions can be reliably achieved using advanced VLMs like GPT-4o for scoring, validated against human judgments.

Explicitly representing object relationships through iterative scene graph construction (RSGAR) helps VLMs decompose complex visual scenes and significantly improves performance on intricate multi-step spatial logical tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.20739.Title: PyVision-RL: Forging Open Agentic Vision Models via RL
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.20739.Summary: PyVision-RL introduces an open-weight reinforcement learning framework for agentic multimodal models, enabling dynamic Python-based tool use for images and videos. The framework effectively counters interaction collapse and achieves state-of-the-art performance on image benchmarks, while significantly improving visual token efficiency for video tasks (e.g., 7.3% accuracy increase on VSI-Bench with an order of magnitude fewer visual tokens).
Problem: Agentic capabilities with dynamic tooling are largely confined to proprietary systems or image-only tasks, limiting the accessibility and advancement of open-weight multimodal large language models (MLLMs).
Reinforcement Learning (RL) fine-tuning for agentic MLLMs often suffers from "interaction collapse," where models learn to minimize tool usage and multi-turn reasoning.
Traditional video MLLMs incur high computational costs due to uniform frame sampling, making efficient and scalable video understanding challenging.
Method: A unified agentic scaffold integrates Python as a primitive tool, enabling dynamic, on-the-fly operation synthesis and iterative reasoning for both image and video tasks.

An accumulative tool reward (only for correct answers) and an oversampling–filtering–ranking strategy for rollouts stabilize RL training and sustain multi-turn tool usage, combating interaction collapse.
For video understanding, an "on-demand context construction" mechanism allows the MLLM to selectively fetch and present task-relevant frames via Python, drastically reducing visual token consumption.
Results: PyVision-Image achieved state-of-the-art results on visual search (e.g., +10.2% on V* avg@32) and multimodal reasoning benchmarks (e.g., +9.6% on WeMath) over previous methods.
PyVision-Video obtained a 7.3% absolute accuracy improvement on VSI-Bench while reducing visual token usage from approximately 45K to 5K tokens per sample.

Ablation studies confirmed that the accumulative tool reward is crucial for sustaining tool usage throughout training, and the oversampling–filtering–ranking rollout strategy significantly improves performance and stability.
Takeaways: Interaction collapse in agentic RL is not an inherent limitation of multi-turn interaction but rather a solvable issue related to insufficient training incentives and unstable rollout selection.

Dynamic tool use, through treating a general-purpose language like Python as a primitive, provides superior expressiveness and compositional reasoning for both image and video understanding in open-weight MLLMs.

On-demand visual processing, where an agent intelligently samples and presents only relevant video frames, is crucial for achieving high performance and efficiency in video reasoning, reducing token consumption by an order of magnitude.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.20687.Title: How Foundational Skills Influence VLM-based Embodied Agents:A Native Perspective
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.20687.Summary: Researchers at the University of Science and Technology of China and Alibaba Group introduced NativeEmbodied, a benchmark for VLM-based embodied agents that uses a low-level action space and a decoupled task hierarchy. The evaluation reveals that while models demonstrate strong perception (GPT-o3 F1: 83.97%) and planning, they face significant challenges in fine-grained spatial alignment and navigation, with many proprietary models achieving single-digit success rates in alignment tasks.
Problem: Existing benchmarks for VLM-based embodied agents often rely on 'non-native' high-level action spaces, abstracting low-level skills and creating a disparity with real-world operational conditions.
Current evaluations focus on coupled, high-level tasks with overall success rates, making it difficult to pinpoint specific foundational skill deficiencies and diagnose performance bottlenecks.
A lack of comprehensive understanding regarding which foundational skills are truly essential and how they impact higher-level task execution for VLM-based agents.
Method: Introduces NativeEmbodied, a benchmark employing a 'native' low-level, primitive action space (e.g., 'MoveAhead x meters', 'RotateRight x degrees') derived from AI2THOR, allowing for fine-grained control.

Features a decoupled task hierarchy with three complex high-level tasks (Exploration, Search, Interaction) and four isolated low-level tasks (Perception, Spatial Alignment, Navigation, Planning) to assess specific foundational skills.
Utilizes an automatic data generation pipeline with human-machine collaborative filtering, built upon AI2-THOR, to create high-quality, challenging scenarios for evaluation.
Results: On high-level tasks, even leading VLMs achieved limited success: the best model (GPT-o3) reached 34.64% success in Search, 38.34% in Interaction, and 52.43% in Exploration.

In low-level skills, models performed comparatively well in Perception (GPT-o3 F1: 83.97%) and Planning (GPT-o3 SR: 72.54%) but struggled significantly with Spatial Alignment (only GPT-o3 above 50% SR) and Navigation (over half of models below 50% SR).

Ablation studies confirmed that navigation and planning are dual bottlenecks for long-horizon tasks, while spatial alignment is crucial for search; enabling 'think mode' improved performance on perception and planning but led to a decrease in success rates for precise actions.
Takeaways: Current VLMs show strong perceptual understanding and planning capabilities but exhibit pronounced deficiencies in fine-grained spatial alignment and precise navigation, which are critical bottlenecks for complex embodied tasks.
Long-horizon tasks (Exploration, Interaction) are dually bottlenecked by both cognitive-level planning and action-level navigation capabilities.

While explicit 'think mode' reasoning enhances cognitive abilities for perception and planning, it can paradoxically interfere with the intuitive and precise execution of fundamental motor controls like alignment and navigation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.20159.Title: A Very Big Video Reasoning Suite
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.20159.Summary: VIDEO-REASON.COM: A Very Big Video Reasoning Suite introduces an extensive, community-curated dataset with over one million video clips and two million images, alongside a verifiable evaluation framework for video reasoning. Training on this suite improved a Wan2.2 model's reasoning performance by 84.6% relative to its baseline, achieving an overall score of 0.685, while revealing persistent challenges in long-horizon reasoning and cross-task generalization.
Problem: Current video generation models lack robust reasoning capabilities, particularly concerning physical world understanding.
Existing video reasoning benchmarks are small, evaluation-heavy, and do not provide sufficient large-scale training data for investigating scaling behaviors.
The absence of verifiable and reproducible evaluation frameworks hinders rigorous diagnosis and comparison of video reasoning models.
Method: Introduction of VBVR-Dataset, an unprecedentedly large-scale resource (1M+ video clips, 2M+ images) featuring 200 diverse reasoning tasks across a cognitive architecture-grounded taxonomy.
Development of VBVR-Bench, a verifiable evaluation framework utilizing rule-based, human-aligned scorers to ensure reproducible and interpretable diagnosis of video reasoning capabilities.
Conducting a large-scale scaling study to analyze emergent generalization to unseen reasoning tasks, leveraging the extensive VBVR suite.
Results: VBVR-Wan2.2, fine-tuned on the dataset, achieved an overall score of 0.685 on VBVR-Bench, representing an 84.6% relative improvement over its base model (0.371) and outperforming other tested state-of-the-art models.
Despite performance improvements with data scaling, a substantial gap to human performance (0.974 overall) and a persistent ~15% gap between in-domain and out-of-domain generalization remain.

The scaling study demonstrated performance plateaus at 400K-500K samples, indicating that current video generation architectures face representational and optimization bottlenecks for complex video reasoning tasks.
Takeaways: Scaling video reasoning data significantly improves both in-domain and out-of-domain performance, yet gains plateau, suggesting fundamental architectural bottlenecks for complex tasks.
Training on VBVR instills a "controllability-first" execution logic in models, enabling precise, verifiable manipulations critical for grounded physical world reasoning.
Analysis of capability correlations among cognitive faculties in AI models reveals non-trivial structural dependencies, such as a strong positive coupling between Knowledge and Spatiality.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.20133.Title: AdaEvolve: Adaptive LLM Driven Zeroth-Order Optimization
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.20133.Summary: AdaEvolve, an adaptive framework developed at UC Berkeley, reframes LLM-driven program evolution as a hierarchical optimization problem, employing an "accumulated improvement signal" to dynamically manage search processes. The framework achieved state-of-the-art results on 4 out of 6 mathematical optimization tasks, surpassing human SOTA on Circle Packing and consistently outperforming baselines across 185 diverse problems.
Problem: Existing LLM-guided search systems use static schedules and fixed hyperparameters, leading to computational waste and premature stagnation in discrete, non-differentiable search spaces.
These systems lack adaptability to the non-stationary dynamics of evolutionary search, often getting trapped in local optima and requiring extensive manual tuning for each new problem.
The semantic capabilities of LLMs are underutilized for overarching search control and strategic redirection beyond simple program mutations.
Method: AdaEvolve introduces a hierarchical adaptive optimization framework that uses an "accumulated improvement signal" to unify and coordinate adaptation across three levels of control.

It dynamically modulates exploration/exploitation within islands, allocates global computational resources to the most productive islands via a multi-armed bandit approach with globally normalized rewards, and spawns new islands during stagnation.
A "System 2" meta-LLM is triggered when global stagnation persists to generate high-level "solution tactics" which are then injected into mutation prompts to shift search strategy.
Results: AdaEvolve consistently outperformed open-sourced baselines (OpenEvolve, GEPA, ShinkaEvolve) across all categories of 185 diverse problems, including mathematical optimization, systems benchmarks, and Frontier-CS tasks.
It achieved state-of-the-art results in 4 of 6 mathematical optimization problems, notably surpassing human SOTA on Circle Packing (Square, N=26) with a score of 2.636 (vs. 2.634).

Comprehensive ablation studies confirmed the individual contributions of all three adaptive control levels, with meta-guidance proving most impactful for enabling breakthroughs by breaking conceptual stalemates.
Takeaways: An "accumulated improvement signal," reflecting the productivity of the search trajectory, can effectively drive multi-level adaptive control in zeroth-order optimization.

Hierarchical adaptation, encompassing local search intensity, global resource allocation, and meta-level strategy shifts, is crucial for breaking both numerical and conceptual local optima in complex search spaces.
Globally normalizing bandit rewards for island selection prevents bias towards trivial improvements on low-performing islands, ensuring resources are directed towards globally significant progress.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.19063.Title: Direction-aware 3D Large Multimodal Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.19063.Summary: Researchers from Nanyang Technological University and The University of Tokyo developed a framework, including PoseRecover and PoseAlign, that integrates explicit ego-pose information into 3D Large Multimodal Models. This approach addresses the ambiguity of directional queries in existing datasets, enhancing spatial reasoning capabilities and achieving up to a 30.0% mIoU increase in referring segmentation on ScanRefer.
Problem: Existing 3D indoor datasets lack explicit ego-pose information, rendering a significant portion of directional queries (e.g., "left," "right") ill-posed for spatial reasoning by 3D LMMs.
Without persistent awareness of ego poses and spatial directions, 3D LMMs struggle with robust and alias-free spatial reasoning, accurate understanding, and safe navigation for embodied agents.

Prior methods either created new datasets with implicit ego-situational information or used 2D image-based approaches, which often introduced textual ambiguity or did not directly rectify the ill-posed nature of 3D point cloud benchmarks.
Method: Developed PoseRecover, an automatic pipeline that retrieves mission-critical ego poses from raw RGB-D sequences by calculating object-frustum intersection rates and employs a robust "Clip" strategy for online pose selection.

Introduced PoseAlign, a method to integrate these identified ego poses into 3D LMMs, with three variants: PoseAlign-Transform (directly transforming point clouds into the camera coordinate frame), PoseAlign-Embed (modulating the projection layer with pose embeddings), and PoseAlign-Prompt (serializing pose info into textual prompts).

Applied the framework to various 3D LMM architectures (e.g., 3D-LLAVA, LL3DA) and fine-tuned the multimodal projector and LLM using LoRA, while typically freezing the 3D encoder to focus improvements on directional awareness.
Results: Achieved substantial performance improvements across multiple 3D LMM backbones and datasets; for 3D-LLAVA with PoseAlign-Transform, mIoU increased by 30.0% (from 42.6% to 55.4%) on ScanRefer and by 12.9% (from 48.1% to 54.3%) on Multi3DRefer.
Improved LLM-as-judge accuracy on question answering and captioning tasks, with a 3.5% increase on ScanQA (to 47.3%) and an 11.7% increase on Scan2Cap (to 31.4%) for 3D-LLAVA.

Qualitative results demonstrated that PoseAlign-enhanced models successfully avoided directional ambiguity, providing robust spatial reasoning and more accurate responses to directional queries compared to baselines.
Takeaways: Directly transforming the input point cloud into the recovered camera coordinate frame (PoseAlign-Transform) is the most effective method for instilling directional awareness and achieves superior performance in refer segmentation tasks.

The systematic integration of explicit ego-pose information through PoseRecover and PoseAlign consistently improves the performance of 3D LMMs across diverse tasks and benchmarks by resolving directional ambiguity.
A significant percentage (40-95%) of queries in current 3D LMM benchmarks are direction-critical, highlighting a fundamental flaw that the proposed ego-pose integration addresses effectively.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.18374.Title: Zero-shot Interactive Perception
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.18374.Summary: Researchers from the University of Surrey and University of Sheffield developed the Zero-Shot Interactive Perception (ZS-IP) framework, enabling robots to extract hidden information and resolve semantic queries in cluttered environments through physical interaction. The system integrates Vision-Language Models with multi-strategy manipulation and memory-guided action planning, achieving high success rates in interactive perception tasks, often outperforming existing methods like MOKA.
Problem: Robots in cluttered or partially observable environments face challenges due to occluded objects, as traditional active perception cannot physically alter the scene to reveal information.

Integrating high-level semantic reasoning from Vision-Language Models (VLMs) with low-level physical interaction remains a bottleneck for generalizable robotic manipulation, especially for tasks requiring temporal context or involving unseen objects.

Existing interactive perception methods struggle with contact-rich actions like pushing in cluttered scenes, often relying on limited 2D spatial annotations that do not effectively capture manipulation affordances.
Method: An iterative Zero-Shot Interactive Perception (ZS-IP) framework that integrates a VLM (GPT-4o) with a robot manipulator, allowing it to dynamically interact with the environment to resolve semantic queries.

Introduction of an Enhanced Observation (EO) module which generates specialized visual augmentations like "pushlines" for robust pushing, grasping keypoints, and a virtual grid for precise robot movements.

A Memory-Guided Action Module that stores interaction history and scene context, enabling context-aware action selection, prevention of redundant actions, and support for multi-step manipulation plans.
Results: The ZS-IP framework achieved high success rates (0.8-1.0 SR) in less complex interactive perception tasks, showcasing its robust reasoning and manipulation capabilities in unstructured scenes.

In complex, multi-step scenarios, ZS-IP (especially "In-Context" configuration) demonstrated an SR of 0.7-0.8, outperforming the MOKA baseline (SR 0.0-0.5) by effectively leveraging memory and strategic action sequencing.

The "pushlines" visual augmentation significantly improved performance in contact-rich pushing tasks (Task VIII SR 0.8), and GPT-4o proved to be the most effective VLM compared to other models within the ZS-IP framework.
Takeaways: Specialized visual augmentations, such as "pushlines" derived from object geometry, are effective in capturing affordances for contact-rich actions, significantly improving pushing performance in cluttered environments.

Integrating a memory-guided action module with a VLM allows robots to retain temporal context from previous interactions, enabling more robust multi-step reasoning, dynamic action selection, and efficient task termination.

Zero-shot interactive perception can be achieved by tightly coupling high-level VLM reasoning with enhanced visual affordances and memory, allowing robots to resolve complex semantic queries in partially observable scenes.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.17270.Title: Unified Latents (UL): How to train your latents
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.17270.Summary: Google DeepMind Amsterdam's Unified Latents (UL) framework introduces a principled method for learning optimal latent representations for diffusion models. This framework achieves state-of-the-art generation quality and pre-training efficiency on datasets like ImageNet-512 and Kinetics-600, while offering interpretable control over latent information content.
Problem: Efficiently scaling diffusion models to high resolutions is challenging without effective latent representations.
Current latent learning strategies often lack principled regularization, making it difficult to control the information content (bitrate) of the latents.
A fundamental trade-off exists between the ease of modeling latent representations for generation and their ability to retain high-frequency details for accurate reconstruction.
Method: Introduces the Unified Latents (UL) framework that jointly trains an encoder, a diffusion prior, and a diffusion decoder in a two-stage process.
Employs a fixed amount of Gaussian noise when encoding latents and aligns the diffusion prior with this minimum noise level using an unweighted ELBO loss.
Utilizes a reweighted ELBO loss with a loss factor for the diffusion decoder, providing explicit and interpretable control over the latent bitrate.
Results: Achieves a state-of-the-art FID of 1.4 on ImageNet-512 and an FVD of 1.3 on Kinetics-600 (medium model), demonstrating superior pre-training efficiency.

Provides interpretable control over latent information content, allowing for optimization of either generation quality (e.g., lower bitrate for smaller models) or reconstruction fidelity (e.g., higher bitrate for larger models).
Demonstrates robust performance and scalability on large text-to-image datasets, yielding better perceptual quality (gFID 4.1) compared to baselines while maintaining high reconstruction PSNR.
Takeaways: Co-training a diffusion prior with an unweighted ELBO loss provides principled regularization for latents, preventing information collapse and improving modelability.
Encoding latents with a fixed amount of Gaussian noise and aligning the prior's minimum noise level simplifies the VAE's KL term and enhances training stability.

Explicit hyperparameters (loss factor and sigmoid bias) in the decoder loss enable interpretable control over the latent bitrate, optimizing the trade-off between reconstruction and generation quality.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.16702.Title: Saliency-Aware Multi-Route Thinking: Revisiting Vision-Language Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.16702.Summary: The Saliency-Aware Multi-Route Thinking (SAP) framework introduces an inference-time optimization approach to enhance vision-language reasoning by addressing text-dominated processing and object hallucination. This method leverages a multi-route, principle-guided evolutionary strategy with saliency-aware evaluation, leading to improved performance, reduced hallucination, and more efficient parallel inference across diverse benchmarks.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) exhibit "text-dominated" reasoning, where visual attention diminishes over long inference sequences, causing an over-reliance on generated text.
Early visual grounding errors accumulate as VLM reasoning progresses, leading to phenomena like object hallucination and reasoning that drifts away from the visual evidence.
Existing guidance signals for visual grounding during VLM inference are often noisy, coarse, and inconsistent, making stable control over discrete, token-level generation challenging.
Method: The Saliency-Aware Principle Selection (SAP) framework is proposed as a model-agnostic, data-free, inference-time optimization approach for VLMs.

Reasoning behaviors are parameterized using high-level textual "reasoning principles" that guide the VLM on *how* to reason, rather than dictating token-level sequences, enabling the generation of multiple distinct reasoning routes.

An evolutionary (μ+λ)(\mu + \lambda)(μ+λ) selection strategy refines these principles, guided by a novel saliency-aware evaluation that assesses consensus, diversity, uncertainty, and crucially, visual evidence validity against external visual grounding services.
Results: The framework achieved a higher average performance of 76.6 across 16 diverse vision-language benchmarks, surpassing standard Instruct (75.4) and LongCoT-style Thinking (75.9) baselines.
Object hallucination was significantly mitigated, with performance on perception-sensitive tasks like POPE-recall improving to 89.9, contrasting with LongCoT's decline to 79.6.

SAP demonstrated enhanced computational efficiency and lower response latency in parallel inference settings, decomposing inference into independent short-route generations, and proved model-agnostic across various VLM scales and architectures.
Takeaways: Extending sequential reasoning (LongCoT) in VLMs exacerbates text-dominated processing and diminishes visual grounding, leading to a "robustness-depth trade-off."
A multi-route, parallel exploration of reasoning paths, guided by high-level principles, offers a more robust and efficient alternative to linear, sequential inference-time scaling for VLMs.

Saliency-aware evaluation, using external visual grounding tools, can provide effective and non-intrusive feedback to maintain visual grounding and reduce hallucination without directly exposing raw saliency information to the VLM during reasoning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.15950.Title: Can Vision-Language Models See Squares? Text-Recognition Mediates Spatial Reasoning Across Three Model Families
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.15950.Summary: This research reveals that Vision-Language Models (VLMs) exhibit a substantial and consistent degradation in spatial localization when processing non-textual visual information compared to text symbols, suggesting a reliance on an internal text-recognition pathway for high-fidelity spatial reasoning. Across Claude Opus, ChatGPT 5.2, and Gemini 3 Thinking, F1 scores for black-cell detection dropped by 34.1 to 53.8 points when grids were presented as abstract squares instead of text.
Problem: A gap exists in understanding the underlying mechanisms of spatial reasoning in VLMs, particularly whether their capabilities are uniform across diverse visual inputs.
The prevailing assumption that VLMs possess robust and generalizable spatial reasoning abilities for arbitrary visual content needed to be critically examined.
There was a need to isolate spatial localization from semantic understanding to probe fundamental limitations in VLM visual processing without confounding factors.
Method: Fifteen 15x15 binary grids were programmatically generated with varying densities.
Each grid was rendered under two visual encoding conditions: as text symbols (periods and hash marks) and as unsegmented abstract squares.
Three frontier VLMs (Claude Opus, ChatGPT 5.2, Gemini 3 Thinking) were prompted to transcribe these grids, and performance was measured using cell accuracy and black-cell F1 score.
Results: All three frontier VLMs showed a substantial performance drop in F1 score for black-cell detection when processing unsegmented squares compared to text symbols, with gaps ranging from 34.1 to 53.8 percentage points.

Claude Opus and ChatGPT 5.2 maintained stable F1 scores across varying densities in the text condition, while Gemini 3 Thinking experienced a catastrophic performance collapse at higher text densities.

In the unsegmented squares condition, Gemini 3 Thinking achieved the highest F1 scores on sparse grids (averaging 68.0% for ≤20% density) but rapidly collapsed at higher densities, frequently generating hallucinated geometric patterns.
Takeaways: VLMs appear to have two distinct implicit processing pathways for spatial information: a robust text-recognition pathway and a significantly weaker visual-feature pathway for non-textual content.
The perceived strong spatial reasoning in VLMs might be largely an artifact of their implicit OCR capabilities, leading to an overestimation of their general visual spatial acuity.

Different VLMs exhibit distinct qualitative failure modes in the non-textual condition, ranging from under-counting and displacement (Claude) to massive over-counting (ChatGPT) and hallucinating stereotyped patterns (Gemini).

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.15918.Title: EarthSpatialBench: Benchmarking Spatial Reasoning Capabilities of Multimodal LLMs on Earth Imagery
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.15918.Summary: EarthSpatialBench introduces a comprehensive benchmark to evaluate the spatial reasoning capabilities of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on Earth imagery. It provides 21,000 images and over 325,000 question–answer pairs, covering quantitative distance and direction, systematic topological relations, and diverse geometric entities like bounding boxes, polylines, and polygons, revealing MLLMs' limitations in precise geospatial reasoning.
Problem: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs), primarily trained on natural images, struggle with the unique characteristics of Earth imagery, such as noise, dense object populations, and diverse geometric representations.

Existing MLLM benchmarks for Earth imagery lack support for quantitative direction (azimuth angle) and distance metrics, systematic topological relations, and complex object geometries beyond bounding boxes.

Current spatial reasoning benchmarks generally do not extensively cover continuous metric reasoning, angular direction estimation, or formal topological relations with polygonal and polyline structures intrinsic to geospatial analysis.
Method: Developed EarthSpatialBench, a comprehensive benchmark comprising 21,000 Earth images and over 325,000 question–answer pairs to evaluate MLLMs' spatial reasoning.

The benchmark systematically assesses MLLMs across four dimensions: spatial relations (distance, direction, topology), geometry types (bounding boxes, polylines, polygons), object representations (text, visual overlays, coordinates), and question formats.

Utilized a multi-stage quality assurance pipeline, combining automated checks with manual review, to ensure the validity and consistency of generated questions and ground-truth labels derived from exact geometry computations.
Results: Proprietary models (e.g., GPT-5, Claude 3.5 Sonnet) achieved higher classification accuracy, while open-source models (e.g., Qwen3-VL variants) demonstrated stronger performance in localization tasks.

Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting generally improved classification and regression performance for most models, particularly in topological reasoning, but had limited or sometimes negative impact on localization tasks.

Heterogeneous geometry pairs (e.g., bounding box-polyline, polygon-polyline) consistently yielded higher errors for distance estimation compared to homogeneous pairs, with polygon-polyline interactions proving most challenging, indicating difficulties in reasoning over irregular region-curve interactions.
Takeaways: Current MLLMs exhibit substantial performance gaps across numerical estimation, spatial grounding, and geometric reasoning tasks on Earth imagery, particularly for precise quantitative and topological queries.

Accurate object localization is a prerequisite for reliable spatial reasoning, yet models often show a disconnect between high-level spatial reasoning capabilities (e.g., classification accuracy) and precise low-level visual grounding.

Performance on spatial reasoning tasks varies significantly with different geometric representations and object reference modalities; heterogeneous geometry pairs and mixed reference types often lead to higher errors, highlighting the challenge of integrating diverse spatial information.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.15727.Title: Spanning the Visual Analogy Space with a Weight Basis of LoRAs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.15727.Summary: LoRWeB introduces a framework for visual analogy learning that dynamically generates task-specific LoRA adapters from a learned basis, enabling models to apply diverse transformations from example pairs. This approach achieves superior generalization to unseen analogy tasks, producing higher quality and more consistent visual outputs compared to methods using single, fixed-capacity adapters.
Problem: Text-based image editing models struggle to articulate complex, nuanced, or abstract visual transformations precisely, limiting creative control for users.

Existing visual analogy learning methods relying on single Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) modules face a fundamental capacity bottleneck, hindering generalization to a vast and diverse range of unseen transformations.

There was a need for a stable and efficient mechanism to dynamically specialize generative models for individual analogy tasks at inference time, avoiding the instability and training difficulties of hypernetworks.
Method: LoRWeB proposes a novel architecture that dynamically composes a task-specific LoRA from a learned basis of multiple low-rank LoRA modules, each associated with a unique, learnable key vector.

A lightweight encoder (router) processes input analogy images using frozen CLIP embeddings to generate a query vector, which then computes scalar coefficients via a softmax function to combine the basis LoRAs.

The resulting dynamically composed "Mixed LoRA" is injected into a pre-trained conditional flow model (FLUX.1-Kontext) to generate analogously transformed images, specializing the model for each specific analogy task.
Results: Qualitative evaluations demonstrate LoRWeB's superior generalization to a wide variety of novel analogy tasks, accurately applying diverse transformations with enhanced detail preservation and consistency.

Quantitative metrics, including VLM-based assessments (Gemma-3), show LoRWeB achieves higher 'Edit Accuracy' and 'Preservation' scores, significantly improving the Pareto front compared to all baselines.

In 2-alternative-forced-choice (2AFC) evaluations, both Gemma-3 and human users strongly preferred LoRWeB's outputs over all baselines, with Gemma-3 preferring LoRWeB over Edit Transfer 83.6% of the time and over the r=128 LoRA baseline 57.6% of the time.
Takeaways: A dynamically composed basis of low-rank LoRAs can effectively span the visual analogy space, overcoming the generalization limitations of single, fixed-capacity adapters.

Separately encoding analogy images (`a`, `a'`, `b`) with a powerful Vision-Language Model (CLIP) provides richer semantic context for the router, leading to better editing accuracy compared to encoding a composite image.
Using a softmax function for combining basis LoRAs is crucial for stability and performance, preventing overly large LoRA norms that can arise with alternative coefficient-weighting functions.

A larger basis of smaller-rank adapters (e.g., N=32, r=4) is more effective for generalization across diverse transformations than a smaller basis of higher-rank adapters or a single high-capacity LoRA.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.15029.Title: Symmetry in language statistics shapes the geometry of model representations
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.15029.Summary: A theoretical framework demonstrates that translation symmetry in pairwise word co-occurrence statistics determines the geometric structures in language model representations. This principle accounts for phenomena like circular embeddings for cyclical concepts and robust, rippled 1D manifolds, consistently observed across various model architectures.
Problem: A clear, unifying theoretical explanation for widely observed geometric patterns (e.g., circles, 1D manifolds) in language model representations has been largely absent.
The lack of an overarching "organizing principle" to explain the apparent universality of these geometric structures across diverse LLM architectures and tasks.
Prior theoretical work did not adequately address how data distribution and unsupervised learning settings drive these specific representational geometries.
Method: Proposed that translation symmetry within pairwise word co-occurrence statistics serves as the universal organizing principle for representational geometry.
Developed a mathematical theory to analytically derive specific manifold geometries (e.g., circles, rippled 1D manifolds) from this symmetry.
Empirically validated these theoretical predictions using both simple word embedding models and complex transformer-based large language models.
Results: Analytically derived and empirically confirmed that translation symmetry in co-occurrence statistics leads to circular representations for periodic concepts (e.g., months) and rippled 1D manifolds for continuous sequences (e.g., years).

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.14697.Title: Evolutionary System Prompt Learning for Reinforcement Learning in LLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.14697.Summary: A framework called Evolutionary System Prompt Learning (E-SPL) jointly optimizes Large Language Model weights using reinforcement learning and system prompts via an evolutionary algorithm, achieving enhanced performance, sample efficiency, and generalization on mathematical reasoning and agentic search tasks.
Problem: Existing LLM self-improvement mechanisms (self-reflection for context updates and reinforcement learning for weight updates) are typically applied in isolation, missing potential synergistic benefits.
There is a representational gap between evolutionary methods, which explore discrete high-level structures like programs, and reinforcement learning, which optimizes continuous policy parameters.
Current RL methods for LLMs often assume a fixed system prompt during training, neglecting the potential for dynamic evolution of declarative knowledge.
The full potential of combining declarative knowledge (prompts) and procedural knowledge (weights) for LLM self-improvement remains largely unexplored.
Method: E-SPL integrates a reinforcement learning (RL) component for updating LLM policy weights and an evolutionary algorithm (EA) for optimizing system prompts.
The RL component conditions the LLM's policy on multiple evolving system prompts in parallel, using rewards from sampled trajectories to compute policy gradients for weight updates.

The EA maintains a population of system prompts, evaluating their fitness using a TrueSkill rating system based on RL rollout performance, and employs LLM-driven mutation and crossover operators to generate new, improved prompts.

Mutation involves the LLM self-reflecting on successful and failed trajectories under a prompt to propose `git diff`-like edits, while crossover uses differential performance information to suggest edits based on problem-wise strengths.
Results: E-SPL consistently outperformed RL-only, evolution-only, and self-reflection baselines across mathematical reasoning (DeepSeek-v3.1) and agentic search (gpt-oss-120b) tasks.

In mathematical reasoning, E-SPL achieved a 60.6% success rate on AIME 25 (vs. 56.3% for RL-only) and demonstrated superior generalization, reaching 45.1% success on BeyondAIME (easy-to-hard) tasks (vs. 38.8% for RL-only).

Analysis of learning dynamics showed E-SPL achieved better sample efficiency and higher asymptotic performance, adapting effectively to leverage either declarative or procedural knowledge for improvement.

Learned system prompts externalized interpretable strategies, such as explicit generative self-verification instructions and codified domain expertise, enhancing the LLM's ability to self-correct and apply sophisticated reasoning principles.
Takeaways: Jointly optimizing LLM weights and system prompts through a tightly coupled RL and EA framework leads to synergistic self-improvement, surpassing methods that optimize either component in isolation.

The E-SPL framework facilitates a natural division of knowledge: explicit, interpretable declarative knowledge is encoded and evolved in system prompts, while implicit, intuitive procedural knowledge is refined in the model's weights.

Evolutionary search, guided by LLM self-reflection for mutation and crossover, can effectively discover and externalize domain-specific strategies and self-verification heuristics into human-readable system prompts.

The explicit nature of learned knowledge in prompts improves interpretability and oversight, as errors or overgeneralizations in declarative statements are more easily identified and corrected by humans than those embedded within model weights.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.13949.Title: Experiential Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.13949.Summary:
Experiential Reinforcement Learning (ERL) from Shi et al. introduces a novel training paradigm that augments standard reinforcement learning with an explicit experience
reflection
consolidation loop. This approach enables large language models to self-improve by transforming environmental feedback into structured behavioral revisions and internalizing these lessons for efficient, durable performance gains at inference time, demonstrating up to an 81% reward increase in complex sparse-reward tasks like Sokoban.
Problem: Large language models (LLMs) struggle to learn effectively as decision-making agents in environments characterized by sparse and delayed feedback.

Current reinforcement learning (RL) paradigms for LLMs compel models to implicitly infer how observed failures should translate into behavioral changes, leading to unstable and sample-inefficient learning.
Traditional RL treats environmental feedback primarily as a scalar optimization signal, failing to leverage LLMs' explicit reflective capacity for systematic behavioral revision during learning.
Method: ERL introduces an explicit experience–reflection–consolidation loop, triggered only when initial attempts fall below a reward threshold, to transform raw feedback into structured behavioral revisions.
The model generates a self-reflection after an initial failure, then produces a refined second attempt, with both the reflection and the second attempt contributing to RL updates.

Successful reflection-guided improvements are internalized into the base policy via selective distillation, ensuring durable behavioral enhancements without requiring the explicit reflection step at inference time.
Results: ERL consistently outperformed standard Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) across all six evaluated settings, including sparse-reward control environments (FrozenLake, Sokoban) and agentic reasoning (HotpotQA).

Achieved substantial performance gains in complex, sparse-reward tasks, such as an 81% increase in Qwen3-4B-Instruct's reward on Sokoban (from 0.06 to 0.87) and a 70% increase on FrozenLake for Olmo3-7B-Instruct.

Demonstrated improved learning efficiency and stability, reaching higher reward levels earlier in training than RLVR, with ablation studies confirming the critical contributions of structured reflection and cross-episode memory.
Takeaways: ERL bridges the gap between LLM self-reflection capabilities and practical RL training by embedding an explicit revision process within each trajectory, making learning more efficient and stable.

The internalization mechanism is crucial, as it distills reflection-driven improvements directly into the base policy, allowing enhanced behaviors to persist without additional inference-time overhead.
A gated mechanism selectively triggers reflection only on suboptimal attempts, conserving computational resources and focusing learning on critical failure cases, thereby concentrating exploration.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12395.Title: What does RL improve for Visual Reasoning? A Frankenstein-Style Analysis
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12395.Summary: This study provides a mechanistic analysis of how Reinforcement Learning (RL) improves Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for visual reasoning tasks. It reveals that RL's primary effect is a focused refinement of mid-to-late transformer layers, which in turn enhances vision-to-reasoning alignment and overall reasoning capabilities.
Problem: Despite empirical gains from Reinforcement Learning (RL) in Vision-Language Models (VLMs), the specific capabilities RL enhances for visual reasoning remain ambiguous.
End-to-end benchmark evaluations conflate various factors, making it difficult to attribute performance improvements to distinct skills like visual perception or language-side reasoning.
Fine-grained metrics for vision ability, reasoning ability, and vision-to-reasoning alignment do not consistently show monotonic improvements from supervised fine-tuning to RL.
Method: Proposing a "Frankenstein-style analysis framework" to mechanistically dissect VLM behavior and causally trace RL's alterations across model architectures.
Localizing vision and reasoning-related computations within transformer layers through causal probing using vision-token interventions and layer-wise causal ablations.

Characterizing parameter updates from supervised fine-tuning and RL by analyzing their energy and diversity using Frobenius norms and singular value spectra, and validating their causal importance and transferability via model merging and freezing experiments.
Results: End-to-end benchmark accuracy improves monotonically from base to RL models, but fine-grained vision ability and standalone reasoning ability do not show consistent monotonic improvements.
Vision computations are predominantly localized in early and mid-transformer layers, while reasoning computations are concentrated in late layers.
Hybrid models incorporating RL-refined mid-to-late layers consistently show improvements in vision-to-reasoning alignment and reasoning performance compared to supervised fine-tuned models.
Freezing late layers during RL training leads to substantial degradation in reasoning and vision-to-reasoning alignment, confirming their causal necessity for RL's gains.
Takeaways: RL consistently induces an increased attention from reasoning tokens to visual tokens, concentrated specifically in the mid-to-late transformer layers.
RL applies less diverse, more focused parameter refinements in the mid-to-late layers compared to supervised fine-tuning, indicating targeted optimization.
RL-induced improvements in vision-to-reasoning alignment and reasoning abilities are modular and transferable, demonstrably encoded within the mid-to-late architectural segments.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12275.Title: On-Policy Context Distillation for Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12275.Summary: On-Policy Context Distillation (OPCD) enables language models to internalize transient in-context knowledge by training student models on their own generations guided by a context-conditioned teacher using reverse KL divergence. This approach yields improved task accuracy, better out-of-distribution generalization, and effective knowledge transfer across model sizes, overcoming limitations of off-policy distillation.
Problem: In-context knowledge in large language models (LLMs) is transient, requiring repeated 're-learning' from prompts, which leads to inefficiencies and increased computational overhead.
Existing off-policy context distillation methods suffer from exposure bias, as models are trained on teacher-generated data but generate their own sequences during inference.
Minimizing forward Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence in off-policy methods can lead to mode-covering behavior, causing student models to produce overly broad distributions or 'hallucinations'.
Method: Introduces On-Policy Context Distillation (OPCD), a framework that trains a student model on its own generated responses to mitigate exposure bias.
Utilizes a context-conditioned teacher model to guide the student's learning by minimizing reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, promoting mode-seeking behavior.

Applies OPCD to two main scenarios: experiential knowledge distillation (internalizing strategies from model-generated solutions) and system prompt distillation (embedding optimized prompt behaviors into model parameters).
Results: OPCD consistently achieved superior task accuracy across mathematical reasoning and text-based games, outperforming off-policy distillation (e.g., Qwen3-8B on Math reached 79.7% with OPCD vs. 78.5% for off-policy distillation).

Demonstrated enhanced out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization, better preserving OOD capabilities compared to off-policy methods, with observed improvements of approximately 4 points in OOD task accuracy for safety distillation.

Enabled effective cross-size distillation, allowing smaller student models (e.g., Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B) to successfully internalize experiential knowledge from larger teachers (Qwen3-8B), often outperforming direct in-context usage for smaller models.
Takeaways: Minimizing reverse KL divergence encourages mode-seeking behavior, prompting the student to focus on high-probability regions of the teacher's context-aware distribution, thus preventing mode-averaging.
On-policy learning, where the student trains on its own generations, aligns training conditions with inference, leading to more robust models with better out-of-distribution generalization.
A fixed, frozen teacher model in teacher-student distillation provides a more stable and consistent learning signal, generally outperforming self-distillation where the teacher's weights evolve.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11858.Title: Zooming without Zooming: Region-to-Image Distillation for Fine-Grained Multimodal Perception
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11858.Summary: Researchers from Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Ant Group developed "Zooming without Zooming" (ZwZ), a paradigm using Region-to-Image Distillation (R2I) to train multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for fine-grained perception. This approach internalizes "zooming" capabilities during training, enabling a single-pass inference that achieves competitive accuracy while being approximately 10 times faster than agentic "Thinking-with-Images" models.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) often lack fine-grained perception, struggling to discern subtle details like tiny text or specific attributes embedded within complex visual contexts.
Current solutions using iterative "zooming" or agentic tool-use ("Thinking-with-Images") suffer from high inference latency, rendering them impractical for real-time applications.
Existing benchmarks for fine-grained perception are often limited in scope, task coverage, or difficulty, hindering robust evaluation of MLLM capabilities.
Method: Developed Region-to-Image Distillation (R2I), an automated pipeline that synthesizes high-veracity, fine-grained VQA data by generating QA pairs from micro-crops using powerful teacher models, then distilling this supervision to full images with visual (bounding box overlay) and textual grounding.

Trained student MLLMs using reinforcement learning (DAPO) on these augmented full-image QA pairs, teaching them to intrinsically "gaze" at relevant micro-evidence from the global context in a single forward pass.

Introduced ZoomBench, a hybrid-annotated benchmark featuring diverse perceptual dimensions and a dual-view evaluation protocol to rigorously assess fine-grained acuity and quantify the "global-regional zooming gap."
Results: ZwZ models, trained with 74K R2I samples, demonstrated leading performance on various fine-grained benchmarks, surpassing larger open-source MLLMs and achieving competitive accuracy with state-of-the-art closed-source models, while performing approximately 10 times faster than agentic baselines.
Region-to-Image Distillation yielded higher-quality, more efficient training data, with models trained on 74K R2I samples outperforming those trained on significantly larger public datasets.

On the novel ZoomBench, ZwZ-8B reduced the "zooming gap" to 15.26%, the smallest among tested models, and exhibited increased relative attention coverage within annotated key regions, confirming improved fine-grained attention.
Takeaways: The benefits of inference-time agentic "zooming" for fine-grained perception can be effectively internalized into an MLLM during training, enabling a single-pass inference that maintains accuracy without high latency.
Synthesizing fine-grained VQA data from micro-crops using powerful teacher models significantly improves data quality and reduces hallucination compared to direct global-to-global synthesis.

Visually augmenting training images with bounding box overlays for specific regions serves as crucial "privileged information," guiding the model's attention to learn intrinsic fine-grained perception.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11737.Title: Mask What Matters: Mitigating Object Hallucinations in Multimodal Large Language Models with Object-Aligned Visual Contrastive Decoding
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11737.Summary: Researchers from ETH Zurich, Amazon, and MBZUAI developed Object-Aligned Visual Contrastive Decoding (OA-VCD), an inference-time method that uses DINO Vision Transformers to create object-aligned auxiliary views for Visual Contrastive Decoding. This approach reduced object hallucination in MLLMs, achieving up to a 1.5% accuracy gain on the POPE benchmark and improving average scores on the MME hallucination subset for models like LLaVA-v1.5 and Qwen-VL.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) frequently generate responses referring to objects not present or incorrectly grounded in images, a phenomenon known as object hallucination.
Existing Visual Contrastive Decoding (VCD) methods often rely on generic, heuristic image-level perturbations that do not precisely target object extents.
Some VCD approaches depend on prompt- and model-specific cross-modal signals, potentially introducing computational overhead, complexity, or circularity.
Method: The work introduces Object-Aligned Visual Contrastive Decoding (OA-VCD), enhancing standard VCD with a novel approach for generating auxiliary views.
Pre-trained DINO Vision Transformers are leveraged to extract object-centric saliency maps from input images, exploiting their inherent ability to identify semantic regions.
Auxiliary views are created by masking out the most salient object regions based on a quantile threshold of these saliency maps, with the masked areas filled by a neutral background.
Results: OA-VCD consistently outperformed baseline methods on the POPE benchmark, achieving up to 1.5% higher Accuracy and 1.6% higher F1 score compared to AGLA on LLaVA-v1.5 (7B).
The method led to improved average scores on the MME hallucination subset, showing notable gains in "Existence" and "Color" categories for both LLaVA-v1.5 and Qwen-VL.
Ablation studies demonstrated the method's robustness to different choices of neutral background (e.g., blur, black, mean color) and masking area ratio (γ\gammaγ).
Takeaways: Object-aligned auxiliary views, derived from self-supervised ViT attention, provide a more semantically targeted and stronger contrast signal for VCD compared to generic perturbations.
The method is prompt-agnostic and model-agnostic, enabling broad applicability across various MLLMs without requiring model-specific fine-tuning or internal states.
Generating these targeted auxiliary views requires only a single cacheable forward pass through a DINO ViT, ensuring computational efficiency during inference.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11635.Title: Do MLLMs Really Understand Space? A Mathematical Reasoning Evaluation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11635.Summary: Lu et al. introduce MathSpatial, a unified framework for evaluating and improving mathematical spatial reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). This framework, comprising a benchmark, training corpus, and structured reasoning traces, reveals a significant gap between human (96.3% accuracy) and top MLLM performance (58.5% for GPT-5) in spatial tasks, while improving fine-tuned open-source models by up to 4.3% accuracy and reducing token usage by 25%.
Problem: MLLMs struggle with "mathematical spatial reasoning," showing a significant performance gap compared to human accuracy (MLLMs typically < 60% vs. human > 95%).
Existing spatial reasoning benchmarks are confounded by visual perception complexities, obscuring the diagnosis of true reasoning failures.
A lack of large-scale, high-quality training data specific to mathematical spatial reasoning hinders systematic MLLM improvement.
Current MLLM approaches for spatial problem-solving are often black-box, lacking interpretability and transparent intermediate reasoning steps.
Method: Developed MathSpatial, a unified framework comprising MathSpatial-Bench (2K problems) for evaluation, MathSpatial-Corpus (8K problems) for training, and MathSpatial-SRT for structured reasoning.

Constructed a large-scale dataset using a semi-automated pipeline that curates and verifies mathematical spatial problems from educational sources, ensuring geometric consistency and solution reliability.

Introduced MathSpatial-SRT (Structured Reasoning Traces) to decompose spatial problem-solving into three atomic, interpretable operations (Correlate, Constrain, Infer) for supervised fine-tuning of MLLMs.
Results: Humans achieved 96.3% average accuracy on MathSpatial-Bench, while the best MLLM (GPT-5) reached only 58.5%, confirming a significant performance deficit.
Fine-tuning open-source MLLMs with MathSpatial-Corpus and SRTs improved accuracy by up to 4.3% (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL-7B to 22.1%) and reduced token consumption by approximately 25%.
MathSpatial-trained models demonstrated consistent accuracy gains (+1.3% to +3.4%) and reduced token usage (7.1%–21.3%) when evaluated on external, out-of-distribution spatial benchmarks.
Error analysis revealed that reasoning gaps (34.4%) and geometry violations (33.0%) were the primary causes of MLLM failures on mathematical spatial tasks.
Takeaways: A profound gap exists between human and MLLM capabilities in mathematical spatial reasoning, underscoring a fundamental limitation of current MLLMs.
Disentangling spatial reasoning from perceptual noise is crucial for accurate diagnosis and targeted improvement of MLLMs' cognitive abilities.
Structured reasoning traces provide an effective method for enhancing both the accuracy and interpretability of MLLM spatial problem-solving, leading to more concise and efficient reasoning.
MLLM failures predominantly stem from core reasoning gaps and violations of geometric rules, highlighting challenges in multi-step logical deduction and consistency enforcement.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11389.Title: Causal-JEPA: Learning World Models through Object-Level Latent Interventions
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11389.Summary: Causal-JEPA presents an object-centric world model integrating Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) with object-level latent interventions, fostering interaction-dependent dynamics learning and efficient planning. It improves counterfactual reasoning accuracy by approximately 20% and accelerates model predictive control planning by over 8 times.
Problem: Existing object-centric world models often fail to inherently capture interaction-dependent dynamics, instead relying on learning object self-dynamics or incidental correlations.
Traditional masked prediction methods (e.g., patch-based) do not explicitly enforce object-level interaction reasoning and can be computationally inefficient for complex dynamic environments.
World models require a deeper, more robust relational understanding for accurate prediction and control, which is not sufficiently induced by current learning objectives alone.
Method: Causal-JEPA leverages a frozen object-centric encoder (e.g., VideoSAUR, SAVi) to transform high-dimensional observations into compact sets of object-level latent representations.
It employs a Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA)-style masked transformer as the core predictor, operating on these object latents and auxiliary variables (actions, proprioception).

A central innovation is the application of object-level masking as a latent intervention, replacing masked object states with an 'identity anchor' from an earlier timestep to force inference based on interactions with other objects.
Results: Achieved an absolute improvement of approximately 20% in counterfactual visual question answering accuracy on the CLEVRER dataset, demonstrating enhanced causal understanding.
Attained comparable task success rates to state-of-the-art patch-based world models on the Push-T robotic manipulation task, while enabling over 8 times faster planning.
Operated on only 1.02% of the input features compared to patch-based models, leading to substantial computational efficiency during Model Predictive Control.
Takeaways: Object-level masking, interpreted as a latent intervention, induces a causal inductive bias that compels the model to learn stable, interaction-dependent predictive relationships.

The masked history prediction objective formally necessitates reliance on a 'minimal sufficient set of contextual variables' (Influence Neighborhood) for optimal inference, making interaction reasoning functionally essential.
Integrating object-centric representations with JEPAs enables efficient world modeling by operating on a significantly reduced latent feature space, without sacrificing performance.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11241.Title: Active Zero: Self-Evolving Vision-Language Models through Active Environment Exploration
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11241.Summary: Active-Zero introduces a framework enabling Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to autonomously improve their reasoning by actively exploring and curating visual data from open-ended environments. This approach allows VLMs to dynamically construct a learning curriculum tailored to their evolving capabilities, achieving superior performance on reasoning and general visual understanding tasks.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language Model (VLM) self-play methods passively interact with static image collections, limiting task diversity and quality.
Reliance on fixed datasets prevents VLMs from truly transcending their initial training distribution as capabilities evolve.
Inefficient learning occurs when VLMs expend computational effort on visual data that is either too easy or too difficult for their current skill set.
Method: A tri-agent framework—comprising a Searcher, Questioner, and Solver—is introduced to create a co-evolutionary cycle for active data acquisition and reasoning enhancement.
The Searcher agent actively explores an open-world visual environment to identify images at the VLM's "capability frontier," using a challenge reward based on Solver uncertainty.
The Questioner synthesizes adaptive, instructionally useful reasoning tasks from these retrieved images, while the Solver optimizes its reasoning abilities on this self-generated curriculum.
Results: Achieved substantial performance gains on 12 benchmarks, with an average 5.7% improvement on reasoning tasks and 3.9% on general visual understanding for the Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct model.
Ablation studies confirm the critical role of the active Searcher, RL optimization, domain-conditioned exploration, and visual redundancy control in driving performance improvements.

The system generates a more effective curriculum, shifting task difficulty towards moderately challenging and higher-consensus questions, while enabling the Searcher to evolve its query strategy over time.
Takeaways: Empowering Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to actively explore and curate visual data from open environments significantly overcomes the limitations of static datasets.
The co-evolutionary training of specialized agents (Searcher, Questioner, Solver) enables the creation of a self-scaffolding curriculum that continuously adapts to the VLM's evolving capabilities.

Optimizing data acquisition for a balance of challenge (based on Solver uncertainty) and diversity (through repetition penalties) is crucial for generating an effective and comprehensive learning trajectory.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11217.Title: The Magic Correlations: Understanding Knowledge Transfer from Pretraining to Supervised Fine-Tuning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11217.Summary: Researchers at Google DeepMind and EPFL systematically analyzed how accuracy and confidence transfer from pretraining to supervised fine-tuning in large language models using correlation protocols. Their findings reveal category-dependent transfer reliability and an inverse scaling dynamic where larger models exhibit stronger accuracy transfer but weaker confidence transfer, indicating significant calibration reorganization.
Problem: LLM development often relies on the untested assumption that pretraining performance reliably predicts post-fine-tuning performance.
Decisions about data curation and resource allocation are frequently based on early-stage evaluations with smaller proxy models, which may lead to suboptimal outcomes if transfer is not stable.
A lack of systematic understanding of how model capabilities, specifically accuracy and confidence, evolve and transfer across pretraining and fine-tuning stages.
Method: Trained decoder-only transformer models (240M and 1B parameters) on 9 distinct pretraining data mixtures, varying proportions of general web, code, and curated knowledge.
Fine-tuned all pretrained checkpoints on the Tulu-v2-mix instruction-following dataset for 5 epochs.
Evaluated models on 20 benchmarks across four capability categories (Commonsense, Scientific, NLI, Semantic) using both accuracy and confidence metrics.
Employed five correlation protocols to quantify the preservation and reorganization of model capabilities across training stages and data mixtures.
Results: Science and Commonsense benchmarks show high cross-stage accuracy correlation (mean r > 0.5), indicating pretraining performance reliably predicts SFT outcomes, unlike NLI and Semantic tasks.
1B models achieve stronger accuracy transfer (r = 0.60) but substantially weaker confidence transfer (r = 0.39) compared to 240M models, which maintain higher confidence transfer (r = 0.68).
Persistent miscalibration is observed in Commonsense and Semantic tasks, exhibiting weak or negative accuracy-confidence alignment (r_align ≈ -0.1 to -0.2) even after SFT.
Benchmarks like WiC and MultiRC show weak cross-stage accuracy correlations (r < 0.3), making them unreliable early-stage predictors of post-SFT success.
Takeaways: Knowledge transfer from pretraining to supervised fine-tuning is not uniform; its reliability varies significantly by capability category and model scale.
Larger models exhibit stronger accuracy transfer from pretraining but weaker confidence transfer, suggesting extensive reorganization of calibration patterns during fine-tuning.
