Pretraining data choices have lasting, scale-dependent effects on model calibration and task performance that supervised fine-tuning does not easily overwrite.
Specific benchmarks can be unreliable early-stage predictors of downstream SFT performance, highlighting the need for careful benchmark selection.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11144.Title: GENIUS: Generative Fluid Intelligence Evaluation Suite
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11144.Summary: Researchers from Peking University, CUHK, StepFun, PolyU, and MSRA introduce GENIUS, the first benchmark dedicated to evaluating Generative Fluid Intelligence (GFI) in Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs). Their work reveals significant GFI deficits in state-of-the-art models and proposes a training-free attention adjustment mechanism that boosts performance by rectifying disordered attention distributions.
Problem: Existing benchmarks for Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) primarily assess "Crystallized Intelligence" (memorization and retrieval), failing to evaluate their ability for dynamic reasoning and adaptation.
A formal definition for Generative Fluid Intelligence (GFI) in visual generation was lacking, hindering systematic assessment and development of truly adaptable AI.
UMMs often exhibit an "illusion of competence," where visually plausible outputs mask a fundamental inability to deeply comprehend context and logically adhere to novel, ad-hoc rules.
Method: Formally defined Generative Fluid Intelligence (GFI) as a synthesis of Inductive Inference, Abstract Dynamic Reasoning, and Adaptive Inhibition, grounded in the Cattell-Horn-Carroll theory.
Introduced GENIUS, a multimodal, expert-curated benchmark with 510 samples across 3 dimensions and 5 tasks, designed to rigorously decouple static knowledge from fluid reasoning.

Proposed a training-free attention adjustment mechanism that distills task-critical keywords, maps their relevance to visual context, and injects a spatial bias into attention logits to focus on critical signals.
Results: Evaluations of 12 UMMs on GENIUS showed widespread GFI deficiencies, with the highest-performing proprietary model (Nano Banana Pro) achieving an overall score of only 57.19%.
The proposed attention adjustment mechanism improved the overall GFI score of an open-source model (Bagel) by 6.18%, demonstrating its effectiveness in activating latent GFI capabilities.
A high Pearson correlation (r = 0.9630 to 0.9659) between LMM-based automated scoring (Gemini-3-Pro) and human expert judgments validated the reliability of the GENIUS evaluation framework.
Takeaways: Current state-of-the-art UMMs exhibit substantial deficits in GFI, with even the best proprietary models scoring below 60%, indicating a significant gap towards general intelligence.
Models suffer from "cognitive inertia," frequently defaulting to pre-trained priors when instructions contradict established world knowledge, rather than adapting to new contextual rules.
There is an "execution gap" where models often demonstrate accurate comprehension of context (via VQA probes) but fail to translate this understanding into compliant visual outputs during generation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11073.Title: Chatting with Images for Introspective Visual Thinking
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11073.Summary: The VILAVT model introduces a "chatting with images" framework, which redefines visual reasoning as language-guided feature modulation for large vision-language models. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on 5 out of 8 benchmarks for general, single-image, multi-image, and video-based spatial reasoning tasks, demonstrating improved versatility and robustness to information loss at lower resolutions.
Problem: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) operating under the 'thinking about images' paradigm suffer irreversible information loss due to single-pass visual encoding.

Existing 'thinking with images' approaches (tool-based, programmatic, generative imagination) often lack expressiveness for high-level relational intent, incur high latency, or struggle with joint reasoning across multiple visual inputs.

Challenges in establishing effective cross-modal alignment and grounding between linguistic semantics and low-level visual manipulation interfaces, especially for complex visual semantics or geometric relationships.
Method: Introduces the 'chatting with images' paradigm, which models visual reasoning as generating an iterative trajectory of textual reasoning, natural language inquiries, and targeted visual region re-examinations.

Develops VILAVT, a novel LVLM featuring a dynamic vision encoder that jointly processes multiple, potentially non-contiguous visual regions conditioned on a natural language inquiry using a hybrid attention strategy.

Employs a two-stage training strategy: Supervised Fine-tuning (SFT) on a multi-domain dataset of repurposed and synthesized reasoning trajectories, followed by Reinforcement Learning (RL) with an outcome-based reward function.
Results: VILAVT achieved state-of-the-art results on 5 out of 8 diverse benchmarks, encompassing General VQA, single-image, multi-image, and video-based spatial reasoning tasks.
Ablation studies confirmed that the 'chatting with images' paradigm and the dynamic vision encoder contributed substantial performance gains over baseline models.
The model demonstrated improved robustness to information loss at lower visual resolutions, achieving 75.9% accuracy on SPAR with 512 visual tokens, a 24.8% gap over a vanilla encoder.
Takeaways: Modeling visual reasoning as language-guided feature modulation enables a more robust and fine-grained visual thinking process, overcoming limitations of static encoding and low-level manipulation.

A dynamic vision encoder with query-conditioned joint encoding across multiple visual inputs is crucial for effective cross-view interaction and detail preservation, especially in multi-image and video reasoning scenarios.

Both supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning stages are essential for bootstrapping the model's ability to generate interactive reasoning trajectories and for refining its strategic problem-solving capabilities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.10675.Title: TwiFF (Think With Future Frames): A Large-Scale Dataset for Dynamic Visual Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.10675.Summary: A collaborative research effort introduces TwiFF (Think With Future Frames), a large-scale dataset (TwiFF-2.7M) and a corresponding model for dynamic visual reasoning, enabling multimodal AI to understand and predict temporal progression in visual tasks. The framework jointly leverages video generation and image comprehension to produce coherent reasoning chains, showing substantial improvements in reasoning plausibility and answer accuracy on dynamic benchmarks.
Problem: Existing Visual Chain-of-Thought (VCoT) methods are confined to static scenarios, unable to reason about temporal progression, future events, or step-by-step instructions.
There is a lack of large-scale, temporally grounded VCoT datasets necessary for training models in dynamic visual reasoning tasks.

Current multimodal benchmarks for dynamic tasks often suffer from small sample sizes, utilize multiple-choice formats, or exclusively focus on final answer accuracy, neglecting the plausibility and coherence of intermediate reasoning steps.
Method: The researchers developed TwiFF-2.7M, the first large-scale, temporally grounded VCoT dataset, constructed from millions of video clips through a three-stage pipeline (coarse filtering, event extraction, and VCoT generation).

They introduced TwiFF-Bench, a novel evaluation benchmark that uses GPT-5.1 as a judge to assess both the plausibility of reasoning trajectories and the correctness of final answers in open-ended dynamic settings.

A unified TwiFF model was proposed, which fine-tunes Bagel-7B to iteratively generate future action frames and accompanying textual reasoning, thereby synergistically combining video generation and image comprehension capabilities.
Results: The TwiFF model achieved a 28.8% improvement in CoT scores (reasoning plausibility) and 41.6% in answer scores on TwiFF-Bench compared to its base model, Bagel-7B.
It demonstrated strong generalization, showing a 21.0% improvement in answer scores on the out-of-distribution Seed-Bench-R1 dataset.

Ablation studies confirmed that the interleaved vision-textual VCoT (TwiFF-Lite) consistently outperformed single-modality variants (TwiFF-Text, TwiFF-Image) in both reasoning plausibility and answer accuracy, especially for out-of-distribution generalization.
Takeaways: Dynamic VCoT demonstrates superior performance over Textual CoT and static VCoT in dynamic reasoning tasks, providing a more effective paradigm for understanding temporal visual information.
The synergistic interaction between textual and visual modalities is crucial for VCoT's effectiveness and generalization, as neither modality alone suffices to achieve full reasoning capability.
Physically plausible and temporally accurate visual cues are paramount for enhancing reasoning performance, while static or misleading cues actively impede the process.
Dynamic VCoT exhibits a potential for information compression, where the first generated visual cue can effectively capture and retain critical contextual information from the input image.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.10551.Title: C^2ROPE: Causal Continuous Rotary Positional Encoding for 3D Large Multimodal-Models Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.10551.Summary: A new positional encoding, C2RoPE, enhances the ability of 3D Large Multimodal Models to perceive and reason about visual information by explicitly modeling spatio-temporal and causal relationships within visual tokens. Applied to the LLaVA-3D baseline, it boosted performance on the ScanQA benchmark with an +18.1 CIDEr score improvement and achieved a +1.2 EM@1 gain on SQA3D.
Problem: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE), designed for 1D text sequences, poorly handles the multi-dimensional spatial and causal relationships inherent in visual data, particularly in 3D Large Multimodal Models (LMMs).
RoPE's raster-scan indexing for visual tokens leads to 'spatial locality loss' by assigning numerically distant positional indices to spatially adjacent tokens along vertical axes.

The inherent temporal-causality assumption in RoPE causes 'visual tokens neglect,' where attention progressively weakens for earlier visual tokens in extended sequences, hindering comprehensive 3D scene understanding.
Method: C2RoPE (Causal Continuous Rotary Positional Encoding) is proposed to explicitly model spatio-temporal and causal relationships for visual tokens, integrating into the LLaVA-3D-7B architecture.

A spatio-temporal continuous positional embedding mechanism combines 1D temporal indices with 2D Cartesian spatial coordinates (x, y) to form a hybrid positional index for each visual token, addressing spatial locality loss through a tailored frequency allocation strategy.

Chebyshev Causal Masking redefines causal dependencies based on spatial (Chebyshev) distance from an image's center, replacing temporal-based masking to mitigate visual token neglect and long-term attention decay.
Results: C2RoPE improved the LLaVA-3D baseline on the ScanQA benchmark, achieving +4.3 EM@1, +8.5 BLEU-4, +13.4 METEOR, +2.5 ROUGE, and +18.1 CIDEr, reaching state-of-the-art among compared 3D LMMs.
On the SQA3D benchmark (test set), C2RoPE enhanced LLaVA-3D by +1.2 EM@1 and +1.2 EM@R.
Ablation studies confirmed C2RoPE's superior performance over other multimodal positional encoding methods like CCA and MCA on SQA3D validation and test subsets.
Takeaways: Direct application of 1D-sequence-centric RoPE to 2D/3D visual data fundamentally limits LMMs' perceptual capabilities, causing issues like spatial locality loss and visual token neglect.
Explicitly integrating 2D spatial coordinates with 1D temporal information, using a strategic frequency allocation, is effective in preserving spatial continuity within visual token representations.

Defining causality based on spatial relationships (e.g., Chebyshev distance) rather than pure temporal distance better reflects visual information dependencies, enabling more comprehensive attention to spatially relevant visual tokens.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.09463.Title: SpotAgent: Grounding Visual Geo-localization in Large Vision-Language Models through Agentic Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.09463.Summary: SpotAgent grounds visual geo-localization in Large Vision-Language Models by formalizing the task as an agent-based decision-making process, integrating external tools for iterative evidence gathering and verification. This framework achieves state-of-the-art performance among retrieval-free methods on the Im2GPS3k benchmark, with 14.12% accuracy at 1km, while effectively reducing spatial hallucinations.
Problem: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) for geo-localization often rely solely on internal knowledge, treating the task as a closed-world problem.
This reliance makes LVLMs prone to generating plausible but spatially incorrect "hallucinations" when visual cues are sparse, ambiguous, or long-tailed.
Existing LVLM approaches lack active external verification, hindering the factual grounding and verifiable precision of geo-localization predictions.
Method: SpotAgent formulates visual geo-localization as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP), enabling an agent to iteratively perform actions based on its current state.
A multi-agent ReAct framework generates high-quality training data, decoupling visual perception (Observer Agent) from strategic planning and tool invocation (Tool-Call Agent).

A 3-stage post-training pipeline (Supervised Fine-Tuning, Agentic Cold Start, and Reinforcement Learning with Spatially-Aware Dynamic Filtering) instills tool-calling expertise and refines reasoning for fine-grained spatial accuracy.
Results: SpotAgent achieved state-of-the-art performance among retrieval-free methods on the Im2GPS3k benchmark, with 14.12% accuracy at 1km and 40.36% at 25km.

The agentic framework demonstrated improved robustness in challenging long-tail scenarios, outperforming a "No Tool" variant by more than double (19.65% vs 9.22% at 1km) on the Street View Text Dataset.

Ablation studies confirmed that each stage of the post-training pipeline progressively contributes to performance gains, with the Agentic Cold Start notably improving tool utilization and the RL stage refining spatial accuracy.
Takeaways: The "Agentic Cold Start" training stage is crucial for activating the LVLM's awareness and robust utilization of external tools, significantly improving tool-call rates and success.
Synergizing diverse external tools like web search, visual zoom, and geo-coding proves essential for achieving precise geo-localization, especially in ambiguous or long-tail scenarios.

Dynamically filtering reinforcement learning samples to prioritize "learnable" examples, rather than perfectly solved or intractable ones, enhances the efficiency and effectiveness of spatial reasoning refinement.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.08346.Title: What, Whether and How? Unveiling Process Reward Models for Thinking with Images Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.08346.Summary: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology and collaborators introduce ThinkWithImages-PRMBENCH, the first benchmark for Process Reward Models (PRMs) in "thinking with images" visual reasoning. The research defines a seven-category error taxonomy and reveals that current Large Vision Language Models (LVLMs) perform poorly as PRMs, exhibiting a strong positive bias and limited ability to detect complex multimodal reasoning errors compared to human performance.
Problem: Large Vision Language Models (LVLMs) utilizing "thinking with images" methods generate complex, multi-step visual reasoning trajectories that are prone to fine-grained errors.

Existing Process Reward Models (PRMs) and their benchmarks primarily focus on text-based reasoning, lacking specific tools to evaluate multimodal reasoning processes involving interleaved text and image interactions.
Current LVLMs struggle to reliably self-correct or receive fine-grained feedback due to the absence of a structured approach to identify and assess errors at each step of dynamic visual reasoning.
Method: A comprehensive taxonomy of seven fine-grained error types in "thinking with images" reasoning was developed through analysis of model trajectories.
ThinkWithImages-PRMBENCH, the first human-annotated multimodal benchmark for Process Reward Models, was constructed from 1,206 visual reasoning questions with detailed step-by-step annotations.
State-of-the-art LVLMs were evaluated on this new benchmark to assess their capabilities as PRMs, focusing on overall accuracy and detection rates for specific error categories.
Results: The ThinkWithImages-PRMBENCH dataset was created, containing 1,206 questions and 12,714 meticulously human-annotated reasoning steps spanning diverse visual reasoning scenarios.

Evaluated LVLMs achieved substantially lower accuracy in detecting correct and incorrect reasoning steps than human annotators, with proprietary models also showing limited performance (e.g., GPT-4o at 31.45% ACC).

Performance of LVLMs as PRMs was highly variable across different error types and reasoning steps, often degrading during image extraction steps, suggesting challenges in consistently evaluating dynamic visual processing.
Takeaways: Integrating PRMs, even generic LVLM-based ones, improves the reasoning accuracy of "thinking with images" models by 1-8%, highlighting the utility of process-level supervision.
Current LVLMs demonstrate limited capability as PRMs for visual reasoning, with the best open-source model achieving only 41.74% accuracy, considerably below human expert performance.
LVLMs exhibit a pronounced "positive bias" in reward assignments and struggle significantly with detecting subtle and complex error types like Tool Invocation and Relationship Understanding.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.08241.Title: Do MLLMs Really See It: Reinforcing Visual Attention in Multimodal LLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.08241.Summary: Ou et al. present SAYO, a reinforcement learning framework designed to strengthen visual attention in multimodal large language models by directly rewarding precise region-level focus on high-entropy visual tokens. This approach leads to improved performance across diverse visual reasoning benchmarks, with SAYO-Qwen-8B achieving an average score of 64.03, and exhibits strong cross-domain generalization.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) frequently exhibit weak and unstable visual attention policies, especially in complex visual scenes.
Early visual misalignment during MLLM inference propagates through Chain-of-Thought reasoning, leading to systematic and uncorrected errors.
Existing MLLM training paradigms suffer from an "optimization deficiency," lacking effective credit assignment signals for learning robust visual attention behaviors.
Method: Introduces SAYO, a reinforcement learning (RL) framework based on Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), to explicitly train MLLMs for stable visual grounding.
Develops an "Entropy-Based Target Attention Reward" that selectively incentivizes MLLMs to allocate more attention to target visual regions for high-entropy (information-rich) tokens.
Constructs specialized training data by aligning textual questions with precise bounding box coordinates, converted to visual token ranges, to emphasize visual attention focus.
Results: SAYO consistently outperforms its base models and other leading open-source MLLMs across diverse visual reasoning benchmarks, with SAYO-Qwen-8B achieving an average score of 64.03.

The method demonstrates strong cross-domain generalization, showing significant performance improvements on mathematical reasoning benchmarks like We-Math and MathVision, despite not being trained on mathematical datasets.

Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of the entropy-based attention reward, which yields substantially larger performance gains compared to conventional or uniformly applied rewards, leading to higher target attention scores and more efficient reasoning.
Takeaways: The primary bottleneck in MLLM performance for complex reasoning is often weak visual grounding and attention rather than insufficient reasoning capacity.
Explicitly rewarding precise, region-level visual attention, particularly for tokens indicating high uncertainty, is critical for learning stable visual focus.
The learned "Look-to-Verify" policy enables MLLMs to proactively consult visual evidence to resolve uncertainty, thus mitigating blind reasoning and hallucinations.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.08236.Title: When and How Much to Imagine: Adaptive Test-Time Scaling with World Models for Visual Spatial Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.08236.Summary: Researchers from UNC Chapel Hill and Nanyang Technological University developed Adaptive Visual Imagination Control (AVIC), a test-time framework that enables multimodal large language models to selectively and efficiently use visual world models for spatial reasoning. AVIC improves visual spatial reasoning accuracy (e.g., GPT-4.1 from 74.0% to 79.3% on SAT-Real) while significantly reducing computational costs, such as decreasing world-model calls by approximately 17 times and language tokens by about 9 times compared to always-on imagination methods.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle with complex visual spatial reasoning tasks that require understanding beyond a single static observation.
Existing visual world models, designed to augment MLLMs with 'imagination,' employ fixed and exhaustive strategies, indiscriminately generating views regardless of necessity.
This 'always-on' imagination leads to high computational overhead and can degrade MLLM performance by introducing misleading or redundant visual evidence.
Method: The Adaptive Visual Imagination Control (AVIC) framework is introduced, which adaptively decides 'when' and 'how much' to invoke a visual world model during test-time inference.
AVIC incorporates a policy model that acts as a gatekeeper, deciding whether to skip imagination or call the world model, and proposing a short, discrete action plan if imagination is needed.
A trajectory-level verification mechanism evaluates entire imagined trajectories to select the most useful one, ensuring temporal and geometric consistency for downstream reasoning.
Results: AVIC consistently improved average accuracy on visual spatial reasoning benchmarks like SAT-Real (e.g., GPT-4.1 from 74.0% to 79.3%) and MMSI-Bench compared to baseline and fixed imagination methods.

AVIC achieved these performance gains with significantly reduced computational resources, using approximately 9 times fewer language tokens and 17 times fewer world-model calls than 'always-on' strategies.
The framework successfully integrated into embodied navigation tasks (R2R), improving key metrics (e.g., Oracle Success Rate, Success Rate) and reducing Navigation Error in MapGPT with GPT-4o.
Takeaways: Indiscriminate, 'always-on' visual imagination is computationally inefficient (e.g., nearly two orders of magnitude more tokens, ~30x higher inference time) and can lead to performance degradation (9% of cases were 'misleading').
Visual imagination is most beneficial for action-conditioned spatial reasoning, yielding the largest accuracy gains in scenarios requiring predictions of future states under hypothetical actions.
Optimal benefits from imagination are achieved with a small, targeted number of imagined views (1-2), beyond which additional imagination provides diminishing returns or can harm performance.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.08234.Title: SkillRL: Evolving Agents via Recursive Skill-Augmented Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.08234.Summary: Researchers from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and collaborators developed SKILLRL, a framework enabling Large Language Model (LLM) agents to learn and recursively evolve abstract skills from diverse experiences. SKILLRL achieves state-of-the-art performance with a 89.9% success rate on ALFWorld, 72.7% on WebShop, and an average score of 47.1% on search-augmented QA tasks, outperforming larger closed-source models and memory-augmented baselines.
Problem: Large Language Model (LLM) agents often operate episodically, failing to learn and generalize from past experiences, which limits their scalability and adaptability.
Existing memory-augmented LLM agents predominantly store raw, verbose, and noisy interaction trajectories, leading to "context bloat" and inefficient extraction of high-level behavioral patterns.
Current memory mechanisms typically function as external references without fundamentally adapting the agent's internal policy or evolving to address new failure modes and challenges.
Method: Employs a teacher model to distill raw interaction trajectories, including both successful episodes and failures, into concise "strategic patterns" and "failure lessons."

Constructs a hierarchical SKILLBANK that organizes distilled knowledge into general skills (universal strategies) and task-specific skills, designed for efficient retrieval and significant token compression.

Utilizes Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) for a cold-start initialization, followed by recursive skill evolution during Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to dynamically refine the skill library and agent policy based on ongoing performance.
Results: Achieved state-of-the-art success rates, including 89.9% on ALFWorld, 72.7% on WebShop, and an average score of 47.1% on search-augmented QA tasks.
Outperformed strong baselines, including GPT-4o by 41.9% and Gemini-2.5-Pro by 29.6% on ALFWorld, demonstrating that intelligent skill learning can compensate for model scale.

Reduced prompt token usage by approximately 10.3% compared to raw memory retrieval, while also exhibiting faster convergence and a dynamic expansion of the skill library from 55 to 100 skills during training.
Takeaways: Abstracting experiences into high-level, hierarchical skills provides superior performance and context efficiency for LLM agents compared to storing or compressing raw interaction trajectories.

A dynamic and recursive skill evolution mechanism, where the skill library co-evolves with the agent's policy, is critical for continuous improvement, adaptability, and effectively addressing emergent failure modes.
Initial Supervised Fine-Tuning on skill-augmented reasoning traces is essential for enabling the base LLM agent to effectively utilize and integrate abstract skills into its decision-making process.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.07605.Title: Fine-R1: Make Multi-modal LLMs Excel in Fine-Grained Visual Recognition by Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.07605.Summary: Researchers from Peking University introduce FINE-R1, a Multi-modal Large Language Model (MLLM) that achieves state-of-the-art performance in Fine-Grained Visual Recognition (FGVR) with only 4-shot training data per category. This MLLM surpasses specialized discriminative models like SigLIP-L by +5.16% on unseen categories and shows a +23.75% semantic similarity improvement in open-world settings, demonstrating strong generalization and efficient knowledge deployment for subtle visual distinctions.
Problem: Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) underperform specialized computer vision models in Fine-Grained Visual Recognition (FGVR) tasks, which require distinguishing subtle visual differences.
Adapting MLLMs for FGVR is data-inefficient, demanding vast amounts of expensive, fine-grained annotated data and often leading to overfitting and poor generalization to unseen categories.
FGVR is inherently challenging due to high intra-class variance (diverse appearances within a category) and low inter-class variance (subtle differences between similar categories).
Method: FINE-R1 employs a two-stage training framework starting with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Supervised Fine-tuning (SFT) to teach structured, human-like reasoning for open-world FGVR.

It then uses Triplet Augmented Policy Optimization (TAPO), a novel reinforcement learning algorithm that augments each image with positive (same category) and negative (most similar distinct category) examples.

TAPO incorporates both intra-class augmentation (hybrid sampling for diversity) and inter-class augmentation (KL divergence loss to enhance discriminative ability between similar categories) to refine knowledge deployment with few-shot data.
Results: FINE-R1-7B achieved state-of-the-art average accuracy of 91.71% on seen categories and 85.70% on unseen categories in closed-world FGVR, surpassing general MLLMs, reasoning MLLMs, and specialized CLIP models.
In open-world evaluation, FINE-R1-7B established a new state-of-the-art with an average relative semantic similarity of 74.80%, representing a +23.75% improvement over Qwen2.5-VL-7B.

The model demonstrates strong generalization to unseen categories, with significant gains (+15.59% over SFT in closed-world for FINE-R1-3B), and also improved performance on related non-classification questions (e.g., +3.60% on ImageWikiQA) while preserving general VQA capabilities.
Takeaways: MLLMs do not necessarily lack fine-grained subcategory knowledge but rather struggle with its effective deployment for specific FGVR tasks, as FINE-R1 shows improved knowledge deployment without altering visual features or subcategory encoding.

Structured Chain-of-Thought reasoning, when learned through SFT, provides a robust foundation for MLLMs to integrate domain knowledge and perform meticulous visual comparisons, outperforming zero-shot or in-context learning CoT strategies.

Reinforcement learning, particularly with triplet-based augmentation, is highly effective in addressing the high intra-class and low inter-class variance challenges of FGVR, leading to superior generalization with limited data.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.06218.Title: Cross-Modal Redundancy and the Geometry of Vision-Language Embeddings
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.06218.Summary: Researchers introduced the Iso-Energy Assumption and an Aligned Sparse Autoencoder (SAE-A) to dissect the geometric structure of Vision-Language Model embeddings. This framework successfully disentangles cross-modal representations into distinct bimodal and unimodal components, enabling the elimination of the modality gap and precise semantic edits without impacting model performance.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) lack a principled understanding of how they achieve cross-modal alignment within their embedding spaces.
Concept-based interpretability methods on VLMs often show a "modality gap," where extracted concepts activate exclusively for either image or text.
Interventions to reduce the modality gap typically degrade VLM cross-modal performance, highlighting a knowledge gap regarding shared vs. modality-specific features.
Method: Introduces the Iso-Energy Assumption, positing that genuinely shared concepts in VLMs should have invariant average activation energy across modalities.
Develops an Aligned Sparse Autoencoder (SAE-A) that incorporates the Iso-Energy Assumption as a soft regularization term during training.
Validates the method on synthetic data and applies it to six foundational dual-encoder VLMs, employing a suite of multimodality-sensitive metrics.
Results: SAE-A achieves comparable reconstruction fidelity to standard SAEs while showing superior performance on multimodality-sensitive metrics, including an order-of-magnitude increase in Functional Alignment ("rho").

Filtering unimodal atoms effectively collapses the modality gap, merging image and text distributions without degrading VLM retrieval or zero-shot performance, surpassing prior "embedding shift" methods.
Semantic vector arithmetic restricted to the bimodal subspace ensures in-distribution edits and improves retrieval performance on benchmarks such as FashionIQ compared to conventional methods.
Takeaways: The Iso-Energy Assumption effectively guides concept learning, allowing the SAE-A to correctly identify bimodal concepts exhibiting consistent activation energy across modalities.

VLM embedding spaces feature a geometric decomposition into sparse bimodal atoms, responsible for cross-modal alignment, and unimodal atoms, which hold modality-specific information and explain the modality gap.
High-energy unimodal features are largely responsible for the observed modality gap, acting as modality-specific biases rather than contributing to cross-modal semantics.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.05986.Title: RISE-Video: Can Video Generators Decode Implicit World Rules?
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.05986.Summary: Researchers from Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Tencent Youtu Lab developed RISE-Video, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating the implicit world reasoning capabilities of Text-Image-to-Video (TI2V) models. This framework, which leverages an LMM-based automated judging pipeline, revealed that even leading TI2V models like Hailuo 2.3 achieved only 22.5% accuracy, consistently struggling with higher-level reasoning despite their visual fidelity.
Problem: Existing video generation benchmarks predominantly emphasize surface-level qualities such as perceptual realism and temporal consistency, lacking diagnostic granularity for higher-level cognitive reasoning.
The capacity of current Text-Image-to-Video (TI2V) models to internalize and reason over implicit world rules (e.g., physical laws, social norms, logical inferences) remains largely unquantified.

Without a dedicated framework, models might generate visually convincing but physically implausible, logically inconsistent, or experientially nonsensical videos, hindering the development of true 'world simulators'.
Method: Introduced RISE-Video, a reasoning-oriented benchmark featuring 467 human-annotated samples across eight distinct reasoning categories, from perceptual to logical knowledge.

Developed a multi-dimensional evaluation protocol using four complementary metrics: Reasoning Alignment, Temporal Consistency, Physical Rationality, and Visual Quality, with specialized handling for abstract tasks.
Proposed an automated and scalable LMM-based judging pipeline, primarily utilizing GPT-5, to efficiently assess videos while maintaining high alignment with human judgments.
Results: The top-performing TI2V model, Hailuo 2.3, achieved only 22.5% accuracy on the RISE-Video benchmark, indicating pervasive deficiencies in implicit reasoning across all 11 evaluated models.
Models performed best on low-level Perceptual Knowledge tasks but showed consistently low performance in Logical Capability, highlighting a fundamental limitation in abstract, rule-based reasoning.
Sora 2 showed notable strength in Temporal Consistency, while Hailuo 2.3 demonstrated a clear advantage in Reasoning Alignment, outperforming the second-ranked model by 6.6% in this metric.
Takeaways: Current state-of-the-art TI2V models, despite their impressive visual fidelity, systematically struggle with implicit world reasoning, particularly in logical and complex experiential scenarios.
There is a significant performance gap between closed-source and open-source models, with open-source models exhibiting more visual artifacts and lower reasoning capabilities.
The LMM-based judging pipeline, validated through ablation studies, demonstrates robust alignment with human preferences, enabling scalable and reliable evaluation for reasoning in video generation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.05547.Title: Multi-Task GRPO: Reliable LLM Reasoning Across Tasks
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.05547.Summary: Researchers from UCL, Huawei Noah’s Ark Lab, UNIST, Edinburgh, and Basel developed Multi-Task GRPO (MT-GRPO), an algorithm for large language model post-training that optimizes for balanced performance across diverse reasoning tasks. MT-GRPO enhances worst-task accuracy by 16-28% over standard GRPO and 6% over DAPO, achieving faster convergence to reliable multi-task reasoning.
Problem: Current LLM post-training methods create "specialist" models, failing to ensure reliable, balanced performance across diverse reasoning tasks required for general-purpose reasoners.
Multi-task optimization often results in imbalanced outcomes, with some tasks dominating and others suffering from negative transfer or stagnation.
In GRPO, tasks exhibit varying rates of "zero advantage" prompts, which distort actual gradient contributions and make the GRPO loss an unreliable signal for effective task reweighting.
Method: Formulated a multi-task post-training objective that maximizes average reward while explicitly constraining performance disparity across tasks, using a max-min optimization framework.

Introduced Improvement-Aware Task Reweighting (IWU) to dynamically adapt task weights based on both current task performance and recent learning progress, preventing weight collapse and ensuring balanced optimization.

Developed a Ratio-Preserving Sampler (RP SAMPLER) to guarantee that intended task weights translate into accurate gradient contributions by correcting for task-dependent rates of zero-gradient prompts.
Results: MT-GRPO achieved 16-28% absolute improvement in worst-task accuracy over standard GRPO and 6% over DAPO in a 3-task reasoning benchmark.
The algorithm demonstrated faster convergence to robust performance, reaching 50% worst-task accuracy in 50% fewer training steps than baselines.
The "lambda" parameter in improvement-aware reweighting effectively controlled the trade-off, allowing tunable emphasis on worst-task robustness versus overall average accuracy.
Takeaways: Robust multi-task LLM reasoning necessitates an explicit objective that balances average performance with worst-task guarantees, moving beyond single-task specialization.
The varying rates of "zero advantage" prompts in GRPO significantly bias effective task gradient contributions, making naive multi-task sampling ineffective.
Dynamic task reweighting benefits from incorporating both absolute task performance and observed improvement signals to prevent optimization from collapsing onto a single task.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.05359.Title: Multimodal Latent Reasoning via Hierarchical Visual Cues Injection
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.05359.Summary: The HIVE framework introduces a multimodal latent reasoning approach that uses a recurrent transformer architecture and hierarchical visual cue injection to achieve deliberate, multi-step inference. This method enhances complex visual-linguistic reasoning capabilities, achieves an F1 score of 91.6% on ScienceQA-Img, and reduces inference computations by up to 43% by enabling faster convergence of latent states.
Problem: Existing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) often employ a 'fast thinking' approach, struggling with complex, compositional questions requiring deeper logical inference.
Current 'slow thinking' MLLMs primarily rely on explicit textual Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, which can be inefficient, verbose, and susceptible to language biases or hallucinations.

Most MLLMs use 'flat' visual feature projections from a single vision encoder layer, proving insufficient for nuanced understanding of complex scenes that need both global context and fine-grained details.
Method: HIVE implements a recurrent visual-language backbone, built on Huginn, that iteratively refines latent representations within a fixed parameter count, allowing for multi-step reasoning.
It integrates hierarchical visual cues by extracting features from multiple layers of a pre-trained vision encoder and adaptively injecting them into recurrent blocks based on an iteration schedule.
The framework incorporates an adaptive computation mechanism that dynamically adjusts recurrence steps during inference using a 'norm diff' metric for early exit, optimizing computational efficiency.
Results: HIVE achieved 91.6% on ScienceQA-Img, outperforming larger MLLMs, and demonstrated the highest score (87.6%) on the POPE benchmark for hallucination mitigation among evaluated models.
Recurrent iterations significantly improved performance, with the hierarchical model climbing from 32.82% at 1 step to 91.57% at 32 steps on ScienceQA-Img, confirming iterative refinement benefits.
Hierarchical visual cues consistently enhanced reasoning, improving metrics across various benchmarks and reducing average inference steps by up to 43% on RealWorldQA (from 25.5 to 14.5 steps).
Takeaways: Deliberate 'slow thinking' in MLLMs can be effectively achieved through latent-space iterative refinement within a recurrent architecture, moving beyond reliance on explicit linguistic chains.
Injecting hierarchical visual cues directly into the latent reasoning process, rather than solely relying on text-derived supervision, is crucial for grounded and robust multimodal understanding.

Combining recurrent architectures with adaptive computation and rich hierarchical visual features leads to substantial inference efficiency gains, reducing computational overhead without sacrificing accuracy.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.04884.Title: Reinforced Attention Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.04884.Summary: Reinforced Attention Learning (RAL) introduces a post-training framework that optimizes internal attention distributions instead of output token sequences in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). This approach leads to consistent performance gains across diverse image and video question answering benchmarks, improving visual grounding and multimodal reasoning.
Problem: Existing reinforcement learning (RL) methods, effective for LLM reasoning, yield only marginal gains or degradation when directly applied to MLLMs for perception-intensive tasks.
Standard RLHF optimizes 'what to generate' (output tokens) rather than 'where to attend' (internal attention distribution), which is crucial for MLLMs to allocate information effectively.
Output-based supervision can lead to issues like 'diversity collapse' or 'reward hacking,' hindering robust cross-modal alignment and genuine multimodal understanding.
Method: Reinforced Attention Learning (RAL) is proposed, reformulating the MLLM's internal attention mechanism as a latent policy space to be directly optimized.
RAL employs an advantage-weighted attention divergence loss, specifically Jensen-Shannon Divergence, to pull current attention policies towards successful patterns and push away from suboptimal ones.

On-Policy Attention Distillation extends this framework by aligning a student model's attention patterns with a teacher model, thereby transferring structural reasoning and fine-grained perceptual behaviors.
Results: RAL consistently outperforms the GRPO baseline and the base Qwen-2.5-VL-7B model across nearly all evaluated image and video VQA benchmarks, including a +5.8% improvement on V*Bench and +3.4% on NExT-QA.

On-Policy Attention Distillation further enhances performance compared to standard token-level distillation, showing gains on 7 out of 8 image benchmarks and all video benchmarks (e.g., +4.4% on NExTQA).

Ablation studies demonstrate RAL's robustness to increasing visual information density, with performance margins widening for higher fidelity inputs, and the RAL-zero variant showing strong visual understanding even without explicit textual rationales.
Takeaways: Optimizing internal attention distributions provides a more potent, stable, and generalizable training signal for MLLMs, particularly for tasks requiring fine-grained perception and long-range multimodal reasoning.
Directly shaping attention patterns effectively improves visual grounding and cross-modal alignment, addressing limitations of token-level optimization.
Attention patterns are a transferable and semantically rich representation of reasoning behavior, enabling more effective knowledge distillation between models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.04879.Title: Rethinking the Trust Region in LLM Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.04879.Summary: Researchers from Sea AI Lab and the National University of Singapore developed Divergence Proximal Policy Optimization (DPPO), a framework for LLM fine-tuning that replaces PPO's heuristic ratio clipping with a principled, divergence-based trust region. This approach delivers improved training stability and efficiency across various LLM architectures and tasks, often reducing the need for external stabilization techniques.
Problem: Proximal Policy Optimization's (PPO) heuristic ratio-clipping mechanism is structurally ill-suited for the vast, long-tailed vocabularies inherent to Large Language Models (LLMs), leading to suboptimal and unstable learning.

LLM fine-tuning with Reinforcement Learning (RL) frequently suffers from training instability, often linked to 'bad updates' that cause catastrophic performance degradation, and inefficiency due to over-constraining critical token updates.

Principled trust region methods, such as TRPO, are computationally prohibitive for LLMs because they require calculating full vocabulary probability distributions, leading to high memory and computational overhead.
Method: Derived new policy improvement bounds tailored for the finite-horizon, undiscounted setting of LLM generation, providing a rigorous theoretical basis for trust-region methods in this context.

Introduced Divergence Proximal Policy Optimization (DPPO), which replaces PPO's ratio clipping with a dynamic mask applied to the policy gradient objective, based on a direct measure of policy divergence (e.g., Total Variation or KL divergence).

Developed memory-efficient approximations for policy divergence calculation (Binary and Top-K Approximations) to ensure the method's scalability and negligible overhead for LLMs with massive vocabularies.
Results: DPPO consistently demonstrated superior training stability and efficiency, achieving faster reward optimization and better converged performance compared to baselines like GRPO-ClipHigher and CISPO across various LLM architectures.

DPPO maintained stable training where baselines frequently exhibited instability or catastrophic collapse, and its inherent stability significantly reduced the reliance on complex external stabilization techniques like Rollout Router Replay (R3).

The simpler 'binary approximation' of TV/KL divergence performed comparably to the richer 'Top-K approximation,' proving to be a sufficient and computationally efficient choice for scalable RL in LLMs across diverse reasoning tasks.
Takeaways: A trust region is essential for stable LLM training even at low learning rates, and it must be correctly anchored to the original behavior policy (μ) rather than a recomputed policy distribution (π).

Training instability in LLM RL is primarily caused by a small fraction (≤ 0.5%) of 'bad updates' on negative samples that aggressively decrease the probability of a sampled token far outside the trust region.

PPO's ratio clipping mechanism 'over-constrains' updates to low-probability, high-entropy tokens, hindering exploration and efficiency, and Truncated Importance Sampling (TIS) can degrade stability rather than improve it.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.04837.Title: Group-Evolving Agents: Open-Ended Self-Improvement via Experience Sharing
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.04837.Summary: Researchers at the University of California, Santa Barbara developed Group-Evolving Agents (GEA), a framework enabling open-ended self-improvement for AI systems by evolving groups of agents that share experiences. This group-centric approach led to a 71.0% success rate on SWE-bench Verified and 88.3% on Polyglot, surpassing individual-centric self-evolving methods and matching human-designed agent performance.
Problem: Traditional AI systems rely on pre-defined architectures and continuous human intervention, limiting their ability for autonomous, open-ended self-improvement.

Existing open-ended self-evolving AI, often inspired by biological evolution, uses individual-centric, tree-structured approaches that isolate evolutionary branches, preventing effective experience sharing and long-term cumulative progress.
Exploratory diversity generated by individual agents in isolation often remains transient, failing to contribute to the collective and sustained advancement of AI capabilities.
Method: GEA introduces a group-centric evolutionary paradigm where a collection of agents, rather than individuals, forms the fundamental unit of evolution.
The framework incorporates a Parent Group Selection mechanism that selects a diverse, high-performing group of agents using a balanced performance-novelty score.

Open-Ended Group Evolution explicitly enables intra-group experience sharing, aggregating all evolutionary traces from the parent group into a shared pool for every agent to utilize in its reflection and evolution modules.
Results: GEA achieved a 71.0% success rate on SWE-bench Verified and 88.3% on Polyglot, significantly outperforming the state-of-the-art individual-centric Darwin Gödel Machine (DGM) baseline (56.7% and 68.3% respectively).
The autonomously evolved GEA agents demonstrated performance competitive with or superior to human-designed state-of-the-art frameworks, such as OpenHands + GPT-5 (71.8%) and Aider + GPT-5 (52.0%).

GEA exhibited enhanced robustness by repairing framework-level bugs in an average of 1.4 iterations, faster than DGM's 5 iterations, and demonstrated transferability of improvements across different backbone models (e.g., GPT and Claude series).
Takeaways: Treating a group of agents as the evolutionary unit, with explicit experience sharing, transforms transient exploratory diversity into sustained, cumulative progress for AI self-improvement.
AI agents, unlike biological organisms, are not bound by lineage and can directly share and aggregate 'trajectories, tools, and learned artifacts,' leading to more efficient evolution.

Meta-learning based self-improvement allows agents to autonomously evolve their own framework-level designs, matching or exceeding the performance of human-designed systems without direct human intervention.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.04413.Title: History-Guided Iterative Visual Reasoning with Self-Correction
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.04413.Summary: The H-GIVR framework enhances multimodal large language models by integrating history-guided iterative visual reasoning and self-correction during inference. This method enables dynamic error correction and repeated visual observation, consistently improving reasoning accuracy across five VQA benchmarks, with accuracy gains exceeding 50% on multiple-choice datasets and requiring an average of 2.57 to 4.04 model calls per question.
Problem: Existing self-consistency methods for MLLMs treat multiple reasoning attempts as independent, failing to leverage historical outputs for dynamic error correction or iterative refinement.
MLLMs generally lack human-like iterative verification and dynamic adjustment of reasoning based on prior iterations and re-examination of visual cues during inference.
Improving MLLM performance often relies on increasing model size, leading to exponentially growing and unsustainable training costs, necessitating efficient inference-time enhancement strategies.
Method: The H-GIVR framework introduces a "Visual Description" component, guiding the MLLM to first generate a detailed image description, serving as explicit visual evidence for subsequent answer generation.

A "Consistency-Iterative Reasoning" component dynamically updates an "Answer List" with past responses, feeding it back into the model's prompt as historical context to encourage reflection and verification.

An "Image Re-observation Mechanism" periodically prompts the model to reprocess the original image and generate an updated visual description, mitigating memory loss and insufficient initial visual understanding.
Results: H-GIVR achieved consistent performance improvements across five VQA benchmarks and three MLLMs, with accuracy gains exceeding 50% on multiple-choice datasets and ranging from 2.8% to 69.2% on open-ended tasks.

The framework demonstrated computational efficiency, requiring an average of 2.57 to 4.04 model calls per question, making it more efficient than some baselines while maintaining competitive or superior accuracy.

Ablation studies confirmed that both the Visual Description and Consistency-Iterative Reasoning modules individually contributed to accuracy improvements, with their combination in H-GIVR yielding the highest overall performance.
Takeaways: Integrating historical reasoning through an iterative feedback loop allows MLLMs to actively correct visual understanding errors and adapt their reasoning dynamically during inference.

Periodically re-observing the visual input during iterative reasoning significantly improves the model's robustness and accuracy by reinforcing attention to key image content and mitigating memory decay.

Achieving internal consistency among iteratively generated answers serves as an effective and computationally efficient stopping criterion, indicating convergence towards a reliable solution without complex training.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.04118.Title: Learning to Reason in 13 Parameters
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.04118.Summary: Meta FAIR researchers developed TinyLoRA, a parameter-efficient finetuning method that enables large language models to acquire complex mathematical reasoning skills by training as few as 13 parameters. This approach, when combined with reinforcement learning, achieved 91% accuracy on GSM8K, demonstrating a significant advancement in ultra-low-capacity model adaptation.
Problem: Finetuning large language models traditionally requires updating billions of parameters, leading to high computational and memory costs.

Existing parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT) methods, while reducing parameters, still operate in the range of millions or tens of thousands, limiting their application in highly constrained environments.
There is a need to understand the fundamental minimum number of parameters necessary for effective adaptation, especially for complex reasoning tasks.
Method: Introduced TinyLoRA, a novel PEFT method that extends LoRA-XS by replacing the trainable r×rr \times rr×r matrix with a low-dimensional trainable vector projected through a fixed random tensor, significantly reducing parameters per module.

Implemented aggressive weight tying strategies, allowing the trainable vector to be shared across multiple or all layers of the model, enabling total trainable parameters to be reduced to single digits.

Utilized Reinforcement Learning (specifically GRPO) as the primary learning algorithm, demonstrating its unique efficiency in leveraging sparse, reward-driven signals for highly constrained parameter updates.
Results: A Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct model achieved 91% accuracy on the GSM8K dataset by training only 13 parameters, marking a 15% absolute improvement over its 76% baseline.
When trained on the more difficult MATH dataset, TinyLoRA with 196 parameters retained 87% of the absolute performance improvement across a suite of six challenging math benchmarks.
Qwen models consistently demonstrated greater parameter efficiency than Llama models in low-parameter finetuning, often requiring 10x fewer parameters to reach equivalent performance levels.
Takeaways: Reinforcement learning exhibits 100-1000x greater parameter efficiency than supervised finetuning in extremely low-parameter regimes, due to its ability to make more 'information-dense' updates.
Larger pre-trained language models are more amenable to ultra-low-parameter adaptation, requiring smaller relative update sizes to achieve performance gains on specific tasks.
The findings empirically support the concept of intrinsic dimensionality, suggesting that complex capabilities can be amplified or 'unlocked' in LLMs with remarkably few trainable parameters.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.03916.Title: SpatiaLab: Can Vision-Language Models Perform Spatial Reasoning in the Wild?
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.03916.Summary: SPATIALAB, a new comprehensive benchmark, rigorously evaluates vision-language models' spatial reasoning in diverse, real-world visual environments across six categories. Its assessment reveals a considerable performance disparity between state-of-the-art models and humans, particularly when tasks require open-ended generative reasoning.
Problem: Vision-language models (VLMs) demonstrate inconsistent spatial reasoning, especially in complex and noisy real-world scenes.
Prior benchmarks for spatial reasoning often rely on simplified, synthetic, or templated datasets, lacking ecological validity and comprehensive task coverage.
Most existing evaluations use closed-ended (multiple-choice or binary) formats, which can overestimate VLM capabilities by allowing models to use shortcuts.
Method: The SPATIALAB benchmark is introduced, comprising 1,400 visual question-answer pairs generated from diverse, unconstrained real-world images.
It employs a hierarchical taxonomy covering six major spatial reasoning categories (e.g., Depth & Occlusion, Spatial Navigation) and thirty fine-grained subcategories.
The benchmark supports both multiple-choice (SPATIALAB-MCQ) and open-ended (SPATIALAB-OPEN) evaluation formats to assess discriminative accuracy and generative reasoning.
Results: State-of-the-art VLMs achieved a maximum of 54.93% accuracy on SPATIALAB-MCQ (InternVL3.5-72B), considerably below the human baseline of 87.57%.
Performance further declined in the open-ended evaluation, with top models reaching only 40.9% accuracy (GPT-5-mini), compared to human performance of 64.9%.
Qualitative error analysis revealed recurring issues including spatial mislocalization, perspective and scale mistakes, occlusion failures, and generating fluent but visually ungrounded narratives.
Takeaways: VLMs exhibit a substantial performance gap, averaging 23.0%, between multiple-choice and open-ended spatial reasoning tasks, suggesting models rely on recognition over genuine generative understanding.
Systematic errors persist across models in areas like occlusion handling, inconsistent scale judgments, and multi-step relational chaining, pointing to limitations in fundamental geometric grounding.

Traditional improvement methods (Chain-of-Thought prompting, supervised fine-tuning, multi-agent systems) provide limited, localized, or inconsistent benefits without resolving core perceptual and reasoning deficiencies.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.03806.Title: Bridging Online and Offline RL: Contextual Bandit Learning for Multi-Turn Code Generation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.03806.Summary: Researchers from The Ohio State University and Microsoft developed COBALT, an efficient reinforcement learning framework that reconfigures multi-turn code generation as a contextual bandit problem, achieving improved performance and training stability. The work also presents a systematic analysis of in-context reward hacking in Large Language Models and introduces a data augmentation strategy to enhance model robustness against incorrect feedback.
Problem: Online Reinforcement Learning (RL) for Large Language Models (LLMs) is computationally expensive and suffers from instability issues like gradient explosion for complex, multi-turn tasks.
Offline RL provides cost-effectiveness and stability but often leads to lower-performing models due to distributional shifts and lack of active environment exploration.
LLMs are vulnerable to 'in-context reward hacking,' where they exploit erroneous feedback to achieve superficial rewards, leading to undesired program behaviors without parameter updates.
Method: The COBALT framework redefines multi-turn code generation as a contextual bandit problem, leveraging the 'one-step recoverability' property of this task to simplify the optimization objective.

It employs a three-stage process: offline trajectory collection from a reference LLM, filtering and segmentation of these trajectories, and online contextual bandit learning using a stepwise objective function.

To mitigate reward hacking, the method incorporates perturbation-based data augmentation, training the LLM with trajectories where public test cases are intentionally perturbed to introduce incorrect feedback.
Results: COBALT achieved notable performance improvements, with R1-Distill 8B-COBALT scoring 31.7 Pass@1 (+9.0 absolute points) and Qwen3 8B-COBALT reaching 38.5 Pass@1 (+6.2 absolute points) on LiveCodeBench, while demonstrating superior training efficiency compared to online RL baselines.

Models trained with COBALT generalized effectively to longer code generation horizons (up to 8 turns) even after training on shorter sequences (up to 3 turns), maintaining significant performance gains.

Perturbation-based data augmentation for COBALT training data substantially reduced in-context reward hacking instances and improved model robustness, with one model seeing errors drop from 855 to 85.
Takeaways: Multi-turn code generation, characterized by 'one-step recoverability,' can be effectively approximated as a contextual bandit problem, allowing for efficient stepwise optimization while retaining strong long-horizon performance.
A theoretical analysis shows that COBALT's contextual bandit objective has a performance difference bound of O(T

An analysis of reward hacking using perturbed test cases revealed its prevalence across open-weight and proprietary LLMs, with "semantic drifting" being the most common behavior, and noted that RL training can increase the frequency of such behaviors.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.03733.Title: RegionReasoner: Region-Grounded Multi-Round Visual Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.03733.Summary: Researchers from the University of Amsterdam, Anhui University, and Westlake University developed REGIONREASONER, a reinforcement learning framework that enables Vision-Language Models to perform multi-round visual reasoning. It enforces explicit spatial grounding and global-local semantic consistency, achieving state-of-the-art performance on a new benchmark, RegionDial-Bench, with detection improvements of up to 17.7 AP in later dialogue turns.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language Models (VLMs) primarily rely on single-step or text-only reasoning, struggling with iterative refinement across multiple visual contexts.
Current VLMs lack explicit spatial grounding within their reasoning processes, leading to issues like 'coordinate hallucinations' and difficulty maintaining verifiable references.
In multi-round interactions, VLMs often suffer from 'semantic drift,' where global scene understanding becomes inconsistent with localized region-specific details.
A lack of standardized benchmarks specifically designed for multi-round, visually-grounded reasoning tasks hinders progress in this area.
Method: Developed an autoregressive VLM policy generating structured text actions at each turn, comprising global context (), local focus (), explicit thinking (), and a final answer ().

Introduced a 'Reference-Grounded Thinking' mechanism that mandates explicit citation of reference bounding boxes from previous turns within the  block to ensure verifiability and prevent hallucination.
Implemented 'Global-Local Semantic Consistency' by enforcing keyword alignment between scene descriptions, localized region captions, and the reasoning trace, preventing semantic drift.
Optimized the VLM using GRPO with novel reinforcement learning rewards: a Reference Citation Reward and a Global-Local Consistency Reward, designed for multi-round interaction.
Created RegionDial-Bench, a new multi-round benchmark derived from RefCOCO+ and RefCOCOg, supporting both referring detection and segmentation tasks with programmatically propagated references.
Results: RegionReasoner-7B achieved state-of-the-art performance on RegionDial-Bench, with 80.7 AP for detection on RefCOCO+ and 78.2 AP on RefCOCOg, outperforming baselines by 4.6-7.6 AP.
For referring segmentation, the model attained 69.6 gIoU on RefCOCO+ and 66.5 gIoU on RefCOCOg, showing improvements of 5.3-9.8 gIoU over prior methods.

The framework demonstrated enhanced robustness to error accumulation, with performance gains up to +17.7 AP over baselines at deeper turns (Round 7), effectively mitigating degradation in longer dialogues.

Ablation studies confirmed the complementary contributions of the Reference Citation Reward and Global-Local Consistency Reward, with their combined use yielding the strongest multi-round performance.

The model exhibited strong generalization, achieving the highest overall performance on the V* benchmark's 'Spatial' dimension among Qwen2.5-VL-based models, indicating transferability of learned reasoning capabilities.
Takeaways: Explicitly requiring VLM reasoning to cite specific reference bounding boxes significantly improves verifiability and prevents coordinate hallucinations in multi-round dialogues.

Enforcing semantic consistency between global scene descriptions, localized region captions, and the reasoning trace is crucial for preventing semantic drift and maintaining coherence over dialogue turns.
Tailored reinforcement learning signals, particularly those rewarding reference citation and global-local consistency, effectively train VLMs to handle complex, iterative visual reasoning tasks.
A structured output format that includes explicit 'thinking' steps enhances the interpretability of the VLM's reasoning process, making it more transparent and auditable.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.03361.Title: Z3D: Zero-Shot 3D Visual Grounding from Images
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.03361.Summary: Z3D introduces a universal zero-shot 3D visual grounding pipeline that localizes objects in 3D scenes from natural language queries using multi-view images. It establishes new state-of-the-art performance in zero-shot 3DVG, including image-only scenarios, by integrating high-quality 3D instance segmentation and advanced Vision-Language Model (VLM) reasoning, achieving significant improvements on ScanRefer and Nr3D benchmarks.
Problem: Existing 3D visual grounding (3DVG) methods often rely on extensive 3D annotations or textual supervision, limiting generalization and increasing data labeling burden.
Prior zero-shot 3DVG methods suffered from insufficient quality of 3D object proposals and did not fully leverage advanced VLM reasoning capabilities.
3DVG from images, a more practical scenario, was largely limited to single-view inputs or required explicit 3D geometry/camera pose supervision, hindering comprehensive scene-level understanding.
Method: Z3D implements a modular pipeline for zero-shot 3DVG from multi-view images, optionally integrating camera poses and depth maps, without requiring geometric supervision or object priors.
The pipeline combines a two-stage view selection (CLIP and VLM), SAM3-Agent for VLM-guided zero-shot 2D object segmentation, and MaskClustering for class-agnostic 3D proposals.
For image-only scenarios, Z3D integrates DUSt3R for zero-shot 3D reconstruction, generating dense depth maps and point clouds from multi-view images to enable subsequent grounding.
Results: Z3D achieved an absolute improvement of +38.7 Acc@0.5 over OpenScene on ScanRefer and 56.8% top-1 accuracy on Nr3D, outperforming prior zero-shot methods like SPAZER (56.0%) and VLM-Grounder (48.0%) with depths.

In the images-only scenario, Z3D with DUSt3R achieved 12.9 Acc@0.5 on ScanRefer, surpassing a DUSt3R 
 SeeGround baseline (8.2 Acc@0.5) and approaching fully supervised VG LLM (14.9 Acc@0.5).

Ablation studies confirmed the critical role of VLM view selection and multi-view aggregation, and showed that reconstruction quality (DUSt3R vs. DROID-SLAM) significantly impacts image-only 3DVG performance.
Takeaways: Combining advanced VLM reasoning for view selection and prompt-guided 2D segmentation with high-quality zero-shot 3D instance segmentation significantly improves zero-shot 3DVG performance.
Robust 3D reconstruction from multi-view images, even without explicit depth or pose supervision, can effectively enable zero-shot 3DVG in challenging image-only settings.
A two-stage view selection approach (initial lightweight filtering followed by VLM refinement) efficiently reduces computational load while maintaining accuracy in VLM-based pipelines.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.03143.Title: Self-Hinting Language Models Enhance Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.03143.Summary: This research introduces SAGE, a reinforcement learning framework that enhances language model training by addressing the problem of collapsed policy gradients under sparse rewards. SAGE utilizes privileged, self-generated hints during training to diversify rollout outcomes, resulting in consistent accuracy improvements across various LLMs and benchmarks, including up to a 2.0% increase over standard GRPO.
Problem: Reinforcement Learning (RL) for Large Language Models (LLMs) faces a "sparse terminal reward" problem, particularly in verifiable tasks with binary (0/1) outcomes.
Policy-gradient methods like GRPO suffer from a "GRPO stall" where, for difficult prompts, all rollouts yield identical zero rewards, leading to zero policy gradients and halting learning.
Existing solutions like data resampling or external guidance can introduce biases, instability, or require dependence on stronger external models.
Method: SAGE (Self-hint Aligned GRPO with Privileged Supervision) injects "privileged hints" (e.g., plans or problem decompositions) into the prompt context during training to reshape the rollout distribution.

Hints are generated online by a copy of the current policy and adaptively scheduled based on whether a probe group of rollouts yields degenerate (all zero) rewards, ensuring hints are applied precisely when needed.
The framework maintains an on-policy objective, evaluating log-probabilities conditioned on the hint, and completely removes hints at inference time.
Results: SAGE achieved the highest average accuracy across three LLMs and eight diverse benchmarks, demonstrating improvements of +1.2% to +2.0% over GRPO on math benchmarks and superior generalization.
The method significantly mitigated the GRPO stall, enabling the utilization of up to 10% more uninformative prompts for learning compared to standard GRPO.

Ablation studies confirmed the critical importance of online self-hinting and on-policy conditioning, with SAGE outperforming baselines that used fixed hints, external hints, or off-policy variants while maintaining stable training.
Takeaways: The "advantage energy" in GRPO (a measure of update magnitude) collapses to zero if and only if all rollouts within a group yield identical rewards, turning training into a gated procedure.

The probability of opening this 'gate' (generating a non-zero gradient) is maximized when the success probability with hints is around 1/2, meaning hints should move sparse outcomes toward this target.
The optimal hint distribution for maximizing gate opening probability is policy-dependent, rigorously justifying the need for online self-hinting to adapt to the learner's evolving capabilities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.03120.Title: Quantized Evolution Strategies: High-precision Fine-tuning of Quantized LLMs at Low-precision Cost
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.03120.Summary: Researchers from UCLA and Cognizant AI Lab introduce Quantized Evolution Strategies (QES), a method for high-precision, full-parameter fine-tuning of quantized Large Language Models directly within their low-precision discrete parameter space. QES achieves significant performance improvements (e.g., up to 31.85% accuracy on Qwen2.5-3B INT4) over prior zeroth-order methods while maintaining an inference-level memory footprint.
Problem: Fine-tuning quantized Large Language Models (LLMs) is difficult because traditional backpropagation methods require high-precision, differentiable operations incompatible with discrete, low-precision weights.

Existing zeroth-order (ZO) optimization and Evolution Strategies (ES) for quantized models suffer from "stagnation" where small gradient signals vanish or become inaccurate in discrete parameter spaces.
Storing high-precision optimizer states (e.g., error vectors or Adam states) for quantized models can negate the memory benefits of quantization, hindering deployment on resource-constrained devices.
Method: QES combines Evolution Strategies with a stochastic discrete perturbation strategy and boundary gating to operate directly within the quantized parameter space.
It implements an accumulated error feedback mechanism, inspired by Delta-Sigma modulation, which accumulates fractional updates in a high-precision residual vector to prevent gradient stagnation.
A Stateless Seed Replay mechanism is used to reconstruct the high-precision error vector on-the-fly from a limited history of random seeds and rewards, drastically reducing memory overhead.
Results: QES significantly improved arithmetic reasoning accuracy on the Qwen2.5-3B INT4 model from a base of 2.80% and QuZO's 14.25% to 31.85%.

The stateless seed replay method achieved performance remarkably close to storing the full high-precision residual (e.g., 31.85% vs. 33.50% for Qwen2.5-3B INT4), demonstrating minimal approximation impact.

Analysis showed that parameter updates are sparse (~10^-2 of parameters change per step), and updates hitting quantization boundaries are extremely rare (<1 	imes 10^-5 for INT4), ensuring high fidelity for stateless reconstruction.
Takeaways: Accumulating fractional update errors over time allows for precise gradient ascent in discrete parameter spaces, enabling effective optimization despite the integer-based parameter updates.
Maintaining a high-precision error state is crucial for optimization in quantized spaces, and this state can be efficiently reconstructed without being stored, trading computation for memory.

Parameter updates in quantized models are sparse, and instances where updates hit quantization boundaries are rare, which validates the high fidelity and low approximation error of the stateless reconstruction method.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.02951.Title: Nüwa: Mending the Spatial Integrity Torn by VLM Token Pruning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.02951.Summary: The paper introduces NÜWA, a training-free, two-stage token pruning framework for Vision-Language Models that addresses the performance degradation of existing methods on visual grounding tasks. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on VQA while dramatically improving visual grounding accuracy, retaining 47.19% performance at an 88.9% token reduction rate on RefCOCO benchmarks, alongside an 89% reduction in TFLOPs.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) incur substantial inference costs due to the high number of visual tokens from high-resolution images, leading to quadratic computational complexity.
Existing visual token pruning methods, while accelerating Visual Question Answering (VQA), cause significant performance degradation on Visual Grounding (VG) tasks.
This degradation stems from pruning methods disrupting the "global spatial reference frame" essential for precise object localization in VG tasks.
Method: A training-free, two-stage token pruning framework called NÜWA is proposed, designed to preserve spatial integrity crucial for visual grounding tasks.

Stage 1, "Spatial Cohesion Pruning," operates in the vision encoder, using a Boids-inspired aggregation strategy to partition tokens into regions and merge features around salient "benchmark tokens" based on semantic similarity and spatial proximity.
Stage 2, "Text-Modulated Pruning," refines the token set within the LLM by selecting only the top-K visual tokens most relevant to a holistic textual query vector.
Results: NÜWA achieves state-of-the-art performance on VQA benchmarks, retaining 94-95% of the vanilla model's performance at an 88.9% token reduction across LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT, and Qwen2.5-VL architectures.

On visual grounding tasks (RefCOCO series), NÜWA dramatically outperforms prior methods, achieving 47.19% average performance retention at an 88.9% token reduction, a substantial improvement over 7.28% for VisionZip.

The framework yields significant efficiency gains, including an 89% reduction in TFLOPs and a 62% reduction in prefill time (e.g., 46ms vs. 124ms for vanilla LLaVA-1.5) with negligible computational overhead.
Takeaways: VLMs process visual information in a multi-stage pipeline, moving from global semantic integration in early layers to fine-grained object-centric focus in middle layers, which is critical for visual grounding.

The poor performance of existing pruning methods on visual grounding tasks is primarily caused by the disruption or loss of the "Global Spatial Reference Frame," built from token positional information.

A Relative Position Mapping Extension (RPME) strategy, which restores continuous spatial coordinates, significantly improves visual grounding performance for existing pruning methods, validating NÜWA's design philosophy.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.02710.Title: Maximum Likelihood Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.02710.Summary: Maximum Likelihood Reinforcement Learning (MaxRL), developed by researchers primarily at Carnegie Mellon University, introduces a sampling-based framework that approximates maximum likelihood optimization for tasks with binary outcome feedback. MaxRL demonstrates superior scaling with increased computational resources, mitigates issues like pass@k degradation in Large Language Models (LLMs), and achieves up to 20x test-time scaling efficiency on mathematical reasoning benchmarks by generating a higher number of correct solutions.
Problem: Many modern learning problems (e.g., code generation, multi-step LLM reasoning) rely on binary outcome feedback, implicitly defining a likelihood of success, but direct maximum likelihood optimization is precluded by non-differentiable sampling.
Standard Reinforcement Learning (RL) is used as a workaround but only optimizes a first-order approximation of the true maximum likelihood objective.
Conventional RL methods lead to issues like underexploration of hard, low-success inputs and 'distribution sharpening' (pass@k degradation) in LLMs, where solution diversity is lost.
Method: MaxRL introduces a compute-indexed family of objectives that smoothly interpolates between standard expected reward and exact maximum likelihood, allowing more faithful approximation with increased sampling compute.

It proposes a simple, on-policy gradient estimator that averages score functions exclusively from successful trajectories, proving it to be an unbiased estimator for the compute-indexed MaxRL objective.
The framework employs a control variate for variance reduction by normalizing rewards with the per-task mean, and provides a unifying weight-function view to characterize various RL objectives.
Results: MaxRL closely matches cross-entropy performance in image classification and significantly outperforms REINFORCE on maze navigation, demonstrating superior scaling with additional training compute.

On GSM8K, MaxRL showed greater resistance to overfitting and pass@k degradation, maintaining healthier output diversity and achieving higher peak performance over longer training durations compared to RLOO and GRPO.

When training Qwen3 models on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, MaxRL consistently Pareto-dominated GRPO, achieving higher pass@1 while simultaneously *improving* pass@k, leading to up to 20x test-time scaling efficiency gains.
