Takeaways: Explicit visual context, rather than textual instructions, provides a more effective control mechanism for guiding generative models in visual reasoning tasks.
Increasing the generated video length during inference ("Visual Test-Time Scaling") improves performance on complex out-of-distribution problems, showing parallels to Chain-of-Thought in LLMs.
Video generation models can learn abstract planning algorithms, enabling generalization to unseen visual elements and irregular spatial layouts, indicating a focus on underlying logic.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.20802.Title: Reinforcement Learning via Self-Distillation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.20802.Summary: The paper introduces Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO), an on-policy reinforcement learning algorithm that leverages rich, tokenized environment feedback to improve Large Language Model (LLM) performance. This method enables LLMs to learn from their own explained mistakes, leading to significantly enhanced sample efficiency and higher final accuracy on complex reasoning and coding tasks.
Problem: Current Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) methods for LLMs primarily rely on sparse, scalar outcome rewards, creating a severe credit-assignment bottleneck.
LLMs struggle to learn effectively from limited information about *why* an attempt failed, leading to slow learning or stalled progress, especially for long and complex generations.
Rich textual feedback (e.g., runtime errors, judge evaluations) is often available in verifiable environments but is largely underutilized by existing RL methods.
Method: **Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO):** An on-policy RL algorithm formalizing Reinforcement Learning with Rich Feedback (RLRF) to leverage detailed, tokenized environment feedback.

**Self-Teacher Mechanism:** Uses the current LLM policy as a 'self-teacher' that, when conditioned on rich feedback from its own previous attempt, retrospectively re-evaluates the log-probabilities of its original generation.

**Logit-Level Distillation Loss:** Minimizes a KL-divergence between the student's next-token distribution and the feedback-informed self-teacher's distribution, providing dense, token-level credit assignment.
Results: SDPO consistently outperforms GRPO baselines in scientific reasoning and competitive programming tasks, achieving higher final accuracy (e.g., 68.8% vs. 64.1% aggregate on SciKnowEval, 48.8% vs. 41.2% on LCBv6) and significantly improved sample efficiency (e.g., 10x speedup on Chemistry, 4x fewer generations on LCBv6).

The method leads to more concise and efficient reasoning in LLM generations, reducing response lengths by over 3x on average while maintaining or improving accuracy, indicating improved reasoning efficiency.

SDPO demonstrates effective bootstrapping, with the self-teacher improving over time and the student's performance surpassing initial capabilities, and efficiently accelerates solution discovery during test-time on very hard binary-reward problems, solving some questions uniquely.
Takeaways: Rich, tokenized environment feedback provides a dense learning signal that effectively overcomes the credit-assignment bottleneck of sparse scalar rewards in LLM fine-tuning.
An LLM can effectively serve as its own 'self-teacher' by leveraging its in-context learning capabilities to infer corrections to past generations when presented with specific error feedback.

Distilling these feedback-informed insights directly into the policy weights provides a more permanent and efficient learning mechanism than merely appending feedback to context for iterative self-correction.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.20540.Title: Advancing Open-source World Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.20540.Summary: Robbyant Team's LingBot-World offers an open-source, interactive world simulator that transcends passive video generation by producing dynamic, controllable environments. It quantitatively outperforms existing models in visual quality, dynamism, and consistency, while operating in real-time.
Problem: Existing "text-to-video" models lack fundamental understanding of physical laws and object permanence, limiting interactive simulation capabilities.
High-quality interactive data for agent-environment interplay is scarce, and traditional diffusion architectures struggle with long-term temporal consistency.
State-of-the-art world models are predominantly closed-source, hindering broader community research and real-time inference remains computationally prohibitive.
Method: A scalable hybrid data engine combines general videos, game data with synchronized controls, and synthetic rendering, enriched with hierarchical semantic captions.

A multi-stage evolutionary training pipeline pre-trains a video generator, middle-trains it into an action-conditioned bidirectional world model with progressive curriculum, and post-trains for real-time autoregressive generation.
Causal architecture adaptation and few-step distillation techniques transform the model for efficient, interactive performance with sub-second latency.
Results: Achieved the highest VBench scores for Imaging Quality (0.6683) and Aesthetic Quality (0.5660) compared to Yume-1.5 and HY-World 1.5.
Demonstrated a superior Dynamic Degree of 0.8857 and the best Overall Consistency of 0.2178 among compared state-of-the-art models.
Generated minute-level, ultra-long videos (up to ten minutes) with robust temporal coherence and physical logic, maintaining 16 fps real-time interaction for 480p.
Takeaways: LingBot-World exhibits emergent memory, maintaining object permanence and reasoning about unobserved states for up to 60 seconds without explicit 3D representations.
Real-time performance is achieved with minimal perceptual degradation, enabling 16 frames per second for 480p videos on a single GPU.
The open-source release of code and model weights aims to democratize access and accelerate research in interactive world models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.20354.Title: Everything in Its Place: Benchmarking Spatial Intelligence of Text-to-Image Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.20354.Summary: This research introduces SpatialGenEval, a novel benchmark designed to evaluate the spatial intelligence of Text-to-Image (T2I) models using information-dense prompts and fine-grained multi-choice questions. The paper reveals that T2I models possess only rudimentary spatial reasoning capabilities, with top models achieving around 60% accuracy, and demonstrates that fine-tuning with the SpatialT2I dataset improves performance by 4.2% to 5.7%.
Problem: State-of-the-art Text-to-Image (T2I) models frequently fail to accurately represent complex spatial relationships, leading to misplaced objects, incorrect orientations, and illogical interactions.
Existing T2I benchmarks are insufficient for diagnosing nuanced spatial deficiencies, as they rely on short prompts and coarse-grained evaluation metrics, overlooking higher-order spatial reasoning.

This limitation points to a fundamental deficit in 'spatial intelligence' (perception, reasoning, interaction) in current T2I models, hindering their ability to generate coherent and logically structured scenes.
Method: Introduces SpatialGenEval, a novel benchmark consisting of 1,230 long, information-dense prompts across 25 real-world scenes, each evaluated with 10 omni-dimensional multi-choice question-answer pairs targeting specific spatial sub-domains.
Develops a hierarchical framework of spatial intelligence encompassing 4 domains and 10 sub-domains (e.g., spatial position, occlusion, causality) for systematic evaluation.

Constructs SpatialT2I, a dataset of 15,400 text-image pairs with carefully rewritten prompts, used for supervised fine-tuning of state-of-the-art foundation models to improve their spatial generation capabilities.
Results: The highest overall score on SpatialGenEval was approximately 60%, with open-source Qwen-Image (60.6%) closely matching closed-source Seed Dream 4.0 (62.7%).

Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) using the SpatialT2I dataset consistently improved the performance of models like Stable Diffusion-XL, UniWorld-V1, and OmniGen2 on SpatialGenEval by +4.2%, +5.7%, and +4.4% respectively.

Ablation studies demonstrate that higher-quality data subsets within SpatialT2I contribute more significantly to performance gains, and increasing the quantity of spatial-aware training data consistently improves spatial intelligence.
Takeaways: Current T2I models exhibit only rudimentary spatial intelligence, with even the most advanced models achieving around 60% accuracy on the SpatialGenEval benchmark, indicating significant room for improvement.
Spatial reasoning, encompassing tasks like spatial comparison and occlusion, is identified as the primary bottleneck, with models often scoring below 30% in these sub-domains.

Models leveraging stronger text encoders (based on LLMs) and unified multimodal architectures generally outperform others, highlighting the importance of robust language understanding for complex spatial generation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.19897.Title: Self-Distillation Enables Continual Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.19897.Summary: Researchers at MIT and ETH Zurich developed Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (SDFT), a method that enables large language models to continually acquire new skills and knowledge from demonstrations without experiencing catastrophic forgetting. SDFT achieves this by using the model itself as an in-context learning teacher, consistently outperforming traditional fine-tuning methods and enhancing generalization capabilities.
Problem: Foundation models suffer from catastrophic forgetting when sequentially learning new skills and knowledge from demonstrations, leading to performance degradation on previously mastered tasks.

Traditional methods like Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) are inherently off-policy, resulting in poor generalization and an inability to adapt to the model's evolving behavior, while on-policy learning from demonstrations typically requires complex Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) or explicit reward functions.
Training reasoning models often requires expensive, explicitly labeled chain-of-thought annotations; using SFT with only final answers can degrade a model's internal reasoning capabilities.
Method: SDFT introduces a novel framework where the foundation model acts as both a student and an in-context learning (ICL) teacher.

The teacher model, conditioned on expert demonstrations, generates an on-policy signal that guides the student through minimizing a reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence objective, with updates based on trajectories the student itself generates.
Teacher parameters are maintained as an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) of the student's parameters to ensure stable and effective training, tracking student progress while smoothing updates.
Results: SDFT consistently achieved superior continual learning, allowing models to acquire new skills (e.g., Tool Use, Science Q&A) while retaining performance on previously learned and general capabilities, in contrast to SFT which exhibited severe catastrophic forgetting.

The method demonstrated enhanced generalization, achieving higher new-task accuracy for in-distribution examples and near-perfect accuracy on 'indirect' out-of-distribution knowledge acquisition questions.

SDFT successfully fine-tuned reasoning models using only final answers, preserving internal reasoning depth and significantly improving accuracy where SFT caused a 'reasoning collapse,' with its effectiveness scaling positively with model size.
Takeaways: The SDFT objective of minimizing reverse KL divergence is mathematically equivalent to an on-policy Reinforcement Learning algorithm that maximizes an implicit reward function derived from the demonstration-conditioned teacher, circumventing the need for explicit reward engineering.

Large pretrained models' inherent in-context learning (ICL) abilities can be effectively leveraged to create high-quality, demonstration-conditioned teaching signals for self-distillation, eliminating reliance on external expert models.
Ablation studies confirm that the on-policy nature of SDFT is critical for mitigating catastrophic forgetting and enhancing generalization, as offline distillation methods consistently underperform.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.19686.Title: Video-KTR: Reinforcing Video Reasoning via Key Token Attribution
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.19686.Summary: A new framework named Video-KTR improves multimodal large language models' video reasoning by selectively reinforcing key tokens identified via visual, temporal, and entropy attributions. This method achieved 42.7% accuracy on the Video-Holmes benchmark, exceeding GPT-4o's performance.
Problem: Existing MLLMs often use coarse sequence-level rewards or simplistic token selection in reinforcement learning (RL) for video, failing to capture fine-grained dependencies.
Current methods neglect intricate relationships between visual inputs, temporal dynamics, and linguistic outputs, leading to poor credit assignment and underutilization of visual/temporal cues.
This leads to models over-relying on linguistic priors, increasing hallucinations, and making the reasoning process less interpretable.
Method: Video-KTR introduces a modality-aware policy shaping framework that leverages token-level attribution signals for selective reinforcement learning in video reasoning tasks.
It identifies "key tokens" using three distinct attribution signals: visual-aware (via counterfactual masking), temporal-aware (via frame shuffling), and entropy-aware (via predictive uncertainty).
Only these identified key tokens contribute to the reinforcement learning update objective, applying a binary mask to focus training on semantically important and modality-sensitive elements.
Results: Video-KTR achieved 42.7% accuracy on the Video-Holmes benchmark, outperforming GPT-4o (42.0%) and all open-source baselines, and scored 53.1% on VideoMMMU and 66.6% on MMVU.
The method consistently surpasses vanilla GRPO and other token-weighted RL baselines in controlled experiments, showing gains in complex tasks like "Timeline Analysis" and "Core Theme Inference."

Analysis confirms that selected tokens are semantically rich, while unselected ones are typically low-information function words; the framework also introduces marginal computational overhead and is effective on smaller MLLMs.
Takeaways: Combining visual, temporal, and entropy-aware attribution signals for token selection provides complementary benefits, yielding the most robust and accurate performance for video reasoning.
Selective reinforcement learning with a "hard top-r%" token selection strategy, based on these attributions, effectively filters noise and concentrates learning on high-value information.

Each attribution strategy targets linguistically distinct token types (e.g., nouns for visual, verbs for temporal), confirming their effectiveness in capturing different aspects of multimodal relevance.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.19204.Title: MATA: A Trainable Hierarchical Automaton System for Multi-Agent Visual Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.19204.Summary: MATA is a trainable hierarchical automaton system for multi-agent visual reasoning that employs an LLM-based hyper agent to learn dynamic transitions between specialized reasoning agents. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across compositional VQA, external knowledge VQA, and referring expression comprehension benchmarks, while providing enhanced transparency and robustness.
Problem: Monolithic Vision-Language Models (VLMs) often produce unexplainable reasoning and hallucinate when dealing with complex visual queries.
Existing compositional and single-agent methods are rigid, lack robustness to errors, and struggle with multi-step, feedback-driven reasoning or flexible collaboration.
Previous automaton-based systems relied on hand-crafted, rule-based transition rules, which are inflexible and difficult to scale with increasing complexity or ambiguous agent selection criteria.
Method: Developed MATA, a multi-agent system structured as a hierarchical finite-state automaton with an LLM-based 'hyper agent' controlling high-level state transitions.
Specialized agents (e.g., ONESHOT, STEPWISE, SPECIALIZED) act as top-level states, each with rule-based sub-automata for micro-control, and communicate via an append-only shared memory.
Introduced a data generation pipeline (MATA-SFT-90K) to create supervised finetuning examples for the hyper agent, enabling it to learn dynamic, context-aware transition policies between agents.
Results: MATA achieved state-of-the-art results, including 64.9% accuracy on GQA (outperforming InternVL3.5 by 1.1%), 76.5% on OK-VQA (surpassing InternVL3.5 by 0.8%), and 96.3% on RefCOCO (exceeding Florence2-L by 1.2%).
Ablation studies confirmed the trainable hyper agent's crucial role, substantially improving accuracy (e.g., 64.9% for MATA vs. 57.7% for exhaustive on GQA) and reducing inference time.

The learned transition policy demonstrated strong cross-task generalization, with a single hyper agent showing robust performance across diverse visual reasoning benchmarks with minimal performance drop.
Takeaways: A trainable hyper agent governing high-level transitions allows dynamic selection and collaboration/competition among specialized agents, enhancing flexibility and robustness in visual reasoning.
The hierarchical design, separating learned high-level control from rule-based low-level execution, provides both adaptive decision-making and an explainable, auditable reasoning trace.
Supervised finetuning the hyper agent with systematically explored optimal reasoning trajectories yields an efficient and generalizable control policy for multi-agent systems.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.19099.Title: m2sv: A Scalable Benchmark for Map-to-Street-View Spatial Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.19099.Summary: The m2sv benchmark is introduced to evaluate Vision-Language Models' spatial reasoning by requiring them to align a north-up overhead map with a Street View image to infer camera orientation. This reveals a substantial performance gap, with human accuracy at 95.0% compared to the best VLM's 65.2%.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) demonstrate brittle performance in spatial reasoning tasks that demand alignment between abstract overhead (allocentric) maps and egocentric ground-level views.
Existing multimodal benchmarks often use synthetic data or simplify real-world complexities, which may overestimate VLMs' true spatial competence.
Current AI systems struggle with fine-grained spatial alignment and 'directional intelligence,' a crucial capability for applications in autonomous navigation and robotics.
Method: A scalable benchmark, m2sv, was developed where models identify which labeled direction on an overhead map corresponds to the orientation of a Street View camera at the same intersection, with 2 to 7 candidate directions.
A 'blueprint metadata' pipeline was implemented to create m2sv-20k, a dataset of 20,000 examples across 32 cities, ensuring scalability and reproducible dataset generation.

Various proprietary and open-source VLMs were evaluated in zero-shot settings, and an open-source model was fine-tuned using Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning (RL) on 11,000 reasoning traces.
Results: Humans achieved 95.0% accuracy on m2sv, significantly outperforming the best proprietary VLM (Gemini-3-Pro) at 65.2% and open models like Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct at 35.5% (random baseline 31.4%).

Supervised Fine-Tuning improved Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct's accuracy from 34.3% to 39.8%, and subsequent Reinforcement Learning further boosted it to 43.9%, yet performance remained substantially below human levels.

Qualitative failure analysis identified common errors including egocentric–allocentric confusion, over-reliance on unreliable or transient visual cues, landmark misbinding, and internal contradictions in reasoning.
Takeaways: A significant performance disparity of over 30 percentage points between human performance (95.0%) and the best VLM (65.2%) highlights that current VLMs lack robust, human-like spatial reasoning for real-world cross-view alignment.

Fine-tuning on specific spatial tasks primarily induces benchmark-specific reasoning policies and can lead to a loss of difficulty-adaptive reasoning depth, rather than developing genuinely transferable spatial representations.

The benchmark serves as a diagnostic tool, revealing recurring VLM failure modes such as egocentric–allocentric confusion (e.g., left-right inversions), over-reliance on unreliable visual cues, and failures to maintain consistent spatial representations.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.18734.Title: Self-Distilled Reasoner: On-Policy Self-Distillation for Large Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.18734.Summary: The paper introduces On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD), a framework enabling a single Large Language Model to improve its mathematical reasoning by simultaneously acting as a teacher and student. OPSD achieves performance comparable to or better than RL-based methods like GRPO while demonstrating 4-8x higher token efficiency on competition-level math benchmarks.
Problem: Existing Reinforcement Learning (RL) methods for LLM reasoning are computationally expensive, requiring multiple rollouts and suffering from sparse reward signals.
Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) can lead to exposure bias, where models trained on expert trajectories struggle with out-of-distribution sequences during inference.
Current on-policy distillation methods require a separate, often larger and costly, teacher LLM, adding complexity and computational overhead to the training process.
Method: A single LLM is instantiated as both a student policy (generating responses from problem context) and a teacher policy (generating responses conditioned on the problem and ground-truth solution).

The student policy samples its own trajectories, and the learning objective minimizes the per-token divergence between the teacher's (ground-truth informed) and student's next-token probability distributions.

Gradients are backpropagated only through the student policy, allowing the model to provide itself with dense, token-level feedback without altering the teacher's 'knowledge' or requiring an external teacher.
Results: OPSD consistently matched or exceeded the performance of RL-based GRPO and outperformed SFT across Qwen3 models (1.7B, 4B, 8B) on competition-level mathematical reasoning benchmarks.
The method demonstrated a 4-8x improvement in token efficiency compared to GRPO, utilizing only one rollout per problem and substantially fewer generated tokens without sacrificing accuracy.
Performance gains from OPSD were more pronounced with larger model scales (4B and 8B parameters), confirming the hypothesis that the framework benefits from increased model capacity.
Takeaways: An LLM can effectively serve as its own teacher by leveraging ground-truth solutions as 'privileged information' for the teacher policy, guiding self-improvement.

On-policy training combined with dense, full-vocabulary token-level feedback provides a superior learning signal compared to sparse rewards or sampled-token distillation, enhancing efficiency and accuracy.

The benefits of On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) scale with model capacity, indicating that sufficiently capable models can better utilize self-rationalization and privileged information for reasoning improvement.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.18631.Title: AdaReasoner: Dynamic Tool Orchestration for Iterative Visual Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.18631.Summary: DAREASONER introduces a framework that enables Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to learn dynamic, iterative tool orchestration for complex visual reasoning tasks. The approach leverages high-quality trajectory data, a tailored reinforcement learning algorithm, and adaptive learning, allowing smaller MLLMs to achieve state-of-the-art performance, outperforming some larger proprietary models on specific benchmarks and demonstrating robust generalization to unseen tools and tasks.
Problem: Existing MLLMs struggle with complex, multi-step visual reasoning requiring fine-grained perception and adaptive problem-solving strategies.
Current tool-use approaches in MLLMs are rigid, lacking dynamic decision-making for tool selection, composition, and multi-turn orchestration.
Tool-using policies often show poor generalization to unseen tools or novel task distributions due to overfitting specific tool APIs or training scenarios.
Method: A three-stage data curation pipeline synthesizes high-fidelity, multi-turn reasoning trajectories, incorporating explicit reflection, backtracking, and tool failure cases for initial supervised fine-tuning.

Multi-Turn Tool Group Relative Policy Optimization (Tool-GRPO), an extension of GRPO, refines the MLLM policy using a multi-component reward function optimized for long-horizon strategic planning in multi-turn tool-calling scenarios.

An Adaptive Learning strategy enhances generalization by applying token-level randomization to functional identifiers and semantic-level paraphrasing to tool descriptions, forcing models to infer functionality rather than memorize syntax.
Results: The DAREASONER framework consistently improved 7B base MLLMs by an average of +38.66% across tasks, enabling them to achieve competitive or superior performance compared to strong proprietary models, such as surpassing GPT-5 on VSP and Jigsaw (96.60% vs. 80.10%).

The model demonstrated adaptive tool usage, including zero-shot adoption of new tools (e.g., `ASTAR` boosting VSP navigation by +17.5 points with 94.53% success rate) and dynamic modulation of tool-use frequency based on task relevance.

Strong generalization was achieved for new tasks and tool definitions through Adaptive Learning, maintaining high tool engagement (e.g., 3.54 calls per sample on Jigsaw) and execution reliability (98.50% success) even when tool APIs were randomized or paraphrased.
Takeaways: Effective tool orchestration fundamentally shifts the MLLM performance bottleneck from intrinsic model scale to the utility of external tools, allowing smaller models to achieve state-of-the-art results.
Learning tool use as a dynamic and generalizable reasoning skill, rather than a rigid, task-specific behavior, is crucial for developing truly adaptive and versatile AI agents.
Explicitly incorporating reflection, backtracking, and the handling of tool failures during data curation and training fosters robust, human-like iterative problem-solving strategies in MLLMs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.16973.Title: VisGym: Diverse, Customizable, Scalable Environments for Multimodal Agents
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.16973.Summary: Researchers from UC Berkeley introduced VisGym, a diverse and customizable benchmark suite, to evaluate and train Vision-Language Models in multi-step visual interaction tasks. Their extensive evaluations reveal that frontier VLMs achieve only 46.61% success on easy tasks, with performance significantly impacted by context length, visual grounding, and a strong reliance on explicit textual feedback.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language Models (VLMs) struggle with multi-step visual interactions, where perception, memory, and action must be integrated over long horizons.
Current VLM benchmarks for interactive decision-making are fragmented, domain-specific, lack fine-grained control for diagnostic analysis, and often do not provide scalable environments for training.
There is a critical gap in systematically characterizing and diagnosing why VLMs fail in dynamic, visually rich environments, moving beyond mere observational studies.
Method: Introduces VisGym, a suite of 17 diverse, visually interactive environments built on the Gymnasium framework, spanning symbolic puzzles, real-image understanding, navigation, and manipulation.
Designed with fine-grained control over factors like task difficulty, input representation, planning horizon, and environmental feedback, enabling systematic diagnostic experiments.
Includes multi-step oracle solvers for each environment capable of generating diverse demonstration trajectories, facilitating supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of VLMs.
Employs a function-conditioned action space and provides function instructions and environment feedback to aid VLM interaction and self-correction.
Results: The top-performing frontier VLM (Gemini-3-Pro) achieved a success rate of 46.61% on easy tasks and 26.00% on hard tasks across VisGym's diverse environments.
Converting visual observations to ASCII text improved performance up to 3-4x for some symbolic tasks, and removing text-based feedback consistently degraded performance across all evaluated models.

Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) using solver-generated demonstrations significantly boosted VLM performance, with newer base models like Qwen3-VL showing nearly double the generalization ability to harder tasks compared to older versions, and the LLM backbone contributing more to gains than the vision encoder.
Takeaways: Frontier VLMs demonstrate limited robust performance in multi-step visual interactions, often struggling beyond 3-5 steps and exhibiting common failures like action looping, state mismanagement, and poor visual/spatial grounding.

Current models heavily rely on explicit textual feedback for action validity and consequences; performance significantly improves when visual observations are replaced with ASCII text, indicating weak visual perception.

Long-term context can be detrimental, and effective supervised fine-tuning benefits from "information-revealing" demonstrations that clarify hidden states or dynamics, rather than just longer or more numerous standard trajectories.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.16538.Title: OnlineSI: Taming Large Language Model for Online 3D Understanding and Grounding
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.16538.Summary: OnlineSI enables multimodal large language models to continuously perceive and understand 3D environments from streaming video by employing a finite spatial memory and fusing point cloud data with semantic information. The framework achieves an average Fuzzy F1-score of 0.4397 on ScanNet++, demonstrating improved 3D object grounding and recognition over baselines.
Problem: Existing MLLMs face prohibitive computational scaling issues and exhaust context windows when processing continuous, streaming 3D data.
MLLMs often lack the ability to continuously learn, refine, and adapt their spatial understanding from dynamic real-world environments.
Evaluating online 3D object detection with partial observations introduces significant ambiguity, making reliable performance assessment challenging.
Method: Introduces OnlineSI, a framework utilizing a finite, explicit spatial memory for continuous 3D point cloud and semantic label fusion from video streams, maintaining a bounded computational budget.
Enhances the base SpatialLM by injecting semantic information, derived from Llama token features, into point cloud features to create unified spatial memory tokens for the MLLM backbone.
Proposes a novel Fuzzy F1-Score metric to robustly evaluate online 3D object detection in scenarios with partial observations, addressing inherent ambiguities.
Results: OnlineSI achieved an average Fuzzy F1-score of 0.4397 on ScanNet++, significantly outperforming baselines such as SpatialLM-Finetune (0.3943) and SpatialLM-Merge (0.3397).

Qualitative results demonstrate OnlineSI's capacity to continuously refine scene understanding, leveraging spatial memory and semantic cues for accurate 3D object localization and recognition in real-world scenes.
Ablation studies confirmed the critical roles of explicit 3D point cloud memory, semantic information injection, and ground-plane aligned coordinate systems for optimal performance.
Takeaways: Maintaining a persistent, explicit 3D spatial memory is crucial for aggregating observations over time and achieving robust online 3D understanding, outperforming implicit 1D latent state representations.
Injecting detailed semantic information, derived from the MLLM's own token features, significantly enhances the model's ability to localize and recognize objects within the 3D point cloud.
Aligning the point cloud with a ground-plane coordinate system is fundamental for the SpatialLM backbone, indicating its strong dependence on axis-aligned input for effective 3D reasoning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.16520.Title: TangramPuzzle: Evaluating Multimodal Large Language Models with Compositional Spatial Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.16520.Summary: Researchers introduced TangramPuzzle, a geometry-grounded benchmark using the Tangram Construction Expression (TCE) to rigorously evaluate compositional spatial reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). This work revealed that while some advanced models like Gemini3-Pro demonstrated robust geometric understanding, many MLLMs struggled with rigid body constraints, often distorting or overlapping pieces to achieve visual fidelity rather than generating physically valid solutions.
Problem: Existing MLLM benchmarks primarily focus on high-level semantic understanding and coarse spatial relations, failing to evaluate precise compositional spatial reasoning under strict geometric and physical constraints.

Spatial problems in current evaluations are often described ambiguously using natural language or multiple-choice formats, relying more on linguistic reasoning than exact visual-geometric understanding.
Evaluation metrics are limited, often using text matching or subjective judgment, and lack mathematically rigorous validation for constructive tasks where multiple valid geometric solutions exist.
Method: The TangramPuzzle benchmark was developed, leveraging the classic Tangram puzzle, which inherently requires multi-step compositional spatial reasoning from local parts to a global shape.

A formal symbolic geometry description language, Tangram Construction Expression (TCE), was introduced to represent tangram configurations with exact algebraic coordinates and structural relations, enabling unambiguous, machine-verifiable evaluation.

Two complementary tasks were designed: Outline Prediction (inferring a global silhouette from local components) and End-to-End Tangram Solution Generation (solving the inverse geometric assembly problem by outputting a complete TCE in JSON format).
Results: Gemini3-Pro consistently outperformed other MLLMs, achieving the highest Validation Pass Rate (VPR) of 22.60% and a Success rate of 21.56% in End-to-End Solution Generation, demonstrating robust geometric reasoning.

Most MLLMs exhibited widespread failures in the End-to-End Solution Generation task, with high rates of Rigid Geometry Errors and Physical Errors, leading to 0% success rates for several top-tier models despite high Intersection over Union (IoU) scores.

Human solvers achieved a 72.67% success rate, rarely violating geometric constraints, which confirms the task's non-trivial difficulty and highlights the current gap in MLLMs' precise spatial intelligence.
Takeaways: Current MLLMs often prioritize visual fidelity (matching a target silhouette) over strict geometric constraints, leading to 'cheating' behaviors like distorting pieces or allowing overlaps to force a visual match.

Advanced MLLMs heavily rely on explicit textual geometric data for spatial reasoning, showing a significant performance drop when these 'textual crutches' are removed, indicating limited ability to ground precise coordinates directly from visual inputs.

In-Context Learning can improve the overall silhouette quality for correctly parsed responses but does not inherently instill a fundamental understanding of rigid body and non-overlap constraints in MLLMs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.16175.Title: Learning to Discover at Test Time
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.16175.Summary: Researchers introduce TTT-Discover, a test-time training framework that enables Large Language Models to learn and adapt during problem-solving, leading to new state-of-the-art solutions in diverse scientific and engineering challenges. The method achieved improved mathematical bounds, faster GPU kernels, and top scores in programming competitions using an open-source model at low computational cost.
Problem: Current AI systems, including powerful Large Language Models (LLMs), struggle with genuine scientific discovery, which requires generating ideas beyond their training data and existing human knowledge.
Traditional test-time search methods with frozen LLMs do not allow the models to internalize new ideas or learn from failed attempts, limiting their adaptive capabilities.

The goal of scientific discovery, which is to find a single, exceptional solution, mismatches the objective of standard Reinforcement Learning (RL) that typically maximizes expected reward for generalization.
Method: The approach formulates scientific discovery problems as Markov Decision Processes, allowing an LLM policy to continuously learn and improve by interacting with the problem environment at test time.
It implements an adaptive entropic objective function, `J_β(θ) = E[log E[e^(βR)]]`, which dynamically adjusts `β` to prioritize finding single maximum reward solutions over average rewards.

A PUCT-inspired (Polynomial Upper Confidence Trees) reuse mechanism selects optimal initial states from a buffer of past solutions, fostering optimistic exploration and leveraging previous high-quality attempts.
Results: Achieved new upper bounds in mathematics, including improving Erdős’ Minimum Overlap Problem (0.380876) and the First Autocorrelation Inequality (1.50286) over previous bests.
Discovered state-of-the-art GPU kernels for the TriMul competition across various hardware, outperforming human experts with up to 2x speedup on A100 and over 15% on H100.
Secured 1st place in two AtCoder Heuristic programming competitions, 'Purse Seine Fishing' and 'Apple Incremental Game,' by outperforming all human submissions and existing AI benchmarks.
Takeaways: Allowing LLMs to continually train and internalize feedback directly from the problem environment at test time enables them to truly adapt and generate novel solutions, moving beyond static search paradigms.

Customizing the RL objective and search strategy, specifically with an adaptive entropic objective and PUCT-inspired reuse, is critical for optimizing for a single, maximum-reward solution in discovery problems.
State-of-the-art scientific discovery can be achieved efficiently with open-source LLMs and modest computational resources, democratizing access to advanced AI-assisted research.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.15275.Title: RayRoPE: Projective Ray Positional Encoding for Multi-view Attention
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.15275.Summary: RayRoPE introduces a projective ray positional encoding for multi-view transformers that represents image patches as geometry-aware ray segments with unsupervised depth prediction, achieving SE(3) invariance, uniqueness, geometry-adaptiveness, and multi-frequency similarity. It demonstrates improved performance in novel-view synthesis, with a 15% relative LPIPS improvement over prior methods on CO3D, and more accurate stereo depth estimation.
Problem: Existing positional encodings for multi-view transformers struggle to simultaneously satisfy four critical desiderata: SE(3) invariance, uniqueness, geometry-adaptiveness, and multi-frequency similarity.
Absolute positional encodings lack SE(3) invariance, causing attention operations to depend on arbitrary global coordinate systems.

Camera-based relative encodings achieve SE(3) invariance but typically lack geometry-adaptiveness and multi-frequency capabilities, or compromise uniqueness when incorporating 2D pixel-based encodings.
Method: Represents each image patch as a geometry-aware ray segment defined by the camera center and a 3D point (at a learned depth), with depth predicted unsupervisedly by a linear layer within each attention layer.

Computes positional encodings in the local frame of the query camera using a projective operator, then applies a multi-frequency Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) to the 6D projected ray for SE(3) invariance and multi-frequency similarity.

Models uncertainty in the predicted depths by having the linear layer also predict an uncertainty value, which is then used in an 'Expected RoPE' mechanism to provide robustness against noisy depth estimations.
Results: Achieved state-of-the-art performance in novel-view synthesis, with a 15% relative improvement in LPIPS over PRoPE on the challenging CO3D dataset, and consistent gains in PSNR and SSIM across Objaverse and RealEstate10K.

Demonstrated more accurate stereo depth estimation, outperforming baseline UniMatch and PRoPE variants across RGBD, SUN3D, and Scenes11 datasets by improving metrics like Abs Rel, Sq Rel, RMSE, and RMSE log.
Ablation studies confirmed that geometry-adaptiveness, uncertainty modeling, and multi-frequency encoding are each critical components contributing to RayRoPE's superior performance in 3D tasks.
Takeaways: The proposed RayRoPE framework effectively fulfills all four critical desiderata for multi-view positional encodings: SE(3) invariance, uniqueness, geometry-adaptiveness, and multi-frequency similarity.
The model can implicitly learn geometrically plausible depth maps and associated uncertainties from the task objective (e.g., image reconstruction) without direct depth supervision.
Explicitly modeling depth uncertainty via the Expected RoPE mechanism is crucial for robust performance, particularly for high-frequency encoding components, as confirmed by ablation studies.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.15224.Title: PROGRESSLM: Towards Progress Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.15224.Summary: Researchers at Northwestern University developed PROGRESSLM, a framework that enables Vision-Language Models to perform progress reasoning for robotic tasks by emulating human-like episodic retrieval and mental simulation. This approach, supported by a new benchmark, allows a 3B-parameter model to surpass larger VLMs like GPT-5 in estimating task completion and recognizing unanswerable scenarios.
Problem: Current Vision-Language Models (VLMs) struggle with long-horizon, dynamic reasoning to estimate task progress from a single, partial observation.
Existing progress estimation methods are often task-specific or rely on indirect VLM approaches, lacking generalizable and direct intermediate progress quantification.
VLMs typically fail to recognize unanswerable cases in progress estimation, providing arbitrary scores even when information is insufficient or inconsistent.
Method: Introduces PROGRESS-BENCH, a systematic benchmark for progress reasoning across demonstration modalities (vision/text), viewpoint correspondence (same/cross-view), and answerability (answerable/unanswerable cases).
Proposes a human-inspired two-stage reasoning paradigm: episodic retrieval for a coarse anchor, followed by mental simulation for fine-grained progress estimation.

Develops PROGRESSLM, a model based on Qwen2.5-VL-3B, trained using a combination of ground-truth guided chain-of-thought supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning on the PROGRESSLM-45K dataset.
Results: PROGRESSLM-3B-RL achieved the best macro-averaged Normalized Score Error (NSE) and Progress Rank Correlation (PRC) on PROGRESS-BENCH, outperforming stronger general-purpose VLMs like GPT-5 and Qwen2.5-VL-72B.
The trained PROGRESSLM demonstrated improved robustness to cross-view observations, maintaining smaller performance gaps between same-view and cross-view settings.
PROGRESSLM consistently identified unanswerable cases across modalities, with PROGRESSLM-3B-RL achieving the strongest or near-strongest unanswerable recognition accuracy among all evaluated models.
Takeaways: Human-inspired two-stage reasoning (episodic retrieval and mental simulation) is effective for teaching VLMs robust dynamic progress understanding for long-horizon tasks.

Targeted supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning can enable smaller VLMs to acquire specialized, generalizable progress reasoning capabilities that outperform much larger, general-purpose models.

Systematic evaluation across demonstration modalities, viewpoint variations, and explicit unanswerable cases is crucial for comprehensively assessing VLM capabilities in dynamic reasoning and uncertainty awareness.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.14514.Title: "Just in Time" World Modeling Supports Human Planning and Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.14514.Summary: Researchers from MIT and UBC developed the "Just-in-Time" (JIT) framework, demonstrating how humans construct simplified environmental representations incrementally during planning and reasoning by integrating simulation, visual search, and dynamic representation modification. This model accurately predicts human memory and attention patterns across both planning and physical reasoning tasks, outperforming alternative models that rely on pre-computed optimal representations.
Problem: Humans fluently plan and reason in complex, detail-rich environments despite severe working memory and computational capacity limitations.

Existing models often assume simplified mental representations are formed *before* simulation, leading to a "pre-computation paradox" where evaluating optimal representations can be more demanding than a full simulation.
A lack of concrete algorithmic accounts explaining *how* these simplified representations are efficiently constructed online by the human mind.
Method: The "Just-in-Time" (JIT) model proposes an iterative process where simulation, local visual search, and dynamic representation modification are interleaved.

The model uses a representational sketchpad, a probabilistic simulator, and a perceptual lookahead module to encode objects only when they become relevant along a simulated trajectory and probabilistically forget irrelevant ones.
The JIT framework was implemented and tested in two distinct domains: a grid-world navigation planning task and a Plinko-like physical prediction task.
Results: The JIT model significantly outperformed the Value Guided Construal (VGC) model in explaining human memory for object locations (r=0.95 vs. VGC r=0.93) and attention patterns (e.g., r=0.88 vs. VGC r=0.65 for Experiment 1D) during planning tasks.

JIT accurately predicted human memory recall (r=0.87) and confidence (r=0.96) for object positions in physical reasoning tasks, explaining substantial unique variance beyond VGC (partial r_JIT|VGC = 0.49).

In specifically designed dissociation experiments (Experiment 2B), JIT aligned with human memory patterns (r=0.84), correctly predicting higher recall for frequently contacted "counterfactually irrelevant" objects, whereas VGC predicted the opposite (r=-0.65).
Takeaways: Humans construct efficient, simplified representations of their environment *online* and *incrementally* during the simulation process itself, rather than through extensive pre-computation.

The "Just-in-Time" approach resolves the paradox of pre-computation by allowing representations to emerge organically as needed, deferring encoding until an object is immediately relevant for the current simulation.
This framework provides a unified algorithmic account for managing representational complexity across diverse cognitive functions, including planning and intuitive physics.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.14339.Title: CityCube: Benchmarking Cross-view Spatial Reasoning on Vision-Language Models in Urban Environments
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.14339.Summary: CityCube is a new benchmark designed by researchers from the National University of Defense Technology and Tsinghua University to evaluate cross-view spatial reasoning capabilities of Vision-Language Models in complex urban environments. It reveals a substantial performance gap between current state-of-the-art VLMs and human intelligence, with VLMs struggling particularly with geometric and multi-view consistency tasks.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language Model (VLM) benchmarks primarily focus on indoor settings or restricted street-level environments, overlooking the unique complexities of open-ended urban spaces.

Embodied AI agents (e.g., autonomous vehicles, drones) operating in cities lack systematic evaluation tools for their spatial understanding and planning capabilities across diverse, multi-scale urban viewpoints.

Current VLMs often prioritize semantic understanding, leading to limitations in precise geometric reasoning, perspective taking, and mental simulation required for complex urban navigation and interaction.
Method: CityCube introduces a systematic benchmark with 5,022 multi-view Question-Answer pairs, integrating real-world (nuScenes, GeoText-1652) and simulated urban imagery (EmbodiedCity, MatrixCity) from over 70 cities.

The benchmark is structured along four dimensions: Viewpoint Dynamics (rotation, orbit, ego-allocentric, dynamic translation), View Perspectives (ground-level, low-altitude, bird-eye), five cognitive Benchmark Tasks (Mental Reconstruction, Perspective Taking, Spatial Relation, Comprehensive Reasoning, World Knowledge), and Spatial Relation Expressions.

A human-AI collaborative approach, leveraging Gemini-2.5 Pro with contextual role-playing and geometric reference injection, along with a two-stage human-AI quality control pipeline, ensures high-quality and challenging QA instances.
Results: The best-performing proprietary VLM achieved only 54.1% accuracy on CityCube, compared to human performance of 88.3%, indicating a substantial 34.2% gap.
Fine-tuning on CityCube significantly improves performance; custom 'CityBot' models, even at 2B parameters, surpassed strong proprietary baselines, with CityBot-8B (CoT) achieving 61.4% accuracy.

Error analysis revealed common VLM failure modes including limited sensitivity to small-scale urban entities, failures in egocentric spatial reasoning, insufficient cross-view consistency, and misinterpretation of motion/scale dynamics.
Takeaways: Current Vision-Language Models exhibit a significant performance gap compared to human spatial reasoning in urban environments, underscoring the fundamental difficulty of cross-view spatial intelligence for AI.

VLMs demonstrate a bias towards semantic understanding (e.g., World Knowledge tasks) while struggling with tasks demanding precise geometric reasoning, viewpoint transformation, and multi-view consistency (e.g., Perspective Taking, Mental Reconstruction).

The low correlation between human and VLM task difficulty suggests that current models may not be leveraging spatial cues and reasoning strategies in the same way as humans, highlighting a divergence in cognitive approaches.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.14127.Title: The Side Effects of Being Smart: Safety Risks in MLLMs' Multi-Image Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.14127.Summary: The paper introduces MIR-SafetyBench, the first benchmark for evaluating safety risks in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) stemming from complex multi-image reasoning, revealing widespread vulnerabilities where models' enhanced capabilities correlate with increased susceptibility to malicious queries. It also demonstrates that many "safe" responses are due to misunderstanding rather than true safety alignment.
Problem: Current MLLM safety evaluations primarily focus on "content-based safety," assessing explicit harmful content in single inputs.
There is a lack of systematic evaluation for "reasoning-based safety," where harm emerges from an MLLM's complex multi-image reasoning and contextual understanding.
Existing multi-image understanding benchmarks do not explicitly center on safety implications, leaving a critical gap in understanding advanced MLLM vulnerabilities.
Method: Developed MIR-SafetyBench, the first comprehensive benchmark for multi-image reasoning safety, featuring instances generated through an iterative AI-driven pipeline across 9 multi-image relation types.
Conducted extensive evaluations on 19 MLLMs, measuring Attack Success Rate (ASR) and qualitatively analyzing the nature of "safe" responses.
Probed internal model states using attention entropy to diagnose underlying mechanisms of safety failures in multi-image contexts.
Results: Most evaluated MLLMs were highly susceptible to multi-image relational reasoning attacks, with ASRs reaching 87.63%, indicating widespread vulnerability beyond content-based safety.
A controlled comparison demonstrated that all tested models became significantly more vulnerable when malicious intent was embedded in multi-image prompts compared to single-image scenarios.

Internal analysis showed that unsafe generations in multi-image tasks exhibited more concentrated attention, suggesting models might under-allocate resources to safety constraints under high cognitive load.
Takeaways: Increased multi-image reasoning capabilities in MLLMs can lead to an expanded attack surface, termed "the side effects of being smart," though frontier models show exceptions.
Many "safe" model responses are superficial, often resulting from "Harmless Misunderstanding" or evasive tactics, rather than genuine safety alignment.
Unsafe multi-image generations are associated with lower attention entropy, suggesting that cognitive load from complex reasoning might lead models to prioritize task completion over safety.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.13942.Title: Glance-or-Gaze: Incentivizing LMMs to Adaptively Focus Search via Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.13942.Summary: Researchers at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology developed Glance-or-Gaze (GoG), a framework that enables Large Multimodal Models to adaptively focus their visual search through a "Selective Gaze" mechanism and dual-stage reinforcement learning. This approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on knowledge-intensive visual question answering by dynamically combining global context with targeted region analysis.
Problem: Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) are limited by static parametric knowledge, leading to "knowledge cutoff" and "long-tail amnesia" for recent or obscure visual information.
Existing search-augmented LMMs use inefficient visual strategies, often relying on indiscriminate whole-image retrieval or converting rich visual details into text, creating information bottlenecks.
Current methods lack deep iterative reflection, preventing LMMs from adaptively refining search strategies, self-correcting, or performing multi-step visual verification.
Method: The Glance-or-Gaze (GoG) framework transforms LMMs into active visual planners through a fully autonomous, dual-stage learning system.
It introduces a "Selective Gaze" mechanism that dynamically decides whether to "glance" at global context or "gaze" into high-value image regions, filtering visual noise.

A two-phase training strategy, comprising Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) for reflective behavior alignment and Reinforcement Learning (RL) for complexity-adaptive policy optimization, instills and refines these capabilities.
Results: GoG-3-8B-Think-RL achieves state-of-the-art performance across six diverse benchmarks, with an average +9.89 gain over the strongest Full-Search Workflow baseline and +19.97 over the previous MMSearch-R1.

RL training dramatically increases "Mix Search" behavior (combining multiple search types) from 28.7% to 76.7% and improves Crop Selection Accuracy by 4.7-6.8% and Reflection Rate on Errors from 30% to 70%.
Ablation studies confirm the necessity of the Selective Gaze mechanism for granular evidence verification and validate the effectiveness of complexity-adaptive RL training on challenging samples.
Takeaways: LMMs can transition from passive image perception to active, dynamic visual planning, enabling them to intelligently focus attention and search efforts based on query complexity.
A dual-stage training approach effectively instills foundational search behaviors via SFT and then refines adaptive, iterative reasoning and robust policy optimization through RL.

Explicitly controlling visual attention with a "Selective Gaze" mechanism provides a physical anchor for reasoning, allowing for granular evidence verification and efficient information filtering before external retrieval.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.13705.Title: Reasoning or Pattern Matching? Probing Large Vision-Language Models with Visual Puzzles
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.13705.Summary: This survey paper from the National Technical University of Athens and Instituto de Telecomunicações recasts visual puzzles as diagnostic instruments to probe whether Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) exhibit genuine reasoning or sophisticated pattern-matching, revealing that current LVLMs often display an "illusion of reasoning" where fluent explanations mask fundamental cognitive limitations across various reasoning types.
Problem: A critical question exists whether LVLMs possess genuine reasoning capabilities or primarily rely on complex pattern-matching, despite impressive performance on multimodal tasks.
Traditional multimodal benchmarks often entangle reasoning with confounding factors, making it difficult to diagnose specific failure modes or ascertain true visual reasoning.
There is a need for robust diagnostic tools to evaluate LVLMs' cognitive foundations beyond perception and high-level recognition.
Method: The authors formally define visual puzzles as diagnostic instruments, characterized by essential reliance on visual information, explicitly constrained structure, and reasoning-centric challenges.
A comprehensive taxonomy organizes existing visual puzzle benchmarks into five distinct reasoning dimensions: inductive, analogical, algorithmic, deductive, and geometric/spatial reasoning.
The paper provides an empirical synthesis of findings across these categories to identify consistent limitations and vulnerabilities in current LVLMs.
Results: LVLMs demonstrate brittle generalization, struggling to induce invariant rules or abstract structural patterns and degrading sharply under minor variations or out-of-distribution shifts.

Models show a perception-reasoning entanglement, where limitations in fine-grained visual perception bottleneck downstream reasoning, and they often fail in multi-step execution and maintaining internal state for algorithmic tasks.

LVLMs struggle with constraint integration in deductive tasks and often rely on superficial spatial cues rather than abstract geometric relations, leading to error accumulation in geometric/spatial reasoning.
Takeaways: Current LVLMs exhibit an "illusion of reasoning," where fluent and rational verbal explanations often do not correspond to faithful execution or comprehension of visual evidence.
Visual puzzles serve as uniquely sharp diagnostic tools by providing isolated environments and controlled conditions that decouple domain knowledge from pure logic.
Future research should focus on multi-agent collaboration, long-horizon training objectives, compositional generalization, and abductive/lateral visual reasoning to foster more reasoning-aware LVLMs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.13633.Title: Scaling Test-time Inference for Visual Grounding
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.13633.Summary: Researchers from NVIDIA, MIT, Oxford, and Tsinghua University developed EGM, a method that enables smaller Visual Language Models to achieve state-of-the-art visual grounding performance, including amodal grounding, by strategically scaling test-time computation. This approach allows 8B parameter models to outperform 235B parameter counterparts while being nearly six times faster, making high-performance VLMs more deployable.
Problem: State-of-the-art visual grounding VLMs are often too large and computationally demanding for practical deployment on edge devices or in latency-sensitive applications.
Smaller VLMs struggle with visual grounding tasks involving complex linguistic prompts due to limitations in their language understanding and multi-modal reasoning capabilities.
Current VLMs lack a robust ability to perform amodal grounding, which requires identifying objects' complete shapes, including occluded parts, based on natural language.
Method: The Efficient visual Grounding language Models (EGM) method scales test-time computation by enabling small VLMs to generate multi-modal reasoning traces, rather than increasing model size.

A two-stage training paradigm is employed: Supervised Fine-tuning (SFT) leveraging proprietary VLM-generated reasoning traces, followed by Reinforcement Learning (RL) specifically targeting challenging examples.
A novel data curation pipeline generates high-quality reasoning traces for both vanilla and amodal grounding tasks, explicitly detailing how to locate and perceive occluded objects.
Results: EGM-Qwen3-VL-8B achieved 91.4% IoU on the RefCOCO benchmark, outperforming the much larger Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B-Instruct (90.5% IoU) while being 5.9 times faster.
The method consistently boosted vanilla visual grounding accuracy across various Qwen3-VL and InternVL models, showing improvements of up to +6.0 percentage points for smaller models.
EGM demonstrated strong capabilities in the novel amodal grounding task, with EGM-Qwen3-VL-8B achieving 73.9% amodal accuracy, comparable to or surpassing larger baseline models.
Takeaways: The primary performance gap between small and large VLMs in visual grounding stems from differences in language understanding and reasoning abilities, rather than inherent visual processing limitations.

Explicitly generating more reasoning tokens with a smaller model during inference is a more efficient strategy for achieving high-performance visual grounding compared to directly running a massive VLM.
Integrating targeted reasoning patterns through SFT and RL, supported by detailed generated data, can effectively teach VLMs to perform both standard and complex amodal grounding tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.13562.Title: Reasoning is a Modality
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.13562.Summary: Researchers from the University of Missouri - Columbia developed a role-separated transformer architecture, grounded in the hypothesis that reasoning functions as a distinct internal modality. This model achieved an average accuracy of 58.8% on ARC-1 and 11.0% on ARC-2, with an ensemble reaching 62.6% on ARC-1, surpassing reported average human performance.
Problem: Modern AI systems, despite their performance, often lack a persistent, readable mental state, primarily excelling at sequence-of-behavior prediction rather than genuine human-like reasoning.
Current AI frequently produces post-hoc rationalizations or 'hallucinations' that are not causally connected to an internal, structured understanding.
The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) tasks, designed to test out-of-distribution generalization and abstract rule understanding, remain a significant challenge for existing AI paradigms.
Method: The authors introduced a role-separated transformer block that segregates 'global controller tokens' (for high-level reasoning) from 'grid workspace tokens' (for low-level grid operations).

A structured attention mechanism was implemented, allowing controller tokens to access all information while restricting workspace tokens to only attend to controllers and local neighborhoods, thereby bottlenecking global information flow through the controller.

A recurrent wrapper was applied to the transformer stack for iterative refinement, and the model adhered to a two-stage training protocol (offline pretraining followed by test-time training for task adaptation).
Results: The top-performing `c-d-4-TTT3` model achieved an average accuracy of 58.8% on ARC-1 and 11.0% on ARC-2, surpassing the VARC-ViT baseline (54.5% on ARC-1, 8.3% on ARC-2).
When combined with the VARC-Unet ensemble technique, the model reached 62.6% accuracy on ARC-1, outperforming the reported average human performance of 60.2%.

Qualitative analysis of attention maps revealed that the proposed architecture maintained stable, structured attention fields across layers, demonstrating coherent spatial primitives and controller-driven rule application, in contrast to the diffused attention seen in standard ViT models.
Takeaways: Architecturally enforcing role separation through a compact global controller and a restricted local workspace creates a more structured and interpretable internal state for abstract reasoning.

While global guidance from the controller is essential, maintaining local consistency and repair capabilities within the workspace through limited neighborhood attention is crucial for effective rule application.

Deeper recurrent unrolling combined with specific test-time training strategies, including auxiliary objectives and pixel-level error emphasis, are key to unlocking the full potential of the structured architecture.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.13304.Title: CausalSpatial: A Benchmark for Object-Centric Causal Spatial Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.13304.Summary: A new diagnostic benchmark, CausalSpatial, evaluates Multimodal Large Language Models' (MLLMs) capacity for causal spatial reasoning, revealing their tendency for spatially ungrounded hallucinations when predicting object interactions. The CAUSAL OBJECT WORLD MODEL (COW) framework is also introduced, providing explicit visual simulation to ground MLLM reasoning in physical reality and improving performance on causal spatial tasks.
Problem: Current Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle with causal spatial reasoning, failing to predict dynamic consequences of actions in 3D environments.
MLLMs over-rely on linguistic priors, leading to 'spatially ungrounded hallucinations' when attempting causal reasoning tasks.
Existing benchmarks do not adequately assess models' ability to reason about dynamic object interactions and causal prediction at an object level.
Method: Developed CausalSpatial, a synthetic, object-centric diagnostic benchmark featuring four causal anticipation tasks (e.g., Collision, Occlusion, Trajectory) across two difficulty levels, using physically simulated 3D scenes.
Created the CAUSAL OBJECT WORLD MODEL (COW) framework, which externalizes 4D trajectory simulation and generates controllable videos to provide MLLMs with explicit visual evidence of causality.
Evaluated MLLMs using True Positive Rate (TPR) and Not Sure Rate (NSR) on multiple-choice questions with 'Not Sure' options to diagnose hallucination bias and epistemic uncertainty.
Results: Humans achieved 84.49% overall accuracy on the CausalSpatial benchmark, while the top-performing MLLM, GPT-5, scored 54.17%.

Collision Anticipation proved most challenging for MLLMs, with many open-source models performing near random guessing on Level 2, whereas Trajectory Anticipation showed the narrowest performance gap (GPT-5 at 64.96% on L2 vs. human 62.50%).

Incorporating three initial frames from COW-generated simulation videos as visual cues led to performance gains for MLLMs, with Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct improving by 2.40% on Collision and 2.20% on Trajectory tasks.
Takeaways: State-of-the-art MLLMs exhibit a substantial performance gap compared to humans in causal spatial reasoning, with GPT-5 scoring 54.17% versus human 84.49%.

MLLMs often display increased confidence (lower Not Sure Rate) without a proportional increase in accuracy, indicating overconfidence in incorrect, ungrounded predictions and a tendency for textual hallucinations.

Explicit visual simulation provided by the COW framework consistently boosts MLLM performance on CausalSpatial tasks, validating that grounding reasoning in dynamic physical reality helps suppress hallucinations.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.13132.Title: GaussExplorer: 3D Gaussian Splatting for Embodied Exploration and Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.13132.Summary: GaussExplorer introduces a unified framework integrating 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to enable embodied exploration and reasoning in 3D scenes. The system achieves state-of-the-art performance in embodied question answering by dynamically adjusting viewpoints for complex natural language queries and significantly improves 3D referring segmentation.
Problem: Existing VLM-based embodied reasoning systems are limited by pre-fixed viewpoints and object-level abstractions, preventing dynamic exploration or fine-grained spatial reasoning.

Current language-driven 3D Gaussian Splatting methods struggle with complex, compositional natural language queries, primarily relying on static embedding similarity for simple category-level matching.

Intelligent embodied agents require both high-level understanding of natural language instructions and precise 3D localization capabilities to reason and interact effectively within complex 3D environments.
Method: Constructs semantic 3D Gaussian representations by integrating object categories or open-set CLIP embeddings into individual Gaussians, enabling rich scene understanding.

Implements an initial view selection process that uses LLMs to extract relevant 'evidence categories' from queries, followed by a Gaussian search and instance-level clustering to identify candidate objects.

Introduces a novel-view adjustment mechanism where VLMs dynamically synthesize and evaluate perturbed camera poses, acting as a 'judge' to select optimal viewpoints that provide the strongest visual evidence for a given query.
Results: Achieved an LLM-Match score of 57.8 on the EM-EQA benchmark for Embodied Question Answering, outperforming the previous state-of-the-art 3D-Mem (54.6) while maintaining comparable VLM processing efficiency (2.6 vs. 2.7 frames).

Demonstrated superior performance in Question-based 3D Referring Segmentation with a 3D mIoU of 12.87 and Acc@10 of 45.71, significantly surpassing Dr. Splat (10.56 3D mIoU) and ReferSplat (2.34 3D mIoU).

Ablation studies confirmed that the proposed visibility score, novel-view adjustment, and VLM-based verification steps are crucial for the observed performance gains in both embodied reasoning and 3D localization tasks.
Takeaways: Dynamic, VLM-guided novel-view synthesis from 3D Gaussian Splatting can overcome the fixed-view limitations of traditional embodied AI systems, leading to more accurate and reliable reasoning.

Integrating semantic embeddings directly into 3D Gaussians enables robust open-vocabulary understanding and fine-grained 3D localization in response to complex, compositional natural language queries.

A 'visibility score' for initial view selection, combined with a 'VLM-as-Judge' mechanism for novel-view adjustment, effectively identifies and leverages informative viewpoints to enhance embodied reasoning accuracy.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.12964.Title: Cross-Scale Pretraining: Enhancing Self-Supervised Learning for Low-Resolution Satellite Imagery for Semantic Segmentation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.12964.Summary: Researchers at Carnegie Mellon University Africa introduced a spatial affinity component for cross-scale pretraining, integrating real high-resolution (HR) and mid-resolution (MR) satellite imagery to improve self-supervised learning. This approach consistently enhanced downstream semantic segmentation performance, achieving higher mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) on MR tasks compared to single-resolution pretraining across various benchmarks.
Problem: Deep learning for remote sensing tasks like semantic segmentation is hampered by the scarcity of expensive, pixel-level annotated datasets.

Current self-supervised learning (SSL) in remote sensing primarily pretrains on readily available mid-resolution (MR) data, which limits the capture of fine spatial details crucial for many applications.

Existing multi-resolution SSL approaches often rely on synthetic downsampling of high-resolution (HR) imagery, failing to replicate the true physical and sensor-specific characteristics of real lower-resolution images.
Method: Developed a pluggable "spatial affinity component" for existing self-supervised learning (SSL) frameworks, enabling cross-scale pretraining.
Utilizes a student-teacher architecture to process real co-located high-resolution (HR) and mid-resolution (MR) image pairs simultaneously.
Employs a gram loss that computes the mean squared error between gram matrices of student and downsampled HR teacher outputs, fostering spatial alignment robust to sensor differences.
Results: The SA-model, incorporating cross-scale pretraining, consistently achieved higher mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) in semantic segmentation across three Geo-Bench datasets compared to models pretrained exclusively on single-resolution HR or MR data.

Pretraining with real high-resolution (HR) data led to significantly superior performance compared to using synthetically interpolated HR data, confirming the importance of actual sensor characteristics.

Qualitative visualizations demonstrated that the SA-model learned more discriminative spatial representations for mid-resolution (MR) imagery, enabling better identification of distinct spatial features.
Takeaways: Real high-resolution (HR) satellite data contains critical physical and sensor-specific characteristics that are essential for learning superior mid-resolution (MR) representations, outperforming synthetically generated HR imagery.

Aligning the spatial structure of features using gram matrices allows effective knowledge transfer between real HR and MR imagery, tolerating sensor differences while enhancing patch-level spatial detail in MR representations.

Integrating a spatial affinity component into existing SSL frameworks enables robust cross-scale pretraining, demonstrating generalizability across different masked image modeling architectures like LatentMIM and I-JEPA.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.12585.Title: Do MLLMs See What We See? Analyzing Visualization Literacy Barriers in AI Systems
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.12585.Summary: Researchers at the University of Toronto introduced the first systematic taxonomy of visualization literacy barriers for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), identifying both common and machine-specific failure patterns. The study found that MLLMs struggle particularly with color-intensive, segment-based visualizations like pie charts and stacked bar charts due to errors in value extraction and reasoning logic.
Problem: There was a lack of systematic understanding regarding the specific reasons why Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) fail in data visualization interpretation tasks.
Prior MLLM evaluations on visualization tasks were susceptible to 'data leakage,' where models might retrieve memorized answers rather than demonstrating genuine interpretive abilities.
A comprehensive framework for MLLM visualization literacy barriers, similar to those established for human cognition, was absent.
Method: A barrier-centric, open-coding methodology, inspired by human visualization literacy research, was applied to analyze MLLM failures systematically.
Four state-of-the-art MLLMs (GPT-5, Claude-Sonnet-4, Gemini 2.5, Qwen3-VL) were evaluated using the reVLAT benchmark, which features synthetic data to mitigate data leakage concerns.

The evaluation process was augmented to collect detailed reasoning rationales and proxy 'points of focus' (x,y coordinates) from MLLMs to enable qualitative analysis of their decision-making processes.
Results: Overall accuracy varied among models: Qwen achieved 86.42%, followed by Claude (74.72%), Gemini (73.21%), and GPT (49.06%).

MLLMs consistently performed poorly on 'color-intensive, segment-based visualizations' such as pie charts (Claude: 46.70% accuracy) and stacked bar charts (Claude: 72.00% accuracy), indicating specific vulnerabilities.
The extended taxonomy categorizes MLLM failures into four classes: Translation Barriers, Visual Perception Barriers, and the machine-specific Visual Reasoning Barriers and Coherence Barriers.
Takeaways: The study developed the first systematic taxonomy of MLLM visualization literacy barriers, extending human-centric frameworks by identifying novel, machine-specific failure modes.

MLLMs exhibit unique 'Visual Reasoning Barriers' (e.g., incorrect comparison, perceptual–logic mismatch) and 'Coherence Barriers' (e.g., self-consistency issues, sensitivity to answer choice ordering) that distinguish their interpretive challenges from human cognition.
The findings provide actionable insights for MLLM developers to enhance model architectures and training objectives, particularly for improving visual reasoning and internal consistency.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.12538.Title: Agentic Reasoning for Large Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.12538.Summary: A comprehensive survey details the rapidly evolving landscape of Large Language Model agents, reframing LLMs as autonomous entities capable of planning, acting, and learning through interaction. It introduces a structured taxonomy for agentic reasoning, encompassing foundational capabilities, self-evolving adaptation, and collective intelligence, while also reviewing diverse applications and identifying critical open challenges.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) traditionally operate as passive sequence generators, struggling with dynamic, open-ended environments despite strong performance in static, closed-world reasoning tasks.
The absence of intrinsic mechanisms for LLMs to continuously act, learn, and improve over time limits their applicability in real-world interactive scenarios.
The rapidly growing research landscape of LLM agents lacked a systematic, unified framework to categorize and understand diverse approaches to agentic reasoning.
Method: A paradigm of "Agentic Reasoning" is introduced, formally defining LLMs as autonomous agents capable of planning, acting, and learning through continuous interaction with an environment.
A three-dimensional taxonomy is established, systematically organizing existing research into foundational agentic reasoning, self-evolving agentic reasoning, and collective multi-agent reasoning.

The framework consistently analyzes mechanisms under two complementary optimization settings: in-context reasoning (inference-time interaction) and post-training reasoning (parameter-updating learning).
Results: A coherent conceptual framework for agentic reasoning is established, defining its core components and their interconnections.
Existing research on single-agent capabilities (planning, tool use, search), self-evolution (feedback, memory), and multi-agent coordination is systematically mapped and categorized.
A comprehensive overview of real-world applications and benchmarks is provided, illustrating the practical instantiation and evaluation of agentic reasoning frameworks.
A clear agenda of future research challenges is articulated, spanning personalization, long-horizon interaction, world modeling, and the governance of agentic systems.
Takeaways: Agentic reasoning fundamentally reframes LLMs from static inference machines to interactive, adaptive entities that bridge internal thought with external action.

The acquisition and refinement of agent capabilities can be systematically understood by distinguishing between inference-time workflow orchestration ("in-context reasoning") and parameter-updating learning ("post-training reasoning").
Effective LLM agents rely on a set of core mechanisms—planning, tool use, search, feedback, and memory—that can evolve through continuous interaction and learning.
