https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.11729.Title: SpaRRTa: A Synthetic Benchmark for Evaluating Spatial Intelligence in Visual Foundation Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.11729.Summary: SpaRRTa, a new synthetic benchmark, evaluates Visual Foundation Models' abstract spatial reasoning abilities by requiring them to identify relative object positions from egocentric and allocentric viewpoints. It reveals that spatial information is distributed within local patch features, and while 3D supervision enhances this, allocentric perspective-taking remains difficult for current models.
Problem: Visual Foundation Models (VFMs) lack robust, abstract spatial reasoning, hindering their application in embodied and interactive AI systems.
Existing benchmarks primarily assess metric 3D perception (e.g., depth, camera pose), not qualitative, relational spatial understanding.
It is unclear if VFMs truly gain general spatial awareness or merely overfit to specific geometric training objectives.
Method: A synthetic benchmark called SpaRRTa was created to specifically evaluate abstract, relational spatial understanding in VFMs, differentiating it from metric 3D tasks.
Unreal Engine 5 was used to generate photorealistic images with precise control over object placement, camera views, and ground-truth spatial annotations across diverse scenes.

Two distinct spatial reasoning tasks were defined: SpaRRTa-ego for egocentric relations and SpaRRTa-allo for allocentric relations, which necessitates implicit perspective-taking from a third object's viewpoint.
Results: Efficient Probing consistently achieved superior performance across all models, confirming that structured aggregation of local patch features is critical for effective spatial reasoning.
VGGT, a 3D-supervised model, significantly surpassed DINO-v2 in accuracy when evaluated with AbMILP and Efficient Probing, indicating that 3D supervision enhances localized geometric structure.
All evaluated models exhibited substantially lower accuracy on the allocentric spatial reasoning task compared to the egocentric task, highlighting the challenge of perspective-taking.
A positive correlation (R² "0.40) was observed between SpaRRTa performance and 3D geometric tasks, while correlation with semantic classification benchmarks was negligible (R² ".00).
Takeaways: Spatial information critical for relational understanding is predominantly embedded within local patch features of VFM representations, often obscured by global pooling methods.

Explicit 3D supervision reorganizes VFM internal representations by increasing cross-object attention and enhancing patch-level geometric structure, making spatial details more accessible to sophisticated probes.
Abstract allocentric reasoning, which demands implicit perspective-taking, poses a significantly greater challenge for current VFMs compared to egocentric spatial understanding.
VFM spatial intelligence is a distinct capability, showing strong correlation with other 3D geometric tasks but negligible correlation with high-level semantic classification.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.11442.Title: Map2Thought: Explicit 3D Spatial Reasoning via Metric Cognitive Maps
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.11442.Summary: The Map2Thought framework enables explicit 3D spatial reasoning in Vision-Language Models by creating a Metric Cognitive Map that unifies discrete symbolic grid representations with continuous metric-scale data. This structured approach, combined with a Cognitive Chain-of-Thought module for deterministic geometric computations, achieves an average accuracy of 61.0% on VSI-Bench and demonstrates superior data efficiency from monocular RGB videos.
Problem: Existing 3D Vision-Language Models (3D-VLMs) rely on implicit latent space fusion, resulting in opaque and uninterpretable spatial reasoning processes.
Current 3D-VLMs often lack precise geometric grounding and metric-scale understanding, limiting their ability to perform fine-grained spatial queries.
Models struggle with data efficiency and generalization across diverse 3D scenes due to reliance on vast annotated datasets and implicit reasoning.
Method: Develops the Metric Cognitive Map (Metric-CogMap), a dual-format spatial representation that integrates discrete symbolic grids for relational understanding with continuous metric-scale data for precise geometric details.
Implements a robust Video-to-Map pipeline that constructs the Metric-CogMap from raw monocular RGB videos using techniques like crucial frame selection and covisibility mapping.
Introduces Cognitive Chain-of-Thought (Cog-CoT), an explicit reasoning module that performs deterministic geometric computations directly on the Metric-CogMap, producing verifiable inference traces.
Results: Achieved an overall average accuracy of 61.0% on the VSI-Bench dataset, positioning it as the top open-source VLM and surpassing several proprietary models.
Exhibited superior data efficiency, reaching 59.9% accuracy with only 50% of the training data, nearly matching the baseline's performance with 100% data.
Demonstrated significant performance improvements in geometry-aware tasks, including Object Count, Absolute Distance, Object Size, Room Size, and Appearance Order.
Takeaways: Explicit, metrically grounded spatial representations, combined with deterministic geometric reasoning, enhance the interpretability and explainability of 3D-VLM outputs.
A unified spatial map that integrates both discrete symbolic relationships and continuous metric-scale information is essential for comprehensive and precise 3D spatial understanding.
Structured reasoning modules dramatically improve data efficiency and generalization capabilities, enabling strong performance with significantly less training data.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.11322.Title: Enhancing Vision Language Models with Logic Reasoning for Situational Awareness
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.11322.Summary: A framework integrates Vision-Language Models with traditional computer vision and explicit logical reasoning to provide justifications for VLM outputs and flag unreliable predictions in situational awareness applications. Its consistency-driven fine-tuning strategy consistently outperforms uninformed tuning, achieving comparable accuracy to label-intensive methods while reducing labeling effort.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) lack fine-grained, quantitative details crucial for precise situational awareness, despite providing rich semantic descriptions.
Fine-tuning VLMs for specific, often rare, events is resource-intensive due to the need for large labeled datasets.
Current VLMs do not provide justifications for their outputs or indicate when predictions might be unreliable, hindering deployment in critical systems.
Method: The proposed framework integrates Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and Traditional Computer Vision (TCV) with explicit logical reasoning using Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT).
It employs a three-task activity categorization (main, auxiliary, proxy) to structure knowledge and facilitate consistency checks between VLM outputs and TCV-derived facts.

A consistency-driven fine-tuning algorithm intelligently selects unlabeled video segments for VLM fine-tuning based on identified logical inconsistencies, reducing reliance on extensive prior labeling.
Results: The consistency-driven directed fine-tuning achieved up to 9 percentage points higher accuracy compared to uninformed (random) fine-tuning (e.g., MiniGPT4 on TU DAT improved from 73.14% to 82.14%).

Directed fine-tuning attained classification accuracy nearly identical to that of an accuracy-driven method requiring prior labels for selection, demonstrating efficiency without sacrificing performance.

The Consistency Improvement Factor (CIF) was significantly higher for directed fine-tuning (e.g., X-CLIP on TU DAT at 74.25%) compared to undirected fine-tuning (54.5%), indicating better resolution of inconsistencies.
Takeaways: Explicit logical reasoning via SMT effectively combines high-level VLM semantic understanding with fine-grained TCV details, enabling both justification for VLM outputs and reliability checks.

Consistency checks, derived from logical rules and TCV groundings, serve as a powerful, label-free signal to guide VLM fine-tuning, leading to substantial accuracy improvements with reduced labeling effort.
The integration of an auxiliary VLM, which performs a simpler related task, enhances the robustness of consistency checks and improves the effectiveness of directed fine-tuning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.10825.Title: Reasoning Models Generate Societies of Thought
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.10825.Summary: This research investigates how advanced large language models (LLMs) achieve complex reasoning, finding that they implicitly simulate multi-agent-like interactions, or "societies of thought," characterized by diverse perspectives and conversational dynamics. This internal social structure is functionally and mechanistically linked to superior reasoning performance, facilitating cognitive strategies and accelerating learning.
Problem: Existing explanations for enhanced reasoning in large language models (LLMs), such as generating longer "chains of thought," offer superficial insights into the underlying qualitative characteristics of their "thinking" processes.
The fundamental mechanisms enabling complex, step-by-step reasoning in LLMs have remained largely opaque.
A lack of understanding exists regarding whether improved LLM reasoning is merely extended computation or involves more complex, qualitative shifts in their internal processes.
Method: Conducted comparative analysis using an "LLM-as-judge" approach to quantify conversational behaviors, socio-emotional roles, and implicit perspective diversity in reasoning models versus instruction-tuned baselines.

Employed mechanistic interpretability with Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and activation steering to causally link specific internal conversational features to reasoning performance and the deployment of cognitive strategies.

Performed controlled reinforcement learning (RL) experiments to observe the spontaneous emergence of conversational behaviors and assess how conversational scaffolding impacts reasoning acquisition in base models.
Results: Reasoning models exhibited significantly more frequent conversational behaviors (e.g., question-answering, perspective shifts, conflicts) and a wider range of reciprocal socio-emotional roles, adaptively increasing these patterns for more complex problems.

Causally steering a specific "conversational surprise" feature in a reasoning model via activation addition improved accuracy on an arithmetic task and simultaneously increased the deployment of effective cognitive strategies like verification and backtracking.

Base models, rewarded solely for accuracy, spontaneously developed conversational behaviors during reinforcement learning, and pre-training with conversational dialogue data accelerated reasoning acquisition and improved accuracy across different tasks.
Takeaways: Advanced reasoning in LLMs is characterized by the implicit simulation of internal "societies of thought" with diverse perspectives and conversational dynamics, rather than merely extended computational steps.

These internal social-like interactions are not just stylistic outputs but are functionally and causally linked to superior reasoning performance, actively scaffolding the deployment of effective cognitive strategies.

Principles of collective intelligence and cognitive diversity, analogous to those observed in human groups, can spontaneously emerge and enhance problem-solving within individual LLMs when rewarded for accuracy.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.10679.Title: Are Your Reasoning Models Reasoning or Guessing? A Mechanistic Analysis of Hierarchical Reasoning Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.10679.Summary: Researchers from the Shanghai Qi Zhi Institute conducted a mechanistic analysis of the Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM), uncovering that its impressive performance stems from a "scaled guessing" dynamic, characterized by fixed-point violations and spurious attractors, rather than gradual reasoning. This understanding led to an "Augmented HRM" achieving 96.9% accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme, a substantial increase from 54.5%.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle with complex "System-2 thinking" tasks like Sudoku, often achieving 0% success rates.

Latent-space reasoning models, such as the Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM), demonstrate high accuracy on these tasks, but the precise mechanisms behind their success and failure modes remain unclear.
A need exists to mechanistically scrutinize the nature of impressive performance in advanced AI reasoning models to determine if they are truly 'reasoning' or employing other strategies.
Method: A mechanistic analysis of the Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM) was performed using the challenging Sudoku-Extreme dataset to probe its internal dynamics.
The methodology involved examining the fixed-point property, analyzing segment-wise loss for 'grokking' patterns, and visualizing latent state trajectories via PCA to classify reasoning modes.
Three performance enhancement strategies were developed and combined: data augmentation, input perturbation (token relabeling), and model bootstrapping, culminating in "Augmented HRM."
Results: Data augmentation (data mixing) restored the fixed-point property, boosting HRM's accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme from 54.5% to 59.9%.
Input perturbation (token relabeling) alone improved accuracy from 54.5% to 73.2%, demonstrating the effectiveness of diversifying input perspectives for generating 'guesses.'
Combining data augmentation, input perturbation, and model bootstrapping in 'Augmented HRM' achieved a new state-of-the-art accuracy of 96.9% on the Sudoku-Extreme dataset.
Takeaways: HRM frequently violates the 'fixed-point property,' failing on extremely simple puzzles despite solving complex ones, indicating a lack of stability in its solutions.
The model exhibits a 'grokking' dynamic in its reasoning steps, where solutions are found abruptly rather than through gradual refinement, suggesting recursive segments scale 'guessing attempts.'

Latent space analysis reveals 'spurious fixed points' as misleading attractors, causing non-trivial failures where the model gets trapped in incorrect solutions corresponding to local minima of a heuristic error function.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.10497.Title: MERGETUNE: Continued fine-tuning of vision-language models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.10497.Summary: MERGETUNE presents a novel "Continued Fine-Tuning" paradigm to recover pre-trained knowledge from Vision-Language Models after task-specific fine-tuning, employing a replay-free, learning-based merging strategy anchored by linear mode connectivity. This approach consistently improves generalization and robustness across diverse benchmarks, for instance, boosting CoOp's harmonic mean by 5.58% in base-to-novel scenarios.
Problem: Fine-tuning Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for downstream tasks often leads to catastrophic forgetting of valuable generalizable pre-trained knowledge.

Existing Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods incompletely preserve pre-trained knowledge and can rely on complex modules, while robust ensembling strategies incur high inference costs or unstable performance.
Direct model merging techniques struggle to integrate knowledge when zero-shot and fine-tuned models are far apart in weight space.
Method: Introduces "Continued Fine-Tuning (CFT)," a post-hoc, learning-based model merging paradigm that actively recovers forgotten knowledge from a fine-tuned VLM.
Formulates a replay-free objective by using a second-order Taylor expansion surrogate for pretraining data constraints, enabling knowledge preservation without needing original pretraining data.
Guides the learning process by explicitly enforcing linear mode connectivity (LMC) to find a new model state that maintains low-loss paths to both the original zero-shot VLM and the task-adapted VLM.
Results: Consistently improved base-to-novel generalization, increasing CoOp's harmonic mean by +5.58% (from 71.66% to 77.24%) and showing similar gains across other baselines, outperforming existing training-free merging methods.

Achieved new state-of-the-art ID-OOD generalization in many-shot settings, with MERGETUNE-enhanced linear probing improving average domain accuracy by +2.27% (from 57.39% to 59.66%) over the base model, surpassing SOTA ensembling methods like VRF.

Demonstrated model-agnostic applicability and robustness across different VLM backbones (CLIP-L/14, Siglip2-B/16, Siglip2-L/16) and hyperparameter choices, while maintaining a single model for efficient inference.
Takeaways: Knowledge lost during VLM fine-tuning can be effectively recovered post-hoc through a dedicated continued fine-tuning process, rather than solely relying on mitigation strategies during initial adaptation.

Linear mode connectivity provides a principled, learning-based approach to integrate knowledge from disparate model states (e.g., zero-shot and fine-tuned) even when they are geometrically distant in the parameter space.

A replay-free surrogate loss can effectively approximate the preservation of pre-trained knowledge, overcoming the major challenge of requiring access to massive pretraining datasets for knowledge recovery.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.10129.Title: LaViT: Aligning Latent Visual Thoughts for Multi-modal Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.10129.Summary: Researchers from City University of Hong Kong developed LaViT, a framework that aligns latent visual thoughts from a large teacher model into a smaller student Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM), addressing a "Perception Gap" in multimodal distillation. LaViT-3B surpassed larger 7B models and proprietary models like GPT-4o on various complex visual reasoning benchmarks, achieving 78.23% on Relative Depth and 32.0% on IQ-Test.
Problem: Existing latent reasoning methods in MLLMs primarily rely on externally provided visual supervision, neglecting the intrinsic, dynamic visual attention mechanisms a model employs during complex reasoning.

Standard knowledge distillation for MLLMs often fails to transfer the teacher's visual attention trajectories to the student, creating a "Perception Gap" where students mimic text but lack genuine visual grounding.

Student models, when merely mimicking textual outputs or static embeddings, frequently rely on linguistic priors rather than genuinely observing relevant visual evidence, leading to unreliable responses.
Method: LaViT introduces "White-box Trajectory Distillation" to autoregressively reconstruct the teacher's dynamic visual gaze (attention trajectories) and contextualized visual thoughts (semantics) using continuous latent tokens.

A "Curriculum Sensory Gating" mechanism dynamically modulates the direct visual perception path with a time-dependent attention bias, compelling the student to internalize latent visual reasoning and preventing shortcut learning.

A dual-stream distillation scheme employs Semantic Reconstruction Loss, Trajectory Alignment Loss, and Next-Token Prediction Loss to jointly train the student in capturing both visual concepts to encode and where to attend during reasoning.
Results: LaViT-3B achieved substantial performance gains over its Qwen2.5-VL-3B baseline (e.g., +16.94% on Relative Depth, +15.67% on Relative Reflectance) and surpassed larger 7B models on multiple benchmarks.
The model demonstrated superior complex visual reasoning, scoring 78.23% on Relative Depth and 32.0% on IQ-Test, outperforming proprietary models like GPT-4o on these perception-intensive benchmarks.

LaViT reduced the information entropy of the student's attention distribution and achieved more stable attention patterns (lower Coefficient of Variation) than the teacher, attributed to Top-K sparsification filtering attentional noise.
Takeaways: Focused visual attention is causally linked to correct multimodal reasoning, and a lack of it leads to hallucinations, as evidenced by higher reasoning accuracy correlating with increased attention mass in ground-truth regions.
Standard knowledge distillation fails to transfer visual attention patterns from teacher to student, confirming that textual mimicry does not guarantee visual understanding or grounding.

Explicitly aligning both visual semantics and attention trajectories via latent tokens can effectively bridge the "Perception Gap," enabling student models to learn both 'what to see' and 'where to look'.
Curriculum Sensory Gating is a robust method to prevent shortcut learning, ensuring student models genuinely internalize latent visual reasoning capabilities rather than bypassing them.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.10094.Title: V-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Reasoning with Zero Annotation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.10094.Summary: V-Zero, a framework developed at Zhejiang University, enables Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to self-improve their reasoning capabilities using only unlabeled images and internal feedback. The approach enhances base models by an average of 2.0 points and notably outperforms fully supervised baselines on various multimodal benchmarks.
Problem: State-of-the-art Vision-Language Models (VLMs) heavily rely on extensive, costly, and labor-intensive human-annotated datasets, particularly for complex Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning tasks.
The domain-specific nature of human-annotated datasets limits the generalization capabilities of VLMs to novel scenarios.
Existing VLM self-improvement methods still necessitate external expert models or curated edited images for data construction.
Method: V-Zero introduces a co-evolutionary loop where a Questioner and a Solver, both initialized from the same VLM, iteratively improve each other using only unlabeled images.

The Questioner is trained using a Dual-Track Reasoning Reward that incentivizes the generation of challenging questions which highlight a divergence between an intuitive guess and a reasoned answer from the Solver.

The Solver is optimized via Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) on a curated dataset, employing Difficulty-Guided Data Sampling to focus on questions that are challenging yet solvable (confidence between 0.3 and 0.8).
Results: V-Zero consistently improved the average score of the Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct base model by +2.0 points (from 49.9 to 51.9) across diverse multimodal benchmarks over two iterations.

The framework notably outperformed a Supervised GRPO baseline (51.9 vs. 50.8 average score) that utilized the same image dataset but with full human annotations, demonstrating the efficacy of self-generated curricula.

Ablation studies confirmed the critical impact of the Dual-Track Reasoning Reward and Difficulty-Guided Data Sampling, with their removal leading to significant performance drops (e.g., General Avg. -2.1 without difficulty sampling).
Takeaways: Self-improvement for Vision-Language Models is achievable with zero human annotation, significantly overcoming the traditional data bottleneck in VLM development.
A dynamically self-curated curriculum, where a continuously improving Questioner generates progressively challenging problems, can be more effective than static, human-designed training data.
Training on abstract visual reasoning tasks, such as geometric figures, leads to strong generalization and robust improvements across broader vision-centric benchmarks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.09859.Title: Breaking the Limits of Open-Weight CLIP: An Optimization Framework for Self-supervised Fine-tuning of CLIP
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.09859.Summary: Researchers from Texas A&M University developed TuneCLIP, a self-supervised fine-tuning framework for open-weight CLIP models that addresses optimization cold-start bias and false negatives. It consistently improved general performance, achieving up to +6.66% in retrieval for OpenAI ViT-B/16 and pushing state-of-the-art for ViT-H/14 by 1.5% on ImageNet classification.
Problem: The prohibitive computational cost of training state-of-the-art CLIP models from scratch restricts innovation and accessibility.
Supervised fine-tuning to specific tasks often compromises a CLIP model's generalization capabilities and robustness to distribution shifts.

Naive application of self-supervised fine-tuning protocols to pretrained CLIP models often leads to initial performance degradation due to cold-start bias in optimizers and over-penalization of false negatives.
Method: TuneCLIP introduces a two-stage self-supervised fine-tuning (SSFT) framework designed to enhance general-purpose performance of existing open-weight CLIP models.

Stage I, Optimizer Statistics Recovery (OSR), mitigates cold-start bias by running the optimization algorithm with frozen model parameters to accurately estimate optimizer statistics (momentum, variance, contrastive loss estimators).

Stage II, Hinged Global Contrastive Loss (HGCL), addresses false negatives by introducing a hinge-based margin into the contrastive loss function, selectively penalizing negative pairs only when their similarity is not sufficiently below positive similarities.
Results: TuneCLIP consistently improved performance across various CLIP architectures and benchmarks, including a +1.69% gain on ImageNet & variants and a +6.66% gain on retrieval for OpenAI ViT-B/16.
Optimizer Statistics Recovery (OSR) was critical for stable training, contributing up to a +4.69% improvement on the DataComp benchmark compared to baselines without OSR.
The Hinged Global Contrastive Loss (HGCL) enhanced retrieval performance in self-supervised settings by intelligently handling false negatives, outperforming standard Global Contrastive Loss.
Takeaways: Standard zero-initialization of optimizer statistics creates significant 'cold-start bias' that destabilizes the fine-tuning process of already powerful pretrained models.
Over-aggressively penalizing semantically similar 'false negatives' in self-supervised contrastive learning distorts the embedding space, particularly harming retrieval performance.
Separating the recovery of accurate optimizer statistics from the actual model parameter updates enables a more stable and effective fine-tuning trajectory, preventing performance drops.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.09667.Title: Collaborative Multi-Agent Test-Time Reinforcement Learning for Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.09667.Summary: The MATTRL framework, developed by researchers from MIT, NUS, and Microsoft, introduces Multi-Agent Test-Time Reinforcement Learning to enhance LLM-driven multi-agent reasoning. It achieves superior accuracy on medical, mathematical, and educational benchmarks by injecting structured textual experience at inference time, avoiding costly weight fine-tuning.
Problem: Traditional Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) for LLMs is resource-intensive and suffers from instability due to non-stationary co-adaptation.
Sparse, delayed, and high-variance rewards in complex reasoning tasks make effective learning challenging for multi-agent LLM systems.
Fine-tuning LLMs extensively for specific MARL domains can erode their general reasoning capabilities, limiting versatility.
Method: MATTRL introduces a Multi-Agent Test-Time Reinforcement Learning framework that injects rich, turn-level, structured textual experience directly during inference.
A three-stage multi-expert team collaboration process is established, involving team formation, consensus-driven dialogue augmented by retrieved experiences, and final report synthesis.
A dynamic experience construction mechanism scores utterances, assigns credit using strategies like Difference Rewards, and distills high-value turns into a retrievable experience pool.
Results: MATTRL achieved the strongest overall retrieval quality (average Hit@k of 0.565 and MRR of 0.51) on the RareBench medical diagnostic task, outperforming existing multi-agent baselines.

The framework improved exact-match accuracy on mathematical reasoning (Humanity's Last Exam) to 0.36 (+0.09 over single-agent) and achieved a 0.33 learning gain (∆Acc) on educational tasks (SuperGPQA), nearly doubling the single-agent improvement.

Difference Rewards consistently yielded the best strict-precision performance for credit assignment (Hit@1/3 of 0.40/0.53 in medicine), demonstrating its ability to isolate decisive contributions and reduce noise compared to Naive and Shapley methods.
Takeaways: Test-time injection of structured textual experience offers a stable, efficient, and robust alternative to traditional weight-update-based MARL training for LLMs.
The choice of group-to-agent credit assignment significantly impacts the quality of the constructed experience pool, with Difference Rewards balancing precision and efficiency effectively.
An adaptive router, which dynamically switches between single-agent and multi-agent MATTRL based on task characteristics, further improves performance by leveraging complementary strengths.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.09536.Title: Omni-R1: Towards the Unified Generative Paradigm for Multimodal Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.09536.Summary: Researchers from The Hong Kong Polytechnic University and collaborators introduced Omni-R1, a framework that enables Multimodal Large Language Models to perform unified generative multimodal reasoning by generating diverse intermediate images during problem-solving. Its zero-shot variant, Omni-R1-Zero, achieves comparable or superior performance to direct supervision by bootstrapping step-wise visualizations, thereby reducing annotation costs, enhancing general multimodal understanding, and reducing hallucination.
Problem: Existing interleaved-modal reasoning methods employ single task-specific patterns, limiting generalizability across diverse multimodal reasoning skills (e.g., zooming, marking, predicting).
MLLMs face challenges in generating "functional images" (e.g., images with marked numbers or highlighted regions) as intermediate reasoning steps, which are often unnatural and task-specific.
Developing generative multimodal reasoning models is hindered by the high cost and scarcity of human-annotated, step-by-step interleaved reasoning traces.
Method: A unified generative multimodal reasoning paradigm is proposed where a single MLLM generates diverse intermediate images (e.g., zoomed views, bounding boxes) as part of its internal reasoning process.

The Omni-R1 framework employs a two-stage optimization: Perception-Aligned Supervised Fine-Tuning (PeSFT) with cross-entropy and perception loss, followed by Perception-Calibrated Relative Policy Optimization (PeRPO) using a composite reward.
Omni-R1-Zero addresses data scarcity by bootstrapping step-wise visualizations from text-only Chain-of-Thought prompts, synthesizing interleaved trajectories for PeSFT without human annotations.
Results: Omni-R1 and Omni-R1-Zero significantly surpassed baseline models (Anole, Zebra-CoT) across all four "Uni-Task" slices of the `Omni-Bench` benchmark, with the most pronounced gains in Vision-Operational Scenes.

Omni-R1-Zero, trained with bootstrapped supervision, yielded stronger overall gains than Omni-R1 (which used limited human annotations), demonstrating effective generative multimodal reasoning without costly human-annotated interleaved rationales.

Both Omni-R1 and Omni-R1-Zero achieved superior performance on general multimodal benchmarks (e.g., MME-P, MM-Vet, POPE), indicating enhanced generalizability, improved perception-oriented capabilities, and reduced object hallucination.
Takeaways: Multimodal Large Language Models can perform unified reasoning by generating diverse intermediate visual evidence (e.g., zoom-ins, markings) within their problem-solving steps, moving beyond mere interpretation.
Perception-aligned supervised fine-tuning and perception-calibrated reinforcement learning are crucial for training MLLMs to generate functional and visually coherent intermediate images.
Bootstrapping synthetic interleaved reasoning traces from text-only Chain-of-Thought data effectively enables advanced generative multimodal reasoning without extensive human annotation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.09430.Title: Video-MSR: Benchmarking Multi-hop Spatial Reasoning Capabilities of MLLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.09430.Summary: Researchers at Baidu Inc., in collaboration with Nanjing University, The University of Queensland, and Peking University, introduced Video-MSR, the first benchmark to evaluate multi-hop spatial reasoning (MSR) in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) using dynamic video. The study revealed that state-of-the-art MLLMs struggle significantly with complex spatial logic, but performance can be substantially improved through specialized instruction tuning with the MSR-9K dataset.
Problem: Existing MLLM benchmarks primarily focus on "single-step perception-to-judgment" tasks, which only evaluate basic object recognition or simple spatial relationships.
The multi-hop spatial reasoning (MSR) capabilities of MLLMs, involving complex 2D/3D spatial relationships and logical chains, remained largely unbenchmarked.
There was a critical gap between MLLMs' superficial visual perception and their deep logical reasoning abilities, limiting their application in advanced embodied AI tasks.
Method: Developed Video-MSR, a novel benchmark featuring four distinct multi-hop spatial reasoning tasks: Constrained Localization, Chain-based Reference Retrieval, Route Planning, and Counterfactual Physical Deduction.

Created a scalable data construction pipeline that combines automated video-QA generation with a dual-phase verification process (automated blind test and manual expert review) to produce 4,993 high-quality video-QA pairs.
Curated MSR-9K, a specialized instruction-tuning dataset of 8,369 MSR QA pairs, designed to enhance MLLMs' capacity for deep spatial reasoning.
Results: State-of-the-art MLLMs achieved overall accuracies between 20% and 44% on Video-MSR, with Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct (43.92%) and GPT-4o (41.87%) being top performers, yet indicating significant MSR limitations.

Performance varied across tasks: Gemini-2.5-Flash excelled at Chain-based Reference Retrieval (66.33%) and Route Planning (61.21%) but performed poorly on Counterfactual Physical Deduction (24.77%) and Constrained Localization.

Fine-tuning models on the MSR-9K instruction-tuning dataset yielded substantial improvements, with Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct showing a +7.82% absolute gain in overall accuracy and a remarkable +48.62% improvement on the Route Planning task.
Takeaways: Current state-of-the-art MLLMs exhibit significant performance drops, spatial disorientation, and hallucination when faced with multi-hop spatial reasoning tasks.

MSR proficiency is not solely an emergent property of model scale; generic enhancement strategies like Chain-of-Thought prompting often prove detrimental, and atomic capability training does not translate to long-horizon spatial reasoning.
Specialized, logically-grounded instruction-tuning data is crucial for fostering deep spatial reasoning, demonstrating substantial performance gains in complex MSR tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.09295.Title: MACRO-LLM: LLM-Empowered Multi-Agent Collaborative Reasoning under Spatiotemporal Partial Observability
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.09295.Summary: The University of Hong Kong researchers developed MACRO-LLM, an LLM-empowered multi-agent framework designed for collaborative reasoning in environments with spatiotemporal partial observability. This system leverages decentralized negotiation, combining semantic reasoning with statistical spatial features, to achieve superior coordination, scalability, and robustness in tasks like cooperative adaptive cruise control and pandemic containment.
Problem: Deploying LLM agents in complex real-world scenarios inherently leads to spatiotemporal partial observability due to physical dispersion.
Spatial partial observability limits agents' local perception, hindering their ability to form a full global understanding.
Temporal partial observability arises from LLMs' fixed context windows, causing uncertainty about future dynamics and limited historical context for aligning long-term objectives.
Method: MACRO-LLM employs a decentralized negotiation framework, where each agent uses three modules: CoProposer, Negotiator, and Introspector.
The CoProposer generates and verifies action proposals by integrating long-term objectives with immediate spatial constraints and mitigating future uncertainty via k-step rollout simulations.

The Negotiator resolves conflicting proposals and updates spatial strategies by exchanging aggregated statistical features (mean-field approximation) with neighbors, followed by proposal regeneration and multi-round negotiation.
Results: MACRO-LLM achieved superior performance in Cooperative Adaptive Cruise Control (CACC), reducing the Standard Deviation of Headway by 86.3% and RMSE of Headway by 24.4% compared to existing baselines.

In Pandemic Control tasks, the framework consistently attained lower normalized infection rates, fewer peak infections, and significantly shorter pandemic durations, reducing cumulative infections by over 99.2% in complex scenarios.

The system demonstrated robust scalability with increasing agent numbers (up to 32) and effective generalization across different LLM backbones, with smaller models performing comparably to larger ones in strategic tasks.
Takeaways: Explicitly decomposing coordination challenges into spatial and temporal dimensions, managed by specialized modules, enhances multi-agent performance under partial observability.
Combining LLM's semantic reasoning with statistical mean-field approximations enables scalable, decentralized neighborhood negotiation without relying on central coordination.
An adaptive learning mechanism, inspired by semantic gradient descent, allows agents to continuously refine their temporal strategies based on historical performance for long-term consistency.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.08499.Title: EfficientFSL: Enhancing Few-Shot Classification via Query-Only Tuning in Vision Transformers
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.08499.Summary: EfficientFSL, developed by researchers from Fudan, Tsinghua, and East China University of Science and Technology, presents a framework for enhancing few-shot classification in Vision Transformers using a query-only tuning paradigm. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse benchmarks and cross-domain tasks with only 1.25M trainable parameters for a ViT-S backbone.
Problem: Utilizing large Vision Transformers (ViTs) for few-shot learning (FSL) is challenging due to their high computational and memory demands for full fine-tuning.
Existing Parameter-Efficient Transfer Learning (PETL) methods often modify the ViT backbone, risking alteration of pre-trained knowledge or overfitting in data-scarce FSL settings.
Few-shot classification frequently struggles with distribution shifts between the limited support set (for prototypes) and the query set, leading to degraded generalization.
Method: EfficientFSL employs a 'query-only' tuning paradigm, completely freezing the pre-trained ViT backbone and training only lightweight, external modules to extract task-relevant features.
It integrates a Forward Block for each ViT layer, where a trainable Active Block generates task-specific queries that interact with the frozen ViT's intermediate features.

A Combine Block adaptively fuses multi-layer, multi-type features using conditional weighting, and a Support-Query Attention Block refines class prototypes by aligning them with query sample distributions.
Results: Achieved state-of-the-art performance on four in-domain few-shot benchmarks (miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, CIFAR, FC100) and six cross-domain datasets, surpassing full fine-tuning and other SOTA FSL methods.
Demonstrated superior parameter efficiency, utilizing only 1.25M trainable parameters for ViT-S and 2.48M for ViT-B, a significant reduction compared to full fine-tuning (e.g., 21.7M for ViT-S).

Ablation studies confirmed the critical roles of the Forward Block's trainable components, the adaptive feature fusion in the Combine Block, and the prototype refinement by the Support-Query Attention Block.
Takeaways: Freezing the entire pre-trained Vision Transformer while tuning external querying modules effectively preserves the model's general knowledge and prevents overfitting in data-limited FSL scenarios.
Adaptive, conditional aggregation of hierarchical features from various ViT layers is crucial for forming robust and generalized representations, especially in few-shot settings.

Dynamically adjusting class prototypes using query-aware attention effectively mitigates distribution shifts between support and query sets, thereby enhancing classification accuracy and generalization.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.07645.Title: PlaM: Training-Free Plateau-Guided Model Merging for Better Visual Grounding in MLLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.07645.Summary: Researchers from Northeastern University, China, and LMU Munich developed PlaM, a training-free model merging framework that addresses linguistic reasoning degradation in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). It consistently improved visual grounding and overall performance across various MLLMs and benchmarks, for instance, boosting MMStar by +1.52 and MME-C by +15.00 for LLaVA-v1.5-7B.
Problem: Multimodal instruction fine-tuning in MLLMs often paradoxically degrades the base language model's inherent linguistic reasoning capabilities.
This degradation leads to poor visual grounding, where MLLMs exhibit scattered attention and make incorrect inferences despite visual input.
Existing solutions to mitigate linguistic reasoning degradation are training-based, requiring substantial computational resources and complex data curation.
Method: PlaM employs a layer-wise vision token masking strategy to diagnose and identify a consistent three-stage pattern of visual information utilization within MLLM decoders.
A training-free, plateau-guided model merging approach selectively injects parameters from the original base language model into the fine-tuned MLLM.

Only the self-attention projection weights of decoder layers from an identified "plateau onset layer" to the final layer are merged via linear interpolation, leaving early layers and the vision encoder/projector fixed.
Results: PlaM consistently improved performance across five MLLM architectures (e.g., LLaVA-v1.5, Qwen2.5/3-VL) and nine diverse vision-language benchmarks, with notable gains on MMStar (+1.52), MME-C (+15.00), and RealWorldQA (+0.26) for LLaVA-v1.5-7B.
The method significantly outperformed alternative merging strategies (early-layer, mid-layer, full-layer merging), confirming the importance of plateau-guided, selective intervention.

Attention analysis revealed that PlaM merging substantially increased attention mass to vision tokens and led to more focused, task-relevant visual grounding in case studies, improving decision-making.
Takeaways: MLLMs exhibit a consistent three-stage pattern in their decoder's visual information processing: early feature separation, mid-layer alignment/fusion, and late-layer feature degradation or plateau.

The performance plateau in late decoder layers is primarily linked to weakened language capabilities rather than insufficient visual information, making these layers ideal targets for restoring linguistic reasoning.
Selective, late-layer parameter merging from the base LLM effectively recovers linguistic abstraction and improves visual grounding without disrupting critical early-to-mid multimodal alignment.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.07055.Title: Dr. Zero: Self-Evolving Search Agents without Training Data
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.07055.Summary: Dr. Zero, a framework developed by Meta Superintelligence Labs and UIUC, enables multi-turn search agents to self-evolve without any human-curated training data. It utilizes a proposer-solver co-evolution mechanism and a novel Hop-Grouped Relative Policy Optimization, allowing agents to match or surpass supervised baselines on open-domain QA tasks while drastically reducing computational overhead.
Problem: Reliance on expensive, human-curated training data for developing advanced search and reasoning large language models (LLMs).
Limitations of prior data-free self-evolution frameworks in generating diverse, challenging open-domain questions for multi-hop reasoning.
Computational inefficiency of existing reinforcement learning methods for optimizing multi-turn search agents that interact with external tools.
Method: A self-evolving proposer-solver framework where both agents learn without human data, relying solely on an external search engine for factual verification.
Introduces Hop-Grouped Relative Policy Optimization (HRPO) for efficient proposer training, clustering questions by hop complexity and using group-level baselines to reduce computational overhead.
Employs a difficulty-guided reward for the proposer to generate diverse, challenging, yet verifiable multi-hop questions, fostering a dynamic curriculum.
Results: Dr. Zero matches or exceeds the performance of supervised baselines and significantly outperforms few-shot and other data-free methods on open-domain QA benchmarks, achieving up to 22.9% higher EM on Natural Questions.
The Hop-Grouped Relative Policy Optimization (HRPO) method reduces computational rollout cost by approximately four times compared to standard GRPO while maintaining or improving performance.
The self-evolving framework consistently showed performance improvements over 2-3 iterations, demonstrating autonomous learning, with optimal curriculum composition adapting to model size.
Takeaways: Complex open-domain reasoning and search capabilities can emerge entirely through self-evolution without human-curated training data, challenging traditional data dependency.
The proposed HRPO method significantly improves the computational efficiency of self-evolution for multi-turn search agents by grouping questions by hop complexity.
A dynamic, difficulty-guided curriculum, where the proposer creates challenging but solvable tasks, is essential for continuous improvement and generalization of the solver agent.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.06993.Title: Can Textual Reasoning Improve the Performance of MLLMs on Fine-grained Visual Classification?
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.06993.Summary: Researchers from Michigan State University empirically identified the 'Cost of Thinking,' where excessive textual reasoning degrades Multi-modal Large Language Model performance on fine-grained visual classification. They developed ReFine-RFT, a reinforcement fine-tuning framework that achieves state-of-the-art results on FGVC benchmarks by constraining reasoning length and using a multi-perspective reward system.
Problem: Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle with fine-grained visual classification (FGVC), a task requiring discrimination of subtle visual differences.
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, while effective for complex linguistic tasks, paradoxically degrades MLLM performance on certain visual perception tasks.
The root cause of this performance degradation from textual reasoning in visual contexts remained undiagnosed across diverse evaluation and training paradigms.
Method: A novel Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RFT) framework, ReFine-RFT, was developed to constrain reasoning length and provide dense, accuracy-oriented feedback for FGVC.
ReFine-RFT incorporates an Ensemble Reward system with five components: format, classification, a novel thinking length reward, MLLM-based accuracy reward, and embedding similarity reward.
Multi-reward Normalization (MRN) is introduced to independently normalize each heterogeneous reward component, ensuring stable and balanced optimization.
Results: ReFine-RFT achieved an average accuracy of 86.5% across FGVC benchmarks, outperforming Visual-RFT (82.9%) and even larger 8B models like Finedefics-8B (82.7%) with a 2B backbone and 4-shot training.
The diagnostic experiments showed a 3-6% average accuracy drop in non-reasoning MLLMs when moving from 'Answer-only' to 'Chain-of-Thought' prompts without explicit training.

Ablation studies confirmed the effectiveness of Multi-reward Normalization (MRN), which consistently improved performance by 0.7% to 2.1% across datasets, and demonstrated the synergistic benefits of the ensemble reward components.
Takeaways: Excessive textual reasoning, termed the 'Cost of Thinking,' consistently degrades MLLM performance on fine-grained visual perception tasks, both in zero-shot settings and with supervised fine-tuning.
During RFT for visual accuracy, MLLMs exhibit 'reasoning collapse,' where they learn to suppress verbose reasoning and stabilize at significantly shorter lengths.
Explicitly controlling reasoning length is crucial: shorter, more concise reasoning traces lead to higher classification accuracy compared to longer, more elaborate ones.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.06803.Title: Forest Before Trees: Latent Superposition for Efficient Visual Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.06803.Summary: Laser introduces a latent superposition paradigm for Vision-Language Models, enabling efficient and multi-step visual reasoning by maintaining a probabilistic distribution of future semantics. This method achieves state-of-the-art performance in latent reasoning, outperforming previous benchmarks by 5.03% overall, while reducing inference tokens by over 97% on key tasks.
Problem: Explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning in VLMs suffers from an information bandwidth bottleneck, losing continuous visual details when discretized into textual rationales.
Current explicit reasoning methods, including CoT and external tools/RL, incur substantial computational costs and high inference latency.

Existing latent reasoning approaches often experience "premature semantic collapse" due to rigid autoregressive objectives that force latent states to predict immediate next tokens, hindering holistic visual context understanding.
Method: Laser (Latent Superposition for Efficient Visual Reasoning) employs a novel paradigm that maintains a probabilistic superposition of global visual features within the latent state before narrowing down to local details.

Dynamic Windowed Alignment Learning (DWAL) redefines the optimization objective, guiding latent states to align with a dynamic validity domain of future visual semantics rather than just the immediate next token.

The approach uses GPT-4o to weakly supervise and synthesize "Cognitive Scanpaths" that follow a "Global-to-Local Scanning Logic," creating a specialized dataset (ScanPath) without extensive human annotation.
Results: Laser achieved a new state-of-the-art among latent reasoning methods, surpassing the previous best (Monet) by +5.03% in overall score across six benchmarks, with notable gains on HallusionBench (+11.36%) and BLINK (+6.21%).
It demonstrated extreme efficiency, reducing average inference tokens by over 97% on BLINK (to 6.0 tokens) and over 89% on HRBench (to 5.7 tokens) compared to the Qwen2.5-VL-7B baseline.

The model preserved general vision-language abilities and showed improvements on out-of-distribution domains like Web (+8.03%) and Chart (+5.18%), with case studies illustrating structured, interpretable multi-hop reasoning within its compact latent space.
Takeaways: Aligning VLM reasoning with a "Forest-before-Trees" cognitive hierarchy, moving from global apprehension to specific details, is crucial for preventing premature semantic collapse and enhancing robust visual understanding.

Performing multi-step visual deduction efficiently within a compact latent space, through probabilistic superposition of future semantics, can outperform verbose explicit reasoning and prior latent methods.

The learned latent states in Laser are inherently interpretable, allowing visualization of the model's "cognitive trajectory" by projecting them onto the vocabulary, thereby demystifying internal reasoning processes.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.06521.Title: BabyVision: Visual Reasoning Beyond Language
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.06521.Summary: BabyVision introduces a benchmark evaluating Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) on foundational visual reasoning tasks, revealing that even state-of-the-art models significantly underperform human children on basic visual perception, often due to a "verbalization bottleneck" that limits true visual understanding.
Problem: Existing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) demonstrate an "inverted profile of competence," excelling at complex, knowledge-intensive tasks but failing at basic, pre-linguistic visual perception.
Current benchmarks primarily evaluate MLLMs on high-level, language-dependent visual reasoning, overlooking foundational visual skills acquired by young children.
MLLMs frequently rely on linguistic priors or exhibit "language leakage," rather than true visual understanding, during visual reasoning.
Method: Developed BABYVISION, a benchmark with 388 questions across 22 subtypes, specifically designed to test MLLMs' foundational visual understanding akin to human children (3-12 years old).
Introduced BABYVISION-GEN, a generative benchmark (280 questions) where models provide visual annotations as answers, addressing tasks more naturally solved through visual actions.
Established human performance baselines using children and adults, and implemented an LLM-as-judge evaluation for model outputs, validated by human experts.
Results: The best MLLM, Gemini3-Pro-Preview, scored 49.7% on BABYVISION, demonstrating a 44.4% absolute performance gap compared to adult humans (94.1%) and lagging behind average 6-year-old children.

MLLMs showed consistent deficits across all four early-vision categories (Fine-grained Discrimination, Visual Tracking, Spatial Perception, Visual Pattern Recognition), with "Count 3D Blocks" (max 20.5%) being especially challenging.

Generative models achieved an average accuracy of 18.3% on BABYVISION-GEN, with visual tracking tasks remaining particularly difficult (6.7% for the best model), suggesting limitations in visual reasoning through direct generation.
Takeaways: The "verbalization bottleneck" is a core reason for MLLMs' failures, as encoding visual information into language for reasoning leads to loss of fine-grained detail, spatial coherence, and continuous identity.
MLLMs exhibit systemic failures in tasks requiring precise fine-grained discrimination, visual tracking, 3D spatial imagination, and abstract visual pattern induction.
Achieving human-level visual intelligence requires moving beyond current vision-language encoders towards natively multimodal architectures that can reason directly in visual space.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.06002.Title: The Molecular Structure of Thought: Mapping the Topology of Long Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.06002.Summary: This research introduces a "molecular structure of thought" framework to mechanistically characterize how Large Language Models (LLMs) learn and represent multi-step reasoning. It identifies stable reasoning topologies formed by distinct interaction "bonds" (Deep-Reasoning, Self-Reflection, Self-Exploration) and develops Mole-Syn, a structure-aware synthesis method, enabling cheaper instruction LLMs to achieve reasoning performance comparable to powerful, specialized models.
Problem: LLMs consistently struggle to acquire robust Long Chain-of-Thought (CoT) capabilities, exhibiting coherence loss and poor generalization, even with standard supervised fine-tuning or in-context learning.
Existing paradigms for modeling CoT (sequences, trees, graphs of logical nodes) lack a mechanistic explanation for the stability and learnability of complex, extended reasoning processes.
Distillation from human rationales or weaker instruction-tuned LLMs often fails to reliably instill effective Long CoT skills, suggesting that surface-level imitation is insufficient.
Method: A "molecular structure of thought" hypothesis was proposed, conceptualizing Long CoT as stable structures formed by three types of interaction bonds: Deep-Reasoning, Self-Reflection, and Self-Exploration.

A structure-aware synthesis framework called Mole-Syn was developed to generate effective Long CoT data by learning behavioral transition graphs from strong reasoning models and guiding cheaper instruction LLMs through controlled trajectory synthesis.

The hypothesis was verified through analysis of stable bond distributions, SFT learning of structures over keywords, visualization of 'logical folding' in 3D semantic space, and quantification of attention energy levels for each bond type.
Results: Strong reasoning LLMs exhibit stable 'transfer graphs' of reasoning behaviors, with Pearson correlations exceeding 0.95 across different models and tasks, indicating a universal underlying reasoning topology.

Mole-Syn successfully synthesizes Long CoT structures that accurately match teacher models' behavior distributions, enabling models fine-tuned on this data to achieve reasoning performance comparable to or exceeding direct distillation from powerful reasoning LLMs.
Mole-Syn-initialized LLMs demonstrate superior and more stable performance in reinforcement learning tasks, providing consistent and sustained gains over extended training periods.

Summarization and reasoning compression techniques effectively protect Long CoT structures from distillation, limiting the replication of internal reasoning processes and safeguarding proprietary model capabilities.
Takeaways: Effective Long CoT reasoning in LLMs is characterized by stable, macromolecular-like organizations, with specific, convergent distributions of Deep-Reasoning, Self-Reflection, and Self-Exploration behaviors across models and tasks.

LLMs learn the underlying structural organization of reasoning trajectories rather than merely memorizing surface-level keywords or specific token sequences, as evidenced by robust performance despite keyword substitutions.

Training LLMs on conflicting or incompatible reasoning structures, even from individually effective models, leads to 'structural chaos' and performance degradation, highlighting the criticality of structural compatibility for robust Long CoT learning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.05877.Title: iReasoner: Trajectory-Aware Intrinsic Reasoning Supervision for Self-Evolving Large Multimodal Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.05877.Summary: The IREASONER framework enhances the implicit reasoning capabilities of Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) by introducing a trajectory-aware intrinsic reward for Chain-of-Thought (CoT) steps within a fully unsupervised self-evolution setting. This approach yielded consistent performance gains across eight diverse multimodal reasoning benchmarks, particularly in visual mathematics.
Problem: Existing self-evolving LMMs primarily rely on "outcome-only" rewards, which provide insufficient supervision for the internal Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning process.
Current methods for optimizing CoT in LMMs typically require labeled data, external judges, or offline supervision, limiting their applicability in unsupervised settings.
Without direct feedback on intermediate steps, LMMs may develop unstable reasoning paths or rely on shortcuts, even if the final answer is correct.
Method: IREASONER integrates a novel trajectory-aware intrinsic reward into a Proposer-Solver self-evolution framework that operates solely on unlabeled images.
It quantifies CoT step agreement by embedding intermediate claims from multiple Solver rollouts and comparing them to dynamically generated per-step prototypes using weighted cosine similarity.
The Solver's training objective combines traditional answer-level consistency rewards with this new step-level agreement reward, gradually introduced via a warmup schedule to foster stable learning.
Results: IREASONER achieved consistent performance gains across eight diverse multimodal reasoning benchmarks, with an average improvement of +1.32 points on general visual understanding and +1.64 points on visual mathematics tasks.

The framework surpassed existing outcome-only self-evolution methods (e.g., EvoLMM) on all general visual understanding benchmarks, showing an average gain of +0.50 points on InfoGraphic-VQA and +0.48 points on AI2D.

Ablation studies confirmed the critical role of the reward warmup schedule, which led to the largest performance regression when removed, and demonstrated the complementary nature of answer stability and step-wise rewards.
Takeaways: Cross-rollout agreement on intermediate Chain-of-Thought (CoT) steps can serve as a robust intrinsic reward signal, enabling step-level supervision without external labels or human intervention.
Combining outcome-level consistency with a continuously applied step-level agreement reward, introduced progressively, is more effective than discrete rewards for improving multimodal reasoning.
Early reasoning steps are particularly influential for overall consistency, and their consistency is emphasized through higher weighting in the intrinsic reward calculation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.05600.Title: SceneAlign: Aligning Multimodal Reasoning to Scene Graphs in Complex Visual Scenes
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.05600.Summary: The paper introduces SceneAlign, a framework designed to enhance multimodal large language models (MLLMs) by aligning their reasoning processes more closely with the visual structure of complex scenes. It employs scene graphs to systematically generate structured counterfactuals for Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), improving both answer accuracy and visually grounded reasoning across various benchmarks.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) frequently exhibit 'reasoning unfaithfulness,' where generated rationales decouple from actual visual evidence despite potentially correct final answers.
This unfaithfulness manifests as object hallucination, relation mis-grounding, skipped reasoning steps, or over-specified details, hindering trustworthiness.
Existing preference-based alignment methods are often 'structure-agnostic,' allowing MLLMs to rely on strong language priors rather than addressing true visual grounding errors directly.
Method: SceneAlign leverages detailed scene graphs to create 'structure-consistent' positive chains of thought, anchoring MLLM reasoning to explicit visual structures.

It constructs 'hard negative rationales' by applying four controlled perturbation strategies (swap, replace, shorten, overthink) to critical elements within the scene graphs, creating linguistically plausible but visually inaccurate counterfactuals.

A two-step filtering process (scene-graph filtering and diversity-based sampling) selects informative hard negative examples, which are then used in a Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) pipeline to fine-tune MLLMs.
Results: SceneAlign consistently outperforms base models and SFT baselines across five MLLMs and seven diverse visual reasoning benchmarks, improving both answer accuracy and reasoning faithfulness.
The approach yields the most pronounced improvements on reasoning-intensive tasks, showing gains up to +23.97% on HallusionBench and +3-5% on EMMA benchmarks for specific models.

Ablation studies confirm that all four perturbation operators are critical for performance, with relation perturbations yielding the largest gains, and that optimizing negative sampling strategies is essential for effectiveness.
Takeaways: Generating hard negative examples through controlled structural perturbations of scene graphs is a highly effective method for explicitly teaching MLLMs to identify and avoid visual grounding errors.

Different perturbation types (swapping roles, replacing entities, shortening details, overthinking) target distinct failure modes in multimodal reasoning, all contributing to overall performance gains.
Careful selection of 'medium-difficulty' negative rationales, balanced by scene-graph similarity and diversity, provides the most potent contrastive supervision for DPO.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.05552.Title: One Language-Free Foundation Model Is Enough for Universal Vision Anomaly Detection
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.05552.Summary: Tencent YouTu Lab introduced UniADet, a universal vision anomaly detection framework that operates without a language encoder, simplifying the process by directly learning decoupled decision weights from a vision foundation model. This approach achieves superior performance, reducing learnable parameters by factors of 300x to 10,000x and demonstrating the first instance of a few-shot method surpassing full-shot state-of-the-art on benchmarks like Real-IAD.
Problem: Traditional anomaly detection (AD) demands extensive, scenario-specific "normal" image training, hindering adaptability and scalability in open-world settings.
Existing zero-shot/few-shot AD methods leveraging Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are complex, requiring elaborate prompt engineering, adaptive modules, and intricate training strategies.

VLM-based approaches face limitations in generality, particularly in transferring to pure vision foundation models, and often suffer from learning conflicts due to shared decision weights across diverse visual features.
Method: UniADet directly learns "normal" and "anomaly" decision weights from frozen vision foundation model features, eliminating the need for a language encoder and textual prompts.
It employs Decoupling Classification and Segmentation (DCS), using separate learned weights for image-level anomaly classification and pixel-level segmentation to mitigate learning conflicts.
The framework also utilizes Decoupling Hierarchical Features (DHF), learning distinct weights for each hierarchical feature layer to fully leverage multi-scale information without interference.
For few-shot scenarios, a multi-scale normal memory bank generates additional anomaly scores, which are then fused with the zero-shot predictions for enhanced performance.
Results: UniADet achieved superior performance across 14 diverse datasets, with its DINOv3 integration outperforming VLM-based methods like Bayes-PFL by 7% P-AUPR in pixel-level segmentation on industrial benchmarks.
The framework significantly reduced learnable parameters by factors of 300x to 10,000x and demonstrated faster inference speeds, showcasing its efficiency.
In a few-shot setting, 4-shot UniADet became the first method to surpass the performance of existing *full-shot* state-of-the-art anomaly detection systems on challenging datasets like Real-IAD.
Takeaways: The language encoder's role in VLM-based AD is essentially to derive decision weights, which can be directly learned in a data-driven manner, making language components expendable.
Shared decision weights between image-level and pixel-level tasks, or across different hierarchical feature layers, create learning conflicts that hinder optimal performance.
Decoupling these weights across tasks and feature hierarchies allows for optimized decision boundaries at each level, fully leveraging the foundation model's diverse representations.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.05344.Title: Coding the Visual World: From Image to Simulation Using Vision Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.05344.Summary: Sagi Eppel from the Weizmann Institute AI Hub developed the Im2Sim methodology and Im2Sim2Im evaluation framework to assess Vision Language Models' capacity for mechanistic understanding by generating simulation code from images. The research shows VLMs can grasp high-level generative processes and build models but often struggle with replicating fine details and exact spatial layouts.
Problem: Current Vision Language Model (VLM) benchmarks primarily assess descriptive and discriminative abilities, failing to probe deeper "world understanding" beyond pattern recognition.
A key challenge is determining if VLMs can infer the underlying causal mechanisms or generative processes responsible for visual patterns.
Existing visual-to-code generation approaches are often limited to structured, man-made visuals, not complex, emergent natural phenomena.
Method: The Im2Sim methodology prompts Vision Language Models (VLMs) to generate executable simulation code that recreates the underlying generative processes observed in natural images.
An Im2Sim2Im evaluation framework quantitatively assesses the similarity between VLM-generated simulations and original images, complemented by qualitative analysis of code and descriptions.
The approach evaluates leading VLMs' ability to explain and reproduce emergent patterns across diverse domains, including physical phenomena, biological structures, and urban layouts.
Results: Leading Vision Language Models achieved 50-80% matching accuracy between their generated synthetic images and original inputs in quantitative evaluations, exceeding random chance.
VLMs successfully generated executable code capable of simulating a wide array of emergent patterns from images, including physical phenomena and biological structures.

Qualitative analysis indicated that while VLMs grasp high-level processes, they sometimes resort to visual pattern replication using procedural functions instead of true physical simulation, especially for intricate details.
Takeaways: VLMs exhibit high-level conceptual understanding, identifying fundamental generative mechanisms and selecting appropriate modeling frameworks (e.g., L-systems for vegetation, Perlin noise for textures).
Models can decompose complex systems into components and apply multi-level abstraction, balancing detailed physics with simpler approximations.

A notable asymmetry reveals strong conceptual grasp of principles but limited capacity to precisely reproduce fine-grained details, exact spatial arrangements, and integrate multi-component simulations with high fidelity.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.05328.Title: Bi-Orthogonal Factor Decomposition for Vision Transformers
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.05328.Summary: Bi-Orthogonal Factor Decomposition (BFD) is introduced as a framework to quantitatively disentangle positional, semantic, and global bias factors within Vision Transformer attention mechanisms. Applying BFD reveals that self-supervised DINOv2 models preserve 2D spatial topology while enriching semantic content, offering a mechanistic explanation for their superior holistic shape processing compared to supervised ViTs.
Problem: Existing interpretability methods for Vision Transformers (ViTs) often highlight where a model attends or what concepts it learns, but lack a mechanistic understanding of *how* information is processed within the self-attention mechanism.

The precise informational factors (e.g., positional, semantic) mediating token communication in ViT self-attention remain opaque, making it difficult to understand the rationale behind attention patterns.
A clear mechanistic explanation for the superior holistic shape processing observed in self-supervised models like DINOv2, differentiating them from supervised counterparts, is currently lacking.
Method: Introduced Bi-Orthogonal Factor Decomposition (BFD), a two-stage analytical framework that statistically factorizes raw token activations and then spectrally decomposes attention mechanisms.
The first stage uses an ANOVA-style decomposition to isolate statistically orthogonal factors for each token: a global layer effect, a positional effect, and a content residual.

The second stage analyzes the query-key interaction of attention heads using Singular Value Decomposition to identify bi-orthogonal communication modes, then projects the previously isolated factors onto these modes to quantify their relative contributions.
Results: Content-based interactions (content-content and content-position coupling) accounted for the majority of attention energy in both architectures, with DINOv2 allocating significantly more energy to content-position coupling across all layers and distributing it across more modes.

DINOv2 models preserved the 2D spatial grid topology of positional information throughout all layers, maintaining neighborhood structure, whereas supervised ViTs progressively collapsed this spatial manifold into a quasi-1D structure.

DINOv2's content factors showed progressive semantic enrichment with depth, indicating a genuine transformation and accumulation of information, while supervised ViTs exhibited limited content evolution across layers.
Takeaways: BFD provides a principled framework to quantitatively attribute the communication strength of attention modes to specific informational factors, moving beyond qualitative interpretations of attention maps.

Self-supervised ViTs (DINOv2) exhibit a 'dual preservation' mechanism, maintaining 2D spatial topology of positional embeddings while concurrently enriching semantic content across layers, which explains their holistic shape processing.

Individual bi-orthogonal modes within attention heads demonstrate strong functional specialization, acting as pure operators primarily dedicated to content-content, position-position, or content-position interactions.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.05244.Title: GREx: Generalized Referring Expression Segmentation, Comprehension, and Generation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.05244.Summary: Fudan University researchers created new generalized referring expression tasks (GREx) for segmentation, comprehension, and generation, accompanied by the gRefCOCO dataset to support multi-target and no-target expressions. Their ReLA baseline model, featuring dynamic region-language attention, showed improved performance on these complex scenarios and established new baselines for classic referring expression tasks.
Problem: Classic referring expression (REx) tasks and datasets were limited to a 'one expression, one object' paradigm, making them impractical for real-world scenarios.
Existing REx methods struggled with expressions referring to multiple objects (multi-target) or no objects at all (no-target), leading to inefficient interactions or undefined behaviors.
The absence of large-scale, high-quality datasets for multi-target and no-target expressions hindered systematic research into these generalized REx challenges.
Method: Introduced Generalized Referring Expression Segmentation (GRES), Comprehension (GREC), and Generation (GREG) benchmarks to accommodate expressions referring to arbitrary numbers of objects.
Constructed gRefCOCO, a large-scale, high-quality dataset extending RefCOCO with 90,064 multi-target and 34,537 no-target expressions, ensuring diverse and realistic annotations.

Proposed ReLA (ReLAtionship modeling block), a transformer-based baseline method with novel Region-Image Cross Attention (RIA) and Region-Language Cross Attention (RLA) to model complex relationships and fine-grained attributes.
Results: ReLA significantly outperformed re-implemented state-of-the-art classic RES methods on gRefCOCO, demonstrating over 4% cIoU improvement for GRES.
The method achieved 61.90% Pr@F1 for GREC on the gRefCOCO validation set, showing strong performance in multi-instance bounding box prediction.
ReLA also established new state-of-the-art results on classic RES benchmarks (RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, G-Ref) when trained on single-target data.
Takeaways: Explicitly modeling complex relationships through dynamic region feature aggregation (RIA) and combined region-word/region-region interactions (RLA) is crucial for generalized referring expression tasks.

The explicit prediction of the number of target objects (
N
O
) is vital for accurate instance-level comprehension, especially for distinguishing multi-target from no-target scenarios.
Classic REx models fail to generalize to multi-target and no-target expressions, highlighting the necessity of dedicated datasets and methodologies for these generalized tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.05242.Title: GDPO: Group reward-Decoupled Normalization Policy Optimization for Multi-reward RL Optimization
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.05242.Summary: GDPO (Group reward-Decoupled Normalization Policy Optimization) improves multi-reward reinforcement learning for large language model alignment by addressing "reward signal collapse" inherent in existing GRPO methods. It achieves this by decoupling the normalization of individual reward components, leading to more stable training and enhanced performance across various tasks, such as increasing mathematical reasoning accuracy by up to 6.3% on AIME.
Problem: Aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) with diverse human preferences (e.g., safety, coherence, efficiency) requires multi-reward reinforcement learning.

Commonly used Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) algorithms suffer from "reward signal collapse" when applied to a sum of multiple rewards, meaning distinct reward combinations can yield identical advantage values.
This reward signal collapse diminishes the resolution of the training signal, leading to suboptimal convergence, reduced training stability, and potential early training failure.
Method: GDPO decouples the normalization of individual reward components, performing group-wise normalization for each reward separately to preserve fine-grained distinctions.
The individually normalized advantages are then summed and subjected to an additional batch-wise normalization to ensure numerical stability for policy updates.
To manage priorities among rewards, GDPO explores reward weighting and advocates for reward function conditioning, where an easier reward is granted only if a harder objective is met.
Results: GDPO consistently preserves a substantially larger number of distinct advantage groups compared to GRPO, demonstrating a more expressive training signal.
Across tool-calling, mathematical reasoning, and coding reasoning tasks, GDPO achieves higher reward scores and exhibits greater training stability, preventing training collapses observed with GRPO.
GDPO improves mathematical reasoning accuracy by up to 6.3% on AIME for DeepSeek-R1-1.5B models while simultaneously reducing the length-exceeding ratio by up to 80%.
Takeaways: Summing individual rewards before group-wise normalization in algorithms like GRPO causes a loss of information (reward signal collapse), leading to a less effective training signal.
Decoupling the normalization process for each reward component preserves a significantly richer and more expressive advantage signal, crucial for accurate multi-objective optimization.

Simply weighting rewards is often insufficient for guiding model behavior when objectives differ greatly in difficulty; instead, conditioning an easier reward on a harder one is more effective for prioritized learning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.05230.Title: Learning Latent Action World Models In The Wild
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.05230.Summary: Researchers at FAIR at Meta developed a method to learn effective latent action world models directly from diverse, unlabeled "in-the-wild" video data. The approach enables planning performance on robotic manipulation and navigation tasks comparable to models trained with explicit action labels.
Problem: Most successful world models rely on explicit action labels, limiting their scalability and generality when applied to the vast amount of unlabeled real-world video data.
Prior latent action models (LAMs) were confined to constrained environments, leading to action spaces that lacked transferability and generalization to varied real-world scenarios.
