"In-the-wild" videos present challenges such as ill-defined actions, environmental noise, and a lack of a common embodiment, making it difficult to extract meaningful action representations.
Method: A joint training framework for a world model and an inverse dynamics model (IDM) on large-scale, unlabeled "in-the-wild" video datasets, leveraging a frozen V-JEPA 2-L visual encoder.

Investigation of information regularization techniques—sparsity, noise addition (VAE-like), and discretization—to control the content of continuous latent actions and prevent encoding irrelevant information.

Evaluation of the learned latent action space through intrinsic metrics like future leakage and action transferability, and practical utility on downstream planning tasks via lightweight controllers and the Cross-Entropy Method.
Results: The world model achieves planning performance on robotic manipulation and navigation tasks (e.g., DROID, RECON) that is competitive with baselines trained on domain-specific, action-labeled data.
Latent actions exhibit minimal future leakage and good transferability, with cycle consistency experiments showing only minor error increases.
Optimal downstream planning performance is attained with a balanced regularization strength, with noise-added continuous latent actions generally yielding the best results.
Takeaways: Continuous latent actions, particularly when regularized with noise or sparsity, effectively capture complex dynamics in uncurated videos, outperforming discrete action representations.
Latent actions learned from diverse "in-the-wild" data encode spatially-localized, camera-relative transformations, enabling broad action transferability across different objects and contexts.

Information regularization is critical for balancing the expressiveness of latent actions, ensuring they capture relevant dynamics without overfitting to environmental noise or encoding excessive future information.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.05172.Title: CoV: Chain-of-View Prompting for Spatial Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.05172.Summary: CoV: Chain-of-View Prompting enhances Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for Embodied Question Answering by enabling active, iterative viewpoint adjustment within 3D environments at inference time. The training-free framework significantly boosts spatial reasoning, achieving an average +11.56% improvement on the OpenEQA benchmark and state-of-the-art results on ScanQA.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and Embodied Question Answering (EQA) methods are limited by a fixed, passive set of input viewpoints in 3D environments.
This passive observation restricts VLMs' ability to acquire sufficient, question-relevant context, especially when information is partially occluded or distributed across multiple views.
Traditional EQA systems struggle with complex spatial reasoning and multi-step inferences due to incomplete visual information derived from static observations.
Method: The Chain-of-View (CoV) prompting framework transforms passive VLMs into active viewpoint reasoners via a two-stage, training-free, test-time approach.
A coarse-grained view selection agent initially filters a large set of egocentric frames to identify a reduced subset most relevant to the question, using the VLM itself.

A fine-grained CoV agent then iteratively adjusts viewpoints by generating discrete camera actions (translation and rotation) to acquire additional environmental details and refine its understanding of the 3D scene.
Results: CoV achieved an average +11.56% improvement in LLM-Match across four mainstream VLMs (Qwen3-VL-Flash, GLM-4.6V, Gemini-2.5-Flash, GPT-4o-Mini) on the OpenEQA benchmark.
The framework secured state-of-the-art results on the ScanQA validation set, achieving 116 CIDEr and 31.9% EM@1, and strong performance on SQA3D with 51.1% EM@1.
Performance scaled with increased exploration budget, showing an average additional +2.51% improvement across models when allowing more action steps compared to a minimum of one.
Takeaways: Active visual exploration, analogous to Chain-of-Thought for language, can significantly improve spatial reasoning in VLMs by dynamically acquiring better-selected visual data.
Endowing AI agents with an "observational agency," allowing them to strategically gather information, is crucial for robust human-like interaction and understanding in complex 3D environments.
The framework demonstrates test-time scaling, where increasing the budget for active exploration steps directly correlates with progressive improvements in the agent's performance.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.04777.Title: GeM-VG: Towards Generalized Multi-image Visual Grounding with Multimodal Large Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.04777.Summary: GeM-VG, a Multimodal Large Language Model, advances multi-image visual grounding by addressing single-target limitations and diverse task scenarios. The model achieves an average performance of 74.65% on MIG-Bench, outperforming UniVG-R1 by 2.0%, and demonstrates robust multi-instance localization with 32.8% AP@50 on MC-Bench, a 9.7% improvement over Migician.
Problem: Existing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) for multi-image visual grounding are biased towards single-target localization, struggling with scenarios requiring identification of multiple object instances.

Current methods lack a unified framework to model diverse multi-image grounding tasks, especially those requiring complex cross-image reasoning or fine-grained visual distinctions that are difficult to verbalize.

The absence of comprehensive datasets supporting multi-target localization and varied image relationships (e.g., semantic, temporal, spatial) limits the development of generalized multi-image grounding models.
Method: GeM-VG utilizes a unified output representation for localizing both single and multiple targets within multiple images, specifying image index, object description, and bounding box coordinates.

The work introduces MG-Data-240K, a new dataset systematically categorizing multi-image grounding tasks based on cognitive demands and image relationships to support multi-target and diverse scenarios.

A three-stage progressive training strategy (Supervised Finetuning, CoT-based SFT, Hybrid Reinforcement Finetuning with GRPO) is employed to develop comprehensive perception, reasoning, and multi-instance localization capabilities.

A reward-modulated hybrid finetuning strategy is implemented during the GRPO phase to dynamically balance Chain-of-Thought reasoning and direct answering, optimizing for complementary strengths in different task types.
Results: GeM-VG achieves 74.65% average performance on MIG-Bench, surpassing UniVG-R1 by 2.0%, and demonstrates superior multi-instance localization with 32.8% AP@50 on MC-Bench, outperforming Migician by 9.7%.

The model shows robust performance on single-image grounding (41.1% on ODINW, a 9.1% improvement over Qwen2-VL-7B) and video grounding, indicating strong generalization across various visual-language tasks.

Ablation studies confirm the critical role of the MG-Data-240K dataset in enhancing multi-instance localization and validate the effectiveness of the multi-dimensional reward design and hybrid finetuning strategy in balancing reasoning and perception.
Takeaways: Developing a unified output representation and curating a systematically categorized dataset (MG-Data-240K) is critical for enabling generalized multi-image visual grounding, especially for multi-instance localization.

A multi-stage progressive training approach, coupled with a multi-dimensional rule-based reward function in reinforcement learning, effectively refines an MLLM's ability to localize an arbitrary number of instances and perform complex reasoning.

Intelligently balancing Chain-of-Thought reasoning and direct answering through reward modulation during reinforcement learning optimizes performance across tasks requiring either explicit reasoning or fine-grained visual perception.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.03872.Title: Atlas: Orchestrating Heterogeneous Models and Tools for Multi-Domain Complex Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.03872.Summary: ATLAS introduces a dual-path framework to dynamically orchestrate diverse large language models and external tools, enabling superior complex reasoning across multiple domains. This system achieved an average accuracy of 63.5% on in-distribution tasks, outperforming RouterDC by 10.1%, and demonstrated robust generalization on out-of-distribution tasks with a 13.1% improvement over baselines through learned model-tool synergies.
Problem: Existing LLM tool usage relies on rigid, pre-configured invocation logic, limiting adaptability to diverse tasks and model capabilities.
Current LLM routing methods select models in isolation, overlooking the performance benefits from synergistic integration with external tools.
Reinforcement Learning applications for LLMs often optimize individual components rather than jointly leveraging the combined strengths of multiple models and tools.
Method: Developed ATLAS, a dual-path framework balancing efficiency for domain-specific tasks with generalization for open-domain reasoning.
Implemented a training-free cluster-based routing mechanism for known domains, which uses query embeddings and empirical statistics to select optimal model-tool pairs.

Introduced an RL-driven multi-step routing approach for open-domain scenarios, modeling reasoning as a sequential decision task with an augmented action space and optimizing policy using PPO with a composite reward function.
Results: Achieved an average accuracy of 63.5% on in-distribution tasks, surpassing the strongest baseline, RouterDC, by 10.1%.
Demonstrated robust generalization on out-of-distribution tasks, with ATLAS(RL) reaching an average accuracy of 59.4%, which was 13.1% higher than RouterDC.
Attained an average accuracy of 68.9% across five multi-modal datasets, outperforming the strongest single-tool baseline by 4.3%, by effectively integrating multi-modal tools.
Takeaways: Strategic orchestration of heterogeneous LLMs and external tools can enable smaller open-source models to rival or exceed larger proprietary systems in complex reasoning.
A dual-path architecture, combining cluster-based routing for efficiency in known domains and RL-driven routing for generalization in open domains, is effective.
Reinforcement learning can teach transferable collaborative decision principles for model and tool selection, leading to robust performance on out-of-distribution tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.03220.Title: From Entropy to Epiplexity: Rethinking Information for Computationally Bounded Intelligence
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.03220.Summary: Researchers from Carnegie Mellon University and New York University introduce epiplexity, a new information measure that quantifies structural content learnable by computationally bounded observers. This framework resolves paradoxes in classical information theory, demonstrating how computation can create information, how data ordering affects learnability, and how models extract emergent structures, showing a correlation between higher epiplexity and improved out-of-distribution generalization.
Problem: Classical information theory (Shannon entropy, Kolmogorov complexity) assumes infinite computational capacity, making it inadequate for explaining phenomena in modern computationally bounded AI.

The inability of classical theory to explain how deterministic processes can yield new information, why factorization order matters, or how likelihood modeling uncovers emergent structures in AI systems.
A lack of a theoretical framework to quantify the 'value of data' for broad generalization and guide data selection, rather than just model selection, in large-scale AI.
Method: Define epiplexity (structural information) and time-bounded entropy (random information) using a time-bounded Minimum Description Length (MDL) principle relative to a computationally bounded observer (probabilistic model).
Empirically estimate these quantities using neural networks (specifically transformers) as the bounded observers, leveraging prequential and requential coding to approximate model description length.
Optimize hyperparameters and training dynamics within given computational budgets (FLOPs) to find the compute-optimal two-part code, analyzing the Pareto frontier of MDL versus compute.
Results: Elementary Cellular Automata (ECA) Rule 54 generates high epiplexity due to complex emergent patterns, while Rule 30 produces high time-bounded entropy (randomness) for a bounded observer.

Experiments with chess data and ECA Rule 30 showed that reversing the data factorization order leads to both higher time-bounded entropy (harder to predict) and higher epiplexity (more complex structures learned).

Models trained on data yielding higher epiplexity (e.g., 'reverse' chess order, OpenWebText) consistently demonstrated improved out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization and downstream task performance, with language models exhibiting higher epiplexity than vision models.
Takeaways: Computationally bounded observers can 'create' new and useful structural information (epiplexity) from deterministic processes, such as complex cellular automata rules, resolving the paradox of information increase.

The order of data factorization significantly impacts the learnable information and epiplexity for bounded observers, as demonstrated by one-way functions and chess game sequences, challenging classical information symmetry.

Likelihood modeling in computationally limited systems can necessitate learning inductive strategies and discovering emergent patterns not explicitly present in the data-generating process, leading to higher epiplexity.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.03193.Title: UniCorn: Towards Self-Improving Unified Multimodal Models through Self-Generated Supervision
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.03193.Summary: UniCorn enhances unified multimodal models by enabling them to autonomously bridge the gap between their comprehension and generation capabilities through a self-contained, post-training framework. The approach leverages a model's internal understanding to guide its own generative processes, resulting in improved performance across various text-to-image synthesis benchmarks.
Problem: Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) often exhibit a significant disparity between their ability to comprehend inputs and generate high-quality outputs, termed "Conduction Aphasia".
Current UMMs struggle to effectively translate their deep internal understanding into faithful, controllable, and coherent generative content.
Existing self-improvement methods for UMMs typically rely on external data, teacher models, or heuristic reward engineering, limiting their scalability and autonomy.
Method: A single UMM is functionally divided into three internal roles—Proposer, Solver, and Judge—to generate high-quality interaction data through structured self-play.

Cognitive Pattern Reconstruction (CPR) distills latent understanding into explicit training signals (Caption, Judgement, Reflection) by transforming self-generated outputs into structured data patterns.
A novel cycle-consistency benchmark, UniCycle, is introduced to holistically evaluate cognitive alignment and information preservation in a Text → Image → Text loop.
Results: UniCorn achieved state-of-the-art performance on several generative benchmarks, including TIIF (73.8), DPG (86.8), CompBench (88.5), and UniCycle (46.5 Hard score).

Ablation studies demonstrated that the Cognitive Pattern Reconstruction components (Caption, Judgement, Reflection) are critical for preventing latent space collapse and driving comprehensive improvements.

The framework generalizes across different UMM architectures and shows efficient scaling, outperforming models trained on larger external datasets with significantly fewer self-generated samples (e.g., 5K samples surpass DALL·E 3 on TIIF).
Takeaways: A UMM's intrinsic capabilities can be leveraged for autonomous self-supervision by functionalizing it into distinct, collaborative agents within its single parameter space.
Explicitly reconstructing cognitive patterns like Caption, Judgement, and Reflection from self-generated data effectively converts latent understanding into a robust, internal training signal.
Restoring cognitive symmetry between comprehension and generation through an internal feedback loop is crucial for advancing general multimodal intelligence and achieving more controllable synthesis.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.03054.Title: IBISAgent: Reinforcing Pixel-Level Visual Reasoning in MLLMs for Universal Biomedical Object Referring and Segmentation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.03054.Summary: Researchers at Zhejiang University and Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory developed IBISAgent, an agentic Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) framework for universal biomedical object referring and segmentation. It reformulates segmentation as a multi-step Markov Decision Process, allowing an MLLM to iteratively refine masks by generating text-based click actions for an external segmentation tool, significantly outperforming existing MLLMs on medical benchmarks with an 85.58% IoU, 92.21% DSC, and 96.39% F1-score on an in-domain test set.
Problem: Existing MLLMs struggle with fine-grained, pixel-level understanding and precise segmentation critical for clinical diagnosis despite strong image-level comprehension.

Current MLLM-based segmentation methods face issues like catastrophic forgetting, limited generalization, and interference with natural language capabilities due to architectural modifications or implicit tokens.
These methods often lack iterative refinement capabilities, relying on single-pass segmentation that is insufficient for complex biomedical image analysis.
Method: Reformulates biomedical segmentation as a vision-centric, multi-step Markov Decision Process, enabling an MLLM to iteratively refine masks.
Trains the MLLM to act as an agent, generating textual reasoning and text-based click actions that invoke an external interactive segmentation tool for mask updates.
Employs a two-stage training strategy: cold-start supervised fine-tuning using automatically generated trajectories, followed by agentic reinforcement learning with fine-grained, rule-based rewards.
Results: IBISAgent achieved state-of-the-art performance, with an 85.58% IoU, 92.21% DSC, and 96.39% F1-score on an in-domain test set, significantly surpassing other MLLMs for biomedical segmentation.
Qualitative analysis revealed that the model generates correct, coherent textual reasoning and precisely grounded, high-quality masks through adaptive, step-by-step refinement.
Ablation studies confirmed the critical contributions of the agentic formulation, the two-stage training protocol (SFT and RL), and the novel fine-grained reward signals to the overall performance.
Takeaways: An agentic, multi-step reasoning framework allows MLLMs to achieve genuine pixel-level visual understanding and adaptive action planning for segmentation.
Decoupling the MLLM from architectural modifications for segmentation preserves its inherent language capabilities and prevents catastrophic forgetting.
The use of specific, fine-grained rewards during reinforcement learning is essential for fostering robust decision-making and efficient iterative mask refinement.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.02771.Title: AbductiveMLLM: Boosting Visual Abductive Reasoning Within MLLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.02771.Summary: Researchers at Beijing Institute of Technology and collaborators introduce AbductiveMLLM, an architecture designed to enhance Multimodal Large Language Models' (MLLMs) capacity for Visual Abductive Reasoning (VAR). The approach integrates human-inspired verbal and pictorial thinking, achieving state-of-the-art results on VAR and YouCookII benchmarks, with improvements such as +15.38 CIDEr over previous traditional models on the VAR dataset.
Problem: Humans readily infer plausible explanations for incomplete visual observations, a process known as Visual Abductive Reasoning (VAR).
Current Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle with high-level abductive inference, often providing textually consistent but visually inconsistent outputs.
Prior specialized VAR models are typically small-scale, task-specific, and rely exclusively on verbal forms of abduction, limiting their generalizability and reasoning depth.
Method: Developed AbductiveMLLM, a unified multimodal network that incorporates two synergistically trained components: REASONER for verbal abduction and IMAGINER for pictorial abduction.

REASONER employs a causality-aware hypothesis generation module to create diverse verbal hypotheses, then prunes them using a cross-modal contrastive learning mechanism to select causally relevant priors for the MLLM.

IMAGINER adapts a text-to-image diffusion model with lightweight visual, temporal, and FFN adapters to 'imagine' plausible visual scenes conditioned on observed video and REASONER's output, providing rich visual context to the MLLM.
Results: AbductiveMLLM achieved state-of-the-art performance across all five evaluation metrics (BLEU@4, METEOR, ROUGE-L, CIDEr, BERT-S) on both the VAR and YouCookII benchmarks.

The method substantially outperformed traditional specialized models (e.g., +1.14 BLEU@4, +15.38 CIDEr on VAR over UPD-Trans) and general MLLMs (e.g., +6.34 ROUGE-L, +27.79 CIDEr over zero-shot MLLMs on VAR).

Ablation studies confirmed that both REASONER and IMAGINER components contribute individually to performance gains, with their synergistic combination yielding the best results and optimal performance achieved with k=3 selected hypotheses.
Takeaways: Mimicking human dual-mode cognition, integrating both verbal and pictorial thinking, significantly boosts MLLMs' capabilities in visual abductive reasoning.
Causality-aware selection of verbal hypotheses, informed by cross-modal alignment, is essential to filter out low-quality or hallucinated explanations generated by LLMs.
Leveraging adapted text-to-image diffusion models for pictorial thinking provides crucial visual contextual grounding, complementing verbal reasoning within the MLLM framework.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.02422.Title: Watch Wider and Think Deeper: Collaborative Cross-modal Chain-of-Thought for Complex Visual Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.02422.Summary: Researchers from Zhejiang University and Fujian Normal University introduced CoCoT, a framework that enhances Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) for complex visual reasoning through dynamic multi-region grounding and relation-aware reasoning. The approach achieved an average accuracy gain of 15.4% for LLaVA-1.5 and 4.0% for Qwen2-VL across diverse visual question answering benchmarks, supported by a new high-quality dataset, CoCoT-70K.
Problem: Existing multi-modal Chain-of-Thought (CoT) methods often rely on single, coarse-grained image regions, leading to diluted or missed critical visual information.
Previous approaches suffer from semantic fragmentation, where successive reasoning steps lack coherent and logical connections, resulting in disjointed thought processes.
A lack of high-quality, large-scale datasets specifically designed for complex, multi-region visual reasoning with structured reasoning chains.
Method: CoCoT developed a Dynamic Multi-Region Grounding mechanism that collaboratively uses MLLMs (Qwen2-VL) and OCR (PaddleOCR) to identify and correct multiple precise bounding boxes for relevant visual elements.

A Relation-Aware Reasoning module was implemented, enabling MLLMs to iteratively select the most relevant regions and infer their relationships (parallel or sequential) to construct a coherent reasoning chain.

The CoCoT-70K dataset was constructed with 74,691 samples from six benchmarks, featuring multi-region annotations and structured reasoning chains specifically for complex visual questions, and utilized in a two-stage progressive training paradigm.
Results: CoCoT enhanced LLaVA-1.5's performance with an average accuracy gain of 15.4% and Qwen2-VL's performance by 4.0% across six diverse visual reasoning benchmarks compared to direct inference.

The CoCoT-70K dataset, comprising 74,691 samples with multi-region annotations and structured reasoning chains, demonstrated its efficacy by enabling a fine-tuned LLaVA-1.5 model (on 20% of the dataset) to achieve comparable performance to a VisCoT model trained on 363,000 samples.

Ablation studies confirmed the necessity of the Relation-Aware Reasoning module; removing it or integrating its function into the grounding stage severely degraded performance, particularly for stronger MLLMs like Qwen2-VL (up to -22.4% accuracy).
Takeaways: Decoupling dynamic multi-region grounding from relation-aware reasoning is crucial for robust performance, as attempting to generate both simultaneously significantly degrades model accuracy.
Weaker MLLMs (like LLaVA-1.5) benefit substantially from explicit, structured reasoning chains, especially when those chains are generated by more capable models (like Qwen2-VL).

High-quality, meticulously annotated datasets like CoCoT-70K can efficiently impart advanced reasoning capabilities, rivaling the performance of models trained on much larger, less structured datasets.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.02356.Title: Talk2Move: Reinforcement Learning for Text-Instructed Object-Level Geometric Transformation in Scenes
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.02356.Summary: TALK2MOVE, developed by researchers at AWS Agentic AI, introduces a reinforcement learning framework for precise, text-instructed geometric transformations of objects within scenes. This method leverages flow-based Group Relative Policy Optimization and spatially grounded reward models, outperforming state-of-the-art models in translation, rotation, and resizing accuracy while maintaining scene coherence.
Problem: Existing graphics-based editing tools require significant human intervention and specialized expertise for object manipulation.
General text-based image editing models struggle with precise geometric commands (e.g., 'rotate 90 degrees') and disentangling specific objects from the background.
Supervised learning for fine-grained geometric transformations is hampered by the scarcity of high-quality paired 'before-and-after' training data.
Reinforcement learning approaches for diffusion models are often computationally expensive due to dense rollout generation.
Method: The work formulates text-guided geometric object transformation as a reinforcement learning problem within a diffusion framework, utilizing flow-based Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO).

It introduces spatially grounded reward models that use specialist off-the-shelf tools (e.g., object localization, depth estimation, orientation estimation) to provide fine-grained feedback on object displacement, rotation, and scaling.
The method incorporates 'off-policy step evaluation' and 'active step sampling' mechanisms to significantly improve GRPO training efficiency by focusing on the most informative denoising steps.
A two-stage training pipeline starts with a small SFT 'cold start' using synthesized paired data, followed by extensive GRPO training with input-only data.
Results: TALK2MOVE consistently achieved superior performance across translation, rotation, and resizing tasks, outperforming state-of-the-art models like GPT-Image-1, with a 76.67% translation accuracy and 29.55% rotation accuracy on synthetic data.

Human evaluation confirmed the method's superiority, with TALK2MOVE achieving the highest winning rates across all three tasks (57.50% translation, 68.75% rotation, 63.89% resizing) due to better editing accuracy and scene coherence.

Ablation studies demonstrated that the active step sampling mechanism reduced training iteration time by 49% compared to full sampling and improved editing correctness, indicating both efficiency and performance gains.
Takeaways: Formulating geometric object transformation as an RL problem, particularly with GRPO, allows effective learning without extensive paired 'before-and-after' data, addressing a major data scarcity challenge.
Spatially grounded reward models, which directly evaluate object-level geometric metrics, are crucial for achieving precise and semantically faithful transformations.
Computational efficiency of RL for diffusion models can be significantly improved by identifying and actively sampling the most informative denoising steps, accelerating convergence and performance.
A small amount of supervised pre-training (SFT cold start) provides beneficial initial priors, improving the stability and quality of subsequent reinforcement learning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.00659.Title: CRoPS: A Training-Free Hallucination Mitigation Framework for Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.00659.Summary: CRoPS is a training-free framework that effectively mitigates hallucinations in Large Vision-Language Models by dynamically integrating a novel text-deficit hallucinated model with a visual-deficit model. The approach consistently reduces hallucination rates by approximately 15-25% on benchmarks like CHAIR for LLaVA-1.5 while maintaining fluency and improving general multimodal reasoning with minimal inference overhead.
Problem: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) frequently generate factually incorrect or inconsistent content (hallucinations), severely hindering their trustworthiness.
Prior training-free hallucination mitigation methods often target a single source of hallucination and lose effectiveness as text generation progresses due to decreasing reliance on visual input.
Current approaches fail to adequately address hallucinations arising from textual context or co-occurrence biases in training data, especially in later stages of generation.
Method: Develops a novel "text-deficit" hallucinated model that removes all visual tokens and selectively retains the least important textual tokens, providing a consistent contrastive signal throughout text generation.
Proposes Generalized Contrastive Decoding, an extended framework capable of integrating multiple distinct hallucinated models to address various sources of errors simultaneously.
Integrates a visual-deficit model (inspired by SID) and the new text-deficit model with dynamically adjusted weights, adapting their influence based on the generation stage.
Results: Demonstrated consistent reduction in hallucination rates across LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT, and Qwen2-VL, with approximately 15-25% reduction on CHAIR for LLaVA-1.5 while maintaining recall.
Achieved superior performance on multi-dimensional hallucination benchmarks like AMBER, showing a 25-30% reduction in overall hallucination and 10-15% reduction in cognitive deviation.
Introduced minimal inference overhead, performing comparably or faster than other training-free methods, confirming its practicality as a plug-and-play solution.
Takeaways: Large Vision-Language Models' reliance on visual input diminishes significantly during later stages of text generation, making purely visual-token-perturbing methods less effective for hallucination mitigation over time.
Hallucinations in LVLMs arise from multifaceted sources, requiring a comprehensive approach that moves beyond single-source mitigation strategies.

A novel "text-deficit" hallucinated model, which removes visual tokens and crucial textual context, consistently produces a distinct contrastive signal crucial for effective and sustained hallucination suppression.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.00561.Title: AEGIS: Exploring the Limit of World Knowledge Capabilities for Unified Mulitmodal Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.00561.Summary: Researchers at multiple Hong Kong universities and Huawei Research introduced AEGIS, a multi-task benchmark, and Deterministic Checklist-based Evaluation (DCE) protocol to rigorously assess the world knowledge and reasoning capabilities of Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs). The evaluation revealed that current UMMs struggle with complex reasoning, and their visual decoders often act as a bottleneck, even when the language component demonstrates understanding.
Problem: Existing multimodal benchmarks are typically siloed, focusing on single tasks and failing to evaluate UMMs' unified operations or inter-task performance gaps.
Current evaluation methods lack fine-grained diagnostics, making it difficult to pinpoint whether model failures stem from understanding (LLM) or generative modules.
Many benchmarks have limited scope and difficulty, often over-representing common questions and neglecting the broad world knowledge and complex reasoning required for real-world scenarios.
Method: Developed AEGIS, a comprehensive multi-task benchmark featuring 1,050 manually verified questions across 21 topics and 6 reasoning types (spatial, temporal, causal, comparative, analogical, logical) for visual understanding, generation, editing, and interleaved generation.

Introduced a novel Deterministic Checklist-based Evaluation (DCE) protocol that uses atomic, verifiable "Y/N" judgment questions, generated by an MLLM from keywords and reference responses, to objectively assess UMM outputs.
Established a robust methodology that includes human-in-the-loop taxonomy construction, prompt generation (clear and reasoning-enhanced), and high-quality input/ground-truth annotation.
Results: Closed-source UMMs like Gemini Nano Banana and GPT-4o+GPT-Image-1 significantly outperformed open-source models, with Gemini Nano Banana achieving the highest scores (e.g., 64.5% in STEM understanding, 42.6% in STEM generation).
The Deterministic Checklist-based Evaluation (DCE) protocol demonstrated high human consistency, achieving 90.7% agreement across all tasks.
Performance consistently degraded with increased task complexity and reasoning demands, with temporal and causal reasoning being the most challenging types for UMMs.
Takeaways: UMMs possess more world knowledge than they can effectively apply when complex reasoning is required, indicating a reasoning bottleneck rather than a pure knowledge deficit.
The visual decoder acts as a significant bottleneck, often failing to render concepts correctly even when the LLM component provides accurate textual attributes.
Higher quality and more abundant training data, rather than just model scale, play a crucial role in enhancing UMMs' world knowledge capabilities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.00215.Title: From Sight to Insight: Improving Visual Reasoning Capabilities of Multimodal Models via Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.00215.Summary: Researchers identified that visual perception, not algorithmic reasoning, primarily limits multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on visual puzzles. They enhanced MLLMs' visual reasoning through a reinforcement learning framework using specially designed reward functions, successfully inducing multi-step, visually-grounded thought processes without reliance on costly human annotations.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) frequently underperform on visual reasoning tasks, such as solving visual puzzles, that demand precise visual perception and complex multi-step reasoning.
MLLMs often exhibit 'weakly grounded' reasoning, failing to consistently interpret visual information and bypassing visual details in favor of abstract reasoning or direct answers.

Existing RL-based approaches for multimodal reasoning often require dense intermediate supervision like executable tool outputs or human-annotated reasoning traces, which are expensive to obtain for complex visual tasks.
Method: Empirically determined that visual perception is the primary bottleneck for MLLMs in solving visual puzzles by comparing performance on multimodal versus text-only inputs.
Utilized Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to fine-tune the Qwen-2.5-VL-7B MLLM using synthetically generated, diverse visual puzzle datasets.

Designed and evaluated six distinct reward functions within a reinforcement learning framework to incentivize structured, multi-step, and explicitly visually-grounded reasoning without requiring costly human-annotated reasoning traces.
Results: MLLMs (Claude-3.5/3.7) showed substantial average performance gains of 23.6 to 26.7 percentage points when visual information was converted to textual descriptions, confirming visual perception as the primary bottleneck.

The 'Mixture' reward function achieved the highest average accuracy (15.56%) on the `Diverse-8k` dataset and successfully encouraged the MLLM to generate longer, structured, and visually-grounded reasoning trajectories across various categories.

RL training on a diverse dataset significantly improved generalization across both in-domain and out-of-domain visual puzzle categories compared to the no-RL baseline, albeit with overall accuracy remaining modest on highly complex tasks.
Takeaways: Visual perception is the fundamental bottleneck limiting MLLM performance on complex visual puzzles, as converting images to text significantly boosts their reasoning accuracy.

Reward-driven reinforcement learning, especially with 'Mixture' and 'Continuous' reward functions, can effectively induce longer, structured, and visually-grounded reasoning chains ('think with image') in MLLMs.

It is possible to foster emergent, multi-step reasoning capabilities in MLLMs purely through careful reward design, reducing dependency on expensive, dense intermediate supervision for complex multimodal tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.00092.Title: Spatial4D-Bench: A Versatile 4D Spatial Intelligence Benchmark
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.00092.Summary: Huawei Technologies researchers and academic collaborators introduced Spatial4D-Bench, a large-scale, multi-task benchmark designed to evaluate 4D spatial intelligence in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Evaluations across 18 tasks revealed a substantial 17-22% performance gap between MLLMs and humans in dynamic reasoning, with models struggling particularly in spatiotemporal continuity and physical plausibility despite proficiency in some basic object perception tasks.
Problem: Existing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle with comprehensive 4D spatial intelligence, often acting as "frame-based observers" rather than understanding dynamic, evolving scenes.

Prior spatial intelligence benchmarks are often limited in scale and diversity, predominantly focusing on static 3D scenes and neglecting the crucial temporal dimension for evaluating spatiotemporal awareness.
There is a lack of rigorous, multi-faceted evaluation tools to precisely diagnose MLLMs' limitations in complex spatial and temporal reasoning, such as route planning and physical plausibility.
Method: Developed Spatial4D-Bench, a versatile 4D spatial intelligence benchmark containing approximately 40,000 question-answer pairs spanning 18 distinct tasks.

Tasks are organized into a hierarchical taxonomy of six cognitive categories, progressing from basic object/scene understanding to advanced spatiotemporal and physical reasoning, utilizing diverse real-world video data.

A four-stage construction pipeline ensures benchmark quality and diversity by unifying data from multiple sources, employing hybrid human and automatic QA generation, and thorough human review processes.
Results: Humans achieved an average score of 78.02% on the benchmark, outperforming the best proprietary MLLM (GPT-5 at 60.90%) by approximately 17% and the best open-source model (Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B at 56.17%) by 22%.

MLLMs showed substantial performance degradation in reasoning tasks, scoring only 32.83% on 'Route Plan' and 30-40% on 'Physical Plausibility Reasoning,' contrasting sharply with human scores of 91.67% and 66.67% respectively.

While MLLMs occasionally surpassed human performance on perception-related tasks like object size estimation (e.g., Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B at 80.10% vs. human 74.61%), they performed near random chance on tasks requiring intuitive physics.
Takeaways: MLLMs exhibit a significant overall gap in 4D spatial intelligence compared to human performance, indicating they lack coherent 4D world models and an intuitive understanding of physics.

MLLMs struggle notably with spatiotemporal continuity and long-term spatial memory, with performance degrading as video length increases, pointing to limitations in current information retrieval and state representation architectures.

Visual ablation studies demonstrated that incomplete visual frames can act as "adversarial distractors," sometimes causing MLLMs to prioritize flawed visual evidence over correct language priors, leading to confident hallucinations.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24880.Title: mHC: Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24880.Summary: Researchers at DeepSeek-AI developed Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC), an architectural modification that stabilizes and enhances the performance of large language models using expanded residual connections. This approach incorporates manifold constraints and infrastructure optimizations to ensure stable signal propagation and achieve higher efficiency, leading to improved downstream task performance with a 6.7% training overhead.
Problem: Advanced deep learning architectures like Hyper-Connections (HC) show performance potential but suffer from severe training instability due to unconstrained learnable mappings.
Unconstrained residual mappings in HC compromise the identity mapping property, leading to exploding or vanishing signals and gradients that hinder large-scale model training.
Expanded residual streams, while powerful, introduce significant memory access overhead and reduce hardware efficiency, posing a 'memory wall' challenge.
Method: Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) project learnable residual mappings onto the Birkhoff polytope, ensuring they are doubly stochastic matrices, which guarantees stable signal propagation.
Non-negativity constraints are applied to pre- and post-mappings using Sigmoid functions to prevent signal cancellation within the expanded residual stream.

Extensive infrastructure optimizations, including kernel fusion, recomputing (gradient checkpointing), and overlapping communication, are integrated to ensure high hardware efficiency and minimize training overhead.
Results: mHC achieves significantly enhanced training stability with smoother loss convergence and stable gradient norms, resolving the instability observed in unconstrained Hyper-Connections.
The approach consistently outperforms baseline models and unconstrained HC on 8 diverse downstream benchmarks, showing gains of 2.1% on BBH and 2.3% on DROP tasks.
mHC demonstrates robust scalability across varying compute and token budgets, introducing only a 6.7% additional training time overhead for an expansion rate of 4, proving its practical efficiency.
Takeaways: Constraining residual mappings to be doubly stochastic matrices effectively restores signal stability by bounding spectral norms and ensuring compositional closure, mitigating gradient explosion/vanishing.
The Sinkhorn-Knopp algorithm can be effectively used to project learnable matrices onto the manifold of doubly stochastic matrices, facilitating robust and stable feature mixing.
Careful co-design of architecture and system infrastructure is crucial for scaling complex network topologies, allowing advanced designs to be practical for large language models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24695.Title: Nested Learning: The Illusion of Deep Learning Architectures
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24695.Summary: Nested Learning introduces a paradigm that reinterprets machine learning as nested, multi-level optimization problems with varying update frequencies, addressing the limitations of static models in continual learning. The proposed Hope architecture and M3 optimizer demonstrate enhanced performance in mitigating catastrophic forgetting and improving long-context understanding across various tasks.
Problem: Modern Multimodal Large Language Models (LLMs) are largely static post-training, experiencing catastrophic forgetting when learning new information continually.
Deep learning architectures often lack true "computational depth" for complex algorithmic tasks, with simply stacking more layers not equating to enhanced dynamic learning.
A unifying theoretical framework is missing to integrate diverse machine learning components for effective continual learning and self-improvement.
Method: Nested Learning (NL) proposes reinterpreting machine learning as a hierarchy of nested, multi-level optimization problems, with components categorized by their update frequencies.
The Hope architecture is developed, combining "self-modifying Titans" for dynamic, context-adaptive learning rules with a "Continuum Memory System (CMS)" for multi-timescale knowledge retention.
Expressive optimizers, such as Multi-scale Momentum Muon (M3), are designed to manage gradient information across multiple timescales for improved parameter updates.
Results: Hope-enhanced Llama models consistently improved accuracy on class-incremental learning benchmarks (e.g., CLINC, Banking), demonstrating superior catastrophic forgetting mitigation.
The Hope architecture achieved competitive performance in long-context understanding, handling up to 10M tokens on BABILong and outperforming attention-free baselines on Needle-in-a-Haystack tasks.
The M3 optimizer exhibited superior training and test loss compared to AdamW when pre-training Vision Transformers on ImageNet-21K, supporting the benefits of multi-timescale gradient memory.
Takeaways: All machine learning components, including neural network layers and optimizers, can be fundamentally viewed as associative memory systems that compress their respective context flows.
The diverse appearance of deep learning architectures is an "illusion," as they are all composed of uniform feedforward layers operating at different levels and frequencies with unique objectives.
Continual learning and adaptation can be achieved through a multi-level, self-referential optimization process that mimics the human brain's multi-timescale information processing.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24601.Title: Recursive Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24601.Summary: Recursive Language Models (RLMs) introduce an inference-time paradigm allowing large language models to process inputs exceeding 10 million tokens, vastly extending their effective context window. This approach achieved 91.3% accuracy on multi-document retrieval tasks where base models failed and dramatically outperformed other long-context methods on information-dense problems.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) are severely limited by finite context windows, experiencing "context rot" and performance degradation with longer prompts.
Existing LLM architectures struggle to effectively process and reason over extremely long inputs, such as millions of tokens required for "long-horizon" tasks.
Conventional methods for handling long contexts often involve lossy compression or architectural changes that require extensive retraining.
Method: Recursive Language Models (RLMs) scaffold a base LLM within a Read-Eval-Print Loop (REPL) programming environment, treating the user prompt as an external object.
The LLM generates code to symbolically interact with, decompose, and transform the long prompt, examining selective portions rather than ingesting the full input directly.
The RLM enables symbolic recursion, allowing the LLM to programmatically invoke itself on arbitrary slices or transformations of the prompt, overcoming output length limitations.
Results: RLMs successfully processed inputs up to 10 million tokens, achieving 91.3% accuracy on a multi-document task (BrowseComp-Plus) where base models scored 0.0%.

They dramatically outperformed vanilla frontier LLMs and common long-context baselines on tasks requiring deep reasoning over extensive inputs, like OOLONG-Pairs (RLM(GPT-5) achieved 58.0% F1 vs. <0.1% for base models).
Post-training smaller models (e.g., RLM-Qwen3-8B) on RLM trajectories from larger models significantly improved their RLM performance, demonstrating a promising path for native RLM capabilities.
Takeaways: Offloading the prompt into a REPL environment is essential for scaling beyond the base LLM's inherent context window.
Symbolic recursion, where the LLM can programmatically invoke sub-LLMs, provides significant performance gains for information-dense and complex tasks.
This inference-time scaling approach enables LLMs to robustly handle increasing task complexity and context length, exhibiting slower performance degradation than base models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24497.Title: What Drives Success in Physical Planning with Joint-Embedding Predictive World Models?
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24497.Summary: This research provides a systematic empirical study of Joint-Embedding Predictive World Models (JEPA-WMs), identifying the specific technical choices that contribute to their success in physical planning. It proposes optimized model configurations that consistently achieve higher success rates compared to existing baselines on diverse simulated and real-world robotic manipulation and navigation tasks.
Problem: A lack of comprehensive understanding regarding the specific technical choices that drive success in physical planning using Joint-Embedding Predictive World Models (JEPA-WMs).
Prior JEPA-WM implementations often rely on ad-hoc design choices, hindering principled advancement and optimization for robotic tasks.
The challenge of developing AI agents that can efficiently solve a wide range of physical tasks and generalize to unseen environments.
Method: Formalize JEPA-WMs as a unified recipe, systematically varying and evaluating key components across model architecture, training objectives, and planning algorithms.
Conduct a component-wise empirical study on diverse simulated (Metaworld, Push-T, Wall, PointMaze, Robocasa) and real-world (DROID) robotic tasks to isolate the impact of each design choice.
Propose optimized JEPA-WM configurations based on the comprehensive analysis, distinguishing between optimal settings for simulated versus complex real-world dynamics.
Results: The proposed optimal JEPA-WM models consistently outperformed established baselines like DINO-WM and V-JEPA-2-AC across most simulated and real-world environments.
Proprioceptive input consistently improved planning success, and a 2-step rollout loss was generally optimal for simulated tasks, while a 6-step rollout was best for complex real-world dynamics.
Nevergrad, a tuning-free planner, performed comparably to CEM on real-world manipulation data (DROID), offering a practical advantage by requiring less hyperparameter tuning.
Takeaways: DINO-style visual encoders consistently outperform V-JEPA encoders due to their superior fine-grained object segmentation capabilities, which are essential for precise manipulation and navigation.

While gradient-based planners excel on tasks with smooth cost landscapes, population-based methods like CEM and Nevergrad are more robust for complex, multi-modal cost landscapes encountered in robotics.

The benefits of model scaling (larger encoders and deeper predictors) are primarily observed in complex real-world data, whereas they offer limited or negative gains in simpler simulated environments.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24385.Title: Forging Spatial Intelligence: A Roadmap of Multi-Modal Data Pre-Training for Autonomous Systems
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24385.Summary: Researchers from Zhejiang University, National University of Singapore, and collaborators present a detailed roadmap for multi-modal data pre-training in autonomous systems, categorizing methods and identifying challenges to achieve robust Spatial Intelligence. The work synthesizes an evolutionary trajectory from single-modality to unified foundation models, underscoring their empirical advantages in 3D perception and generative world modeling.
Problem: Autonomous systems require deep environmental understanding, but face challenges integrating heterogeneous sensor data (camera, LiDAR, radar, event cameras) for holistic perception.
Large-scale datasets for autonomous systems rely heavily on costly manual annotations, leading to scalability and generalization bottlenecks.
While foundation models excel in single-modal contexts, their effective integration across diverse, heterogeneous sensors for autonomous systems remains a significant challenge.
Method: Developed a unified taxonomy categorizing multi-modal pre-training techniques, from single-modality baselines to unified frameworks and foundation model integration.
Performed an extensive literature review and chronological analysis of state-of-the-art methods, synthesizing empirical performance on key 3D perception tasks.

Identified critical bottlenecks and proposed a clear roadmap for future research, including physically consistent world simulators and 4D semantic-geometric unification, aiming for general-purpose multi-modal foundation models.
Results: Quantitative analysis on benchmarks like nuScenes demonstrates that multi-modal and unified pre-training significantly outperform single-modality baselines in 3D object detection and LiDAR semantic segmentation.
Foundation models, particularly Vision-Language Models (VLMs), enable auto-labeling and self-supervised 3D occupancy prediction, addressing annotation bottlenecks.

Generative world models, such as OccWorld and GenAD, predict 4D occupancy flows conditioned on ego-actions, showing improved planning fidelity and safety, moving towards unified Vision-Action (VA) and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) frameworks.
Takeaways: Representation learning in autonomous systems is evolving from single-modality self-supervision to cross-modal synergy and unified pre-training frameworks, leveraging foundation models.

Modern datasets increasingly incorporate planning trajectories, logic, and language, facilitating the training of embodied AI and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, alongside a growing reliance on synthetic and generative data.

Achieving 'true Spatial Intelligence' requires shifting from specialized, task-specific models to holistic, multi-modal foundation models capable of learning generalizable world knowledge and enabling end-to-end planning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24331.Title: Spatial-aware Vision Language Model for Autonomous Driving
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24331.Summary: Researchers at Motional and the University of Amsterdam developed LVLDrive, a framework that integrates LiDAR point clouds into Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to enhance 3D metric spatial understanding for autonomous driving. This system employs a Gradual Fusion Q-Former and a specialized Spatial-Aware Question-Answering (SA-QA) dataset, leading to improved open-loop planning performance on nuScenes with a reduced collision rate of 0.25%.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for autonomous driving predominantly rely on 2D imagery, leading to a lack of robust 3D metric spatial understanding essential for safe navigation.

The inability to accurately infer 3D geometry results in unreliable estimations of distances, object dimensions, and collision risks, which directly impacts the safety and effectiveness of driving policies.
Directly incorporating disparate 3D LiDAR data into pre-trained VLMs can cause "catastrophic disturbance," disrupting their learned visual-linguistic alignments and degrading performance.
Method: LVLDrive integrates LiDAR point clouds, camera images, and text prompts into a VLM using a novel Gradual Fusion Q-Former architecture.

A zero-initialized multi-head gating mechanism is implemented within the Gradual Fusion Q-Former to enable stable and adaptive integration of LiDAR features, preserving the VLM's pre-trained knowledge.

The SA-QA dataset was created from nuScenes and OpenLane ground-truth annotations to explicitly teach the model advanced 3D spatial perception and reasoning through structured question-answering tasks.
Results: LVLDrive achieved an average L2 displacement error of 0.29 meters, an average collision rate of 0.25%, and an average road boundary intersection rate of 2.59% on the nuScenes open-loop planning benchmark, outperforming existing LLM-based driving models.

On the DriveLM dataset, LVLDrive obtained a CIDEr score of 21.65, demonstrating superior content relevance and more accurate spatial and semantic understanding in its generated answers compared to baselines.

Ablation studies confirmed that the zero-initialized multi-head gate is critical for stable LiDAR integration and robust planning, while the SA-QA dataset's spatial perception and reasoning components are essential for achieving the best overall 3D grounding and planning performance.
Takeaways: Explicitly providing 3D metric spatial understanding and reasoning capabilities to Vision-Language Models is crucial for improving their performance and safety in autonomous driving applications.

A controlled, gradual integration mechanism, like the zero-initialized multi-head gate within a unified Q-Former, can effectively incorporate LiDAR data into pre-trained VLMs without disrupting their existing knowledge.
A targeted dataset that includes both fundamental 3D spatial perception and complex spatial reasoning questions is vital for training VLMs to leverage multimodal 3D data comprehensively.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24330.Title: SenseNova-MARS: Empowering Multimodal Agentic Reasoning and Search via Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24330.Summary: Developed by SenseTime Research, Tsinghua University, and USTC, SenseNova-MARS is a multimodal agentic reasoning and search framework enabling Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to dynamically integrate image search, text search, and image crop tools via a novel Reinforcement Learning algorithm, BN-GSPO. This framework achieves state-of-the-art performance, including a score of 41.64 on the new HR-MMSearch, matching Gemini-3-Flash, and excels across various search-oriented and fine-grained visual understanding benchmarks.
Problem: Traditional Vision-Language Models (VLMs) primarily rely on text-based reasoning, struggling to seamlessly integrate visual analysis directly into the reasoning process.
Existing VLM agents often invoke external tools in an isolated or sequential manner, hindering their ability to handle complex, multi-step problems requiring adaptive tool use.

Human-like proficiency in real-world tasks demands coordinating external tools with iterative reasoning for both extensive knowledge retrieval and precise visual perception, particularly with high-resolution images.
Method: Introduces SenseNova-MARS, a multimodal agentic framework that dynamically integrates image search, text search, and image crop tools into a continuous, multi-turn reasoning process.

Employs a two-stage training pipeline, beginning with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) for basic tool usage, followed by Reinforcement Learning (RL) to refine multi-tool collaboration and adaptive reasoning.

Develops BN-GSPO (Batch-Normalized Group Sequence Policy Optimization), a novel RL algorithm that uses a two-stage normalization method to stabilize training and ensure consistent learning signals across diverse multi-tool trajectories.
Results: SenseNova-MARS-8B achieved leading performance on search-oriented benchmarks, scoring 67.84 on MMSearch and 41.64 on the new HR-MMSearch, matching Gemini-3-Flash.
The model demonstrated superior fine-grained visual understanding with state-of-the-art scores of 92.2 on V* Bench, 83.1 on HR-Bench 4K, and 78.4 on HR-Bench 8K.

The proposed BN-GSPO algorithm significantly improved the stability and effectiveness of multi-tool RL training, outperforming GRPO and GSPO in ablation studies and leading to more streamlined, efficient tool usage.
Takeaways: Dynamically interleaving tool invocation (search and image manipulation) with continuous reasoning enables VLMs to address complex visual and knowledge-intensive tasks more effectively than isolated tool use.
Reinforcement Learning, specifically with robust algorithms like BN-GSPO, is crucial for teaching VLM agents adaptive and efficient multi-tool collaboration strategies in dynamic environments.

A hybrid training data distribution, combining both search-oriented and fine-grained perception tasks, is essential for developing a unified multi-tool policy that balances external knowledge retrieval with precise visual analysis.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24297.Title: Figure It Out: Improve the Frontier of Reasoning with Executable Visual States
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24297.Summary: FIGR, developed by WeChat AI, Tencent Inc., enhances large language models' reasoning by integrating executable visual construction into multi-turn inference via reinforcement learning. It improves problem-solving involving implicit spatial and geometric relationships, achieving an an average accuracy of 74.11% on mathematical benchmarks, marking a 6.77% gain over its base policy and over 11% on complex geometric reasoning tasks.
Problem: Text-only reasoning methods (e.g., Chain-of-Thought) struggle with complex problems requiring implicit spatial or geometric understanding, leading to errors due to the high cognitive burden on internal representations.

Unconstrained visual generation models (Large Vision-Language Models) lack precise control over their visual outputs, often generating noisy or spatially imprecise images that are unreliable for tasks demanding fine-grained geometric accuracy.

Tool-augmented visual reasoning models operate on given images with fixed sets of predefined transformations, preventing them from autonomously constructing novel, task-specific diagrams or abstract visual representations from scratch.
Method: Introduces an executable visual construction within the reasoning loop, where the model dynamically generates code to construct and refine diagrams, with a sandboxed interpreter providing precise visual and textual feedback.

Employs a reinforcement learning procedure with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to train the model, optimizing long-horizon, multi-turn reasoning trajectories using a combined reward for final answer correctness, output format, and visual construction appropriateness.

Utilizes an Adaptive Reward Mechanism (ARM) to guide purposeful visual thinking by conditionally rewarding diagrammatic reasoning based on a predicted suitability for the given problem, encouraging effective use of visual construction.
Results: FIGR achieved an average accuracy of 74.11% across seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks (e.g., AIME, BeyondAIME, MATH 500), representing a 6.77% improvement over its base policy and a 4.88% gain over a text-only reinforcement learning baseline.
Demonstrated substantial performance gains on benchmarks requiring complex geometric and structural understanding, with increases of 13.12% on AIME 2025 and 11.00% on BeyondAIME.

Ablation studies confirmed that the Adaptive Reward Mechanism is critical for guiding purposeful visual construction, and that explicit, executable visual feedback is superior to passively injected visual information or static image generation.
Takeaways: Human reasoning for complex problems involving spatial or structural relationships benefits from externalizing information visually, a capability that AI models need to emulate more effectively.

Active, executable construction and iterative refinement of visual states within the reasoning loop are crucial for enforcing geometric consistency and providing actionable feedback, unlike static or passively injected images.

End-to-end reinforcement learning, particularly with an adaptive reward mechanism, can effectively teach AI models when and how to judiciously invoke multimodal (visual construction) capabilities without relying on extensive supervised visual reasoning annotations.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24119.Title: GeoBench: Rethinking Multimodal Geometric Problem-Solving via Hierarchical Evaluation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24119.Summary: Researchers developed GeoBench, a hierarchical benchmark with formally verified synthetic data, to diagnostically evaluate multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on geometric reasoning. The framework revealed that MLLMs struggle significantly with self-reflective reasoning, while capacities for sub-goal decomposition and irrelevant premise filtering are strong determinants of problem-solving success.
Problem: Existing geometric problem-solving benchmarks suffer from potential data contamination, leading to overestimation of MLLM capabilities due to memorization.
Current evaluations focus solely on final answers, neglecting the logical steps and reasoning processes crucial for rigorous geometric problem-solving.
Benchmarks lack diagnostic granularity, making it difficult to pinpoint specific points of failure (e.g., visual perception, planning, theorem application) in MLLM reasoning.
Method: GeoBench introduces a hierarchical evaluation framework, inspired by the van Hiele model, to assess geometric reasoning across four levels: Visual Perception, Goal-Oriented Planning, Rigorous Theorem Application, and Self-Reflective Backtracking.
The benchmark utilizes formally verified synthetic geometric problems generated by `TrustGeoGen`, ensuring correctness, eliminating data contamination risks, and providing detailed reasoning graphs.

Six distinct multiple-choice tasks are operationalized within the framework (e.g., Numerical Perception, Sub-Goal Decomposition, Faulty Branch Localization) to enable fine-grained diagnostic assessment of MLLMs.
Results: All MLLMs, including top proprietary models like OpenAI-o1, showed profound limitations in the Faulty Branch Localization task, with highest accuracy at 27.89%, only slightly above random guessing.
Reasoning MLLMs (e.g., OpenAI-o3, Gemini-2.5-pro) consistently outperformed general MLLMs, with OpenAI-o3 achieving 91.00% accuracy on Sub-Goal Decomposition.

The identified correlations between GeoBench tasks and overall problem-solving generalized robustly to out-of-distribution datasets, confirming the benchmark's ability to measure genuine geometric reasoning.
Takeaways: MLLMs' performance consistently declines with increasing task complexity, with self-reflective backtracking presenting the most significant challenge.
Sub-Goal Decomposition and Irrelevant Premise Filtering are identified as critical reasoning bottlenecks, exhibiting the strongest correlations with overall geometric problem-solving success.

Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting does not universally improve performance and can even degrade results in tasks like faulty branch localization, challenging its presumed efficacy in all complex reasoning scenarios.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.23676.Title: Web World Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.23676.Summary: Researchers at Princeton University and collaborators introduce Web World Models (WWMs), a new architectural paradigm that integrates standard web development with large language models to create persistent, interactive environments for language agents. WWMs offer a hybrid neuro-symbolic approach that combines the reliability of traditional web applications with the open-endedness and scalability of generative AI, exemplified through diverse applications such as explorable atlases and dynamic game generation.
Problem: Existing environments for language agents either offer highly reliable but bounded contexts (conventional web frameworks) or unlimited but uncontrollable and costly generative worlds.
There is a lack of a 'middle ground' solution that combines the reliability and controllability of traditional web applications with the open-endedness and scalability of generative AI.
Language agents require persistent and evolving environments that can dynamically expand their state space while ensuring logical coherence and predictability over extended periods.
Method: Introduces Web World Models (WWMs), a hybrid neuro-symbolic architecture that leverages standard web development practices alongside large language models (LLMs).

Employs four core design principles: Separation of Concerns (deterministic 'Physics Layer' by code, stochastic 'Imagination Layer' by LLM), Typed Interfaces for neuro-symbolic contracts, Infinite Worlds via Deterministic Hashing, and Graceful Degradation.
Implements diverse WWMs across various domains using a modern web stack (TypeScript, HTTP streaming, serverless architecture) to demonstrate the concept's feasibility and versatility.
Results: Successfully implemented a suite of diverse Web World Models, including the Infinite Travel Atlas, Galaxy Travel Atlas, WWMPedia, Bookshelf, AI Spire, AI Alchemy, and Cosmic Voyager, demonstrating the paradigm's versatility across different applications.

The implemented WWMs effectively hosted controllable yet open-ended environments, showcasing the ability to blend code-governed logic with LLM-generated narratives and content while maintaining consistency.
The framework proved robust and practical, maintaining logical continuity and application functionality even under constraints or LLM unavailability through the principle of graceful degradation.
Takeaways: Explicitly separating the deterministic, rule-based 'Physics Layer' from the stochastic, LLM-driven 'Imagination Layer' ensures logical consistency and controllability while enabling rich content generation.

Utilizing typed interfaces (e.g., JSON schemas) as a 'neuro-symbolic contract' makes LLM outputs transparent and debuggable, preventing structural hallucinations and ensuring compatibility with the physics engine's logic.
Procedural generation combined with deterministic hashing allows for effectively unbounded, consistent world states that maintain 'object permanence' without requiring infinite storage.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.23453.Title: CoFi-Dec: Hallucination-Resistant Decoding via Coarse-to-Fine Generative Feedback in Large Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.23453.Summary: CoFi-Dec introduces a training-free decoding framework for Large Vision-Language Models, leveraging coarse-to-fine generative self-feedback and a Wasserstein-based fusion mechanism to reduce visual hallucinations. The approach consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple hallucination benchmarks, enhancing factual consistency and visual grounding of generated content.
Problem: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) frequently generate content inconsistent with visual input, known as hallucinations, limiting their trustworthiness and real-world applicability.
Existing training-time hallucination mitigation methods are resource-intensive and unscalable for rapidly evolving foundation models.
Prior decoding-time strategies often process visual information at a single resolution and apply feedback post-hoc, lacking fine-grained, step-by-step integration during token generation.
Method: The framework performs hierarchical visual decomposition, generating coarse-grained (downsampled) and fine-grained (cropped salient regions) views of the input image.
It employs a text-to-image generative model to synthesize pseudo-images from initial textual hypotheses derived from both coarse and fine visual conditions, creating 'generative self-feedback'.

A Wasserstein barycenter optimization is used to fuse the conditional probability distributions from the original image and the synthesized multi-granular pseudo-images, guiding token generation at each step.
Results: Achieved state-of-the-art accuracy, precision, and F1 scores on the POPE benchmark for object hallucination, demonstrating robustness against challenging negative sampling strategies.

Significantly reduced CHAIR
S
and CHAIR
I
scores on the CHAIR benchmark, indicating a substantial decrease in subject and instance hallucinations in free-form image captions.
Outperformed competitors on MME-Hallucination and MMBench, showing improved object-level and attribute-level hallucination mitigation, alongside gains in general multimodal reasoning accuracy.
Takeaways: Mimicking human coarse-to-fine visual perception by integrating multi-granular feedback during autoregressive decoding significantly improves visual grounding.
Leveraging text-to-image generative models to create 'pseudo-visual' feedback from textual hypotheses offers an effective self-verification mechanism for LVLMs.
A principled Wasserstein-based fusion across diverse semantic probabilities leads to more robust and accurate token predictions by respecting the underlying semantic space.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.23365.Title: SpatialMosaic: A Multiview VLM Dataset for Partial Visibility
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.23365.Summary: Researchers from Seoul National University and collaborators introduce SpatialMosaic, a multi-view dataset and benchmark comprising 3 million QA pairs, specifically designed to train and evaluate multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on 3D spatial reasoning tasks under partial visibility, occlusion, and low-overlap conditions. Their proposed SpatialMosaicVLM, a hybrid VLM integrating 3D geometric encoders, achieves 81.8% average accuracy on the new benchmark and demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization to another temporal spatial reasoning benchmark, outperforming larger proprietary and open-source models.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) lack robust 3D spatial reasoning capabilities when processing multi-view images, particularly under real-world conditions of partial visibility, occlusion, and low-overlap.
Existing approaches often depend on costly explicit 3D representations or struggle to consistently integrate fragmented visual information across sparse viewpoints.
Current MLLMs do not achieve human-like implicit 3D scene reconstruction or reliable reasoning about unseen objects from imperfect, limited observations.
Method: A scalable multi-view data generation pipeline was developed, leveraging ScanNet++ to automatically construct 3 million geometrically grounded spatial reasoning question-answer pairs.

The SpatialMosaic dataset was introduced, a large-scale instruction-tuning dataset specifically designed to train MLLMs on tasks involving partial visibility, occlusion, and low-overlap conditions from multi-view inputs.

SpatialMosaicVLM, a hybrid framework, was proposed, which integrates 3D reconstruction models as explicit geometry encoders to provide geometry-aware representations and improve cross-view alignment for robust spatial reasoning.
Results: SpatialMosaicVLM achieved an average accuracy of 81.8% on the SpatialMosaic-Bench, significantly outperforming existing MLLM baselines (e.g., LLaVA-NeXT-Video-7B at 47.8%).
The model demonstrated strong zero-shot generalization to VSTI-Bench, securing the top rank with 46.8% average accuracy and surpassing larger proprietary models like GPT-4o and Gemini-1.5 Flash.

Diagnostic analysis confirmed that performance degrades with increased occlusion and reduced view overlap, but SpatialMosaicVLM consistently maintained superior robustness across all difficulty levels and task types compared to baselines.
Takeaways: Explicitly addressing scenarios of partial visibility, occlusion, and low-overlap through tailored data generation is crucial for advancing MLLMs' 3D spatial reasoning capabilities.

Integrating 3D reconstruction models as geometry encoders within a VLM architecture provides explicit geometric priors, which are essential for achieving robust cross-view alignment and consistent object understanding.
Training on a large-scale, diagnostically challenging dataset fosters a more generalized spatial intelligence, enabling strong zero-shot performance on diverse, unseen spatial reasoning tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.23169.Title: REVEALER: Reinforcement-Guided Visual Reasoning for Element-Level Text-Image Alignment Evaluation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.23169.Summary: REVEALER presents a reinforcement-guided visual reasoning framework that evaluates text-image alignment at an element level, achieving over 85% accuracy across multiple benchmarks. This approach provides fine-grained interpretability by explicitly localizing semantic elements and generating natural language rationales, with an inference time of 1.2s-1.6s per sample.
Problem: Existing text-to-image (T2I) alignment metrics provide only coarse-grained evaluations, often failing to identify specific mismatches related to individual objects, attributes, or relationships.
Automated evaluation methods typically lack interpretability, offering numerical scores without detailed explanations, which hinders effective debugging and improvement of T2I models.
Current iterative visual reasoning methods for T2I alignment suffer from efficiency issues and are prone to error propagation due to unreliable object localization.
Method: A three-stage 'grounding–reasoning–conclusion' visual reasoning paradigm evaluates each semantic element, explicitly localizing it with bounding boxes and generating natural language explanations.

A high-quality dataset of visual reasoning trajectories is curated using a combination of Grounding DINO, GPT-4o, and Gemini 2.5 Pro, incorporating a Strict Grounding Strategy to prevent error propagation from ambiguous elements.

A two-stage training pipeline fine-tunes a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) first with Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and then with Reinforcement Learning via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), guided by a composite reward function.
Results: REVEALER achieves state-of-the-art accuracy, with over 85% ACC across EvalMuse-40K, RichHF, MHaluBench, and GenAI-Bench benchmarks.

Reinforcement learning (GRPO) improves accuracy by over 13% (e.g., +13.1% ACC on EvalMuse-40K) compared to supervised fine-tuning alone, demonstrating its effectiveness in aligning with human judgment.
The framework achieves inference times of 1.2s–1.6s per sample, offering substantial efficiency gains compared to iterative reinforcement learning methods which range from 4.1s to 7.3s.
Takeaways: The structured 'grounding–reasoning–conclusion' paradigm inherently enhances interpretability and forms an effective foundation for T2I alignment evaluation.

Reinforcement learning, specifically GRPO with a composite reward function, is essential for refining MLLM reasoning capabilities and aligning its judgments more closely with human preferences beyond SFT.
Implementing a 'Strict Grounding Strategy' that allows MLLMs to abstain from grounding ambiguous elements and instead rely on global context significantly reduces hallucination and error propagation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.23167.Title: SPIRAL: Symbolic LLM Planning via Grounded and Reflective Search
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.23167.Summary: Researchers from Vanderbilt University and IBM T.J. Watson Research Center introduced SPIRAL, a framework that enhances LLM planning by integrating specialized agents for planning, grounded simulation, and reflective feedback into a modified Monte Carlo Tree Search. The system achieved 83.61% accuracy on the DailyLifeAPIs dataset, outperforming state-of-the-art methods like LATS (67.39%) and demonstrating superior token efficiency.
Problem: Linear LLM planning approaches (e.g., Chain-of-Thought) are brittle and prone to errors in complex, multi-step tasks due to a lack of self-correction and structured deliberation.
