Progressive analysis across RL stages confirmed that RLHF improves token efficiency and accuracy, while subsequent domain-specific RL stages further enhance reasoning and problem-solving without degrading prior domain performance.
Takeaways: Cascade RL effectively addresses the heterogeneity of multi-domain LLM training by enabling sequential specialization, minimizing catastrophic forgetting, and reducing engineering complexity.

Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), when applied as an initial step, unexpectedly boosts reasoning performance in subsequent math and code tasks, improving the efficiency of later RL stages.

A unified model, trained with a specific 'Half-Half' RLHF strategy, can successfully operate in both 'instruct' and 'deep thinking' modes, challenging the necessity for separate specialized reasoning models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13564.Title: Memory in the Age of AI Agents
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13564.Summary: This survey provides a comprehensive analysis of memory systems in AI agents, introducing a novel "Forms–Functions–Dynamics" taxonomy to categorize and understand current research. It clarifies conceptual boundaries with related areas and identifies promising future research directions, establishing a unified framework for the field.
Problem: The rapid expansion of AI agent research has led to fragmentation and conceptual ambiguity regarding memory systems.
Existing taxonomies, like the simple long-term/short-term dichotomy, are insufficient to capture the diversity of modern agent memory.
A lack of clear distinctions between agent memory, LLM memory, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and context engineering hinders systematic progress.
Method: The authors introduce a multidimensional taxonomy for agent memory based on "Forms, Functions, and Dynamics" (FFD).
They rigorously define agent memory and delineate its boundaries from related concepts such as LLM memory, RAG, and context engineering.
The survey systematically categorizes existing research within this FFD framework and outlines emerging research frontiers.
Results: The survey identifies token-level memory as the most prevalent form, detailing its structural variations (1D flat, 2D planar, 3D hierarchical) alongside parametric and latent memory forms.

It presents a functional taxonomy distinguishing factual memory (user/environment consistency), experiential memory (case-based, strategy-based, skill-based learning), and working memory (single/multi-turn context management).

Memory dynamics are decomposed into formation (summarization, distillation, structured construction), evolution (consolidation, updating, forgetting), and retrieval (timing, query construction, strategies, post-processing), each with detailed sub-processes.
Takeaways: Agent memory differs from LLM memory, RAG, and context engineering by focusing on an external, evolving cognitive state for persistent, adaptive decision-making.

Memory forms are classified by *where it resides* and *how it's represented* (token-level, parametric, latent), with token-level memory further structured into flat, planar, and hierarchical organizations.
Memory functions are categorized by *purpose* (factual, experiential, working memory), while dynamics cover the lifecycle of memory via *formation*, *evolution*, and *retrieval* processes.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.12822.Title: Lemon: A Unified and Scalable 3D Multimodal Model for Universal Spatial Understanding
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.12822.Summary: LEMON, a unified transformer architecture, directly processes 3D point cloud patches and language tokens as a single sequence to achieve universal spatial understanding. This model sets new state-of-the-art results in 3D embodied interaction and scene spatial awareness benchmarks, outperforming existing 3D multimodal models and demonstrating competitive performance with 2D vision-language models.
Problem: Existing 3D Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) use fragmented architectures with separate, modality-specific encoders, leading to architectural imbalances and representational bottlenecks.
3D encoders typically suffer from limited pretraining on smaller datasets, hindering generalization and end-to-end optimization of 3D representations.
The inherent irregularity, sparsity, and unordered nature of 3D point cloud data complicates its effective integration into deep learning models and large language models.
Method: A unified transformer architecture processes both 3D point cloud patches and natural language tokens as a single, concatenated sequence, integrating 3D spatial information directly within the language model framework.

A hierarchical spatial partitioning scheme dynamically divides point clouds along Z, Y, and X axes into patches, which are then tokenized with specialized separator tokens to preserve spatial context and structure.

A progressive three-stage training curriculum systematically builds 3D spatial understanding, starting with object recognition, moving to object captioning, and culminating in scene spatial question answering.
Results: LEMON-7B achieved the highest GPT-4 score of 57.22 on 3D MM-Vet for embodied object QA and established new state-of-the-art on 3D-GRAND (74.32% binary accuracy), substantially outperforming previous 3D LMMs.

The model demonstrated strong 3D object generative recognition (59.20% accuracy, comparable to GPT-4V) and significantly surpassed other 3D multimodal models in object captioning using semantic metrics like Sentence-BERT and SimCSE.

Ablation studies confirmed the effectiveness of the unified architecture, the three-stage training curriculum, and the Z-Y-X spatial tokenization, with the model also showing robustness to sparse/noisy data and superior computational efficiency.
Takeaways: Unified transformer architecture consistently outperforms modular designs, demonstrating that separate 3D encoders often create a representational bottleneck and can even degrade performance.
LEMON provides the first systematic evidence of power-law scaling behavior in 3D LMMs, indicating predictable performance gains with increased model size and training data.

The proposed Z-Y-X hierarchical spatial ordering of patches with explicit separator tokens is crucial for effective scene-level spatial reasoning and significantly outperforms other tokenization strategies.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.12690.Title: Reassessing the Role of Supervised Fine-Tuning: An Empirical Study in VLM Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.12690.Summary: This study empirically re-evaluates Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning (RL) for Vision-Language Model (VLM) reasoning, demonstrating that SFT can be more effective for weaker models and data-efficient, while RL scales better with stronger models but is susceptible to deceptive rewards. It identifies conditional advantages for each approach, challenging the general "RL over SFT" belief.
Problem: The prevailing 'RL over SFT' narrative in VLM reasoning often claims RL is inherently superior for generalization, potentially underestimating SFT's role.
A lack of systematic, controlled comparisons between SFT and RL for VLM reasoning leads to potentially confounded results due to differing data sources or model setups.
Concerns exist that SFT might merely 'memorize' and potentially hinder subsequent RL optimization rather than fostering true reasoning capabilities.
Method: Conducted a systematic empirical study comparing SFT and RL using identical training data sources (up to 50K samples) and matched optimization setups to ensure fair evaluation.
Utilized open-source QwenVL series models (Qwen2-VL-2B/7B and Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B) to evaluate performance across different model capacities.
Implemented SFT (negative log-likelihood) and two representative RL algorithms (GRPO, DAPO) with verifiable, task-level rewards (exact correctness, format consistency).
Results: SFT consistently outperforms RL (GRPO) by approximately 2% on weaker VLMs (e.g., Qwen2-VL-2B/7B), while RL shows advantages primarily with stronger models (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL-7B).
SFT achieves reasoning performance comparable to or better than RL trained on 20K samples, using only 2K samples, highlighting its data efficiency.
RL training exhibits consistently increasing rewards, but test set accuracy often plateaus or declines, indicating 'deceptive rewards' and overfitting, a phenomenon stabilized by SFT pre-training.
Takeaways: The relative effectiveness of SFT and RL for VLM reasoning is conditional, depending on factors like model capacity and data scale, rather than one being universally superior.
SFT demonstrates high data efficiency, achieving strong reasoning performance with significantly less data than RL, and shows robust cross-modal transferability under appropriate data conditions.

RL optimization can be plagued by 'deceptive rewards,' where increasing training rewards do not consistently correlate with improved reasoning accuracy on unseen data due to reward hacking, though SFT initialization can mitigate this.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.12633.Title: DiG: Differential Grounding for Enhancing Fine-Grained Perception in Multimodal Large Language Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.12633.Summary: The DiG framework enhances Multimodal Large Language Models' fine-grained visual perception and precise spatial reasoning through a differential grounding task, leveraging an automated 3D rendering pipeline and curriculum-based reinforcement learning. This approach consistently improves performance across various perception, general multimodal, and visual grounding benchmarks.
Problem: Current Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle with fine-grained visual perception and precise spatial reasoning, often overlooking subtle visual details or changes.

Existing MLLM training methods and proxy tasks either lead to overspecialized models, rely on costly and limited manual annotations, or are not specifically designed to strengthen fine-grained perceptual sensitivity.
MLLMs frequently exhibit issues like visual hallucination or inaccurate localization due to insufficient supervision for discerning nuanced visual information.
Method: Introduces 'Differential Grounding (DiG)', a novel proxy task requiring MLLMs to identify and localize all subtle visual discrepancies between two highly similar images.

Develops a fully automated data generation pipeline using Blender 3D rendering to create scalable, perfectly annotated training data with controllable difficulty by programmatically modifying scene attributes.

Employs a reinforcement learning framework with a multi-component reward function, combining format adherence, F1 score (detection completeness), and mean IoU (spatial precision), optimized via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO).

Integrates a curriculum learning strategy that progressively increases task complexity, starting with single-difference, then multi-difference, and finally mixed-difficulty scenarios to ensure stable optimization and robust learning.
Results: DiG consistently improved the performance of Qwen3-VL models on perception-oriented benchmarks (e.g., +3.4 on HalBench and +2.1 on V* for the 8B model), demonstrating enhanced sensitivity to visual cues and reduced hallucination.

Models trained with DiG showed strong transferability, achieving consistent gains on general multimodal benchmarks (e.g., +2.2 on MMBench and +17.5 on MME for the 8B model), indicating improved overall multimodal reasoning.

DiG-trained models significantly outperformed baselines on fine-grained visual grounding benchmarks (RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, RefCOCOg) with average improvements of 2-3 points, confirming enhanced spatial localization capabilities.
Takeaways: Training MLLMs to explicitly localize subtle visual differences between similar images directly enhances their fine-grained perceptual and spatial reasoning abilities.

Automated 3D rendering is a scalable and cost-effective method for generating high-quality, diverse datasets with precise ground-truth annotations for fine-grained visual tasks, circumventing manual annotation limitations.

A curriculum-based reinforcement learning approach effectively mitigates sparse reward challenges in complex visual tasks, allowing MLLMs to acquire sophisticated perceptual skills incrementally and stably.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.12623.Title: Reasoning Within the Mind: Dynamic Multimodal Interleaving in Latent Space
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.12623.Summary: The DMLR framework, developed by researchers from UCSB, Stanford, and UCSC, introduces a test-time, training-free approach that dynamically refines latent representations and selectively injects visual information based on internal confidence to enhance Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) reasoning. It consistently outperformed baselines across seven diverse benchmarks, achieving, for example, average improvements of +4.5% in mathematics and +3.45% in visual reasoning for the R1-OneVision-7B model.
Problem: Existing textual-only MLLM reasoning (Semantic CoT) suffers from language bias and insufficient visual grounding, leading to hallucinations.
Tool-augmented reasoning methods introduce computational overhead and unstable tool invocation due to explicit visual generation or manipulation.
Prior latent MLLM reasoning relies on extra training or fixed visual injection positions, preventing adaptive allocation of reasoning effort based on actual need.
Method: A training-free, test-time framework that optimizes 'latent think tokens' within the MLLM's internal representation space using a REINFORCE-based policy gradient.
A confidence-guided reward function, derived from truncated entropy, provides intrinsic feedback to continuously refine these latent tokens, mimicking human self-correction.
A Dynamic Visual Injection Strategy (DVIS) allows the model to autonomously determine when and which relevant visual patches to revisit and inject, optimizing for confidence.
Results: DMLR-integrated models consistently outperformed all baselines across seven diverse multimodal reasoning benchmarks (e.g., MathVista, HallusionBench, ScienceQA), achieving the best performance on over 95% of tasks.

Demonstrated average performance gains of +4.5% in mathematics reasoning and +3.45% in visual reasoning for the R1-OneVision-7B model, while maintaining a more favorable balance between accuracy and inference efficiency.
Qualitative analyses showed DMLR enhanced visual grounding with stable, focused attention on relevant regions, and formed a compact, modality-independent cluster of optimized latent think tokens.
Takeaways: MLLMs exhibit uneven visual dependency during reasoning; only a small subset of tokens requires visual information, and stronger visual reliance correlates with higher accuracy.
The model's internal confidence, quantifiable via truncated entropy, serves as a reliable intrinsic signal for indicating reasoning quality, faithfulness, and visual grounding.
Dynamic interleaving of latent reasoning and selective visual attention, inspired by human cognition, can significantly enhance MLLM performance and efficiency without additional model training.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.11141.Title: Learning complete and explainable visual representations from itemized text supervision
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.11141.Summary: ItemizedCLIP provides a framework for learning complete and explainable visual representations from itemized text supervision, where each text item describes distinct visual findings. It achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot performance across medical imaging datasets like Brain MRI, Head CT, and Chest CT, demonstrating superior item independence and interpretability.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are primarily designed for 'multi-positive text supervision' where captions provide redundant descriptions of similar visual content.
Critical visual domains like medical imaging and remote sensing use 'itemized text supervision,' where multiple independent text items describe distinct visual findings within the same image.
Current VLM methods fail to capture both item independence (differentiating distinct findings) and representation completeness (encoding all findings) from such itemized annotations.
Method: ItemizedCLIP introduces a VLM framework with a multi-headed cross-attention module to generate text item-conditioned visual embeddings from visual patch representations.
It employs a suite of SigLIP-based objectives including Itemized Local Alignment (ILA) with Upweighting Worst Positive (UWP) and Masked Attention for completeness and robustness.
Inter-Item Separation (IIS) loss is specifically designed to enforce item independence by pushing apart text-conditioned visual representations from different items within the same image.
Results: ItemizedCLIP achieved significant gains in zero-shot performance, including a +6.8% mean AUC increase on UM220K Brain MRI and a +9.3% mean AUC increase on HeadCT240K, often surpassing linear probing of recent foundation models.
The model demonstrated strong item-level explainability, naturally generating attention maps that accurately localize text descriptions to corresponding visual regions.
Inter-Item Separation (IIS) loss quantitatively reduced mean Attention Map Similarity between different positive items, improving item differentiability and leading to more focused visual grounding.
Takeaways: Formalizing 'itemized text supervision' as a distinct VLM paradigm is crucial for domains where annotations describe independent visual findings rather than redundant ones.

Achieving both 'item independence' (differentiating distinct visual features for each item) and 'representation completeness' (encoding all items) is vital for accurate and trustworthy AI in high-stakes fields like medical diagnostics.

Tailored loss functions, such as Inter-Item Separation and Upweighting Worst Positive, are effective in learning fine-grained, localized, and comprehensive visual representations without explicit region supervision.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.10950.Title: E-RayZer: Self-supervised 3D Reconstruction as Spatial Visual Pre-training
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.10950.Summary: E-RayZer introduces a self-supervised framework for 3D reconstruction, employing explicit 3D Gaussian Splatting to learn camera parameters and scene geometry directly from unlabeled multi-view images. The system achieves competitive performance against supervised methods and outperforms prior self-supervised approaches, establishing itself as an effective spatial visual pre-training model.
Problem: Existing 3D vision models heavily rely on supervised learning, necessitating costly and often imperfect 3D annotations like ground-truth camera poses or dense depth maps.
Previous self-supervised 3D methods often learn 'superficial 3D awareness,' resorting to shortcut solutions like view interpolation rather than genuinely understanding physical 3D geometry.
There is a critical need for a foundation model in 3D vision that can effectively leverage vast quantities of unlabeled multi-view data to learn robust and transferable spatial representations.
Method: E-RayZer proposes a self-supervised feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting model that directly predicts camera intrinsics and extrinsics, alongside explicit 3D scene geometry, from unlabeled multi-view inputs.
The framework removes image index embeddings from the camera estimation transformer and utilizes a VGGT-style multi-view transformer, promoting true 3D understanding over view interpolation.

A novel learning curriculum, based on the visual overlap between input views, is introduced to stabilize training and ensure convergence for explicit 3D models, progressively introducing more challenging samples.
Results: E-RayZer significantly outperforms prior self-supervised methods like RayZer in camera pose estimation accuracy across multiple datasets and achieves comparable novel-view synthesis quality.
The model demonstrates performance on par with or superior to a re-implemented supervised VGGT* model on several out-of-domain datasets, particularly for stricter pose estimation metrics.

Pre-training with E-RayZer's learned weights leads to substantial performance improvements for supervised models and results in superior feature generalization on downstream tasks, including multi-view depth, pose, and flow estimation.
Takeaways: Explicit 3D geometry modeling with 3D Gaussian Splatting, coupled with differentiable rendering, compels the model to learn truly 3D-aware and geometrically grounded representations, effectively preventing shortcut solutions.
A fine-grained, visual-overlap-based learning curriculum is essential for stabilizing and efficiently training self-supervised explicit 3D reconstruction models from scratch.

Self-supervised pre-training with explicit 3D representations can yield performance comparable to, or even surpass, supervised methods on various 3D tasks, providing robust and transferable features for diverse downstream applications.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.10942.Title: VL-JEPA: Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture for Vision-language
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.10942.Summary: Researchers at Meta FAIR developed VL-JEPA, a Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture for vision-language tasks, which predicts abstract semantic embeddings rather than explicit tokens. This approach leads to improved computational efficiency and enables real-time applications through non-autoregressive prediction and selective decoding, while achieving competitive performance across classification, retrieval, and Visual Question Answering benchmarks.
Problem: Generative Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are computationally expensive and introduce high latency, making them unsuitable for real-time applications.
Existing generative VLMs complicate the learning process by predicting high-dimensional, surface-level linguistic variability in raw token space.
A unified, efficient architecture capable of handling diverse vision-language tasks in dynamic, real-time settings was lacking.
Method: VL-JEPA introduces a Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture that focuses on predicting abstract, low-dimensional latent space embeddings instead of explicit text tokens.
The model utilizes a four-component architecture: a visual X-Encoder, a query-conditioned Predictor, a textual Y-Encoder (for ground truth embeddings), and an inference-only Y-Decoder.
It employs an InfoNCE loss function for latent-space prediction, trained in two stages: query-free large-scale pretraining for alignment, followed by supervised finetuning for VQA capabilities.
Results: VL-JEPA achieved an average accuracy of 46.4% across 8 video classification datasets and an average recall@1 of 58.4% across 8 text-to-video retrieval datasets, outperforming existing generalist models with substantially less training data.
The 1.6B parameter `VL-JEPA_SFT` demonstrated competitive performance on discriminative VQA tasks (GQA, TallyQA, POPE), matching or outperforming many established VLM families.

Embedding-guided selective decoding reduced the number of text decoding operations by approximately 2.85x for long-form video streams while maintaining similar performance for action sequence recovery.
Takeaways: Predicting abstract embeddings in a latent space simplifies the learning objective by discarding task-irrelevant linguistic variability, enhancing computational efficiency and sample efficiency.
The non-autoregressive nature of embedding prediction, combined with selective decoding, significantly reduces latency, enabling real-time multimodal understanding for streaming data.
A unified JEPA framework successfully generalizes across diverse vision-language tasks, including classification, retrieval, and VQA, without requiring task-specific architectural modifications.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.10938.Title: Stronger Normalization-Free Transformers
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.10938.Summary: Researchers from Princeton, NYU, and Carnegie Mellon introduced Dynamic erf (Derf), a point-wise function that replaces traditional normalization layers in Transformers. Derf consistently achieved higher accuracy or lower error rates across various modalities, including an average of 0.6 percentage points higher top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K for ViT-Base/Large models and improved FID scores for Diffusion Transformers.
Problem: Traditional normalization layers (e.g., Batch Norm, Layer Norm) introduce computational overhead (memory, synchronization) and exhibit sensitivity to batch size, hindering efficiency and scalability.
Previous normalization-free methods primarily aimed to match the performance of normalization layers rather than surpass them, limiting their impact.
The underlying mathematical properties that make point-wise functions effective replacements for normalization were not fully understood.
Method: A systematic analysis of point-wise function properties (zero-centeredness, boundedness, center sensitivity, monotonicity) was conducted to derive design principles for stable training.

An extensive empirical search was performed for optimal point-wise functions based on these principles, leading to the identification of the error function (erf) with learnable parameters, termed Dynamic erf (Derf).
Derf was rigorously evaluated as a drop-in replacement for normalization layers across diverse Transformer architectures and tasks, including vision, speech, DNA, and language models.
Results: Derf consistently outperformed LayerNorm, RMSNorm, and Dynamic Tanh across all evaluated architectures and tasks, including ViT (ImageNet-1K), DiT (image generation), wav2vec 2.0 (speech), HyenaDNA/Caduceus (DNA), and GPT-2 (language).
On ViT-Base/Large models, Derf achieved up to 0.6 percentage points higher top-1 classification accuracy on ImageNet-1K compared to LayerNorm.
For Diffusion Transformers (DiT-L/4), Derf yielded a Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) score of 43.94, compared to 45.91 for LayerNorm, indicating superior image generation quality.
Takeaways: Effective normalization-free point-wise functions must be near zero-centered, bounded, center-sensitive, and monotonic to ensure stable convergence and high performance.
Point-wise functions like Derf exhibit reduced fitting capacity (higher training loss) compared to normalization layers, yet achieve superior downstream performance due to stronger generalization.
The specific mathematical form of the error function (erf), beyond a simple S-shape, contributes unique beneficial properties for model performance.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.10863.Title: MMSI-Video-Bench: A Holistic Benchmark for Video-Based Spatial Intelligence
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.10863.Summary: Researchers from Shanghai AI Laboratory and several universities developed MMSI-Video-Bench, a holistic and human-annotated benchmark for video-based spatial intelligence. The benchmark evaluates multimodal large language models (MLLMs) across perception, planning, prediction, and cross-video reasoning tasks, revealing that current MLLMs achieve only 38.0% accuracy compared to 96.4% for human performance.
Problem: Existing benchmarks for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) lack comprehensive evaluation of spatial intelligence from continuous video inputs, often focusing on discrete images or limited aspects of spatial understanding.

Many current benchmarks rely on automatic question generation, which can lead to limited diversity, biases, and susceptibility to template overfitting, thereby hindering the assessment of true reasoning capabilities.

There is a need for a rigorous, holistic benchmark that can assess a full spectrum of spatial cognitive abilities, including perception, planning, prediction, and complex cross-video reasoning, crucial for developing embodied AI assistants.
Method: Developed MMSI-Video-Bench, a multi-level benchmark featuring 1,106 fully human-annotated multiple-choice questions designed by 3DV experts, covering five main categories of spatial intelligence.
Curated a diverse dataset of approximately 20,000 video clips from 25 public sources and newly recorded in-house videos, ensuring broad coverage of real-world scenarios (indoor, outdoor, robotics).
Established a multi-stage cross-evaluation protocol with 100% approval from reviewing researchers to ensure high-quality, unambiguous, and challenging questions requiring non-trivial reasoning.
Results: The best-performing MLLM, Google’s Gemini 3 Pro, achieved only 38.0% accuracy on MMSI-Video-Bench, while human performance averaged 96.4%.

A detailed error analysis showed that Geometric Reasoning Errors were the most prevalent, particularly in Spatial Construction tasks, highlighting persistent struggles with inferring basic spatial relations.

Uniform frame sampling significantly outperformed consecutive sampling or adaptive keyframe sampling, demonstrating that broad temporal coverage is crucial for complex spatial and temporal reasoning in video-based tasks.
Takeaways: Current state-of-the-art MLLMs exhibit a substantial performance gap of nearly 60% compared to human ability on video-based spatial intelligence tasks, indicating significant room for improvement.

MLLMs struggle across all categories of spatial intelligence, including Spatial Construction, Motion Understanding, Planning, Prediction, and Cross-Video Reasoning, with Prediction tasks being the most challenging.

Neither providing more visual information (Sufficient-Coverage) nor using Chain-of-Thought prompting consistently improved MLLM performance, and attempts to integrate 3D spatial cues or use spatially fine-tuned models did not generalize effectively.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.10554.Title: Grounding Everything in Tokens for Multimodal Large Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.10554.Summary: GETok enhances Multimodal Large Language Models' 2D spatial reasoning by introducing a lexical spatial representation with learnable grid and offset tokens for native object grounding. The method achieves state-of-the-art performance in referring expression segmentation and demonstrates improvements in complex real-world driving tasks.
Problem: Existing MLLMs struggle with precise 2D spatial grounding due to the loss of fine-grained spatial information during image tokenization.
Current spatial representations (text-based, patch-based, 1D bin-based) are inefficient, ambiguous, lack unified handling for various formats, and often require architectural modifications.
MLLMs typically make one-shot spatial predictions without an inherent mechanism for iterative self-correction, limiting precision in complex scenarios.
Method: GETok augments MLLM vocabulary with learnable Grid Tokens for coarse spatial anchoring and Offset Tokens for fine-grained, iterative refinement and self-correction, directly integrating into autoregressive architectures.
A novel greedy mask-to-token conversion algorithm and an offset-aware dataset construction method are used for Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) without altering the MLLM architecture.

A self-improving Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework employs two-stage GRPO optimization with geometry-aware reward functions to leverage GETok's structured 2D lattice for stable policy learning and efficient exploration.
Results: GETok-RL achieved state-of-the-art performance in Referring Expression Segmentation, showing a +4.5% gain over GETok-SFT on ReasonSeg and RefCOCO datasets, with offset tokens improving performance by +1.0% (SFT) and +1.5% (RL).

In a real-world driving case study, GETok outperformed traditional visual prompts, improving traffic sign color recognition by +12.24% and achieving a +10% F1-score gain for curved lane polyline detection over coordinate-based methods.

A 32x32 grid with offset tokens achieved comparable or superior performance to a 64x64 grid while significantly reducing token length and vocabulary overhead, demonstrating the efficiency of the offset mechanism.
Takeaways: GETok's 2D grid tokens natively encode spatial topology, outperforming 1D text coordinates and bin tokens by enabling smoother, topology-aware attention maps and reducing format brittleness.

Offset tokens provide fine-grained precision and iterative self-correction with minimal vocabulary overhead, achieving performance comparable to higher-resolution grids at a significantly reduced computational cost.

The structured 2D lattice of GETok creates a low-entropy action space, making it highly amenable to GRPO, leading to accelerated convergence and consistently higher reward levels in RL for spatial reasoning tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.10359.Title: Tool-Augmented Spatiotemporal Reasoning for Streamlining Video Question Answering Task
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.10359.Summary: Tsinghua University researchers developed the "STAR" framework, which augments Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) with a Video Toolkit and a spatiotemporal reasoning strategy to enhance video question answering. This approach yielded an 8.2% accuracy increase over GPT-4o on the VideoMME dataset and achieved substantial efficiency gains by reducing runtime and processed frames across various benchmarks.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle with simultaneously discerning spatial relationships within frames and understanding complex temporal dynamics across video frames.
Existing tool-augmented LLMs for VideoQA often use unidimensional tools, lack balanced tool management, and have insufficient scheduling strategies, leading to inefficiencies and reasoning shortcuts.
The inability to progressively localize a 3D Region of Interest (RoI) in video content hinders deep understanding and robust, step-by-step reasoning.
Method: A comprehensive and extensible Video Toolkit was constructed, comprising approximately 22 plug-and-play tools categorized into temporal, spatial, and general-purpose functionalities, using lightweight specialized CV models and natural language interfaces.
The Spatiotemporal Reasoning Framework (STAR) was proposed, an agentic and iterative framework built on ReAct principles, which strategically controls tool invocation using GPT-4o as an LLM Planner.

STAR employs an alternating spatiotemporal tool invocation pattern to progressively narrow down the 3D Region of Interest in the video, guiding the MLLM through deliberate, step-by-step visual reasoning to overcome 'toolchain shortcuts'.
Results: STAR achieved a 70.0% accuracy on VideoMME, an 8.2% gain over GPT-4o (61.8%), with comparable input frames and reducing runtime from several minutes to 15.8 seconds per video.
On challenging LongVideoBench, STAR improved accuracy by 4.6% over GPT-4o (57.2% vs. 52.6%) while significantly reducing the number of processed frames and overall runtime for long-form videos.

Ablation studies confirmed the spatiotemporal-interleaved strategy outperformed 'No Constraints' (61.2% accuracy) and 'Spatiotemporal Disentanglement' (68.6% accuracy), achieving the highest accuracy (70.0%) and frame efficiency (30.2 frames processed) on VideoMME.
Takeaways: Interleaving spatial and temporal tool invocation is crucial for effective video understanding, facilitating progressive 3D Region of Interest (RoI) localization and preventing reasoning shortcuts by forcing comprehensive analysis.

Augmenting MLLMs with specialized perception tools leads to more accurate and robust outputs for specific tasks (e.g., object detection, action localization) compared to relying solely on direct MLLM inference.

A training-free, agentic framework that strategically manages a diverse toolkit can significantly boost MLLM performance and efficiency on complex video understanding tasks without requiring core model retraining.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.09924.Title: ReViSE: Towards Reason-Informed Video Editing in Unified Models with Self-Reflective Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.09924.Summary: The ReViSE framework from HKUST, Zhejiang University, Fudan University, and Tongyi Lab enables video models to perform edits requiring implicit reasoning by introducing a self-reflective learning paradigm. It achieved a 32% improvement in the "Overall score" on its new RVE-Bench for reason-informed editing and demonstrated robust performance on conventional video editing tasks.
Problem: Existing instruction-guided video editing models struggle with "reason-informed" editing, which demands deeper understanding of physical plausibility, causal dynamics, and common sense.
Current video editing datasets primarily focus on literal transformations, lacking the complexity needed to train and evaluate models for reasoning-aware tasks.
A disconnect exists between a model's internal Vision-Language Model (VLM) for understanding and its generative components, preventing effective transfer of semantic and world knowledge.
Method: The paper introduces the Reason-Informed Video Editing (RVE) task and constructs RVE-Bench, a new benchmark and training dataset created by re-captioning existing data with reasoning prompts and generating from movie data.
It proposes ReViSE, a Self-Reflective Reasoning framework built on a unified model architecture that leverages pre-trained VLMs and generative diffusion models.
ReViSE employs its internal VLM as a critic, providing intrinsic, QA-based feedback to refine the generator's reasoning behavior through Unified Semantic Optimization (USO).
Results: ReViSE achieved a 32% improvement in the "Overall score" on the RVE-Bench's "Reasoning-Informed Video Editing" subset, with a 38% improvement specifically for temporal reasoning.

It consistently outperformed state-of-the-art baselines across all reasoning categories (Causal, Temporal, Spatial, Commonsense) on RVE-Bench and demonstrated generality on conventional Ditto-1M data with a 36.7% gain in Overall score.
Ablation studies confirmed the superiority of the Unified Semantic Optimization (USO) approach and validated the internal VLM's reliability as a critic, showing 74.6% decision agreement with GPT-4o.
Takeaways: Integrating an internal VLM as a self-reflective critic effectively bridges the gap between understanding and generation in video editing, eliminating the need for expensive external reward models.
The Unified Semantic Optimization (USO) objective, which combines flow matching loss with a distinct reasoning loss, is crucial for balancing generative fidelity with high-level semantic alignment.

Reason-informed video editing necessitates explicit evaluation metrics beyond pixel-level accuracy, leading to the development of a GPT-4o-based framework assessing semantic consistency and perceptual quality.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.09441.Title: Representation Calibration and Uncertainty Guidance for Class-Incremental Learning based on Vision Language Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.09441.Summary: Researchers from Sun Yat-sen University and HKUST developed a VLM-based class-incremental learning framework that mitigates cross-task class confusion and enables robust inference in exemplar-free settings. The method, employing a Mixture of Projectors for representation calibration and uncertainty guidance during inference, consistently surpassed existing methods on benchmarks like CIFAR100 and ImageNet-R, improving Last-A on CIFAR100 by 6.62% over memory-based methods.
Problem: Deep learning models struggle with catastrophic forgetting when acquiring knowledge about new classes sequentially in Class-Incremental Learning (CIL).
Task-wise fine-tuning of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) often creates disparate feature spaces, leading to cross-task class confusion and image-text misalignment during inference.

Selecting the most appropriate task-specific feature representation for a test image is challenging when its originating task is unknown, particularly in exemplar-free CIL settings where no old data is retained.
Method: A two-stage training framework utilizing task-specific adapters to learn new knowledge for each incremental task while keeping the pre-trained CLIP VLM frozen.
Cross-task representation calibration is performed using a Mixture of Projectors (MoP), which maps features from diverse task-specific spaces into a unified, task-shared feature space.
An uncertainty-guided inference strategy leverages prediction entropy to select the most appropriate calibrated feature from multiple task-specific branches for final classification.
Results: Achieved state-of-the-art performance across diverse benchmarks including CIFAR100, ImageNet-R, Cars196, and Skin40, consistently outperforming both memory-based and exemplar-free baselines.

On CIFAR100 in a 10-task setting, the method improved Last-A by 6.62% and 7.09% over memory-based PROOF and PR-CLIP, respectively, and by over 10% Last-M on ImageNet-R (20-task) compared to prompt-based methods.

The framework demonstrated robustness to varying hyperparameters and generalized effectively to different VLM backbones (OpenCLIP, SigLip), maintaining efficiency with a moderate number of trainable parameters.
Takeaways: Task-specific adapters, while efficient for individual tasks, necessitate a subsequent calibration step to unify their disparate feature spaces and alleviate cross-task confusion.

Pseudo-features, sampled from approximated Gaussian distributions of past class embeddings, can effectively substitute real data for training a shared representation module (MoP) in exemplar-free CIL.
Prediction uncertainty, quantified by entropy, serves as a reliable mechanism to guide the selection of the most suitable task-specific model output during inference in multi-task continual learning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.09322.Title: Self-Supervised Learning with Gaussian Processes
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.09322.Summary: This work introduces Gaussian Process Self-Supervised Learning (GPSSL), a framework that integrates Gaussian Processes and generalized Bayesian inference to learn data representations without relying on explicit data augmentation. It explicitly quantifies uncertainty in these representations, leading to improved performance in downstream classification tasks, particularly for tabular and spatial transcriptomics data.
Problem: Most Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) methods heavily depend on data augmentation for positive pair generation, limiting their applicability to diverse data types like tabular data, time series, or text where augmentations are difficult to define.

Existing SSL approaches produce deterministic point estimates for representations, lacking uncertainty quantification, which leads to overconfidence and hinders their utility in risk-sensitive applications.
Method: GPSSL employs Gaussian Processes (GPs) with a generalized Bayesian inference framework to learn a distribution over representation functions rather than deterministic mappings.
The GP prior's kernel function intrinsically encodes data similarity, eliminating the need for explicit data augmentation to create positive pairs.
A VICReg-inspired loss function (variance and covariance terms) is minimized using generalized variational inference, augmented with inducing points for scalability to larger datasets.
Results: GPSSL successfully provides meaningful uncertainty quantification, with standard deviations in learned representations varying inversely with training data density on synthetic tasks.

Across UCI tabular datasets and real-world spatial transcriptomics data, GPSSL-full consistently achieved the best performance in downstream classification based on accuracy, ROC AUC, and Area Under Risk-Coverage (AURC) metrics.

In spatial transcriptomics applications, GPSSL effectively integrated multi-modal features, produced interpretable cell-type predictions with informative uncertainty maps, and demonstrated the lowest mean squared error for predicted probabilities.
Takeaways: The Gaussian Process prior, through its kernel, implicitly acts as an invariance loss, enforcing smoothness and similarity in representations based on input similarity, thereby removing the need for augmentation-based invariance terms.

GPSSL establishes a theoretical connection to classical Kernel PCA, demonstrating that for a 1D representation, its maximum a posteriori estimate is equivalent to the first principal component of Kernel PCA.

Propagating the full uncertainty from the learned representation distribution (GPSSL-full) consistently yields superior performance in downstream tasks compared to using only deterministic mean representations (GPSSL-mean).

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.08889.Title: No Labels, No Problem: Training Visual Reasoners with Multimodal Verifiers
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.08889.Summary: VALOR, developed at Caltech, presents an annotation-free framework that trains visual reasoners by employing multimodal verifiers to jointly tune an LLM for reasoning and specialized vision tools for visual grounding. This approach achieves superior performance on various visual reasoning benchmarks, including a 6.5% average improvement over direct-answer VLMs on OMNI3D-BENCH.
Problem: Existing visual reasoning methods, like language-only CoT, often exhibit weak visual understanding and logical errors, requiring extensive and costly labeled supervision data.
Program-synthesis approaches struggle with faulty program logic and misaligned pre-trained vision specialists, limiting their adaptability to complex spatial reasoning tasks.

The high cost and labor involved in collecting large-scale, high-quality, and domain-specific labeled data for both reasoning and object annotations bottleneck the development of robust visual reasoning systems.
Method: VALOR proposes an annotation-free training framework that jointly optimizes an LLM for complex reasoning (generating plans and executable programs) and vision specialist tools for accurate visual grounding.

An LLM verifier (Gemini-2.5-Flash) provides structured reward signals based on six criteria (e.g., logic, spatial adherence) to guide the training of the reasoning LLM (Qwen3-8B) via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO).

A VLM verifier (GPT-5-mini) generates high-quality pseudo-annotations for object detection by filtering and refining initial detector (GroundingDINO) predictions through a three-stage pipeline, enabling scalable, label-free fine-tuning of the grounding model.
Results: VALOR achieved an average 6.5% accuracy improvement on OMNI3D-BENCH compared to state-of-the-art direct-answer VLMs, scoring 44.0% versus 35.0% for GPT-4o, demonstrating superior 3D spatial reasoning.
The framework consistently outperformed other program synthesis methods and RL-tuned VLMs on benchmarks like OMNI3D-BENCH (44.0% vs. 38.9% for VADAR) and ROBOSPATIAL (69.5% vs. 64.9% for ViGoRL).

The VLM verifier pipeline generated 30,826 high-quality pseudo-annotations from unlabeled images, leading to substantial gains in visual grounding accuracy, with an 8.3% increase on COUNTBENCHQA and 7.7% on ROBOSPATIAL compared to reasoning-only training.
Takeaways: Powerful generative models, even when imperfect as generators, can serve as highly effective 'critics' or 'verifiers' to provide structured feedback for training without requiring ground truth labels.

A synergistic, multimodal approach that uses LLM verifiers to refine high-level reasoning and VLM verifiers to improve low-level visual grounding can lead to robust and accurate visual reasoning capabilities.

Reinforcement learning, specifically GRPO, is a more effective optimization strategy than supervised fine-tuning for leveraging sparse, verifier-generated reward signals to enhance complex reasoning skills in LLMs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.08511.Title: Thinking with Images via Self-Calling Agent
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.08511.Summary: Researchers at the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences developed the Self-Calling Chain-of-Thought (sCoT) paradigm, which reformulates interleaved multimodal reasoning as a language-only CoT where a main MLLM agent self-calls virtual subagent replicas for visual subtasks. The approach achieved 1.2% higher performance on the V* benchmark and 1.9% higher on HR-Bench 4K compared to DeepEyes, utilizing approximately 75% fewer GPU hours during training.
Problem: Optimizing interleaved multimodal Chain-of-Thought (iMCoT) for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) through reinforcement learning is highly challenging and resource-intensive.
There is a scarcity of high-quality, tightly interleaved multimodal reasoning corpora needed for training advanced MLLMs.
MLLMs often experience performance degradation and heavy computational burden when processing ultra-high-resolution images or integrating cues across multiple images in iMCoT.
Method: The Self-Calling Chain-of-Thought (sCoT) paradigm re-conceptualizes iMCoT into a language-only CoT, where visual interactions are mediated by 'self-calling' to virtual subagent replicas.

A main MLLM agent decomposes complex visual queries into atomic subtasks (e.g., grounding, OCR) and invokes subagents, which are weight-shared replicas, using a structured tool-calling protocol with parameters like task type, prompt, and bounding box.

An end-to-end agentic reinforcement learning framework, utilizing Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and a specifically designed reward function, optimizes the main agent's planning and orchestration of these self-calling interactions.
Results: SubagentVL (sCoT) consistently outperformed state-of-the-art iMCoT approaches like DeepEyes, achieving a 1.2% improvement on the V* benchmark and 1.9% on HR-Bench 4K.
The sCoT framework demonstrated significant training efficiency, achieving better results with approximately 75% fewer GPU hours and more constrained resources compared to DeepEyes.

SubagentVL showed a notable improvement in hallucination benchmarks (POPE) and exhibited distinct training dynamics that evolved from direct problem-solving to learning diverse subagent calling strategies.
Takeaways: The performance improvement in complex visual reasoning largely stems from learning an effective subagent-calling strategy and orchestration of existing visual capabilities, rather than directly enhancing the base MLLM's low-level perception.

Strict constraints on tool-calling arguments (task type, prompt, bounding box) and an ordering constraint in the reward function (tool calls must precede the final answer) are essential for stable and non-degenerate agentic learning.

Training data focused on fine-grained visual discrimination and spatially localized structures is most beneficial for sCoT's region-based perception and tool-calling strategies, while abstract reasoning data can be detrimental.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.08228.Title: MM-CoT:A Benchmark for Probing Visual Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Multimodal Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.08228.Summary: Researchers from Sun Yat-sen University and industry partners introduced MM-CoT, a diagnostic benchmark designed to evaluate visual grounding and logical coherence in Chain-of-Thought reasoning for multimodal models. The benchmark reveals that state-of-the-art models like GPT-5 achieve only 19.47% accuracy on verification tasks, highlighting a substantial gap between their generative fluency and genuine reasoning fidelity.
Problem: Existing multimodal Chain-of-Thought benchmarks primarily focus on generating plausible answers and fluent rationales, overlooking the verification of visual grounding and logical coherence.
Multimodal models often produce explanations that are linguistically plausible but unfaithful to visual evidence, leading to hallucination or misinterpretation of visual cues.
Current evaluation methods fail to diagnose specific reasoning failures where models might rely on linguistic shortcuts or dataset priors without true visual understanding.
Method: MM-CoT was developed as a novel, large-scale diagnostic benchmark that re-frames multimodal CoT reasoning as a discriminative verification task.
A triadic event-chain format (A→B→C) was designed, requiring models to simultaneously satisfy visual grounding and logical coherence for each step.

The benchmark uses a 'Generate-then-Disturb' pipeline, leveraging GPT-4o for generating valid chains and adversarial distractors (visually inconsistent or logically incoherent), followed by rigorous human verification.
Results: Leading multimodal models, including proprietary ones like GPT-5 (19.47% accuracy) and open-source models like Qwen2.5-VL-72B (32% accuracy), perform significantly below human experts (82.57% accuracy) on MM-CoT.
Performance on video tasks notably degrades with increased temporal span and complexity, indicating limitations in current LVLMs for genuine causal event reconstruction.

Utilizing Chain-of-Thought and Reflective Reasoning paradigms consistently improved model performance (e.g., GPT-5's video extreme tasks improved from 7.54% to 13.82% with Reflective Reasoning), validating the benchmark's sensitivity to enhanced reasoning structures.
Takeaways: Despite their generative fluency, current state-of-the-art multimodal models demonstrate significant deficiencies in verifying true visual grounding and logical coherence, falling far behind human performance.
MM-CoT successfully differentiates model capabilities, exposing specific challenges in multi-step reasoning for images and cross-frame state tracking for videos.
The benchmark tasks genuinely require multimodal perception, as removing visual signals dramatically reduces model accuracy, preventing reliance on purely linguistic patterns.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.07733.Title: SpatialDreamer: Incentivizing Spatial Reasoning via Active Mental Imagery
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.07733.Summary: SpatialDreamer presents a reinforcement learning framework that endows multimodal large language models with active spatial mental simulation capabilities via iterative exploration and visual imagination. This approach, incorporating a Geometric Policy Optimization algorithm, established new top performances on various spatial reasoning benchmarks.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) exhibit fragility in complex spatial reasoning tasks demanding mental simulation, such as object counting with occlusions or perspective-taking.

Current methods either rely on passive observation of spatial data or employ external, manually configured test-time scaling approaches, failing to internalize active spatial mental imagery within the MLLM.

Training MLLMs for multi-step, long-horizontal reasoning via standard Reinforcement Learning (RL) is hindered by sparse trajectory-level reward signals, making efficient learning of exploration policies difficult.
Method: The SpatialDreamer framework implements an agentic reinforcement learning approach that enables MLLMs to actively explore and reason through an iterative `think-imagine-answer` loop, leveraging an external world model (Stable Virtual Camera) to generate novel egocentric views.

Geometric Policy Optimization (GeoPO) introduces a tree-structured sampling scheme and a hybrid reward design, incorporating dense step-level rewards and geometric penalties, to stabilize training and encourage geometrically plausible action sequences.

A Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) dataset, SpatialDreamer-SFT, is constructed using single-pass and error-injection-based reflective reasoning samples to bootstrap the MLLM with preliminary agentic imagination behaviors.
Results: SpatialDreamer achieved state-of-the-art performance on the SAT benchmark, with 93.9% average accuracy on SAT-Real and 92.5% on SAT-Synthesized, surpassing generalist and specialized MLLMs.

The model established a new state-of-the-art overall score of 84.9% on MindCube-Tiny, representing a 55.6% absolute improvement over the Qwen2.5-VL-7B baseline, demonstrating strong active mental imagery capabilities.

Ablation studies confirmed that GeoPO significantly outperforms standard GRPO (e.g., +5.5% on MindCube-Tiny) and that both the geometric penalty and the comprehensive SFT dataset are critical for achieving optimal performance and efficient training.
Takeaways: Equipping MLLMs with active mental imagery, where they iteratively imagine and integrate novel views generated by a world model, allows them to overcome the limitations of static single-view perception for complex spatial reasoning.

Geometric Policy Optimization (GeoPO)'s hybrid reward system, which provides dense step-level feedback and penalizes geometrically sub-optimal actions, effectively addresses reward sparsity and ensures efficient, stable learning for multi-step reasoning.

A carefully curated Supervised Fine-Tuning dataset, including reflective reasoning samples, is essential for pre-training MLLMs to adopt the iterative `think-imagine-answer` agentic reasoning paradigm and develop self-correction capabilities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.07203.Title: MMRPT: MultiModal Reinforcement Pre-Training via Masked Vision-Dependent Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.07203.Summary: A multimodal reinforcement pre-training framework, MMRPT, enhances visual reasoning in MLLMs by integrating masked vision-dependent reasoning and reinforcement learning during the pre-training phase. This method demonstrates consistent zero-shot performance gains across various benchmarks and significantly improves model robustness by preventing degradation on out-of-distribution tasks after specialized fine-tuning.
Problem: Current MLLMs exhibit descriptive bias from image-caption pair pre-training, leading to reliance on surface linguistic cues over genuine visual understanding.
This bias manifests as visual hallucination, shallow cross-modal alignment, and limited abstraction abilities when reasoning about visual content.
Pre-training objectives often fail to adequately foster active, inference-driven visual reasoning, hindering deeper understanding of fine-grained or implicit visual information.
Method: A novel masked multimodal reinforcement pre-training (MMRPT) framework is introduced, operating in two main stages: data construction and reinforcement-guided pre-training.
An automated, attention-driven data construction pipeline identifies and masks vision-dependent language units in captions, ensuring that masked segments genuinely require visual reasoning.

Reinforcement learning is integrated directly into pre-training, rewarding explicit reasoning traces and accurate reconstruction of masked visual content, using metrics like exact match and strict prefix token matching.
Results: MMRPT-enhanced models achieved consistent zero-shot performance gains, typically 0.5-1% absolute improvement, across most multimodal reasoning benchmarks.
Crucially, MMRPT pre-training provided a more robust initialization, preventing "pronounced degradation" on out-of-distribution tasks after supervised fine-tuning, unlike standard base models.
When fine-tuned on domain-specific data, MMRPT-pretrained models maintained strong out-of-distribution generalization while still achieving comparable or superior in-domain performance.
Takeaways: Cross-attention patterns in specific MLLM decoder layers (upper-middle) are highly indicative of vision-dependent textual segments, enabling effective automated data construction.
Employing a high-capacity text-only LLM to refine mask targets alongside MLLM cross-attention ensures that masked tokens truly necessitate visual evidence, preventing reliance on linguistic priors.

Directly incorporating reinforcement learning during pre-training, guided by structured outputs and a reward function combining format and answer correctness, fosters active visual inference and deeper semantic grounding.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.06835.Title: Decouple to Generalize: Context-First Self-Evolving Learning for Data-Scarce Vision-Language Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.06835.Summary: The DoGe framework from Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory and collaborators introduces a context-first self-evolving learning approach that decouples cognitive processes for data-scarce vision-language reasoning. It achieves stable performance improvements of 5.7% for 3B-series models and 2.3% for 7B-series models across seven benchmarks, while enhancing policy exploration and mitigating reward hacking.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) struggle with data scarcity in specialized domains, making RL post-training prohibitively expensive due to high annotation costs.
Existing data synthesis and self-rewarding methods for VLMs suffer from limited data distributions, poor alignment with reasoning objectives, and 'reward hacking' leading to policy entropy collapse.
Current VLM supervision often overlooks rich contextual information in problem statements, reducing learning to superficial question-answering loops without fostering generalizable reasoning.
Method: Introduces DoGe (Decouple to Generalize), a dual-decoupling framework that separates the VLM's cognitive process into a Thinker and a Solver component.
Employs a two-stage Reinforcement Learning (RL) post-training approach, where the Thinker is trained on question-masked context and the Solver evaluates its generated analysis.
Implements an iterative curriculum data synthesis pipeline to continuously generate diverse and challenging multimodal training data, adapting to the model's evolving capabilities.
Results: DoGe achieves stable self-evolution with an average performance increase of 5.7% for 3B-series models and 2.3% for 7B-series models across seven benchmarks after three iterations.
The framework enhances general visual reasoning capabilities and reduces hallucination, demonstrating an average improvement of 2.0% on the HallBench benchmark.
DoGe effectively increases initial policy entropy and maintains higher entropy throughout training compared to naive GRPO, promoting better exploration and preventing policy entropy collapse.
Takeaways: Decoupling the cognitive process into a context-analyzing Thinker and a problem-solving Solver helps prevent reward hacking and fosters deeper, more generalizable reasoning.
Training the Thinker to first understand contextual information, rewarded by the Solver's performance on the original problem, guides the model toward high-level thinking patterns.
Continuously synthesizing challenging, domain-specific data, informed by both general knowledge and 'occasionally solvable' problems, enables stable self-evolution in data-scarce environments.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.06281.Title: Unleashing the Intrinsic Visual Representation Capability of Multimodal Large Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.06281.Summary: A framework named LaVer strengthens the intrinsic visual modeling capability of Multimodal Large Language Models by integrating direct visual supervisory signals in the LLM's latent semantic space. This approach enhances visual reasoning, improves visual attention, and yields consistent performance improvements across various multimodal benchmarks, including a 19.22% gain on OCR-Bench.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) exhibit a "modality imbalance," often underutilizing visual information and prioritizing textual cues.
This imbalance leads to degraded visual performance and an increased propensity for visual hallucinations not grounded in the visual input.

Current MLLM training paradigms, reliant on "next-text-token-prediction," cause visual tokens to lose discriminative power in deeper layers, resulting in "progressive visual representation homogenization."
Method: Introduces Latent Visual Reconstruction (LaVer), a masked image modeling approach applied to vision tokens within the LLM's joint latent semantic space, leveraging an EMA teacher for direct visual supervision.
Incorporates a mixed attention mechanism and 2D-Rotary Position Embeddings (2D-RoPE) to enhance spatial awareness and better align visual processing with image structure.
Employs Clipped Gram-Anchoring (CGA), an asymmetric regularizer, to prevent visual feature inconsistency and foster the learning of discriminative visual representations.
Results: LaVer consistently achieved performance improvements across diverse multimodal benchmarks, including a 19.22% gain on OCR-Bench and 6.72% on MMVP when using SigLIP 2.
The framework demonstrated broad generalizability across various vision encoders and robust scalability across different model sizes (1.5B, 3B, 7B) and data volumes.
Qualitative and quantitative analyses confirmed enhanced visual attention allocation and improved cross-modal synergy, while preserving the model's core language capabilities.
Takeaways: The "modality imbalance issue" in MLLMs stems from insufficient direct visual supervision, leading to a loss of discriminative power in visual representations over deeper layers.
Masked Image Modeling (MIM) at the latent semantic level of the LLM, coupled with a student-teacher framework, offers effective direct visual supervision.

Direct reconstruction loss alone can lead to "visual feature inconsistency," highlighting the need for asymmetric regularization like Clipped Gram-Anchoring to encourage discriminative feature learning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.06104.Title: ARC-AGI Without Pretraining
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.06104.Summary: CompressARC, developed by researchers at Carnegie Mellon University, addresses the ARC-AGI benchmark by achieving 20% accuracy on evaluation puzzles without any pretraining, learning entirely at inference time from the target puzzle. It leverages a custom equivariant neural network and the Minimum Description Length principle to discover abstract reasoning patterns with extreme data efficiency.
Problem: The ARC-AGI benchmark poses a challenge for abstract visual reasoning, requiring rapid skill acquisition and generalization from minimal input-output examples.
Prevailing state-of-the-art methods, particularly those based on Large Language Models, heavily rely on massive pretraining data and extensive computational resources.
Directly applying information-theoretic principles like Minimum Description Length (MDL) for program discovery is computationally intractable.
Method: CompressARC reframes ARC-AGI as a "code-golfing" problem, aiming to find the shortest self-contained program capable of generating a given puzzle, guided by the Minimum Description Length (MDL) principle.

It employs an inference-time learning approach for each individual puzzle, approximating MDL optimization using a differentiable loss function composed of KL divergence (for seed length) and cross-entropy (for reconstruction error).

A custom, parameter-efficient (76K parameters) neural network architecture is utilized, featuring strong inductive biases such as equivariance to permutations, rotations, and flips, and processing information across "multitensors" of varying ranks.
Results: The model correctly solved 20% of evaluation set puzzles and 34.75% of training set puzzles (with 2 allowed guesses) without any pretraining or use of the ARC-AGI training set.
CompressARC demonstrates extreme data efficiency, performing all its "learning" purely at inference time, using only the single target puzzle as input data.

Qualitative analysis shows the system generalizes to a diverse range of ARC-AGI puzzles, performing tasks like color assignment, infilling, cropping, connecting dots, and identifying pixel adjacencies.
Takeaways: Abstract reasoning and generalization can be achieved with extreme data efficiency, challenging the conventional necessity of massive pretraining for complex AI capabilities.

The Minimum Description Length principle can be effectively operationalized in deep learning through differentiable approximations, providing a practical link between information compression and intelligent behavior.
Carefully engineered architectural inductive biases, such as equivariance and multitensor processing, are crucial for enabling rapid, few-shot generalization from extremely limited data.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.05665.Title: Interleaved Latent Visual Reasoning with Selective Perceptual Modeling
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.05665.Summary: Researchers from a collaborative team including China University of Geosciences and the University of Southern California developed Interleaved Latent Visual Reasoning (ILVR), a framework that enables Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to perform dynamic, multi-step visual reasoning by operating entirely in a latent space. This approach reduces inference latency by 8x to 18x compared to pixel-based methods while achieving state-of-the-art performance and strong generalization across various reasoning benchmarks.
Problem: Existing interleaved image-text reasoning approaches in MLLMs are computationally expensive due to repeated re-encoding of pixel-dense images during multi-step processes.

Current latent visual reasoning methods are typically single-step or over-compress visual features, failing to capture dynamic intermediate state evolution or retaining crucial fine-grained perceptual details.
The trade-off between generative fidelity and reasoning performance limits dynamic visualization methods in MLLMs.
Method: The Interleaved Latent Visual Reasoning (ILVR) framework processes dynamic visual feedback entirely in a continuous latent space, generating and updating latent representations without pixel-level re-encoding.

A self-supervised strategy with a momentum teacher model constructs context-aware queries to perform selective perceptual modeling, extracting and supervising the MLLM with only the most relevant visual features.

A two-stage learning process trains the model first for precise perceptual grounding (latent alignment) and then for flexible self-generated latent states (latent relaxation) to serve as internal priors for textual generation.
Results: ILVR achieved state-of-the-art accuracy on in-distribution tasks, outperforming the Mirage latent reasoning method by up to 5.2% on the COMT benchmark using the Qwen3-VL-8B backbone.

The framework demonstrated robust generalization, surpassing Mirage by an average of 3.2% and outperforming state-of-the-art multimodal reasoning models like VisionR1 (by 8.0%) and PixelReasoner (by 5.9%) on diverse out-of-distribution benchmarks.
ILVR exhibits significantly lower inference latency, achieving an 8x to 18x speedup compared to competing methods by eliminating costly pixel-level re-encoding and intermediate image generation.
Takeaways: Dynamic visual reasoning in MLLMs can be efficiently achieved by interleaving textual generation with evolving latent visual representations, bypassing the computational bottleneck of explicit image processing.

A teacher-guided selective perceptual modeling approach can effectively preserve fine-grained visual details by focusing on context-aware feature extraction, preventing information loss from over-compression.
Allowing the model to self-generate and utilize latent states as internal priors (latent relaxation) during the second training stage enhances overall reasoning performance and adaptability.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.04563.Title: COOPER: A Unified Model for Cooperative Perception and Reasoning in Spatial Intelligence
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.04563.Summary: COOPER, developed by researchers from Chinese Academy of Sciences and Baidu Inc., introduces a unified multimodal large language model that intrinsically generates auxiliary visual cues, such as depth and segmentation maps, and adaptively integrates them with textual reasoning. The model achieves an average 6.91% improvement in spatial reasoning and a 4.47% gain on general multimodal benchmarks, surpassing several larger and proprietary models on specific spatial tasks.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) exhibit limited 3D-aware reasoning, struggling to infer geometry, depth, and spatial relationships from 2D images.

Existing MLLM approaches typically treat perception enhancement (e.g., using auxiliary modalities) and reasoning enhancement (e.g., textual Chain-of-Thought) as separate processes, hindering their interdependent benefits.
Current unified MLLMs lack the ability to internally generate non-RGB auxiliary modalities and adaptively interleave such generation with textual reasoning during problem-solving.
Method: COOPER extends a unified MLLM to intrinsically generate depth estimation and semantic segmentation maps by representing these non-RGB auxiliary modalities as RGB-compatible pseudo-images.
An adaptive interleaved reasoning framework is implemented using Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) to teach basic dynamic behavior and Reinforcement Learning (RL) for refinement.
A novel Cooperative Perception–Reasoning (CPR) reward, incorporating an exploration-guided component, optimizes the model's adaptive scheduling of visual assistance during problem-solving.
Results: COOPER demonstrates an average 6.91% improvement in spatial reasoning tasks and a 4.47% improvement on general multimodal benchmarks compared to its base model.
The model surpasses proprietary GPT models and the 38B-parameter open-source InternVL3.5-38B on fine-grained spatial perception benchmarks like Q-SpatialBench.

Ablation studies show that learning auxiliary modality generation (Stage 1) alone provides a 7.92% gain on Q-SpatialBench, indicating internalized spatial knowledge, and the exploration-guided reward (`r_e`) component effectively refines adaptive reasoning.
Takeaways: Unifying intrinsic perception (generating auxiliary spatial cues) and adaptive reasoning within a single MLLM leads to superior spatial intelligence compared to approaches that treat these capabilities in isolation.
Learning to generate auxiliary visual modalities inherently strengthens an MLLM's internal spatial understanding and knowledge, even before explicit reasoning supervision.

An adaptive 'Multimodal Chain-of-Thought,' where the model dynamically decides when to generate and incorporate visual information with textual reasoning, mirrors human-like cognitive processes and enhances problem-solving.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.03746.Title: Thinking with Programming Vision: Towards a Unified View for Thinking with Images
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.03746.Summary: Researchers from Zhejiang University and ByteDance introduced CodeVision, a "code-as-tool" framework that equips Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to programmatically interact with images. The approach significantly improves MLLM robustness by correcting common image corruptions and enables state-of-the-art multi-tool reasoning through emergent tool use and error recovery.
Problem: State-of-the-art MLLMs exhibit surprising brittleness to simple real-world visual perturbations like image rotations and flips, leading to significant performance degradation.
Existing tool-augmented MLLMs often lack flexibility and scalability, relying on brittle, hand-specified tool interfaces that hinder generalization.
Current MLLM tool-use paradigms frequently offer only marginal performance gains, raising questions about the genuine necessity and utility of tools for many tasks.
Method: The CodeVision framework employs a two-stage training process: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) to teach fundamental tool-use syntax and multi-tool sequences, followed by Reinforcement Learning (RL) for strategic decision-making.
A "code-as-tool" paradigm allows MLLMs to generate code as a universal interface to invoke any image operation, moving beyond fixed tool registries for greater flexibility and scalability.

A dense, multi-component reward function for RL training guides the agent in achieving correct answers, mastering strategic tool selection (including discovery of emergent tools), and ensuring robust error recovery.
Results: CodeVision models consistently and substantially outperform baseline MLLMs on transformed OCRBench and ChartQAPro, achieving an average score of 73.4 on transformed OCRBench with CodeVision-7B, a +17.4 improvement over its base model.
The framework establishes a new state-of-the-art on the novel MVToolBench for multi-tool composition, with CodeVision-7B scoring 60.1, nearly doubling the performance of Gemini2.5-Pro (32.6).

Qualitative results demonstrate CodeVision's emergent capabilities, including the discovery and use of beneficial tools not explicitly trained, efficient chaining of multiple operations, and sophisticated error handling by revising incorrect tool calls based on runtime feedback.
Takeaways: State-of-the-art MLLMs show significant vulnerability (up to 80% performance drop) to simple image orientation changes, highlighting a fundamental robustness issue that necessitates tool use.

A "code-as-tool" approach, combined with a multi-stage training methodology and dense reward, enables emergent behaviors like the discovery of unseen tools, efficient tool chaining, and robust error recovery.

Carefully curated SFT data with metadata-conditioned image transformations and a rich RL reward function are crucial for bootstrapping the model and guiding it towards strategic, multi-tool reasoning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.03442.Title: PretrainZero: Reinforcement Active Pretraining
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.03442.Summary: PretrainZero introduces a self-supervised reinforcement active pretraining framework that enables large language models to acquire general reasoning capabilities directly from real-world, noisy data like Wikipedia. This method achieved substantial performance improvements across diverse reasoning benchmarks, including MMLU-Pro and various math tasks, by allowing models to actively learn from self-generated, verifiable challenges.
Problem: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) and Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) in post-training are bottlenecked by costly human annotations or domain-specific verifiers, creating a 'data-wall' for scaling reasoning abilities.

Existing Reinforcement Learning Pre-Training (RLPT) methods often rely on synthetic, high-quality data or external dependencies like supervised fine-tuning (SFT) cold-starts, and fail when applied to noisy, real-world corpora.
Passive self-supervised pretraining alone does not effectively foster the explicit and robust Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning abilities desired in advanced LLMs.
Method: A reinforcement active learning framework is proposed, where a unified LLM policy performs two coupled tasks: mask generation (proposing challenging word spans to mask) and mask prediction (recovering the masked content with a CoT reasoning process).

An adversarial min-max objective governs the interaction: the predictor maximizes its accuracy, while the generator minimizes the predictor's accuracy by creating increasingly challenging but verifiable masks.

Both mask generation and prediction tasks are optimized using the Group Reward-driven Policy Optimization (GRPO) algorithm, training directly on general-domain Wikipedia data without external supervision or SFT cold-starts.
Results: PretrainZero significantly outperformed base models and random RLPT baselines across diverse benchmarks; for example, a Qwen3-4B-Base model improved by 8.43 points on MMLU-Pro and 10.60 points on the math average benchmark.

Models pretrained with PretrainZero exhibited explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, exploring multiple possibilities and verifying steps, which contrasts with the direct answer generation observed in baseline models.
PretrainZero models served as stronger 'reasoning foundation models,' yielding sustained and significant improvements over base and random RLPT models after subsequent general RLVR post-training.
