Takeaways: Vanilla RLPT methods, including entropy-based masking strategies successful on synthetic data, fail or collapse when applied to noisy, real-world pretraining corpora like Wikipedia due to uninformative or genuinely unlearnable targets.

An active learning mechanism that allows the model to dynamically identify and prioritize informative, verifiable, and moderately challenging content is crucial for robust and efficient reinforcement learning from noisy general-domain data.

The reinforcement active pretraining process fosters the emergence of explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning patterns in LLMs, demonstrating the development of genuine reasoning capabilities rather than just statistical pattern matching.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.02472.Title: Guided Self-Evolving LLMs with Minimal Human Supervision
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.02472.Summary: The R-FEW framework introduces a method for Large Language Models to self-evolve stably and controllably using minimal human supervision, achieving performance comparable to or surpassing models trained with 20 times more human data. It effectively mitigates issues like concept drift and diversity collapse by integrating few-shot grounding and an online curriculum.
Problem: Unguided self-evolving LLMs suffer from concept drift, causing models to reinforce biases and stray from factual correctness.
These systems often face diversity collapse, leading to self-generated challenges converging to familiar, low-entropy regions and hindering novel skill acquisition.
Uncontrolled self-play can lead to mis-evolution or reward hacking, where models exploit superficial features instead of genuinely improving reasoning.
Method: R-FEW proposes a guided Self-Play Challenger–Solver framework for LLMs, iteratively co-evolving a Challenger for question generation and a Solver for task solving.
A Few-Shot Grounded Challenger uses a small number of human-labeled 'anchor' examples (1-5% of a dataset) as in-context demonstrations to guide diverse and aligned synthetic question generation.

An Online Curriculum Solver selects tasks of moderate difficulty for training, filtering both synthetic and human questions within a specific success rate quantile (e.g., [0.3, 0.7]) and upweighting human anchor examples.
Results: R-FEW consistently outperformed existing self-play baselines (R-Zero, Absolute Zero, SPICE) across mathematical and general reasoning benchmarks, demonstrating an average score of 56.7 (Qwen3-8B-Base, 5% data) compared to R-Zero's 53.7.
The framework achieved performance on par with or superior to General-Reasoner, a model trained on 20 times more human data (232k examples), showcasing remarkable data efficiency.

R-FEW successfully mitigated instability issues, maintaining stable question diversity and appropriate question lengths throughout training, unlike unguided systems prone to diversity collapse and reward hacking.
Takeaways: Integrating lightweight human supervision through few-shot grounding is crucial for stabilizing LLM self-evolution, preventing concept drift and maintaining task diversity.
An online curriculum that adaptively selects tasks within the 'zone of proximal learning' significantly enhances the efficiency and stability of the Solver's learning process.
The Challenger's ability to generate a guided, diverse, and appropriately difficult curriculum, rather than simply maximizing internal rewards, is central to achieving meaningful self-improvement.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.01374.Title: Stabilizing Reinforcement Learning with LLMs: Formulation and Practices
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.01374.Summary: The Qwen Team at Alibaba Inc. developed a theoretical formulation that justifies token-level optimization for sequence-level rewards in Large Language Model (LLM) reinforcement learning, identifying training–inference discrepancy and policy staleness as key instability factors. Their work also provides empirically validated strategies, including Routing Replay and clipping, to achieve stable and high-performing RL training for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs.
Problem: Applying reinforcement learning (RL) to Large Language Models (LLMs) often suffers from instability due to the mismatch between sequence-level rewards and token-level optimization objectives.
The theoretical soundness of optimizing sequence-level rewards via token-level objectives in LLMs was not clearly established, leading to empirical instability and potential training collapse.
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures introduce further complexities, as dynamic expert routing can invalidate standard importance sampling ratios and exacerbate RL training instability.
Method: A novel theoretical formulation is proposed, demonstrating that a token-level objective can serve as a first-order approximation to the true expected sequence-level reward under conditions where training-inference discrepancy and policy staleness are minimized.

The 'MiniRL' algorithm is introduced, incorporating importance sampling (IS) correction to address training-inference discrepancy, group-normalization for variance reduction, and a PPO-inspired clipping mechanism to restrain policy staleness.
Specific 'Routing Replay' techniques (Vanilla R2 and Rollout R3) are developed to stabilize RL training for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models by managing expert routing during gradient updates.
Results: On-policy training demonstrated the highest stability and performance with basic MiniRL (including IS correction), while off-policy training critically required Routing Replay and clipping to prevent collapse and sustain performance.

Rollout Routing Replay (R3) proved superior under high off-policiness (larger global batch sizes), whereas Vanilla Routing Replay (R2) performed better under low off-policiness conditions for MoE models.

Stable RL training consistently led to comparable final model performance across various cold-start initializations, indicating that long-term training stability can mitigate the impact of initial model quality.
Takeaways: The stability of token-level RL optimization for sequence-level rewards hinges on minimizing the gap between the target policy and the rollout policy, primarily affected by training–inference discrepancy and policy staleness.
Importance sampling correction for the training–inference discrepancy is a fundamental requirement for the first-order approximation to hold, preventing rapid training collapse in LLM-RL.

For MoE models, dynamic expert routing amplifies instability, necessitating specific mitigation strategies like Routing Replay to preserve the validity of importance sampling and enable stable training.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.21688.Title: G$^2$VLM: Geometry Grounded Vision Language Model with Unified 3D Reconstruction and Spatial Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.21688.Summary: G G ²VLM integrates 3D reconstruction and spatial reasoning within a single Vision-Language Model, addressing the spatial intelligence limitations of current VLMs. It learns explicit visual geometry from 2D data using a Mixture-of-Transformer-Experts architecture, leading to robust spatial understanding and strong performance on both 3D reconstruction and complex spatial reasoning benchmarks.
Problem: Current Vision-Language Models (VLMs) often lack robust spatial intelligence, struggling with tasks requiring a deep understanding of 3D space.
VLMs traditionally learn implicit knowledge of the physical world from 2D image-text datasets, without explicit learning of visual geometry to lift 2D perceptions into coherent 3D representations.
Existing feedforward visual geometry models focus solely on 3D reconstruction, neglecting higher-level scene understanding and reasoning capabilities.
Method: Introduces G G ²VLM, a unified framework with a Mixture-of-Transformer-Experts (MoT) architecture, comprising a Geometric Perception Expert and a Semantic Perception Expert.

Employs a two-stage training strategy: initial pretraining of the geometric expert on 3D-annotated datasets, followed by joint training of both experts on spatial understanding and general VQA datasets.
The geometric expert predicts 3D attributes like depth, point clouds, and camera poses, with all tokens from both experts engaging in shared multi-modal self-attention.
Results: Achieves competitive visual geometry performance, reducing the Absolute Relative Error (Abs Rel) for monocular depth estimation on Sintel from VGGT’s 0.335 to 0.297.
Demonstrates state-of-the-art spatial reasoning, with G G ²VLM-SR surpassing GPT-4o by 18.48 points on the SPAR-Bench and achieving the best results on MindCube and OmniSpatial benchmarks.

Ablation studies confirm the positive impact of explicit geometry pretraining and the dual-encoder design, showing that better geometric features directly correlate with improved spatial reasoning performance.
Takeaways: Unifying low-level 3D reconstruction and high-level spatial understanding within a single VLM architecture significantly enhances the model's spatial intelligence.
A dual-expert design with shared attention allows for a rich interplay between geometric and semantic representations, enabling mutual improvement.

Explicitly learning 3D visual geometry from abundant 2D multi-view image and video data offers a scalable method to imbue VLMs with a genuine understanding of the 3D world, bypassing extensive 3D annotation needs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.21471.Title: SpatialBench: Benchmarking Multimodal Large Language Models for Spatial Cognition
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.21471.Summary: Researchers introduced SpatialBench, a cognitively grounded, hierarchical evaluation framework and a large-scale dataset for benchmarking Multimodal Large Language Models' (MLLMs) spatial cognition. The study found MLLMs excel at basic spatial perception but exhibit significant limitations in higher-level symbolic reasoning, causality, and planning, revealing a substantial performance gap when compared to human intelligence which achieved a near-perfect 96.40% overall score.
Problem: Existing MLLM benchmarks for spatial abilities are fragmented, task-oriented, and rely on simplified datasets, failing to capture the hierarchical and interdependent nature of spatial cognition.
Prior evaluations provide only a partial view of MLLMs' spatial intelligence, making it difficult to systematically diagnose deficiencies or analyze cognitive processes comprehensively.
A lack of robust, diagnostically powerful methods for evaluating MLLM spatial cognition hinders the development of AI systems capable of effective interaction with the physical world.
Method: A five-level hierarchical framework for spatial cognition was established, decomposing spatial intelligence into observation, topology and relation, symbolic reasoning, causality, and planning.

A new, large-scale, and fine-grained benchmark dataset named SpatialBench was constructed, comprising 1,347 question-answer pairs across 15 tasks derived from real-world, egocentric videos with LiDAR ground truth.

A novel, high-level capability-oriented metric was introduced, which assigns adaptive weights to each cognitive level to provide a holistic and complexity-aware assessment of overall spatial reasoning ability.
Results: MLLMs generally performed well on Level 1 (Observation) and Level 2 (Topology and Relation) tasks but exhibited a sharp performance drop for Levels 3 (Symbolic Reasoning), 4 (Causality), and 5 (Planning).
Proprietary models like Gemini-2.5-pro consistently secured top positions, demonstrating up to 15.6% higher average accuracy on higher-level tasks compared to open-source models.

One-shot evaluation revealed varied generalization capabilities across models, with some weaker models showing substantial performance improvements, indicating the potential of in-context learning to boost higher-level cognitive capabilities.
Takeaways: MLLMs demonstrate strong performance on lower-level spatial cognition tasks (observation, topology & relation) but show a significant decline in higher-level tasks (symbolic reasoning, causality, planning).
Leading proprietary MLLMs consistently achieved substantially higher overall scores than open-source counterparts, particularly in complex cognitive tasks.

Human participants achieved a near-perfect overall score of 96.40%, significantly outperforming all MLLMs and highlighting their superior goal-directed reasoning and robust egocentric perspective taking.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.21395.Title: Monet: Reasoning in Latent Visual Space Beyond Images and Language
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.21395.Summary: Monet, a framework developed by researchers from Peking University, ByteDance's Kling Team, and Amazon, enables multimodal large language models to perform abstract visual reasoning by directly operating within a continuous latent visual space. The approach achieves superior performance on real-world perception and reasoning benchmarks and demonstrates strong out-of-distribution generalization capabilities.
Problem: Existing "thinking with images" methods for MLLMs are rigid, tool-dependent, and lack generalization to complex visual operations beyond trained toolsets.
Prior "reasoning in latent space" approaches for MLLMs suffer from poor scalability, loss of visual detail, and insufficient optimization for continuous latent embeddings.
MLLMs generally lack a flexible, internal perceptual space for abstract visual thinking akin to human cognition.
Method: Introduces a three-stage Supervised Fine-tuning (SFT) pipeline to equip MLLMs with the ability to generate and reason with continuous latent embeddings.
Develops the Monet-SFT-125K dataset, providing high-quality, fine-grained supervision for learning latent visual observations.
Proposes Visual-latent Policy Optimization (VLPO), a novel reinforcement learning algorithm tailored for optimizing continuous latent embeddings.
Results: Monet-7B consistently outperforms Qwen2.5-VL-7B and other state-of-the-art open-source methods on benchmarks including V*, HRBench, and MME-RealWorld-Lite.
Achieves the best performance among open-source models on the VisualPuzzles benchmark, showcasing strong out-of-distribution generalization for abstract visual reasoning.
Ablation studies confirm that dual supervision, latent-only backpropagation, and VLPO are crucial for the framework's effectiveness in learning and optimizing latent visual reasoning.
Takeaways: MLLMs can learn to generate and leverage internal continuous latent embeddings for abstract visual reasoning, eliminating the reliance on explicit external tools or auxiliary images during inference.
Dual supervision with representation-alignment loss on crucial observation tokens and direct attention from latent embeddings to auxiliary images is vital for effective latent feature learning.
Restricting gradients to flow solely through generated latent embeddings (latent-only backpropagation) is essential for genuinely improving latent representations during training.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.20844.Title: Pre-train to Gain: Robust Learning Without Clean Labels
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.20844.Summary: This work explores how self-supervised pre-training (SSL) can enhance deep learning model robustness to noisy labels without requiring clean data subsets. Researchers demonstrate that SSL pre-training consistently improves classification accuracy on clean test sets and label error detection when models are trained on corrupted datasets.
Problem: Deep neural networks are prone to memorizing incorrect labels when trained on noisy datasets, leading to poor generalization.

Many existing Learning with Noisy Labels (LNL) methods rely on restrictive assumptions, such as access to clean label subsets or prior knowledge of noise distribution, limiting their real-world applicability.
Obtaining large, high-quality, meticulously labeled datasets for deep learning is often expensive, time-consuming, or impossible in practical applications.
Method: Implement a two-stage training pipeline: first, self-supervised pre-training (using SimCLR or Barlow Twins) on the entire noisy dataset without labels, then supervised fine-tuning on the same noisy dataset.
Evaluate the approach on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 with synthetic uniform noise, and CIFAR-10N, CIFAR-100N with real-world human annotation noise.
Compare SSL pre-training against training from scratch and against models initialized with ImageNet pre-trained weights.
Results: SSL pre-training consistently increased classification accuracy on clean test sets by 5-30% on CIFAR-10/100 (synthetic noise) and 5-8% on CIFAR-10N/100N (real-world noise), particularly under high noise rates.
Models pre-trained with SSL improved label error detection (F1 Score and Balanced Accuracy) by 4-7 percentage points, showing enhanced ability to distinguish correct from incorrect labels.

SSL pre-trained models demonstrated greater resistance to overfitting during prolonged supervised training, maintaining higher accuracy and slower loss increase compared to models trained from scratch.
Takeaways: Self-supervised pre-training enables models to learn robust, noise-invariant feature representations by completely bypassing the label space during the initial training phase.
The benefits of SSL pre-training emerge rapidly (e.g., within 10 epochs) and tend to plateau around 50 epochs, indicating computational efficiency.
Domain-aligned self-supervised pre-training offers a substantial advantage over generic external pre-training (like ImageNet) under high label noise conditions.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.20836.Title: Structured Prompting Enables More Robust Evaluation of Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.20836.Summary: A framework from Stanford University researchers, DSPy+HELM, integrates structured prompting into language model evaluation, revealing that fixed-prompt benchmarks often yield unrepresentative performance estimates and lead to altered leaderboard rankings. The study found LMs achieved an average +4% absolute accuracy increase across diverse tasks when using structured prompting, with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning identified as the main contributor to performance improvements.
Problem: Fixed, hand-crafted prompts in existing benchmarks frequently underestimate the true capabilities of large language models (LLMs).
LLMs are highly sensitive to prompt design, leading to unreliable performance comparisons and potentially inaccurate leaderboard rankings.
Manual prompt engineering for optimal performance is labor-intensive, requires domain expertise, and does not scale across many models or tasks.
Method: Developed a reproducible DSPy+HELM framework that integrates DSPy's declarative structured prompting methods into HELM's comprehensive evaluation suite.
Systematically evaluated various structured prompting methods, including Zero-Shot CoT, Bootstrap Few-Shot with Random Search (BFRS), and MIPROv2, against HELM's baseline fixed prompts.
Conducted experiments on four frontier LLMs across seven diverse general and medical benchmarks to quantify the impact of optimized prompting.
Results: Structured prompting methods consistently improved LM performance, yielding an average +4% absolute accuracy gain across the seven benchmarks compared to the HELM baseline.
Leaderboard rankings were altered on 3 out of 7 benchmarks, and the average performance gap between the top two models (o3 Mini and Claude 3.7 Sonnet) shrank from 6% to 3% under structured prompting.
Zero-Shot CoT achieved most of the performance improvements with only 164 additional prompt tokens, whereas more complex few-shot methods required up to 1,700 tokens for marginal additional gains.
Takeaways: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning is the dominant driver of performance gains, significantly reducing an LM's sensitivity to further prompt optimization, as explained by a theoretical model.
Fixed-prompt benchmarks provide unrepresentative performance estimates and can lead to materially altered leaderboard rankings and performance gap assessments between models.
While few-shot optimizers achieve the performance ceiling, Zero-Shot CoT provides most of the gains with minimal computational overhead, making it a cost-effective method for robust evaluation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.20814.Title: SPHINX: A Synthetic Environment for Visual Perception and Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.20814.Summary: SPHINX is a new synthetic environment designed by researchers at RIT and the University of Washington to evaluate and advance visual perception and reasoning in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs). It features 25 procedurally generated task types with verifiable ground truth, revealing that state-of-the-art LVLMs achieve only 51.1% accuracy compared to 75.4% for humans, and demonstrating that Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) significantly improves LVLM performance and generalization.
Problem: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) significantly lag behind Large Language Models (LLMs) in complex reasoning tasks, particularly those involving genuine visual understanding.

Existing multimodal benchmarks often prioritize perception-focused tasks, allow models to bypass true visual reasoning, or lack systematic evaluation of fundamental cognitive primitives essential for fluid intelligence.
There is a need for scalable, diverse, and verifiable datasets to thoroughly diagnose LVLM limitations and facilitate advanced training paradigms like reinforcement learning.
Method: SPHINX introduces a novel synthetic environment with a modular, programmatic framework capable of generating diverse visual reasoning data through factorized control of appearance (motifs), spatial layout (tilings), and reasoning rules (tasks).

It features 25 distinct task types categorized into five broad families (Geometric Reasoning, Counting, Symmetry & Pattern Recognition, Sequence & Transformation, Topological & Graph Reasoning), each with a deterministic checker for unambiguous ground-truth answers.

The environment includes 'difficulty knobs' for precise control over problem complexity, enabling tailored dataset generation and making it suitable for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR).
Results: State-of-the-art proprietary LVLMs like GPT-5 achieved only 51.1% accuracy across SPHINX's 25 tasks, notably lower than human performance at 75.4%.

RLVR consistently improved performance on in-distribution SPHINX tasks and demonstrated generalization, with RL-trained models showing an average accuracy improvement across eight external visual reasoning benchmarks (e.g., +2.8% for Qwen3-VL-8B).
Model accuracy consistently decreased as task complexity increased across all evaluated models, validating SPHINX's ability to provide a tunable difficulty axis for evaluation.
Takeaways: Current state-of-the-art LVLMs, including powerful proprietary models, still exhibit significant gaps in fundamental visual reasoning capabilities compared to human performance, especially in tasks requiring accurate low-level visual extraction and counting.

The modular design and verifiable ground truth of SPHINX enable systematic evaluation of cognitive primitives and provide a robust platform for diagnosing specific failure modes in multimodal AI systems.

Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), applied using SPHINX-generated data, is an effective paradigm for substantially improving LVLM accuracy on in-distribution tasks, enhancing generalization to held-out tasks, and yielding consistent gains on external visual reasoning benchmarks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.20639.Title: Latent Collaboration in Multi-Agent Systems
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.20639.Summary: LatentMAS, a framework by researchers from Princeton, UIUC, and Stanford, enables large language model agents to collaborate purely within their continuous latent space, rather than using text. This approach substantially improves problem-solving accuracy by up to 14.6% and achieves 4x to 4.3x faster inference speeds while reducing output token usage by 70-80% compared to text-based multi-agent systems.
Problem: Existing LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) primarily use text for communication and reasoning, which is computationally expensive and leads to slow inference.
Text-based communication creates information bottlenecks, as rich continuous latent information is compressed and potentially lost when converted into discrete tokens.
Errors in reasoning can easily propagate and amplify in sequential text-based MAS, as subsequent agents explicitly inherit textual mistakes.
Method: LatentMAS introduces an end-to-end, training-free framework where LLM agents generate and communicate continuous "latent thoughts" (last-layer hidden states) auto-regressively.
It preserves and transfers an agent's complete "latent working memory" (accumulated KV caches from all transformer layers) directly to subsequent agents, enabling lossless information transfer.
An input-output alignment operator is employed to ensure distributional consistency when feeding latent states as inputs, preventing hidden state drift.
Results: LatentMAS achieved an average of +13.3% higher accuracy compared to single-model baselines and up to +14.6% improvement over text-based MAS on various benchmarks.
It reduced total output token usage by 70.8% to 83.7% and accelerated end-to-end inference speed by 4x to 4.3x compared to text-based MAS.

Empirical analysis validated that latent thoughts maintain semantic consistency, offer broader expressive capacity, and the alignment operator is critical for performance, improving accuracy by 2.3% to 5.3%.
Takeaways: Latent thoughts are theoretically more expressive and carry significantly more information than discrete text tokens, offering a richer communication medium.
Direct transfer of Key-Value (KV) caches facilitates "lossless information transfer" between agents, preserving the full context of prior reasoning steps without re-encoding.
The framework inherently reduces computational complexity compared to text-based methods, bypassing tokenization and decoding overheads, as supported by theoretical analysis.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.20351.Title: Thinking in 360°: Humanoid Visual Search in the Wild
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.20351.Summary: This research prototypes humanoid visual search, enabling multimodal large language models to actively explore 360° panoramic environments for object and path finding, similar to human perception. A new benchmark, H*Bench, evaluates models in complex real-world scenarios, revealing that post-training significantly improves open-source models, allowing them to outperform proprietary models in object search.
Problem: Most multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are passive observers, analyzing static 2D images, which fundamentally differs from active human visual search in 3D environments.
Current embodied AI research often relies on expensive 3D simulators or physical hardware, limiting scalability and generalization to complex "in-the-wild" human environments.
Existing models lack the ability to dynamically change their perspective or couple visual reasoning with physical actions in a closed-loop manner.
Method: Developed Humanoid Visual Search (HVS) where an MLLM agent actively rotates a virtual "head" within 360° panoramic images to perform object and path finding tasks.
Introduced H*Bench, a benchmark comprising 3,000 richly annotated real-world panoramic task instances across diverse scene types to evaluate embodied visual search in complex scenarios.
Employed a two-stage post-training pipeline, combining Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning (RL), to adapt and enhance MLLMs for HVS tasks.
Results: State-of-the-art proprietary MLLMs like Gemini2.5-Pro and GPT-4o achieved only approximately 30% success rates on both Humanoid Object Search (HOS) and Humanoid Path Search (HPS) tasks on H*Bench.

The proposed HVS-3B model (a Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct model with post-training) improved its HOS success rate over threefold from 14.83% to 47.38%, surpassing the best proprietary model, Gemini2.5-Pro (31.96%).
HVS-3B's HPS success rate increased over threefold from 6.44% to 24.94%, demonstrating significant gains, though it still trailed Gemini2.5-Pro's performance on this more demanding task.
Takeaways: MLLMs trained primarily on static 2D data exhibit a substantial performance drop when transferred to active 3D embodied visual search tasks, indicating a significant gap between passive reasoning and embodied interaction.

Active visual search, where the agent dynamically changes its perspective, is empirically superior to passive analysis of a full panorama, mimicking human visual efficiency and reducing reliance on models' generalization to distorted wide-angle views.

While post-training significantly enhances MLLMs for embodied tasks, higher-order spatial and commonsense reasoning, especially for complex path search, remains a persistent challenge, exposing limitations in current learning paradigms.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.19900.Title: Agent0-VL: Exploring Self-Evolving Agent for Tool-Integrated Vision-Language Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.19900.Summary: Agent0-VL from UNC-Chapel Hill introduces a self-evolving vision-language agent that integrates tool usage into both reasoning and its self-evaluation processes, resolving issues with purely text-based self-critique in multimodal tasks. This framework enables continuous self-improvement without external human reward signals, achieving substantial performance improvements and outperforming closed-source systems like GPT-4o on MathVista, HallBench, and ChartQA.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and agents heavily rely on human-annotated preference data or external reward signals, which limits their capabilities and hinders adaptation in sparse feedback environments.

Existing self-rewarding/self-evolving methods, primarily text-based, struggle with complex visual reasoning due to limited evaluation capabilities and unreliable evaluation processes (hallucinations).
Purely textual reflection in multimodal contexts is insufficient for accurately verifying intricate multi-step computations, spatial relationships, or precise numerical and geometric reasoning.
Method: Introduces a unified Large Vision-Language Model (LVLM) architecture that assumes dual roles: a 'Solver' for multimodal task execution and a 'Verifier' for introspective, step-wise evaluation.

The Verifier provides tool-grounded feedback (score, confidence, critique) and can re-invoke tools for cross-checking, triggering a confidence-gated self-repair mechanism when confidence in a step falls below a threshold.

Employs a Self-Evolving Reasoning Cycle (SERC) which iteratively updates the unified policy using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), leveraging self-generated rewards for continuous learning without external supervision.
Results: Agent0-VL achieved substantial performance improvements, with the 7B model showing a 12.5% gain over its Qwen2.5-VL-7B base model and outperforming closed-source systems like GPT-4o on MathVista, HallBench, and ChartQA.

The framework demonstrated strong domain-specific enhancements, achieving 18.1% improvement on MathVista (7B model) and reducing visual hallucinations on perception-heavy tasks like HallusionBench (12.2% improvement).

Ablation studies confirmed the critical roles of the Self-Evolving Reasoning Cycle (SERC), tool use, and self-repair, with SERC removal leading to an 8.7% performance drop. The Verifier module also generalized effectively as a standalone Process Reward Model, improving Best-of-N performance by 7.3% for other VLMs.
Takeaways: Integrating tool usage directly into the self-evaluation and self-repair mechanisms of a VLM enables evidence-grounded analysis, overcoming the limitations of purely textual self-critique in complex visual reasoning tasks.
A unified Solver-Verifier architecture within a single LVLM can synergistically align and optimize both task execution and internal self-evaluation behaviors through an iterative self-evolving cycle.

Continual self-improvement for VLMs with zero external rewards is achievable by transforming the learning objective into a dynamic process of self-consistency and refinement, driven by verifiable self-generated feedback.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.19820.Title: CropVLM: Learning to Zoom for Fine-Grained Vision-Language Perception
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.19820.Summary: CropVLM introduces an external, lightweight network that leverages reinforcement learning to dynamically generate relevant image crops, thereby enhancing existing Vision-Language Models' (VLMs) fine-grained perception on high-resolution inputs. This method consistently improves VLM performance across diverse benchmarks and target models by mitigating computational overhead and removing the need for direct bounding box supervision.
Problem: Mainstream Vision-Language Models (VLMs) struggle with fine-grained visual perception due to low input resolution constraints, leading to loss of crucial details.
Existing solutions like uniformly increasing resolution or architectural modifications are computationally prohibitive, risk catastrophic forgetting, or are infeasible for proprietary VLMs.
Many fine-grained perception methods rely on expensive human-labeled bounding box annotations, limiting their scalability and generalizability.
Method: CropVLM employs a lightweight, external cropping network, initialized from a SmolVLM Instruct model, designed to output bounding box coordinates for a given image-question pair.

The cropping network is trained using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), which utilizes objective reward signals (accuracy or log-likelihood) from the target VLM's performance, eliminating the need for explicit bounding box supervision.

The generated high-resolution crop, alongside the original image, is then fed to any VLM (open-source or proprietary) to enhance its fine-grained understanding without altering its internal architecture or weights.
Results: CropVLM consistently delivered significant performance gains across all evaluated target VLMs (SmolVLM, LLaVA 1.5 7B, Qwen 2.5 VL 3B, GPT 4.1 nano) and various fine-grained VQA benchmarks, including strong out-of-domain generalization.
The method outperformed alternative cropping strategies like ViCrop and UV-CoT, demonstrating superior results despite CropVLM being a much smaller model trained on less data.
CropVLM exhibited lower GPU memory usage compared to ViCrop and UV-CoT, and enabled a 1024x1024 base VLM to achieve higher average performance than a 2048x2048 baseline without CropVLM.
Takeaways: Reinforcement learning with VLM-derived objective rewards offers a scalable and cost-effective method for training cropping networks, outperforming approaches reliant on explicit bounding box annotations.
Log-likelihood based rewards provide more nuanced feedback and consistently yield superior performance compared to accuracy-based rewards during GRPO training.

VQA performance does not directly correlate with high Intersection over Union (IoU) scores; instead, achieving sufficient context through larger crops with higher recall proves more beneficial for VQA accuracy.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.19418.Title: Chain-of-Visual-Thought: Teaching VLMs to See and Think Better with Continuous Visual Tokens
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.19418.Summary: The Chain-of-Visual-Thought (COVT) framework equips Vision-Language Models (VLMs) with continuous visual tokens, distilled from lightweight vision experts, to improve reasoning in dense perceptual space. This approach yields performance gains across vision-centric benchmarks and enhances interpretability.
Problem: Current Vision-Language Models (VLMs) struggle with perception-intensive tasks (e.g., precise counting, depth estimation) due to the loss of rich perceptual cues when continuous visual information is compressed into discrete text tokens.

Existing VLM reasoning is predominantly language-bound, limiting their ability to reason about fine-grained spatial and geometric details, with text-only Chain-of-Thought often degrading visual reasoning performance.
External tool-augmented methods for VLMs introduce computational overhead and still often project tool outputs back into the text space, reintroducing information loss and delegating core perception.
Method: Introduce Chain-of-Visual-Thought (COVT), a framework enabling VLMs to generate and process "continuous visual tokens"—compact latent representations encoding fine-grained perceptual cues—directly within their autoregressive sequence.

Distill knowledge from specialized, lightweight vision experts (e.g., SAM for segmentation, DepthAnything v2 for depth, PIDINet for edges, DINOv2 for semantics) into these visual tokens using tailored, task-oriented alignment strategies.

Employ a four-stage training pipeline (comprehension, generation, reasoning, efficient reasoning) to progressively teach the VLM to effectively utilize and reason with visual tokens, complementing its text-space abilities.
Results: COVT consistently improved performance across diverse vision-centric benchmarks (e.g., CV-Bench, BLINK, RealWorldQA), achieving a 5.5% overall gain on CV-Bench and a 14.0% improvement on its Depth sub-task with Qwen2.5-VL-7B.
Demonstrated strong generalization by outperforming prior latent reasoning methods (e.g., Aurora) on LLaVA-v1.5-13B, with gains such as 12.9% on BLINK relative-depth and 26.6% on BLINK count.

Enabled enhanced interpretability through optional decoding of visual tokens into human-readable outputs (segmentation masks, depth maps, edge maps), providing a visual window into the model's intermediate reasoning process.
Takeaways: Integrating continuous visual tokens allows VLMs to "think visually," directly addressing the limitations of language-bound reasoning and providing a more faithful bridge between continuous visual perception and higher-level cognition.

Tailored alignment strategies, particularly projecting visual tokens into the decoder prompt space of vision experts, are crucial for effectively distilling dense perceptual information into the compact token representations.

Unlike text-only Chain-of-Thought, which can degrade performance on vision-centric tasks, COVT's continuous visual tokens consistently enhance performance, empirically validating the necessity of direct visual grounding.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.19261.Title: LAST: LeArning to Think in Space and Time for Generalist Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.19261.Summary: The LAST framework enhances generalist Vision-Language Models (VLMs) with advanced 3D spatial understanding and long video comprehension by integrating "visual thinking trajectories" through external visual tools. This extension of Chain-of-Thought reasoning yields substantial performance increases on relevant benchmarks for both powerful proprietary models and fine-tuned open-source VLMs.
Problem: Generalist Vision-Language Models (VLMs) demonstrate limitations in tasks requiring robust 3D spatial reasoning and comprehension of long video sequences.

Existing solutions for 3D and long video understanding are often specialized, relying on additional 3D inputs or task-specific architectures, hindering the development of unified general-purpose VLMs.

Traditional, language-centric Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning is insufficient for visually complex tasks, as it "lacks visual engagement" and can lead to incorrect reasoning when deep visual understanding is required.
Method: Introduces "visual thinking trajectories" to extend Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, enabling VLMs to dynamically interact with visual information for spatial and temporal analysis.

Leverages a curated set of external visual tools, including frame selection, object tracking, temporal grounding, image grounding, and depth estimation, to generate intermediate visual observations and augment VLM reasoning.

The approach is implemented via zero-shot prompting for proprietary models (e.g., GPT-4o) and through a two-stage data curation and fine-tuning pipeline for open-weight models (e.g., LAST-7B based on Qwen2.5-VL-7B).
Results: GPT-4o with LAST achieved up to a 15.8% accuracy gain on EgoSchema (from 69.6% to 85.4%) and an 11.4 points CIDEr improvement on ScanQA (from 65.4% to 76.8%), outperforming some specialized 3D models.
The fine-tuned LAST-7B model, built on Qwen2.5-VL-7B, showed an 8.3% accuracy increase on VSI-Bench (from 33.0% to 41.3%) and a 14-point gain on EgoSchema (from 55.0% to 69.0%) with 16 frames.
LAST consistently outperformed text-only CoT, which often resulted in performance degradation (e.g., EgoSchema baseline 69.6% vs. 62.7% with text CoT, while LAST achieved 85.4%).
Takeaways: Integrating external visual tool use directly into a VLM's reasoning process allows it to effectively acquire advanced spatial and temporal understanding from sequential 2D image observations without specialized architectures.
Purely textual Chain-of-Thought reasoning is inadequate and often degrades performance on visually complex spatial and temporal tasks, underscoring the critical need for visually-engaged reasoning.

A dedicated two-stage data curation process, generating visual thinking trajectories, can successfully fine-tune open-source VLMs to achieve significant performance gains on advanced visual reasoning benchmarks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.18538.Title: From Code Foundation Models to Agents and Applications: A Comprehensive Survey and Practical Guide to Code Intelligence
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.18538.Summary: A comprehensive synthesis of Large Language Models for automated software development covers the entire model lifecycle, from data curation to autonomous agents, and offers practical guidance derived from empirical experiments on pre-training, fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning, alongside a detailed analysis of challenges and future directions.
Problem: The rapid, fragmented advancements in code LLMs lacked a systematic, unified analysis, making it difficult for researchers and practitioners to keep pace.
A significant gap existed between academic benchmarks for code LLMs and the complex demands of real-world software development, including code correctness, security, and contextual understanding.
Developers and researchers lacked comprehensive, data-driven guidelines for effectively building, optimizing, and deploying top-tier code LLMs.
Method: Provided a comprehensive survey that systematically analyzes the entire lifecycle of code LLMs, from data curation and pre-training to advanced alignment techniques, evaluation, applications, and safety.

Conducted a series of analytical and probing experiments to establish practical guidelines on distributed training frameworks, pre-training scaling laws across languages, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) hyperparameter sensitivity, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR).
Developed a unified taxonomy of contemporary code LLMs, comparing both general-purpose and code-specialized models, and detailed the evolution of their architectures and alignment strategies.
Results: Established Chinchilla-style scaling laws for programming languages, demonstrating varying sensitivities to model size and data volume (e.g., Python benefits more from scaling than statically-typed languages).

Provided SFT guidelines, identifying global batch size as a dominant factor, highlighting MoE models' increased hyperparameter sensitivity, and confirming the superiority of datasets with executable supervision for robust performance.

Offered RLVR guidelines, recommending the `REINFORCE++_baseline` estimator for stability and efficiency, and detailing optimal `MAX_RESPONSE_LENGTH` and `N_RESP_PER_PROMPT` settings based on target metrics (Pass@1 vs. Pass@5).
Takeaways: Data quality is paramount for code LLM performance and safety, requiring rigorous curation and governance, while architectural diversity beyond dense models (e.g., MoE, recurrent) optimizes for efficiency and specialized tasks.

Code LLMs are inherently insecure by default due to training on vulnerable public corpora, necessitating proactive safety measures across pre-training, post-training, red-teaming, and agentic execution.

Autonomous Software Engineering (SWE) agents and the use of code as a generalist agent medium are expanding across the entire software development lifecycle, moving beyond simple code generation to complex planning and interaction.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.18373.Title: MASS: Motion-Aware Spatial-Temporal Grounding for Physics Reasoning and Comprehension in Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.18373.Summary: A new framework, MASS (Motion-Aware Spatial–temporal Grounding), and its accompanying benchmark, MASS-Bench, enable Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to better comprehend physics-driven reasoning in videos by injecting explicit spatial-temporal and motion cues. Models enhanced with MASS showed up to an 8.7% improvement over prior open-source state-of-the-art on physics-related tasks and matched or exceeded closed-source models on physical abnormality detection.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) frequently struggle with complex physics-driven reasoning involving fine-grained 3D spatial layouts, intricate motion patterns, and precise temporal dynamics.
Existing datasets lack the dense spatiotemporal and motion-level annotations required to train VLMs for robust physics-grounded reasoning.
VLMs often rely on implicit priors, leading to physically implausible interpretations or overlooking abnormalities, especially in AI-generated content (AIGC) videos.
Method: Introduced MASS-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark comprising 4,350 real-world and AIGC videos with 8,361 physics-related QA pairs and dense entity-level motion-grounded annotations.
Developed MASS, a model-agnostic approach that injects explicit spatial-temporal signals into the VLM's language space using depth-based 3D encoding, visual grounding, and a motion tracker.
Employed Reinforcement Fine-tuning (RFT) with Temporal Group Relative Policy Optimization (T-GRPO) to strengthen cross-modal alignment and multi-stage physics reasoning in VLMs.
Results: MASS-augmented VLMs achieved up to an 8.7% improvement over the previous best open-source model (Qwen3-VL-8B) on physics reasoning tasks.
Qwen2.5-VL-7B + MASS demonstrated performance comparable to closed-source state-of-the-art VLMs like Gemini-2.5-Flash, and surpassed it in Physical Abnormality Detection.
The framework also showed strong generalization, outperforming all baselines on general-purpose real-world video QA benchmarks such as MVBench.
Takeaways: Explicit motion-aware spatial-temporal grounding is crucial for robust physics reasoning in VLMs, demonstrating more impact than simply increasing model scale.
High-quality, densely annotated datasets like MASS-Bench are essential for effectively training VLMs to perform physics-related comprehension and abnormality detection tasks.

Reinforcement Fine-tuning (RFT) significantly enhances VLMs' ability to integrate grounded visual cues with spatial-temporal structures for complex physics reasoning, outperforming Supervised Fine-tuning (SFT).

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.17487.Title: Downscaling Intelligence: Exploring Perception and Reasoning Bottlenecks in Small Multimodal Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.17487.Summary: Researchers from Stanford University systematically investigate how reducing large language model capacity affects small multimodal models, pinpointing perception and reasoning as key bottlenecks. They introduce EXTRACT+THINK, a two-stage framework that achieves up to 19.5% higher performance on the MMStar benchmark while utilizing 73% fewer visual training samples compared to existing smaller models.
Problem: Large multimodal models (MLLMs) are computationally demanding, restricting their deployment in resource-limited settings like edge devices.
A systematic understanding of how MLLM capabilities, specifically perception and reasoning, degrade when the underlying large language model (LLM) capacity is reduced is lacking.
Inconsistent findings in previous studies on the impact of LLM size on perceptual abilities necessitate a principled investigation into these effects.
Method: Conducted a systematic empirical study by downscaling Qwen3 series LLMs in multimodal models and evaluating performance across a diverse set of visual tasks.
Utilized a decoupled framework, adapting the Prism method, to independently analyze the impact of LLM downscaling on perception and reasoning modules.
Developed EXTRACT+THINK, a two-stage framework employing "Visual Extraction Tuning" to enhance perception and "Chain-of-Thought reasoning" to improve the LLM's reasoning capabilities.
Results: The EXTRACT+THINK framework achieved state-of-the-art efficiency, with its smaller variant surpassing LLaVA-OneVision-0.5B by up to 19.5% on MMStar while using 73% fewer visual training samples.

Visual extraction tuning significantly enhanced perceptual performance, yielding up to +5.2 accuracy for the 0.6B perception module on in-domain data and +4.6 on the MMStar benchmark compared to a captioning baseline.
Chain-of-Thought reasoning effectively boosted the reasoning module's capabilities, leading to substantial improvements in out-of-domain performance across various LLM scales.
Takeaways: Performance degradation from LLM downscaling is most pronounced in visually demanding tasks, suggesting that core vision-centric capabilities are disproportionately affected.

The perception module's capacity, alongside the reasoning module's, represents a critical bottleneck in smaller multimodal models, challenging prior assumptions about perception's robustness to LLM scale.
Training the perception module with visual extraction tuning, which emphasizes fine-grained, question-relevant detail extraction, significantly improves performance and data efficiency.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.17473.Title: Masked-and-Reordered Self-Supervision for Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.17473.Summary: This work introduces Masked-and-Reordered Self-Supervision for Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (MR-RLVR), a two-stage framework enhancing large language models' mathematical reasoning by integrating self-supervised process-level rewards. It achieves average relative gains of +9.86% Pass@1 and +5.27% Pass@5 over standard RLVR, demonstrating improved performance and data efficiency on challenging mathematical benchmarks.
Problem: Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) suffers from sparse supervision, as it relies only on terminal verification, leading to 'process hallucinations' in intermediate reasoning steps.
Process supervision, which provides fine-grained step-level feedback, is prohibitively expensive due to the need for extensive human annotation for complex mathematical tasks.
Traditional supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on chain-of-thought data often leads to rote memorization of solution patterns rather than generalizable reasoning strategies.
Method: A two-stage training framework: an initial RLVR phase uses process-level rewards from self-supervised tasks, followed by fine-tuning with outcome-only rewards for final answer accuracy.

Automatic curation of process-aware self-supervised data using two tasks: 'Masked-Then-Fill' to reconstruct missing elements in reasoning steps and 'Step Reordering' to recover the correct logical sequence of permuted steps.

Design of process-level rewards (ranging from 0 to 1) for each self-supervised task, measuring semantic match for masked elements and position-based distance for reordered steps, combined into a single `r_proc` signal.
Results: MR-RLVR achieved average relative gains over standard RLVR of +9.86% Pass@1, +5.27% Pass@5, and +4.00% Pass@8 across mathematical benchmarks.
Less optimized base models (e.g., Qwen2.5-3B) showed substantially larger improvements, with up to +35.98% Pass@1 and +22.44% Pass@5 on AIME25.
The method demonstrated better sample efficiency, consistently outperforming standard GRPO even with limited training data (1k and 3k samples), particularly enhancing Pass@5 and Pass@8.
Takeaways: Dense, structured process-level signals can be automatically extracted from existing mathematical reasoning trajectories, overcoming the cost and scalability limitations of human-centric process supervision.

Integrating these self-supervised process signals into RLVR significantly enriches the learning process by providing fine-grained guidance for intermediate steps, leading to more robust and interpretable reasoning.

The two-stage approach effectively combines the benefits of fine-grained process quality with outcome-oriented precision, enabling models to generate structurally sound reasoning while optimizing for accurate final answers.
Process-level self-supervision enhances sample efficiency, allowing models to learn more effectively even in low-data regimes and generalize better to complex, unseen problems.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.16901.Title: R-AVST: Empowering Video-LLMs with Fine-Grained Spatio-Temporal Reasoning in Complex Audio-Visual Scenarios
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.16901.Summary: Researchers introduce R-AVST, the first dataset specifically designed for fine-grained audio-visual spatio-temporal reasoning in complex scenarios, and AVST-Zero, a reinforcement learning-based Video-LLM. AVST-Zero demonstrates competitive and often superior performance across new spatio-temporal reasoning tasks, outperforming existing models on the R-AVST benchmark.
Problem: Existing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle with fine-grained spatio-temporal reasoning in complex, real-world audio-visual events, often operating in simpler video scenarios.
Current audio-visual datasets are fragmented, lacking comprehensive integration of fine-grained temporal boundaries, spatial localization, and rich audio-visual dynamics for diverse event types.

Existing Video-LLMs often rely on extensive high-quality labeled data and lack sufficient exploration capacity, while reinforcement learning approaches for Video-LLMs lack dedicated reward designs for complex audio-visual spatio-temporal tasks.
Method: Constructed R-AVST, a novel dataset comprising 5,237 untrimmed videos with fine-grained temporal and spatial annotations for 27,253 objects across over 100 audio-visual event types, generating 8,166 task-specific question-answer (QA) pairs.
Defined three core tasks for audio-visual spatio-temporal reasoning: Audio-Visual Temporal Reasoning (AVTR), Audio-Visual Spatial Reasoning (AVSR), and Audio-Visual Spatio-Temporal Reasoning (AVSTR).

Developed AVST-Zero, a Video-LLM fine-tuned using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) combined with a multi-dimensional reward system tailored for format, object, temporal, and spatial accuracy in audio-visual contexts.
Results: R-AVST is the first dataset to combine fine-grained temporal boundaries and spatial localization for over 100 types of audio-visual events in untrimmed videos, offering a robust benchmark.

AVST-Zero (7B) achieved the highest mean temporal IoU (m tIoU) of 47.96% on Audio-Visual Temporal Reasoning (AVTR) and superior joint grounding with 46.04% m tIoU and 8.59% mean visual IoU (m vIoU) on Audio-Visual Spatio-Temporal Reasoning (AVSTR).

Ablation studies confirmed the critical contribution of each multi-dimensional reward component and the GRPO fine-tuning strategy, with GRPO improving AVTR m tIoU from 42.84% (SFT) to 48.17% (AVST-Zero).
Takeaways: A comprehensive dataset like R-AVST, uniquely combining fine-grained temporal and spatial annotations with diverse audio-visual events, is crucial for advancing models beyond simple video understanding.

Reinforcement learning, specifically GRPO with a carefully designed multi-dimensional reward system, significantly enhances Video-LLM performance in fine-grained spatio-temporal reasoning tasks over supervised fine-tuning.
Accurate spatio-temporal reasoning for both audible and visible objects in complex real-world scenarios requires a holistic integration of audio and visual cues, revealing their interdependencies.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.16674.Title: Dataset Distillation for Pre-Trained Self-Supervised Vision Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.16674.Summary: The Massachusetts Institute of Technology developed Linear Gradient Matching (LGM), a dataset distillation method for pre-trained self-supervised vision models. This approach synthesizes a single, highly discriminative synthetic image per class, enabling efficient training of linear classifiers and providing insights into model representations and biases.
Problem: Traditional dataset distillation (DD) methods primarily focus on training models from scratch, which is misaligned with the modern computer vision paradigm of using large, pre-trained self-supervised models.

There was a lack of DD techniques specifically designed to efficiently train lightweight linear probes on top of these frozen pre-trained vision models for downstream tasks, which can still be computationally intensive.

Scaling existing DD methods to achieve high performance with ultra-small datasets (e.g., one image per class) for large-scale tasks like ImageNet has been challenging due to memory constraints and instability.
Method: Introduced Linear Gradient Matching (LGM), a method that distills synthetic images by aligning the gradients of a randomly initialized linear classifier trained on synthetic features with those derived from real data, using a frozen pre-trained backbone.
Employed a pyramid representation for each synthetic image, optimizing multi-scale components progressively to prevent adversarial patterns, improve realism, and enhance generalization across models.

Incorporated multi-round differentiable augmentations during distillation, applying transformations like cropping, flipping, and noising to multiple copies of synthetic data per iteration to boost robustness and cross-model transferability.
Results: LGM achieved test accuracy up to 75% on ImageNet-1k with DINO-v2 using just one synthetic image per class, closely approaching the 83% accuracy from the full 1.3 million real images, and consistently outperformed real-image baselines.

Distilled images revealed that MoCo-v3's poor performance on adversarial datasets like Spawrious stemmed from prioritizing spurious background elements over foreground objects, unlike robust models like DINO-v2.

The method's regularization techniques, especially differentiable augmentations and pyramid representation, were critical for achieving high performance and ensuring good generalization across different pre-trained backbone models.
Takeaways: LGM distills highly discriminative synthetic images that effectively train linear probes, often representing extreme class features rather than averages, which is particularly effective for fine-grained classification.

The distilled images serve as an interpretability tool, visually diagnosing model biases (e.g., reliance on spurious correlations on datasets like Spawrious) and offering insights into the distinct representational strategies of different pre-trained backbones.

Distilled datasets exhibit cross-model transferability, and this transferability correlates with the alignment of embedding spaces between different pre-trained models, supporting the 'Platonic Representation Hypothesis'.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.16672.Title: EvoLMM: Self-Evolving Large Multimodal Models with Continuous Rewards
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.16672.Summary: Researchers from Mohamed bin Zayed University of AI present EvoLMM, a framework enabling Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) to autonomously improve their reasoning capabilities without human supervision. It utilizes a continuous self-consistency reward and an entropy-guided question generation mechanism, achieving consistent absolute accuracy gains of +2-3% across various multimodal reasoning benchmarks.
Problem: Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) heavily depend on human-annotated data, metadata, or external reward models for training and fine-tuning.
This dependency creates scalability bottlenecks, restricts generalization to novel domains, and increases the cost and effort of model development.
Prior self-improvement techniques for LMMs often rely on discrete rewards, which are unstable and sub-optimal in multimodal settings, especially during early training.
Method: EvoLMM instantiates two cooperative roles, a Proposer and a Solver, from a single LMM backbone, operating in a closed-loop fashion.
The Solver is trained using a novel continuous self-consistency reward, calculated from the agreement among multiple answers generated by the model itself, providing stable gradients.
The Proposer's reward is guided by the Solver's consensus entropy, encouraging it to generate questions of moderate difficulty, thereby establishing an automatic curriculum for the Solver.
Results: EvoLMM achieved consistent gains of approximately +2-3% absolute accuracy across a broad suite of multimodal mathematical and visual reasoning benchmarks (e.g., ChartQA from 84.00% to 86.70%).
The continuous self-consistency reward approach proved superior to discrete majority-vote rewards, which offered only marginal gains (+0.3-0.6%) and sometimes degraded performance.

The framework demonstrated robust performance and architecture-agnostic improvements (+1-3% accuracy) across different LMM backbones (e.g., Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, InternVL3-8B) and positive scaling with larger model sizes.
Takeaways: A continuous self-consistency reward is more stable and effective for LMM self-improvement than discrete rewards, leading to consistent learning progression.
An entropy-guided Proposer reward mechanism can dynamically adjust question difficulty, fostering an emergent curriculum that drives the Solver to develop more structured reasoning.
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning strategies like LoRA are crucial for stabilizing the self-evolution process and preserving the LMM's general multimodal capabilities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.16160.Title: Video2Layout: Recall and Reconstruct Metric-Grounded Cognitive Map for Spatial Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.16160.Summary: Researchers from several Chinese institutions developed a framework, Video2Layout, that equips multimodal large language models with a metric-grounded cognitive map, enabling precise spatial reasoning by converting video inputs into continuous Bird's-Eye View object coordinates. This system demonstrates enhanced accuracy on spatial benchmarks and improves generalization to real-world environments through a two-stage training approach.
Problem: Existing multimodal large language models (MLLMs) struggle with precise spatial perception and reasoning, particularly in forming coherent global spatial representations from multi-frame visual inputs.

Previous attempts to integrate cognitive maps into MLLMs relied on discrete, grid-based representations, which led to coarse positional descriptions, inaccuracies in real-world metrics, and object overlaps.
The inherent ambiguity of natural language descriptions for spatial relationships hinders fine-grained, quantitative spatial computation required for advanced embodied AI tasks.
Method: The Video2Layout framework constructs a metric-grounded cognitive map from video inputs, representing spatial layouts using continuous Bird's-Eye View (BEV) bounding box coordinates for precise object localization and size.

A structured Chain-of-Thought (COT) process explicitly decouples spatial perception (Map Module) from mathematical and logical deduction (Think Module) to perform rigorous numerical spatial computation.

A two-stage training paradigm utilizes Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on simulated data to instill foundational spatial perception and a structured output format, followed by Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RFT) on real-world data to enhance generalization and bridge the sim-to-real gap.
Results: V2LO-7B achieved an average accuracy of 47.46% across mainstream spatial reasoning benchmarks, demonstrating an absolute improvement of 3.29% over its base model and 4.92% over grid-map-trained counterparts.

The framework outperformed leading closed-source models like GPT-4o (46.25% overall) and Gemini 2.0 Flash (32.56% on ViewSpatial-Bench), with V2LO-7B achieving 40.18% on ViewSpatial-Bench and slightly surpassing GPT-4o's overall average.

Analysis on the QVS-Bench diagnostic benchmark revealed that cognitive map accuracy and overall spatial task performance peak with 4-8 input images (e.g., 61.32% map accuracy with 4 images), indicating an optimal range for visual information aggregation, and V2LO-7B consistently outperformed baselines across varying image quantities.
Takeaways: Metric-grounded cognitive maps, using continuous object coordinates, offer a significantly more powerful foundation for fine-grained spatial knowledge learning compared to discrete grid-based representations.

Transforming abstract spatial problems into explicit mathematical deductions via a structured numerical Chain-of-Thought enhances reasoning accuracy by overcoming the imprecision of purely linguistic spatial descriptions.

The synergistic combination of SFT with precisely annotated synthetic data and RFT with real-world data effectively generalizes MLLM spatial reasoning capabilities to diverse real-world scenarios without requiring explicit ground-truth coordinates during reinforcement learning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.16077.Title: VideoSeg-R1:Reasoning Video Object Segmentation via Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.16077.Summary: VideoSeg-R1 introduces the first framework to integrate reinforcement learning (RL) with large language models for referring video object segmentation, enabling explicit, interpretable reasoning in dynamic video environments. It achieves new state-of-the-art performance across multiple video and image reasoning segmentation benchmarks, including a 4.1 J&F point increase over prior SOTA on ReVOS.
Problem: Existing Referring Video Object Segmentation (RVOS) methods, primarily based on supervised fine-tuning, generalize poorly to out-of-distribution data and lack explicit, interpretable reasoning chains.
Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) often struggle with long-form videos and complex language queries that demand multi-step temporal reasoning.

Applying reinforcement learning to video reasoning segmentation faces challenges such as an exploding action space with temporal length and the need for complex reward functions balancing spatial accuracy and temporal consistency.
Method: VideoSeg-R1 proposes an RL-driven framework with a decoupled three-stage architecture: Hierarchical Text-guided Frame Sampler (HTFS), a Reasoning Model, and a Segmentation and Propagation stage.
The Reasoning Model utilizes an MLLM (Qwen2.5-VL) optimized with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to generate explicit spatial cues and a Chain-of-Thought (CoT).
Novel reward functions, including a negative point distance reward and a task-difficulty-aware soft length penalty, guide the RL agent to balance accuracy, efficiency, and reasoning depth.
Results: VideoSeg-R1 achieved new state-of-the-art J&F scores on Ref-YouTube-VOS (81.3), Ref-DAVIS17 (79.8), MeViS (55.3), and notably 61.1 J&F on the ReVOS reasoning benchmark, surpassing the best prior method by 4.1 points.
It also set new SOTA on reasoning-intensive image segmentation datasets like ReasonSeg (69.8 gIoU, 68.2 cIoU), demonstrating strong reasoning capabilities in static contexts.

Ablation studies confirmed the critical roles of RL training, the Hierarchical Text-guided Frame Sampler (HTFS), synergistic spatial prompts (bounding box, positive/negative points), and the soft length penalty in improving performance and efficiency.
Takeaways: Reinforcement learning can effectively instill explicit, interpretable reasoning capabilities in MLLMs for complex, dynamic video object segmentation tasks, surpassing the generalization limitations of supervised fine-tuning.

A decoupled, multi-stage architecture, combining efficient frame sampling, RL-driven reasoning, and specialized segmentation/propagation models (SAM2, XMem), effectively handles the computational complexity of long videos.

Adaptive control of reasoning depth through a soft length penalty, guided by estimated task difficulty, improves both segmentation performance and computational efficiency by preventing unnecessary reasoning steps.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.16043.Title: Agent0: Unleashing Self-Evolving Agents from Zero Data via Tool-Integrated Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.16043.Summary: Agent0, developed by researchers at UNC-Chapel Hill, Salesforce Research, and Stanford University, introduces a fully autonomous framework for evolving high-performing LLM agents from scratch, without human-curated data. The system achieves substantial improvements, such as an 18% increase in mathematical reasoning and a 24% boost in general reasoning for Qwen3-8B-Base models, through a co-evolutionary loop and tool-integrated learning.
Problem: Current LLM agents, especially those trained with Reinforcement Learning (RL), heavily depend on massive, high-quality human-curated datasets, creating scalability and cost bottlenecks.
Existing self-evolution frameworks often suffer from "learning stagnation," as the tasks they generate rarely surpass the model's current capabilities, limiting continuous improvement.
Many frameworks struggle to foster complex multi-step reasoning and effective external tool integration, often limited to single-round interactions.
Method: A fully autonomous, iterative co-evolutionary framework where a Curriculum Agent generates increasingly challenging tasks and an Executor Agent learns to solve them, both initialized from a base LLM.
Seamless integration of an external code interpreter tool, where the Curriculum Agent is explicitly rewarded for generating tasks that require tool use, establishing a "virtuous cycle."

Ambiguity-Dynamic Policy Optimization (ADPO) for Executor training, which employs ambiguity-aware advantage scaling and dynamically modulated trust regions to handle noisy pseudo-labels from self-generated data.
Results: Agent0 achieved an 18% average improvement in mathematical reasoning and a 24% boost in general-domain reasoning on Qwen3-8B-Base models, consistently outperforming existing self-evolutionary and tool-integrated baselines.
The co-evolutionary loop demonstrated stable, progressive performance improvement over multiple iterations, with the curriculum agent successfully generating more difficult, tool-reliant tasks.
Ablation studies confirmed the critical roles of Curriculum Agent training, the explicit tool reward, repetition penalty, ADPO, and multi-turn reasoning for the framework's overall effectiveness.
Takeaways: A symbiotic co-evolutionary process between a task-generating Curriculum Agent and a task-solving Executor Agent can drive continuous, autonomous improvement from zero human data.

Deeply integrating external tools into the curriculum generation process itself creates a self-reinforcing cycle, leading to the discovery and mastery of increasingly complex, tool-aware reasoning skills.

Addressing ambiguity and noise in self-generated training data through mechanisms like ambiguity-aware advantage scaling and dynamic trust regions is crucial for stable and effective self-evolutionary learning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.15703.Title: Think Visually, Reason Textually: Vision-Language Synergy in ARC
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.15703.Summary: A multimodal framework strategically combines visual abstraction for pattern recognition with textual reasoning for precise execution, enhancing abstract reasoning capabilities on ARC-AGI benchmarks. The approach achieves up to a 7.25% improvement on ARC-AGI and enables smaller open-source models to outperform larger closed-source ones by integrating vision-language synergy.
Problem: State-of-the-art foundation models exhibit significant limitations in abstract reasoning from minimal examples, a core challenge in Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) as tested by ARC-AGI.
Most existing ARC-AGI approaches treat it as a purely textual task, overlooking the visual nature of the puzzles and losing intuitive spatial information critical for human problem-solving.
Naive integration of visual inputs can paradoxically degrade performance due to the imprecision of pixel-based rule execution, highlighting the need for a more strategic multimodal approach.
Method: The research conducts a systematic comparative analysis of visual and textual modalities, empirically decomposing ARC-AGI into 'rule summarization' and 'rule application' to identify modality-specific strengths and weaknesses.

Vision-Language Synergy Reasoning (VLSR) is proposed, which strategically routes visual representations to rule summarization (pattern recognition) and textual representations to rule application (precise manipulation).

Modality-Switch Self-Correction (MSSC) is introduced, allowing models to generate output textually and then visualize it to detect inconsistencies with examples, providing effective iterative refinement through cross-modal verification.
Results: The combined VLSR+MSSC approach yields substantial gains across various models and benchmarks, achieving up to a 7.25% improvement (Gemini-2.5-Pro on ARC-AGI) and an average of 4.33% over text-only baselines.

Modality-Switch Self-Correction (MSSC) demonstrates consistent monotonic gains through iterative rounds of correction, improving GPT-4o's performance from 8.25% to 12.0% in three rounds, significantly surpassing text-only self-correction.
Applying vision-language synergy during fine-tuning allows a smaller open-source model (Qwen3-8B) to achieve 13.25% on ARC-AGI, outperforming closed-source baselines like GPT-4o (8.25%) by 3.5%.
Takeaways: Vision excels in holistic pattern recognition, 2D structure preservation, and encoding efficiency for summarizing abstract rules, while textual reasoning provides fine-grained precision for applying discrete transformation rules.
A simple addition of visual inputs is insufficient; a strategic, task-decomposed integration of modalities is necessary to leverage their complementary strengths for abstract reasoning.

Intrinsic self-correction is significantly enhanced by switching modalities (e.g., visual verification of text-generated outputs), enabling models to identify and rectify errors more effectively than text-only self-correction.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.15661.Title: VisPlay: Self-Evolving Vision-Language Models from Images
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.15661.Summary: The VisPlay framework enables Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to autonomously enhance their reasoning and factual grounding by learning from unlabeled image data, eliminating the need for human annotations. This approach achieves consistent performance gains across diverse visual reasoning tasks, including reducing hallucination for Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct from 32.81% to 94.95%, and demonstrates competitive average accuracy compared to models trained with human-curated data.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) heavily depend on costly, labor-intensive human-annotated datasets, limiting their scalability and continuous improvement.
The successful self-evolving paradigm observed in Large Language Models (LLMs) has not been widely adapted to VLMs due to the complexities of integrating visual modalities.
Existing reinforcement learning methods for VLMs typically require external, verifiable rewards derived from human annotations or specific heuristics, reintroducing scalability issues.
Method: Introduces VisPlay, a self-evolving reinforcement learning framework that operates a single VLM in a closed-loop, self-play system using only unlabeled images.
Decomposes the VLM into two interacting roles: an Image-Conditioned Questioner (generating diverse, challenging questions) and a Multimodal Reasoner (answering these questions).
Employs Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with internal uncertainty and diversity rewards to train the Questioner, and uses filtered, moderately confident pseudo-labels to train the Reasoner.
Results: Demonstrated consistent overall performance improvements across various VLM architectures, with Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct's average score increasing from 30.61% to 47.27% over three iterations.
Achieved a substantial reduction in visual hallucination, improving the hallucination score for Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct from 32.81% to 94.95% by the second iteration.
Showed competitive average accuracy compared to models trained on human-curated data, validating the quality and effectiveness of self-generated supervision for VLM enhancement.
Takeaways: The self-evolving paradigm, successful in LLMs, can be effectively adapted to Vision-Language Models by establishing a closed-loop self-play system with internal reward mechanisms.
Designing an Image-Conditioned Questioner that generates tasks based on the Reasoner's uncertainty and diversity can autonomously drive progressive learning without human supervision.
Filtering self-generated question-answer pairs to include only those with moderate confidence allows the Reasoner to learn from challenging yet attainable examples, improving overall robustness.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.13876.Title: QwenCLIP: Boosting Medical Vision-Language Pretraining via LLM Embeddings and Prompt tuning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.13876.Summary: Researchers at LIPADE, Université Paris Cité, developed QwenCLIP, a medical vision-language pretraining framework that integrates dedicated Large Language Model embeddings and a hybrid prompt tuning strategy. This approach effectively processes lengthy clinical texts, achieving state-of-the-art performance in medical image retrieval tasks with improvements in CUI@K and Precision@K across multiple benchmarks.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language Pretraining (VLP) models like CLIP struggle with limited text input length (77 tokens), failing to process the often hundreds of tokens in detailed medical reports.
Even domain-specific BERT encoders used in medical CLIP variants face context limits (e.g., 512 tokens), leading to significant information loss in comprehensive clinical narratives.
Prior attempts to integrate Large Language Models (LLMs) often involve complex, computationally intensive two-stage training to adapt generative LLMs for discriminative embedding tasks.
Method: Replaces the traditional CLIP text encoder with a frozen Qwen3-embedding-8B model, a dedicated LLM embedding model designed for dense representation learning and long context windows.
Implements a hybrid prompt tuning strategy, combining static explicit instructions with learnable soft prompt vectors, to optimally guide the LLM for cross-modal medical tasks.
Utilizes a learnable Vision Transformer (ViT-B/16) as the image encoder, trained with the LLM embeddings via a standard InfoNCE contrastive loss to align visual and textual modalities.
Results: QwenCLIP achieved state-of-the-art CUI@K scores on the ROCOv2 dataset (e.g., 45.96 @5, 52.47 @50), indicating enhanced alignment between medical images and their associated concepts.

The framework demonstrated superior performance across all zero-shot image-to-image retrieval benchmarks, including ROCOv2 (Modality, Organ, Modality & Organ) and IRMA, with leading Precision@K scores (e.g., 96.24 @5 for Modality on ROCOv2, 98.49 @5 for Organ on IRMA).
