Ablation studies confirmed that both the dedicated LLM embedding model and the learnable prompt tuning strategy independently and synergistically contribute to the observed performance improvements.
Takeaways: Dedicated Large Language Model embedding models significantly improve semantic understanding of medical texts and boost cross-modal alignment performance compared to generic or BERT-based text encoders.
A hybrid prompt tuning strategy, combining static instructions with learnable soft prompts, is crucial for optimally adapting the LLM's representations to specific medical vision-language tasks.
Integrating a dedicated embedding LLM is more efficient and architecturally suitable for VLP than repurposing generative LLMs, reducing complexity and computational cost.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.13787.Title: Exploring Transferability of Self-Supervised Learning by Task Conflict Calibration
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.13787.Summary: Researchers from the Institute of Software Chinese Academy of Sciences and the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences developed Task Conflict Calibration (TC²), a framework enhancing the transferability of self-supervised learning representations by addressing gradient conflicts in multi-task training. This approach consistently improves performance in unsupervised, semi-supervised, and various transfer learning scenarios, including notable gains in out-of-distribution generalization and visual understanding tasks.
Problem: Existing self-supervised learning (SSL) methods often struggle to transfer learned representations effectively to out-of-distribution data or diverse downstream tasks.
A direct integration of meta-learning principles into SSL, while conceptually promising for transferability, leads to unstable and inconsistent performance due to conflicting gradients between tasks.
Task-specific causal factors from other tasks can act as confounders, 'contaminating' the feature representations for a target task.
Method: The Task Conflict Calibration (TC²) framework is introduced, which reformulates SSL training from an instance-centric to a task-centric perspective by splitting mini-batches into distinct SSL tasks.
TC² learns a union of global causal generative factors and identifies task-specific relevant factors for each sample, using these to calibrate representations by filtering out irrelevant semantics.

A two-stage bi-level optimization framework integrates TC² into the SSL pipeline, optimizing both the factor extraction networks and the SSL model to ensure transferability and mitigate task conflicts.
Results: TC² consistently improved unsupervised classification performance across various datasets, with SimCLR+TC² achieving approximately 4.74% higher Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-100.
In semi-supervised learning, Barlow Twins+TC² showed a ~2.9% Top-1 accuracy improvement on ImageNet with 1% labeled data, from 55.0% to 57.9%.

The method enhanced transfer learning capabilities across diverse tasks, including up to a ~3.3% boost in VOS (J-mean) for video tasks and significant gains in object detection/instance segmentation and out-of-distribution generalization (e.g., ~2.5% average accuracy on PACS for MAE+TC²).
Takeaways: Empirical experiments demonstrate that a simple multi-task SSL setup, though yielding average improvements, suffers from significant instability due to frequent and detrimental 'task conflicts' arising from gradient misalignment.
Causal analysis using Structural Causal Models (SCMs) reveals that task-specific causal factors from other tasks act as confounders, degrading target task representation learning.
Calibrating sample representations to retain only task-relevant semantics, by learning and selectively applying causal generative factors, effectively alleviates these identified task conflicts.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.13054.Title: ViSS-R1: Self-Supervised Reinforcement Video Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.13054.Summary: ViSS-R1 introduces a self-supervised reinforcement learning framework to enhance visual understanding in Multimodal Large Language Models for video reasoning. This approach achieved state-of-the-art performance on four out of six video benchmarks, including a 7.2% gain on VSI-Bench, while improving model robustness to visual transformations.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) for video reasoning often exhibit a "text-centric bias," underutilizing rich spatio-temporal visual information.
This bias leads to shortcut learning, where models rely on sparse cues rather than deep visual understanding.
The over-reliance on textual reasoning increases the susceptibility of MLLMs to generating hallucinated or factually incorrect responses in video tasks.
Method: Developed Pretext-GRPO, a self-supervised reinforcement learning method that provides a "warm start" by training the policy model on pretext tasks involving various visual transformations (e.g., rotation, reversal, shuffle).
Introduced the ViSS-R1 framework, which integrates pretext-task-based self-supervised learning (SSL) directly into a unified Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) pipeline.
ViSS-R1 utilizes a novel training approach where models simultaneously reason about both visual transformations (identified via new tags) and real user queries, guided by a composite reward function.
Results: ViSS-R1 achieved state-of-the-art performance on 4 out of 6 widely-used video reasoning and understanding benchmarks, including VSI-Bench, VideoMMMU, TempCompass, and VideoMME.
The framework delivered substantial performance improvements, with ViSS-R1 showing gains up to +7.2% on VSI-Bench and +6.1% on MMVU compared to the base Qwen2.5-VL-7B model.

ViSS-R1 models demonstrated enhanced robustness to various visual transformations, incurring minimal accuracy loss (e.g., -1.1% on VSI-Bench) compared to prior R1 models which saw drops of -3.2% to -6.0%.
Takeaways: Integrating self-supervised visual pretext tasks directly into MLLM reinforcement learning shifts the reasoning paradigm from text-centric to a more robust, visual-centric approach.
Training models to identify various spatio-temporal visual transformations provides a strong "warm start" and enhances the MLLM's ability to deeply process and understand video content.

A unified framework (ViSS-R1) with simultaneous reasoning for pretext tasks and user queries, guided by a multi-component reward, is effective in improving both reasoning and perceptual understanding.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.11113.Title: VIDEOP2R: Video Understanding from Perception to Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.11113.Summary: This research introduces VIDEOP2R, a process-aware reinforcement fine-tuning framework for Large Video Language Models (LVLMs) that explicitly disentangles video perception from reasoning. The framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on six out of seven video understanding benchmarks, demonstrating an average accuracy improvement of 1.3% over prior top methods and 5.8% over its base model.
Problem: Existing reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) frameworks for Large Video Language Models (LVLMs) are process-agnostic, treating video understanding as a single, undifferentiated procedure.

This monolithic approach leads to blurred credit assignment in reinforcement learning, making it difficult to pinpoint whether errors stem from visual misinterpretation (perception) or faulty inference (reasoning).
Current Chain-of-Thought (CoT) data and coarse reward signals conflate perception and reasoning, hindering targeted error correction and efficient learning in LVLMs.
Method: VIDEOP2R employs a two-stage reinforcement fine-tuning framework based on a Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct base model, explicitly modeling perception and reasoning as distinct processes.

The first stage involves Supervised Fine-Tuning with VIDEOP2R-CoT-162K, a new, automatically generated dataset featuring process-aware CoT annotations that clearly separate visual observations from subsequent reasoning.

The second stage utilizes Process-Aware Group Relative Policy Optimization (PA-GRPO), an extension of GRPO that provides distinct reward signals for perception tokens and reasoning tokens, enabling fine-grained credit assignment.
Results: VIDEOP2R achieved state-of-the-art results on six out of seven diverse video understanding benchmarks (VSI-Bench, VideoMMMU, VCR-Bench, MVBench, TempCompass, VideoMME), with an average accuracy gain of 1.3% over previous state-of-the-art methods and 5.8% over its base model.

Ablation studies confirmed the synergistic effect of both the process-aware Supervised Fine-Tuning and Reinforcement Learning stages, yielding an average improvement of 5.8% compared to 2.7% (SFT-only) and 3.1% (RL-only).

Process-aware SFT outperformed process-agnostic SFT by 2.1%, and PA-GRPO achieved a 2.3% average accuracy gain over process-agnostic GRPO, with all components of the process-aware reward function proving essential for optimal performance.
Takeaways: Explicitly modeling and training perception and reasoning separately significantly enhances video understanding and reasoning capabilities in LVLMs, outperforming process-agnostic alternatives.
A process-aware reward mechanism (PA-GRPO) improves RL training efficiency by mitigating 'advantage collapse' and reduces the 'Think-Answer Mismatch' rate by promoting faithful reasoning traces.

The textual perception outputs generated by VIDEOP2R are information-sufficient, demonstrating that the model effectively extracts and verbalizes semantically rich visual evidence, often leading to better downstream reasoning than raw video input for a base model.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.11007.Title: VisMem: Latent Vision Memory Unlocks Potential of Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.11007.Summary: Researchers from NUS, Fudan, Tsinghua, and vivo developed VisMem, a framework that integrates a dual latent vision memory system inspired by human cognition into Vision-Language Models. This approach alleviates the visual processing bottleneck, yielding an average 11.8% performance increase across visual understanding, reasoning, and generation tasks with minimal added inference latency.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) suffer from a "visual processing bottleneck," leading to a loss of visual grounding and contextualized visual experience during multi-step generation.
This bottleneck impairs VLM performance on complex tasks requiring fine-grained perception, multi-step reasoning, and visual fidelity, often resulting in visual hallucinations.

Prior attempts to address this, such as direct training or image/token-level paradigms, incur issues like catastrophic forgetting, high computational costs, or limitations in generating new visual information.
Method: VisMem introduces a cognitively-aligned framework for VLMs, integrating dynamic short-term (perceptual) and long-term (semantic) latent vision memories, inspired by human cognitive theory.

A dynamic memory invocation mechanism, using special tokens, seamlessly triggers and inserts memory content generated by a Query Builder and specialized LoRA-based Memory Formers into the VLM's autoregressive inference.
A two-stage Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) training strategy is used to optimize both the utility of the generated memory content and the efficiency of the memory invocation process.
Results: VisMem achieved an average performance increase of 11.8% across 12 visual benchmarks, outperforming 15 baseline methods in understanding (+8.9%), reasoning (+16.4%), and generation (+10.6%) tasks.
The framework exhibited robust cross-domain generalization and effectively mitigated catastrophic forgetting, showing superior knowledge retention compared to direct training methods.

VisMem maintained broad compatibility across nine diverse base VLM architectures (3B to 38B parameters) and incurred only insignificant additional inference latency, comparable to direct training optimization methods.
Takeaways: Translating human cognitive memory structures, distinguishing between short-term visually-dominant and long-term semantically-dominant memory, offers an effective paradigm for enhancing VLM visual processing.

Dynamically invoking specialized latent vision memories based on the model's cognitive state allows for efficient and context-aware retention and utilization of visual information during complex tasks.

Integrating memory through lightweight, non-intrusive components (e.g., LoRA adapters) allows for substantial VLM capability enhancements while preserving base model generalization and maintaining minimal computational overhead.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.10648.Title: Enhancing the Outcome Reward-based RL Training of MLLMs with Self-Consistency Sampling
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.10648.Summary: This research introduces Self-Consistency Sampling (SCS) to improve the faithfulness of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) trained with outcome-reward reinforcement learning. SCS addresses unfaithful reasoning, where models arrive at correct answers via flawed logic, by integrating a differentiable consistency reward, leading to an average absolute performance gain of 7.7 percentage points for Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct.
Problem: Outcome-reward reinforcement learning (RL) in multiple-choice MLLM tasks often reinforces "unfaithful trajectories" where models guess correct answers despite flawed or hallucinatory reasoning.
This leads to limited performance gains in multiple-choice benchmarks compared to open-ended question-answering, indicating a failure to develop robust reasoning abilities.
Qualitative analysis revealed MLLMs frequently produced incorrect rationales while selecting correct options, and truncated rationales often led to divergent answers, highlighting unstable reasoning.
Method: The Self-Consistency Sampling (SCS) framework is proposed, which integrates a differentiable consistency reward into outcome-reward RL training for MLLMs.

SCS explores "neighboring trajectories" via two mechanisms: Truncation–Resampling (TR), where initial reasoning is truncated and re-sampled, and Visual-Perturbation (VP), which introduces small visual noise to input images.

A consistency reward is calculated based on the number of distinct answers from resampled trajectories, then combined with standard accuracy and format rewards to update the MLLM policy, penalizing inconsistent reasoning.
Results: SCS consistently improved MLLM performance, achieving an average absolute gain of 7.7 percentage points for Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct over the RLOO baseline across six multimodal benchmarks.
Models trained with SCS demonstrated a 13.6% to 15.2% reduction in unfaithful reasoning occurrences compared to baselines, validated by human and strong LLM evaluations.

The method generalized across different model scales (3B, 7B, 8B parameters) and various RL algorithms, with both Truncation–Resampling and Visual Perturbation components synergistically contributing to performance gains.
Takeaways: Outcome-reward alone is insufficient for distinguishing genuinely correct reasoning from unfaithful lucky guesses in multiple-choice MLLM tasks.
Perturbing reasoning trajectories through truncation and visual noise can effectively assess and, subsequently, improve the robustness and faithfulness of MLLM reasoning during RL training.
Integrating a consistency reward into existing outcome-reward RL frameworks provides a computationally efficient method to enhance reasoning fidelity without requiring complex process reward models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.10395.Title: AgentEvolver: Towards Efficient Self-Evolving Agent System
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.10395.Summary: AgentEvolver presents a self-evolving agent system that leverages large language models for autonomous task generation, efficient exploration, and fine-grained credit assignment. The framework demonstrated an average performance improvement of 29.4 percentage points for its 7B model and reduced training steps for convergence by up to 67% on standard benchmarks.
Problem: The high cost and scarcity of manually crafted, diverse task datasets for training LLM-powered agents.
Inefficient exploration strategies in reinforcement learning (RL) for LLM agents, leading to slow convergence in complex, tool-augmented environments.
Low sample utilization in RL, where sparse terminal rewards fail to provide fine-grained credit assignment for individual actions within a trajectory.
Method: Self-Questioning: Enables autonomous generation of diverse training tasks and reference solutions by leveraging LLMs for curiosity-guided environment exploration and adaptive task synthesis.
Self-Navigating: Boosts exploration efficiency by distilling and reusing structured natural language 'experiences' from past successful or failed trajectories to guide future rollouts.
Self-Attributing: Improves sample efficiency through LLM-based retrospective analysis to assign fine-grained, step-wise attribution rewards to individual actions within a trajectory.
Results: Achieved a 29.4 percentage point improvement in average task goal completion (avg@8) for the 7B model and 27.8 percentage points for the 14B model on AppWorld and BFCL v3 benchmarks.
Reduced training steps for convergence by 55% on AppWorld and 67% on BFCL v3 compared to baselines, demonstrating significantly enhanced sample efficiency.
Synthetic training data generated by the system proved as effective as, or superior to, human-curated data, facilitating cross-domain generalization.
Takeaways: Large Language Models possess sufficient reasoning capabilities to autonomously drive their own learning process, encompassing task generation, exploration guidance, and reward attribution.
High-quality synthetic training data, generated by LLMs with robust curation and a reference-based LLM Judge, can effectively replace or augment human-curated datasets for agent training.
Combining curiosity-driven task generation, experience-guided exploration, and fine-grained credit assignment mechanisms creates a synergistic system for efficient and scalable agent self-evolution.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.10279.Title: PROPA: Toward Process-level Optimization in Visual Reasoning via Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.10279.Summary: A framework called PROPA is introduced by the University of Melbourne to enhance complex visual reasoning in Vision-Language Models by combining Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) for dense, process-level reward generation with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and an interleaved Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) scheme. This approach achieves state-of-the-art accuracy across seven benchmarks, demonstrating up to a 21.0% gain on out-of-domain tasks, by specifically optimizing intermediate reasoning steps.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) struggle with complex, multi-step visual reasoning tasks, where errors in early stages can propagate and lead to incorrect final answers.
Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) methods for reasoning require costly, dense step-level human annotations, or suffer from error propagation and overfitting when using auto-generated data.

Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) approaches typically use sparse, outcome-level feedback, making it difficult to pinpoint errors in intermediate steps and leading to unstable training and inefficient exploration.
Method: PROPA employs Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to automatically generate dense, process-level reward estimates for each intermediate reasoning step, eliminating the need for human annotations.

It utilizes Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to refine the VLM's policy using these MCTS-generated process rewards, enhanced with localized updates, group-level filtering, and a log-based nonlinear reward transformation.

An interleaved training scheme dynamically combines GRPO updates (on successful MCTS trajectories) with SFT updates (on trajectories where MCTS fails or for initial stabilization) to address the cold-start problem and maintain robust learning.
A dedicated Process Reward Model (PRM) is trained to predict node scores, which then guides MCTS efficiently during test-time inference, replacing computationally expensive simulations.
Results: PROPA consistently achieves the highest accuracy across all seven visual reasoning benchmarks (both in-domain and out-of-domain) and four VLM backbones, outperforming competitive baselines like Reason-RFT.

The framework demonstrates substantial quantitative gains, including an average accuracy improvement of 7.9% and 10.1% on Qwen2.5-VL-3B and Intern2.5-VL-2B backbones, respectively, over Reason-RFT, with a peak gain of 21.0% on the TranceL (Out-of-Domain) benchmark.

Ablation studies confirm the critical role of the interleaved training scheme, the log-based nonlinear reward transformation, and the Process Reward Model in PROPA's superior performance, stability, and effective test-time search.
Takeaways: Automatically generated, dense process-level rewards are highly effective for optimizing intermediate reasoning steps in VLMs, moving beyond sparse outcome-based feedback.

An interleaved training strategy, blending reinforcement learning with supervised fine-tuning, stabilizes the learning process and effectively mitigates the cold-start problem often associated with pure RL approaches.
A learned Process Reward Model can accurately guide efficient MCTS at inference time, aligning test-time search with the optimized training signal without incurring high computational costs.
Non-linear transformations applied to process rewards amplify their disparities, allowing GRPO to more effectively differentiate between high- and low-quality reasoning paths.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.10055.Title: Image Aesthetic Reasoning via HCM-GRPO: Empowering Compact Model for Superior Performance
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.10055.Summary: Researchers from Tsinghua University and Alibaba Health developed HCM-GRPO, an enhanced reinforcement learning framework, along with a novel dataset, to improve image aesthetic reasoning in multimodal large language models. This approach enabled compact models to achieve over 20 points higher performance on image screening tasks compared to leading large-scale MLLMs, demonstrating superior physical and spatial understanding.
Problem: State-of-the-art Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) exhibit unsatisfactory performance in image aesthetic reasoning, often failing to identify objective flaws like appearance deformation or illogical extensions in generated content.

A scarcity of specialized datasets exists to effectively train and evaluate MLLMs on objective image quality assessment, particularly concerning verifiable physical transformations rather than subjective artistic preferences.
The uncontrolled nature of AI-generated images necessitates a robust and automated post-generation screening mechanism to ensure quality and consistency in real-world applications.
Method: A large-scale image screening dataset was constructed, comprising over 128,000 samples and approximately 640,000 images, specifically designed to evaluate MLLMs on four objective aesthetic dimensions.

A two-stage training methodology was implemented, starting with Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) to establish basic spatial understanding, followed by reinforcement fine-tuning using the proposed HCM-GRPO framework.

The HCM-GRPO (Hard Cases Mining with Dynamic Proportional Accuracy Reward in Group Relative Policy Optimization) method was developed, incorporating a novel DPA reward function and a strategy to identify and re-sample hard cases, thereby focusing learning on model weaknesses.
Results: Compact MLLMs fine-tuned with HCM-GRPO achieved an overall score of 64.74 on the image screening dataset, demonstrating over 20 points higher performance than the best large-scale open-source and leading closed-source MLLMs (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct at 39.74, GPT4o at 34.62).

Hard Cases Mining proved effective, with the HCM-GRPO approach (InternVL3-2B) outperforming variants without hard case augmentation, confirming that targeted learning from difficult examples improves reasoning.

The proposed methodology generalized well to public benchmarks, improving InternVL3-2B's accuracy on RealWorldQA by 2.62 points and BLINK by 8.92 points, indicating its robustness for broader physical reasoning and multi-image understanding tasks.
Takeaways: Existing MLLMs, including large closed-source models, exhibit performance akin to random guessing on objective image aesthetic reasoning tasks, revealing a significant deficiency in their physical and spatial understanding.

Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), particularly with human-answer-guided Chain-of-Thought data, is crucial for equipping MLLMs with foundational instruction-following and basic spatial understanding, serving as an effective "cold start."

The combination of a dynamic proportional accuracy reward for multi-choice questions and a hard cases mining strategy within a reinforcement learning framework effectively focuses MLLM learning on challenging examples, leading to substantial performance improvements.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.09158.Title: Efficient Reasoning via Reward Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.09158.Summary: Researchers from City University of Hong Kong and Huawei Research developed a Conciseness Reward Model (CRM) and an innovative Conciseness Reward Function (CRF) to enable Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) to generate more efficient and accurate solutions. This approach delivered an 8.1% improvement in Pass@1 accuracy and a 19.9% reduction in token length on the Qwen2.5-7B model, successfully mitigating common issues like length and training collapse.
Problem: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) frequently exhibit "overthinking," producing verbose and redundant reasoning steps that increase computational costs and latency.

Existing length penalty methods designed to encourage conciseness often lead to "length collapse," where reasoning quality suffers, or "training collapse," indicating a breakdown in the learning process.
The absence of reliable and scalable methods to quantitatively evaluate reasoning path conciseness without extensive human annotation hindered the development of efficient LRMs.
Method: A Conciseness Reward Model (CRM) was trained using an innovative LLM-powered data augmentation pipeline, scoring reasoning paths based on factors like repetition, irrelevance, and token length.
A novel Conciseness Reward Function (CRF) was designed, incorporating an explicit dependency where conciseness is rewarded only when the reasoning outcome is correct, preventing reward hacking.

The CRF integrated an annealing coefficient for training stability and a difficulty coefficient to adapt conciseness expectations based on problem complexity, applied within a Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) framework.
Results: The method achieved an 8.1% absolute improvement in Pass@1 accuracy and a 19.9% reduction in average token length compared to original GRPO on the Qwen2.5-7B backbone.
Consistent performance gains were observed across diverse LLM backbones, including Llama3.1-8B and Mistral-7B-v0.1, confirming the framework's generalizability.
Ablation studies demonstrated that the explicit dependency within the CRF is essential for robust training, preventing a 9.8% drop in outcome reward compared to a simple weighted sum approach.
Takeaways: An explicit dependency between outcome correctness and conciseness in the reward function is crucial for preventing "length collapse" and "training collapse," common pitfalls of simpler length penalties.
Leveraging powerful LLMs for data augmentation and conciseness scoring provides a scalable and robust alternative to human annotation for training effective reward models.

The proposed Conciseness Reward Function theoretically reduces the variance of the stochastic gradient estimator and improves convergence properties, leading to more stable and efficient reinforcement learning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.09057.Title: PAN: A World Model for General, Interactable, and Long-Horizon World Simulation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.09057.Summary: PAN, a world model from MBZUAI's Institute of Foundation Models, employs a Generative Latent Prediction (GLP) architecture to enable open-domain, action-conditioned simulation with coherent, long-term dynamics. The model achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-source models, demonstrating 70.3% accuracy in agent simulation and improving planning success by 26.7% in open-ended tasks when integrated with an external VLM.
Problem: Current high-fidelity video generation models lack causal control, interactivity, and long-horizon consistency, operating in an open-loop manner without explicit state or action representations.

Existing world models are typically confined to restricted domains (e.g., game environments) and struggle to generalize across diverse scenarios, provide deep interactive control, or unify different capabilities.

Purely latent-space predictive models are susceptible to representational collapse, where their learned latent transitions do not reliably correspond to observable and physically grounded world dynamics.
Method: Introduces the Generative Latent Prediction (GLP) architecture, unifying a vision encoder, an autoregressive world model backbone (based on a large language model), and a video diffusion decoder.

Utilizes a generative supervision objective (flow matching loss) that explicitly anchors latent space predictions to observable data, ensuring that learned world dynamics are perceptually grounded and interpretable.

Integrates a Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct-based LLM as the latent dynamics backbone for general knowledge and long-horizon reasoning, alongside an enhanced Causal Shift-Window Denoising Process Model (Causal Swin-DPM) for high-fidelity, temporally coherent video generation.
Results: Achieved state-of-the-art performance among open-source world models and is competitive with leading commercial models across action simulation fidelity, long-horizon forecast, and simulative reasoning benchmarks.

Demonstrated superior action simulation fidelity with 70.3% accuracy on agent simulation and 47.0% on environment simulation, along with leading long-horizon forecasting (53.6% transition smoothness, 64.1% simulation consistency).

Improved planning performance when integrated with an external VLM agent, leading to a 26.7% increase in task success for Open-Ended Planning and a 23.4% increase for Structured Planning compared to a VLM-only baseline.
Takeaways: Explicit generative supervision through observable data reconstruction is essential for preventing representational collapse in world models, ensuring that abstract latent dynamics correspond to real-world changes.

Leveraging large language models as the core for latent world dynamics enables the integration of vast real-world knowledge and facilitates open-domain, natural language-conditioned interaction and long-horizon reasoning.

A hierarchical generative approach, combining an LLM for global causal dynamics with a video diffusion model for local perceptual detail, effectively bridges abstract causal reasoning and high-fidelity visual simulation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.09018.Title: Causally-Grounded Dual-Path Attention Intervention for Object Hallucination Mitigation in LVLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.09018.Summary: Researchers from the University of Electronic Science and Technology of China and the University of Auckland developed Owl, a causally-grounded dual-path attention intervention that employs a Structural Causal Model and the Visual-to-Textual Attention Contribution Ratio (VTACR) to mitigate object hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models. This method reduces sentence-level hallucination by up to 22.1% and instance-level hallucination by up to 36.7% on CHAIR benchmarks, while preserving general vision-language understanding.
Problem: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) frequently suffer from "object hallucination," generating content inconsistent with visual input.
This issue severely compromises LVLM trustworthiness and limits their deployment in safety-critical applications.
Prior attention-based mitigation methods often address visual or textual attention in isolation, failing to account for their complex, interactive causal relationship in driving hallucinations.
Method: Formalizes the object hallucination process using a Structural Causal Model (SCM), treating visual and textual attention as explicit mediators for intervention.
Introduces the Visual-to-Textual Attention Contribution Ratio (VTACR) to dynamically quantify the cross-modal attention balance and identify hallucination risk.
Implements an adaptive, token- and layer-wise attention modulation within a dual-path contrastive decoding strategy to enhance visual grounding and suppress textual over-reliance.
Results: The Owl framework achieved state-of-the-art hallucination mitigation on CHAIR benchmarks, reducing sentence-level hallucinations by up to 22.1% and instance-level by up to 36.7%.
General vision-language understanding was preserved or enhanced across multiple VQA benchmarks, with LLaVA-1.5 showing a +3.7 gain on TextVQA and +7.6% on VizWiz.
Owl demonstrated robust generalization against object hallucinations on the POPE benchmark, consistently outperforming other baselines, particularly in adversarial settings.
Takeaways: Object hallucination is causally linked to an imbalance in visual and textual attention, where over-reliance on textual context (linguistic priors) overrides visual evidence.
The Visual-to-Textual Attention Contribution Ratio (VTACR) provides a dynamic, layer-wise signal to identify insufficient visual grounding during token generation.
Intervening on visual and textual attention as explicit mediators within a Structural Causal Model allows for targeted, interpretable control over the hallucination process.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.08585.Title: Simulating the Visual World with Artificial Intelligence: A Roadmap
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.08585.Summary: Researchers from Carnegie Mellon University, Nanyang Technological University, and Kuaishou Technology present a conceptual roadmap for evolving video generation models into comprehensive artificial intelligence world models. This work introduces a four-generation taxonomy, defines key concepts like "physical world models" and "navigation modes," and outlines a structured progression towards physically plausible, highly interactive, and planning-capable simulations.
Problem: The term "world model" in AI research lacks a precise and unified definition, leading to ambiguity in evaluating progress and aligning research efforts.
The rapidly advancing field of video generation, despite its potential for world models, lacks a structured taxonomy to categorize model capabilities and delineate future research trajectories.

Current video generation models face limitations such as restricted video length, challenges in maintaining 3D consistency, and insufficient real-time interaction, hindering their development into comprehensive world simulators.
Method: A four-generation taxonomy (Faithfulness, Interactiveness, Planning, Stochasticity) is proposed to systematically categorize the evolutionary stages of video generation models transitioning into world models.

A formal definition for a "physical world model" is established as a digital simulation engine for next-scene video prediction, distinct from 'mental world models', alongside the introduction of "navigation modes" to characterize interactive control signals.

Existing video generation methods are analyzed and mapped across various application domains (robotics, autonomous driving, gaming) within this new taxonomic framework to illustrate progress and identify gaps.
Results: The paper categorizes current high-profile video generation models, such as Sora and Kling 1.0/2.1 Master, within the first two generations (Faithfulness and Interactiveness), highlighting their advancements in visual realism, consistency, and basic control.

It identifies the third generation (Planning) as an emerging stage, with models like NWM and Genie 3 demonstrating complex task planning, self-evolving scenarios, and physically intrinsic faithfulness.

The fourth generation (Stochasticity) is presented as a largely underexplored frontier, emphasizing the need for future research into simulating low-probability events and multi-scale spatiotemporal dynamics.
Takeaways: Modern video generation models implicitly function as world models, inherently capable of simulating physical dynamics, temporal causality, and agent-environment interactions.
The development of world models follows a progressive evolutionary ladder, building capabilities in faithfulness, interactiveness, and planning across distinct generations.
"Navigation modes," defined by temporality, content independence, and spatial reasoning, are critical for discerning true interactive controls from static spatial conditions in generative models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.08577.Title: Think-at-Hard: Selective Latent Iterations to Improve Reasoning Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.08577.Summary: Researchers from Tsinghua University developed Think-at-Hard (TaH), a framework that improves reasoning in large language models by selectively applying deeper latent iterations only to tokens identified as challenging. This approach prevents 'latent overthinking,' achieving accuracy gains of 4.0-5.4% over single-iteration baselines while maintaining computational efficiency.
Problem: Small LLMs struggle to achieve deep reasoning, often hitting performance ceilings when mimicking larger models' Chain-of-Thought trajectories.

Existing recurrent transformers uniformly apply a fixed number of latent iterations to all tokens, leading to 'latent overthinking' where correct predictions for easy tokens are sometimes revised into errors.
Enhancing LLM reasoning typically requires increased parameters or heavy computation, limiting practical deployment in resource-constrained environments.
Method: Introduced Think-at-Hard (TaH), which employs a neural decider to dynamically trigger deeper latent iterations only for tokens identified as 'hard,' avoiding unnecessary computation on 'easy' tokens.
Implemented Duo-causal Attention, allowing tokens to access hidden states from previous positions across all shallower iteration depths, ensuring comprehensive context flow.

Utilized a stable two-stage training scheme: first, supervising the backbone LLM at oracle-determined depths, then training the iteration decider to imitate the oracle's policy with a frozen backbone.
Results: TaH achieved average accuracy gains of 4.0-5.4% over strong single-iteration LLM baselines and 8.1-12.6% over fixed-depth recurrent transformers on reasoning benchmarks.
The method efficiently exempts approximately 94% of tokens from deeper iterations, resulting in per-token FLOPs comparable to single-iteration models while outperforming them.
Ablation studies confirmed the critical roles of duo-causal attention, depth-specific LoRA, and the two-stage training scheme in TaH's superior performance and stability.
Takeaways: Fixed-depth latent iterations can degrade performance due to 'latent overthinking,' as easy tokens may be incorrectly revised by redundant deeper computation.
Selectively allocating deeper computation only to challenging tokens (hard tokens) leads to substantial improvements in reasoning accuracy and computational efficiency.

Depth-aware LoRA adapters and Duo-causal Attention are critical architectural elements for enabling stable cross-depth information flow and specializing model behavior across different computational stages.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.08544.Title: LeJEPA: Provable and Scalable Self-Supervised Learning Without the Heuristics
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.08544.Summary: LeJEPA (Latent-Euclidean Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture) introduces a self-supervised learning framework based on a provably optimal isotropic Gaussian embedding distribution. It utilizes a heuristics-free regularization method, SIGReg, achieving robust and scalable performance, including superior results in in-domain pretraining compared to larger, generically pretrained models.
Problem: Existing Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) rely on numerous brittle, ad-hoc heuristics (e.g., stop-gradients, teacher-student networks, negative samples) to prevent representation collapse.
The prevalent heuristic-driven approach makes JEPA training complex, hard to tune, and lacks a clear theoretical understanding, hindering broader adoption and development.
There was no clear, theoretically optimal statistical distribution identified for encoder embeddings that would intrinsically minimize downstream prediction risk.
Method: Theoretically proving that the isotropic Gaussian distribution is the unique optimal target for encoder embeddings to minimize downstream prediction risk for both linear and non-linear probes.

Introducing Sketched Isotropic Gaussian Regularization (SIGReg), a novel, provable, and scalable method that enforces the isotropic Gaussian distribution using random projections and the Epps-Pulley characteristic function test.

Designing LeJEPA, a simplified self-supervised learning framework that combines a standard JEPA predictive loss with SIGReg, operating with a single hyperparameter and eliminating the need for common heuristics.
Results: LeJEPA demonstrates exceptional stability and versatility across over 50 diverse architectures and a wide range of hyperparameters, successfully operating without common heuristics like stop-gradients or teacher-student networks.

It achieves superior performance for in-domain pretraining, consistently outperforming larger, state-of-the-art foundation models (e.g., DINOv2/v3) on specialized datasets such as Galaxy10 and Food101.

The framework scales effectively to models with up to 1.8 billion parameters on ImageNet-1K, maintaining competitive linear probe accuracies (e.g., 78.5% for ConvNeXtV2-Huge) and an informative training loss highly correlated with downstream performance.
Takeaways: The isotropic Gaussian distribution is theoretically optimal for encoder embeddings, minimizing integrated squared bias and variance for various downstream evaluation tasks.

High-dimensional distribution matching can be achieved scalably and stably by testing one-dimensional projections of embeddings (via a modified Cramér-Wold theorem), particularly with the Epps-Pulley test which ensures uniformly bounded gradients.

A principled, theoretically-grounded distribution regularization strategy effectively prevents representation collapse and achieves strong performance without requiring the complex, brittle heuristics common in other SSL methods.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.07317.Title: RLVE: Scaling Up Reinforcement Learning for Language Models with Adaptive Verifiable Environments
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.07317.Summary: RLVE introduces adaptive verifiable environments that procedurally generate an unbounded supply of dynamically challenging problems for language models. This approach enables continuous learning, improving generalizable reasoning by 3.37% over a data-saturated baseline and achieving 2% higher average performance than a strong RLVR baseline in compute-constrained settings.
Problem: Existing reinforcement learning (RL) methods for language models (LMs) face high costs and scarcity of diverse datasets with ground-truth answers for verifiable rewards.
Traditional RL training suffers from learning signal vanishing, where static problem distributions lead to data saturation on easy tasks or stalled learning on overly difficult ones.
Current RL training paradigms for LMs struggle with scalability and efficient continuous improvement due to finite data and inefficient learning signals.
Method: Introduction of "verifiable environments" that procedurally generate an unbounded number of problems, each defined by an input template, problem generator, and an algorithmic verifier.
Implementation of an adaptive difficulty mechanism that dynamically adjusts the problem distribution based on the language model's evolving performance, maintaining a challenging learning frontier.
Creation of RLVE-GYM, a large suite of 400 manually engineered verifiable environments designed for pedagogical reasoning and leveraging the solving-verification asymmetry.
Results: RLVE achieved a 3.37% absolute average improvement on six reasoning benchmarks for a data-saturated 1.5B LM, outperforming continued traditional RL training by over 7x in improvement per compute.
For compute-constrained scenarios, RLVE training from an SFT model yielded approximately 2% absolute average improvement over using the high-quality DeepMath-103K dataset for the same training steps.
Scaling the number of diverse training environments from 1 to 256 consistently improved performance on 50 held-out reasoning environments across various language models.
Takeaways: Dynamically adapting problem difficulty to the model's capabilities is essential for continuous, efficient learning and preventing data saturation.
Scaling the diversity of training environments, rather than just data volume, is crucial for developing generalizable reasoning abilities in language models.
"Environment engineering," focusing on designing adaptive and verifiable problem spaces, offers a new foundational paradigm for scalable language model development.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.06908.Title: Mono3DVG-EnSD: Enhanced Spatial-aware and Dimension-decoupled Text Encoding for Monocular 3D Visual Grounding
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.06908.Summary: Mono3DVG-EnSD improves monocular 3D visual grounding by introducing a CLIP-Guided Lexical Certainty Adapter to enhance spatial text comprehension and a Dimension-Decoupled Module to mitigate cross-dimensional interference in feature interaction. This framework achieved state-of-the-art performance on the Mono3DRefer dataset, showing an 8.60% improvement in overall Acc@0.5 and a 13.54% increase in the challenging "Far" scenario.
Problem: Existing Monocular 3D Visual Grounding (Mono3DVG) models tend to over-rely on explicit keywords, neglecting crucial implicit spatial descriptions in natural language.

Current methods suffer from cross-dimensional interference when generalized textual features (combining 2D and 3D attributes) interact with dimension-specific visual features (e.g., 2D image or 3D depth).
Accurate 3D object localization from a single RGB image guided by text remains challenging due to the inherent lack of explicit depth information.
Method: A CLIP-Guided Lexical Certainty Adapter (CLIP-LCA) dynamically masks high-certainty words during training, forcing the text encoder to learn implicit spatial relationships from low-certainty descriptors.
A Dimension-Decoupled Module (D2M) disentangles generalized textual features into 2D-specific and 3D-specific representations using coarse decoupling and a novel reverse cross-attention mechanism.
The refined dimension-specific textual features (T2D, T3D) then guide their corresponding 2D and 3D visual features, ensuring dimensionally consistent cross-modal interactions.
Results: Mono3DVG-EnSD achieved state-of-the-art performance on the Mono3DRefer dataset, improving overall Acc@0.5 by 8.60% (from 44.25% to 52.85%) compared to the baseline Mono3DVG-TR.
The method demonstrated a notable +13.54% increase in Acc@0.5 for the challenging "Far" scenario (objects >35m), highlighting enhanced ability to localize distant objects.

Ablation studies confirmed that both CLIP-LCA (+5.04% Acc@0.5) and D2M (+6.83% Acc@0.5) individually contribute to performance, with their combined use yielding synergistic improvements (+8.60% Acc@0.5).
Takeaways: Dynamically adjusting the saliency of high-certainty keywords during training can force a model to develop a deeper understanding of implicit spatial relationships in text.
Decoupling generalized textual features into dimension-specific (2D and 3D) representations is crucial for mitigating cross-dimensional interference during multimodal feature interaction.
A reverse cross-attention mechanism can effectively refine dimension-specific features by emphasizing unique information not shared with other dimensions, leading to more precise guidance.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.06411.Title: SofT-GRPO: Surpassing Discrete-Token LLM Reinforcement Learning via Gumbel-Reparameterized Soft-Thinking Policy Optimization
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.06411.Summary: SofT-GRPO, a new reinforcement learning algorithm, enables large language models using the "soft-thinking" paradigm to achieve superior reasoning accuracy compared to discrete-token methods reinforced with GRPO. It demonstrates average accuracy improvements of +0.13% on Pass@1 and up to +2.19% on Pass@32 across numerical, scientific, and code reasoning benchmarks.
Problem: Despite the theoretical advantages of "soft-thinking" over discrete-token Chain-of-Thought (CoT), prior attempts to apply Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) to soft-thinking models failed to match or surpass discrete-token GRPO.
Introducing controllable stochasticity into continuous soft-thinking tokens for effective exploration was challenging, often leading to generated inputs outside the pre-trained embedding space.
Developing an effective policy optimization approach for continuous soft-thinking tokens, capable of accurate gradient estimation for reward attribution, proved difficult.
Method: Developed SofT-GRPO, a novel RLVR algorithm specifically tailored for "soft-thinking" LLMs, integrating Gumbel-reparameterized policy optimization.

Employed **Group Rollout with Gumbel Noise** by injecting Gumbel noise into log probabilities and applying Gumbel-Softmax to create stochastic, continuous soft-thinking tokens while maintaining valid input representations.
Utilized **Gumbel Reparameterization** within a modified GRPO loss function to enable accurate gradient estimation and policy updates for these continuous soft-thinking trajectories.
Results: SofT-GRPO achieved +0.13% higher average accuracy on Pass@1 and a notable +2.19% on Pass@32 compared to discrete-token GRPO across numerical reasoning benchmarks.
The method significantly surpassed prior soft-thinking + GRPO attempts and demonstrated improved out-of-domain generalization on scientific and code reasoning tasks.
SofT-GRPO reduced thinking length for correct queries, leading to improved token efficiency during training, and further boosted performance when combined with majority voting.
Takeaways: Gumbel reparameterization is an effective technique for introducing controllable stochasticity and estimating gradients for continuous, non-discrete representations in LLM reasoning.
Successfully applying RL to continuous reasoning processes requires careful consideration to ensure that generated representations remain within the meaningful pre-trained embedding space of the LLM.

When properly reinforced, continuous "soft-thinking" can surpass the performance of discrete-token Chain-of-Thought, especially for tasks benefiting from deeper exploration and diverse reasoning paths.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.05491.Title: Visual Spatial Tuning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.05491.Summary: Researchers from HKU, ByteDance Seed, and Tsinghua University developed Visual Spatial Tuning (VST), a framework that cultivates human-like visuospatial abilities in general Vision-Language Models without architectural modifications, utilizing extensive spatial datasets and a progressive training pipeline. The approach achieves state-of-the-art spatial understanding across various benchmarks and improves Vision-Language-Action models by 8.6% on robotic manipulation tasks, while preserving general multi-modal capabilities.
Problem: Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) demonstrate limitations in capturing precise spatial relationships and understanding 3D environments from visual inputs.
Existing methods to improve VLM spatial awareness often involve additional expert encoders, which introduce computational overhead and can degrade general capabilities.
Prior spatial datasets for VLMs typically focus on narrow aspects of spatial understanding or are limited to supervised fine-tuning, lacking diversity and comprehensive training strategies.
Method: A comprehensive Visual Spatial Tuning (VST) framework is proposed, integrating spatial perception and reasoning into general VLM architectures.
Two large-scale, diverse datasets, VST-Perception (VST-P) and VST-Reasoning (VST-R), were created, covering single-image, multi-image, and video spatial tasks.
A three-stage progressive training pipeline is employed, involving Supervised Fine-tuning (SFT), Chain-of-Thought (CoT) cold start, and Reinforcement Learning (RL) using the GRPO algorithm.
The spatial-enhanced VST model is adapted for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) tasks by discretizing the action space and fine-tuning the VLM for robotic manipulation.
Results: VST models consistently achieved state-of-the-art performance across various spatial benchmarks, with VST-7B-RL reaching an average spatial score (S-AVG) of 61.2%.
The VST-7B-RL model demonstrated superior 3D object detection, achieving 44.2% AP@15 on SUN RGB-D without a specialized 3D encoder, outperforming existing general and specialized models.

The framework successfully preserved general multi-modal capabilities, and VST-enhanced Vision-Language-Action models showed an 8.6% improvement in average success rate on the LIBERO robotic manipulation benchmark.
Takeaways: Comprehensive spatial intelligence, encompassing both perception and reasoning, can be effectively cultivated in general VLM architectures without relying on specialized 3D encoders.
Constructing large-scale, diverse datasets that cover single-image, multi-image, and video-based spatial tasks is essential for holistic visuospatial understanding.
A progressive training pipeline, starting with supervised fine-tuning for perception and advancing to reinforcement learning for reasoning, proves effective for instilling complex spatial abilities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.04670.Title: Cambrian-S: Towards Spatial Supersensing in Video
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.04670.Summary: Researchers from NYU and Stanford introduce a "spatial supersensing" hierarchy for video-based Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) and new VSI-SUPER benchmarks to reveal current models' limitations in genuine spatial and temporal reasoning. They develop Cambrian-S, a specialized MLLM trained on a large spatial dataset achieving state-of-the-art on VSI-Bench, and prototype a "predictive sensing" paradigm that leverages prediction error ("surprise") to robustly improve memory management and event segmentation in arbitrarily long videos.
Problem: Current MLLMs primarily offer semantic perception, treating video as discrete frames rather than continuous 3D world projections, limiting deeper visual-spatial and temporal reasoning.
Existing video benchmarks often permit MLLMs to rely on linguistic priors or context expansion, failing to rigorously assess genuine spatial cognition or world modeling.
Even leading MLLMs struggle with long-horizon spatial memory, continuous counting, and proactive understanding of dynamic environments from unbounded video streams.
Method: Propose a four-stage "spatial supersensing" hierarchy for video understanding, moving beyond semantic perception to predictive world modeling.

Introduce VSI-SUPER, a benchmark featuring Visual Spatial Recall (VSR) and Visual Spatial Counting (VSC) tasks, designed to challenge MLLMs on long-horizon spatial memory and cumulative reasoning in extended videos.

Develop Cambrian-S, a specialized video MLLM, and curate the VSI-590K dataset to enhance spatial understanding, alongside a "predictive sensing" paradigm leveraging "surprise" to optimize memory and event processing.
Results: Benchmarks like VSI-SUPER demonstrated that even advanced proprietary MLLMs like Gemini-2.5-Flash struggle with long-horizon spatial recall and continuous counting in extended videos.

Cambrian-S achieved state-of-the-art performance on the VSI-Bench dataset, scoring 67.5% and outperforming prominent open-source and proprietary models, showcasing its enhanced spatial cognition capabilities.

The proposed predictive sensing paradigm, utilizing surprise-driven memory management and event segmentation, enabled Cambrian-S to maintain stable accuracy on VSR across arbitrary video lengths and significantly improve VSC performance compared to vanilla MLLMs.
Takeaways: Existing MLLMs, despite large context windows, fall short on tasks demanding genuine spatial-temporal reasoning across long videos, often relying on linguistic shortcuts or brute-force context expansion.

Achieving "spatial supersensing" requires moving beyond scaling current MLLM paradigms; true understanding necessitates models that proactively build and update internal representations of the 3D world.

Leveraging "surprise" (prediction error in latent frame prediction) provides an effective mechanism for intelligent memory management and event segmentation, enabling more robust processing of unbounded video streams.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.02779.Title: When Visualizing is the First Step to Reasoning: MIRA, a Benchmark for Visual Chain-of-Thought
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.02779.Summary: The MIRA benchmark introduces 546 multimodal problems requiring intermediate visual representations for reasoning, revealing that state-of-the-art MLLMs achieve only 16.5% average accuracy without visual guidance. However, providing human-annotated visual chain-of-thought improves performance by a relative 33.7%, indicating a critical need for models capable of integrating visual generation into complex problem-solving.
Problem: Current Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) primarily rely on text-only chain-of-thought reasoning, which is inefficient and limited for problems with intrinsic visual or spatial components.

Existing benchmarks for MLLMs mainly evaluate visual perception or superficial reasoning, failing to assess models' ability to generate and utilize intermediate visual representations for complex problem-solving.
MLLMs lack the human-like cognitive ability to "draw to think," creating visual aids to guide reasoning for visually-intensive tasks.
Method: Introduction of MIRA, a benchmark featuring 546 multimodal problems across 20 task types, explicitly designed to require intermediate visual information for successful reasoning.
Each problem in MIRA is meticulously constructed with human-annotated, step-wise visual clues to facilitate evaluation in a Visual Chain-of-Thought (Visual-CoT) setting.
A three-level diagnostic evaluation protocol (Direct, Text-CoT, and Simulated Visual-CoT) is established to provide granular insights into MLLM capabilities and the impact of visual guidance.
Results: Advanced closed-source MLLMs, including GPT-5, achieve an average accuracy of only 16.5% on MIRA with direct inputs, highlighting their limitations in visual reasoning.
Standard Text-CoT proves insufficient for visually-intensive tasks on MIRA, offering minimal gains and sometimes leading to performance degradation (e.g., Gemini 2.5 Pro saw an 18.3% drop).
Providing models with human-annotated intermediate visual cues (Simulated Visual-CoT) consistently improved performance, yielding an average relative gain of 33.7% across models and tasks.
Takeaways: Current state-of-the-art MLLMs exhibit a fundamental lack of capability for complex visual reasoning that necessitates "drawing to think," struggling significantly on the MIRA benchmark.
Text-only Chain-of-Thought (CoT) is largely ineffective for MIRA's visually-intensive problems and can sometimes degrade MLLM performance compared to direct answering.
Providing explicit human-annotated intermediate visual cues, as in the Simulated Visual-CoT setting, substantially enhances MLLM reasoning capabilities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.01833.Title: TIR-Bench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Agentic Thinking-with-Images Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.01833.Summary: Researchers at Shanghai AI Laboratory and collaborating institutions developed TIR-BENCH, a comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate multimodal large language models' ability to 'think with images' by dynamically manipulating visual inputs with tools. The benchmark revealed that models with explicit agentic tool-use capabilities achieved up to 46% accuracy, significantly outperforming non-agentic models on tasks requiring active visual interaction.
Problem: Existing MLLM benchmarks primarily evaluate static visual input and recognition, neglecting dynamic, tool-based image manipulation capabilities.
Current MLLMs often treat visual inputs as unalterable, limiting their reasoning to linguistic domains despite the emergence of agentic functionalities.
There was a lack of a comprehensive evaluation framework for "thinking-with-images" where models actively transform visual information to inform subsequent reasoning.
Method: Introduced TIR-BENCH, a benchmark featuring 13 diverse tasks spanning spatial reasoning, visual perception, and mathematics, requiring active, tool-based visual manipulation (e.g., drawing lines, pixel analysis, image enhancement).
Designed tasks to be inherently difficult, demanding multi-step, programmatic strategies to differentiate genuine "thinking-with-images" from superficial recognition.
Evaluated 22 leading MLLMs, including open-source, proprietary, and explicit tool-using models, using objective accuracy metrics and pilot studies on function-calling and fine-tuning strategies.
Results: TIR-BENCH proved universally challenging, with the highest overall accuracy being 46% achieved by o3-TU, underscoring its effectiveness in assessing advanced reasoning.
Agentic tool-using MLLMs (e.g., o3-TU) demonstrated substantially higher performance, outperforming the best non-tool-using model (Gemini-2.5-pro) by nearly 17% on average.

Pilot studies showed o3 had superior function-calling ability, explicit prompting strategies improved performance, and "Tool-use SFT" significantly surpassed "Direct SFT" on the Rotated Image OCR task.
Takeaways: Agentic tool-use capabilities are essential for solving tasks requiring dynamic visual interaction, with models like o3-TU significantly outperforming non-tool-using MLLMs.
Complex tasks, such as the Jigsaw Game, remain highly challenging even for advanced tool-using models, indicating specific areas for future development in multimodal reasoning.
"Tool-use SFT" (fine-tuning models to leverage tools) is more effective and scales better with data size than "Direct SFT" for image-operation tasks, suggesting a promising training paradigm.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.01758.Title: RLAC: Reinforcement Learning with Adversarial Critic for Free-Form Generation Tasks
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.01758.Summary: RLAC (Reinforcement Learning with Adversarial Critic) introduces a framework to fine-tune large language models for open-ended generation tasks by employing a dynamically adapting adversarial critic that identifies failure modes. The method improved factuality in text generation and achieved higher Pass@1 scores in code generation, notably reducing verification costs by up to 97.5% compared to prior approaches.
Problem: Existing LLM post-training paradigms like SFT, RLHF, and reward models struggle with the scalability and cost of human data, or are susceptible to 'reward hacking' for complex, open-ended generation.
Defining a singular, clear reward function for free-form outputs with numerous, often implicit, evaluation rubrics is challenging and prone to misalignment.
Exhaustive verification of all possible criteria for generated outputs (e.g., test cases for code) is computationally intractable, creating a significant bottleneck for practical application.
Method: RLAC reformulates the training objective as an adversarial min-max game between a generator (the LLM being fine-tuned) and a critic (an LLM that learns to propose failure-mode rubrics).
The critic adversarially generates natural language rubrics that represent properties the generated output is likely to violate, focusing verification efforts on weaknesses.
An objective, external validator provides binary ground-truth feedback on these proposed rubrics, which is then used to update both the generator and critic via Direct Preference Optimization (DPO).
Results: RLAC achieved the highest FactScore (e.g., 0.889) in factual text generation tasks, simultaneously reducing the number of verification calls by up to 5.7 times compared to alternative methods.

In code generation, RLAC consistently produced superior average Pass@1 scores (e.g., 53.2 for Base models) while reducing verification costs (total test cases executed) by 97.5% compared to enumerative RL baselines.

Ablation studies demonstrated that an adversarial critic is crucial; static critics led to generator exploitation and diminished performance, validating the need for dynamic adaptation to maintain effective supervision.
Takeaways: The dynamic, adversarial nature of the critic enables it to continuously adapt to the generator's evolving capabilities, providing 'on-policy' feedback that mitigates reward hacking and drives genuine quality improvement.

Framing the problem as an adversarial game with targeted, verifiable feedback from an external validator allows for scalable reinforcement learning post-training in domains where exhaustive verification is impractical.
DPO provides a stable and effective mechanism for policy optimization for both the generator and critic, directly leveraging binary preference signals derived from validator checks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.01618.Title: Actial: Activate Spatial Reasoning Ability of Multimodal Large Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.01618.Summary: Actial, a framework developed by researchers including those from Nanjing University and The Chinese University of Hong Kong, activates latent 3D spatial reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models by explicitly training them on foundational viewpoint understanding. It achieves 92.2% accuracy on its new Viewpoint-100K dataset and secures an 83.5% average score on CV-Bench, outperforming leading proprietary models such as GPT-4o and Gemini-1.5-Pro.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle with understanding fine-grained 3D spatial information and cross-view consistency, often defaulting to superficial 2D continuity.
Existing MLLMs lack foundational spatial skills, such as precise viewpoint understanding and spatial transformations, leading to unreliable performance in real-world 3D scenarios.
The inherent "visual-spatial intelligence" of MLLMs is underexploited due to a lack of targeted training strategies for 3D perception from 2D inputs.
Method: Actial introduces a "Viewpoint Learning" task that simplifies 3D consistency evaluation into multiple-choice questions about relative horizontal translation and rotation between object-centric image pairs.
A new Viewpoint-100K dataset, comprising 100,000 object-centric image pairs with automatically generated question-answer pairs for relative viewpoints, is created to support this task.

A two-stage fine-tuning strategy is employed: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) with hybrid cold-start initialization for foundational knowledge injection, followed by Reinforcement Learning using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) for generalization enhancement.
Results: Actial-7B achieved 92.2% accuracy on the Viewpoint-100K dataset, a substantial improvement from the baseline's 12.9%.
On the CV-Bench, Actial-7B scored an average of 83.5%, surpassing leading models like GPT-4o (79.4%) and Gemini-1.5-Pro (77.7%).

The model demonstrated near-mastery of foundational viewpoints with 99.2% accuracy on BLINK's multi-view component and showed comprehensive improvements across many subtasks on the challenging MMSI-Bench.
Takeaways: MLLMs, despite primary training on 2D data, possess significant latent potential for 3D spatial perception that can be activated through targeted training.
Explicitly training MLLMs on basic spatial skills like viewpoint understanding effectively "activates" and substantially enhances their broader spatial reasoning capabilities across diverse tasks.

A hybrid cold-start initialization during SFT, combining new dataset training with human-assisted pseudo Chain-of-Thoughts, is crucial for preserving instruction-following and coherent reasoning while injecting foundational knowledge.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.01191.Title: Self-Harmony: Learning to Harmonize Self-Supervision and Self-Play in Test-Time Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.01191.Summary: The Self-Harmony framework enhances Large Language Model reasoning at test-time without external supervision by leveraging cooperative self-play and a theoretically grounded harmonic mean for robust pseudo-label selection. This method, which utilizes a single LLM in dual roles, consistently outperforms existing approaches across diverse benchmarks and models.
Problem: Enhancing Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning capabilities traditionally requires costly human-curated datasets for supervised fine-tuning.
Existing Test-Time Reinforcement Learning (TTRL) methods using majority voting for pseudo-labeling are prone to reinforcing systematic reasoning errors, creating an 'echo chamber' effect.
A lack of robust, self-contained mechanisms for generating reliable, label-free learning signals within test-time adaptation paradigms without external verifiers.
Method: A cooperative self-play framework where a single LLM dynamically takes on two roles: a 'Solver' for problem-solving and a 'Reframer' for generating semantically equivalent paraphrases.
Generates multiple 'views' of a problem by having the Reframer create stylistically diverse reformulations, acting as an online data augmentation mechanism.
Applies a theoretically justified harmonic mean for pseudo-label selection, identifying answers that are both frequently generated and consistent across original and reframed problem views.
Results: Self-Harmony achieved state-of-the-art performance across 28 of 30 configurations, encompassing 5 open-source LLMs and 6 challenging reasoning benchmarks.
Performance improved substantially; for example, Llama-3.1-8B's accuracy on GSM8K increased from 60.5% to 91.6% with only 16 original and 16 reframed rollouts.
The framework demonstrated robust training stability with zero failures and consistently produced pseudo-labels with higher accuracy (80-85%) throughout training compared to competing methods.
Takeaways: Accurate answers demonstrate inherent stability and robustness when confronted with semantically equivalent yet stylistically varied problem rephrasings.

The harmonic mean score, theoretically justified by a View-Invariant Infomax objective, offers a principled method for selecting high-quality pseudo-labels by rewarding consistency across diverse problem views.
Optimizing the cooperative self-play process by fusing reframing and solving actions into a single generative step enhances computational efficiency at test-time.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.27606.Title: Spatial-SSRL: Enhancing Spatial Understanding via Self-Supervised Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.27606.Summary: Spatial-SSRL introduces a self-supervised reinforcement learning framework that enhances the spatial understanding capabilities of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs). This approach utilizes intrinsic signals from ordinary RGB and RGB-D images to generate verifiable rewards, achieving average accuracy gains of 4.63% on spatial benchmarks for its 3B model while preserving general visual abilities.
Problem: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) struggle with robust 2D and 3D spatial understanding, limiting their application in real-world scenarios like robotics and autonomous systems.
Existing supervised fine-tuning (SFT) methods for spatial tasks are costly, rely on potentially noisy human annotations, and lack scalability.
Current reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) approaches are often confined to specific environments and require complex engineering, limiting broad applicability.
Method: A two-stage self-supervised reinforcement learning paradigm is implemented, utilizing five automatically generated pretext tasks for spatial understanding.
Depth-free tasks (shuffled patch reordering, flipped patch recognition, cropped patch inpainting) are designed for 2D spatial consistency from RGB images.
Depth-based tasks (regional depth ordering, relative 3D position prediction) leverage RGB-D data for 3D scene comprehension, with GRPO used to optimize LVLM policy using accuracy and format rewards.
Results: Spatial-SSRL models achieved average accuracy gains of +4.63% (3B model) and +3.89% (7B model) across seven spatial understanding benchmarks.
General visual question answering (VQA) and fine-grained perception capabilities were preserved or improved, with the 3B model showing an average gain of +2.02% across four general VQA benchmarks.
The framework enhanced the LVLMs' ability to generate coherent spatial reasoning, outperforming baselines when explicit reasoning was required.
Takeaways: Intrinsic consistency signals within ordinary RGB/RGB-D images can serve as naturally verifiable, scalable, and cost-effective ground truth for self-supervised reinforcement learning.
A diverse set of complementary 2D and 3D self-supervised tasks leads to more holistic spatial intelligence, rather than single-task optimization.
Self-supervised reinforcement learning can cultivate genuinely productive spatial reasoning in LVLMs, enabling better performance even when models are prompted to generate explicit reasoning chains.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.27492.Title: ThinkMorph: Emergent Properties in Multimodal Interleaved Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.27492.Summary: A unified model named ThinkMorph, developed by researchers from National University of Singapore, Zhejiang University, University of Washington, Stanford University, and The Chinese University of Hong Kong, utilizes multimodal interleaved chain-of-thought reasoning to generate progressive text-image steps, leading to substantial performance gains on vision-centric tasks and revealing emergent properties such as unseen visual manipulations and autonomous mode switching.
Problem: Multimodal reasoning tasks often require iterative coordination, but existing models struggle to genuinely integrate visual and linguistic thoughts beyond superficial correlation.
Current interleaved Chain-of-Thought approaches are either brittle (tool-augmented) or produce isomorphic representations, failing to leverage the complementary strengths of text and image.
There is a lack of a unified, generalizable framework to enable and investigate genuinely iterative and coordinated reasoning between language and vision.
Method: Developed ThinkMorph, a unified multimodal model based on Bagel-7B, capable of generating progressive, interleaved text and image tokens for reasoning.
Constructed a meticulously curated dataset of approximately 24,000 high-quality text-image reasoning traces, emphasizing complementary modality interactions across diverse vision-centric tasks.
Fine-tuned the model with dual loss functions (Mean Squared Error for images, negative log-likelihood for text) to jointly optimize both visual generation and textual coherence.
Results: ThinkMorph achieved an average performance gain of 34.74% on vision-centric benchmarks compared to its base model, with an 85.84% improvement on Spatial Navigation.
The 7B-parameter model performed comparably to or better than models an order of magnitude larger, surpassing Qwen2.5-VL-72B by 34% on VSP and GPT-4o by 24.67% on SAT.

Three emergent properties were identified: the generation of unseen visual manipulations, autonomous switching to text-only reasoning for certain samples (achieving 81.25% accuracy when switching), and superior test-time scaling through diversified multimodal thoughts.
Takeaways: Text and image thoughts are most effective when they function as complementary modalities, each advancing the reasoning process beyond what the other could achieve alone.
Fine-tuning on carefully curated interleaved reasoning traces enables generative models to develop and utilize task-effective visual manipulations (e.g., zoom, inpainting) not explicitly trained.
Unified multimodal models can develop emergent properties, including autonomous mode switching between textual and visual reasoning, and diversified test-time exploration of solution spaces.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.27363.Title: ToolScope: An Agentic Framework for Vision-Guided and Long-Horizon Tool Use
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.27363.Summary: Researchers from Renmin University of China developed ToolScope, a training-free multimodal agent framework, that integrates global planning with local multimodal perception for complex Vision Question Answering tasks. It consistently outperformed existing baselines across four VQA datasets, achieving gains such as +9.12% on MAT-Search and +4.67% on ScienceQA, by using a strategic navigator and a native visual "Perceive" tool to manage long-horizon reasoning and visual context.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle with complex Vision Question Answering (VQA) tasks requiring dynamic reasoning and external knowledge.
Existing training-free multimodal agents suffer from "local reasoning traps" due to a lack of high-level global planning for long-horizon decision-making.
Multi-step multimodal reasoning often leads to "visual context degradation," where crucial visual information is lost or not revisited dynamically.
Method: Introduces ToolScope, a plug-and-play, training-free framework comprising a Global Navigator, Agentic Executor, and Response Synthesizer.
The Global Navigator performs high-level task analysis to select relevant tools and generate a strategic, long-term reasoning plan.
The Agentic Executor employs specialized tools, including a novel native "Perceive Tool" for dynamic visual re-attention, a Search Tool for knowledge retrieval, and a Code Tool for computation.
Results: ToolScope consistently outperformed all prompt-based and tool-augmented baselines across four VQA benchmarks (VQA 2.0, ScienceQA, MAT-Search, MathVista).
Achieved performance gains up to +9.12% on MAT-Search, +4.67% on ScienceQA, and +1.4% on VQA 2.0 and MathVista when integrated with MiMo-VL-7B-RL.

Demonstrated strong generalization across different MLLM backbones and scales, with an average accuracy improvement of +6.69% for MiMo-VL-7B-RL and +6.33% for InternVL3-78B, validating its robustness and scalability.
Takeaways: Integrating explicit global planning with local multimodal perception significantly improves coherence and effectiveness in complex VQA tasks.
A native "Perceive Tool," allowing the MLLM to dynamically query and re-attend to visual information, effectively mitigates visual context degradation without external vision models.
A modular, training-free design can achieve robust and generalizable performance gains across various MLLM backbones and tasks, making advanced agentic capabilities more accessible.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.26788.Title: Defeating the Training-Inference Mismatch via FP16
