https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.26788.Summary: This research from Sea AI Lab and the National University of Singapore demonstrates that using FP16 precision for both training and inference fundamentally resolves the numerical discrepancies causing instability in Reinforcement Learning (RL) fine-tuning of Large Language Models. Employing FP16 drastically reduces the training-inference mismatch, leading to more stable optimization, faster convergence, and superior performance compared to existing BF16-based methods and complex algorithmic corrections.
Problem: Reinforcement Learning (RL) fine-tuning of Large Language Models (LLMs) often suffers from instability, training collapse, and sub-optimal performance.
The 'training-inference mismatch,' caused by numerical discrepancies between fast inference and gradient computation engines, leads to biased gradients and a 'deployment gap'.

Existing solutions, such as importance sampling corrections or manual engineering alignments, are computationally expensive, complex, or only address symptoms without eliminating the fundamental mismatch.
Method: The paper hypothesizes and confirms that low floating-point precision, specifically BF16, is the root cause of the training-inference mismatch due to accumulated rounding errors.
The core solution involves switching from BF16 to FP16 precision for both the inference policy and the training engine in RL fine-tuning.

FP16's higher numerical precision (more mantissa bits) ensures that minor implementation differences are absorbed, preventing policy divergence, with standard loss scaling addressing its limited dynamic range.
Results: FP16 reduced the training-inference mismatch in sequence-level log-probability ratios by approximately 24 times compared to BF16.

Switching to FP16 precision enabled traditional RL algorithms (e.g., GRPO, PG-Seq-IS) to converge stably and achieve nearly 100% training accuracy on a challenging dataset, while BF16-based methods frequently collapsed or converged slowly.

The benefits of FP16 generalized across diverse settings, including Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, LoRA-based fine-tuning, larger dense models, and different LLM architectures, consistently leading to higher training rewards and validation performance.
Takeaways: BF16's lower precision (7 mantissa bits) is a primary source of numerical instability in RL fine-tuning, causing policies to diverge even with identical model weights.
FP16's significantly higher precision (10 mantissa bits) effectively eliminates the training-inference mismatch by ensuring numerical consistency between inference and training policies.

By addressing the root cause of the mismatch, FP16 simplifies RL fine-tuning, allowing even simple, unbiased policy gradient estimators to perform robustly and effectively, rendering complex algorithmic corrections less necessary.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.26583.Title: Emu3.5: Native Multimodal Models are World Learners
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.26583.Summary: BAAI's Emu3.5 introduces a native multimodal model trained extensively on internet videos, capable of understanding and generating interleaved vision-language sequences across long horizons. The model achieves strong performance in various multimodal tasks, including complex image generation with accurate text rendering and embodied AI scenarios, while accelerating image inference by approximately 20x using a novel Discrete Diffusion Adaptation (DiDA) technique.
Problem: Large language models are inherently limited by their text-only input, offering a restricted view of the world and hindering comprehensive understanding.
Many existing vision-language models employ separate encoders or adapter-based approaches, lacking deep, native integration of vision and language for unified prediction.
Autoregressive models suffer from slow, token-by-token inference, creating a practical bottleneck for generating high-resolution images in real-time applications.
Method: Develop Emu3.5, a 34.1 billion parameter decoder-only transformer, designed for native multimodal prediction of the 'next state across vision and language' using a unified next-token prediction objective.
Pre-train the model on over 13 trillion multimodal tokens, primarily sourced from ~63 million internet videos, to learn long-horizon spatiotemporal continuity and cross-modal alignment.
Introduce Discrete Diffusion Adaptation (DiDA), a technique that converts autoregressive image generation into bidirectional parallel prediction, significantly accelerating inference.

Apply extensive post-training through two-stage supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and large-scale reinforcement learning (RL) guided by comprehensive multimodal rewards to enhance reasoning and generation.
Results: Emu3.5 achieves strong performance in Any-to-Image (X2I) generation, including open-world image editing, precise control, and complex text-rich image rendering, outperforming various state-of-the-art T2I models on benchmarks like LeX-Bench and CVTG-2K.

The model demonstrates generalizable world-modeling abilities, achieving a 65.5% win rate against Gemini 2.5 Flash Image for world exploration and a 67.1% win rate for embodied manipulation in automated preference evaluations.

Discrete Diffusion Adaptation (DiDA) accelerates per-image inference by approximately 20x (reducing generation time for a 1024x1024 image from 120s to 10s) without sacrificing performance on T2I and X2I tasks, making it competitive with fast-sampling diffusion models.
Takeaways: Native multimodal architectures, when trained on vast quantities of long-horizon interleaved vision-language data, move closer to learning a 'world model' that captures temporal dynamics and rich context.

The Discrete Diffusion Adaptation (DiDA) method effectively transforms sequential autoregressive image generation into an efficient parallel process, addressing a major practical limitation for high-resolution output.

A unified post-training strategy, incorporating large-scale SFT and RL with a comprehensive multimodal reward system, is crucial for aligning model outputs with human preferences and improving generalization across diverse tasks.
Scaling pre-training compute with high-quality, meticulously filtered and annotated internet video data leads to progressively stronger generalization capabilities across multimodal tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.26493.Title: Context Engineering 2.0: The Context of Context Engineering
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.26493.Summary: Researchers from Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory redefine context engineering, tracing its two-decade evolution from ubiquitous computing to modern LLMs, and propose a unified 'entropy reduction' framework. The work introduces a four-stage evolutionary model and detailed design considerations for optimizing context within AI systems.
Problem: The narrow perception that 'context engineering' is a recent innovation primarily associated with modern LLM prompt engineering, overlooking its rich history.
Limited definitions of 'context' often confined to dialogue history or system prompts, failing to capture its broader significance.
The inherent 'cognitive gap' between human and machine intelligence, where machines struggle with 'entropy reduction' to infer missing context from high-entropy human intentions.
Method: Developing a formal, technology-agnostic definition of context engineering, grounded in an 'entropy reduction' perspective to unify diverse practices.
Presenting a comprehensive historical analysis that traces the field's evolution through a four-stage model, from primitive computation to superhuman intelligence.

Outlining systematic design considerations for the entire context lifecycle, covering collection, storage, management (including abstraction), and usage, to guide future intelligent system development.
Results: Established a formal, broad definition of context engineering and a unifying theoretical framework centered on the concept of 'entropy reduction'.
Introduced a four-stage evolutionary model (Context Engineering 1.0 to 4.0) that integrates historical practices with future projections of AI capabilities.

Provided a comprehensive categorization of design considerations across the entire context lifecycle, including advanced techniques for context abstraction and strategies for lifelong context preservation and update.
Takeaways: Context engineering is a continuous, evolving discipline with a history spanning over two decades, rooted in ubiquitous computing and human-computer interaction, not solely a modern LLM-era concept.

The fundamental essence of context engineering is 'entropy reduction,' bridging the cognitive gap by transforming high-entropy human intentions into low-entropy machine-understandable representations.

The field's progression can be systematically modeled through four evolutionary stages, where increasing machine intelligence leads to greater context-processing ability and reduced human-AI interaction costs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.25992.Title: Supervised Reinforcement Learning: From Expert Trajectories to Step-wise Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.25992.Summary: The Supervised Reinforcement Learning (SRL) framework enables smaller Large Language Models (LLMs) to learn complex multi-step reasoning by providing dense, step-wise similarity rewards from expert demonstrations. It notably improved greedy average accuracy on math reasoning benchmarks by 3.0% over the base model, and showed a 74% relative improvement in resolve rate on agentic software engineering tasks.
Problem: Small-scale, open-source LLMs struggle to solve challenging multi-step reasoning problems effectively with current training paradigms.
Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) often leads to overfitting on complex expert demonstrations, sometimes causing performance degradation for smaller models.
Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) faces sparse reward signals on difficult problems, hindering effective learning due to a lack of positive advantage estimates.
Method: Introduced Supervised Reinforcement Learning (SRL), which reformulates problem-solving as a sequential decision-making process by decomposing expert solutions into logical 'actions'.
Generated step-wise training data from expert trajectories and provided a dense sequence similarity reward based on the model's predicted action, allowing for flexible internal monologues.
Optimized the policy using a Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) objective with dynamic sampling and explored a curriculum learning strategy combining SRL with RLVR.
Results: SRL alone achieved a 27.6% greedy average accuracy on math reasoning benchmarks, a 3.0% increase over the base Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct model.
The SRL → RLVR pipeline delivered the strongest performance, reaching 28.3% greedy average accuracy, a 3.7% increase over the base model and outperforming all baselines.
SRL generalized to agentic software engineering tasks, achieving a 14.8% resolve rate in an oracle file editing setting, representing a 74% relative improvement over an SFT baseline.
Takeaways: Dense, step-wise supervision, through sequence similarity rewards on discrete actions, effectively guides LLMs on complex problems where sparse rewards or rigid imitation fail.
SRL encourages flexible and sophisticated reasoning patterns, including planning, on-the-fly adjustments, and reflective verification, without merely increasing output length.
The combination of SRL for initial robust guidance and subsequent RLVR refinement forms a powerful curriculum learning approach for maximizing performance on challenging tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.25741.Title: Scaling Latent Reasoning via Looped Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.25741.Summary: Ouro, a family of Looped Language Models (LoopLMs), embeds iterative computation directly into the pre-training process through parameter reuse, leading to enhanced parameter efficiency and reasoning abilities. These models achieve the performance of much larger non-looped Transformers while demonstrating improved safety and a more causally faithful internal reasoning process.
Problem: Large Language Model scaling strategies primarily focused on increasing model size and data, leading to high deployment costs, latency, and diminishing returns from data scarcity.
Existing inference-time reasoning techniques like Chain-of-Thought (CoT) expand context length and often reflect post-hoc rationalization rather than intrinsic, efficient internal reasoning.
A need for LLM architectures capable of adaptively allocating computational depth based on input complexity to optimize resource usage.
Method: Developed Ouro, a family of LoopLMs that recursively apply a shared block of Transformer layers to integrate iterative computation into the model's latent space during pre-training.
Implemented a two-stage training scheme with an entropy-regularized objective and focused adaptive gate training, enabling the model to learn adaptive computation and dynamic early exiting.
Trained Ouro models (up to 2.6B parameters) on an extensive 7.7 trillion token dataset, demonstrating the efficacy of the LoopLM architecture at a frontier-level scale.
Results: Ouro models achieved significant parameter efficiency gains, with Ouro 1.4B matching or exceeding 4B parameter dense models, and Ouro 2.6B outperforming 8B parameter dense models on reasoning benchmarks like BBH, GSM8K, and MATH500.

The adaptive computation mechanisms, particularly the two-stage gate training, enabled efficient and dynamic compute allocation, consistently yielding optimal accuracy across various computational budgets.

LoopLMs showed improved safety, with harmfulness decreasing as recurrent steps increased, and demonstrated more causally faithful reasoning through observable evolution of intermediate latent state predictions.
Takeaways: Loop depth serves as a distinct and powerful third scaling axis for LLMs, complementing model size and data volume to unlock enhanced capabilities.
LoopLMs improve model capabilities primarily by enhancing *knowledge manipulation* (reasoning, application of rules) rather than increasing raw *knowledge storage* capacity.
Adaptive computation, facilitated by learned gating mechanisms, allows LoopLMs to dynamically adjust their computational effort, optimizing performance-cost trade-offs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.24684.Title: SPICE: Self-Play In Corpus Environments Improves Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.24684.Summary: A research team from FAIR at Meta and NUS developed SPICE, a reinforcement learning framework that enables large language models to continuously enhance their reasoning abilities through adversarial self-play grounded in a vast external document corpus. The method consistently improved performance on mathematical and general reasoning benchmarks by up to 11.9% compared to base models.
Problem: Existing reinforcement learning methods for large language models (LLMs) often rely on human supervision, curated datasets, or domain-specific reward engineering, limiting scalability and generalizability.
Ungrounded self-play techniques (e.g., R-Zero) suffer from hallucination amplification, where factual errors compound, degrading performance over time.
These methods also face information symmetry, making it difficult to create genuinely challenging and diverse tasks when both the problem generator and solver share the same internalized knowledge.
Method: SPICE employs a single LLM that dynamically switches between two adversarial roles: a Challenger that generates tasks and a Reasoner that solves them, both grounded in an external document corpus.
The Challenger samples passages from a vast corpus to create diverse, multi-format tasks (multiple-choice or free-form) with verifiable gold answers, ensuring factual accuracy.
A variance-based curriculum reward guides the Challenger to generate tasks at an optimal difficulty level, specifically targeting a 50% Reasoner success rate, to drive continuous learning.
Results: SPICE consistently outperformed state-of-the-art self-play methods and strong supervised baselines, achieving average performance gains from +5.7% to +11.9% across multiple base models (Qwen3, OctoThinker families).
The framework demonstrated broad applicability, improving mathematical reasoning benchmarks by an average of +8.9% and general reasoning tasks by +9.8%, indicating generalizable skill development.

Ablation studies confirmed the critical role of corpus grounding and adversarial co-training, showing that their absence leads to significantly lower performance (e.g., 40.7% vs. 43.9% on Qwen3-4B-Base without grounding).

Qualitative analysis revealed that Challengers evolved to generate complex, multi-step tasks from the same documents, while Reasoners developed highly structured and sophisticated problem-solving patterns.
Takeaways: Corpus grounding is critical for sustained self-improvement in LLMs, effectively addressing hallucination amplification and providing an inexhaustible, verifiable knowledge source.
The adversarial co-evolution of the Challenger and Reasoner components creates an automatic and adaptive curriculum that continuously pushes the Reasoner's capabilities.
Establishing information asymmetry, where the Reasoner solves tasks without access to the source document, ensures genuine challenge and fosters authentic reasoning development.
The variance-based reward mechanism for the Challenger is crucial for calibrating task difficulty, optimizing the learning rate for the Reasoner across various tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.24285.Title: ViPER: Empowering the Self-Evolution of Visual Perception Abilities in Vision-Language Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.24285.Summary: ViPER, a self-evolutionary framework, iteratively enhances Vision-Language Models' fine-grained visual perception by autonomously generating high-quality training data and employing a two-stage reinforcement learning strategy. This approach enables average performance gains of 1.6-1.7% on comprehensive multimodal benchmarks and reduces hallucination rates in the resulting ViPER-trained models.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) possess limited capacity for fine-grained visual perception, hindering their utility in real-world applications.
Acquiring vast amounts of precisely annotated data for fine-grained perception is costly and time-consuming, while existing data scaling methods yield diminishing returns.

Current fine-tuning paradigms (SFT, RFT) often compromise VLM general capabilities or fail to enhance intrinsic visual understanding, frequently focusing on superficial textual reasoning or tool manipulation.
Method: ViPER introduces a self-evolutionary, closed-loop framework that progressively refines VLM perceptual abilities through self-critiquing and self-prediction.
It employs a two-stage task formulation: 'Caption Self-Refining' for holistic image reasoning and 'Visual-Operation Predicting' for fine-grained understanding.

The framework integrates a data synthesis module using a VLM and a diffusion model to autonomously generate perception-intensive training data (Viper10K) for both image-level and instance-level reconstruction, alongside a tailored two-stage reinforcement learning strategy.
Results: ViPER-trained models (Qwen-Viper-3B/7B) achieved average performance gains of 1.7% and 1.6% respectively across seven comprehensive multimodal benchmarks.
Demonstrated substantial improvements in fine-grained perception tasks, with gains of 4.4% for Qwen-Viper-3B and 6.0% for Qwen-Viper-7B.

The models exhibited reduced hallucination rates, enhanced generalizability across domains (e.g., 3.6% gain in Science & Technology for 7B), and validated the efficacy of the two-stage reinforcement learning strategy over mixed training approaches.
Takeaways: A progressive coarse-to-fine learning strategy, moving from holistic scene understanding to instance-level perception, effectively enhances VLM visual abilities.
The reciprocal relationship between visual generation and self-critique profoundly improves VLM visual understanding, enabling a self-bootstrapping paradigm without relying on external annotations.
The self-synthesized training data effectively eliminates the dependency on expensive cold-start data and large-scale external data distillation for VLM enhancement.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.23925.Title: Latent Chain-of-Thought for Visual Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.23925.Summary: A new framework for Large Vision-Language Models, Latent Chain-of-Thought (LaCoT), reformulates visual reasoning as a posterior inference problem, using Generative Flow Networks for efficient training and Bayesian inference for optimal answer selection. The LaCoT-Qwen-7B model demonstrated a 6.6% improvement over its base model and surpassed existing methods by 10.6% on various visual reasoning benchmarks.
Problem: Current Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) using Chain-of-Thought (CoT) often struggle with generalization across diverse visual reasoning tasks and tend to produce limited, deterministic rationales.
Existing reinforcement learning approaches for CoT generation depend on external, potentially biased reward models, leading to issues like reward hacking and constrained exploration.
Traditional inference-time scaling methods (e.g., Best-of-N, Beam Search) for CoT are computationally expensive for long multimodal sequences and also rely on potentially biased critic models.
Method: LaCoT reformulates CoT reasoning as a posterior inference problem over latent variables (Z) given question-answer pairs (X,Y), leveraging Amortized Variational Inference (AVI) with Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets).

A Reference-Guided GFlowNet Fine-tuning (RGFN) algorithm is introduced for efficient training, utilizing a token-level marginal reward approximation and guiding exploration with reference rationales to improve efficiency and quality.

A principled Bayesian Inference over N latent rationales (BiN) strategy is proposed for optimal rationale and answer selection at inference time, which estimates marginal likelihood without an explicit critic model.
Results: The LaCoT-Qwen-7B model achieved state-of-the-art performance among open-source LVLMs, outperforming its base Qwen2.5-VL-7B by 6.6% and GRPO by 10.6% across seven visual reasoning benchmarks.
LaCoT models generate rationales with higher diversity and log-likelihood compared to SFT baselines, contributing to better posterior coverage and a higher probability of sampling correct answers.

The Bayesian Inference (BiN) method consistently outperformed Best-of-N (BoN) for optimal rationale and answer selection, demonstrating improved accuracy, generalizability, and a notable ability to mitigate hallucination issues with increased rationale candidates.
Takeaways: Treating CoT reasoning as a probabilistic inference problem over latent variables allows for capturing uncertainty and diverse reasoning paths more effectively than deterministic or purely reward-maximizing approaches.

Combining GFlowNets with targeted approximations (token-level marginal reward) and guided exploration (RGFN) makes advanced probabilistic modeling computationally feasible for long multimodal reasoning sequences.
Bayesian inference over sampled latent rationales offers a statistically robust, scalable, and principled alternative to heuristic inference-time scaling methods, enhancing output reliability.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.23603.Title: PixelRefer: A Unified Framework for Spatio-Temporal Object Referring with Arbitrary Granularity
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.23603.Summary: PixelRefer presents a unified framework for fine-grained spatiotemporal object understanding in images and videos, achieving state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks. The framework incorporates a scale-adaptive object tokenizer and an efficient object-centric infusion module, alongside a new 2.2 million-sample instruction-tuning dataset, enabling significant computational cost reductions for video processing.
Problem: Existing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) excel at holistic scene understanding but lack precise, fine-grained, object-centric reasoning capabilities, crucial for detailed visual referring tasks.
Previous region-level MLLMs were often task-specific, leading to high computational overhead and sacrificing the general-purpose capabilities and flexibility of foundational MLLMs.
A shortage of high-quality, diverse instruction-tuning datasets exists for truly fine-grained, pixel-level object understanding, particularly for complex spatiotemporal reasoning in videos.
Method: Introduces the Vision-Object Framework (PixelRefer) featuring a Scale-Adaptive Object Tokenizer (SAOT) that dynamically processes objects of arbitrary granularity to generate semantically rich and compact representations.

Develops the Object-Only Framework (PixelRefer-Lite) with an Object-Centric Infusion (OCI) module that pre-integrates hierarchical local and global visual context into object tokens, significantly reducing LLM computational load.

Curates PixelRefer-2.2M, a comprehensive open-source instruction-tuning dataset for foundational object perception and visual instruction tuning, addressing the data scarcity for fine-grained spatiotemporal tasks.
Results: Achieved state-of-the-art performance across numerous benchmarks, including a +12.7% improvement on Ferret-Reasoning and outperforming GPT-4o by 8.1% on VideoRefer-Bench Q for multi-choice QA in videos.
PixelRefer-Lite demonstrated dramatic efficiency gains, reducing FLOPs by approximately 100x and memory usage by 5x for video inputs, making advanced region-level MLLM capabilities more practical.

The Scale-Adaptive Object Tokenizer (SAOT) significantly outperformed baseline methods, especially for small regions (+15.6% on LVIS), and the Object-Centric Infusion (OCI) module synergistically improved performance by effectively infusing local and global context into object tokens.
Takeaways: An LLM's attention mechanisms predominantly focus on region-level tokens for answer generation, highlighting the importance of rich, compact object representations for object-centric tasks.

Global visual tokens primarily contribute in early LLM layers, with their activity diminishing in deeper layers, suggesting that pre-fusing essential global context into object tokens can drastically improve efficiency without compromising semantic fidelity.
The curated PixelRefer-2.2M dataset, through its diverse and progressive inclusion of data types, systematically enhances the model's capabilities across various fine-grained visual reasoning tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.23596.Title: Think Twice: Branch-and-Rethink Reasoning Reward Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.23596.Summary: The Branch-and-Rethink Reasoning Reward Model (BR-RM) introduces a two-turn framework to improve Large Language Model evaluation by mitigating "judgment diffusion." This approach adaptively focuses on critical evaluation criteria and performs a conditioned re-evaluation, achieving a new state-of-the-art average score of 84.2% across RewardBench, RM-Bench, and RMB benchmarks.
Problem: Existing reward models (RMs) for LLMs suffer from "judgment diffusion," where attention is spread thinly across evaluation criteria, leading to shallow analysis and missed subtle errors.

While LLM solvers benefit from multi-step "think-twice" reasoning strategies, most reward models operate in a "one-shot" manner, lacking instance-adaptive focus or a conditioned second pass for deep scrutiny.
Traditional scalar RMs and current generative/reasoning RMs often fail to detect nuanced factual errors, local contradictions, or logical inconsistencies in LLM outputs.
Method: A two-turn Branch-and-Rethink Reasoning Reward Model (BR-RM) is proposed, reframing reward modeling as a structured reasoning and generation task.

The first turn involves "Adaptive Branching" where the model selects a small subset of instance-critical evaluation criteria and generates an "issue sketch" for each response, focusing its initial analysis.

The second turn, "Branch-Conditioned Rethinking," re-evaluates responses through the lens of the issues and criteria identified in the first turn, guided by task-specific evaluation hierarchies, to produce a detailed comparative judgment and final decision.
Results: The BR-RM-Qwen-14B model achieved state-of-the-art performance, with an average score of 84.2% across RewardBench, RM-Bench, and RMB benchmarks, and the highest accuracy on RM-Bench (85.9%).
Ablation studies confirmed that both the "rethinking" turn and its "conditioned" nature are critical, with their removal causing significant performance drops (up to 3.7 and 2.8 points respectively).

The smaller BR-RM-Qwen-8B model outperformed much larger single-turn baselines (e.g., GPT-4o, 70B scalar models) in average score, demonstrating the efficiency benefits of targeted two-turn reasoning.
Takeaways: Applying a structured, adaptive "think-twice" reasoning process from LLM solvers to reward models (judges) effectively mitigates "judgment diffusion" and enhances evaluation sensitivity.
A two-turn reasoning structure provides the optimal balance between reasoning depth and stability, as increasing the number of turns beyond two leads to performance degradation.
A straightforward reward function combining a binary outcome reward with strict format checks is most effective for training the structured generative reward model.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.23595.Title: Multi-Agent Evolve: LLM Self-Improve through Co-evolution
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.23595.Summary: A framework called Multi-Agent Evolve (MAE) enables large language models (LLMs) to improve their reasoning abilities through a co-evolutionary process involving self-generated questions, answers, and evaluations, eliminating the need for human-curated data or external verifiable rewards. The method significantly outperforms existing baselines, with the MAE (half reference) setting achieving an overall average score of 59.87 on diverse benchmarks using a Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct model.
Problem: Current reinforcement learning methods for LLMs rely heavily on expensive human-curated datasets and domain-specific verifiable rewards, limiting their scalability and generality.
Self-play paradigms for LLMs often require 'grounded environments' that provide objective feedback, which is difficult to apply in open-ended, general reasoning domains.
Integrating LLM-as-a-Judge mechanisms into robust, general self-improvement loops for continuous training has faced challenges in stability and implementation complexity.
Method: MAE instantiates three interacting roles (Proposer, Solver, Judge) from a single, shared LLM backbone, forming a closed self-improving loop for generating training data and reward signals.
The Proposer generates questions, the Solver answers them, and the Judge evaluates both questions and answers, providing numerical reward signals without human ground truth.
All three roles are trained simultaneously using Task-Relative REINFORCE++, performing synchronized parameter updates on the uniform shared model to foster co-evolution and stable learning.
Results: MAE (zero), starting with only 16 self-generated questions, improved the base model's overall average score from 55.33 to 58.51, surpassing the strong AZR baseline (57.72) without relying on verifiable environments.
All MAE variants, which do not use ground-truth answers, consistently outperformed Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on the same seed dataset, demonstrating the framework's data efficiency and robustness.
The MAE (half reference) setting achieved the highest overall average score of 59.87, showing strong performance on both in-distribution (68.95) and out-of-distribution (43.96) benchmarks.
Takeaways: A 'beyond-zero-sum' reward design, incentivizing the Proposer to generate challenging yet solvable questions for the Solver while ensuring intrinsic question quality, is crucial for stable and effective co-evolution.
Maintaining high-quality training data through a Judge-based question quality filtering mechanism is essential to prevent degradation of the question dataset and ensure sustained learning.

A balanced approach that combines exploring novel self-generated questions with referencing an existing, diverse distribution of unlabeled seed questions (MAE (half reference)) is most effective for general reasoning improvement.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.23569.Title: EgoThinker: Unveiling Egocentric Reasoning with Spatio-Temporal CoT
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.23569.Summary: EgoThinker enhances Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) with robust egocentric reasoning, leveraging a novel 5-million-sample dataset, EgoRe-5M, and a two-stage supervised and reinforcement fine-tuning curriculum. The framework achieves state-of-the-art performance across various egocentric benchmarks, including an 8.4% improvement on cross-view skill transfer, and significantly boosts fine-grained spatio-temporal grounding while maintaining general video understanding capabilities.
Problem: Current Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) primarily operate from an observer-centric, third-person viewpoint, lacking the embodied cognitive processes crucial for genuine first-person understanding.
Existing MLLMs struggle with complex egocentric tasks requiring causal inference, precise hand-object interaction recognition, and multi-horizon temporal integration across long video durations.
A lack of large-scale, richly annotated egocentric datasets with explicit reasoning chains and fine-grained spatio-temporal grounding hinders the development of robust egocentric AI.
Method: Developed EgoRe-5M, a novel 5-million-sample egocentric QA dataset, featuring diverse egocentric video clips with explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) rationales, dense hand-object grounding, and multi-minute segments.

Introduced a two-stage learning curriculum, combining Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) for foundational reasoning and language skills, with Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RFT) using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) for precise spatio-temporal localization.
Utilized Qwen2-VL-7B as the backbone, adapting it with specialized training data and reward functions to acquire embodied cognitive skills from an egocentric perspective.
Results: EgoThinker achieved state-of-the-art performance on egocentric reasoning benchmarks, including a 4.4% absolute gain on EgoPlan (long-horizon planning) and an 8.4% improvement on the Referenced Egocentric Skill benchmark.
Demonstrated substantial improvements in fine-grained spatio-temporal localization, notably achieving an 80.3% Localization Accuracy on EK-Visor for hand-object grounding, surpassing larger models.

Maintained or improved performance on general video understanding benchmarks (e.g., +1.8% on MVBench), indicating that specialized egocentric training enhances broader video comprehension without degradation.
Takeaways: MLLMs can be effectively endowed with robust egocentric reasoning and precise spatio-temporal grounding capabilities through a carefully designed data collection and two-stage fine-tuning approach.

The combination of supervised instruction tuning and reinforcement fine-tuning, particularly with rule-based reward functions for grounding, is crucial for simultaneously improving high-level reasoning and low-level localization in egocentric contexts.

Explicit Chain-of-Thought rationales and fine-grained grounding annotations in large-scale egocentric datasets significantly improve a model's ability to understand complex human-object interactions and temporal causality.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.23473.Title: Video-Thinker: Sparking "Thinking with Videos" via Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.23473.Summary: VIDEO-THINKER, a new framework, empowers Multimodal Large Language Models to reason with videos by intrinsically developing temporal grounding and captioning abilities. The model establishes new state-of-the-art performance on various video reasoning benchmarks, achieving up to an 11.44% improvement on the VRBench out-of-domain dataset, while showcasing enhanced temporal localization (48.22% mIoU) and descriptive captioning.
Problem: Extending the 'Thinking with Images' paradigm to videos poses challenges due to inherent temporal dependencies and dynamic content.
Existing MLLMs often treat videos as static inputs or rely on rigid, pre-designed prompting strategies, limiting dynamic manipulation and reasoning over temporal sequences.
Many video reasoning models struggle to seamlessly integrate temporal grounding into the full chain-of-thought process and typically demand extensive datasets.
Method: A Hindsight-Curation Reasoning pipeline synthesizes the Video-Thinker-10K dataset, providing structured reasoning traces with explicit temporal (``), captioning (``), and thinking (``) tags.
A two-stage training strategy is employed, beginning with Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) to teach the MLLM to generate reasoning in the specified format.

The SFT stage is followed by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), a reinforcement learning technique, to intrinsically strengthen grounding and captioning capabilities for autonomous temporal navigation and robust reasoning.
Results: Video-Thinker-7B achieves new state-of-the-art results among 7B-sized MLLMs across in-domain and challenging out-of-domain video reasoning benchmarks, with up to an 11.44% improvement on VRBench.

The model demonstrates superior intrinsic grounding abilities with an mIoU of 48.22% (a 75.5% relative improvement over Qwen2.5-VL-7B) and enhanced captioning, showing a 31.2% relative enhancement in overall captioning performance.

Video-Thinker exhibits emergent 'aha moments' and self-reflective behaviors during reasoning, suggesting dynamic internal feedback mechanisms and metacognitive capabilities acquired with high data efficiency.
Takeaways: Empowering MLLMs with intrinsic temporal grounding and captioning allows them to autonomously 'think with videos,' moving beyond passive video processing to active, dynamic reasoning.
The hindsight-curation data synthesis, combined with the two-stage SFT and GRPO training, efficiently instills complex video reasoning abilities using a relatively small 10K sample dataset.
The GRPO stage is crucial for developing robust reasoning and out-of-domain generalization, transforming basic format-following into effective autonomous temporal navigation and understanding.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.23038.Title: Incentivizing Agentic Reasoning in LLM Judges via Tool-Integrated Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.23038.Summary: TIR-Judge, developed by researchers from Google and Emory University, introduces an LLM judge framework that integrates code execution tools through an end-to-end reinforcement learning approach. This method enhances judging accuracy on reasoning benchmarks by up to 7.7% and demonstrates self-evolution capabilities without relying on distilled data.
Problem: Traditional LLM judges, relying solely on text-based reasoning, struggle with tasks requiring precise computation, symbolic reasoning, or verifiable constraint checking.
Existing tool-augmented LLM judges often treat tool invocation as an inference-time add-on, failing to deeply integrate tool-use strategies into the model's core reasoning process.
Prior tool-assisted approaches were often limited by narrow task coverage, which hindered their general applicability across diverse evaluation domains.
Method: An end-to-end Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework, based on DAPO, trains LLM judges to strategically generate and execute Python code during the training phase.
The judgment trajectory interleaves natural language reasoning, generated code, and execution results from an external interpreter, allowing for iterative refinement of decisions.
A structured reward system incentivizes correctness, proper output formatting, and error-free, budget-constrained tool execution, promoting effective and efficient tool integration.
Results: TIR-Judge consistently achieves superior judging accuracy, with gains of up to 6.4% (pointwise) and 7.7% (pairwise) over baselines on reasoning-focused benchmarks, and an 8B parameter model often surpasses 32B parameter reasoning reward models.

The `TIR-Judge-Zero` variant, trained entirely without distilled judge trajectories, delivers comparable or even better performance than its distilled counterpart, demonstrating effective self-bootstrapping.

When used for best-of-N inference, TIR-Judge consistently surpasses strong baselines, achieving absolute gains of 3.9–6.7% on challenging code generation and math problems, validating its utility in enhancing policy model performance.
Takeaways: Reinforcement learning is essential for effectively unlocking and optimizing tool-use capabilities in LLM judges, as merely providing tool access to base LLMs yields negligible gains.
Tool-augmented judges can self-evolve and self-improve their reasoning and tool-use skills through iterative RL (TIR-Judge-Zero), reducing reliance on costly supervision from frontier models.
Training with a diverse mixture of verifiable and non-verifiable tasks is crucial for the judge's generalization abilities and robust development of tool-use skills.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.22832.Title: HRM-Agent: Training a recurrent reasoning model in dynamic environments using reinforcement learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.22832.Summary: Melbourne, Australia, and Cerenaut AI researchers adapted the Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM) for reinforcement learning in dynamic maze environments, demonstrating that its recurrent internal state can maintain and adapt learned plans across environmental changes. The HRM-Agent achieved approximately 99% success rates in navigation tasks while efficiently reusing prior computations through its carried-forward latent state.
Problem: Existing reasoning models like Large Language Models (LLMs) are often inefficient and struggle with adaptive, sustained reasoning in dynamic and partially observable environments.
The Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM) was previously limited to supervised, static, and fully-observable problems, restricting its real-world applicability.
Reinforcement learning agents require mechanisms to effectively handle hierarchical, long-horizon planning and maintain consistent internal states across dynamic environmental changes.
Method: Adapted the Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM) by replacing its output head with a Deep Q-Network (DQN) head for action value prediction.
Trained the HRM-Agent entirely from scratch using reinforcement learning, without any supervised losses or human-defined problem decompositions.
Introduced a "Carry Z" mechanism where the agent's recurrent latent state from the previous environment step is carried forward to the next, promoting computational reuse.
Results: The HRM-Agent achieved a high success rate of approximately 99% in goal navigation within both dynamic Four-Rooms and random maze environments.
Demonstrated efficient path planning, with mean episode lengths approaching theoretical optimums, indicating learned deliberate reasoning.
The "Carry Z" variant consistently led to faster convergence of the recurrent latent state and exhibited greater consistency in internal plans compared to the "Reset Z" variant.
Takeaways: The intrinsic recurrent reasoning capabilities of HRM can be successfully leveraged within an RL framework to develop adaptive agents for dynamic and uncertain environments.

Carrying forward the recurrent latent state (z) allows the agent to efficiently reuse computations, accelerate internal plan convergence, and maintain consistency in its reasoning across environmental timesteps.
The agent's recurrent state appears to function as an internal "plan" or "belief state" that dynamically adapts to environmental changes without being reset.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.22512.Title: Transitive RL: Value Learning via Divide and Conquer
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.22512.Summary: Researchers at UC Berkeley introduce Transitive RL (TRL), a divide-and-conquer value learning algorithm for offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning, which mitigates the "curse of horizon" by employing a transitive Bellman update with in-trajectory subgoals and expectile regression. This method achieves leading performance on long-horizon robotic tasks and competitive results across various standard benchmarks.
Problem: Traditional temporal difference (TD) learning in offline goal-conditioned RL suffers from severe bias accumulation, leading to the "curse of horizon" in long-horizon tasks.
Monte Carlo (MC) methods for value learning exhibit high variance, particularly for long trajectories, limiting their practicality.

Prior approaches leveraging the triangle inequality in goal-conditioned RL for value learning have not successfully scaled to complex, high-dimensional robotic environments without additional planning.
Method: Develops Transitive RL (TRL), an algorithm leveraging a divide-and-conquer approach to value learning, specifically designed for offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning.

Employs a transitive Bellman update rule that uses soft expectile regression to approximate maximization, and critically restricts intermediate subgoals to those observed within the training trajectories.
Utilizes distance-based re-weighting to stabilize training by prioritizing the learning of values for shorter trajectory segments.
Results: TRL demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on demanding long-horizon robotic tasks like `humanoidmaze-giant` and `puzzle-4x6`, outperforming previous TD-based, MC-based, and other GCRL methods.
The algorithm achieves the best average performance across 10 standard OGBench environments and 50 evaluation tasks, showing strong general competitive capability.

Key components like expectile regression (with $ \kappa > 0.5 $ ), restricting subgoals to in-trajectory states, and distance-based re-weighting were experimentally validated as crucial for TRL's stable and high performance.
Takeaways: A divide-and-conquer approach to value learning can fundamentally address the "curse of horizon" by reducing recursive dependencies from O(T) to O(log T) steps, combining benefits of TD and MC methods.

Preventing value overestimation is critical for scaling transitive value updates; this is effectively achieved by restricting intermediate subgoals to only those present within observed dataset trajectories.

The inherent triangle inequality property of goal-conditioned reinforcement learning can be practically leveraged for complex tasks through careful algorithmic design, specifically using expectile regression and in-trajectory subgoals.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.21890.Title: The Principles of Diffusion Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.21890.Summary: Authored by leading researchers from Sony AI, OpenAI, and Stanford, this monograph synthesizes the rapidly evolving field of diffusion models by clarifying their theoretical foundations and unifying diverse formulations into a single continuous-time generative framework. It systematically covers the origins, unifies variational, score-based, and flow-based perspectives, and outlines advancements in sampling and generation techniques.
Problem: The rapid proliferation of diverse diffusion model formulations (e.g., DDPM, NCSN, Flow Matching) led to a fragmented literature.
Researchers and practitioners found it challenging to grasp the underlying mathematical connections and theoretical coherence across different approaches.
A lack of a systematic and unified understanding hindered entry into the field and efficient progress in research.
Method: The monograph provides a comprehensive and authoritative review, acting as a pedagogical guide for the field of diffusion models.
It rigorously demonstrates the mathematical equivalence of variational, score-based, and flow-based approaches under a continuous-time framework.

It clarifies the theoretical underpinnings, including the central roles of the score function, SDEs, ODEs, and the Fokker-Planck equation, and systematically covers practical advancements like guidance and efficient sampling.
Results: The monograph conclusively demonstrates the mathematical equivalence between DDPM, NCSN/Score SDE, and Flow Matching paradigms, showing they are manifestations of a unified continuous-time generative process.

It establishes the Fokker-Planck equation as the universal underlying law governing the evolution of marginal probability densities in diffusion models, regardless of stochastic or deterministic dynamics.

The work systematically categorizes and explains advancements in diffusion models, including guidance mechanisms for controllable generation, training-free acceleration methods (numerical solvers), and training-based acceleration techniques (distillation, learning from scratch like Consistency Models).
Takeaways: Variational, score-based, and flow-based diffusion models are mathematically equivalent formulations of a single continuous-time generative process, all implicitly or explicitly learning a time-dependent vector field.
The 'conditioning trick,' which transforms intractable marginal objectives into tractable conditional ones, is a foundational enabler for training across all major diffusion model formulations.
The generation process can be fundamentally understood as solving a differential equation (SDE or Probability Flow ODE), providing a principled basis for analyzing and accelerating sampling.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.21501.Title: GranViT: A Fine-Grained Vision Model With Autoregressive Perception For MLLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.21501.Summary: Researchers from Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Huawei Inc. developed GranViT, a fine-grained vision model for MLLMs, by constructing the Gran-29M dataset and proposing a two-stage pretraining-adaptation framework. GranViT achieves state-of-the-art performance in fine-grained recognition and OCR understanding, demonstrating enhanced regional perception and strong transferability to larger language models.
Problem: Existing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) primarily rely on global image representations, leading to a neglect of fine-grained regional analysis.
A significant scarcity of large-scale, high-quality datasets explicitly annotated with region-level details (e.g., bounding boxes for objects or text) for training vision encoders.
The absence of a dedicated pre-training paradigm designed to instill fine-grained perception capabilities into vision encoders while maintaining effective alignment with LLMs.
Method: Introduced Gran-29M, a large-scale dataset comprising 29.51 million natural and OCR images with over 183 million high-quality, region-level bounding box and caption annotations, formatted into question-answer pairs.

Developed a two-stage pretraining-adaptation framework: Stage 1 focuses on pretraining the vision encoder for Bbox2Caption regression and localized self-distillation, while Stage 2 adapts the LLM for Caption2Bbox regression with the frozen vision encoder.

Incorporated a localized self-distillation mechanism during pre-training to impose explicit localization constraints on the vision encoder, ensuring features are aligned with ground truth localized regions.
Results: Achieved state-of-the-art average top-1 scores of 80.78 on fine-grained recognition benchmarks (2.83 points relative improvement) and 55.97 on OCR understanding tasks (2.64 points relative improvement), outperforming previous leading models.

Demonstrated strong transferability, with the GranViT vision encoder effectively integrating with larger LLMs (Qwen2.5-3B/7B) to maintain superior performance on fine-grained tasks and achieve competitive results on multimodal VQA benchmarks.

Ablation studies confirmed that each component of the proposed framework, including the Gran-29M dataset, Bbox2Caption and Caption2Bbox tasks, and localized self-distillation, progressively contributes to significant performance gains in fine-grained and OCR capabilities.
Takeaways: Explicit region-level supervision via Bbox2Caption tasks, coupled with self-distillation, is crucial for compelling the vision encoder to learn generic and precise fine-grained visual features.
A decoupled two-stage training approach efficiently optimizes both the vision encoder's fine-grained feature extraction and the LLM's capability to accurately localize and utilize these features.

The creation of a vast, high-quality dataset with multi-granularity annotations (Gran-29M) is fundamental for overcoming data scarcity and enabling the training of robust fine-grained perception in MLLMs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.21311.Title: FineRS: Fine-grained Reasoning and Segmentation of Small Objects with Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.21311.Summary: FINERS introduces a multi-modal large language model framework designed for instruction-guided reasoning and pixel-level segmentation of ultra-small objects within high-resolution images. The model achieves state-of-the-art gIoU/cIoU scores of 55.1/46.5 on the new UAV-captured 4K dataset, FINERS-4k, and generalizes robustly to other high-resolution visual question answering benchmarks.
Problem: Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle with fine-grained perception and precise localization of small objects in high-resolution images due to input resolution limitations, leading to a loss of critical visual details through downsampling.

Existing high-resolution MLLM approaches often lack pixel-level segmentation capabilities, typically providing only coarse visual reasoning or question answering without precise spatial grounding for referred objects.

There is a scarcity of large-scale, high-quality benchmark datasets specifically designed for fine-grained reasoning and segmentation of ultra-small objects in complex, high-resolution imagery, particularly from UAVs.
Method: A two-stage coarse-to-fine pipeline combines a Global Semantic Exploration (GSE) module for identifying broad target regions and a Localized Perceptual Refinement (LPR) module for fine-grained localization, with a frozen SAM2 model generating final pixel-level segmentation masks.

A reinforcement learning strategy based on GRPO is employed, featuring a novel locate-informed retrospective reward for GSE, which leverages the already trained LPR module to provide robust supervision for coarse region prediction.

Task-specific multi-task reward functions are designed for both GSE and LPR, guiding optimization towards accurate textual answers, precise bounding boxes, and segmentation points, enabling unified reasoning and segmentation capabilities.
Results: FINERS achieved gIoU/cIoU scores of 55.1/46.5 on the FINERS-4k test set for instruction-guided segmentation, outperforming the next best baseline (Seg-zero† 7B) by 8.5/7.9 points, with particularly strong performance on extra-small and extra-extra small objects.

The model demonstrated strong generalization to other high-resolution VQA benchmarks, achieving 77.5% accuracy on V* (outperforming SEAL's 75.4%) and significantly surpassing baselines on HR-Bench 4K (63.8% vs. DC2's 50.0%) and HR-Bench 8K (58.1% vs. DC2's 40.8%).

Ablation studies confirmed the critical contributions of the two-stage design, the locate-informed retrospective reward mechanism for GSE, the random input region augmentation for LPR, and the comprehensive multi-task reward functions for both stages.
Takeaways: A coarse-to-fine MLLM architecture effectively addresses the challenge of small object perception in high-resolution images by sequentially identifying broad areas and then refining details within localized views.

Reinforcement learning, particularly with a retrospective reward mechanism, can efficiently fine-tune MLLMs for complex multi-task vision-language problems like simultaneous reasoning and fine-grained segmentation, even with limited direct supervision for intermediate steps.

The creation of specialized, high-resolution datasets, such as the UAV-captured FINERS-4k, is essential for pushing the boundaries of MLLMs in challenging domains involving small object detection and segmentation in cluttered visual environments.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.21223.Title: Model Merging with Functional Dual Anchors
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.21223.Summary: Functional Dual Anchors (FDAs) introduce a method for model merging that operates by modeling knowledge in the input-representation space, rather than the parameter space. This approach generates synthetic inputs whose induced gradients align with task vectors, leading to consistent performance improvements over parameter-centric methods and effectively refining models merged by existing techniques across vision and language tasks.
Problem: Existing model merging methods primarily operate in the parameter space, facing challenges with parameter inconsistency and conflicts when combining diverse task-specific knowledge.

There is a need for efficient post-training strategies to consolidate knowledge from multiple specialized (finetuned) models into a single, unified model without the high cost of full multi-task retraining.
Parameter-space task vectors can be sensitive to initialization and prone to drift, limiting the robustness and reliability of merged models.
Method: The paper proposes Functional Dual Anchors (FDAs), synthetic inputs constructed by matching their induced gradients on a pretrained model to the task vector (parameter difference) of a finetuned model, effectively projecting task knowledge into the input-representation space.
A principled initialization scheme for FDAs, derived from linear model analysis, ensures efficient and stable convergence during their construction, limiting energy in the tail subspace.

Once constructed, FDAs are used to optimize the merged model parameters by minimizing representation discrepancies across tasks, or to refine existing parameter-centric merged models by fine-tuning their task vector adjustments.
Results: FDAs consistently outperform basic parameter-centric methods like Task Arithmetic, achieving an average performance improvement of nearly 18% on ViT-B/16 and 15.4% in average GLUE score on RoBERTa-Large.

FDAs are complementary to existing data-free parameter-centric merging methods, providing further performance improvements of up to ~5.10% on ViT-B/16, ~13% on RoBERTa-Large, and 10% on auto-regressive models when used as a refinement step.

The layer-wise FDA construction and adaptation strategy, combined with effective initialization schemes like "Linear Weight Sampling," enables practical application and scalability to large foundation models across diverse vision and language tasks.
Takeaways: Modeling knowledge in the input-representation space via synthetic inputs (FDAs) offers a robust and flexible alternative to direct parameter-space manipulation for model merging, effectively bridging multi-task training and post-hoc merging paradigms.

FDAs exhibit a long-tailed singular value spectrum and their high-energy subspace progressively aligns with that of real task-specific data, indicating they capture salient functional characteristics.

FDA-induced parameter adaptations (gradients) align with those induced by real data, validating their effectiveness as a proxy for real data in guiding model changes and mitigating representation bias in merged models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.20994.Title: VESSA: Video-based objEct-centric Self-Supervised Adaptation for Visual Foundation Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.20994.Summary: VESSA enables visual foundation models to specialize in new, label-scarce domains through a self-supervised adaptation strategy that utilizes object-centric videos. This method, a collaboration between UFMG, UNICAMP, and Google DeepMind, integrates parameter-efficient fine-tuning and uncertainty-weighted self-distillation, yielding consistent improvements in downstream classification performance.
Problem: Visual Foundation Models (VFMs) often face performance degradation when applied to specialized target domains due to distribution shifts and the scarcity of labeled data.

Existing supervised fine-tuning methods for VFMs are resource-intensive and impractical in label-scarce environments, while naive self-supervised adaptation for vision encoders is ineffective and can lead to catastrophic forgetting.
A gap exists for an effective self-supervised fine-tuning strategy that can directly specialize pre-trained VFMs to unlabeled target domains for downstream tasks.
Method: VESSA introduces a video-based object-centric self-supervised adaptation strategy for VFMs, using short multi-view videos as the sole source of unlabeled adaptation data.
The method employs an Uncertainty-Weighted Self-Distillation (UWSD) loss, which assigns higher importance to 'harder' examples based on teacher model entropy, to guide the student network.

It integrates Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) using LoRA with a careful, staged unfreezing schedule: initial projection head adaptation followed by gradual fine-tuning of early and late backbone layers.
Results: VESSA consistently improved kNN classification accuracy across DINO, DINOv2, and TIPS models on the MVImageNet and CO3D datasets, with DINOv2 showing a 4% absolute gain on CO3D (from 87.86% to 91.85%).
The approach significantly outperformed image-based self-supervised adaptation methods and other video-based baselines like ExPLoRA in most comparative experiments.

The adaptation process is computationally efficient, requiring only 1.97 hours of training for the CO3D dataset with a ViT-Base backbone, though it entails an expected trade-off in catastrophic forgetting of original general-purpose capabilities.
Takeaways: Object-centric videos, with their inherent spatio-temporal consistency and diverse viewpoints, provide rich implicit supervisory signals for effective self-supervised adaptation of VFMs.

A carefully designed training schedule, including initial adaptation of the prediction head and selective unfreezing of backbone layers via LoRA, is crucial to stabilize fine-tuning and prevent catastrophic forgetting of pre-trained knowledge.

Uncertainty weighting in the self-distillation loss effectively guides the model to focus on more challenging examples, leading to more robust and discriminative feature learning in the target domain.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.20817.Title: KL-Regularized Reinforcement Learning is Designed to Mode Collapse
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.20817.Summary: Researchers from NYU and EPFL demonstrate that KL-regularized reinforcement learning objectives inherently lead to mode collapse, proving that optimal solutions are often unimodal by design rather than due to optimization failures. They introduce Mode Anchored Reward Augmentation (MARA), a simple algorithm that modifies rewards to foster diverse, high-quality outputs across generative AI applications.
Problem: Diversity collapse (mode collapse) is a pervasive issue in reinforcement learning post-training of foundation models, leading to models producing similar outputs despite multiple valid solutions.
Existing approaches to combat diversity collapse are often heuristic and address symptoms rather than the fundamental theoretical cause.
A lack of rigorous understanding of why diversity collapse occurs inherently within KL-regularized reinforcement learning objectives.
Method: The authors conducted a rigorous theoretical analysis using variational inference to derive the globally optimal target distributions implicitly defined by KL-regularized RL objectives.

They developed Mode Anchored Reward Augmentation (MARA), a simple algorithm that redefines the reward function to ensure the optimal target distribution places uniformly high mass over all high-quality samples.
The theoretical claims and MARA's efficacy were validated through didactic simulations and experiments on Large Language Models (LLMs) and Chemical Language Models (CLMs).
Results: Theoretical analysis revealed that optimal KL-regularized policies exhibit exponential sensitivity to even minor reward differences and merely preserve reference policy ratios for equally rewarded samples, thereby leading to mode collapse.

MARA successfully maintained diversity and quality in LLM post-training, outperforming baselines in tasks like verifiable integer generation and creative question answering by achieving higher entropy and distinctness.
Applied to Chemical Language Models for drug discovery, MARA significantly increased the
Takeaways: KL-regularized RL objectives, under common settings, are intrinsically designed to yield unimodal optimal policies, indicating that diversity collapse is an inherent outcome rather than an optimization failure.

The choice between reverse and forward KL regularization does not primarily determine mode coverage; instead, the regularization strength (β), and relative magnitudes of rewards and reference probabilities are the dominant factors.

The proposed MARA algorithm promotes multimodality by modifying the reward function to equalize the effective reward-to-reference-probability ratio for all high-quality samples, thus directly shaping the target distribution.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.20607.Title: Generalizable Reasoning through Compositional Energy Minimization
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.20607.Summary: Researchers from Harvard University and the University of Barcelona developed a framework for generalizable reasoning that learns modular energy functions for subproblems and combines them, utilizing Parallel Energy Minimization to solve complex tasks. This approach demonstrates strong generalization capabilities, often outperforming state-of-the-art methods in benchmarks like N-Queens, 3-SAT, Graph Coloring, and Crosswords.
Problem: Machine learning models, especially end-to-end approaches, exhibit poor generalization to structurally more complex or out-of-distribution reasoning problems.
Combinatorial optimization problems often require extensive, diverse datasets for effective training, limiting scalability and robustness.
Current AI methods lack the compositional reasoning abilities seen in human intelligence, struggling to apply learned rules to novel, harder tasks.
Method: Formulates reasoning as minimizing a neural Energy-Based Model (EBM) trained using a denoising diffusion objective and an additional contrastive loss.
Decomposes complex problems into subproblems, learning modular EBMs for each, and then optimizes the sum of these EBMs for a complete solution.

Employs Parallel Energy Minimization (PEM), an algorithm that uses multiple parallel particles, importance sampling, resampling, and noise injection to effectively navigate and optimize complex energy landscapes.
Results: Achieved 97 out of 100 correct solutions for the 8-Queens problem, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art combinatorial optimization methods and generalizing to N-Queens for N=7-10.
Outperformed neural SAT solvers on 3-SAT, solving 91 out of 100 instances for 20 variables/91 clauses, and 43 out of 100 for 50 variables/218 clauses.
Demonstrated superior performance in Graph Coloring over GNN-based and RL-guided methods across various graph types, notably improving generalization to larger and denser graphs.
Showed competitive results on Crosswords, reaching an 80.4% letter success rate, comparable to Tree-of-Thought LLM strategies.
Takeaways: Learning modular energy functions for subproblems allows for compositional generalization to significantly harder and larger problem instances beyond training data.

Reasoning can be effectively framed as an energy minimization problem, where increasing computational effort during inference (e.g., via more PEM particles) directly improves solution quality for complex tasks.
Parallel Energy Minimization (PEM) provides a robust strategy for optimizing over high-dimensional, non-convex energy landscapes, successfully avoiding local minima and enhancing solution discovery.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.19307.Title: Unified Reinforcement and Imitation Learning for Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.19307.Summary: The Unified Reinforcement and Imitation Learning (RIL) framework enhances lightweight Vision-Language Models (VLMs) through an efficient training algorithm, allowing them to match or surpass the performance of larger state-of-the-art models. This enables practical deployment in resource-constrained environments while maintaining original inference speeds.
Problem: State-of-the-art Vision-Language Models are too large and computationally demanding for efficient deployment on resource-constrained edge devices.
Traditional methods for improving VLM performance, such as scaling model size or adding complex architectural components, exacerbate problems with inference latency and memory footprint.
Existing reinforcement learning approaches for VLMs often rely on conventional answer parsing for rewards, limiting their applicability to open-ended visual question answering.
Method: A Unified Reinforcement and Imitation Learning (RIL) framework is proposed, combining Dr.GRPO (a reinforcement learning algorithm) with an adversarial imitation learning component inspired by GAIL.

The framework employs a dual reward system: a similarity reward from an LLM-based discriminator assessing how closely student responses mimic teacher responses, and an answer reward from an LLM-as-a-Judge for factual correctness.

RIL leverages responses from multiple large teacher VLMs to provide diverse exemplars and a more robust discriminator, while avoiding explicit 'think' phases to preserve the student VLM's original inference speed.
Results: RIL-trained student VLMs consistently outperform RL-only baselines (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL-7B saw approximately 8.2% improvement on MathVista and 12.3% on ChartQA over Dr.GRPO).

RIL-applied models achieve competitive performance against leading open-source models and in several cases surpass closed-source models like GPT-4o, Gemini-1.5-Pro, and Claude-3.5 Sonnet on benchmarks like MathVista.

The framework effectively trains lightweight VLMs suitable for edge deployment, with RIL-trained models maintaining their original inference speeds without additional architectural complexity or verbose reasoning steps.
Takeaways: Combining reinforcement learning with adversarial imitation learning through a dual reward system is crucial for transferring sophisticated generation capabilities to smaller VLMs, significantly outperforming RL-only approaches.
Utilizing multiple diverse large teacher VLMs provides a richer source of knowledge, leading to substantially better student VLM performance than training with a single teacher.

An LLM-as-a-Judge offers a flexible and robust mechanism for evaluating factual correctness in open-ended visual question answering, overcoming limitations of conventional parsing methods for reward computation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.19245.Title: See, Think, Act: Online Shopper Behavior Simulation with VLM Agents
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.19245.Summary: A team including researchers from Amazon and academic institutions introduced a VLM-driven framework to simulate online shopper behavior, integrating visual webpage screenshots alongside text to create more cognitively aligned and realistic action sequences. The multimodal approach achieved 44.57% exact match accuracy, a 6% improvement over text-only methods, demonstrating enhanced fidelity in capturing human decisions influenced by visual cues.
Problem: Existing human behavior simulation methods for web interactions rely solely on text-based inputs (HTML, action histories), neglecting the visual context.
Real human users heavily depend on visual perception for decision-making on image-rich webpages, considering aspects like product layouts and button salience.
This reliance on text-only input limits the fidelity and cognitive alignment of simulated behavior, failing to capture the full nuances of human interaction.
Method: Developed a GUI-aware simulation framework for online shopper behavior that integrates current webpage screenshots alongside simplified HTML and past actions as input to a VLM agent.
The OPeRA dataset was post-processed and augmented with LLM-synthesized rationales to provide suitable training data for multimodal learning.

Employed a two-stage training scheme involving Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) followed by Reinforcement Learning (RL) with a hierarchical, difficulty-aware reward system to refine action and rationale generation.
Results: The multimodal VLM agent trained with SFT+RL achieved 44.57% exact match accuracy, outperforming text-only methods by over 6% (38.44%) and image-only methods by nearly 20% (24.71%).

Reinforcement Learning (RL) significantly improved exact match accuracy and helped calibrate action distributions, increasing the proportion of 'scroll' actions to a more realistic 41.04% (Text + Image) and 55.00% (Text-only).

Fine-tuning via SFT and RL drastically reduced structured output formatting errors to under 0.2%, while zero-shot Claude-3.5-Sonnet exhibited very low exact match accuracy due to a strong bias towards 'click' actions (over 96%).
Takeaways: Integrating visual input is essential for high-fidelity human behavior simulation in visually rich web environments, validating that human users "see" before "acting."

Combining Supervised Fine-Tuning with Reinforcement Learning, particularly with a hierarchical and difficulty-aware reward structure, significantly enhances both semantic understanding and sequence-level action precision.
Even advanced generalist LLMs exhibit prediction biases and underutilize cross-modal signals without explicit, task-aware fine-tuning for structured interaction tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.18927.Title: BAPO: Stabilizing Off-Policy Reinforcement Learning for LLMs via Balanced Policy Optimization with Adaptive Clipping
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.18927.Summary: BAPO introduces an adaptive clipping mechanism for off-policy Reinforcement Learning in Large Language Models, which dynamically re-balances optimization signals and preserves policy entropy. This method achieves state-of-the-art performance on AIME reasoning benchmarks, outperforming comparable open-source models and demonstrating competitiveness with proprietary systems.
Problem: Off-policy Reinforcement Learning (RL) for Large Language Models (LLMs) suffers from optimization instability, leading to erratic training and performance collapse, particularly with increasing data staleness.

A rapid and sharp decline in policy entropy during off-policy RL reduces the LLM's exploratory capacity, driving it towards over-exploitation and potentially hindering the discovery of better behaviors.

Fixed clipping mechanisms in PPO-like objectives lead to imbalanced optimization, disproportionately penalizing negative samples while blocking beneficial updates from low-probability positive tokens that are crucial for entropy preservation.
Method: BAPO employs a novel adaptive clipping mechanism that dynamically adjusts the upper (`c_high`) and lower (`c_low`) bounds of the PPO objective for each update step and batch.

The adjustment aims to ensure that the contribution of positive signals to the policy gradient loss meets a predefined target threshold, `ρ₀`, thereby re-balancing the influence of positive and negative samples.

This iterative adjustment process expands `c_high` to include more low-probability positive tokens and adjusts `c_low` to filter out excessively negative tokens, promoting entropy maintenance and preventing gradient explosions.
Results: BAPO achieved significantly more stable training dynamics, maintaining stable policy entropy, steady gradient normalization, and balanced positive token contributions, preventing the collapse observed in baselines.

The method demonstrated superior robustness to data staleness, consistently outperforming base models, standard clipping, and empirically tuned asymmetric clipping on both AIME 2024 and AIME 2025 benchmarks.

BAPO-trained BP-Math-32B models scored 87.1 on AIME 2024 and 80.0 on AIME 2025, setting state-of-the-art among open-source models of comparable scale and achieving results competitive with proprietary systems like Gemini-2.5-Flash-Thinking.
Takeaways: Optimization in PPO-like objectives for LLMs is often imbalanced, with negative-advantage samples disproportionately dominating policy gradient updates, which can lead to instability and suppressed exploration.

A newly derived "Entropy-Clip Rule" reveals that fixed clipping systematically blocks entropy-increasing updates from low-probability positive tokens, leading to a continuous decline in policy entropy.

Preliminary experiments with asymmetric clipping confirmed that increasing the upper bound (`c_high`) improves performance and counteracts entropy decline, motivating the need for an adaptive mechanism.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.18873.Title: DSI-Bench: A Benchmark for Dynamic Spatial Intelligence
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.18873.Summary: A new benchmark, DSI-Bench, assesses dynamic spatial intelligence in Vision-Language Models and 3D expertise models by evaluating their comprehension of simultaneous motion between observers and objects in 3D environments. Evaluations reveal that current state-of-the-art models significantly struggle with dynamic tasks, exhibit limited robustness, and often suffer from biases like forward prediction or conflating rotation with translation, even as model scale increases.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and benchmarks are primarily limited to static or semi-dynamic 3D environments, neglecting scenarios where both observer and observed objects are in motion.
Current models demonstrate significant accuracy degradation, hallucinations, and biases when faced with complex, dynamic 3D scenes requiring simultaneous understanding of multiple moving entities.
The absence of a comprehensive benchmark for "Dynamic Spatial Intelligence" prevents rigorous evaluation and targeted development of AI systems for real-world dynamic interactions.
Method: DSI-Bench was introduced, a novel benchmark comprising nearly 1,000 dynamic scene videos and over 1,700 manually annotated Vision-Question-Answering (VQA) pairs covering diverse motion patterns.
A task taxonomy for dynamic spatial intelligence was developed, categorizing questions into object-scene, observer-scene, and observer-object relationships.
Spatio-temporal flip augmentation with a group-wise evaluation strategy was implemented to rigorously assess model robustness and mitigate biases from 3D motion patterns.
Results: State-of-the-art VLMs consistently showed a decline in accuracy when tested on dynamic scenarios compared to static ones, with performance degradation sometimes exceeding 10% on specific tasks.

VLMs exhibited a substantial drop in performance (e.g., up to 20-30% on some tasks) when evaluated group-wise (requiring consistency across flipped variants) compared to sample-wise accuracy, indicating a lack of robustness.

Models frequently displayed a "forward bias" (disproportionately selecting "forward" options) and confusion between rotational and translational movements, leading to hallucinations where objects were perceived as moving even when fixed.
Takeaways: Current VLMs lack true dynamic spatial intelligence, demonstrating significant performance drops and limited robustness when both observer and objects are in simultaneous motion.
