Simply increasing VLM scale improves sample-wise accuracy but does not consistently enhance, and can sometimes decrease, robustness against spatio-temporal transformations and inherent biases.

Language-based free-form reasoning (FFR) provides only marginal and inconsistent benefits for dynamic spatial tasks, suggesting a fundamental limitation in visual perception rather than purely reasoning capabilities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.18091.Title: Accelerating Vision Transformers with Adaptive Patch Sizes
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.18091.Summary: Researchers from Carnegie Mellon University and KAIST developed Adaptive Patch Transformers (APT) to accelerate Vision Transformers by dynamically adjusting patch sizes based on image content. This approach yields substantial speedups in both training and inference across various visual tasks while fully maintaining or slightly improving downstream performance.
Problem: Vision Transformers (ViTs) suffer from quadratic computational complexity due to self-attention, making them slow and expensive for high-resolution images.
Standard ViTs use fixed-size image patches, wasting computation on visually homogeneous or redundant regions and failing to allocate finer-grained attention to complex areas.

Existing token reduction methods often introduce practical inefficiencies (e.g., irregular shapes, padding) or require extensive fine-tuning, limiting their real-world applicability and training speedups.
Method: APT implements a content-aware, multi-scale patchification strategy, using entropy to dynamically assign larger patches to homogeneous regions and smaller patches to detailed areas.

A novel patch aggregation mechanism employs a zero-initialized MLP to convert variable-sized patches into uniform embeddings, enabling APT to rapidly adapt to pre-trained ViT models with minimal fine-tuning.
Dynamic token counts are efficiently handled through sequence packing and block-diagonal attention masks, which are optimized by modern attention backends like FlashAttention.
Results: Achieved up to an 86% speedup in ImageNet training for ViT-L at 448x448 resolution and up to 23% throughput increase for LLaVA-1.5-13B on VQA benchmarks, maintaining or exceeding baseline performance.
Reduced input tokens by 30% and attained a 30% speedup in object detection (COCO) and an 11% speedup in semantic segmentation (ADE20K) using EVA-02 backbones, matching baseline accuracy.

APT effectively allocates patches, using fewer tokens for homogeneous regions and more for complex areas, confirming its content-aware processing and achieving rapid convergence (1 epoch) for fine-tuning pre-trained models.
Takeaways: Adopting a variable-granularity, content-aware tokenization strategy, similar to those in NLP, can drastically improve the computational efficiency of Vision Transformers.
A zero-initialized MLP enables a "plug-and-play" capability, allowing APT to be applied to existing pre-trained ViT backbones and converge in as little as one fine-tuning epoch.
Input-level token reduction, when guided by image content, provides more robust and practical speedups compared to fixed-ratio or layer-level token merging/pruning methods.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.17045.Title: Video Reasoning without Training
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.17045.Summary: V-Reason is an inference-time optimization framework that enhances video reasoning in Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) without additional training, achieving an average accuracy gain of +1.4% on certain benchmarks while reducing output tokens by 58.6% and inference time by up to 37% compared to RL-trained models. This approach leverages an entropy-based objective to steer the model's internal thinking process, scaling effectively to larger LMMs.
Problem: Existing video reasoning methods for LMMs incur high computational costs during both training and inference due to complex architectures, extensive datasets, or verbose reasoning traces.
There is a limited understanding of the internal reasoning mechanisms within LMMs, making it difficult to interpret, control, or optimize their 'thinking' process effectively.
Conventional approaches like Chain-of-Thought prompting or reinforcement learning with human feedback exacerbate computational overhead, particularly for high-resolution video data.
Method: V-Reason introduces a training-free, inference-time optimization framework that modifies LMM behavior by dynamically controlling the model's output distribution entropy.
It employs a small, trainable Value-Cache Controller (∆V) added only to the value cache of the last decoder layer for video tokens, preserving the base model's frozen weights.

A novel Entropy Switching Loss optimizes ∆V, adaptively encouraging either micro-exploration (increasing entropy) or micro-exploitation (decreasing entropy) based on the exponential moving average of entropy.
Results: V-Reason consistently improved baseline accuracy, achieving average gains of +1.0% to +1.4% on various video reasoning benchmarks for the Qwen2.5-VL-7B model, and +3.9% on the challenging MMVU dataset.
The method drastically reduced output token length by 58.6% compared to RL-trained Video-R1-7B and 21.4% compared to the base Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, leading to up to 37% lower inference time.

V-Reason scaled effectively to larger models, providing a +3.0% gain for Qwen2.5-VL-32B on MMVU and a +0.4% improvement even for the Qwen2.5-VL-72B model, demonstrating its generalizability and efficiency benefits across scales.
Takeaways: LMMs exhibit distinct macro-exploration (increasing entropy) and macro-exploitation (decreasing entropy) phases during token generation, observable via output distribution entropy.
Higher-quality reasoning models demonstrate lower and delayed entropy maxima during exploration, alongside more pronounced micro-exploration/exploitation cycles, indicating 'deeper thinking'.
These internal entropy dynamics can be directly manipulated at inference time to steer an LMM's reasoning process towards higher performance without requiring extensive retraining.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.16714.Title: SceneCOT: Eliciting Grounded Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in 3D Scenes
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.16714.Summary: SCENECOT introduces a framework that facilitates step-by-step, grounded Chain-of-Thought reasoning within 3D scenes, supported by the creation of the SCENECOT-185K dataset. The approach enhanced grounding–QA coherence and yielded competitive question-answering results on 3D reasoning benchmarks, notably outperforming baselines on the Beacon3D benchmark.
Problem: Existing 3D vision-language models (3D-LLMs) exhibit 'poor grounding–QA coherence,' often generating verbally fluent answers without explicit connections to visual evidence in the 3D scene.
Complex 3D reasoning, particularly in embodied and situated settings, lacks principled task decomposition and step-by-step processes, unlike human cognitive approaches.
There is an absence of large-scale, high-quality datasets that provide explicit, stepwise reasoning traces necessary for training models capable of grounded 3D reasoning.
Method: SCENECOT establishes a four-stage reasoning process: Task Recognition, Task-relevant Region Localization, Entity Grounding, and Grounded Reasoning, each designed to produce explicit grounding signals.
The framework integrates a Multi-modal Large Language Model (LLaVA-1.5) with specialized 3D-VL and 2D-VL models, along with symbolic engines, into a modular learning and inference pipeline.
The SCENECOT-185K dataset, the first large-scale 3D-CoTs dataset with 185K instances, was created to provide high-quality supervision for learning grounded, step-by-step reasoning in 3D scenes.
Results: SCENECOT achieved competitive overall performance on the MSQA benchmark (55.6 GPT-Score) and demonstrated superior results on the Beacon3D benchmark for object-centric reasoning (58.9 Case and 23.2 Obj. GPT-Scores), surpassing all baselines.

The framework exhibited enhanced grounding–QA coherence, securing the highest Good Coherence (GC) score of 34.7% on Beacon3D, a considerable improvement over previous methods (e.g., LEO: 1.6%, Chat-Scene: 19.5%).

Ablation studies confirmed the importance of key components, showing that removing question type recognition or region localization led to substantial performance drops across various sub-tasks (e.g., ~20% drop in overall GPT-Score for forced question typing).
Takeaways: Explicitly decomposing 3D reasoning into human-like, step-by-step stages with clear grounding signals substantially improves both question-answering accuracy and the coherence between answers and their visual evidence.

Task-specific components, such as question type recognition and relevant region localization, are crucial for effectively narrowing the reasoning scope, reducing noise, and strengthening grounding in complex 3D environments.

Applying a dedicated grounding loss during training is important for ensuring accurate object grounding, which is vital for maintaining the consistency and overall correctness of the step-by-step reasoning process.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.16596.Title: SHIELD: Suppressing Hallucinations In LVLM Encoders via Bias and Vulnerability Defense
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.16596.Summary: SHIELD introduces a training-free framework that effectively mitigates object hallucinations in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) by targeting specific issues within their visual encoders, including statistical bias, inherent bias, and vulnerability. The method achieves substantial reductions in hallucination metrics, such as an 18% improvement over previous training-free approaches on CHAIR benchmarks, while also enhancing general perception capabilities across various LVLM architectures.
Problem: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) frequently generate object hallucinations, producing plausible but factually inaccurate descriptions of objects, which compromises their reliability and safety in critical applications.
Current hallucination mitigation strategies primarily focus on the Large Language Model (LLM) component of LVLMs or require computationally expensive retraining/fine-tuning.
The direct contributions of the visual encoder—the component responsible for processing image information—to the problem of object hallucination in LVLMs remained largely unaddressed.
Method: SHIELD proposes a training-free framework that intervenes on visual tokens extracted by the encoder and adjusts the decoding process to suppress hallucinations.
It implements Token Re-weighting to mitigate statistical bias by redistributing attention across object-relevant visual tokens, leveraging a similarity matrix derived from a naive image caption.

The framework incorporates Token Subtraction to reduce inherent bias by removing noise-derived erroneous features, and utilizes Contrastive Decoding with adversarial attacks and an adaptive plausibility constraint to address visual encoder vulnerability and suppress hallucination-prone tokens.
Results: SHIELD significantly outperformed existing training-free methods, achieving an 18% improvement over the second-best method (OPERA) in reducing sentence-level hallucinations on CHAIR benchmarks for LLaVA-1.5.

Consistent and substantial reductions in object, attribute, and relational hallucinations were observed across multiple LVLM architectures (LLaVA-1.5, InstructBLIP, Qwen-VL) and various benchmarks, including GPT4o-aided LLaVA-Bench and POPE.

The framework also improved general perception capabilities, showing gains in subtasks like OCR and Posters on the MME benchmark, indicating that addressing visual encoder issues enhances overall visual understanding beyond just hallucination suppression.
Takeaways: Object hallucinations in LVLMs are directly linked to specific issues within their visual encoders: statistical bias (overemphasis on frequent patterns), inherent bias (generating dominant objects regardless of input), and vulnerability (sensitivity to minor input perturbations).
Targeting these visual encoder-specific biases and vulnerabilities at the feature processing level can effectively reduce hallucinations without requiring modifications to the core model parameters.

Interventions like re-weighting visual tokens based on textual context and subtracting bias-induced features, combined with contrastive decoding, improve factual consistency and overall visual understanding in LVLMs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.16416.Title: SSL4RL: Revisiting Self-supervised Learning as Intrinsic Reward for Visual-Language Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.16416.Summary: The SSL4RL framework reinterprets self-supervised learning tasks as intrinsic, verifiable reward signals for reinforcement learning, providing a scalable method for post-training vision-language models. This approach consistently improves visual grounding and reasoning capabilities across diverse multimodal benchmarks and also generalizes effectively to graph learning.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) often over-rely on linguistic priors, underutilizing visual evidence and resorting to 'textual shortcuts' in reasoning.

Applying Reinforcement Learning (RL) to VLMs is limited by the scarcity of scalable, reliable, and verifiable reward mechanisms, with human preferences or explicit verifiers being costly or unavailable.

The traditional use of Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) is primarily for pre-training, leaving its potential as a source of intrinsic, verifiable targets for fine-tuning behavioral alignment largely unexplored.
Method: Reformulates established SSL tasks (e.g., Rotation, Jigsaw, Contrastive, Patch Position) to provide dense, automatic, and intrinsically verifiable reward signals for RL-based post-training.
Utilizes Grouped Reinforcement Policy Optimization (GRPO) to fine-tune multimodal models, maximizing the SSL-derived intrinsic rewards.
Trains models to generate natural language reasoning paths that accurately predict the ground truth labels of the self-supervised tasks, thereby reinforcing visual grounding and reasoning.
Results: SSL4RL models achieve substantial performance gains on vision-language reasoning benchmarks, with average improvements of 7.39% on MMBench and 8.94% on SEED-Bench for the Qwen2.5-VL-3B model.
The framework demonstrates enhanced robustness against various image perturbations and consistently improves performance on open-ended image captioning tasks.
SSL4RL successfully generalizes to graph-structured data, showing improvements in node classification and link prediction tasks, confirming its domain-agnostic applicability.
Takeaways: Self-supervised learning tasks can effectively serve as intrinsic, verifiable reward signals for reinforcement learning, addressing the reward scarcity bottleneck in VLM alignment.
The effectiveness of SSL tasks as RL rewards adheres to a 'Goldilocks principle,' where task difficulty must be appropriately matched to model capacity for optimal performance.
SSL4RL fosters stronger visual grounding by compelling models to derive answers directly from image content, leading to reduced reliance on linguistic priors and more robust reasoning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.16333.Title: RL makes MLLMs see better than SFT
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.16333.Summary: Research from KAIST and NAVER AI Lab demonstrates that Reinforcement Learning (RL) with Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) fundamentally enhances vision encoders within Multimodal Language Models (MLLMs) more effectively than Supervised Finetuning (SFT). This approach yields stronger visual representations and improves MLLM performance on vision-centric tasks, leading to the development of PIVOT, an efficient method for evolving existing vision models.
Problem: A prevailing assumption that MLLM performance primarily inherits from the Large Language Model (LLM) backbone, leading to an oversight of the vision encoder's independent role.
A lack of systematic understanding of how different MLLM post-training strategies (SFT vs. RL) specifically impact the underlying visual representations of the vision encoder.
The absence of an efficient framework to specifically optimize existing vision encoders for optimal performance within MLLMs, beyond traditional vision pre-training methods.
Method: Conducted a systematic comparison of Supervised Finetuning (SFT) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) as post-training strategies on MLLMs across varying vision encoder and LLM scales.
Analyzed the impact of these strategies on vision encoder capabilities through vision-only benchmarks (ImageNet, semantic segmentation) and gradient visualizations (Grad-CAM).
Developed PIVOT (Preference-Instructed Vision OpTimization), an RL-driven auxiliary training process to efficiently enhance existing vision encoders for MLLM applications.
Results: DPO consistently outperformed SFT on MLLM performance, particularly on vision-centric tasks like OCR & Chart VQA (+4.2%p) and Vision-Centric VQA (+2.4%p), while showing marginal gains on weakly vision-related tasks.

DPO-trained vision encoders demonstrated superior performance on vision-only benchmarks, including a +1.83%p improvement in ImageNet Top-1 accuracy and +1.08%p increase in patch-level recall for semantic segmentation, over SFT-trained encoders.

PIVOT-enhanced vision encoders achieved significant performance boosts within MLLMs, with a PIVOT-enhanced SigLIP1-So/14 surpassing a more recent SigLIP2-So/16 (53.2%p vs. 52.4%p average VQA score) at less than 1% of standard vision pre-training computational cost.
Takeaways: MLLM post-training, particularly with DPO, actively reshapes and significantly enhances the intrinsic visual representations within the vision encoder, rather than merely aligning an LLM with a frozen vision component.

DPO's contrastive nature generates more precise, fine-grained gradient signals that focus on semantically relevant regions, leading to improved object localization and stronger vision-language alignment compared to SFT.
Larger LLM backbones provide more informative optimization signals during MLLM training, resulting in vision encoders that achieve higher performance on vision-only tasks after post-training.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.15242.Title: Dual-Weighted Reinforcement Learning for Generative Preference Modeling
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.15242.Summary: Dual-Weighted Reinforcement Learning (DWRL) enables Generative Preference Models (GPMs) to integrate Chain-of-Thought reasoning into human preference tasks by preserving Bradley-Terry inductive bias. This approach, evaluated on Qwen2.5 and Llama3 models, consistently surpassed existing GPMs and standard preference models with up to a 9.1% improvement in accuracy on math reasoning benchmarks.
Problem: Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) for Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning is limited to tasks with objective, verifiable answers, struggling with subjective human preferences.
Existing Generative Preference Models (GPMs) often underperformed simpler scalar preference models by failing to incorporate the crucial inductive bias of preference data when integrating CoT.
Prior GPMs required costly supervised thought data for training and faced fragility due to strict output formatting for preference scores, limiting practical applicability.
Method: Introduced a dialog-based GPM architecture that separates latent thought generation from final preference scoring, deriving scores from designated token logits to avoid formatting fragility.

Developed Dual-Weighted Reinforcement Learning (DWRL), an RL algorithm that approximates the Bradley-Terry loss gradient using two complementary weighting terms: an instance-wise misalignment weight and self-normalized conditional preference scores.
Employed an alternating optimization strategy to update preference scoring and thought generation components, ensuring stable training by emphasizing misaligned preference pairs.
Results: DWRL consistently outperformed all baselines across Helpfulness & Harmlessness, Instruction Following, and Math Reasoning tasks, achieving accuracy gains of up to 4.8%, 2.7%, and 9.1% respectively.
Prior GRPO-based GPMs performed significantly worse than simple Bradley-Terry models, achieving near-random accuracy (50-53%) on Math Reasoning compared to BT's 76-84%.
Ablation studies confirmed the critical role of the instance-wise misalignment weight; its removal led to substantial performance drops (e.g., from 70.5% to 59.1% on Helpfulness & Harmlessness).
Takeaways: Explicitly incorporating the Bradley-Terry inductive bias through an instance-wise misalignment weight is critical for effectively training GPMs, as naive RL applications discard this bias.
GPMs can learn to generate genuinely informative thoughts that enhance preference prediction accuracy, rather than merely leveraging pre-existing LLM reasoning capabilities.
Pointwise preference modeling demonstrates greater robustness for complex, reasoning-intensive tasks compared to pairwise GPMs, which can be less generalizable.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.14901.Title: Reasoning with Sampling: Your Base Model is Smarter Than You Think
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.14901.Summary: Researchers at Harvard University developed power sampling, a training-free method leveraging the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm to sample from a sharpened distribution of a base large language model. This technique unlocks latent reasoning capabilities, achieving single-shot performance comparable to or exceeding reinforcement learning post-training methods across various tasks, while also preserving generation diversity.
Problem: A lack of clarity on whether reinforcement learning (RL) fundamentally teaches new reasoning skills to LLMs or merely sharpens existing, latent capabilities.
High computational costs, reliance on curated datasets, and the need for external verifiers inherent in current RL-based LLM post-training methods.
RL-posttrained models often suffer from a 'collapse in diversity,' sacrificing multi-shot reasoning performance (pass@k) for single-shot gains.
Method:
Samples from a 'power distribution'
p
α
(where
α≥1) of the base LLM, which mathematically reweights the original distribution to favor higher-likelihood sequences.
Employs the Metropolis-Hastings (MH) algorithm, a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) technique, to enable approximate sampling from the unnormalized power distribution.
Introduces an iterative, block-wise autoregressive MCMC approach to progressively refine sequence segments, managing complexity and improving mixing times for long-sequence generation.
Results: Achieved single-shot reasoning performance comparable to or surpassing state-of-the-art RL-posttraining methods (like GRPO) on in-domain (e.g., MATH500) and out-of-domain (e.g., HumanEval, GPQA) tasks, with Phi-3.5-mini-instruct showing a +51.9% accuracy gain over its base model on HumanEval.
Demonstrated performance gains are training-free, dataset-free, and verifier-free, offering a significantly more efficient and broadly applicable approach than RL-based methods.
Maintained and improved multi-shot generation diversity (pass@k accuracy) compared to both base models and GRPO, effectively avoiding the 'collapse in diversity' common in RL-posttraining approaches.
Takeaways:
Sampling from the power distribution
p
α
is fundamentally distinct from traditional low-temperature sampling, as it focuses on upweighting tokens with 'few but high likelihood future paths' essential for reasoning.

Base large language models possess greater latent reasoning capabilities than conventionally assumed, which can be effectively elicited purely through sophisticated inference-time sampling without additional training.

The success of power sampling reinforces the 'distribution sharpening' hypothesis, suggesting that much of the improvement from RL-posttraining comes from refining the model's likelihood of selecting existing high-quality solutions.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.13800.Title: Reasoning in Space via Grounding in the World
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.13800.Summary: The GS-Reasoner framework enables 3D Large Language Models to intrinsically perform 3D visual grounding by predicting bounding boxes autoregressively as an intermediate step for spatial reasoning, without requiring external modules. This approach, supported by a novel semantic-geometric hybrid representation and the Grounded Chain-of-Thought dataset, achieves state-of-the-art performance in 3D dense captioning and complex spatial reasoning tasks, with competitive results in 3D visual grounding.
Problem: Existing 3D LLMs lack a unified representation that effectively captures both semantic and geometric information, leading to compromises in fidelity or weak integration of 3D cues.

Current 3D LLMs heavily rely on external pre-trained modules (e.g., 3D detectors) for visual grounding, preventing intrinsic 3D scene understanding and seamless integration with higher-level reasoning.

A scarcity of high-quality datasets exists that explicitly link 3D visual grounding with spatial reasoning through step-by-step annotations, hindering the training of models for complex, interpretable reasoning.
Method: Developed the Grounded-Spatial Reasoner (GS-Reasoner), an end-to-end framework enabling autoregressive 3D visual grounding as an intermediate Chain-of-Thought step within the LLM's output for spatial reasoning.

Introduced a novel semantic-geometric hybrid 3D scene representation, utilizing Dual-Path Pooling to unify semantic, geometric, and positional features from multi-view images and point clouds, resolving feature misalignment.

Created the Grounded Chain-of-Thought (GCoT) dataset, which provides step-by-step reasoning paths with explicit 3D bounding box annotations, teaching the model to autonomously determine when and how to perform grounding during reasoning.
Results: GS-Reasoner is the first 3D LLM to achieve autoregressive 3D visual grounding without external modules, demonstrating performance comparable to state-of-the-art proposal-based methods and setting a new SOTA F1@25 on Multi3DRef.

The framework achieved state-of-the-art performance on various spatial reasoning tasks within VSI-Bench, particularly for Relative Direction and Absolute Distance, and established a new SOTA for 3D dense captioning on Scan2Cap.
GS-Reasoner exhibited strong zero-shot generalization capabilities, performing comparably to SOTA expert models on unseen 3D scenes from ARKitScenes and ScanNet++ validation splits.
Takeaways: Intrinsic, autoregressive 3D visual grounding by an LLM is achievable and leads to a more unified and robust understanding of 3D scenes without the need for external detection modules.

A hybrid 3D scene representation, combining semantic and geometric features with a dual-path pooling mechanism, effectively resolves misalignment issues and is crucial for accurate 3D localization and comprehensive scene understanding.

Explicitly integrating 3D visual grounding as an intermediate step within a Chain-of-Thought framework, supported by a tailored dataset like GCoT, significantly enhances the interpretability and accuracy of complex spatial reasoning tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.12798.Title: Detect Anything via Next Point Prediction
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.12798.Summary: Researchers at the International Digital Economy Academy (IDEA) introduced Rex-Omni, a 3-billion-parameter Multimodal Large Language Model capable of unifying various visual perception tasks. The model achieves state-of-the-art or highly competitive performance across 11 diverse benchmarks by integrating robust language understanding with precise object localization.
Problem: Traditional regression-based object detectors, despite their localization precision, possess limited language understanding for complex or nuanced textual descriptions.

Existing MLLM-based detectors often suffer from low recall rates, coordinate misalignment, and duplicate predictions due to geometric discretization of continuous coordinates and limitations of supervised fine-tuning (SFT).
A need existed for a single, versatile MLLM to handle a broad range of visual perception tasks with both deep language comprehension and accurate spatial localization.
Method: Rex-Omni, a 3B-parameter MLLM, unifies diverse visual perception tasks under a direct coordinate prediction framework using a quantized relative coordinate representation with special tokens.

A two-stage training paradigm is employed, combining initial Supervised Fine-tuning (SFT) with GRPO (Group-based Reinforcement Learning with Policy Optimization) for precision and behavioral correctness.

Custom-designed data engines (Grounding, Referring, Pointing, OCR) generate 13.1 million high-quality samples, augmenting 8.9 million public datasets, to ensure extensive and fine-grained spatial and language supervision.
Results: Rex-Omni achieves superior or competitive F1-scores across 11 diverse visual perception tasks, often outperforming other MLLMs and traditional open-set detectors in zero-shot settings.

The GRPO post-training stage dramatically mitigates common MLLM failures, reducing duplicate predictions (e.g., SFT removal gain 1.23-15.3% vs. GRPO 0.06-0.08%) and large-box predictions (20.5% for SFT vs. 3.5% for GRPO).

The model demonstrates unique generalization capabilities in complex tasks like layout grounding, OCR, and spatial pointing, outperforming previous specialized models and MLLMs in interpreting and grounding nuanced spatial relationships.
Takeaways: Quantizing relative coordinates and representing them with dedicated special tokens significantly reduces the learning complexity and improves token efficiency for MLLM-based object detection.

GRPO-based reinforcement post-training is effective in correcting SFT-induced behavioral deficiencies, such as duplicate and overly large predictions, by providing geometry-aware rewards and encouraging policy exploration.

High-quality, large-scale synthetic data generated by specialized engines is crucial for training MLLMs to achieve fine-grained spatial reasoning and robust language grounding across various perception tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.12603.Title: Reasoning in the Dark: Interleaved Vision-Text Reasoning in Latent Space
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.12603.Summary: Researchers developed Interleaved Vision-Text Latent Reasoning (IVT-LR), a framework that performs multimodal reasoning entirely within an MLLM's latent space, without explicit intermediate steps. This approach achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on M3CoT and ScienceQA benchmarks while reducing inference latency by 3-8 times and requiring 9 times fewer autoregressive steps compared to explicit reasoning methods.
Problem: Existing multimodal reasoning methods often require labor-intensive annotations for explicit intermediate reasoning steps.
Generating explicit reasoning steps leads to significant inference latency, hindering real-time applications.
Prior latent reasoning efforts for MLLMs struggled to unify interleaved vision-text interaction truly within the latent space.
Method: The IVT-LR framework introduces multimodal latent reasoning, where both 'latent text' (hidden states) and 'latent vision' (dynamically selected image embeddings) interact implicitly.
An attention-based mechanism dynamically selects the most relevant visual features at each reasoning step, fusing them with latent textual information.
A progressive multi-stage training strategy incrementally replaces explicit reasoning steps with latent ones, using NLL loss supervision only on remaining explicit outputs and the final answer.
Results: IVT-LR achieved state-of-the-art accuracy, outperforming the strongest baseline (Chain-of-Focus) by 7.5% on M3CoT and 3.4% on ScienceQA using a Qwen2-VL backbone.
The method demonstrated a ~9x reduction in autoregressive steps and was 3 to 8 times faster in inference latency (e.g., 0.65-0.67s for IVT-LR vs. 2.09s-5.31s for baselines).

Ablation studies confirmed that both latent text and latent vision components are crucial, with their removal causing substantial accuracy drops (e.g., 19.63% without latent text, 25.19% without latent vision on M3CoT).
Takeaways: Truly unified, interleaved vision-text reasoning can be effectively performed implicitly within an MLLM's latent space, avoiding explicit token generation.
Latent reasoning not only drastically improves inference efficiency but can also lead to higher accuracy compared to methods relying on explicit rationales.
Dynamic attention analysis within the latent process reveals a sophisticated, adaptive shift from visual focus to textual refinement, indicating robust internal problem-solving.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.12276.Title: Spatial Forcing: Implicit Spatial Representation Alignment for Vision-language-action Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.12276.Summary: A new method, Spatial Forcing (SF), implicitly develops 3D perception in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for robotic manipulation by aligning their internal visual representations with geometric knowledge from a pretrained 3D foundation model. This approach achieves state-of-the-art performance in robotic manipulation benchmarks, enhancing training efficiency by 3.8 times and data efficiency by 5.9 times compared to baselines.
Problem: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, primarily pretrained on 2D image data, lack the precise 3D spatial awareness essential for robust physical interaction in the real world.

Existing methods for integrating 3D information (e.g., explicit 3D sensor inputs, depth map estimation) face practical issues such as sensor noise, hardware heterogeneity, data scarcity, and inherent performance limitations.
Empirical analysis reveals that VLA visual embeddings, without specific guidance, do not encode meaningful spatial structures required for accurate action generation.
Method: Spatial Forcing (SF) implicitly instills spatial comprehension in VLA models by supervising their intermediate visual embeddings with geometric representations.
The method aligns the VLA's visual embeddings with features from a pretrained 3D foundation model (VGGT), which provides rich, normalized spatial information, using a cosine similarity loss.
Alignment is applied to specific causal attention layers of the VLA's backbone, augmented with positional embeddings, and introduces no additional computational overhead during inference.
Results: Spatial Forcing achieved an average success rate of 98.5% on the LIBERO benchmark, outperforming both 2D-based and explicit 3D-based VLA methods.
SF demonstrated significant training efficiency, converging to the same success rates 3.8 times faster, and improved data efficiency by being 5.9 times more efficient than baselines.
Real-world experiments across single-arm and dual-arm tasks showed consistently higher success rates, affirming SF's robustness and strong data utilization even with limited training data.
Takeaways: Intermediate visual tokens within VLA models can be effectively guided to encode richer spatial information, thereby enhancing action precision without relying on explicit 3D inputs.
Aligning VLA visual representations with a powerful 3D foundation model (VGGT) offers a robust and universal pathway to impart 3D spatial understanding.

The optimal integration point for spatial supervision is not the deepest or shallowest layer but rather an intermediate causal attention layer (e.g., 24th layer) to balance feature richness and spatial integration.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.12225.Title: HoneyBee: Data Recipes for Vision-Language Reasoners
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.12225.Summary: Researchers at FAIR at Meta and UCLA conducted a systematic investigation into the construction of high-quality training datasets for Vision-Language Models (VLMs), identifying key data curation strategies. Their empirically-derived HoneyBee dataset enables smaller VLMs to achieve state-of-the-art reasoning performance, often outperforming larger existing models, and introduces an efficient inference method reducing decoding cost by 73%.
Problem: The underlying principles for constructing performant multimodal Chain-of-Thought (CoT) datasets for Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are poorly understood.
Training datasets and curation methodologies for state-of-the-art VLMs are often proprietary, creating a "black box" scenario that hinders scientific understanding and reproducibility.

Prior work on VLM reasoning datasets often conflates the impact of different factors (e.g., context sources, teacher models, filtering techniques), making it difficult to isolate true drivers of performance improvements.
Method: A systematic data curation pipeline was developed, encompassing controlled context sourcing, targeted data interventions (perception and problem-solving), and scaling along diverse data axes.

A fixed, performant Llama4-Scout generator model was used to create all Chain-of-Thought (CoT) annotations, ensuring consistency for knowledge distillation to student Perception Language Models (PLMs).

The HoneyBee dataset (2.5M instances) was constructed based on empirical insights, integrating high-quality ViRL data, scaled questions and CoTs, "caption and solve" auxiliary signals, and re-annotated text-only reasoning data.
Results: VLMs trained with the HoneyBee dataset achieved best-in-class performance across diverse benchmarks, with a 1B-parameter PLM-HoneyBee model showing a 28 percentage point relative improvement over InternVL-3-1B-Instruct.

Augmenting multimodal data with text-only reasoning data resulted in a 7.5 percentage point average accuracy gain on VL reasoning tasks and enhanced generalization to text-only benchmarks like MATH500.
A novel "shared caption" decoding strategy reduced VLM test-time scaling decoding cost by 73% without any loss in accuracy, improving inference efficiency.
Takeaways: The choice of the initial (image, question) context source critically impacts VLM performance, with naive mixing of diverse sources not outperforming the single best source.

Integrating auxiliary visual signals via image captions ("Caption and Solve") and augmenting with high-quality text-only reasoning data yielded significant improvements in VLM performance and generalization.
Scaling data along unique images, unique questions per image, and unique CoTs per (image, question) pair consistently improves the reasoning capabilities of VLMs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.11549.Title: ODI-Bench: Can MLLMs Understand Immersive Omnidirectional Environments?
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.11549.Summary: Researchers from Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Shanghai AI Laboratory introduce ODI-BENCH, a rigorous benchmark for evaluating multi-modal large language models' understanding of 360-degree omnidirectional images. They also present Omni-CoT, a training-free framework that substantially enhances MLLMs' capabilities, particularly in spatial reasoning, within these immersive environments.
Problem: Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) demonstrate advanced capabilities in 2D image understanding but their performance in comprehending immersive 360-degree omnidirectional environments remains largely unassessed.

Existing benchmarks for omnidirectional images (ODIs) suffer from low resolution, limited scene diversity, restricted question domains, and insufficient evaluation of complex spatial reasoning or varied viewpoints.
Current MLLMs generally fail to effectively process the unique challenges of ODIs, such as inherent distortions from equirectangular projection and the need for higher-level 3D spatial reasoning.
Method: The team developed ODI-BENCH, a new benchmark featuring 2,000 high-resolution, real-world omnidirectional images with over 4,000 human-annotated question-answer pairs across 10 fine-grained general and spatial understanding tasks.

ODI-BENCH incorporates dual evaluation settings (close-ended and open-ended) and questions are designed to mimic immersive first-person perspectives, using a combination of automated pipelines with human refinement and expert manual annotation.

A training-free framework called Omni-CoT is introduced, which employs viewpoint-guided textual captions, relevant cropped visual cues with refinement, and a final response refinement step to enhance MLLM comprehension of ODIs.
Results: State-of-the-art MLLMs exhibit unsatisfactory performance on ODI-BENCH, with the top proprietary model achieving only 62.62% accuracy in close-ended evaluation, reflecting a significant struggle with omnidirectional environments.

MLLMs demonstrated particularly poor performance on spatial-level understanding tasks, often scoring only marginally above or below the "Blind GPT-4o" baseline for tasks like allocentric view orientation and scene simulation.

The Omni-CoT framework consistently enhanced MLLM performance across various models, with viewpoint guiding proving to be a critical component for substantial gains, especially in spatial-related tasks.
Takeaways: MLLMs primarily perceive omnidirectional images as warped 2D visual inputs rather than integrated 360-degree immersive environments, leading to poor spatial reasoning.
Spatial-level understanding tasks (e.g., view orientation, scene simulation) present a significantly greater challenge for MLLMs compared to general-level tasks (e.g., object attributes).
Evaluation in both close-ended and open-ended formats is crucial, as multiple-choice options can sometimes provide hints or introduce "option anchoring bias," affecting comprehensive assessment.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.11106.Title: Compositional Zero-Shot Learning: A Survey
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.11106.Summary: This survey paper presents the first comprehensive taxonomy for Compositional Zero-Shot Learning (CZSL) methods, categorizing them based on their disentanglement strategies for attributes and objects. It consolidates existing knowledge, reviews benchmarks, and identifies key performance trends, open challenges, and future research directions in the field.
Problem: Machine learning models struggle to recognize novel combinations of known attributes and objects (e.g., 'striped elephant') without specific training data, due to the combinatorial explosion of possibilities.
The rapidly growing and diverse field of Compositional Zero-Shot Learning (CZSL) lacked a systematic and comprehensive overview or unified analytical framework.
Understanding how different CZSL methods balance learning distinct primitive representations versus modeling their contextual interactions was fragmented across various publications.
Method: Developed the first comprehensive taxonomy for CZSL methods, classifying them into categories like no explicit disentanglement, textual, visual, and cross-modal disentanglement.
Conducted a systematic review of state-of-the-art CZSL approaches, benchmark datasets (e.g., MIT-States, UT-Zappos), and standard evaluation protocols.
Performed an empirical comparative analysis of method performance across closed-world and open-world CZSL settings, utilizing different architectural backbones like ResNet, ViT, and CLIP.
Results: Methods leveraging CLIP-based encoders consistently achieve superior performance across all CZSL categories and evaluation settings, highlighting the impact of large-scale vision-language pretraining.

Visual disentanglement methods, especially those with augmentation or prototype-centric designs, generally demonstrate the strongest performance, particularly in the more challenging open-world setting.
While cross-modal disentanglement approaches show strong potential in controlled closed-world scenarios, they often trail leading visual disentanglement methods in the open-world setting.
Takeaways: Disentanglement, the explicit separation and representation of constituent primitives (attributes and objects), serves as a fundamental organizing principle for understanding CZSL methods.
The visual appearance and semantics of primitives are highly contextual, requiring robust models to effectively disentangle and combine them.
There is a clear need for methods that can handle unfeasible attribute-object combinations and generalize to truly unseen primitives in real-world scenarios.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.10606.Title: ViSurf: Visual Supervised-and-Reinforcement Fine-Tuning for Large Vision-and-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.10606.Summary: ViSurf introduces a unified, single-stage post-training framework that integrates supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) for large vision-and-language models (LVLMs). The method consistently outperforms existing paradigms across diverse visual perception and reasoning tasks, achieving an average relative gain of 38.6% and mitigating catastrophic forgetting.
Problem: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) often leads to sub-optimal performance and catastrophic forgetting in Large Vision-and-Language Models (LVLMs).
Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) struggles with tasks requiring knowledge beyond the model's pre-existing base, particularly when self-generated rollouts are unreliable.
Sequential SFT RLVR pipelines are computationally expensive, complex, and still prone to catastrophic forgetting during the initial SFT phase.
Method: ViSurf proposes a unified, single-stage post-training paradigm that integrates SFT and RLVR objectives, leveraging a theoretical analysis of their gradient similarity.
The method constructs an augmented rollout set that includes both model-generated rollouts and ground-truth labels, with rewards computed for both to influence advantage calculations.

Three novel reward control strategies are introduced: aligning ground-truth labels with model preference, eliminating thinking reward for ground-truth, and adaptively smoothing ground-truth rewards to balance external supervision with internal reinforcement.
Results: ViSurf achieved superior performance across diverse visual-language tasks, demonstrating an average relative gain of 38.6% over the baseline and outperforming SFT, RLVR, and sequential SFT RLVR methods.
The framework effectively mitigated catastrophic forgetting, maintaining or improving performance on VQA tasks while fine-tuning for new perception tasks, unlike SFT and sequential methods.

Ablation studies confirmed the critical contribution of each reward control strategy to improved performance, training stability, and entropy behavior, additionally showing reduced dependence on meticulous prompt design.
Takeaways: The gradients of SFT and RLVR objectives share a similar structural form, which enables their effective integration into a single, unified objective function.

Adaptive reward control strategies, particularly smoothing the ground-truth reward, allow ViSurf to dynamically adjust the influence of external supervision based on the model's internal generative capabilities.

Injecting ground-truth labels directly into the RL framework within a single training loop provides robust guidance, mitigating catastrophic forgetting and enhancing performance on out-of-distribution tasks more effectively than multi-stage approaches.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.10487.Title: Towards Self-Refinement of Vision-Language Models with Triangular Consistency
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.10487.Summary: This research introduces a self-refinement framework for Vision-Language Models (VLMs) that utilizes a "Triangular Consistency" principle to autonomously generate, filter, and learn high-quality supervision from unlabeled images. The approach achieved consistent performance improvements, averaging 1.22% on VQA tasks and 2.1% on MMBench, across various VLM architectures and benchmarks without external supervision.
Problem: Acquiring high-quality supervised visual instruction data (image-question-answer triplets) is costly, time-consuming, and labor-intensive.
Existing synthetic data generation methods often depend on expensive proprietary "teacher" VLMs or inefficient environmental feedback.
The potential for VLMs to autonomously learn and refine themselves from readily available unlabeled images remains largely unexplored.
Method: A three-stage iterative self-refinement framework is proposed: enhancing instruction generation, applying Triangular Consistency filtering, and then instruction tuning.
The "Triangular Consistency" principle serves as an internal mechanism to validate the quality of self-generated IQA triplets by checking consistency between original and reconstructed elements.
The VLM is fine-tuned with a multi-task objective (I→QA, IQ→A, IA→Q) to improve its capability to generate diverse and precise IQA pairs from unlabeled images.
Results: SRF-LLaVA-1.5 consistently improved performance, achieving an average 1.22% gain on VQA tasks and 2.1% on MMBench, 1.7% on MM-VET, and 3.5% on LLaVA-Wild benchmarks.

Triangular Consistency filtering was critical, with ablated studies showing that filtered data led to improvements while unfiltered data (or low-quality data) provided only marginal gains or degradation.

The framework generalized across different VLM architectures (MobileVLM-1.7B, QWen2.5-VL 3B), demonstrating consistent improvements and producing significantly higher quality (85.3% GPT-4o accuracy) and more diverse self-generated QA pairs.
Takeaways: Vision-Language Models possess an inherent capability for self-refinement, enabling them to improve autonomously without relying on external supervision or superior teacher models.

The Triangular Consistency principle effectively identifies and filters high-quality synthetic data, demonstrating that model-intrinsic signals can reliably guide self-improvement in multimodal contexts.

Causal analysis provides a theoretical justification for VLM self-refinement, suggesting that incorporating additional unlabeled images helps refine the model's empirical estimate of conditional distributions for better inference.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.09733.Title: VisRAG 2.0: Evidence-Guided Multi-Image Reasoning in Visual Retrieval-Augmented Generation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.09733.Summary: The EVisRAG framework enhances visual retrieval-augmented generation by guiding Vision-Language Models through explicit observe, record, reason, and answer phases for multi-image reasoning. It achieves substantial performance gains, with an average +19% accuracy and +27% F1 score over its 7B parameter backbone, across five visual question answering benchmarks.
Problem: Existing Visual RAG systems struggle to effectively integrate and reason over evidence distributed across multiple retrieved images.
Vision-Language Models (VLMs) often exhibit weak grounding, leading to hallucinations and erroneous conclusions despite access to relevant visual information.
Current VLM training strategies suffer from intertwined perception and reasoning reward signals, complicating credit assignment and training stability in multi-step visual tasks.
Method: EVisRAG introduces an evidence-guided reasoning paradigm that explicitly sequences visual processing into 'observe,' 'record evidence' from each image, 'reason,' and 'answer' steps.

The framework employs a novel Reward-Scoped Group Relative Policy Optimization (RS-GRPO) algorithm, which assigns fine-grained, distinct rewards (format, perception, derivation) to specific token spans within the generated output.
A two-stage training strategy involves initial supervised fine-tuning followed by RS-GRPO to jointly optimize both visual perception and logical reasoning capabilities.
Results: EVisRAG achieves an average of +19% accuracy and +27% F1 score improvement over its Qwen2.5-VL-7B backbone across five VQA benchmarks, outperforming larger 32B models and other state-of-the-art methods.

Ablation studies confirm that the evidence-guided reasoning paradigm, dedicated perception reward, and Reward-Scoped Group Relative Policy Optimization (RS-GRPO) are critical components for the framework's superior performance.

The framework demonstrates improved visual attention, focusing more precisely on relevant image regions, and exhibits superior robustness to varying evidence densities and a controlled reduction in hallucinations.
Takeaways: An explicit, structured approach to perceiving and recording evidence from each image before reasoning significantly improves a VLM's ability to synthesize information from multiple visual sources.

Assigning distinct reward signals to specific components of the generated output (reward scoping) is crucial for sharpening credit assignment, stabilizing reinforcement learning, and effectively training complex, multi-stage visual reasoning tasks.
Enhanced fine-grained visual attention, guided by dedicated perception rewards, is fundamental for robust multi-image reasoning and effectively mitigating hallucination in VLMs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.09606.Title: SpaceVista: All-Scale Visual Spatial Reasoning from mm to km
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.09606.Summary: SpaceVista introduces a comprehensive solution for advancing spatial reasoning capabilities in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) across physical scales ranging from millimeters to kilometers. This work provides a new dataset, SpaceVista-1M, and a model, SpaceVista-7B, demonstrating superior performance on the accompanying SpaceVista-Bench evaluation benchmark, outperforming existing proprietary and open-source models by over 3%.
Problem: Existing spatial reasoning research, particularly with MLLMs, is largely confined to constrained environments and limited physical scales, hindering generalization to diverse real-world applications.
Current spatial reasoning datasets are costly, rely on laborious manual annotations, and lack diversity across broad scales and 'in-the-wild' scenes.

MLLMs lack effective architectures and training paradigms to handle vast differences in object sizes, scene layouts, and semantic complexities across scales, leading to 'knowledge conflict' in reasoning.
Method: An automated, specialist-driven pipeline curates SpaceVista-1M, a dataset of 1 million spatial Question-Answer pairs from 38,000 video scenes, spanning five distinct scales and 19 task types.

SpaceVista-7B, an MLLM, integrates dense visual inputs (DINOv3), employs LoRA-like 'scale experts' with a dynamic router to mitigate cross-scale knowledge conflicts, and utilizes a progressive reward system for Reinforcement Learning training.
SpaceVista-Bench, a high-fidelity, hand-crafted evaluation benchmark, ensures accurate, physically grounded assessment across all scales using real-world measurements and human annotation.
Results: SpaceVista-7B achieves over 3% higher overall performance on the new SpaceVista-Bench compared to state-of-the-art proprietary and open-source models, demonstrating robust all-scale reasoning capabilities.

The model shows significantly higher scores in challenging scenarios like Tiny Tabletop, Tabletop, and Outdoor scenes within SpaceVista-Bench, delivering around 6% improvement over other open-source models.

Ablation studies confirm the critical role of scale experts, progressive rewards, and dense visual inputs in improving performance and mitigating cross-scale knowledge conflicts, with performance generally improving with more experts.
Takeaways: Integrating dense geometric features from self-supervised vision models (e.g., DINOv3) into MLLMs significantly enhances spatial perception beyond purely semantic understanding.

Scale-aware expert architectures, such as LoRA-like experts with a dynamic router, effectively mitigate 'knowledge conflicts' and enable MLLMs to specialize knowledge for reasoning across vastly different physical scales.
A progressive reward mechanism using semantic, scale, and answer anchors during reinforcement learning guides the model's Chain-of-Thought, promoting human-like, scale-centric spatial reasoning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.09586.Title: Vision Language Models: A Survey of 26K Papers
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.09586.Summary: A quantitative analysis of 26,104 papers from top-tier AI conferences (CVPR, ICLR, NeurIPS 2023-2025) reveals a substantial shift towards multimodal Vision-Language Models, which increased from 16% to 40% of papers, alongside a steady expansion of diffusion models and a focus on instruction-following capabilities.
Problem: The overwhelming volume of research publications in rapidly evolving AI fields makes it challenging to quantitatively identify genuine trends and allocate resources effectively.
Reliance on anecdotal evidence and qualitative observations for understanding research shifts lacks the rigor and reproducibility needed for strategic decision-making.
A transparent, data-driven approach is needed to map the trajectory of computer vision and machine learning research, rather than subjective interpretations.
Method: A lexicon-driven quantitative survey analyzes titles and abstracts of 26,104 papers from CVPR, ICLR, and NeurIPS (2023-2025), plus 8,424 from 2022 for longitudinal trends.
The methodology involves text processing, categorizing papers using 35 regular-expression-based topic labels, and calculating prevalence and TF-IDF mass for trend analysis.
Fine-grained mining is applied to Vision-Language Models to detail specific shifts in architectures, tasks, training paradigms, loss functions, dataset usage, and co-mentioned modalities.
Results: Vision-Language Model (VLM) papers showed a sharp rise, increasing from 16% of publications in 2023 to 40% in 2025 across the analyzed conferences.
Diffusion models continued their steady expansion, accounting for 8% of papers in 2023 and growing to 19.2% in 2025, with research consolidating around controllability, distillation, and speed.

Instruction tuning saw a substantial increase of 3.9 percentage points, becoming a primary paradigm for developing conversational VLMs, while the use of purely contrastive objectives in new VLM works markedly declined.
Takeaways: Multimodal Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are becoming a central organizing paradigm, increasingly reframing classic perception tasks as instruction-following and multi-step reasoning problems.
Research is consolidating around large-scale pre-trained models, with parameter-efficient adaptation methods like prompt/prefix tuning and LoRA dominating VLM development.

Traditional learning paradigms (e.g., self-supervised learning, meta-learning) are increasingly integrated as modules within larger systems rather than being standalone contributions, while engineering concerns like efficiency and robustness gain prominence.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.09312.Title: Verifying Chain-of-Thought Reasoning via Its Computational Graph
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.09312.Summary: Researchers from FAIR at Meta and the University of Edinburgh developed Circuit-based Reasoning Verification (CRV), a white-box method that analyzes the computational graph of a Large Language Model to verify its Chain-of-Thought reasoning. This approach demonstrated superior performance in identifying reasoning errors and provided insights into the causal mechanisms of these failures through structural 'fingerprints' and targeted interventions.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) employing Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning can produce complex, multi-step solutions that are sometimes plausible but fundamentally flawed.

Existing black-box and gray-box verification methods can detect correlations with errors but lack the ability to explain *why* an LLM's reasoning fails or to pinpoint the exact computational malfunction.
A deeper, mechanistic approach was needed to move beyond error detection to a causal understanding and potential intervention for LLM reasoning failures.
Method: Introduced Circuit-based Reasoning Verification (CRV), a four-stage white-box pipeline that modifies an LLM (Llama 3.1 8B Instruct) by replacing its MLP modules with interpretable transcoders.
Constructed sparse, weighted, directed attribution graphs for each CoT reasoning step, capturing causal information flow between model components and active transcoder features.

Extracted a fixed-size feature vector (structural fingerprint) from each attribution graph, comprising global, node influence, and topological statistics, which was then used to train a Gradient Boosting Classifier to predict step correctness.
Results: CRV consistently outperformed all black-box and gray-box baselines across synthetic (Boolean, Arithmetic) and real-world (GSM8K) datasets, achieving an AUROC of 92.47 on the Arithmetic task compared to the strongest baseline's 76.45.
Leave-one-out ablation studies revealed that features related to Node Influence & Activation were most critical for verification performance, contributing the largest share to predictive accuracy.

Proof-of-concept causal interventions, such as manually suppressing or amplifying specific transcoder features, successfully corrected faulty reasoning paths, providing strong evidence that CRV's identified structural signatures are causally implicated in reasoning errors.
Takeaways: Reasoning failures in LLMs manifest as distinct structural "fingerprints" within the model's computational graph, making direct white-box verification feasible and effective.

The identified error signatures are highly domain-specific, meaning that distinct computational patterns characterize failures in different reasoning tasks (e.g., arithmetic vs. general problem-solving).

Analysis of feature importance and distributions confirmed that the structural properties captured by CRV distinguish correct from incorrect reasoning, delineating a "zone of computational integrity."

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.09201.Title: Multimodal Prompt Optimization: Why Not Leverage Multiple Modalities for MLLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.09201.Summary: Researchers at KAIST developed a Multimodal Prompt Optimizer (MPO) framework that optimizes both textual and non-textual prompt components for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). This approach consistently achieves superior performance across diverse tasks and modalities while significantly improving the efficiency of prompt discovery, addressing the limitations of text-only prompt engineering.
Problem: Existing prompt optimization methods for MLLMs are limited to text-only inputs, preventing these models from fully leveraging their inherent multimodal capabilities.
Manual prompt engineering is labor-intensive, requires significant expertise, and often leads to suboptimal performance for MLLMs designed to process diverse modalities.
The restricted search space of text-only prompts fails to exploit the rich contextual signals available in non-textual forms.
Method: Introduced the Multimodal Prompt Optimizer (MPO) framework to jointly optimize prompts across textual and non-textual modalities.

Utilized alignment-preserving exploration through cohesive backpropagation and joint multimodal updates, ensuring semantic consistency between modalities, along with diverse exploration operators (generation, edit, mix) for non-textual prompts.
Implemented Prior-Inherited Bayesian UCB for efficient prompt selection, which warm-starts evaluations for new candidates based on parent prompt performance, reducing the evaluation budget needed.
Results: MPO consistently and significantly outperformed manual prompts and leading text-only automatic prompt optimization methods across 10 diverse datasets, achieving an average accuracy of 65.1%, compared to 60.0% for the best text-only method.
The Prior-Inherited Bayesian UCB strategy reduced the evaluation budget by 70% compared to a uniform selection strategy, while achieving similar performance levels.
Visualization of MLLM hidden states demonstrated that full multimodal prompts shift internal representations into distinct regions, indicating richer reasoning influenced by non-textual components.
Takeaways: Optimizing prompts with both textual and non-textual components unlocks the full potential of MLLMs, yielding substantial performance improvements over text-only approaches.
Maintaining cross-modal alignment during prompt generation is critical for producing effective and coherent multimodal prompts.
Leveraging prior performance information from parent prompts dramatically increases the efficiency of searching in the vast multimodal prompt space.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.09001.Title: DARO: Difficulty-Aware Reweighting Policy Optimization
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.09001.Summary: DARO introduces an adaptive reweighting algorithm for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) that dynamically adjusts loss contributions based on sample difficulty, achieving state-of-the-art performance and faster convergence in large language model mathematical reasoning tasks. It resolves the "loss scale issue" found in previous GRPO-based methods by employing learnable weights to balance training signals across different problem difficulties.
Problem: Existing Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) algorithms, particularly GRPO-based methods, rely on static or overly simplistic weighting schemes for training samples.
This leads to a "loss scale issue" where the magnitude of the loss varies dramatically across different problem difficulty levels, causing unbalanced training.
Such imbalances hinder efficient learning, slow convergence, and lead to suboptimal performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) in complex reasoning tasks.
Method: DARO provides a unified mathematical framework for GRPO-based RLVR algorithms, revealing their underlying static weighting mechanisms.
It introduces dynamic, learnable weights for different difficulty groups (defined by empirical pass rates), which are optimized jointly with the LLM's policy parameters.
The loss function is designed with a regularization term to ensure weights are inversely proportional to their group's loss, thereby balancing training signals across difficulty levels.
Results: DARO consistently achieves the highest average accuracy across three base LLMs and six diverse math reasoning benchmarks, with peak performance of 50.8% for Qwen2.5-Math-7B.
The algorithm demonstrates significantly faster convergence rates and reaches higher final performance levels that are often unattainable by other static-weighting methods.

Ablation studies confirm the crucial role of DARO's dynamic weights, showing substantial performance gains (e.g., +2.7 over GRPO baseline for Llama3.1-8B) compared to static or simplistic weighting strategies.
Takeaways: Prior GRPO-based RLVR methods (GRPO, DAPO, LIPO, Dr. GRPO) can be unified and mathematically shown to employ static or predefined weighting schemes tied to sample difficulty.
The "loss scale issue" formally demonstrates that loss magnitude in RLVR is inherently imbalanced across different empirical pass rates (difficulty levels), impeding balanced learning.
Dynamically adapting loss weights based on the inverse of their group's loss magnitude effectively mitigates this imbalance, promoting more stable and efficient training.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.08696.Title: Don't Waste Mistakes: Leveraging Negative RL-Groups via Confidence Reweighting
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.08696.Summary: This research introduces Likelihood Estimation with Negative Samples (LENS), a method that enhances Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) by deriving a confidence-weighted penalty from a maximum likelihood objective, allowing large language models to learn from previously discarded incorrect responses. LENS consistently improves performance on the MATH benchmark, particularly for harder problems, yielding gains of up to 2.54 Pass@1 and 2.64 Pass@16 percentage points for a Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct model.
Problem: Existing RLVR methods like Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) discard 'negative groups' (batches of responses where none are correct), leading to wasted computation and reduced learning signals.
Negative groups constitute a substantial portion of samples (up to 45% early in training), representing a major inefficiency, especially when models struggle with challenging problems.
Traditional GRPO provides zero advantage for entirely incorrect groups, failing to offer fine-grained feedback or encourage exploration on difficult items.
Method: A theoretical framework is developed that reformulates policy learning as a Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) problem for a reward model, connecting it to policy gradients.
LENS introduces a 'calibrated reward' that assigns a non-zero, confidence-dependent penalty to incorrect responses, even within negative groups, turning wasted computation into a learning signal.

The method integrates as a plug-and-play modification into GRPO, using length-normalized probabilities for confidence and estimating a question difficulty factor to generate confidence-weighted advantages.
Results: LENS consistently outperforms the GRPO baseline across all evaluation metrics and models (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen-2.5-3B-Base) on the MATH benchmark.
Performance gains are most pronounced on harder subsets of the MATH benchmark (Levels 4-5), demonstrating LENS's ability to foster exploration and improve on problems where the baseline saturates.

LENS achieved Pass@1 improvements from 54.09% to 56.63% and Pass@16 from 72.70% to 75.34% for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, indicating both single-shot accuracy and broader quality improvements in generated responses.
Takeaways: Policy learning can be expressed as a statistical task of estimating a reward probability function, whose MLE gradient naturally provides a confidence-weighted learning signal for both correct and incorrect answers.
A model's confidence in its incorrect predictions provides a valuable signal; highly confident wrong answers should incur a larger penalty to encourage exploration and better policy calibration.
Leveraging even purely negative groups significantly contributes to performance gains, particularly on challenging reasoning tasks where initial correct answers are scarce.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.08673.Title: Thinking with Camera: A Unified Multimodal Model for Camera-Centric Understanding and Generation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.08673.Summary: Puffin, a unified multimodal model, integrates camera-centric understanding and generation by interpreting camera parameters as a "first-class modality" within a linguistic reasoning framework. The model demonstrates superior performance in both estimating camera parameters from images and generating visual content with precise viewpoint control, achieving enhanced spatial intelligence.
Problem: Camera understanding (e.g., pose estimation) and camera-controllable generation (e.g., text-to-image with viewpoint control) were traditionally treated as isolated tasks, limiting mutual benefits.
Existing large multimodal models (LMMs) struggled with precise geometric control, often ignoring or misinterpreting abstract numerical camera parameters, leading to spatially inconsistent outputs.
A scarcity of large-scale, high-quality datasets linking vision, language, and detailed camera parameters hindered progress in multimodal spatial intelligence.
Method: Developed Puffin, a unified model combining a geometry-aligned vision encoder, a large language model, and a diffusion model, connected by an adaptive module.

Introduced the "thinking with camera" paradigm, which processes camera parameters as language, maps them to professional photographic terms, and uses structured textual reasoning to bridge the modality gap.
Constructed Puffin-4M, a 4 million vision-language-camera triplet dataset with detailed camera parameters, scene captions, and spatial reasoning annotations, built through a multi-stage process.
Results: Puffin significantly outperforms state-of-the-art specialized methods in camera understanding, achieving lower median angular errors and higher AUC scores on benchmarks like MegaDepth and Puffin-Und.

Demonstrates high spatial consistency and realism in camera-controllable image generation, drastically outperforming powerful multimodal models (e.g., GPT-4o) and specialized generators like PreciseCam.

Exhibits versatile adaptability to downstream cross-view tasks, including spatial imagination, world exploration, and photography guidance, extending LMM capabilities to tasks like 3D object insertion.
Takeaways: Integrating camera parameters as a "first-class modality" and leveraging a linguistic reasoning paradigm ("thinking with camera") enables LMMs to robustly interpret and generate scenes with precise geometric control.

Pixel-wise continuous camera maps are critical for fine-grained spatial control during image generation, preventing geometric distortions and inverted spatial illusions under challenging camera configurations.

Jointly optimizing camera understanding and generation within a unified framework leads to mutual enhancement, with auxiliary generation losses implicitly improving geometric perception for understanding tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.08638.Title: Into the Rabbit Hull: From Task-Relevant Concepts in DINO to Minkowski Geometry
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.08638.Summary: Researchers at the Kempner Institute, Harvard University, and collaborators investigated DINOv2's internal representations, revealing that they form convex combinations of archetypal landmarks rather than solely sparse linear features. This work introduces the Minkowski Representation Hypothesis, which describes representations residing in Minkowski sums of convex polytopes, explaining phenomena like interpolative geometry and observed deviations from the Linear Representation Hypothesis.
Problem: Understanding the internal workings and representational geometry of powerful self-supervised vision transformers like DINOv2 remains largely opaque.
The prevailing Linear Representation Hypothesis (LRH) might be insufficient to fully describe the complexity of learned concepts in advanced AI models.
There is a need to identify the functional specialization of visual concepts recruited by DINOv2 for different downstream tasks.
Method: Overcomplete Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) were trained on DINOv2-B to extract a dictionary of 32,000 visual concepts.
Empirical analysis examined concept recruitment across classification, segmentation, and depth estimation tasks, as well as the geometric and statistical properties of the learned concepts.
The Minkowski Representation Hypothesis (MRH) was proposed, grounded in multi-head attention mechanisms and Gärdenfors' conceptual spaces, to provide a refined geometric understanding.
Results: Downstream tasks recruit differentially specialized concepts: classification uses a broader set, while segmentation relies on 'Border concepts' and depth estimation leverages distinct 'Monocular Depth Cue concepts' (projective, shadow, frequency).

Analysis revealed a partly dense representation with three outlier concepts encoding persistent positional information (left, right, bottom) and an anisotropic dictionary with a sharp singular value decay.

Empirical signals like piecewise-linear interpolation paths staying close to the data manifold and Archetypal Analysis achieving comparable reconstruction to SAEs support the proposed Minkowski sum structure.
Takeaways: DINOv2's representations exhibit a more complex, anisotropic geometry with coherent subspaces and antipodal concept pairs, challenging the purely sparse and orthogonal view of the Linear Representation Hypothesis.
Multi-head attention naturally generates Minkowski sum structures, where individual heads form convex hulls of value vectors, and their aggregation creates larger convex polytopes.

Concepts are better understood as archetypal points or bounded convex regions in a latent space, implying that interventions and interpretability methods should consider this non-linear, interpolative geometry.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.08558.Title: Agent Learning via Early Experience
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.08558.Summary: The "early experience" paradigm enables autonomous language agents to learn and continuously improve from their own interactions with the environment, leveraging implicit feedback from observed future states rather than explicit reward signals. This approach consistently improves task effectiveness, enhances out-of-domain generalization, and provides a robust foundation for subsequent reinforcement learning.
Problem: Existing language agent training (supervised fine-tuning) is limited by expensive, non-scalable human expert data, leading to brittle agents with poor generalization.
Applying reinforcement learning to complex, real-world language agent tasks is challenging due to absent/sparse reward signals and inefficient long-horizon rollouts.
There is a critical need for language agents to learn continuously from their own interactions and consequences in reward-free, unstructured environments.
Method: The "early experience" paradigm collects interaction data by executing alternative agent actions and observing the resulting future states, forming a reward-free `D_rollout` dataset.
Implicit World Modeling (IWM) trains the agent to predict future states from current states and actions, thereby implicitly learning environment dynamics directly within the policy.

Self-Reflection (SR) generates natural language chain-of-thought explanations that compare expert actions to suboptimal alternatives based on their observed outcomes, providing contrastive supervision for refining agent reasoning.
Results: Both IWM and SR consistently improve agent success rates across eight diverse language-agent environments and multiple model sizes, with gains ranging from +2.3% to +18.4% success rate.
Early experience methods substantially enhance out-of-domain generalization, helping agents recover a significant portion of performance loss in novel scenarios compared to imitation learning.
Models pre-trained with early experience provide a superior initialization for subsequent reinforcement learning, achieving higher ultimate performance ceilings during the RL phase.

The paradigm reduces reliance on expert data, demonstrating comparable or superior performance with significantly fewer human demonstrations, and scales effectively across various model sizes (3B to 70B parameters).
Takeaways: Agents can achieve substantial self-improvement and develop a deeper understanding of environment dynamics by learning from the observed consequences of their own actions, even without explicit reward signals.
Integrating implicit world modeling and grounded self-reflection provides scalable, reward-free supervision that enhances policy robustness and decision-making beyond rote imitation.

"Early experience" serves as a practical, effective bridge, enabling experience-driven learning before full reinforcement learning infrastructure is available and providing a superior warm-start for downstream RL.
The effectiveness of these methods stems from converting off-expert rollouts into grounded supervision derived from actual environment outcomes, unlike ungrounded reasoning methods.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.08191.Title: Training-Free Group Relative Policy Optimization
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.08191.Summary: Researchers from Tencent Youtu Lab developed Training-Free Group Relative Policy Optimization, a method that enhances LLM agent performance in specialized tasks by learning and integrating experiential knowledge as a token prior without modifying model parameters. This approach achieved substantial performance gains on mathematical reasoning and web searching benchmarks with significantly reduced data and computational costs, leveraging the full capabilities of frozen large LLMs.
