Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle to perform optimally in specialized real-world domains, often lacking deep domain knowledge and effective tool integration.
Existing agentic reinforcement learning (RL) methods, which rely on fine-tuning LLM parameters, incur prohibitive computational costs and environmental impact, especially for very large models.
Parameter-tuned LLM agents often exhibit poor generalization across different domains and require large volumes of expensive, high-quality data, leading to a "cost-performance dilemma".
Method: Introduces Training-Free GRPO, which adapts LLM agents to specialized tasks by learning "experiential knowledge" in natural language, avoiding direct parameter updates.
The method leverages the base LLM itself to generate "group relative semantic advantages" for its own outputs, identifying reasons for success or failure.
This distilled knowledge is then used as a dynamic "token prior" in subsequent prompts, guiding the frozen LLM's inference to improve its policy in a cost-effective manner.
Results: Achieved substantial performance gains on mathematical reasoning (AIME24, AIME25) and web searching (WebWalkerQA) benchmarks, with DeepSeek-V3.1-Terminus showing improvements like +5.4% on AIME25.
These gains were realized with exceptional data efficiency (100 training examples) and a minimal training cost of approximately $18, an order of magnitude less than traditional RL approaches.

Demonstrated superior cross-domain generalization and transferability, adapting a single frozen LLM to diverse tasks by simply integrating domain-specific learned experiences, and showed robustness to the absence of ground truth labels.
Takeaways: Policy optimization effects analogous to traditional reinforcement learning can be achieved by learning and integrating experiential knowledge into the LLM's context, rather than modifying its parameters.
Encoding "group relative semantic advantages" in natural language allows for efficient distillation of high-quality experiential knowledge from LLM rollouts.
The approach enables powerful, frozen LLMs (including API-based models) to be adapted to specialized tasks, circumventing the computational and data demands of fine-tuning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.08189.Title: R-Horizon: How Far Can Your Large Reasoning Model Really Go in Breadth and Depth?
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.08189.Summary: Researchers from Fudan University and Meituan LongCat Team developed R-HORIZON, a method and benchmark to evaluate and enhance Large Reasoning Models' (LRMs) long-horizon reasoning capabilities. Their work demonstrates that state-of-the-art LRMs exhibit significant performance degradation on complex, interdependent multi-step tasks but can achieve substantial improvements through reinforcement learning with R-HORIZON-generated data.
Problem: Current benchmarks for Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) primarily focus on isolated, single-horizon tasks, failing to reflect the complexity of real-world multi-step problems.
Real-world AI applications, especially agentic systems, require sequential planning and problem-solving over extended periods where previous outputs critically influence subsequent steps.
Existing evaluation methods do not adequately assess LRMs' ability to perform sustained, interdependent reasoning across a 'long reasoning horizon'.
Method: The R-HORIZON methodology systematically transforms existing single-horizon problems into complex, multi-step scenarios with explicit dependencies, tailored for mathematical, code, and agentic tasks.
A novel R-HORIZON benchmark was constructed using these composed datasets, covering 6 domains, to rigorously evaluate LRMs' 'actual accuracy' compared to 'theoretical accuracy' on long-horizon tasks.

Reinforcement Learning with Verified Rewards (RLVR) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) were applied using R-HORIZON data, incorporating distinct `R_last` and `R_all` reward schemes to train models for multi-horizon reasoning.
Results: Across 25 mainstream LRMs, performance degraded significantly with increased reasoning horizon; DeepSeek-R1's AIME25 accuracy dropped from 87.3% (1 query) to 24.6% (5 queries).
RLVR training with R-HORIZON data yielded substantial improvements, with R1-Qwen-7B showing a +17.4 point increase on AIME24 (2 queries) and a +7.5 point improvement on single-horizon tasks.
Trained models demonstrated enhanced efficiency with shorter responses, learned to allocate their 'thinking budget' more appropriately, and engaged in more frequent and longer-range reflections.
Takeaways: Even advanced LRMs exhibit a limited 'effective reasoning length,' with performance degrading significantly as the number of interdependent queries increases.
LRMs struggle with 'thinking budget' allocation and localized reflection, often 'overthinking' early reasoning stages and failing to identify/rectify errors from earlier steps in a long chain.
Explicitly training models with R-HORIZON-composed, sequentially dependent data via RLVR can substantially improve both multi-horizon and single-horizon reasoning performance and efficiency.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.07242.Title: Hybrid Reinforcement: When Reward Is Sparse, It's Better to Be Dense
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.07242.Summary: The Hybrid Ensemble Reward Optimization (HERO) framework integrates sparse, deterministic verifier signals with dense, continuous reward model scores to enhance large language model reasoning. This method, from FAIR at Meta and the University of Wisconsin–Madison, consistently outperforms both verifier-only and reward model-only baselines on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, achieving up to +11.7 points over RM-only training on hard-to-verify tasks, by providing stable and informative supervisory signals.
Problem: Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) suffers from reward sparsity and brittleness, leading to stalled learning when all generated responses are uniformly correct or incorrect.
Reward Models (RMs) provide dense, continuous scores but can be noisy and misaligned with true correctness, potentially destabilizing training.
Neither sparse, reliable signals nor dense, noisy signals alone are sufficient for robustly guiding Large Language Models (LLMs) on complex reasoning tasks, especially those that are hard to verify.
Method: HERO (Hybrid Ensemble Reward Optimization) combines sparse rule-based verifiers with dense reward models using a two-pronged approach.

Stratified normalization partitions responses into correct/incorrect groups based on verifier feedback, then normalizes reward model scores within each group to ensure correct responses always score higher while retaining nuance.
Variance-aware weighting dynamically adjusts prompt importance during training, up-weighting challenging, high-variance prompts to focus learning on more informative examples.
Results: HERO consistently outperformed RM-only and verifier-only baselines across all training regimes and task types on mathematical reasoning benchmarks.

On hard-to-verify tasks, HERO achieved an average of 66.3 accuracy for Qwen3-4B-Base when trained on easy-to-verify data, representing an +11.7 point improvement over RM-only (54.6) and +9.2 points over verifier-only (57.1) training.

Ablation studies confirmed that dense negative ranges and variance-aware reweighting were critical, with variance-aware reweighting adding +3.8 points, and that larger reward models (72B vs 7B) provided only marginal or no additional benefits, highlighting HERO's efficiency.
Takeaways: Integrating sparse and dense reward signals through structured methods (stratified normalization) provides more effective gradients and prevents learning from stalling, especially when rule-based rewards are uniform.
Providing dense rewards within the 'negative' (incorrect) response range is crucial for stabilizing training and improving learning efficiency by guiding the model to better distinguish among errors.

Dynamically reweighting prompts based on the variance of candidate response scores (variance-aware weighting) improves robustness and generalization by prioritizing ambiguous and challenging examples.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.06783.Title: TTRV: Test-Time Reinforcement Learning for Vision Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.06783.Summary: TTRV introduces the first test-time reinforcement learning framework for decoder-based Vision-Language Models, enabling unsupervised adaptation on unlabeled test data by combining frequency-based and entropy-controlled self-supervised rewards with GRPO. This method yields substantial accuracy gains, averaging 28.97% on image recognition and 17.50% on VQA for InternVL3-8B, often outperforming GPT-4o.
Problem: Current Vision-Language Models (VLMs) remain static post-training and struggle to adapt to new or out-of-distribution data without costly, labeled fine-tuning.
Existing reinforcement learning methods for VLM adaptation rely on labeled data or curated training splits to generate reward signals, limiting their real-world applicability.
Many Test-Time Training (TTT) approaches are not directly applicable to autoregressive, decoder-based VLMs, which generate token sequences, or rely on class-level distributions.
Method: TTRV adapts pre-trained decoder-based VLMs on-the-fly at inference time using only unlabeled test data by integrating Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO).
It generates multiple candidate responses for each input to form an empirical output distribution and derives a novel self-supervised reward from this distribution.
The reward mechanism combines a frequency-based signal to encourage consistency and an entropy-based signal for diversity control, guiding the VLM policy optimization via GRPO.
Results: TTRV consistently improved Top-1 accuracy across 16 diverse benchmarks, with average gains of 28.97% for InternVL3-8B on image recognition and 17.50% on VQA tasks.
The method enabled open-source InternVL3-8B to surpass GPT-4o by an average of 2.3% on image recognition and remain highly competitive on VQA tasks.
Impressive gains were achieved with remarkable data efficiency, using only 20 randomly chosen test instances per dataset, with non-trivial improvements observed even with a single adaptation sample.
Takeaways: Effective unsupervised adaptation of Vision-Language Models is achievable at test-time, enabling continuous model refinement without reliance on external labels.
Latent visual recognition and reasoning capabilities within large pre-trained VLMs can be significantly activated and amplified through self-supervised reinforcement learning.
A sophisticated self-supervised reward combining consistency (frequency) and certainty (low entropy) proves effective for guiding policy optimization in autoregressive multimodal models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.06673.Title: Heptapod: Language Modeling on Visual Signals
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.06673.Summary: Heptapod introduces "next 2D distribution prediction," a novel generative learning paradigm that enables causal Transformers to learn holistic visual semantics. It achieves state-of-the-art performance for causal autoregressive image generation on ImageNet-1K without relying on classifier-free guidance or semantic tokenizers, demonstrating intrinsic semantic learning from reconstruction-focused visual tokens.
Problem: Existing visual generative models often rely on external semantic crutches like Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) or pre-trained semantic tokenizers, masking intrinsic model limitations and compromising reconstruction fidelity.

Applying 1D language modeling directly to 2D images is challenging due to the lack of intrinsic sequential order and the "curse of locality," which leads models to learn only local interpolations rather than global semantics.

The research aimed to develop a visual generative learning paradigm that adheres to LLM "first principles": a tokenizer focused solely on faithful reconstruction and complex semantics emerging implicitly within the Transformer.
Method: Heptapod redefines "next token" for visual data by training a causal Transformer to predict the token distribution over the entire remaining 2D spatial grid in parallel at each timestep.
The framework employs reconstruction-focused visual tokenizers (discrete VQ-VAE or continuous VAE) to decouple compression from semantic learning, aligning with LLM tokenizer principles.
A standard 1D causal Transformer backbone is used in conjunction with specialized 2D prediction heads (Global or Chunk-based) to map its output to a full 2D spatial distribution prediction.
Results: Heptapod-H (941M parameters) achieved an FID of 2.70 and IS of 229.8 on ImageNet 256x256 class-conditional generation, dramatically outperforming prior causal autoregressive models like LlamaGen-3B (3B parameters, FID 9.38) with fewer parameters.

The model's strong performance is achieved without Classifier-Free Guidance or semantic tokenizers, demonstrating that visual semantics can emerge intrinsically from a well-posed generative objective within a causal Transformer.

The "next 2D distribution prediction" objective demonstrated a substantial performance gain, achieving FID 3.97 and IS 185.3, significantly outperforming traditional 1D next-token prediction methods (e.g., FID 13.07 for 1D-random scan order).
Takeaways: Predicting the entire 2D spatial distribution compels the model to learn holistic global structures and semantics, effectively overcoming the "curse of locality" observed in 1D next-token prediction for images.

The approach implicitly unifies autoregressive modeling with Masked Autoencoding, combining the strengths of both paradigms by having the causal prefix act as context for predicting all future tokens.

Reconstruction-focused tokenizers are viable, with continuous VAE tokenizers ultimately yielding superior generative quality due to their better reconstruction fidelity, even with slower initial convergence than discrete VQ-VAE tokenizers.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.06499.Title: Webscale-RL: Automated Data Pipeline for Scaling RL Data to Pretraining Levels
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.06499.Summary: Salesforce AI Research developed an automated Webscale-RL data pipeline to generate 1.2 million verifiable QA pairs from web-scale pretraining data, enabling efficient reinforcement learning for large language models. This approach enhanced general reasoning capabilities and improved data efficiency by over 100x compared to continual pretraining.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) trained via imitation learning often exhibit a 'training-generation gap' and limited robust reasoning abilities, especially when faced with distribution shifts.

The application of Reinforcement Learning (RL) to LLMs at web-scale is severely constrained by a critical data bottleneck, as existing high-quality RL datasets are vastly smaller and less diverse than pretraining corpora.
Generating high-quality, verifiable question-answering (QA) pairs for RL training is exceptionally costly and time-consuming through traditional human annotation methods.
Method: An automated, multi-stage 'Webscale-RL data pipeline' was developed to systematically convert vast, unstructured web-scale pretraining documents into millions of diverse, verifiable question-answer pairs.
The pipeline employs LLM-based filtering to select high-quality documents, followed by domain classification and persona assignment to enrich question diversity.
A powerful LLM generates questions and short, verifiable answers entirely grounded in the source documents, with a subsequent LLM-based quality check for correctness and leakage prevention.
Results: The Webscale-RL model consistently outperformed all baselines, achieving an average improvement of 3.4 points over the strongest baseline (GDR) across a suite of diverse benchmarks, with most pronounced gains in general knowledge and reasoning tasks.
RL training demonstrated over a 100x improvement in data efficiency, with approximately 10 million tokens achieving MMLU-pro performance similar to continual pretraining with 1 billion tokens.
The 3B model fine-tuned with Webscale-RL narrowed the average performance gap to a larger 7B model from 10.6 points to 6.1 points, indicating enhanced capabilities for smaller models.
Takeaways: Automating RL data generation from existing web-scale pretraining corpora is a viable and highly effective strategy for overcoming data scarcity and improving LLM capabilities.
Reinforcement Learning, when supplied with web-scale, grounded data, dramatically boosts general reasoning and knowledge application across diverse domains in LLMs.
The approach achieves exceptional data efficiency, allowing RL training to reach comparable performance with orders of magnitude fewer tokens than traditional continual pretraining.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.05069.Title: SwiReasoning: Switch-Thinking in Latent and Explicit for Pareto-Superior Reasoning LLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.05069.Summary: The SWIREASONING framework enhances large language models' reasoning by dynamically switching between explicit and latent thinking modes, leading to Pareto-superior performance with up to 2.8% average accuracy improvement and 56-79% better token efficiency across various benchmarks.
Problem: Explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) methods discard information by committing to discrete tokens, limiting exploration and leading to suboptimal reasoning paths.

Training-free latent reasoning, while promising, can suffer from uncontrolled "drift," diffused probability mass, and "overthinking" due to a lack of explicit training for long-horizon continuous inputs.
Existing LLM reasoning paradigms often face a trade-off, where improving accuracy comes at the expense of token efficiency or vice-versa, hindering practical deployment.
Method: A dynamic mode-switching mechanism leverages Shannon entropy to estimate block-wise confidence, enabling LLMs to intelligently alternate between exploratory latent thinking and consolidating explicit CoT.

Asymmetric dwell windows prevent rapid mode oscillations, allowing immediate latent-to-explicit switches when confidence rises but requiring sustained explicit reasoning before re-entering latent mode.
An overthinking suppression mechanism, controlled by a maximum number of latent-to-explicit switches, injects `` tokens to encourage timely convergence and efficiently produce a final answer.
Results: Achieved Pareto-superior performance, demonstrating average accuracy gains of 1.5-2.8% and token efficiency improvements of 56-79% (up to 84% AUC over CoT) on mathematics and STEM benchmarks.
Showed enhanced performance on challenging tasks like AIME (up to +5.00% accuracy) and GPQA Diamond, indicating better deep deductive reasoning capabilities.

Demonstrated faster convergence to peak accuracy, reaching maximal performance with significantly fewer samples (e.g., 72% fewer on AIME 2024 than CoT), and generalized improvements across coding, multi-hop QA, and commonsense reasoning tasks.
Takeaways: Combining the strengths of continuous latent exploration and discrete explicit consolidation through dynamic, confidence-aware switching can overcome individual limitations of each reasoning mode.
Estimating a model's confidence in its reasoning path via entropy provides an effective, training-free signal for adaptive self-correction and optimal resource allocation.
Controlling the extent of internal deliberation (overthinking) is crucial for achieving high token efficiency while maintaining or even improving reasoning accuracy in LLMs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04871.Title: Less is More: Recursive Reasoning with Tiny Networks
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04871.Summary: The Tiny Recursive Model (TRM) demonstrates that a simplified recursive architecture can tackle complex reasoning tasks with higher efficiency and generalization than larger models and its predecessor, the Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM). For instance, TRM-MLP attained an 87.4% test accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme, a substantial increase from HRM's 55.0%, utilizing significantly fewer parameters.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) often struggle with complex puzzle-solving tasks such as Sudoku, Maze pathfinding, and Abstract Reasoning Corpus (ARC-AGI), exhibiting error propagation and costly inference.
The Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM), a previous alternative, was overly complex, relied on questionable theoretical assumptions for gradient approximation, and its performance driver was unclear.
There was a need for a simpler, more robust, and parameter-efficient model that could achieve better generalization on these challenging reasoning benchmarks.
Method: Developed the Tiny Recursive Model (TRM), utilizing a single 2-layer network for both latent reasoning and output refinement, replacing HRM's dual, more complex network structure.
Implemented full backpropagation through all recursive steps during deep supervision, abandoning the Implicit Function Theorem and 1-step gradient approximations used by HRM.
Streamlined the Adaptive Computational Time (ACT) mechanism by removing the "continue loss" component, which eliminated expensive extra forward passes during training.
Results: TRM-MLP achieved 87.4% test accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme, marking a substantial increase from HRM's 55.0%.
TRM-Att demonstrated improved performance on Maze-Hard with 85.3% accuracy (vs. HRM's 74.5%) and on ARC-AGI-1 with 44.6% accuracy (vs. HRM's 40.3%).
The model achieved exceptional parameter efficiency, with TRM-Att using only 7 million parameters, approximately four times fewer than HRM's 27 million, while consistently outperforming it.
Takeaways: Full backpropagation through the entire recursive process is crucial for performance, leading to a substantial increase in accuracy over HRM's 1-step gradient approximation.

A simplified architecture with a single 2-layer network significantly improves generalization and reduces overfitting, particularly on small datasets, by condensing the two 4-layer networks of its predecessor.
Reinterpreting latent features as a general reasoning feature ("z") and current embedded solution ("y") provides an optimal balance for iterative problem-solving.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04618.Title: Agentic Context Engineering: Evolving Contexts for Self-Improving Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04618.Summary: The Agentic Context Engineering (ACE) framework dynamically evolves and curates comprehensive 'playbook' contexts for large language models, allowing them to continuously improve performance. This enables smaller, open-source models to match or exceed proprietary LLM agent performance on benchmarks like AppWorld, simultaneously reducing adaptation latency by up to 91.5% and token cost by 83.6%.
Problem: Current prompt optimizers often prioritize concise instructions, leading to a "brevity bias" that discards valuable domain-specific heuristics and detailed failure modes essential for complex tasks.

Iterative rewriting of contexts by LLMs frequently results in "context collapse," where detailed information is compressed into shorter, less informative summaries, causing performance degradation over time.
Achieving scalable and self-improving LLM systems for complex tasks and autonomous agents requires efficient context adaptation without constant reliance on expensive human-labeled supervision.
Method: ACE employs a modular agentic architecture with a Generator for task execution, a dedicated Reflector for critically analyzing traces and distilling insights, and a Curator for synthesizing lessons into compact context items.

Context is represented as structured, itemized "bullets" (delta context items) that enable localized, incremental updates rather than monolithic rewrites, preserving past knowledge and reducing computational overhead.
A "grow-and-refine" mechanism continuously appends new insights (growth) and periodically prunes redundancy using semantic embeddings (refinement) to maintain comprehensive yet relevant contexts.
Results: On the AppWorld benchmark, ACE improves ReAct's accuracy by an average of 17.0% offline and 7.6% online over Dynamic Cheatsheet, with a smaller open-source model matching or surpassing GPT-4.1 powered agents.
ACE achieves an average performance gain of 8.6% on financial reasoning tasks (FiNER and Formula), outperforming ICL, MIPROv2, and GEPA by an average of 10.9% in offline adaptation.

The framework dramatically reduces adaptation overhead, showing an 82.3% reduction in latency and 75.1% fewer rollouts compared to GEPA in offline settings, and a 91.5% reduction in latency and 83.6% reduction in token dollar cost compared to Dynamic Cheatsheet in online settings.
Takeaways: LLMs benefit significantly from comprehensive, detailed contexts, from which they can autonomously distill relevance, countering the common assumption that shorter prompts are always better.

Separating the generation, reflection, and curation processes through a specialized agentic architecture leads to higher-quality context evolution and prevents the information loss seen in monolithic context rewriting.
Efficient and robust self-improvement for LLMs can be achieved by leveraging natural execution feedback and environment signals, reducing the need for expensive ground-truth labels during adaptation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.03259.Title: Meta-Awareness Enhances Reasoning Models: Self-Alignment Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.03259.Summary: Researchers from KAIST and AITRICS developed Meta-Awareness via Self-Alignment (MASA), a reinforcement learning framework that enhances large language models' reasoning capabilities by cultivating intrinsic meta-awareness through self-generated signals. MASA achieved up to a 19.3% accuracy gain on mathematical benchmarks and an average of 2.08% on diverse out-of-domain tasks, while its efficient variant reduced training time by 34.5%.
Problem: Large language models (LLMs) for reasoning often exhibit a misalignment between their internal meta-information (e.g., predicted solution length, difficulty) and the actual characteristics of their problem-solving processes.

Existing meta-cognitive approaches for LLMs frequently rely on external supervision (datasets, human pipelines) or tie meta-cognitive rewards solely to final solution success, limiting scalability and adaptability.
Current RL-based post-training methods for LLMs can be computationally inefficient, with some self-improving agents intermixing control mechanisms with reasoning, leading to unstable training.
Method: Introduces Meta-Awareness via Self-Alignment (MASA), an RL framework that generates parallel solution paths and meta-paths for each task.

Employs a self-alignment reward (`r_meta`) for meta-predictions, calculated by comparing predicted length, difficulty, and relevant notions with statistics derived from the model's *own* solution rollouts.

MASA-efficient further enhances training by dynamically collecting expert meta-trajectories (Behavior Cloning), implementing predictive gating to filter prompts, and using early cutoff for unproductive rollouts based on predicted length.
Results: MASA achieved an average accuracy gain of 6.2% (Pass@1) for Qwen3-8B on six in-domain mathematical benchmarks, including a 19.3% gain on AIME’25.
MASA demonstrated strong out-of-domain generalization, yielding an average 2.08% accuracy gain across 13 benchmarks spanning logical, scientific, and coding domains.

MASA-efficient reduced total training time by 34.5% compared to MASA and achieved baseline performance 1.28 times faster than standard GRPO training, largely maintaining performance while filtering out approximately 37% of prompts.
Takeaways: Explicitly aligning an LLM's meta-predictions with its actual problem-solving statistics directly leads to significant performance gains in reasoning tasks.
Notion-awareness, or the ability to predict and leverage relevant mathematical concepts, is the most dominant factor in performance improvement, explaining over two-thirds of the variance.

Training efficiency can be substantially improved (up to 34.5% faster) by dynamically filtering out trivial/unsolvable prompts and curtailing unproductive rollouts based on stable meta-predictions without significant performance degradation on most tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.03222.Title: Low-probability Tokens Sustain Exploration in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Reward
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.03222.Summary: Researchers from Tencent's LLM Department and collaborating universities introduced Low-probability Regularization (Lp-Reg) to overcome exploration collapse in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) for Large Language Models by specifically preserving valuable low-probability "reasoning sparks". This approach enabled continuous on-policy training for 3,000 steps and achieved a 2.66% average accuracy improvement on challenging mathematical reasoning benchmarks.
Problem: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) for Large Language Models (LLMs) suffers from a scalability bottleneck.
This bottleneck is characterized by "policy entropy collapse," where models lose exploration capacity and plateau or degrade in complex reasoning tasks.
Prior entropy-centric solutions often fail by indiscriminately boosting both valuable and irrelevant exploratory tokens, leading to training instability.
Method: Developed Low-probability Regularization (Lp-Reg), an algorithm integrated into policy gradient methods like Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO).
Constructed a "less-noisy proxy distribution" by filtering out irrelevant low-probability tokens from the current policy using adaptive or fixed probability thresholds.

Applied a selective regularization penalty using forward KL divergence to protect identified valuable low-probability tokens ("reasoning sparks") specifically when they receive negative advantage signals.
Results: Enabled sustained on-policy training for 3,000 steps, accumulating over 81,204 GPU-hours, showcasing a substantial improvement in training stability and scalability.
Achieved state-of-the-art performance on five mathematical reasoning benchmarks, with an average accuracy of 60.17% on the Qwen3-14B-Base model, outperforming the previous best by 2.66%.

Ablation studies validated core design choices, confirming the necessity of noise filtering, selective regularization of tokens with negative advantage, and the use of forward KL divergence for effective training.
Takeaways: The core issue in RLVR scalability is the systematic elimination of specific valuable low-probability exploratory tokens, termed "reasoning sparks," rather than a general loss of policy entropy.
"Reasoning sparks" are qualitatively different from high-entropy tokens and exhibit statistically higher average probabilities than irrelevant noise within the low-probability spectrum.
Sustained, stable exploration in RL for LLMs requires a targeted approach to preserve these meaningful low-probability tokens, avoiding indiscriminate entropy boosting.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.02665.Title: Self-Improvement in Multimodal Large Language Models: A Survey
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.02665.Summary: Researchers from UT Dallas, University of Toronto, University of Notre Dame, and MBZUAI present the first comprehensive survey on self-improvement in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), systematizing current methodologies for data collection, organization, and model optimization. The work provides a structured overview of techniques enabling MLLMs to autonomously enhance their capabilities, identifies unique challenges, and outlines future research directions in this area.
Problem: High costs and human effort dependency in training and scaling Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs).
Performance limitations and efficiency challenges of traditional, static training paradigms for MLLMs.
Absence of a comprehensive, structured overview of self-improvement methodologies specifically within the MLLM domain.
Method: Formal definition of self-improvement for MLLMs and a five-level spectrum of autonomy, distinguishing it from self-refinement.

A three-step iterative framework comprising data collection (e.g., guided generation, negative sampling), data organization (e.g., rule/model/environment-based verification), and model optimization (e.g., SFT, RL, DPO).
Comprehensive review of seed models, evaluation benchmarks, applications, and challenges unique to MLLM self-improvement.
Results: Delivered the first comprehensive survey structuring the nascent field of self-improvement in Multimodal Large Language Models.
Systematized methodologies into a clear framework encompassing data collection, organization, and model optimization techniques.
Identified persistent MLLM limitations, such as fine-grained spatial reasoning and long-horizon temporal grounding, even with self-improvement efforts.
Delineated unique challenges and future research directions like achieving 'Omni I/O' and enhancing robust, generalizable self-improvement mechanisms.
Takeaways: Self-improvement offers a scalable pathway to reduce human annotation costs and enhance MLLM capabilities, including hallucination reduction.
The quality and organization of self-generated data, through verification and arrangement, are crucial for effective model enhancement.
Performance improvements from self-improvement are typically method-task specific, with limited universal generalization across diverse MLLM capabilities.
Evaluation integrity requires preventing 'Judge/Reward Leakage' by ensuring strict separation between data generation/curation and benchmark evaluation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.02292.Title: From Behavioral Performance to Internal Competence: Interpreting Vision-Language Models with VLM-Lens
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.02292.Summary: VLM-LENS provides a unified, extensible toolkit for systematically extracting and analyzing the internal representations of diverse Vision-Language Models. It enables a shift from evaluating behavioral performance to understanding a VLM's internal competence, as demonstrated by insights into how models encode primitive concepts and process ambiguous multimodal inputs.
Problem: Current VLM evaluation primarily relies on superficial, exact-match accuracy metrics, overlooking the richness of internal representations and potentially leading to misleading assessments.
The research landscape lacks comprehensive and extensible interpretability toolkits for VLMs, making systematic cross-model analysis challenging due to proprietary nature or limited model support.
Researchers face substantial hurdles in extracting intermediate representations from diverse VLM architectures beyond basic layer-wise outputs.
Method: VLM-LENS employs PyTorch's `hook` mechanism to extract internal representations from any specified layer during a VLM's forward pass, capturing output tensors.
It provides a unified, YAML-configurable interface that abstracts model-specific complexities, streamlining model loading, preprocessing, and inference across diverse architectures.
The toolkit supports 16 base VLMs and over 30 variants, offering isolated, model-specific environment setups for easy installation and reproducibility.
Results: Probing experiments revealed significant differences in internal competence across VLMs, with Qwen2-VL-7B and MiniCPM-o achieving near-perfect accuracy for primitive concepts, while LLaVA-1.5-7B showed weaker competence.

Concept similarity analysis with Stroop-like stimuli demonstrated that lexical content (the written word) can influence VLM color perception more prominently than the actual font color, with background color being the most dominant visual cue.

System evaluation showed generative VLM inference times ranging from 0.092s/instance (MiniCPM-V-2) to 0.623s/instance (InternVL) and peak GPU memory usage varying from 7GB to over 34GB, indicating architectural efficiency differences.
Takeaways: Evaluating internal competence, not just behavioral performance, is crucial for truly understanding VLM capabilities and limitations, distinguishing genuine understanding from shortcut learning.
Standardizing access to VLM internal states significantly lowers the technical barrier for interpretability research, accelerating scientific understanding and improvement of these models.
Different VLMs exhibit varied internal competence in encoding primitive concepts like color, material, and shape within their hidden states, complementing traditional output-based evaluations.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.02263.Title: RLAD: Training LLMs to Discover Abstractions for Solving Reasoning Problems
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.02263.Summary: The RLAD framework enables large language models to self-discover and leverage high-level reasoning abstractions, leading to substantial improvements in accuracy and compute efficiency on challenging mathematical reasoning tasks. This approach teaches models to propose and utilize concise procedural and factual knowledge to guide complex problem-solving.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) often engage in verbose or degenerate exploration, leading to 'underthinking' and inconsistent logic switches during complex reasoning.
Current reinforcement learning approaches for LLMs incentivize 'depth' (longer reasoning chains) over 'breadth' (diverse solution strategies), limiting exploration of alternative paths.
LLMs struggle to consistently capture, reuse, or generalize fundamental procedural and factual knowledge, hindering truly algorithmic reasoning.
Method: Introduces 'reasoning abstractions' as concise natural language descriptions of procedural and factual knowledge to guide LLM reasoning.
Develops RLAD, a novel two-player reinforcement learning framework that jointly trains an 'abstraction generator' and an 'abstraction-conditioned solution generator'.
Employs a modified reward function for the solution generator and curriculum training to ensure effective abstraction utilization and learning on challenging problems.
Results: RLAD consistently outperformed state-of-the-art RL methods (e.g., DAPO) on math reasoning benchmarks, showing an average 44% improvement on AIME 2025.
Abstractions proposed by the RLAD-trained generator improved a stronger solution model's (o4-mini) pass@1 accuracy from 80.38% to 85.83% without further fine-tuning.
Solutions generated with different abstractions exhibited increased semantic diversity and significantly higher adherence to their respective abstraction's guidance.
Takeaways: Self-discovered reasoning abstractions, even from weaker models, can significantly improve the accuracy of LLM solutions and generalize to guide stronger models.
Allocating test-time compute to generating diverse abstractions is more efficient for performance gains than solely increasing the number of solution samples per abstraction.
Training with abstractions enhances an LLM's general reasoning capabilities and generalization, even when abstractions are not provided during inference.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.02245.Title: ExGRPO: Learning to Reason from Experience
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.02245.Summary: EXGRPO is a framework that improves large language model reasoning by intelligently managing and replaying high-quality past experiences within reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR). It yielded average performance gains of +3.5 points on in-distribution math benchmarks and +7.6 points on out-of-distribution general reasoning benchmarks, while also substantially enhancing training stability for weaker models.
Problem: Traditional on-policy Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) for Large Language Models (LLMs) is computationally inefficient, discarding valuable reasoning trajectories after a single update.
RLVR training suffers from instability, particularly for weaker LLMs, often leading to performance collapse or slow convergence due to the constant generation and discarding of new experiences.
Prior RLVR methods lacked a systematic approach to identify and leverage "valuable" self-generated reasoning experiences within a replay buffer.
Method: EXGRPO introduces an experience management layer that intelligently handles a replay buffer, partitioning it dynamically based on question correctness rates.
The framework prioritizes questions of medium difficulty (25-75% correctness rate) and selects the lowest-entropy successful reasoning trajectories for replay, aiming for higher CoT quality.

It integrates a mixed-policy optimization objective that combines on-policy samples with replayed experiential samples, utilizing importance reweighting and a non-linear policy shaping function for stable training.
Results: EXGRPO achieved average performance gains of +3.5 points on in-distribution mathematical reasoning benchmarks and +7.6 points on out-of-distribution general reasoning benchmarks across five diverse LLM backbones.
It dramatically enhanced training stability for weaker models (e.g., Llama-3.1 8B Base), improving average out-of-distribution performance from 1.3 to 30.8, where on-policy RLVR failed.

Ablation studies confirmed that selecting medium-difficulty questions, lowest-entropy trajectories, and utilizing policy shaping are crucial components, preventing performance degradation observed without them.
Takeaways: Medium-difficulty questions and low-entropy reasoning trajectories represent the most valuable learning signals for enhancing LLM reasoning in RLVR.
Principled experience management, which strategically identifies and reuses high-quality experiences, significantly boosts both sample efficiency and training stability in RLVR.
Prioritizing low-entropy trajectories effectively counters the "snowball effect," where repeatedly sampling misguided, high-entropy experiences can degrade reasoning capabilities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.01265.Title: RLP: Reinforcement as a Pretraining Objective
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.01265.Summary: Researchers developed RLP (Reinforcement as a Pretraining Objective), which integrates reinforcement learning directly into the pretraining of Large Language Models to encourage Chain-of-Thought generation by rewarding information gain. This method enhances base model reasoning, showing a 19% average performance increase over conventional methods on an 8-benchmark math-science suite for a 1.7B model and achieving a 35% relative improvement for a 12B model with reduced training data.
Problem: The dominant next-token prediction objective in LLM pretraining does not explicitly foster long-range reasoning or deep integration of world knowledge.
Reasoning abilities are primarily induced in costly, late-stage post-training phases like RLHF/RLAIF/RLVR, creating a disconnect from foundational learning.
Current pretraining methods do not adequately reflect active human cognitive processes where internal deliberation precedes external expression.
Method: RLP introduces an information-driven reinforcement pretraining objective into the last phase of pretraining, leveraging exploration.
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) generation is treated as an explicit exploratory action, sampled by a 'thought policy' before predicting the next token.
A verifier-free, dense reward signal is computed as the log-likelihood increase of the next token when conditioned on the sampled CoT compared to a no-think baseline.
Results: RLP-trained base models consistently outperformed baselines, with a 1.7B model showing a 19% average improvement on an 8-benchmark math-science suite.
A 12B hybrid Mamba-Transformer model (Nemotron-Nano-12B-v2) achieved a 35% relative improvement with RLP using only 250 million tokens, compared to a baseline trained on 20 trillion tokens.
RLP demonstrated superior performance (+4.0% overall average) compared to Reinforcement Pre-training (RPT) under matched compute, attributing gains to its dense, per-token information-gain reward.
Takeaways: Integrating reinforcement learning directly into pretraining, using an intrinsic information-gain signal, can effectively teach models 'independent thinking behavior' earlier.
The dense, continuous, and verifier-free reward allows RLP to learn powerful reasoning signals from diverse, ordinary text corpora without specialized datasets.
The reasoning foundations established by RLP compound with subsequent post-training, leading to more capable and robust aligned models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.01135.Title: Prompt Curriculum Learning for Efficient LLM Post-Training
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.01135.Summary: Researchers from Meta Superintelligence Labs and Cornell University developed Prompt Curriculum Learning (PCL), an efficient framework for post-training large language models with reinforcement learning. PCL uses a learned value model to dynamically select prompts of intermediate difficulty, which accelerates training by up to 16.9x in filtering time while achieving higher performance.
Problem: High computational cost and hyperparameter sensitivity of reinforcement learning (RL) for post-training large language models (LLMs).
Inefficiency of current curriculum learning methods for LLMs, which either waste computation on unselected prompts or suffer from off-policy issues.
Limited understanding of the impact of key hyperparameters like batch size and prompt selection on LLM RL training dynamics.
Method: Conducted systematic preliminary investigations to identify optimal batch sizes and the effectiveness of intermediate-difficulty prompts in LLM RL.
Developed Prompt Curriculum Learning (PCL), which leverages a concurrently updated value model to predict prompt difficulty with a single forward pass.
PCL dynamically selects prompts of intermediate difficulty for policy updates, avoiding costly rollouts or stale dictionary lookups.
Results: PCL consistently achieved higher final performance or reduced training time, outperforming GRPO, DS, SPEED, and GRESO on mathematical and reasoning tasks.
Prompt filtering using PCL's value model was 12.1x faster on MATH and 16.9x faster on DeepScaleR compared to rollout-based methods.
The framework maintained a high effective ratio throughout training and adaptively focused on prompts of intermediate difficulty, requiring only slightly higher generation time than standard methods.
Takeaways: An optimal batch size exists where generation time scales sublinearly, leading to maximally fast convergence for LLM RL.
Prompts where the current policy achieves approximately 50% success yield the highest effective learning signals and gradient magnitudes.
A learned value model can accurately predict prompt difficulty comparable to multiple generations, enabling efficient on-policy curriculum learning without wasteful rollouts.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.01132.Title: A Practitioner's Guide to Multi-turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.01132.Summary: Researchers at UCSD and NVIDIA present a systematic guide for training large language models as agents in multi-turn interactive environments. The work outlines a practical recipe leveraging curriculum learning, stabilized policy optimization, and verified dense rewards, demonstrating improved skill acquisition and generalization across diverse tasks like text adventures and software engineering.
Problem: The field of multi-turn Reinforcement Learning (RL) for LLM agents lacks systematic understanding and consistent definitions, leading to fragmented approaches.
Existing RL methods are primarily optimized for single-turn scenarios, struggling with sparse terminal rewards and imprecise turn-level credit assignment in multi-turn interactions.
A lack of comprehensive analysis on effective design choices hinders practitioners from developing robust and generalizable LLM agents for complex interactive environments.
Method: Frames multi-turn agentic tasks as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) with a key innovation of token-level credit assignment for rewards.
Systematically deconstructs the complex problem into three core, interdependent pillars: Environment, Reward, and Policy, for structured analysis.
Conducts extensive empirical investigations across diverse benchmarks (TextWorld, ALFWorld, SWE-Gym) to derive a practical, empirically-backed training recipe for LLM agents.
Results: The proposed recipe, emphasizing Curriculum + Stabilized Policy + Verified Dense Reward, substantially enhances LLM agent performance and generalization across various task complexities and types.
PPO demonstrated superior sample efficiency and robustness compared to other RL algorithms (RLOO, Reinforce++, GRPO) in TextWorld, with GRPO proving effective for SWE-Gym.

Dense, turn-level rewards significantly accelerated training, and fine-grained verifier rewards boosted SWE-Gym success rates from 4.2% (sparse binary) to 22%, highlighting the necessity of execution-based feedback.
Takeaways: Multi-turn RL for LLM agents requires careful co-design across environment setup, policy initialization, and reward engineering, rather than a simple extension of single-turn methods.
A strong Supervised Fine-tuning (SFT) prior dramatically accelerates RL efficiency, with an optimal SFT-to-RL ratio crucial for in-domain success and generalization.
Dense, turn-level rewards and fine-grained, execution-based verified rewards are essential for effective learning in complex tasks, significantly outperforming sparse or model-based proxy rewards.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.00855.Title: Can World Models Benefit VLMs for World Dynamics?
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.00855.Summary: The research introduces Dynamic Vision Aligner (DyVA), a World-Language Model that integrates dynamics-aware features from a generative world model into a VLM framework. This approach enables emergent zero-shot multi-frame reasoning from single-image training and consistently enhances spatial understanding across various benchmarks.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) relying on static vision encoders often struggle with understanding dynamic information, temporal reasoning, and robust spatial grounding across multiple views.
Current VLMs are limited in comprehending motion, causality, and intricate dynamic spatial relationships critical for real-world reasoning tasks.
Method: A framework called World-Language Models (WorldLMs), with Dynamic Vision Aligner (DyVA) as a variant, integrates dynamics-aware priors from a frozen, pre-trained Stable Video Diffusion (SVD) model.
SVD is repurposed as a 'Generative Encoder' where a single Euler integration step of its U-Net denoiser extracts low-dimensional, dynamics-aware latents without full video generation.

These dynamic features are combined with static semantic features from a text-aligned vision encoder (e.g., SigLIP) and fed into a frozen LLM via separate, lightweight MLP projectors after concatenation.
Results: DyVA achieved state-of-the-art performance on the MindCube benchmark for multi-frame reasoning, surpassing models like GPT-4o overall and leading by 28.3% on specific subtasks.

It consistently outperformed baselines on single-image spatial reasoning tasks (e.g., VSR, TallyQA, 3DSR-Bench-real), demonstrating improved 3D awareness, relational understanding, and object counting.
The framework is highly efficient, utilizing single-stage instruction tuning of only lightweight projectors and the LLM, completing training in approximately 10.3 hours on 16xA800 GPUs.
Takeaways: Generative world models, specifically their U-Net's intermediate activations from a single denoising step, implicitly capture sufficient dynamics-aware priors that significantly benefit VLM understanding.
The fusion of these dynamic latents with static visual tokens enables emergent zero-shot multi-frame reasoning capabilities in VLMs, despite being trained solely on single images.

Effective integration requires complementary text-aligned semantic encoders (like SigLIP), as purely self-supervised vision encoders (like DINOv2) do not yield optimal performance when combined with world model priors.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.00219.Title: Thoughtbubbles: an Unsupervised Method for Parallel Thinking in Latent Space
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.00219.Summary: Thoughtbubbles presents an unsupervised Transformer architecture capable of dynamically creating and pruning parallel computational streams in its latent space, trained solely using the standard language modeling loss. This approach facilitates adaptive resource allocation during inference, leading to lower perplexity than larger baseline models and enhanced zero-shot reasoning performance by focusing computation on areas of higher uncertainty.
Problem: Standard Transformer architectures employ a fixed computational budget, processing all tokens with uniform effort regardless of their complexity, limiting their capacity for intricate, multi-step reasoning.

Current adaptive reasoning methods, such as Chain-of-Thought, are inherently serial, often necessitate explicit supervision or specific prompting, and are not natively integrated into unsupervised pretraining.
Transformers lack intrinsic mechanisms to adaptively allocate computational resources during pretraining, hindering their ability to develop native reasoning strategies from scratch.
Method: The architecture integrates special "forking layers" into a GPT-2 style Transformer, allowing tokens to dynamically duplicate their residual streams into "bubbles" or delete less important ones, all governed by learned scores.
Cumulative scores, indicating the importance of each residual stream, modulate both attention mechanisms and residual updates in subsequent Transformer blocks to guide computation.

A specialized Rotational Position Embedding (RoPE) variant and final weighted averaging of output distributions based on cumulative scores are used to manage forked tokens and produce a single output.
Results: Thoughtbubbles models consistently achieved lower perplexity on OpenWebText and peS2o validation sets; for instance, a 319M parameter model outperformed a 772M parameter baseline.
The method demonstrated improved performance on zero-shot tasks requiring reasoning and context extraction, such as LAMBADA and HellaSwag, across various model scales.
Qualitative analysis showed computation being allocated to uncertain regions and coreferent entities, and dynamic budget scaling enabled sustained performance in autoregressive generation.
Takeaways: Dynamic, parallel adaptive computation in a Transformer's latent space can be learned in an unsupervised manner using only the standard language modeling loss during pretraining.
This adaptive computation enables models to achieve superior performance in language modeling and reasoning tasks with fewer parameters, outperforming larger, non-adaptive baselines.
The model learns to interpretably allocate more computational resources (forks) to regions of higher uncertainty within the input sequence, demonstrating task-relevant adaptivity.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.00034.Title: Review of Hallucination Understanding in Large Language and Vision Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.00034.Summary: This review from Nanyang Technological University introduces the Model–Observer–World–Input (MOWI) framework to systematically define and categorize hallucinations in Large Language, Vision-Language, and Text-to-Vision Models. It maps these phenomena to their underlying causes across the entire model lifecycle, aiming to provide a unified understanding beyond reactive mitigation.
Problem: Existing research largely focuses on mitigating AI hallucinations, lacking a principled understanding of their underlying causes.
The field suffers from fragmented conceptualizations of hallucinations, often using narrow or task-specific definitions.
This fragmentation impedes the development of generalizable and robust solutions for generative AI risks.
Method: Proposes the Model–Observer–World–Input (MOWI) framework, a general, multi-level definition for characterizing both image and text hallucinations across diverse applications.

Systematically surveys hallucination causes by tracing them across five distinct stages of a model's operational lifecycle: training data, architectural limitations, inference mechanisms, loss and optimization, and misleading evaluations.

Unifies the four levels of the MOWI framework into a formal probabilistic definition to quantify the divergence between learned, real, and observer-perceived distributions, accounting for world uncertainty and input quality.
Results: Models tend to hallucinate when operating outside their training data distributions, exacerbated by data scarcity, limited diversity, structural misalignment, or memorization over generalization.
Hallucinations are significantly driven by inherited biases present in training data, evaluation processes, and model interactions, including effects from self-consumption and multi-agent debates.

Fine-grained internal dynamics, such as architectural flaws (e.g., attention glitches, autoregressive constraints) and optimization trajectories (e.g., oscillatory knowledge acquisition, reward hacking), critically shape hallucination patterns.
Takeaways: Hallucinations are systematic, predictable outcomes deeply rooted in the entire lifecycle of generative AI models, from data and architecture to training and evaluation.
Current evaluation practices are often misleading, propagating a false sense of progress and failing to detect or address hallucinatory tendencies effectively.
Addressing hallucinations requires a shift from reactive symptom management to proactive, principle-driven prevention grounded in a unified understanding.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.26626.Title: Recursive Self-Aggregation Unlocks Deep Thinking in Large Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.26626.Summary: This research introduces Recursive Self-Aggregation (RSA), an inference-time method for Large Language Models that enhances reasoning by iteratively refining and recombining multiple candidate solutions. When combined with aggregation-aware reinforcement learning, RSA consistently improves performance across various complex tasks, enabling smaller models to achieve reasoning capabilities comparable to larger, specialized models.
Problem: Existing test-time scaling methods for LLMs often focus solely on sequential refinement, which can propagate errors, or parallel exploration, which lacks iterative recombination of promising fragments.
There was no universal and effective test-time scaling method that allowed reuse of promising fragments from multiple candidate solutions without relying on external verifiers.

Standard Reinforcement Learning (RL) fine-tuning for LLMs did not explicitly train models on the task of aggregating multiple candidate solutions, potentially degrading performance when used with aggregation-based inference strategies.
Method: Recursive Self-Aggregation (RSA): An iterative, evolutionary-inspired algorithm that maintains a population of candidate reasoning chains and repeatedly forms aggregation sets, instructing an LLM to analyze these sets and generate improved, refined solutions.

Aggregation-Aware Reinforcement Learning (RL): A novel training approach that augments RL datasets with "aggregation prompts" alongside standard prompts, explicitly teaching the LLM to effectively combine multiple candidate solutions.

The method is parameterized by population size (N), aggregation set size (K), and number of recursive steps (T), allowing for flexible control over the breadth and depth of reasoning during inference.
Results: RSA consistently outperformed all evaluated sequential and parallel baselines (e.g., self-refinement, majority voting) across diverse tasks, including math (AIME-25, HMMT-25), general reasoning, and code generation.

RSA yielded substantial Pass@1 improvements across various LLM architectures (e.g., Qwen3, gpt-oss, Nemotron), enabling a 4B parameter model to achieve reasoning performance comparable to, or exceeding, much larger, dedicated reasoning models.

Performance generally improved monotonically with an increasing number of RSA steps (T) and aggregation set size (K), while the proposed aggregation-aware RL consistently boosted RSA performance compared to using the base model or standard RL-tuned models.
Takeaways: LLMs can implicitly verify and effectively aggregate intermediate reasoning steps from multiple candidate solutions to construct superior final answers, eliminating the need for external verifiers.
Iterative, recursive refinement and recombination of candidate reasoning chains lead to monotonic performance improvements, allowing LLMs to achieve deeper, more robust problem-solving capabilities.

Aligning LLM training objectives with specific inference strategies, such as using aggregation-aware RL for RSA, is crucial, as a mismatch between training and inference can paradoxically lead to degraded performance.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.26625.Title: Learning to See Before Seeing: Demystifying LLM Visual Priors from Language Pre-training
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.26625.Summary: Researchers at Meta Superintelligence Labs and University of Oxford empirically demonstrate that Large Language Models acquire separable visual perceptual and reasoning abilities from text-only pre-training, identifying optimal data mixtures for cultivating these "visual priors" and showing improved multimodal performance. The work introduces the Multi-Level Existence Bench (MLE-Bench) for fine-grained perceptual evaluation.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs), despite text-only training, surprisingly develop latent visual capabilities or "visual priors."
The specific textual data sources and pre-training mechanisms contributing to these emergent visual priors remain largely unexamined.
There is a need for a systematic methodology to deliberately cultivate and enhance visual priors within LLMs for building more capable Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs).
Method: The research employs a rigorous data-centric and controlled ablation study methodology, training over 100 LLMs across five scales (340M to 13B parameters) and 16 diverse text sources, consuming over 500,000 GPU-hours.

LLMs are adapted into MLLMs using a standard two-stage process (visual alignment and supervised multimodal fine-tuning) and evaluated on a comprehensive suite of 16 public VQA benchmarks, categorized by task type.

Pre-training data is classified into "reasoning-centric" and "visual world" categories to conduct grid searches on mixing ratios, identifying optimal blends for cultivating visual priors, and introducing the Multi-Level Existence Bench (MLE-Bench) for fine-grained perception evaluation.
Results: An optimal "vision-favorable" data mixture, comprising approximately 60% reasoning and 15% visual content, maximizes downstream MLLM VQA performance.

Perception priors, loosely correlated with general and OCR VQA, emerge from broad data and show scale-dependency, while reasoning priors, related to knowledge and vision-centric VQA, are robustly cultivated by reasoning-centric data and are universally transferable.
A 7B LLM pre-trained on 1T tokens using the proposed "balanced mixture" achieved superior visual task performance and improved language proficiency compared to a "language-favorable" baseline.
Takeaways: Visual priors in LLMs are not monolithic but decompose into separable perception and reasoning components, each with distinct origins and scaling trends.

Reasoning-centric language data (e.g., code, math) primarily cultivates visual reasoning abilities, while diverse language descriptions of the visual world contribute to basic perception, with different saturation points.
The findings strongly support the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, suggesting that LLMs learn an underlying, modality-agnostic statistical model of reality from text alone.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.26346.Title: EditReward: A Human-Aligned Reward Model for Instruction-Guided Image Editing
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.26346.Summary: A human-aligned reward model, EDITREWARD, accurately assesses instruction-guided image edits, leveraging a meticulously annotated 200K preference pair dataset. This model achieves state-of-the-art evaluation performance and enables the curation of high-quality training data, significantly advancing open-source image editing capabilities.
Problem: Open-source instruction-guided image editing models lag behind proprietary solutions due to a lack of reliable, human-aligned reward mechanisms.
Existing evaluation methods like perceptual scores, feature scores, and general Vision-Language Models (VLMs) fail to capture precise editing semantics or align with nuanced human preferences.
Fine-tuning general VLMs for this task is hindered by noisy, low inter-annotator agreement in crowd-sourced annotations or biased pseudo-labels from proprietary models.
Method: Constructed EDITREWARD-DATA, a large-scale (over 200K preference pairs) and high-fidelity human preference dataset annotated by experts across two dimensions: Instruction Following and Visual Quality.
Developed EDITREWARD, a specialized reward model using VLM backbones, a multi-dimensional uncertainty-aware ranking framework, and a novel strategy to disentangle ties in human preferences.
Introduced EDITREWARD-BENCH, a robust benchmark with challenging multi-way preference comparison tasks to more accurately evaluate and differentiate reward models.
Results: EDITREWARD achieved new state-of-the-art results on GenAI-Bench (65.72% accuracy) and AURORA-Bench (63.62% accuracy), outperforming proprietary models like GPT-5 and OpenAI-GPT-4o.
On the challenging EDITREWARD-BENCH, EDITREWARD scored 38.42%, surpassing leading proprietary models like Gemini-2.5-Flash (38.02%) and GPT-5 (37.81%).

Utilizing EDITREWARD for data curation, fine-tuning the Step1X-Edit model on a 20K high-quality subset improved its GEdit-Bench score from 6.444 to 7.086, making it competitive with top-tier editors like Doubao.
Takeaways: Multi-dimensional human annotation and uncertainty-aware ranking are critical for accurately capturing the nuanced quality of instruction-guided image edits.
Decomposing tied preference pairs into distinct dimensional preferences provides richer supervisory signals, leading to more stable and performant model training.
Data quality, as assessed by a highly human-aligned reward model, is more impactful than mere data quantity for training superior downstream image editing models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.26074.Title: Limited Preference Data? Learning Better Reward Model with Latent Space Synthesis
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.26074.Summary: A research team from University of Wisconsin-Madison and Nanyang Technological University introduced LENS, a framework that synthesizes preference data directly in the latent embedding space of large language models, enhancing reward model accuracy and reducing computational generation time by 18x compared to text-based methods.
Problem: Aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) with human preferences requires vast amounts of human feedback data, which is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming to collect.
Existing methods that synthesize preference data in the textual space using other LLMs are computationally intensive due to the costs of text generation and quadratic scaling of LLM-based annotation.
Limited initial preference data restricts the generalization capabilities and robustness of reward models, hindering effective LLM alignment.
Method: LENS employs a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) to learn a structured latent representation from existing LLM embeddings of preferred and non-preferred responses.
A divergence-aware learning objective is integrated into the VAE training, which maximizes the separation between the latent distributions of positive and negative samples.
New preference data is synthesized by perturbing latent codes in this learned space and decoding them into new embeddings, which are then used to train a lightweight reward model.
Results: LENS consistently outperforms all textual synthesis methods and simpler latent space baselines across HH-RLHF and TL;DR summarization benchmarks, improving reward model performance.

The framework achieves an 18x faster sample generation time and a 13x reduction in total processing time on a single A100 GPU, using a generator model with 16,000x fewer parameters (0.5M vs 8B) compared to text-based synthesis.

Reward models trained with LENS-augmented data lead to better downstream Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) outcomes, with SFT models achieving a 61% win rate against those trained with text-synthesis-derived rewards when evaluated by GPT-4.
Takeaways: Synthesizing preference data directly in the latent embedding space can significantly reduce computational overhead while effectively expanding the dataset for reward model training.
A carefully designed VAE with a divergence-aware loss function is crucial for learning a discriminative and smooth latent space that preserves underlying preference relationships.
Theoretical analysis supports that synthetic data generated by LENS can preserve preference ordering and reduce the estimation error of the reward model, improving its learnability.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.25849.Title: Knapsack RL: Unlocking Exploration of LLMs via Optimizing Budget Allocation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.25849.Summary: Knapsack RL introduces an optimization framework for dynamically allocating exploration budgets in Large Language Model (LLM) reinforcement learning, improving training efficiency and performance by focusing computational resources on tasks that yield the most informative gradients. This leads to consistent performance gains on reasoning benchmarks and achieves comparable results with half the computational budget of uniform allocation.
Problem: Existing Large Language Model (LLM) reinforcement learning (RL) methods use a uniform exploration budget per task, leading to inefficient computation.
Uniform allocation causes "zero-gradient" scenarios for very easy or very hard tasks, where all rollouts succeed or fail, halting learning for those tasks.
The high computational cost of generating exploratory trajectories (rollouts) for LLMs necessitates more efficient resource management.
Method: The method reframes exploration budget allocation as a knapsack optimization problem, where tasks are "items" with a computational "cost" and a "value" representing learning potential.
A novel value function is introduced, combining the probability of yielding a non-zero gradient (for algorithms like GRPO) with an estimate of information gain based on task success rates.
An efficient dynamic programming solver adaptively distributes the total computational budget among tasks, employing a fallback strategy to ensure even extremely hard tasks receive exploration.
Results: Knapsack-GRPO consistently improved LLM performance on reasoning benchmarks, with average gains of 2-4 points and peak gains of 9 points on specific tasks.
The "effective gradient ratio" increased by 20-40% compared to uniform allocation, demonstrating more efficient use of computational resources throughout training.
The approach achieved performance equivalent to standard GRPO while using roughly half the computational budget, indicating substantial resource savings.
Takeaways: A significant portion (over 40%) of rollouts in uniform exploration yield "zero gradients," hindering learning and wasting computational resources.
Dynamically allocating exploration budgets based on a task's current success rate (its "learnability") is critical to maximizing the effectiveness of each sampled trajectory.
Reconceptualizing exploration as a resource optimization problem allows for a "computational free lunch," enhancing LLM RL performance without increasing total compute.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.25541.Title: Vision-Zero: Scalable VLM Self-Improvement via Strategic Gamified Self-Play
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.25541.Summary: VISION-ZERO introduces a zero-human-in-the-loop, gamified self-play framework for Vision-Language Models, enabling them to autonomously generate training data and improve multimodal reasoning. This approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on various reasoning and vision-centric tasks while drastically reducing data annotation costs.
Problem: VLM training heavily relies on massive, human-curated datasets, leading to prohibitive annotation costs and data scarcity that limit scalability and diversity.
Models trained exclusively on human data are bounded by a 'knowledge ceiling,' preventing them from discovering novel reasoning strategies or emergent capabilities beyond human expertise.
Existing self-play paradigms for VLMs are largely unexplored and lack comprehensive solutions for scalable difficulty, task alignment, and minimal external data dependency.
Method: A novel gamified self-play environment, 'Who Is the Spy?', compelling VLMs to engage in strategic reasoning, visual analysis, and coherent language generation across multiple roles.
Employs label-free and domain-agnostic image pairs, generated automatically from synthetic scenes, chart data, and real-world image editing, eliminating the need for human annotation.

Utilizes an Iterative Self-Play Policy Optimization (Iterative-SPO) algorithm that dynamically alternates between self-play (Clue Stage) and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (Decision Stage) to ensure sustained performance growth.
Results: Achieved state-of-the-art accuracy on multiple reasoning, chart question answering, and vision-centric benchmarks, surpassing baselines trained on expensive human-labeled datasets.

Demonstrated sustained performance growth throughout training, with VLM win rates against fixed baselines increasing from 50% to 71% and average token lengths increasing significantly, indicating more complex reasoning.

Reduced dataset construction costs to tens of GPU hours and minimal monetary expense, a stark contrast to traditional methods requiring months or years of manual annotation and validation, and showed strong generalization with an average 1% improvement on vision-centric tasks.
Takeaways: Gamified self-play in a strategic social deduction game can effectively create a continuously challenging environment for VLMs to autonomously develop complex multimodal reasoning skills.

Iterative optimization, by alternating between self-play for strategic generation and verifiable reward-based reinforcement learning for decision-making, overcomes limitations of pure self-play and enables sustained performance improvement.

Completely eliminating human-in-the-loop data generation and training drastically reduces VLM development costs and fosters enhanced generalization and mitigation of negative transfer across diverse tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.25454.Title: DeepSearch: Overcome the Bottleneck of Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards via Monte Carlo Tree Search
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.25454.Summary: DeepSearch introduces a framework integrating Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) into the Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) training loop to enhance Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, demonstrating up to a 72x efficiency improvement in GPU hours compared to prior methods for similar performance gains.
Problem: Current Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) methods for LLMs often reach training plateaus despite significant computational investment.
Existing RLVR practices rely on sparse exploration patterns from direct rollouts, failing to systematically uncover diverse and effective reasoning paths.
LLMs are expected to exhibit complex search behaviors during inference, yet they are not explicitly trained with such structured exploration mechanisms.
Method: DeepSearch embeds a modified Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) directly into the RLVR training loop, enabling systematic exploration of multi-step reasoning trajectories.
It employs a hybrid MCTS selection strategy with 'global frontier selection' and an uncertainty bonus to efficiently identify and expand promising or uncertain nodes across the entire search tree.
An adaptive training strategy utilizes a replay buffer for caching verified solutions and progressively filters for 'hard' problems, focusing MCTS computation on the most challenging examples.
Results: DeepSearch-1.5B achieved a new state-of-the-art average accuracy of 62.95% on a suite of mathematical reasoning benchmarks, surpassing all prior baselines for models of its size.

The framework demonstrated remarkable computational efficiency, achieving its superior performance with only 330 GPU hours, representing a 5.7x reduction compared to extended training and a 72x efficiency improvement over the full training of the previous SOTA model for equivalent gains.

Ablation studies confirmed the positive contributions of key components, with global frontier selection and the strategy of learning from the most confident incorrect trajectories being particularly impactful for efficiency and performance.
Takeaways: Systematic training-time exploration, or scaling training 'breadth' through algorithmic innovation, is a more efficient path to improving LLM reasoning than simply scaling training 'depth' via extended optimization steps.
Integrating MCTS provides fine-grained credit assignment to intermediate reasoning steps within a trajectory, offering richer supervision than solely relying on outcome-based rewards.
Selecting the 'most confident incorrect trajectory' (lowest average entropy) for supervision proves highly effective for targeted learning, as it focuses on systematic, high-confidence mistakes.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.25373.Title: From Perception to Cognition: A Survey of Vision-Language Interactive Reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.25373.Summary: This survey analyzes Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) through a "From Perception to Cognition" framework, charting their evolution, challenges, and future directions by examining the integration between visual information acquisition and higher-order reasoning. It identifies a shallow and incoherent integration between perception and cognition as a key bottleneck in current MLLMs.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) exhibit limitations such as hallucination and biases, stemming from a disjointed integration between visual perception and cognitive reasoning.
Prior surveys on MLLMs often categorize models or tasks but lack a unified analytical framework to understand the interplay between perception and cognition.
Current MLLMs struggle to translate low-level pixel processing into robust, coherent internal world models for advanced reasoning.
Method: The authors introduce a "From Perception to Cognition" framework, deconstructing vision-language understanding into distinct yet interdependent layers: Perception and Cognition.
Challenges and existing methodologies for MLLMs are systematically categorized and analyzed under this framework, addressing issues from low-level visual extraction to dynamic reasoning.
The paper reviews relevant benchmarks and applications to evaluate how well MLLMs perform on tasks requiring different levels of perceptual and cognitive capabilities.
Results: Proprietary models generally outperform open-source counterparts in complex cognitive tasks, attributed to their scale and advanced architectures like Mixture-of-Experts.
