Open-source models like InternVL3 and Qwen2.5-VL exhibit strong performance in targeted areas through innovations such as process supervision and dynamic resolution.
Current MLLMs still fall considerably short of human performance in highly specialized cognitive tasks, underscoring ongoing limitations in knowledge integration and reasoning capabilities.
Takeaways: Robust cognitive abilities in MLLMs are fundamentally contingent on the quality of their low-level visual perception and fine-grained vision-language alignment.
The field is transitioning towards dynamic perception and dynamic forensics, allowing MLLMs to actively re-examine visual evidence and engage in iterative, multi-step problem decomposition.
Hallucinations in MLLMs can be attributed to identifiable deficiencies within either the perceptual (e.g., weak visual extraction) or cognitive (e.g., static memory, poor task decomposition) layers.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.25140.Title: ReasoningBank: Scaling Agent Self-Evolving with Reasoning Memory
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.25140.Summary: A novel memory framework, ReasoningBank, coupled with Memory-aware Test-Time Scaling (MaTTS), enables large language model agents to distill generalizable reasoning strategies from both successes and self-judged failures, facilitating continuous self-evolution and enhancing performance by up to 8.3% on web-based tasks and reducing interaction steps.
Problem: LLM agents struggle to learn from past experiences, repeating errors and discarding valuable insights, limiting their self-evolving capabilities.
Existing agent memory systems primarily store raw trajectories or specific successful routines, which often lack high-level, transferable reasoning patterns.
Current approaches often neglect the rich learning opportunities presented by failures, focusing predominantly on successful experiences.
Test-time scaling (TTS) has not been synergistically integrated with memory to create a positive feedback loop for continuous agent learning and performance enhancement.
Method: ReasoningBank introduces a structured memory framework that distills generalizable reasoning strategies (Title, Description, Content) from an agent's self-judged successful and failed experiences.

Memory-aware Test-Time Scaling (MaTTS) instantiates parallel and sequential scaling mechanisms to generate diverse exploration histories, which are then used to synthesize higher-quality, transferable memory.
The framework integrates a closed-loop process of memory retrieval, construction from new experiences (including self-judged failures), and consolidation.
MaTTS fosters a bidirectional synergy where memory guides test-time exploration, and the enriched exploration yields better memory curation.
Results: ReasoningBank consistently outperformed memory-free and other memory baselines (Synapse, AWM) across WebArena, Mind2Web, and SWE-Bench-Verified, achieving up to an 8.3% absolute improvement in overall success rate on WebArena.
The framework enhanced agent efficiency, reducing the average number of interaction steps by up to 1.4 on WebArena and 2.8 on SWE-Bench-Verified.

MaTTS, leveraging both parallel (k=5) and sequential scaling, further improved success rates (e.g., from 49.7% to 55.1% with parallel scaling on WebArena-Shopping) and consistently surpassed vanilla test-time scaling.

Learning from failures significantly contributed to ReasoningBank's performance, improving its success rate from 46.5% (success-only) to 49.7% (with failures), demonstrating robust knowledge acquisition.
Takeaways: Distilling high-level, transferable reasoning patterns from both successful and self-judged failed experiences is crucial for LLM agents to generalize and adapt effectively.

A bidirectional synergy exists between memory and test-time computation: high-quality memory enables more effective scaling, and scaling generates richer experiences that lead to better memory curation.
Learning from self-judged failures significantly boosts agent robustness, transforming counterfactual signals into constructive strategies and preventing future errors.
ReasoningBank's memory items demonstrate emergent behaviors, evolving from simple execution steps to complex, adaptive, and compositional reasoning strategies over time.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.25133.Title: Rethinking Entropy Regularization in Large Reasoning Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.25133.Summary: This paper introduces SIREN (SelectIve entRopy rEgularizatioN), a method designed to mitigate entropy collapse in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for large reasoning models. It significantly improved mathematical reasoning abilities, achieving an average maj@k of 54.6 on Qwen2.5-Math-7B across five benchmarks and promoting stable, effective exploration.
Problem: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) in Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) suffers from entropy collapse and premature convergence, limiting exploration and performance.
Naive entropy regularization fails in LRMs due to their vast action space (diffusing probability mass) and long trajectories (propagating uncertainty, leading to global entropy explosion).
Traditional regularization exhibits high hyperparameter sensitivity, offering minimal gains with small coefficients or rapid, uncontrollable entropy explosions with large ones.
Method: Proposed SIREN (SelectIve entRopy rEgularizatioN), built upon Dr.GRPO, to selectively apply and stabilize entropy regularization in LRMs.

Implemented a two-step entropy masking mechanism: a top-p mask within a token (action space level) to focus on meaningful tokens, and a peak-entropy mask for a trajectory (trajectory level) to target logically critical positions.

Introduced Self-Anchored Regularization, transforming the objective to maintain entropy at an appropriate, stable level by using an 'entropy anchor' initialized from the pre-trained policy, rather than simply maximizing it.
Results: SIREN achieved an average maj@k of 54.6 and avg@k of 46.1 on Qwen2.5-Math-7B across five mathematical reasoning benchmarks, including a +6.6 maj@k improvement on AIME24/25 over baselines.

The method demonstrated generalizability, consistently outperforming baselines on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B and LLaMa3.1-8B models, while increasing perplexity in generated responses, indicating greater diversity.

Ablation studies confirmed that all three components (top-p mask, peak-entropy mask, and self-anchored regularization) are crucial, with self-anchored regularization being particularly critical for stabilizing training and preventing excessive entropy.
Takeaways: Naive entropy regularization is ineffective for LRMs because their vast action space and long autoregressive trajectories lead to either diluted, uninformative entropy or an explosive, incoherent state.
Effective exploration in LRMs requires targeted regularization, focusing entropy control on semantically meaningful tokens and logically critical positions within reasoning trajectories.

Stabilizing the regularization objective by anchoring the target entropy to the model's initial state prevents extreme fluctuations, ensuring both sufficient exploration and robust training without premature convergence or uncontrolled entropy explosion.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.24981.Title: Random Policy Valuation is Enough for LLM Reasoning with Verifiable Rewards
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.24981.Summary: Researchers at Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Kuaishou Technology, and StepFun developed ROVER, a minimalist reinforcement learning algorithm for LLM math reasoning, which leverages uniform policy valuation to enhance solution quality and reasoning diversity. It consistently achieved higher pass@1 and pass@k scores across various benchmarks while reducing training instability compared to existing RL methods.
Problem: General-purpose RL algorithms (like PPO) are often applied to LLM reasoning tasks, leading to training instability, reliance on complex heuristics, and non-stationary learning targets.

These existing methods frequently suffer from "diversity collapse" or entropy collapse, where LLMs converge on a few high-reward solutions, limiting their ability to explore multiple valid reasoning paths.

A critical mismatch exists between the complex, stochastic MDPs for which general RL was designed and the simpler, deterministic, tree-structured MDPs underlying LLM math reasoning with binary terminal rewards.
Method: ROVER introduces a theoretical framework proving that optimal actions for LLM math reasoning's specialized MDPs can be derived by evaluating the Q-function of a fixed uniformly random policy.
It employs a softmax policy over these uniform-policy Q-values to stochastically sample actions, which effectively balances solution quality with desired reasoning diversity.

For practical LLM training, ROVER uses an intrinsic relative Q-function parameterization, mean-centered rewards, and broadcasts the reward signal to tokens, simplifying the optimization objective and avoiding separate value networks.
Results: ROVER consistently outperformed all RL baselines in pass@1 and pass@k metrics across various math benchmarks, achieving an average +8.2 pass@1 and +16.8 pass@256 improvement over the strongest baseline on competition-level tasks for Qwen3-8B-Base.
It significantly preserved policy entropy and demonstrated superior diversity, finding considerably more distinct reasoning strategies per question (e.g., 17 vs. 3 for GRPO on a sample problem).
The method exhibited stronger generalization capabilities on out-of-distribution tasks and enabled models to generate enhanced reflection behaviors and discover novel reasoning strategies.
Takeaways: In finite-horizon, deterministic, tree-structured MDPs with binary terminal rewards, the optimal policy can be recovered by merely evaluating the Q-function of a uniformly random policy.

Introducing stochasticity via softmax over uniform-policy Q-values can effectively maintain reasoning diversity without a catastrophic loss of optimal performance, enabling a trade-off between quality and exploration.
Leveraging the unique structural properties of LLM reasoning MDPs allows for a minimalist RL approach that is more stable, efficient, and performant than complex, general-purpose RL algorithms.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.24726.Title: Socratic-Zero : Bootstrapping Reasoning via Data-Free Agent Co-evolution
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.24726.Summary: SOCRATIC-ZERO introduces a data-free framework enabling large language models to autonomously improve their reasoning capabilities through the co-evolution of Solver, Teacher, and Generator agents. This system creates adaptive, high-quality training curricula from minimal seed examples, achieving state-of-the-art performance in mathematical reasoning and demonstrating transferability to general cognitive tasks.
Problem: State-of-the-art LLMs for reasoning heavily rely on massive, high-quality human-annotated datasets, creating a fundamental bottleneck for scalability and accessibility.
Current LLM training paradigms are static, unable to adapt the curriculum to evolving model capabilities or exploit rich feedback for targeted weakness remediation.
Existing data synthesis methods often struggle with inconsistent data quality and lack dynamic adaptation to a model's current abilities, leading to suboptimal training signals.
Method: A multi-agent co-evolutionary framework (Solver, Teacher, Generator) bootstraps reasoning skills by autonomously generating high-quality training data from minimal seed examples.
The Solver refines its reasoning policy using Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), learning from feedback generated by the Teacher based on its own attempts.

The Teacher (a fixed, high-capacity LLM) verifies solutions, refines problems based on Solver failures, and dynamically adapts the curriculum by categorizing problems and generating new, targeted challenges based on the Solver's 'zone of proximal development'.

The Generator learns to mimic the Teacher's problem design strategy via Value-Weighted Supervised Fine-Tuning (WSFT), using a utility function to ensure generated problems are optimally challenging for the current Solver.
Results: The Socratic-Solver-8B achieved 56.1% average accuracy across seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks, representing a +20.2 percentage point gain over prior data synthesis methods.

The Socratic-Generator-32B produced synthetic data with a 95.6% validity rate and enabled a student LLM to achieve superior downstream training effectiveness (37.72%) compared to data generated by larger commercial LLMs (e.g., GPT-5, Claude-4.1-Opus).

Ablation studies confirmed the critical role of initial supervised fine-tuning for foundational capabilities and validated the effectiveness of the Gaussian reward function in guiding the Generator to produce optimally challenging problems.
Takeaways: Autonomous, data-free co-evolution of specialized LLM agents can effectively generate high-quality training data and adaptive curricula, significantly reducing reliance on expensive human annotation.

Integrating preference learning (DPO) with dynamic curriculum adaptation driven by a 'Teacher' and a 'Generator' learning problem-design principles enables continuous, targeted self-improvement in reasoning.

Maintaining an optimal challenge level for the learner (Solver), guided by an adaptive curriculum that provides problems at its 'zone of proximal development', is crucial for efficient and robust skill bootstrapping.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.24251.Title: Latent Visual Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.24251.Summary: Latent Visual Reasoning (LVR) enables Multimodal Large Language Models to perform autoregressive reasoning directly within a shared visual-semantic embedding space, alternating with text generation. This approach substantially improves performance on tasks requiring fine-grained visual understanding and perception, outperforming methods that rely solely on textual reasoning or external visual tools.
Problem: Most MLLMs primarily conduct reasoning in the language space, leading to a 'semantic gap' where crucial visual nuances relevant to a query may be missed.
Visual information, once encoded, often remains static during the reasoning process, and even tool-augmented methods treat visual input as something external to be pre-processed or re-encoded.
Reliance on external visual tools for 'thinking with images' introduces rigidity, overhead, and bypasses the potential for MLLMs to inherently manipulate or explore visual semantics.
Method: LVR introduces a 'latent reasoning mode' triggered by special tokens, allowing the MLLM to propagate its last hidden states as input embeddings to reconstruct visual semantics relevant to the query.

A two-stage training pipeline is employed: Supervised Fine-tuning (SFT) uses visual reconstruction loss and next-token prediction loss with annotated regions of interest to teach latent visual reasoning.

Reinforcement Learning (RL) with an adapted GRPO_latent algorithm refines the LVR process, using text-based accuracy rewards and a format reward to encourage and optimize latent visual reasoning without explicit intermediate visual supervision.
Results: LVR achieved state-of-the-art performance, demonstrating significant gains on perception-intensive benchmarks, including a 2.7% improvement on V*D.A. and a 5.3% improvement on V*R.P. subsets.

The method consistently outperformed both 'Thinking with Images' (e.g., PixelReasoner) and 'Thinking about Images' (e.g., PAPO) paradigms across various visual tasks like Counting, IQ-Test, JigSaw, and Spatial Relation.
Reinforcement Learning with GRPO_latent further boosted performance over the SFT stage, and the 'Fixed Token' decoding strategy for LVR mode was found to be the most stable and effective.
Takeaways: Enabling MLLMs to actively reason over visual information by reconstructing latent visual thoughts in a shared embedding space is more effective than indirectly referencing it via textual Chain-of-Thought or external tool calls.
The core LLM can natively align visual and textual semantics in the joint latent space, as adding extra architectural heads for latent reasoning did not yield superior performance.
Reinforcement learning, guided by explicit format rewards for activating latent reasoning, successfully encourages and refines the model's ability to perform internal visual computations.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.24207.Title: Humanline: Online Alignment as Perceptual Loss
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.24207.Summary: A paper from researchers at Princeton, Stanford, and the University of Chicago explains the performance advantage of online LLM alignment methods through a human-centric lens based on prospect theory. It introduces "humanline variants," a practical design pattern incorporating perceptual biases, which enables offline training to match online performance while substantially reducing computational demands.
Problem: Online on-policy alignment methods for LLMs consistently achieve higher performance ceilings than offline off-policy methods.
Existing explanations for this performance gap are predominantly based on reinforcement learning theory (e.g., data coverage, search space).
Online methods are computationally expensive, slow, and unstable, limiting their scalability and widespread adoption.
Method: The research introduces a human-centric theoretical framework based on Prospect Theory, arguing that online sampling inadvertently better approximates the human-perceived distribution of model outputs.
It proposes the "humanline" design pattern, which integrates explicit perceptual biases into existing alignment objectives like DPO, KTO, and GRPO.
This pattern involves "humanline syncing" (periodically updating the reference model) and "humanline clipping" (asymmetrically clipping token-wise likelihood ratios upstream of the loss function).
Results: "Offline+humanline" variants matched the performance of online alignment methods on instruction-following tasks (Llama3-8B-Instruct), closing the performance gap using the same offline data.
Humanline GRPO achieved comparable Pass@1 accuracy to fully online GRPO on mathematical reasoning tasks while using 64x less frequent data sampling.
The humanline variants provided substantial computational efficiency, with "offline+humanline GRPO" reducing wall-clock time by over 6x compared to "online GRPO" for instruction-following.
Takeaways: The superior performance of online alignment methods can be attributed to their better approximation of human-perceived output distributions, rather than solely RL-theoretic reasons.
Standard RL clipping mechanisms (e.g., PPO/GRPO) can be reinterpreted as implicitly recovering a specific type of perceptual bias formalized in prospect theory.
By explicitly incorporating perceptual biases via syncing and clipping, offline alignment methods can effectively bridge the performance gap with online methods.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.23250.Title: Training Vision-Language Process Reward Models for Test-Time Scaling in Multimodal Reasoning: Key Insights and Lessons Learned
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.23250.Summary: This research details Vision-Language Process Reward Models (VL-PRMs) trained using a hybrid data synthesis framework, integrating strong VLM judgments and structured reasoning traces. The approach leads to consistent performance enhancements for policy VLMs across various multimodal reasoning tasks during test-time scaling, notably revealing latent reasoning capacities in larger models.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language Process Reward Models (VL-PRMs) relied heavily on Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) for data generation, yielding noisy supervision and limited generalization across diverse tasks.
VL-PRMs lacked effective mechanisms to detect early-stage perception errors, a crucial bottleneck in multimodal reasoning that can propagate through subsequent steps.
There was a need for systematic evaluation of test-time scaling strategies for VL-PRMs and broader assessment of their effectiveness beyond math-specific benchmarks.
Method: Developed VL-PRM300K, a hybrid data synthesis framework combining MCTS with strong VLM (o4-mini) judgments to create 1.32 million accurate step-level labels for multimodal reasoning traces.
Trained QWEN-VL-PRM-3B and QWEN-VL-PRM-7B with structured reasoning, explicitly separating and supervising perception steps to enhance early error detection.
Systematically investigated three test-time scaling strategies: Guided Greedy Search, One-shot Search, and Step-Score Aggregation, to integrate VL-PRM guidance into policy VLM inference.
Results: VL-PRMs consistently boosted policy VLM performance, achieving 7-20% gains on abstract, algorithmic, and mathematical reasoning tasks (e.g., PuzzleVQA, AlgoPuzzleVQA, MathVista, MathVision).
QWEN-VL-PRM-3B demonstrated a 16% gain in macro-F1 score for step-level error detection on VisualProcessBench, even outperforming the larger QWEN-VL-PRM-7B by 5%.
The models successfully unlocked latent reasoning capabilities in larger policy VLMs (e.g., Qwen-2.5-VL-32B, Gemma3-27B), yielding disproportionately substantial gains under test-time scaling.
Takeaways: One-shot search, where VL-PRMs evaluate entire solutions (acting as Outcome Reward Models), proved to be the most effective test-time scaling strategy, often outperforming step-by-step guidance.
Smaller VL-PRMs, specifically QWEN-VL-PRM-3B, achieved competitive or even superior step-level error detection performance compared to larger models or general VLMs.
Explicit perception-focused supervision during VL-PRM training is critical for detecting visual grounding errors, leading to substantial improvements in test-time scaling performance.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.23236.Title: Self-Consistency as a Free Lunch: Reducing Hallucinations in Vision-Language Models via Self-Reflection
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.23236.Summary: A method for reducing hallucinations in Vision-Language Models leverages internal self-consistency, using simple binary questions to identify and correct inconsistencies in detailed generative responses. This approach decreases the hallucination rate on the AMBER benchmark from 36.4% to 10.3% for LLaVA-v1.5-7B, improving factual grounding without external supervision or human annotations.
Problem: Vision-Language Models frequently generate "hallucinations," producing details not present in visual inputs, which undermines their reliability.
Hallucinations arise from noisy pretraining data and linguistic priors, leading models to favor fluent narratives over visual factual grounding.
Existing mitigation strategies often require extensive human annotations or computationally expensive external model supervision, posing scalability and practicality challenges.
Method: The Self-reflection Preference Optimization framework generates detailed responses and atomic binary questions from a VLM's own outputs.
The same VLM self-queries these binary questions to identify factual inconsistencies within its initial detailed responses.
Candidate responses are ranked by factual inconsistency, and preferred (more consistent) pairs are used to fine-tune the VLM via Direct Preference Optimization (DPO).
Results: Reduced VLM hallucination rates across multiple benchmarks; for LLaVA-v1.5-7B, the AMBER hallucination rate decreased from 36.4% to 10.3% while maintaining coverage.
Achieved improved factual grounding and trustworthiness on Object HalBench, ROPE, and MMHal-Bench, often outperforming larger models and those using external feedback.
Maintained or improved general instruction-following and question-answering capabilities on LLaVA-Bench and MMBench, confirming no compromise to overall helpfulness.
Takeaways: VLMs tend to provide more factually accurate answers to simple binary questions compared to complex, open-ended generative tasks.
This "behavioral consistency gap" between simple queries and elaborate generations serves as a reliable, internal self-supervisory signal for detecting hallucinations.
Negative binary responses from the VLM itself are highly precise indicators of hallucinations (e.g., 94% for object-existence claims).

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.22638.Title: Language Models Can Learn from Verbal Feedback Without Scalar Rewards
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.22638.Summary: This research introduces the Feedback-Conditional Policy (FCP) framework, enabling Large Language Models to learn directly from verbal feedback without converting it into scalar rewards. The FCP, particularly when enhanced with an online bootstrapping stage, achieves performance comparable to or exceeding established scalar-based reinforcement learning methods while preserving the richness of feedback.
Problem: Reliance on scalar rewards in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) causes information loss from rich, nuanced verbal feedback.
Mapping complex, mixed, or ambiguous human and AI feedback to precise scalar values is inherently ambiguous and arbitrary.
Maintaining consistent reward scales across diverse tasks (e.g., math, coding) is difficult, leading to imbalanced learning signals and potential biases.
Method: A Feedback-Conditional Policy (FCP) is proposed, treating verbal feedback as a direct conditioning signal for LLMs, similar to captions in text-to-image generation.
An offline training stage initializes the FCP by maximizing the likelihood of observed response-feedback pairs, utilizing diverse feedback types.
An online bootstrapping stage iteratively refines the policy by generating responses conditioned on desired positive feedback and updating with fresh, real-world verbal feedback from an environment.
Results: FCP+Bootstrap achieved an average accuracy of 38.7% on mathematical reasoning and 47.8% on general reasoning benchmarks, matching or surpassing leading scalar-based baselines like GRPO and RFT.

The model demonstrated strong controllability, significantly increasing accuracy when conditioned on 'fully_positive' feedback (68.5% on MATH500) and adapting to stylistic requests like 'has_code' (74.3% of responses containing code).
FCP exhibited robustness against reward hacking, maintaining high accuracy with lower assigned scalar rewards compared to GRPO, suggesting it learns a more direct alignment to desired behavior.
Takeaways: Large Language Models can effectively learn and be aligned directly from verbal feedback, challenging the long-standing necessity of scalar rewards in language-centric systems.
Direct verbal conditioning preserves the full nuance and context of feedback, avoiding information loss and ambiguity inherent in scalarization.
The framework enables fine-grained control over LLM behavior and stylistic attributes at inference time by leveraging diverse feedback without explicit categorization of positive/negative signals.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.22637.Title: Variational Reasoning for Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.22637.Summary: A variational reasoning framework is introduced for large language models, treating thinking traces as latent variables within a probabilistic objective. This approach consistently improves accuracy over supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning methods across various reasoning benchmarks, while also demonstrating enhanced training stability and generalization.
Problem: Supervised Finetuning (SFT) for LLM reasoning demands expensive, meticulously curated thinking traces, leading to generalization issues and catastrophic forgetting.

Reinforcement Learning (RL) approaches for reasoning often exhibit training instability, reduced output diversity, and a bias towards easier questions, resulting in suboptimal performance on complex tasks.
Existing methods lack a principled, robust training objective that can effectively scale and generalize reasoning capabilities across diverse and challenging problem types.
Method: A variational inference framework treats thinking traces as latent variables to maximize the marginal log-likelihood of correct answers for a given input.

An Importance-Weighted Autoencoder (IWAE)-style multi-trace Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) objective is employed to provide a tighter lower bound and improve gradient estimation, utilizing an accuracy-based estimator for answer probability.
The variational posterior is stabilized by optimizing it with a forward-KL divergence, which prevents mode collapse and leverages answer hints to guide the generation of high-quality thinking traces.
Results: The method consistently achieved over 8.5% higher average accuracy than strong SFT baselines and over 14% higher than RL baselines across various reasoning benchmarks, including competitive math, coding, and general knowledge.
Training dynamics showed improved stability, characterized by lower average training loss and reduced gradient norm spikes compared to baseline methods.

Significant generalization improvements were observed on out-of-distribution tasks like GPQA-Diamond and MMLU-Pro, despite training data focusing on math and code, indicating robust transferability of reasoning skills.
Takeaways: The variational framework unifies existing methods like Rejection Sampling Finetuning and binary-reward RL, showing they can be re-expressed as local forward KL optimizations implicitly weighted by model accuracy.
Common RL-style methods exhibit an unnoticed systematic bias towards easier questions, as their optimization inherently prioritizes problems where the model already performs well.

An accuracy-based estimator for the probability of a correct answer given a thought process is theoretically and empirically superior, offering lower variance and more robust training compared to likelihood-based methods.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.21128.Title: RL Squeezes, SFT Expands: A Comparative Study of Reasoning LLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.21128.Summary: Researchers from The University of Tokyo quantitatively compared reasoning in large language models after Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning (RL), establishing that RL prunes incorrect reasoning paths and concentrates functionality, while SFT expands the diversity of correct trajectories and distributes functional importance. This work provides a mechanistic explanation for the empirical success of combined SFT+RL training strategies in enhancing LLM reasoning.
Problem: Existing research predominantly relies on outcome-based metrics like Pass@k, overlooking the qualitative changes in the underlying reasoning processes of LLMs.
The distinct and complementary roles of SFT and RL in shaping LLM reasoning mechanisms remain largely unclarified, leading to 'trial-and-error' approaches in current training methodologies.
A debate persists regarding whether RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) develops new reasoning capabilities or primarily elicits existing ones from pre-trained base models.
Method: The authors developed a novel analytical framework to investigate LLM reasoning paths at two granularities: a trajectory-level analysis and a step-level analysis.
Trajectory-level analysis involved clustering unique correct and incorrect reasoning outputs based on character n-gram similarity (chrF) to quantify their diversity.

Step-level analysis constructed 'reasoning graphs' by segmenting responses into logical expressions, embedding them into a shared space, and then analyzing their global topological properties and local graphlet structures.
Results: RL consistently reduced the number of unique incorrect trajectories and, notably, also reduced the number of unique correct trajectories, which helps explain why base models might outperform RL models at high Pass@k values.

RL models exhibited significantly steeper exponential decay rates (e.g., ~2.5 times higher than Base models) for reasoning graph metrics, indicating a concentration of key functionalities into fewer steps.

SFT models showed flatter decay rates (e.g., reduced to about one-third of Base models), signifying a more uniform distribution of reasoning functionalities and a shift from modular to globally connected graph structures.
Takeaways: RL 'squeezes' reasoning by pruning incorrect trajectories and concentrating functional importance into a smaller, more specialized subset of reasoning steps, leading to a hub-centralized graph structure.

SFT 'expands' reasoning by increasing the diversity of correct trajectories and distributing functional importance more uniformly across a broader range of reasoning steps, creating a globally connected graph.

The two-stage SFT+RL procedure achieves maximal Pass@1 performance by first leveraging SFT to expand the repertoire of correct solution paths, then using RL to effectively compress and eliminate incorrect ones.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.20357.Title: Language Models that Think, Chat Better
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.20357.Summary: Princeton University researchers developed Reinforcement Learning with Model-rewarded Thinking (RLMT), an approach that enables large language models to employ explicit reasoning for diverse, open-ended conversational tasks. An 8B parameter model trained with RLMT achieved a 58.7 score on AlpacaEval2 and 50.4 on WildBench, outperforming larger 70B models and, in some cases, even frontier models like GPT-4o on chat and creative writing benchmarks.
Problem: Existing Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) models, despite strong performance in specific domains like math and code, demonstrate limited generalization of their reasoning abilities to open-ended, subjective tasks.
Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle to engage in robust, human-like "system 2 thinking" for diverse, general-purpose chat and creative problem-solving.
Current LLM alignment methods like RLHF primarily optimize final outputs, often neglecting to explicitly encourage or optimize the internal reasoning processes that lead to high-quality responses.
Method: RLMT trains LLMs to generate an explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning trace prior to the final response, extending structured thinking to general conversational tasks.

This approach leverages a preference-based reward model to evaluate the final response, enabling supervision for thinking in subjective, open-ended domains where rule-based verification is impractical.

The framework was evaluated with various online RL algorithms, with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) demonstrating superior performance, and tested on models both with and without initial Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT).
Results: RLMT models consistently outperformed RLHF baselines by 1.5–4 points across benchmarks, achieving average gains of 3–8 points in chat and creative writing tasks.

The top 8B RLMT model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with GRPO) scored 58.7 on AlpacaEval2 and 50.4 on WildBench, surpassing 70B instruction-tuned models by 9–22 points and outperforming GPT-4o on specific general chat and creative writing benchmarks.

Applying RLMT directly to base models without prior Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) yielded substantial improvements, with Llama-3.1-8B-Base-RLMT outperforming its SFT-trained counterpart by 5.5 points on chat benchmarks.
Takeaways: Reinforcement Learning with Model-rewarded Thinking (RLMT) effectively bridges the generalization gap of prior reasoning-focused methods by applying explicit Chain-of-Thought training to subjective, open-ended domains.

The research indicates that superior performance in general chat and creative tasks is not solely dependent on model scale, as smaller models with RLMT can outperform significantly larger and frontier LLMs.
RLMT demonstrates the potential to simplify the LLM post-training pipeline, achieving strong results by directly training base models without extensive Supervised Fine-Tuning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.19349.Title: ShinkaEvolve: Towards Open-Ended And Sample-Efficient Program Evolution
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.19349.Summary: ShinkaEvolve combines large language models with advanced evolutionary computation to create an open-source framework for efficient, open-ended program discovery. This approach achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse tasks while dramatically reducing the number of computational evaluations required.
Problem: Existing LLM-driven program evolution methods are sample-inefficient, demanding thousands of evaluations and incurring substantial computational costs and execution times.
Many leading LLM-based code evolution systems remain closed-source, which hinders reproducibility, limits community adoption, and restricts scientific collaboration and extensions.
Method: An adaptive parent and LLM sampling strategy balances exploration and exploitation, leveraging an archive of evaluated programs and an island model for diversity.
Code Novelty Rejection Sampling uses embeddings and an LLM-as-judge to prevent redundant evaluations of semantically similar program proposals, improving efficiency.
A bandit-based adaptive LLM ensemble dynamically prioritizes models based on their relative improvement contributions, complemented by a meta-scratchpad for online refinement and knowledge diffusion.
Results: Achieved a new state-of-the-art solution for the 26-circle packing problem using only 150 program evaluations, an improvement of orders of magnitude over prior methods.
Evolved agent scaffolds for AIME mathematical reasoning problems that significantly outperformed hand-designed baselines, demonstrating strong generalization to unseen tasks.
Improved high-performing C++ solutions for 10 competitive programming tasks (ALE-Bench) by an average of 2.3%, with one solution potentially ranking second on the AtCoder leaderboard.
Discovered a novel load balancing loss function for Mixture-of-Experts LLMs that yielded lower perplexity and improved downstream task performance on a 2.7B-parameter model.
Takeaways: Systematically balancing exploration and exploitation through weighted sampling and adaptive LLM prioritization is crucial for achieving high sample efficiency in evolutionary search.
The iterative composition of "stepping stones"—suboptimal intermediate solutions—is a vital mechanism for reaching complex, high-quality solutions in program evolution.
Integrating robust novelty assessment, such as code embedding-based rejection, dramatically improves efficiency by filtering out redundant program explorations before evaluation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.15194.Title: Evolving Language Models without Labels: Majority Drives Selection, Novelty Promotes Variation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.15194.Summary: EVOL-RL introduces an evolutionary, label-free reinforcement learning framework for large language models, mitigating the prevalent 'entropy collapse' by balancing majority-driven selection with novelty-promoting variation. The Tencent AI Lab and University of Notre Dame collaboration achieves over 20 percentage points improvement in pass@16 accuracy on challenging benchmarks and robust out-of-domain generalization.
Problem: Existing label-free LLM self-improvement methods, like Test-Time Reinforcement Learning (TTRL), suffer from 'entropy collapse' due to over-reliance on self-confirmation signals, suppressing solution diversity.
This leads to degraded `pass@n` performance, shorter reasoning chains, and a loss of exploratory capability, hindering long-term autonomous learning.
The challenge is to enable LLMs to continuously self-improve without ground-truth labels while maintaining robust diversity and avoiding premature convergence.
Method: EVOL-RL proposes a framework based on Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), guided by a novel three-part reward function inspired by biological evolution.

The reward function incorporates validity checks, majority-based selection for correctness, and a semantically-aware novelty incentive for reasoning paths, with separate normalization for majority and minority groups.
Supporting mechanisms include asymmetric clipping in GRPO and a token-level entropy regularizer to further promote diversity and preserve beneficial 'mutation' signals.
Results: EVOL-RL consistently and substantially improves `pass@16` performance over TTRL, with gains often exceeding 20 percentage points on challenging benchmarks like AIME24, and enhances `pass@1` accuracy.

The method demonstrates strong cross-difficulty robustness and out-of-domain generalization, transferring learned reasoning skills effectively across mathematical and non-mathematical tasks (e.g., GPQA).

Ablation studies confirm the critical role of the novelty reward and exploration mechanisms in fostering long-term performance and maintaining diversity, even providing synergistic benefits to supervised RLVR.
Takeaways: Label-free self-improvement requires explicitly balancing 'selection' (reinforcing majority consensus) with 'variation' (promoting novel reasoning paths) to prevent degenerative feedback loops.
The novelty reward creates an inherently unstable state for uniform solution populations, continuously driving the policy away from homogeneity and promoting diverse reasoning.

Entropy collapse observed in majority-only methods is not permanent; EVOL-RL demonstrates a distinct 'evolving point' after which policy entropy and reasoning length recover, leading to sustained performance gains.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.15172.Title: Internalizing Self-Consistency in Language Models: Multi-Agent Consensus Alignment
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.15172.Summary: Researchers at Meta AI and collaborating institutions developed Multi-Agent Consensus Alignment (MACA), a post-training framework that internalizes self-consistency in large language models by leveraging self-generated debate signals. This approach significantly boosts reasoning accuracy and generalization across various benchmarks, with preference learning methods achieving up to +23.7% on MATH.
Problem: Large language models often generate inconsistent or contradictory responses, especially under stochastic sampling, due to a lack of intrinsic reasoning stability.
Existing inference-time methods for consistency, such as self-consistency prompting, only aggregate or refine outputs externally without modifying the model's internal reasoning policy.
The absence of a framework to formally establish and optimize self-consistency as an intrinsic property hinders the development of fundamentally reliable and trustworthy LLMs.
Method: Introduces Multi-Agent Consensus Alignment (MACA), a reinforcement learning framework that simulates multi-agent debates to generate rich, self-supervised training signals.
Utilizes multi-round debates among cloned LLM agents where peers observe and update their reasoning, producing consensus-supporting and dissenting trajectories.
Applies four post-training objectives (MV-SFT, MV-GRPO, MV-DPO, MV-KTO) to learn from these self-generated preference signals, guiding the model to inherently favor consistent reasoning pathways.
Results: MACA improved single-agent zero-shot accuracy by up to +23.7% on MATH (Llama-8B) and +22.71% on GSM8K (Qwen-2B) compared to baselines.
Unanimous multi-agent debate agreement (3/3 agents) on GSM8K tripled for Qwen-2B, increasing from 13.4% to 43.4%, while non-parseable responses significantly decreased.
Demonstrated strong generalization, boosting performance on unseen benchmarks such as GPQA (+16.3% for Qwen2B) and CommonsenseQA (+11.6% for Llama3B) after mathematical reasoning training.
Takeaways: Self-generated consensus signals from multi-agent debates provide effective supervision for LLM alignment, often performing comparably to or surpassing oracle ground-truth supervision.
Internalizing self-consistency through post-training fundamentally enhances reasoning capabilities, leading to robust generalization across diverse, unseen tasks beyond the training domain.

Preference learning methods like DPO and KTO are particularly effective at leveraging debate-derived signals to modify model policy, fostering increased decisiveness, conciseness, and peer insight utilization.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.15155.Title: Self-Improving Embodied Foundation Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.15155.Summary: Researchers from Google DeepMind developed a two-stage post-training framework that integrates online reinforcement learning with embodied foundation models, utilizing the model's self-predicted "steps-to-go" as a data-driven reward signal. This approach allows robots to autonomously refine existing skills and acquire novel behaviors, demonstrating substantial performance gains and superior sample efficiency across various robotic tasks.
Problem: Embodied Foundation Models (EFMs) relying solely on behavioral cloning are limited to imitating demonstrated behaviors and struggle with acquiring novel skills or improving beyond initial data.
The 'reward engineering problem' poses a significant challenge for applying reinforcement learning (RL) to real-world robotics, requiring complex and often task-specific reward functions.
Current EFM training paradigms lack the crucial RL-tuning stage, a method that has proven highly effective in boosting performance for large language models (LLMs).
Method: A two-stage post-training framework combines initial supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with an auxiliary objective of predicting 'steps-to-go' to a given goal.
An online reinforcement learning stage is introduced where the EFM autonomously improves using a self-predicted, data-driven reward function derived from its 'steps-to-go' predictions.
The system uses a robust success detector based on thresholding the predicted 'steps-to-go', eliminating the need for manual reward engineering or external success labels.
Results: Self-improvement consistently boosted policy success rates; for example, from approximately 62-63% to 87-88% on real-world LanguageTable tasks.

The method demonstrated superior sample efficiency, with policies trained on 10% of imitation data plus 1% additional robot interaction time outperforming behavioral cloning policies trained on 80% of the imitation dataset.

Multimodal foundation model pretraining was essential for effective and sample-efficient self-improvement, enabling the acquisition of novel skills such as effectively manipulating a banana (BananaTable task) with success rates increasing from ~63% to ~85%.
Takeaways: Large foundation models can leverage their learned representations to self-generate dense and well-shaped reward signals and success detectors, addressing a major hurdle in robot reinforcement learning.

Combining web-scale foundation model pretraining with a minimal amount of online self-improvement data dramatically enhances sample efficiency, outperforming models trained with significantly more imitation data alone.

The framework enables embodied agents to learn genuinely novel behaviors and generalize effectively to tasks not present in their initial training datasets, pushing beyond semantic understanding to behavioral adaptation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.14760.Title: Reasoning over Boundaries: Enhancing Specification Alignment via Test-time Deliberation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.14760.Summary: Researchers introduce "specification alignment" to address large language models' adherence to dynamic, scenario-specific behavioral and safety requirements. They propose ALIGN3, a lightweight test-time deliberation method, and SPECBENCH, a unified evaluation benchmark, demonstrating ALIGN3 improves Specification Alignment Rate (SAR) by up to 11.89% for models like Qwen3-14B with minimal computational cost.
Problem: Current LLM alignment methods often fail to adhere to dynamic, fine-grained, and scenario-specific behavioral and safety requirements in real-world applications.
Prior instruction-following research focuses on isolated or single-constraint instructions, lacking the complexity required for real-world, scenario-level tasks.
Existing safety alignment approaches utilize uniform standards across contexts, proving inflexible and costly to adapt to evolving, scenario-dependent safety boundaries.
Method: Formalized "specification alignment" as the ability of LLMs to satisfy dynamic, scenario-specific safety and behavioral specifications, highlighting the inherent safety-behavior trade-off.
Developed ALIGN3, a lightweight, three-step Test-Time Deliberation (TTD) method, which integrates specifications into the LLM's reasoning process during inference to enhance alignment.
Created SPECBENCH, a unified benchmark encompassing five diverse real-world scenarios with 103 specifications and attack-enhanced prompts, for comprehensive evaluation of specification alignment.
Results: The SPECBENCH benchmark revealed substantial alignment gaps across current LLMs, with most models scoring below 65% in Specification Alignment Rate (SAR), while GPT-5-chat achieved the highest SAR at 82.14%.

ALIGN3 significantly boosted SAR by up to 11.89% (e.g., Qwen3-14B from 51.03% to 62.92%) across various LLMs, achieving superior performance among TTD methods with minimal token overhead (< 2,000 tokens).

Reasoning-capable LLMs consistently outperformed their instruct-tuned counterparts in SAR, and models trained for safety often showed high safety scores but lower behavioral scores, demonstrating the safety-behavior trade-off.
Takeaways: Test-Time Deliberation (TTD) methods can be effectively extended beyond cognitive tasks to significantly enhance LLM adherence to complex, multi-faceted behavioral and safety specifications during inference.

An inherent trade-off exists between maximizing an LLM's helpfulness and ensuring its harmlessness, where optimizing one dimension often impacts the other, revealing over-refusal or safety violations.
Models with explicit internal reasoning capabilities (e.g., Chain-of-Thought) consistently outperform instruct-tuned models in understanding and adhering to complex alignment specifications.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.14252.Title: LLM-JEPA: Large Language Models Meet Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.14252.Summary: LLM-JEPA introduces a Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA)-based training objective for Large Language Models, enhancing fine-tuning and pretraining by improving accuracy, robustness against overfitting, and fostering more structured abstract representations. This method achieved superior performance across models like Llama, Gemma, and OpenELM on datasets including NL-RX-SYNTH, GSM8K, and Spider, while mitigating computational costs with a novel 'loss dropout' mechanism.
Problem: A methodological gap exists between vision and language model training, where vision tasks benefit from JEPAs for robust representation learning, but language tasks predominantly rely on reconstruction-based generative objectives.

Current LLM training, focused on generative capabilities like next-token prediction, may not optimally foster the abstract and robust representations needed for complex reasoning and perception tasks.
Generative models can be computationally intensive due to full input-space reconstruction and may inadvertently learn biases from surface-level features.
Method: Introduced LLM-JEPA, a novel training objective that combines the standard autoregressive language modeling loss with a Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) loss.
Designed the JEPA component to leverage 'multi-view' data (e.g., natural language descriptions and corresponding code or paraphrases) by predicting embeddings of one view from another.

Implemented the JEPA objective with minimal architectural overhead by reusing the LLM's internal transformer layers as both encoder and predictor, facilitated by a special `[PRED]` token and custom attention mask, and introduced 'loss dropout' to reduce computational cost.
Results: Achieved consistent and statistically significant accuracy improvements across various models (e.g., Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, Gemma-2-2b-it) and datasets (e.g., NL-RX-SYNTH, GSM8K, Spider) in fine-tuning, with enhanced robustness against overfitting.

Demonstrated encouraging results in pretraining, leading to improved representation quality and better downstream task performance (e.g., statistically significant improvements on Rotten Tomatoes and Yelp sentiment classification) while maintaining generative abilities.
The 'loss dropout' technique effectively reduced computational overhead by up to 50% for LD=0.5 and enabled faster convergence and higher accuracy under equivalent compute budgets.
Takeaways: Minimizing the standard autoregressive LLM loss does not implicitly minimize the JEPA objective, underscoring the explicit need for a JEPA term to learn robust and abstract representations.
LLM-JEPA induces a clearer, more structured organization in the latent space, making mappings between different views (e.g., Text and Code) approximately linear and confined to a narrow subspace.
The JEPA objective functions as a powerful regularization and representation-structuring mechanism, complementing LLMs' generative capabilities without diminishing them.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.14234.Title: Compute as Teacher: Turning Inference Compute Into Reference-Free Supervision
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.14234.Summary: A new method, Compute as Teacher (CaT), generates supervision signals for large language models in post-training scenarios lacking traditional ground truth or programmatic verifiers. It leverages inference compute to synthesize reference-free supervision, leading to relative performance increases of up to 33% on MATH-500 and 30% on HealthBench.
Problem: Post-training large language models (LLMs) often lack sufficient human-labeled reference data or external programmatic verifiers for specialized tasks.
This data scarcity is particularly acute in "non-verifiable" domains like creative writing or open-ended dialogue, where objective ground truth is elusive.
Existing alternatives like costly human annotation or LLM-as-a-judge methods suffer from inconsistencies and can introduce biases.
Method: Compute as Teacher (CaT) synthesizes a high-quality reference by leveraging multiple parallel rollouts generated by the current policy for a given prompt.
A frozen anchor policy then integrates evidence from these rollouts to construct an improved reference response, without seeing the original prompt.

This synthesized reference is converted into reward signals (binary for verifiable tasks, rubric-based for non-verifiable tasks) to fine-tune the policy using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO).
Results: CaT-RL consistently improved model performance across tasks, achieving up to 33% relative gain on MATH-500 and 30% on HealthBench for Llama 3.1 8B, surpassing the initial policy and its own inference-time teacher signal.

Self-proposed rubrics for non-verifiable tasks were highly effective, outperforming direct LLM-as-a-judge methods and demonstrating quality comparable to, or sometimes exceeding, human expert annotations.

CaT exhibited a unique self-correction ability, producing correct answers that disagreed with all of the initial rollouts it was conditioned on in approximately 1% of questions, demonstrating its generative power beyond simple selection.
Takeaways: CaT synthesizes entirely new reference answers by reconciling multiple rollouts, enabling it to correct errors even when individual model generations are flawed or disagree with the majority.

For non-verifiable tasks, the method uses self-proposed rubrics, decomposing complex judgments into atomic, verifiable criteria, which leads to more robust and less biased reward signals than direct LLM judging.
The approach fosters a virtuous learning cycle where an improving policy generates higher quality rollouts, leading to better synthesized supervision and further model enhancement.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.13351.Title: Teaching LLMs to Plan: Logical Chain-of-Thought Instruction Tuning for Symbolic Planning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.13351.Summary: PDDL-INSTRUCT introduces an instruction tuning framework that enhances Large Language Models' symbolic planning capabilities by integrating explicit logical chain-of-thought reasoning. The approach leads to substantially improved plan validity and accuracy across multiple planning domains, demonstrating up to a 66% absolute improvement over baseline LLMs in plan accuracy.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) often fail to perform rigorous, multi-step logical reasoning required for automated symbolic planning, leading to unreliable plan generation.
Current LLM-based planning approaches lack intrinsic mechanisms for systematically verifying action preconditions, effects, and overall plan validity.
Applying Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting alone has not been consistently sufficient to impart the logical rigor needed for robust formal planning in LLMs.
Method: Introduces PDDL-INSTRUCT, a three-phase instruction tuning framework, to teach LLMs explicit logical Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning for symbolic planning.
Incorporates an iterative training loop that leverages an external PDDL plan validator (VAL) to provide ground-truth feedback on action validity and state transitions.
Utilizes a two-stage optimization process focusing on improving reasoning chain quality and end-task planning performance, with an emphasis on detailed error feedback.
Results: PDDL-INSTRUCT improved plan accuracy by an average of 66% absolute percentage points over baseline LLMs, achieving up to 94% validity for Llama-3 and 91% for GPT-4 in Blocksworld.
Detailed feedback on logical errors consistently outperformed binary feedback, leading to up to a 15 percentage point increase in plan accuracy across domains.

The approach demonstrated strong generalization and substantial improvements across diverse planning domains, including a 64-fold accuracy increase for Llama-3 in the complex Mystery Blocksworld domain.
Takeaways: Explicitly integrating logical Chain-of-Thought reasoning into LLM instruction tuning, combined with external validation, is effective in teaching formal symbolic planning.
Providing detailed feedback on specific logical errors during training leads to more robust planning capabilities in LLMs compared to binary validity feedback.
The method demonstrates strong cross-domain generalization, substantially improving planning accuracy and robustness even in complex and diverse planning scenarios.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.12132.Title: Look Again, Think Slowly: Enhancing Visual Reflection in Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.12132.Summary: A two-stage training strategy, Reflection-V, enhances visual reflection in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) by first generating vision-centered reasoning data and then applying reinforcement learning with a visual attention-based reward. This approach significantly improves reasoning performance across various benchmarks, reduces visual hallucinations, and enables 7B-scale models to achieve performance competitive with much larger proprietary and open-source models.
Problem: While large language models (LLMs) excel at iterative 'slow-thinking' reasoning, transferring this capability to Vision-Language Models (VLMs) often results in a superficial understanding that relies on image descriptions rather than direct visual interaction.
Existing Vision Reasoning Models (VRMs) exhibit 'textual hallucinations and visual neglect,' with their attention to visual information rapidly diminishing as reasoning chains lengthen.
Traditional reinforcement learning techniques, when applied to VRMs, can inadvertently reinforce an over-reliance on previously generated text, further detaching models from actual visual content.
Method: A two-stage training strategy, Reflection-V, is proposed to embed and reinforce visual reflection capabilities in VRMs.

The first stage involves a 'cold-start' initialization using specially constructed reasoning data with visual reflection, generated via orchestrated LLM-VLM interaction to ensure continuous visual access and re-checking.

The second stage fine-tunes the VRM with Reinforcement Learning (using GRPO), incorporating a novel visual attention-based reward that specifically encourages sustained attention to visual tokens throughout the generated response, provided the answer is correct.
Results: Reflection-V-7B achieved superior performance across mathematical, multi-disciplinary, and general reasoning benchmarks (e.g., MathVision, MathVista, MMMU), outperforming state-of-the-art open-source vision-language reasoning models.

The model demonstrated competitive or superior performance compared to significantly larger proprietary models like GPT-4o and GPT-4V, as well as large open-source models such as InternVL2.5-38B and LLaVA-OneVision-72B on various tasks.

Reflection-V significantly reduced visual hallucinations on the HallBench dataset and maintained consistently higher visual attention and dependency throughout reasoning processes, exhibiting explicit 'Aha moments' of visual re-engagement.
Takeaways: True 'slow-thinking' in visual contexts requires active visual reflection, where models critically re-evaluate and refine reasoning steps based on the visual input itself, not just textual descriptions.

Current VRMs suffer from a quantifiable deficiency in sustained visual attention and dependency, which can even be exacerbated by traditional RL methods that do not specifically incentivize visual grounding.

Explicitly designing training data to embed visual reflection patterns and developing a targeted visual attention-based reward function are crucial for mitigating visual neglect and hallucinations, leading to more robust multimodal reasoning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.11452.Title: Learning to Optimize Multi-Objective Alignment Through Dynamic Reward Weighting
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.11452.Summary: This research introduces dynamic reward weighting mechanisms for multi-objective alignment of large language models (LLMs) during online reinforcement learning. The methods, which include hypervolume-guided and gradient-based approaches, enable LLMs to achieve superior Pareto fronts across multiple objectives like accuracy, conciseness, and clarity, while also demonstrating faster convergence rates.
Problem: Fixed-weight linear reward scalarization in multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL) is theoretically limited, unable to capture non-convex regions of the Pareto front in complex, stochastic online RL for LLMs.

Different objectives in LLM alignment (e.g., accuracy, conciseness, clarity) often have varying learning difficulties and saturation points, leading to inefficient resource allocation with static weighting schemes.
Heuristic rules for combining objectives lack flexibility and generalizability, requiring significant manual effort for new tasks or domains.
Method: Developed hypervolume-guided weight adaptation, which uses a meta-reward based on hypervolume contribution to amplify scalarized rewards, proactively pushing the Pareto front in desired directions when human preferences are available.

Introduced gradient-based weight optimization, dynamically adjusting objective weights using an 'influence signal' derived from per-objective gradients, effectively reallocating learning effort towards objectives with greater potential.
Integrated these dynamic weighting mechanisms with standard online RL algorithms (GRPO, REINFORCE, RLOO) and validated them on mathematical reasoning tasks with various LLM architectures.
Results: Hypervolume-guided weight adaptation consistently achieved Pareto dominant solutions, often outperforming fixed-weight baselines in average scores across accuracy, conciseness, and clarity simultaneously.
The gradient-based weight optimization consistently yielded superior Pareto fronts, largely dominating baselines across GRPO, REINFORCE, and RLOO training setups.

Dynamic weighting methods demonstrated improved training efficiency, with the gradient-based method reducing the average number of training steps to reach Pareto fronts by 8.9 steps for GRPO and 8.2 steps for RLOO.
Takeaways: Dynamic reward weighting methods consistently achieve Pareto dominant solutions that are unattainable by static, fixed-weight scalarization approaches in multi-objective LLM alignment.

The gradient-based approach dynamically adjusts weights based on individual objective learning contributions, revealing that objectives like conciseness saturate quickly, while accuracy requires sustained learning, and clarity is synergistic with accuracy.
Careful calibration of meta-rewards is necessary for stability, as overly aggressive exploration in hypervolume-guided methods can lead to suboptimal performance.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.09284.Title: Tree-OPO: Off-policy Monte Carlo Tree-Guided Advantage Optimization for Multistep Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.09284.Summary: Tree-OPO introduces a framework that enhances large language model reasoning by integrating MCTS-derived partial trajectories with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), leveraging a novel Staged Advantage Estimation (SAE) method. This approach allows a Qwen2.5-1.5B model to achieve 77.63% accuracy on the GSM8K mathematical reasoning benchmark.
Problem: Standard on-policy reinforcement learning methods are inefficient for complex, multi-step reasoning tasks due to sparse rewards and high sample costs.
The rich, structured information from Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) rollouts, particularly partial trajectories, is underutilized for direct policy improvement in Large Language Models (LLMs).

Group-based reinforcement learning struggles to compute meaningful advantages when training samples originate from heterogeneous prefixes with disparate expected returns within a reasoning tree, leading to biased gradients and increased variance.
Method: Tree-OPO extends GRPO by creating a reverse curriculum from offline, teacher-generated MCTS prefixes, which are then used for online student policy rollouts.
It introduces Staged Advantage Estimation (SAE), a constrained quadratic program, to calculate prefix-aware advantages by incorporating tree-consistency inductive biases.

Efficient heuristic baselines, such as the Empirical (Expectation) baseline, are employed to approximate prefix-conditioned advantages, reducing computational intensity while maintaining effective learning signals.
Results: Tree-OPO, particularly with the Empirical (Expectation) heuristic, achieved the highest accuracy of 77.63% on GSM8K, outperforming standard GRPO (76.27%) and other variants.
The SAE (Soft Constraints) formulation demonstrated improved stability and performance (77.41%) compared to hard constraints, validating the theoretical convex formulation for advantage estimation.

The framework enables a smaller student model (Qwen2.5-1.5B) to achieve strong reasoning performance comparable to or exceeding larger models or more resource-intensive training regimes, highlighting its efficiency.
Takeaways: MCTS-derived partial trajectories can be effectively repurposed for *direct policy learning* in an off-policy setting, providing a structured supervision signal beyond just reward modeling or inference.

Explicitly accounting for prefix-conditioned values and hierarchical relationships within reasoning trees (via SAE) is crucial for stable and efficient advantage estimation in staged learning environments.

The 'Empirical (Expectation)' heuristic for SAE, which accurately estimates the empirical success rate of subtrees, offers the most effective and stable learning signal for policy optimization in this context.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.08827.Title: A Survey of Reinforcement Learning for Large Reasoning Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.08827.Summary: This survey paper systematically synthesizes advancements in Reinforcement Learning (RL) for Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), moving beyond human alignment to focus on enhancing intrinsic reasoning capabilities through verifiable rewards. It identifies key components, challenges, and future directions for scaling RL towards Artificial SuperIntelligence (ASI).
Problem: The rapid success of RL in transforming LLMs into LRMs faces significant hurdles concerning computational resources, optimal algorithm design, and scalable, high-quality training data.
Existing RL applications for LLMs primarily focused on human alignment, neglecting the potential of RL to fundamentally improve complex reasoning abilities.
A lack of a unified framework to understand and navigate the complex, rapidly evolving landscape of RL for reasoning models hinders systematic research and development.
Method: The authors conduct a comprehensive literature review, systematizing the field into foundational components: reward design, policy optimization, and sampling strategies.
The survey introduces and emphasizes "Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR)" as a key paradigm for enhancing reasoning in tasks with objective feedback.
It identifies and discusses foundational problems and ongoing debates, such as RL's role in "sharpening vs. discovery" and the interplay between RL and Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT).
Results: The survey demonstrates RL's broad impact across diverse applications, including coding, agentic tasks, multimodal understanding, robotics, and medical applications, achieving superior performance compared to non-RL methods.
Analysis of foundational problems reveals that RL can enable "discovery" of new capabilities beyond mere "sharpening," and hybrid SFT+RL paradigms often yield the best generalization.
Future research directions include continual RL, memory-based RL, and model-based RL, alongside architectural co-design and applications to pre-training and scientific discovery.
Takeaways: RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) provides a scalable path to improve complex reasoning in LLMs, especially for tasks like math and coding, by leveraging automated feedback.
Effective RL for LRMs relies on a careful combination of dense/unsupervised rewards, efficient off-policy optimization, and dynamic/structured sampling strategies.
The field is shifting from static datasets to dynamic environments and robust open-source infrastructure, which are crucial for scaling RL training for reasoning tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.07980.Title: Parallel-R1: Towards Parallel Thinking via Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.07980.Summary: Parallel-R1, a reinforcement learning framework developed by a collaborative team including Tencent AI Lab Seattle, teaches large language models to perform parallel thinking for complex mathematical reasoning tasks. The method effectively addresses cold-start challenges and achieves robust performance gains, including a 42.9% improvement on the AIME25 benchmark by utilizing parallel thinking as a mid-training exploration scaffold.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle to engage in "parallel thinking," which involves exploring multiple reasoning paths concurrently, a capability inspired by human cognition.

Existing methods, such as test-time strategies (e.g., CoT, ToT) or Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), are computationally intensive at inference or lead to superficial imitation, failing to instill intrinsic, generalizable parallel thinking.

Applying reinforcement learning (RL) to teach novel complex behaviors like parallel thinking faces a "cold-start" problem, where the model cannot initially generate the target behavior, and challenges in designing effective generalizable reward functions.
Method:
Parallel-R1 formalizes LLM parallel thinking into explicit exploration (generating N independent paths for a critical step) and summary phases, controlled by specific architectural tags (e.g., , ,
).

A scalable data pipeline generates high-quality parallel thinking data for easier problems (Parallel-GSM8K) to teach the model the format and basic behavior, effectively addressing the cold-start problem for subsequent RL.

The framework employs Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a progressive training curriculum, including a crucial Stage 1 RL on easy math to stabilize parallel thinking, followed by Stage 2 RL on general math with nuanced reward designs that balance task accuracy and explicit parallel behavior.
Results: Parallel-R1 consistently outperformed all baselines, with the Parallel-R1-Seen (causal) variant achieving the highest average score of 48.9 across mathematical reasoning benchmarks.

Stage 1 RL on GSM8K was crucial for causal models, improving performance by 2.3% on average, but was detrimental for structured models, indicating that attention masks learned on easy tasks do not generalize well to harder problems.

The "alternating accuracy and parallel" reward schedule for Parallel-R1-Unseen achieved a high parallel ratio (63.0%) while maintaining strong task performance, and as an exploration scaffold, it led to a 42.9% improvement on AIME25 over baseline GRPO models.
Takeaways: The progressive curriculum effectively overcomes the cold-start problem, enabling LLMs to learn structured reasoning behaviors from scratch, demonstrating that initial SFT for format followed by staged RL is a practical approach.

Analysis of LLM behavior during RL training reveals a strategic evolution: models shift from using parallel paths for early-stage computational exploration to late-stage multi-perspective verification as their core reasoning improves.

Parallel thinking can serve as a "mid-training exploration scaffold," where temporarily forcing diverse exploration during RL leads to higher performance ceilings even if the final policy relies less on explicit parallel structures.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.07979.Title: Visual Representation Alignment for Multimodal Large Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.07979.Summary: Researchers from KAIST AI and collaborators introduced VIsual Representation ALignment (VIRAL), a novel regularization strategy that directly supervises the visual pathway in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by aligning internal representations with Vision Foundation Models. This approach prevents the loss of fine-grained visual information, leading to consistent performance improvements of up to 17.3% on specific vision-centric tasks and a 9.4% average gain over baselines like LLaVA-1.5.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) often underperform on vision-centric tasks demanding fine-grained visual understanding and are prone to visual hallucinations.
The dominant text-only supervision paradigm for MLLMs indirectly supervises the visual pathway, leading to the loss of critical fine-grained visual information within the model.
Internal visual representations in MLLMs exhibit "visual representation misalignment," diverging significantly from initial vision encoder features in deeper layers.
Method: A regularization strategy named VIsual Representation ALignment (VIRAL) is introduced to directly supervise the internal visual pathway of MLLMs.

VIRAL aligns the MLLM's intermediate visual representations with features extracted from a robust pre-trained Vision Foundation Model (VFM) using a learnable projection and a negative cosine similarity loss.
This alignment is applied to specific intermediate layers of the MLLM, integrating rich, vision-centric knowledge from models like DINOv2 to prevent the loss of fine-grained visual details.
Results: VIRAL achieved consistent performance gains, with an average improvement of 9.4% over LLaVA-1.5 baselines and up to 17.3% on specific multimodal benchmarks.
The approach substantially enhanced vision-centric reasoning, showing over 5% gains on tasks like MMVP which demand fine-grained visual understanding.
VIRAL proved robust across diverse vision encoders and LLM backbones, demonstrating broad applicability and achieving faster convergence with only a 3% increase in training overhead.
Takeaways: MLLMs' reliance on text-only supervision causes them to implicitly discard fine-grained visual details, leading to limitations in vision-centric tasks.
Directly supervising internal visual pathways by aligning them with features from Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) like DINOv2 can effectively preserve detailed visual semantics.
Applying alignment loss at specific intermediate layers (e.g., the 16th layer of LLaVA-1.5) is critical for optimal visual information retention and processing within MLLMs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.07969.Title: Mini-o3: Scaling Up Reasoning Patterns and Interaction Turns for Visual Search
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.07969.Summary: Mini-o3, developed by ByteDance and The University of Hong Kong, significantly enhances open-source Vision-Language Models for complex visual search tasks by enabling multi-turn, exploratory reasoning and scaling interaction depth at inference. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on challenging benchmarks like VisualProbe-Hard, demonstrating its capacity for deeper thinking paths.
Problem: Current open-source Vision-Language Models (VLMs) exhibit monotonous reasoning patterns and allow only a limited number of interaction turns, hindering their performance on difficult visual search tasks.
Challenging visual problems requiring fine-grained perception, such as small targets or numerous distractors, demand iterative exploration and trial-and-error, which existing open-source models lack.
There is a notable gap between the advanced multi-turn reasoning and tool-use capabilities of proprietary models (e.g., OpenAI o3) and open-source alternatives.
Method: Mini-o3 utilizes an iterative Thought-Action-Observation loop, allowing the VLM to generate internal thoughts, execute grounding actions (e.g., zoom-in), and observe cropped image patches over multiple turns.
A two-phase training procedure combines Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on a dataset of diverse multi-turn trajectories with Reinforcement Learning (GRPO) using verifiable rewards to optimize policy.

The approach introduces the challenging VisualProbe dataset for complex visual search and employs a novel "over-turn masking" strategy during RL to enable deeper test-time reasoning without excessive training costs.
Results: Mini-o3 achieves state-of-the-art performance among 7B-sized open-source models, reaching 48.0% accuracy on VisualProbe-Hard, 50.4% on VisualProbe-Medium, and 67.0% on VisualProbe-Easy, significantly outperforming baselines like DeepEyes.

The model demonstrates the ability to naturally scale interaction turns at test time; accuracy on VisualProbe-Hard continues to improve as the upper limit on interaction turns increases from 4 to 32 during inference.

Ablation studies confirm the necessity of cold-start SFT, hard RL data, and over-turn masking for high performance and deep reasoning, with over-turn masking alone improving VisualProbe-Hard accuracy from 32.2% to 44.4% and increasing average turns for correct responses.
Takeaways: A "cold-start" Supervised Fine-Tuning phase is essential to bootstrap multi-turn agentic behaviors in VLMs, as base models lack intrinsic capabilities for long-horizon, interactive problem-solving.

The "over-turn masking" strategy effectively addresses the premature policy termination problem in RL, allowing models trained with limited turn budgets (e.g., 6 turns) to naturally scale to tens of turns at inference time with improved accuracy.

The design of challenging datasets, such as VisualProbe, featuring small targets, numerous distractors, and high-resolution images, is critical for training robust, exploratory visual agents capable of human-like iterative analysis.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.07414.Title: Language Self-Play For Data-Free Training
