https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.07414.Summary: Meta Superintelligence Labs developed Language Self-Play (LSP), a reinforcement learning framework that enables large language models to improve autonomously without external training data. LSP-trained models achieved performance comparable to or exceeding data-intensive methods on instruction-following, math, and coding benchmarks, with a self-rewarding mechanism crucial for stable and high-quality learning.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) face an increasing data bottleneck as continued improvements demand vast quantities of high-quality, complex training data.
Current LLM training paradigms, including supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) techniques, fundamentally depend on external query-answer pairs or prompts.
This data dependency creates a ceiling on model improvement and poses sustainability challenges for future AI scaling due to finite data resources.
Method: Language Self-Play (LSP) formulates LLM training as a competitive minimax game where a single pre-trained LLM acts as both a 'Challenger' (generating queries) and a 'Solver' (responding to them).

The training employs a Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) variant to update the model's parameters, using rewards derived from external reward models or verification for Solver answers and negative Solver performance for the Challenger.

A crucial self-rewarding mechanism is integrated, where the model itself evaluates the quality of interactions, preventing self-play degeneration and guiding the learning process towards meaningful, high-quality instruction-following.
Results: LSP achieved an AlpacaEval win rate of 36.4%, closely matching data-intensive GRPO (38.8%) and significantly outperforming the base Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct model (26.5%) without using any external training data.

The self-rewarding mechanism was critical for robust learning, improving LSP's performance by 4.4 percentage points (from LSP-Zero's 32.0% to LSP's 36.4%) and preventing adversarial nonsense generation.

When used as a pre-training stage (LSP+RL), performance on AlpacaEval further improved to 39.5%, surpassing standalone GRPO, demonstrating its effectiveness as a complementary component to traditional RL fine-tuning.
Takeaways: LLMs can achieve substantial performance gains through a data-free, autonomous self-play mechanism, generating their own learning curriculum and improving continuously.
Incorporating a quality self-reward within the self-play loop is essential to prevent learning degeneration, ensuring stable training and generation of coherent, high-quality interactions.

The Challenger-Solver dynamic effectively stress-tests and enhances the Solver's capabilities, particularly in open-ended and conversational tasks, by adaptively generating diverse and challenging prompts.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.06870.Title: The Majority is not always right: RL training for solution aggregation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.06870.Summary: Researchers at FAIR at Meta introduce AggLM, a method that fine-tunes a language model using Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) to synthesize a single solution from multiple LLM-generated candidates. AggLM consistently surpasses majority voting and reward-model-based selection on math reasoning benchmarks, demonstrating improved accuracy, token efficiency, and generalization across diverse solution models.
Problem: Standard majority voting methods for LLM-generated solutions often fail when the correct answer is a minority view among candidates, leading to overlooked valuable insights.
Existing model-based selection approaches (e.g., reward models) only pick the best candidate and cannot synthesize a novel, correct solution from partially accurate or complementary components.
Fixed heuristics for aggregating solutions lack the adaptive reasoning required to intelligently reconcile and combine diverse outputs from LLMs.
Method: AggLM (Aggregation Language Model) is trained using Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) to take a problem and multiple candidate solutions as input, then output a single, synthesized solution.

A carefully balanced training dataset is constructed by mixing 'hard' examples (where the majority candidate is incorrect) with 'easy' examples (where it's correct), enabling AggLM to learn both selection and synthesis skills.
AggLM is optimized using Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a binary reward signal for exact match to the ground-truth solution.
Results: AggLM-1.7B consistently outperforms majority voting and reward-model baselines by 3 to 7 percentage points on all four MathArena benchmarks.
The method demonstrates strong generalization, maintaining top performance when aggregating solutions from a stronger Qwen3-8B model or from non-thinking mode solutions.

AggLM achieves higher accuracy with superior token efficiency, using roughly one-third fewer tokens per inference compared to baselines relying on generating a larger number of samples for majority voting.
Takeaways: Aggregation can be learned as an explicit reasoning skill through RLVR, moving beyond fixed heuristics to intelligently review, reconcile, and synthesize information from multiple sources.
Balancing easy and hard examples in the training data is crucial for the aggregation model to effectively learn to recover minority-but-correct answers while also handling straightforward cases.
The learned aggregation skill generalizes robustly across different base models (weaker or stronger) and solution generation modes, indicating broad applicability.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.06806.Title: MachineLearningLM: Scaling Many-shot In-context Learning via Continued Pretraining
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.06806.Summary: A continued pretraining framework, MACHINELEARNINGLM, enhances a general-purpose LLM with robust many-shot in-context learning capabilities for tabular data, achieving monotonic accuracy scaling and performance comparable to Random Forest. The approach maintains the LLM's general knowledge while outperforming vanilla LLMs by 12-16% in high-shot tabular tasks.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle with effective many-shot in-context learning (ICL) for numerical tabular data, showing quick accuracy plateaus and sensitivity to example order.
Specialized tabular models (e.g., TabPFN) excel at tabular ICL but lack the broad world knowledge, general reasoning, and multimodal perception inherent in LLMs.
A gap exists in creating a unified model that combines the robust numerical modeling of specialized methods with the versatility and general intelligence of LLMs without performance degradation.
Method: A continued pretraining framework, MACHINELEARNINGLM, is applied to a general-purpose LLM (Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct) using LoRA, framing the task as conditional sequence modeling.
Millions of diverse, synthetic binary/multiclass tabular prediction tasks are generated from Structural Causal Models (SCMs) for pretraining, ensuring out-of-distribution generalization.

Token-efficient prompting strategies, including tabular encoding, compact integer representation, and sequence-level batch prediction, maximize the number of in-context examples within the context window.
Results: MACHINELEARNINGLM exhibits a striking monotonic many-shot scaling law, with accuracy increasing consistently from 8 to 1,024 in-context demonstrations, outperforming vanilla LLMs (e.g., GPT-5-mini by ~12%, o3-mini by ~16%) in high-shot settings.

The model achieves accuracy levels comparable to Random Forest (within 2% relative) and surpasses instance-based learners (kNN by >4% relative) on diverse tabular tasks, without task-specific fine-tuning.

Continued pretraining successfully preserves the LLM's general knowledge and reasoning abilities, demonstrating comparable performance to its strong base model on the MMLU benchmark (e.g., 73.2% 0-shot, 75.4% 50-shot).
Takeaways: Training on diverse synthetic tasks derived from SCMs effectively instills tree-inductive biases and robust numerical modeling capabilities into an LLM.
Token-efficient encoding and batch prediction significantly overcome LLM context length limitations, allowing an order of magnitude more demonstrations and improved throughput.
A Random Forest mimic warm-start stabilizes training, and confidence-aware, order-robust self-consistency at inference time improves prediction accuracy and mitigates position bias.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.06040.Title: BranchGRPO: Stable and Efficient GRPO with Structured Branching in Diffusion Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.06040.Summary: BranchGRPO introduces a tree-structured policy optimization framework for generative diffusion and flow models, which significantly enhances human preference alignment while boosting training efficiency. The method achieved up to a 4.7x speedup in training time and improved alignment scores on HPS-v2.1 by up to 16% over existing Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) variants.
Problem: Existing GRPO methods suffer from computational inefficiency due to sequential, independent rollouts for each generated sample, leading to O(N*T) complexity.
Sparse terminal rewards, uniformly assigned across all denoising steps, result in unreliable credit assignment and unstable optimization for diffusion models.
Traditional GRPO struggles to attribute outcome rewards to specific intermediate denoising steps that critically shape final output quality.
Method: A tree-structured branching rollout algorithm replaces sequential rollouts, allowing early denoising steps to be shared across multiple diverging trajectories for computational efficiency.
A novel reward fusion and depth-wise advantage estimation method transforms sparse terminal rewards into dense, step-level signals, improving credit assignment.
Structured pruning strategies (width and depth pruning) are applied during backpropagation to selectively reduce gradient computation and accelerate training.
Results: BranchGRPO achieved a 4.7x speedup in training time over DanceGRPO, with its best variant reducing per-iteration time to 148s while increasing HPS-v2.1 alignment scores from 0.360 to 0.369.
Qualitatively, BranchGRPO generated images with sharper details and better semantic alignment, and produced more temporally consistent and coherent videos than baseline models.

The method maintained high sample diversity and demonstrated a favorable scaling law, with increased branching factors and steps consistently leading to higher reward growth and better final performance.
Takeaways: Restructuring the generative process into a tree enables efficient exploration and computational amortization by sharing early denoising prefixes.
Propagating and normalizing aggregated rewards backward through the tree provides finer-grained, more stable, and balanced advantage signals for policy optimization.
Strategic pruning of gradients during backpropagation can significantly speed up training without compromising the forward rollout's exploration breadth.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.04501.Title: Understanding Reinforcement Learning for Model Training, and future directions with GRAPE
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.04501.Summary: Rohit Patel, independently of Meta Superintelligence Labs, clarifies core Reinforcement Learning for Model Training algorithms for Large Language Models with a detailed, intuitive exposition. The work also proposes GRAPE (Generalized Relative Advantage Policy Evolution), a framework for LLM alignment that integrates AI feedback and process supervision to create more scalable and transparent evaluation.
Problem: Existing Reinforcement Learning (RL) literature is often inaccessible to LLM practitioners due to complex notation and abstract theoretical concepts not directly grounded in LLM mechanics.

Current Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) methods for LLM alignment face challenges with high computational cost, reliance on extensive human data, and difficulties in assigning credit for complex reasoning tasks.
Method: Offers a self-contained, step-by-step exposition of core RLMT algorithms (e.g., SFT, PPO, DPO) tailored for LLMs, using simplified notation and grounding concepts in LLM mechanics.
Provides a comprehensive literature review of emerging LLM alignment approaches, including RLAIF, process supervision, and self-play, to inform practitioners about state-of-the-art methods.

Proposes the Generalized Relative Advantage Policy Evolution (GRAPE) framework, integrating AI-generated critiques, category-specific rubrics, and group-relative advantage functions for scalable and transparent LLM alignment.
Results: Successfully clarified core RLMT algorithms (SFT, PPO, DPO, etc.) through a comprehensive, step-by-step exposition, making them accessible to LLM practitioners.
Provided a structured overview of the current LLM alignment research landscape, categorizing and synthesizing emerging approaches like RLAIF and process supervision.

Proposed the GRAPE framework, aiming to enhance transparency and efficiency in LLM alignment by leveraging AI-generated critiques, confidence-weighted scoring, and group-relative advantages, potentially reducing reliance on explicit reward and value models.
Takeaways: Complex Reinforcement Learning algorithms can be effectively demystified for LLM practitioners through intuitive, step-by-step explanations grounded in LLM-specific mechanics and consistent notation.
The current landscape of LLM alignment is shifting towards more scalable, granular, and dynamic methods, moving beyond traditional RLHF to approaches like RLAIF, process supervision, and self-play.

Integrating AI-generated critiques, confidence-weighted scoring, and group-relative advantages can potentially streamline the LLM alignment pipeline by simplifying or eliminating separate reward and value model training.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.04259.Title: RL's Razor: Why Online Reinforcement Learning Forgets Less
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.04259.Summary: Online reinforcement learning (RL) consistently causes less catastrophic forgetting in foundation models compared to supervised fine-tuning (SFT), across both language and robotics tasks. The paper identifies the forward KL divergence between the fine-tuned and base policy, measured on the new task, as a universal predictor for the degree of forgetting and proposes "RL's Razor," which suggests that online RL implicitly seeks KL-minimal solutions.
Problem: Foundation models, despite their capabilities, suffer from catastrophic forgetting, losing previously acquired knowledge when continually adapting to new tasks or environments.
Existing methods for mitigating catastrophic forgetting often rely on heuristic strategies, lacking a fundamental, universal principle to explain its underlying causes.
A clear understanding of the mechanistic differences between SFT and RL that lead to varying levels of forgetting when fine-tuning foundation models was needed.
Method: The research extensively compares the forgetting susceptibility of SFT and on-policy RL across large language models and robotic foundation models through empirical experimentation.
It systematically evaluates various candidate metrics to identify a universal predictor for catastrophic forgetting, focusing on distributional and parameter-level changes.
A theoretical framework is developed to explain why on-policy RL inherently converges to solutions that minimize KL divergence from the base model, thereby preserving prior knowledge.
Results: RL fine-tuning consistently exhibited significantly less catastrophic forgetting than SFT, achieving performance gains on new tasks with minimal degradation of prior capabilities across diverse LLM and robotics benchmarks.

Forward KL divergence between the fine-tuned and base policy demonstrated a strong functional relationship with prior-task performance, serving as a robust predictor for forgetting (e.g., R² = 0.96 in a controlled setting).

A theoretical analysis validates that policy gradient methods, particularly with binary rewards, implicitly converge to the KL-minimal optimal policy, providing a formal basis for the "RL's Razor" principle.
Takeaways: Catastrophic forgetting across different fine-tuning algorithms and tasks is consistently predictable by a single metric: the forward KL divergence between the fine-tuned and base policy on the new task, establishing an "empirical forgetting law."

"RL's Razor" postulates that online reinforcement learning inherently prefers solutions that are closest in KL divergence to the original model, explaining its superior knowledge retention compared to SFT.
The on-policy nature of the training data, rather than the use of negative gradients, is the critical factor responsible for RL's reduced KL divergence and subsequent lower forgetting.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.03646.Title: Emergent Hierarchical Reasoning in LLMs through Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.03646.Summary: This research reveals an emergent hierarchical reasoning structure in Large Language Models during reinforcement learning, where initial procedural consolidation is followed by strategic planning exploration. It introduces Hierarchy-Aware Credit Assignment (HICRA), an algorithm that enhances reasoning performance by focusing optimization efforts on high-level planning tokens.
Problem: Despite empirical success, the mechanistic understanding of how Reinforcement Learning (RL) improves complex reasoning in LLMs remained opaque.
Puzzling phenomena during RL training, such as 'aha moments' and 'length-scaling' effects, lacked a unifying explanation.
Existing RL algorithms often apply optimization pressure indiscriminately across all generated tokens, leading to inefficient learning.
Method: Functionally decomposed LLM-generated tokens into high-level planning tokens (e.g., logical maneuvers) and low-level execution tokens (e.g., calculations).
Introduced "Strategic Grams" (SGs), a data-driven method to empirically identify planning tokens, avoiding subjective manual annotation.
Developed Hierarchy-Aware Credit Assignment (HICRA), an RL algorithm that amplifies the advantage signal for identified planning tokens to concentrate optimization.
Results: HICRA consistently outperformed baseline GRPO, achieving performance gains (e.g., +5.4% to +6.1% on AIME24 for Qwen3-4B models) across text-only and multimodal reasoning benchmarks.
Error analysis revealed that RL primarily improves reasoning by rectifying 'Planning & Strategy' errors, showing a more pronounced reduction in high-level strategic faults.
Semantic entropy accurately correlated with improved validation accuracy, demonstrating that targeted strategic exploration leads to better performance than indiscriminate token-level diversity.
Takeaways: LLM reasoning under RL exhibits a two-phase learning dynamic: initial procedural consolidation followed by an emergent phase of strategic planning exploration.
The learning bottleneck dynamically shifts from procedural correctness to high-level strategic planning, which becomes the primary driver for advanced reasoning.
"Semantic entropy" serves as a more reliable diagnostic metric for tracking genuine strategic exploration compared to traditional token-level entropy or Pass@K.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.03518.Title: Can LLMs Lie? Investigation beyond Hallucination
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.03518.Summary: Carnegie Mellon University researchers distinguish LLM lying from hallucination, identifying a 'dummy token' rehearsal mechanism and sparse neural circuits responsible for deceptive behavior. They develop both bottom-up mechanistic interpretability and top-down representation steering methods to precisely control an LLM's propensity to lie, even improving the honesty-task performance trade-off in goal-oriented scenarios.
Problem: The increasing autonomy of LLMs in agentic roles raises concerns about intentional deceptive behavior, which is distinct from unintentional factual errors (hallucinations).
Current methods often conflate LLM lying with hallucination, and primarily focus on detecting falsehoods *after* generation, lacking mechanistic understanding and proactive control.
Ensuring trustworthiness in LLMs, especially in high-stakes applications, requires moving beyond error identification to understanding and managing deliberate misrepresentation.
Method: Systematically define and quantify LLM lying, differentiating it from hallucination, and investigate its manifestations across various interaction scenarios.
Employ mechanistic interpretability techniques, including Logit Lens analysis and causal interventions (zero-ablation), to pinpoint specific neural pathways and computations underlying deception.

Develop control mechanisms, such as targeted attention head ablation and representation steering vectors, to precisely suppress or enhance lying behavior and improve honesty-task performance trade-offs.
Results: Causal interventions demonstrated that ablating early-to-mid layer MLPs at dummy tokens significantly degrades lying, causing the model to revert to truth-telling.
Targeted ablation of a small number of critical attention heads (e.g., 12 out of 1024) reduced lying to baseline hallucination levels, showing precise control over deceptive circuits.

Honesty-promoting steering vectors increased the LLM's honesty rate (e.g., from 20% to 60% even when prompted to lie) with minimal impact on general capabilities, and improved the Pareto frontier between honesty and task performance in a simulated salesperson agent.
Takeaways: LLMs utilize 'dummy tokens' (non-content chat template tokens) as an internal computational 'scratchpad' for rehearsing and formulating potential lies at intermediate layers before generating deceptive outputs.

Lying behavior is mediated by sparse and localizable neural circuits, with early-to-mid layer MLPs at dummy tokens initiating lies and specific attention pathways linking subject information and lying intent.

Lying-related activations are linearly separable in the LLM's latent space, allowing for effective control of deceptive behavior and even specific lie subtypes (e.g., white vs. malicious) through contrastive representation steering.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.03113.Title: Mitigating Multimodal Hallucinations via Gradient-based Self-Reflection
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.03113.Summary: Researchers from NVIDIA, Data61, CSIRO, and ANU present Gradient-based Influence-Aware Constrained Decoding (GACD), an inference-based method that leverages gradient information to dynamically rebalance cross-modal influence and mitigate multimodal hallucinations in MLLMs. The approach effectively reduces co-occurrence and text-visual biases by up to 57% on co-occurrence metrics while improving accuracy and preserving informativeness across various MLLM architectures.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) frequently generate 'hallucinations' (factually incorrect or ungrounded content), particularly due to text-visual and co-occurrence biases, limiting their trustworthiness and adoption.
Existing hallucination mitigation strategies often require expensive retraining, rely on auxiliary models, or lack the granularity to address biases at a token or object level during inference.
Current inference-based methods provide limited insight into the sample-dependent severity of underlying biases, making targeted adjustments challenging.
Method: Proposes Gradient-based Influence-Aware Constrained Decoding (GACD), an inference-time solution that operates without finetuning or auxiliary models.

Employs first-order Taylor expansion to compute token-wise Jacobians (gradients) that quantify the influence of individual visual features, prompt tokens, and prior output tokens on the next predicted token's logits.

Implements Influence-Aware Constrained Decoding by dynamically adjusting output logits, partitioning visual tokens into object-related and unrelated groups to target co-occurrence bias, and adaptively amplifying visual influence to counteract text-visual bias.
Results: Achieved significant reductions in hallucination rates, including up to 33% for sentence-level and 57% for co-occurrence hallucinations on the AMBER dataset, and up to a 92% increase in accuracy on the LLaVA-QA90 dataset.
Maintained or enhanced informativeness; recall dropped by an average of only 1.1% across models, and detailedness improved by up to 45% on LLaVA-QA90, demonstrating a balanced performance.

Demonstrated broad applicability and superior performance across various MLLMs (e.g., LLaVA-v1.5, InstructBLIP, mPLUG-Owl2, Intern-VL2, Qwen2-VL) and benchmarks, consistently outperforming leading state-of-the-art mitigation methods.
Takeaways: Gradients can provide a principled, granular, and sample-dependent measure of individual input token influence on MLLM outputs, enabling a 'self-reflective' understanding of model biases.

Multimodal hallucinations can be effectively mitigated at inference time by dynamically rebalancing cross-modal contributions and suppressing spurious visual correlations through adaptive logit adjustments.

Partitioning visual tokens based on their relevance to previously mentioned objects allows for targeted reduction of co-occurrence bias, while a dynamic amplification factor helps rebalance visual vs. textual influence.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.02722.Title: Planning with Reasoning using Vision Language World Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.02722.Summary: The Vision Language World Model (VLWM) introduces a foundation model for language-based world modeling from natural videos, enabling high-level task planning. It leverages natural language as an abstract world state representation and achieves state-of-the-art performance on visual planning benchmarks and human-preferred plans in evaluations.
Problem: Traditional world models are limited to low-level, continuous control and struggle with high-level task planning that requires semantic and temporal abstraction.
Existing LLMs lack direct grounding in sensory experience, leading to hallucinations in real-world planning, while VLMs are not designed for action-conditioned world state prediction.
Generating future observations (e.g., raw pixels) is computationally inefficient for long-horizon roll-outs and often captures task-irrelevant details.
Method: A Vision Language World Model (VLWM) is developed, using natural language as an abstract world state representation, trained on a large corpus of natural videos.
A two-stage data generation pipeline compresses raw video into a "Tree of Captions" and extracts structured goal-plan trajectories using LLM self-refinement.
A dual-system planning approach combines efficient reactive plan generation (System-1) with reflective reasoning via cost minimization using a self-supervised critic (System-2).
Results: Achieved new state-of-the-art performance on Visual Planning for Assistance (VPA) benchmarks, with absolute gains of +3.2% in Success Rate and +3.9% in Mean Accuracy.
Secured the highest Elo score (1261) in human evaluations with PlannerArena, demonstrating superior plan quality, and System-2 planning improved Elo by +27% over System-1.
Attained a state-of-the-art BLEU-4 score of 55.6 on the RoboVQA benchmark, and the self-supervised critic model achieved 98.4% accuracy in goal achievement detection on in-domain data.
Takeaways: Natural language provides an efficient, semantically rich, and interpretable interface for abstract world states, effectively bridging the gap between perception and reasoning.
Combining fast reactive planning with a deliberative, cost-minimizing reflective system significantly improves plan quality and robustness in complex, long-horizon tasks.
Self-supervised training of a critic model enables objective evaluation of candidate plans without relying on explicit, engineered reward functions or perfect demonstrations.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.02547.Title: The Landscape of Agentic Reinforcement Learning for LLMs: A Survey
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.02547.Summary: A comprehensive survey formally defines Agentic Reinforcement Learning (RL) for Large Language Models (LLMs) using Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes, distinguishing it from conventional LLM RL. It offers a detailed taxonomy of RL-enhanced agentic capabilities and application domains, providing a structured overview of the field and identifying future research directions.
Problem: The rapidly evolving field of Agentic Reinforcement Learning for LLMs lacked a unified conceptual framework, consistent terminology, and systematic categorization.
Prior Reinforcement Learning approaches for LLMs often treated them as static generators for single-turn text outputs, not as adaptive agents in dynamic, multi-step sequential decision processes.
LLM agents, while showing capabilities like tool use and planning, frequently relied on heuristic pipelines or supervised fine-tuning, missing a unified, adaptive learning mechanism.
Method: Formally defined Agentic RL using temporally extended Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs), contrasting it with conventional LLM RL (PBRFT) modeled as degenerate MDPs.

Developed a comprehensive two-fold taxonomy: one based on RL-optimizable agentic capabilities (e.g., planning, tool use, memory) and another on diverse application domains (e.g., code, math, embodied agents).
Consolidated over 500 recent works, identifying key trends, methodologies, and advancements, alongside a compendium of open-source environments, benchmarks, and frameworks.
Results: Presented a formal distinction between conventional LLM RL (PBRFT, a degenerate MDP) and Agentic RL (a POMDP), clarifying the theoretical underpinnings of treating LLMs as interactive agents.

Provided a systematic taxonomy categorizing existing research across six core agentic capabilities (e.g., Planning, Tool Use, Self-Improvement) and seven application domains (e.g., Code Agents, Embodied Agents).

Compiled a comprehensive list of open-source environments and frameworks, offering practical resources for researchers, and outlined a roadmap for future research by identifying key challenges and opportunities.
Takeaways: Agentic RL fundamentally shifts LLMs from static conditional generators to active, autonomous decision-makers capable of sustained interaction and adaptation within complex, dynamic environments.

Reinforcement learning acts as a critical mechanism for transforming heuristic agentic modules into adaptive, robust, and learnable behaviors, optimizing capabilities through environmental interaction.

Significant challenges for Agentic RL include ensuring trustworthiness (e.g., security, hallucination), efficiently scaling training and environments, and developing a mechanistic understanding of how RL installs or amplifies capabilities in LLMs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.02534.Title: Jointly Reinforcing Diversity and Quality in Language Model Generations
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.02534.Summary: Meta FAIR researchers developed Darling (Diversity-Aware Reinforcement Learning), an online RL framework that integrates a learned semantic diversity signal with standard quality rewards to jointly optimize for both objectives in large language model generations. This approach enabled Llama-3.1-8B models to achieve a 55.2% win rate on AlpacaEval 2.0 and a 68.8% win rate on ArenaHard v2.0, alongside substantially higher semantic diversity on NoveltyBench compared to quality-only baselines.
Problem: Post-training methods for Large Language Models (LLMs), such as RLHF, often lead to 'diversity collapse,' resulting in highly similar, predictable, or repetitive responses.
Existing diversity-enhancing techniques typically involve a trade-off with quality, or only achieve superficial lexical variations rather than true semantic diversity.
The lack of diverse outputs limits LLMs' utility in creative, exploratory, and complex problem-solving applications where a wide range of distinct, high-quality ideas is essential.
Method: Darling integrates a learned semantic diversity signal directly into an online reinforcement learning objective, specifically by modifying the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) algorithm.
A learned binary classifier determines the semantic equivalence of generated responses, enabling a definition of diversity based on the average pairwise semantic distance within a group of outputs.

This semantic diversity signal is multiplicatively aggregated with the standard quality reward, creating a 'diversity-aware reward' that amplifies reinforcement for responses that are both high-quality and semantically distinct.
Results: Darling-trained Llama-3.1-8B models achieved a 55.2% win rate on AlpacaEval 2.0 and a 68.8% win rate on ArenaHard v2.0, while simultaneously showing a semantic diversity of 5.49 distinct generations on NoveltyBench, outperforming GRPO baselines on both quality and diversity.

In competition math, Darling improved Pass@1 (solution quality) by an average of +3.51% for 4B models and +1.90% for 14B models, and significantly enhanced Pass@128 (solution diversity/exploration) by +7.62% and +10.16% respectively, across challenging benchmarks.

Ablation studies confirmed that multiplicative reward fusion consistently outperformed additive aggregation, and using a semantic diversity metric was crucial for performance, as lexical diversity could harm quality in tasks like competition math.
Takeaways: Optimizing for semantic diversity acts as an exploration catalyst in online RL, leading to an unexpected but significant improvement in overall response quality, rather than a trade-off.
Semantic diversity, measured by a learned classifier, is critical; purely lexical diversity metrics can lead to 'reward hacking' and degrade performance, especially in verifiable tasks.

Multiplicative aggregation of diversity and quality rewards is an effective and robust strategy, outperforming additive methods by naturally balancing objectives without complex hyperparameter tuning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.02479.Title: SimpleTIR: End-to-End Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Turn Tool-Integrated Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.02479.Summary: The paper introduces SimpleTIR, an end-to-end Reinforcement Learning (RL) approach that stabilizes multi-turn Tool-Integrated Reasoning (TIR) in Large Language Models (LLMs) under the Zero RL setting. SimpleTIR resolves training instability and gradient explosions by filtering problematic 'void turns,' achieving state-of-the-art performance on mathematical reasoning benchmarks and fostering diverse, emergent reasoning patterns.
Problem: Multi-turn Tool-Integrated Reasoning (TIR) with Reinforcement Learning (RL) suffers from training instability and performance collapse.
External tool feedback causes distributional drift, leading to the generation of low-probability tokens and catastrophic gradient explosions during RL training.
Existing "Zero RL" approaches for TIR struggle with this instability, often relying on Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) which can constrain emergent reasoning capabilities.
Method: The interaction process is formally modeled as a Hierarchical Markov Decision Process (H-MDP), with a single policy trained using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO).
Introduces "void turn" filtering, where entire trajectories are discarded if any turn contains neither executable code nor a final answer, preventing large gradients.
Applies feedback masking, calculating policy loss only for the LLM's generated tokens, to ensure correct credit assignment and avoid penalizing environmental observations.
Results: Achieved remarkable training stability by completely resolving gradient explosions and performance collapse, a common issue in multi-turn RL for LLMs.

Set new state-of-the-art performance on challenging mathematical reasoning benchmarks (e.g., AIME24 score improved from 22.1 to 50.5 with Qwen2.5-7B), outperforming all Zero RL baselines and some SFT-based methods.

Demonstrated the emergence of diverse and sophisticated reasoning patterns (e.g., higher frequencies of progressive reasoning and error correction) compared to SFT-based models, validating the benefits of the Zero RL approach.
Takeaways: Multi-turn TIR instability stems from distributional drift caused by out-of-distribution (OOD) external tool feedback, leading to low-probability token generation and catastrophic gradient explosions in policy gradient methods.
A simple filtering mechanism for "void turns" effectively prevents high-magnitude gradients and corrects misaligned credit assignment, leading to stable RL training for TIR.
Stable Zero RL training, by avoiding SFT, encourages the emergence of diverse and sophisticated reasoning patterns such as cross-validation, progressive reasoning, and error correction.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.02350.Title: Implicit Reasoning in Large Language Models: A Comprehensive Survey
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.02350.Summary: A comprehensive survey organizes research on implicit reasoning in Large Language Models (LLMs) by proposing a new execution-centric taxonomy and consolidating evidence for how multi-step reasoning unfolds internally without generating explicit text. The work highlights critical challenges and future directions to foster more efficient and robust LLM reasoning systems.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) often rely on explicit reasoning methods like Chain-of-Thought (CoT), which are inefficient due to generating lengthy textual intermediate steps, leading to high computational costs and inference latency.

The rapidly expanding field of implicit reasoning in LLMs, where multi-step computation occurs internally, lacks a unified conceptual framework and systematic categorization of its diverse approaches.
There is an underexplored need for a mechanism-level understanding of *how* internal reasoning unfolds within LLMs, beyond general discussions of latent representations.
Method: The survey introduces a novel, execution-centric taxonomy that categorizes implicit reasoning methods based on *how* and *where* internal computation takes place, rather than solely on representational forms.

It systematically details three primary execution paradigms: Latent Optimization (manipulating internal representations), Signal-Guided Control (using specialized non-textual tokens), and Layer-Recurrent Execution (iterative re-use of layers).
The authors synthesize structural, behavioral, and representation-based evidence to empirically demonstrate the presence and dynamics of implicit multi-step reasoning within LLMs.
Results: The survey establishes a novel, three-part execution-centric taxonomy for implicit reasoning: Latent Optimization, Signal-Guided Control, and Layer-Recurrent Execution, providing a unified framework for the field.
It compiles and synthesizes comprehensive mechanistic and behavioral evidence, confirming the existence and operation of implicit reasoning within LLMs.

The work provides a structured overview of over 70 benchmark datasets and evaluation metrics, highlighting the inconsistencies in current practices and the need for standardized assessment of implicit reasoning methods.
Takeaways: Implicit reasoning offers advantages over explicit methods, including lower generation costs, faster inference, and a potentially better alignment with the internal computational processes of LLMs.

LLMs exhibit verifiable patterns in their internal layers, observable behaviors, and detectable information in hidden states, all indicative of internal multi-step computations and implicit reasoning.

Current implicit reasoning methods face significant challenges related to interpretability, control, a performance gap compared to explicit CoT for complex tasks, and a lack of standardized evaluation protocols.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.02333.Title: DCPO: Dynamic Clipping Policy Optimization
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.02333.Summary: Researchers from Baichuan.inc developed Dynamic Clipping Policy Optimization (DCPO), a method to enhance Large Language Models using Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR). DCPO achieved state-of-the-art mathematical reasoning performance across various Qwen2.5 models, improving average scores on benchmarks by up to 6.5 points compared to previous methods, while doubling training efficiency and significantly reducing token clipping.
Problem: Existing RLVR methods like GRPO suffer from 'zero gradients' and 'entropy collapse' when all responses in a batch have identical rewards, halting learning and limiting exploration.
Prior approaches inefficiently utilize generated responses, discarding over half of them in some cases (e.g., GRPO), leading to prolonged training times and wasted computational resources.

Fixed or uniformly asymmetric clipping bounds for token-level probability ratios (in GRPO, DAPO) are suboptimal, as they restrict exploration for low-probability, high-entropy tokens crucial for complex reasoning.
Method: Introduces Dynamic-Adaptive Clipping Bounds (DAC) that vary with the old token probability, granting wider clipping for low-probability tokens to encourage greater policy exploration.
Employs Smooth Advantage Standardization (SAS) by computing advantage statistics cumulatively across all responses for a prompt, preventing zero advantages and reducing fluctuations.

Proposes Only Token Mean (OTM) Loss, which averages advantage-weighted token losses only within each individual response, maintaining relative advantage structure and avoiding dilution from batch-level averaging.
Results: DCPO achieved superior mathematical reasoning performance, improving average scores by up to 6.5 Avg@1 and 7.7 Avg@32 points on Qwen2.5-14B models over GRPO across various benchmarks.
The method reduced the Token Clipping Ratio (TCR) by an order of magnitude compared to GRPO and DAPO, discarding fewer tokens and allowing more complete response sequences to contribute to updates.

DCPO significantly improved the Response Utilization Ratio (RUR) to approximately 70% (a 28% absolute increase over GRPO), doubling training efficiency compared to DAPO by requiring 3 to 5 times fewer generated responses for the same number of parameter updates.
Takeaways: Adaptive clipping, where bounds are dynamically adjusted based on token probabilities, is crucial for balanced exploration, allowing models to leverage rare but informative tokens without destabilizing updates.

Aggregating reward statistics cumulatively across training steps, rather than just within the current batch, prevents premature entropy collapse and ensures more consistent gradient signals for policy updates.

The way loss is aggregated (per token within a response) significantly impacts training stability and efficiency, with response-centric averaging preserving the relative importance of individual response advantages.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.01656.Title: Reinforced Visual Perception with Tools
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.01656.Summary: Researchers from ONE Lab, HUST, University of Washington, and Zhejiang University developed Reinforced Visual Perception with Tools (ReV PT), a framework that trains multimodal language models (MLLMs) to adaptively use visual tools via reinforcement learning. This method achieves state-of-the-art performance on perception-heavy visual reasoning benchmarks by learning to strategically select and interpret tool outputs, overcoming limitations of supervised finetuning approaches.
Problem: Bridging the gap between verbal reasoning in large language models (LLMs) and specialized computer vision (CV) for robust, general visual reasoning remains challenging.

Prior tool-augmented MLLMs primarily relied on supervised finetuning (SFT), which is costly for data curation, requires extensive data filtering, and limits generalization to novel tool-use scenarios.
MLLMs often struggle with complex visual perception tasks requiring granular analysis, such as spatial relationships, object counting, and depth estimation.
Method: ReV PT introduces a two-stage reinforcement learning (RL) framework, built upon Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), to teach MLLMs adaptive visual tool usage.

A "cold-start" phase leverages GPT-4.1 to synthesize high-quality, tool-augmented reasoning data, followed by SFT on this data, to establish a robust initial policy for sequential vision-tool invocation.

The system integrates four perception-oriented visual tools (Object Detection, Zoom In, Edge Detection, Depth Estimation) and a simple binary reward function to guide RL training and optimize tool selection.
Results: ReV PT achieves state-of-the-art performance on several perception-intensive benchmarks, including MMVP, MMStar, CV-Bench, BLINK, and BLINK-Hard, with an average improvement of over 5% compared to instruct-tuned base models.

The method outperforms SFT baselines and text-based RL agents, and surpasses commercial models like GPT-4.1 and Gemini-2.0-Flash on challenging visual reasoning subsets (e.g., BLINK-Depth and Relation).

Ablation studies confirm that both the cold-start process and the integration of specific tools like object detection and depth estimation are critical for the framework's effectiveness, with their removal leading to significant performance degradation.
Takeaways: Reinforcement learning, particularly with the GRPO algorithm, offers a more adaptive and scalable approach to training MLLMs for visual tool use compared to supervised finetuning.

A "cold-start" phase, involving initial SFT on synthetically generated tool-use data, is crucial for preventing MLLMs from neglecting visual tools and for preserving their general capabilities during RL training.
ReV PT learns to optimize the strategic selection of visual tools, resulting in higher accuracy when tools are used, even if the overall frequency of tool calls decreases after RL optimization.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.01644.Title: OpenVision 2: A Family of Generative Pretrained Visual Encoders for Multimodal Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.01644.Summary: OpenVision 2 introduces a family of generative pretrained visual encoders that simplify multimodal learning by exclusively using a caption-only generative objective, abandoning contrastive learning. This approach maintains or improves performance on multimodal benchmarks while reducing training time by up to 50% and memory consumption by 1.8x, enabling billion-parameter scale vision encoders.
Problem: Prohibitively expensive computational cost and extensive resource requirements for training large contrastive Vision-Language Pretraining (VLP) models.
Overly complex architectures in many advanced VLP models, often involving multiple components and intricate loss designs.
A mismatch between the contrastive objective of pretraining and the generative objectives commonly found in downstream multimodal tasks.
Method: Implemented a minimalist, purely generative architecture, removing the text encoder and all contrastive learning objectives.
Utilized an image encoder and text decoder to predict high-quality synthetic captions autoregressively from visual tokens.
Incorporated efficiency techniques such as random visual token masking and an improved ReCap-DataComp-1B v2 synthetic caption dataset.
Results: Achieved comparable or superior performance on a wide range of multimodal benchmarks against previous OpenVision and CLIP-based models.
Reduced wall-clock training time by up to 50% and peak memory usage by approximately 1.8x, allowing for significantly larger batch sizes.
Demonstrated scalability by successfully training vision encoders exceeding 1 billion parameters, validating its efficiency for larger foundation models.
Takeaways: A purely generative, caption-only objective can effectively train high-performance vision encoders, challenging the necessity of contrastive learning.
High-quality synthetic captions generated by MLLMs significantly outperform raw web alt-text as a supervisory signal, improving multimodal performance.
Randomly masking a portion of visual tokens during pretraining enhances efficiency and acts as a regularization method, optimizing feature learning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.01321.Title: Towards High Data Efficiency in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Reward
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.01321.Summary: The DEPO (Data-Efficient Policy Optimization) framework significantly improves the data efficiency of Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) for large reasoning models by implementing a two-stage data selection pipeline. This approach achieves comparable performance to training on full datasets while substantially reducing training time by up to 1.85x and using less than 60% of total training time and 40% of rollout budgets.
Problem: Current Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) methods for Large Language Models (LLMs) rely on extensive data and numerous reasoning rollouts, leading to prohibitively high computational costs and low data efficiency.

Previous offline data selection techniques often require initial training or extensive rollouts on the full dataset to compute selection metrics, while online methods lack fine-grained metrics for evaluating the exploration potential of samples.
The scaling strategy of simply increasing training data and rollouts introduces significant drawbacks, making advanced LLM training resource-intensive and environmentally costly.
Method: DEPO introduces a two-stage pipeline combining offline data curation and online rollout pruning to optimize data efficiency in RLVR training.

The offline stage utilizes a PageRank-weighted Determinantal Point Process (DPP) on a representation-augmented sample graph to prune data for diversity and influence, followed by difficulty-aware normal distribution sampling to create a high-quality, compact training subset.

The online stage dynamically prunes rollouts during training using a novel explorability metric to prioritize samples with high exploration potential, complemented by a dynamic replay mechanism for under-explored samples and an adaptive decay rate for high-explorability focus.
Results: DEPO, using only 20% of the training data, achieved performance nearly matching GRPO trained on the full dataset, outperforming all other offline baselines across five reasoning benchmarks.

When combined with online pruning, DEPO demonstrated a 1.85x speed-up on AIME24 and 1.66x speed-up on AIME25, using less than 60% of total training time and only 40% of rollout budgets while maintaining comparable accuracy.

Ablation studies confirmed that all DEPO components, particularly difficulty-aware sampling and explorability measurement, are critical for its efficiency and performance, with under-explored sample replay being especially beneficial for challenging tasks.
Takeaways: Curating a dataset based on sample diversity, influence, and especially moderate difficulty (via normal distribution sampling) can achieve performance similar to full datasets with significantly fewer samples.

Dynamically measuring and prioritizing samples with high "explorability" (based on entropy and recent rewards) during online training can drastically reduce the number of computational rollouts without sacrificing model performance.
Integrating a mechanism to dynamically replay under-explored samples is crucial to prevent valuable samples from being permanently ignored, particularly for more challenging tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.01092.Title: REFRAG: Rethinking RAG based Decoding
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.01092.Summary: REFRAG introduces an efficient decoding framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) that exploits the sparse attention patterns unique to RAG contexts. This approach, which involves context compression and selective expansion, achieves a 30.85x Time-To-First-Token acceleration and extends the effective context window by 16x, while maintaining or improving perplexity and accuracy across diverse long-context applications.
Problem: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems using Large Language Models (LLMs) face significant system latency and high memory consumption when processing long retrieved contexts.
This leads to a trade-off where enhancing knowledge through longer contexts often degrades system efficiency and throughput.
Generic LLM long-context inference optimizations do not adequately address the specific "block-diagonal attention patterns" and redundant computations inherent in RAG contexts.
Method: A framework using a lightweight encoder compresses RAG context into chunk embeddings, significantly reducing the effective input sequence length for the decoder-only LLM.
The encoder and decoder are aligned through a Continual Pre-training (CPT) regimen involving next-paragraph prediction and reconstruction tasks, employing curriculum learning to manage complexity.

A reinforcement learning policy dynamically identifies and "expands" critical context chunks to full token sequences, while "sensing" (compressing) less important ones, allowing flexible, arbitrary-position compression.
Results: REFRAG delivered a 30.85x acceleration in Time-To-First-Token (TTFT) and up to 6.78x overall throughput acceleration, surpassing previous state-of-the-art methods for TTFT by 3.75x.
The framework successfully extended the effective context window of Large Language Models by 16x, maintaining or improving perplexity and accuracy across various long-context applications.

Its reinforcement learning-based selective compression policy consistently achieved lower perplexity and enhanced performance compared to heuristic selection methods across RAG, multi-turn conversations, and summarization tasks.
Takeaways: RAG contexts possess a unique "block-diagonal attention pattern" and often low semantic similarity between retrieved passages, leading to substantial redundant computation.
Optimizing LLM decoding for RAG requires specialized consideration of its context structure, as generic long-context methods are suboptimal for these specific inefficiencies.
Intelligent, dynamic compression and selective expansion of context chunks, guided by a reinforcement learning policy, is effective for balancing efficiency and performance in RAG systems.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.01055.Title: VerlTool: Towards Holistic Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Tool Use
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.01055.Summary: VERLTOOL introduces a unified, open-source framework for Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Tool use (ARLT), addressing fragmentation and inefficiency in current systems. It achieves near 2x speedup in rollout execution through asynchronous processing and demonstrates competitive performance across six diverse tasks, including mathematical reasoning, knowledge QA, and visual reasoning, while supporting multimodal tool integration.
Problem: Existing Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) for LLMs operates in closed, single-turn settings, limiting interaction with the external world.
Prior LLM tool-use approaches rely on supervised imitation learning, lacking adaptive agentic autonomy from environmental feedback.

The Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Tool use (ARLT) landscape suffers from fragmented, task-specific codebases, synchronous execution bottlenecks leading to inefficient resource utilization, and limited support for multimodal tool interactions.
Method: VERLTOOL provides a modular, open-source framework extending RL with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) to Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Tool use (ARLT), allowing multi-turn, feedback-rich interactions.
It introduces an asynchronous rollout mechanism to eliminate synchronous execution bottlenecks, enabling independent tool interactions for each trajectory and improving computational efficiency.
The framework implements a plugin-based design for tool management with standardized APIs, supporting diverse tools and multimodal interactions, alongside a consistent tokenization strategy.
Results: VERLTOOL-trained models achieved competitive performance, matching or surpassing specialized baselines across six diverse ARLT tasks, including mathematical reasoning, knowledge QA, and software engineering.
The asynchronous rollout mechanism delivered substantial efficiency gains, resulting in nearly 2x speedup in rollout execution and improved computational resource utilization.
The framework demonstrated robust support for multimodal tools, seamlessly integrating vision processing and system-level tools, expanding capabilities beyond text-centric RL.
Agents exhibited sophisticated emergent behaviors, such as self-correction, iterative refinement, and strategic tool selection, in complex, multi-turn problem-solving scenarios.
Takeaways: Effective Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Tool use (ARLT) necessitates combining feedback-driven learning with external tool interaction to foster robust agentic behaviors.
Infrastructure limitations like fragmented codebases, synchronous execution, and single-modality support hinder the broader adoption and advancement of ARLT.
Asynchronous rollout mechanisms significantly boost efficiency by enabling concurrent tool interactions, reducing idle computation time.
Tool usage patterns in ARLT are highly dynamic and task-specific, with effective deployment requiring appropriate reward design and careful initialization strategies.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.00421.Title: Memory Limitations of Prompt Tuning in Transformers
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.00421.Summary: This research provides the first formal proof for the empirically observed memory degradation in transformers with extended contexts, demonstrating that prompt tuning's memorization capacity scales at most linearly with prompt length and is subject to an intrinsic upper bound regardless of context size. The work offers a theoretical justification for why large language models struggle to retain information from very long prompts.
Problem: Lack of a formal theoretical explanation for the empirically observed performance degradation in transformers when handling extended contexts and very long prompts.
Absence of a rigorous understanding of prompt tuning's inherent memory limitations within arbitrary (not synthetically constructed) transformer architectures.
Unclear whether transformers have fundamental architectural limitations regarding the amount of information that can be effectively transferred or memorized via pre-prompts.
Method: Employs a purely theoretical and mathematical approach, leveraging concepts from metric space theory, information theory, and Lipschitz continuity of neural networks.
Utilizes the mean-field generalization of transformers and q-Wasserstein distance to analyze prompts of arbitrary length and model sequences as empirical probability measures.
Applies covering and packing numbers to quantify and compare the total target output space with the limited output space accessible through prompt tuning.
Results: The maximum number of memorizable input/output pairs (k) scales at most linearly with prompt length (k ∈ O(m_p/m)), with the proportion of accessible output sequences decreasing exponentially for k exceeding this linear bound.

Transformers exhibit an intrinsic memory limitation for prompt tuning, where beyond a certain threshold of information, the proportion of accessible output distributions decreases exponentially, independent of the prompt length (m_p).
For single-layer transformers, prompt tuning restricts accessible outputs to a severely limited subspace, making it impossible to even approximately memorize certain target input/output pairs.
Takeaways: Prompt tuning's ability to facilitate memorization is fundamentally constrained by the transformer's Lipschitz continuity and the finite capacity of the prompt space to encode new information.
There is an intrinsic upper bound on the total diversity or complexity of information that can be encoded and retrieved through prompt tuning, which is independent of the context or prompt length.
For shallow architectures like single-layer transformers, prompt tuning severely restricts the accessible output space, rendering many desired input/output pairs fundamentally unreachable.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.20722.Title: rStar2-Agent: Agentic Reasoning Technical Report
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.20722.Summary: Microsoft Research introduces rStar2-Agent, an agentic reasoning model that enables large language models to "think smarter" by autonomously interacting with Python coding tools. The 14B parameter model achieves state-of-the-art mathematical reasoning on AIME24, surpassing much larger models while utilizing significantly less computational resources and producing more concise responses.
Problem: Existing large language model (LLM) reasoning, primarily relying on extended Chain-of-Thought (CoT), often fails to self-correct effectively for complex problems requiring precise calculations or creative shifts in reasoning.

Integrating external tools and developing agentic capabilities in LLMs has been hindered by "environment noise" from tool execution errors and the substantial infrastructure demands of large-scale agentic reinforcement learning.
Current outcome-only reward systems in agentic RL do not effectively penalize inefficient intermediate behaviors, potentially leading to lengthy and low-quality reasoning trajectories.
Method: Introduces rStar2-Agent, an agentic paradigm that trains LLMs to autonomously interact with Python coding tools in a multi-turn, interactive process.

Develops GRPO-RoC (Group Relative Policy Optimization with Resampling on Correct), an agentic RL algorithm that mitigates environment noise and promotes high-quality reasoning by selectively sampling successful trajectories.

Designs a custom, large-scale RL infrastructure featuring a reliable, high-throughput code execution environment and a dynamic, load-balanced rollout scheduler to manage computational demands and asynchronous tool calls.
Employs an efficient multi-stage training recipe, starting with lightweight instruction-following SFT, followed by three incremental RL stages on a curated math dataset.
Results: The rStar2-Agent-14B model achieved 80.6% accuracy on AIME24, outperforming models like OpenAI o3-mini (79.6%) and DeepSeek-R1 (671B, 79.8%).
This performance was attained with a 14B parameter model using only 510 RL training steps over one week on 64 MI300X GPUs, demonstrating superior computational efficiency compared to larger models.

The model produced significantly more concise responses, averaging 9339.7 tokens on AIME24, and exhibited strong generalization, improving GPQA-Diamond accuracy from 42.1% to 60.9% despite math-only agentic RL training.
Takeaways: Agentic reinforcement learning, when coupled with external tools and robust feedback mechanisms, can dramatically improve an LLM's reasoning abilities, even starting from a model with minimal explicit reasoning pre-training.

Careful management of "environment noise" through asymmetric trajectory sampling (GRPO-RoC) is crucial for stable and efficient agentic RL, enabling the model to learn from high-quality reasoning paths rather than distracting errors.

A specialized, high-throughput infrastructure with isolated tool execution and dynamic load balancing is essential for scaling agentic RL and effectively managing the complexity of multi-turn interactions and concurrent tool calls.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.19652.Title: Self-Rewarding Vision-Language Model via Reasoning Decomposition
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.19652.Summary: Vision-SR1 introduces a self-rewarding reinforcement learning framework for Vision-Language Models (VLMs) that guides visual perception through reasoning decomposition. This approach significantly improves visual reasoning capabilities, reduces visual hallucinations and language shortcuts, and better balances multimodal and text-only reasoning.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) frequently generate visual hallucinations and rely on language shortcuts, diminishing their trustworthiness.
Current VLM training methods, especially R1-style RL, offer sparse visual signals, causing models to overemphasize linguistic reasoning at the expense of genuine visual understanding.
External visual supervision is unscalable due to high annotation costs and can introduce biases or lack adaptability to evolving model policies.
Method: Decomposes VLM reasoning into distinct visual perception and language reasoning stages, requiring the VLM to first generate a self-contained visual description.
Implements a two-pass self-reward mechanism where the VLM in a second pass verifies if its own generated visual perception is sufficient to derive the correct answer without re-accessing the image.
Employs Multimodal GRPO with a composite reward function, incorporating rewards for visual perception fidelity, answer accuracy, and structured output adherence.
Results: Vision-SR1 achieved an average performance score of 58.8 (with Qwen2.5-VL-7B) across 24 diverse VLM benchmarks, surpassing Vision-R1 (57.4) and SFT-tuned models (55.1).
The self-reward mechanism demonstrably reduces the Language Shortcut Rate (LSR), lowering it from 7.9 to 6.7 for the 7B model, indicating improved visual grounding over linguistic priors.

The framework helps mitigate "text-only forgetting" in multimodal RL, preserving text-only reasoning capabilities on math tasks and showing larger gains on general knowledge benchmarks compared to Vision-R1.
Takeaways: Self-rewarding frameworks can effectively provide adaptive and dense supervision for intermediate visual perception in VLMs, addressing scalability and bias issues of external methods.
Explicitly decomposing VLM reasoning into visual perception and language reasoning steps fundamentally strengthens visual grounding and reduces reliance on linguistic shortcuts.
The Language Shortcut Rate (LSR) serves as a quantifiable metric to diagnose instances where VLMs produce correct answers despite flawed visual perceptions, highlighting spurious correlations.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.19229.Title: StepWiser: Stepwise Generative Judges for Wiser Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.19229.Summary: STEPWISER introduces a method for training generative judges that meta-reason about an LLM's intermediate reasoning steps, significantly improving judgment accuracy and enabling more capable policy models for multi-step tasks. It achieves this by combining online reinforcement learning with dense, relative reward signals for individual reasoning chunks.
Problem: Current Process Reward Models (PRMs) function as "black-box" classifiers, lacking transparency and interpretability in their step-by-step evaluations.
Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) for PRMs relies on expensive, static human annotations, which limits scalability and generalization.
Ensuring the logical validity of intermediate reasoning steps in LLM Chain-of-Thought (CoT) is critical, but traditional step segmentation often leads to incoherent units.
Method: Develops a self-segmentation method to create "Chunks-of-Thought," training the policy LLM to generate reasoning in logically coherent units.
Automates stepwise data annotation using Monte Carlo Q-value estimation, which are then converted into binary labels with novel "relative reward" thresholding strategies (Rel-Effective, Rel-Ratio).
Trains a generative judge model via online Reinforcement Learning (GRPO), which first generates its own Chain-of-Thought (meta-reasoning) to justify its verdict before providing a binary judgment.
Employs prompt dataset balancing and stability enhancements during RL training to address class imbalance and prevent model collapse.
Results: STEPWISER judges achieved substantially higher accuracy on ProcessBench (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B-chunk with Rel-Effective scored 61.9), outperforming all SFT-trained and sparse RL-trained baselines.
Using STEPWISER for inference-time "Chunk-Reset Reasoning" improved policy model accuracy (e.g., 7B model from 57.4% to 63.3%), demonstrating its utility in real-time self-correction.
Policy models fine-tuned on data selected by STEPWISER judges achieved superior performance (63.0% average accuracy for 7B model), showcasing its effectiveness in data curation.
Ablation studies confirmed the critical roles of online RL, generative meta-reasoning by the judge, and prompt dataset balancing for the framework's superior performance.
Takeaways: Generative judges that explicitly meta-reason about intermediate steps (generating their own CoT for evaluation) are significantly more accurate and transparent than discriminative black-box judges.
Dense, step-level supervision derived from Monte Carlo rollouts, especially using relative reward signals, provides a superior learning signal compared to sparse, outcome-only rewards.
Online Reinforcement Learning is crucial for training robust stepwise judges, overcoming the generalization limitations of SFT on static datasets.
Self-segmentation into "chunks-of-thought" creates more coherent and evaluable reasoning units, improving annotation efficiency and judge context.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.18966.Title: USO: Unified Style and Subject-Driven Generation via Disentangled and Reward Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.18966.Summary: Researchers from ByteDance's Intelligent Creation Lab developed USO, a unified framework that seamlessly integrates style-driven and subject-driven image generation by treating them as complementary tasks. The model, leveraging a novel cross-task co-disentanglement paradigm and Style Reward Learning, achieves state-of-the-art performance on a newly introduced USO-Bench benchmark across subject consistency, style fidelity, and text controllability.
Problem: Existing generative methods treat style-driven and subject-driven image generation as separate, disjoint tasks, leading to sub-optimal feature disentanglement.
This isolated approach results in challenges such as content leakage from style references and difficulty in maintaining subject identity across varying styles or poses.
A lack of unified frameworks capable of simultaneously handling diverse conditioning, including text, style references, and subject references, within a single model.
Method: A "Cross-Task Triplet Curation" framework was developed to generate a large, high-quality dataset comprising content, style, and stylized content images, crucially including both layout-preserved and layout-shifted variations.

The Unified Style-Subject Optimized (USO) model employs a two-stage training process: Style Alignment Training (SAT) using a SigLIP semantic encoder for style, followed by Content-Style Disentanglement Training (CSDT) with a separate VAE encoder for content.
Style Reward Learning (SRL) is integrated during fine-tuning, using a VLM-based reward to explicitly disentangle style from content and optimize for style similarity.
Results: USO consistently surpasses competing open-source models, achieving the highest DINO (0.793) and CLIP-I (0.623) scores for subject consistency and a leading CSD (0.557) score for style similarity on the new USO-Bench.

Qualitative evaluations and a user study confirm USO's superior performance in maintaining subject identity, preserving intricate style details, and aligning with complex textual prompts across individual and combined tasks.

Ablation studies validate the critical contributions of Style Reward Learning, Style Alignment Training, and the disentangled encoder design, demonstrating their necessity for USO's enhanced performance and artifact reduction.
Takeaways: Style-driven and subject-driven generation are complementary tasks that benefit from a shared "cross-task co-disentanglement paradigm," where improving one task mutually reinforces the model's ability to perform the other.

Explicitly disentangling content and style features through separate encoding pathways (SigLIP for style, VAE for content) and a hierarchical style projector is crucial for achieving high-fidelity control and mitigating content leakage.
Style Reward Learning not only enhances style fidelity but also has a positive, unexpected impact on subject consistency, reducing common generative artifacts like a "plastic appearance."

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.18588.Title: History Rhymes: Accelerating LLM Reinforcement Learning with RhymeRL
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.18588.Summary: RhymeRL is an LLM reinforcement learning (RL) system that leverages historical rollout information to accelerate training. It achieves up to 2.6x end-to-end performance improvement over state-of-the-art methods while maintaining algorithmic accuracy and demonstrating scalability in production environments.
Problem: The rollout phase in LLM RL training consumes 84% to 91% of total processing time, driven by autoregressive generation of long reasoning chains and memory-bandwidth-bound token generation.
GPU underutilization occurs due to 'GPU bubbles' where varying response lengths within a batch cause workers to idle, waiting for the longest rollout to complete.
Existing solutions like partial rollouts, batch size adjustments, and asynchronous execution offer limited improvements or compromise accuracy by using highly stale model weights.
Method: RhymeRL introduces HistoSpec, a history-based speculative decoding mechanism that uses past successful rollouts as drafts to predict and verify multiple tokens in a single forward pass, accelerating generation.

It implements HistoPipe, a two-tier, distribution-aware scheduling strategy that exploits historical rollout length distributions for inter-step workload complementarity and includes migration-based rebalancing for outliers.
The system uses a streaming pipeline architecture with asynchronous weight updates and dedicated history workers on idle CPU resources to manage and index historical rollout information efficiently.
Results: RhymeRL achieves up to 2.6x end-to-end performance improvement over state-of-the-art LLM RL training systems, with approximately 1.9x to 2.3x average throughput gains for 8K and 16K max response lengths.
It maintains training accuracy, with reward curves closely overlapping those of baseline systems, confirming that its optimizations do not introduce algorithmic degradation.

The system demonstrates scalability from dozens to over a thousand GPUs in a real production environment, with HistoSpec providing up to 1.86x per-step rollout throughput gains and HistoPipe reducing training time per 10 steps by up to 1.68x.
Takeaways: Rollout responses and their length distributions exhibit remarkable similarity across adjacent training epochs for the same prompts, a previously overlooked characteristic of LLM RL.
This historical consistency is primarily due to clipping operations in mainstream RL algorithms (e.g., PPO) that ensure stable model evolution, preventing erratic changes between epochs.

Systematically leveraging this historical information allows for significant acceleration of the rollout process and effective load balancing without compromising algorithmic integrity or training accuracy.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.17971.Title: Neural Algorithmic Reasoners informed Large Language Model for Multi-Agent Path Finding
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.17971.Summary: Beihang University researchers developed LLM-NAR, a framework integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) with Graph Neural Network-based Neural Algorithmic Reasoners (NARs) for Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF). This approach improves LLMs' ability to generate collision-free and efficient paths by leveraging GNNs for spatial and algorithmic reasoning, achieving higher success rates and reduced execution times.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit limited capabilities in complex Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) tasks, particularly in understanding intricate spatial constraints and coordinating multiple agents precisely.
Traditional MAPF algorithms, while often optimal, suffer from high computational costs and scalability issues as the number of agents and map complexity increase.
Existing learning-based MAPF methods typically demand extensive training data and computational resources, hindering their efficiency and broad applicability.
Method: The LLM-NAR framework combines an LLM for high-level understanding, a pre-trained GNN-based Neural Algorithmic Reasoner (NAR) for spatial comprehension, and a cross-attention mechanism for information fusion.
A GNN-based NAR is pre-trained using optimal path data generated by Conflict-Based Search (CBS), enabling it to learn and represent map information and agent relationships effectively.

A cross-attention mechanism efficiently fuses the linguistic outputs from the LLM with the spatial representations from the pre-trained GNN-NAR, with only the cross-attention network being trained on optimal actions in a few thousand steps.
Results: LLM-NAR consistently achieved higher success rates and produced paths with fewer average steps compared to baseline LLMs (e.g., GPT-3.5-turbo, LLaMA3) across various simulated MAPF scenarios.
The framework demonstrated superior performance in real-world experiments with LIMO mobile robots, successfully guiding all agents with shorter paths in scenarios where other LLM baselines failed.

LLM-NAR exhibited significant efficiency gains, requiring only 5,000 training steps (compared to 300,000 for RL methods) and achieved substantially faster execution times than classical optimal planning algorithms like CBS (e.g., ~2.0s vs ~32.3s for 16 agents).
Takeaways: Integrating GNN-based Neural Algorithmic Reasoners provides LLMs with the structured spatial knowledge and algorithmic reasoning capabilities essential for precise multi-agent path planning.

A focused training strategy for the cross-attention mechanism allows for highly efficient fusion of LLM and GNN-NAR outputs, drastically reducing the required training steps compared to end-to-end learning methods.

Augmenting LLMs with explicit spatial reasoning enables them to overcome inherent limitations in combinatorial planning, leading to more accurate, collision-free, and efficient paths in complex multi-agent environments.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.17784.Title: Proximal Supervised Fine-Tuning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.17784.Summary: Proximal Supervised Fine-Tuning (PSFT) introduces a PPO-inspired clipped objective to stabilize large language model fine-tuning, preventing entropy collapse and catastrophic forgetting. This approach yields a more robust and generalized base model, serving as a superior "cold start" for subsequent reinforcement learning from human feedback or direct preference optimization, which ultimately leads to enhanced performance across various tasks.
Problem: Standard Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) often leads to "catastrophic forgetting" or "capability erosion," resulting in poor generalization to out-of-domain tasks.
SFT can cause "entropy collapse," making the model overly confident and reducing its exploration capacity, which is detrimental for subsequent reinforcement learning (RL) stages.
SFT-trained models provide a suboptimal "cold start" for RL-based alignment, limiting the effectiveness and stability of advanced post-training techniques like RLHF or DPO.
Method: Proximal Supervised Fine-Tuning (PSFT) adapts the clipped surrogate objective from Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) to the SFT setting, drawing inspiration from trust-region methods.
The method frames SFT as a special case of policy gradient with constant positive advantages, enabling the application of stability-enhancing principles from RL.
