PSFT regularizes SFT updates by limiting how much the probability of an action under the new policy can deviate from its probability under a previous policy, preventing drastic changes.
Results: PSFT consistently maintains smoother entropy curves and matches or slightly surpasses standard SFT on in-domain math reasoning tasks while significantly improving out-of-domain generalization and instruction-following capabilities.
Models initialized with PSFT achieve higher entropy during subsequent RL training, leading to superior final performance on both in-domain and out-of-domain tasks compared to SFT-initialized models.
PSFT reduces the "alignment tax" and enables more effective Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), resulting in better human alignment on benchmarks like AlpacaEval2 and MT-Bench.
Takeaways: Supervised Fine-Tuning can be theoretically understood as a policy gradient method where expert actions are treated with a constant positive advantage.
Applying a PPO-like clipped surrogate objective to SFT effectively prevents entropy collapse and preserves generalization capabilities by constraining policy updates.
A more robust and entropy-preserving SFT output provides a significantly better initial policy, leading to greater exploration and superior final performance in subsequent RL-based alignment stages.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.17692.Title: LLM-based Agentic Reasoning Frameworks: A Survey from Methods to Scenarios
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.17692.Summary: Researchers from multiple international institutions propose a unified methodological taxonomy and formal language for LLM-based agentic reasoning frameworks, systematically surveying their progress, application scenarios, and evaluation strategies across diverse domains like scientific research and healthcare. This work provides a structured view of single-agent, tool-based, and multi-agent approaches, clarifying the rapidly evolving landscape.
Problem: The explosive growth of LLM-based agent systems has led to blurred conceptual boundaries, making it difficult to differentiate them from traditional multi-agent or autonomous systems.
It is challenging to attribute performance enhancements in agent systems to specific framework designs versus underlying model improvements or other technological advancements.
Existing surveys are often either model-centric, focusing on training or planning abilities, or domain-specific, lacking a unified taxonomic approach for framework-side developments.
Method: Developed a three-level progressive taxonomy (Single-Agent, Tool-Based, Multi-Agent methods) to systematically organize and analyze agentic reasoning frameworks.
Introduced a unified formal language and a general reasoning algorithm to precisely describe complex, multi-step reasoning processes within these frameworks.

Conducted a scenario-driven review of applications, analyzing representative works and their evaluation strategies across scientific research, healthcare, software engineering, and social simulations.
Results: A novel three-level taxonomy (Single-Agent, Tool-Based, Multi-Agent methods) was successfully proposed and elaborated, providing an organizational framework for the field.
A unified formal language and a general reasoning algorithm were introduced, offering a rigorous foundation for understanding and analyzing agentic systems.

The utility of the proposed framework was demonstrated through a comprehensive review of diverse methodologies and their application across high-impact scenarios, including scientific research, healthcare, and software engineering.
Takeaways: LLM-based agentic reasoning can be systematically deconstructed into single-agent, tool-based, and multi-agent components, each contributing progressively to complex task execution.
A formal language and algorithm can rigorously define how different methodologies enhance an agent's multi-step reasoning cycle.
Effective agent systems often integrate methods from multiple taxonomic levels, demonstrating synergistic potential for addressing complex, real-world problems.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.17445.Title: TreePO: Bridging the Gap of Policy Optimization and Efficacy and Inference Efficiency with Heuristic Tree-based Modeling
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.17445.Summary: TreePO is a framework designed to enhance Large Language Model alignment by integrating segment-based tree search for rollouts with a hierarchical advantage estimation function. It reduces GPU training hours by 22-43% and increases inference throughput by up to 40% while improving policy optimization and achieving higher accuracy in complex reasoning tasks.
Problem: Standard RL methods for LLM alignment are computationally inefficient due to redundant on-policy rollouts and poor Key-Value (KV) cache utilization.
Attributing sparse, delayed rewards accurately to specific tokens in long generated sequences remains challenging, hindering effective exploration and credit assignment.
Existing tree search methods are often inefficient for LLMs due to sequential rollouts, while segment-level RL methods might be dependent on prior supervised fine-tuning.
Method: Introduces a segment-based tree-structured search for rollouts, maximizing KV cache reuse by sharing common prefixes and enabling dynamic branching for diverse exploration.
Develops a tree-based advantage estimation function that aggregates relative advantages from nested sub-groups, providing granular credit assignment for policy optimization.
Implements mechanisms for early stopping of low-value paths and a depth-first search fallback to ensure sufficient trajectory generation.
Results: Achieved a reduction of 12% to 43% in GPU training hours and an average increase of 40% in Trajectories per Second and 30% in Tokens per Second throughput.
Boosted overall accuracy on complex reasoning tasks from 46.63% (GRPO baseline) to 58.21% with TreePO's full configuration, demonstrating enhanced policy optimization.
Identified that optimal efficiency and performance are achieved at intermediate depth-segment configurations, highlighting a trade-off between KV cache prefilling and decoding parallelism.
Takeaways: Replacing sequential sampling with TreePO's tree-based sampling alone substantially boosts performance and training stability for existing RL algorithms.
The hierarchical advantage estimation provides a more precise reward signal, effectively enabling "RL-zero" training directly from base models.
Simple averaging of subgroup advantages proved more effective than size-weighting, and rejecting all-positive/all-negative subgroups negatively impacted performance.
Heuristic probability-based branching strategies did not improve performance, indicating that meaningful and balanced exploration is more effective than simply increasing diversity.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.17298.Title: Explain Before You Answer: A Survey on Compositional Visual Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.17298.Summary: A survey charts the recent trajectory of Compositional Visual Reasoning (CVR) from 2023 to 2025, introducing a five-stage taxonomy to explain its evolution and distinct advantages over monolithic approaches. The work systematically reviews over 260 papers, identifying key benefits such as enhanced interpretability and robustness, while also outlining persistent open challenges and future research directions for the field.
Problem: Traditional monolithic visual reasoning models struggle to replicate human-like intelligence, often relying on superficial correlations and lacking explicit mechanisms for decomposition and relational understanding.
These models face limitations such as reliance on dataset biases, diminishing returns with increased reasoning complexity, and poor generalization to novel compositions.
Existing literature lacked a dedicated and comprehensive synthesis of the rapidly expanding compositional visual reasoning paradigm, particularly recent advancements from 2023-2025.
Method: The authors conducted a systematic review of over 260 papers from leading AI venues between 2023 and 2025, focusing on methods emphasizing explicit intermediate "thought" steps and structured decomposition.
The paper introduces a unified five-stage taxonomy, tracing CVR's evolution from prompt-enhanced language-centric methods to unified agentic Vision-Language Models (VLMs).
It catalogues over 60 benchmarks and evaluation metrics and identifies persistent open challenges with corresponding future research directions for the field.
Results: The survey formally defines CVR, robustly articulates its benefits, and presents a five-stage evolutionary roadmap for the field's architectural and methodological progression.
It catalogs a comprehensive list of over 60 benchmarks and their corresponding evaluation metrics designed to probe various dimensions of compositional visual reasoning.

The paper identifies six core challenges (e.g., LLM reasoning limitations, hallucinations, data scalability, benchmark limitations) and proposes actionable future research directions to advance CVR capabilities.
Takeaways: Compositional Visual Reasoning (CVR) offers advantages over monolithic approaches, including better cognitive alignment with human reasoning, enhanced interpretability, improved generalization, and reduced data requirements.

The field has evolved through distinct architectural stages, progressing from LLM-centric approaches with external vision tools to unified VLM architectures that integrate perception and inference for explicit intermediate thought processes.
Current benchmarks and evaluation protocols are often insufficient, lacking explicit assessment of intermediate reasoning steps, quantified difficulty levels, and comprehensive diagnostic insights.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.16546.Title: RL Is Neither a Panacea Nor a Mirage: Understanding Supervised vs. Reinforcement Learning Fine-Tuning for LLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.16546.Summary: This research uses spectral analysis to reveal that Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) causes out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization loss in Large Language Models primarily through rotations of singular vectors, while Reinforcement Learning Fine-Tuning (RL-FT) acts as a restorative mechanism for these rotations, recovering up to 99% of lost OOD performance in some cases. The study identifies that restoring singular vector directions in low-rank components or early layers can recover 70-80% of OOD performance, offering efficient alternatives to full RL-FT.
Problem: The precise parameter-level dynamics of how SFT and RL-FT impact LLM performance, particularly out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization, were not well understood.
Existing literature lacked a mechanistic explanation for SFT's tendency to improve in-distribution (ID) performance while often degrading OOD generalization.
The fundamental role of RL-FT in LLMs, specifically whether it creates new generalization abilities or merely restores those compromised by SFT, remained unclear.
Method: Conducted two-stage fine-tuning (SFT followed by PPO-based RL) on Llama and Qwen LLMs using a controlled out-of-distribution (OOD) variant of the GeneralPoints card game.

Employed spectral analysis via Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) and Principal Angles Between Subspaces (PABS) to track parameter-level dynamics and geometric shifts in weight matrices during fine-tuning.
Performed targeted ablation studies by selectively restoring singular vector directions layer-wise and rank-wise to causally investigate their impact on OOD performance.
Results: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) caused significant OOD performance degradation, with Llama-3.2-11B dropping from 17.52% to 8.97% and Qwen-2.5-7B experiencing a 13% decline.
Reinforcement Learning Fine-Tuning (RL-FT) substantially restored OOD performance, recovering up to 99% for Qwen-2.5-7B and 85% for Llama-3.2-11B.
Targeted restoration of singular vector directions in the top 20% of singular values or the first 25% of layers successfully recovered 70-80% of a model's OOD performance.
Takeaways: Reinforcement Learning Fine-Tuning (RL-FT) primarily functions as a 'memory restoration' mechanism, counteracting the out-of-distribution (OOD) performance decay caused by Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT).
Changes in OOD generalization are predominantly driven by rotations of singular vectors within weight matrices, rather than significant alterations in singular value magnitudes.
Restoring singular vector directions in low-rank components (e.g., top 20% of singular values) or early layers (e.g., first 25% of layers) is surprisingly effective for OOD recovery.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.16204.Title: Competition and Attraction Improve Model Fusion
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.16204.Summary: The M2N2 framework from Sakana AI refines model fusion by incorporating dynamic merging boundaries, implicit fitness sharing, and attraction-based parent selection within an evolutionary algorithm. This method improves the combination of pre-trained LLMs and diffusion models, and can even evolve models from an initial state, demonstrating comparable performance to direct weight optimization but with higher computational efficiency.
Problem: Existing model merging techniques often require manual partitioning of model parameters into fixed groups (e.g., layers), which limits the exploration of potential parameter combinations.
Preserving diversity in evolutionary algorithms for high-dimensional deep learning models is challenging due to the difficulty in defining meaningful distance metrics for complex parameter spaces.
Inefficient parent selection in evolutionary algorithms can hinder performance, particularly when crossover operations like model merging are computationally expensive.
Method: M2N2 introduces dynamically evolved split-points that define where two models' parameters are merged, allowing for flexible exploration of merging boundaries.

It implements a competition-based mechanism for diversity preservation, where a modified fitness function encourages models to find 'uncontested resources' (data points other models struggle with) via implicit fitness sharing.
A heuristic-based 'attraction score' guides parent selection, prioritizing the fusion of models that exhibit complementary strengths on different data points.
Results: M2N2 successfully evolved MNIST classifiers from scratch, achieving performance comparable to CMA-ES while being significantly more computationally efficient (1 hour vs. 15 hours).
When merging pre-trained LLMs, M2N2 achieved the highest average score of 63.49% on combined math and agentic benchmarks, surpassing individual models and other merging baselines.

For diffusion models, M2N2 produced images with superior quality (NCS, FID) and demonstrated robust preservation of capabilities, including emergent cross-lingual understanding with a CLIP cosine-similarity of 0.787.
Takeaways: Dynamically evolving merging boundaries significantly enhances the flexibility and effectiveness of model fusion, moving beyond static architectural divisions.
Implicit fitness sharing, inspired by natural resource competition, provides a scalable and effective method for maintaining diversity in high-dimensional AI model populations.
Heuristic-driven parent selection based on complementary performance can substantially improve the efficiency and quality of offspring in computationally intensive model merging operations.
Model merging, when enhanced by these evolutionary principles, can serve as a viable gradient-free mechanism for training deep learning models entirely from scratch.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.15568.Title: Backpropagation-Free Test-Time Adaptation via Probabilistic Gaussian Alignment
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.15568.Summary: A method named ADAPT, developed by researchers at Sungkyunkwan University, improves Vision-Language Model robustness to distribution shifts through a backpropagation-free, probabilistic Gaussian alignment approach. It achieves an average accuracy of 66.53% in online settings on natural distribution shifts, outperforming prior methods while reducing inference time on ImageNet to 1h 11m, compared to over 9 hours for optimization-based techniques.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) like CLIP experience significant performance degradation when encountering real-world data outside their pre-training distribution.
Current Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) methods often rely on computationally intensive backpropagation or iterative optimization, limiting real-time deployment and resource efficiency.
Gradient-free TTA approaches frequently lack explicit modeling of class-conditional feature distributions, leading to unstable decision boundaries and less calibrated predictions.
Method: ADAPT reframes Test-Time Adaptation as a probabilistic inference task, utilizing Gaussian Discriminant Analysis (GDA) to model class-conditional feature distributions.
It employs "knowledge banks" which are dynamically updated buffers storing high-confidence samples to guide source-free and unsupervised adaptation.
The method derives a closed-form label estimator and parameter updates, enabling a one-pass, backpropagation-free solution for efficient inference without iterative optimization.
Results: ADAPT achieved an average accuracy of 66.53% in online settings and 67.09% in transductive settings on natural distribution shift benchmarks, outperforming all prior state-of-the-art methods.

It significantly improved corruption robustness, reaching 28.56% accuracy online on ImageNet-C, and reduced inference time on ImageNet to 1h 11m, dramatically faster than optimization-based alternatives.

The method demonstrated consistent performance gains and generalizability across various VLM backbones (CLIP-RN50, BLIP, ALBEF) and in challenging fine-grained categorization and few-shot adaptation tasks.
Takeaways: Pre-trained Vision-Language Model features, when conditioned on their respective classes, can be effectively approximated by Gaussian distributions, facilitating efficient probabilistic inference.

Utilizing dynamically maintained "knowledge banks" of high-confidence pseudo-labeled samples provides stable, source-free, and supervision-free statistics for robust adaptation, mitigating noise from early predictions.

A closed-form solution for parameter estimation and label prediction can achieve state-of-the-art accuracy, delivering significant computational efficiency over iterative, backpropagation-based Test-Time Adaptation methods.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.15260.Title: Deep Think with Confidence
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.15260.Summary: Researchers from UCSD and Meta AI developed DeepConf, a method that enhances Large Language Model reasoning efficiency and performance by leveraging local confidence signals to dynamically prune low-quality reasoning traces and weight final answer aggregation. DeepConf achieved up to 84.7% reduction in generated tokens and improved accuracy, reaching 99.9% on AIME 2025 with GPT-OSS-120B, without requiring additional model training.
Problem: Existing LLM reasoning methods, particularly those using parallel thinking like self-consistency, incur high computational overhead due to generating numerous traces.
Standard majority voting suffers from diminishing returns and suboptimal performance because it treats all reasoning traces equally, irrespective of quality.
Prior global confidence measures fail to detect localized reasoning breakdowns and cannot enable early stopping, thus missing crucial efficiency gains.
Method: DeepConf introduces a suite of confidence metrics, emphasizing *local* signals like Group Confidence, Bottom 10% Group Confidence, and Lowest Group Confidence.
In an offline setting, DeepConf improves answer aggregation by confidence-weighted majority voting and filtering a predefined pool of traces based on their quality.
In an online setting, DeepConf dynamically terminates low-confidence traces during generation using an adaptively set threshold, enabling real-time early stopping to save computational resources.
Results: Offline DeepConf achieved significant accuracy gains, for instance, boosting GPT-OSS-120B to 99.9% accuracy on AIME 2025, an improvement over 97.0% for standard self-consistency.
Online DeepConf-low reduced generated tokens by 43% to 84.7% across various benchmarks while maintaining or improving accuracy compared to full parallel thinking.
The method demonstrates robust benefits across a range of models (from 8B to 120B parameters) and challenging mathematical and STEM reasoning tasks.
Takeaways: Local confidence measures are more effective than global averages at identifying critical reasoning breakdowns and differentiating between correct and incorrect reasoning paths.
Dynamically pruning low-confidence reasoning paths during generation (online filtering) substantially reduces computational cost while preserving or improving accuracy.
Weighting votes based on trace confidence and selectively filtering out low-quality traces leads to more robust and accurate final answers than unweighted majority voting.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.14460.Title: DuPO: Enabling Reliable LLM Self-Verification via Dual Preference Optimization
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.14460.Summary: DuPO introduces a self-supervised dual preference optimization framework that enables reliable LLM self-verification without external annotations by utilizing a generalized duality principle based on complementary tasks. The method achieves substantial performance gains in multilingual translation and mathematical reasoning, bringing smaller models to state-of-the-art levels and significantly improving inference-time reranking.
Problem: Existing LLM alignment techniques like RLHF and RLVR rely on costly human annotations or restrictive verifiable answers, limiting scalability and general applicability.
Traditional dual learning is restricted to strictly invertible task pairs and suffers from bidirectional competence asymmetry, making it unsuitable for most non-invertible LLM tasks.
Many real-world LLM tasks, such as creative writing or mathematical reasoning, are non-invertible, preventing the use of self-supervised methods that require full input reconstruction.
Method: DuPO redefines task duality using a 'complementary consistency principle' where a primal task input is decomposed into known and unknown components, and a dual task reconstructs only the unknown component.

Self-supervised reward signals are generated based on the consistency between the original and reconstructed unknown components, incentivizing the LLM to produce outputs that facilitate accurate reconstruction.

The self-supervised rewards are integrated into a preference optimization framework, specifically Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), to continually improve the LLM without external supervision.
An inference-time reranking mechanism leverages the dual task to select the best reasoning trajectory from multiple LLM samples, boosting performance without additional training.
Results: DuPO boosted the Seed-X-7B-Instruct model by an average of 2.13 COMET points across 756 translation directions, making it comparable to ultra-large state-of-the-art systems.
It achieved consistent performance improvements in mathematical reasoning, increasing scores by 6.4 percentage points for OpenReasoning-Nemotron-7B and Qwen3-4B on challenging benchmarks.
DuPO lifted the average score of vanilla LlaMA-3.1-8B by 24.0 percentage points on AMC23 and MATH500 benchmarks, surpassing oracle-labeled SimpleRL-Zoo by 13.1%.
As an inference-time reranking mechanism, DuPO improved the average performance of Qwen3-4B by 9.3 points on AIME benchmarks, outperforming larger models like DeepSeek-R1 without additional training.
Takeaways: Generalized duality, based on complementary consistency rather than strict invertibility, effectively extends self-supervised learning to a broad range of non-invertible LLM tasks.
Decomposing task inputs into known and unknown components provides a strong contextual anchor for the dual task, mitigating competence asymmetry and ensuring reliable self-supervision signals.

Dual preference optimization can activate and enhance complex reasoning capabilities even in base models without initial supervised fine-tuning, demonstrating the method's ability to unlock latent skills.
Reliable self-verification can be used effectively as a training-free inference-time reranking strategy, significantly improving model performance and extracting more capability from existing LLMs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.14313.Title: Your Reward Function for RL is Your Best PRM for Search: Unifying RL and Search-Based TTS
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.14313.Summary: The AIRL-S framework unifies reinforcement learning (RL) and search-based test-time scaling (TTS) by learning a dynamic, policy-independent Process Reward Model (PRM) directly from correct reasoning traces, circumventing the need for expensive step-wise labels. This approach enhances LLM reasoning, achieving an average 9% performance gain over its base model and matching GPT-4o's overall accuracy with a 7B-parameter model across eight diverse reasoning benchmarks.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle with complex reasoning tasks, with existing Test-Time Scaling (TTS) approaches primarily relying on two separate, often limited, paradigms.
Reinforcement Learning (RL) methods for LLMs suffer from training instability and low sample efficiency due to sparse, outcome-based rewards.
Search-based TTS techniques require Process Reward Models (PRMs) that are expensive to label for intermediate steps and prone to reward hacking or performance degradation under distribution shifts.
Method: AIRL-S unifies RL and search-based TTS by learning a dense, dynamic, policy-independent Process Reward Model (PRM) from correct reasoning traces using Adversarial Inverse Reinforcement Learning (AIRL), eliminating the need for step-wise labels.
The LLM policy is optimized using a composite objective function that combines AIRL-derived dense process rewards with sparse outcome-based rewards from Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO).

The learned PRM is directly reused at inference time to guide various search-based TTS methods, including Best-of-N sampling, Beam Search, and Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS), for verifying and steering the reasoning process.
Results: The AIRL-S trained policy (Qwen2.5-7B) achieved an average 9% performance improvement over its base model across eight benchmarks, with a 13% gain in mathematical and scientific reasoning, and matched the overall accuracy of GPT-4o.
The Qwen2.5-AIRL-S-PRM consistently improved Best-of-N search performance for various generative LLMs, outperforming PRMs trained on labeled data and implicit PRMs by 1.4% to 2.4% on average.

The learned PRM effectively guided MCTS, Beam Search, and Best-of-N methods, outperforming Self-Consistency and demonstrating enhanced inference computation scaling by generating longer, more elaborate responses.
Takeaways: The reward function learned during RL training inherently represents an ideal, dynamic Process Reward Model (PRM) for guiding downstream search, naturally unifying two distinct LLM reasoning paradigms.

Adversarial Inverse Reinforcement Learning (AIRL) can effectively learn a policy-independent, step-wise PRM from only correct final reasoning traces, eliminating the need for expensive intermediate process data labeling.

Combining dense, process-based rewards (from AIRL) with sparse, outcome-based rewards (from GRPO) during RL training leads to more stable policy learning, improved sample efficiency, and enhanced reasoning capabilities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.13755.Title: Depth-Breadth Synergy in RLVR: Unlocking LLM Reasoning Gains with Adaptive Exploration
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.13755.Summary: A new framework, DARS-Breadth, improves large language model reasoning in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Reward (RLVR) by adaptively focusing on difficult problems and expanding training batch sizes. This dual approach boosts both Pass@K and Pass@1 performance across mathematical reasoning benchmarks.
Problem: Existing Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Reward (RLVR) methods, particularly GRPO variants, exhibit a "cumulative advantage bias" that neglects hard-to-solve problems.
This bias prevents large language models (LLMs) from effectively learning complex reasoning paths and limits their Pass@K performance.
The impact of training "breadth" (batch size) in RLVR on LLM reasoning capabilities, especially Pass@1, has been largely underexplored, often defaulting to small fixed sizes.
Method: Proposed Difficulty Adaptive Rollout Sampling (DARS) to re-balance cumulative advantage by adaptively performing multi-stage rollouts for low-accuracy, high-difficulty problems.
Systematically scaled the training batch size ("breadth") and utilized full-batch updates to enhance gradient stability and sustained exploration.
Integrated DARS with large-breadth training into a unified "DARS-Breadth" framework to leverage the complementary benefits of both dimensions.
Results: DARS substantially improves Pass@K performance across mathematical reasoning benchmarks (e.g., Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B and 7B models) with a 25.3% reduction in inference cost compared to naive rollout scaling.
Scaling training breadth dramatically boosts Pass@1 performance and sustains higher token-level entropy, indicating improved exploration.

The DARS-Breadth framework achieves simultaneous improvements in both Pass@1 and Pass@K, outperforming individual optimizations and demonstrating generalized effectiveness on models like Llama-3.1-8B.
Takeaways: Current GRPO-based RLVR algorithms suffer from a "cumulative advantage bias" that underweights high-difficulty problems, hindering Pass@K gains.
Adaptively allocating more computational resources (multi-stage rollouts) to hard problems can efficiently rebalance the learning signal, improving Pass@K without excessive cost.
Increasing training "breadth" (batch size) acts as an implicit entropy regularization mechanism, stabilizing training, sustaining exploration, and boosting Pass@1 performance.
Optimizing "depth" (focus on hard problems) and "breadth" (data quantity per iteration) are orthogonal yet synergistic approaches to unlocking greater LLM reasoning capabilities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.13167.Title: Chain-of-Agents: End-to-End Agent Foundation Models via Multi-Agent Distillation and Agentic RL
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.13167.Summary: The OPPO AI Agent Team developed Chain-of-Agents (CoA), a paradigm enabling a single large language model (LLM) to perform end-to-end complex problem-solving by simulating multi-agent collaboration. This approach, trained via multi-agent distillation and agentic reinforcement learning, achieves state-of-the-art performance across various agentic tasks while reducing inference cost by 84.6% compared to traditional multi-agent systems.
Problem: Traditional Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) suffer from high computational overhead, generalization issues, and a lack of end-to-end data-centric learning, as their LLM backbones are not natively trained for multi-turn, multi-agent workflows.
Existing Tool-Integrated Reasoning (TIR) models are limited by a rigid 'Think-Action-Observation' workflow, preventing them from natively supporting flexible multi-agent collaboration patterns.
Neither MAS nor TIR paradigms effectively leverage end-to-end training to learn complex, dynamic multi-agent and multi-tool orchestration within a single, unified LLM.
Method: The Chain-of-Agents (CoA) paradigm unifies multi-agent collaboration within a single LLM's decoding process, dynamically activating various role-playing (e.g., Thinking, Plan, Reflection) and tool agents (e.g., Search, Crawl, Code Generate).

An Agentic Supervised Fine-tuning (SFT) framework distills expert multi-agent system trajectories into CoA-compatible training data, using progressive quality filtering to ensure high-quality, complex problem-solving patterns.

Agentic Reinforcement Learning (RL) further refines the LLM's multi-tool orchestration policy through outcome-driven rewards, enhancing strategic tool usage and adaptive reasoning on challenging, task-specific queries.
Results: Agent Foundation Models (AFMs) achieve new state-of-the-art performance across multi-hop question answering, complex web tasks, mathematical reasoning (up to 78.0% accuracy with AFM-RL-32B), and code generation benchmarks.
AFMs demonstrate an 84.6% reduction in inference cost (token consumption) compared to traditional multi-agent systems while maintaining or exceeding competitive performance.

The models exhibit strong generalization capabilities, adapting to unseen multi-hop QA datasets and effectively orchestrating novel tool agents when provided with explicit descriptions and invocation schemas.
Takeaways: A single LLM can effectively internalize and dynamically orchestrate complex multi-agent workflows, significantly reducing computational overhead and token consumption compared to traditional multi-agent systems.
Multi-agent distillation, paired with rigorous data filtering, is a highly effective method for teaching an LLM agentic capabilities and sequential decision-making patterns.

Reinforcement learning, with carefully designed reward functions and strategic data sampling, is crucial for optimizing an agent's policy for multi-tool orchestration and achieving robust performance on verifiable tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.13142.Title: Holistic Evaluation of Multimodal LLMs on Spatial Intelligence
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.13142.Summary: SenseTime Research and NTU introduce EASI, a framework for holistically evaluating spatial intelligence in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), revealing that while models like GPT-5 achieve new benchmarks, a substantial performance gap of over 30 percentage points generally persists compared to human capabilities, particularly in complex reasoning tasks.
Problem: State-of-the-art Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) exhibit a surprising inability to perform basic spatial tasks, despite advanced capabilities in other multimodal domains.

Spatial intelligence, crucial for Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) and embodied agents interacting with the physical world, remains a fundamentally underexplored and fragmented area in MLLM evaluation.
Existing benchmarks for spatial understanding are inconsistent and lack a unified framework for systematic assessment, hindering comparable progress across models.
Method: EASI (Evaluation of Multimodal LLMs on Spatial Intelligence) is proposed as a comprehensive framework to systematically assess MLLMs' spatial intelligence.

A unified taxonomy of six fundamental spatial capabilities (Metric Measurement, Mental Reconstruction, Spatial Relations, Perspective-Taking, Deformation and Assembly, Comprehensive Reasoning) is developed to categorize and integrate diverse spatial tasks.

Eight representative benchmarks are incorporated and evaluated under standardized EASI protocols, including a unified zero-shot Chain-of-Thought (CoT) system prompt, to ensure consistent and comparable assessment of leading MLLMs.
Results: GPT-5 establishes a new state of the art in spatial intelligence, consistently ranking as the best performer across evaluated benchmarks, yet lags human performance by over 30 percentage points on average in complex SI tasks.

Models show relative proficiency in Metric Measurement and Spatial Relations, achieving human-level or superior performance in some object/room size estimations, but fail significantly in areas like Perspective-Taking and Mental Reconstruction.

Qualitative analysis confirms that even advanced models like GPT-5 struggle with complex visual illusions, misinterpretations of transformations, and failure to infer hidden objects, highlighting a lack of fundamental spatial representations.
Takeaways: Spatial intelligence tasks expose greater deficiencies in MLLM capabilities compared to non-spatial tasks, with performance gaps often exceeding 76 percentage points against human baselines on SI-specific benchmarks.

The advantage of proprietary models over open-source counterparts diminishes significantly on the most challenging spatial intelligence tasks, suggesting that breakthroughs in these hard areas may not solely depend on proprietary scaling.

Despite progress, fundamental weaknesses persist in MLLMs, particularly in Perspective-Taking, Mental Reconstruction, Deformation and Assembly, and Comprehensive Reasoning, which often require integrated capabilities and multi-stage logical deduction.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.12790.Title: Reinforcement Learning with Rubric Anchors
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.12790.Summary: Rubicon extends Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) to handle subjective and open-ended tasks in Large Language Models (LLMs) by introducing a scalable rubric-based reward system. The framework achieved an average absolute improvement of 5.2% on humanities-centric benchmarks with only 5K+ training samples and enhanced stylistic control, outperforming a significantly larger 671B model.
Problem: Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) is inherently limited to tasks with objectively verifiable, programmatic outcomes.
Many real-world LLM applications involve subjective, open-ended, or multi-dimensional outputs lacking unambiguous correctness, restricting RLVR's applicability.
Achieving fine-grained stylistic control and generating human-like, emotionally expressive outputs without generic "AI-like" tones remains a challenge for LLMs.
Method: Rubicon formalizes rubrics as multi-dimensional evaluation criteria, comprising criterion descriptions, ordered score tiers, and associated weights, to provide structured, model-interpretable reward signals.

The framework employs advanced reward aggregation strategies, including veto mechanisms, saturation-aware aggregation, and targeted reward shaping, to derive scalar rewards from multi-dimensional rubric scores.

A multi-stage RL protocol and an adaptive defense mechanism against reward hacking are used to mitigate the "seesaw effect" and ensure stable, productive training across diverse and sometimes conflicting task objectives.
Results: The 30B-A3B Rubicon-preview model achieved an average 5.2% absolute improvement across diverse open-ended and humanities-centric benchmarks with only 5K+ training samples.

Rubicon-preview outperformed the 671B DeepSeek-V3 model by 2.4 percentage points on these benchmarks and demonstrated enhanced stylistic control, generating more human-like and emotionally expressive responses.

The model preserved its general and reasoning abilities, surprisingly yielding modest improvements on mathematical reasoning benchmarks (+4.17% on AIME 2024, +0.83% on AIME 2025) while specializing in open-ended tasks.
Takeaways: Formalized rubrics act as scalable and reliable "anchors" for guiding LLM learning in subjective domains, enabling fine-grained control over output style, tone, and content adherence.

A multi-stage RL approach, combined with robust data filtering and an adaptive reward-hacking defense, effectively mitigates performance trade-offs (the "seesaw effect") when training on diverse, conflicting objectives.

Significant performance gains and enhanced stylistic control can be achieved with relatively few training samples (5K+) when coupled with a large, diverse set of rubrics, suggesting new token-efficient scaling dynamics for post-training LLMs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.12587.Title: Multimodal Chain of Continuous Thought for Latent-Space Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.12587.Summary: Researchers from Harvard Medical School and Knovel Engineering Lab introduced MCOUT, a framework that enables Vision-Language Models to perform iterative reasoning directly in a continuous latent space. This approach improved multimodal reasoning accuracy by up to 8.23% on MMMU and 4.79% on ScienceQA, with a 1B-parameter model often outperforming larger VLM baselines.
Problem: Traditional Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, designed for text-only models, struggles with dynamically aligning and integrating heterogeneous visual and textual information in multimodal contexts.
Current VLM reasoning methods often rely on discrete token sequences and static vision features, leading to computational inefficiency and hindering truly dynamic cross-modal interaction.
Existing VLM approaches lack a continuous, iterative refinement process in a unified latent space, unlike human reflective cognition where thoughts are continuously validated against sensory inputs.
Method: MCOUT introduces a framework for iterative reasoning directly within a VLM's continuous latent space, refining 'thought embeddings' rather than generating discrete language tokens.

Two variants are proposed: MCOUT-Base directly reuses the language model's last hidden state as the continuous thought, while MCOUT-Multi integrates multimodal latent attention to explicitly combine the hidden state with visual embeddings.

The reasoning process involves N_t iterative steps where each newly generated thought embedding is appended to the input sequence and fed back into the language model for further refinement, guided by an auxiliary loss on intermediate thoughts.
Results: MCOUT-Base achieved a 58.86% accuracy on ScienceQA, representing a 4.79% increase over the baseline, and 27.53% accuracy on MMMU, an 8.21% increase.
The 1B-parameter MCOUT variants consistently outperformed several larger models (e.g., LLaVA-7B/13B, MiniGPT-4-13B, Kosmos-2) on ScienceQA, MMMU, and MMStar benchmarks.

An auxiliary weight of 0.3 for intermediate thought losses yielded the highest performance gains, and full finetuning of both VLM components with LoRA provided additional performance boosts across benchmarks.
Takeaways: Continuous latent reasoning provides a robust and efficient paradigm for enhancing VLM performance, demonstrating that iterative refinement in a hidden space can be more effective than language-bound discrete CoT.

The 1B-parameter MCOUT models achieved strong performance, frequently matching or exceeding much larger state-of-the-art VLMs, highlighting the efficiency and scalability benefits of latent continuous thought.

Analysis revealed a 'modality collapse' in MCOUT-Multi, where the multimodal attention mechanism, despite normalization, provided a static, low-variance contribution from visual inputs, suggesting challenges in truly integrating diverse visual context for continuous reasoning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.12466.Title: Inverse-LLaVA: Eliminating Alignment Pre-training Through Text-to-Vision Mapping
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.12466.Summary: Researchers at Vanderbilt University present Inverse-LLaVA, a novel architecture for Large Vision-Language Models that eliminates the typically costly alignment pre-training stage by mapping discrete text embeddings into continuous visual representation space. This approach reduces computational requirements by 45% and achieves competitive performance, particularly excelling in complex reasoning tasks.
Problem: Current Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) rely on a computationally expensive and data-intensive two-stage training paradigm, beginning with alignment pre-training.
The standard practice of mapping continuous visual features into discrete text token space may lead to information loss and representational bottlenecks.
High computational costs and vast data requirements create barriers for developing multimodal models.
Method: Inverse-LLaVA proposes an inverse modality mapping, projecting discrete text embeddings from the Large Language Model (LLM) into the continuous visual feature space.
It integrates visual and text features within selected transformer layers of a frozen LLM using lightweight, additive fusion components, trained in a single stage.
The method utilizes frozen pre-trained LLM and vision encoder components, only training small projection matrices to connect the modalities.
Results: Inverse-LLaVA eliminates 100% of alignment pre-training data and reduces overall computational requirements by 45% compared to LLaVA-1.5.
The model shows superior performance in reasoning-intensive tasks, achieving a +27.2% higher overall cognition score on the MME benchmark and up to +125% improvement in text translation.

Performance decreases were observed in perception-heavy tasks that rely on memorized visual-text associations (e.g., celebrity recognition, OCR), though richer visual features partially mitigated these gaps.
Takeaways: Alignment pre-training, a cornerstone of existing LVLMs, is not strictly necessary for achieving effective multimodal learning, particularly for reasoning tasks.
Preserving the continuous nature of visual information by projecting text into visual space can unlock deeper cognitive reasoning abilities in multimodal AI.
The conventional vision-to-text mapping paradigm might introduce a 'representational bias' that favors 'textual puzzle-solving' over genuine continuous visual understanding.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.12137.Title: Infusing fine-grained visual knowledge to Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.12137.Summary: A research collaboration between CTU and Google DeepMind introduces a fine-tuning pipeline for Vision-and-Language Models (VLMs) that infuses fine-grained visual knowledge without causing catastrophic forgetting of general-purpose visual understanding or cross-modal retrieval capabilities. The method combines parameter and embedding regularization with a dual-component validation strategy, achieving up to +29.9 mAP@20 in-domain on fine-grained tasks like SOP while largely preserving out-of-domain performance (e.g., -0.1 mAP@20 and -0.9 R@1).
Problem: Fine-grained open-set visual retrieval tasks often yield suboptimal performance when using general-purpose Vision-and-Language Models (VLMs) directly.

Standard fine-tuning of VLM vision encoders on domain-specific data leads to catastrophic forgetting, significantly degrading general-purpose visual understanding and cross-modal (image-text) alignment.
The necessity of maintaining multiple specialized VLM instances for different tasks creates operational inefficiencies in terms of computational resources, storage, and model management.
Method: The authors propose a fine-tuning pipeline for the VLM's visual encoder that combines two regularization techniques: L2 parameter regularization and embedding regularization, the latter distilling embeddings towards a frozen pre-trained encoder using samples from an external generic dataset (ImageNet).
A total objective function weights domain-specific classification loss with both parameter and embedding regularization losses to balance specialization and knowledge retention.

A principled, dual-component validation strategy averages in-domain retrieval metrics (e.g., mAP@20 on fine-grained dataset) and out-of-domain retrieval metrics (e.g., mAP@20 on a generic dataset like ImageNet) to guide hyperparameter tuning and early stopping.
Results: The proposed method successfully mitigated catastrophic forgetting, achieving +29.9 mAP@20 in-domain on Stanford Online Products (SOP) while only incurring -0.1 mAP@20 out-of-domain for image-image and -0.9 R@1 for text-image retrieval on SigLIP, a substantial improvement over standard fine-tuning's -6.0 mAP@20 and -12.8 R@1 drops.

The combined regularization approach consistently outperformed various baselines, including L2-SP, WISE-FT, and variants of LDIFS, in achieving a superior balance between in-domain specialization and out-of-domain knowledge retention across five diverse fine-grained datasets and two VLM architectures (SigLIP, TIPS).

The study demonstrated that ImageNet serves as an effective external dataset for embedding regularization, outperforming LAION in maintaining a strong trade-off between in-domain adaptation and out-of-domain retention.
Takeaways: Parameter regularization alone (L2-SP) is largely insufficient to prevent catastrophic forgetting of out-of-domain performance, especially in fine-grained retrieval contexts.
Embedding regularization, particularly when applied to embeddings from an *external generic dataset* (like ImageNet), is crucial for maintaining general-purpose knowledge and cross-modal alignment.
A rigorous, dual-component validation strategy that jointly optimizes for in-domain specialization and out-of-domain retention is essential for developing robust and adaptable foundation models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.12109.Title: Simple o3: Towards Interleaved Vision-Language Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.12109.Summary: Simple o3 is an open-source framework designed to enhance Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by enabling dynamic, interleaved vision-language reasoning through the use of visual tools. It includes a scalable data synthesis pipeline to create a high-quality dataset, TWI-Tools-146K, and demonstrates superior performance across diverse multimodal benchmarks, including a 27-point lead over GPT-4o on MME reasoning and a 12.9% improvement on VStarBench.
Problem: Existing MLLMs struggled with long Chain-of-Thought reasoning in multimodal scenarios due to fixed visual perception and the separation of perception from reasoning.
A lack of scalable data generation pipelines and systematic methodologies hindered the development of tool-augmented reasoning for hierarchical task decomposition in multimodal settings.
There was insufficient understanding of how different visual tools and varying input resolutions impact MLLM performance in interleaved vision-language reasoning.
Method: Simple o3 introduces an end-to-end open-source framework that integrates dynamic visual tools (cropping, zooming, reusing) into MLLMs via supervised fine-tuning to enable iterative "thinking with images."
It develops an automated, scalable data synthesis pipeline to generate high-quality interleaved vision-language reasoning chains, curating the TWI-Tools-146K dataset from diverse sources.

The framework employs a multi-step inference process where the model iteratively generates reasoning, executes visual tool commands (e.g., cropping images), and appends the transformed visual input as new observations.
Results: Simple o3 achieved 702.1 points on the MME reasoning subset, outperforming its base model by nearly 50 points and GPT-4o by 27 points, demonstrating enhanced multimodal reasoning.
The framework showed substantial improvements in fine-grained perception (+7.4% on HR-Bench 4K, +12.9% on VStarBench) and spatial reasoning (+16.6% on MMVet, +10.3% on LogicVista).
It demonstrated improved robustness by reducing hallucination rates by 1.6% on POPE and 2.3% on HallusionBench, indicating better grounding in visual reality.
Takeaways: Dynamic interaction with visual inputs through tools like image cropping (`focus_area`) and re-attending to the original image (`reuse`) significantly enhances both fine-grained perception and complex multimodal reasoning capabilities.

A scalable, automated data synthesis pipeline using an MLLM orchestrator and a two-step verification module is effective for generating high-quality tool-augmented reasoning data, circumventing the need for expensive human annotation or RL.

Training with diverse, heterogeneous datasets (e.g., mathematical reasoning, perceptual reasoning) is crucial for fostering higher-order iterative reasoning, improving logical inter-object relations and strategic planning.

Optimal `focus_area` implementation involves image cropping during inference, and while high input resolution is beneficial for perception-oriented tasks, it can sometimes be detrimental to certain reasoning tasks due to an "explosion of visual tokens."

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.11737.Title: Ovis2.5 Technical Report
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.11737.Summary: Ovis2.5, developed by the Ovis Team at Alibaba Group, advances multimodal large language models by integrating native-resolution visual processing and reflection-oriented reasoning. The model achieved a state-of-the-art score of 78.3 on the OpenCompass leaderboard for open-source MLLMs under 40B parameters, demonstrating enhanced capabilities in fine-grained visual understanding and deep reasoning.
Problem: Fixed-resolution vision encoders in MLLMs lose fine-grained details and global context for high-resolution or visually dense content, like charts or documents.
Current MLLMs often lack deep, reflective reasoning capabilities such as self-checking and revision, limiting performance on complex, multi-step problems.
Structural misalignment exists between the continuous nature of visual embeddings and the discrete structure of textual embeddings in many MLLM architectures.
Method: Integrates a Native-Resolution Vision Transformer (NaViT) to process images at their original, variable resolutions, preserving fine-grained details and global layout.
Implements reflection-oriented training to enable an optional 'thinking mode' at inference time, allowing for self-checking and iterative refinement of reasoning.
Utilizes a learnable Visual Embedding Table (VET) to structurally align visual and textual embeddings, building on the Ovis architecture, and upgrades the LLM backbone to Qwen3.

Employs a comprehensive five-phase training curriculum (pre-training and post-training with DPO and RL) on a large-scale, high-quality multimodal dataset, supported by an optimized, high-efficiency infrastructure.
Results: Ovis2.5-9B achieved an average score of 78.3 on the OpenCompass leaderboard, setting a new state-of-the-art for open-source MLLMs in the sub-40B parameter range.

The models demonstrated leading capabilities in visual and structured mathematics, ranking first on MathVista (83.4) and WeMath (66.7), and showed strong performance on academic reasoning benchmarks like MMMU (71.2).
Ovis2.5-9B outperformed all leading open-source competitors and GPT-4o on OCRBench v2 (63.4 EN, 58.0 CN) and achieved an impressive average grounding score of 90.1 across RefCOCO datasets.
Takeaways: Native-resolution vision processing combined with Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) in a ViT significantly improves MLLMs' ability to perceive and reason about fine details and spatial layouts in dense visual content.
Explicitly training MLLMs for reflection and self-correction, including the use of '...' tags, enables deeper and more robust reasoning, extending beyond linear chain-of-thought.
The sustained 'small model, big performance' philosophy, exemplified by the Ovis2.5-2B model, shows that highly capable multimodal AI can be made accessible for resource-constrained environments.
A multi-stage, data-rich training curriculum, including DPO and RL with verifiable rewards, is crucial for progressively building strong perceptual and advanced reasoning skills in MLLMs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.11630.Title: Thyme: Think Beyond Images
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.11630.Summary: Thyme introduces a paradigm for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to enhance reasoning and perception by autonomously generating and executing code for image manipulation and computation. This approach achieves substantial performance improvements across nearly 20 benchmarks, frequently outperforming larger models in high-resolution perception tasks.
Problem: Existing open-source MLLMs offer limited functionality for visual information processing, typically restricted to simple cropping or generating auxiliary images with quality issues and high computational cost.
Proprietary MLLMs demonstrate rich image manipulation and computational capabilities through code generation, a feature largely absent in open-source alternatives.
MLLMs often struggle with precise high-resolution perception and complex multi-step reasoning tasks, due to static input interpretation and lack of dynamic interaction with visual data.
Method: Thyme enables MLLMs to autonomously generate and execute Python code for diverse image operations (e.g., cropping, rotation, contrast enhancement) and mathematical computations.
A robust, secure external sandbox is employed to execute the generated code, handle errors, and feed results back to the model for iterative reasoning and problem-solving.

A two-stage training strategy (Supervised Fine-Tuning followed by Reinforcement Learning) is used, featuring specialized data construction and GRPO-ATS for efficient acquisition of tool-use capabilities.
Results: Thyme-7B achieves substantial performance improvements across nearly 20 benchmarks, notably outperforming larger models like Qwen2.5-VL-32B and InternVL3-8B in high-resolution perception tasks.
Significant gains are observed in challenging reasoning domains, including MathVision Mini and LogicVista, by externalizing complex calculations into executable Python code.

Ablation studies confirm the efficacy of masking sandbox content and the 'only last round' training strategy in SFT, while case studies visually demonstrate successful autonomous cropping, rotation, contrast enhancement, and complex calculations.
Takeaways: Masking sandbox execution results during Supervised Fine-Tuning is crucial; it prevents the model from predicting outputs directly and forces it to learn underlying reasoning for code generation.

The GRPO-ATS (Adaptive Temperature Sampling) in RL, using `τ=0.0` for code generation and `τ=1.0` for text, effectively balances precision for executable code with exploration for natural language responses.

A composite reward function, which includes a consistency reward applied only for correct answers, is more effective for guiding complex reasoning than direct rewards for process quality or successful code execution.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.11616.Title: Controlling Multimodal LLMs via Reward-guided Decoding
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.11616.Summary: The research introduces Multimodal Reward-Guided Decoding (MRGD), the first method to enable dynamic, inference-time control over Multimodal Large Language Models. It significantly reduces visual hallucinations and allows users to balance object precision, object recall, and computational cost for image captioning tasks.
Problem: Current Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) offer limited or no dynamic, fine-grained control over their outputs at inference time.
MLLMs frequently suffer from visual hallucinations, generating descriptions of objects not present in the input image, which compromises reliability.
Existing alignment methods like SFT and RLHF produce static MLLMs, while adapting reward-guided decoding from text-only LLMs to multimodal scenarios presents unique challenges.
Method: The Multimodal Reward-Guided Decoding (MRGD) strategy is introduced, enabling dynamic control during the MLLM's autoregressive generation process.
Two distinct multimodal reward models are developed: r_hal to penalize object hallucinations and r_rec to reward the mention of present objects, composed from off-the-shelf tools.
A search-based decoding algorithm combines these reward models using a configurable weight w to balance object precision and recall, with parameters k and T controlling compute-quality trade-offs.
Results: The object hallucination reward model (r_hal) achieved 82.05% validation accuracy in distinguishing hallucinated from factual responses.

MRGD reduced instance-level visual hallucinations by approximately 70% on the COCO benchmark (from 15.05% to 4.53%) when prioritizing precision, while also enabling state-of-the-art object recall when prioritizing coverage.

The approach consistently surpassed existing hallucination mitigation methods, including fine-tuning and other guided decoding strategies, across multiple MLLMs like LLaVA-1.5, Llama-3.2-Vision, and SmolVLM-2, demonstrating robustness and generalizability.
Takeaways: Multimodal reward models, specifically designed for object hallucination and recall, can effectively steer MLLM generation towards desired visiolinguistic properties.
Inference-time dynamic control allows for a flexible trade-off between object precision (reducing hallucinations) and object recall (improving comprehensiveness) based on user-defined priorities.
The proposed search-based decoding strategy, when combined with intermittent reward evaluation, offers a more computationally efficient means of guiding MLLMs than naive rejection sampling.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.10874.Title: SSRL: Self-Search Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.10874.Summary: Self-Search Reinforcement Learning (SSRL) allows large language models to act as internal search engines during training, significantly reducing the reliance on costly external search engines. This method improves training efficiency by 5.53x compared to prior approaches and demonstrates effective generalization to real-world search scenarios during inference.
Problem: Large language models (LLMs) used as agents incur high costs and logistical complexity when frequently interacting with external search engines during reinforcement learning (RL) training.
Existing full-real and semi-real search methods for LLM agents require extensive rollouts and multi-turn API calls, leading to substantial computational and financial overhead.
Current retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approaches rely on static knowledge bases, lacking the dynamic and noisy characteristics of real-time web search.
Method: SSRL introduces a "Full-Sim Search" paradigm where the LLM policy model functions as both the reasoning agent and the internal search engine, generating queries and information from its parametric knowledge.
The training methodology includes an information token mask to encourage comprehensive reasoning and a composite reward function (outcome + format rewards) to guide adherence to structured output.

An on-policy RL approach is used, where the policy model itself acts as the information provider, allowing the model to simultaneously enhance its reasoning and internal knowledge retrieval capabilities.
Results: SSRL achieves a 5.53x reduction in training time compared to simulated search baselines like ZeroSearch, while maintaining robust and steady reward growth.
SSRL-trained models consistently outperform baselines that utilize external or separately simulated search engines, as well as RAG-based methods, on various information-seeking QA benchmarks.

The approach demonstrates effective sim-to-real generalization, allowing SSRL-trained models to seamlessly integrate with real external search engines during inference, with an entropy-guided strategy reducing external search frequency by 20-42% without performance loss.
Takeaways: Large language models possess substantial intrinsic world knowledge that can be effectively elicited and scaled via repeated sampling, with smaller models sometimes rivaling larger ones with sufficient samples.
Instruction-tuned LLMs demonstrate a stronger ability to utilize their internal knowledge for self-search compared to base models, highlighting the impact of fine-tuning on knowledge elicitation.
The use of format-based rewards is critical for guiding LLMs to produce structured, multi-step reasoning trajectories that effectively integrate internal search capabilities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.09834.Title: Speed Always Wins: A Survey on Efficient Architectures for Large Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.09834.Summary: This survey provides a systematic, unified taxonomy of efficient architectural designs and optimization strategies for Large Language Models (LLMs), addressing the computational and memory inefficiencies of traditional Transformers. It synthesizes current progress across diverse approaches, including linear and sparse models, optimized full attention, Mixture-of-Experts, and emerging Diffusion LLMs, also demonstrating their applicability to various modalities.
Problem: The Transformer architecture's quadratic computational and memory complexity with respect to sequence length creates significant barriers for training and deploying LLMs, especially for long-context and multimodal applications.
The rapid proliferation of efficiency-enhancing techniques for LLMs has led to a fragmented research landscape, making it difficult to navigate and understand the broader trends.
There is a critical need to reconcile the immense power of large foundation models with the practical demands of efficiency, scalability, and resource consciousness for sustainable AI development.
Method: The authors conduct a comprehensive literature review, categorizing efficient LLM architectures into a systematic taxonomy with seven main categories: Linear Sequence Modeling, Sparse Sequence Modeling, Efficient Full Attention, Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE), Hybrid Architectures, Diffusion LLMs, and Applications to Other Modalities.
The survey delves into the technical details, mathematical formulations, key innovations, and representative models within each category, providing a structured overview.
It emphasizes the practical aspects of hardware-efficient implementations and critically analyzes the design principles, performance benefits, and limitations of each approach.
Results: The survey maps a trend of 'linearization' of pre-trained Transformer models into efficient recurrent structures, often achieved via finetuning or distillation, to leverage existing model capabilities while gaining efficiency.

It demonstrates that Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers are a powerful paradigm for scaling model capacity without a proportional increase in computational cost, detailing advancements in routing and load balancing.

The research highlights the broad cross-modal transferability of these efficient architectural principles, with SSMs and MoE architectures being effectively adapted for diverse tasks in computer vision, audio processing, and complex multimodal settings.
Takeaways: Linear Attention, Linear RNNs, and State Space Models (SSMs) show a convergent evolutionary trajectory, increasingly adopting similar mathematical formulations and optimization objectives to achieve linear complexity and constant memory.

Significant efficiency gains for standard softmax attention are achieved through hardware-aware optimizations (e.g., IO-aware attention like FlashAttention) and inference-time reductions (e.g., grouped attention, quantization) even without altering quadratic complexity.

Hybrid architectures, combining efficient linear models with attention mechanisms, and the emergence of non-autoregressive Diffusion LLMs represent promising directions for balancing performance and efficiency.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.09736.Title: Seeing, Listening, Remembering, and Reasoning: A Multimodal Agent with Long-Term Memory
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.09736.Summary: M3-Agent, developed by ByteDance Seed, introduces a multimodal AI agent framework that processes continuous video and audio streams, constructs an entity-centric long-term memory, and performs multi-turn reasoning. The system achieves 30.7% accuracy on the M3-Bench-robot dataset and 48.9% on M3-Bench-web, demonstrating enhanced person understanding and cross-modal reasoning capabilities.
Problem: Existing multimodal agents struggle to process infinitely long input streams and are limited by finite context windows or ineffective feature compression.
Current AI memory systems often fail to form consistent, entity-centric world knowledge from diverse multimodal content, leading to ambiguity in long-term understanding.
Standard Long Video Question Answering (LVQA) benchmarks primarily assess low-level visual tasks, lacking the evaluation of higher-level cognitive abilities essential for truly intelligent agents.
Method: M3-Agent employs an entity-centric multimodal graph as long-term memory, continuously generating episodic and semantic memories from incoming video and audio streams.
It integrates external tools for facial and speaker recognition to assign and maintain consistent character identities (e.g., , ) across different modalities and clips.
A reinforcement learning (DAPO) based control workflow enables multi-turn reasoning, allowing the agent to iteratively query its comprehensive memory to answer complex, instruction-based questions.
Results: M3-Agent achieved an overall accuracy of 30.7% on the M3-Bench-robot dataset, surpassing the strongest baseline, MA-LMM, by 6.3%.
On M3-Bench-web, it obtained 48.9% accuracy, outperforming the Gemini-GPT4o-Hybrid baseline by 7.7%, with notable improvements of 15.5% in Person Understanding and 6.7% in Cross-modal Reasoning.

Ablation studies demonstrated that removing character identity equivalence or semantic memory resulted in substantial accuracy drops (e.g., up to 19.2% on M3-Bench-web), affirming their critical roles.
Takeaways: Explicitly managing character identity equivalence and integrating multimodal features into memory is crucial for maintaining long-term consistency and improving agent understanding.
The construction of detailed semantic memory, including character attributes, relationships, and general world knowledge, is essential for enabling higher-level cognitive reasoning in agents.
Reinforcement learning, specifically DAPO, is effective in training agents to perform flexible, multi-turn reasoning and strategic memory retrieval in complex, dynamic environments.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.09726.Title: Sample More to Think Less: Group Filtered Policy Optimization for Concise Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.09726.Summary: Researchers at Microsoft Research developed Group Filtered Policy Optimization (GFPO), an RL fine-tuning method that addresses response length inflation in large language models by integrating rejection sampling into the training process. This approach enables models to generate substantially shorter and more concise reasoning chains while preserving or improving accuracy, leading to significant inference-time compute savings across various reasoning and coding benchmarks.
Problem: Large language models fine-tuned with Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) often suffer from "length inflation," producing excessively verbose responses that do not correlate with improved accuracy.
This verbosity leads to increased inference-time compute costs, slower response times, and a higher carbon footprint, hindering practical deployment.
Existing solutions like token-level loss normalization can inadvertently reinforce verbosity for long correct answers or have limited effectiveness in addressing the core issue.
Method: Group Filtered Policy Optimization (GFPO) modifies GRPO by sampling a larger group of candidate responses during training and then filtering them based on desirable attributes like brevity or "token efficiency" (reward per token ratio).

Only the top-k most desirable responses from the filtered group are used to compute policy gradients, effectively zeroing out gradients for rejected samples and implicitly guiding the policy towards conciseness.

An adaptive variant of GFPO dynamically adjusts the number of retained responses (k) based on real-time estimates of question difficulty, allowing for more exploration on harder problems and more aggressive shortening on easier ones.
Results: GFPO achieved significant Excess Length Reductions (ELR) across benchmarks, including 70.9% on AIME 25 and 84.6% on AIME 24 with Token Efficiency GFPO, while maintaining or improving pass@1 accuracy compared to the GRPO baseline.

Adaptive Difficulty GFPO delivered superior ELR on 4 out of 5 benchmarks and improved accuracy on the hardest AIME 25 questions (27%), demonstrating effective resource allocation for diverse problem difficulties.

GFPO variants generalized robustly to out-of-distribution tasks like LiveCodeBench, mitigating length inflation (up to 79.7% ELR) and sometimes even improving accuracy (e.g., Shortest 8/24 GFPO at 59.2% vs. 56.7% GRPO).
Takeaways: Strategically increasing compute during the training phase by sampling more responses directly translates to continuous and substantial reductions in inference-time compute, creating more efficient LLMs for deployment.
The ratio of retained responses (k/G) acts as a critical control knob to precisely balance the trade-off between response length reduction and reasoning accuracy.
GFPO primarily prunes verbosity in the "Solution" and "Verification" phases of reasoning, indicating it targets redundant steps and filler content without compromising core problem-solving logic.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.08221.Title: Part I: Tricks or Traps? A Deep Dive into RL for LLM Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.08221.Summary: Researchers systematically analyzed reinforcement learning techniques for enhancing large language model reasoning, demonstrating that a minimalist combination of two empirically validated methods can consistently outperform more complex, multi-trick algorithms. The work clarifies the conditional effectiveness of various RL components across different model scales, alignment statuses, and data difficulties.
Problem: The rapidly growing "RL for LLM" (RL4LLM) field suffers from fragmented understanding and inconsistent recommendations, stemming from varied experimental setups and training data.
A lack of standardized guidelines and deep mechanistic analysis makes it challenging for practitioners to select and apply effective RL techniques for LLM reasoning.
Conflicting conclusions across studies regarding the utility of different RL "tricks" (e.g., normalization, clipping, loss aggregation) create ambiguity and hinder progress.
Method: Conducted rigorous reproductions and isolated evaluations of prominent RL techniques within the unified, open-source ROLL framework to ensure consistency and reproducibility.
Performed fine-grained experiments across diverse base models (Qwen3-4B/8B, aligned and non-aligned) and varied mathematical reasoning datasets (easy, medium, hard) to analyze internal mechanisms.

Investigated four key categories of RL techniques: normalization strategies, clipping strategies, loss aggregation granularity, and filtering strategies, primarily using PPO with critic-free REINFORCE.
Results: The proposed "Lite PPO," combining group-level mean/batch-level standard deviation advantage normalization with token-level loss aggregation, consistently outperformed complex algorithms like GRPO and DAPO.

Removing the standard deviation term in advantage normalization significantly stabilizes training and improves effectiveness when reward distributions are highly concentrated (e.g., on easy datasets).
Token-level loss aggregation proved more effective for base models, improving convergence and robustness, while sequence-level loss often performed better for aligned models.
The optimal `Clip-Higher` parameter for performance showed a scaling law for smaller aligned models but not for larger ones, indicating model-dependent behavior for clipping ranges.
Takeaways: The effectiveness of RL techniques like advantage normalization and loss aggregation is highly conditional on reward distribution characteristics, model alignment status, and reasoning task complexity.

Relaxing the PPO `Clip-Higher` bound (as in DAPO) can facilitate exploration for already aligned models by shifting the focus of token-level clipping from discourse connectives to high-frequency functional tokens.

A simple, "minimalist" combination of just two empirically validated techniques (e.g., hybrid normalization and token-level loss aggregation) can surpass the performance of more intricate, multi-trick RL algorithms.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.08189.Title: Reinforcement Learning for Large Model: A Survey
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.08189.Summary: A comprehensive survey maps the rapidly expanding landscape of visual Reinforcement Learning (RL) applied to large multimodal models, systematically categorizing over 250 recent works and detailing algorithmic advancements, evaluation methods, and persistent challenges. This work aims to provide a coherent guide for researchers and practitioners in this rapidly evolving interdisciplinary field.
Problem: The rapidly growing and fragmented research landscape at the intersection of reinforcement learning (RL) and large multimodal models (LMMs) lacks a comprehensive, up-to-date synthesis, especially for advancements since 2024.

Significant challenges exist in applying RL to visual domains, including stabilizing policy optimization with complex reward signals, handling high-dimensional visual inputs, and designing scalable reward functions for long-horizon decision-making.
There is a need for a structured overview to guide future research and practical deployment of RL techniques for visual tasks, covering areas from perception to generation and interaction.
Method: Conducted an extensive and systematic literature review, synthesizing over 250 representative works, predominantly focusing on research advancements since 2024.

Formalized visual RL problems by casting text/image generation as an episodic Markov Decision Process and detailing key alignment paradigms (RLHF, DPO, RLVR) and policy optimization algorithms (PPO, GRPO).

Organized the vast literature into a clear taxonomy across four thematic pillars: Multi-Modal Large Language Models (MLLMs), Visual Generation, Unified Model Frameworks, and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, analyzing algorithmic design, reward engineering, and benchmarking within each.
Results: A structured synthesis identifies RLHF and its variants, along with GRPO, as dominant approaches for aligning and optimizing large multimodal models, providing a clear map of algorithmic evolution.
The survey successfully categorizes over 250 works into four key application areas, detailing their specific algorithmic designs, reward engineering strategies, and progress in benchmarking for each.

A principled taxonomy for evaluating visual RL methods is introduced, differentiating between set-level, sample-level, and model-state metrics, alongside a clear articulation of critical open challenges and promising future research directions.
Takeaways: RLHF principles and its variants, such as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), are profoundly influencing reward signal design for visual RL.

Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) emerges as a particularly effective policy optimization algorithm for visual RL, offering stable, low-variance learning signals and reducing memory consumption by discarding the value network.

The field's research landscape is structured into four primary thematic areas: MLLMs, Visual Generation, Unified Models, and VLA Models, each presenting unique algorithmic adaptations and reward design considerations.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.07976.Title: Beyond Ten Turns: Unlocking Long-Horizon Agentic Search with Large-Scale Asynchronous RL
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.07976.Summary: The ASearcher project, from Tsinghua University and Ant Group, introduces an open-source, large-scale asynchronous reinforcement learning framework that enables LLM agents to perform long-horizon web search and exhibit advanced search intelligence. This system sets new state-of-the-art performance for open-source models on challenging benchmarks like GAIA and xBench-DeepSearch, facilitating learning of multi-step strategies spanning over 100 turns.
Problem: Existing open-source online RL methods for LLM search agents often enforce strict turn limits (e.g., ≤ 10 turns), preventing the learning of complex, multi-step search strategies essential for real-world problems.
