Problem: CLIP's features, while excellent for semantic understanding, inherently lack the fine-grained pixel details required for high-fidelity image reconstruction.

Existing unified models either sacrifice CLIP's understanding capabilities for reconstruction fidelity (e.g., quantization-based) or yield inconsistent, computationally expensive generative results (e.g., diffusion decoders on frozen CLIP).
Fixed-length query embeddings often create information bottlenecks in generative models, leading to loss of crucial visual details necessary for robust and consistent image editing.
Method: A two-stage training scheme with self-distillation is applied to finetune CLIP for image reconstruction, ensuring pixel-level detail injection while preserving original semantic understanding by preventing catastrophic forgetting.

A novel dual-condition architecture is introduced for image generation and editing, leveraging both multimodal hidden states from a large language model and learnable query embeddings as conditions for the diffusion transformer.

The UniLIP framework is built upon InternVL3 (InternViT as CLIP encoder) and SANA (a linear diffusion transformer) with a pixel decoder initialized from DC-AE, trained on extensive datasets for broad applicability.
Results: Achieved state-of-the-art image reconstruction among CLIP-based tokenizers with significantly lower rFID (0.79 at 256x256) and higher PSNR/SSIM compared to previous methods.
Preserved and improved CLIP's multimodal understanding, with UniLIP-1B scoring 1499 on MME-P, surpassing the frozen CLIP's 1492, demonstrating enhanced detail capture without semantic degradation.

Set new state-of-the-art in image generation (GenEval 0.90, WISE 0.63) and image editing (ImgEdit 3.94), often outperforming larger unified models like OmniGen2 and BAGEL with competitive inference speeds.
Takeaways: A carefully designed two-stage training scheme with self-distillation effectively allows CLIP to acquire high-fidelity reconstruction capabilities while remarkably preserving, and in some cases even enhancing, its original understanding performance.

Infusing pixel-level details into CLIP's visual representations can surprisingly improve its ability to answer detail-oriented understanding queries, suggesting a richer, more versatile internal representation.

The dual-condition architecture successfully decouples contextual extraction and reasoning (MLLM) from image synthesis (DiT), ensuring lossless information propagation crucial for consistent and high-fidelity image editing.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.23276.Title: How Far Are AI Scientists from Changing the World?
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.23276.Summary: This survey critically assesses the capabilities of large language model-powered AI Scientist systems, introducing a unique framework to map current achievements and identify gaps in scientific research automation. An empirical evaluation of 28 AI-generated papers revealed severe limitations, including "Experimental Weakness" in 100% of the assessed works, underscoring the distance from autonomous scientific discovery.
Problem: Traditional human-centric scientific research is constrained by limited time and cognitive capacity, leading to inefficiencies in discovery and hypothesis generation.
The rapidly evolving field of LLM-powered AI Scientist systems lacked a structured, prospect-driven review and a clear roadmap for their development.
There was an absence of rigorous identification of key bottlenecks and missing components required for AI Scientists to achieve truly autonomous research capabilities.
Method: A novel "capability-level framework" (knowledge acquisition, idea generation, verification and falsification, and evolution) was introduced to systematically analyze AI Scientist system development.
Existing literature on AI Scientist systems was thoroughly reviewed and synthesized within this framework, categorizing methods and evaluation benchmarks.
An empirical assessment utilized an advanced AI reviewer model, DeepReviewer-14B, to quantitatively evaluate 28 AI-generated research papers for quality and prevalent defects.
Results: An evaluation of 28 AI-generated research papers found low quality scores (highest average 4.63/10), with "Experimental Weakness" present in 100% of the assessed papers and "Methodological Unclarity/Flaws" in 96.4%.
Underlying LLMs showed low accuracy on practical implementation benchmarks, such as OpenAI's "o1-preview" achieving only 16.90% success on MLE-Bench tasks.

Identified research capability gaps include insufficient precision in information retrieval, difficulty generating truly novel hypotheses, weak multi-agent collaboration, and underdeveloped dynamic planning mechanisms.
Takeaways: Despite advancements in LLM technology, AI Scientist systems face fundamental limitations such as hallucination, high costs for knowledge updating, and catastrophic forgetting, hindering scientific accuracy.
Current AI Scientists excel in foundational knowledge acquisition and idea generation but demonstrate severe deficiencies in rigorous verification, experimental design, and autonomous evolution.

The empirical evaluation confirmed that AI-generated research papers frequently fail to meet established scientific standards, particularly regarding experimental soundness and methodological clarity.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.23070.Title: Vocabulary-free Fine-grained Visual Recognition via Enriched Contextually Grounded Vision-Language Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.23070.Summary: The E-FineR framework from MBZUAI introduces a fully automated and training-free method for vocabulary-free fine-grained visual recognition, leveraging VQA, LLMs, and VLMs to dynamically discover and classify subtle visual categories. It achieves state-of-the-art performance in vocabulary-free settings, with an average of 58.4% Clustering Accuracy and 66.3% Semantic Accuracy across five standard datasets, while also showing competitive results in zero-shot and few-shot scenarios.
Problem: Traditional Fine-grained Visual Recognition (FGVR) methods depend on fixed vocabularies, extensive labeled datasets, and expert annotations, hindering scalability and adaptability to emerging classes.

Current Vision-Language Model (VLM) approaches for open-set recognition provide insufficient semantic context for fine-grained distinctions and struggle with truly vocabulary-free scenarios where class names are unknown a priori.
Automated label discovery often results in noisy labels that can propagate errors in training-based methods, while manual prompt engineering is infeasible for dynamic, vocabulary-free environments.
Method: A fully automated and training-free framework, E-FineR, integrates Visual Question Answering (VQA) models, Large Language Models (LLMs), and Vision-Language Models (VLMs).

The method employs a "Class Names Reasoning" step to generate initial candidate class names, followed by "Class-specific Contextual Grounding" using an LLM to enrich these names with detailed, context-aware sentences.

An "Advanced Class Names Refinement" component filters candidates based on visual relevance, and "Vision-Language Prompt Coupling" combines enriched text embeddings with augmented visual prototypes for robust classification.
Results: E-FineR achieves state-of-the-art in vocabulary-free FGVR, with average 58.4% Clustering Accuracy and 66.3% Semantic Accuracy across five fine-grained datasets, outperforming the FineR baseline by +2.5% cACC and +2.0% sACC.
In zero-shot classification, the framework leads among automated and train-free methods, scoring 72.04% on Oxford Flowers and 90.30% on Oxford Pets, closely competing with training-based approaches.

E-FineR demonstrates strong few-shot performance, surpassing other train-free baselines across ImageNet (70.59%), Stanford Cars (72.24%), and Oxford Pets (92.53%), highlighting its adaptability to low-data regimes.
Takeaways: Leveraging the synergy of VQA, LLMs, and VLMs allows for dynamic discovery of fine-grained class names and enrichment of their semantic context in a training-free manner.
A soft filtering strategy for candidate class names, based on visual relevance, is more effective than rigid selection, preserving label diversity and improving recall in fine-grained settings.

Combining contextually grounded text embeddings with augmented visual prototypes yields robust, coupled vision-language classifiers, mitigating issues from noisy auto-discovered labels and limited pseudo-labeled data.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.22844.Title: RLVMR: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Meta-Reasoning Rewards for Robust Long-Horizon Agents
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.22844.Summary: RLVMR integrates verifiable meta-reasoning rewards into reinforcement learning to enhance long-horizon Large Language Model agents, enabling superior performance and generalization on unseen tasks while drastically reducing inefficient exploration. The framework improves success rates on challenging benchmarks like ALFWorld by up to 16.4 percentage points and reduces repetitive actions by tenfold, allowing smaller models to outperform larger commercial LLMs.
Problem: Large Language Model agents often suffer from "inefficient exploration" and brittle reasoning when tackling complex, long-horizon tasks due to reliance on sparse, outcome-only rewards.
Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) leads to policies that are poor at generalizing to novel situations, while traditional Reinforcement Learning (RL) can reinforce illogical or repetitive action sequences.
The lack of interpretable and robust internal reasoning processes makes agents unreliable and difficult to debug, hindering their deployment in dynamic real-world environments.
Method: RLVMR operationalizes metacognitive behaviors (planning, exploration, reflection, monitoring) through explicit, verifiable XML-style tags within the agent's thought process.
It employs a two-phase training strategy: an initial supervised fine-tuning "cold start" to teach meta-reasoning syntax, followed by online reinforcement learning.
A custom GRPO-MR algorithm combines a dense, step-level reward for the quality of meta-reasoning with sparse, global outcome rewards, guiding the agent towards robust problem-solving processes.
Results: RLVMR achieves new state-of-the-art success rates, improving performance on unseen task categories (ALFWorld Unseen-L2) by 16.4 percentage points over the next best baseline.

The framework drastically reduces inefficient exploration behaviors, with repetitive actions decreasing tenfold (e.g., 2.3% vs. 21.5% for GRPO) and invalid actions also significantly cut, leading to shorter episode lengths.
Smaller RLVMR-trained models (e.g., Qwen-1.5B) outperform larger commercial LLMs (e.g., GPT-4o) on complex, long-horizon tasks, demonstrating a more efficient path to high performance.
Takeaways: Directly rewarding the explicit process of reasoning, rather than solely the final outcome, is essential for cultivating robust and generalizable problem-solving skills in LLM agents.
Incorporating metacognitive functions via structured tags provides a verifiable and dense feedback signal, effectively mitigating inefficient exploration and promoting self-correction.
A targeted training approach that bootstraps meta-reasoning through a small SFT dataset before engaging in a specialized RL phase leads to stable and efficient learning, even for smaller models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.22607.Title: VL-Cogito: Progressive Curriculum Reinforcement Learning for Advanced Multimodal Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.22607.Summary: VL-Cogito, developed by researchers from DAMO Academy, Alibaba Group, Hupan Lab, and Fudan University, introduces a Progressive Curriculum Reinforcement Learning (PCuRL) framework to enhance multimodal reasoning in large language models. The framework enables adaptive reasoning depth and efficiency, achieving state-of-the-art or highly competitive performance on 6 out of 10 mainstream multimodal benchmarks, including significant gains over its Qwen2.5-VL-Instruct-7B backbone model.
Problem: Current Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) exhibit unstable performance across diverse domains and difficulty levels due to the inherent complexity and heterogeneity of multimodal tasks.
Existing MLLMs struggle with the semantic richness and varied problem formulations in multimodal contexts, leading to inconsistent performance.
Conventional reasoning models often extend reasoning length indiscriminately, potentially compromising efficiency by over-thinking simple tasks.
Method: The paper introduces VL-Cogito, an MLLM trained with a novel Progressive Curriculum Reinforcement Learning (PCuRL) framework built upon GRPO-based Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR).
PCuRL employs Online Difficulty Soft Weighting (ODSW) to dynamically adjust the importance of prompts based on their difficulty across three progressive training stages (Easy, Medium, Hard).
PCuRL incorporates Dynamic Length Reward (DyLR) during the hard stage to incentivize the model to adapt its reasoning path length based on individual problem demands.
Results: VL-Cogito achieved state-of-the-art or highly competitive performance on 6 out of 10 mainstream multimodal benchmarks, including Geometry@3k, MathVista, LogicVista, ScienceQA, EMMA, and MMStar.
The model demonstrated substantial absolute performance gains over its Qwen2.5-VL-Instruct-7B backbone, with improvements of 7.6% on Geometry@3K and 5.5% on MathVista.

Ablation studies confirmed that PCuRL's components (curriculum, ODSW, and DyLR) contribute to performance improvements, with DyLR effectively promoting adaptive reasoning length and depth when integrated within the progressive curriculum.
Takeaways: Progressive curriculum learning, when guided by online difficulty soft weighting, effectively stabilizes RL training and systematically fosters complex reasoning skills in MLLMs.

Dynamically incentivizing reasoning length, rather than fixed-length rewards, allows MLLMs to develop adaptive thought processes, generating concise responses for simple tasks and longer, in-depth reasoning for complex ones.

The stabilizing effect of the multi-stage curriculum is crucial for Dynamic Length Reward to function effectively, preventing unstable performance from premature over-lengthening on misclassified difficult tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.22448.Title: Falcon-H1: A Family of Hybrid-Head Language Models Redefining Efficiency and Performance
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.22448.Summary: The Falcon LLM Team introduces Falcon-H1, a series of hybrid-head language models that integrate parallel Transformer attention and Mamba State Space Models for improved efficiency and performance. The flagship Falcon-H1-34B-Instruct model rivals or outperforms leading 70B-scale purely Transformer models on various benchmarks while demonstrating up to 4x input and 8x output throughput improvements at long sequence lengths.
Problem: Traditional Transformer architectures face quadratic computational complexity with respect to input sequence length, limiting efficiency for very long contexts.
Existing large language models often require increasingly larger parameter counts and extensive training data to achieve higher performance, leading to high computational and memory costs.
A need exists for LLMs that balance high performance across diverse tasks with exceptional computational and memory efficiency for broader deployment scenarios.
Method: Developed a novel parallel hybrid mixer block that concurrently integrates Transformer-based attention with Mamba-2 State Space Models, allowing independent tuning of component channel ratios.

Employed a comprehensive pretraining strategy including a massive, diverse corpus (up to 18 Teratokens), a dynamic data mixture with an 'anti-curriculum' approach, and aggressive up-sampling of high-quality data.
Introduced an in-house distributed training framework (Mambatron) with 5D parallelism, including novel Context Parallelism and Mixer Parallelism, to optimize training for hybrid architectures.
Results: The Falcon-H1-34B-Instruct model rivals or outperforms leading 70B-scale models (e.g., Qwen3-32B, Qwen2.5-72B, Llama3.3-70B) across complex reasoning, scientific knowledge, and code generation benchmarks, despite being half the size.
Achieved up to a 4x improvement in input throughput and an 8x speedup in output throughput at 262k token sequence lengths compared to Transformer-based counterparts like Qwen2.5-32B.
Smaller models like Falcon-H1-0.5B-Instruct deliver performance comparable to typical 7B models from 2024, demonstrating leading results in Math, Science, and Code among sub-1B models.
Takeaways: A parallel hybrid architecture combining attention and Mamba SSMs can achieve superior performance and efficiency compared to monolithic Transformer designs, especially for long-context tasks.
Deeper model architectures can yield better quality for a fixed parameter budget (e.g., Falcon-H1-1.5B-Deep), challenging simple width-scaling conventions.

Careful tuning of tokenizer components (e.g., individual digit/punctuation splitting, LaTeX tokens) and mitigation of SSM-specific loss spikes (by clipping 'dt' values) are crucial for robust performance and training stability.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.22062.Title: Meta CLIP 2: A Worldwide Scaling Recipe
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.22062.Summary: FAIR (Meta) researchers introduce a transparent, open-sourced methodology for pre-training CLIP on native worldwide web-scale image-text pairs. This approach overcomes the "curse of multilinguality," allowing a ViT-H/14 model to surpass its English-only counterpart by 0.8% on zero-shot ImageNet and establish new state-of-the-art results across multilingual benchmarks like CVQA (57.4%) and Babel-ImageNet (50.2%).
Problem: Most CLIP variants rely on English-only data, discarding over 50% of global web content and introducing challenges for worldwide scaling.
Existing multilingual CLIP methods often rely on less robust approaches like distillation, machine translation, or proprietary datasets, leading to biases and limited transparency.
Multilingual models typically exhibit degraded performance on English tasks, known as the "curse of multilinguality," hindering truly universal foundation models.
Method: Developed a three-step "worldwide scaling recipe" based on English Meta CLIP, incorporating per-language metadata for 300+ languages from expanded sources like Multilingual WordNet and Wikipedia.
Designed a novel, language-by-language curation algorithm that uses language identification, language-specific substring matching, and adaptive concept balancing (t_lang) for diverse data.
Adapted the training framework by integrating a multilingual text tokenizer (XLM-V), scaling seen training pairs (2.3x), and identifying a crucial model capacity (ViT-H/14) to leverage global data.
Results: A Meta CLIP 2 ViT-H/14 model trained on worldwide data achieved 81.3% accuracy on zero-shot ImageNet classification, outperforming its English-only counterpart by 0.8%.

Established new state-of-the-art performance on multilingual benchmarks, including 57.4% averaged answer accuracy on CVQA, 50.2% on Babel-ImageNet, and 64.3% recall@1 for image-to-text retrieval on XM3600.
Demonstrated improved understanding of cultural diversity, leading to better performance on geographically and culturally diverse benchmarks like Dollar Street, GeoDE, and GLDv2.
Takeaways: The "curse of multilinguality" can be overcome with sufficient model capacity (ViT-H/14) and scaled training, enabling non-English data to mutually benefit and even improve English performance.
Language-specific metadata and adaptive concept balancing are critical for effectively curating and processing the vast diversity and varying scales of multilingual web data.
A transparent and open-sourced recipe for training CLIP on native worldwide data is achievable, providing a generalizable framework without reliance on machine translation or distillation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.22003.Title: See Different, Think Better: Visual Variations Mitigating Hallucinations in LVLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.22003.Summary: Researchers from Shanghai University developed ViHallu, a vision-centric framework that mitigates hallucinations in Large Vision-Language Models by generating visual variations and tailored instructions to improve visual-semantic alignment. The approach resulted in up to a 14.4-point overall performance gain on LLaVA-Bench and reduced hallucination rates by up to 5.9% on MMHal-Bench across various LVLM architectures.
Problem: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) frequently hallucinate, generating text inconsistent with visual content, especially when dealing with fine-grained visual distinctions.
Existing
text-centric
hallucination mitigation methods often fail to fundamentally enhance visual comprehension, instead focusing on language generation adjustments.
There is a scarcity of naturally occurring datasets with sufficient fine-grained visual variations needed to train LVLMs to discriminate subtle visual features.
Method: The ViHallu framework generates high-quality visual variation images using ControlNet++ by editing captions and preserving original image structure, including counterfactual interventions.
It constructs tailored visual instructions using an LLM (DeepSeek-chat V2) for question generation and a VQA model (InternVL2.5) for ground-truth answers based on original and varied image pairs.
A multi-model consensus approach, employing LLaVA-1.5, MiniCPM-V 2.6, and mPLUG-OWL3, validates the quality of the generated Question-Answer pairs for the ViHallu-Instruction dataset.
Results: Improved F1 scores on the POPE dataset across LLaVA-1.5, MiniGPT4 v2, and Qwen2-VL, with MiniGPT4 v2 showing the most significant gains of 2.93-5.23% in accuracy and outperforming other text-centric methods.
Enhanced overall performance on the LLaVA-Bench (in-the-wild) dataset, with Qwen2-VL achieving an impressive 14.4-point increase and MiniGPT-4 V2 gaining 10.4 points in conversation.

Reduced hallucination rates on the MMHal-Bench dataset by up to 5.9% (Qwen2-VL) and 5.7% (LLaVA-1.5), alongside increased overall scores across all evaluated models, particularly in challenging categories like Adversarial and Environment.
Takeaways: Directly enhancing visual-semantic alignment through synthetically generated and controlled visual variations is more effective for hallucination mitigation than relying solely on text-centric adjustments.
Counterfactual interventions in visual data generation, such as placing objects in uncommon contexts, force LVLMs to learn from visual evidence rather than spurious linguistic or statistical priors.

A robust pipeline leveraging advanced generative models and multi-model consensus for quality control can create high-quality, targeted instruction datasets to improve fine-grained visual understanding in LVLMs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.21848.Title: EDGE-GRPO: Entropy-Driven GRPO with Guided Error Correction for Advantage Diversity
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.21848.Summary: Researchers at Beihang University developed EDGE-GRPO, an algorithm that combines Guided Error Correction for response diversity and Entropy-Driven Advantage for signal refinement to overcome the "advantage collapse problem" in Group Relative Policy Optimization for LLMs. This approach yields over 20% performance gains on mathematical reasoning benchmarks while requiring only 1K training samples for competitive results.
Problem: The "advantage collapse problem" in Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) for LLMs, where sparse, rule-based reward functions lead to uniform rewards and zero advantages within sampled response groups.
This collapse halts effective policy gradient updates, severely limiting sample efficiency and hindering performance on challenging reasoning problems.

Existing methods for enhancing response diversity or augmenting training signals are often inconclusive, insufficient for limited capacity models, or miscalibrated with respect to response correctness.
Method: Guided Error Correction (GEC) enhances response diversity by strategically introducing external guidance (reflection prompts, direct answer injection, or reference solution replacement) for incorrect responses within a group.
Entropy-Driven Advantage (EDA) refines advantage signals by scaling GRPO advantages with policy entropy, providing finer-grained differentiation among responses.
The EDGE-GRPO algorithm integrates GEC and EDA to simultaneously enhance response diversity and advantage diversity, fundamentally alleviating the advantage collapse problem.
Results: EDGE-GRPO consistently achieved over 20% performance improvement compared to baseline Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B and Qwen2.5-Math-7B models on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, with the 7B model reaching 53.21% average accuracy on DeepScaleR-Hard-1K.

Ablation studies confirmed that both GEC and EDA contribute to performance gains, and their combination effectively mitigates the advantage collapse problem by maintaining consistently higher intra-group advantage variance.
The method demonstrated exceptional data efficiency, achieving competitive results using only 1K training samples for one epoch, significantly less than other state-of-the-art open-source models.
Takeaways: Relying solely on model reflection for self-correction is often ineffective for LLMs, especially those with limited capacity, and spontaneous reflection can even correlate with lower accuracy.
Policy entropy can be miscalibrated, with models showing overconfidence in incorrect answers and underconfidence in correct ones, making simple entropy-based adjustments insufficient.
A dual intervention strategy, addressing both response generation diversity and the granularity of advantage signals, is necessary to effectively overcome the advantage collapse problem in GRPO.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.21053.Title: Flow Matching Policy Gradients
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.21053.Summary: Flow Policy Optimization (FPO) integrates flow-based generative models into on-policy reinforcement learning by using conditional flow matching loss as a proxy for action likelihoods, enabling policies to learn expressive, multimodal action distributions. This approach demonstrated improved performance over traditional Gaussian policies and prior diffusion-RL methods on various continuous control tasks, including challenging high-dimensional humanoid control in under-conditioned settings.
Problem: Integrating expressive flow-based generative models as policies into reinforcement learning systems.
The computational intractability of calculating exact action likelihoods for flow-based and diffusion models, which is a fundamental requirement for policy gradient methods like PPO.
Limitations of prior diffusion-RL methods, which often reformulate denoising as an MDP, increasing credit assignment complexity and coupling training to specific stochastic sampling procedures.
Method: Introduces Flow Policy Optimization (FPO), an on-policy reinforcement learning algorithm that extends PPO to optimize flow-based policies.
Proxies the log-likelihood ratio in the PPO objective using the difference in Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) loss between the current and old policies.
Treats the flow sampling process as a black box during rollouts, making the method agnostic to the choice of diffusion or flow integration method (deterministic or stochastic, varying steps).
Results: In a GridWorld task, FPO learned multimodal action distributions at saddle points, enabling diverse and optimal trajectories towards multiple goal regions.
Outperformed both Gaussian PPO and DPPO in 8 out of 10 continuous control tasks from the MuJoCo Playground benchmark.

Achieved significantly higher success rates in high-dimensional, under-conditioned humanoid control scenarios, achieving 70.6% (vs 46.5% for Gaussian PPO) with root + hands conditioning and 54.3% (vs 29.8% for Gaussian PPO) with root-only conditioning.
Takeaways: The weighted denoising loss (which includes CFM loss) is equivalent to the negative Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) plus a constant, allowing its use as a proxy for the likelihood ratio.
Constructing the PPO ratio based on the difference in CFM losses enables gradient-based optimization of flow-based policies without requiring exact likelihood computations.

Flow-based policies can effectively learn and represent complex, multimodal action distributions, which is advantageous in under-determined or ambiguous environments where single-modal policies struggle.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.21046.Title: A Survey of Self-Evolving Agents: What, When, How, and Where to Evolve on the Path to Artificial Super Intelligence
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.21046.Summary: This survey paper from a global collaboration of institutions introduces a comprehensive framework for self-evolving agents, unifying research around the "What, When, How, and Where to Evolve" dimensions. It identifies critical evaluation gaps in adaptivity, retention, generalization, efficiency, and safety, while also outlining emergent risks and mitigation strategies for these dynamic AI systems.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) are static and cannot adapt their internal parameters or reasoning processes in real-time to novel tasks, evolving knowledge, or dynamic environments.
The lack of a unified theoretical framework for self-evolving agents leads to fragmented research and inconsistent terminology.
Existing evaluation benchmarks and metrics are insufficient for assessing continuous learning, long-term adaptivity, and safety in dynamic AI systems.
Method: The paper provides the first systematic and comprehensive review of self-evolving agents, establishing a structured framework around four core questions: "What to Evolve?", "When to Evolve?", "How to Evolve?", and "Where to Evolve?".

It critically analyzes existing evaluation methodologies, proposing five core evaluation goals (Adaptivity, Retention, Generalization, Efficiency, Safety) and advocating for standardized, longitudinal protocols.

The survey identifies and categorizes emergent risks unique to self-evolving agents, such as uncontrolled behavior drift and deployment-time reward hacking, along with prescriptive guardrails and mitigation strategies.
Results: The survey presents a unified taxonomy for self-evolving agents, categorizing evolutionary mechanisms by *what* (models, context, tools, architecture), *when* (intra-test-time, inter-test-time), and *how* (reward-based, imitation, population-based methods) they evolve.

It highlights significant gaps in current evaluation, particularly regarding retention and long-horizon safety, and proposes new evaluation goals and standardized protocols for measuring adaptivity, generalization, and efficiency.

The paper outlines critical future research directions, including personalization in open-ended environments, achieving robust generalization while avoiding catastrophic forgetting, and ensuring safety, control, and governance in increasingly autonomous multi-agent ecosystems.
Takeaways: Self-evolution encompasses changes across an agent's entire system, including models, context (memory/prompts), tools (acquisition/mastery), and even architectural designs (single/multi-agent).
Evolutionary processes occur both intra-test-time (real-time, task-specific adaptation) and inter-test-time (retrospective, generalized learning between tasks), leveraging various learning paradigms.

The development of truly adaptive and safe self-evolving agents requires a fundamental shift in evaluation, moving beyond episodic metrics to assess long-term adaptivity, catastrophic forgetting, generalizability under distribution shifts, resource efficiency, and evolving safety alignment.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.21045.Title: Reconstructing 4D Spatial Intelligence: A Survey
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.21045.Summary: Researchers from Nanyang Technological University, HKUST, and Texas A&M University present a survey introducing a new five-level hierarchical taxonomy for 4D spatial intelligence, systematically categorizing reconstruction methods from visual observations. The work consolidates recent advancements, identifies challenges across each level, and outlines future research directions in this evolving field.
Problem: Rapid advancements in 3D representations and deep learning for 4D spatial intelligence have quickly outdated existing survey literature.
Previous surveys provided fragmented views, lacking a comprehensive, hierarchical analysis of how different aspects of 4D scene reconstruction build upon each other.
There was a need for an up-to-date, structured overview to guide researchers through the increasingly complex landscape of 4D spatial intelligence.
Method: The authors introduce a novel, five-level hierarchical taxonomy to systematically organize 4D spatial intelligence, progressing from low-level 3D attributes to complex physical interactions.

They conduct a comprehensive review of methods at each level, primarily focusing on reconstructing 4D scenes from video inputs and leveraging cutting-edge techniques like NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting.
An accompanying up-to-date GitHub project page is maintained to track and consolidate ongoing developments in the fast-evolving field.
Results: The survey consolidates advancements in 4D spatial intelligence, detailing methods for reconstruction of low-level 3D attributes, 3D scene components, 4D dynamic scenes, and interactions among scene components.

It identifies specific challenges at each of the five hierarchical levels, such as the difficulty in recovering fine-scale geometry, modeling complex dynamic phenomena, and ensuring physical plausibility.

The work outlines promising future directions for research, including the development of multimodal representations, physics-informed priors, differentiable physics engines, and integration with world models.
Takeaways: 4D spatial intelligence can be effectively understood and categorized through a progressive hierarchical structure, revealing how foundational elements underpin more complex systems.
The field has moved from independent estimation of low-level cues to joint, end-to-end approaches and sophisticated modeling of dynamic scenes, interactions, and physical plausibility.

Despite rapid progress, common challenges like handling occlusions, generalizing to diverse unconstrained inputs, and achieving real-time, robust, and physically accurate simulations persist across all levels.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.20766.Title: Learning Only with Images: Visual Reinforcement Learning with Reasoning, Rendering, and Visual Feedback
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.20766.Summary: The Reasoning-Rendering-Visual-Feedback (RRVF) framework enables Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to acquire complex visual reasoning and code generation capabilities from raw images, circumventing the need for extensive image-text supervision. This approach achieves a 97.83% code execution rate on chart-to-code tasks, demonstrates strong generalization to unseen data, and allows a smaller policy model to outperform its larger teacher model.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) heavily depend on costly and time-consuming curated image-text datasets for training, leading to a significant data bottleneck.
Existing MLLM training methods often struggle to foster deep visual reasoning, such as understanding complex spatial relationships and generative logic, beyond basic perception.
Supervised learning in image-to-code generation faces challenges with "semantic equivalence," where valid code variants producing identical visual outputs are often incorrectly penalized.
Method: Introduces the Reasoning-Rendering-Visual-Feedback (RRVF) framework, employing an iterative MLLM reasoner that generates code, which is then rendered by external tools.
Implements a visual feedback mechanism where a powerful MLLM compares the rendered output with the input image and provides natural language feedback to guide the next reasoning step.

Utilizes Reinforcement Learning, specifically the GRPO algorithm, optimized with a hybrid reward function derived from visual similarity, format correctness, and tool-use incentives, leveraging an MLLM-based visual judge.
Results: Achieved a 97.83% code execution rate and an overall score of 64.36 on the ChartMimic benchmark, outperforming all other open-source models and even the larger 72B model used for feedback.
Demonstrated strong zero-shot generalization on the Plot2Code dataset, maintaining a 96.21% execution rate and significantly surpassing Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) methods.

Delivered competitive performance in the web-to-code task on the WebSight benchmark, achieving CLIP and GPT scores of 88.29 and 91.50 respectively, purely from visual feedback without ground-truth HTML.
Takeaways: The "Asymmetry of Verification" principle provides a powerful foundation for MLLM training, where easily verifiable visual outputs can guide complex generative tasks through reinforcement learning.

Visual feedback, generated by comparing a rendered image from MLLM-produced code with the original input, offers an effective and scalable reward signal for autonomous learning, eliminating dependence on image-text pairs.
A closed-loop reasoning, rendering, and feedback system enables MLLMs to iteratively self-correct and learn deep, transferable generative logic directly from raw pixel data.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.20673.Title: Geometric-Mean Policy Optimization
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.20673.Summary: Geometric-Mean Policy Optimization (GMPO) stabilizes reinforcement learning for large language models (LLMs) by employing a geometric mean for token-level reward aggregation. This approach yielded an average 4.1% improvement in Pass@1 accuracy over GRPO on mathematical reasoning benchmarks and showed gains in multimodal and Mixture-of-Experts settings, demonstrating more stable training and enhanced policy exploration.
Problem: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) for LLMs suffers from training instability due to its arithmetic mean objective being highly susceptible to outlier importance-weighted rewards.
Extreme importance sampling ratios can lead to aggressive and unstable policy updates, hindering consistent learning and model performance.
Clipping mechanisms used in GRPO to mitigate instability often restrict policy exploration, potentially limiting the discovery of optimal reasoning paths.
Method: GMPO replaces the arithmetic mean of token-level rewards in GRPO's objective function with a geometric mean to inherently suppress the influence of extreme importance-weighted rewards.
It applies clipping at the individual token-level, rather than sequence-level, which provides a more stable range of importance sampling ratios and avoids discarding valuable update signals.
GMPO utilizes a significantly wider clipping range, leveraging the robustness of the geometric mean to encourage greater policy exploration without reintroducing instability.
Results: GMPO improved average Pass@1 accuracy by 4.1% (63.4% vs. 59.3%) over GRPO on five mathematical reasoning benchmarks using DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, outperforming several state-of-the-art methods.

The method demonstrated consistent performance gains across different model scales, including a 2.1% improvement on MATH500 with a Qwen-32B Mixture-of-Experts model and a 1.4% gain in multimodal reasoning on Geometry3K.

GMPO exhibited significantly higher token entropy, more stable gradient norms, and lower KL divergence throughout training compared to GRPO, confirming its superior stability and exploration capabilities.
Takeaways: The geometric mean inherently offers a narrower objective value range and less sensitivity to outliers than the arithmetic mean, leading to more stable policy updates.

GMPO's gradient updates are more balanced because each token's gradient is weighted by the geometric mean of all importance sampling ratios in a sequence, making it robust to individual outlier tokens.

GMPO maintains higher token entropy and a smaller KL divergence from the pre-trained model during training, indicating enhanced exploration capabilities while preserving stability and preventing premature convergence.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.20534.Title: Kimi K2: Open Agentic Intelligence
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.20534.Summary: Moonshot AI developed Kimi K2, a 1 trillion-parameter Mixture-of-Experts large language model, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance in agentic intelligence tasks, including software engineering and tool use. The model, which incorporates the novel MuonClip optimizer for training stability and a multi-stage reinforcement learning framework, establishes a new benchmark for open-source LLMs.
Problem: Large language models faced limitations in performing complex, interactive agentic behaviors, primarily due to reliance on static training data for planning and autonomous action.
Scaling LLM pre-training encountered challenges related to token efficiency and training instability, particularly when using token-efficient optimizers like Muon.
Generating high-quality, diverse data for advanced agentic capabilities, such as multi-tool use, was difficult and costly to obtain from natural human-generated datasets.
Method: Kimi K2 utilizes a 1.04 trillion-parameter Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) transformer architecture with 384 experts, enabling efficient scaling for agentic tasks.
The novel MuonClip optimizer, featuring a QK-Clip mechanism, ensures stable pre-training on 15.5 trillion tokens by preventing attention logit explosions and loss spikes.

A multi-stage post-training process incorporates a large-scale agentic data synthesis pipeline for tool use and a comprehensive reinforcement learning framework with verifiable rewards and a self-critique rubric reward.
Results: Kimi K2-Instruct achieved state-of-the-art results in agentic benchmarks, scoring 71.6% on SWE-bench Verified (Agentic-Multi-Attempt) and 66.1% micro Pass@1 on Tau2-Bench, surpassing open-source baselines.
The model was ranked as the top open-source LLM and 5th overall on the LMSYS Arena (July 17, 2025) based on over 3,000 user votes, indicating strong real-world preference.

Kimi K2-Base set new state-of-the-art records for open-source models on 10 out of 12 English language benchmarks (e.g., MMLU 87.79%), and led across all coding and most mathematical reasoning benchmarks.
Takeaways: The QK-Clip mechanism within the MuonClip optimizer is crucial for stabilizing ultra-large-scale LLM pre-training, preventing attention logit explosions and enabling stable learning over trillions of tokens.

Large-scale agentic data synthesis, combined with a sophisticated reinforcement learning framework incorporating both verifiable and self-critique rubric rewards, can effectively imbue LLMs with complex interactive and reasoning capabilities.

Scaling sparse MoE architectures by increasing the number of experts while optimizing attention heads proves effective for improving performance and inference efficiency under fixed computational budgets.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.20529.Title: Enhancing Spatial Reasoning through Visual and Textual Thinking
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.20529.Summary: The SpatialVTS method enhances Vision Language Models (VLMs) for spatial reasoning by integrating visual and textual thinking without requiring explicit depth or mask information. It achieved an 82.03% average accuracy on qualitative spatial benchmarks and demonstrated quantitative performance comparable to models that utilize additional depth cues.
Problem: Vision Language Models (VLMs) struggle with complex spatial reasoning, particularly interpreting implicit spatial cues and performing multi-step inference.
Existing spatial reasoning datasets often suffer from incorrect labels, templated questions, and a lack of explicit reasoning processes (Chain-of-Thought), hindering effective VLM training.
Many approaches for enhanced spatial reasoning rely on additional, often costly to acquire, visual information like depth maps or segmentation masks, limiting their generality.
Method: Introduces SpatialVTS (Spatial reasoning through Visual and Textual thinking Simultaneously), a method that integrates Spatial Visual Thinking for identifying relevant explicit and implicit visual cues and Spatial Textual Thinking for logical, step-by-step inference.
Employs a "seeking the cause by grasping the result" strategy during dataset reconstruction to generate high-quality, process-oriented Chain-of-Thought rationales for training.

Reconstructs and manually corrects existing spatial reasoning datasets (SpatialRGPT, VPT) to improve data quality, add annotations for "potential targets," and convert them to a purely image-text format suitable for generalized VLMs.
Results: SpatialVTS achieved an 82.03% average accuracy on qualitative spatial reasoning benchmarks (WhatsUP, VSR, BLINK-Spatial, SRGPT-QUAL), outperforming all other baselines.
The model demonstrated quantitative spatial perception (Q-Spatial++, SRGPT-QUAN) almost on par with SpatialRGPT, a baseline that specifically utilizes depth information and segmentation masks.

Ablation studies confirmed that the textual thinking (CoT) phase is critical, with its removal leading to a 3-7% performance drop, and that the reconstructed dataset effectively contributes to improved performance with larger data sizes.
Takeaways: Spatial reasoning in VLMs can be significantly enhanced by explicitly integrating both visual cue identification (including implicit cues) and multi-step textual reasoning.
High-quality, process-oriented training data, particularly with Chain-of-Thought rationales, is crucial for developing robust and generalized spatial reasoning capabilities in VLMs.

Achieving advanced spatial perception in VLMs is possible using only standard RGB images and text, without the need for additional modalities like depth maps or segmentation masks, making the approach more versatile.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.19849.Title: Agentic Reinforced Policy Optimization
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.19849.Summary: Agentic Reinforced Policy Optimization (ARPO) trains Large Language Models to act as agents in multi-turn tool interaction scenarios. The method leverages observed increases in token entropy after tool calls to adaptively branch sampling, which leads to superior performance on 13 reasoning and deep search benchmarks while achieving comparable accuracy with half the tool-call budget of previous methods.
Problem: Existing Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) methods for Large Language Models (LLMs) are primarily effective for single-turn reasoning tasks.

Current trajectory-level agentic RL algorithms struggle to effectively balance an LLM's long-horizon reasoning with dynamic, multi-turn tool interactions, often overlooking crucial stepwise behaviors.
LLMs exhibit significant uncertainty (high token entropy) immediately following external tool-call feedback, which prior RL methods do not adequately address for fine-grained exploration.
Method: ARPO introduces an entropy-based adaptive rollout mechanism that dynamically branches exploration paths at high-uncertainty tool-call steps, balancing global trajectory sampling with fine-grained step-level exploration.

It employs an Advantage Attribution Estimation method, specifically a soft setting, to enable LLMs to better internalize the advantage differences of stepwise tool-use interactions within branched trajectories.
The framework integrates a hierarchical reward design, inspired by Tool-Star, which considers correctness, adherence to tool invocation format, and a bonus for effective multi-tool collaboration.
Results: ARPO consistently outperformed trajectory-level RL algorithms (GRPO, Reinforce++, DAPO) across 13 benchmarks in computational reasoning, knowledge reasoning, and deep search, demonstrating an average accuracy improvement of approximately 4%.

The algorithm achieved superior overall accuracy using only half the tool-call budget compared to GRPO during training, highlighting significant efficiency gains through its selective exploration strategy.

ARPO-aligned models demonstrated robust scaling and generalization, achieving high Pass@K scores (e.g., 61.2% Pass@5 on GAIA for Qwen-14B) and showing effectiveness on deep search tasks with limited training data.
Takeaways: LLMs consistently show a sharp increase in token entropy immediately after receiving feedback from external tools, signaling significant uncertainty and critical decision points for exploration.

Balancing broad trajectory exploration with adaptive, step-level exploration guided by this observed uncertainty is crucial for efficiently training LLM agents for complex multi-turn tool interaction.

Attributing advantage at a fine-grained, stepwise level, particularly within branched reasoning paths, facilitates better learning of complex tool-use strategies compared to relying solely on trajectory-level rewards.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.19468.Title: Back to the Features: DINO as a Foundation for Video World Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.19468.Summary: Meta FAIR's DINO-world introduces an efficient generalist video world model by leveraging a frozen DINOv2 encoder to predict future states in a semantic latent space, outperforming pixel-based models in dense feature forecasting and enabling effective action-conditioned planning from uncurated video data.
Problem: Traditional pixel-space generative world models are computationally expensive and require vast resources for training.
Many existing world models are specialized for narrow domains and struggle to generalize due to limited or domain-specific training data.
High-quality, large-scale video datasets annotated with actions are scarce and costly, limiting progress in action-conditioned world modeling.
Method: A two-stage approach: pre-training an unconditional video world model in a latent space and then fine-tuning it with action conditioning for specific control tasks.
Utilizes a frozen, pre-trained DINOv2 ViT-B/14 as the frame encoder to map input video frames to a high-level, semantic latent space of patch tokens.

Employs a lightweight cross-attention predictor architecture trained with a smooth L1 loss on next-frame prediction, incorporating Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) for spatiotemporal reasoning and variable frame rates.
Results: DINO-world consistently outperforms pixel-based (COSMOS) and jointly-trained (V-JEPA) models in dense feature forecasting, achieving 47.0% mIoU on VSPW segmentation (vs. 40.7% for COSMOS) and lower RMSE on KITTI depth.
The model demonstrates strong intuitive physics understanding, achieving 91.3% accuracy on IntPhys, comparable to or better than other large-scale models.
Pre-training substantially improves action-conditioned planning, with fine-tuned DINO-world achieving a 93.8% success rate on the Wall environment compared to 87.1% for training from scratch.
Takeaways: Leveraging strong, frozen self-supervised image features (DINOv2) is effective for building efficient latent-space video world models, significantly reducing computational overhead.
Learning general temporal dynamics from massive uncurated video datasets is crucial for broad applicability and reduces reliance on expensive action-annotated data.
Operating in a semantic latent space (DINOv2 features) improves computational efficiency and prediction quality compared to pixel-based approaches, allowing the model to focus on meaningful dynamics.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.19457.Title: GEPA: Reflective Prompt Evolution Can Outperform Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.19457.Summary: GEPA is a novel prompt optimizer for large language model (LLM) systems that employs reflective prompt evolution and Pareto-based candidate selection. It achieves superior performance and up to 35 times greater sample efficiency compared to reinforcement learning methods for adapting complex, modular LLM workflows.
Problem: Prevailing reinforcement learning methods for adapting Large Language Models (LLMs) to complex tasks are highly sample-inefficient, requiring tens to hundreds of thousands of expensive 'rollouts'.
Scalar rewards provide sparse learning signals for LLMs, limiting their ability to diagnose and correct errors effectively in complex, modular AI systems.
Current LLM adaptation methods often struggle with robust generalization or incur high computational costs due to lengthy prompts.
Method: GEPA employs an iterative genetic optimization loop that manages a pool of candidate prompt sets for modular AI systems.
It leverages natural language reflection, where a meta-LLM analyzes detailed execution traces and textual feedback to propose refined instructions for module prompts.
A Pareto-based candidate selection strategy maintains a diverse set of high-performing prompt configurations, balancing exploration and exploitation across individual task instances.
Results: GEPA outperforms Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) by an average of +10% and achieves up to 35 times greater sample efficiency across diverse tasks.
GEPA surpasses MIPROv2, a joint instruction and few-shot optimizer, with aggregate gains of +14.29% for GPT-4.1 Mini and +12.44% for Qwen3 8B, while generating prompts up to 9.2 times shorter.
Pareto-based candidate selection yields an aggregate +6.4% improvement over naive selection strategies, promoting more robust generalization and higher final performance.
Takeaways: Natural language reflection, using detailed execution traces and textual feedback, provides a more effective and sample-efficient learning signal for LLMs than sparse scalar rewards.
Pareto-based candidate selection is crucial for robust optimization, enabling exploration of diverse high-performing strategies and preventing convergence to local optima.

Instruction-only prompt optimization, when paired with strong reflective capabilities, can outperform methods that jointly optimize instructions and few-shot examples, leading to shorter and more efficient prompts.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.18391.Title: Revisiting LLM Reasoning via Information Bottleneck
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.18391.Summary: This paper from The University of Sydney, ByteDance, and NTU introduces IB-aware Reasoning Optimization (IBRO), an information-theoretic framework grounded in the information bottleneck principle, to enhance the reasoning capabilities of large language models during reinforcement learning-based post-training. The method consistently improved average `top@1` reasoning scores by 2 points across multiple mathematical benchmarks and RL algorithms compared to vanilla training.
Problem: Current reinforcement learning-based post-training methods for LLM reasoning are largely heuristic-driven, lacking a rigorous theoretical framework.

Conflicting empirical findings exist regarding the optimal management of generation entropy during training, with some advocating for high entropy for exploration and others for reduced entropy for focused prediction.
There is a need for a principled methodology to understand and optimally manage entropy and information flow within LLMs to enhance reasoning capabilities.
Method: Introduces IB-aware Reasoning Optimization (IBRO), an information-theoretic framework based on the Information Bottleneck principle, to formally define optimal LLM reasoning as a trade-off between informativeness and generalizability.
Derives a practical, token-level surrogate objective by approximating mutual information terms using readily available token entropy and advantage, making direct optimization tractable.

Proposes IB regularization, an efficient method that seamlessly integrates into standard RL objectives (e.g., PPO, DAPO) by adding a single line of code, introducing negligible computational overhead.
Results: The proposed IB regularization consistently improved LLM reasoning performance, increasing average `top@1` scores by 2 points across PPO and DAPO algorithms on mathematical reasoning benchmarks (AMC23, AIME24, AIME25).

Naive entropy regularization consistently degraded performance compared to no regularization, while IB regularization delivered substantial gains, particularly on more challenging tasks like AIME24 and AIME25.

Analysis showed IB regularization maintained a stable and controlled entropy profile throughout training, unlike naive regularization which caused excessive entropy or entropy collapse, and effectively mitigated premature response truncation.
Takeaways: Optimal LLM reasoning requires a principled trade-off: maximizing informativeness about the correct answer while simultaneously reducing dependence on irrelevant input details for improved generalization.

Uniformly increasing generation entropy during LLM post-training is detrimental, often leading to reduced reasoning performance; instead, selective, advantage-aware entropy modulation is crucial for effective exploration.

IB regularization achieves this by encouraging higher entropy for tokens that significantly contribute to positive rewards (critical tokens) while suppressing entropy for less informative tokens, maintaining coherent and effective reasoning trajectories.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.18074.Title: AlphaGo Moment for Model Architecture Discovery
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.18074.Summary: ASI-ARCH, developed by Shanghai Jiao Tong University and collaborators, is an autonomous system that discovers novel neural architectures by leveraging large language models for design, implementation, and analysis. It successfully identified 106 state-of-the-art linear attention architectures that outperform human-designed baselines and demonstrated the first empirical scaling law for scientific discovery, showing that architectural breakthroughs can be scaled computationally.
Problem: The pace of AI research is linearly bounded by human cognitive capacity, creating an increasingly severe development bottleneck despite exponential improvements in AI capabilities.

Traditional Neural Architecture Search (NAS) methods are confined to optimizing within human-defined search spaces, lacking the ability for true innovation or hypothesizing novel architectural concepts.
Designing efficient neural architectures, particularly for complex attention mechanisms, is a challenging and time-consuming task for human experts.
Method: ASI-ARCH is a closed-loop evolutionary system comprising three interconnected LLM-driven modules: the Researcher (proposes novel architectures), the Engineer (implements and empirically evaluates), and the Analyst (synthesizes results and extracts insights).

It employs an 'exploration-then-verification' strategy to efficiently identify promising candidates with smaller models and then rigorously validate them at scale, using a robust self-revision mechanism for iterative debugging.
A comprehensive fitness function combines quantitative performance with qualitative architectural quality (scored by an LLM-as-judge) to drive the evolutionary improvement strategy.
Results: ASI-ARCH autonomously discovered 106 novel, state-of-the-art linear attention architectures, consuming approximately 20,000 GPU hours, which are publicly available.

Five top-performing AI-discovered architectures consistently outperformed human-designed baselines like DeltaNet, Gated DeltaNet, and Mamba2 on various language modeling and common-sense reasoning benchmarks.

The system established the 'first empirical scaling law for scientific discovery,' demonstrating a strong linear relationship between computational resources consumed and the rate of SOTA architectural discoveries.
Takeaways: Architectural breakthroughs can be scaled computationally, evidenced by a linear relationship between the cumulative count of discovered SOTA architectures and total computing hours consumed.

AI-discovered architectures exhibit 'emergent design principles' and 'Move 37' moments, revealing novel strategies that systematically surpass human intuition, such as breaking traditional trade-offs in gating mechanisms.

Top-performing AI-discovered architectures rely more on insights derived from the AI's own empirical 'analysis' (44.8% of design components) than on 'cognition' from human literature (48.6%), indicating a deeper level of understanding from self-experimentation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.18071.Title: Group Sequence Policy Optimization
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.18071.Summary: Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO) introduces a sequence-level approach to importance sampling in reinforcement learning, stabilizing the training of large language models and enabling more efficient policy updates. This method resolves the instability and model collapse observed in prior token-level algorithms, particularly benefiting Mixture-of-Experts architectures by simplifying their training infrastructure, and has been applied to Qwen3 models.
Problem: Existing reinforcement learning algorithms like GRPO face instability and catastrophic model collapse when applied to very large language models, particularly with long generated responses.
The token-level importance sampling used in prior methods introduces high-variance noise, which accumulates and is amplified by clipping, leading to unreliable gradient estimates.

Training Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models with reinforcement learning is challenging due to "expert-activation volatility," causing token-level importance ratios to fluctuate drastically and hindering convergence.
Method: Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO) redefines importance ratios based on the likelihood of the entire generated sequence, applying a length normalization for variance reduction.
The algorithm performs clipping and optimization at the sequence level, ensuring the unit of optimization aligns with the sequence-level reward and objective.
GSPO's gradient derivation ensures all tokens within a response are weighted equally by the sequence-level importance ratio, thereby eliminating instability from token-specific weighting.
Results: GSPO achieved superior training stability and continuous performance improvement across mathematical reasoning (AIME’24) and programming (LiveCodeBench, CodeForces) benchmarks, outperforming GRPO.
The algorithm inherently resolved expert-activation volatility in Mixture-of-Experts models, eliminating the need for complex stabilization techniques like "Routing Replay."
Successfully applied to the Qwen3 models, GSPO led to notable performance enhancements, validating its effectiveness in practical, state-of-the-art large language model development.
Takeaways: The instability of prior RL algorithms like GRPO is rooted in the misapplication of importance sampling at the token level, creating high-variance noise in gradient estimates.
Aligning importance sampling and policy optimization with the entire sequence unit provides a more stable and effective learning signal, addressing challenges unique to Mixture-of-Experts models.

High-quality, sequence-level gradient signals can lead to superior training efficiency even when fewer individual tokens contribute to gradient estimation, demonstrating the importance of principled importance sampling.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.18009.Title: GRR-CoCa: Leveraging LLM Mechanisms in Multimodal Model Architectures
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.18009.Summary: GRR-CoCa, developed at Rice University, integrates modern architectural features from Large Language Models (LLMs) into the CoCa multimodal model, specifically updating its Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder and textual decoders. This enhanced model demonstrated consistent performance improvements in contrastive and generative image-text tasks, indicating that LLM mechanisms can benefit multimodal architectures without substantially increasing parameters.
Problem: Leading foundational multimodal models, such as CoCa, have architectural designs that lag behind the advancements seen in contemporary Large Language Models (LLMs).
Architectural enhancements like GEGLUs, RMSNorm, and RoPe, proven effective in LLMs, have not been widely adopted in multimodal vision-language models, particularly within their visual encoders.
There is a need to enhance the Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder in multimodal models to produce more feature-rich image latent representations for improved multimodal tasks.
Method: Developed GRR-CoCa, an enhanced version of the CoCa model, by systematically integrating Gaussian Error Gated Linear Units (GEGLUs), Root Mean Squared Normalization (RMSNorm), and Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPe) into its textual decoders and Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder.
Established a 'Baseline CoCa' model for comparison, which incorporated the modern LLM architectures only into its textual decoders, isolating the impact of modifications to the visual encoder.

Rigorously benchmarked GRR-CoCa against Baseline CoCa using a standard pretraining-to-fine-tuning workflow on the CC12M dataset for pretraining and MSCOCO, ROCO, and Flickr30K for fine-tuning, evaluating across contrastive, generative, and combined CoCa loss metrics.
Results: During pretraining on the CC12M dataset, GRR-CoCa achieved a 27.25% improvement in contrastive loss and a 3.71% reduction in perplexity compared to Baseline CoCa.

GRR-CoCa consistently outperformed Baseline CoCa during fine-tuning across MSCOCO, ROCO, and Flickr30K datasets, showing average improvements of 13.66% in contrastive loss, 5.18% in perplexity, and 5.55% in CoCa loss.
These performance gains were achieved with GRR-CoCa having only a marginal 0.17% increase in trainable parameters (394.5M vs 393.8M) compared to Baseline CoCa.
Takeaways: Architectural mechanisms from LLMs (GEGLUs, RMSNorm, RoPe) can be effectively applied to multimodal models, including their visual encoders, leading to performance gains.
Integrating RoPe throughout the Vision Transformer blocks likely helps preserve positional information more effectively in deeper layers, improving spatial understanding.
GEGLUs and RMSNorm contribute to faster learning, better generalization, and more refined manipulation of embeddings by filtering noise and magnifying relevant features.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.17746.Title: Rubrics as Rewards: Reinforcement Learning Beyond Verifiable Domains
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.17746.Summary: The 'Rubrics as Rewards' (RaR) framework enables reinforcement learning for large language models (LLMs) in complex, real-world reasoning tasks that traditionally lack single verifiable answers. This approach uses instance-specific, LLM-generated rubrics as structured reward signals, resulting in improved model performance and enhanced LLM judge alignment with human preferences across various tasks.
Problem: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) is constrained to tasks with clear, binary correctness signals, limiting its application in nuanced, real-world reasoning domains.
Existing reward mechanisms for complex, subjective tasks (e.g., preference models) often lead to learning superficial artifacts, are costly to annotate, and lack transparency.
A scalable and interpretable method for providing multi-criteria feedback to LLMs in expert domains, such as medicine and science, is needed where 'correctness' is multifaceted.
Method: Introduces the Rubrics as Rewards (RaR) framework, formalizing instance-specific rubrics as the core mechanism to generate structured reward signals for on-policy reinforcement learning.
Leverages powerful LLMs (e.g., GPT-4o) to synthetically generate dynamic, instance-specific rubrics at scale, grounded by golden reference answers, for comprehensive and weighted feedback.

Explores two reward aggregation strategies—Explicit (weighted sum of criteria) and Implicit (holistic LLM-as-judge scoring)—to convert multi-criteria rubric feedback into a single scalar reward for GRPO-based policy updates.
Results: RaR-Implicit achieved relative performance gains of up to 31% on rubric-based evaluations (HealthBench) and up to 7% on verifiable multiple-choice tasks (GPQA-Diamond) over Likert-based baselines.

Policies trained with LLM-generated, reference-guided synthetic rubrics performed comparably to those trained with human-authored rubrics, validating the scalability and quality of the rubric generation process.
Rubric guidance consistently improved LLM-judge pairwise preference accuracy with human judgments across all judge model sizes, with the most notable improvements observed for smaller judge models.
Takeaways: Effective reinforcement learning in complex, non-verifiable domains critically depends on instance-specific rubrics that are tailored to the prompt's context, rather than generic criteria.

Structured rubric guidance significantly improves the alignment of LLM judges (especially smaller models) with human preferences, indicating rubrics act as valuable scaffolding for nuanced evaluation.

Implicit aggregation of rubric criteria by a powerful LLM judge generally yields stronger training outcomes than explicit weighting, suggesting advanced LLMs can effectively integrate complex criteria.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.17634.Title: WSM: Decay-Free Learning Rate Schedule via Checkpoint Merging for LLM Pre-training
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.17634.Summary: Warmup-Stable and Merge (WSM) introduces a decay-free learning rate schedule for LLM pre-training that achieves the benefits of learning rate decay through principled checkpoint merging. This approach consistently outperforms the Warmup-Stable-Decay (WSD) baseline, demonstrating average improvements of +1.3 points across benchmarks and significant gains such as +3.5% on MATH, +2.9% on HumanEval, and +5.5% on MMLU-Pro.
Problem: Conventional learning rate (LR) schedules (e.g., cosine decay) require pre-specifying the total training duration, making training extensions or data changes computationally prohibitive due to mandatory restarts.
The Warmup-Stable-Decay (WSD) strategy, while more flexible, still demands manual decisions for decay initiation, duration, and function, hindering autonomous and continuous training.
A lack of a robust, general, and decay-free LR scheduling mechanism that simplifies LLM pre-training while maintaining or improving performance.
Method: WSM eliminates explicit LR decay during live training by employing a Warmup-Stable phase where the learning rate remains constant at its peak value.
It strategically merges periodically saved model checkpoints (an asynchronous, post-hoc process) using mathematically derived weights to emulate the effects of various LR decay curves.

A formal theoretical connection (Theorem 3.1) is established, mapping desired gradient decay coefficients to unique, non-negative checkpoint merge weights, enabling WSM to approximate traditional decay strategies.
Results: WSM consistently outperforms the WSD baseline across diverse tasks, achieving an average improvement of +1.3 points, with specific gains of +3.5% on MATH, +2.9% on HumanEval, and +5.5% on MMLU-Pro.
Models initialized from WSM checkpoints maintain their performance advantage after supervised fine-tuning, demonstrating sustained benefits for downstream tasks.
Merging algorithms derived from the theoretical framework (e.g., 1-sqrt or mean averaging) perform significantly better than Exponential Moving Average (EMA) for checkpoint merging.
Takeaways: Learning rate decay can be formally linked to and emulated by a principled weighted merging of model checkpoints, transforming an empirical heuristic into a systematic approach.

A decay-free, constant LR during live training combined with post-hoc checkpoint merging provides greater flexibility, enabling continuous training and exploration of annealing strategies without costly restarts.
The duration of the merging window is the most critical hyperparameter for WSM's performance, analogous to the total annealing data used in traditional LR decay schedules.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.17520.Title: InstructVLA: Vision-Language-Action Instruction Tuning from Understanding to Manipulation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.17520.Summary: InstructVLA presents an end-to-end Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model that maintains vision-language reasoning capabilities while achieving strong robotic manipulation performance. It utilizes a two-stage training paradigm and a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) adaptation to enable dynamic switching between textual reasoning and action generation, yielding a 92% improvement over a fine-tuned OpenVLA on the SimplerEnv-Instruct benchmark and improved real-world performance.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models suffer from catastrophic forgetting, where fine-tuning on robotic data degrades their pre-trained vision-language reasoning capabilities.
Large-scale real-world robotic datasets often lack diverse human instructions, limiting models to simple, templated commands and hindering their ability to handle free-form directives.
Prior approaches struggle to seamlessly integrate high-level vision-language understanding with precise low-level action generation within a single, unified framework.
Method: A unified VLM architecture based on Eagle2-2B is introduced, capable of generating both textual outputs and latent action representations, featuring learnable action queries and a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) adaptation for dynamic mode switching.

A two-stage training paradigm is employed: Stage 1 for 'Action Pretraining' aligns a VLM-driven action expert with latent actions, and Stage 2 for 'Vision-Language-Action Instruction Tuning' (VLA-IT) reactivates and aligns VLM reasoning with embodied tasks while freezing the action expert.

A 650K-sample VLA-IT dataset is curated, annotating diverse hierarchical language instructions for embodied scene understanding and latent action planning, complemented by the SimplerEnv-Instruct benchmark for evaluating zero-shot instruction following and situated reasoning.
Results: InstructVLA (Generalist, 2B parameters) outperforms larger VLMs on multimodal benchmarks and achieves a 92% improvement over a fine-tuned OpenVLA on the SimplerEnv-Instruct benchmark (46.0% vs 23.9% average success rate).

In real-world zero-shot and few-shot experiments, InstructVLA shows superior performance (41.7% to 46.7% improvement over OpenVLA on reasoning instructions) and robustness to out-of-distribution conditions.

Ablation studies validate design choices: language motion data boosts success by 10.5%, FiLM enhancement improves performance by 15.3%, and internal 'test-time thinking' provides a 36.1% performance gain on SimplerEnv-Instruct.
Takeaways: A Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) adaptation within a two-stage training paradigm effectively mitigates catastrophic forgetting, preserving a VLM's general multimodal understanding while achieving strong manipulation performance.

Integrating textual descriptions of low-level actions ('language motion') during pre-training significantly boosts overall success rates, enabling a better association of visual cues with manipulation primitives.

Allowing the model to generate internal textual analyses ('test-time thinking') during manipulation yields substantial performance gains on complex reasoning tasks, demonstrating the value of integrated, internal reasoning over external LLM assistance.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.16815.Title: ThinkAct: Vision-Language-Action Reasoning via Reinforced Visual Latent Planning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.16815.Summary: A dual-system framework named ThinkAct enables Multimodal Large Language Models to perform long-horizon planning and guide robotic actions through reinforced visual latent planning. This approach achieves success rates up to 15.5% higher than baselines on SimplerEnv robot manipulation tasks and demonstrates emergent capabilities like few-shot adaptation and self-correction.
Problem: End-to-end Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models often lack explicit reasoning, limiting their ability to handle complex instructions and long-horizon tasks.
Supervised chain-of-thought (CoT) methods for VLA require expensive, high-quality reasoning annotations, hindering scalability and generalization.
Reinforcement Learning (RL) for MLLM reasoning in embodied tasks typically uses abstract, QA-style rewards that lack direct grounding in physical actions and visual outcomes.
Method: A dual-system framework integrates a 'slow thinking' Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) for high-level planning and a 'fast control' action model for low-level execution.
The MLLM is fine-tuned using reinforced visual latent planning, employing novel action-aligned rewards that measure visual goal completion and trajectory consistency.
MLLM reasoning is compressed into a compact 'visual plan latent' which explicitly conditions the downstream action model, effectively bridging high-level deliberation and low-level control.
Results: ThinkAct achieved improved success rates on robot manipulation benchmarks, including a 15.5% increase over its base policy on SimplerEnv Google-VM split and an 84.4% overall success rate on LIBERO, outperforming CoT-VLA and OpenVLA.
It demonstrated higher accuracy on embodied reasoning tasks, achieving 48.2% on EgoPlan-Bench2 and a BLEU score of 59.8 on RoboVQA, surpassing competitive MLLMs like GPT-4V and fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL.

The framework exhibited emergent capabilities such as few-shot adaptation to novel skills with limited demonstrations and the ability to self-correct from execution errors by detecting failures and generating revised plans.
Takeaways: Reinforcement learning with action-aligned visual feedback effectively grounds MLLM reasoning in embodied tasks, enabling robust long-horizon planning.
Compressing complex MLLM reasoning into a visual plan latent provides a crucial interface for explicitly steering and enhancing downstream action execution.
A dual-system architecture with asynchronous reasoning and acting can elicit emergent capabilities such as few-shot adaptation to new tasks and self-correction from execution failures.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.16814.Title: Semi-off-Policy Reinforcement Learning for Vision-Language Slow-Thinking Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.16814.Summary: SOPHIA introduces a semi-off-policy reinforcement learning framework that enhances large vision-language models' (LVLMs) slow-thinking reasoning by leveraging the LVLM's own visual perception to ground external language model reasoning. The framework achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-source LVLMs, surpassing some closed-source models on challenging benchmarks like MathVision and OlympiadBench, while also reducing visual hallucinations.
Problem: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) struggle with complex, multi-step "slow-thinking" reasoning tasks, often exhibiting pattern memorization rather than deep understanding.

On-policy reinforcement learning for LVLMs is limited by the current policy's output space, making it difficult to explore and reinforce truly novel reasoning behaviors if initial capabilities are low.

Direct off-policy reinforcement learning exacerbates visual hallucinations in LVLMs due to mismatches between visual features in external reasoning trajectories and the target LVLM's own visual perception.
Method: SOPHIA employs a semi-off-policy sampling method where the trainable LVLM generates its own visual description (on-policy), which then conditions an external reasoning LLM to generate slow-thinking trajectories (off-policy).
