It implements a novel reward propagation mechanism, assigning an outcome-based reward to the reasoning trajectory and propagating an averaged reward to the LVLM's visual description to incentivize useful visual grounding.

An off-policy dataset is constructed by selecting correct and visually grounded trajectories, prioritizing shorter paths, to fine-tune only the language backbone of the LVLM while keeping the visual transformer frozen to maintain alignment.
Results: InternVL3.0-38B + SOPHIA achieved an average gain of +8.50% over its base model, attaining state-of-the-art performance among open-source LVLMs on most multimodal reasoning benchmarks.
SOPHIA outperformed closed-source models like GPT-4.1 on MathVision (49.08% pass@1) and OlympiadBench (49.95% pass@1), demonstrating enhanced capabilities in complex problem-solving.

Qualitative analysis showed a significant reduction in both visual hallucinations (from 38% to 16%) and logical inconsistencies (from 54% to 44%) on MMMU Pro cases, validating the approach's effectiveness in improving reasoning quality.
Takeaways: Decoupling visual perception (from the target LVLM) and logical inference (from a powerful external LLM) during trajectory generation effectively mitigates visual hallucinations and optimization conflicts in multimodal RL.
Propagating rewards back to the LVLM's visual descriptions ensures that the model is incentivized to produce not just accurate, but also *reasoning-relevant* visual interpretations.

Freezing the Visual Transformer (ViT) during the RL fine-tuning process is crucial for maintaining vision-language alignment, preventing long reasoning trajectories from degrading the model's visual understanding.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.16806.Title: Beyond Binary Rewards: Training LMs to Reason About Their Uncertainty
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.16806.Summary: Researchers at MIT developed Reinforcement Learning with Calibration Rewards (RLCR), an approach that trains large language models to concurrently improve answer accuracy and calibrate their confidence. RLCR integrates a Brier score into the RL reward function, enabling models to generate accurate answers alongside well-calibrated uncertainty estimates, reducing Expected Calibration Error on HotpotQA from 0.37 to 0.03 while maintaining task accuracy.
Problem: Standard reinforcement learning with binary rewards for large language models (LMs) often leads to overconfidence and increased hallucination, degrading calibration.
Existing RL-based calibration methods frequently optimize solely for calibration, potentially sacrificing task accuracy.
LMs struggle to reliably communicate uncertainty, undermining their trustworthiness in critical applications.
Method: Introduces RLCR (Reinforcement Learning with Calibration Rewards), which trains LMs to generate reasoning chains, answers, and explicit numerical confidence scores.
Employs an augmented reward function combining a binary correctness reward with a negative Brier score to incentivize both accuracy and calibration.
Theoretically proves that this bounded proper scoring rule encourages both accurate predictions and calibrated confidence matching the true probability of correctness.
Results: RLCR matches the task accuracy of standard binary-reward RL (RLVR) on in-domain datasets (e.g., 62.1% vs. 63.0% on HotpotQA), while dramatically improving calibration.
On HotpotQA, RLCR reduces Expected Calibration Error (ECE) from 0.37 (RLVR) to 0.03, and on math datasets from 0.26 to 0.10.
RLCR consistently and substantially improves calibration on out-of-distribution tasks, outperforming all baselines without sacrificing accuracy.
Takeaways: It is possible to jointly optimize large language models for both task correctness and calibrated confidence without compromising accuracy.
Integrating explicit, textual uncertainty analysis within Chain-of-Thought reasoning can contribute to better calibration.
Training LMs to reason about and express uncertainty improves their generalization and robustness, particularly on out-of-distribution tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.16746.Title: Zebra-CoT: A Dataset for Interleaved Vision Language Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.16746.Summary: Zebra-CoT is a large-scale, diverse dataset created to train vision-language models for native, interleaved visual chain of thought (CoT) reasoning. Fine-tuning models like Anole-7B and Bagel-7B on Zebra-CoT enhanced their visual reasoning abilities, with Anole-7B showing a 4-fold relative improvement on an in-distribution test set and Bagel-7B gaining the capability to intrinsically generate visual aids during problem-solving.
Problem: Large vision-language models (VLMs) predominantly rely on textual reasoning, lacking the ability to natively generate and integrate explicit visual aids (Visual Chain of Thought) into their problem-solving process.
There is a severe lack of high-quality, large-scale, and diverse training data specifically designed for interleaved text and image reasoning, hindering the development of generalizable visual CoT.

Existing visual CoT approaches are either complex agentic pipelines leveraging external tools or domain-specific models, preventing broad application and inherent visual reasoning capabilities in foundation models.
Method: Developed Zebra-CoT, a dataset comprising 182,384 multimodal reasoning traces that explicitly link textual explanations with intermediate visual aids across diverse domains and over 50 distinct tasks.

Implemented a hybrid data curation pipeline that combines real-world problem sourcing with synthetic example generation, critically augmented by frontier VLMs (Gemini-2.5, GPT-4.1) to ensure logical coherence and rich multimodal reasoning traces.

Categorized the dataset into four major areas: Scientific Questions, 2D Visual Reasoning, 3D Visual Reasoning, and Visual Logic & Strategic Games, to ensure breadth and depth in visual reasoning challenges.
Results: Zebra-CoT is the most comprehensive dataset for interleaved text-image reasoning, containing 182,384 reasoning traces across 18 distinct domains and over 50 unique tasks.

Fine-tuning Anole-7B on Zebra-CoT led to a 4-fold relative improvement in accuracy on its in-distribution test set (from 4.2% to 16.9%) and an average 4.9% improvement across seven external VLM benchmarks.

Fine-tuning Bagel-7B on Zebra-CoT enabled the model to intrinsically generate high-quality visual CoT during its reasoning process, although quantitative evaluation indicated challenges with image generation hallucinations.
Takeaways: Proprietary frontier models demonstrate limited performance in zero-shot settings on Zebra-CoT tasks (average 31.51% accuracy), highlighting the inherent difficulty of complex interleaved visual reasoning problems.

Providing even a few initial multimodal reasoning steps (scaffolding) substantially improves the performance of advanced VLMs, with two steps increasing average accuracy by 25.19% (to 56.70%), underscoring the value of explicit visual CoT.

Training on Zebra-CoT enables existing VLMs to natively generate interleaved visual CoT, transforming them from models that merely process visual inputs to those capable of actively producing visual 'thoughts' during problem-solving.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.16663.Title: Turning Internal Gap into Self-Improvement: Promoting the Generation-Understanding Unification in MLLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.16663.Summary: Researchers from The University of Hong Kong, Carnegie Mellon University, RIKEN AIP, Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, and Alibaba Group introduce a self-improvement framework for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) that leverages their stronger internal understanding capabilities to enhance their weaker generation performance. This internal, self-contained approach substantially improves generation quality by up to 20% and reduces the internal non-unification gap by 16% across various tasks, while simultaneously boosting understanding abilities.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) exhibit a pervasive 'internal gap' or 'non-unification,' where their understanding capabilities consistently outperform their generation capabilities.
Existing methods to mitigate this gap often rely on external reward models, additional supervised datasets, or human feedback, introducing complexity and computational overhead.
A systematic quantification and root cause analysis of this internal imbalance across a diverse range of MLLMs and tasks was lacking.
Method: The authors introduce a 'non-unification score,' an internal consistency metric, to systematically quantify the discrepancy between an MLLM's generated content and its understanding of the original prompt.

A self-improvement framework is developed where the MLLM's own stronger understanding branch evaluates its generated images, classifying them as 'aligned' or 'misaligned' to create data for Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) or Direct Preference Optimization (DPO).

A curriculum learning strategy is incorporated, enabling the MLLM to dynamically expand its post-training data by revisiting and utilizing samples that were initially difficult to generate or understand as its capabilities improve.
Results: The internal self-improvement framework achieved up to +20% generation performance gains and a 16% reduction in the non-unification score on benchmarks like T2I-CompBench++.

Understanding capabilities improved concurrently, with up to 80% of gains from 'false positive correction' and up to 3% accuracy increases on standard understanding benchmarks (POPE, MMB, SEED, GQA, MMMU).

The curriculum learning strategy dynamically expanded post-training data by up to 50% and delivered further performance gains across generation, understanding, and unification, often outperforming baselines that use external reward models.
Takeaways: The internal gap in MLLMs is widespread, with non-unification scores up to 60%, and is predominantly caused by 'weak generation' rather than misunderstanding.

A 'co-improvement effect' is empirically discovered, where generation-targeted self-improvement not only enhances generation but also significantly boosts the MLLM's understanding capabilities, particularly in correcting false positives.

Theoretical analysis, extending learning dynamic theory to MLLMs, reveals that generation and understanding learning dynamics are coupled through shared empirical neural tangent kernels (eNTK), explaining the co-improvement effect.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.16518.Title: C2-Evo: Co-Evolving Multimodal Data and Model for Self-Improving Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.16518.Summary:
The C
2
-Evo framework introduces an automatic, closed-loop approach for jointly evolving multimodal data and model capabilities, specifically improving complex geometric reasoning in MLLMs. It achieves notable performance improvements, increasing geometric reasoning accuracy on Geo-Sub-Aux from 40.4% to 54.9% while utilizing less than 1% of the training data compared to prior methods.
Problem: High demand for costly, manually curated, and scale-challenged high-quality multimodal datasets for MLLM training, especially for complex reasoning tasks.
Current self-improvement methods for MLLMs often result in misaligned complexity between visual and textual components of generated data.
A static or unadaptive difficulty progression in existing self-improvement frameworks leads to inefficient training due to a mismatch between model capabilities and task complexity.
Method:
An automatic, closed-loop C
2
-Evo framework with interleaved co-evolution loops for multimodal data and model capabilities.
A Cross-Modal Data Evolution Loop utilizes advanced LLMs (GPT-4o, Doubao, DeepSeek-R1) and an image editing tool to generate visually and textually complex, aligned geometric reasoning problems.

A Data and Model Co-evolution Loop refines MLLMs through SFT to standardize reasoning and GRPO with accuracy/format rewards, applying adaptive error-based filtering (error rate ">= 0.3") to select optimal training data.
Results:
The Qwen2-VL-7B model, enhanced by C
2
-Evo, improved geometric reasoning accuracy on the Geo-Sub-Aux benchmark from 40.4% to 54.9% across three iterations.

C
2
-Evo achieved strong performance using less than 1% of the training data typically required by many prior reasoning models.

Qualitative assessments confirmed that C
2
-Evo models generate more structured and logically sound step-by-step reasoning traces, reducing inaccuracies seen in base models.
Takeaways: Synchronous complexification of both visual and textual data components is vital for fostering robust, integrated multimodal reasoning in MLLMs.
Aligning training data difficulty with the model's current capability through adaptive error-based filtering is key for efficient and effective self-improvement.
Cumulative learning is maximized by iteratively refining the model (SFT followed by RL) and building upon the previously evolved model rather than restarting.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.16003.Title: Learning without training: The implicit dynamics of in-context learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.16003.Summary: This research from Google Research demonstrates that In-Context Learning (ICL) in Large Language Models (LLMs) can be theoretically explained as an implicit, low-rank update to the weights of the MLP layer within a transformer block. Experiments confirm that the model's predictions with an in-context prompt are identical to those made by explicitly applying these derived weight updates without the prompt.
Problem: The underlying mechanisms of In-Context Learning (ICL) in Large Language Models (LLMs) remained a theoretical mystery, despite its practical utility.

Prior theoretical models attempting to explain ICL often relied on highly restrictive assumptions, such as linear-attention layers or specific regression tasks, limiting their applicability to complex, real-world LLMs.
It was unclear whether ICL represented 'true learning' or merely sophisticated retrieval, and how it connected to traditional optimization-based learning paradigms.
Method: The authors generalized the concept of a transformer block to a 'contextual block' and mathematically proved that the effect of contextual information on its output is equivalent to an implicit, low-rank weight update of the first dense layer in the subsequent neural network (MLP).

They derived an explicit formula for this rank-1 weight update and demonstrated that the sequential processing of context tokens can be interpreted as an implicit, online gradient descent-like learning process.

Empirical validation was conducted using a simplified transformer trained on linear functions, comparing model predictions with full in-context prompts against predictions made with explicitly computed implicit weight updates.
Results: Experimental results showed a 'remarkable agreement' where the validation loss from a model using an in-context prompt was nearly identical to that of a model with its weights explicitly modified by the derived implicit update formula.

The magnitude of the marginal implicit weight changes was observed to decrease and vanish as more context was processed, indicating a convergence behavior consistent with an implicit gradient descent process.
The implicit learning dynamics were found to minimize loss in 'similar ways' to explicit fine-tuning via gradient descent, suggesting a functional analogy between these two forms of learning.
Takeaways: In-Context Learning in a transformer block fundamentally operates by implicitly modifying the first dense layer's weights of the MLP, where the context effectively loads a rank-1 update matrix into these weights.

The iterative consumption of context tokens during ICL mimics an online gradient descent process, where each token contributes to an implicit 'gradient step' that refines the model's effective internal parameters.

This theoretical framework significantly broadens the understanding of ICL beyond simplified linear-attention models to encompass generic contextual layers and prompts, bridging the gap towards real-world LLMs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.15857.Title: Diffusion Beats Autoregressive in Data-Constrained Settings
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.15857.Summary: Researchers at Carnegie Mellon University found that masked diffusion models achieve lower validation loss and better downstream task performance than autoregressive models in data-constrained environments with extensive compute for repeated training. Diffusion models demonstrated a data reuse half-life of approximately 494 epochs compared to 31 for autoregressive models, highlighting their superior sample efficiency.
Problem: The impending exhaustion of high-quality human-generated data poses a bottleneck for further scaling of large language models.
Autoregressive (AR) models, the dominant paradigm, exhibit poor sample efficiency and quickly overfit when repeatedly exposed to limited datasets.
Existing comparisons inaccurately suggested masked diffusion models require significantly more compute than AR models, conflating compute efficiency with sample efficiency in single-epoch training.
Method: Trained hundreds of masked diffusion and autoregressive models with shared Transformer backbones across varying model sizes, unique data budgets, and high epoch counts.
Used the C4 corpus and GPT-2 tokenization, training models up to 800 epochs with unique token budgets from 25M to 100M tokens.
Applied a data-constrained scaling law framework to analyze model performance as a function of effective unique data and total compute, isolating data reuse efficiency.
Results: Masked diffusion models achieved substantially lower validation loss and superior performance on downstream tasks in data-constrained, high-compute environments, outperforming AR models.
Diffusion models exhibited an R*D (data reuse half-life) of approximately 494, indicating effective learning from repeated data for hundreds of epochs, unlike AR models which saturated around 31.
A critical compute point C_crit(U) = 2.12 × 10^1.956 * U^2.174 was identified, providing a guideline for when diffusion models become the preferable choice based on unique data size.
Explicitly permuting token orderings during AR training significantly improved their performance, corroborating that diffusion's randomized masking objective enables better generalization.
Takeaways: The core advantage of masked diffusion models in data-constrained settings stems from their implicit exposure to diverse conditional prediction orders via random masking.
This randomized masking acts as a powerful implicit data augmentation, enabling diffusion models to continuously learn from repeated data without overfitting.
Previously observed compute inefficiency of diffusion models was an artifact of single-epoch training, where sample efficiency was not a primary concern.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.14172.Title: Self-Improving Language Models for Evolutionary Program Synthesis: A Case Study on ARC-AGI
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.14172.Summary: SOAR (Self-improving Operators for Automated program Refinements) is a framework that enables large language models (LLMs) to learn to improve their program synthesis and refinement capabilities from their own search experience. Applied to the ARC-AGI benchmark, SOAR achieves 52.00% accuracy on the public test set, establishing a new state-of-the-art for open-source LLM-based inductive methods and demonstrating continuous performance gains beyond fixed model capacities.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) often struggle with complex program synthesis tasks, especially those requiring abstract reasoning, failing to provide correct solutions in a single attempt.
Integrating LLMs into traditional evolutionary search methods leads to performance plateaus, as the LLM's generative and refinement capabilities remain static after initial training.
Existing LLM-based program synthesis often relies on extensive human-curated datasets for finetuning or hand-crafted domain-specific languages (DSLs), limiting autonomy and scalability.
Method: SOAR integrates LLMs into an iterative self-improving evolutionary loop that alternates between a Sample&Refine phase for program generation and a Learning phase for model updates.
The Sample&Refine phase uses an LLM to generate initial program candidates and iteratively refine them based on execution feedback within a multi-armed bandit framework (REX).

The Learning phase fine-tunes the LLM using data generated during its own search attempts, leveraging "hindsight relabeling" to create synthetic training examples from both successful and unsuccessful programs.
Results: SOAR dramatically improves LLM performance on ARC-AGI; for instance, the Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B model's accuracy increases from 14.25% (search-only) to 36.25% (SOAR), a 2.5-fold gain.

The framework achieves a peak accuracy of 52.00% on the public ARC-test set by ensembling solutions from various SOAR-trained open-source LLMs, setting a new state-of-the-art for open-source inductive methods.

SOAR successfully breaks through performance ceilings observed when merely increasing LLM size or search budget with fixed models, demonstrating sustained improvements through iterative learning and test-time adaptation.
Takeaways: Self-improvement allows LLMs to overcome performance plateaus tied to fixed model size or search budget, continuously elevating performance ceilings through adaptive learning.

Hindsight relabeling is an effective technique for generating diverse and relevant training data from self-generated search traces, enabling autonomous learning without relying on human-curated datasets.
Jointly finetuning LLMs for both program sampling and refinement capabilities (rather than separately) leads to better overall performance, indicating a synergistic relationship between these tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.13362.Title: Enhancing Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models via Chain-of-Thought Prompting and Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.13362.Summary: This research from NYU's Courant Institute systematically enhances the spatial reasoning capabilities of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) by investigating structured Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting and Reinforcement Learning. The study demonstrates that Scene Graph CoT significantly improves VLM performance on spatial tasks, and fine-tuning with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) leads to superior out-of-distribution generalization compared to supervised fine-tuning.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) often struggle with complex spatial reasoning tasks, including interpreting object locations, relative depths, and geometric relationships.
Current VLM limitations in spatial understanding hinder their deployment in real-world applications like robotics and autonomous navigation.
Traditional supervised fine-tuning (SFT) frequently leads to overfitting and poor generalization in VLMs, especially under out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions.
Method: The research develops and evaluates structured Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting strategies, specifically Scene Graph CoT, to guide VLMs in explicit spatial decomposition.
It leverages Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), a reinforcement learning algorithm, to fine-tune VLMs for improved spatial reasoning and enhanced robustness.

A two-step prompting approach (scene graph generation followed by answer generation) is formalized, along with dynamic sampling within GRPO, to encourage genuine reasoning and mitigate reward hacking.
Results: Structured Scene Graph CoT yielded significant gains (5-15%) across spatial reasoning tasks, with Llama-4-Scout-17B-16E-Instruct + 4-shot Conversational CoT achieving 77.69% total accuracy on CVBench.

GRPO-v2 achieved 72.38% Pass@1 accuracy on CVBench, outperforming supervised fine-tuning (66.79%), and demonstrated superior robustness under out-of-distribution conditions (e.g., +19.5% gain on Depth OOD compared to base model, while SFT degraded).

Fine-tuning with segmentation-aware data improved counting accuracy by 43.16% on CV-Bench (SpaceQwenVL-2.5-3B improved from 21.05% to 64.21%), suggesting encoder segmentation limitations are a key factor in 'off-by-one' counting errors.
Takeaways: Naive Chain-of-Thought prompting can be detrimental to VLM spatial reasoning, underscoring the necessity for structured, domain-specific approaches.
Structured Scene Graph CoT consistently improves VLM performance on spatial tasks by enabling compositional reasoning cues.

Reinforcement learning via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) fosters a deeper, more generalizable understanding of spatial relationships in VLMs, exhibiting superior robustness to out-of-distribution linguistic shifts compared to supervised fine-tuning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.13348.Title: VisionThink: Smart and Efficient Vision Language Model via Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.13348.Summary: VisionThink is a Vision-Language Model that dynamically adjusts its visual input resolution using reinforcement learning. It achieves substantial computational savings by processing low-resolution images by default and requesting higher resolution only when necessary, while maintaining performance and outperforming fixed-compression methods on detail-intensive visual tasks.
Problem: State-of-the-art Vision-Language Models (VLMs) consume excessive visual tokens, leading to high computational costs and limiting practical deployment.
Existing efficient VLM methods apply fixed compression ratios, which causes performance degradation on tasks requiring fine-grained visual details, such as OCR.
Applying reinforcement learning to general VQA tasks is challenging due to their open-ended nature and the difficulty of defining precise reward functions.
Method: VisionThink introduces a two-stage dynamic processing pipeline: an initial low-resolution image analysis, followed by an autonomous decision to request a high-resolution image if needed.
It leverages Reinforcement Learning with an "LLM-as-Judge" strategy to train the VLM on general VQA, where an external LLM evaluates answer correctness to provide rewards.

A multi-turn Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) algorithm combined with a balanced reward function (accuracy, format, and control penalty) guides the model to optimize both performance and efficiency in its resolution choices.
Results: VisionThink achieved comparable or superior performance on general VQA benchmarks, including a 3.7% gain on MathVerse and an 8.9% gain on MMVet over its base model.
It significantly reduced inference time on most benchmarks (e.g., more than twice as fast on DocVQA) compared to full-resolution models, while maintaining accuracy.

The model intelligently requests high-resolution images for detail-dependent tasks (e.g., 79% for ChartQA, 62% for OCRBench) and uses low-resolution for the majority of general VQA queries (e.g., 93% for DocVQA).
Takeaways: Dynamically adjusting visual input resolution based on query needs significantly improves VLM efficiency without compromising accuracy on detail-intensive tasks.
Reinforcement learning, particularly with an "LLM-as-Judge" approach, can effectively train VLMs for complex, open-ended general VQA tasks, overcoming reward definition challenges.
A carefully balanced reward mechanism is crucial for RL agents to make intelligent trade-offs between computational efficiency and answer accuracy in multimodal settings.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.13334.Title: A Survey of Context Engineering for Large Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.13334.Summary: Mei et al. formalize "Context Engineering" as a systematic discipline for optimizing information supplied to Large Language Models, proposing a comprehensive taxonomy that unifies fragmented research domains. Their analysis identifies a critical "comprehension-generation asymmetry," where LLMs demonstrate strong understanding but limitations in generating equally sophisticated long-form outputs.
Problem: The explosive growth of LLM research has led to fragmented, specialized domains (e.g., prompt engineering, RAG, memory systems) that lack a unified understanding.
LLMs face computational bottlenecks with long contexts due to quadratic scaling of self-attention, alongside reliability issues such as hallucinations and unfaithfulness to context.
Traditional prompt engineering is often heuristic and subjective, lacking a systematic and formalized approach for optimizing LLM performance.
Method: Conducted a comprehensive and systematic literature review, synthesizing over 1400 research papers to provide a holistic view of LLM context utilization.
Developed a novel, structured taxonomy that formally defines and categorizes the diverse techniques within "Context Engineering" into foundational capabilities and their architectural integrations.
Formally defined Context Engineering, re-conceptualizing the traditional LLM input context as a dynamically structured set of information components subject to optimization.
Results: Formalization of "Context Engineering" as a systematic discipline, moving beyond heuristic prompt design to a principled approach for optimizing LLM information payloads.

Introduction of a comprehensive taxonomic framework that organizes the field into Foundational Components (Context Retrieval/Generation, Processing, Management) and System Implementations (RAG, Memory Systems, Tool-Integrated Reasoning, Multi-Agent Systems).

Identification of the "comprehension-generation asymmetry" as a pivotal finding, highlighting that while LLMs understand complex contexts well, their ability to generate equally sophisticated long-form outputs from this understanding remains a significant challenge.
Takeaways: The performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) is fundamentally determined by the contextual information provided during inference.
A critical 'comprehension-generation asymmetry' exists, where LLMs excel at understanding complex contexts but exhibit limitations in generating equally sophisticated, long-form outputs.
Unifying fragmented research domains under a systematic framework like Context Engineering is crucial for advancing LLM capabilities and addressing current limitations.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.12508.Title: MindJourney: Test-Time Scaling with World Models for Spatial Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.12508.Summary: MindJourney enhances Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in spatial reasoning tasks by enabling them to interactively explore imagined 3D environments using controllable video diffusion models. The framework yields an average 7.7% top-1 accuracy gain on the SAT benchmark, pushing models like OpenAI o1 from 74.6% to 84.7% accuracy on SAT-Real.
Problem: Current Vision-Language Models (VLMs) struggle with understanding 3D dynamics and anticipating egocentric motion from static 2D images.
This limitation hinders the development of robust embodied AI agents that require deep spatial reasoning for navigation, manipulation, and planning in physical environments.
VLMs lack an inherent internal model for simulating interactions and changes within a 3D world, unlike human cognition.
Method: MindJourney introduces a test-time scaling framework that couples VLMs with controllable video diffusion models, functioning as egocentric 3D 'world models'.
A 'Spatial Beam Search' algorithm guides the VLM to iteratively plan exploratory trajectories, which the world model then uses to generate corresponding imagined multi-view observations.

The accumulated multi-view evidence, including generated frames and natural language trajectory descriptions, is then provided to a Question-Answering VLM to produce a final answer without requiring VLM fine-tuning.
Results: Achieved an average 7.7% top-1 accuracy improvement across diverse VLMs on the SAT spatial reasoning benchmark, with individual gains exceeding 10%.
Established a new state-of-the-art on the SAT-Real dataset, raising the accuracy of the OpenAI o1 model from 74.6% to 84.7% when augmented with MindJourney's Search World Model (SWM).

Demonstrated consistent performance gains across both real-world (SAT-Real) and synthesized (SAT-Synthesized) scenarios, validating its generalizability across different types of spatial reasoning tasks.
Takeaways: Granting VLMs a 'physically consistent simulator' for test-time imagination offers a powerful and orthogonal method for enhancing reasoning capabilities beyond traditional text-centric approaches.
The framework is model-agnostic and training-free, demonstrating its plug-and-play compatibility with various VLM backends (e.g., GPT-4o, InternVL) and world models.
MindJourney effectively complements existing advanced reasoning techniques, such as RL-based chain-of-thought scaling, further boosting their performance in spatial tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.12507.Title: Scaling Up RL: Unlocking Diverse Reasoning in LLMs via Prolonged Training
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.12507.Summary: Researchers at NVIDIA demonstrate that prolonged reinforcement learning, coupled with specific algorithmic enhancements, can enable a 1.5 billion parameter language model to achieve significant improvements across diverse reasoning tasks like mathematics, coding, and logical puzzles. This work shows sophisticated reasoning can be unlocked in smaller, more resource-efficient models by refining training stability and duration rather than solely scaling model size.
Problem: Developing small language models with sophisticated, diverse reasoning capabilities without relying solely on increased model size, which is computationally expensive.

Addressing common challenges in large-scale Reinforcement Learning for LLMs, such as entropy collapse, maintaining an exploration-exploitation balance, and overcoming performance plateaus during extended optimization.
The lack of stable and scalable methodologies for prolonged RL training that can reliably enhance reasoning in general-purpose models across multiple domains.
Method: Applied prolonged Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to a 1.5 billion parameter Qwen-based model, enhancing it with novel stability mechanisms for extended training durations.
Integrated decoupled clipping for PPO-style objectives and dynamic prompt sampling to promote exploration, maintain entropy, and improve sample efficiency.

Introduced controlled KL regularization between the current and reference policies, alongside periodic hard resets of the reference policy and optimizer states, to prevent policy drift and overcome performance plateaus during long training runs.
Results: The Nemotron-Research-Reasoning-Qwen-1.5B model achieved substantial performance gains over its baseline, including +14.7% in mathematics, +13.9% in coding, +54.8% in logic puzzles, and +25.9% in STEM reasoning.

The trained model demonstrated strong generalization, performing competitively with larger or domain-specialized baselines (like DeepScaleR-1.5B and DeepCoder-1.5B) despite its smaller size and generalist approach.

Ablation studies confirmed the critical contributions of controlled KL regularization, decoupled clipping, dynamic sampling, and periodic reference policy resets in ensuring stable and continuous performance improvements over prolonged training.
Takeaways: Controlled KL regularization and periodic resets of the reference policy are critical for mitigating entropy collapse and achieving stable, prolonged training in reinforcement learning for large language models.

A higher rollout sampling temperature (e.g., 1.2) and decoupled clipping (with higher upper bounds) effectively promote exploration and prevent early training instability, leading to better performance.
Utilizing dynamic sampling, which focuses on prompts of intermediate difficulty, improves sample efficiency and accelerates learning by providing a more informative signal.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.12006.Title: Frequency-Dynamic Attention Modulation for Dense Prediction
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.12006.Summary: Researchers from Beijing Institute of Technology and RIKEN AIP developed Frequency-Dynamic Attention Modulation (FDAM) to counteract the low-pass filtering effect of self-attention in Vision Transformers. This approach, inspired by circuit theory, dynamically modulates frequency responses, leading to performance gains across dense prediction tasks, such as a +1.6 AP_box improvement for Mask DINO on COCO object detection.
Problem: Vision Transformer (ViT) self-attention mechanisms inherently act as low-pass filters, causing a loss of high-frequency information (fine details, textures, edges) across layers.
This 'frequency vanishing' leads to 'representation collapse,' resulting in blurred feature maps and reduced discriminability.
The degradation of fine-grained details significantly impairs performance on dense prediction tasks like semantic segmentation and object detection, which require precise spatial understanding.
Method: The authors propose Frequency-Dynamic Attention Modulation (FDAM), a circuit-theory-inspired strategy to dynamically manage ViTs' frequency responses.
FDAM includes Attention Inversion (AttInv), which generates complementary high-pass filtering by dynamically combining original low-pass attention with its inverted high-pass counterpart.

It also incorporates Frequency Dynamic Scaling (FreqScale) to adaptively re-weight different frequency bands within feature maps, enabling fine-grained amplification of suppressed high-frequency signals.
Results: FDAM consistently improved semantic segmentation performance, achieving a +2.4 mIoU gain for SegFormer-B0 and +2.6 mIoU for DeiT-T on ADE20K.
For object and instance segmentation, FDAM boosted Mask DINO's AP_box by +1.6 (from 45.5 to 47.1) and AP_mask by +1.4 (from 41.2 to 42.6) on COCO with minimal overhead.
The method prevents representation collapse, maintaining a higher effective rank and reducing patch-wise cosine similarity by up to 35% in deeper layers compared to baseline ViTs.
Takeaways: ViT self-attention mechanisms exhibit a low-pass filtering characteristic that exponentially suppresses high-frequency components, causing feature blurring in deeper layers.
A dynamic combination of low-pass and high-pass filters, inspired by circuit theory and adapted per spatial location, can effectively counteract frequency vanishing.
Adaptive, input-dependent scaling of frequency bands allows for precise control over the spectral content of features, preserving fine-grained details throughout the network.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.11988.Title: Aime: Towards Fully-Autonomous Multi-Agent Framework
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.11988.Summary: ByteDance researchers developed Aime, a multi-agent framework that overcomes limitations of traditional static planning by enabling dynamic, reactive adaptation and on-demand agent specialization. It achieves superior performance across general reasoning, software engineering, and web navigation benchmarks, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art specialized agents.
Problem: Existing multi-agent systems (MAS) based on 'plan-and-execute' frameworks suffer from rigid plan execution, making them unable to adapt to real-time feedback or unexpected events.
Current MAS often use agents with static, predefined roles and fixed toolkits, limiting their extensibility and ability to handle unforeseen or novel tasks.
Inefficient communication and lack of a centralized state management system lead to context loss, redundant work, and coordination failures between agents.
Method: Aime introduces a Dynamic Planner that continuously assesses the global task list and execution history to produce both strategic updates and tactical next actions, allowing for real-time re-planning.

The Actor Factory implements Dynamic Actor Instantiation, constructing specialized agents on-demand by selecting relevant tool bundles and generating customized prompts based on specific subtask requirements.

A centralized Progress Management Module serves as a shared memory, maintaining a hierarchical 'progress list' for real-time status tracking and facilitating structured, explicit communication between components.
Results: Aime achieved a 77.6% success rate on the GAIA benchmark, outperforming leading general-purpose agent frameworks like Langfun (71.5%) and Trase (70.3%).
It successfully resolved 66.4% of issues on SWE-bench Verified, surpassing specialized code agents such as OpenHands (65.8%) and SWE-agent (62.4%).
Aime demonstrated a 92.3% success rate on WebVoyager, exceeding strong baselines like Browser use (89.1%) and Operator (87%) in live web environments.
Takeaways: Continuous re-planning and dynamic task dispatch are essential for adaptability in multi-agent systems, moving beyond rigid, static plans.
On-demand agent specialization, enabled by dynamically selecting tools and generating prompts, significantly enhances flexibility and robustness to unforeseen tasks.
A centralized progress management module acts as a single source of truth, improving communication coherence and reducing context loss among agents.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.11932.Title: Hyperphantasia: A Benchmark for Evaluating the Mental Visualization Capabilities of Multimodal LLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.11932.Summary: The Hyperphantasia benchmark evaluates multimodal large language models' (MLLMs) mental visualization capabilities through synthetic interpolation and extrapolation puzzles. It reveals that current MLLMs largely lack robust internal visual construction and simulation, performing significantly below human levels and often resorting to brittle heuristics.
Problem: Existing benchmarks for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) primarily assess passive visual perception, such as visual question answering or object recognition.

There is a gap in evaluating MLLMs' active cognitive processes like mental visualization, which involves internally constructing, manipulating, and simulating visual representations without direct external stimuli.

Human intelligence relies heavily on mental visualization for complex tasks like spatial reasoning, trajectory prediction, and problem-solving through imaginative simulation, a capability not systematically tested in MLLMs.
Method: Researchers developed Hyperphantasia, a new synthetic benchmark comprising four procedurally generated puzzle types designed to test interpolation and extrapolation abilities.

The benchmark includes tasks like 'Seven Segments' (inferring digits from partial connections), 'Connect the Dots' (identifying objects from sparse contours), 'Linear Trajectory' (extrapolating lines), and 'Parabolic Trajectory' (predicting ball impact points).

Reinforcement learning (RL) was applied to a Qwen-VL 2.5 7B model on extrapolation tasks to investigate whether training can enhance mental visualization, using varied datasets in terms of difficulty and composition.
Results: Most MLLMs achieved near 0% accuracy on the 'Seven Segments' task, and even with explicit visual cues, many still failed, indicating issues with basic visual interpretation of out-of-distribution patterns.
On extrapolation tasks, MLLMs often performed near random guessing on medium and hard difficulties, frequently employing overly simplistic and incorrect heuristics for trajectory prediction.

Reinforcement learning on diverse, moderately difficult datasets significantly improved Qwen-VL 2.5 7B's performance, for example, achieving 40% accuracy on Hard Parabolic Trajectory after training on a 'Parabolic Medium' mix, demonstrating some cross-task transfer.
Takeaways: Current state-of-the-art MLLMs exhibit a profound deficiency in mental visualization, with performance significantly deteriorating as task difficulty increases, contrasting sharply with high human accuracy.
Failure modes extend beyond a mere lack of mental visualization, with models often unable to interpret even simple geometric patterns when presented in slightly out-of-distribution visual formats.

Reinforcement learning can improve generalization for mental visualization, particularly when models are trained on diverse and moderately challenging problems rather than just easy examples, which tend to foster brittle, non-transferable heuristics.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.11851.Title: Your LLM Knows the Future: Uncovering Its Multi-Token Prediction Potential
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.11851.Summary: A framework developed by researchers at Apple enables pretrained autoregressive large language models to perform multi-token prediction, yielding inference speedups of up to 5.35x for code and math tasks and approximately 2.5x for general tasks while preserving generation quality.
Problem: High latency and computational cost of autoregressive LLM inference due to its inherent sequential, token-by-token generation process.
Difficulty in efficiently adapting existing powerful pretrained autoregressive LLMs for multi-token generation without degrading their original next-token prediction capabilities.
The need for practical, efficient methods to unlock and utilize the implicit future token knowledge already encoded within pretrained autoregressive models.
Method: A masked-input formulation using special mask tokens appended to the input, enabling the LLM to predict multiple future tokens in parallel within a single inference step.
Gated LoRA, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique that applies low-rank adaptations only when processing mask tokens, preserving the original model's next-token prediction capabilities.

A lightweight, learnable sampler module and Latent Consistency Matching (LCM) loss used during training to improve the coherence and alignment of multi-token predictions with ground-truth autoregressive outputs, enhancing speculative decoding acceptance rates.
Results: The framework achieved significant inference speedups, with acceptance rates translating to nearly 5.0x to 5.35x for code and math tasks, and approximately 2.5x for general chat and knowledge tasks, averaging 3.17x across benchmarks.
Gated LoRA successfully preserved the original model's next-token prediction (NTP) accuracy and cross-entropy loss, demonstrating no degradation of baseline performance.

Ablation studies confirmed that Quadratic Decoding, the lightweight sampler head, and Latent Consistency Matching (LCM) loss each contribute to improved speedup and acceptance rates, with their combined use showing the strongest performance.
Takeaways: Existing autoregressive LLMs implicitly contain knowledge about future tokens, which can be explicitly leveraged for multi-token prediction.
It is possible to adapt pretrained LLMs for new capabilities like multi-token prediction without degrading their original performance by using gated adaptation mechanisms such as Gated LoRA.

Carefully designed decoding strategies, such as Quadratic Decoding, combined with coherence-enhancing components like a sampler head and Latent Consistency Matching loss, are crucial for maximizing the efficiency and reliability of multi-token generation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.10548.Title: EmbRACE-3K: Embodied Reasoning and Action in Complex Environments
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.10548.Summary: Researchers introduced EmbRACE-3K, a dataset featuring 3,000 embodied reasoning and action tasks in photorealistic Unreal Engine environments, notable for its fine-grained, step-wise natural language rationales. Training vision-language models on this dataset significantly enhances their performance in complex interactive tasks like exploration and dynamic spatial reasoning, demonstrating improved generalization to unseen environments.
Problem: Current Vision-Language Models (VLMs) excel in "passive" visual understanding but perform poorly in "embodied" settings due to a training-deployment mismatch.
Existing VLMs exhibit short-sighted exploration, dynamic spatial-semantic drift, and target forgetting when applied to interactive environments.
Many existing embodied benchmarks lack photorealism, sufficient fine-grained supervision, or truly online, closed-loop interaction.
Method: Introduced EmbRACE-3K, a dataset of 3,000 multi-stage, language-guided tasks in 24 diverse, photorealistic Unreal Engine environments, collected via human demonstrations.
Captured human demonstrations including egocentric views, executed actions, and precise pose trajectories within a closed-loop perception-action cycle.
Generated step-wise natural language "thinking" rationales for every decision point in the human demonstrations using Gemini, providing fine-grained, temporally grounded supervision for reasoning.
Results: State-of-the-art VLMs like GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Pro show very low zero-shot success rates on EmbRACE-3K, validating the dataset's challenge.

Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-VL on EmbRACE-3K (Qwen2.5-VL-sft-rl) leads to substantial performance gains, achieving 30.9% SR on out-of-domain Exploration tasks and 42.4% SR on Dynamic Spatial-Semantic tasks, significantly outperforming zero-shot VLMs.

Models trained with step-wise reasoning supervision and reinforcement learning demonstrate improved generalization to unseen environments, with the sft-rl model showing better robustness compared to sft-only variants.
Takeaways: Explicit, step-wise natural language reasoning annotations ("thinking" rationales) are crucial for training VLMs to make more stable and coherent decisions in embodied tasks.
Integrating reinforcement learning with supervised fine-tuning significantly improves the generalization capabilities of embodied agents to unseen environments.
High-fidelity, interactive environments with diverse tasks and fine-grained supervision are essential for developing robust embodied reasoning in VLMs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.10532.Title: Reasoning or Memorization? Unreliable Results of Reinforcement Learning Due to Data Contamination
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.10532.Summary: The research investigates why Qwen2.5 LLMs show performance gains from random rewards on math benchmarks, concluding that these gains stem primarily from test data contamination and memorization. Only accurate reward signals led to genuine improvements in mathematical reasoning on a novel, leakage-free benchmark called RandomCalculation.
Problem: Unreliable results were observed when applying reinforcement learning with spurious (random or incorrect) rewards to the Qwen2.5 series of large language models, particularly in mathematical reasoning tasks.
A debate existed on whether reported performance gains with random rewards indicated genuine reasoning enhancements or were artifacts of data contamination.
There was a lack of truly contamination-free benchmarks to reliably evaluate the impact of reinforcement learning on LLM reasoning capabilities.
Method: The study systematically audited existing mathematical benchmarks (e.g., MATH-500, AMC) for data contamination using novel partial-prompt completion and answer accuracy metrics.
A novel, automatically generated, leakage-free dataset named *RandomCalculation* was introduced to provide an unbiased evaluation of arithmetic reasoning.

Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) was empirically evaluated with correct, random, inverted, and majority-voted incorrect reward signals on both contaminated and the clean *RandomCalculation* benchmarks.
Results: Qwen2.5-Math-7B exhibited partial-prompt completion rates exceeding 50% and answer accuracy over 50% on MATH-500 when prompted with only 60% of a problem, demonstrating high memorization.

On the contamination-free *RandomCalculation* dataset, only correct reward signals improved Qwen2.5-Math-7B's performance, while random or incorrect rewards resulted in unstable training and no consistent improvements.

Analysis revealed significantly higher lexical overlap (ROUGE-L) and lower KL divergence between model outputs before and after RL training on contaminated benchmarks, indicating memory retrieval rather than genuine policy shifts due to spurious rewards.
Takeaways: Widely used mathematical benchmarks, such as MATH-500, are significantly contaminated, causing models like Qwen2.5 to exhibit high memorization of problems and solutions from their pre-training data.

The apparent effectiveness of spurious rewards on contaminated benchmarks is largely due to an 'exploitation bias' in the GRPO algorithm, which reinforces the retrieval of existing memorized content rather than fostering novel reasoning.

On clean, leakage-free data, only genuinely correct and continuous reward signals lead to stable and consistent improvements in mathematical reasoning, while random or incorrect rewards provide no reliable gains.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.10524.Title: Mixture-of-Recursions: Learning Dynamic Recursive Depths for Adaptive Token-Level Computation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.10524.Summary: Mixture-of-Recursions (MoR) introduces a unified framework for language models that combines parameter efficiency, adaptive computation, and efficient KV caching. It achieves strong performance, outperforming vanilla Transformers with nearly 50% fewer parameters and reducing training FLOPs by 25%, while increasing inference throughput by up to 2.06x.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) face high computational and memory costs during training and deployment, hindering accessibility and sustainability.
Existing approaches to efficiency, such as parameter sharing and adaptive computation, often operate in isolation or introduce practical hurdles like complex training procedures.
Traditional Recursive Transformers use fixed recursion depths for all tokens, ignoring varying computational needs, while KV caches consume vast GPU memory during inference.
Method: Mixture-of-Recursions (MoR) integrates dynamic, token-level computation within a parameter-shared architecture, leveraging the "Middle-Cycle" strategy for efficient weight reuse.
Lightweight routers, either Expert-choice (selecting top-k tokens for continued processing) or Token-choice (assigning fixed recursion depth per token), enable adaptive computational allocation.
Two KV caching strategies, Recursion-wise (selective storage) and Recursive KV Sharing (single computation and reuse), optimize memory usage during inference.
Results: MoR models achieve lower validation NLL (2.7511) and higher average few-shot accuracy (43.1%) compared to Vanilla Transformers (NLL 2.7824, accuracy 42.3%), utilizing nearly 50% fewer parameters under equivalent training FLOPs.
Processing the same amount of data (20B tokens), MoR reduces training FLOPs by 25%, leading to a 19% reduction in training time and 25% less peak memory usage.
Inference throughput is boosted by up to 2.06x over vanilla baselines when MoR is combined with continuous depth-wise batching.
Takeaways: The unification of parameter efficiency, adaptive computation, and efficient KV caching within a single framework establishes a new Pareto frontier for LLM efficiency.
Dynamic, token-level routing allows models to adaptively allocate computational resources, enabling deeper "thinking" on complex tokens while optimizing overall compute.
MoR exhibits compute-optimal scaling behavior that prioritizes increases in model capacity (parameter count) over extending training length under isoFLOPs constraints.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.10442.Title: Response Wide Shut? Surprising Observations in Basic Vision Language Model Capabilities
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.10442.Summary: Researchers from UBC, Vector Institute, IIT Hyderabad, and Microsoft Research India introduce a "three-space analysis" to diagnose Vision-Language Model (VLM) limitations, revealing that fine-grained visual information often exists in early processing stages but is lost by the language decoder. The study shows that VLMs exhibit a stronger reliance on texture over shape for object recognition, suggesting key areas for improving VLM architectures and training strategies.
Problem: Despite advanced capabilities, VLMs often exhibit surprising shortcomings in basic visual understanding (e.g., counting, fine-grained recognition, spatial relations).

Existing evaluations primarily focus on final VLM textual responses, offering limited insight into which architectural component (visual encoder, projection, or language decoder) is responsible for deficiencies.
Prevailing hypotheses sometimes attribute VLM visual shortcomings solely to limitations of their visual encoders, without detailed investigation of later stages.
Method: The paper introduces a "three-space analysis" methodology, dissecting VLMs into visual latent, vision-language shared latent, and language response spaces to probe information flow.

Linear probes are trained on intermediate feature representations and output token representations to assess what information is implicitly captured at each stage for object recognition, counting, and spatial understanding tasks.

A diverse set of VLMs (contrastive, encoder-decoder generative, instruction-tuned) are evaluated, and robustness to visual corruptions, background transformations, and the impact of language priors and model scale are analyzed.
Results: Fine-grained object recognition accuracy drops by at least 45% in the response space compared to >90% in intermediate spaces, attributed to ineffective joint fine-tuning.
Object counting similarly shows at least a 14% performance degradation in the response space despite high accuracy in earlier stages.

For spatial understanding, visual latent representations perform worst, with performance improving in the VL projection and response spaces, suggesting the language decoder's role in compensating for initial visual encoder weaknesses.
Takeaways: For fine-grained recognition and counting, crucial visual information is well-encoded in the visual and vision-language projection spaces but is significantly lost or poorly utilized by the language decoder.
Visual encoders initially exhibit weaker performance for spatial understanding, but the language decoder, when appropriately fine-tuned, can partially compensate.
VLMs demonstrate a critical reliance on texture cues over shape information for object recognition, a divergence from human perception that impacts generalization.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.10434.Title: CLA: Latent Alignment for Online Continual Self-Supervised Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.10434.Summary: The paper introduces Continual Latent Alignment (CLA), a self-supervised learning strategy designed for online continual learning from unlabeled, non-stationary data streams. CLA consistently surpasses existing online continual self-supervised learning methods on benchmarks like Split CIFAR-100 and Split ImageNet100, and is shown to be a more efficient early-stage pretraining protocol than traditional i.i.d. training.
Problem: Most self-supervised learning (SSL) methods assume i.i.d. (independent and identically distributed) data and offline access to all training data, which is often unrealistic for continuous data streams.
Existing continual self-supervised learning (CSSL) primarily focuses on "offline" scenarios with explicit task boundaries, allowing for multiple epochs of training per task.

The challenging "Online Continual Self-Supervised Learning (OCSSL)" setting, characterized by continuous, one-pass data streams, no task boundaries, and strict computational budgets, remains largely underexplored.
Method: The proposed Continual Latent Alignment (CLA) strategy aims to mitigate catastrophic forgetting by aligning the current model's representations with past representations, using either an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) network or stored past targets from a memory buffer.
CLA includes variants like CLA-b (base, no replay), CLA-E (EMA with FIFO replay buffer), and CLA-R (stored targets with FIFO replay buffer) to adapt to different online learning conditions.
The novel Cumulative Backward Passes (CBP) metric is introduced to provide a fair and hardware-agnostic comparison of computational costs across various online continual learning methods.
Results: CLA variants consistently achieve state-of-the-art performance in both Final Accuracy and Average Accuracy on Split CIFAR-100 and Split ImageNet100 benchmarks across varying computational budgets.
CLA demonstrates faster adaptation and stable convergence, sometimes surpassing the performance of conventional i.i.d. training under limited Cumulative Backward Passes (CBP) conditions.
Models initially pretrained with CLA show superior generalization capabilities to novel downstream tasks (SVHN, Stanford Cars) when compared to models undergoing full i.i.d. pretraining.
Takeaways: Continuously aligning current features with a dynamically evolving 'past' representation (via EMA or stored targets) effectively mitigates catastrophic forgetting and promotes stable, fast convergence in online SSL without explicit task boundaries.

A First-In-First-Out (FIFO) memory buffer, which prioritizes uniform training iterations for replayed samples, proves more effective than a reservoir buffer in OCSSL when integrated with an alignment mechanism.

OCSSL strategies, specifically CLA, can be more efficient for early-stage pretraining compared to traditional i.i.d. training, potentially leading to better final models with reduced overall computational cost.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.10302.Title: DisCo: Towards Distinct and Coherent Visual Encapsulation in Video MLLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.10302.Summary: DisCo introduces a visual encapsulation method for video Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) that generates semantically distinct and temporally coherent visual tokens. This approach achieves state-of-the-art performance across various video understanding benchmarks while significantly improving token efficiency.
Problem: Existing visual encapsulation methods for video MLLMs often produce semantically indistinct tokens, leading to redundancy and increased computational load.
Current approaches struggle with temporal incoherence, failing to consistently track specific entities or actions across video frames.
The inefficient use of visual tokens hinders the LLM's comprehensive understanding of dynamic video content and increases inference costs.
Method: A Visual Concept Discriminator (VCD) employs GPT-4 for semantic concept extraction and uses bipartite matching with contrastive and matching losses to align visual token groups with distinct semantic concepts.

A Temporal Focus Calibrator (TFC) module ensures consistency by supervising each visual token to maintain focus on its corresponding semantic concept across all video frames through a frame-level focus alignment loss.
The method integrates these modules into a two-stage training scheme: initial vision-text alignment on dense captions, followed by instruction tuning with diverse video QA data.
Results: DisCo achieves new state-of-the-art performance on multiple video question-answering benchmarks, including MVBench (68.2%), STAR (77.7%), and EgoSchema (72.2%) when integrated with InternVideo2-HD.
It demonstrates enhanced token efficiency, with a 16-token DisCo model outperforming a 64-token traditional resampler baseline on MVBench, reducing token count by 75%.
Qualitative evaluations show improved correctness, stronger temporal coherence, and richer detail in video captions and conversational responses compared to baselines.
Takeaways: Explicitly enforcing semantic distinctiveness and temporal coherence in visual tokens is crucial for improving video MLLM understanding beyond simple token compression.
Leveraging large language models like GPT-4 to curate non-overlapping semantic concepts provides effective supervision for differentiating visual tokens.
Using feature centroids to anchor temporal alignment enables more robust and consistent tracking of objects or actions across variable video segments.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.10203.Title: Improving Multimodal Learning via Imbalanced Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.10203.Summary: Researchers at the University of Electronic Science and Technology of China introduce a theoretical re-evaluation showing that optimal multimodal learning benefits from imbalanced modality contributions, inversely proportional to their prediction variances. Their Asymmetric Representation Learning (ARL) strategy implements this principle, achieving state-of-the-art performance with improvements up to 3.02% macro F1 on CREMA-D and consistent gains across diverse multimodal tasks and architectures.
Problem: Multimodal models frequently exhibit an "under-optimized problem," where individual modality encoders within a fused model perform below their unimodal potential.
A prevailing hypothesis attributes this to "modality imbalance," suggesting a stronger modality suppresses weaker ones during joint training.
Existing solutions largely focus on rebalancing learning across modalities, often through unimodal assistance, gradient modulation, or alternating learning.
Method: The authors theoretically demonstrate, via bias-variance decomposition, that optimal multimodal decision dependency should be inversely proportional to each modality's prediction variance.
They propose Asymmetric Representation Learning (ARL), which uses auxiliary regularizers to estimate modality variance (uncertainty) without adding extra parameters.
ARL then dynamically modulates gradients to each modality encoder based on their inverse variance ratio and incorporates unimodal bias regularization to minimize individual modality biases.
Results: ARL consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance across various multimodal tasks and datasets, including a 3.02% macro F1 improvement on CREMA-D, 2.28% on AVE, and 3.01% on Kinetics-Sounds.

The method demonstrates strong generalization capabilities, performing effectively with more than two modalities (MOSI), on large datasets (UCF-101), and when integrated with diverse architectures like CNN-based and Transformer-based models.
Ablation studies confirm that both Unimodal Bias Regularization and Asymmetric Learning components, along with the Gradient Residual, synergistically contribute to the observed performance gains.
Takeaways: Optimal multimodal learning is achieved not through balanced contributions, but by an imbalanced dependency where modalities with lower prediction variance contribute more to the final decision.
The 'under-optimized problem' can be effectively addressed by simultaneously minimizing individual modality biases and the variance of the fused multimodal prediction.
A residual connection in gradient modulation is crucial to prevent training stagnation in modalities with very small modulation factors, ensuring continuous optimization.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.10202.Title: A Training-Free, Task-Agnostic Framework for Enhancing MLLM Performance on High-Resolution Images
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.10202.Summary: The Extract Candidate then Predict (ECP) framework enables existing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to effectively process high-resolution images (e.g., 4K, 8K) by employing a training-free, two-stage coarse-to-fine approach. It demonstrates substantial accuracy improvements on tasks such as 4K GUI grounding and 4K/8K MLLM perception, making MLLMs viable for scenarios requiring fine-grained visual detail.
Problem: Current Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) perform poorly on tasks requiring fine-grained localization and reasoning within high-resolution images (e.g., 4K, 8K).
This limitation stems from a train-test resolution discrepancy, where downsampling high-resolution images for MLLM input results in a significant loss of crucial fine-grained visual details.

Prior approaches either demand computationally expensive re-training with specialized high-resolution datasets or are limited by manually crafted heuristics specific to particular tasks, lacking generalizability.
Method: The Extract Candidate then Predict (ECP) framework is a training-free, two-stage approach that utilizes existing pre-trained MLLMs.

In the 'Extract Candidate' (EC) stage, a downsampled version of the high-resolution image is fed to an MLLM to obtain a coarse localization cue (point or bounding box), from which a high-resolution candidate region is extracted.

In the 'Predict' (P) stage, the original high-resolution image is cropped to this candidate region, which is then provided to an MLLM (along with the instruction and optionally the downsampled full image) to generate the final, precise prediction.
Results: On the 4K GUI grounding ScreenSpot-Pro benchmark, ECP improved OS-Atlas-7B's accuracy from 19.1% to 40.4%, an absolute increase of 21.3%.
For 4K and 8K MLLM perception on the HR-Bench, ECP boosted Qwen2-VL-7B's overall accuracy by 5.8% on 4K (to 68.3%) and 5.2% on 8K (to 60.3%).

Ablation studies confirmed that leveraging the MLLM's instruction-guided coarse localization in the first stage is critical, with random sampling for candidate region selection significantly degrading performance.
Takeaways: Existing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), even when processing downsampled images, possess an implicit coarse localization ability that can be effectively leveraged to identify instruction-relevant regions.

A training-free, two-stage coarse-to-fine processing strategy can successfully overcome the resolution discrepancy faced by MLLMs without requiring additional training, fine-tuning, or architectural modifications.

Developing task-agnostic frameworks allows for broad applicability across diverse vision-language tasks involving high-resolution imagery, enhancing practical utility and reducing deployment barriers.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09961.Title: Text-Driven Causal Representation Learning for Source-Free Domain Generalization
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09961.Summary: Researchers from the Chinese Academy of Sciences, University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, University of Surrey, Shenzhen University, and University of Rochester introduced Text-Driven Causal Representation Learning (TDCRL), a framework integrating causal inference into Source-Free Domain Generalization (SFDG). It learns robust, domain-invariant features by mitigating domain-specific confounders through text-simulated visual representations from VLMs, achieving state-of-the-art performance on various benchmarks.
Problem: Traditional Domain Generalization (DG) methods are resource-intensive, requiring extensive, costly collection and annotation of diverse multi-source image datasets.

Existing Source-Free Domain Generalization (SFDG) approaches, while leveraging Vision-Language Models (VLMs), struggle with domain-specific confounders that lead to overfitting styles and poor generalization to unseen target domains.
The powerful theoretical framework of causal inference, effective in traditional DG for explicit confounder removal, had not yet been successfully applied within the SFDG setting.
Method: The method efficiently generates diverse text embeddings by combining class names with augmented style word vectors, encoded by CLIP's text encoder, to simulate rich visual data without actual source images.

A Causal Intervention Network (CIN) is designed to perform a "do-operation" on these features, explicitly intervening on style components using a learned confounder dictionary to disentangle domain-invariant features from spurious style correlations.

A classifier is trained on the intervened, domain-invariant features, with the entire model (CIN and classifier) optimized jointly using a contrastive loss for intervention and a cross-entropy loss for classification.
Results: TDCRL achieved state-of-the-art average Top-1 accuracy across four challenging benchmarks (PACS, VLCS, OfficeHome, DomainNet) using various CLIP backbones, notably reaching 84.6% with ViT-L/14, outperforming prior SFDG and many source-dependent DG methods.

Ablation studies empirically confirmed the crucial role of the causal intervention module, demonstrating accuracy improvements of up to 3.4% and showing effective removal of domain styles in both text and image features.

The framework exhibits enhanced computational efficiency, requiring less training time than comparable SFDG methods, and t-SNE visualizations confirm its ability to merge domain-specific feature clusters into cohesive, domain-invariant representations.
Takeaways: Causal intervention, traditionally complex for image data, can be effectively implemented in a source-free manner using VLM-driven text prompts, allowing precise control over style components to isolate category-specific information.

The causal intervention network, trained exclusively on text embeddings, successfully transfers its ability to remove domain-specific style information from *image* embeddings during inference, enhancing cross-modal transferability.

Explicitly modeling and intervening on domain-specific confounders through a theoretically grounded causal framework significantly improves out-of-distribution generalization, moving beyond purely empirical solutions in SFDG.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09876.Title: ViTCoT: Video-Text Interleaved Chain-of-Thought for Boosting Video Understanding in Large Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09876.Summary: ViTCoT introduces a Video-Text Interleaved Chain-of-Thought paradigm for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), integrating key visual information directly into the step-by-step reasoning process. The approach consistently improves video understanding accuracy by an average of 3.5% across various MLLMs and mainstream CoT methods, supported by a newly constructed, human-verified benchmark.
Problem: Existing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) for video understanding predominantly rely on text-only reasoning, treating visual data as an initial input rather than an iterative reference point.
This text-only reasoning paradigm overlooks the human cognitive tendency to re-examine visual content during complex comprehension tasks.
A lack of dedicated benchmarks exists to evaluate models capable of true video-text interleaved reasoning.
Method: Introduces ViTCoT, a two-stage video-text interleaved reasoning paradigm: initial text reasoning followed by refined reasoning with key-videos integrated into the textual thought process.
Constructs the Video-Text Interleaved Benchmark (ViTIB) by leveraging MLLM-assisted key-video selection from VideoEspresso, followed by rigorous human verification to ensure quality.
Enables MLLMs to refine their understanding by iteratively interacting with both textual and key visual information, mimicking human cognitive patterns during problem-solving.
Results: ViTCoT consistently improved video understanding accuracy by an average of 3.5% across diverse MLLMs (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL, Gemini-2.0-Flash) and mainstream CoT methods compared to text-only approaches.
The interleaving process itself contributed an average 2.8% performance gain over vanilla methods, even when baselines were provided with both original and key videos, suggesting its critical role.
Qualitative analysis revealed ViTCoT activated more neuron values across attention heads and layers within MLLMs, indicating deeper and more intensive multimodal engagement.
Takeaways: Integrating visual information iteratively into the reasoning process, rather than just as initial input, significantly enhances MLLM video understanding.
The act of interleaving visual and textual cues during reasoning is critical, providing substantial benefits beyond merely providing additional visual input.
High-quality, condensed "key-videos" can effectively capture essential information for reasoning, sometimes outperforming reliance on full, longer videos.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09662.Title: Towards Concise and Adaptive Thinking in Large Reasoning Models: A Survey
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09662.Summary: This survey provides a comprehensive overview of methods for achieving concise and adaptive thinking in Large Reasoning Models (LRMs). It categorizes existing research into training-free and training-based approaches, detailing how models can shorten verbose reasoning chains and dynamically adjust their 'thinking' depth based on input difficulty, thereby improving efficiency and practical usability.
Problem: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) like OpenAI O1 and DeepSeek R1 generate excessively long and redundant Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning sequences, even for simple queries.
This 'overthinking' leads to substantial waste of inference resources, increased response times, and higher computational costs, hindering practical LRM deployment.
LRMs lack the ability to adapt their reasoning depth based on input difficulty, failing to balance 'fast' (System 1) and 'slow' (System 2) thinking.
Method: The survey categorizes and analyzes existing methodologies into two main approaches: training-free methods and training-based methods.

Training-free methods include prompt-guided, pipeline-based architectures, decoding manipulation techniques, and model merging strategies to control reasoning length without additional model training.

Training-based methods involve fine-tuning strategies (e.g., data construction, variable-length datasets, DPO variants) and reinforcement learning (e.g., with length penalties, difficulty awareness) to learn adaptive reasoning.
Results: Training-free methods offer ease of implementation but often exhibit inconsistent performance (e.g., prompt-guided), introduce latency (pipeline-based), or require careful design to avoid errors (decoding manipulation).
Training-based methods, while powerful for teaching adaptive length, are heavily reliant on high-quality variable-length CoT data and face challenges like 'Format Collapse' in RL approaches.
A lack of unified evaluation standards across research efforts, including inconsistent base models, datasets, and metrics, hinders direct comparison and standardization of findings in the field.
Takeaways: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) widely exhibit an 'overthinking phenomenon,' generating unnecessarily lengthy reasoning chains for many tasks.
Optimal reasoning lengths are non-uniform and vary with input difficulty, necessitating adaptive thinking to balance performance and efficiency.

Current research on concise and adaptive LRM thinking falls into two main paradigms: training-free methods (e.g., prompting, pipeline-based, decoding manipulation) and training-based methods (e.g., fine-tuning, reinforcement learning).

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09615.Title: Towards Fine-Grained Adaptation of CLIP via a Self-Trained Alignment Score
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09615.Summary: A framework called Fine-grained Alignment and Interaction Refinement (FAIR) enhances the performance of Vision-Language Models like CLIP in unsupervised fine-grained classification by introducing a learned alignment score and adaptively refining cross-modal interactions. The approach achieved an average accuracy gain of 2.78% over the prior state-of-the-art, DPA, across 13 fine-grained datasets.
Problem: Pretrained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) like CLIP struggle with fine-grained classification due to their reliance on global features and generic text prompts, failing to capture subtle visual distinctions.
Acquiring labeled data for fine-grained domains is often costly or infeasible, necessitating effective unsupervised adaptation (UA) methods.
Existing UA methods use fixed alignment scores, limiting their adaptability to evolving class distinctions, or computationally expensive localized feature processing for pseudo-labeling.
