Method: Introduces Fine-grained Alignment and Interaction Refinement (FAIR), an unsupervised adaptation framework for CLIP that dynamically aligns localized image features with adaptive language embeddings.
Employs learnable Class Description Anchors (CDAs) initialized by an LLM, which adapt concurrently with the image encoder during self-training to capture evolving class semantics.
Utilizes selective crop relevance weighting to choose only the top-k most informative localized image crops, significantly reducing computational cost while enhancing local feature utilization.
Integrates a confidence-adjusted weighting mechanism during self-training to refine pseudo-labels, especially for visually similar classes, thereby mitigating ambiguity.
Results: FAIR improved average classification accuracy by 2.78% across 13 fine-grained datasets compared to the state-of-the-art DPA, and by over 9% compared to zero-shot CLIP and CuPL.

The framework achieved a notable performance of 91.92% accuracy on the EuroSAT dataset, significantly outperforming DPA's 79.94%, demonstrating strong capability in distinguishing highly similar classes.

FAIR exhibited computational efficiency, achieving competitive performance with only 45.1K trainable parameters (for ViT-B/32 on EuroSAT) and faster convergence (15 epochs), while also outperforming prior methods in transductive settings.
Takeaways: Dynamically learning and adapting class representations through a Learned Alignment Score (LAS) is critical for capturing fine-grained distinctions, contributing a 7.04% performance boost.
Refining pseudo-labels with an adaptive confidence-adjusted weighting mechanism significantly enhances self-training robustness by 1.84%, particularly for ambiguous fine-grained classes.
Selectively weighting and utilizing only the most relevant localized image crops ([CLS]-based top-k selection) provides a computationally efficient way to leverage fine-grained visual cues.
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning of only layer normalization weights and Class Description Anchors enables competitive performance with a small number of trainable parameters.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.08979.Title: PRISM: Reducing Spurious Implicit Biases in Vision-Language Models with LLM-Guided Embedding Projection
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.08979.Summary: Queen’s University researchers developed PRISM, a data-free and task-agnostic framework that leverages large language models to identify spurious correlations and projects VLM embeddings to mitigate implicit biases. This method achieved state-of-the-art worst-group accuracy on Waterbirds (84.2%) and CelebA (84.0%) datasets, maintaining high overall performance and reducing reliance on confounding background features.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) inherit and amplify spurious correlations from pre-training data, leading to biased, inaccurate, and non-robust predictions.
Existing debiasing methods often require predefined bias categories, external visual data, or compromise the VLM's overall accuracy.
There is a lack of truly data-free and task-agnostic debiasing solutions that preserve core semantic information and overall performance.
Method: PRISM, a two-stage data-free and task-agnostic framework, is introduced to mitigate VLM biases without predefined categories or external visual data.
Large Language Models (LLMs) are prompted to dynamically identify spurious attributes and generate controlled scene descriptions encoding both the true class and spurious context.
A learnable projection matrix is optimized using a novel Latent space Debiasing (LD) loss, designed to minimize spurious attribute influence while preserving core semantic alignment.
Results: PRISM achieved state-of-the-art worst-group (WG) accuracy of 84.2% on Waterbirds and 84.0% on CelebA, outperforming all data-free baselines and many image-based methods.
The method preserved high overall accuracy (93.6% on Waterbirds, 86.9% on CelebA), effectively balancing fairness gains with general performance.

Qualitative analysis through representation maps confirmed that PRISM successfully disentangles features, leading to more structured and separated clusters with reduced influence from background information.
Takeaways: LLMs can be effectively leveraged to dynamically identify spurious correlations from textual co-occurrence statistics, removing the reliance on human-defined bias categories.
A targeted projection of the VLM's embedding space, rather than full model fine-tuning, can effectively remove spurious biases while preserving semantic information and computational efficiency.
The novel Latent space Debiasing (LD) loss, with its intra-class invariance and inter-class separation components, is crucial for learning a robust debiasing projection.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.08838.Title: wd1: Weighted Policy Optimization for Reasoning in Diffusion Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.08838.Summary: wd1 introduces a weighted policy optimization approach for diffusion-based Large Language Models (dLLMs) that reformulates the reinforcement learning objective to require only a single likelihood approximation. This method achieves up to a 100% accuracy improvement on reasoning and planning benchmarks while reducing training costs by eliminating the need for supervised fine-tuning.
Problem: Diffusion-based Large Language Models (dLLMs) face challenges in applying reinforcement learning due to the intractability of their sequence-level likelihood functions.
Existing RL methods for dLLMs require approximating likelihoods for multiple policies (current, old, reference), leading to high computational overhead.
These multi-policy likelihood approximations, particularly in policy ratios used for importance sampling, introduce bias and training instability.
Method: wd1 reformulates the reinforcement learning objective by leveraging reverse-KL regularization, deriving a weighted log-likelihood objective that avoids explicit policy ratios.
The approach significantly reduces computational overhead by requiring the approximation of only the current policy's likelihood, unlike previous methods that need multiple policy likelihoods.
It incorporates both positive and negative weights derived from group-relative advantages, ensuring robust learning by amplifying beneficial samples and explicitly penalizing low-advantage ones.
Results: The method achieved up to a 100% relative gain on planning tasks like Countdown (51.2% accuracy) and a 43% relative gain on Sudoku (25.2% accuracy) compared to existing methods, without requiring supervised fine-tuning.

Training costs were reduced by eliminating the two-hour supervised fine-tuning phase and achieving faster reinforcement learning training times (82.16 seconds per global step vs. 103.5 seconds for baselines).
It demonstrated superior sample efficiency with faster training reward increases and converged to shorter, more token-efficient output sequences on mathematical reasoning tasks.
Takeaways: Reformulating the RL objective using reverse-KL regularization can bypass the need for explicit policy ratios, enabling stable policy optimization for dLLMs with intractable likelihoods.
Reducing the number of required likelihood approximations to only the current policy substantially boosts training efficiency and stability for dLLMs.
The explicit inclusion of negative weights for low-advantage samples is crucial for effective policy optimization, demonstrating the value of leveraging all training data.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.08664.Title: Introspection of Thought Helps AI Agents
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.08664.Summary: The Introspection of Thought (INoT) framework introduces an "LLM-Read code" called PromptCode, embedding structured iterative reasoning and multi-agent debate directly within the prompt. This approach enables AI agents to perform complex introspection, yielding an average 7.95% performance improvement over baselines while reducing token costs by 58.3% across diverse language and multimodal tasks.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) and Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) inherently struggle with complex reasoning tasks that require deep planning or self-correction.
Existing iterative reasoning frameworks incur high computational costs and inefficiency from multiple external interactions with the LLM, leading to substantial token consumption.
Natural language prompts can be ambiguous, leading to LLM misinterpretations and a lack of universal applicability across different task types and modalities.
Method: The Introspection of Thought (INoT) framework proposes "PromptCode," an LLM-readable, XML-structured code that embeds complete reasoning logic directly within the prompt.
PromptCode combines Python-like syntax with natural language to provide precise, unambiguous instructions for LLM introspection and decision-making.
A virtual multi-agent debate mechanism, simulated internally within the LLM using PromptCode, enables iterative reflection, critique, and self-correction without external orchestration.
Results: The INoT framework achieved an average performance improvement of 7.95% across six diverse benchmarks, outperforming the best baseline method by 6.41 percentage points.
INoT significantly reduced token costs by an average of 58.3% compared to the best-performing baseline methods, demonstrating superior operational efficiency.

The framework consistently enhanced performance in tasks including Code (HumanEval 95.9%, MBPP 84.3%), Math (MATH 53.4%, GSM8K 93.3%), QA (HotpotQA 72.2%, SQuAD 88.8%), and Image QA (e.g., 6.0% gain on LLaVA-Bench In-the-Wild).
Takeaways: Embedding programmatic reasoning logic directly into the prompt allows LLMs to perform complex, iterative introspection and multi-agent debates internally, significantly reducing the need for external orchestrators.
A hybrid "PromptCode" that integrates Python syntax with natural language offers a precise yet flexible method for guiding LLM reasoning and decision-making.
Structuring prompts with XML and including an Image Augment Module for MLLMs standardizes visual analysis, leading to more robust and accurate multimodal understanding.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.08306.Title: M2-Reasoning: Empowering MLLMs with Unified General and Spatial Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.08306.Summary: Inclusion AI, Ant Group developed M2-Reasoning-7B, a Multimodal Large Language Model capable of unified general and spatial reasoning, which achieved state-of-the-art performance across 8 diverse benchmarks, including an average score of 45.0 on general reasoning and 82.3 on image-based spatial reasoning.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle with understanding dynamic spatial interactions, including motion, orientation, and physical interactions.
There is a scarcity of high-quality, logically coherent datasets specifically designed for spatial reasoning, especially dynamic interactions.
Training MLLMs on diverse tasks like general and specialized spatial reasoning leads to conflicts due to data heterogeneity and varying reward signals.
Method: A multi-stage data construction pipeline synthesizes high-quality general reasoning (168K CoT instances) and spatial reasoning data (26.2K RLVR instances, image- and video-based).
A two-stage training framework starts with cold-start Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and proceeds to dynamic multi-task Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR).

The RLVR stage utilizes a GRPO variant with task-specific reward formulations, including Exponential Decay Numeric Matching (EDNM) for continuous spatial answers, and dynamic hyper-parameter adjustments for stable training.
Results: M2-Reasoning-7B achieved state-of-the-art performance across 8 diverse benchmarks, demonstrating advancements in both general and spatial reasoning.

For general reasoning, it secured an average score of 45.0, outperforming prior base-scale MLLMs like InternVL3-8B (41.4) and WeThink-VL-7B (44.3), with specific strengths in MathVista (75.0) and DynaMath (26.8).

In spatial reasoning, it scored 82.3 on CV-Bench (image-based) and 42.3 on VSI-Bench (video-based), establishing new SOTA records for inferring Room Size (55.4) and Relative Direction (47.3) in video-based tasks.
Takeaways: The two-stage training paradigm of Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) followed by Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) effectively enhances reasoning capabilities in MLLMs.
Explicitly synthesizing high-quality, logically coherent data, particularly for dynamic spatial interactions, is crucial for improving MLLM's spatial understanding.

Adaptive training strategies, including task-specific reward functions like Exponential Decay Numeric Matching (EDNM) and dynamic hyper-parameter adjustments, are necessary to unify and optimize diverse reasoning tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.08068.Title: Quantile Reward Policy Optimization: Alignment with Pointwise Regression and Exact Partition Functions
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.08068.Summary: Researchers at CLAIRE, EPFL, developed Quantile Reward Policy Optimization (QRPO), a new policy fitting method that allows large language models to be aligned directly with pointwise absolute rewards. This approach makes the intractable partition function analytically tractable, leading to strong performance in chat and coding tasks while exhibiting reduced length bias compared to previous methods.
Problem: Policy Improvement (PI) methods for LLM alignment (e.g., PPO, RLHF) can use pointwise absolute rewards but are computationally intensive and complex, requiring online sampling.

Policy Fitting (PF) methods (e.g., DPO) are simpler and more stable, but are limited to using relative reward signals (e.g., preference pairs) because their objective formulation relies on canceling out an intractable partition function.

This limitation prevents PF methods from directly utilizing powerful pointwise absolute reward signals from advanced reward models or verifiable metrics, often necessitating the use of more complex PI approaches.
Method: QRPO introduces a novel transformation that converts raw, pointwise absolute rewards into "quantile rewards," defined as the cumulative distribution function (CDF) value of the original reward under the reference policy.

This quantile reward, when sampled from the reference policy, is uniformly distributed, allowing the intractable partition function in the KL-regularized RL objective to become analytically tractable and a constant.
The simplified objective can then be optimized directly via a simple Mean Squared Error (MSE) regression loss, enabling efficient policy fitting using pointwise absolute rewards.
Results: QRPO consistently achieves top-tier performance on chat benchmarks (e.g., 0.2005 ArmoRM reward, 50.6% AlpacaEval 2 win rate with Llama 8B) and significantly outperforms baselines on a LeetCode coding task with a 32.7% pass rate.

The method demonstrates efficient scalability, with performance improving as more reference rewards are used for quantile estimation, and it achieves near-optimal results with very few reference rewards in offline settings.

QRPO exhibits significantly less length bias in generated responses compared to DPO and SimPO, attributed to its direct utilization of robust absolute reward models designed to counteract such biases.
Takeaways: The partition function in the KL-regularized RL objective can be re-expressed as the moment generating function of the reference reward distribution, highlighting the challenge of its unknown form.
By transforming original rewards into quantile rewards, the resulting distribution becomes uniform, regardless of the original reward distribution's complexity.

A uniform reward distribution yields an analytically tractable and constant partition function, fundamentally simplifying the policy fitting problem for absolute rewards into a direct regression task.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.07998.Title: PyVision: Agentic Vision with Dynamic Tooling
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.07998.Summary: The PyVision framework equips multimodal large language models with the ability to autonomously generate, execute, and refine Python code for visual reasoning tasks. This approach leads to consistent performance improvements across various benchmarks, including a 7.8% gain on fine-grained visual search with GPT-4.1 and a 31.1% increase on symbolic vision tasks with Claude-4.0-Sonnet.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle with novel or complex visual reasoning due to reliance on static, predefined toolsets.
Current MLLM agents lack the ability to dynamically generate custom computational tools, limiting their adaptability to diverse visual tasks.
Prior approaches lacked sufficient interpretability and verifiability for complex, compositional visual reasoning tasks.
Method: An interactive, multi-turn framework empowers MLLMs to dynamically generate and execute Python code for visual reasoning.
Python and its rich ecosystem of libraries (e.g., OpenCV, NumPy) serve as the exclusive primitive for tool creation, enabling dynamic composition of task-specific solutions.
The framework ensures robust multi-turn interaction through process isolation, cross-turn state persistence, and secure I/O for iterative refinement.
Results: PyVision-GPT-4.1 achieved performance increases of +1.8% on MathVista, +2.4% on MMMU, and +7.8% on V* benchmarks.
PyVision-Claude-4.0-Sonnet showed significant gains, including +4.8% on MathVista, +8.3% on Visual Puzzles, and +31.1% on VLMsAreBlind-mini.
Analysis of dynamically generated code revealed adaptive tool usage, with specific tool types predominantly invoked according to task demands and domain characteristics.
Takeaways: MLLMs can move beyond static tool usage to dynamically invent task-specific computational tools using a Python-based framework.
The framework provides enhanced interpretability and verifiability by allowing inspection of the AI's generated Python code and execution steps.
PyVision's dynamic tooling complements and amplifies the inherent strengths of its backend MLLMs, leading to varied performance boosts depending on the model's core capabilities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.07969.Title: Reinforcement Learning with Action Chunking
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.07969.Summary: Researchers at UC Berkeley developed Q-chunking, a method integrating action chunking into temporal difference (TD) reinforcement learning to enable unbiased n-step value backups and enhance online exploration. This approach significantly improved sample efficiency and performance on challenging long-horizon, sparse-reward robotic manipulation tasks compared to existing offline-to-online methods.
Problem: Reinforcement learning agents struggle with effective exploration and sample efficiency in complex, long-horizon tasks, especially with sparse rewards.
Existing offline-to-online RL methods often suffer from distributional shift and overly pessimistic policies during online fine-tuning.
Traditional n-step Temporal Difference (TD) learning introduces off-policy bias, making it unstable for accelerating value propagation from diverse data.
Method: Introduce Q-chunking, which redefines the Q-function and policy to operate on temporally extended action sequences (chunks) of 'h' actions.
Utilize this chunked Q-function to enable theoretically unbiased n-step value backups, accelerating value propagation without off-policy bias.
Employ behavior regularization, constraining the policy towards temporally coherent action sequences learned from offline data, to guide online exploration.
Results: Q-chunking methods achieved state-of-the-art online sample efficiency, significantly outperforming prior offline-to-online baselines on challenging long-horizon, sparse-reward robotic manipulation tasks.
The proposed approach consistently outperformed both 1-step TD and naive n-step return variants, demonstrating the stability and effectiveness of its unbiased n-step value estimation.
Empirical analysis confirmed that Q-chunking generates more temporally coherent action sequences, leading to more structured and diverse exploration compared to single-step baselines.
Takeaways: Learning a Q-function directly on action chunks enables unbiased n-step value propagation, resolving issues of off-policy bias in traditional multi-step TD learning.
Constraining policies to generate temporally coherent action sequences, derived from offline data, facilitates more effective and structured online exploration.
Action chunking offers a simple yet powerful form of temporal abstraction, potentially simplifying the development of multi-step behaviors compared to complex hierarchical methods.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.07101.Title: Small Batch Size Training for Language Models: When Vanilla SGD Works, and Why Gradient Accumulation Is Wasteful
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.07101.Summary: Researchers from NYU and Columbia demonstrated that small batch sizes, even down to one, can stably and effectively train large language models when Adam's beta2 parameter is properly scaled, revealing that gradient accumulation is often inefficient and vanilla SGD can be competitive. This approach enables memory-efficient full fine-tuning on resource-constrained hardware, challenging the conventional necessity of large batches for LLM training.
Problem: Conventional wisdom in LLM training suggests that large batch sizes are crucial for stable and efficient training.
Gradient accumulation is widely adopted to simulate large batch sizes, often assumed necessary despite its memory overheads.
Small batch sizes were generally considered unstable or underperforming for LLMs, frequently necessitating complex adaptive optimizers like Adam.
Method: Conducted extensive empirical studies on decoder-only transformer models ranging from 30M to 4B parameters across diverse datasets.
Performed exhaustive hyperparameter tuning, especially for Adam's decay parameters (β1 and β2), introducing a 'moment half-life' metric for principled scaling.
Compared the performance and memory footprint of various optimizers (SGD, Adam, Adafactor, Muon) across a wide spectrum of batch sizes, incorporating bfloat16 training with stochastic rounding.
Results: Small batch sizes, including batch size one, achieved performance on par with or superior to larger batch sizes when hyperparameters were correctly tuned.
Vanilla SGD, even without momentum, performed competitively with sophisticated adaptive optimizers like Adam for models up to 1.3 billion parameters when utilizing small batches.
Gradient accumulation was found to be generally unnecessary and memory-inefficient, with direct small batch training recommended instead.
Combining small batch sizes with memory-efficient optimizers like Adafactor enabled full fine-tuning with a memory footprint comparable to LoRA.
Takeaways: Small batch sizes exhibit significantly greater robustness to hyperparameter choices, offering a broader optimal performance region than large batches.
The optimal learning rate for small batches scales more slowly than the commonly assumed square-root rule.
Scaling Adam's β2 parameter by maintaining a constant 'token half-life' is critical for stabilizing small batch training, while β1 can often remain at its default value.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.06261.Title: Gemini 2.5: Pushing the Frontier with Advanced Reasoning, Multimodality, Long Context, and Next Generation Agentic Capabilities
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.06261.Summary: Google's Gemini 2.X model family substantially progresses AI capabilities by delivering state-of-the-art performance in advanced reasoning, coding, and multimodality, notably processing up to 3 hours of video and featuring a novel "Thinking" mechanism. Designed for next-generation agentic systems, the models underwent extensive safety evaluations, confirming no critical capability level risks.
Problem: Limitations in processing extremely long contexts and natively integrating diverse multimodal inputs (text, image, audio, video) in existing AI models.
The demand for AI systems capable of advanced, multi-step reasoning and autonomous agentic behaviors in complex, dynamic environments.
The challenge of delivering highly capable AI while maintaining practical efficiency and cost-effectiveness for widespread real-world deployment.
Method: Introduction of the Gemini 2.X model family, based on sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) transformers with native multimodal support for text, image, audio, and video inputs.
Development of a novel "Thinking" mechanism, allowing models to utilize additional inference-time compute through multiple forward passes for improved answer accuracy.
Leveraging Google's TPUv5p architecture and advanced training infrastructure (e.g., Slice-Granularity Elasticity, Split-Phase SDC Detection) for large-scale and robust model training.
Results: Gemini 2.5 Pro achieved state-of-the-art performance, with scores like 74.2% on LiveCodeBench (from 30.5%) and 88.0% on AIME 2025 (from 17.5%), and demonstrated processing of up to 3 hours of video.
The models exhibited advanced agentic capabilities, successfully completing complex tasks such as autonomously playing and completing Pokémon Blue in 406.5 hours.

Rigorous safety evaluations using the Frontier Safety Framework confirmed Gemini 2.5 Pro did not reach Critical Capability Levels for severe risks, while also showing improved helpfulness and reduced memorization.
Takeaways: The combination of sparse Mixture-of-Experts architecture and enhanced large-scale training stability is key to achieving substantial performance gains in frontier models.
A novel "Thinking" mechanism, employing additional inference-time compute, demonstrably improves reasoning accuracy and problem-solving, offering a direct pathway to more capable AI agents.
Comprehensive, native multimodal pre-training and advanced post-training techniques enable deep understanding across extended contexts, including 3-hour long videos and complex code repositories.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.06203.Title: A Survey on Latent Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.06203.Summary: This comprehensive survey from a large multi-institutional collaboration examines "Latent Reasoning" in Large Language Models, an emerging paradigm that performs multi-step inference entirely within the model's high-bandwidth continuous hidden states to overcome the limitations of natural language-based explicit reasoning. It highlights the significant bandwidth advantage of latent representations (approximately 2700x higher) and provides a unified taxonomy of current methodologies.
Problem: Large Language Models primarily rely on explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, which verbalizes intermediate steps in natural language.
This reliance on discrete tokens limits the model's expressive bandwidth compared to its continuous hidden states, which are significantly richer.
Forcing LLMs to verbalize every reasoning step introduces computational redundancy, as much of their complex processing occurs internally within hidden states.
Method: Defines and systematically surveys "Latent Reasoning" or "Latent Chain-of-Thought (Latent CoT)" as a paradigm for multi-step inference within an LLM's continuous hidden state.

Presents a comprehensive taxonomy that categorizes existing latent reasoning approaches based on how information is propagated, including vertical and horizontal recurrence, mechanistic interpretability, and infinite-depth reasoning.
Unifies disparate research efforts under a coherent conceptual framework to foster a clearer understanding of latent reasoning and chart future research directions.
Results: Latent representations offer an approximately 2700 times higher bandwidth compared to explicit tokens, enabling richer internal expressivity.

The survey consolidates latent reasoning into two main paradigms: Vertical Recurrence (e.g., architectural loops like Universal Transformer, or training-induced recurrence like Coconut) and Horizontal Recurrence (e.g., Linear-State models like Mamba-2, or Gradient-State models like TTT).

Analysis of mechanistic interpretability shows that LLM layers exhibit specialized roles, with intermediate layers central to latent Chain-of-Thought, and highlights advanced paradigms for infinite-depth reasoning through spatial (text diffusion) and temporal (optimization-based) approaches.
Takeaways: Latent reasoning, operating within high-bandwidth continuous hidden states, offers a significant improvement over the low-bandwidth discrete tokens used in explicit reasoning.
Latent reasoning methodologies can be categorized into vertical recurrence (iterative refinement of activations) and horizontal recurrence (evolution of hidden states across sequences).
Mechanistic interpretability reveals that different LLM layers specialize in distinct aspects of latent reasoning, with intermediate layers performing core computational steps.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.06187.Title: The Delta Learning Hypothesis: Preference Tuning on Weak Data can Yield Strong Gains
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.06187.Summary: Proposes the delta learning hypothesis, demonstrating that preference tuning on pairs of individually weak model outputs, where one is marginally better than the other, can lead to performance comparable to models trained with expensive, strong supervision. This approach significantly reduces the cost and complexity of post-training language models, matching the performance of a Tulu 3 model without relying on frontier LLM judges like GPT-4o.
Problem: The high cost and scarcity of strong supervision (e.g., human annotations, frontier LLM distillation) limit the development of more capable and accessible large language models (LLMs).
Current LLM alignment methods often rely on training data quality that exceeds or matches the model's target capability, creating a bottleneck for further improvement.
Existing approaches struggle to enable models to surpass the quality of their training data, especially when strong supervision is unavailable.
Method: Proposes the "delta learning hypothesis," asserting that preference tuning can leverage the relative quality difference between paired responses, even if both are individually weak.

Develops a "simple recipe" for preference data generation by using a smaller LLM to generate chosen responses and an even smaller one for rejected responses, eliminating reliance on strong LLM judges (e.g., GPT-4o).
Applies Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to tune models on these "weak-over-weaker" preference pairs, demonstrating that the directional signal is sufficient for learning.
Results: A "simple recipe" using weak model outputs for preference data generation matched the performance of the Tulu 3 model on an 11-benchmark suite, which originally relied on expensive, strong LLM judges (GPT-4o).

Controlled experiments demonstrated that preference tuning on a "delta" can cause a model to extrapolate far beyond the absolute quality of chosen responses, such as increasing generated bold sections from a baseline of 5.9 to 81.1.

DPO tuning a model to prefer its own outputs over those of a weaker sibling model consistently yielded small but positive gains across various semantic benchmarks, whereas supervised finetuning on the same (weak) chosen responses degraded performance.
Takeaways: Preference tuning, unlike supervised finetuning, can effectively learn from the relative quality difference (delta) between paired responses, even when the chosen response's absolute quality is low or below the model's current capability.
The magnitude of the quality delta between chosen and rejected responses is a strong predictor of preference tuning performance, with gains saturating beyond a certain delta threshold.
A theoretical analysis confirms that even with individually suboptimal teachers, the difference in their signals provides a directionally correct learning signal, enabling student model improvement.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.05920.Title: High-Resolution Visual Reasoning via Multi-Turn Grounding-Based Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.05920.Summary: This paper introduces Multi-turn Grounding-based Policy Optimization (MGPO), a reinforcement learning framework that allows Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) to perform high-resolution visual reasoning by iteratively focusing on key image regions. The approach enables LMMs to implicitly learn visual grounding capabilities from a simple binary reward, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy on challenging high-resolution benchmarks like V* Bench and MME-Realworld while surpassing large commercial models.
Problem: State-of-the-art Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) struggle with high-resolution images due to the massive number of visual tokens generated, leading to computational inefficiency and a 'needle-in-a-haystack' problem.
LMMs face maximum pixel constraints, often requiring aggressive resizing of high-resolution images, which results in the loss of critical fine-grained details necessary for many tasks.
Integrating visual grounding into LMMs typically relies on supervised fine-tuning (SFT) which demands costly and scarce explicit bounding box annotations.
Method: The paper proposes Multi-turn Grounding-based Policy Optimization (MGPO), an end-to-end reinforcement learning framework that extends Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to a multi-turn conversational setting.

MGPO enables iterative visual search by having the LMM generate grounding coordinates in one turn, which are then used to crop a high-resolution sub-image from the original input for the subsequent turn.

A simple binary reward function (1 for correct final answer, 0 for incorrect) is used to optimize the LMM's policy across all intermediate grounding and reasoning steps, eliminating the need for explicit grounding annotations.
Results: Multi-turn Grounding-based Policy Optimization (MGPO) achieved 76.4% accuracy on the out-of-distribution V* Bench, a 5.2% absolute improvement over the GRPO baseline (71.2%), and 60.5% accuracy on MME-Realworld, a 5.4% gain over GRPO (55.1%).
The MGPO post-trained model, based on a 7B Qwen2.5-VL, surpassed OpenAI’s o1 (69.7%) and GPT-4o (73.9%) models on the out-of-distribution V* Bench.

During RL training, MGPO showed a steady increase in valid grounding coordinate generation, and 65.2% of its generated grounding sub-images from the test set were sufficient to directly answer the question, demonstrating robust emergent grounding ability.
Takeaways: Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) can develop robust visual grounding capabilities through reinforcement learning, leveraging only a binary reward signal from the final answer's correctness, without needing explicit grounding annotations.
Iteratively focusing on high-resolution sub-regions, mimicking human foveal vision, significantly improves an LMM's performance on fine-grained visual reasoning tasks.

A fixed multi-turn dialogue template can effectively guide an LMM to perform grounding actions in an RL setup, mitigating the 'cold start' problem without requiring extensive pre-training on grounding-annotated data.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.05707.Title: Agentic-R1: Distilled Dual-Strategy Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.05707.Summary: Researchers at Carnegie Mellon University's LTI developed Agentic-R1, a language model trained with the DualDistill framework to adaptively combine long chain-of-thought and tool-augmented reasoning. The model achieved 65.3% accuracy on DeepMath-L and 52.0% on Combinatorics300, demonstrating improved performance over specialized baselines on complex mathematical tasks.
Problem: Long Chain-of-Thought (CoT) models struggle with numerical accuracy and efficiency for computations, often "overthinking" when exact results are needed.
Tool-augmented agentic models excel at precise computation but falter on abstract, complex logical reasoning problems without clear tool interfaces.
Combining these complementary strengths often relies on computationally expensive and unstable reinforcement learning or heuristic methods.
Method: The DualDistill framework distills complementary reasoning strategies from two specialized teacher models (an Agentic Teacher and a Reasoning Teacher) into a unified student model.
A Trajectory Composition process generates solutions for each problem from both teachers sequentially and composes informative training trajectories, including explicit strategy transition segments.

A Self-Distillation phase refines the student's strategy selection by generating its own candidate trajectories, evaluating them, and learning from both successful and corrected unsuccessful attempts with teacher feedback.
Results: Agentic-R1-SD achieved 65.3% accuracy on DeepMath-L and 52.0% on Combinatorics300, outperforming specialized long-CoT and tool-augmented baselines by significant margins (e.g., 9.0% and 7.5% respectively over DeepSeek-R1-Distill-7B).

The model demonstrated adaptive tool usage, invoking code tools in 79.2% of Combinatorics300 problems (computation-heavy) but only 52.0% in simpler AMC problems, reflecting an implicit understanding of task demands.
Ablation studies confirmed that the proposed trajectory composition strategy is crucial for teaching strategy adaptation, consistently outperforming non-compositional training across benchmarks.
Takeaways: A distillation framework can effectively unify heterogeneous reasoning strategies, such as text-based reasoning and tool-augmented execution, into a single student model without relying on reinforcement learning.
The model learns adaptive strategy selection, dynamically choosing between complex textual reasoning and precise tool-assisted computation based on problem characteristics.
The approach enables learning robust agentic behaviors even from imperfect teacher models, with the student model surpassing the agentic teacher's performance on certain tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.05258.Title: Spatio-Temporal LLM: Reasoning about Environments and Actions
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.05258.Summary: Researchers at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign developed the Reasoning about Environments and Actions (REA) dataset and two Spatio-Temporal LLM (STLLM) baselines to enable large language models to jointly understand 3D environments and egocentric video actions. The STLLM models achieved up to 46.50% overall accuracy on REA, outperforming existing multimodal LLMs on complex spatio-temporal reasoning tasks.
Problem: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) struggle with jointly understanding 3D environments (point clouds) and dynamic egocentric video actions.
Existing MLLMs often simplify videos as sequences of independent frames or neglect deeper temporal dynamics, failing to integrate global spatial context with local actions.
A comprehensive benchmark dataset specifically designed for evaluating this joint spatio-temporal reasoning capability was lacking.
Method: A novel dataset, Reasoning about Environments and Actions (REA), was created with 24,371 question-answer pairs requiring joint understanding of 3D point clouds and egocentric video clips, derived from EPIC-KITCHENS, VISOR, and EPIC-FIELDS.

Two baseline Spatio-Temporal LLM (STLLM) architectures were proposed: STLLM-3D, which directly concatenates 3D features with image and text embeddings, and STLLM-Aligner, which uses a cross-modal alignment module to create compact spatial representations.

The REA dataset includes five distinct tasks: Relative Direction, Relative Distance, Find My Item, Furniture Affordance Prediction, and Action Planning, to probe various aspects of spatio-temporal reasoning.
Results: Existing MLLMs achieved low overall LLM-Judge accuracies on the REA dataset, ranging from 23.85% to 31.46% (ChatGPT-4o judge) and 35.74% to 39.50% (Gemini 2.0 Flash judge).

The proposed STLLM baselines significantly outperformed finetuned existing models on REA, with STLLM-Aligner achieving the highest overall accuracy of 41.89% (ChatGPT-4o) and 46.50% (Gemini 2.0 Flash).

In zero-shot cross-dataset evaluation on SQA3D, STLLM baselines and models finetuned on REA showed consistent improvements over vanilla counterparts, demonstrating generalization capabilities for 3D reasoning.
Takeaways: Off-the-shelf multimodal LLMs demonstrate limited capabilities in spatio-temporal reasoning, confirming that current models struggle to effectively integrate 3D environmental context with egocentric actions.

Specialized architectural designs that explicitly integrate 3D information are crucial for improving spatio-temporal understanding in MLLMs, as evidenced by the superior performance of STLLM baselines.
The REA dataset effectively serves as a benchmark for training and evaluating models on complex spatio-temporal prompts, with finetuning on REA showing transferability to other 3D reasoning tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.05255.Title: Open Vision Reasoner: Transferring Linguistic Cognitive Behavior for Visual Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.05255.Summary: Researchers developed Open-Vision-Reasoner (OVR), an MLLM that transfers linguistic cognitive behaviors to the visual domain, achieving state-of-the-art results on visual reasoning benchmarks such as 51.8% on MathVision and 54.6% on MathVerse for 7B models. This approach clarifies how cognitive patterns emerge and scale in multimodal contexts, using a two-stage training process.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) often lack the advanced reasoning capabilities (e.g., backtracking, self-verification) seen in Large Language Models (LLMs).
Previous MLLM reinforcement learning efforts predominantly used RLHF, which is susceptible to 'reward hacking,' unlike the more robust Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Reward (RLVR) paradigm.
A systematic understanding of how linguistic cognitive behaviors from LLMs transfer to MLLMs for complex visual reasoning tasks was missing.
Method: A two-stage training paradigm was developed using Qwen2.5-VL-7B, starting with a 'linguistic cold start' fine-tuning on over 2 million language-only reasoning examples.
The linguistic cold start was followed by large-scale multimodal Reinforcement Learning (RL) using the Open-Reasoner-Zero framework on over 0.3 million mixed-modality examples.
A minimalist, rule-based binary reward function was employed during RL, providing a clear and unhackable signal for correct answers, aligning with the RLVR paradigm.
Results: OVR-7B achieved state-of-the-art visual reasoning among 7B models, scoring 51.8% on MathVision, 54.6% on MathVerse, and 33.5% on DynaMath, demonstrating successful cross-modal transfer.
The model exhibited enhanced language reasoning, outperforming other 7B open-source models by over 10% on challenging math reasoning tasks like AIME 2024 (63.5%) and AIME 2025 (52.1%).

Linguistic cold-start initially impaired visual perception but long-term multimodal RL effectively recovered and enhanced perceptual performance, while RL alone showed limitations for pure perceptual tasks.
Takeaways: Visual-specific cognitive behaviors, such as visual reflection, emerge remarkably early in the linguistic cold-start phase due to 'mental imagery' encoded in linguistic patterns.

The linguistic cold-start phase broadly familiarizes the model with diverse cognitive behaviors, while large-scale multimodal RL critically discerns and strategically amplifies only the most effective ones for generalization.

The transfer of cognitive behaviors is strategic, with behaviors like backtracking showing significant growth in transfer rate (from 2.5% to 17.3%) due to their higher utility in complex visual reasoning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.04590.Title: VLM2Vec-V2: Advancing Multimodal Embedding for Videos, Images, and Visual Documents
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.04590.Summary: VLM2Vec-V2, developed by researchers from Salesforce Research and collaborating universities, introduces a unified multimodal embedding model capable of processing and aligning videos, images, and visual documents with text. The model achieves the highest overall score of 58.0 on the newly introduced MMEB-V2 benchmark, which expands evaluation to 78 tasks across these diverse visual modalities.
Problem: Existing state-of-the-art multimodal embedding models predominantly focus on natural images and text, limiting their applicability to real-world scenarios involving diverse visual content.
There is a lack of unified support for dynamic content like videos and structured visual forms such as documents (PDFs, slides) within a single multimodal embedding framework.
A comprehensive and standardized benchmark was missing to effectively evaluate embedding models across images, videos, and visual documents.
Method: The paper introduces VLM2Vec-V2, a unified multimodal embedding model trained using an instruction-guided contrastive learning approach on the Qwen2-VL backbone.
A new comprehensive benchmark, MMEB-V2, is developed with 9 meta-tasks and 78 specific tasks to evaluate multimodal embeddings across text, images, videos, and visual documents.
Sophisticated data sampling strategies, including on-the-fly batch mixing and interleaved sub-batching, are employed during multi-task training to handle heterogeneous data sources.
Results: VLM2Vec-V2 achieves the highest overall average score of 58.0 across all 78 datasets in the MMEB-V2 benchmark, outperforming existing generalist models like GME and previous VLM2Vec versions.

It demonstrates strong performance on image tasks (average 64.9), competitive results on video tasks (average 34.9), and significantly improved performance on visual document retrieval (65.4) compared to other generalist VLMs.

Ablation studies confirm that training with all three modalities (images, videos, visual documents) consistently leads to the best overall performance and that increased training steps further improve results.
Takeaways: Comprehensive multi-modal training across images, videos, and visual documents is crucial for achieving broad generalization in embedding models.
Instruction-guided contrastive learning with a robust Vision-Language Model backbone (Qwen2-VL) enables effective alignment of diverse visual and textual data into a unified embedding space.
Data sampling strategies like interleaved sub-batching and specific LoRA ranks are important for optimizing performance across heterogeneous modalities during training.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.04511.Title: FA: Forced Prompt Learning of Vision-Language Models for Out-of-Distribution Detection
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.04511.Summary: The paper introduces the "Forced prompt leArning" (FA) framework, a new approach for Out-of-Distribution (OOD) detection using Vision-Language Models (VLMs) like CLIP. It improves OOD detection by deeply enriching the model's understanding of in-distribution (ID) data through a novel forced prompt learning strategy, achieving state-of-the-art performance across various benchmarks, with up to a 16.09% increase in average AUROC and a 38.7% reduction in average FPR95 on challenging datasets in few-shot settings.
Problem: Existing OOD detection methods, particularly those based on Vision-Language Models (VLMs), frequently rely on resource-intensive external OOD datasets or struggle with generalizing OOD-related knowledge.
Current VLM-based OOD detection approaches often focus on explicitly acquiring 'OOD-related knowledge,' which is limited in its ability to generalize to diverse, unseen OOD data.

Many traditional and VLM-based OOD methods face challenges such as high computational costs, reliance on extensive labeled in-distribution (ID) datasets, or difficulties in effectively generalizing, especially in few-shot learning scenarios.
Method: Introduces "Forced prompt leArning" (FA), a CLIP-based framework that utilizes both frozen "original prompts" and learnable "forced prompts" for each in-distribution (ID) class to enhance OOD detection.

Employs a novel Forced Cross-Entropy (FCE) loss function (
L
FCE−K
) to compel the learnable forced prompts to capture richer, more diversified, and salient semantic descriptions of ID classes.
Maintains parameter efficiency comparable to existing prompt learning methods like CoOp by freezing original prompts and sharing learnable context vectors across classes for the forced prompts.
Results: Achieves state-of-the-art OOD detection performance across conventional and challenging benchmarks (e.g., ImageNet-1k, OpenImage-O, NINCO), consistently outperforming baselines, particularly in few-shot settings.
In the 1-shot setting, FA_GL reduced average FPR95 from 31.62% to 27.81% and improved average AUROC from 92.01% to 93.26% on ImageNet-1k OOD benchmarks.

Demonstrates robustness and insensitivity to the forced coefficient
K, and maintains in-distribution classification accuracy while outperforming baselines on diverse ID datasets, including challenging low-resolution ones like EuroSAT, with improvements of up to 16.09% in average AUROC.
Takeaways: Superior OOD detection can be achieved by thoroughly exploiting and enriching in-distribution (ID) knowledge, rather than explicitly attempting to acquire OOD-related knowledge.
Compelling Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to learn more discriminative and detailed features for ID classes implicitly enhances the separation between ID and OOD samples in the embedding space.

The use of a 'forced coefficient' within the FCE loss function prompts the learnable prompt to significantly surpass the generic representation provided by a stable, frozen original prompt, thereby deepening ID understanding.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.04380.Title: Transferring Visual Explainability of Self-Explaining Models through Task Arithmetic
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.04380.Summary: Researchers at STAIR Lab and ZOZO Research developed a method using task arithmetic to transfer visual explainability to self-explaining models without requiring target domain explanation data. The approach achieves explanation quality comparable to Kernel SHAP with 150 times fewer inferences, while maintaining classification accuracy at 90% of a prediction-only baseline model.
Problem: Developing and deploying visual explainability in AI systems faces high computational and labeling costs.
Training self-explaining models, while efficient at inference, demands expensive ground-truth explanation data or numerous model passes.
Post-hoc explanation methods are computationally intensive during inference, limiting their use in real-time or resource-constrained applications.
Method: The method uses task arithmetic to algebraically extract and transfer an 'explainability vector' from a source self-explaining model to a target domain model.
It extends vision-language pretrained models (e.g., CLIP ViT-B/32) to generate both predictions and patch-level attributions in a single forward pass.

Target model parameters are constructed by combining a target-specific classification task vector with the source-learned explainability vector, bypassing the need for explanation data in the target domain.
Results: The transferred models maintained high classification accuracy (average 0.876) close to target-finetuned prediction-only models (0.890), while significantly improving explanation quality (e.g., E-RMSE decreased from 1.599 to 0.943).
Explanation generation achieved IoU@10 scores comparable to Kernel SHAP with approximately 150 times fewer model inferences, demonstrating a substantial reduction in computational cost.
An explainability vector learned from ImageNet+X proved robust, improving explanation quality across 9 out of 10 diverse target datasets.
Takeaways: An 'explainability vector' can be mathematically isolated and transferred between models using task arithmetic, representing specific knowledge for explanation generation.
This explainability knowledge can be effectively transferred to models in a target domain that were only trained for prediction, without requiring ground-truth explanations for the target tasks.
The similarity between classification-only task vectors from source and target domains can moderately predict the success of explainability transfer.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.03657.Title: Dynamic Multimodal Prototype Learning in Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.03657.Summary: Researchers from USTC, NTU, and collaborators developed ProtoMM, a training-free framework that constructs and dynamically updates multimodal prototypes by integrating textual descriptions with visual knowledge from streaming test data. This method improved average zero-shot classification accuracy by 0.93% on 11 cross-domain datasets using CLIP-RN50 and achieved 1.08% higher accuracy on OOD benchmarks with CLIP-ViT-B/16 compared to previous state-of-the-art baselines.
Problem: Textual prototypes in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) suffer from semantic ambiguity, leading to confusion between visually distinct classes with similar textual names (e.g., 'sword lily' vs. 'blackberry lily').
Existing VLM test-time adaptation methods primarily focus on textual prompt refinement and largely overlook crucial visual information present in streaming test images.
VLMs struggle to dynamically and continuously adapt to evolving, streaming test data distributions without expensive, gradient-based re-training or complex updates.
Method: ProtoMM constructs multimodal prototypes by combining LLM-enhanced textual descriptions with dynamically updated visual 'particles' extracted from the test stream.

It re-conceptualizes images and prototypes as discrete distributions in the CLIP embedding space, assigning importance weights to individual visual augmentations and prototype components via Optimal Transport.

Visual 'particles' within the multimodal prototypes are dynamically updated through a weighted moving average of high-confidence visual features from incoming test samples, enabling continuous, training-free adaptation.
Results: ProtoMM achieved an average zero-shot classification accuracy of 63.10% across 11 cross-domain datasets with a CLIP-RN50 backbone, representing a 0.93% improvement over the previous best training-free method, AWT.
The method demonstrated robust generalization to out-of-distribution data, achieving an OOD average accuracy of 65.69% with a CLIP-ViT-B/16 backbone, surpassing the training-based DPE by 1.03%.

Ablation studies confirmed the critical contributions of both the distributed feature construction and the dynamic multimodal prototype learning modules, showing incremental performance gains with each component.
Takeaways: Augmenting textual prototypes with dynamically acquired visual knowledge is crucial for resolving semantic ambiguities and significantly enhancing VLM generalization to both in-distribution and out-of-distribution data.

Optimal Transport provides an effective and interpretable mechanism for quantifying the importance of diverse visual features and prototype components, guiding the intelligent integration of multimodal information.

A training-free framework for dynamic multimodal prototype learning offers an efficient and robust approach for VLMs to continuously adapt and improve their zero-shot classification performance during inference.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.03458.Title: Helping CLIP See Both the Forest and the Trees: A Decomposition and Description Approach
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.03458.Summary: Researchers from Tianjin University and collaborators developed 'Decomposition and Description' (D&D), a method to enhance Vision-Language Models like CLIP by integrating fine-grained local visual semantics with detailed textual descriptions. D&D achieves an average top-1 accuracy improvement of 1.85% in zero-shot classification and up to 1.95% in test-time adaptation over strong baselines.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) like CLIP exhibit a strong inherent bias towards global image patterns, hindering their effective processing of fine-grained local semantics.
A widely held assumption that VLMs inherently recognize local visual details when provided with descriptive text was found to be flawed.
Existing VLM adaptation strategies struggle to effectively integrate both global image patterns and fine-grained local attributes for improved understanding.
Method: Introduces "Decomposition and Description" (D&D), a plug-and-play approach that decomposes images into multiple stochastic local regions using multi-crop augmentation.
Utilizes Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate sets of fine-grained textual descriptors for each candidate class.
Employs Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) to compute set-level similarity between the set of local visual features and the set of textual descriptors, finding optimal latent correspondences.
Results: Achieved an average top-1 accuracy of 60.62% in zero-shot classification across 11 datasets, representing a 1.85% improvement over Zero-Shot CLIP and 1.17% over CALIP.
Improved few-shot learning performance, reaching an average top-1 accuracy of 71.46% (16-shot setting) when integrated with Tip-Adapter, surpassing original Tip-Adapter by 1.14%.

Attained state-of-the-art test-time adaptation, outperforming the strongest baseline TDA by 1.95% (69.48% vs. 67.53% average accuracy with ViT-B/16 backbone) across cross-domain benchmarks, with a notable +27.87% on Aircraft.
Takeaways: Empirical evidence disproves the common assumption that VLMs inherently process fine-grained local details, revealing a fundamental bias towards global semantics.
Explicitly decomposing visual inputs into local regions and aligning them with detailed textual descriptions via EMD effectively activates CLIP's latent capacity for localized feature analysis.
The D&D method is highly adaptable and can be integrated into existing VLM adaptation paradigms (zero-shot, few-shot, test-time adaptation) without architectural modifications.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.03302.Title: Leveraging Out-of-Distribution Unlabeled Images: Semi-Supervised Semantic Segmentation with an Open-Vocabulary Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.03302.Summary: A new framework, SemiOVS, allows semi-supervised semantic segmentation models to utilize abundant out-of-distribution unlabeled images by employing an open-vocabulary model for robust pseudo-label generation. The approach achieved state-of-the-art performance on Pascal VOC, with up to a 12.6% mIoU improvement over FixMatch in low-label settings, and consistently enhanced results on Pascal Context.
Problem: Semantic segmentation requires extensive pixel-level annotations, which are costly and time-consuming to acquire.

Current semi-supervised semantic segmentation (SSSS) approaches mainly utilize unlabeled data assumed to be in-distribution, limiting their applicability to real-world scenarios with diverse data sources.
Naively incorporating abundant out-of-distribution (OOD) unlabeled images can lead to noisy pseudo-labels, misguiding model training and degrading performance due to distribution shifts.
Method: A framework called SemiOVS is introduced, integrating a standard semi-supervised segmentation model with a pretrained open-vocabulary segmentation (OVS) model.
The OVS model is strategically deployed to generate pseudo-labels for unlabeled out-of-distribution (OOD) images, leveraging its strong generalization capabilities.
OVS pseudo-label generation is optimized with an extended text prompt set (including potential OOD classes) and a refinement process to align output with the target label space.
Results: SemiOVS established new state-of-the-art performance on Pascal VOC, demonstrating a 12.6% mIoU improvement over FixMatch and a 3.0 mIoU gain over SemiVL in low-label settings (e.g., 92 labeled images).

The framework consistently delivered substantial performance enhancements on the more complex Pascal Context dataset, showing gains of 6.6% to 10.2% in the 1/32 protocol, and achieved SOTA on Pascal VOC Blended and Priority protocols.

Ablation studies confirmed that leveraging an OVS model for OOD pseudo-labeling consistently improved performance across all label settings, contrasting with the detrimental effects of directly using standard semi-supervised models for OOD data.
Takeaways: Abundant out-of-distribution (OOD) unlabeled images, often neglected, can significantly improve semi-supervised semantic segmentation when effectively utilized.
Open-vocabulary segmentation (OVS) models possess the generalization capacity to generate robust and accurate pseudo-labels for OOD images, overcoming limitations of standard segmentation models.
Optimizing OVS pseudo-label generation through extended text prompts and label space refinement is critical for successfully incorporating OOD data into semi-supervised learning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.02978.Title: Ascending the Infinite Ladder: Benchmarking Spatial Deformation Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.02978.Summary: This research introduces Inf-Bench, the first comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate Vision-Language Models' capabilities in spatial deformation reasoning across 2D, 2.5D, and 3D contexts. The study reveals that current VLMs exhibit significant limitations in understanding and executing multi-step spatial transformations, particularly in three dimensions, where their performance lags far behind human capabilities.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language Model (VLM) benchmarks primarily assess static spatial relationships, navigation, or general scene understanding, largely overlooking complex spatial deformation reasoning.
A critical gap exists in evaluating how VLMs understand, predict, and execute dynamic transformations that alter an object's intrinsic form and topological properties.
Traditional static benchmarks quickly become obsolete as VLMs rapidly improve, failing to continuously challenge and differentiate model capabilities over time.
Method: Introduces Inf-Bench, a novel benchmark evaluating spatial deformation reasoning across 2D, 2.5D (layered 2D), and 3D (Rubik's Cube) tasks, assessing both forward (predicting outcome) and inverse (inferring operations) reasoning.
Develops an automated shape generation engine to produce an unlimited supply of unique problem pairs, ensuring data quality, diversity, and preventing data leakage.

Proposes an 'Infinite Ladder Competition' framework that dynamically adjusts task difficulty based on model performance (number of deformation steps), enabling continuous assessment and preventing performance saturation.
Results: Human evaluators consistently and significantly outperform all 18 tested VLMs across all spatial dimensions (2D, 2.5D, 3D) and reasoning types, with the largest gap in 3D tasks.

Models achieve competitive performance in 2D and 2.5D deformation but show severe limitations in 3D, with most models failing even basic single-step deformations, though select models like OpenAI O3/O4-mini and Gemini-2.5-pro show limited ability.

Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) significantly boosts reasoning depth in 2D and 2.5D tasks, but 3D forward reasoning performance remains limited (rarely exceeding five steps), and general reasoning enhancement methods offer only marginal improvements.
Takeaways: Vision-language models exhibit two main reasoning strategies: 'direct pairing' and 'step-by-step reasoning execution', with stronger models favoring the latter.
Perceptual encoding is a significant bottleneck; providing pre-encoded textual input substantially improves VLM performance in 2D/2.5D spatial deformation tasks.
Current VLMs fundamentally struggle with 3D spatial deformation reasoning due to complex coupled shape states and cumulative errors, indicating a need for new architectural approaches.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.02199.Title: Latent Chain-of-Thought? Decoding the Depth-Recurrent Transformer
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.02199.Summary: A study investigated whether depth-recurrent Transformers, exemplified by Huginn-3.5B, perform structured "latent chain-of-thought" reasoning, finding limited evidence for such a mechanism. The research revealed inconsistencies in interpretability tool behavior across the model's distinct architectural blocks and showed that increased recurrence depth yields only marginal performance improvements compared to explicit Chain-of-Thought prompting.
Problem: Explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, while effective for complex reasoning in LLMs, introduces verbosity and slows inference, limiting real-world application.

The nature of "latent reasoning" in recurrent architectures, designed to enhance internal processing, remains ambiguous; it's unclear if performance gains stem from genuine structured reasoning or merely iterative computation.
Existing interpretability techniques struggle to consistently explain the internal workings of complex, novel LLM architectures, leaving their internal reasoning mechanisms as a black box.
Method: Employs a systematic probing approach targeting Huginn-3.5B, a depth-recurrent Transformer, focusing on arithmetic tasks where explicit Chain-of-Thought is suppressed.

Utilizes and adapts interpretability techniques, including the standard Logit Lens and a novel "Coda Lens" specific to Huginn's architecture, to decode and analyze hidden states across unrolled recurrent layers.
Traces the rank trajectories of intermediate and final result tokens within arithmetic problems and benchmarks model accuracy on GSM8K with varying recurrence depths against explicit CoT performance.
Results: Huginn's internal representations showed sharp discontinuities and periodic oscillations in decoded token rank trajectories, with interpretability varying significantly by layer and probing method.

Analysis of token rank trajectories offered limited evidence for structured latent Chain-of-Thought, as final answers converged quickly, and no clear "phase separation" for intermediate reasoning steps was observed.

On the GSM8K benchmark, increasing recurrence depth yielded only marginal accuracy gains (e.g., from 3.11% to 4.93%) when explicit CoT was suppressed, falling substantially short of performance achieved with explicit CoT (24.87%).
Takeaways: Interpretability methods must be carefully adapted for complex, non-standard Transformer architectures, as tools like Logit Lens can show inconsistent behavior across different recurrent blocks.
The specific design of recurrent blocks can lead to distinct encoding patterns, with modules like Huginn's R4 block playing a unique dual role in processing and output, requiring tailored probing.

Simply increasing computational depth through recurrence does not automatically induce structured, interpretable latent Chain-of-Thought reasoning that rivals the efficacy of explicit, language-based CoT.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.02092.Title: Energy-Based Transformers are Scalable Learners and Thinkers
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.02092.Summary: This paper introduces Energy-Based Transformers (EBTs), a new class of models that enable scalable System 2 thinking through unsupervised learning by reframing prediction as an optimization process over a learned energy function. EBTs demonstrate superior scaling rates compared to standard Transformers in language and video, improve performance by up to 29% with increased inference-time computation, and achieve better generalization on out-of-distribution data across diverse modalities.
Problem: Current Transformer-based models and LLMs excel at 'System 1 thinking' (fast pattern recognition) but struggle with 'System 2 thinking' (slow, deliberate reasoning, complex math, OOD data).
Existing System 2 approaches are often modality/problem-specific, require additional supervision (e.g., RL, human feedback), or lack dynamic computation allocation.
Traditional EBMs have faced issues with scalability, stability, and long training times, preventing their use in foundation models.
Method: Develop Energy-Based Transformers (EBTs) that combine the scalability of Transformers with the verification capabilities of Energy-Based Models (EBMs).
Implement prediction as an iterative gradient descent optimization on a learned energy function, allowing for dynamic computation per prediction and explicit uncertainty modeling.

Introduce energy landscape regularization techniques (e.g., replay buffer, Langevin Dynamics, varying optimization paths) and optimize training for second-order derivatives to ensure scalable and stable EBM learning.
Results: Energy-Based Transformers (EBTs) show up to a 35% higher scaling rate with respect to data than Transformer++ on autoregressive language modeling, indicating improved data efficiency.

EBTs improve language modeling performance by up to 29% and significantly outperform Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) in image denoising (99% fewer forward passes) and representation learning (10x higher ImageNet-1k accuracy) by leveraging inference-time 'thinking'.
EBTs exhibit greater performance improvements on out-of-distribution data (e.g., in language tasks and image denoising), demonstrating enhanced generalization capabilities.
Takeaways: Reframing prediction as an iterative optimization process over a learned energy function allows models to exhibit System 2 thinking facets: dynamic computation allocation, uncertainty modeling, and intrinsic prediction verification.
Energy-Based Models (EBMs) can be scaled using Transformer architectures and novel regularization techniques, overcoming historical scalability and stability challenges.
The ability to 'think longer' and self-verify through energy minimization leads to improved generalization, particularly on out-of-distribution data.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.01955.Title: How Well Does GPT-4o Understand Vision? Evaluating Multimodal Foundation Models on Standard Computer Vision Tasks
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.01955.Summary: EPFL researchers assessed the visual comprehension of Multimodal Foundation Models (MFMs) like GPT-4o across standard computer vision tasks using a novel "prompt chaining" framework. Their evaluation revealed that MFMs, despite being strong generalists, fall short of specialist vision models, exhibiting particular weaknesses in geometric understanding while performing better on semantic tasks; GPT-4o consistently outperformed other non-reasoning MFMs.
Problem: Lack of comprehensive quantitative evaluation for Multimodal Foundation Models (MFMs) on detailed, pixel-level computer vision tasks.
Incompatibility of text-output MFMs with traditional vision tasks requiring dense pixel predictions (e.g., masks, depth maps).
Proprietary nature of leading MFMs (API-only access) prevents direct architectural modification or fine-tuning for standard vision benchmarks.
Method: Developed a "prompt chaining" framework that translates complex vision tasks into multiple simpler, text-promptable sub-tasks for MFMs.

Implemented specific prompt chaining strategies for tasks like object detection (recursive zooming), semantic segmentation (superpixel classification with multi-scale pyramids), and depth/surface normal prediction (pairwise relative ranking).
Established control baselines, including specialist vision models, specialists constrained by prompt chaining, and an oracle, for fair and calibrated comparisons.
Results: GPT-4o emerged as the top performer among non-reasoning MFMs, leading in 4 out of 6 evaluated tasks, followed by Gemini 2.0 Flash and 1.5 Pro.
MFMs exhibit a notable performance gap compared to state-of-the-art specialist models across all tasks, even when specialists operate under identical prompt chaining constraints.
Image generation capabilities of GPT-4o (DALL-E 3) for dense vision outputs show significant limitations, including spatial misalignments, hallucinations, and lack of precise correspondence.
Takeaways: Current MFMs serve as respectable generalists but significantly underperform specialized vision models, even when subjected to the same methodological constraints.
MFMs demonstrate stronger capabilities in semantic tasks (e.g., classification, segmentation) compared to geometric tasks (e.g., depth, surface normals).
Enhanced reasoning capabilities in newer MFM architectures (e.g., OpenAI's o1, o3, o4-mini) correlate with improved performance on geometric understanding tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.01949.Title: Kwai Keye-VL Technical Report
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.01949.Summary: Kuaishou Group's Keye Team developed Kwai Keye-VL, an 8-billion-parameter multimodal foundation model that achieves leading performance in short-video understanding while retaining robust general vision-language capabilities. It significantly outperforms existing models on video-centric benchmarks and a new real-world short-video dataset (KC-MMBench).
Problem: Existing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle to fully comprehend dynamic, information-dense short-form videos, often optimized for static images.
Current MLLMs typically fail to capture the rich temporal, contextual, and sequential information inherent in video content, including event sequences and audio integration.
A lack of tailored benchmarks exists for rigorously evaluating MLLMs on real-world short-video scenarios.
Method: Introduces Kwai Keye-VL, an 8-billion-parameter MLLM with a native-resolution Vision Transformer using 2D and 3D Rotary Position Embeddings for unified processing of text, image, and video.
Constructs a massive, diverse corpus exceeding 600 billion tokens, including MLLM-recaptioned images, synthesized OCR data, and extensive video data with interleaved ASR.

Employs a sophisticated multi-stage training methodology, combining a four-stage progressive pre-training with a two-phase post-training that includes Supervised Fine-Tuning, Mixed Preference Optimization, Chain-of-Thought cold-start, Mix-Mode Reinforcement Learning, and Iterative Alignment.
Results: Achieves leading performance on short-video benchmarks, including 57.6% on Video-MMMU (an 8.7% absolute improvement) and 66.1% on MMVU.
Outperforms the second-best model by over 10% on the newly released Kuaishou Community Multimodal Benchmark (KC-MMBench), scoring 68.03%, validating its practical value for commercial applications.
Demonstrates competitive or state-of-the-art results on general vision-language tasks such as MMMU (71.4%) and AI2D (86.7%), while also showing lower hallucination rates.
Takeaways: A multi-stage training approach combining extensive pre-training and reasoning-focused post-training (including Chain-of-Thought and Reinforcement Learning) effectively cultivates comprehensive multimodal capabilities.
Training on Chain-of-Thought reasoning data mutually enhances both reasoning and non-reasoning abilities, leading to improved general perceptual performance.
The model can spontaneously select appropriate reasoning depths (Auto-Think mode), demonstrating adaptive cognitive processing for varying task complexities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.01701.Title: Exploring Advanced LLM Multi-Agent Systems Based on Blackboard Architecture
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.01701.Summary: Researchers from the Chinese Academy of Sciences propose LbMAS, a Large Language Model multi-agent system built on the classical blackboard architecture. This system enables dynamic agent collaboration and shared information access, achieving superior performance on complex reasoning and mathematical tasks while significantly reducing token consumption by avoiding pre-training requirements.
Problem: Existing LLM multi-agent systems often use fixed architectures, limiting their generality and adaptability to diverse tasks.
Dynamic LLM multi-agent systems frequently require a costly pre-optimization or supervised training phase to define their workflows, restricting real-time adaptation and generalizability.
Many LLM multi-agent systems struggle with complex, ill-structured problems due to insufficient shared information and rigid collaboration mechanisms.
Method: Proposing the blackboard-based LLM multi-agent system (bMAS) framework, with LbMAS as its first implementation, which centralizes information sharing and communication through a shared 'blackboard'.
Developing an LLM-based 'Control Unit' that dynamically selects suitable agents based on the query and current blackboard content, enabling flexible and adaptive collaboration.

Incorporating a mix of dynamically generated expert agents and predefined operational agents (e.g., Decider, Planner, Critic, Conflict-Resolver, Cleaner) to facilitate iterative problem-solving and self-correction on the blackboard.
Results: LbMAS achieved the best average performance across six diverse benchmarks (MMLU, ARC-Challenge, GPQA-Diamond, BBH-dateunderstand, MATH, GSM8K), outperforming Chain-of-Thought methods by an average of 4.33% and static Multi-Agent Systems by 5.02%.

On the MATH benchmark, LbMAS incurred the second lowest total token cost (4,721,489 tokens) while achieving the best performance (72.60%), demonstrating significant token efficiency compared to training-based autonomous MASs.
Ablation studies confirmed the crucial role of the LLM-based control unit in token efficiency and the necessity of active blackboard content management (cleaning) for maintaining performance.
Takeaways: Revitalizing the classical blackboard architecture effectively enables LLM-based multi-agent systems to achieve dynamic, adaptive collaboration.

The blackboard serves as a highly efficient shared context mechanism, allowing agents to dynamically adjust their contributions and significantly reducing token consumption compared to other dynamic multi-agent systems.
Integrating an LLM-based control unit facilitates autonomous agent selection and execution, leading to robust performance without the need for pre-training or fixed workflows.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.01679.Title: Blending Supervised and Reinforcement Fine-Tuning with Prefix Sampling
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.01679.Summary: Researchers introduce Prefix Reinforcement Fine-tuning (Prefix-RFT), a hybrid post-training approach for large language models that unifies supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT). The method consistently outperforms existing SFT, RFT, and two-staged baselines on mathematical reasoning benchmarks and general domain tasks, while demonstrating data efficiency and robustness across different model scales.
Problem: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) often leads to problematic generalization, suboptimal solution paths, and reduced robustness in complex reasoning tasks due to its behavioral cloning nature.

Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RFT) struggles with sparse reward signals, high sensitivity to initial policies, and might primarily refine existing capabilities rather than instilling fundamentally new knowledge.

The traditional sequential 'SFT-then-RFT' pipeline is a heuristic approach, lacking a principled framework to formally integrate the complementary strengths of SFT's dense supervision and RFT's goal-oriented optimization.
Method: Prefix-RFT unifies SFT and RFT training objectives by introducing a hybrid loop where a prefix from an expert demonstration guides an on-policy continuation by the model, creating a blended trajectory.

An entropy-based clipping mechanism is applied during training, incorporating only a top-k% of high-entropy demonstration tokens in the gradient calculation to ensure stable updates and target critical learning junctures.

A cosine decay scheduler dynamically adjusts the length of the sampled prefix, starting with longer, more guiding prefixes and gradually decreasing their length to encourage exploration and mitigate positional bias.
