Results: Prefix-RFT consistently achieved superior performance over standalone SFT, RFT, and sequential SFT-then-RFT baselines across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks (e.g., AIME 2024/2025) and three general domain reasoning tasks.

The method demonstrated significant data efficiency, maintaining strong performance even with a 99% reduction in training data (from 45k to 0.45k samples), and showed robustness to the quality of demonstration generators.

Ablation studies confirmed that the entropy-based clipping (top 20% high-entropy tokens) and the cosine decay scheduler were critical components, outperforming alternative strategies and contributing to the method's stable and superior outcomes.
Takeaways: SFT and RFT, despite their distinct origins, share a consistent underlying optimization structure, enabling their principled integration within a single training objective.
Providing high-quality prefixes effectively guides exploration, offering constrained autonomy to the model to begin on a promising path while still allowing it to discover superior continuations.

Targeting high-entropy demonstration tokens for reinforcement updates is crucial for stable learning, preventing overfitting and focusing learning on ambiguous steps where the model is most uncertain.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.01643.Title: SAILViT: Towards Robust and Generalizable Visual Backbones for MLLMs via Gradual Feature Refinement
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.01643.Summary: SAILViT introduces a three-stage 'gradual feature refinement' training pipeline for Vision Transformers, yielding visual backbones that are more robust and generalizable for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). This method systematically bridges modality semantic gaps and improves MLLM performance across various benchmarks, including multidisciplinary multimodal Q&A and logical reasoning.
Problem: Existing visual encoders in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) often suffer from parameter initialization conflicts and semantic gaps when integrated with LLMs.
Current visual backbone pre-training methods (e.g., multimodal contrastive learning, autoregressive modeling) struggle to incorporate comprehensive 'world knowledge' into visual features.
Suboptimal visual backbones create performance bottlenecks in MLLMs, limiting their potential in complex visual understanding and reasoning tasks.
Method: SAILViT proposes a novel three-stage 'gradual feature refinement' training pipeline for Vision Transformers (ViTs), building on architectures like AIMv2.
Stage 1 focuses on 'Coarse-grained Modality Alignment', training only the MLP connector to establish initial links between visual and linguistic representations.

Stage 2 performs 'Fine-grained Modality Alignment', optimizing both the visual backbone and connector, followed by Stage 3, 'World Knowledge Infusion', which jointly trains the visual backbone, connector, and LLM on diverse, complex data.
Results: SAILViT-Large achieved average relative performance improvements of 2.3% on InternLM2.5, 5.5% on Qwen2.5, and 5.4% on Qwen3 series compared to baselines on the OpenCompass benchmark.
The method demonstrated strong generalizability, showing consistent performance gains across different LLM families and sizes, and proved effective when applied to other ViT architectures.
On standard visual recognition tasks (ImageNet-1k, ImageNet-A/R/V2), SAILViT-Large and SAILViT-Huge improved average performance by 1.5% and 2.11% respectively, compared to their AIMv2 counterparts.
Takeaways: A progressive, hierarchical training process effectively aligns visual features with linguistic semantics and infuses world knowledge directly into the visual backbone.
Jointly training the visual backbone, connector, and LLM in the final 'World Knowledge Infusion' stage is crucial for comprehensive cross-modal reasoning and overall MLLM performance.
The 'gradual feature refinement' strategy yields visual backbones that not only enhance MLLMs but also extract more effective general-purpose visual features for traditional computer vision tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.01544.Title: MARVIS: Modality Adaptive Reasoning over VISualizations
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.01544.Summary: MARVIS introduces a training-free method that extends Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to predict across diverse data modalities, including vision, audio, biological, and tabular data, by transforming data embeddings into visualizations for VLM interpretation. The approach achieves performance within 2.5% of specialized models and significantly outperforms other generalist foundation models by an average of 16.7%, while also enhancing data privacy by avoiding direct exposure of raw data.
Problem: Large foundation models often underperform specialized models on non-traditional data modalities (e.g., audio, tabular) and 'long-tail' domains.

There is no straightforward or efficient way to input many data modalities directly into text-centric foundation models, and existing serialization methods for data like tabular information suffer from privacy concerns and inefficient scaling.
A gap exists between the high performance of specialized machine learning models within their narrow scope and the desired versatility of foundation models across diverse data types.
Method: A training-free, four-stage pipeline: (1) specialized embedding models generate dense vector representations from raw input data of any modality.
(2) Dimensionality reduction (primarily t-SNE) converts high-dimensional embeddings into 2D scatter plot visualizations, preserving local relationships.

(3) A VLM (Qwen 2.5 VL 3B) queries the visualization, leveraging its pre-trained visual reasoning capabilities with in-context learning to make predictions based on spatial relationships and provided semantic context.
(4) A robust parser extracts the final prediction from the VLM's natural language response, handling consistent color schemes and legend naming.
Results: MARVIS-3B achieves performance within 2.5% of best specialized models and improves upon other foundation models by an average of 16.7% across vision, audio, biological, and tabular data modalities.
For tabular data classification (OpenML CC18), MARVIS-3B attains 84.5% mean accuracy, outperforming other LLM-based tabular methods by 34-44 percentage points.

VLMs demonstrate adaptive reasoning; correct predictions are associated with more sophisticated responses, increased spatial analysis (33% more color mentions, 18% more distance reasoning), and distinct reasoning styles are observed for different visualization methods.
Takeaways: Vision-Language Models' (VLMs) pre-trained ability to reason over spatial relationships in images can serve as a "skeleton key" to interpret abstract data from any modality.

Transforming complex, high-dimensional data embeddings into human-interpretable 2D visualizations (e.g., using t-SNE) enables VLMs to make predictions without needing modality-specific projection layers or fine-tuning.
Empirical evidence suggests that VLMs engage in genuine, adaptive spatial reasoning over these abstract visual representations, adapting their analysis based on the visual information presented.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.01006.Title: GLM-4.5V and GLM-4.1V-Thinking: Towards Versatile Multimodal Reasoning with Scalable Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.01006.Summary: The GLM-V Team from Zhipu AI and Tsinghua University developed GLM-4.5V and GLM-4.1V-Thinking, a family of vision-language models designed for versatile multimodal reasoning. These models, trained with a scalable reinforcement learning framework, achieve state-of-the-art performance across 42 diverse public benchmarks, including complex STEM problem-solving, GUI agents, and VLM coding, while maintaining competitive results against closed-source models.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language Models (VLMs) often specialized in narrow domains, lacking general-purpose reasoning capabilities for complex tasks.
There was a need for VLMs capable of advanced multimodal reasoning in areas such as STEM problem-solving, autonomous GUI agents, coding from designs, and interpreting long documents.

Unlocking the full potential of strong vision foundation models required sophisticated and scalable reinforcement learning (RL) techniques, which were primarily explored for large language models (LLMs).
Method: A three-stage, reasoning-centric training framework was employed, including vision foundation model pre-training, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL).
Pre-training involved a unified architecture with an AIMv2-Huge vision encoder and GLM-4-9B-0414 or GLM-4.5-Air LLMs, supporting arbitrary resolutions and diverse multimodal data.

The core Reinforcement Learning stage combined Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) and Human Feedback (RLHF) with a multi-domain reward system and Reinforcement Learning with Curriculum Sampling (RLCS) for efficiency and stability.
Results: GLM-4.5V achieved state-of-the-art performance on nearly all 42 public benchmarks among open-source models of comparable size, outperforming models like Step-3 (321B-A38B) and Qwen-2.5-VL-72B.
The model demonstrated competitive or superior results compared to closed-source models such as Gemini-2.5-Flash on challenging tasks including VLM Coding and GUI Agents.
The smaller GLM-4.1V-9B-Thinking model achieved superior results to the much larger Qwen2.5-VL-72B on 29 out of 42 benchmarks, highlighting an excellent balance of performance and efficiency.
Takeaways: Multi-domain reinforcement learning promotes robust cross-domain generalization and mutual facilitation, where training on one domain positively impacts performance in others.
Dynamically selecting informative rollout problems through Reinforcement Learning with Curriculum Sampling (RLCS) is critical for maximizing learning gains and overall efficiency.
A precise and hack-resistant multi-domain reward system is essential for the stability and effectiveness of large-scale RL training across diverse multimodal tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.00994.Title: Should We Still Pretrain Encoders with Masked Language Modeling?
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.00994.Summary: This paper presents a controlled study comparing Masked Language Modeling (MLM) and Causal Language Modeling (CLM) as pretraining objectives for text encoders across various model sizes and a fixed data budget. The research finds that while MLM generally yields stronger representations for downstream tasks, a two-stage CLM then MLM approach or continuing pretraining with MLM from a CLM checkpoint delivers optimal performance and improved fine-tuning stability.
Problem: The observed superior performance of CLM-pretrained decoder models, when repurposed as encoders, might stem from their typically larger scale rather than an inherent advantage of the CLM objective, creating ambiguity in optimal pretraining strategies.
A lack of controlled studies makes it difficult to disentangle the specific contributions of Masked Language Modeling (MLM) and Causal Language Modeling (CLM) for learning text representations.

There is a need to identify more efficient and effective pretraining strategies for encoder models, particularly by exploring hybrid approaches or leveraging existing large language model checkpoints.
Method: Conducted a large-scale controlled study (38 models, 110,000 GPU hours) using identical encoder architectures and sizes (210M, 610M, 1B parameters) trained on a fixed 100 billion unique tokens.
Investigated various pretraining objectives: Masked Language Modeling (MLM) with different masking ratios, Causal Language Modeling (CLM), and a two-stage sequential CLM followed by MLM.

Explored two pretraining scenarios: training from scratch (PFS) and Continued PreTraining (CPT) from existing CLM or MLM checkpoints, followed by extensive fine-tuning across four categories of NLP tasks (SC, TC, QA, IR).
Results: MLM generally outperformed CLM for text representation tasks (e.g., Sequence Classification, Question Answering) when models were pretrained exclusively from scratch.
A two-stage pretraining protocol (CLM followed by MLM) consistently achieved better downstream performance compared to MLM-only training under fixed computational budgets.

Applying MLM Continued Pretraining (CPT) to a CLM-pretrained model resulted in superior downstream performance compared to CPT on an already MLM-pretrained model, demonstrating an efficient pathway to strong encoders.
CLM-pretrained models showed better data efficiency in early training stages and improved fine-tuning stability, exhibiting lower sensitivity to fine-tuning learning rates.
Takeaways: CLM offers benefits beyond raw performance, such as better data efficiency in early training stages and improved fine-tuning stability.
Combining CLM and MLM, either through a two-stage protocol or by adapting existing CLM models with MLM, can leverage the strengths of both objectives for superior encoder performance.
Existing large CLM-pretrained decoder models can serve as computationally efficient starting points for developing strong encoder models via MLM continued pretraining.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.00898.Title: ONLY: One-Layer Intervention Sufficiently Mitigates Hallucinations in Large Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.00898.Summary: This research from Carnegie Mellon University introduces ONLY, an efficient method to mitigate hallucinations in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) by employing a one-layer intervention and a single-query approach. The method reduces hallucination rates across multiple LVLM backbones and benchmarks while maintaining general multimodal understanding and achieving a minimal 1.07x increase in inference latency, addressing a key efficiency bottleneck of prior techniques.
Problem: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) frequently generate content inconsistent with visual input (hallucinations), undermining their reliability.
Existing training-based hallucination mitigation methods are computationally expensive and impractical for most users.
Inference-time contrastive decoding methods for LVLMs require multiple forward passes, significantly increasing inference time (2x+) and GPU memory, making them unsuitable for real-time applications.
Method: ONLY proposes a training-free decoding algorithm that intervenes with a single additional Transformer layer computation, rather than multiple full forward passes.

It introduces a 'textual enhancement' process that selectively deactivates attention heads based on their Text-to-Visual Entropy Ratio (TVER) to prioritize text-focused information and reduce language bias.

An adaptive decoding strategy then dynamically combines original and textually-enhanced logits, switching between collaborative (reinforcing consistent predictions) and contrastive (suppressing biased predictions) modes based on distribution divergence.
Results: ONLY consistently outperformed state-of-the-art baselines like VCD and M3ID across POPE, CHAIR, and MME-Hallucination benchmarks, achieving superior hallucination reduction (e.g., 89.10% F1 on LLaVA-1.5/MS-COCO Random POPE, and lowest CHAIR rates).
The method maintained or improved general multimodal understanding on MMBench and MM-Vet, demonstrating that hallucination mitigation did not degrade performance on other tasks.

ONLY achieved exceptional efficiency with a minimal 1.07x increase in inference latency and negligible additional GPU memory (1.00x) compared to regular decoding, significantly faster than VCD and M3ID (2.0x+ latency).
Takeaways: Language biases within the attention mechanism are a significant contributor to hallucinations in LVLMs, and targeted intervention at the attention head level can effectively address this.
A Text-to-Visual Entropy Ratio (TVER) can be used to identify and selectively amplify textual information to mitigate hallucinations with minimal computational overhead.
An adaptive decoding strategy, combining collaborative and contrastive modes based on the divergence between original and textually-enhanced outputs, improves hallucination mitigation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.00754.Title: Language-Unlocked ViT (LUViT): Empowering Self-Supervised Vision Transformers with LLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.00754.Summary: Language-Unlocked ViT (LUViT) proposes a self-supervised pre-training strategy that synergistically co-adapts Vision Transformers (ViTs) and Large Language Model (LLM) blocks, enabling LLMs to enhance visual features for discriminative tasks. The model achieves 83.6% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K and notable improvements in robustness benchmarks like ImageNet-A (+2.2%) compared to MAE-ViT.
Problem: Integrating pre-trained Large Language Models (LLMs) directly with Vision Transformers (ViTs) for discriminative computer vision tasks is challenging due to inherent modality mismatch.
Exploiting the rich semantic knowledge of LLMs to enhance vision-only models is difficult, as LLMs are optimized for linguistic structures while ViTs are optimized for pixels.
Adapting massive pre-trained LLMs to a new modality is computationally prohibitive and can lead to training instabilities or catastrophic forgetting if done without parameter efficiency.
Method: Proposed LUViT (Language-Unlocked ViT), an architecture combining a ViT encoder, an LLM Fusion Block (with linear projections and a pre-trained LLM block), and a lightweight MAE decoder for pre-training.
Introduced a synergistic pre-training strategy where both the ViT backbone and the LoRA-adapted LLM block are jointly optimized using the same MAE reconstruction loss, enabling co-adaptation.
Modified the LLM block for visual processing by replacing causal attention with bidirectional attention and removing Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE) to align with visual characteristics.
Results: Achieved a new state-of-the-art of 83.6% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K among comparable LLM-augmented models, surpassing the MAE-pretrained ViT/B baseline by 0.4%.
Demonstrated enhanced robustness and generalization, with a +2.2% absolute improvement on ImageNet-A (36.0%) and gains on ImageNet-SK (+0.8%), ImageNet-V2 (+0.7%), and ImageNet-C (+0.5%).
Outperformed the MAE ViT/B baseline on MS COCO, achieving a +0.5 AP improvement for object detection (51.1 AP) and a +0.2 AP improvement for instance segmentation (45.1 AP).
Takeaways: A synergistic pre-training strategy using a shared Masked Auto-Encoding (MAE) objective for both the Vision Transformer (ViT) backbone and the LoRA-adapted Large Language Model (LLM) block effectively bridges the modality gap.
Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is crucial for efficiently and stably adapting pre-trained LLM blocks to process visual features, significantly improving performance over frozen LLMs.

Integrating LLM knowledge leads to more focused attention patterns on foreground regions and substantially improves robustness against out-of-distribution data and adversarial backgrounds for discriminative vision tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.00748.Title: Improving the Reasoning of Multi-Image Grounding in MLLMs via Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.00748.Summary: Researchers from Xiaohongshu Inc. and affiliated universities developed a two-stage training framework that combines Chain-of-Thought Supervised Fine-tuning (CoT-SFT) and Reinforcement Learning (RL) to enhance multi-image grounding reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). This approach achieved state-of-the-art performance, including a 9.04% improvement over the SFT baseline on MIG-Bench and outperforming GPT-4o on the BLINK multi-image understanding benchmark, demonstrating robust generalization.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle with complex real-world tasks that require reasoning across multiple images and intricate multi-modal instructions.
Existing supervised fine-tuning (SFT) methods for multi-image grounding often lead to pattern memorization rather than robust, generalizable reasoning, limiting performance on novel scenarios.
Direct application of Reinforcement Learning (RL) to MLLMs for complex multi-image queries faces instability, as base models lack the foundational capacity to handle such tasks.
Method: A two-stage training framework was developed, starting with a Qwen2.5-VL-7B base model.

Stage 1: Cold-start CoT-SFT initialization. A high-quality Chain-of-Thought (CoT) dataset was synthesized using Qwen2.5-VL-72B and filtered for accuracy, then used to fine-tune the base MLLM via LoRA.

Stage 2: Rule-based Reinforcement Learning (RL) using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Rejection sampling was applied to curate informative training samples, and a combined accuracy and format reward function guided the learning process.
Results: Achieved state-of-the-art results on multi-image grounding benchmarks, with a 9.04% improvement over the SFT baseline on MIG-Bench (58.83% accuracy) and a 6.37% gain on MC-Bench (58.49% accuracy).
Demonstrated superior generalization, outperforming the 72B-scale Qwen2.5-VL-72B and even the closed-source GPT-4o model on the BLINK multi-image understanding benchmark (61.18% average accuracy).

Ablation studies confirmed the critical contributions of the cold-start CoT-SFT initialization, the rejection sampling strategy for efficient RL training, and the optimized KL divergence weight in the GRPO objective.
Takeaways: A structured two-stage approach, initiating with CoT-SFT, is essential for stabilizing and effectively applying RL to MLLMs for complex multi-image reasoning tasks.

Reinforcement Learning, specifically GRPO with targeted reward design and rejection sampling, can transition MLLMs from rote memorization to robust, generalizable reasoning capabilities in multimodal contexts.

Enhancing MLLM reasoning through RL in multi-image grounding tasks leads to improved performance across broader multi-image understanding, zero-shot grounding, and out-of-domain object detection tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.00505.Title: LLaVA-SP: Enhancing Visual Representation with Visual Spatial Tokens for MLLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.00505.Summary: LLaVA-SP, developed by researchers from Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications and Beihang University, enhances multimodal large language models by introducing a novel projector that efficiently captures visual spatial information. The method adds only six spatial visual tokens, enabling significant improvements across 10 out of 11 multimodal benchmarks, including visual grounding and hallucination mitigation, while maintaining inference efficiency comparable to LLaVA-1.5.
Problem: Mainstream MLLMs using CLIP-ViT vision encoders struggle to capture fine-grained perceptual details and suffer from disrupted spatial relationships due to ViT's patch flattening.
Existing methods to improve visual understanding often lead to a significant increase in visual token counts, resulting in substantially higher training and inference costs.
Deficiencies in visual representation contribute to issues like visual hallucinations and poor performance in tasks requiring precise spatial reasoning or object localization.
Method: LLaVA-SP enhances the standard MLLM architecture (CLIP-ViT + Projector + LLM) by introducing a novel Projector design with two components: a Spatial Feature Extractor (SFE) and a Detail Feature Integrator (DFI).
The SFE uses convolutional kernels to generate a small set of visual spatial tokens (six) by either progressively cropping or adaptively pooling multi-scale 2D features from the ViT encoder's output.
The DFI employs a cross-attention mechanism to integrate fine-grained details from a broader feature map into these spatial tokens, enriching their information content without increasing their count.
Results: LLaVA-SP outperforms LLaVA-1.5 on 10 out of 11 multimodal benchmarks (e.g., +5.9% on VizWiz, +2.5% on TextVQA), achieving a 1.5-1.6% average normalized score improvement.
The model maintains nearly identical inference latency compared to LLaVA-1.5 (approx. 20.5 tokens/s vs. 20.76 tokens/s), adding only six spatial visual tokens.

LLaVA-SP-Cropping improved visual grounding on RefCOCO and demonstrated better performance in spatial relation, object localization, and physical relation tasks, while both variants showed improved scores on hallucination mitigation benchmarks (POPE, MMVP).
Takeaways: Re-introducing 2D spatial relationships and fine-grained details via a specialized projector can significantly enhance MLLM visual understanding without substantially increasing token count or inference latency.
Convolutional kernels are more effective than transformer blocks for extracting spatial information within the projector, while the optimal number of spatial tokens is small (e.g., six).

The Detail Feature Integrator (DFI) effectively enhances 'cropping'-based spatial features but can negatively impact 'pooling'-based features, highlighting different mechanisms for detail integration.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.00462.Title: Unleashing the Potential of All Test Samples: Mean-Shift Guided Test-Time Adaptation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.00462.Summary: Researchers at Xi'an Jiaotong University developed Mean-Shift Guided Test-Time Adaptation (MS-TTA), a training-free method that refines Visual-Language Model feature embeddings using Mean-Shift clustering to leverage all test samples. MS-TTA achieved an average accuracy of 69.48% on cross-domain benchmarks with a ViT-B/16 backbone, outperforming previous methods by 0.81%, and demonstrated improved robustness on out-of-distribution datasets.
Problem: Visual-Language Models (VLMs) like CLIP experience significant performance degradation when encountering distribution shifts at test time, despite strong zero-shot generalization.

Current training-free Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) methods for VLMs rely on CLIP's original feature space and selectively utilize only high-confidence samples, overlooking the potential of "low-quality" data.
This selective sample usage and dependence on the original feature space limit adaptation effectiveness and can be sensitive to noisy pseudo-labels under strong distribution shifts.
Method: Introduce MS-TTA (Mean-Shift Guided Test-Time Adaptation), a training-free framework that refines feature embeddings and leverages all test samples for adaptation.
Employ a single-step k-nearest neighbors (kNN) Mean-Shift operator to refine initial CLIP embeddings, creating "mean-shifted embeddings" that are more compact and discriminative.
Utilize a dynamic cache to store high-confidence mean-shifted embeddings and their pseudo-labels, which are then combined with original CLIP logits for final, robust predictions.
Results: MS-TTA achieved 69.48% average accuracy on cross-domain benchmarks (ViT-B/16), surpassing BoostAdapter by 0.81%, with notable gains of +3.99% on EuroSAT.
The method demonstrated robust performance on out-of-distribution benchmarks, achieving 65.65% average OOD accuracy (ViT-B/16), outperforming previous approaches.
t-SNE visualizations showed that mean-shifted embeddings have significantly more compact and distinct clusters, improving class separability and resolving ambiguities between challenging classes.
Takeaways: Visual-Language Models' original feature space is not always optimal for test-time adaptation and can be enhanced for better class separability and compactness.
All test samples, including those initially deemed "low-quality" or low-confidence, can be refined and contribute positively to the adaptation process.
Mean-Shift clustering provides an efficient, training-free method to refine feature embeddings, improving their discriminability and robustness to distribution shifts.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.00432.Title: Does Math Reasoning Improve General LLM Capabilities? Understanding Transferability of LLM Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.00432.Summary: This research investigates how fine-tuning methods for math reasoning affect the broader capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs), revealing that Reinforcement Learning (RL) approaches foster superior generalization across diverse reasoning and non-reasoning tasks compared to Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT). RL-tuned models successfully transfer math gains and preserve performance on general tasks, while SFT models often exhibit narrow specialization and degradation in other domains.
Problem: It is unclear whether impressive gains in specialized math reasoning translate into broader, general problem-solving abilities in LLMs or merely reflect narrow overfitting.
Current post-training recipes, particularly those relying on Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) with distilled data, might lead to catastrophic forgetting or reduced versatility in other tasks.
A lack of mechanistic understanding exists regarding why certain fine-tuning paradigms succeed or fail in generalizing LLM knowledge across diverse domains.
Method: An initial audit of over 20 open-weight LLMs was conducted across math, other reasoning, and non-reasoning benchmarks, utilizing a novel Transferability Index (TI) to quantify generalization.
Controlled experiments on Qwen3-14B compared Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning (RL) using identical math-only data to isolate the effects of each tuning method.

Mechanistic analyses, including latent-space PCA and token-space distribution analysis (KL-divergence, rank shifts), were performed to understand internal model changes induced by different fine-tuning approaches.
Results: RL-tuned models exhibited superior generalization, showing a +17.1% improvement on tasks like LiveCodeBench2 over SFT variants, and recovered or exceeded base performance on non-reasoning tasks where SFT models often declined.

PCA analysis revealed RL caused significantly lower latent-space shifts across all task categories, indicating better preservation of the model's internal representation structure than SFT, which induced substantial, scattered shifts.

KL-divergence analysis demonstrated that RL models had significantly lower token distribution shifts from the backbone and selectively adjusted a small set of task-relevant tokens, unlike SFT which perturbed a much larger number of irrelevant tokens.
Takeaways: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) for math reasoning often leads to narrow specialization, failing to transfer gains to other domains and frequently causing performance degradation on non-reasoning tasks.

Reinforcement Learning (RL) consistently promotes broad generalization, improving math reasoning while positively transferring gains to other reasoning tasks and maintaining or improving performance on non-reasoning tasks.

RL-based fine-tuning induces significantly smaller latent-space shifts and less perturbation to output token distributions compared to SFT, better preserving the model's original feature geometry and overall competence.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.00417.Title: ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.00417.Summary: AI at Meta and University of Washington researchers introduce ASTRO, a three-stage framework that teaches large language models to reason by reflecting and backtracking in-context. It instills search-like reasoning via synthetic data generation, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning, leading to absolute performance gains of up to 26.9% on challenging mathematical reasoning benchmarks.
Problem: Open-source large language models (LLMs) often lack the advanced search-like reasoning capabilities (e.g., self-reflection, backtracking) observed in state-of-the-art proprietary models.

Current methods for enhancing LLM reasoning often rely on distillation from already strong models or external inference-time scaffolds, rather than enabling LLMs to internalize and generate complex search procedures themselves.
It has been unclear how to robustly enhance the reasoning capabilities of general-purpose LLMs, such as the Llama 3 family, which may not inherently demonstrate such advanced behaviors.
Method: Generates a synthetic dataset of high-quality 'long Chain-of-Thoughts' (CoTs) that encode diverse search behaviors, including self-reflection and backtracking, derived from Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) trajectories and linearized into natural language.
Applies Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) to a target LLM (Llama-3.1-70B-instruct) on this curated dataset for a single epoch to instill autoregressive search priors.

Utilizes a modified Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) for Reinforcement Learning (RL) to further refine and optimize the SFT-tuned model's reasoning capabilities, leveraging verifiable binary rewards.
Results: Llama-3.1-70B-ASTRO-RL achieved significant absolute performance gains on mathematical benchmarks: 81.8% on MATH-500 (+16.0% over baseline), 64.4% on AMC 2023 (+26.9%), and 30.0% on AIME 2024 (+20.0%).
ASTRO-RL models consistently outperformed strong baselines, including Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and other Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct variants fine-tuned with Step-KTO and SPOC.

Control experiments confirmed that explicitly infused search priors from SFT are essential, as ASTRO-RL models consistently and significantly outperformed 'Direct-RL' models across all benchmarks, which lacked these priors.
Takeaways: Explicitly teaching search priors, such as self-reflection and backtracking, during Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is crucial for the efficacy and performance ceiling of subsequent Reinforcement Learning (RL) in reasoning tasks.

The models learn to generate longer, more detailed Chain-of-Thought (CoT) traces and increase their frequency of backtracking during RL training, which directly correlates with improved problem-solving performance.
The framework enables LLMs to internalize complex search procedures, allowing them to autoregressively generate full search trajectories, including recoveries from errors.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.24119.Title: SPIRAL: Self-Play on Zero-Sum Games Incentivizes Reasoning via Multi-Agent Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.24119.Summary: The SPIRAL framework trains Large Language Models (LLMs) to acquire transferable reasoning skills by engaging in self-play on two-player zero-sum language games. This approach automates curriculum generation and leads to substantial improvements, such as an 8.6% increase in mathematical reasoning and 8.4% in general reasoning for a Qwen3-4B model.
Problem: Existing Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) methods for LLM reasoning suffer from a 'scalability bottleneck,' relying heavily on human-curated problem-answer pairs, domain-specific reward engineering, and expert supervision.

Prior applications of self-play to language models were limited to offline updates, simple word games, or single-turn tasks, failing to leverage the full potential of multi-turn competitive dynamics for extended strategic reasoning.
The challenge of developing an autonomous and scalable method to enhance generalizable reasoning capabilities in LLMs without continuous human intervention.
Method: The SPIRAL framework implements a fully online, multi-turn, multi-agent reinforcement learning system for LLMs using two-player zero-sum language games.
It frames learning as a turn-level Markov Decision Process, where each action is a complete, multi-token response, and both players share a single, role-conditioned policy.

A key technical innovation, Role-conditioned Advantage Estimation (RAE), uses separate, exponentially moving average baselines for each game and player role to stabilize training and reduce variance in multi-agent REINFORCE.
Results: SPIRAL, trained exclusively on Kuhn Poker, improved Qwen3-4B-Base's mathematical reasoning by 8.6% and general reasoning by 8.4%, demonstrating transferability of skills from games to standard reasoning benchmarks.
Self-play significantly outperformed training against fixed opponents, which either led to 'thinking collapse' with random opponents or exploitation and overfitting with strong fixed opponents.

Multi-game training (TicTacToe + Kuhn Poker + Simple Negotiation) achieved superior average performance on out-of-distribution games (44.9% vs. 27.1-34.4% for single-game specialists) and improved even a stronger DeepSeek-Distill-Qwen-7B model by 2.0 percentage points.

Role-conditioned Advantage Estimation (RAE) was essential for stable self-play, preventing 'thinking collapse' (where reasoning traces ceased to be generated) and ensuring stable policy gradient norms.
Takeaways: Competitive pressure within self-play on zero-sum games forces Large Language Models (LLMs) to develop genuine, transferable reasoning abilities rather than memorization or exploitation of static strategies.
Self-play's automatic, adaptive curriculum consistently outperforms fixed-opponent training, which leads to overfitting and poor generalization in LLMs.

Different types of zero-sum games cultivate specialized reasoning skills in LLMs, and training across multiple games yields synergistic benefits, enhancing performance on novel, composite reasoning challenges.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.23918.Title: Thinking with Images for Multimodal Reasoning: Foundations, Methods, and Future Frontiers
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.23918.Summary: A comprehensive survey introduces "Thinking with Images," a new paradigm where AI models use visual representations as dynamic, manipulable intermediate steps in reasoning, moving beyond static visual inputs. It proposes a three-stage evolutionary framework—Tool-Driven Visual Exploration, Programmatic Visual Manipulation, and Intrinsic Visual Imagination—to categorize and guide the development of AI systems capable of active visual cognition.
Problem: Current Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) primarily "Think about Images," encoding visual inputs into static features, with subsequent reasoning conducted almost exclusively within the textual domain.
This creates a "semantic gap" where the richness of continuous visual data is compressed and becomes a passive, fixed context for discrete symbolic thought.
This limitation leads to brittleness in tasks requiring iterative visual engagement, fine-grained detail analysis, or complex physical reasoning.
Method: The paper defines the "Thinking with Images" paradigm, where vision transitions from a passive input to a dynamic, manipulable cognitive workspace, akin to a human's mental sketchpad.

It proposes a three-stage evolutionary framework—Tool-Driven Visual Exploration, Programmatic Visual Manipulation, and Intrinsic Visual Imagination—to categorize and guide the development of AI systems capable of active visual cognition.
The survey systematically reviews core methods (prompt-based, SFT-based, RL-based) for implementing these stages and analyzes relevant evaluation benchmarks and applications.
Results: The survey formally establishes and distinguishes the "Thinking with Images" paradigm, defining it by its core principle: utilizing visual representations as manipulable and verifiable intermediate steps in a cognitive process.
It proposes a three-stage evolutionary framework for increasing cognitive autonomy: Tool-Driven Visual Exploration, Programmatic Visual Manipulation, and Intrinsic Visual Imagination.

The paper identifies unique challenges to the "Thinking with Images" paradigm, including high computational cost, error propagation due to visual information density, architectural divides between modalities, and challenges in cross-task generalization.
Takeaways: The transition from "Thinking about Images" to "Thinking with Images" is crucial for overcoming the "semantic gap" in multimodal reasoning and achieving more robust, human-aligned AI.

The proposed three-stage evolutionary framework (Tool-Driven Visual Exploration, Programmatic Visual Manipulation, Intrinsic Visual Imagination) provides a novel taxonomy for understanding how Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) can develop active visual reasoning capabilities.

"Thinking with Images" enables dynamic perceptual exploration, structured visual reasoning (using images as cognitive scratchpads), and goal-oriented generative planning, which are key for advanced multimodal intelligence.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.23822.Title: Interpretable Zero-Shot Learning with Locally-Aligned Vision-Language Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.23822.Summary: A training-free framework, LaZSL, developed by researchers from MBZUAI and collaborators, enhances interpretable zero-shot learning by employing Optimal Transport to align local visual regions with LLM-generated semantic attributes. This approach achieves state-of-the-art accuracy across diverse benchmarks, including 69.7% on average with a ViT-B/16 backbone, while providing human-understandable explanations for predictions.
Problem: Current Vision-Language Models (VLMs) like CLIP offer limited interpretability in Zero-Shot Learning (ZSL), providing global similarity scores without explaining specific visual cues for predictions.
Global image-text alignment struggles with fine-grained classification and shows poor generalization across domain shifts, leading to suboptimal accuracy for challenging distinctions.

Existing interpretable ZSL methods typically align entire images with attributes, failing to establish fine-grained local correspondences between visual regions and specific semantic attributes, particularly with frozen pre-trained VLM encoders.
Method: Employs Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate sets of discrete semantic attributes for each class, providing fine-grained textual descriptions.
Constructs a diverse 'region vision set' from multi-scale cropped image patches to capture local visual information.

Leverages Optimal Transport (OT) to establish fine-grained alignment between local visual features and semantic attributes, minimizing the cost of transforming visual distributions to semantic ones, enhanced by a vision selection mechanism and a region-global hybrid cost.
Results: LaZSL achieved state-of-the-art average accuracy on five diverse image classification benchmarks, demonstrating a 69.7% average accuracy with a ViT-B/16 backbone and outperforming direct interpretable baselines like DCLIP by up to 3.8%.

The method showcased superior domain generalization capabilities on ImageNet variants (V2, R, Sketch, A), achieving an average accuracy of 60.9% with ViT-B/16, surpassing both training-required and training-free baselines.
Provides explicit, human-understandable interpretations for predictions by aligning specific local visual regions with discrete semantic attributes, illustrating *why* a particular class was chosen.
Takeaways: Establishing fine-grained, local visual-semantic alignment is essential for truly interpretable Zero-Shot Learning, moving beyond black-box global similarity scores.
Optimal Transport offers an effective training-free mechanism to achieve precise local alignment between visual regions and discrete semantic attributes derived from LLMs.
A balanced integration of local visual information, LLM-generated attributes, and global VLM context is key to boosting accuracy and domain generalization in ZSL while maintaining interpretability.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.23785.Title: Visual Textualization for Image Prompted Object Detection
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.23785.Summary: VisTex-OVLM is a novel image-prompted object detection method that projects visual exemplars into the text feature space of Object-level Vision-Language Models (OVLMs). This approach enhances detection capabilities for rare or novel categories without altering the OVLM's original architecture, thereby preserving its pre-trained object-text alignment and generalization.
Problem: OVLMs demonstrate suboptimal performance on rare or underrepresented objects not sufficiently covered in their vast pre-training datasets.
Text prompts for object detection can suffer from granularity limitations, semantic bias, or omissions, making fine-grained object distinction challenging.
Existing few-shot methods for OVLMs often disrupt the models' pre-trained object-text alignment and generalization capabilities when adapting to new data.
Method: A 'visual textualization' process is introduced to convert visual information from support images into a textualized feature format compatible with OVLM text prompts.

Multi-scale Textualizing Blocks (MSTB) extract and map multi-scale visual features from image-engineered support images into the OVLM's text feature space, using a parameter-sharing strategy for efficiency.
Textualized visual tokens are consolidated via non-parametric Multi-Stage Fusion (MSF) and concatenated directly with original text prompts, then fed into an unmodified and frozen pre-trained OVLM.
Results: VisTex-GLIP achieved state-of-the-art performance on PASCAL VOC (e.g., 74.8 AP50 on Split 1, 10-shot) and MSCOCO few-shot object detection benchmarks, outperforming prior VLM-based methods.

The method demonstrated superior detection for novel categories across open-set scenarios including LVIS MiniVal, 11 ODinW35 datasets, and 5 challenging medical datasets (MoNu, CCRCC, ConSep, LIDC, Deeplesion).

Ablation studies confirmed that multi-scale textualization, parameter-sharing in MSTB, and non-parametric multi-stage fusion are critical components that synergistically enhance performance and maintain OVLM integrity.
Takeaways: Projecting visual semantics from few-shot exemplars directly into the text feature space enables seamless integration with text-prompt-exclusive OVLMs without architectural modifications.

Employing background blur in image prompt engineering effectively highlights target objects, and multi-scale visual textualization leverages diverse feature representations for robust object learning.

Strictly preserving the pre-trained OVLM architecture and its object-text alignment is crucial for maintaining strong generalization capabilities across both base and novel categories, preventing performance degradation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.23639.Title: Unified Multimodal Understanding via Byte-Pair Visual Encoding
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.23639.Summary: A framework unifies multimodal understanding by applying a byte-pair encoding (BPE) strategy to visual tokens, which are derived from quantized images and incorporate spatial consistency. This approach achieves performance competitive with leading continuous representation MLLMs on diverse vision-language tasks and contributes to reduced visual hallucinations.
Problem: Conventional Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) using continuous visual representations suffer from a "modality gap" with discrete text tokens and an "information bottleneck" leading to visual hallucinations.
Existing discrete visual tokenization methods often quantize images into fixed-size tokens without fully capturing semantic structure or incorporating crucial spatial relationships.
Prior work on visual BPE was primarily frequency-based, overlooking spatial consistency, and lacked effective training procedures for practical multimodal models.
Method: Transforms images into discrete BPE visual tokens using a pre-trained VQ-GAN for initial quantization, followed by a BPE process that adapts text-based BPE for visual data.
Introduces a priority-guided encoding scheme for visual BPE that considers both co-occurrence frequency and a novel measure of spatial consistency to form semantically meaningful tokens.

Employs a multi-stage training pipeline with curriculum-based data composition (progressing from foundation to instruction data) and progressive parameter unfreezing to optimize learning with hierarchical BPE tokens.
Results:
Proposed models (Being-VL-0.5 and Being-VL-0.5
+
) achieve performance comparable to leading continuous embedding-based MLLMs (e.g., Being-VL-0.5
+
reaches 80.6 on VQAv2 and 72.1 on MMBench).
The approach significantly outperforms previous discrete token methods (Being-VL-0) across benchmarks and shows reduced visual hallucination on POPE (84.3 for Being-VL-0.5).

Ablation studies demonstrate that both curriculum-based data composition and progressive parameter unfreezing are essential, with the multi-stage strategy outperforming single-stage training by over 12% on perception and reasoning tasks.
Takeaways: Applying byte-pair encoding (BPE) to visual data, guided by both frequency and spatial consistency, helps bridge the representation gap between visual and textual modalities.
A multi-stage training strategy, combining curriculum-based data composition and progressive parameter unfreezing, is crucial for effectively training models with hierarchical BPE visual tokens.
BPE tokenization enables a more unified multimodal knowledge space by balancing the activation magnitudes of visual and text token embeddings.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.23529.Title: When Test-Time Adaptation Meets Self-Supervised Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.23529.Summary: Korea University and NAVER AI Lab researchers developed a Self-Supervised Test-Time Adaptation (SSTTA) protocol and an 'Adapt Without Source pretraining' (AWS) framework that enables effective online adaptation of self-supervised models. This approach eliminates the need for expensive labeled source pretraining, improving DINO's performance on ImageNetC by 16.2% and iBOT's by 19.9% while also achieving competitive results with supervised baselines.
Problem: Traditional Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) methods depend heavily on costly, label-intensive source-pretrained models, posing significant computational and data acquisition challenges.
The computational expense of source pretraining, often overlooked, makes TTA less practical for real-world deployments.
Existing TTA techniques struggle when directly applied to self-supervised models due to their lower initial accuracy and the unreliability of generated pseudo-labels.
Method: Introduced the Self-Supervised Test-Time Adaptation (SSTTA) protocol, which leverages a self-supervised model and an efficient prototype classifier instead of labeled source pretraining.
Proposed 'Adapt Without Source pretraining' (AWS), a collaborative learning framework consisting of Contrastive Learning, Knowledge Distillation, and Mutual Learning components.
Designed a prototype classifier that computes class prototypes using only forward passes of the self-supervised model, allowing for efficient adaptation without backpropagation or high memory usage.
Results: SSTTA significantly reduces pretraining computational cost; for ImageNet, classifier construction takes 36m25s compared to '1h8m23s x 300 epochs' for conventional pretraining.
AWS improved DINO's error rate on ImageNetC by 16.2% (from 69.2% to 53.0%) and iBOT's error rate by 19.9% (from 68.0% to 48.1%), demonstrating strong adaptation performance for SSL models.
AWS achieves state-of-the-art results even on traditionally source-pretrained models, recording a mean error of 39.4% on ImageNet-to-ImageNetC, outperforming the previous best of 42.5%.
Takeaways: The substantial computational cost of traditional source pretraining in TTA necessitates a shift towards label-free pretraining paradigms.
Self-supervised models, while powerful, require a tailored adaptation strategy due to their initial accuracy and pseudo-label characteristics that differ from supervised models.

A multi-component collaborative learning framework that includes robust contrastive learning, knowledge preservation through distillation, and mutual information maximization can effectively adapt self-supervised models to dynamic environments.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.23235.Title: Generalist Reward Models: Found Inside Large Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.23235.Summary: Researchers at Nanjing University reveal that a powerful, generalist reward model is latently present within any LLM trained via standard next-token prediction, which they term the 'endogenous reward.' They provide theoretical proof that this endogenous reward can be directly extracted from the LLM's logits and empirically demonstrate that using it for reinforcement learning fine-tuning yields a +5.8% average performance gain on math reasoning benchmarks while outperforming explicitly trained reward models.
Problem: Aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) with human values and instructions is costly and slow, primarily due to the expense and scalability issues of collecting human preference data for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF).
Alternative methods like Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback (RLAIF) or 'LLM-as-a-judge' are often heuristic, lack robust theoretical foundations, and can inherit biases from the judging LLM.
Existing LLM alignment techniques heavily rely on external feedback or new preference datasets, indicating a bottleneck in achieving efficient and scalable alignment.
Method: The paper proposes that a generalist reward model, termed the 'endogenous reward,' is latently present within any Large Language Model (LLM) trained via standard next-token prediction.

A theoretical framework is established that proves the LLM's logits are a solution to an offline Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) objective, enabling direct extraction of a principled reward signal without further training or external data.

The extracted endogenous reward can then be used to fine-tune the LLM through reinforcement learning, aiming to mitigate compounding errors and enhance performance in a more efficient and scalable manner.
Results: EndoRM significantly outperformed all other training-free baselines and four top-performing, explicitly trained reward models on RM-Bench and Multifaceted-Bench, demonstrating superior accuracy and robustness in evaluating diverse preference pairs.

Experiments on the Domain-Specific Preference dataset confirmed that EndoRM acts as a dynamic and promptable judge, adapting its evaluation criteria based on natural language system prompts, achieving highest accuracy (e.g., 76.89% on academic data for EndoRM-Academy) in corresponding domains.

Reinforcement learning fine-tuning with the endogenous reward improved the base model (Qwen2.5-Math-7B) by an average of +5.8% across five math reasoning benchmarks (e.g., +10.7% on Minerva, +7.1% on AMC), empirically validating the theoretical gains against compounding errors.
Takeaways: The logits of an LLM trained via next-token prediction are theoretically equivalent to the optimal Q-function derived from an offline Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) objective, meaning the LLM implicitly learns a reward function.

The 'endogenous reward' can be directly recovered from the LLM's logits without additional training, and subsequent reinforcement learning (RL) using this reward leads to a policy with a provably superior linear error bound (O(H*ε_π)) compared to the quadratic error (O(H^2*ε_π)) of the base model from imitation learning.
The endogenous reward is dynamic and can be controlled at inference time by providing natural language instructions, enabling a promptable and generalist reward model.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.23156.Title: Self-Supervised Contrastive Learning for Multi-Label Images
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.23156.Summary: A research effort from Hohai University introduces a self-supervised contrastive learning framework specifically tailored for multi-label images, incorporating a block-wise augmentation module and an image-aware contrastive loss to enhance representation learning. The method achieves competitive performance on multi-label classification and transfer learning tasks using the COCO2017 dataset, often surpassing baselines pre-trained on ImageNet with significantly fewer samples.
Problem: Current self-supervised learning (SSL) approaches heavily rely on massive, single-label datasets like ImageNet, leading to high computational costs and resource dependency.

Multi-label images, which are common in real-world applications and possess rich semantic information, are often overlooked in mainstream SSL, as standard augmentation strategies struggle to generate semantically consistent positive pairs.
Traditional linear evaluation protocols for SSL are insufficient for accurately assessing performance on multi-label classification tasks, as they lose crucial spatial structural information.
Method: A Block-wise Augmentation Module (BAM) is introduced, which partitions images into overlapping blocks and applies independent augmentations to generate a richer set of semantically similar positive view pairs.

An Image-Aware Contrastive Loss (IA-CLoss) is proposed to establish semantic connections among all views originating from the same multi-label image, treating them as positives regardless of their specific visual content.

An improved fine-tuning validation framework, Global Average Pooling Minus Global Max Pooling (GAMP), is developed to replace the final pooling layer, retaining more spatial information for effective multi-label classification.
Results: The proposed method achieved a 64.0% mAP on COCO2017 multi-label classification at 224x224 input scale, outperforming ImageNet-pretrained MoCoIN (63.3% mAP), and reached 68.5% mAP at 448x448, surpassing MoCoIN (68.1% mAP).

BAM and IA-CLoss contributed to faster convergence of the similarity contrastive loss during pre-training and demonstrated sustained performance improvements over longer training epochs compared to baselines.

In transfer learning tasks, the framework showed competitive performance on VOC object detection (79.4 AP) and COCO object detection (42.4 AP) and segmentation (37.8 AP), often outperforming or matching ImageNet-pretrained baselines despite pre-training on a smaller, multi-label dataset.
Takeaways: Dividing multi-label images into overlapping blocks and augmenting them independently provides a more effective strategy for generating semantically consistent positive view pairs compared to random cropping.

Establishing a contrastive objective where all views derived from a single original image are considered positive samples allows the model to learn robust representations by explicitly linking co-occurring concepts.

The combination of global average and max pooling during linear evaluation significantly enhances the assessment of SSL-learned features for multi-label classification by better preserving discriminative spatial information.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.23120.Title: Enhancing Spatial Reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models through Reasoning-based Segmentation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.23120.Summary: Researchers from Harbin Institute of Technology, Pengcheng Laboratory, and The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen developed Relevant Reasoning Segmentation (R^2S), a framework that enhances 3D multimodal large language models' spatial reasoning by decomposing complex instructions into identifying relevant objects and prior-guided refinement. The method, along with a new 3D ReasonSeg dataset, improved Acc@50 on ScanRefer by over 10 percentage points compared to the baseline and achieved 33.1 gIoU on the challenging 3D ReasonSeg dataset.
Problem: Existing 3D Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle with complex spatial reasoning tasks, failing to accurately localize targets when instructions involve intricate inter-object relationships, attributes, or functionality.
Current 3D MLLMs primarily rely on direct instruction tuning, which is insufficient for capturing the nuanced spatial cues inherent in 3D point cloud data.

Available datasets like ScanRefer and ScanQA contain oversimplified or ambiguous spatial relations, limiting the effective training and comprehensive evaluation of sophisticated spatial reasoning capabilities.
Method: The authors proposed Relevant Reasoning Segmentation (R^2S), a two-step framework that mimics human cognition by first identifying "question-related objects" as reasoning priors, then using these priors to guide the MLLM's refinement for precise target localization.

They introduced the 3D ReasonSeg dataset, comprising 25,185 training and 3,966 validation samples, which focuses on object functionality, visual attributes, and complex spatial relationships, to specifically train and assess advanced spatial reasoning.

R^2S integrates a baseline MLLM with a segmentation head, where the MLLM is prompted to first generate segmentation masks for relevant objects, and these visual features are then incorporated into a refined instruction for final target prediction.
Results: R^2S achieved 59.5 Acc@25 and 48.7 Acc@50 on the ScanRefer benchmark, marking an improvement of over 10 percentage points in Acc@50 compared to the baseline and outperforming previous state-of-the-art specialized models.
On the newly introduced 3D ReasonSeg dataset, R^2S obtained a gIoU of 33.1, demonstrating its effectiveness in handling challenging questions requiring complex spatial reasoning.

Ablation studies confirmed that the Prior-guided Refinement step is essential, with its removal leading to degraded performance, and that visual feature-based priors derived from segmentation masks are more effective than text-only priors for enhancing reasoning.
Takeaways: Decomposing complex spatial reasoning into identifying relevant elements (reasoning priors) and then refining the target based on these priors (Prior-guided Refinement) significantly improves 3D MLLMs' performance compared to concurrent object prediction and instruction processing.

Explicitly leveraging precise instance-level visual features from segmented relevant objects as reasoning priors is crucial for accurate target localization, outperforming approaches that only use textual representations of relevant objects.

Developing a dedicated, reasoning-intensive dataset like 3D ReasonSeg is essential for pushing the boundaries of 3D MLLMs, as existing datasets do not adequately challenge or evaluate models on complex spatial understanding tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.23115.Title: MoCa: Modality-aware Continual Pre-training Makes Better Bidirectional Multimodal Embeddings
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.23115.Summary: MoCa is a two-stage framework that transforms pre-trained causal Vision-Language Models (VLMs) into robust bidirectional multimodal embedding models by applying modality-aware continual pre-training on unlabeled data and heterogeneous contrastive fine-tuning. The MoCa-7B model achieved a state-of-the-art 71.5 average Precision@1 on the MMEB benchmark and strong performance on ViDoRe-v2, demonstrating improved generalization and scalability.
Problem: Many state-of-the-art Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are designed with causal attention for generation, which is suboptimal for embedding tasks requiring comprehensive context understanding.

Current multimodal embedding methods heavily rely on large, costly labeled image-text pairs, limiting scalability and preventing the effective use of vast amounts of readily available unlabeled multimodal data.

Existing VLM-based embedding approaches often use a single contrastive objective on relatively narrow datasets, which can lead to models that overfit and struggle to generalize to diverse multimodal scenarios beyond simple image-caption pairs.

Method: MoCa adapts pre-trained causal VLMs to a bidirectional attention mechanism by removing causal masks and applying mean pooling for embedding extraction.

It introduces Modality-aware Continual Pre-training (MCPT) with a joint denoising objective (Masked Language Modeling for text and Masked Autoencoding for images) on massive unlabeled multimodal data.

The framework incorporates Heterogeneous Contrastive Fine-tuning (HCFT) using a broad range of supervised data, including long-form multimodal documents, curated pairs, and text-only pairs, along with task-aware batching.

The framework incorporates Heterogeneous Contrastive Fine-tuning (HCFT) using a broad range of supervised data, including long-form multimodal documents, curated pairs, and text-only pairs, along with task-aware batching.
Results: MoCa-7B achieved a state-of-the-art average Precision@1 score of 71.5 on the Massive Multimodal Embedding Benchmark (MMEB), surpassing prior models like mmE5 (69.8) and VLM2Vec (62.9).
MoCa-3B, a smaller model, achieved an average 67.5 on MMEB and 59.8 NDCG@5 on ViDoRe-v2, demonstrating that the framework enables smaller models to match or exceed larger baselines.

Ablation studies confirmed the individual contributions of Modality-aware Continual Pre-training (MLM and MAE) and Heterogeneous Contrastive Fine-tuning (diverse data types and task-aware batching) to the overall performance gains.

Takeaways: Transforming causal VLMs into bidirectional encoders via continual pre-training with joint reconstruction (MLM+MAE) on unlabeled data significantly enhances multimodal embedding quality and scalability.
Leveraging diverse heterogeneous data sources and task-aware batching during contrastive fine-tuning is crucial for improving model generalization and robustness across various multimodal tasks.

The benefits of large-scale unlabeled continual pre-training can enable smaller models (e.g., 3B) to achieve performance comparable to or exceeding larger models (e.g., 7B) trained with less comprehensive methods.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.23061.Title: Empowering Small VLMs to Think with Dynamic Memorization and Exploration
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.23061.Summary: Researchers from The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) introduced DyME (Dynamic Memorize–Explore), a novel training paradigm that empowers Small-scale Vision-Language Models (SVLMs) with robust thinking capabilities. DyME achieves this by dynamically integrating supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, leading to significant performance improvements and allowing SVLMs to match or even surpass some much larger models in reasoning tasks. For instance, DyME improved SmolVLM's medical VQA score by 6.0% and chart understanding by 6.5%.
Problem: Small-scale Vision-Language Models (SVLMs) struggle to perform complex, multi-step reasoning tasks, which are typically exclusive to Large-scale VLMs (LVLMs) due to their limited parameter capacity.

Existing training paradigms for reasoning, such as Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on Chain-of-Thought (CoT) data and Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Reward (RLVR), are ineffective for SVLMs, often leading to 'pseudo thinking traces' or 'advantage collapse'.
Combining SFT and RLVR in a two-stage pipeline is difficult for SVLMs due to their susceptibility to local optima, making it hard to balance memorization and exploration effectively.
Method: DyME introduces a dynamic training paradigm that adaptively switches between a memorization mode (SFT) and an exploration mode (Group Relative Policy Optimization - GRPO) at each training step based on the model's performance.
In memorization (SFT) mode, a 'Visual Refiner' enriches ground-truth thinking traces by injecting concrete, image-grounded details to ensure genuine visual grounding and prevent shallow memorization.

In exploration (GRPO) mode, a 'Visual Checker' assesses the generated thinking trace's alignment with actual visual content and integrates this relevance score into the reward, guiding the model to produce visually grounded reasoning.
Results: DyME consistently delivered substantial performance gains across medical VQA, chart understanding, and geometry problem solving for all tested SVLMs, with SmolVLM (0.5B) showing an average improvement of 5.7%.
Existing training paradigms (SFT on CoT, standalone GRPO, and two-stage SFT+RL) were found to degrade or offer only marginal gains for SVLMs, validating DyME's core hypothesis.
DyME-trained SVLMs achieved performance levels comparable to or even surpassed some Large-scale VLMs (LVLMs); for example, SmolVLM (0.5B) with DyME outperformed MoVA (10B).
Takeaways: SFT and GRPO gradients are mathematically compatible, allowing seamless, dynamic interleaving of these two objectives within a unified training framework for SVLMs.

A dynamic selection mechanism that switches between SFT (when struggling) and GRPO (when partially competent) is critical for stabilizing learning, mitigating pseudo thinking, and preventing advantage collapse in SVLMs.
Explicit visual supervision, integrated via both a Visual Refiner (for SFT targets) and a Visual Checker (for GRPO rewards), ensures that SVLM reasoning is truly grounded in visual evidence.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.23044.Title: Ovis-U1 Technical Report
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.23044.Summary: Ovis-U1, a 3-billion-parameter unified model from Alibaba Group, integrates multimodal understanding, text-to-image generation, and image editing capabilities, achieving competitive performance across these tasks through a six-stage unified training approach that simultaneously optimizes all components.
Problem: Developing AI models capable of seamlessly integrating and operating across multiple modalities (text, image) for both understanding and generation tasks.
Endowing multimodal understanding models with image generation capabilities without relying on frozen or decoupled components.
Designing an effective unified training approach that allows for collaborative improvement across understanding and generation tasks, rather than separate or sequential optimization.
Method: Introduced Ovis-U1, a 3-billion-parameter unified model architecture built on Qwen3-1.7B, incorporating a visual encoder, a diffusion transformer (MMDiT) as a visual decoder, and a novel bidirectional token refiner.

Implemented a six-stage progressive unified training procedure, updating the LLM and other components using a diverse dataset that includes multimodal understanding, text-to-image generation, and various image editing data.
Utilized architectural elements like an adaptive visual encoder for arbitrary image resolutions and a learnable `[CLS]` token in the refiner for improved cross-modal interaction.
Results: Ovis-U1 achieved an average score of 69.6 on OpenCompass Multi-modal Academic Benchmarks for understanding, outperforming other open-source models in its parameter range.
Demonstrated strong generative capabilities, scoring 0.89 on GenEval and 83.72 on DPG-Bench for text-to-image generation.
Secured competitive results in image editing, with a score of 4.00 on ImgEdit-Bench and 6.42 on GEdit-Bench-EN, comparable to larger proprietary models in some aspects.
Takeaways: Training a unified model from a language model, with collaborative optimization across understanding and generation tasks, improves performance in both domains.
A bidirectional token refiner enhances interaction between visual and textual embeddings, contributing to better conditional guidance in generation and reducing reliance on external models like CLIP.
Progressive training stages, particularly incorporating image editing data late in the pipeline, can synergistically boost overall multimodal capabilities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.22992.Title: MARBLE: A Hard Benchmark for Multimodal Spatial Reasoning and Planning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.22992.Summary: Researchers from EPFL and ETH Zurich developed MARBLE, a new benchmark designed to assess multi-step multimodal spatial reasoning and planning in large language models using game-inspired tasks. Evaluations revealed that current state-of-the-art models perform near-randomly on core tasks like distinguishing correct multi-step plans or assembling 3D puzzles, demonstrating limitations in both structured perception and combinatorial reasoning capabilities.
Problem: Existing multimodal benchmarks often focus on shallow forms of reasoning or conflate perception with deeper multi-step reasoning, failing to rigorously challenge multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on complex planning and spatial understanding.

There is a critical gap in hard benchmarks that specifically stress multi-step planning and spatial reasoning under physical constraints, which is essential for developing intelligent systems that can generalize and interact adaptively with complex environments.

MLLMs' capacity for complex reasoning that integrates diverse modalities, especially vision and spatial understanding, remains nascent and poorly understood, hindering progress towards human-like intelligence.
Method: Introduces MARBLE, a challenging game-inspired multimodal reasoning benchmark with two distinct tasks: M-Portal (abstracted *Portal 2* spatial planning) and M-Cube (3D mechanical puzzle assembly).

M-Portal requires MLLMs to evaluate the correctness of multi-step solution plans or fill in missing steps, incorporating screenshots and textual instructions, and evaluating the entire reasoning process.

M-Cube challenges models to assemble a 3D cube from rendered images of interlocking pieces, with a programmatic solution validator provided to assess the correctness of proposed assemblies and support iterative refinement.
Results: On M-Portal's `plan correctness` task, all evaluated MLLMs and text-only LLMs achieved near-random F1 scores of approximately 6%, indicating an inability to reliably distinguish correct from incorrect multi-step plans.

All advanced MLLMs completely failed on the harder `CUBE` task within M-Cube, achieving 0% accuracy, and even on the simplified `CUBE-easy` task, only one model (GPT-o3) achieved a substantial accuracy (72.0%), while others performed significantly lower.

A specific perception task for M-Cube revealed that models achieved 0% accuracy in perfectly extracting structured visual information (5x5 array) from a single 3D-rendered jigsaw piece image, highlighting a foundational perceptual limitation.
Takeaways: Current MLLMs exhibit fundamental weaknesses in structured visual perception, unable to perfectly extract structured information from images (e.g., converting a 3D-rendered piece to a 2D array representation).
Navigating vast combinatorial search spaces for multi-step planning and problem-solving remains a significant bottleneck for state-of-the-art MLLMs, even when perceptual challenges are simplified.

While tool use and iterative feedback can offer marginal improvements on simplified tasks, they do not compensate for a lack of fundamental reasoning capability in highly complex multimodal scenarios.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.22982.Title: Revisiting CroPA: A Reproducibility Study and Enhancements for Cross-Prompt Adversarial Transferability in Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.22982.Summary: A study on Cross-Prompt Attack (CroPA) for Vision-Language Models validates the original framework's claims and introduces methodological enhancements. These improvements boost attack success rates, accelerate convergence, and enhance cross-model and cross-image transferability of adversarial examples.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) face vulnerabilities to adversarial attacks that perturb images to mislead models across various text prompts.
The foundational Cross-Prompt Attack (CroPA) framework required thorough reproduction and validation to confirm its claims and understand its limitations.
Existing CroPA methods exhibited limitations in attack success rate, convergence efficiency, and generalizability across diverse images and VLM architectures.
Method: A rigorous reproducibility study confirmed CroPA's core claims regarding cross-prompt transferability and performance across prompt numbers and few-shot settings.
A semantically informed noise initialization strategy, leveraging diffusion models, was developed to guide adversarial perturbations more effectively.
A novel loss function was introduced to target the vision encoder's value vectors, enhancing architectural sensitivity and improving attack generalization.
Image augmentation techniques (SCMix, CutMix) were integrated during perturbation generation to improve the cross-image transferability of adversarial examples.
Results: Reproducibility experiments validated CroPA's superior targeted ASR (Attack Success Rate) compared to baselines, demonstrating consistent cross-prompt misleading of VLMs.
The CroPA+Init method, with diffusion-based initialization, achieved a 6-15% average increase in overall ASR and faster convergence on BLIP-2.
CroPA+D-UAP (value vector guidance) boosted targeted ASR by over 10% on BLIP-2 and OpenFlamingo and improved intra-family cross-model transferability by 17-18%.
SCMix augmentation increased untargeted cross-image ASR from 43.55% (base CroPA) to 70.55%, showing progress in learning universal perturbations.
Takeaways: The cross-prompt adversarial transferability of visual perturbations against VLMs is a verifiable and robust vulnerability.
Intelligent initialization, rather than random noise, is crucial for improving the efficacy and speed of bi-level adversarial optimization.
Targeting specific architectural components, like vision encoder value vectors, can create more potent and transferable adversarial examples, especially within similar VLM families.
Data augmentation during adversarial training partially enables the learning of universal perturbations that generalize across multiple images.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.22880.Title: Decoupled Seg Tokens Make Stronger Reasoning Video Segmenter and Grounder
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.22880.Summary: DeSa2VA presents a novel framework that decouples textual and visual information within multimodal large language models, significantly enhancing grounded image and video segmentation performance. The method achieves state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks by pre-training the segmentation model for text understanding and employing a robust decoupling scheme, while maintaining strong performance on question answering tasks.
Problem: Existing multimodal approaches integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) with segmentation models often suffer from information entanglement, where dynamic visual information and static semantics become indistinguishably fused.
Prompts generated by LLMs for segmentation models lack sufficient semantic detail, limiting precise alignment and fine-grained guidance for pixel-level predictions.
Foundation segmentation models like SAM-2 are primarily designed for visual prompts and lack inherent capabilities for directly interpreting complex text-based information.
Method: Introduces a multi-modal decoupling module that uses linear layers, adversarial training with discriminators, and mutual information minimization to separate MLLM-generated hidden states into distinct textual and visual feature subspaces.
Implements a novel pre-training paradigm for SAM-2, enabling it to directly learn text understanding by processing real textual labels converted into interpretable point prompts.
Incorporates an improved dense prompting mechanism through self-feedback generation, where an initial predicted mask is reused as a dense prompt for iterative refinement of segmentation quality.
Results: Achieved state-of-the-art image segmentation on RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, and RefCOCOg, with gains of 3.7, 6.1, and 5.1 percentage points respectively over the Sa2VA baseline.

Maintained comparable performance to Sa2VA on image and video question answering benchmarks (SEED-Bench and Video-MME), demonstrating that segmentation improvements do not compromise language understanding.
Outperformed baselines in Grounded Caption Generation, indicating stronger cross-modal association and robust performance in both segmentation and text generation.
Takeaways: Decoupling textual and visual modalities using adversarial training and mutual information minimization effectively mitigates information entanglement, leading to more precise multimodal understanding.
