Pre-training foundation segmentation models like SAM-2 directly on textual labels is crucial for enabling explicit text understanding and bridging the modality gap between language and vision models.
Iterative self-feedback, where an initial mask is reused as a dense prompt, consistently improves segmentation performance without adding parameters.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.22819.Title: Prompting without Panic: Attribute-aware, Zero-shot, Test-Time Calibration
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.22819.Summary: Researchers from IIT Delhi and TCS Research Labs developed Test-time Calibration via Attribute Alignment (TCA), a method to improve confidence calibration in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) during zero-shot, test-time prompt tuning. The approach achieved an average Expected Calibration Error (ECE) of 4.11 for CLIP-RN50 and 4.05 for CLIP-ViT-B/16 across 11 fine-grained classification datasets, outperforming prior methods while maintaining or improving predictive accuracy.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) adapted with Test-Time Prompt Tuning (TPT) often suffer from miscalibration, leading to overconfident predictions despite improved accuracy.
Traditional calibration methods require labeled validation data or retraining, making them incompatible with the zero-shot, test-time adaptation paradigm.
Naive prompt initialization in TPT can cause prompts to overfit to single test samples, further exacerbating miscalibration and eroding model trustworthiness.
Method: The method, Test-time Calibration via Attribute Alignment (TCA), employs attribute-aware prompt initialization using LLM-generated visual attributes to create semantically rich starting points for prompts.

A novel contrastive regularization loss is introduced, comprising intra-class attribute contraction (pulling attributes of a class closer) and inter-class text feature dispersion (pushing different class representations apart).
This approach operates entirely in a zero-shot, test-time setting, freezing the VLM encoders and updating only soft prompts, without requiring any labeled data or model fine-tuning.
Results: TCA consistently achieved substantially lower Expected Calibration Error (ECE) compared to state-of-the-art TPT methods, reporting average ECEs of 4.11 (CLIP-RN50) and 4.05 (CLIP-ViT-B/16) across 11 fine-grained datasets.

The method demonstrated superior robustness to natural distribution shifts, achieving significantly lower average ECEs on ImageNet variants (e.g., 8.24 for CLIP-RN50 Ensemble and 3.81 for CLIP-ViT-B/16 Ensemble).

Ablation studies confirmed that attribute-aware initialization alone reduced ECE by 20.6%, while the proposed contrastive regularization loss further led to a 3.65x ECE reduction, with both components synergistically yielding a 4.59x overall reduction.
Takeaways: Leveraging LLM-extracted, ranked visual attributes for prompt initialization significantly mitigates overfitting and enhances calibration in TPT by providing more informed semantic anchors.

Explicitly structuring the prompt embedding space through contrastive regularization, which simultaneously encourages intra-class cohesion and inter-class separation, is effective for optimizing confidence calibration without labeled data.

It is possible to simultaneously improve both predictive accuracy and confidence calibration in VLMs within a practical zero-shot, test-time adaptation framework by combining attribute-aware prompt initialization with targeted regularization.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.22624.Title: Seg-R1: Segmentation Can Be Surprisingly Simple with Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.22624.Summary: Seg-R1 introduces a reinforcement learning-based framework that enables large multimodal models (LMMs) to perform pixel-level segmentation by generating sparse mask prompts for an external segmenter like SAM2. This approach achieves state-of-the-art performance in salient object detection, demonstrates robust zero-shot generalization to referring and reasoning segmentation tasks, and crucially, preserves the LMM's general-purpose capabilities.
Problem: LMMs typically require complex architectural modifications and specialized segmentation tokens to achieve pixel-level understanding, disrupting their inherent causal structure.
Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) for LMM segmentation leads to high data annotation costs, lengthy training, and catastrophic forgetting of the model's general-purpose visual comprehension.
Integrating robust and generalizable pixel-level segmentation into LMMs without compromising their existing reasoning abilities or increasing architectural complexity remains a challenge.
Method: The LMM is trained to generate a sequence of sparse mask prompts (points, bounding boxes, labels) for an external foundation model like SAM2, rather than directly predicting dense pixel masks.
Reinforcement learning, specifically Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), is used to train the LMM, leveraging its efficiency for large-scale models.

A composite reward function combining format adherence and a weighted sum of IoU (0.7) and S-Measure (0.3) guides the RL process to ensure both structural fidelity and global accuracy of generated masks.
Results: Seg-R1 achieves state-of-the-art performance in salient object detection, reaching an S-measure (Sα) of 0.878 and E-measure (Eφ) of 0.911 on DUT-OMRON.

The model exhibits remarkable zero-shot generalization, achieving a cIoU of 71.4 on RefCOCOg for referring segmentation and a gIoU of 56.7 on ReasonSeg for reasoning segmentation, outperforming prior supervised models.
Pure reinforcement learning training preserves the LMM's general-purpose capabilities across multimodal benchmarks, whereas supervised fine-tuning results in a noticeable performance degradation.
Takeaways: Reinforcement learning allows LMMs to acquire robust pixel-level segmentation capabilities by learning to generate mask prompts without requiring architectural modifications or specialized tokens.
Pure RL training effectively preserves the LMM's general-purpose visual comprehension and reasoning abilities, circumventing the catastrophic forgetting observed with supervised fine-tuning.

Training an LMM to generate sparse, human-like prompts via RL results in strong zero-shot generalization across various segmentation tasks, including referring and reasoning segmentation, despite being trained only on foreground tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.22434.Title: MiCo: Multi-image Contrast for Reinforcement Visual Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.22434.Summary: MiCo (Multi-image Contrast) introduces a self-supervised reinforcement learning framework for Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to enhance their Chain-of-Thought reasoning across multiple images without relying on human-annotated reasoning steps. The framework leverages inherent visual constraints from video frames and image editing datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance on multi-image reasoning benchmarks like VLM2-Bench and generalizing effectively to a range of other vision tasks.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) struggle to robustly link fine-grained visual cues and perform complex logical reasoning when presented with multiple related images.

Existing methods for improving VLM reasoning, especially those using reinforcement learning, heavily depend on prohibitively expensive and time-consuming human-annotated question-answer pairs with ground-truth reasoning steps.
Current VLMs often lack the "meta-cognitive" ability to effectively compare and connect visual information across different views, leading to failures or hallucinations in multi-image tasks.
Method: MiCo develops a self-supervised framework that constructs challenging visual comparison tasks by selecting visually similar but meaningfully different image pairs from video frames and image editing datasets.
It formulates training triplets using augmented views of these image pairs, implicitly supervising the VLM to identify subtle differences and similarities.

An Augmented Group Reinforcement Policy Optimization (GRPO) strategy is employed, where reasoning trajectories sampled from weakly augmented inputs are used to optimize the VLM's policy for stronger augmentations, improving generalization.
Results: MiCo-7B achieved state-of-the-art performance on the VLM2-Bench benchmark with an average accuracy of 61.06%, outperforming the Qwen2.5-VL-7B baseline by +12.93% and surpassing larger models like GPT-4o in multi-image comparison.

The framework demonstrated strong performance on other multi-image benchmarks (MuirBench, BLINK) in correspondence and spatial relation tasks, and showed steady improvements across general vision benchmarks (MMStar, MMMU, HallusionBench, MathVista).

Ablation studies confirmed the critical roles of CoT reinforcement learning, diverse data sources, the Augmented GRPO strategy, and varied prompt templates in achieving robust and generalized multi-image reasoning capabilities.
Takeaways: Self-supervised learning, leveraging inherent visual constraints, can effectively instill complex multi-image Chain-of-Thought reasoning capabilities in VLMs without the need for explicit human labels.

The Augmented GRPO strategy successfully transfers high-quality CoT reasoning behaviors learned from simpler visual conditions (weak augmentations) to more challenging ones (strong augmentations), significantly improving model generalization.

Training VLMs on visual comparison skills through contrastive learning not only enhances multi-image reasoning but also generalizes to a broader range of general vision tasks, indicating the acquisition of a fundamental "meta-cognitive" visual skill.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.22419.Title: The Automated LLM Speedrunning Benchmark: Reproducing NanoGPT Improvements
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.22419.Summary: Researchers at Meta introduce the Automated LLM Speedrunning Benchmark to evaluate AI agents' capacity for reproducing documented improvements in LLM training efficiency. The study finds that even state-of-the-art models and scaffolds struggle to consistently replicate human-achieved speedups, often recovering less than half of the original performance gains even with explicit guidance.
Problem: Automated scientific discovery requires AI agents to reliably reproduce existing experimental findings, a capability currently underevaluated.
There is a lack of specialized benchmarks focusing on sequential, code-level reproducibility of complex improvements within dynamic fields like LLM training.
Understanding the limitations of current LLM-based AI research agents in this foundational task is crucial for advancing autonomous research.
Method: Developed the Automated LLM Speedrunning Benchmark, comprising 19 tasks derived from the NanoGPT Speedrun, where agents reproduce successive LLM training time records from previous versions.
Implemented a flexible AI agent scaffold, extending the AIDE framework, enabling iterative code generation, execution, and analysis using various LLM backbones.

Agents are evaluated primarily by the Fraction of Speedup Recovered (FSR), measuring their ability to match human-achieved performance, with different levels of textual and pseudocode hints available.
Results: AI agents recovered under 20% of the speedup on average without hints; the best model (o3-mini) achieved up to 46% FSR with a combination of hints and Multi-AIDE search.
o3-mini generally outperformed other LLMs, while Gemini-2.5-Pro and Claude-3.7-Sonnet showed near 0% FSR in interquartile mean evaluation, and DeepSeek-R1 benefited from combined hints.
Performance declined sharply in cumulative tasks (o3-mini's FSR dropped from 60% for the 2nd record to 20% for the 3rd), and external documentation negatively impacted results.
Takeaways: Current LLM agents struggle to reproduce scientific improvements, achieving less than 20% of the speedup without hints, highlighting a fundamental challenge for automated science.
Explicit hints, especially pseudocode, are crucial for improving agent performance, though the best agents still recover less than half of the human-achieved speedups.
Agents exhibit difficulty integrating external knowledge and show significant performance degradation when attempting to cumulatively reproduce multiple successive findings.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.22395.Title: Test-Time Consistency in Vision Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.22395.Summary: Researchers from the University of British Columbia and Vector Institute introduce a test-time consistency framework that adaptively tunes Vision-Language Model parameters at inference. This approach significantly improves semantic consistency and overall performance on the MM-R3 benchmark across various models and tasks.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) often produce inconsistent or contradictory outputs when presented with semantically equivalent inputs, such as rephrased questions or restyled images.
This semantic inconsistency undermines the reliability, interpretability, and trustworthiness of VLMs, particularly in high-stakes applications.

Existing consistency-enhancing methods typically involve computationally intensive training-time solutions like architectural modifications or large-scale fine-tuning, which are impractical for many deployment scenarios or proprietary models.
Method: A lightweight, post-hoc test-time consistency framework that applies a small number of gradient-based updates to the VLM's language modeling head at inference time, using only the single test input.

The method uses two complementary objectives: Cross-Entropy Agreement Loss (L_CE) to align token-level output distributions across semantically equivalent input variants, and Pseudo-Label Consistency Loss (L_PL) to guide predictions towards a dominant self-consistent pseudo-label.
An adaptive step selection mechanism automatically determines the optimal number of update steps per test instance by maximizing an internal consistency score, eliminating the need for manual tuning.
Results: The proposed test-time consistency framework achieved substantial gains in semantic consistency and overall performance across LLaVA 1.5M, LLaVA-Next, and Qwen2-VL models on the MM-R3 benchmark.
For LLaVA-1.5M, the overall score (O_all) improved from 52.73 to 64.08 on Question Rephrasing, with consistency (Con) rising from 48.55 to 79.11.

The test-time approach yielded performance competitive with, and in some cases superior to, resource-intensive full fine-tuning, while demonstrating that consistency gains did not degrade base model accuracy on unperturbed data.
Takeaways: Semantic consistency in Vision-Language Models can be improved at inference time through lightweight, instance-specific parameter adaptation without requiring supervised retraining.
Combining token-level distributional alignment (Cross-Entropy Agreement Loss) with sequence-level pseudo-label guidance (Pseudo-Label Consistency Loss) effectively enforces VLM consistency.
An adaptive selection of update steps is important to prevent over-adaptation and optimize consistency for individual test instances, while generally preserving or improving base model accuracy.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.22355.Title: Embodied AI Agents: Modeling the World
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.22355.Summary: Meta AI Research proposes a world-modeling approach for embodied AI agents, arguing it addresses limitations of current generative models by enabling agents to understand, simulate, and reason about physical and mental environments. Their work highlights existing AI models' struggles on new benchmarks for physical and causal reasoning while demonstrating improved performance in visual understanding and planning assistance with their integrated systems.
Problem: Existing 'disembodied' AI systems, like large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs), lack a fundamental understanding of the physical world and direct means of interaction.

Generative models are often inefficient and prone to hallucination when applied to embodied tasks, as their next-token/pixel prediction objective often misses essential information for robust reasoning and planning.
There is a need to develop AI agents capable of natural, intuitive interaction with both users and environments, similar to human learning and engagement.
Method: Meta AI proposes developing embodied AI agents centered on a 'world modeling' approach, which enables agents to understand, simulate, and reason about their environment.

The approach integrates multimodal perception (image, video, audio, speech, touch) and focuses on building distinct 'physical world models' (e.g., JEPA-based in latent space) and 'mental world models' (for human intentions).

The research involves creating novel, rigorous benchmarks (e.g., Minimal Video Pairs, IntPhys 2, CausalVQA, WorldPrediction) to evaluate physical and causal reasoning capabilities beyond traditional metrics.
Results: Meta AI's new benchmarks reveal significant performance gaps: SOTA video-language models achieve 40.2% on Minimal Video Pairs (MVP) compared to 92.9% human, and 38% on WorldPrediction-PP (procedural planning) versus near-perfect human scores.
Perception Language Models (PLMs) demonstrate state-of-the-art visual understanding, with improvements over open models (e.g., +39.8 CIDEr for video captioning).
Vision-Language World Models (VLWM) for wearable agents show improved planning assistance (e.g., +20% success rate, +10% mean action accuracy) over prompting-based baselines.
Takeaways: True intelligence in AI requires grounding in real-world interaction, moving beyond disembodied models.
World models are essential for robust reasoning, planning, and overcoming the limitations (inefficiency, hallucination) of purely generative models in embodied contexts.
Proactive consideration of ethical implications like privacy and anthropomorphism is critical for responsible embodied AI development.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.21872.Title: A Survey of Continual Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.21872.Summary: This survey paper provides a comprehensive review of Continual Reinforcement Learning (CRL), introducing a novel taxonomy that categorizes methods based on whether they primarily store and transfer knowledge related to policies, experiences, environment dynamics, or reward signals. It identifies the unique challenges of CRL, such as the stability-plasticity-scalability dilemma, and outlines future research directions and applications across various domains.
Problem: Traditional Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) agents suffer from "catastrophic forgetting," losing previously acquired knowledge when learning new tasks.
DRL often requires extensive training data and computational resources, limiting its efficiency and generalization in dynamic, real-world, non-stationary environments.
Agents struggle to continuously learn and adapt to new tasks while retaining knowledge from prior experiences, necessitating relearning from scratch for each new task.
Method: Continual Reinforcement Learning (CRL) aims to enable agents to learn new tasks sequentially while retaining knowledge and leveraging prior experiences more efficiently.

This survey proposes a novel taxonomy that classifies CRL methods based on *what knowledge* is stored and transferred (policy, experience, dynamics, reward) to provide a structured understanding of the field.
The paper provides a comprehensive review of existing CRL methods within this new framework, standardizes scenario settings and evaluation metrics, and outlines open challenges.
Results: The survey classified existing CRL methods into four main categories based on knowledge management: policy-focused (e.g., reuse, decomposition, merging), experience-focused (e.g., direct, generative replay), dynamic-focused (e.g., direct, indirect modeling), and reward-focused (e.g., shaping, intrinsic rewards).

Key challenges and future research directions were identified, including task-free CRL, the need for improved evaluation and benchmarks, interpretable knowledge, integration with large-scale pre-trained models (including LLMs), and application to embodied agents.
Common application areas for CRL were summarized, spanning robotics, game playing, natural language processing, medical imaging, finance, and autonomous driving.
Takeaways: Continual Reinforcement Learning (CRL) extends traditional Continual Learning by explicitly addressing a "triangular balance" among plasticity (learning new tasks), stability (retaining old knowledge), and scalability (resource efficiency for many tasks).
A novel taxonomy categorizes CRL methods based on the type of knowledge they manage for transfer and retention: policy-focused, experience-focused, dynamic-focused, and reward-focused.

Standardized scenario settings (Lifelong Adaptation, Non-Stationarity Learning, Task Incremental Learning, Task-Agnostic Learning) and evaluation metrics (average performance, forgetting, transfer, efficiency) are essential for consistent assessment of CRL systems.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.21734.Title: Hierarchical Reasoning Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.21734.Summary: The Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM), developed by researchers from Sapient Intelligence and Tsinghua University, introduces a recurrent architecture designed for deep algorithmic reasoning. The model, trained on minimal data, achieves near-perfect accuracy on complex tasks like Sudoku-Extreme and Maze-Hard, where leading large language models fail, and outperforms them on the ARC-AGI challenge, while also demonstrating emergent brain-like hierarchical processing.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) based on Transformer architectures possess a "paradoxically shallow" computational depth (AC0 or TC0), limiting their ability to perform complex algorithmic reasoning, planning, or symbolic manipulation.

Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, while used to enable LLMs to tackle complex problems, suffers from brittleness, high data requirements, increased latency, and a dependence on explicit linguistic patterns for reasoning.

Standard recurrent neural networks (RNNs) struggle to achieve deep latent reasoning due to premature convergence (states settling too quickly) and high memory costs (O(T)) associated with Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT).
Method: A novel recurrent architecture with two interdependent modules: a high-level (H) module for slow, abstract planning and a low-level (L) module for rapid, detailed computations, updated through a hierarchical convergence mechanism.

A memory-efficient "one-step gradient" training approach, inspired by Deep Equilibrium Models, which approximates gradients without requiring Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT), maintaining O(1) memory complexity.

Incorporates Adaptive Computational Time (ACT) using a Q-learning head, allowing the model to dynamically determine the number of computational steps based on task complexity, and enables performance scaling during inference by simply increasing the maximum step limit.
Results: Achieved near-perfect accuracy (e.g., 55.0% on Sudoku-Extreme 9x9 and 74.5% on Maze-Hard 30x30) with only 1000 training samples, tasks on which state-of-the-art CoT-based LLMs failed completely (0% accuracy).
Outperformed significantly larger CoT-based LLMs on the ARC-AGI-1 challenge (40.3% vs. Claude 3.7's 21.2% and o3-mini-high's 34.5%), trained only on the official dataset (~1000 examples).

Showed an emergent dimensionality hierarchy akin to the mouse cortex, with the high-level module (zH) exhibiting a much higher participation ratio (PR = 89.95) than the low-level module (zL, PR = 30.22) during task execution, a property that was learned during training.
Takeaways: HRM achieves significant computational depth through hierarchical convergence, where the high-level module provides fresh context, effectively 'resetting' the low-level module's path and enabling a sequence of distinct, stable computations over an effective depth of N*T steps.

The model demonstrates an emergent hierarchical dimensionality organization in its hidden states, with the high-level module operating in a significantly higher-dimensional space than the low-level module, mirroring observations in biological neural systems.

HRM can learn complex algorithmic solutions from minimal data (e.g., 1000 examples) and parameters (27M), challenging the paradigm that requires massive datasets and pre-training for advanced reasoning tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.21710.Title: FOCUS: Internal MLLM Representations for Efficient Fine-Grained Visual Question Answering
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.21710.Summary: Researchers from Technical University of Berlin, Technical University of Munich, CARIAD SE, and Volkswagen AG developed FOCUS, a training-free visual cropping method that enhances multimodal large language model (MLLM) performance on fine-grained Visual Question Answering (VQA). This approach achieved up to 42% higher accuracy on LLaVA-1.5 and 17% higher on LLaVA-OneVision for fine-grained tasks, while requiring 3 to 6.5 times less computational effort than existing methods.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle with fine-grained visual details in high-resolution images due to downscaling, leading to information loss.
Existing visual cropping techniques are often computationally inefficient, require extensive task-specific fine-tuning, or are incompatible with modern efficient attention mechanisms.
Global-local-view MLLMs, while using local crops, still face challenges in identifying the few truly relevant visual tokens amidst a large volume of visual input.
Method: FOCUS extracts target objects from VQA prompts using in-context learning, then constructs object relevance maps by comparing cached MLLM internal value features (V-V pseudo-attention) from multiple transformer layers.
The method proposes and expands potential image regions of interest (ROIs) around high-relevance anchor points, applying non-maximum suppression for redundancy reduction.
It re-ranks proposed ROIs based on MLLM's confidence scores for object existence within each region, then performs VQA on the top-ranked or combined relevant regions.
Results: FOCUS improved LLaVA-1.5 accuracy by an average of 42% and LLaVA-OneVision by 17% on fine-grained VQA benchmarks (V*Bench, HRBench-4K, HRBench-8K).

The method achieved comparable or superior accuracy to existing state-of-the-art baselines like ZoomEye, while requiring 3 to 6.5 times fewer forward passes (compute) and significantly faster inference.
When integrated with Qwen-2.5-VL, FOCUS set new state-of-the-art accuracy on HRBench-4K (79.25%) and HRBench-8K (76.25%).
Takeaways: MLLMs' internal KV-cache value features can be effectively repurposed to construct object relevance maps, enabling precise localization without explicit attention weights or additional training.
A confidence-based re-ranking mechanism for proposed ROIs significantly improves the robustness and accuracy of fine-grained detail identification by filtering out noisy relevance scores.

Leveraging combined relevance maps and existence confidence allows for an efficient and training-free visual cropping approach that dramatically reduces computational overhead while boosting MLLM fine-grained perception.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.21656.Title: Fine-Grained Preference Optimization Improves Spatial Reasoning in VLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.21656.Summary: SpatialReasoner-R1, a Vision-Language Model, introduces enhanced capabilities for fine-grained, multi-step spatial reasoning from 2D images. The model achieved new state-of-the-art accuracy on the SPATIALRGPT-BENCH dataset, demonstrating a 15.8% improvement in quantitative spatial tasks through novel fine-grained Direct Preference Optimization (fDPO) and Multi-Model Monte Carlo Tree Search (M3CTS) for data generation.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language Models (VLMs) demonstrate limitations in performing fine-grained, multi-step spatial reasoning from 2D images, particularly for precise object relationships and quantitative estimations.
The scarcity of high-quality, structured Long Chain-of-Thought (LongCoT) supervision data specifically designed for complex spatial reasoning hinders the development of robust VLMs in this domain.

Traditional preference optimization methods (e.g., DPO) apply uniform learning signals across entire responses, which is suboptimal for multi-component reasoning where different segments (e.g., visual descriptions vs. logical inferences) require distinct optimization strategies.
Method: Introduced `SpatialReasoner-R1`, a VLM based on the Sa2VA architecture, designed to generate structured LongCoT responses that decompose complex spatial queries into verifiable steps.

Developed `Multi-Model Monte Carlo Tree Search (M3CTS)` to generate a diverse and high-quality `OPEN SPATIAL REASONING dataset`, leveraging multiple VLMs and fine-grained spatial rewards to create LongCoT preference pairs.

Proposed `fine-grained Direct Preference Optimization (fDPO)`, an off-policy preference learning algorithm that applies segment-specific preference granularity and adaptively tuned parameters to optimize distinct components of spatial reasoning (description and inference) within LongCoT.
Results: SpatialReasoner-R1 fDPO 8B achieved state-of-the-art performance on the SPATIALRGPT-BENCH dataset, with a 9.4% improvement in average accuracy over the strongest baseline, SpatialRGPT-8B.
The model demonstrated a 15.8% improvement in accuracy on spatial quantitative tasks and a 2.9% improvement on spatial qualitative tasks compared to SpatialRGPT-8B.

fDPO significantly outperformed standard DPO, showing a relative gain of 9.0% on quantitative tasks and 4.1% on qualitative tasks, validating the effectiveness of segment-specific optimization for complex reasoning.
Takeaways: Decomposing complex spatial reasoning into explicit, verifiable LongCoT steps, guided by a robust, fine-grained spatial reward mechanism, substantially improves VLM capabilities beyond superficial visual understanding.

A multi-model Monte Carlo Tree Search (M3CTS) approach effectively addresses data scarcity by generating high-quality, diverse, and logically consistent LongCoT data for specialized domains like spatial reasoning.

Applying adaptive, segment-specific preference optimization (fDPO) significantly enhances model alignment and performance for multi-step reasoning tasks by differentiating the learning signals for distinct semantic components of a generated response.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.21495.Title: Bridging Offline and Online Reinforcement Learning for LLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.21495.Summary: Researchers at FAIR at Meta and NYU demonstrated that Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), when adapted to online or semi-online training, consistently outperforms offline DPO and performs comparably to online GRPO for LLM alignment, achieving up to a 56.6% increase in AlpacaEval LC winrate for non-verifiable tasks. They also showed the feasibility of training a single LLM on both verifiable and non-verifiable tasks simultaneously to improve generalization.
Problem: Traditional offline reinforcement learning methods for LLM alignment (like DPO) often underperform compared to online methods, but fully online methods (like PPO/GRPO) are computationally expensive due to frequent model synchronization.
There is a lack of systematic comparison and understanding of the trade-offs between offline, semi-online, and fully online LLM alignment training paradigms across diverse tasks.

Training LLMs on different types of rewards (e.g., human preferences for open-ended tasks vs. binary correctness for verifiable tasks) can lead to models specialized in one domain but lacking generalization to others, or even exhibiting 'reward hacking'.
Method: The researchers systematically explored three training regimes for LLM alignment – offline, semi-online (periodic synchronization), and fully online (per-step synchronization) – varying the `s` parameter for synchronization frequency.

They adapted Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and utilized Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) across these regimes, comparing their performance on both verifiable math problems and non-verifiable open-ended instruction following tasks.

They investigated multi-task training by sequentially fine-tuning and jointly fine-tuning a base Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct model with mixed reward signals from both verifiable (Math-Verify) and non-verifiable (Athene-RM-8B) sources.
Results: Semi-online and fully online DPO consistently and significantly outperform offline DPO across both verifiable math tasks and non-verifiable instruction following, with online DPO showing up to a 56.6% increase in AlpacaEval LC winrate over offline DPO for non-verifiable tasks.
Online DPO achieves performance comparable to or marginally better than online Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) in both verifiable and non-verifiable settings.

Jointly training a single LLM with both verifiable and non-verifiable reward signals yields performance gains across both task types, demonstrating the feasibility of developing more general-purpose models without performance degradation in specific domains.
Takeaways: Semi-online training (periodic generator synchronization) achieves performance comparable to fully online methods while offering substantial computational efficiency gains by enabling asynchronous response generation.

Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), traditionally an offline algorithm, can achieve performance comparable to or better than on-policy methods like GRPO when adapted to online or semi-online settings.

To develop general-purpose LLMs, exposure to both verifiable (e.g., math) and non-verifiable (e.g., instruction following) reward signals is crucial, and joint training with mixed rewards is feasible and beneficial.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.21458.Title: Spatial Mental Modeling from Limited Views
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.21458.Summary: Researchers introduce MINDCUBE, a benchmark for evaluating Vision-Language Models' spatial mental modeling from limited views, revealing that current models struggle with inferring hidden information. They demonstrate that supervised fine-tuning combined with reinforcement learning, teaching models to internally generate cognitive maps and reasoning chains, significantly improves spatial reasoning, boosting performance from 47.62% to 70.67% accuracy.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language Models (VLMs) struggle with spatial reasoning from limited views, exhibiting near-random performance on tasks requiring inferring hidden information or maintaining cross-view consistency.

Current VLM benchmarks primarily focus on passive perception, failing to adequately evaluate models' ability to build and leverage robust internal "spatial mental models" for dynamic, partially observable environments.

VLMs lack the ability to effectively synthesize spatial information across sparse viewpoints, reason about objects not directly visible, or perform "what-if" simulations of viewpoint changes, critical for embodied AI.
There is a need to understand whether cognitive-inspired scaffolding and advanced training paradigms can bridge the gap between current VLM capabilities and human-like spatial understanding.
Method: The paper introduces MINDCUBE, a new benchmark with 21,154 questions across 3,268 images, designed to specifically evaluate VLMs' spatial mental modeling from limited views, including reasoning about unseen elements and dynamic viewpoint changes.
It proposes training VLMs to explicitly generate internal spatial representations, specifically 2D cognitive maps and free-form reasoning chains, as a means to foster robust spatial understanding.

The research employs a multi-stage training paradigm: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to teach VLMs to internalize and generate these spatial representations, followed by reinforcement learning (RL) to refine their spatial reasoning for higher accuracy.

Different cognitive scaffolding approaches are explored, including view interpolation, direct input of cognitive maps, and Chain-of-Thought prompting, to understand their effects on VLM spatial reasoning.
Results: State-of-the-art VLMs performed poorly on the MINDCUBE benchmark, with the best model achieving only 47.62% accuracy against a ~32% chance baseline, confirming a significant spatial reasoning gap.

Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on joint cognitive map generation and free-form reasoning chains boosted VLM accuracy to 60.76% (+22.95% over baseline), with generated maps achieving 88.79% overall similarity to ground truth.
Reinforcement learning (RL) warm-started from the best SFT checkpoint further improved accuracy to 70.67% (+9.91% over best SFT, +32.86% over baseline), producing high-quality plain cognitive maps.

A bottleneck analysis revealed that fine-tuning only the LLM component of the VLM captured nearly all performance gains (51.43% vs. 52.28% for full fine-tuning), whereas fine-tuning only the vision encoder yielded no improvement.

Providing pre-computed augmented cognitive maps as direct input to frozen VLMs degraded performance, while prompting for free-form reasoning or map generation offered modest gains (e.g., +3.62% for Plain-CGMap-FFR-Out prompting).
Takeaways: The Large Language Model (LLM) component, not the vision encoder, is the primary bottleneck for spatial reasoning in VLMs, indicating reasoning capabilities are key.
Teaching VLMs to explicitly generate and reason over internal cognitive maps, inspired by human spatial models, significantly improves their spatial understanding.

Combining supervised fine-tuning (SFT) for initial learning with reinforcement learning (RL) for refinement proves highly effective, achieving a "1+1 > 2" synergy in developing robust spatial intelligence.
Models trained to jointly generate cognitive maps and reasoning chains achieve superior performance in spatial reasoning tasks compared to models trained on raw QA pairs or map generation alone.
Simpler, object-only cognitive maps (Plain-CGMap) are more effective for SFT than augmented maps that include camera views, likely due to reduced complexity in learning internal representations.

RL significantly refines spatial reasoning when warm-started from a strong SFT checkpoint, boosting accuracy by nearly 10% over the best SFT results, indicating its role in polishing learned behaviors rather than building from scratch.

The act of prompting frozen VLMs to generate free-form reasoning or cognitive maps, even imperfectly, improves their QA accuracy, suggesting that explicit internal thought processes aid spatial understanding.

The study confirms that state-of-the-art VLMs perform near-randomly on complex spatial tasks requiring inference about unseen elements and cross-view consistency, highlighting a critical gap in their capabilities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.21215.Title: Unveiling Causal Reasoning in Large Language Models: Reality or Mirage?
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.21215.Summary: A study from the National University of Defense Technology and collaborators assessed large language models' causal reasoning capabilities, revealing their reliance on memorized patterns rather than genuine understanding when evaluated on the novel CausalProbe-2024 benchmark. The proposed G2-Reasoner, which integrates external general knowledge and goal-oriented prompts, improved performance on these fresh causal tasks.
Problem: Determining whether large language models exhibit genuine causal reasoning or merely sophisticated pattern matching based on training data.
The inadequacy of existing causal reasoning benchmarks due to potential data contamination, hindering accurate evaluation of LLMs' generalization abilities.
Understanding the theoretical limitations of autoregressive transformer-based LLMs in performing true causal inference.
Method: Differentiating between Level-1 (retrieval-based) and Level-2 (deductive, genuine) causal reasoning to categorize LLM capabilities.
Constructing CausalProbe-2024, a novel causal reasoning benchmark utilizing news articles published after LLM training cut-offs, to mitigate data contamination.
Designing G2-Reasoner, a method that combines retrieved external general knowledge with goal-oriented prompting to guide LLMs toward more robust causal inference.
Results: Large language models experienced a substantial decline in exact match accuracy on the novel CausalProbe-2024 benchmark (e.g., Claude 3 Opus from 0.991 to 0.758 EM on CausalProbe-E), confirming their struggle with unseen causal reasoning tasks.

G2-Reasoner consistently improved LLM performance on causal reasoning, including on challenging fresh and counterfactual scenarios (e.g., LLaMA 2 7B improved on CausalProbe-H from 0.565 to 0.582 EM), surpassing baseline prompting and RAG-only approaches.
The goal-oriented prompting component of G2-Reasoner proved crucial, as retrieval-augmented generation alone did not consistently lead to performance gains for causal inference.
Takeaways: Large language models predominantly perform Level-1 causal reasoning by retrieving patterns from training data, rather than deep Level-2 deduction.
The autoregressive nature of LLMs inherently limits their capacity for genuine causal inference, as sequential dependencies do not directly equate to logical causality.
Effective integration of external knowledge for causal reasoning requires specific goal-oriented prompting to guide the LLM's inference process.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.21046.Title: Boosting Generative Adversarial Transferability with Self-supervised Vision Transformer Features
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.21046.Summary: The Beijing Institute of Technology research presents dSVA, a generative adversarial attack leveraging self-supervised Vision Transformer (ViT) features for enhanced black-box transferability. This approach, which exploits ViT facet-level features, self-attention saliency maps, and jointly disrupts both global structural and local textural representations, achieves superior performance, outperforming state-of-the-art attacks by an average of 13.70% and robust defenses by 32.98% against diverse models.
Problem: Generating highly transferable adversarial examples for black-box attacks, where the adversary has no access to the target model's internal parameters.
Existing black-box adversarial attacks predominantly relied on features from supervised Convolutional Neural Networks (ConvNets).
The rich, semantically meaningful representations learned by self-supervised Vision Transformers (ViTs) remained largely unexplored for boosting adversarial transferability.
Method: Developed dSVA, a generative adversarial attack that exploits specific facet-level features within self-supervised Vision Transformers (ViTs).
Utilized self-attention saliency maps from ViTs as 'dense semantic guides' to focus adversarial perturbations on semantically important image regions.
Jointly optimized the attack by disrupting complementary features from both Contrastive Learning (DINO) and Masked Image Modeling (MAE) self-supervised ViT models.
Results: The dSVA attack achieved state-of-the-art black-box transferability, outperforming existing generative and gradient-based attacks on ImageNet.
dSVA (Joint) improved attack success rates by an average of 13.70% over single-model variants and by 32.98% against adversarially trained defense models.

Facet-level exploitation (keys for DINO, queries for MAE) and self-attention saliency maps in the penultimate layer (l=10) were found to be most effective for maximizing transferability across diverse target architectures.
Takeaways: Exploiting granular 'facet-level' features (queries and keys) within ViT attention blocks yields more generalizable adversarial perturbations than aggregated layer outputs.
Self-attention saliency maps from self-supervised ViTs provide effective semantic guidance for regularizing attacks, focusing on perceptually important regions.
Features learned by Contrastive Learning (global structure) and Masked Image Modeling (local texture) are complementary, and jointly disrupting both leads to superior adversarial transferability.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.20134.Title: From 2D to 3D Cognition: A Brief Survey of General World Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.20134.Summary: This survey provides a structured and forward-looking review of general world models, emphasizing their transition from primarily 2D visual perception to comprehensive 3D spatial cognition. It highlights how advancements in 3D representations and the integration of physical and learned world knowledge are enabling models to achieve 3D physical scene generation, spatial reasoning, and interaction, outlining critical challenges and future research directions.
Problem: Prior world models primarily focused on 2D visual perception, which limited their ability to accurately simulate motion, physical interactions, and causal reasoning in true 3D environments.
A lack of systematic analysis existed to categorize emerging techniques and clarify their roles in advancing 3D cognitive world models, despite rapid progress in 3D-aware generative models.
Existing surveys often focused on rendering realism or abstract structural modeling without a unified perspective on the transition to comprehensive 3D cognition and active interaction.
Method: The survey introduces a conceptual framework to systematically review world models as they evolve from 2D perception to 3D cognition, organizing various components and capabilities.

It dissects core cognitive capabilities—3D Physical Scene Generation, 3D Spatial Reasoning, and 3D Spatial Interaction—analyzing how models achieve these by leveraging 3D representations and world knowledge.
The paper examines real-world applications and identifies open challenges and promising future directions across data, modeling, and deployment, providing a roadmap for research.
Results: The survey established that the field of world models is undergoing a paradigm shift towards 3D cognitive systems, recognizing that understanding and interacting with a geometrically consistent 3D world is fundamental for general intelligence.
It synthesized that advanced 3D representations and the integration of physical and learned world knowledge are the two fundamental pillars enabling this transition.

The work structured advancements around three core cognitive capabilities: 3D physical scene generation, 3D spatial reasoning, and 3D spatial interaction, demonstrating their broad applicability across embodied AI, autonomous driving, digital twins, and gaming/VR.
Takeaways: The transition to 3D cognition in world models is driven by advancements in 3D representations (e.g., NeRF, 3DGS) and the integration of diverse world knowledge (physical laws via differentiable simulations and learned commonsense from large pretrained models like LLMs/VLMs).

Three interdependent cognitive capabilities underpin 3D world modeling: 3D physical scene generation (creating physically plausible environments), 3D spatial reasoning (interpreting and analyzing 3D dynamics), and 3D spatial interaction (enabling goal-directed physical engagement).

Identifying persistent challenges in data heterogeneity, model scalability, and real-time performance is crucial, alongside proposing breakthrough paths like standardized data formats and advanced fusion techniques.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.19360.Title: SoK: Can Synthetic Images Replace Real Data? A Survey of Utility and Privacy of Synthetic Image Generation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.19360.Summary: Chung et al. present a Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) that empirically evaluates the utility and privacy of various synthetic image generation models and mitigation strategies. Their analysis establishes that synthetic data can offer a favorable utility-privacy tradeoff, often outperforming DP-SGD on real data for downstream tasks, with diffusion models generally demonstrating superior performance.
Problem: A lack of comprehensive, unified analysis and empirical benchmarking for synthetic image data regarding its utility and privacy. Existing literature focused more on tabular data or had limited scope.

Inconsistencies and fragmentation in prior empirical studies on privacy-preserving image generation, making it difficult to compare different generative models and privacy attacks under unified conditions.
Absence of a systematic framework to categorize and analyze methods, attacks, and mitigations across different stages of privacy-preserving data synthesis for image data.
Method: Introduced a novel "generation-sampling-classification pipeline" to systematically analyze information release stages and evaluate methods, attacks, and mitigations.
Conducted a broad empirical evaluation across diverse generative models (GANs, VAEs, Diffusion Models, Data Condensation) and privacy mitigation strategies (DP, adversarial training).

Employed three distinct, model-agnostic Membership Inference Attacks (MIAs) to measure privacy and standardized classification performance metrics (F1-score, Accuracy, AUC) for utility across three varied datasets.
Results: Diffusion-based models (e.g., SMP-LoRA, LoRA, TI) consistently achieved more favorable utility-privacy tradeoffs compared to GANs and VAEs across both image-based and classifier-based attacks.

Classifiers trained on high-quality synthetic data, especially from advanced diffusion models, showed superior utility for a given privacy level compared to classifiers trained directly on real data using DP-SGD.

Several synthetic data generation methods (e.g., TI, SMP-LoRA) demonstrated a better capacity to maintain or improve performance on minority groups, potentially mitigating the disparate impact sometimes observed with direct DP applications.
Takeaways: The optimal strategy for privacy-preserving synthetic image generation (e.g., sharing synthetic images vs. classifiers) is highly dependent on dataset characteristics, specific utility requirements, and privacy goals.
Synthetic data can provide superior utility-privacy tradeoffs compared to directly applying differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) to real data for classifier training.

Diffusion models generally offer more favorable utility-privacy tradeoffs, and implicit privacy gains can be achieved through careful hyperparameter tuning or specific generative process designs like multi-instance synthesis.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.18945.Title: Chain-of-Experts: Unlocking the Communication Power of Mixture-of-Experts Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.18945.Summary: The Chain-of-Experts (CoE) architecture enhances Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models by enabling sequential communication and iterative processing among experts within each layer. This approach improves performance, particularly for reasoning tasks, and offers an efficient scaling method that achieves the capabilities of deeper models with less memory.
Problem: Traditional Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models feature experts operating independently and in parallel within a layer, limiting their ability to leverage complementary reasoning patterns.
Existing MoE scaling primarily relies on increasing model depth, width, or the total number of experts, often leading to substantial computational and memory costs.
Complex tasks that benefit from multi-expert coordination may not fully utilize the capacity of MoE models due to the lack of explicit intra-layer expert interaction.
Method: A Chain-of-Experts (CoE) architecture is introduced, which processes tokens through `C` sequential communication steps within a single Transformer layer.
Each iterative step utilizes a dedicated router to dynamically select a new subset of `K/C` experts, allowing for adaptive processing based on the progressively refined token representation.
Inner residual connections are incorporated at each iterative step to ensure stable updates and preserve information throughout the multi-step refinement process.
Results: CoE (C=2, K=4 experts/iteration) consistently outperformed traditional MoE (C=1, K=8 experts) under matched per-token compute, achieving faster convergence and reduced validation loss on math reasoning tasks.
A 4-layer CoE model with 2 iterations matched the performance of significantly deeper MoE models (8 or 12 layers) while reducing memory usage by up to 42%.
Ablation studies confirmed that removing iteration-specific gating or inner residual connections severely degraded performance, underscoring their necessity for CoE's effectiveness and stability.
Takeaways: Enabling sequential communication and dynamic, iteration-specific routing among experts within a layer significantly enhances the model's capacity for compositional reasoning and expert specialization.

Introducing 'depth through expert iteration' offers an efficient new axis for scaling MoE models, capable of achieving performance comparable to much deeper or wider models with reduced resource requirements.

Both iteration-specific gating and inner residual connections are critical architectural components, preventing performance degradation and ensuring training stability in the iterative expert refinement process.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.18504.Title: Generalizing vision-language models to novel domains: A comprehensive survey
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.18504.Summary: This survey offers the first comprehensive review of knowledge transfer and generalization strategies for pretrained Vision-Language Models (VLMs), including recent Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). It systematically categorizes adaptation methods, compares their performance across diverse transfer learning settings, and identifies critical future research challenges.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs), despite strong zero-shot performance, often perform poorly on domain-specific or out-of-distribution (OOD) data.
Directly fine-tuning large pretrained VLMs with limited target data can disrupt their carefully aligned multimodal representations, leading to performance degradation.
There was a lack of a comprehensive overview of strategies for efficient knowledge transfer and generalization of VLMs to novel domains and tasks.
Method: Conducted the first comprehensive survey dedicated to VLM knowledge transfer and generalization, analyzing existing literature and methodologies.
Proposed a novel classification framework categorizing VLM adaptation methods into prompt-based, parameter-based, and feature-based approaches.
Reinterpreted traditional transfer learning settings (UDA, DG, TTA, FSL) through the unique lens of VLM-based generalization and integrated discussion of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs).
Results: The survey successfully established a novel categorization of VLM generalization methods: prompt-based, parameter-based, and feature-based.
Performance comparisons indicate that Vision Transformer (ViT) backbones achieve approximately 15% higher generalization accuracy than ResNet-based ones within VLMs.

Test-Time Adaptation methods prove superior on hard Out-of-Distribution datasets, while Few-Shot Learning methods generally yield the best overall performance when limited labeled target data is available.
Takeaways: Pretrained VLMs, especially those with Vision Transformer backbones, fundamentally reshape transfer learning, often providing robust baselines in various adaptation settings.

Generalization methods demonstrate varying strengths: Test-Time Adaptation excels on hard Out-of-Distribution datasets, Few-Shot Learning achieves top performance with labeled data, and robust fine-tuning is effective for significant domain shifts.
The emergence of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) marks a crucial advancement in VLM generalization, showcasing broad capabilities across diverse multimodal tasks via multi-stage training.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.18254.Title: RLPR: Extrapolating RLVR to General Domains without Verifiers
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.18254.Summary: Researchers from Tsinghua University and NUS developed RLPR, a verifier-free reinforcement learning framework that enhances Large Language Model reasoning across general domains by using an intrinsic probability-based reward. This method achieved an average 24.9% improvement on general-domain benchmarks and consistently outperformed existing RLVR and concurrent verifier-free approaches by removing the need for external verification.
Problem: Existing Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) methods for LLMs heavily rely on domain-specific external verifiers.
Handcrafting rule-based verifiers is laborious, complex, and leads to brittle systems, while training LLM-based verifiers introduces high annotation costs and complexity.
Applying RLVR to general, open-ended natural language reasoning is difficult due to the inability to devise general-purpose verifiers, limiting scalability.
Method: RLPR introduces a 'Probability-based Reward' (PR) that uses the mean of an LLM's per-token decoding probabilities for a ground-truth reference answer as a reward signal.

A 'Reward Debiasing' mechanism is employed to calculate the reward as the improvement in probability gained by generating reasoning, by subtracting a base score obtained without intermediate reasoning.
A 'Standard Deviation Filtering' approach dynamically filters out training prompts with low reward standard deviation, focusing learning on more informative samples and stabilizing training.
Results: RLPR achieved an average 24.9% improvement on four general-domain benchmarks using Qwen2.5-7B, demonstrating its ability to extend RL to broader reasoning tasks.
The framework consistently outperformed traditional RLVR baselines and specialized model-based verifiers, for example, surpassing General Reasoner-7B by 1.6 average points across seven benchmarks.
Quantitative analysis showed the Probability-based Reward (PR) achieved high discrimination (e.g., 0.95 ROC-AUC on math data), significantly outperforming rule-based verifiers (0.61 on general data).
Takeaways: An LLM's intrinsic probability of generating a correct free-form answer can serve as an internal evaluation of reasoning reward.
The mean of per-token probabilities for a reference answer is a more robust reward signal than naive sequence likelihood, which is highly sensitive to minor variations.
Debiasing the reward by subtracting a base score (probability without reasoning) isolates the contribution of the generated reasoning process.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.17901.Title: PostAlign: Multimodal Grounding as a Corrective Lens for MLLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.17901.Summary: The PostAlign framework enhances Multimodal Large Language Models' (MLLMs) visual understanding and reduces hallucinations by incorporating multimodal grounding as a corrective lens. This approach employs explicit visual and textual grounding mechanisms, enabling MLLMs to anchor responses more faithfully to visual evidence.
Problem: MLLMs frequently over-rely on spurious correlations and linguistic priors, leading to generated content inconsistent with actual visual information.
A direct consequence of linguistic biases is multimodal hallucination, where MLLMs generate objects, attributes, or actions not present in the input image.
Current MLLMs often struggle with fine-grained visual understanding and complex reasoning, tending to prioritize text-driven generalizations over specific visual evidence.
Method: Introduced MMGrounded-PostAlign, a post-multimodal alignment framework that integrates an MLLM backbone, a visual grounding encoder, and a multi-task decoder.
Developed a negative rejection mechanism where the MLLM predicts a special `` token for non-existent objects, preventing visual hallucinations by explicitly signaling absence.
Implemented a selective reasoning mechanism, training the MLLM to dynamically assess query complexity and generate textual rationales only for complex queries, optimizing efficiency and accuracy.
Results: The negative rejection mechanism provided the most significant improvement in mitigating hallucinations on the HaloQuest benchmark, particularly in anti-concept scenarios.
MMGrounded-PostAlign outperformed bounding-box-as-language token methods on the POPE benchmark, achieving superior reduction of object and attribute hallucinations.

The framework preserved or improved the general reasoning abilities of the underlying MLLM backbone on datasets like VQAv2, MME, and MMBench (e.g., MMBench score of 1514.3 for 7B model vs. baseline 1504.6).
Takeaways: Linguistic priors can progressively override visual information during MLLM decoding, leading to hallucinations that persist even when visual evidence contradicts them.
Explicit visual grounding, particularly the negative rejection mechanism, significantly mitigates hallucinations by enforcing stronger multimodal alignment between text and image.

The framework allows MLLMs to retain or enhance general reasoning capabilities, suggesting a balanced approach that avoids the degradation seen when over-biasing models towards specific visual tokens.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.17629.Title: CLiViS: Unleashing Cognitive Map through Linguistic-Visual Synergy for Embodied Visual Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.17629.Summary: CLiViS introduces a training-free framework for embodied visual reasoning, synergistically combining Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) via a dynamic Cognitive Map. The method achieves state-of-the-art accuracy across benchmarks, including 55.4% on OpenEQA, 23.0% on EgoTempo, and 69.4% on EgoSchema, demonstrating enhanced performance with longer video durations and robustness across various VLM backbones.
Problem: Embodied Visual Reasoning (EVR) tasks struggle with accurate spatiotemporal perception from long, egocentric videos due to limited fields of view and complex dynamics.
Complex, free-form user instructions in EVR demand sophisticated compositional reasoning that existing methods often lack.
Prior Socratic-based approaches lose crucial fine-grained visual details through fixed captions, while end-to-end VLMs generally lack robust high-level logical planning capabilities.
Method: CLiViS is a training-free framework orchestrating an iterative linguistic-visual synergy between LLMs (for reasoning) and VLMs (for perception).
It dynamically constructs and updates a 'Cognitive Map' (composed of a Scene Navigation Graph and an Object Relation Graph) and an 'Evidence Memory' module to represent the evolving embodied scene.
The LLM generates precise sub-instructions for the VLM to perform focused perception on specific video segments, then parses VLM responses to update the cognitive map and evidence memory.
Results: CLiViS achieved state-of-the-art average accuracy across all evaluated benchmarks: 55.4% on OpenEQA, 23.0% on EgoTempo, and 69.4% on EgoSchema, with an overall average of 48.4%.
The framework outperformed Socratic-based models by 20.2% and end-to-end VLMs by 2.9%, showcasing superior logical planning and retention of visual detail.

It demonstrated more pronounced improvements with increasing video duration (e.g., a 6.5% accuracy gain for videos ">= 30s" on OpenEQA) and exhibited model-agnostic effectiveness across various VLM backbones.
Takeaways: Synergistically combining LLMs for high-level reasoning and VLMs for fine-grained perception effectively bridges the perception-reasoning gap in embodied visual reasoning.
A dynamic and structured 'Cognitive Map' provides an evolving semantic representation of the scene, crucial for integrating long-term spatiotemporal cues and supporting compositional reasoning.
Iterative LLM-VLM dialogue, guided by prompt engineering, enables robust multi-step inference, enhanced interpretability, and a self-correcting mechanism for VLM-generated descriptions.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.17608.Title: HIRE: Lightweight High-Resolution Image Feature Enrichment for Multimodal LLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.17608.Summary: Adobe's Media and Data Science Research Lab developed HIRE, a lightweight feature enrichment pipeline for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to achieve high-resolution visual understanding. This method attains competitive performance on fine-grained tasks, reducing computational costs by up to 35% and inference times by over 50% compared to existing multi-crop approaches.
Problem: Existing high-resolution MLLMs rely on processing multiple crops of an image through a large vision encoder, leading to substantial computational costs and extended inference times.
Achieving fine-grained visual understanding in MLLMs typically incurs a quadratic increase in FLOPs, hindering practical deployment and scalability, especially with larger vision backbones.
A challenge exists in balancing high accuracy for detailed visual tasks with the necessity for computational efficiency and real-time application in MLLMs.
Method: HIRE employs a lightweight feature enrichment pipeline that directly generates high-resolution visual features from a single low-resolution vision encoder output, eliminating the need for multiple, computationally expensive ViT forward passes.
It utilizes a compact UNet module (approximately 250k parameters) to extract multi-scale semantic and high-frequency details from the original high-resolution image as guidance signals.

A stack of Joint Bilateral Upsampling (JBU) modules progressively enriches the low-resolution features, guided by the UNet's multi-scale outputs, with the final enriched features average-pooled and concatenated with original features to prevent quadratic scaling of LLM context length.
Results: HIRE reduces computational costs (FLOPs) by up to 35% and accelerates inference time by over 50% on benchmarks like VQA_T compared to existing multi-crop high-resolution MLLM methods.

The framework demonstrates approximately 10-15% improvements in fine-grained tasks such as pixel-level localization and animal keypoint detection, and about a 5% reduction in hallucination, on the MMT-Bench.

HIRE's computational overhead remains nearly constant across different scales of ViT backbones and input resolutions, showcasing superior scalability compared to methods whose overhead increases significantly with larger backbones.
Takeaways: High-resolution visual understanding in MLLMs can be efficiently achieved by enriching features from a single low-resolution vision encoder pass, rather than through multiple, independent crop processing.

A small, specialized UNet module can effectively extract crucial multi-scale semantic guidance from high-resolution images, facilitating accurate and efficient feature upsampling without adding significant computational overhead.

Strategically average-pooling high-resolution enriched features before concatenation and projection to the LLM is critical for maintaining overall computational efficiency by avoiding a quadratic increase in the LLM's context length.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.17219.Title: No Free Lunch: Rethinking Internal Feedback for LLM Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.17219.Summary: This study reveals a "no free lunch" principle for Reinforcement Learning from Internal Feedback (RLIF) in LLM reasoning, showing it initially benefits base models by reducing underconfidence but degrades performance with prolonged training by inducing overconfidence. RLIF effectively improves instruction following in models with high initial policy entropy but offers little benefit and can be detrimental to already instruction-tuned models.
Problem: Existing RL approaches for LLMs (RLHF, RLVR) are heavily reliant on costly and labor-intensive external supervision.
RLVR, while improving single-answer accuracy (pass@1), often struggles to fundamentally enhance broader multi-step reasoning capabilities (pass@N).

A systematic understanding of Reinforcement Learning from Internal Feedback (RLIF) was lacking, specifically regarding its conditions for effectiveness, optimal internal signals, and long-term training dynamics.
Method: Conducted theoretical analysis demonstrating that diverse internal feedback signals are partially equivalent and fundamentally minimize policy entropy.
Empirically evaluated RLIF using various Qwen models on challenging math reasoning benchmarks (AIME2025, MATH500, GSM8K) within a reinforcement learning framework.

Employed diagnostic techniques including policy entropy tracking, "transitional word" analysis, and model merging experiments to understand the training dynamics and the relationship between initial policy entropy and RLIF effectiveness.
Results: RLIF initially boosts reasoning performance for base LLMs, but performance consistently declines with prolonged training, sometimes leading to "training collapse".
RLIF provides minimal to no improvement and often degrades performance for already instruction-tuned models.
All three investigated RLIF methods (self-certainty, token-level entropy, trajectory-level entropy) consistently reduce the model's policy entropy during training, confirming theoretical predictions.
RLIF training significantly decreases the frequency of "transitional words," indicating a shift from mitigating underconfidence to inducing overconfidence in reasoning processes.
Takeaways: RLIF's effectiveness is inversely related to a model's initial policy entropy: base models with high entropy benefit, while low-entropy instruction-tuned models do not and may degrade.
Internal feedback signals fundamentally operate by minimizing policy entropy, making the model more confident and deterministic in its outputs.

The performance dynamics of RLIF are characterized by a two-stage process: initial gains from mitigating underconfidence (reducing excessive deliberation) followed by degradation due to inducing overconfidence (suppressing beneficial deliberation).

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.17218.Title: Machine Mental Imagery: Empower Multimodal Reasoning with Latent Visual Tokens
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.17218.Summary: Researchers from UMass Amherst and MIT developed Mirage, a framework that enables Vision-Language Models to perform multimodal reasoning by interleaving compact latent visual tokens with text. This approach, inspired by human mental imagery, significantly outperforms text-only baselines and explicit image-generating models on spatial reasoning tasks, showing an 11% accuracy gain on VSP Spatial Planning.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are limited in tasks requiring "visual imagination" or manipulation (e.g., spatial reasoning) due to their reliance on text-only decoding, which forces verbose verbalization of visual thought.

Unified multimodal models that generate explicit images suffer from heavy pre-training demands, potentially hindering reasoning ability and leading to a trade-off between generation fidelity and reasoning quality.
Existing VLMs lack the ability to produce fluid, interleaved multimodal reasoning trajectories, where visual cues are seamlessly integrated alongside textual thought.
Method: Integrate special "latent visual tokens" into VLM decoding, allowing the model to generate compact visual embeddings interleaved with text instead of explicit images.

Implement a two-stage fine-tuning process: Stage 1 grounds latent tokens to visual representations using cosine similarity loss, while Stage 2 allows these tokens to adapt for task-specific reasoning via text-only cross-entropy loss.
Apply Reinforcement Learning (GRPO) with accuracy and format rewards to further optimize the end-to-end multimodal reasoning trajectory for task success.
Results: Mirage consistently surpassed text-only baselines and unified models that generate explicit images across spatial reasoning benchmarks (VSP, BLINK-Jigsaw, SAT, COMT).
Achieved an 11% improvement on VSP Spatial Planning (58% accuracy compared to 47% for CoT SFT) and a 3% gain on VSP Spatial Reasoning (87% accuracy compared to 84% for CoT SFT).
Ablation studies confirmed the criticality of both training stages, and the framework demonstrated robustness to hyperparameter changes and showed enhanced benefits for smaller model sizes.
Takeaways: Emulating human "mental imagery" through compact latent visual tokens enables effective multimodal reasoning in VLMs without the computational burden of explicit pixel-level image generation.

A two-stage fine-tuning process, involving initial latent grounding followed by relaxation, is essential for enabling the model to generate flexible yet visually meaningful latent tokens that adapt for downstream reasoning tasks.

Interleaving these learned latent visual tokens within the reasoning chain consistently enhances VLM performance on complex spatial reasoning tasks, surpassing methods that rely solely on textual chains or explicit image generation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.17202.Title: UniFork: Exploring Modality Alignment for Unified Multimodal Understanding and Generation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.17202.Summary: UNIFORK, developed by HKUST, Shanghai AI Lab, and SJTU, introduces a Y-shaped Transformer architecture for unified multimodal understanding and generation that resolves the inherent representational conflict between these tasks. The model achieves competitive performance across vision-language benchmarks like MME-P and VQAv2 for understanding, and GenEval and MJHQ for generation, by separating deeper layers into task-specific branches based on observed distinct modality alignment patterns.
Problem: Existing unified multimodal models using fully shared Transformer backbones face a "representational compromise," where understanding and generation tasks have conflicting demands on feature alignment in deeper layers.

Image understanding benefits from monotonically increasing modality alignment across network depth, while image generation requires alignment to decrease in deeper layers for synthesizing spatial details.
Prior unified approaches often introduce architectural complexity or compromise performance by forcing a single, suboptimal alignment strategy across inherently divergent tasks.
Method: A Y-shaped Transformer backbone that features shared early layers for joint semantic representation and independent deeper branches specialized for understanding and generation.
A shared visual tokenizer based on residual vector quantization is used for both tasks, converting images into 1D token sequences for the Transformer.
A three-stage training pipeline is employed: visual alignment pretraining, joint optimization of the full model, and task-specific fine-tuning where only the respective branches are updated.
Results: UniFork consistently outperformed fully shared Transformer backbones on both understanding (e.g., MME-P, VQAv2) and generation (e.g., GenEval, MJHQ) benchmarks.
Achieved performance comparable to or surpassing task-specific expert models, with up to 10% gains on MME-P over some unified baselines and a FID score of 10.6 on MJHQ-30K for generation.

The final UniFork model's modality alignment analysis empirically confirmed its successful recovery of the desired distinct patterns: monotonically increasing for understanding and "rise-then-fall" for generation.
Takeaways: Image understanding models exhibit a progressively increasing modality alignment with network depth, crucial for comprehensive semantic comprehension.

Image generation models show a "rise-then-fall" alignment pattern, where early layers establish semantic grounding, and deeper layers reduce alignment to enable high-fidelity spatial detail synthesis.

Fully shared unified models trained on both tasks demonstrate a "representational compromise," where their internal modality alignment patterns converge, preventing optimal performance for either task.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.16895.Title: With Limited Data for Multimodal Alignment, Let the STRUCTURE Guide You
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.16895.Summary: Researchers at EPFL developed a framework for multimodal alignment that achieves high performance with limited paired data by using "STRUCTURE" regularization and similarity-based layer selection. The method yields average relative improvements of 51.6% in zero-shot classification and 91.8% in cross-modal retrieval, requiring less than 1% of the data typically used by state-of-the-art models.
Problem: State-of-the-art multimodal models rely on vast amounts of paired training data, often hundreds of millions of samples, which are prohibitive to collect in many specialized scientific and real-world domains.

Existing methods for parameter-frozen modality alignment either lack coherence in shared embedding spaces (unsupervised) or still require millions of paired samples (supervised), limiting their use in low-data settings.
Efficiently leveraging powerful, pre-trained unimodal foundation models for multimodal tasks is difficult when paired data for alignment is scarce.
Method: A modular alignment strategy is introduced, combining "STRUCTURE" regularization with a similarity-based layer selection mechanism.
"STRUCTURE" regularization prevents distortion of unimodal latent structures by preserving multi-scale neighborhood geometry through a Jensen-Shannon divergence-based loss.
A data-driven method selects the optimal intermediate layers from pretrained unimodal encoders for alignment based on their representational similarity, rather than defaulting to final layers.
Results: The framework yields average relative performance gains of 51.6% for zero-shot classification and 91.8% for cross-modal retrieval tasks.
It achieves high-quality multimodal alignment with limited paired data (tens of thousands of samples), requiring up to 23 times fewer samples than baseline methods.
The proposed solution generalizes across various unimodal foundation models (e.g., RoBERTa, DINOv2) and diverse modalities beyond vision-language, including audio-text and single-cell biology.
Takeaways: Preserving the intrinsic multi-scale neighborhood geometry of pretrained unimodal representations is crucial for effective multimodal alignment in low-data environments.
Selecting the most representationally similar intermediate layers from unimodal encoders, rather than just the final layers, leads to improved alignment performance.
The judicious inclusion of a very small number of in-domain paired samples can drastically enhance performance, sometimes outperforming models trained on orders of magnitude more general data.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.16691.Title: LaVi: Efficient Large Vision-Language Models via Internal Feature Modulation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.16691.Summary: LaVi, from researchers primarily at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, introduces a novel Feature Modulation Injection paradigm for large vision-language models (LVLMs) that significantly reduces computational overhead and memory usage. The approach achieves up to a 94.0% reduction in FLOPs and a 3.1x inference speedup while maintaining or improving performance on various image and video understanding benchmarks.
Problem: Integrating visual information into large language models (LLMs) often compromises their pre-trained linguistic knowledge or introduces excessive computational burden.
Existing "architectural injection" methods like Flamingo disrupt the LLM's internal structure, potentially degrading its core language capabilities.
"In-context injection" methods, such as LLaVA, lead to prohibitive computational costs (FLOPs, latency, memory) due to the quadratic complexity of self-attention with long visual token sequences.
Method: Introduces Feature Modulation Injection (FMI), a novel paradigm that directly modulates the Large Language Model's (LLM) internal hidden states with visual information.
