Develops Vision-Infused Layer Normalization (ViLN) that dynamically adjusts the LLM's standard Layer Normalization parameters using vision-guided deltas (Δαv, Δβv).
Employs a lightweight conditioning module, typically attention-based, to generate these deltas, with zero-initialization to facilitate stable adaptation and preserve linguistic priors.
Results: Achieved up to a 94.0% reduction in FLOPs, a 3.1x inference speedup, and a 51.5% memory reduction compared to state-of-the-art LLaVA models of similar scale.
Outperformed or matched LLaVA baselines on 9 image understanding benchmarks (e.g., VQAv2, MMBench) with up to 19.4x FLOPs reduction.
Showed 6x to 7x reduction in FLOPs on 6 video understanding benchmarks (e.g., EgoSchema, MVBench) while maintaining or improving performance.
Takeaways: Feature Modulation Injection (FMI) significantly improves computational efficiency and convergence speed while better preserving the LLM's linguistic proficiency compared to prior integration methods.
Both multiplicative (scaling) and additive (shifting) modulations of Layer Normalization parameters based on visual input are crucial for effective vision-language integration.
Applying modulation to a moderate, uniformly distributed subset (e.g., 25%) of LLM layers provides optimal performance and scalability without compromising linguistic priors.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.16673.Title: Extracting Multimodal Learngene in CLIP: Unveiling the Multimodal Generalizable Knowledge
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.16673.Summary: Researchers from Southeast University developed Multimodal Learngene (MM-LG), a framework that extracts generalizable knowledge from CLIP, enabling efficient initialization of diverse multimodal and unimodal models. The method reduces pre-training costs by 2.8 times and parameter storage by 75% compared to full pre-training, while achieving comparable or superior performance across various tasks, notably improving image captioning.
Problem: Large multimodal foundation models like CLIP require significant computational resources for pre-training and necessitate repetitive large-scale pre-training when different model scales or architectures are needed for downstream applications.

Existing 'Learngene' paradigms, which aim to extract generalizable knowledge for efficient initialization, primarily focused on unimodal scenarios and lacked mechanisms to handle the unique characteristics of multimodal knowledge within models like CLIP.
There was a need for a method to efficiently extract and transfer the powerful cross-modal understanding capabilities of CLIP into smaller, task-specific models without redundant training.
Method: Introduces Multimodal Learngene (MM-LG), a framework that extracts multimodal generalizable knowledge from a large CLIP model, comprising a 'Block Part' (vision, language, multimodal blocks) and a 'Coefficient Part' (learnable coefficients).

An auxiliary model is constructed whose layer parameters are formed as a weighted sum of these extracted learngene blocks and trained using knowledge distillation from the ancestry CLIP model, combining CLIP's contrastive loss with a logit distillation loss.

The extracted learngene is used to numerically initialize descendant models of various scales and modalities, followed by a brief 'parameter activation' training phase on a small fraction of the pre-training dataset.
Results: MM-LG consistently outperforms existing unimodal Learngene approaches (He-LG, TLEG) across cross-modal retrieval, image classification, and image captioning, with up to +4.13% I2T Recall@1 on Flickr30k over TLEG.
The framework achieves performance comparable to or superior to the traditional Pre-training and Fine-tuning (PT-FT) paradigm, notably outperforming PT-FT in image captioning by over 5 CIDEr points.
MM-LG significantly reduces parameter storage by 75% and pre-training costs by approximately 2.8 times compared to PT-FT, while maintaining or improving task performance.
Takeaways: Generalizable knowledge within large multimodal models like CLIP can be effectively decomposed and extracted into distinct unimodal (vision, language) and multimodal interaction components.

A knowledge distillation approach can be used to train an auxiliary model that learns to compose these fundamental 'learngene' components, capturing the behavior of the large ancestry model efficiently.
A brief parameter activation step using a small subset of data is crucial after numerical initialization from the extracted learngene to effectively prepare descendant models for downstream tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.16141.Title: GRPO-CARE: Consistency-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Multimodal Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.16141.Summary: Researchers from ARC Lab, Tencent PCG, The University of Hong Kong, and The Chinese University of Hong Kong introduce GRPO-CARE, a consistency-aware reinforcement learning framework that enhances both answer correctness and reasoning coherence in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) without explicit process supervision. The method, evaluated on their new SEED-Bench-R1 benchmark, boosts reasoning consistency by 24.5% (to 82.4%) and achieves a 6.7% performance gain on challenging cross-environment and cross-task scenarios.
Problem: Existing outcome-supervised reinforcement learning methods for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) improve accuracy but often degrade the logical coherence between reasoning steps and final answers, leading to issues like "Thought Collapse."
Current MLLM evaluation benchmarks are too narrow, focusing either on perception or reasoning, and lack structured assessment of generalization across diverse real-world scenarios.
It is challenging to develop MLLMs that can genuinely integrate sophisticated perception with robust logical reasoning while maintaining interpretable Chain-of-Thought outputs.
Method: A new comprehensive benchmark, SEED-Bench-R1, is introduced for MLLM post-training on video understanding, featuring real-world inputs, complex questions, large-scale training data, and hierarchical generalization assessment.
GRPO-CARE, a novel reinforcement learning framework, is proposed to jointly optimize for answer correctness and reasoning consistency in MLLMs without requiring explicit process supervision.

GRPO-CARE employs a two-tiered reward system, combining a base correctness reward with an adaptive consistency bonus derived from a slowly evolving reference model, while removing restrictive KL divergence penalties.
Results: GRPO-CARE significantly outperforms standard GRPO on the SEED-Bench-R1 benchmark, achieving a 6.7% performance gain on the challenging Level-3 (cross-environment & cross-task) evaluation.
The method dramatically improves reasoning consistency, boosting the consistency rate from 57.9% (for standard GRPO) to 82.4% for MLLMs.
Ablation studies confirm that removing the standard KL divergence penalty and utilizing GRPO-CARE's sparse, adaptive consistency bonus are crucial for performance and consistency.
Models trained with GRPO-CARE demonstrate strong transferability, showing significant performance improvements across six diverse general video understanding benchmarks.
Takeaways: Standard outcome-supervised reinforcement learning, while improving MLLM accuracy, often compromises the logical coherence between the reasoning steps and the final answer, exhibiting a low consistency rate (e.g., 57.9% for GRPO).

Standard KL divergence penalties, typically used in RL, can excessively restrict MLLM exploration and hinder the model's ability to adaptively adjust reasoning paths, thereby limiting performance and interpretability.

A sparse, group-relative consistency bonus, adaptively estimated from a slowly evolving reference model, effectively improves reasoning coherence without requiring explicit step-wise supervision, proving more robust than dense or noisy consistency signals.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.16112.Title: Loss-Oriented Ranking for Automated Visual Prompting in LVLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.16112.Summary: An automated visual prompting framework, AutoV, dynamically selects optimal visual cues from a candidate pool to enhance Large Vision-Language Model performance. It consistently improves accuracy across diverse LVLMs and benchmarks, achieving up to 10.2% higher accuracy on VizWiz and demonstrating strong transferability to various model architectures, including closed-source ones.
Problem: Existing visual prompting methods for Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) rely on heuristic, fixed designs that lack adaptability.
These static prompts are often sub-optimal, showing inconsistent performance across different tasks and requiring extensive manual tuning for specific benchmarks or instances.
Efficiently and effectively guiding LVLM attention for diverse image-query contexts without laborious manual intervention remains a challenge.
Method: AutoV introduces an automated framework that dynamically selects the most appropriate visual prompt for any given textual query and input image from a pre-defined pool of candidates.
It employs a lightweight ranking network, trained using the first layer of the LVLM's language decoder for modality interaction, to evaluate and score the relevance of each candidate prompt.
An innovative automated data generation pipeline is used, leveraging LVLM prediction loss as a scalable, reward-based supervision signal to train the ranking network, avoiding manual annotation.
Results: AutoV consistently outperforms existing heuristic visual prompting methods, achieving average accuracy gains of 2.2% to 4.2% across various open-source LVLMs (LLaVA-1.5, InternVL2, Qwen2.5-VL) and benchmarks, with notable improvements such as 10.2% on VizWiz and 3.8% on MMMU.
The framework demonstrates strong transferability, boosting closed-source models like Gemini-Pro (+6.4 points) and GPT-4o (+6.0 points) on VizWiz and LLaVA-Wild benchmarks without specific training.
AutoV enhances model efficiency by enabling smaller 7B LVLMs to achieve performance levels competitive with larger 13B models, while introducing minimal inference latency (e.g., 6.9 ms for LLaVA-7B).
Takeaways: Dynamically selecting visual prompts tailored to specific image-query pairs yields superior and more robust LVLM performance compared to static, heuristic prompting methods.
LVLM prediction loss can serve as an effective and scalable reward signal for training prompt selection models, enabling automated data generation without costly human labeling.

A lightweight, trained ranking network can generalize its prompt selection strategy across diverse LVLM architectures, acting as a model-agnostic enhancement without requiring fine-tuning of the base models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.15757.Title: Weakly-supervised VLM-guided Partial Contrastive Learning for Visual Language Navigation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.15757.Summary: The Weakly-supervised Partial Contrastive Learning (WPCL) framework enhances Visual Language Navigation (VLN) agents by improving viewpoint-invariant object recognition using pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for weak supervision without fine-tuning. This method achieves state-of-the-art performance on R2R, REVERIE, and SOON benchmarks, notably reaching 78% Success Rate and 70% SPL on R2R val unseen, while operating on a single 24GB GPU.
Problem: VLN agents struggle to robustly identify the same objects from different dynamic viewpoints due to the sensitivity of existing vision models.
Integrating powerful pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) into VLN is computationally expensive if fine-tuned, or suboptimal if used in a zero-shot manner.
Directly relying on VLM outputs in a fully supervised way can introduce biases from their general pre-training data that may not align with specific VLN tasks.
Method: Developed Weakly-supervised Partial Contrastive Learning (WPCL) that leverages pre-trained VLMs (like LLaVA v1.5) to extract object lists from observations as weak supervisory signals.

Introduced a Partial Contrastive Learning mechanism that splits visual feature vectors into object-centric and flexible segments, applying contrastive loss only to the object segment to encourage viewpoint-invariant learning.
Integrated this mechanism into a VLN agent architecture (DUET-based) guided by a sample selection matrix generated from VLM-extracted objects, without fine-tuning the VLM itself.
Results: WPCL consistently achieved state-of-the-art results across R2R, REVERIE, and SOON benchmarks, with an R2R val unseen Success Rate of 78% and SPL of 70%, outperforming prior methods.
The method demonstrates computational efficiency, running on a single 24GB NVIDIA TITAN RTX GPU, in contrast to VLM fine-tuning approaches that require significantly more powerful and numerous GPUs.

Performance remains robust across different VLM choices for generating weak supervision (e.g., LLaVA 1.5, LLaVA 1.6, OpenFlamingo), indicating its generalizability and insensitivity to specific VLM architectures.
Takeaways: High performance in Visual Language Navigation can be achieved by carefully integrating VLM knowledge through weak supervision, circumventing the high computational cost of VLM fine-tuning.

A causal framework informs the design of a partial contrastive learning approach, allowing for specific invariance to shared objects across viewpoints while maintaining flexibility for other visual information.
Careful prompt engineering for VLM-based object extraction is crucial for generating effective weak supervisory signals, ensuring relevant object pairs for contrastive learning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.15692.Title: MLE-STAR: Machine Learning Engineering Agent via Search and Targeted Refinement
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.15692.Summary: MLE-STAR is an LLM-based agent that automates machine learning engineering tasks by leveraging web search for up-to-date models and implementing a targeted, ablation-guided code refinement process. This framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on a benchmark of 22 Kaggle competitions, outperforming existing LLM agents and specialized AutoML tools.
Problem: Existing LLM-based ML agents often propose familiar or outdated ML methods due to their training data, limiting the use of state-of-the-art approaches.
Current agents perform coarse, broad modifications to code, hindering deep and iterative optimization of specific ML pipeline components.
Many LLM agents face scalability and generalizability issues due to reliance on manually curated knowledge bases or case banks.
LLM-generated code can exhibit 'misbehaviors' like data leakage or incomplete data utilization, compromising solution robustness.
Method: A multi-agent framework that uses a retriever agent with web search to identify state-of-the-art ML models and example code relevant to a given task.
A targeted code block refinement mechanism where an extractor agent, guided by ablation studies, identifies and iteratively refines high-impact ML components.
A novel, LLM-guided ensemble strategy that proposes and evaluates various ensemble plans to combine multiple candidate solutions.
Auxiliary modules for debugging, data leakage checking, and data usage checking to ensure the robustness and correctness of generated ML solutions.
Results: Achieved a 63.6% medal rate (36.4% gold medals) on 22 Kaggle competitions within the MLE-bench Lite benchmark using Gemini-2.5-Pro.
Outperformed the leading LLM agent, AIDE, by 18.1 percentage points in 'Any Medal' rate (43.9% vs 25.8%) using the same Gemini-2.0-Flash model.
Demonstrated superior performance against DS-Agent and AutoGluon on most tabular tasks, without relying on manually curated case banks.
The proposed ensembling method significantly improved the 'Any Medal' rate from 37.9% to 43.9% and the 'Gold Medal' rate from 25.8% to 30.3%.
Takeaways: Integrating external web search allows LLM agents to overcome knowledge biases and dynamically incorporate up-to-date, task-specific ML models and practices.
Focusing refinement efforts on specific, high-impact code blocks identified through ablation studies leads to more efficient and effective performance gains.
Proactive detection and correction of common LLM code misbehaviors (like data leakage) are critical for generating robust and reliable ML solutions.
Intelligent, LLM-guided ensembling can further boost model performance by effectively combining diverse candidate solutions.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.15679.Title: Dense SAE Latents Are Features, Not Bugs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.15679.Summary: This research redefines dense latents in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) from perceived training artifacts to functional features, demonstrating they reflect intrinsic, frequently activating computations within large language models. The study reveals these latents perform diverse, interpretable roles, including tracking token position, binding contextual information, and regulating output entropy, and persist across different model architectures.
Problem: Interpreting individual neurons in large language models (LLMs) is challenged by polysemanticity, where a single neuron may activate in semantically unrelated contexts.
Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) aim to extract monosemantic features, but frequently activating 'dense latents' are consistently observed and often dismissed as undesirable artifacts.
The prevailing assumption that all interpretable features must be sparse has led to efforts to suppress dense latents, potentially obscuring meaningful LLM computations.
Method: The authors conducted systematic ablation experiments across Gemma 2 2B, GPT-2, and LLaMA 3.2 to test if dense latents are intrinsic to the residual stream or merely training artifacts.
They analyzed the geometric properties of dense latents, identifying an 'antipodality' structure using cosine similarities and validating it with an `AbsoluteTopK` SAE.

A comprehensive taxonomy of dense latents was developed through various analyses including correlating activations with token positions, using LLM-based interpretation, performing steering experiments, and assessing alignment with the W _U quasi-nullspace.
Results: Ablation experiments showed that removing the subspace of dense latents prevents their re-emergence in retrained SAEs, confirming their intrinsic nature and persistence across various LLMs.
Dense latents frequently form antipodal pairs, a geometric structure eliminated in `AbsoluteTopK` SAEs, which inherently allow for bidirectional use of a single latent direction.

A functional taxonomy identified specific dense latent types: Position Latents (tracking token location), Context-Binding Latents (influencing semantic completion), Nullspace Latents (regulating output entropy), Alphabet Latents (lexical signaling), and Meaningful-Word Latents (tracking linguistic categories).

Layer-wise analysis revealed that dense latent fractions and their underlying subspaces evolve, transitioning from early-layer structural features to mid-layer semantic features and final-layer output-oriented signals.
Takeaways: Dense latents are not optimization artifacts but intrinsic properties of the LLM's residual stream, representing robust, densely represented information.
Dense latents often form 'antipodal pairs' with nearly opposite encoder and decoder vectors, suggesting they encode single 1-dimensional directions in the residual stream.
Dense latents serve diverse, interpretable functional roles within LLMs, evolving across layers from structural tracking to semantic binding and output regulation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.15564.Title: Show-o2: Improved Native Unified Multimodal Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.15564.Summary: Show Lab and ByteDance researchers developed Show-o2, a native unified multimodal model capable of both understanding and generating text, images, and videos within a single architecture. The model achieves state-of-the-art or highly competitive performance across various multimodal benchmarks, supported by a novel dual-path visual representation and an efficient two-stage training strategy.
Problem: Existing large multimodal models (LMMs) primarily focus on text and images, often lacking comprehensive and native handling of dynamic video content.
A challenge in achieving true unification of multimodal understanding and generation within a single, cohesive architecture, rather than assembling disparate specialized models.

The difficulty of efficiently training powerful generative LMMs to cultivate visual generation abilities while preserving extensive pre-trained language model (LLM) knowledge without relying on prohibitively expensive, web-scale text corpora.
Method: Introduces a native unified multimodal architecture that leverages a 3D causal VAE for efficient visual encoding/decoding of both images and videos.
Employs a dual-path Unified Visual Representation (UVR) with Spatial (-Temporal) Fusion to integrate both high-level semantic and low-level structural features for visual inputs.

Utilizes a two-stage training recipe: an initial visual generation pre-training phase, followed by full model fine-tuning, designed to efficiently impart visual generation skills while preserving the LLM's language knowledge.
Results: Achieves state-of-the-art or highly competitive performance on image understanding benchmarks (e.g., MME-p, GQA, MMMU-val) and image generation benchmarks (GenEval, DPG-Bench, OneIG-Bench).

Outperforms models with more parameters (e.g., TokenFlow-XL 14B) on several image understanding tasks and demonstrates strong text-to-video and image-to-video generation on VBench with a 2B parameter model.

The two-stage training successfully preserves LLM language knowledge, maintaining performance comparable to original Qwen2.5-1.5B and Qwen2.5-7B Instruct models on text-only tasks like MMLU and GSM8K.
Takeaways: The dual-path Spatial (-Temporal) Fusion mechanism is crucial for effectively integrating both high-level semantic and low-level structural features, significantly improving both multimodal understanding and generation.

A two-stage training strategy effectively cultivates strong visual generation capabilities and adapts visual components to the LLM's embedding space, critically maintaining the pre-trained LLM's language proficiency without requiring massive text-only datasets.
Unified visual representations, designed to be scalable for both images and videos, enable robust multimodal understanding and generation within a single, coherent framework.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.15211.Title: ProtoReasoning: Prototypes as the Foundation for Generalizable Reasoning in LLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.15211.Summary: The ProtoReasoning framework enhances Large Language Models' (LLMs) generalizable reasoning by training them on abstract, verifiable prototypes derived from formal logic (Prolog) and planning (PDDL). This approach led to performance improvements of up to 6.4% on planning tasks and 4.7% on logical reasoning, demonstrating that learning structural reasoning patterns facilitates cross-domain transfer.
Problem: Despite empirical success in complex reasoning tasks, the underlying mechanisms enabling cross-domain generalization in Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) remain poorly understood.
There is a need to develop a systematic framework to enhance LLMs' generalizable reasoning abilities beyond empirical observation.
Current methods often lack scalable and verifiable means of generating high-quality reasoning data to train models effectively.
Method: The ProtoReasoning framework leverages abstract, verifiable prototypes (Prolog for logical reasoning and PDDL for planning) to represent fundamental reasoning patterns.
An automated, model-driven pipeline constructs diverse and verifiable prototype-based reasoning problems, using interpreters like SWI-Prolog and VAL for ground-truth derivation and verification.

A three-phase Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) recipe on a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture (teacher model distillation, difficulty stratification, quality filtration) is used to train LLMs on these datasets.
Results: ProtoReasoning improved logical reasoning performance on Enigmata-Eval by 4.7% (from 37.3% to 42.0%).
Planning tasks showed gains of 6.4% on Nexus-Hard (from 53.1% to 59.5%) and 6.3% on Dedicated Task Planning (from 46.7% to 53.0%).
The framework demonstrated out-of-domain generalization, achieving a 4.0% gain on MMLU (from 82.7% to 86.7%) and a 1.0% gain on AIME2024 (from 72.0% to 73.0%).
Takeaways: Cross-domain generalization in Large Language Models (LLMs) originates from shared abstract reasoning prototypes, which represent fundamental, domain-agnostic reasoning patterns.
Training LLMs on formal prototype representations (e.g., Prolog, PDDL) is as effective as direct natural language training for enhancing generalizable reasoning on structurally similar problems.
Effective generalization through prototype training requires explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, as it homogenizes and reinforces reasoning paths.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.15050.Title: Truncated Proximal Policy Optimization
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.15050.Summary: Truncated Proximal Policy Optimization (T-PPO) significantly enhances the training efficiency of large language models for complex reasoning tasks by enabling progressive policy updates on incomplete trajectories. The method achieved up to 2.5x higher training efficiency, leading to a 60% reduction in wall-clock time while securing a 62 pass@1 score on the AIME 2024 benchmark.
Problem: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), a standard for fine-tuning LLMs, suffers from computational inefficiency due to its on-policy nature, requiring new, lengthy trajectory collection for each policy update, especially for long Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning.
The 'barrel effect' in distributed PPO training leads to low GPU utilization, as the system waits for the longest generated response in a batch to complete, leaving other resources idle.
Achieving high reasoning performance in LLMs typically demands generation of very long sequences, exacerbating the PPO efficiency problem and increasing training costs.
Method: Introduces Extended Generalized Advantage Estimation (EGAE), which allows the calculation of advantage estimates on truncated trajectories by approximating the value of future, ungenerated states, enabling progressive policy updates.

Implements a token filtering strategy with successive batching: generation is truncated by a window length, and completed sequences are dynamically replaced with new prompts to maintain constant batch size and maximize GPU throughput.

Employs a dual optimization mechanism where the policy model is updated on currently generated tokens using EGAE, while the value model is updated using Monte Carlo returns only from fully completed trajectories to ensure unbiased value predictions.
Results: T-PPO achieved a 62 pass@1 score on the AIME 2024 benchmark, outperforming existing baselines like DeepSeek-R1-Zero-Qwen-32B (47), DAPO (50), GePPO (50), PPO-EWMA (52), and slightly exceeding VAPO (60).
It demonstrated up to 2.5x higher training efficiency, resulting in a 60% reduction in wall-clock time compared to prior state-of-the-art synchronization algorithms.

Hardware utilization significantly improved, reaching 249 operations/byte in policy rollout on an Nvidia H800 GPU, compared to PPO's 84 operations/byte, indicating better compute resource utilization.
Takeaways: Policy optimization for large language models (LLMs) can be effectively performed on truncated, incomplete reasoning trajectories, significantly reducing idle compute time.
Dynamic batch management and successive batching, where new prompts fill slots left by completed sequences, substantially improve GPU utilization during LLM generation.

Decoupling policy updates (using Extended Generalized Advantage Estimation on current tokens) from value updates (using Monte Carlo on completed trajectories) allows for both efficient training and stable, unbiased value predictions.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.14965.Title: Revisiting Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning from A Cross-Domain Perspective
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.14965.Summary: The paper introduces GURU, a multi-domain reinforcement learning corpus with 92K verifiable examples across six distinct reasoning domains, enabling the training of GURU-7B and GURU-32B models. These models achieve state-of-the-art general reasoning capabilities among open RL-trained LLMs, demonstrating how multi-domain RL can lead to robust, generalized reasoning abilities.
Problem: Current reinforcement learning (RL) for large language model (LLM) reasoning predominantly focuses on mathematics and programming code, limiting the generalizability of understanding how RL improves reasoning and hindering the development of versatile models.
A significant bottleneck exists due to the scarcity of high-quality, diverse, and verifiable datasets suitable for RL training across a broad spectrum of reasoning domains beyond math and code.
Existing RL-trained LLMs tend to be highly specialized, often exhibiting performance degradation when applied to diverse reasoning tasks outside their specific training distribution.
Method: Introduced GURU, a multi-domain reinforcement learning corpus comprising 92K verifiable examples across six diverse reasoning domains: Math, Code, Science, Logic, Simulation, and Tabular.

Developed a meticulous five-stage data curation pipeline for GURU, including data sourcing from multiple datasets, conservative deduplication, domain-tailored binary reward design, heuristic filtering, and a crucial difficulty filtering stage.

Performed large-scale RL training experiments using the GRPO algorithm on single-domain and mixed-domain subsets of GURU, leveraging Qwen2.5-7B-Base and Qwen2.5-32B-Base models, and systematically evaluated them on comprehensive benchmark suites.
Results: GURU-7B and GURU-32B models establish new state-of-the-art performance among open models RL-trained with publicly available data, achieving average scores of 43.29% (+9.0% over best baselines) and 54.24% (+6.7% over best baselines) respectively across a 17-task evaluation suite.

Unlike domain-specific baselines, GURU models demonstrate superior and well-balanced performance across all evaluated domains (Math, Code, Science, Logic, Simulation, Tabular) and unseen generalization tasks.

Pass@k analysis indicates task-dependent patterns where RL expands the reasoning boundary on complex, less pretraining-exposed tasks like the synthetic Zebra Puzzle, providing evidence of genuine skill acquisition, while on tasks like AIME (Math), it aligns with knowledge elicitation.
Takeaways: RL's impact on LLM reasoning is highly domain-dependent: it primarily elicits existing knowledge in domains frequently encountered during pretraining (Math, Code, Science) and facilitates genuine skill acquisition in less-exposed domains (Logic, Simulation, Tabular).

Training on a uniformly mixed, diverse dataset is remarkably effective, enabling models to achieve performance comparable to, and often surpassing, those trained exclusively on single-domain data, indicating enhanced general reasoning with minimal apparent interference.

Training on difficulty-filtered (harder) in-domain data consistently improves in-domain performance but can lead to degradation on easier cross-domain tasks, suggesting a risk of negative transfer if not carefully managed for beneficial cross-domain transfer.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.14728.Title: AgentDistill: Training-Free Agent Distillation with Generalizable MCP Boxes
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.14728.Summary: AgentDistill presents a training-free framework for distilling advanced problem-solving capabilities from large language model (LLM) agents into smaller, more efficient student LLMs. It achieves this by having a teacher agent generate reusable Model–Context–Protocols (MCPs) which are then consolidated into an 'MCP-Box' that student agents directly leverage for tool-use, leading to substantial performance gains and enabling them to perform comparably to larger, more expensive systems.
Problem: Large language models (LLMs) used in agents incur substantial inference costs, limiting their widespread and continuous deployment.
Existing agent distillation methods often require computationally expensive fine-tuning on full teacher trajectories and struggle to generalize to novel environments or tasks.
Current distillation approaches frequently overlook inherent capability differences between teacher and student models, hindering effective knowledge transfer for adaptive problem-solving.
Method: A training-free agent distillation framework called AgentDistill is introduced, centered on Model–Context–Protocols (MCPs) generated by a teacher agent.
The teacher agent identifies subtasks requiring tool-use and generates structured, self-contained MCPs from successful reasoning trajectories.

These collected MCPs are then abstracted, clustered by functionality, and consolidated into a compact, parameterized 'MCP-Box' by a high-capacity instruction-tuned LLM, which student agents directly utilize during inference.
Results: Student agents demonstrated high MCP-Box calling rates (24.3% to 100%) across benchmarks, confirming broad applicability and reuse of distilled MCPs without additional training.
AgentDistill led to substantial performance improvements for student agents, including gains of +7.0% on PathVQA for GPT-3.5-turbo and +48.4% on Game of 24 for GPT-3.5-turbo.
Distilled student agents achieved performance comparable to or sometimes surpassing teacher agents and strong retrieval-based baselines like OctoTools with GPT-4o on tasks like PathVQA.
Takeaways: Teacher-generated Model–Context–Protocols (MCPs) can effectively encapsulate generalizable and reusable tool-use logic from complex tasks.
Distilling knowledge into structured, parameterized MCPs and packaging them into an 'MCP-Box' allows for a training-free transfer of sophisticated capabilities.

Small language models can achieve performance comparable to larger LLMs by leveraging a pre-validated, pre-packaged library of functional tools, without needing to learn tool implementations or elaborate reasoning chains through fine-tuning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.14641.Title: Revisiting Chain-of-Thought Prompting: Zero-shot Can Be Stronger than Few-shot
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.14641.Summary: This study demonstrates that for recent, powerful large language models, Zero-shot Chain-of-Thought prompting often outperforms Few-shot variants in mathematical reasoning tasks after correcting evaluation biases, suggesting exemplars primarily serve to standardize output format rather than enhance core reasoning abilities.
Problem: The prevailing assumption that Few-shot Chain-of-Thought (CoT) universally improves Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning, largely derived from experiments on older, weaker models.
A lack of clarity regarding the actual role and effectiveness of CoT exemplars for newer, intrinsically stronger LLMs.
Potential evaluation biases in standard benchmarks that could obscure the true reasoning capabilities of Zero-shot CoT.
Method: Systematically compared Few-shot and Zero-shot CoT across a range of strong, instruction-tuned LLMs (e.g., Qwen2.5, LLaMA3) on mathematical reasoning benchmarks like GSM8K and MATH.
Identified and corrected a critical evaluation bias in GSM8K, ensuring accurate extraction of boxed answers from CoT outputs to enable fair comparisons.
Conducted extensive ablation studies, including varying exemplar content, retrieval methods, noise injection, and attention visualizations to understand exemplar utility.
Results: After correcting a prevalent evaluation bias, Zero-shot CoT consistently achieved substantial performance gains and frequently surpassed Few-shot CoT for strong models on GSM8K.
Few-shot CoT for strong models generally yielded comparable or worse performance than Zero-shot CoT on both GSM8K and MATH, failing to demonstrate reasoning enhancement.

Attention visualizations and noisy exemplar ablation studies showed that strong models allocated consistently low attention to exemplar content, suggesting reliance on internal capabilities rather than explicit examples for reasoning.
Takeaways: The primary function of Few-shot CoT exemplars for strong LLMs shifts from enhancing reasoning to mainly aligning output formats for reliable evaluation.
Zero-shot CoT, when properly evaluated, can be as strong as or stronger than Few-shot CoT for modern, capable LLMs in mathematical reasoning tasks.
The utility of CoT exemplars is model-dependent, still providing reasoning benefits for weaker models but being largely ignored semantically by stronger ones.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.14245.Title: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards Implicitly Incentivizes Correct Reasoning in Base LLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.14245.Summary: Researchers at Microsoft Research Asia and collaborating universities demonstrate that Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) fundamentally enhances Large Language Model reasoning capabilities, extending their problem-solving boundaries beyond improved sampling efficiency. The work introduces CoT-Pass@K to rigorously evaluate reasoning and provides a theoretical framework explaining how answer-based rewards implicitly incentivize correct intermediate thought processes.
Problem: The ongoing debate regarding whether Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) genuinely improves Large Language Model (LLM) intrinsic reasoning or merely boosts sampling efficiency for existing reasoning paths.
Limitations of standard evaluation metrics like Pass@K, which can be inflated by LLMs producing correct final answers through flawed intermediate reasoning, especially in mathematical tasks.
A lack of a comprehensive theoretical framework explaining how RLVR implicitly incentivizes correct reasoning, particularly when rewards are solely based on final answer correctness.
Method: Introduced CoT-Pass@K, a refined evaluation metric that verifies both the final answer and the correctness of intermediate Chain-of-Thought (CoT) steps, leveraging an LLM-as-a-CoT-Judge paradigm for scalable verification.

Developed a theoretical framework demonstrating that RLVR, under a 'Logic Prior' assumption (correct CoTs more likely to yield correct answers), implicitly incentivizes the generation of correct CoTs, even with binary answer-based rewards.

Conducted empirical analyses of RLVR training dynamics and evaluated the quality of RLVR-generated CoTs through supervised fine-tuning experiments, using generalization performance as a proxy for CoT quality.
Results: RLVR models (e.g., DAPO-Qwen-32B) showed a consistent and significant performance gap over base LLMs on math benchmarks (AIME 2024/2025) across large sampling numbers (up to K=1024) when measured by CoT-Pass@K.

The theoretical framework proved that the GRPO policy gradient positively biases correct CoTs and negatively biases incorrect ones, leading to a monotonic increase in the probability of generating correct CoTs.

Supervised fine-tuning on CoTs generated by the final RLVR model (DAPO CoTs) nearly replicated the Pass@1 performance of the RLVR-tuned model, demonstrating a fundamental enhancement in the quality of reasoning paths.
Takeaways: RLVR fundamentally extends the reasoning capabilities of LLMs beyond mere sampling efficiency, as evidenced by consistent performance gaps over base models on challenging benchmarks when evaluated with CoT-Pass@K.

The 'Logic Prior' assumption, combined with the GRPO algorithm, explains how even binary answer-level rewards can implicitly and monotonically increase the probability of generating correct intermediate reasoning steps.

RLVR produces high-quality reasoning CoTs that can be used to significantly improve other models via supervised fine-tuning, nearly replicating the performance of computationally expensive RLVR-tuned models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13925.Title: Segmenting Visuals With Querying Words: Language Anchors For Semi-Supervised Image Segmentation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13925.Summary: HVL, a framework developed by researchers from the University of Regina, University of Western Australia, and University Canada West, enhances semi-supervised semantic segmentation by integrating hierarchical vision-language synergy. It leverages VLM text embeddings as dynamic, context-aware object queries, achieving state-of-the-art performance with less than 1% labeled data across major benchmarks.
Problem: Acquiring pixel-level annotations for semantic segmentation is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming, necessitating label-efficient methods.

Existing semi-supervised semantic segmentation (SSS) methods, relying primarily on visual features, often struggle with semantic ambiguities (e.g., distinguishing visually similar classes) and are vulnerable to domain shifts.
Vision-Language Models (VLMs) offer robust, domain-invariant semantic understanding but lack the fine-grained spatial precision required for pixel-level dense prediction tasks like segmentation.
Method: HVL introduces a transformer-based framework that integrates domain-invariant text embeddings from VLMs as hierarchical object queries for semi-supervised semantic segmentation.
A Hierarchical Textual Query Generator (HTQG) creates multi-level, image-relevant, and semantically rich class queries by filtering classes present in an image and capturing intra-class variations.

A Pixel-Text Refinement Module (PTRM) mutually refines visual pixel features and textual queries using bidirectional cross-attention, while a Dual-Query Transformer Decoder (DQTD) combines these class-level textual queries with instance-level visual queries, supported by regularization losses to maintain vision-language alignment.
Results: HVL achieved new state-of-the-art mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) across four major benchmarks, including a +9.3% mIoU gain on COCO with 232 labeled images and +13.5% mIoU on ADE20K with 158 labeled images.

Qualitative results demonstrate enhanced class discrimination for visually similar objects, reduced over-segmentation, sharper object boundaries, and more accurate instance recognition compared to prior methods.

Ablation studies confirmed that the Hierarchical Textual Query Generator and Pixel-Text Refinement Module contribute the most significant performance gains, particularly in low-label settings, with all regularization losses collectively boosting performance by 2.4 mIoU on Pascal VOC.
Takeaways: Directly leveraging VLM text embeddings as hierarchical, image-context-aware object queries significantly enhances semantic grounding and generalization in low-supervision segmentation settings.

The explicit mutual refinement between global semantic textual queries and local spatial visual features (PTRM) effectively bridges the modality gap, improving both semantic clarity and spatial precision.

Combining domain-invariant class-level textual queries with instance-level visual queries in a dual-query decoder effectively captures both high-level semantic understanding and fine-grained intra-class variations for robust segmentation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13923.Title: Adaptive Guidance Accelerates Reinforcement Learning of Reasoning Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13923.Summary: This paper investigates how large language models learn complex reasoning when trained with Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), formally decomposing performance gains into 'self-distillation' and 'capability gain'. The authors introduce 'Guide-GRPO,' an adaptive online RL algorithm that strategically injects natural language hints when unguided attempts fail, demonstrating superior generalization on mathematical reasoning benchmarks and a consistent performance lead across model scales up to 72B parameters.
Problem: The precise mechanisms driving performance gains in Large Language Models (LLMs) trained with Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) were poorly understood, particularly the balance between refining existing knowledge and acquiring new capabilities.

Accelerating the acquisition of genuinely new problem-solving abilities in LLMs during RLVR training remained a challenge, as existing methods often struggled to efficiently help models overcome problems they could not initially solve.
Developing an effective and scalable method to inject targeted learning signals that improve LLMs' reasoning without requiring constant guidance or relying solely on off-policy data was needed.
Method: The paper formally decomposes RLVR's performance gains into 'self-distillation' (improving pass@k to pass@1) and 'capability gain' (solving previously unsolvable problems), enabling a quantitative understanding of learning mechanisms.

A new class of online RL training algorithms, 'Guide' (specifically Guide-GRPO), is introduced, which adaptively injects natural language hints into the model's context only for problems where all initial unguided rollouts fail.

Guide-GRPO uses importance sampling to optimize the policy for contexts where hints are absent, ensuring that learning from guided trajectories translates to improved performance in unguided inference scenarios.
Results: Empirical analysis confirmed that self-distillation is the dominant driver of RLVR learning across Qwen 2.5 models (0.5B to 72B parameters), with capability gain being a minority contributor.

Guide-GRPO consistently achieved superior performance on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, outperforming standard GRPO, Filter-GRPO, and SFT, with a macro-average Pass@1 of 51.03% and Pass@16 of 70.15%.

Guide-GRPO demonstrated robust scalability, maintaining its performance lead over vanilla GRPO with increased context length (4K to 8K) and model size (7B to 32B), achieving 3.39 percentage points higher macro-average Pass@1 for the 32B model with 8K context.
Takeaways: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) performance gains are predominantly driven by 'self-distillation,' where models learn to convert problems solvable with multiple attempts (pass@k) into single-attempt solutions (pass@1).
Genuine 'capability gain,' solving problems previously unsolvable even with multiple attempts, contributes a smaller but present portion to RLVR's learning progress across various model scales.

Adaptive, in-context guidance applied selectively when all unguided rollouts fail, combined with importance sampling, accelerates the acquisition of new problem-solving abilities without requiring hints at inference time.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13888.Title: VL-GenRM: Enhancing Vision-Language Verification via Vision Experts and Iterative Training
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13888.Summary: VL-GENRM enhances Vision-Language Reward Models (VL-RMs) through a novel iterative training framework that incorporates external vision experts and Chain-of-Thought rationales. The approach improves hallucination detection and general instruction following in VL-RMs, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance on relevant benchmarks and boosting the Best-of-N accuracy of base Vision-Language Models.
Problem: Training high-quality Vision-Language Reward Models (VL-RMs) faces a "bootstrapping" dilemma, requiring strong VL models to generate training data, leading to a circular dependency.

VL-RMs suffer from inherited modality bias and negative example amplification when trained on responses from VLMs, reinforcing existing hallucinations rather than truly addressing visual-textual inconsistency.
Existing VL-RM training methods struggle to provide structured, verifiable feedback for effectively aligning multimodal Large Language Models (LLMs).
Method: A two-phase data collection process leverages external vision experts (e.g., object detection models) to filter and augment negative responses, ensuring visual grounding and breaking the bootstrapping cycle.
VL-GENRM is trained with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) rationales, where the model first generates a step-by-step reasoning explanation before outputting a binary correctness assessment.

An iterative optimization framework refines the VL-GenRM by self-generating CoT rationales and applying margin-based rejection sampling to select informative examples for subsequent lightweight fine-tuning.
Results: VL-GenRM (7B) achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-source VLMs in general QA and hallucination robustness on VLRewardBench, outperforming much larger models.
It consistently outperforms baseline reward modeling methods, including Bradley-Terry RM and VLM-as-a-Judge, across General, Hallucination, and Reasoning evaluation categories.
When used as a test-time verifier, VL-GenRM consistently improves Best-of-N accuracy across different base VLMs, demonstrating its effectiveness in enhancing the quality of VLM outputs.
Takeaways: Leveraging external, specialized vision expertise is crucial for generating high-quality, visually grounded negative examples, mitigating inherited biases in Vision-Language Reward Model (VL-RM) training.
Integrating Chain-of-Thought (CoT) rationales into VL-RM training enables more structured reasoning and verifiable feedback, improving both hallucination control and general instruction following.
An iterative self-improvement process, guided by margin-based rejection sampling of self-generated rationales, can progressively refine VL-RM capabilities and enhance reward alignment.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13759.Title: Discrete Diffusion in Large Language and Multimodal Models: A Survey
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13759.Summary: This survey provides a systematic overview of Discrete Diffusion Language Models (dLLMs) and Multimodal Language Models (dMLLMs), detailing their mathematical foundations, modeling innovations, and diverse applications. It highlights how these models achieve up to 10 times faster inference and offer enhanced control compared to traditional autoregressive models, establishing them as a promising paradigm for future generative AI.
Problem: Autoregressive (AR) models suffer from slow sequential inference, preventing parallel generation of output tokens.
AR models exhibit limited fine-grained control over output attributes, often requiring complex prompt engineering.
The static, one-pass perception of input contexts in AR models hinders dynamic, task-aware comprehension.
Method: Discrete diffusion models reframe generation as an iterative denoising process over discrete token sequences, enabling parallel decoding for faster inference.
These models provide enhanced controllability over output properties by treating generation as a denoising or infilling task.
Bidirectional attention in discrete diffusion models allows for continuous revision of context perception throughout the generation process.
Results: The survey systematically consolidates fragmented research on discrete diffusion models, tracing their evolution and categorizing their mathematical frameworks, architectures, and techniques.

It details sophisticated training paradigms, such as diverse masking strategies, reweighting techniques, distillation, and reinforcement learning, alongside innovative inference methods like unmasking, remasking, and various guidance mechanisms.

The work identifies critical future research directions, including the development of robust infrastructure, further optimization of inference efficiency, and improved security and privacy safeguards tailored for d(M)LLMs.
Takeaways: Discrete diffusion models offer a viable alternative to autoregressive models, providing up to 10x faster inference speeds and improved control over generation.
The field is built on diverse mathematical foundations, including D3PMs, simplified masked diffusion, and continuous-time frameworks, each offering distinct approaches to the denoising process.

Discrete diffusion models have rapidly scaled and diversified across language and multimodal tasks, showcasing competitive performance and expanding applications in areas like reasoning, robotics, and drug discovery.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13723.Title: OTFusion: Bridging Vision-only and Vision-Language Models via Optimal Transport for Transductive Zero-Shot Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13723.Summary: OTFusion unifies Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and Vision-only Foundation Models (VFMs) using Optimal Transport to enhance Transductive Zero-Shot Learning (ZSL). The training-free framework achieves an average accuracy improvement of nearly 10% over the CLIP baseline across 11 datasets, often surpassing training-based methods.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) excel at semantic alignment but struggle with fine-grained visual distinctions and domain shifts in Zero-Shot Learning (ZSL).
Vision-only Foundation Models (VFMs) provide rich, discriminative visual features but inherently lack semantic grounding for direct ZSL.
Existing methods to combine these models are often computationally expensive, require extensive training, or lack broad generalizability across different foundation models.
Method: OTFusion proposes a training-free framework that models both VLM and VFM outputs as probability distributions over class labels.
A Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) is fitted to VFM features to generate a visual prior, while VLM predictions provide a semantic prior.
Optimal Transport is employed to fuse these visual and semantic priors, creating a unified probabilistic representation through an alternating optimization scheme with mutual reinforcement.
Results: The framework achieves an average accuracy improvement of nearly 10% over the CLIP baseline across 11 diverse benchmark datasets.
OTFusion frequently outperforms state-of-the-art training-based ZSL methods by over 10% on average, demonstrating high efficiency without additional training.
The method exhibits fast convergence (typically within 5 iterations) and robust performance across a range of hyperparameters, particularly the entropy regularization strength.
Takeaways: VLMs and VFMs offer complementary strengths: VLMs provide semantic structure, while VFMs offer fine-grained visual discrimination.
Optimal Transport effectively bridges these diverse foundation models by operating in the probability space, allowing for training-free and model-agnostic integration.
A joint optimization that mutually reinforces GMM parameter updates with the evolving Optimal Transport plan ensures that visual clusters are not only coherent but also semantically aligned.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13585.Title: MiniMax-M1: Scaling Test-Time Compute Efficiently with Lightning Attention
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13585.Summary: MiniMax developed MiniMax-M1, a large reasoning model leveraging a hybrid Mixture-of-Experts architecture with Lightning Attention to enable efficient scaling of test-time compute for extremely long contexts. It supports up to 1 million input tokens and 80,000 generation tokens while achieving substantial FLOPs reduction and competitive performance across various reasoning benchmarks.
Problem: The quadratic computational complexity of traditional softmax attention limits the ability to continuously extend reasoning processes and support very long context lengths in large language models (LLMs).
Existing large reasoning models (LRMs) struggle with high computational costs during inference for extended generations, making them prohibitively expensive for complex real-world applications.
There was a lack of open-weight, large-scale reasoning models that effectively leverage and validate computationally efficient attention mechanisms for long-context tasks.
Method: The model employs a hybrid Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture with 456 billion total parameters, integrating Lightning Attention (an I/O-aware linear attention variant) in most blocks, interspersed with standard softmax attention blocks.

A multi-stage training pipeline was used, including continual pre-training on a reasoning-intensive corpus, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with long Chain-of-Thought examples, and extensive reinforcement learning (RL).

A novel RL algorithm, ClippedIS-weight Policy Optimization (CISPO), was introduced to clip importance sampling weights rather than token updates, enhancing training stability and achieving a 2x speedup over DAPO.
Results: MiniMax-M1 achieved a significant FLOPs reduction during inference, consuming less than 50% of FLOPs compared to DeepSeek R1 at 64K generation length and approximately 25% at 100K tokens.
The model natively supports input contexts up to 1 million tokens and generation lengths of 80,000 tokens, demonstrating an 8x context size increase over DeepSeek R1.

MiniMax-M1-80k outperformed other open-weight models and even some closed-weight models (like OpenAI o3 and Claude 4 Opus) on long-context understanding benchmarks (e.g., OpenAI-MRCR at 128k and 1M tokens), while performing comparably on general coding and agentic tool use benchmarks.
Takeaways: Efficient linear attention mechanisms, when integrated into a hybrid architecture, can achieve competitive performance at frontier model scales while providing substantial efficiency gains for long-context reasoning.

The novel CISPO reinforcement learning algorithm, which clips importance sampling weights instead of token updates, significantly improves training efficiency and stability for complex reasoning behaviors.

Scaling context lengths during training for hybrid attention models requires a gradual, multi-staged approach and careful management of precision mismatches and pathological generation patterns to ensure stability.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13351.Title: Direct Reasoning Optimization: Constrained RL with Token-Level Dense Reward and Rubric-Gated Constraints for Open-ended Tasks
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13351.Summary: Researchers from Microsoft and UCLA developed Direct Reasoning Optimization (DRO), an RL-based framework that allows large language models to self-refine their reasoning for open-ended tasks by using a novel internal Reasoning Reflection Reward (R3). This method leverages the model's self-certainty about a reference outcome given its Chain-of-Thought, leading to superior reasoning quality on tasks like paragraph revision and comparable performance to explicit verifiers on structured QA.
Problem: Existing Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) struggles with open-ended, long-form reasoning tasks due to the lack of objective, scalable reward signals.
Training separate reward models is computationally expensive and requires extensive human preference data, while "LLM-as-a-judge" introduces biases and prompt sensitivity.
Traditional metrics like ROUGE fail to capture logical coherence or reasoning quality in open-ended generations.
Method: Direct Reasoning Optimization (DRO), an RL-based fine-tuning framework, is introduced to enable self-reward and self-refinement for LLMs on open-ended tasks.
A novel internal reward signal, Reasoning Reflection Reward (R3), quantifies the consistency between a model's Chain-of-Thought and a reference outcome by emphasizing "reasoning-reflective tokens."
R3 addresses log-probability aggregation issues by weighting crucial tokens and subtracting a masked-CoT baseline, while a dynamic data filtering mechanism optimizes training efficiency.
Results: On the open-ended ParaRev dataset, DRO-R3 achieved higher win rates against GPT-4o than all baselines, including ROUGE-rewarded and aggregate-certainty models, as evaluated by GPT-4o and Claude 3.7 Sonnet.
For the structured FinQA task, DRO-R3 demonstrated performance comparable to an ideal correctness-based reward, falling just 0.9% short on Pass@1 and surpassing it for Pass@k (k 2).
The dynamic data filtering mechanism reduced training time by approximately 45% while maintaining similar final reward scores and ensuring smoother convergence.
Takeaways: Large Language Models can effectively reward and refine their own reasoning for open-ended tasks using internal self-certainty signals, eliminating reliance on external feedback.

Not all tokens contribute equally to reflecting reasoning quality; emphasizing "reasoning-reflective tokens" via variance weighting provides a more precise reward signal than naive log-probability aggregation.
Dynamically filtering training data based on model difficulty and reasoning variation significantly improves training efficiency and focuses learning on impactful samples.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13331.Title: Mixture of Cognitive Reasoners: Modular Reasoning with Brain-Like Specialization
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13331.Summary: Researchers from EPFL, MIT, and Harvard developed Mixture of Cognitive Reasoners (MICRO), a modular LLM architecture that explicitly incorporates specialized "expert" modules aligned with human brain networks. The model demonstrates interpretable, brain-like functional specialization, enhanced alignment with human behavior on the COGBENCH benchmark, and competitive performance on various reasoning tasks, enabling dynamic control over its cognitive processes.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) possess largely unstructured internal organizations, contrasting with the human brain's clear functional specialization across distinct cognitive networks.
Existing LLMs, despite exhibiting implicit specialization, lack explicit interpretability and fine-grained controllability over their reasoning processes.
Bridging the gap between AI models and human cognition requires architectures that not only perform well but also mechanistically align with human brain organization and behavior.
Method: A Mixture-of-Blocks (MOB) transformer architecture, MICRO, is introduced, where each layer's entire transformer block is duplicated into four "expert" modules aligned with human cognitive networks (Language, Logic, Social, World).

A three-stage training curriculum induces specialization: experts are first primed on a small, pseudo-labeled dataset with deterministic token routing, then a router learns to assign tokens, and finally, the whole model is finetuned end-to-end on a large instruction dataset.
An MLP-based router dynamically assigns each token to a single expert module at every layer, enabling context-dependent activation of specialized reasoning paths.
Results: MICRO models exhibit clear domain-specific token routing and an emergent hierarchical processing structure, with router probabilities correlating with human behavioral judgments (e.g., social expert selectivity with mental state content, r=0.7).

Mechanistic ablations confirmed the causal role of individual experts, with Logic expert ablation significantly reducing accuracy on math tasks and Social expert ablation sometimes improving performance on purely logical problems.

The framework achieved superior alignment with human behavior on the COGBENCH benchmark and matched or outperformed non-modular and general-purpose modular baselines on various reasoning tasks including GSM8K, MATH, MMLU, and BBH.
Takeaways: Explicitly incorporating cognitive inductive biases into LLM design, coupled with a targeted training curriculum, effectively induces interpretable, brain-like functional specialization in models.

The Mixture-of-Blocks (MOB) architecture, where entire transformer blocks function as experts, is crucial for achieving clear and reliable specialization, particularly in larger models, outperforming traditional Mixture-of-Experts.

Functionally specialized modules in AI models offer a computational framework to test hypotheses about human brain network interactions and provide enhanced interpretability and dynamic control over AI reasoning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13284.Title: AceReason-Nemotron 1.1: Advancing Math and Code Reasoning through SFT and RL Synergy
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13284.Summary: NVIDIA researchers developed AceReason-Nemotron 1.1, a Qwen2.5-7B based model, by systematically investigating the synergy between supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) to enhance math and code reasoning. The model achieved new state-of-the-art performance for its size on challenging benchmarks like AIME25 (64.8%) and LiveCodeBench v6 (52.1%).
Problem: Prior research lacked a systematic study on the synergy between supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) in developing reasoning models.
Technical reports from frontier models often omitted detailed insights into how SFT and RL post-training techniques interact and influence each other's effectiveness.
Optimizing training pipelines required a better understanding of SFT data scaling strategies, RL hyperparameter tuning, and stage-wise curriculum design.
Method: NVIDIA researchers developed a comprehensive, stage-wise training pipeline combining Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and GRPO-based Reinforcement Learning (RL), building upon a Qwen2.5-Math-7B base model.
They systematically investigated SFT data scaling by constructing various datasets to analyze the impact of unique prompts versus responses per prompt on performance.

Extensive RL ablation studies were conducted on factors such as initial SFT model strength, sampling temperature, strategies for handling overlong responses, and the necessity and duration of an initial warm-up RL stage.
Results: AceReason-Nemotron-1.1-7B achieved new state-of-the-art pass@1 performance among Qwen2.5-7B-based models, including 64.8% on AIME25 and 52.1% on LiveCodeBench v6.
The model demonstrated absolute performance gains of 10.6% on AIME24, 16.4% on AIME25, 8.4% on LiveCodeBench v5, and 8.3% on LiveCodeBench v6 over its strong SFT starting model.
RL training enabled the model to solve a 'long tail' of harder problems that the initial SFT model struggled with, particularly evident on LiveCodeBench where it solved over ten additional problems.
Takeaways: Scaling the number of unique prompts in supervised fine-tuning (SFT) had a more significant impact on reasoning performance than increasing the number of generated responses per prompt, as indicated by higher regression coefficients.

Reinforcement learning (RL) consistently improved performance even when starting from strong SFT baselines, and while a stronger SFT initialization led to better final results, RL training effectively narrowed initial performance gaps between different SFT models.

An initial 'Math-only Stage-1' in the RL curriculum, despite a temporary performance dip, was crucial for learning concise reasoning and enabling higher gains in subsequent stages, facilitating a smoother transition from SFT to RL.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13131.Title: AlphaEvolve: A coding agent for scientific and algorithmic discovery
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13131.Summary: AlphaEvolve, from Google DeepMind, combines large language models with an evolutionary search framework to autonomously discover novel algorithms and optimize code. This system identified a faster procedure for 4x4 complex matrix multiplication, improved state-of-the-art for several open mathematical problems, and delivered tangible optimizations for Google's computing ecosystem, including recovering 0.7% of fleet-wide compute resources.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) often struggle to generate entirely novel and verifiable scientific or algorithmic discoveries in a single attempt, frequently producing "hallucinations."
Automated discovery systems need to move beyond simple code generation to enable continuous, iterative improvement of complex algorithms based on empirical feedback.

Optimizing critical computational infrastructure and solving open scientific problems often require designing sophisticated, multi-stage search algorithms or making subtle, high-impact code changes that are difficult for humans or prior AI systems to identify.
Method: AlphaEvolve implements a distributed, asynchronous evolutionary pipeline that orchestrates state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs) within a continuous feedback loop.
LLMs are prompted to propose targeted code modifications (diff blocks) to existing programs, which are then automatically evaluated against user-defined metrics.

The system maintains a 'Program database' inspired by MAP-elites to balance exploration and exploitation, iteratively refining solutions, and utilizes an ensemble of LLMs for high-throughput and high-quality generation.
Results: Discovered a procedure for multiplying 4x4 complex matrices using 48 scalar multiplications, improving upon Strassen’s 49-multiplication algorithm (a first in 56 years) and enhancing 14 other matrix multiplication algorithms.
Achieved new state-of-the-art results in approximately 20% of over 50 open mathematical problems, including improving the lower bound for the kissing number in 11 dimensions from 592 to 593.

Deployed optimizations across Google's computing ecosystem, recovering 0.7% of fleet-wide compute resources in data center scheduling, accelerating Gemini training kernels by 23%, and contributing to TPU hardware circuit design.
Takeaways: Integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) into an evolutionary feedback loop allows for continuous, iterative refinement of code, transforming LLMs from one-shot generators into active agents for discovery.
LLMs can automate the design of complex 'evolution operators' and even evolve entire heuristic search algorithms, enabling adaptive, multi-stage problem-solving previously difficult to achieve.

Combining an ensemble of LLMs with efficient, parallelized evaluation cascades and multi-objective optimization strategies significantly boosts the system's ability to explore complex search spaces and identify subtle improvements.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13056.Title: Metis-RISE: RL Incentivizes and SFT Enhances Multimodal Reasoning Model Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13056.Summary: Meituan introduces Metis-RISE, a hybrid training framework that first uses Reinforcement Learning to activate latent multimodal reasoning in MLLMs, then applies Supervised Fine-Tuning to refine these abilities. The approach yields state-of-the-art performance on reasoning benchmarks for both 7B and 72B parameter open-source models, demonstrating competitive results against leading proprietary models.
Problem: Existing Reinforcement Learning (RL) only methods for MLLMs are sample-inefficient and struggle to activate reasoning abilities not already somewhat present in the base model.
Conventional Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) before RL restricts a model's exploratory capacity, limiting discovery of new reasoning pathways during the RL phase.
Models, even after RL, often exhibit inconsistent application of correct logic (inefficient trajectory sampling) or completely lack fundamental reasoning capabilities for certain problems.
Method: A two-stage hybrid training framework: Reinforcement Learning (RL) for incentivization, followed by Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) for enhancement, notably omitting an initial cold-start SFT.

The initial RL phase, using a modified Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and a hybrid format/accuracy reward, directly encourages exploration and activates latent reasoning without prior SFT constraints.

The subsequent SFT phase uses a curated dataset combining self-distilled successful trajectories (for consistent application) and expert-augmented solutions (for absent capabilities) to refine and solidify the model's reasoning.
Results: Metis-RISE-7B achieved an average score of 46.4 on multimodal reasoning benchmarks, establishing state-of-the-art performance among open-source models in the ≤10B parameter category.

Metis-RISE-72B reached an average score of 56.6, becoming the top-performing open-source model in the >10B category and demonstrating competitiveness with proprietary models like ChatGPT-4o and Gemini-2.0-Pro.

Ablation studies confirmed that the initial RL phase boosted performance by 4.8 points, and the subsequent SFT enhancement phase further improved it by 2.4 points, validating the cumulative benefits of the proposed two-stage approach.
Takeaways: Initiating training with Reinforcement Learning (RL) is more effective for activating latent reasoning and encouraging exploration in MLLMs than starting with Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT).
A targeted SFT phase, following RL, can specifically address inconsistent reasoning application and fill fundamental knowledge gaps, further enhancing overall model performance.
The synergistic combination of RL-first incentivization and problem-specific SFT enhancement leads to cumulative improvements in multimodal reasoning capabilities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13018.Title: Symmetry in Neural Network Parameter Spaces
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13018.Summary: This survey paper systematically consolidates fragmented knowledge on parameter space symmetry in neural networks, defining its various forms and demonstrating its pervasive influence on loss landscape geometry, optimization dynamics, and generalization. It provides a unified framework for understanding how transformations of parameters, which leave the network's output function or loss unchanged, shape deep learning theory and practice across diverse architectures.
Problem: Modern deep learning models exhibit pervasive overparameterization, leading to numerous parameter configurations that yield functionally identical outputs.
A unified theoretical understanding of how parameter space symmetry impacts loss landscapes, optimization, and generalization in neural networks has been lacking.
Existing deep learning theory often focuses on data space symmetry, leaving the critical role of parameter space symmetry relatively underexplored despite its empirical relevance.
Method: The authors conduct a comprehensive review, formally defining various types of parameter space symmetries (e.g., functional, loss, data-dependent, distribution-dependent) using group theory.
The survey illustrates the ubiquity of these symmetries with concrete examples across diverse neural network components and modern architectures like Transformers.

It synthesizes the literature by organizing the impact of symmetry into distinct thematic areas: loss landscapes, optimization algorithms, learning dynamics, and connections to internal representations and data space symmetries.
Results: The survey demonstrates that actively addressing or "removing symmetry" can simplify loss landscapes, facilitate model compression, and potentially improve optimization efficiency.

Understanding parameter symmetries enables advanced optimization techniques, such as "neural teleportation" to navigate orbits for better gradient properties, and the design of symmetry-invariant algorithms like Path-SGD.

The work establishes connections between parameter symmetries and equivariance in internal representations, also showing how parameter symmetries become "data symmetries" in weight space learning for improved meta-architectures and data augmentation.
Takeaways: Functional parameter space symmetries, including continuous (e.g., scaling, orthogonal transformations) and discrete (e.g., neuron permutations), are ubiquitous across various neural network architectures.

These symmetries fundamentally shape loss landscapes by explaining mode connectivity through continuous manifolds of equivalent minima and the combinatorial replication of minima via discrete transformations.
Continuous parameter symmetries give rise to conserved quantities in gradient flow, analogous to Noether's theorem, providing insights into implicit bias and constraining learning trajectories.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.12776.Title: Native Visual Understanding: Resolving Resolution Dilemmas in Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.12776.Summary: This research introduces RC-Bench, a resolution-centric benchmark, and NativeRes-LLaVA, an open-source training framework, to enable Vision-Language Models to process images at their native resolutions and aspect ratios. The NativeRes-LLaVA framework demonstrates improved accuracy and robustness on tasks requiring fine-grained visual details, particularly for images with extreme resolutions or aspect ratios.
Problem: Most Vision-Language Models (VLMs) process images at a fixed, often low resolution, leading to a loss of fine-grained visual details crucial for tasks like OCR, chart interpretation, or medical image analysis.

Existing multimodal benchmarks are 'Semantic-Centric' and do not adequately evaluate VLM performance under varying resolution and aspect ratio conditions, hindering the development of robust visual encoding strategies.
The open-source ecosystem for native-resolution VLMs is fragmented, lacking unified frameworks that allow for systematic research and comparison of dynamic visual encoding approaches.
Method: Introduction of RC-Bench, a new Resolution-Centric benchmark specifically designed to evaluate VLMs' visual encoding capabilities under diverse resolutions and aspect ratios, using a balanced distribution of image areas and aspect ratios with human-annotated QA pairs.

Development of NativeRes-LLaVA, an open-source, end-to-end training framework featuring a Native Resolution Vision Encoder (ViT), a compression module, and a two-layer MLP connecting to an LLM backbone (Qwen2-7B-Instruct).

Implementation of Multimodal Sequence Packing ('Patch n' Pack') to efficiently handle variable-length visual token sequences generated by the native resolution encoder, using Variable Length Flash Attention for parallel processing without redundant padding.
Results: NativeRes-LLaVA, trained on 1.34M samples, achieved top results on several resolution-centric benchmarks, including TextVQA (74.0%), ChartQA (79.0%), DocVQA (89.7%), and OCRBench (705), outperforming many models trained on larger datasets.

On the newly introduced RC-Bench, the native resolution strategy consistently showed higher average accuracy and greater robustness (lower Coefficient of Variation for Area Accuracy and Ratio Accuracy) compared to cropping-based and fixed-resolution methods.

The native resolution method demonstrated a significant advantage in processing images with extreme aspect ratios (e.g., very high or very wide) or ultra-large areas, highlighting its superior generalization to diverse visual data.
Takeaways: Native resolution visual encoding provides inherent advantages for Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in handling diverse image resolutions and aspect ratios, leading to improved accuracy on fine-grained visual tasks.

Existing VLM benchmarks often lack sufficient resolution and aspect ratio diversity, and a resolution-centric benchmark is crucial for accurately evaluating a VLM's ability to process varied visual inputs.

The proposed NativeRes-LLaVA framework's open-source nature and modular design, along with its multimodal sequence packing, offer an efficient and accessible pathway for researchers to develop and experiment with native resolution VLMs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.12698.Title: Unsupervised Contrastive Learning Using Out-Of-Distribution Data for Long-Tailed Dataset
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.12698.Summary: Researchers from Seoul National University of Science and Technology and Chung-Ang University developed KDUP, a two-step framework for unsupervised contrastive learning on long-tailed datasets using out-of-distribution data. This method improved classification accuracy by up to 7.11% on CIFAR-10-LT and learned more balanced, well-separated embedding spaces.
Problem: Self-supervised learning (SSL) methods, while powerful, show significant performance degradation when applied to real-world long-tailed datasets due to inherent class imbalance.
