The high cost and impracticality of collecting and annotating sufficient in-domain data, particularly for rare 'tail' classes, hinders the application of SSL in many real-world scenarios.
Traditional SSL struggles to learn robust representations for tail classes, leading to biased models that perform poorly on underrepresented categories.
Method: Introduces KDUP, a two-step knowledge distillation framework that strategically leverages abundant unlabeled out-of-distribution (OOD) data to address class imbalance.

In Step 1, a 'guiding network' is pre-trained using in-domain (ID) data and OOD data sampled based on a KL divergence-based clustering and instance-wise 'tailness' scores, employing a pseudo semantic discrimination loss (L_PSD) and a domain discrimination loss (L_DD).

In Step 2, a 'training network' is initialized from the guiding network and refined solely on ID data through knowledge distillation, utilizing a novel guided contrastive loss (L_GCL) with force-controlling weights and an embedding space distillation loss (L_DL).
Results: Achieved state-of-the-art classification performance on long-tailed datasets, with up to 7.11% higher overall accuracy on CIFAR-10-LT and 4.9% on CIFAR-100-LT compared to prior methods like COLT.

Produced demonstrably better-structured embedding spaces, characterized by improved class separability and compactness, as evidenced by higher Calinski-Harabasz Index and lower Davies-Bouldin Index scores, and clearer t-SNE visualizations.

Ablation studies confirmed the individual contributions of key components, including KL divergence-based clustering, the pseudo semantic discrimination loss, and the guided contrastive loss, to the overall performance gains and balancedness.
Takeaways: Integrating OOD data in a preliminary stage to establish a balanced and well-separated embedding space, followed by knowledge distillation to refine the model for in-domain data, yields superior representations for long-tailed distributions.

Dynamic and selective sampling of OOD data, guided by cluster-wise tailness scores derived from KL divergence clustering, effectively rebalances the representation learning process towards underrepresented classes.

A guided contrastive loss that weights attractive and repulsive forces based on similarities from a frozen guiding network enables effective transfer of robust, balanced representation knowledge to the final model.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.12609.Title: Not All Tokens and Heads Are Equally Important: Dual-Level Attention Intervention for Hallucination Mitigation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.12609.Summary: Peking University researchers developed VisFlow, a training-free, dual-level attention intervention framework that modulates attention patterns during inference to mitigate visual hallucinations in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs). This method significantly improved factual grounding on benchmarks like POPE and CHAIR, reducing hallucination rates while maintaining decoding efficiency comparable to standard beam search.
Problem: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) frequently generate visual hallucinations, producing descriptions inconsistent with or inaccurately reflecting visual input.
Existing hallucination mitigation strategies are often computationally expensive (e.g., fine-tuning, contrastive decoding) or introduce latency (e.g., auxiliary modules).
LVLMs suffer from insufficient visual attention, often focusing on uninformative visual tokens, and an over-reliance on linguistic priors and generic system prompts.
Method: VisFlow introduces a dual-level attention intervention framework applied at inference time, directly modulating attention patterns within the LVLM decoder.
Token-level Attention Intervention (TAI) enhances attention to visual salient tokens and attenuates attention to visual sink tokens, correcting RoPE-induced positional biases.
Head-level Attention Intervention (HAI) identifies and suppresses over-attention in system-dominant and text-dominant attention heads, reducing the influence of linguistic priors.
Results: VisFlow achieved state-of-the-art performance on the POPE benchmark, improving the Adversarial F1 score for LLaVA-1.5 from 73.54 to 84.35, significantly outperforming contrastive decoding methods.
On the CHAIR benchmark, VisFlow reduced sentence-level (CHAIR_s) hallucinations for LLaVA-1.5 from 6.8 to 3.8 and instance-level (CHAIR_i) hallucinations from 20.0 to 15.0.

The framework maintained decoding speed comparable to standard beam search, demonstrating significantly higher efficiency (Tokens Per Second) compared to other decoding-based hallucination mitigation methods requiring multiple forward passes.
Takeaways: Not all tokens and attention heads are equally important; targeted intervention at these fine-grained levels can more effectively and efficiently mitigate hallucinations.
Analysis of information flow reveals sparse visual attention, layer-wise decay of visual information, and RoPE-induced positional biases contribute to hallucinations.
Specific attention heads within the LVLM decoder specialize in visual processing versus relying on language priors, allowing for targeted modulation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.12508.Title: AgentOrchestra: Orchestrating Multi-Agent Intelligence with the Tool-Environment-Agent(TEA) Protocol
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.12508.Summary: The AgentOrchestra framework, based on the Tool-Environment-Agent (TEA) protocol, introduces a unified approach to managing and orchestrating multi-agent intelligence by treating tools, environments, and agents as first-class, versioned resources. It achieved state-of-the-art performance on benchmarks like GAIA (89.04%), SimpleQA (95.3%), and Humanity’s Last Exam (37.46%), demonstrating enhanced capabilities for complex tasks.
Problem: Existing LLM-based agent protocols suffer from fragmented lifecycle and context management, leading to monolithic agent compositions and brittle integration code.
Current approaches lack built-in mechanisms for feedback-driven self-evolution and traceable versioning of prompts and resources.
Computational environments are often treated as application-specific runtimes rather than first-class managed components, limiting reusability and flexible agent deployment.
Method: The Tool–Environment–Agent (TEA) Protocol is introduced, unifying the management of tools, environments, and agents as first-class, versioned resources with explicit lifecycles and robust context management.

The TEA Protocol includes Basic Managers for foundational services, Core Protocols (TCP, ECP, ACP) to formalize interactions, Protocol Transformations for dynamic entity conversion, and a Self-Evolution Module.

AGENTORCHESTRA, a hierarchical multi-agent framework, is developed as an instantiation of TEA, employing specialized sub-agents orchestrated by a central Planning Agent for complex task decomposition.
Results: AGENTORCHESTRA achieved state-of-the-art performance on GAIA (89.04% on Test set), SimpleQA (95.3% accuracy), and Humanity’s Last Exam (37.46%), significantly surpassing existing baselines.
Ablation studies confirmed that specialized sub-agents provide substantial performance gains, with the Deep Researcher and Browser Use agents increasing GAIA performance by approximately 56%.

The self-evolution module, utilizing TextGrad and self-reflection, consistently improved reasoning performance, and the Tool Generator autonomously created over 50 specialized tools with a 30% reuse rate.
Takeaways: Treating Tools, Environments, and Agents as first-class, versioned resources through a unified protocol provides a principled foundation for building traceable, reproducible, and robust multi-agent systems.
Hierarchical orchestration with specialized sub-agents and localized tool ownership effectively reduces planning complexity and context management overhead for long-horizon tasks.
Integrating a self-evolution module at the protocol level, leveraging TextGrad and self-reflection, enables agent components to continuously refine and adapt based on execution feedback.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.11991.Title: VGR: Visual Grounded Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.11991.Summary: VGR introduces a framework that enables Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to perform self-driven, selective visual analysis and integrate fine-grained visual details directly into their reasoning processes. This approach improves performance on perception-heavy tasks, such as achieving +4.5 on MMStar and +9.0 on ChartQA, while utilizing 70% fewer image tokens compared to baselines.
Problem: Existing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) suffer from an inherent 'language bias,' often relying predominantly on reasoning within the pure language space.
Current multimodal reasoning approaches struggle with 'perception-heavy' tasks due to limited fine-grained visual understanding and an inability to comprehensively utilize intricate image details.
Direct application of chain-of-thought (CoT) paradigms to MLLMs often leads to performance degradation in perception-heavy tasks due to the accumulation of this language bias.
Method: Introduces VGR, a framework featuring a 'self-driven selective visual replay' mechanism, enabling MLLMs to autonomously generate signals for specific bounding boxes and retrieve corresponding fine-grained visual features.
Integrates these replayed visual features directly into the Large Language Model's input sequence, augmenting its reasoning with precise visual clues at relevant steps.

Develops VGR-SFT, a large-scale, multi-stage supervised fine-tuning dataset specifically designed to train MLLMs for reasoning with mixed vision grounding and language deduction, using a cold-start, reject sampling, and annotation model pipeline.
Results: VGR-7B consistently outperforms a wide range of existing MLLMs on multimodal benchmarks, achieving gains such as +4.5 on MMStar (41.7) and +9.0 on ChartQA (67.7) compared to the LLaVA-NeXT-7B baseline.
The framework achieves these performance improvements with high computational efficiency, utilizing only 30% of the image token count (864 tokens) compared to the LLaVA-NeXT baseline (2880 tokens).

Ablation studies confirm that both explicit visual grounding cues, structured reasoning processes, and an auxiliary detection loss for bounding box prediction are critical for effective multimodal understanding and accurate spatial localization.
Takeaways: Explicitly grounding reasoning steps in selected visual regions effectively mitigates language bias in MLLMs, leading to improved performance on perception-heavy tasks.

A self-driven selective visual replay mechanism, allowing the model to autonomously choose when and which fine-grained visual details to integrate, enhances perception while significantly improving computational efficiency.

The VGR-SFT data curation pipeline, involving cold-start generation, multi-step rejection sampling, and an annotation model, is crucial for creating high-quality, visually grounded reasoning data that enables autonomous region attention.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.11976.Title: How Visual Representations Map to Language Feature Space in Multimodal LLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.11976.Summary: Researchers from the University of Oxford, McGill University, and Meta, along with a mechanistic interpretability expert, employed Sparse Autoencoders to reveal that visual representations in multimodal LLMs gradually align with language features, converging in the middle-to-later layers around layer 18 of the Gemma-2-2b-it model.
Problem: The internal mechanisms by which multimodal LLMs achieve robust cross-modal understanding remain largely opaque, posing a 'black box' problem.
A core challenge in multimodal AI is understanding how different sensory inputs (e.g., visual pixels, text tokens) are transformed into a shared, semantically rich representation space.
Existing interpretability methods like 'logit lens' are limited, as they cannot capture meaningful representational alignment in earlier or intermediate layers of LLMs.
Method: Employed a constrained multimodal LLM architecture using the LiMBeR framework, featuring a frozen vision transformer (CLIP ViT-L/14) and a frozen language model (Gemma-2-2b-it).
A trainable linear adapter was used to map visual features from the frozen ViT into the fixed input token space of the frozen LLM.
Utilized pre-trained Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), specifically GemmaScope SAEs, to conduct a layer-wise mechanistic analysis of visual-to-linguistic feature alignment across all 26 layers of the LLM.
Results: The constrained VLM achieved competitive performance on standard benchmarks (MME, LLaVA Bench, GQA, POPE), confirming its functional integration of modalities.
SAE reconstruction error and feature sparsity for visual tokens significantly decreased, and semantic alignment increased, converging around layers 18-20 of the Gemma-2-2b-it LLM.

A fundamental misalignment was identified between ViT outputs and the early LLM layers, indicating that the linear adapter alone is insufficient to perfectly translate visual information into the early conceptual representations of the language model.
Takeaways: Cross-modal alignment is a gradual process within the LLM, not an instantaneous event, with convergence primarily occurring in the middle-to-later layers.
Visual information, even after adapter projection, initially remains out-of-distribution for the early language feature space of the LLM.
Sparse Autoencoders offer a robust tool for deep, layer-wise mechanistic interpretability in complex multimodal models, effectively probing internal representations beyond surface-level observations.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.11967.Title: Visual Pre-Training on Unlabeled Images using Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.11967.Summary: Annotation Bootstrapping, developed by UC Berkeley researchers, recasts visual pre-training as a reinforcement learning problem, framing image transformations as a Markov Decision Process to learn representations from unlabeled images. This approach improves performance, showing gains on diverse datasets like COCO and EpicKitchens where invariance-based methods struggle, and achieving up to 4% higher ImageNet probing performance over vanilla CLIP in a weakly-supervised setting.
Problem: Current self-supervised learning (SSL) methods relying on 'invariance' (e.g., SimCLR, DINO) struggle with 'in-the-wild' datasets where random crops may capture semantically different content.

Combining weak supervision (e.g., text captions) with self-supervised losses in vision-language pre-training (VLP) often requires complex tuning and can degrade performance if invariance assumptions do not hold.
Self-distillation methods for SSL can be unstable and prone to representation collapse.
Method: The method frames visual pre-training as a Markov Decision Process (MDP), where image views are states, controllable transformations are actions, and semantic annotations provide rewards.
It learns a general value function (Q-function) to predict the maximum expected future likelihood of eliciting specific semantic annotations across sequential image transformations.

The approach decouples reward learning from value bootstrapping, using an existing self-supervised or weakly-supervised objective to define the reward function and optimizing the Q-function to predict Bellman targets.
Results: Annotation Bootstrapping (AB) consistently improved representations across diverse datasets, including ImageNet, CC12M, COCO, and EpicKitchens.

AB variants (AB_SimCLR, AB_DINO) alleviated performance degradation seen with invariance-based methods on non-object-centric datasets like COCO and EpicKitchens for tasks such as object detection and action recognition.
AB_CLIP achieved substantial gains (e.g., 4% on ImageNet probing) over vanilla CLIP and other combined CLIP+SSL methods, particularly on COCO where other methods degraded performance.
Takeaways: Visual pre-training can be effectively re-framed as a reinforcement learning problem using value-based methods, offering a fresh theoretical lens to approach representation learning.

Learning equivariant representations, where features change predictably with transformations, is more suitable for diverse, non-object-centric "in-the-wild" image data than strictly invariant representations.

The framework allows for a clear separation between defining 'what to learn' (via reward function and semantic annotations) and 'how to learn from unlabeled data' (via value function), providing flexible guidance.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.11902.Title: TreeRL: LLM Reinforcement Learning with On-Policy Tree Search
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.11902.Summary: TreeRL, developed by researchers from Tsinghua University and Caltech, introduces an on-policy reinforcement learning framework that integrates tree search to enhance large language model reasoning. It achieves superior performance over traditional ChainRL on challenging math and code benchmarks by leveraging an efficient entropy-guided tree search (EPTree) and deriving fine-grained process supervision from the generated reasoning trees.
Problem: Traditional Reinforcement Learning for LLMs (ChainRL) relies on sparse, delayed rewards from final outcomes, making it difficult to learn from intermediate reasoning steps.

Existing tree search applications for LLMs are often used for inference-time enhancement or offline data generation, leading to potential distribution mismatch and reward hacking during online training.
Inefficient exploration of the vast reasoning space by independent chain sampling and the computational inefficiency of classical MCTS for modern LLM inference engines.
Method: Introduces EPTree (Entropy-Guided Tree Search), an efficient and parallelizable tree search algorithm that iteratively expands branches from high-uncertainty (high-entropy) tokens, optimizing for diversity and PassRate under a given inference budget.

Develops an on-policy process supervision mechanism that derives fine-grained reward signals for each reasoning step by calculating global and local advantages based on the success rate of descendant nodes in the EPTree.

Integrates EPTree and its derived process rewards directly into the LLM's on-policy reinforcement learning loop, updating the policy using a policy gradient method while re-weighting rewards for non-leaf steps.
Results: EPTree consistently achieved a 3% higher PassRate compared to independent multi-chain sampling under the same inference cost, demonstrating superior efficiency and diversity in generation.

TreeRL outperformed traditional ChainRL across all evaluated math and code reasoning benchmarks (e.g., MATH500, AIME2024, LiveCodeBench), showing consistent performance gains after approximately 100 training steps.

Ablation studies confirmed the effectiveness of entropy-guided forking and the combined global and local advantage signals for process supervision, both of which were crucial for optimal RL training performance.
Takeaways: Entropy-guided forking (EPTree) efficiently generates more diverse and high-quality responses than traditional sampling methods, leading to improved search PassRate.
Deriving on-policy process supervision signals, using a combination of global and local advantages re-weighted by subtree size, provides effective and stable feedback for LLM reinforcement learning.
Directly integrating tree search into the on-policy RL loop mitigates issues of distribution mismatch and reward hacking often seen with offline reward models or static data generation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.11515.Title: Manager: Aggregating Insights from Unimodal Experts in Two-Tower VLMs and MLLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.11515.Summary: Researchers from Harbin Institute of Technology, Central South University, and National University of Singapore developed "Manager," a plugin that adaptively aggregates multi-level insights from unimodal encoders to enhance vision-language understanding. This approach boosted Two-Tower VLM performance on tasks like VQAv2 to 79.15% accuracy and improved MLLM zero-shot capabilities across 20 diverse datasets by over 1% on average, demonstrating powerful synergy with multi-grid algorithms.
Problem: Existing Two-Tower Vision-Language Models (VLMs) like BridgeTower ineffectively utilize multi-level semantic knowledge from unimodal encoders due to fixed layer-by-layer connections.
Prior multimodal fusion architectures suffered from rigid coupling between cross-modal and unimodal layers, limiting scalability and increasing computational costs.

The evolving Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) architecture and its challenges with high-resolution images via multi-grid algorithms were not adequately addressed by previous VLM-focused research.
Method: Introduced "Manager," a lightweight plugin for adaptively aggregating insights from diverse levels of pre-trained unimodal experts.
Developed the Adaptive Aggregation Unimodal Manager (AAUM) which dynamically generates token-level weights from a cross-modal fused query for flexible knowledge integration.
Integrated managers into both Two-Tower VLMs (ManagerTower) and Multimodal Large Language Models (LLaVA-OV-Manager) to enhance vision-language understanding across different architectural paradigms.
Results: ManagerTower achieved state-of-the-art performance in Two-Tower VLMs, surpassing strong baselines like METER and BridgeTower on VQAv2 (79.15% accuracy) and Flickr30K (95.64% TR@1).
Managers consistently improved LLaVA-OV's zero-shot performance across 20 diverse MLLM datasets, yielding an average +1.06% score with minimal overhead.

Combining Manager with multi-grid algorithms resulted in the highest overall performance, with a +4.60% increase over the baseline, effectively mitigating semantic ambiguity in high-resolution image processing.
Takeaways: Adaptive aggregation, particularly with token-level dynamic weighting guided by a cross-modal query, is crucial for effectively leveraging multi-level unimodal semantic knowledge.
Managers increase the diversity of internal model representations and attention patterns, facilitating richer information flow and preventing over-focusing on redundant features.
The "Manager" plugin offers an efficient solution, providing substantial performance gains with negligible additional parameters (0.08M) or computational overhead (1.03-1.04x).

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.11136.Title: JAFAR: Jack up Any Feature at Any Resolution
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.11136.Summary: A new method named JAFAR enhances features from foundation vision encoders, enabling them to produce sharp, high-resolution representations for dense prediction tasks without requiring task-specific training. It leverages a lightweight attention mechanism and generalizes effectively across different output scales, leading to improved accuracy in semantic segmentation, depth estimation, and open-vocabulary segmentation.
Problem: Foundation Vision Encoders produce semantically rich but spatially coarse features due to aggressive downsampling.
This low spatial resolution severely limits their performance on dense prediction tasks demanding pixel-level accuracy.
Current feature upsampling techniques often introduce blurriness, are computationally intensive, or lack generalization across tasks and resolutions.
Method: A lightweight, attention-based architecture uses the original high-resolution image as guidance to upsample coarse features.
It employs an asymmetric query-key design, where keys are semantically enriched through Spatial Feature Transform (SFT) modulation using foundation encoder features.
An annotation-free training scheme with multi-resolution views allows the model to generalize from moderate training upsampling ratios to significantly higher inference scales.
Results: JAFAR significantly improves semantic segmentation performance, achieving an average of +1.63 mIoU over leading baselines, including a +5.41 mIoU increase on Cityscapes.
It generates sharper and more semantically faithful Class Activation Maps (CAMs), with an 8-point higher aggregate ADCC score compared to the second-best method.
The method consistently enhances performance in zero-shot open-vocabulary segmentation and complex Bird's-Eye View (BeV) segmentation, yielding up to +5 points in vehicle-IoU.
Takeaways: JAFAR's ability to generalize from training at moderate upsampling ratios to substantially higher inference scales reduces training memory and computational costs.
Spatial Feature Transform (SFT) modulation of keys, enriched by foundation encoder features, is critical for achieving robust semantic and spatial alignment.
The absence of a learned value projection layer in the cross-attention mechanism helps preserve the original feature content, enabling resolution-agnostic generalization.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10979.Title: How Well Can Reasoning Models Identify and Recover from Unhelpful Thoughts?
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10979.Summary: Yang et al. investigate large language models' capacity for self-reevaluation by testing their ability to identify and recover from various injected "unhelpful thoughts." The research finds a substantial gap between thought recognition and effective recovery, particularly noting an inverse scaling trend where larger models demonstrate reduced robustness to certain unhelpful thought injections, impacting their reliability and safety.
Problem: The true effectiveness and generality of LLMs' meta-cognitive abilities, such as self-reevaluation and self-correction within chains of thought, remained underexplored.

It was unclear how well LLMs could identify and effectively recover from various types of internal "unhelpful thoughts," ranging from uninformative ramblings to incorrect or misdirecting reasoning paths.

Understanding the limitations in self-reevaluation is crucial for assessing potential vulnerabilities in reasoning models, particularly concerning adversarial attacks through thought injection and interactions with external tools.
Method: A two-part evaluation framework was developed, assessing models' ability to *identify* unhelpful thoughts via binary classification and their capacity to *recover* from them by measuring task performance after injection.

Four distinct categories of unhelpful thoughts (uninformative rambling, irrelevant, misdirecting, incorrect) were generated and programmatically injected into LLMs' thinking processes across five diverse reasoning datasets.

Experiments were conducted on multiple sizes of three LLM families (DeepSeek R1-Distill, s1.1, EXAONE Deep), including tests with explicit recovery cues and a novel "attack-in-thought" jailbreak scenario to examine practical vulnerabilities.
Results: Models demonstrated high accuracy in identifying unhelpful thoughts (e.g., near-perfect for irrelevant thoughts) but showed severe performance drops (e.g., up to 70% decrease in accuracy) across all unhelpful thought types during recovery.

For short irrelevant thoughts, larger models like DeepSeek R1-Distill 70B exhibited significantly lower recovery performance compared to smaller models (e.g., 7B), a trend consistently observed across three model families.

Explicit cues to encourage recovery, such as additional instructions or "aha moment" triggers, provided only negligible to modest improvements, failing to restore baseline performance after thought injection.

The inverse scaling trend for recovery translated to jailbreak scenarios, where smaller models were more robust to "attack-in-thought" injections (harmful content within internal thought processes) than larger models.
Takeaways: There is a significant discrepancy between LLMs' strong ability to *identify* unhelpful thoughts when explicitly prompted and their struggle to *recover* from them when those thoughts are injected into their reasoning process.
The observed "meta-cognitive" awareness in LLMs is often local, leading to self-reevaluation within an unhelpful trajectory rather than a global re-grounding of reasoning to the original problem.

Larger models exhibit an unexpected non/inverse-scaling trend for recovery from short irrelevant thoughts, performing worse than smaller models and suggesting increased brittleness in specific adversarial contexts.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10967.Title: Beyond Attention or Similarity: Maximizing Conditional Diversity for Token Pruning in MLLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10967.Summary: Researchers from Peking University and ByteDance propose CDPruner, a training-free token pruning method for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) that dynamically selects visual tokens by maximizing their conditional diversity, leading to over 94% token reduction while preserving more than 94% of original accuracy on various benchmarks and achieving up to a 10x reduction in FLOPs.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) generate a high number of visual tokens (hundreds to thousands) from image/video inputs, leading to prohibitive inference costs due to the quadratic complexity of attention mechanisms.
Existing attention-based token pruning methods often retain redundant visual tokens and can be incompatible with efficient attention implementations like FlashAttention.
Existing similarity-based pruning methods fail to consider the user's instruction, leading to static pruning that may discard visual information relevant to the specific query.
Method: Introduces CDPruner, a training-free and model-agnostic visual token pruning method that maximizes conditional diversity.
Calculates a conditional kernel matrix by weighting visual token feature similarities with their relevance to the input text instruction.
Leverages Determinantal Point Processes (DPPs) with a greedy algorithm to select a diverse subset of visual tokens that are most relevant to the given instruction.
Results: CDPruner maintains 94.3% of original accuracy on LLaVA-1.5 even with a 94.4% reduction in visual tokens (from 576 to 32), outperforming other methods by up to 3%.
Achieves up to a 10x reduction in FLOPs, 6.6x faster prefill latency, 1.3x faster decode latency, and over 88% KV cache reduction for MLLMs like LLaVA-NeXT-7B.
Demonstrates strong generalizability and superior performance across diverse MLLM architectures (LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT, LLaVA-Video, Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL3) and various vision-language tasks.
Takeaways: Jointly maximizing feature diversity and instruction relevance is crucial for effective visual token pruning, leading to dynamic and context-aware selection.
Determinantal Point Processes (DPPs) are an effective mathematical framework for modeling and selecting diverse subsets of visual tokens, outperforming traditional similarity-based methods.

A training-free and model-agnostic pruning approach can significantly reduce MLLM inference costs while maintaining high performance and compatibility with various architectures and optimizations like FlashAttention.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10947.Title: Spurious Rewards: Rethinking Training Signals in RLVR
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10947.Summary: This study demonstrates that Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) can significantly improve mathematical reasoning in Qwen models even when using "spurious" reward signals, challenging the necessity of high-quality, task-specific rewards. It further reveals that these gains are highly dependent on the base model's pretraining and do not generalize to other LLM architectures.
Problem: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) for Large Language Models typically relies on high-quality, task-specific reward signals, which are costly to obtain.
The precise mechanisms by which RLVR enhances LLM capabilities are not fully understood, specifically whether it teaches new skills or primarily surfaces existing ones.
Conclusions about RLVR's effectiveness and generalizability might be skewed if research relies heavily on models with unique pretraining characteristics, leading to potentially misleading results.
Method: Conducted systematic experiments using GRPO with a range of binary reward functions, from high-quality ground truth to increasingly spurious signals like format-based, random, and deliberately incorrect rewards.

Evaluated the impact of these reward functions across diverse LLM architectures, including Qwen2.5-Math, general-purpose Qwen2.5, Llama3, and OLMo2 variants, on standard mathematical reasoning benchmarks.

Analyzed changes in model reasoning strategies, particularly code reasoning frequency, and performed intervention experiments to understand their causal impact; also investigated algorithmic mechanisms like GRPO's clipping bias.
Results: Qwen2.5-Math models achieved substantial performance gains on mathematical reasoning benchmarks (e.g., up to +24.1% absolute accuracy on MATH-500) using various spurious reward signals, comparable to gains from ground truth rewards.

These gains were highly model-dependent; Llama3 and OLMo2 variants showed minimal improvement or even performance degradation when trained with spurious rewards, highlighting a lack of generalization.
For Qwen2.5-Math, spurious rewards amplified its pre-existing code reasoning strategy, increasing its frequency from 65% to over 90%, which accounted for a majority of performance improvements.

The clipping mechanism within the GRPO algorithm was identified as a key driver for performance improvements from random rewards, creating a non-zero gradient bias that amplified existing high-probability behaviors.
Takeaways: RLVR, particularly with weak signals, primarily acts as an elicitation mechanism for pre-existing latent capabilities within the base model, rather than teaching new reasoning skills.
The success of RLVR, even with spurious rewards, is highly dependent on the model's pretraining distribution and inherent reasoning priors, such as a robust code reasoning ability in Qwen models.

Algorithmic artifacts, specifically the clipping mechanism in GRPO, can inadvertently provide a training signal that amplifies existing high-probability behaviors, explaining performance gains with seemingly random rewards.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10943.Title: Self-Adapting Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10943.Summary: Researchers from MIT's Improbable AI Lab developed Self-Adapting Language Models (SEAL), a framework enabling LLMs to autonomously generate optimized finetuning data and adaptation strategies for internal parameter updates. The approach substantially improved few-shot learning success rates and boosted knowledge incorporation accuracy to 47.0%, outperforming synthetic data produced by GPT-4.1 in single-passage scenarios.
Problem: Large language models (LLMs) are inherently static after training, leading to inefficiencies in adapting to new tasks, integrating novel knowledge, or refining reasoning skills without extensive, costly retraining.
Current adaptation methods often consume training data 'as-is,' failing to critically evaluate or restructure information for optimal learning.

The AI field is approaching a 'data wall' where high-quality human-generated text for pretraining is becoming scarce, necessitating models to generate their own high-utility training signals for continued improvement.
Method: SEAL implements a meta-learning framework featuring two nested loops: an inner loop where the LLM generates 'self-edits' (synthetic data and/or hyperparameters) for supervised finetuning (SFT) updates, and an outer reinforcement learning (RL) loop to optimize this self-edit generation policy.

The model is trained to produce natural-language self-edits that define synthetic training data (e.g., implications for knowledge, tool configurations for few-shot learning) and configure LoRA finetuning parameters.
An on-policy RL algorithm, specifically Rejection Sampling + SFT (ReST_EM), is used to train the model to generate self-edits that maximize a binary reward based on downstream task performance.
Results: SEAL achieved a 72.5% success rate in few-shot learning on a simplified ARC-AGI subset, significantly outperforming In-Context Learning (0%) and Test-Time Training with base model self-edits (20%).
For knowledge incorporation, SEAL using Qwen2.5-7B achieved 47.0% accuracy on SQuAD passages without explicit context, surpassing the 46.3% accuracy obtained from synthetic data generated by GPT-4.1.

The relative improvement of SEAL over base model self-edits increased with model capacity (2.04x for 7B vs. 1.75x for 3B), indicating compounding benefits, though the system currently faces high computational costs and susceptibility to catastrophic forgetting.
Takeaways: LLMs can be trained to autonomously generate effective finetuning data and adaptation strategies, transforming them from passive data consumers into active, self-improving learners.

Optimizing the *generation* of synthetic training data through RL can lead to more effective model updates than using fixed prompting strategies or even data from larger, off-the-shelf proprietary models like GPT-4.1.
The framework provides a foundational step towards continuous learning and the development of agentic systems capable of structured self-modification and incremental knowledge acquisition.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10910.Title: Magistral
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10910.Summary: Mistral AI introduces Magistral, its inaugural reasoning model, which leverages a custom Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) pipeline to significantly enhance the reasoning abilities of its base models. Magistral Medium, trained purely with RL, achieved a nearly 50% increase on AIME '24 (pass@1), while Magistral Small demonstrated that RL effectively boosts distilled models and both models showed surprising improvements in multimodal reasoning despite text-only training.
Problem: Traditional large language models (LLMs) often struggle with multi-step logical deduction and complex problem-solving tasks.
Developing scalable and efficient reinforcement learning pipelines for LLMs, particularly from scratch, poses significant engineering and algorithmic challenges.
Ensuring that specialized reasoning training does not degrade other essential LLM capabilities like instruction following and function calling.
Method: Developed Magistral, Mistral AI's first reasoning model, using a custom-built, scalable Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) pipeline.
Employed a modified Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) algorithm with key changes like eliminating KL divergence and relaxing the trust region's upper bound to foster exploration.
Implemented a meticulous reward system considering formatting, correctness (math/code verification), length penalties, and a novel language consistency reward for multilingual reasoning.
Results: Magistral Medium achieved a nearly 50% increase on AIME '24 (pass@1), improving from 26.8% to 73.6%, and a 30% increase on LiveCodeBench (v5), from 29.1% to 59.4%.
Magistral Small, a 24B model, demonstrated that RL provided substantial performance boosts even after distillation (SFT) from a larger teacher model, achieving 70.7% on AIME '24 pass@1 with SFT+RL.
Despite being trained on text-only data, Magistral models showed improved performance on multimodal reasoning benchmarks like MathVista, MMMU, and MMMU-Pro.
Takeaways: Pure Reinforcement Learning (RL) alone can achieve substantial reasoning performance gains on large models without initial distillation from other reasoning models.
Text-only RL training not only preserves but surprisingly improves multimodal reasoning capabilities, suggesting deep generalization of learned reasoning patterns.
Detailed ablations revealed that controlling exploration via the PPO-like clip-higher threshold was more stable than entropy bonuses, and specific batching strategies influenced training stability.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10159.Title: Probabilistic Variational Contrastive Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10159.Summary: Variational Contrastive Learning (VCL) introduces a probabilistic framework for contrastive representation learning, enabling uncertainty quantification for embeddings through a decoder-free Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) maximization. The method consistently matches or exceeds the classification performance of deterministic baselines while effectively mitigating dimensional collapse and providing interpretable posterior uncertainty measures.
Problem: Existing contrastive learning methods learn deterministic point embeddings, lacking principled uncertainty quantification, which is crucial for trustworthy AI applications.
The theoretical foundation of contrastive learning, often relying on InfoNCE loss, lacks a direct connection to a robust probabilistic framework like Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) maximization.
Self-supervised contrastive learning frequently suffers from dimensional collapse, where embeddings occupy only a low-dimensional subspace, underutilizing representational capacity.
Method: VCL frames contrastive learning as decoder-free ELBO maximization, using the InfoNCE loss as a surrogate for the intractable reconstruction term.
It models embeddings as projected normal distributions, allowing for explicit prior distributions (e.g., uniform on the unit hypersphere) and enabling the computation of an approximate KL divergence.
The framework integrates uncertainty quantification by outputting mean and covariance parameters for each embedding, trainable via reparameterization and a normalized Gaussian KL regularizer.
Results: VSimCLR and VSupCon consistently achieve classification accuracy comparable to or better than their deterministic counterparts (SimCLR, SupCon) across datasets like CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Caltech-256.

VSimCLR significantly mitigates dimensional collapse, producing a flatter singular-value spectrum of the embedding covariance matrix and nearly doubling the number of dominant components compared to SimCLR.
Leveraging posterior dispersion, VCL methods in a label-scarce setting improve accuracy on CIFAR-100 by upweighting more certain samples, demonstrating practical utility for downstream tasks.
Takeaways: InfoNCE loss can be interpreted as a surrogate for the reconstruction term within a variational ELBO framework, providing a strong probabilistic foundation for contrastive learning without requiring a generative decoder.
Posterior dispersion (quantified by log det(K)) serves as an interpretable measure, inversely correlating with typicality within a class and with label ambiguity or corruption severity.
Explicitly enforcing a uniform prior on the hypersphere via KL regularization effectively mitigates dimensional collapse, promoting a more isotropic use of the embedding space.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10139.Title: Unsupervised Elicitation of Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10139.Summary: This paper presents Internal Coherence Maximization (ICM), an unsupervised algorithm for fine-tuning language models by having them generate and refine their own labels based on internal consistency and mutual predictability. The research demonstrates that this method can match or surpass human supervision on various tasks, including the successful training of a production-scale Claude 3.5 Haiku assistant that performs competitively against its human-supervised counterpart.
Problem: Prevailing language model alignment methods (e.g., SFT, RLHF) heavily rely on human supervision.
As language models develop superhuman capabilities, obtaining high-quality and reliable human supervision becomes difficult or impossible, creating a bottleneck.
Human supervision can lead to models mimicking human mistakes, reward hacking, or failing to fully unlock their latent superhuman potential.
Method: Introduces Internal Coherence Maximization (ICM), an unsupervised algorithm that enables language models to fine-tune themselves by generating and refining their own labels.
ICM defines a scoring function combining "mutual predictability" (how well the pretrained model can infer labels from other labels) and "logical consistency" to evaluate label set quality.
An iterative search procedure, inspired by simulated annealing, is employed to construct and refine the label set, including a critical "ConsistencyFix" step to resolve inconsistencies.
Results: ICM-trained models achieved performance comparable to or surpassing models trained on human supervision across various tasks, including TruthfulQA, GSM8K-verification, and Alpaca (helpfulness/harmlessness).
The method successfully elicited superhuman capabilities, matching golden supervision and outperforming human annotators on a gender prediction task.

Anthropic applied ICM to train a Claude 3.5 Haiku-based assistant without human supervision; its unsupervised reward model (75.0% accuracy) outperformed a human-supervised one (72.2%), and the resulting assistant policy won 60% of head-to-head comparisons against a human-supervised policy.
Takeaways: Powerful pretrained language models inherently possess a rich understanding of complex concepts like correctness and helpfulness, which can be "elicited" rather than "taught."
Mutual predictability, measuring how well a model can infer labels from other labels within a dataset, is the critical component for driving internal coherence in unsupervised elicitation.
Unsupervised methods can match or surpass human supervision for aligning LLMs, especially on tasks where human judgment is suboptimal or limited by the models' superhuman capabilities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10128.Title: ViCrit: A Verifiable Reinforcement Learning Proxy Task for Visual Perception in VLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10128.Summary: A novel reinforcement learning proxy task, ViCrit, enhances Vision-Language Models' fine-grained visual perception by training them to identify subtle hallucinations in captions. This method, developed by researchers from the University of Maryland, Microsoft, and University of Michigan, effectively reduces visual hallucinations and improves general VLM performance across diverse benchmarks, while ViCrit-Bench serves as a new diagnostic tool for evaluating these capabilities.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) frequently suffer from visual hallucinations and often lack truly fine-grained visual perception, relying on shallow object recognition.

The success of Reinforcement Learning (RL) in LLMs (e.g., for math or code) has not extended to VLM visual perception due to a lack of visual tasks that are both challenging and automatically verifiable.
Existing VLM training, such as supervised fine-tuning on captioning data, often leads to superficial understanding rather than deep, transferable perceptual strategies.
Method: Introduces ViCrit, a reinforcement learning proxy task where a VLM must identify a single, subtly injected visual hallucination within an almost-correct, long image caption.
Employs an exact string match reward for the identified hallucinated span, providing a precise and automatically verifiable signal crucial for scalable RL training.

Develops ViCrit-Bench, a human-curated diagnostic benchmark featuring fine-grained hallucinations across diverse image domains (natural, document, scene-text, abstract) to systematically evaluate VLM perception.
Results: ViCrit RL training significantly reduces visual hallucinations, with ViCrit-RL-72B improving CHAIRs/CHAIRi from 28.0/5.1 (baseline) to 21.0/3.9 and MMHal from 3.74 to 3.91.

Models trained with ViCrit show consistent average accuracy gains of 2.4% (7B) and 3.4% (72B) across eight diverse general VLM benchmarks, including strong generalization to out-of-domain tasks like visual math and document analysis.
ViCrit-Bench is a challenging diagnostic for current VLMs, with top proprietary models achieving less than 50% accuracy, and it strongly predicts overall VLM capabilities.
Takeaways: Reframing fine-grained visual perception into a "hallucination criticism" task allows for scalable reinforcement learning, bridging the gap between perceptual difficulty and verifiable reward signals.

The ViCrit task design encourages VLMs to internalize transferable "how to perceive" strategies, prompting them to cross-check textual claims against visual evidence rather than relying on superficial object memorization.
Performance on the ViCrit-Bench diagnostic benchmark shows a strong positive linear correlation (r = 0.96) with overall VLM performance across diverse general reasoning tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09985.Title: V-JEPA 2: Self-Supervised Video Models Enable Understanding, Prediction and Planning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09985.Summary: FAIR at Meta developed V-JEPA 2, a self-supervised video model that learns a general world model from over 1 million hours of internet video, then adapts this model with a small amount of unlabeled robot data to enable zero-shot robot control and strong performance in video understanding and prediction tasks. The model achieves 80% success for pick-and-place tasks with a cup in novel environments and sets new benchmarks in video question-answering, demonstrating the efficacy of learning predictive world models in representation space.
Problem: AI agents struggle to understand and interact with the physical world primarily through observation, often relying on costly interaction data or explicit rewards.

Traditional world models, particularly those based on generative approaches, are computationally expensive and may focus on unpredictable pixel-level details rather than robust underlying dynamics relevant for planning.
Robotics faces data scarcity, requiring vast amounts of expensive, labeled interaction data for task-specific training, which limits scalability and generalization to novel environments.
Method: V-JEPA 2, a self-supervised video model, is pre-trained on over 1 million hours of diverse internet video using a mask-denoising objective in a learned representation space.
An action-conditioned predictor (V-JEPA 2-AC) is then post-trained on a small amount (62 hours) of unlabeled robot video to learn the causal effects of actions for predicting future states.

For robotic control, V-JEPA 2-AC is integrated into a Model Predictive Control (MPC) loop, where it plans actions by minimizing a goal-conditioned energy function defined by the L1 distance between imagined future state representations and goal image representations.
Results: V-JEPA 2 ViT-g achieved 77.3% top-1 accuracy on Something-Something v2 (SSv2), outperforming other vision encoders and demonstrating superior motion understanding.

The model attained state-of-the-art results for its model class on several video question-answering benchmarks (e.g., 84.0% on PerceptionTest, 44.5% on MVP) when aligned with an LLM, despite being pre-trained without language supervision.

V-JEPA 2-AC demonstrated zero-shot robotic manipulation with high success rates (e.g., 80% for pick-and-place with a cup) on Franka arms in novel environments, significantly outperforming baselines using only 62 hours of unlabeled robot video for post-training.
Takeaways: Large-scale self-supervised pre-training on general internet video effectively builds a robust "world model" that captures predictable dynamics without explicit action or language supervision.
Predicting in a learned representation space (JEPA) is more efficient and robust for learning world dynamics compared to pixel-level generation, especially for planning.
A powerful visual foundation model, even without language pre-training, can achieve state-of-the-art video question-answering performance when aligned with a large language model.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09967.Title: Resa: Transparent Reasoning Models via SAEs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09967.Summary: Resa introduces SAE-Tuning, a two-stage training procedure that efficiently elicits strong reasoning abilities in language models using only verified question-answer data. The method reduces training costs by over 2000x and time by over 450x compared to RL-based approaches, achieving comparable performance while offering transparency into reasoning features.
Problem: Existing LLM reasoning elicitation methods (RL-based) are computationally intensive, demanding vast resources and long training times.
Traditional fine-tuning methods (RL or SFT) are largely 'black boxes,' obscuring how reasoning abilities are instilled and activated within the model.
Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) often relies on costly and labor-intensive Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning traces, limiting scalability.
Method: Resa introduces SAE-Tuning, a novel two-stage training procedure that leverages Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) with only verified, CoT-free question-answer data.
Stage I: Train an SAE on a source model's internal layer activations to explicitly extract and capture reasoning-related features.
Stage II: Elicit reasoning abilities in a target model by guiding its Low-Rank Adapters (LoRA) based SFT with the frozen, pre-trained SAE, which is removed at test time.
Results: Resa-STILL-v5 achieves 48.06% average performance, nearly matching the RL-trained Tina-STILL (48.16% avg) while reducing training costs by over 2000x (to ~$1) and time by over 450x (to under 20 minutes).

Reasoning abilities extracted from one dataset generalize to different, even non-overlapping, elicitation datasets, with Resa-STILL2DeepScaleR (48.77% avg) performing on par with Tina-DeepScaleR (48.38% avg).
Reasoning abilities captured in low-rank adapters during SAE-guided SFT can be treated as portable modules, demonstrating competitive performance when attached to different base models at test time.
Takeaways: SAEs can extract and explicitly represent latent reasoning abilities from language model activations, enabling transparent analysis of how reasoning is encoded.
Reasoning capabilities can be modularized and transferred as portable adapters, suggesting a composable AI system architecture where abstract abilities are separate from foundational knowledge.

The overall structural organization of reasoning features across model layers correlates with the final reasoning performance, providing a data-driven path to optimizing SAE-Tuning by strategically selecting SAE hookpoints.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09965.Title: Reinforcing Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models with Interwoven Thinking and Visual Drawing
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09965.Summary: This work introduces VILASR, a Vision-Language Model capable of spatial reasoning by generating and interpreting visual drawing operations directly within its reasoning process. The model, developed by researchers at Institute of Automation, CAS, Ant Group, CUHK MMLab, and Nanjing University, consistently outperforms existing methods by an average of 18.4% across various spatial reasoning benchmarks, including maze navigation and video analysis.
Problem: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) exhibit limited spatial reasoning capabilities, often relying on text-centric processing that loses fine-grained visual details.
Existing approaches that integrate external visual tools for LVLMs suffer from black-box limitations, offering fixed perception capabilities and leading to fragmented reasoning.
LVLMs lack intrinsic visual manipulation abilities, hindering their capacity for iterative refinement and dynamic interaction with visual information during reasoning.
Method: A novel "drawing to reason in space" paradigm enables LVLMs to decompose complex spatial tasks into interleaved steps of natural language reasoning and visual drawing operations (bounding boxes and auxiliary lines).
The model utilizes two fundamental drawing operations: `T_box` for localizing objects with bounding boxes and `T_line` for visualizing spatial relationships and trajectories with auxiliary lines.

A three-stage training framework progressively builds capabilities: cold-start training with synthetic data, reflective rejection sampling to cultivate self-correction, and reinforcement learning (GRPO) to optimize for accuracy and efficient visual thinking using a rule-based reward function.
Results: VILASR consistently outperforms existing methods across five diverse spatial reasoning benchmarks, achieving an average improvement of 18.4% over strong baselines.
The model achieves 98.2% on MAZE navigation and state-of-the-art results on video and multi-view spatial reasoning benchmarks like VSI-Bench (45.4%), SPAR-Bench (37.6%), and MMSI-Bench (30.2%).

Ablation studies confirm the critical role of each training stage: cold-start for foundational drawing, reflective rejection sampling for self-correction (reducing reflection patterns by 96.5% without it), and reinforcement learning for efficiency and precise numerical reasoning.
Takeaways: Direct visual manipulation via elementary drawing operations allows Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) to reason about fine-grained spatial details and dynamic changes more effectively than text-centric methods.

A progressive three-stage training framework, incorporating supervised fine-tuning, reflective rejection sampling, and reinforcement learning, is essential for cultivating robust, self-correcting, and efficient spatial reasoning.
Empowering LVLMs with an intrinsic visual workspace enables them to express and analyze spatial relationships more naturally, drawing parallels to human cognitive processes.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09691.Title: Adding simple structure at inference improves Vision-Language Compositionality
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09691.Summary: An inference-time approach enhances the Vision-Language Compositionality of dual-encoder models like CLIP and SigLIP 2 by decomposing images into crops and text into segments, then matching them. This method consistently improves retrieval performance across datasets, achieving gains such as over 22 absolute points on BIVLC and up to 90 points on controlled compositional benchmarks without additional training.
Problem: Dual-encoder Vision-Language Models (VLMs) like CLIP exhibit "bag-of-words-like" behavior, failing to understand Vision-Language Compositionality.
These models struggle with attribute-object binding and complex relational understanding in image-text retrieval tasks.
Current approaches to improve VLM compositionality often involve expensive end-to-end training or are not specifically designed for retrieval.
Method: A novel inference-time approach that processes input images by generating diverse smaller crops and texts by segmenting them into hierarchical object-attribute-relation units.
Utilizes the pretrained dual-encoder VLM to compute fine-grained similarities between each image crop and text segment, creating best matching pairs.
Aggregates these fine-grained match similarities by averaging them to determine the final image-text alignment score.
Results: The inference-time approach consistently and significantly improved retrieval performance for CLIP and SigLIP 2 across all evaluation datasets without additional training.
SigLIP 2-Giant with the approach achieved over 22 absolute points improvement in group score on BIVLC and up to 90 absolute points on controlled BISCOR-CTRL benchmarks.
Ablation studies confirmed that decomposing images into crops is essential for performance gains, while text-only segmentation provided minimal benefit.
Takeaways: Pretrained dual-encoder Vision-Language Models contain latent compositional representations that are not fully leveraged by standard global embedding comparisons.
Enhancing compositional reasoning can be achieved through inference-time modifications, challenging the reliance on extensive retraining.
Decomposing images into smaller crops is crucial for improving compositional understanding, as confirmed by ablation studies.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09522.Title: Revisit What You See: Disclose Language Prior in Vision Tokens for LVLM Decoding
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09522.Summary: ReVisiT, from Yonsei University, proposes a decoding strategy that leverages intrinsic object-level semantics within Large Vision-Language Model (LVLM) vision tokens to reduce visual hallucinations. The method enhances visual grounding and general VQA performance across models, achieving this with negligible computational overhead compared to greedy decoding.
Problem: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) frequently suffer from "visual hallucination," generating text descriptions of objects or attributes not present in the input image.
Existing methods to mitigate hallucinations often incur significant computational overhead, requiring multiple forward passes or complex interventions during decoding.
The intrinsic semantic information within LVLM "vision tokens"—visual embeddings projected into the text embedding space—is often latent and under-leveraged by conventional decoding processes.
Method: ReVisiT employs a training-free, model-agnostic decoding strategy that dynamically refines output logits at each generation step.
It constructs an adaptive, context-aware vocabulary subset and projects relevant vision tokens from specific decoder layers over this subset.

The method combines the vanilla output probability distribution with the selected vision token's projected distribution (chosen by minimizing Jensen-Shannon Divergence) to guide text generation, amplifying visually grounded tokens.
Results: ReVisiT significantly reduced hallucination rates across benchmarks (e.g., HallusionBench qAcc improved from 11.55% to 20.22% for LLaVA-1.5-7B) and consistently improved general VQA performance (e.g., VQAv2 accuracy for LLaVA-1.5-7B from 69.47% to 70.40%).
The method maintains inference efficiency comparable to greedy decoding, with only a marginal runtime increase (+1.9% for LLaVA-1.5-7B), substantially outperforming other intra-alignment techniques.
It demonstrated broad applicability and scalability, improving performance across various LVLM architectures (LLaVA-1.5, Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL) and model sizes (7B to 32B).
Takeaways: Even at hallucinated steps, ground-truth visual information often remains present among the LVLM's high-probability output candidates.
Vision tokens intrinsically encode meaningful object-level semantics, but their interpretability becomes explicit only when projected onto a semantically coherent, constrained vocabulary subset.
The presence of vision tokens significantly contributes to visual grounding, with their removal leading to a reversal in probability mass distribution between ground-truth and hallucinated objects.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09477.Title: On a few pitfalls in KL divergence gradient estimation for RL
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09477.Summary: A paper from Meta FAIR and Meta GenAI identifies widespread implementation errors in KL divergence gradient estimation, a crucial component in reinforcement learning, particularly for large language models. It demonstrates that common methods yield biased gradients or optimize the unintended reverse KL, and provides correct, unbiased estimators, showing their efficacy in tabular and LLM experiments including Llama 3 models.
Problem: Widespread implementation practices for KL divergence gradient estimation in reinforcement learning, particularly in large language models, often result in incorrect or biased gradients.
Current methods frequently fail to properly account for the auto-regressive sequential dependencies in LLM outputs when computing sequence-level KL divergence gradients.
Many open-source projects and influential papers contain these pitfalls, leading to the intended KL regularization not being enforced effectively.
Method: The paper theoretically derives and explains the correct, unbiased gradient estimate for KL divergence, showing it can be obtained by differentiating the squared KL estimate or by using a stop-gradient operation on the ratio term.

It proposes unbiased sequence-level KL gradient estimates for auto-regressive models, including a vanilla sequence-level form and two variance-reduced variants (leave-one-out control variate and cumulative estimate) to account for full sequential dependencies.

The authors provide empirical validation in both controlled tabular settings and realistic large language model fine-tuning experiments to demonstrate the impact of the identified pitfalls and the efficacy of the proposed correct methods.
Results: Tabular experiments demonstrated that common incorrect KL gradient estimates exhibit significant bias, fail to minimize the target KL, or inadvertently minimize the reverse KL, unlike correctly derived estimates.

In LLM experiments (e.g., Llama 3), correct vanilla token-level gradient estimates effectively reduced KL divergence, whereas incorrect variance-reduced methods showed little progress on the target metric, especially in high-KL regimes.

Properly implemented sequence-level KL gradient estimates (vanilla, leave-one-out, cumulative) significantly outperformed token-level implementations in minimizing sequence-level KL divergence for LLMs, showing faster convergence and better overall performance.
Takeaways: Auto-differentiating common Monte-Carlo estimates of KL divergence (e.g., vanilla or variance-reduced) as a loss function yields biased gradients, often resulting in no effective regularization or minimizing the unintended reverse KL divergence.
For sequence generation tasks like those with large language models, token-level KL losses produce only partial gradients, as they fail to account for the auto-regressive dependencies between tokens.

Correctly estimating the KL divergence gradient requires specific forms derived from the score function, and for sequences, unbiased sequence-level estimators that capture full temporal dependencies are crucial for effective optimization.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09278.Title: UFM: A Simple Path towards Unified Dense Correspondence with Flow
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09278.Summary: A single transformer-based model, Unified Flow & Matching (UFM), integrates optical flow and wide-baseline matching, achieving state-of-the-art performance in both domains. The model demonstrates significant error reduction, such as 62% less End-Point Error compared to RoMa for wide-baseline matching, and improved efficiency through joint training on diverse datasets.
Problem: Dense image correspondence has been traditionally split into two separate domains: optical flow estimation (small temporal displacements) and wide-baseline matching (large viewpoint changes).
Existing specialized models are suboptimal for real-world scenarios that often present mixed challenges, limiting their generalization across both small and large displacement conditions.
Previous attempts to unify these tasks had limited success, failing to match the performance of state-of-the-art specialized methods in their respective domains.
Method: The Unified Flow & Matching (UFM) model employs a simple, end-to-end transformer-based architecture that directly regresses dense pixel displacements and covisibility masks.

It utilizes shared DINOv2 ViT-L encoders for feature extraction, followed by 12 layers of self-attention transformers for feature fusion, with separate Dense Prediction Transformer (DPT) heads for flow and covisibility prediction.

The model is trained on a comprehensive dataset compiled from 12 diverse sources covering both optical flow and wide-baseline domains, using robust loss functions and supervising only co-visible pixels.
Results: UFM560 achieves a 62% reduction in End-Point Error and is 6.7x faster compared to RoMa on wide-baseline dense correspondence benchmarks (ETH3D, DTU, TA-WB), and 60x faster than MASt3R with comparable precision.
UFM980 achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot performance on the Sintel-Final and KITTI datasets for optical flow, and competitive performance on Sintel-Clean.
The model demonstrates state-of-the-art accuracy for relative pose estimation on ETH3D and TA-WB benchmarks, indicating its learned correspondences are robust for 3D reconstruction.
Takeaways: Joint training on diverse optical flow and wide-baseline data leads to mutual performance improvements, with optical flow benefiting from wide-baseline data and wide-baseline matching benefiting from optical flow data.

The UFM architecture demonstrates superior scalability compared to existing specialized methods, showing significant performance gains with increased computational resources when trained on unified datasets.
Analysis of DINOv2 layers reveals that intermediate layers (L9-L11) encode the most effective features for correspondence, supporting the decision to fine-tune the encoder during training.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09047.Title: Same Task, Different Circuits: Disentangling Modality-Specific Mechanisms in VLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09047.Summary: Researchers from Technion and UC Berkeley investigated the persistent performance gap in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) between visual and textual tasks, finding that visual representations align slowly with textual ones. They propose an inference-time intervention called "back-patching" that re-injects later-layer visual activations into earlier layers, closing approximately 32% of this performance gap by improving visual task accuracy by an average of 4.6%.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) consistently exhibit a performance gap, achieving higher accuracy on textual inputs than on analogous visual inputs for the same task.
The underlying computational mechanisms and reasons for this modality-specific performance discrepancy within VLMs are not fully understood.
Improving VLM performance on visual tasks typically requires computationally intensive retraining or fine-tuning, lacking insights for training-free interventions.
Method: A custom dataset of five analogous visual and textual question-answering tasks was created to precisely compare VLM performance and internal processing across modalities.
Mechanistic interpretability techniques, specifically Attribution Patching with Integrated Gradients, were used to identify and compare modality-specific computational "circuits" within VLMs.
A training-free, inference-time intervention called "back-patching" was developed, which records and re-injects textually-aligned visual token activations from later layers back into earlier layers.
Results: Back-patching achieved an average absolute accuracy gain of 4.6% on visual prompts across various tasks and models, effectively closing approximately 32% of the performance gap between analogous visual and textual tasks.
Control experiments confirmed that back-patching's improvements for visual tasks stemmed from accelerating textual alignment rather than merely adding computation.

The intervention's efficacy was validated on general VQA benchmarks (VQAv2 and RealWorldQA) with statistically significant accuracy increases, and it generally improved performance across different scales of PaliGemma2 models.
Takeaways: VLMs utilize largely disjoint sets of computational components (circuits) for processing analogous visual and textual tasks, with only 18% average overlap.

While data processing sub-circuits are modality-specific and functionally non-interchangeable, query processing and answer generation sub-circuits, despite structural differences, are functionally equivalent across modalities.
Visual token representations align gradually and slowly with their analogous textual counterparts across model layers, with robust alignment typically achieved only in later stages of processing.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09033.Title: Router-R1: Teaching LLMs Multi-Round Routing and Aggregation via Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09033.Summary: Router-R1, developed by researchers at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, introduces a reinforcement learning framework that trains an LLM to perform multi-round routing and aggregation of other LLMs for complex tasks. This approach enables dynamic coordination of multiple models, yielding improved performance on diverse QA benchmarks, robust generalization to unseen models and data, and controllable trade-offs between accuracy and computational cost.
Problem: Existing LLM routing strategies are limited to single-round, one-to-one model selection, failing to address tasks requiring iterative interaction and complementary strengths of multiple LLMs.
Complex reasoning tasks, such as multi-hop question answering, demand a sequential orchestration of multiple LLMs, which single-shot routing cannot provide.
Optimizing discrete routing decisions in a multi-round, sequential process is intractable for traditional gradient-based end-to-end training methods.
Method: Router-R1 formulates multi-LLM routing and aggregation as a sequential decision process, optimizing an LLM acting as the router using a cost-aware reinforcement learning (PPO) framework.

The router LLM interleaves internal 'think' actions with external 'route' actions to dynamically select and invoke candidate LLMs, integrating their responses over multiple rounds to refine the answer.
A hierarchical reward function includes format adherence, final answer correctness (Exact Match), and a novel cost reward to balance task performance with the computational cost of LLM invocations.
Results: Router-R1 consistently outperformed over ten competitive baselines across seven diverse QA benchmarks, achieving average Exact Match scores of 0.416 (Qwen) and 0.409 (Llama).
It demonstrated robust generalization, maintaining strong performance on five out-of-domain QA datasets and effectively incorporating unseen LLM candidates without additional fine-tuning.
The framework learned controllable performance-cost trade-offs, enabling reduced average LLM invocation cost while maintaining competitive accuracy by prioritizing cheaper models when appropriate.
Takeaways: Reinforcement learning effectively teaches an LLM to dynamically coordinate other LLMs in a multi-round fashion, enabling complex problem decomposition and iterative answer refinement.

Introducing a cost reward allows the router to learn strategies that balance answer quality with the computational expense of querying different LLMs, creating controllable performance-cost trade-offs.
An LLM acting as a router can generalize to unseen candidate LLMs without retraining by leveraging simple textual descriptors of their capabilities and costs provided at inference time.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09026.Title: e3: Learning to Explore Enables Extrapolation of Test-Time Compute for LLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09026.Summary: The e3 training recipe enables Large Language Models to truly extrapolate their reasoning performance by effectively utilizing increased test-time computation. A 1.7B parameter model trained with e3 outperforms much larger models in the extrapolation regime on mathematical reasoning benchmarks.
Problem: Most existing Large Language Models (LLMs) trained for reasoning do not effectively extrapolate their performance, showing diminishing returns and plateauing even when given significantly more compute at test time.

Current methods often fail to enable LLMs to perform genuine 'in-context exploration,' such as planning or self-correction, which is needed to leverage extended inference budgets for complex problem-solving.
Achieving true extrapolation from LLMs is hindered by training regimes that either penalize longer, exploratory traces or lead to optimization instability with overly large training budgets.
Method: Introduces `e3` (in-context exploration enables extrapolation), a novel training recipe designed to train LLMs for effective in-context exploration.
Leverages the chaining of asymmetric capabilities within the model, particularly the verification-generation gap, to provide a natural pathway for iterative search and refinement.

Employs negative gradients in Reinforcement Learning to incentivize longer, more exploratory traces and uses a coupled curriculum that dynamically adjusts both task difficulty and training token budget.
Results: Most tested open-source reasoning models fail to extrapolate effectively beyond their training token budgets, showing significant performance plateaus.

The e3-1.7B model achieves state-of-the-art performance for models under 2B parameters on mathematical reasoning benchmarks (AIME'25, HMMT'25) and consistently outperforms larger models (7B, 32B) in the extrapolation regime (16k to 32k test tokens).

Negative gradients promote diverse responses and increase the chaining of asymmetric skills within generated traces, while the coupled curriculum effectively structures exploration, balancing training efficiency with the ability to extrapolate.
Takeaways: The presence of asymmetric competencies, such as a verification-generation gap, within a base model is crucial for enabling effective in-context exploration.

Negative gradients in Reinforcement Learning are essential for driving models to explore longer, diverse reasoning paths by redirecting probability mass from incorrect, short traces to longer, exploratory ones.
A coupled curriculum that coordinates increases in task difficulty with an adaptive training token budget is necessary to efficiently foster and maintain in-context exploration for extrapolation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08989.Title: SwS: Self-aware Weakness-driven Problem Synthesis in Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08989.Summary: The SwS framework enhances Large Language Model reasoning by enabling self-aware, weakness-driven problem synthesis for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR). It generates targeted, high-quality training data, leading to substantial performance gains on mathematical benchmarks compared to baseline RL.
Problem: High scarcity and cost of acquiring high-quality, human-labeled, verifiable data for training Large Language Models (LLMs) via Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR).
Existing synthetic datasets are often suboptimal for RLVR due to a lack of rigorous verification for reference answers, which are crucial for generating robust training signals.

Inefficient problem augmentation strategies that indiscriminately expand datasets, resulting in problems that are either too trivial (no learning signal) or too challenging (gradient vanishing), hindering effective RL training.
Method: The SwS framework employs a three-stage pipeline: self-aware weakness identification, targeted problem synthesis, and augmented RLVR training.
It identifies an LLM's weaknesses by analyzing consistently failed problems during a preliminary RL training phase, classifying problems with low and decreasing accuracy as targets.

New problems are generated by extracting and recombining concepts from these failed problems, with the augmentation budget dynamically allocated based on category-specific failure rates, and then rigorously filtered for quality, verifiable answers, and appropriate difficulty.
Results: SwS consistently yielded average absolute performance improvements of +10.0% for 7B models and +7.7% for 32B models across a range of mathematical reasoning benchmarks (e.g., GSM8K, MATH, AIME).
The framework effectively mitigated identified weaknesses, showing significant gains of +20% in 'Intermediate Algebra' and +5% in 'Geometry' for previously failed problems.

Ablation studies confirmed that 'Medium' and 'Hard' synthetic problems provided more sustained and significant performance gains compared to 'Simple' problems, highlighting the importance of appropriate challenge levels.
Takeaways: Consistently failed problems in initial RL training reveal specific model weaknesses that can be systematically leveraged to guide more efficient and focused learning.
