Targeted problem synthesis, by extracting and recombining concepts from identified weaknesses, creates high-quality, difficulty-tailored training data that significantly enhances an LLM's reasoning abilities and generalization.

Rigorous filtering of synthetic problems based on solvability and appropriate difficulty (e.g., accuracy within 25%-75%) ensures that the generated data provides meaningful gradient signals and prevents issues like gradient vanishing.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08552.Title: Efficient Post-Training Refinement of Latent Reasoning in Large Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08552.Summary: Researchers from Arizona State University developed a post-training framework to refine latent reasoning in large language models by integrating contrastive feedback and residual embedding refinement. The method yields accuracy gains of 2-5% across various reasoning tasks while drastically reducing token overhead compared to explicit Chain-of-Thought approaches.
Problem: Explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting incurs substantial token overhead and generates fixed, often irreversible, reasoning trajectories.
Existing latent reasoning models lack explicit directional guidance for consistent progression and suffer from instability with recursive embedding updates.
Improving LLM reasoning often requires expensive retraining or architectural modifications, limiting practical deployment for frozen models.
Method: A training-free framework enhances latent reasoning during inference by integrating two novel strategies without modifying model parameters.
Contrastive Reasoning Feedback Search uses auxiliary 'strong' and 'weak' models to infer a gradient-based directional update for current latent embeddings.
Residual Embedding Refinement stabilizes latent state evolution by blending previous and current embeddings with a fixed 'memory rate' to prevent semantic drift.
Results: Achieved absolute accuracy gains of +1.95% to +3.67% over latent-only reasoning (Coconut) and outperformed explicit CoT on four out of five reasoning benchmarks.
Reduced average generated tokens per query by over 92% compared to CoT, demonstrating superior cost-efficiency during inference.
Demonstrated robust generalization across different LLM backbones (GPT-2, Qwen-2.5, LLaMA-3.2) with consistent accuracy improvements and efficient inference.
Takeaways: Refining latent reasoning through post-training, inference-only mechanisms is highly effective and significantly more efficient than continued training.
Both contrastive directional feedback and residual context preservation are crucial and synergistic for maintaining stable and accurate latent reasoning trajectories.
The proposed framework acts as a plug-and-play component, enabling performance enhancement for frozen LLMs without requiring retraining or architectural changes.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08429.Title: Better Reasoning with Less Data: Enhancing VLMs Through Unified Modality Scoring
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08429.Summary: Researchers developed SCALE, an automated pipeline that curates high-quality multimodal instruction tuning datasets by integrating unimodal and cross-modal quality assessments. This method allows Visual Language Models trained on less than 10% of the original data to achieve superior performance compared to models trained on full, uncurated datasets across various benchmarks.
Problem: Visual Language Model instruction tuning datasets suffer from noisy image-text correspondences.
Existing datasets contain ambiguous or misleading textual descriptions, degrading overall data quality.
Manually curating large-scale, high-quality multimodal datasets is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming.
Method: Introduced SCALE, a five-stage automated pipeline for comprehensive data quality assessment, integrating unimodal (image and text) and multimodal alignment evaluations.
Utilized large language models (Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct) for predicting data tasks and rating text and multimodal quality.

Employed a lightweight VLM (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) to generate general and task-specific image captions, unifying visual and linguistic representations into a text-only format for streamlined multimodal comparison.
Results: Models fine-tuned on less than 10% of SCALE-curated data consistently outperformed models trained on the full 500K instruction tuning dataset.
SCALE achieved an average score of 84.23 across various benchmarks, surpassing the full data baseline (83.94) and all other data selection baselines.
The internal task prediction component using Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct achieved over 80% accuracy for all defined sub-tasks, demonstrating its robustness in categorizing data.
Takeaways: Training VLMs on a significantly smaller, quality-curated subset of data can lead to superior performance compared to using the entire, uncurated dataset.
Unimodal data quality assessments (image-only or text-only) are insufficient and can bias selection by overlooking crucial, task-specific aspects or discarding valuable lower-fidelity samples.
Generated image captions effectively transform complex image-text multimodal alignment into a unified text modality, simplifying the evaluation process and improving efficiency.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08391.Title: SECOND: Mitigating Perceptual Hallucination in Vision-Language Models via Selective and Contrastive Decoding
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08391.Summary: Researchers from Seoul National University's AIDASLab developed SECOND (Selective and Contrastive Decoding), a training-free framework that addresses object hallucination in Vision-Language Models by mimicking human visual perception. The method uses selective multi-scale processing and multi-stage contrastive decoding, leading to consistent reductions in hallucination (e.g., POPE F1 scores improved from 86.5 to 89.2 for LLaVA-NeXT) while also improving general VLM task performance.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) frequently generate confident but factually incorrect responses about objects not present in an image, a phenomenon known as object hallucination.
Existing multi-scale VLM approaches integrate visual information uniformly, which can introduce irrelevant background noise and dilute object-specific context, worsening hallucination.
The unreliability caused by hallucination limits the deployment of VLMs in sensitive, high-stakes applications requiring factual accuracy.
Method: SECOND employs a training-free, human-inspired multi-scale processing pipeline that selectively integrates visual information based on dynamic patch selection.
Visual patches for higher-resolution processing are chosen based on attention scores and entropy calculations, preserving object-relevant details while filtering out irrelevant background.

A novel multi-stage contrastive decoding formulation amplifies distinctions between sparse and dense visual information from different processing stages, leveraging a coarse-to-fine understanding to refine outputs.
Results: SECOND consistently reduced hallucination on the POPE benchmark, improving F1 scores (e.g., from 86.5 to 89.2 for LLaVA-NeXT on MSCOCO) across 11 out of 12 configurations.
The framework also improved performance on general VLM tasks, increasing VQAv2 accuracy from 76.4 to 77.5, MMStar from 37.3 to 38.6, and MMBench from 75.8 to 80.0 for LLaVA-NeXT.
Ablation studies confirmed that the dynamic patch selection based on visual attention entropy and the multi-stage contrastive decoding were crucial for the observed performance gains.
Takeaways: VLM object hallucination is inversely correlated with visual attention alignment, meaning models are more likely to hallucinate when their attention poorly aligns with ground truth objects.
Indiscriminate integration of visual information across multiple scales can dilute object-specific context and increase hallucination, indicating a need for selective processing.
A multi-stage contrastive decoding approach, leveraging hierarchical visual representations, can effectively amplify visual evidence and reduce hallucination without retraining.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08388.Title: Reinforcement Learning Teachers of Test Time Scaling
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08388.Summary: Researchers at Sakana AI developed Reinforcement-Learned Teachers (RLTs), a framework that trains specialized language models to generate high-quality, step-by-step explanations for known solutions instead of solving problems from scratch. This approach produces superior distillation datasets, enabling smaller student models to outperform those trained with existing pipelines based on much larger LMs, and achieves significant computational efficiency with an RLT training costing 280.4 GPU-hours.
Problem: Traditional reinforcement learning for reasoning Language Models (LMs) struggles with sparse, one-hot correctness rewards, leading to exploration challenges, instability, and high computational costs, often only benefiting very large models.

Current supervised distillation methods for LMs face an objective mismatch where teachers optimized for problem-solving do not optimally generate instructive explanations for students, necessitating extensive heuristic postprocessing.
Existing distillation pipelines are inefficient and rely on prohibitively large LMs or costly manual/LLM-based postprocessing for data refinement.
Method: Redefine the teacher's role by training Reinforcement-Learned Teachers (RLTs) to generate step-by-step explanations for given question-solution pairs, rather than solving problems independently.

Introduce a dense, two-part reward function (r_SS for student understanding and r_KL for explanation interpretability) to provide continuous feedback on the quality and utility of the generated explanations for student learning.
Employ a computationally efficient training paradigm using the GRPO algorithm with a small 7B base model, requiring minimal pre-training and a short reinforcement learning phase.
Results: Raw explanations from a 7B RLT consistently led to higher student performance on challenging reasoning tasks (AIME, MATH, GPQA) compared to distillation from larger LMs (e.g., DeepSeek R1) with extensive postprocessing.

RLT-generated traces proved more effective for cold-starting traditional reinforcement learning and exhibited strong zero-shot transferability, enabling successful distillation for out-of-domain tasks.

The framework achieved substantial computational efficiency, with training a 7B RLT and generating its dataset requiring only a fraction of the GPU hours compared to existing large-scale reasoning LM pipelines.
Takeaways: Reframing the reinforcement learning objective to focus on explanation generation for known solutions effectively circumvents the severe exploration challenges faced by traditional RL with sparse correctness rewards.

Aligning the teacher's training objective directly with its downstream distillation role, by optimizing for explanation quality, yields superior and more efficient knowledge transfer to student models.
Even relatively small language models possess latent 'teaching skills' that can be effectively elicited and refined through purpose-aligned dense reward functions.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08257.Title: Highly Compressed Tokenizer Can Generate Without Training
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08257.Summary: Researchers from MIT and Meta FAIR demonstrated that highly compressed 1D image tokenizers, particularly TiTok, can perform image editing and text-to-image synthesis through test-time optimization of their latent codes, removing the need for a separate generative model. Their approach achieved competitive generation quality and revealed that generative performance improves with higher compression ratios and discrete token representations.
Problem: Modern image generation pipelines traditionally rely on a dedicated, complex generative model in addition to an image tokenizer, often requiring extensive training.
The inherent generative capabilities of image tokenizers, especially highly compressed one-dimensional ones, have largely been unexplored.
Existing methods for "generation without training" often still rely on pre-trained generative models or 2D latent spaces that are not as highly compressed.
Method: The approach utilizes a pre-trained, highly compressed one-dimensional (1D) tokenizer (e.g., TiTok) as the sole "generative" component.

It employs gradient-based test-time optimization of the tokenizer's continuous latent codes using plug-and-play loss functions, such as CLIP similarity for text guidance or L1 reconstruction for inpainting.
Simple heuristic manipulations, like copying and pasting tokens based on discovered semantic disentanglement, enable fine-grained image editing.
Results: Confirmed semantic disentanglement in 1D latent space through importance metrics and single-token perturbations, enabling effective heuristic image editing by copying single tokens.
Successfully performed training-free text-guided image editing, text-to-image generation from scratch, and inpainting with realistic and diverse outputs.

Demonstrated that generative performance improved with fewer tokens and smaller codebook sizes, and that discrete VQ tokens significantly outperformed continuous VAE tokens, achieving competitive FID scores (e.g., 8.2 on ImageNet with 1000 seed images).
Takeaways: Highly compressed 1D latent spaces exhibit semantic disentanglement, allowing specific token positions to control global image attributes like subject type, background material, or lighting.
The generative capabilities of these tokenizers are enhanced by higher compression ratios (fewer tokens, smaller codebook sizes) and the use of discrete tokens (Vector Quantization).

The tokenizer's decoder implicitly performs a generative task when input from a highly compressed latent space, suggesting generation can be inherent in the compression mechanism itself rather than a separate model.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08011.Title: Play to Generalize: Learning to Reason Through Game Play
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08011.Summary: Researchers from Rice University, Johns Hopkins University, and NVIDIA developed Visual Game Learning (ViGaL), a post-training method that uses simple visual games as surrogate tasks for reinforcement learning, to enhance multimodal large language models (MLLMs) reasoning capabilities. The approach achieved superior zero-shot generalization to diverse multimodal reasoning tasks, outperforming specialist models trained on domain-specific data, while preserving general visual capabilities.
Problem: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) struggle with robust, multi-step reasoning and generalization to out-of-domain scenarios.
Existing methods, like supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or reinforcement learning (RL) with domain-specific data, often lead to task specialization and can degrade general visual understanding.
Creating high-quality, human-annotated datasets for complex reasoning tasks is expensive, labor-intensive, and limits scalability.
Method: Introduced Visual Game Learning (ViGaL), a post-training paradigm that applies reinforcement learning on simple, synthetic visual games (Snake and Rotation) to cultivate transferable reasoning skills.
Designed game environments as Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) where MLLMs receive multimodal observations, output actions and reasoning traces, and receive rule-based rewards.

Employed a specific reward function incentivizing both 'best' and 'worst' moves in the Snake game, and incorporated explicit reasoning instructions within prompts generated by GPT-4o to guide the model's thinking processes.
Results: ViGaL outperformed proprietary models (GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Pro) in game performance and demonstrated significant zero-shot generalization to 7 unseen Atari games, nearly doubling the cumulative reward compared to the base model.

The model achieved 0.5% higher accuracy on multimodal math benchmarks and 5.4% higher on multi-discipline QA (MMMU) benchmarks compared to specialist models, despite having no explicit math-specific training data.

ViGaL improved 3D spatial reasoning by 2.0% on VSI-Bench and maintained general visual understanding across diverse perception benchmarks, demonstrating enhanced reasoning without degrading other visual capabilities.
Takeaways: Simple, synthetic arcade-style games can serve as scalable and controllable pretext tasks for RL post-training, effectively developing foundational, transferable reasoning skills in MLLMs.
Reinforcement Learning is crucial for this paradigm; unlike RL which boosts reasoning, supervised fine-tuning with game data actually degrades the MLLM's performance on downstream reasoning tasks.

Specific design choices such as explicit reasoning instructions in prompts and a contrastive reward system (predicting best and worst actions) significantly enhance the transferability of learned skills to unseen domains.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08008.Title: Hidden in plain sight: VLMs overlook their visual representations
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08008.Summary: UC Berkeley researchers found that Vision-Language Models frequently underperform on vision-centric tasks because their language model components fail to fully leverage the high-quality visual representations available from their vision encoders, instead often defaulting to linguistic priors. The study demonstrated that fine-tuning the LLM significantly improves visual utilization and reduces reliance on these priors.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) exhibit significantly worse performance on vision-centric tasks compared to their standalone vision encoders, often performing near random chance.
There is an unreliable rank-ordering of vision encoders when integrated into VLMs; top-performing standalone encoders do not consistently yield the best VLMs.
The underlying reason for VLMs failing to effectively use demonstrably rich visual information from their encoders remained unclear.
Method: Developed a dual evaluation strategy comparing direct visual encoder readouts with full VLM performance on a suite of "vision-centric" tasks.
Conducted diagnostic analyses to probe potential bottlenecks: degradation of visual representations, brittleness to linguistic prompts, and the LLM's ability to utilize visual information.
Systematically fine-tuned individual VLM components (vision encoder, projector, LLM) on vision-centric tasks to isolate the source of performance limitations.
Results: A universal and substantial performance drop was observed from direct vision encoder evaluation to full VLM evaluation across all vision-centric tasks, often to near-chance levels.
VLMs' answer distributions closely matched those generated when given blank visual inputs, confirming a reliance on linguistic priors over visual evidence.

Fine-tuning the LLM component on vision-centric tasks yielded the largest performance improvements, alongside improved visual attention and mitigation of language biases, compared to fine-tuning other VLM components.
Takeaways: Task-relevant visual information is largely preserved within the VLM's internal representations, indicating that the visual input itself is not degraded by the projector or LLM layers.
VLMs often default to "blind" language priors or biases when answering, ignoring available visual evidence, which significantly contributes to their underperformance.
The language model (LLM) component is the primary bottleneck, as it fails to effectively attend to, integrate, and reason over the rich visual features it receives.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08007.Title: Reinforcement Pre-Training
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08007.Summary: Reinforcement Pre-Training (RPT) introduces a novel paradigm for pre-training large language models by reframing next-token prediction as a reasoning task, utilizing on-policy reinforcement learning with verifiable, rule-based rewards. This approach enhances next-token prediction accuracy and improves zero-shot performance on diverse downstream tasks by fostering deeper reasoning capabilities from the foundational training stage.
Problem: Standard self-supervised next-token prediction in LLM pre-training primarily optimizes for statistical likelihood, which may not foster deeper reasoning or robust understanding.

Current reinforcement learning methods for LLMs (like RLHF and RLVR) are mostly confined to post-training fine-tuning due to their reliance on costly human preference data or limited domain-specific annotations.
A significant gap exists in applying scalable and general reinforcement learning techniques to the foundational, general-purpose pre-training phase of LLMs using vast amounts of unannotated text.
Method: Reinforcement Pre-Training (RPT) reframes the ubiquitous next-token prediction task as a 'next-token reasoning process,' requiring the model to generate a chain-of-thought before predicting the final token.
The approach employs an on-policy reinforcement learning framework, where the language model performs multiple 'thinking trajectories' for each context.

A deterministic prefix matching reward (1 for exact prefix match, 0 otherwise) is used to verify the correctness of the predicted next token, leveraging unannotated text data for verifiable intrinsic rewards.
Results: Reinforcement Pre-Training (RPT)-14B achieved higher next-token prediction accuracy across all difficulty levels on OmniMATH, reaching 23.75% accuracy on 'Hard' tokens, outperforming a 14B baseline and matching a 32B baseline.
Models pre-trained with RPT provided a stronger foundation for subsequent reinforcement fine-tuning, reaching 58.3% accuracy after RLVR on Skywork-OR1, compared to 52.7% for the baseline.

RPT-14B showed enhanced zero-shot performance on general downstream tasks, with approximately 7 points gain on SuperGPQA and 22 points gain on MMLU-Pro over a 32B standard next-token prediction baseline.
Takeaways: Reframing pre-training as an active reasoning task, where the model explicitly generates a chain-of-thought to predict the next token, enables LLMs to develop deeper understanding and reasoning capabilities directly.

Leveraging objective, rule-based rewards derived from the correctness of next-token predictions on abundant unannotated text provides a scalable and general approach for applying reinforcement learning during pre-training, bypassing data scarcity and reward hacking issues.

Incentivizing reasoning during pre-training not only fosters complex abilities and generalizable intelligence but also inherently improves fundamental next-token prediction accuracy, suggesting a deeper understanding enhances core language modeling.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07966.Title: SpaCE-10: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Multimodal Large Language Models in Compositional Spatial Intelligence
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07966.Summary: SpaCE-10, a new benchmark, evaluates Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) in compositional spatial intelligence by defining 10 atomic spatial capabilities and 8 complex question-answer types across over 800 real indoor scenes. Evaluations showed current MLLMs achieved a maximum of 55.0% accuracy, significantly below human performance of 91.2%, with particular struggles in counting and integrating multiple spatial skills.
Problem: Existing MLLM benchmarks lack comprehensive and systematic evaluation of compositional spatial intelligence, often focusing on isolated or less complex spatial capabilities.
Many current benchmarks are limited in terms of scenario diversity, scale, modalities, and question types, hindering thorough assessment of advanced MLLMs.
A clear framework was missing to explicitly define and systematically combine atomic spatial capabilities for rigorous evaluation of real-world spatial reasoning.
Method: Introduced SpaCE-10, a comprehensive benchmark featuring 10 atomic spatial capabilities and 8 compositional QA types, built upon 811 diverse real indoor scenes from multiple 3D datasets.

Developed a dataset of over 5,000 high-quality question-answer pairs, supporting both 2D imagery and 3D point cloud inputs, annotated through a five-stage hierarchical pipeline combining human expertise and advanced LLMs.
Conducted extensive evaluations on nearly 50 MLLMs, encompassing both open-source and closed-source models, to establish current performance levels in compositional spatial intelligence.
Results: InternVL3.5-241B-A28B was the top open-source MLLM with 55.0% overall accuracy, outperforming leading closed-source models like GPT-5 (53.4%) and GPT-4o (49.0%).
2D MLLMs generally outperformed 3D MLLMs on the benchmark, suggesting greater proficiency in inferring spatial intelligence from image-based inputs.

MLLM accuracy declined significantly for multiple-answer questions and when more atomic capabilities were integrated into a task, showing an average accuracy decrease of up to 42.9% for functional reasoning tasks requiring multiple integrations.
Takeaways: Current MLLMs are significantly behind human performance in compositional spatial intelligence, with the best model achieving 55.0% accuracy compared to human experts' 91.2%.
Integrating multiple atomic spatial capabilities into tasks leads to substantial drops in MLLM accuracy, highlighting a fundamental difficulty in compositional reasoning.
The 'Counting' (C5) capability consistently emerged as the weakest across all evaluated MLLMs, indicating a persistent challenge in discrete numerosity, especially in complex spatial contexts.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07936.Title: Mimicking or Reasoning: Rethinking Multi-Modal In-Context Learning in Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07936.Summary: Researchers at Georgia Institute of Technology challenge the assumption that Vision-Language Models (VLMs) genuinely learn from in-context examples, finding that they often mimic superficial patterns rather than acquire deeper reasoning capabilities. Their work demonstrates that current VLMs generally do not achieve consistent performance gains over zero-shot baselines, even when provided with explicit reasoning demonstrations and under controlled distribution shifts.
Problem: A prevailing assumption exists that Vision-Language Models (VLMs) possess multi-modal in-context learning (MM-ICL) capabilities akin to large language models, but the depth of this learning (mimicking vs. reasoning) is unclear.

VLMs often resort to shallow heuristics like copying answers or majority voting when learning from demonstrations, especially in out-of-distribution (OOD) settings where performance can plateau or degrade.
Existing MM-ICL benchmarks may not rigorously distinguish between superficial pattern matching and genuine task understanding, leading to ambiguous conclusions about VLM capabilities.
Method: The study rigorously evaluates MM-ICL capabilities under distribution shifts by comparing VLM performance in In-Distribution (ID) vs. Out-of-Distribution (OOD) settings for support examples.

A novel MM-ICL with Reasoning pipeline is introduced that provides information-enriched demonstrations, including explicit step-by-step rationales alongside answers, to provide a stronger learning signal.

Comprehensive experiments are conducted on a diverse range of modern open-source and proprietary VLMs, including their 'reasoner' variants, assessing sensitivity to factors like shot count, retrieval methods, rationale quality, and support set distribution.
Results: Current VLMs and VLM reasoners generally do not derive consistent or substantial benefit from MM-ICL over zero-shot performance across a majority of perception and reasoning datasets, often failing to significantly exceed or sometimes falling below the zero-shot baseline.

The performance of VLM reasoners significantly improved (e.g., up to +8.71% on M3CoT) when demonstrations included both rationales and answers, ensuring format consistency with the model's expected output.

Improving the quality of rationales (via filtering incorrect samples or using ground-truth rationales) within demonstrations did not consistently lead to improved performance, and multimodal retrievers often underperformed random selection for reasoning models, indicating insensitivity to reasoning quality and complex interactions with retrieval.
Takeaways: Current Vision-Language Models (VLMs) frequently rely on superficial pattern matching or 'mimicking' rather than genuine in-context reasoning from demonstrations.
Format consistency between demonstration structure (e.g., including rationales) and the VLM's expected output format is crucial for effective in-context learning by reasoner models.

The quality of rationales within demonstrations, even if ground-truth or filtered for correctness, often does not consistently improve VLM performance, indicating insensitivity to deeper informational content.

Multimodal retrievers can be counterproductive for VLM reasoners by selecting examples with similar inputs but potentially inconsistent reasoning paths, hindering learning from diverse logical structures.

Modern VLMs are more robust to distribution shifts (Out-of-Distribution vs. In-Distribution support sets) in demonstrations, but this robustness does not equate to effective in-context learning gains over zero-shot performance itself, rather it suggests less susceptibility to superficial patterns based on data distribution.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07850.Title: SAM2Auto: Auto Annotation Using FLASH
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07850.Summary: SAM2Auto introduces a fully automated and training-free pipeline for video annotation, leveraging robust object detection and real-time multi-object video instance segmentation. This system reduces false positives in object detection by 57% and improves Multiple Object Tracking Accuracy (MOTA) by 1393% on the MOT17 dataset, establishing a new baseline for scalable Vision-Language Model dataset creation.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) face a 'dataset bottleneck' due to the scarcity of high-quality, large-scale paired visual and textual video annotations.
Traditional manual video annotation is labor-intensive, expensive, time-consuming, and prone to inconsistencies, especially for maintaining consistent object IDs across frames.
Existing open-world detection and tracking methods often require human intervention or dataset-specific training, limiting their scalability and generalizability for diverse video datasets.
Method: SAM2Auto is an end-to-end automated pipeline consisting of SMART-OD for robust open-vocabulary object detection and FLASH for real-time multi-object video instance segmentation.
SMART-OD integrates SAM2 for mask generation, YOLO-World for object detection on masked inputs, and a robust verification stage using SAHI and dynamic thresholding to minimize false positives.

FLASH leverages ByteTrack for multi-object tracking with a memory-based SAM2 (ASH module) to propagate polygon segmentations across frames, ensuring temporal consistency and employing post-processing for quality refinement.
Results: SMART-OD reduced false positives by 57% (from 5,861 to 2,516) and improved precision from 59.4% to 72.8% on MOT17 training sets compared to a YOLO-World baseline.
The full SAM2Auto pipeline increased MOTA by 1393% (from -0.014 to 0.181) and recall by 52.2% on the MOT17 training set when applying FLASH to SMART-OD detections.
FLASH achieved the highest IDF1 score (72.5%) and ranked second in HOTA (62.0%) on the DanceTrack dataset, and the highest mHOTA (53.7%) on BDD100K using curated detections.
Takeaways: It is feasible to achieve fully automated, training-free video annotation, providing a new paradigm for VLM dataset creation that eliminates human intervention.

The primary bottleneck for end-to-end automated tracking performance is the quality of initial object detections, particularly the suppression of false positives, rather than the tracking component itself.

Memory-based segmentation trackers like SAM2ASH can achieve competitive performance in specific scenarios, such as DanceTrack, where objects have distinctive visual characteristics and tracking protocols align with its design.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07751.Title: AbstRaL: Augmenting LLMs' Reasoning by Reinforcing Abstract Thinking
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07751.Summary: The ABSTRAL framework augments Large Language Models' reasoning capabilities by training them to perform abstract thinking using structured data and reinforcement learning. It notably improves model robustness to various input perturbations and boosts out-of-distribution generalization on mathematical and general reasoning benchmarks.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit fragility and poor out-of-distribution generalization, especially when faced with subtle shifts in problem statements like varied numbers, rephrasing, or distracting information.
LLMs experience significant performance degradation on reasoning tasks due to 'instantiation shifts' and more challenging 'interferential shifts'.
Current data augmentation methods aimed at improving robustness are computationally intensive, demanding vast amounts of varied training instances.
Method: Introduction of the AbstRaL framework, which integrates neural language understanding with symbolic reasoning through a four-step pipeline: Condition Recognition, Abstract Reasoning, Abstraction Retrieval, and Symbolic Derivation.
Development of Granularly-decomposed Abstract Reasoning (GranulAR) data to teach LLMs to generate abstract answers with explicit reasoning steps and symbolic derivations.

Application of Reinforcement Learning (RL) using GRPO with novel model-free rewards, specifically a binary answer correctness reward and a symbolic distance reward, to guide the learning of faithful abstractions.
Results: AbstRaL almost entirely reverted performance drops on instantiation shifts, achieving a -1.27% change for Qwen2.5-0.5B on GSM-Symbolic (compared to a 10.58% drop for CoT-8S).
Significantly mitigated the negative impact of distracting information (interferential shifts), raising accuracy for Qwen2.5-0.5B to 36.5% on GSM-Plus 'Distract' versus 15.2% for CoT-RL.

Demonstrated improved zero-shot performance across a wide range of out-of-distribution datasets, including diverse mathematical (e.g., MATH, Minerva MATH) and general reasoning tasks (e.g., MMLU, BBH).
Takeaways: Explicitly teaching LLMs to identify and operate on the abstract, high-level reasoning schema underlying problems significantly improves their invariance to surface-form variations.
The GranulAR data format, which provides fine-grained sub-questions and explicitly quotes input conditions, is crucial for structured planning and effectively filtering out distracting information.

Reinforcement learning with specific model-free rewards (answer correctness and symbolic distance) is vital for training LLMs to generate faithful and accurate abstract reasoning, moving beyond supervised fine-tuning limitations.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07468.Title: Chasing Moving Targets with Online Self-Play Reinforcement Learning for Safer Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07468.Summary: Researchers from the University of Washington and Stanford University developed SELF-REDTEAM, an online multi-agent reinforcement learning framework, to enhance large language model safety by allowing a single LLM to continuously co-evolve as both attacker and defender. This approach achieves up to a 95% reduction in attack success rates on safety benchmarks and generates more diverse adversarial attacks, all while preserving the model's general capabilities.
Problem: Existing LLM safety alignment relies on reactive patching against static vulnerabilities, creating an inefficient 'cat-and-mouse game' where defenders perpetually lag behind emerging threats.
Traditional safety training against fixed datasets limits a model's ability to adapt to novel threats or continuously improve its safety posture.
Current methods often lead to a trade-off where aggressive safety alignment can degrade an LLM's general conversational quality or lead to undesirable 'over-refusal' of benign queries.
Method: SELF-REDTEAM utilizes an online multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) framework, where a single LLM policy dynamically alternates between attacker and defender roles, grounded in a two-player zero-sum game theory.

The framework employs a 'Hidden Chain-of-Thought' mechanism, allowing agents to develop private strategic reasoning without exposing internal thought processes to their opponents, encouraging diverse adversarial behaviors.

A composite reward structure guides both attacker and defender, incorporating game outcomes (response harmfulness, refusal appropriateness), formatting, and revision faithfulness, with optional auxiliary Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) to maintain general capabilities.
Results: SELF-REDTEAM achieves up to a 95% reduction in Attack Success Rates (ASR) across 12 safety benchmarks on Llama-3.1 and Qwen2.5 models, outperforming 'Defender-Only + SFT' methods by an average of 17.33%.

Adversarial attacks generated by the self-play mechanism exhibit greater semantic and lexical diversity, as evidenced by T-SNE visualizations and quantitative metrics, compared to 'Attacker-Only' approaches.

The framework maintains general conversational quality and instruction-following capabilities (e.g., stable or improved AlpacaEval-2 scores) and prevents over-refusal on benign queries, demonstrating a balanced safety-utility outcome.
Takeaways: Framing LLM red-teaming as a two-player zero-sum game provides a theoretical safety guarantee: convergence to a Nash Equilibrium ensures the defender generates safe responses.
Online co-evolution in self-play is critical for uncovering more diverse adversarial attacks and preventing overfitting to static attack patterns, leading to more generalizable defenses.
The 'Hidden Chain-of-Thought' mechanism significantly enhances attack diversity and enables more nuanced decision-making for appropriate compliance versus refusal, mitigating over-refusal issues.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07413.Title: Variational Supervised Contrastive Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07413.Summary: VarCon (Variational Supervised Contrastive Learning) unifies supervised contrastive learning with variational inference, providing a probabilistic framework for representation learning. It achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming SupCon on ImageNet-1K with 79.36% Top-1 accuracy, and demonstrates superior few-shot learning and robustness across various benchmarks while reducing batch size dependency.
Problem: Existing contrastive learning methods often lack explicit embedding distribution regulation, relying on heuristic energy functions without clear statistical meaning.
Current approaches heavily depend on large in-batch negative samples and tailored data augmentations, hindering generalization and increasing computational costs.
Traditional pairwise comparison in contrastive learning leads to quadratic computational complexity with respect to batch size.
Method: VarCon reformulates supervised contrastive learning as variational inference, maximizing a posterior-weighted Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) to provide explicit probabilistic semantics to the representation space.

It replaces exhaustive pairwise comparisons with efficient class-level centroids and defines a loss function that balances KL divergence (for distribution alignment) and negative log-posterior (for classification).

A confidence-adaptive temperature mechanism is introduced, dynamically adjusting the learning intensity for intra-class dispersion based on the model's prediction confidence, providing sharper supervision for difficult samples.
Results: VarCon achieves state-of-the-art Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K (79.36%) and CIFAR-100 (78.29%), surpassing SupCon by 0.64% and 1.72% respectively.
It demonstrates faster convergence (200 epochs vs. SupCon's 350 epochs on ImageNet) and reduced batch size dependency, maintaining high performance with smaller batch sizes.

The framework exhibits superior performance in few-shot learning scenarios (e.g., 1.24% higher accuracy at N=100 on ImageNet) and enhanced robustness to image corruptions on ImageNet-C across all severity levels.
Takeaways: Reinterpreting supervised contrastive learning as variational inference provides a rigorous probabilistic foundation, bridging the gap between contrastive and generative paradigms.

Dynamically adjusting supervision strength with a confidence-adaptive temperature allows for fine-grained control over intra-class dispersion, focusing learning on challenging samples while relaxing constraints for easy ones.
Utilizing class-level centroids for computing posteriors significantly improves computational efficiency, reducing the dependency on large batch sizes.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07326.Title: Reward Model Interpretability via Optimal and Pessimal Tokens
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07326.Summary: Researchers from the University of Oxford investigated the interpretability of reward models by analyzing their scoring of optimal and pessimal tokens and multi-token sequences. This analysis exposed significant heterogeneity and systematic biases across models, including the devaluation of identity group references and sexual content, suggesting a misalignment with human preferences.
Problem: Reward models (RMs), foundational for LLM alignment via RLHF, are typically treated as 'disposable intermediaries,' with their internal workings, biases, and fidelity to human values largely unexplored.
A lack of systematic understanding regarding how RMs translate complex human value judgments into scalar representations hinders the development of robust and truly aligned AI systems.
The potential for unintended biases within RMs, which could propagate into widely deployed LLMs, remained understudied despite their critical role in encoding human values.
Method: An exhaustive search methodology was pioneered to compute reward model scores for every single token in a model's vocabulary in response to value-laden prompts.
Quantitative analysis, including sentiment lexicons, frequency bias investigation, and external validation with human preference data (EloEverything), was employed to interpret RM behaviors.
The analysis was extended to multi-token sequences using discrete optimization methods like Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) to explore longer 'optimal' and 'pessimal' responses.
Results: Reward models showed only moderate alignment with independent human preferences from the EloEverything platform, with an average Kendall’s τ correlation of 0.29, and stronger agreement for highly-rated human items.
All reward distributions exhibited a positive skew, and a 'mere-exposure effect' was observed where models assigned higher scores to more frequent words, even after controlling for sentiment.

Identity group references and sexual content were consistently devalued by RMs compared to human rankings, with terms like 'Jews' appearing among pessimal multi-token sequences, indicating concerning biases.
Takeaways: Reward models exhibit substantial heterogeneity and idiosyncratic biases, challenging the assumption of their interchangeability and demonstrating how base models and alignment performance shape token valuations.

Systematic asymmetries and framing effects exist, with RMs showing greater sensitivity to positive-sentiment tokens in positively framed prompts, potentially undermining the objective of effectively steering away from harmful responses.

A 'linguistic erasure effect' was identified, where RMs systematically undervalue identity group references (e.g., "homosexuals," "Black people") and sexual content, likely an unintended consequence of harmlessness training.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07254.Title: A Stable Whitening Optimizer for Efficient Neural Network Training
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07254.Summary: From UC Berkeley, SPlus introduces a stable whitening optimizer that improves the efficiency of training large Transformer models by addressing common issues in second-order methods. It enables faster loss decrease, matching Adam's validation performance in 44-58% fewer gradient steps and 62-83% less wall-clock time.
Problem: Existing whitening-based optimizers like Shampoo are prone to divergence, particularly when computationally expensive matrix inversions are cached.
Optimal learning rates for these optimizers often lack transferability across different neural network widths, complicating hyperparameter tuning.
Whitening-based optimizers can suffer from significant parameter noise and oscillations at high learning rates, which can degrade final validation performance.
Method: Instant-sign normalization is introduced to bound update magnitudes, preventing divergence and allowing eigendecomposition results to be cached for over 100 steps.
A symmetric shape-aware scaling factor (2 / (m + n)) is applied per-layer to standardize update magnitudes, making learning rates robust and transferable across network widths.
Iterate averaging (Exponential Moving Average) is incorporated to reduce parameter noise at high learning rates, allowing fast learning without compromising final validation performance.
Results: SPlus consistently achieved faster loss decrease across language modeling, image classification, and diffusion modeling tasks, reaching Adam's performance in 44-58% fewer gradient steps and 62-83% less wall-clock time.
Instant-sign normalization eliminated divergence, allowing SPlus to remain stable with eigendecomposition cached for over 100 gradient steps, significantly improving wall-clock efficiency.

The symmetric shape-aware scaling enabled learning rate transfer across different network widths, and iterate averaging consistently improved final validation loss by mitigating parameter noise at higher learning rates.
Takeaways: Divergence in whitening optimizers can be effectively addressed by bounding update magnitudes through an instant-sign normalization on rotated gradients.
Achieving learning rate transferability across network widths is possible with a symmetric shape-aware scaling, which simplifies hyperparameter tuning for adaptive optimizers.

Iterate averaging provides an effective annealing mechanism, enabling aggressive learning rates for rapid training while preserving or enhancing final model performance by smoothing parameter updates.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07235.Title: Multi-Step Visual Reasoning with Visual Tokens Scaling and Verification
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07235.Summary: Researchers develop VTS-V (Visual Token Scaling with Verification), a framework that enables multimodal language models to perform iterative visual reasoning through dynamic interaction with visual tools, achieving 6.90-point improvements on BLINK benchmark for GPT-4o and consistent gains across open-source models (4.18-7.58 points) through a Markov Decision Process formulation where a reasoner proposes visual actions from ten tool types (depth, cropping, OCR, segmentation) while a verifier trained on 301K preference pairs via direct preference optimization determines reasoning termination, supported by a novel VTS-SFT dataset of 315K tool-grounded reasoning trajectories that enables open-source models to transition from static "look once" visual encoding to adaptive "look deeper and verify" inference patterns with theoretical guarantees for bounded reasoning steps.
Problem: Current multimodal large language models use static visual inference, processing entire images into fixed visual tokens upfront, limiting their ability to iteratively refine understanding or adapt to visual ambiguities during reasoning
Existing visual reasoning approaches focus primarily on scaling text tokens or using predefined visual tools in fixed pipelines, neglecting dynamic scaling of visual tokens based on reasoning context
Available datasets lack multi-step, tool-grounded reasoning trajectories with preference labels needed to train models for dynamic visual interaction and verification
Method: Formulate visual reasoning as a Markov Decision Process with a reasoner that proposes visual actions and a verifier that evaluates reasoning quality and determines termination
Introduce ten diverse visual tools (grounding, depth, zoom, visual search, crop, OCR, segmentation, captioning, similarity, overlay) that enable fine-grained visual interaction
Create VTS-SFT dataset with 315K verified tool-grounded reasoning trajectories and VTS-DPO dataset with 301K preference pairs for training reasoner and verifier components respectively
Train verifier using multi-step Direct Preference Optimization to learn when reasoning should terminate based on diminishing reward differences between consecutive states
Results: GPT-4o with VTS-V achieves 69.15% average accuracy on BLINK benchmark, outperforming base GPT-4o (62.25%), Chain-of-Thought (64.96%), Set-of-Mark (60.13%), and Visual Sketchpad (66.78%) approaches
Fine-tuned open-source models show consistent improvements: Qwen2.5VL-7B increases from 49.07% to 56.65%, Qwen2VL-7B from 48.01% to 52.19%, and LLaMA3.2-11B from 47.98% to 50.32% on BLINK
Ablation studies confirm verifier's critical role, with removal causing accuracy drops across all models (e.g., Qwen2.5VL drops from 54.44% to 47.09% without verifier)

Generalization validated across diverse benchmarks including V*Bench, MMStar, and MathVista, with enhanced interpretability through explicit step-by-step visual evidence backing each reasoning decision
Takeaways: Open-source models require supervised fine-tuning on tool-grounded trajectories before they can effectively utilize verifier signals and external visual tools, unlike closed-source models that demonstrate inherent tool-use capabilities
Dynamic visual token scaling enables models to focus computational resources on relevant image regions rather than uniformly processing all pixels, leading to more efficient and accurate reasoning

Verifier-guided termination prevents infinite reasoning loops while ensuring sufficient exploration, with theoretical guarantees that total reasoning steps form a finite stopping time under mild conditions
Complex compositional tasks benefit most from iterative visual reasoning, with largest improvements observed in counting, functionally-correlated, and visually-correlated reasoning categories

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07227.Title: Hallucination at a Glance: Controlled Visual Edits and Fine-Grained Multimodal Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07227.Summary: A framework integrates controlled visual editing with fine-grained multimodal learning to reduce hallucinations in MLLMs. It generates the Micro Edit Dataset (MED) of 50K image-text pairs and a benchmark, using supervised fine-tuning with a feature-level consistency loss, enabling fine-tuned open-source models to match or exceed commercial MLLMs like GPT-4o on fine-grained visual tasks.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) frequently hallucinate, generating factually incorrect responses, especially when confronted with subtle visual details or fine-grained differences.
A scarcity of suitable training data exists that contains tightly controlled, minimal semantic differences with precisely aligned textual descriptions.
Existing MLLM learning objectives do not explicitly enforce feature-level stability across small visual perturbations, leading to brittle visual embeddings.
Method: Developed the Micro Edit Dataset (MED) through a pipeline involving MLLM-guided data filtering, controlled visual editing with Gemini Flash 2.0, and caption alignment, producing over 50K high-quality minimally edited image-text pairs.

Constructed the Micro Edit Detection (MED) benchmark, comprising 165 machine-generated questions and 35 real-world examples, specifically designed to assess fine-grained visual reasoning and difference detection.

Introduced a supervised fine-tuning (SFT) strategy incorporating a feature-level consistency regularization term, explicitly training MLLMs to align visual feature differences with natural language descriptions of changes.
Results: Fine-tuned open-source MLLMs demonstrated significant performance improvements on the MED benchmark; for example, Qwen2.5-VL-7B improved from 40.24% to 51.61% accuracy (+11.37 percentage points).
The fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL-7B achieved 51.61% accuracy on the MED benchmark, comparable to or slightly surpassing leading commercial models like GPT-4o (51.32%) and Doubao-1.5-Vision-Pro (51.81%).

Generalizable performance gains were observed across various multimodal benchmarks (MMStar, BLINK, POPE, MME), with the fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL-7B achieving the highest average score (58.52) among open-source models, indicating enhanced numeracy, spatial grounding, and hallucination resistance.
Takeaways: MLLM hallucinations regarding subtle visual changes stem from inadequate fine-grained training data and learning objectives that fail to encourage stable feature representations under minor perturbations.
Controlled generation of minimally different image-text pairs with precise semantic descriptions can effectively teach MLLMs to detect and reason about fine-grained visual distinctions.
A feature-level consistency loss during fine-tuning promotes more robust visual embeddings and improves the MLLM's ability to ground language in subtle visual cues, directly mitigating hallucination.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07218.Title: Perception-R1: Advancing Multimodal Reasoning Capabilities of MLLMs via Visual Perception Reward
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07218.Summary: Perception-R1 enhances the multimodal reasoning abilities of Multimodal Large Language Models by explicitly integrating a novel visual perception reward into the Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards framework. This approach yields new state-of-the-art performance on various multimodal benchmarks while achieving remarkable data efficiency, using only 1,442 training samples.
Problem: Existing Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) methods for MLLMs primarily focus on logical reasoning and neglect the foundational aspect of multimodal perception.
MLLMs trained with accuracy-only RLVR can "guess" correct answers without genuinely understanding the visual context, leading to brittle reasoning.
Reward sparsity in accuracy-only RLVR training makes it difficult for MLLMs to learn and correct underlying visual perception flaws.
Method: Perception-R1 introduces a visual perception reward to explicitly guide MLLMs towards improved multimodal perception during RLVR training.
High-quality "visual annotations" are curated from powerful proprietary MLLM Chain-of-Thought trajectories, serving as ground-truth references for critical visual elements.

A "judging LLM" assesses the consistency between the MLLM's generated response and these visual annotations, contributing to an enhanced reward function that includes format, accuracy, visual perception, and repetition penalty components.
Results: Achieves new state-of-the-art performance across numerous multimodal reasoning benchmarks, including MathVista, MathVerse, MMMU, and MMStar.

Demonstrates statistically significant improvements in multimodal perception capabilities, particularly on vision-only subsets of MathVerse and MMMU-Pro, validating the effectiveness of the visual perception reward.
Obtains SOTA results using an exceptionally small dataset of only 1,442 training samples, showcasing remarkable data efficiency compared to previous methods.
Takeaways: Multimodal perception is a critical bottleneck for robust MLLM reasoning, often overlooked by existing accuracy-only RLVR methods.
Explicitly rewarding accurate visual perception, grounded in verifiable annotations, significantly improves MLLM reasoning capabilities and robustness.
Intelligent reward design, by incorporating richer, perception-focused signals, can dramatically enhance data efficiency in MLLM development.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07138.Title: Learning Compact Vision Tokens for Efficient Large Multimodal Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07138.Summary: Researchers from Central South University developed a two-stage token fusion strategy, Spatial Token Fusion (STF) and Multi-Block Token Fusion (MBTF), to enhance the efficiency of large multimodal models. This method significantly reduces vision token sequence length by 75% and improves average performance by 0.8% over the LLaVA-1.5-7B baseline across eight vision-language benchmarks.
Problem: Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) suffer from high computational costs, particularly due to the quadratic complexity of self-attention mechanisms when processing long sequences of vision tokens.
Vision encoders processing high-resolution images generate hundreds to thousands of redundant vision tokens, limiting LMM deployment and scalability.
Existing vision token reduction methods often introduce complex mechanisms, risk compromising fine-grained visual details, or rely on text tokens in the pruning process.
Method: A Multi-Block Token Fusion (MBTF) module extracts and fuses multi-granularity features from various intermediate blocks of the vision encoder to enrich visual context.
A Spatial Token Fusion (STF) module applies a convolutional operation with a stride to effectively merge spatially adjacent vision tokens, reducing their count by 75%.
The method integrates MBTF and STF as a learnable visual projector between the frozen vision encoder and the Large Language Model (LLM), requiring no retraining of the vision encoder.
Results: The proposed method achieved an average performance of 66.3% across 8 vision-language benchmarks, outperforming the original LLaVA-1.5-7B by 0.8% while using 75% fewer vision tokens.
Ablation studies showed MBTF alone improved LLaVA-1.5 performance by 1.1%, demonstrating the benefit of multi-granularity features, and STF alone maintained baseline performance with reduced tokens.
Qualitative case studies illustrated improved detail recognition, counting accuracy, and detailed image descriptions compared to the LLaVA-1.5 baseline.
Takeaways: LMMs exhibit substantial inherent spatial redundancy in their vision tokens, which can be exploited for significant compression without major performance degradation.
Integrating multi-granularity features from different layers of a vision encoder significantly enriches the visual representation, leading to improved performance in multimodal tasks.
A learnable and adaptive spatial token fusion mechanism outperforms simpler, static strategies like average pooling or concatenation for reducing vision token sequence length.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.06499.Title: SPARQ: Synthetic Problem Generation for Reasoning via Quality-Diversity Algorithms
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.06499.Summary: SPARQ introduces an algorithm for generating high-quality and diverse synthetic math problems by leveraging Quality-Diversity methods and a model-centric "solve-rate" to filter problem quality. The approach improved a Gemma-2-9b model's math reasoning accuracy by 9% and enabled successful recursive self-improvement where the model generated its own training data.
Problem: A scarcity of high-quality and diverse training data for large language models (LLMs) performing complex reasoning tasks, particularly in domains like mathematics.

Existing synthetic data generation methods often rely on large "teacher" models, generate only solutions for fixed problems, or lack robust mechanisms to filter out illogical or invalid generated problems.
The absence of a reliable ground truth signal makes it challenging to assess the quality and correctness of newly generated problem statements for LLM training.
Method: Introduces SPARQ, an iterative pipeline that generates and filters synthetic math problem-solution pairs using a single student model for quality assessment.

Defines a novel "solve-rate" metric, representing the student model's average success at solving a problem, which serves as an internal proxy for problem difficulty and quality to filter out trivial, impossible, or potentially invalid problems.

Integrates Quality-Diversity (QD) algorithms to explicitly promote the generation of problems diverse in their required skill-sets, alongside quality optimization, within the iterative generation process.
Results: SPARQ improved the Gemma-2-9b model's pass@1 accuracy on the MATH test set by 9% (from 38% to 47%) when using the static uniform generation method.
Training on the synthetic data also enhanced out-of-distribution generalization, boosting AIME pass@n accuracy from 20% to 25% (with K=96 inference samples).
Successfully demonstrated recursive self-improvement, with a Gemma-2-9b model showing a 20% relative performance increase over its baseline when generating and learning from its own problems.
Takeaways: The "solve-rate" metric, while effective for filtering, is a noisy proxy for true logical validity, especially for harder problems, yet LLM fine-tuning proved robust to this moderate level of noise in training data.
Post-generation filtering strategies, specifically those that jointly optimize for quality and diversity, can achieve strong performance comparable to larger datasets with fewer samples.
Data quality primarily correlates with improvements in in-distribution performance, while data diversity is crucial for enhancing out-of-distribution generalization.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.06279.Title: CoMemo: LVLMs Need Image Context with Image Memory
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.06279.Summary: Chinese Academy of Sciences and Shanghai AI Lab researchers develop CoMemo, a dual-path architecture that addresses the "lost in the middle" phenomenon and positional encoding limitations in Large Vision-Language Models by combining a Context path (autoregressive processing) with an Image Memory path (cross-attention retrieval) alongside RoPE-DHR positional encoding that preserves 2D spatial relationships in high-resolution images, achieving 17.2% relative improvement on caption tasks and 7.0% on long-generation tasks compared to single-paradigm baselines while demonstrating superior performance across seven benchmark categories including multi-image reasoning where CoMemo maintains higher accuracy for information placed in middle sequences compared to conventional LVLM-S models, with the framework employing a three-stage training strategy that prevents optimization bias between pathways through gate freezing and validates consistent improvements at both 2B and 8B parameter scales across diverse fine-tuning datasets.
Problem: LVLMs exhibit "lost in the middle" phenomenon inherited from LLMs, where attention distribution becomes bimodal and neglects information in middle of long input sequences

Conventional 1D positional encoding schemes like RoPE fail to preserve 2D spatial relationships in high-resolution images, leading to sparse encodings and remote decay when processing numerous image patches
Method: Dual-path architecture combining Context path (LVLM-S-like autoregressive processing) with Image Memory path (LVLM-X-like cross-attention) using shared image representations
RoPE-DHR positional encoding that maps high-resolution image tiles to thumbnail coordinates, preserving 2D spatial awareness while preventing sparse encoding
Three-stage training strategy with projector/mixin tuning, gate freezing, and full-parameter finetuning to balance pathway optimization
Results: 17.2% relative improvement on caption tasks and 7.0% on long-generation tasks compared to single-paradigm baselines
Superior performance across multi-image reasoning, long-context comprehension, and Needle-in-a-Haystack tasks with 5.6% improvement on long-context benchmarks
Consistent improvements at both 2B and 8B parameter scales while maintaining comparable training and inference efficiency to LVLM-S models
Takeaways: Both LVLM-X and LVLM-S paradigms have complementary strengths that can be effectively combined through dual-stream processing
Positional encoding compression and 2D spatial preservation are crucial for handling dynamic high-resolution images in vision-language models
Training stage management prevents over-reliance on single pathways and ensures balanced multimodal representation learning

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.06122.Title: Reinforcement Learning Optimization for Large-Scale Learning: An Efficient and User-Friendly Scaling Library
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.06122.Summary: Alibaba Group's ROLL is a comprehensive framework designed for large-scale Reinforcement Learning (RL) training of Large Language Models (LLMs), capable of supporting models over 200 billion parameters. It demonstrated robust scalability by training an MoE model on thousands of GPUs for two weeks uninterrupted and achieved significant performance improvements on RLVR and agentic RL tasks.
Problem: Applying Reinforcement Learning (RL) to Large Language Models (LLMs) introduces significant system-level challenges due to complex multi-model, multi-stage pipelines (generation, inference, training).

Existing RL-LLM frameworks often present trade-offs in efficiency, scalability, and usability, especially when dealing with the increasing size of LLMs and the complexity of RL tasks like multi-turn agentic interactions.

Users across different scales (from thousands of GPUs to single GPUs) lack a unified, fault-tolerant, and easy-to-use solution for large-scale RL training, leading to high engineering overhead and limited experimentation.
Method: ROLL employs a modular, single-controller architecture that abstracts complex distributed RL workflows into manageable components, leveraging a `Parallel Worker` abstraction for resource orchestration.

It integrates leading LLM optimization systems (MegatronCore, DeepSpeed for training; vLLM, SGLang for inference) to support advanced 5D parallelism and efficient serving, along with a `Transfer Protocol` for fast data re-sharding.

The framework incorporates an `AutoDeviceMapping` module and `Rollout Scheduler` to efficiently manage CPU/GPU resources, enable dynamic sampling, and support dedicated `Environment` and `Reward Workers` for scalable agentic interactions and diverse reward computations.
Results: ROLL successfully facilitated the in-house training of a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with over 200 billion total parameters, scaling to thousands of GPUs and running for approximately two weeks without interruption.

On multi-domain RL with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) tasks, Qwen2.5-7B-Base showed an average accuracy improvement from 0.18 to 0.52 (a 2.89x increase), while Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base improved from 0.27 to 0.62.

For agentic RL tasks, LLM-based agents achieved substantial improvements, such as increasing the WebShop success rate from 37% to over 85% and reducing average actions per episode from over 7 to approximately 4.
Takeaways: Large-scale RL training for LLMs requires a comprehensive system that unifies efficient resource management, advanced parallelization, and flexible workflow orchestration across multiple stages and models.

Different user groups (tech pioneers, product developers, algorithm researchers) have distinct needs for RL-LLM frameworks, necessitating a solution that balances scalability, usability, and flexibility.

Asynchronous processing of samples and dynamic resource allocation are crucial for maximizing throughput and reducing GPU idle time in complex, multi-stage RL pipelines involving heterogeneous computational demands.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.06105.Title: Text-to-LoRA: Instant Transformer Adaption
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.06105.Summary: Sakana AI researchers developed Text-to-LoRA (T2L), a hypernetwork that dynamically generates task-specific Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) weights for large language models from natural language descriptions. The method enables efficient, zero-shot adaptation, outperforming established baselines and achieving performance comparable to fine-tuned adapters on unseen tasks.
Problem: Adapting large language models (LLMs) to new, specific tasks requires resource-intensive processes like full fine-tuning or parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), demanding careful dataset curation and lengthy training.
Existing PEFT methods, such as LoRA, still necessitate 'one-LoRA-per-task', leading to significant engineering overhead and limiting agile knowledge transfer.
Prior hypernetwork-based LLM adaptation approaches often rely on learned task identifiers or few-shot examples, which inherently limit zero-shot generalization to entirely unseen tasks.
Method: Introducing Text-to-LoRA (T2L), a hypernetwork-based model that generates task-specific LoRA adapter weights for a base LLM solely based on a natural language description of the target task.

T2L leverages a shared backbone architecture with specific output heads (L, M, S variants) that take concatenated embeddings of task description, module type, and layer index as input to generate LoRA matrices.

The model is trained using two schemes: LoRA Reconstruction (minimizing L1 distance to pre-trained LoRAs) and Supervised Fine-Tuning (directly optimizing the base LLM's loss when adapted by generated LoRAs).
Results: T2L trained via SFT consistently generates useful LoRAs that outperform strong baselines like multi-task LoRA and state-of-the-art zero-shot routing methods on 10 unseen benchmark tasks.

When trained via reconstruction, T2L fully recovers or even exceeds the performance of oracle task-specific LoRA adapters on multiple benchmarks, demonstrating effective compression and potential regularization benefits.
T2L reduces adaptation cost by over 4x compared to 3-shot in-context learning, highlighting its efficiency for instant, on-the-fly LLM specialization.
Takeaways: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) of the hypernetwork, directly optimizing for downstream task performance, is crucial for strong zero-shot generalization, outperforming LoRA reconstruction training.
Text-to-LoRA (T2L) effectively learns to compress knowledge from hundreds of task-specific LoRAs, exhibiting a regularization effect that can sometimes outperform individual oracles.

The model learns semantically meaningful representations of tasks, clustering task encoder activations and generated LoRA outputs based on task type, allowing it to synthesize novel adapters for unseen tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.05316.Title: Improving Data Efficiency for LLM Reinforcement Fine-tuning Through Difficulty-targeted Online Data Selection and Rollout Replay
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.05316.Summary: This research introduces a method to enhance the data efficiency of Large Language Model (LLM) reinforcement learning fine-tuning by combining difficulty-targeted online data selection and rollout replay. The approach reduces total training time by an average of 40.7% while achieving comparable or superior performance on mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks.
Problem: Reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning for Large Language Models (LLMs) is computationally very expensive, demanding significant GPU resources and time.
Existing on-policy RL methods for LLMs are data inefficient, often discarding valuable generated rollouts after a single training step.
The high cost hinders research iteration speed and limits broader accessibility to developing advanced LLM capabilities.
Method: A Difficulty-targeted Online Data Selection (DOTS) framework that adaptively predicts the optimal difficulty (failure rate near 0.5) for questions using a lightweight attention-based model and a small reference set.
A Rollout Replay (RR) mechanism that reuses previously generated rollouts from a FIFO buffer for on-policy GRPO training, using importance sampling to maintain stability.
The combined DOTS and RR approach is integrated within the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) framework, commonly used for LLM reasoning tasks.
Results: The combined DOTS+RR method reduced total RL fine-tuning time by an average of 40.7% (ranging from 23% to 62%) across various LLMs and datasets, achieving comparable or better performance.
DOTS alone enabled convergence with 13.33% to 56.67% fewer training steps by increasing the ratio of informative "effective questions" in each batch by an average of 25.4%.
Rollout Replay reduced per-step training time by 11-13% by reusing past rollouts, without compromising the stability or final performance of the fine-tuning process.
Takeaways: Training samples with an adaptive difficulty (failure rate) around 0.5 yield the most effective learning signal, maximizing the expected squared norm of the policy gradient.
Adaptive difficulty can be accurately and efficiently predicted using an attention-based framework, avoiding costly full rollouts for all questions.
Rollout replay, when combined with importance sampling, can stably and effectively reduce the per-step computational cost in on-policy LLM RL fine-tuning without performance degradation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.05302.Title: Perceive Anything: Recognize, Explain, Caption, and Segment Anything in Images and Videos
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.05302.Summary: The Perceive Anything Model (PAM) extends the Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM 2) framework to achieve comprehensive region-level visual understanding, performing recognition, explanation, captioning, and segmentation in both images and videos. PAM operates 1.2-2.4 times faster and consumes less GPU memory than prior models, while achieving state-of-the-art performance across various image and video benchmarks, including novel streaming video region captioning tasks.
Problem: Modern segmentation models like SAM 2 excel at localizing objects but lack deep semantic understanding and cannot explain 'what' an object is or 'how' it functions.

Existing region-level Vision-Language Models (VLMs) often provide limited semantic output granularity (basic categories, short captions) and lack a unified, efficient framework for both images and videos.
There is a scarcity of high-quality, fine-grained datasets, particularly for region-level understanding in streaming video, hindering the development of continuous, detailed visual analysis.
Method: The Perceive Anything Model (PAM) extends the pre-existing SAM 2 framework with a lightweight Semantic Perceiver and a Qwen2.5 Large Language Model (LLM) as a semantic decoder, keeping SAM 2's parameters frozen.
PAM features a parallel design for its mask and semantic decoders, allowing for simultaneous generation of region masks and diverse semantic content, improving computational efficiency.

A three-stage curriculum learning approach (image pretraining, video-enhanced pretraining, multimodal fine-tuning) progressively trains the model, coupled with a novel data refinement pipeline that creates a high-quality, multi-granularity, and bilingual dataset, including pioneering region-level streaming video captions.
Results: PAM runs 1.2 to 2.4 times faster and consumes less GPU memory than prior models, demonstrating superior efficiency for both image and video processing.
PAM-3B achieves optimal performance on the PACO benchmark and outperforms DAM-8B on LVIS for regional recognition and explanation, while also showing strong scene text recognition capabilities.

PAM-3B sets new state-of-the-art performance on Elysium, BensMOT, and HC-STVG for video region captioning, and achieves optimal performance on the novel GPT-4o-evaluated Spatio-Temporal Description Continuity Score for streaming video region captioning.
Takeaways: Efficiently extending the frozen SAM 2 framework with a Semantic Perceiver allows direct bridging of its rich visual features to an LLM for comprehensive semantic understanding.
A parallel decoding design for mask and semantic generation significantly enhances computational efficiency, enabling simultaneous segmentation and detailed content output.

The development of a high-quality, multi-granularity dataset, including pioneering region-level streaming video captions, is critical for training a model capable of diverse and complex visual understanding tasks.
A staged curriculum learning approach, progressing from image to video understanding, optimizes the training process for robust spatio-temporal comprehension.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.04713.Title: Enabling Validation for Robust Few-Shot Recognition
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.04713.Summary: VEST (Validation-Enabled Stage-wise Tuning) introduces a novel validation strategy for adapting Vision-Language Models in few-shot recognition, addressing the absence of dedicated validation sets. The framework, which integrates retrieval-based augmentation and adversarial perturbation, achieved state-of-the-art performance on ImageNet Out-Of-Distribution (OOD) benchmarks, improving ID accuracy by up to 2.16% and OOD average accuracy by 1.02% in 16-shot settings.
Problem: Few-Shot Recognition (FSR) lacks dedicated validation data for hyperparameter tuning and checkpoint selection in realistic settings.

Directly using noisy, retrieved Out-Of-Distribution (OOD) data for validation is counterproductive, as models finetuned on In-Distribution (ID) data often degrade on OOD, favoring the unfinetuned base model.
Existing VLM adaptation methods for FSR often struggle with robust generalization to OOD data, which is critical for real-world applications.
Method: Proposed the `gF1` score, a novel validation metric that harmonizes performance gains on ID training data and OOD retrieved data to guide robust checkpoint and hyperparameter selection.

Developed VEST (Validation-Enabled Stage-wise Tuning), a three-stage framework that integrates `gF1`-enabled layer selection, partial finetuning with retrieval-based augmentation, and partial finetuning with adversarial perturbation.
Applied adversarial perturbation on features (via PGD) rather than raw images to enhance model robustness and OOD generalization.
Results: VEST achieved state-of-the-art performance on ImageNet OOD benchmarks, with improvements up to 2.16% on ID accuracy and 1.02% on OOD average accuracy over strong baselines in the 16-shot setting.
The `gF1` validation strategy successfully identified optimal finetuning depths (e.g., top-4 layers for CLIP ViT-B/16) and hyperparameters, leading to better robustness and generalization.
The stage-wise training within VEST demonstrated superior ID and OOD accuracies and reduced computational costs compared to a one-stage joint training approach.
Takeaways: The `gF1` score effectively resolves the validation data paradox in FSR, enabling robust selection of models that generalize well to both ID and OOD data without a dedicated validation set.

A stage-wise finetuning approach, sequentially combining retrieval-based augmentation and adversarial perturbation, is more effective and computationally efficient than joint training for improving both ID and OOD generalization.
Adversarially perturbed features can act as an effective 'bridge' between ID training features and OOD test features, intuitively explaining improved OOD generalization.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.04411.Title: Self-Supervised Contrastive Learning is Approximately Supervised Contrastive Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.04411.Summary: This research from Texas A&M University establishes a theoretical duality between self-supervised Decoupled Contrastive Learning (DCL) and a supervised counterpart, demonstrating that DCL implicitly approximates a supervised objective whose global minimizers exhibit neural collapse properties. The work explains how self-supervised models learn class-aware representations effective for few-shot learning, showing that semantic structure emerges without explicit labels.
