Problem: A formal understanding of why self-supervised contrastive learning (CL) effectively learns semantic, class-aware representations without explicit label supervision was missing.

The theoretical connection between the empirical success of CL in producing high-quality features and well-understood phenomena in supervised learning, such as neural collapse, was not fully established.
Identifying and quantifying the specific properties of learned representations that enable effective few-shot transfer learning in self-supervised settings needed further theoretical grounding.
Method: A theoretical duality was established by proving that the self-supervised Decoupled Contrastive Loss (DCL) approximates a Negatives-Only Supervised Contrastive Loss (NSCL), with the approximation gap diminishing as the number of semantic classes increases.

The global minimizers of the NSCL were analyzed under an unconstrained features model, demonstrating that they achieve augmentation collapse, within-class collapse, and a Simplex Equiangular Tight Frame (ETF) structure.

A novel metric called 'directional CDNV' was introduced to measure feature variability along class-discriminative directions, and a refined bound on m-shot classification error was derived, emphasizing the importance of this directional variability.
Results: Empirical evaluations confirmed that the gap between DCL and NSCL losses decreases at an O(1/C) rate as the number of classes (C) increases, validating the theoretical bound.

DCL-trained models achieved low few-shot classification errors on diverse datasets (e.g., CIFAR10, ImageNet-1K), which were accurately predicted by the newly derived error bound based on directional CDNV.

Experiments showed DCL-trained representations exhibit properties consistent with neural collapse, including high cosine similarity for positive pairs (0.90) and low similarity for negative pairs, along with clear semantic clustering in UMAP visualizations.
Takeaways: Self-supervised contrastive learning, specifically DCL, implicitly minimizes a supervised loss (NSCL) that explicitly excludes same-class negatives, thus explaining its capability to learn class-aware features without direct label supervision.

The global minimizers of the approximated supervised loss (NSCL) inherently exhibit neural collapse phenomena, including augmentation collapse, within-class feature collapse, and class-center features forming an optimal Simplex ETF structure.

Effective few-shot transfer learning performance in self-supervised models is primarily driven by low feature variability along the directions separating class centers (directional CDNV), rather than uniform isotropic clustering.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.04374.Title: A Statistical Physics of Language Model Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.04374.Summary: Researchers at MIT developed a statistical physics framework to model large language model (LLM) reasoning as a low-dimensional stochastic dynamical system. Their Switching Linear Dynamical System (SLDS) can effectively capture and predict complex reasoning pathways, including critical transitions into misaligned states, with a one-step-ahead prediction R^2 of 0.68.
Problem: Understanding the emergent reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) remains challenging due to their opaque, high-dimensional internal dynamics, making mechanistic interpretability difficult.
Current interpretability methods struggle to explain long-range, multi-step semantic transitions that characterize complex LLM reasoning chains.
Predicting and understanding how LLMs transition into 'misaligned states' or generate factual errors is a critical open problem in AI safety.
Method: Researchers propose modeling sentence-level LLM hidden states as a continuous-time stochastic process governed by a low-dimensional Itô stochastic differential equation (SDE).
They employ Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to project high-dimensional hidden states onto a tractable low-rank manifold (rank 40) while preserving significant variance.
A Switching Linear Dynamical System (SLDS) is formulated, using a K-component Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) to identify and model transitions between four distinct latent reasoning regimes.
Results: The Switching Linear Dynamical System (SLDS) model achieved a one-step-ahead predictive R^2 of approximately 0.68 on held-out trajectories, outperforming simpler global linear models (R^2 ","0.51).
Ablation studies confirmed the necessity of regime switching, low-rank projection, and state-dependent drift for the SLDS model's performance.

The SLDS framework successfully modeled and predicted LLM belief shifts induced by adversarial prompts, achieving approximately 0.72 R^2 for Llama-2-70B and 0.69 R^2 for Gemma-7B-IT, and predicting ultimate misinformation acceptance with high accuracy (around 0.88 for Llama-2-70B).
Takeaways: LLM reasoning trajectories, when analyzed at the sentence level, exhibit multimodal structures in their hidden state dynamics, suggesting the existence of distinct, metastable reasoning regimes akin to multi-well potentials in statistical physics.

A relatively low-dimensional manifold (rank 40 PCA projection) can capture approximately 50% of the variance in high-dimensional LLM hidden state transitions, enabling tractable modeling of complex reasoning dynamics.

The evolution of LLM reasoning states can be effectively modeled as a continuous-time stochastic process, where internal shifts between distinct reasoning regimes are crucial for explaining observed behaviors.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.04277.Title: RSVP: Reasoning Segmentation via Visual Prompting and Multi-modal Chain-of-Thought
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.04277.Summary: RSVP introduces a two-stage framework that integrates multi-modal large language model reasoning with precise visual segmentation. It achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot performance on reasoning segmentation benchmarks by leveraging structured visual prompting and a multi-modal chain-of-thought to bridge the gap between high-level reasoning and pixel-level grounding.
Problem: Bridging the gap between the high-level cognitive reasoning abilities of Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) and the need for precise, low-level visual grounding in segmentation tasks.
Existing reasoning segmentation methods often require extensive and costly fine-tuning of large models, limiting their scalability, adaptability, and computational efficiency.
Lack of interpretability in many end-to-end reasoning segmentation models makes it difficult to understand how decisions are reached for complex queries.
Method: RSVP employs a two-stage structuralized framework: a Reasoning Stage using Multi-modal Chain-of-Thought Visual Prompting with an MLLM for coarse localization.
The Reasoning Stage guides the MLLM to infer object properties, identify relevant image regions via structured visual prompts (grid IDs), and output a bounding box and reasoning rationale.

A Vision-Language Segmentation Module (VLSM) then refines the MLLM-generated coarse region proposal into a precise segmentation mask by integrating BEiT-3 for multi-modal feature encoding with SAM for mask prediction.
Results: RSVP-GPT achieved 60.3 gIoU and 60.0 cIoU on the ReasonSeg-Test dataset in a zero-shot setting, outperforming other zero-shot baselines by up to +9.2 cIoU and showing competitive performance against fine-tuned LISA models.

Ablation studies confirmed that stronger MLLMs, multimodal information distillation, and a carefully designed multi-modal Chain-of-Thought prompt significantly improve reasoning segmentation performance.
The framework demonstrated strong generalization to open-world segmentation tasks, achieving a mean Average Precision (mAP) of 49.7 across 25 diverse categories on the SegInW zero-shot benchmark.
Takeaways: Multi-modal Chain-of-Thought Visual Prompting effectively guides MLLMs to perform complex reasoning and coarse localization by generating interpretable region proposals and rationales.
A modular, two-stage framework enables zero-shot reasoning segmentation, leveraging pre-trained MLLMs and a segmentation module without requiring additional fine-tuning on specific datasets.
The strength of the initial MLLM, the detailed design of CoT prompts, and appropriate visual prompting density are crucial for achieving high reasoning segmentation performance.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.04220.Title: Struct2D: A Perception-Guided Framework for Spatial Reasoning in MLLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.04220.Summary: Struct2D introduces a perception-guided framework enabling Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to perform 3D spatial reasoning using structured 2D representations, bypassing direct 3D input. The framework, along with its automatically generated instruction tuning dataset Struct2D-Set, achieves an average score of 43.6% on VSI-Bench for open-source MLLMs and competitive performance on other 3D scene understanding benchmarks.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) traditionally struggle with robust 3D spatial reasoning and typically require explicit 3D representations like point clouds as direct inputs.
Existing 3D-input methods for MLLMs face limitations in adaptability, generalization across diverse textual queries, and architectural complexity.
Prior 2D-based approaches for inferring 3D spatial cues often omit crucial object appearance details and explicit spatial priors (e.g., coordinates, categories), limiting their effectiveness.
Method: Struct2D proposes a perception-guided prompting strategy that transforms raw egocentric RGB-D video inputs into structured 2D representations, including Bird's-Eye-View (BEV) images with object marks, object-centric metadata (category, 3D coordinates), and intelligently selected egocentric keyframes.

A large-scale instruction tuning dataset, Struct2D-Set, is automatically generated from over 6K indoor scenes, designed for open-source MLLMs to acquire robust 3D spatial reasoning skills using only 2D projected inputs during training.
The framework is applied in a zero-shot setting to closed-source MLLMs (e.g., GPT-o3) and also used to fine-tune an open-source MLLM (Qwen2.5VL) on the Struct2D-Set.
Results: In zero-shot analysis, GPT-o3 achieved high scores with Struct2D inputs on VSI-Bench (e.g., 96.5% on relative distance and 94.4% on relative direction with ground-truth object annotations).

The Qwen2.5VL model fine-tuned on Struct2D-Set attained the highest average score (43.6%) among open-source MLLMs on VSI-Bench, with notable gains in relative direction (45.9%) and route planning (35.8%).

The instruction-tuned model demonstrated competitive performance on standard 3D question answering and visual grounding benchmarks (ScanQA, SQA3D, Scan2Cap, ScanRefer, Multi3DRefer), often outperforming methods reliant on explicit 3D point cloud inputs.
Takeaways: MLLMs can achieve strong 3D spatial reasoning capabilities by leveraging carefully constructed structured 2D inputs, even without direct 3D features as input.

Object-centric metadata and filtered object marks are crucial for effectively grounding spatial context and reducing ambiguity, while guide prompts and rotation-aligned BEV images are essential for complex reasoning tasks like relative direction.
Large-scale instruction tuning with step-by-step reasoning traces (using augmented QA pairs and `` tokens) substantially enhances an MLLM's ability to perform complex spatial reasoning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.04209.Title: Language-Image Alignment with Fixed Text Encoders
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.04209.Summary: Researchers at UC Berkeley developed LIFT, a framework for language-image alignment that leverages a fixed, pre-trained Large Language Model as the text encoder, rather than training it jointly with the image encoder. This approach improves compositional understanding and robustness to long captions while significantly reducing computational costs compared to traditional joint training paradigms like CLIP.
Problem: Existing language-image alignment models, such as CLIP, require computationally expensive joint training of large text and image encoders on massive datasets.

These models often struggle with compositional understanding, such as accurately encoding object-attribute associations or spatial relationships, due to the nature of general-purpose retrieval datasets.
CLIP's zero-shot performance can degrade when trained on full-length, synthetically generated long captions, a phenomenon referred to as the 'inverse effect'.
Method: Introduces LIFT, a dual-encoder framework that leverages a pre-trained and *frozen* Large Language Model (LLM) as the text encoder, rather than training it jointly with the image encoder.
Performs offline pre-computation and storage of all text embeddings using the fixed LLM-based text encoder, eliminating the need for real-time forward and backward passes through it during training.
Trains only the image encoder (a Vision Transformer) and a small projection head to align with these fixed text embeddings, using a contrastive InfoNCE loss or a simplified cosine similarity loss.
Results: LIFT achieves a 6.8% average accuracy gain over CLIP on compositional SugarCrepe tasks (7.9% with long captions), demonstrating improved compositional understanding.
It mitigates the 'inverse effect' with long synthetic captions, outperforming CLIP by an average of 11.0% on zero-shot classification and retrieval tasks.
LIFT reduces FLOPs by 25.5% for short captions and 35.7% for long ones, and lowers GPU memory usage by 6.8% for short captions and 12.6% for long ones.
Takeaways: Pre-trained and contrastively fine-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) can effectively serve as fixed text encoders for vision-language alignment, challenging the necessity of joint training.

A simple cosine similarity loss on positive pairs can perform comparably to InfoNCE contrastive loss for compositional understanding tasks, though InfoNCE remains superior for general zero-shot retrieval.
The inherent linguistic understanding of LLMs provides robustness against the 'inverse effect' of long, synthetically generated captions, which often degrade performance in jointly trained models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.04207.Title: Advancing Multimodal Reasoning: From Optimized Cold Start to Staged Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.04207.Summary: Chinese researchers develop ReVisual-R1, a 7B multimodal reasoning model that achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-source MLLMs through a three-stage Staged Reinforcement Optimization (SRO) framework combining text-centric cold start initialization, multimodal reinforcement learning with novel Prioritized Advantage Distillation (PAD) to address gradient stagnation in GRPO, and textual RL refinement to prevent capability decay, achieving 53.1% average across 10 challenging benchmarks (+16.8 points over previous open-source SOTA) and outperforming GPT-4o on several tasks including 89.2% on MATH500 and substantial gains on AIME mathematical reasoning benchmarks, supported by the carefully curated GRAMMAR dataset containing 99K samples designed for complex multimodal reasoning development.
Problem: Existing multimodal large language models struggle with complex reasoning despite successful reinforcement learning applications in text-only models
Standard Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) suffers from gradient stagnation in multimodal settings with sparse rewards
Conventional multimodal pre-training provides inadequate cold start initialization for sophisticated reasoning tasks
Intensive multimodal RL training leads to textual capability decay, degrading abstract reasoning abilities
Method: Develop three-stage Staged Reinforcement Optimization framework starting with high-difficulty text-centric cold start using 40K pure text reasoning samples
Introduce Prioritized Advantage Distillation (PAD) that filters effective samples based on advantage ranges and prioritizes high-value sequences to prevent gradient stagnation
Apply textual RL refinement phase with frozen vision tower to restore and enhance linguistic reasoning while preserving multimodal gains
Create GRAMMAR dataset with 99K diverse samples through multi-stage curation including difficulty classification and topic balancing
Results: Achieves 53.1% average performance across 10 benchmarks, +16.8 points improvement over previous open-source 7B SOTA
Outperforms GPT-4o on multiple tasks including MATH500 (89.2% vs 74.6%) and shows substantial leads on AIME24/AIME25 mathematical reasoning
Secures top position among open-source models on 9 out of 10 individual benchmarks including MathVerse (+5.4%), MathVision (+13.9%), and LogicVista (+9.6%)
Ablation studies confirm effectiveness of three-stage curriculum and PAD's role in improving training stability with higher reward accuracy and faster convergence
Takeaways: Text-centric cold start outperforms traditional multimodal initialization for complex reasoning, establishing foundational reasoning templates before visual grounding
Gradient stagnation in GRPO occurs when uniform rewards across response groups yield near-zero advantages, which PAD addresses through selective sampling
Sequential training (textual → multimodal → textual RL) proves more effective than alternative orderings for balancing visual grounding with abstract reasoning
Efficient-length reward function prevents uncontrolled response verbosity while maintaining reasoning depth and training stability

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.04005.Title: Vocabulary-free few-shot learning for Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.04005.Summary: This research defines and addresses vocabulary-free few-shot learning for Vision-Language Models, where target class names are absent. It introduces Similarity Mapping (SiM), an efficient and interpretable method that classifies new instances by learning a linear mapping from generic prompt similarity scores to target classes, achieving performance competitive with zero-shot CLIP and outperforming existing label mapping techniques.
Problem: Existing few-shot Vision-Language Model (VLM) adaptation methods heavily rely on predefined, explicit class names, limiting their applicability in real-world scenarios.
Class names can be ambiguous, require complex descriptions, or may not exist for novel concepts, making traditional prompt-based adaptation difficult or impossible.
A fundamental gap exists in adapting powerful VLMs to new tasks using only visual examples, without the need for corresponding textual labels.
Method: The authors introduce Similarity Mapping (SiM), which uses a fixed set of generic textual or visual prompts (e.g., ImageNet class names or embeddings) instead of target class-specific names.
SiM learns a linear mapping matrix by minimizing a regularized least-squares objective, translating similarity scores between few-shot examples and generic prompts into target class probabilities.

For new images, their similarity scores with the generic prompts are computed and then transformed by the learned matrix to predict the target class, enabling classification without explicit class vocabulary.
Results: SiM consistently outperformed existing vocabulary-free baselines, such as One-to-One mapping and Bayesian Label Mapping, across 10 evaluated datasets and two CLIP backbones.

With 16 shots per class using the ViT-L/14 backbone, SiM achieved an average accuracy of 83.9%, surpassing zero-shot CLIP on 8 out of 10 datasets and significantly narrowing the performance gap with label-dependent few-shot VLM methods.
The learning process for the mapping matrix is highly efficient, typically completing in under one second, demonstrating the method's practicality for rapid adaptation.
Takeaways: A simple linear mapping from generic VLM similarity scores can effectively classify novel, unnamed visual categories in a few-shot setting, establishing a robust baseline for vocabulary-free learning.
The choice of generic prompt source (e.g., ImageNet text, ImageNet images, Wordnet) impacts performance but the method remains effective and scales with different modalities and sizes of prompt sets.
The learned weights of the mapping matrix provide interpretability, allowing for a semantic understanding of target classes by linking them to the most relevant generic concepts.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.03642.Title: Spatial Understanding from Videos: Structured Prompts Meet Simulation Data
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.03642.Summary: A framework from Harbin Institute of Technology and Pengcheng Laboratory enhances 3D spatial understanding in pre-trained Vision-Language Models by integrating a structured Chain-of-Thought prompting strategy and a large-scale synthetic dataset, yielding consistent performance improvements on spatial reasoning tasks without architectural modifications.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) struggle with spatial uncertainty, inferring coherent 3D scene structure from limited 2D observations (scanning videos) due to occlusions and perspective distortions.
A scarcity of large-scale, diverse, and scalable datasets for 3D spatial reasoning from scanning videos limits VLMs from acquiring robust spatial knowledge.
Existing solutions often involve specialized 3D sensors or complex architectural modifications to VLMs, limiting broad applicability.
Method: **SpatialMind:** A novel structured Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting strategy that guides VLMs through scene decomposition (generating textual descriptions of object relations) and question decomposition.
**ScanForgeQA:** A large-scale, scalable synthetic question-answering dataset created from diverse 3D simulation scenes using an automated pipeline for fine-tuning VLMs.
The framework non-invasively enhances pre-trained VLMs, leveraging both explicit reasoning guidance and comprehensive data-driven knowledge acquisition without modifying core VLM architectures.
Results: Textual descriptions as scene representations consistently outperformed 3D map and 2D grid formats, becoming the default for the SpatialMind strategy.

Both SpatialMind prompting and ScanForgeQA fine-tuning individually improved visual-spatial understanding across diverse VLMs, with combined strategies yielding further improvements (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL-72B improved by 7.9% when both strategies were combined).

The framework demonstrated strong generalizability, leading to performance gains on external spatial benchmarks (OpenEQA, ScanQA, SQA3D) and showing robustness to varying input frames and resolutions.
Takeaways: Current VLMs are more interpretable with textual descriptions of 3D scenes than with raw 3D maps or 2D grids for spatial reasoning tasks.
The structured prompting (SpatialMind) and synthetic data fine-tuning (ScanForgeQA) are complementary, with their combined application yielding superior performance in visual-spatial understanding.
Larger VLMs benefit more from structured prompting, while smaller VLMs show greater improvements from fine-tuning on specialized synthetic data.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.03637.Title: RewardAnything: Generalizable Principle-Following Reward Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.03637.Summary: "RewardAnything" introduces a new paradigm for reward models that can interpret and follow natural language principles, allowing them to generalize to diverse and unseen evaluation criteria without retraining. This generative model, trained with Group Relative Policy Optimization, achieves state-of-the-art performance on the challenging RM-Bench (86.4% accuracy) and strong generalization on the new RABENCH (81.9% accuracy, Kendall's "u03c4" 65.27).
Problem: Traditional Reward Models (RMs) are rigid, struggling to generalize to diverse human preferences and requiring costly retraining for new scenarios.
Existing RMs often learn implicit biases from static preference datasets, leading to issues like favoring response length over factual accuracy, and lack interpretability.
The need for continuous data collection and retraining for each new preference limits the scalability and efficiency of LLM alignment.
Method: Proposed a "principle-following" reward model paradigm, where RMs interpret natural language principles to guide evaluation.
Introduced REWARDANYTHING, a generative reward model that outputs structured evaluations (reasoning, scores, rankings) in a single pass.
Developed Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a comprehensive reward function (format and accuracy components) for training, fostering better generalization.
Created RABENCH, a new benchmark with a robust LLM-consensus judgment pipeline, to evaluate principle-following capabilities on unseen principles.
Results: Achieved state-of-the-art performance on the challenging RM-Bench (86.4% overall accuracy, 84.4% on "hard" setting), demonstrating effective bias mitigation through principles.
Demonstrated strong generalization on the novel RABENCH benchmark with 81.9% overall accuracy (Kendall's "u03c4" 65.27), performing comparably to powerful general-purpose LLMs like GPT-4.1.
Successfully aligned a Qwen3-8B LLM using only a natural language safety principle and GRPO, resulting in improved refusal behavior and maintaining general response quality.
Takeaways: Natural language principles are crucial for guiding reward models, enabling strong generalization to unseen evaluation criteria and mitigating biases inherent in traditional preference datasets.
Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) significantly outperforms Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) for training principle-following RMs, facilitating better generalization.
Generating explicit reasoning alongside evaluations is integral to the model's accuracy and interpretability in applying principles.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.03596.Title: ControlThinker: Unveiling Latent Semantics for Controllable Image Generation through Visual Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.03596.Summary: ControlThinker enhances controllable image generation by leveraging a Multimodal Large Language Model to interpret abstract control images and enrich text prompts. This approach results in higher fidelity and semantic consistency in generated images without requiring modifications to the core image generator.
Problem: Existing controllable image generation models suffer from a semantic gap between sparse text prompts and abstract control images.
Text prompts provide insufficient semantic detail for pixel-wise synthesis, while control images lack color, texture, and contextual cues.
This often leads to generated images that maintain layout but are semantically misaligned, lack visual quality, or contain artifacts.
Method: Introduces a "comprehend-then-generate" paradigm, where a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) acts as a semantic interpreter.
Developed ControlThink-50K, a specialized Chain-of-Thought dataset, to train the MLLM to effectively reason from abstract control images.
Employs a two-phase MLLM training strategy (Supervised Fine-Tuning followed by Reinforcement Fine-Tuning) and an inference-time output reward model for selecting optimal reasoning trajectories.
Results: Achieved superior layout consistency across multiple control types, including a 2.17 mIoU increase for segmentation and a 3.49 RMSE reduction for depth tasks.
Demonstrated state-of-the-art Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) scores across various control conditions, indicating improved image quality and realism without fine-tuning the generator.
Ablation studies confirmed the effectiveness of both the MLLM's two-phase training and the inference-time scaling mechanism in enhancing visual quality and structural adherence.
Takeaways: MLLMs can effectively bridge the semantic gap in controllable image generation by actively enriching sparse prompts with latent semantics from control images.
Specialized training for MLLMs on abstract visual reasoning using a high-quality CoT dataset is crucial for accurately interpreting structurally sparse control signals.
Optimizing input semantics through an MLLM-based interpreter can significantly improve the quality and consistency of generated images without altering the underlying image synthesis model.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.03569.Title: MiMo-VL Technical Report
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.03569.Summary: Xiaomi's LLM-Core division develops MiMo-VL-7B, a compact vision-language model that achieves state-of-the-art performance across 50+ multimodal benchmarks through a four-stage training process consuming 2.4 trillion tokens and novel Mixed On-policy Reinforcement Learning (MORL) framework, with the resulting MiMo-VL-7B-RL model outperforming Qwen2.5-VL-7B on 35 out of 40 tasks and surpassing much larger models (up to 78B parameters) on complex reasoning benchmarks like OlympiadBench (59.4 score) and GUI grounding tasks like OSWorld-G (56.1 score), while achieving 95.4% on MATH500 and maintaining the highest Elo rating among open-source VLMs in user preference evaluations, accomplished through strategic incorporation of high-quality Chain-of-Thought reasoning data directly into late pre-training stages rather than only post-training fine-tuning.
Problem: Existing compact vision-language models lag behind larger proprietary models on complex multimodal reasoning and agentic tasks
Current VLM training approaches primarily incorporate reasoning capabilities through post-training fine-tuning rather than pre-training
Limited availability of comprehensive, standardized evaluation frameworks for fair VLM comparison across diverse tasks
Challenge of integrating multiple reward signals (verifiable rewards and human feedback) in reinforcement learning for VLMs
Method: Four-stage pre-training architecture with strategic data progression from basic alignment to complex reasoning integration
Mixed On-policy Reinforcement Learning (MORL) framework combining rule-based verifiable rewards with human feedback through "Reward-as-a-Service" system
Direct incorporation of high-quality synthetic reasoning data with long Chain-of-Thought into Stage 4 pre-training rather than only fine-tuning
Comprehensive open-source evaluation suite covering 50+ multimodal benchmarks with standardized prompts and protocols
Results: MiMo-VL-7B-RL achieves 59.4 on OlympiadBench, surpassing models up to 72B parameters and setting new standards for multimodal reasoning
Outperforms specialized GUI models on OSWorld-G (56.1 score) despite being a general-purpose VLM, demonstrating strong agentic capabilities
Maintains excellent text-only performance (95.4% MATH500, 85.1% DROP) while excelling across diverse multimodal tasks including video understanding and document analysis
Achieves highest Elo rating among open-source VLMs in user preference evaluation, approaching proprietary model performance levels
Takeaways: Incorporating reasoning data with long Chain-of-Thought directly into late pre-training stages yields substantial performance gains (+9 MMMU, +14 OSWorld-G, +16 OlympiadBench) compared to post-training only approaches
On-policy reinforcement learning variants demonstrate superior scaling properties and training stability compared to vanilla GRPO, showing continuous improvement without early saturation
Task interference remains a significant challenge in mixed RL objectives, with disparities in response length requirements across different task types limiting unified optimization
Compact 7B parameter models can achieve competitive performance with much larger models through sophisticated training methodologies and high-quality data curation

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.03525.Title: Video-Skill-CoT: Skill-based Chain-of-Thoughts for Domain-Adaptive Video Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.03525.Summary: The VIDEO-SKILL-COT (VIDEO-SKOT) framework enhances Multimodal Large Language Models for video reasoning by automatically generating skill-aware Chain-of-Thought supervisions and employing skill-specific expert modules. This approach leads to average performance improvements of up to 5.70 accuracy points over baselines on benchmarks like VSI-Bench, alongside more accurate and coherent reasoning traces as rated by human evaluators.
Problem: Existing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning struggle to adapt to the diverse and domain-specific reasoning skills required for various video understanding tasks.
Current CoT methods often rely on fixed, general-purpose reasoning traces that are insufficient for tasks demanding specialized skills like temporal, spatial, or narrative understanding.
Manually annotating skill-specific reasoning traces for video QA datasets is labor-intensive and not scalable, limiting the development of adaptable video reasoning systems.
Method: An automated two-step process to generate skill-based CoT annotations, involving MLLMs to extract, cluster, and produce skill-conditioned rationales from video QA pairs.

Skill-specific expert learning where N_experts LoRA modules are trained to specialize in distinct question groups, allowing the MLLM backbone (e.g., LLaVA-Video) to adapt efficiently to varied reasoning capabilities.
A combined training objective that minimizes cross-entropy loss for both the final answer and the skill-grounded CoT tokens, fostering explicit and verifiable multi-step reasoning.
Results: VIDEO-SKOT consistently improved accuracy across diverse benchmarks, including a +4.10 point gain on E.T.Bench, +5.70 on VSI-Bench, and +1.59 on CinePile compared to fine-tuned LLaVA-Video baselines.
Ablation studies confirmed that both skill-based CoT and skill-specific expert modules are essential and contribute synergistically to the framework's overall performance.
Human evaluation showed skill-based CoT significantly outperformed regular CoT, scoring higher in correctness (+2.09), relevance (+1.64), and coherence (+1.93) on a 1-5 Likert scale.
Takeaways: Effective video reasoning in MLLMs requires domain-adaptive, skill-aware Chain-of-Thought processes, moving beyond generic reasoning traces.
High-quality, interpretable, and skill-conditioned CoT supervisions can be automatically constructed at scale using advanced MLLMs, eliminating the need for manual annotation.
Modularizing MLLM fine-tuning with lightweight LoRA experts for specific skill sets enables efficient specialization and enhances the model's adaptability across diverse video domains.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.03295.Title: Unleashing the Reasoning Potential of Pre-trained LLMs by Critique Fine-Tuning on One Problem
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.03295.Summary: One-shot Critique Fine-Tuning (CFT) activates latent reasoning abilities in pre-trained large language models using a single problem, outperforming supervised fine-tuning and matching reinforcement learning with 1/15th to 1/20th the computational cost. This approach trains models to critique diverse incorrect solutions, fostering a deeper understanding of reasoning patterns.
Problem: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) methods, though effective for reasoning, are computationally expensive (hundreds of GPU hours for one problem) and suffer from unstable training dynamics.
Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) requires vast, high-quality, and expensive datasets to prevent overfitting and achieve strong generalization, which are scarce for complex reasoning tasks.
There is a need for a more efficient and stable post-training method to unleash the latent reasoning potential of pre-trained LLMs with minimal data and computational resources.
Method: Construct a 'one-shot CFT dataset' by having 10 diverse 'student' LLMs generate 100 candidate solutions for a single seed reasoning problem.
Employ 7 high-performing 'teacher' LLMs to provide detailed critiques for each of the 100 candidate solutions, yielding 600 filtered critiques per problem.
Fine-tune pre-trained LLMs using this compact critique dataset, training the model to generate critiques (problem + candidate solution -> critique) rather than direct solutions.
Results: One-shot Critique Fine-Tuning (CFT) improved Qwen2.5-Math-7B's average accuracy on math benchmarks from 32.2% to 42.2% (+10.0 points).
CFT achieved performance comparable to or superior to 1-shot RLVR while requiring significantly less compute, using approximately 5 GPU hours compared to over 120 GPU hours for RLVR.

The method consistently outperformed 1-shot SFT and even full-dataset SFT, demonstrating strong generalization across mathematical and logic reasoning tasks (e.g., +16% average gain on BBEH logic tasks for Qwen2.5-Math-7B).
Takeaways: Learning from critiques of diverse incorrect solutions provides a richer and more effective supervisory signal for reasoning than directly learning from correct solutions.

A minimal, qualitatively rich dataset derived from a single problem can efficiently activate latent reasoning capabilities in LLMs, outperforming methods requiring large datasets or complex reinforcement learning.
Critique fine-tuning offers a significantly more computationally efficient and stable approach compared to reinforcement learning for improving LLM reasoning performance.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.03195.Title: Unlabeled Data Improves Fine-Grained Image Zero-shot Classification with Multimodal LLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.03195.Summary: Researchers at UCLA developed AutoSEP, a self-supervised prompt learning framework that improves fine-grained image classification performance of Multimodal Large Language Models using only unlabeled data and black-box access. The framework consistently boosted classification accuracy by an average of 13% over standard zero-shot performance across various MLLMs and datasets.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) generally struggle with fine-grained image classification tasks, often overlooking subtle yet discriminative visual details.
Existing methods to improve MLLM performance on fine-grained tasks typically rely on expensive, large-scale labeled datasets for training or fine-tuning, which are resource-intensive to acquire.

Current prompt optimization techniques often require labeled data for supervision or are designed for text-only tasks, making them less effective for black-box multimodal scenarios without label access.
Method: AutoSEP employs an iterative self-supervised 'Reflect-and-Modify' strategy to optimize a description-generation prompt without using any labeled data.
The MLLM first generates a detailed textual description of an image using the optimized prompt, then performs classification by combining the image with its generated description.

Prompt optimization is guided by an unsupervised scoring function based on instance-level classification, which measures how well the MLLM can correctly distinguish an image's own generated description from those of other images.
Results: AutoSEP consistently achieved an average improvement of 13% over standard zero-shot classification and 3% over the best unsupervised baselines across eight fine-grained datasets and three state-of-the-art MLLMs (Gemini 1.5 Flash, GPT-4o, Qwen2-VL-72B-Instruct).

The proposed instance-level classification accuracy as an unsupervised scoring signal significantly outperformed other prompt optimization strategies that used pseudo-labeling or pairwise output evaluations.
The framework demonstrated consistent performance gains with increasing unlabeled sample sizes, showing reliable improvements even when utilizing as few as 60 unlabeled images for optimization.
Takeaways: Principled optimization of description-generation prompts is crucial for MLLMs to produce task-relevant, discriminative descriptions, as unoptimized prompts often yield marginal or negative performance changes.
Instance-level classification accuracy provides a robust and effective unsupervised signal for guiding prompt optimization in MLLMs, outperforming alternative self-supervised scoring strategies.
The iterative prompt refinement process leads to increased prompt diversity and semantic richness, which positively correlates with improved fine-grained classification performance.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.03147.Title: UniWorld-V1: High-Resolution Semantic Encoders for Unified Visual Understanding and Generation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.03147.Summary: UniWorld-V1 introduces a unified generative model that integrates vision-language understanding, image generation, perception, and manipulation within a single framework. It achieves competitive performance across these diverse visual tasks, notably excelling in image manipulation and perception, using only 2.7 million training samples.
Problem: Existing unified models often lack comprehensive capabilities for both image perception (e.g., detection, segmentation) and fine-grained image manipulation (e.g., precise editing, style transfer).
The impressive capabilities of proprietary multimodal models like GPT-4o-Image are not openly accessible, limiting scientific scrutiny, reproducibility, and broader community innovation.
Prevailing approaches for unified image manipulation frequently rely on VAEs for visual feature extraction, which may not be optimal for semantic-level understanding and diverse manipulation tasks.
Method: A unified architecture is designed by integrating a pre-trained multimodal large language model (Qwen2.5-VL-7B), a high-resolution contrastive semantic encoder (SigLIP), and a Diffusion Transformer (FLUX).

A two-stage training recipe is employed: first, pretraining for semantic alignment of VLM features with the generative backbone, followed by fine-tuning to incorporate SigLIP features for consistent generation.
An adaptive editing region weighting strategy is introduced to prioritize loss signals from small edited regions during image manipulation training, ensuring focus on fine-grained changes.
Results: Achieves the highest overall performance among open-source models on the ImgEdit-Bench for image manipulation, scoring 3.26, surpassing models like BAGEL and Step1X-Edit.

Demonstrates strong text-to-image generation capabilities on GenEval, with an overall score of 0.80, becoming competitive with GPT-4o-Image and BAGEL despite using orders of magnitude less training data.

Exhibits highly competitive performance in diverse image perception tasks, including canny edge detection, normal map generation, and segmentation, making it the first open-source unified model to cover this broad range.
Takeaways: Empirical analysis suggests that proprietary models like GPT-4o-Image may leverage semantic encoders, not VAEs, for effective visual feature injection in image manipulation tasks.
High-resolution contrastive semantic encoders (e.g., SigLIP) prove more effective than VAEs for generalizable image manipulation and perception within a unified framework.
Competitive performance across diverse multimodal tasks can be achieved with significantly less training data through an optimized architecture and a two-stage training strategy.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.03096.Title: FuseLIP: Multimodal Embeddings via Early Fusion of Discrete Tokens
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.03096.Summary: FuseLIP proposes a single-encoder architecture for vision-language models that processes both images and text through early fusion of discrete tokens. This approach enables modality interaction at every layer of the transformer encoder, achieving superior performance on tasks requiring fine-grained visual-textual understanding while reducing trainable parameters by more than 50% compared to competitive baselines.
Problem: Traditional vision-language models like CLIP use separate encoders for images and text, preventing deep, unified interaction between modalities for tasks requiring joint understanding of image-text pairs.

Existing late fusion methods for multimodal tasks limit modality interaction to the final processing stages, hindering the development of deeply integrated representations necessary for fine-grained visual-textual understanding.
Multimodal sequence-to-sequence models, while versatile, often lack the strong zero-shot generalization capabilities of CLIP or incur high computational costs due to their size.
Method: FuseLIP introduces a single transformer-based encoder that processes both images and text by converting them into unified sequences of discrete tokens through early fusion.
It employs a novel tokenization strategy that combines standard text tokens with discrete visual tokens from TiTok family image tokenizers into a single, extended vocabulary.

The model is trained with a dual-objective strategy that combines a modified Sigmoid contrastive loss with a masked multimodal modeling (MMM) objective, where masking applies to the same input used for contrastive learning.
Results: FuseLIP-B achieved top performance across nearly all evaluation benchmarks, leading on 8 out of 9 tasks when trained on CC3M+MM and 7 out of 9 tasks for CC12M+MM training.
The model demonstrated significantly fewer trainable parameters (65.6M for FuseLIP-B vs. 149.7M for SigLIP-B_SF), resulting in faster training and reduced GPU memory requirements.

FuseLIP-S outperformed late fusion baselines by 9-24% on text-guided transformation tasks like CC3M-TGIT, showing particular strength in understanding fine-grained visual changes such as cropping, rotation, and flipping operations.
Takeaways: Early fusion of discrete image and text tokens within a single encoder enables richer, layer-wise modality interaction, leading to superior performance on tasks requiring fine-grained understanding.
A single encoder can effectively process both unimodal and multimodal data in a CLIP-like framework, challenging the established dual-encoder paradigm for vision-language models.

Seamless integration of masked multimodal modeling (MMM) alongside contrastive learning within a single encoder improves performance across tasks and simplifies the training process by eliminating the need for separate passes or auxiliary modules.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.02843.Title: Random Registers for Cross-Domain Few-Shot Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.02843.Summary: This study reveals that learnable prompts can hinder Vision Transformer generalization in cross-domain few-shot learning, while randomly initialized prompts, termed random registers, improve it. A two-stage method, Random Registers Enhanced Attention Perturbation (REAP), is proposed to leverage this insight, achieving state-of-the-art performance by enhancing attention perturbation and adapting effectively to new target domains.
Problem: Vision Transformers (ViTs) struggle to generalize effectively across significant domain gaps when very few labeled examples are available in the target domain.
Standard prompt tuning strategies, commonly used for adapting pre-trained ViTs, unexpectedly degrade performance in cross-domain few-shot learning (CDFSL) scenarios.
There is a lack of understanding regarding how prompt tuning mechanisms specifically influence ViT transferability when confronting substantial domain shifts.
Method: Observed that random Gaussian noise (random registers) appended to input tokens consistently improves ViT transferability in CDFSL, contrasting the negative effect of learnable prompts.
Interpreted the role of random registers as implicitly performing sharpness-aware minimization (SAM), guiding the model to flatter, more generalizable minima in the loss landscape.

Developed Random Registers Enhanced Attention Perturbation (REAP), a two-stage strategy that perturbs clustered semantic image regions with random noise during source training and utilizes learnable registers for efficient target-domain adaptation.
Results: REAP achieved state-of-the-art average performance across four diverse target-domain datasets (CropDiseases, EuroSAT, ISIC2018, ChestX) in both 1-shot and 5-shot settings.

Quantitative analysis using Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) demonstrated that random registers significantly increase the similarity between source and target domain features, confirming improved domain-agnostic learning.
Qualitative visualizations of attention maps showed that REAP leads to more focused and valid attention on semantic objects within target images, indicating enhanced generalization capabilities.
Takeaways: Learnable prompts, when trained on the source domain, can absorb domain-specific information, leading to overfitting and sharper loss landscapes, which ultimately harms ViT generalization to new target domains.

Random registers introduce controlled perturbations that push the model towards flatter loss minima, functioning as a form of sharpness-aware minimization to learn more robust and domain-agnostic features.

Perturbing semantically meaningful clustered regions of image patches with random noise during source training is more effective for enhancing transferability than random masking, and learnable registers are optimal for rapid adaptation during target-domain fine-tuning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.02557.Title: Kernel-based Unsupervised Embedding Alignment for Enhanced Visual Representation in Vision-language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.02557.Summary: Researchers at The Chinese University of Hong Kong and Shanghai AI Laboratory developed Kernel-based Unsupervised Embedding Alignment (KUEA) to improve CLIP's fine-grained visual perception by aligning its visual embeddings with a vision-centric model like DINOv2. This method, which enhanced CLIP ViT-L-14's zero-shot accuracy by 1.28% and boosted downstream Multi-modal Large Language Models like LLaVA-1.5-7B by 1.66% on average, preserves the crucial image-text alignment while being computationally lightweight.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) like CLIP, while strong in semantic understanding, struggle with fine-grained visual perception (e.g., spatial reasoning, counting) due to training with global image-caption supervision.
This limitation propagates to Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) that rely on CLIP as their visual backbone, hindering their performance on visually nuanced tasks.

Existing solutions to improve fine-grained perception are often computationally prohibitive (requiring full retraining) or risk disrupting CLIP's crucial pre-existing image-text alignment, making them incompatible with downstream MLLMs.
Method: Proposes Kernel-based Unsupervised Embedding Alignment (KUEA) to enhance CLIP's visual encoder by aligning its feature space with a vision-centric model like DINOv2.

The method minimizes the squared difference between the kernel matrices of CLIP's visual embeddings and the target model's embeddings, encouraging CLIP to capture more fine-grained visual similarities.

An L2 regularization term is applied to CLIP's visual embeddings, constraining them to remain close to their original pre-trained state, thereby preserving the vital visual-text alignment without needing text data during fine-tuning.
Results: Achieved consistent improvements in CLIP's zero-shot object recognition (e.g., 1.28% average increase for ViT-L-14 on CLIP-Benchmark) and enhanced performance on tasks requiring fine-grained perception (e.g., 5.51% average increase for linear probing on counting/spatial tasks).
Maintained original image-text retrieval performance on datasets like Flickr30K and MSCOCO, confirming that the alignment process does not compromise CLIP's core visual-text compatibility.

Improved performance of downstream MLLMs (LLaVA-1.5-7B, OpenFlamingo-3B) when integrating the aligned CLIP visual encoder, with LLaVA showing an average score increase of 1.66% on vision-language benchmarks, especially strong in localization.
Takeaways: Aligning embeddings in a higher-dimensional kernel space allows for flexible adjustments of similarity relationships, enhancing fine-grained perception without drastically altering the feature space.
An L2 regularization term on visual embeddings is sufficient to maintain cross-modal (image-text) alignment, even without explicit text-based supervision during fine-tuning.
Efficient stochastic optimization for kernel alignment is feasible, enabling lightweight and scalable fine-tuning on large image-only datasets.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.02359.Title: Auto-Labeling Data for Object Detection
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.02359.Summary: A method called "Auto-Labeling" uses pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to automatically generate pseudo ground truth labels for object detection training data, achieving a 5,000x speedup and 100,000x cost reduction compared to human annotation while yielding competitive downstream model performance.
Problem: Training object detection models requires vast amounts of labeled data, leading to prohibitive human annotation costs.
Manual labeling for large-scale applications can reach hundreds of thousands of dollars.
Human annotation is time-consuming, ranging from 7 seconds to 1.5 hours per bounding box.
Method: Introduces "Auto-Labeling" (AL), a method that leverages pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to automatically generate pseudo ground truth labels for object detection training data.
VLMs such as YOLO-World, YOLOE, and Grounding DINO-T are used as "label generators" to create training data for lightweight detection models.
The auto-labeling function utilizes a confidence threshold (α) and an ordered set of text prompts (T) to map class names to predicted object indices.
Results: Auto-labeling was ~5,000x faster and ~100,000x cheaper than human annotation services, costing $1.18 and taking 1.27 hours for entire datasets.
On general datasets like PASCAL VOC and COCO, models trained on auto-labels achieved 70-80% of the performance of models trained on human labels.
YOLO-World consistently performed best as the foundation model for label generation, with a confidence threshold of 0.2 proving optimal across datasets and downstream models.
Takeaways: The confidence threshold (α) is critical for balancing label quantity and quality; lower α values generating more labels with higher recall proved more beneficial for downstream model training.
Reinvesting the cost savings from auto-labeling into training larger downstream models can yield superior performance compared to training smaller models on human labels.
High auto-label recall is the strongest predictor of success for the downstream object detection model.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.02153.Title: Small Language Models are the Future of Agentic AI
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.02153.Summary: Researchers from NVIDIA and Georgia Institute of Technology contend that Small Language Models (SLMs) are the optimal choice for agentic AI systems, possessing sufficient power while delivering superior operational suitability and economic benefits over Large Language Models (LLMs) for a majority of tasks. The work advocates for a paradigm shift towards more efficient, sustainable, and democratized AI agent development.
Problem: The prevalent LLM-centric paradigm for AI agents incurs high economic costs due to significant computational demands for inference.
Generalist LLMs exhibit operational inefficiency and increased latency when performing repetitive, specialized sub-tasks common in agentic workflows.
The massive energy consumption associated with running LLMs raises environmental sustainability concerns, and they often lack precise specialization for narrow agentic tasks.
Method: The paper proposes a paradigm shift towards specialized Small Language Models (SLMs) as the primary computational units for most agentic invocations.
It advocates for heterogeneous agent architectures that leverage SLMs for routine, specialized tasks and reserve LLMs for complex, general reasoning.
A practical, six-step algorithm is provided for converting LLM-centric agentic applications to SLM specialists, involving data collection, task clustering, fine-tuning, and continuous refinement.
Results: Evidence from various SLMs demonstrates capabilities (e.g., commonsense reasoning, tool calling, code generation) on par with or exceeding much larger LLMs, often with substantial efficiency gains.
Case studies on open-source agents (MetaGPT, Open Operator, Cradle) estimate that 40-70% of LLM queries could be effectively handled by specialized SLMs.

The paper argues that current barriers to SLM adoption, such as existing LLM infrastructure investments and generalist benchmarks, are practical and being addressed by ongoing technological advancements and industry recognition.
Takeaways: Modern SLMs, including models like Microsoft Phi and NVIDIA Nemotron-H, are already sufficiently powerful to handle the language modeling requirements of most agentic applications.
SLMs offer inherent operational advantages for agentic systems, such as significantly lower latency, greater flexibility for fine-tuning, and closer behavioral alignment for structured outputs.
SLMs are inherently more economical, providing 10-30 times cheaper inference, reducing infrastructure costs, and promoting more sustainable and accessible AI development.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.02138.Title: Revisiting LRP: Positional Attribution as the Missing Ingredient for Transformer Explainability
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.02138.Summary: Tel Aviv University researchers develop Positional-Aware LRP (PA-LRP), a framework for Transformer explainability that explicitly attributes relevance to positional encoding components alongside token embeddings, addressing a fundamental flaw in existing Layer-wise Relevance Propagation methods that violate conservation properties by ignoring positional information, achieving consistent performance improvements across NLP (7-51% AU-MSE reduction on IMDB classification, 3-8% gains on LLaMA-3 zero-shot tasks) and vision tasks (4-point average improvement on ImageNet perturbation tests, 2-3% gains in segmentation metrics) by introducing specialized LRP rules for various positional encoding types (learnable, sinusoidal, RoPE, ALiBi) and reformulating the input space as position-token pairs with per-layer positional sinks, with empirical analysis revealing that positional relevance constitutes 9-22% of total model relevance in vision transformers, demonstrating that structural and spatial cues carry distinct explanatory value complementary to semantic attributions.
Problem: Existing LRP methods for Transformers ignore positional encoding during relevance propagation, violating the conservation property and losing significant relevance information (9-22% of total relevance)
Current explainability approaches fail to attribute the distinct structural and spatial information encoded in positional components, leading to incomplete and potentially unfaithful explanations
State-of-the-art methods like AttnLRP produce fragmented attribution maps that miss holistic object-level patterns captured by positional encoding
Method: Reformulate input space as position-token pairs with separate "sinks" for positional relevance at each layer to prevent information loss during backward propagation

Design specialized LRP rules for different positional encoding types: standard LRP-ε for input-level PE (learnable/sinusoidal), matrix multiplication rules for attention-level PE (RoPE), and addition rules for bias-based PE (ALiBi)
Aggregate final relevance by summing positive contributions from both semantic embeddings and all per-layer positional components using multi-sink approach
Results: Consistent improvements across diverse tasks: 14.5-51% AU-MSE reduction on IMDB classification with LLaMA models, 3.2% AUAC and 7.7% AU-MSE gains on zero-shot question answering
Superior segmentation performance on ImageNet with 1.8-3% improvements in pixel accuracy and mIoU across DeiT models, demonstrating better object boundary detection

Empirical validation of theoretical claims showing positional relevance constitutes 9.22-22.39% of total model relevance in vision transformers, confirming conservation property violations in existing methods
Takeaways: Positional encoding carries substantial and unique relevance signal that complements semantic attributions, with "PE Only" explanations often matching full AttnLRP baseline performance
Positional relevance captures broader spatial and structural patterns (entire objects, sequential relationships) while semantic relevance focuses on specific discriminative features
Conservation property violation in existing methods represents a significant theoretical flaw that impacts explanation faithfulness, particularly when positional cues are dominant

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.02126.Title: Knowledge or Reasoning? A Close Look at How LLMs Think Across Domains
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.02126.Summary: Researchers from UC Santa Cruz, Stanford University, and Tongji University developed a fine-grained evaluation framework to dissect Large Language Model reasoning into factual knowledge and logical inference components. Their analysis shows that while Supervised Fine-Tuning improves knowledge, Reinforcement Learning enhances reasoning by refining knowledge application across medical and mathematical domains.
Problem: Existing LLM evaluation methods largely focus on final-answer accuracy, obscuring the intricate interplay between factual knowledge and logical inference in their step-by-step reasoning processes.

Earlier fine-grained reasoning metrics (e.g., ROSCOE) can be unreliable because LLMs often generate reasoning from internal knowledge, not just by rephrasing input, leading to potentially misleading similarity scores.

A lack of transparent understanding of LLM 'thinking trajectories' makes it difficult to discern whether correct answers stem from robust factual recall, sound logical inference, or a fortuitous combination.
Method: Developed a novel, fine-grained three-stage evaluation framework that decomposes LLM responses into explicit, successive logical steps.
Introduced the 'Information Gain (InfoGain)' metric to quantify reasoning efficiency by measuring how much each step reduces uncertainty towards the correct solution using step-wise perplexity.

Established the 'Knowledge Index (KI)' metric to evaluate the factual correctness of knowledge within each reasoning step by extracting knowledge points and judging their consistency against external ground truth databases.
Results: Trained Qwen-Base models consistently outperformed DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B in the medical domain, indicating that pre-training optimized for reasoning (like math/code) does not effectively transfer to knowledge-intensive domains.

Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) increased average Knowledge Index (KI) by 6.2% on medical tasks but resulted in a significant average 38.9% reduction in Information Gain (reasoning efficiency) compared to untrained models.

Reinforcement Learning (RL) consistently enhanced Information Gain across both domains and boosted Knowledge Index (average 12.4 points gain for Qwen-Base in medicine) primarily by guiding models to discard incorrect or irrelevant knowledge in reasoning paths.
Takeaways: Knowledge and reasoning are distinct evaluation dimensions that should be measured independently, as models can have similar overall accuracy but differing strengths in factual correctness (Knowledge Index) and reasoning efficiency (Information Gain).
Domain demands vary, with medical tasks being more knowledge-intensive (Knowledge Index strongly correlates with accuracy), while mathematical tasks are more reasoning-intensive.

Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) primarily boosts factual knowledge but can compromise reasoning clarity, whereas Reinforcement Learning (RL) enhances reasoning quality by guiding models to prune inaccurate or irrelevant knowledge.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.02096.Title: SynthRL: Scaling Visual Reasoning with Verifiable Data Synthesis
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.02096.Summary: NUS-TRAIL researchers develop SynthRL, an automated three-stage pipeline that synthesizes more challenging visual reasoning problems while preserving original answers to enhance reinforcement learning training for vision-language models, generating 3,380 verified harder questions from 8,072 MMK12 seed samples through difficulty-based selection, Gemini-2.5-Flash synthesis, and guaranteed verification using Monte Carlo rollouts, achieving consistent +1.0% average accuracy gains across five out-of-domain benchmarks (MathVerse, MathVision, MathVista, WeMath, DynaMath) with pronounced improvements on medium (+1.7%) and hard (+1.6%) evaluation samples, demonstrating that strategically augmenting training distributions with verifiably correct yet more complex variants provides richer learning signals for RLVR than traditional data scaling approaches.
Problem: RLVR shows promise for enhancing VLM reasoning but faces data scalability challenges, as existing selection methods are constrained by original dataset volume and bias
Creating challenging yet verifiable training data for visual reasoning requires expensive human annotation and step-by-step reasoning supervision
Traditional data augmentation lacks correctness guarantees and difficulty calibration needed for effective RL training where unreliable rewards lead to suboptimal policies
Method: Three-stage automated pipeline: difficulty-based seed selection using Monte Carlo rollouts to identify easy questions, synthesis using powerful VLMs prompted to create harder variants without seeing answers, and guaranteed verification ensuring correctness and increased difficulty
Target model-aligned verification using rollout pass counts with dual criteria: correctness (C_cand ≥ 4) and difficulty enhancement (C_cand ≤ C_ori - 2)
Augmentation strategy combining original and synthesized data rather than replacement to create richer training distributions
Results: Generated 3,380 verified challenging questions from 8,072 seeds, achieving 58.0% average accuracy versus 57.0% baseline across five benchmarks
Largest improvements on medium (+1.7%) and hard (+1.6%) evaluation samples while showing slight decrease (-0.5%) on easy samples, confirming targeted enhancement of complex reasoning
Ablation studies confirm necessity of verification (1.4% drop without), multi-pass evaluation (0.7% drop with single-pass), and augmentation over replacement strategy (1.1% performance difference)
Takeaways: More challenging yet still correct training samples provide richer learning signals for RLVR than volume increases alone
Verification alignment with target model capabilities is crucial - using non-target verifiers reduces performance by 1.5%
Benefits scale with seed dataset size, widening from +0.2% at 2K samples to +1.0% at 8K samples, indicating complementary value to traditional scaling

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.02095.Title: Cycle Consistency as Reward: Learning Image-Text Alignment without Human Preferences
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.02095.Summary: Researchers at MIT CSAIL introduced CycleReward, a self-supervised reward model for image-text alignment, by generating preference signals entirely from cycle consistency without relying on human or proprietary AI feedback. This approach achieved an average 65% agreement with human judgments and outperformed prior state-of-the-art methods on detailed captioning benchmarks with 60.50% pairwise accuracy, effectively aligning generative models through direct preference optimization.
Problem: Existing state-of-the-art image-text alignment metrics are costly and difficult to scale due to their reliance on expensive human preferences or proprietary AI feedback.
Current preference datasets and alignment metrics often lack the granularity to robustly evaluate and improve models handling long, descriptive captions or complex text prompts.

Direct cycle consistency methods for alignment, while conceptually appealing, are computationally inefficient and often non-differentiable, limiting their use for direct optimization of generative models.
Method: Defined cycle consistency scores by reconstructing images from text using DreamSim for image similarity (I2T) and text from images using SBERT for semantic text similarity (T2I), then converted these into pairwise preferences.

Generated a large-scale, self-supervised preference dataset, CyclePrefDB, by using diverse I2T/T2I models to create candidates and powerful generative models (e.g., Stable Diffusion 3, LLaVA-1.5-13B) for reconstruction.
Trained CycleReward, a lightweight and differentiable reward model, using a BLIP backbone and Bradley-Terry loss on the CyclePrefDB dataset, creating I2T, T2I, and combined variants.
Results: CycleReward-Combo achieved a 65% average agreement rate with human preferences and significantly outperformed existing methods on the DetailCaps-4870 benchmark with 60.50% pairwise accuracy for detailed captioning.

Using CycleReward for Best-of-N sampling led to substantial relative performance gains on detailed captioning and text-to-image generation benchmarks, demonstrating its effectiveness in selecting high-quality outputs.

Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) of Qwen-VL-Chat and Stable Diffusion 1.5 using the CyclePrefDB dataset improved model performance across diverse tasks, matching or surpassing models aligned with costly human preference data.
Takeaways: Cycle consistency provides a robust and scalable self-supervised signal for learning image-text alignment, eliminating the need for expensive human or proprietary AI supervision.

The quality of cycle consistency signals heavily depends on the choice of perceptual similarity metrics (e.g., DreamSim for images, SBERT for text) and the capabilities of the underlying generative models used for reconstruction.

Distilling cycle consistency into a fast, differentiable reward model (CycleReward) enables its practical application in downstream tasks like Best-of-N sampling and Direct Preference Optimization, improving generative model quality.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.01939.Title: Beyond the 80/20 Rule: High-Entropy Minority Tokens Drive Effective Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.01939.Summary: Research from Alibaba Inc.'s Qwen Team and Tsinghua University's LeapLab reveals that in large language models, only a small fraction of high-entropy tokens are critical for reasoning improvements during Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR). By focusing policy gradient updates exclusively on these minority tokens, models achieve superior performance, including setting new state-of-the-art scores on mathematical benchmarks while reducing computational overhead and improving generalization.
Problem: Existing Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) methods improve LLM reasoning empirically, but lack a mechanistic understanding of how or why.
Current RLVR training applies uniform policy gradient updates across all generated tokens, without distinguishing their individual contributions to reasoning.
The internal dynamics of how RLVR enhances Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning at a token-level remained largely unexplored.
Method: The authors analyzed token-level generation entropy within LLM Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning to identify distinct functional roles for tokens.
They adapted the Dynamic sAmpling Policy Optimization (DAPO) algorithm to restrict policy gradient updates to only a predefined proportion (e.g., 20%) of the highest-entropy tokens.
Evaluations were conducted across Qwen and Llama models on multiple mathematical reasoning and out-of-distribution benchmarks to assess the impact of this targeted training.
Results: Focusing policy gradient updates on the top 20% highest-entropy tokens improved reasoning performance, achieving gains of +7.71 on AIME’24 and +11.04 on AIME’25 for Qwen3-32B, setting new state-of-the-art scores.
Conversely, training on the 80% lowest-entropy tokens resulted in a notable decline in reasoning performance, indicating these tokens contribute little or negatively to effective learning.

The optimized approach also demonstrated enhanced generalization, with models trained on high-entropy tokens significantly outperforming vanilla RLVR on the out-of-distribution LiveCodeBench benchmark.
Takeaways: LLM Chain-of-Thought reasoning is driven by a sparse minority of high-entropy "forking tokens" that represent critical decision points, while most tokens are low-entropy "following tokens" completing linguistic structures.

Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) primarily increases the entropy of these existing high-entropy tokens, preserving the base model's inherent entropy patterns and focusing on refining existing uncertainty.

Uniform policy gradient updates are suboptimal; focusing training on high-entropy minority tokens leads to better performance and generalization, suggesting these tokens are key to adaptable reasoning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.01850.Title: MoDA: Modulation Adapter for Fine-Grained Visual Grounding in Instructional MLLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.01850.Summary: MoDA (Modulation Adapter) enhances Multimodal Large Language Models by dynamically refining pre-aligned visual features through instruction-guided modulation, improving fine-grained visual grounding and reducing hallucinations. Integrating MoDA into the LLaVA-1.5 pipeline boosted MMVP accuracy by 12.0 percentage points and achieved competitive or superior performance against recent MLLMs on various benchmarks.
Problem: MLLMs often struggle with fine-grained visual grounding due to entangled semantic elements within patch-based visual encoder representations.
Poor visual grounding leads to frequent hallucinations, where MLLMs generate text inconsistent with image semantics.
Existing solutions to these issues typically incur substantial computational overhead, require large-scale retraining, or introduce architectural complexity.
Method: MoDA, a lightweight, plug-and-play module, refines pre-aligned visual features using instruction-guided modulation.
It employs a cross-attention mechanism to estimate a soft modulation mask, dynamically weighting visual features based on the input language query.
MoDA integrates into the standard LLaVA two-stage training pipeline and is fine-tuned jointly with the LLM during the instruction-tuning phase without additional supervision.
Results: MoDA integration improved LLaVA-1.5's accuracy on the MMVP hallucination benchmark by 12.0 percentage points, from 24.0% to 36.0%.
LLaVA-MoRE SigLIP-S2 + MoDA achieved 65.4% on GQA and 81.9% on ScienceQA, outperforming Qwen-2.5-VL by +4.0 and +11.7 percentage points respectively, while matching its POPE score of 87.7%.

Ablation studies confirmed cross-attention without L1 regularization as the optimal MoDA architecture, and demonstrated that applying MoDA only at the beginning of the LLM is more effective and efficient than layer-wise application.
Takeaways: Dynamically modulating visual features based on language instructions effectively disentangles semantic elements and enhances fine-grained visual grounding in MLLMs.
A lightweight, modular adapter can significantly improve MLLM reliability by reducing hallucinations without requiring major architectural overhauls or extensive retraining.
The effectiveness of instruction-guided feature modulation is amplified when combined with richer base visual features (e.g., SigLIP-S2) and more powerful LLM backbones (e.g., LLaMA 3.1).

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.01724.Title: Active Learning via Vision-Language Model Adaptation with Open Data
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.01724.Summary: Active Learning with Open Resources (ALOR) enhances active learning by integrating open-source Vision-Language Models with their vast pretraining datasets. The framework significantly improves data efficiency, achieving state-of-the-art performance with approximately 7.2% higher accuracy over baselines by adopting contrastive tuning and a novel tail-first sampling strategy.
Problem: Minimizing the high costs and efforts associated with manual data labeling for specific downstream tasks in active learning.
Underutilization of the massive open pretraining datasets (e.g., LAION-400M) of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in existing VLM-based active learning methods.
A prevalent assumption that prompt tuning is the most suitable VLM adaptation strategy for active learning, potentially limiting performance.
Addressing inherent biases and long-tailed distributions within real-world and retrieved data, which can hinder fair and robust model performance.
Method: Introduces Active Learning with Open Resources (ALOR), a framework integrating Retrieval-based Data Augmentation (RDA) and Tail First Sampling (TFS).

Employs Retrieval-based Data Augmentation (RDA) to augment limited labeled data with relevant examples from VLM pretraining datasets via efficient string-matching and filtering, with hard-capping to balance retrieved data.
Proposes Tail First Sampling (TFS), an active learning strategy that prioritizes selecting highly uncertain examples from underrepresented "tail" classes identified through pseudo-labeling.

Rigorously evaluates VLM adaptation strategies in active learning contexts, identifying Contrastive Tuning (CT) as the superior approach over Prompt Tuning (PT), Linear Probing (LP), and Finetuning (FT).
Results: Retrieval-based Data Augmentation (RDA) consistently boosted performance, achieving 1.7 times higher accuracy in Round-0 and over 8% accuracy gains in subsequent rounds for all active learning methods.
Tail First Sampling (TFS) consistently outperformed all other state-of-the-art active learning baselines when VLM adaptation was performed via prompt tuning.
Contrastive Tuning (CT) proved to be the superior VLM adaptation approach, outperforming all other strategies across initial low-data regimes and subsequent active learning rounds.
The full ALOR framework, combining CT, RDA, and TFS, achieved state-of-the-art performance with average accuracy gains of approximately +7.2% over strong baselines across five benchmark datasets.
Takeaways: Open pretraining data of Vision-Language Models is a valuable, underutilized resource that can universally and significantly boost active learning performance.

Contrastive Tuning (CT) is a more effective VLM adaptation strategy for active learning than Prompt Tuning (PT), challenging existing assumptions about lightweight adaptation in limited-data scenarios.

Explicitly addressing data imbalance by prioritizing sampling from underrepresented 'tail' classes, guided by insights from retrieved data, is critical for improving overall model robustness and performance.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.01716.Title: Self-Challenging Language Model Agents
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.01716.Summary: The Self-Challenging Agent (SCA) framework enables Large Language Model (LLM) agents to self-improve by generating high-quality, verifiable training tasks through a "Code-as-Task" (CaT) formalism. This approach improved a Llama-3.1-8B model's success rate by 20.2% via distillation and doubled its success rate in self-improvement settings on multi-turn tool-use benchmarks compared to zero-shot performance.
Problem: Manually creating diverse, high-quality training data for multi-turn, open-ended LLM tool-use is costly, labor-intensive, and unscalable.
Prior self-generation methods often produce low-quality, infeasible, or unverifiable tasks, hindering effective LLM agent training.
A general, robust pipeline for synthesizing challenging tasks for multi-turn tool-use LLM agents was largely missing.
Method: An LLM agent is used in two roles: a task challenger that generates tasks and a task executor that attempts them.
Tasks are formalized as "Code-as-Task" (CaT), comprising a natural language instruction, an executable verification function, an example solution, and specific failure cases.
