An automatic filtering mechanism ensures task quality by verifying that the example solution passes and failure cases fail the associated verification function.
The executor agent learns from these self-generated tasks through either self-improvement (Rejection Fine-Tuning) or distillation (Supervised Fine-Tuning on a stronger model's trajectories).
Results: The SCA framework improved the Llama-3.1-8B model's average success rate on multi-turn tool-use benchmarks by 20.2% (from 12.0% to 32.2% Pass@1) through distillation of a larger model.
In a self-improvement setting, SCA doubled the Llama-3.1-8B model's average success rate from 12.0% to 23.5% Pass@1, outperforming the PAE baseline by a 10.6% absolute margin.

Ablation studies confirmed that the full "Code-as-Task" (CaT) formalism, including failure cases, was essential for generating high-quality tasks, effectively eliminating false positives and significantly reducing false negatives.
Takeaways: The "Code-as-Task" formalism, especially the inclusion of explicit failure cases, is critical for synthesizing high-quality, verifiable, and challenging tasks, effectively mitigating issues like task ambiguity or triviality.
Automated self-challenging methods can yield substantial performance gains for LLM agents in tool-use environments, surpassing alternative self-supervision techniques.
Scaling the diversity and coverage of self-generated tasks is more impactful for generalizing agent performance than merely increasing the number of rollout trajectories per task.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.01663.Title: Zoom-Refine: Boosting High-Resolution Multimodal Understanding via Localized Zoom and Self-Refinement
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.01663.Summary: A training-free framework called Zoom-Refine enhances Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) in interpreting high-resolution images by integrating localized region zooming with a self-refinement stage. This method improved accuracy on MME-Realworld reasoning tasks by 3.60% to 5.07% and on HR-Bench by 2.1% to 5.0% for leading MLLMs, offering greater efficiency than comparable training-free approaches.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle to effectively process and interpret high-resolution images.
Downsampling or cropping high-resolution inputs by MLLMs leads to significant loss of fine-grained details.
This information loss hinders MLLM performance on tasks requiring discernment of small objects, intricate textures, or subtle textual cues.
Method: A training-free framework named Zoom-Refine, inspired by human visual cognition, uses a two-stage process.
The 'Localized Zoom' stage involves preliminary assessment, identifying a task-relevant region, and extracting a high-resolution crop from the original image.
The 'Self-Refinement' stage integrates the high-resolution crop and conversational history to guide the MLLM in re-evaluating and refining its initial answer.
Results: On the MME-Realworld reasoning benchmark, Zoom-Refine boosted InternVL3-78B's weighted average accuracy by 3.60% and unweighted average accuracy by 4.39%.
It achieved a 5.0% average accuracy increase on HR-Bench 8K for InternVL3-78B and 2.9% for InternVL2.5-78B, demonstrating effectiveness with extreme high-resolution images.

Zoom-Refine outperformed other training-free methods like DC^2 and ZoomEye by 2.87% and 2.92% respectively on MME-Realworld reasoning, while being significantly more inference-efficient (447 minutes vs. ~3500-3800 minutes).
Takeaways: The framework draws inspiration from human visual cognition, mimicking how humans selectively attend to and refine understanding of complex scenes.
It uniquely incorporates a self-refinement step based on new, detailed visual evidence, moving beyond simple region selection.

The method leverages the MLLM's intrinsic capabilities for spatial localization, contextual reasoning, and comparative analysis solely through prompt engineering, requiring no additional training or external modules.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.01622.Title: General agents contain world models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.01622.Summary: This research from Google DeepMind formally proves that agents capable of generalizing to multi-step, goal-directed tasks inherently learn an accurate predictive model of their environment. The paper demonstrates that this world model is extractable from the agent's policy, with its accuracy directly tied to the agent's competence in achieving complex objectives.
Problem: The ongoing debate concerning whether world models are a necessary component for flexible, goal-directed behavior in AI, contrasting model-based and model-free learning paradigms.
The challenge of understanding what an agent must implicitly learn about its environment to generalize effectively to novel, complex, and multi-step tasks.
The need for a formal theoretical answer to whether a 'model-free shortcut' exists for achieving human-level AI capabilities.
Method: The authors developed a formal proof by reduction, defining the environment as a controlled Markov process and goals using Linear Temporal Logic (LTL).
They rigorously characterized a 'bounded goal-conditioned agent' as one satisfying a regret bound for a diverse set of composite goals up to a specified depth.
An algorithm was constructed to query such an agent's policy with specially crafted composite LTL goals, enabling the inference and extraction of the environment's true transition probabilities.
Results: Theorem 1 formally establishes that for any bounded goal-conditioned agent capable of multi-step tasks (n > 1), a predictive world model can be extracted with an error scaling as O(δ/√n) + O(1/n), where δ is the agent's regret and n is the maximum goal depth.
Theorem 2 provides a counterpoint, proving that world models are not necessary for myopic agents (n=1), as their policies offer no information to bound the environment's transition probabilities.

Experimental validation demonstrated the practical recovery of world models from trained agents, confirming that the error in the recovered transition function decreased with increasing goal depth, aligning with theoretical predictions.
Takeaways: Any agent capable of generalizing to multi-step goal-directed tasks (beyond a single step) must internally contain an accurate predictive model of its environment, refuting the possibility of a purely model-free path to general AI.

The accuracy of this implicitly learned world model is directly proportional to the agent's ability to achieve increasingly complex and long-horizon goals, scaling with its performance and goal depth.
For myopic agents, which optimize only for immediate, one-step goals, a world model is not necessary, as their policies provide no non-trivial information about the underlying environmental dynamics.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.01247.Title: Visual Sparse Steering: Improving Zero-shot Image Classification with Sparsity Guided Steering Vectors
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.01247.Summary: Rutgers University researchers developed Visual Sparse Steering (VS2), a suite of methods that leverage sparse autoencoders to directly steer Vision Foundation Models at inference time, leading to absolute top-1 accuracy gains of up to 4.12% with VS2 and over 21% with its retrieval-augmented variant (VS2++) in zero-shot image classification across various datasets.
Problem: Traditional fine-tuning of Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) is computationally expensive and data-intensive, limiting their adaptability for new tasks.
Applying 'steering vectors' to the vision domain is challenging due to the redundancy of visual representations and the lack of clear, interpretable 'anchors' to define steering directions.
Existing VFM control methods often rely on external language signals or aggregate class-level statistics from training data, limiting test-time unsupervised operation.
Method: Visual Sparse Steering (VS2) extracts sparse concept activations from VFM embeddings using a Top-k Sparse Autoencoder and amplifies these features to create an inference-time steering vector.
VS2++ extends VS2 by leveraging cached unlabeled data to construct more precise, contrastive steering vectors based on pseudo-labeled positive and negative neighbors.

Prototype-Aligned Sparse Steering (PASS) enhances SAEs by incorporating a prototype-alignment loss during training, aligning learned sparse features with class-discriminative information for improved downstream relevance.
Results: Visual Sparse Steering (VS2) improved zero-shot top-1 accuracy over CLIP by up to 4.12% on CIFAR-100 and 1.84% on Tiny-ImageNet without external data.
The retrieval-augmented VS2++ achieved up to 21.44% absolute top-1 accuracy gain over CLIP in an oracle setting and generally outperformed standard CLIP Steering Vectors in realistic conditions.
Per-class accuracy for confusing categories increased by up to 25% with VS2 and 38% with VS2++, demonstrating targeted disambiguation of fine-grained visual concepts.
Takeaways: Sparse autoencoder (SAE) features capture interpretable, disentangled visual concepts within Vision Foundation Models (VFMs), enabling principled steering.

Steering vectors derived from amplifying these sparse features effectively modulate VFM behavior at inference time without requiring explicit positive/negative concept pairs or additional supervision.
The proposed sparse steering methods primarily improve classification accuracy for visually or taxonomically similar categories, disambiguating fine-grained confusions.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.01097.Title: Generic Token Compression in Multimodal Large Language Models from an Explainability Perspective
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.01097.Summary: This research introduces an explainability-guided method for visual token compression in Multimodal Large Language Models, enabling efficient processing by identifying and retaining only semantically important visual information. The approach demonstrates that significant compression at the MLLM input stage can maintain over 98% of original performance on image tasks and over 99% on video tasks, even with 50% token retention, offering improved computational efficiency and practical deployment.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) face significant computational burden due to the exponential growth of visual tokens with increasing image resolutions and video lengths.
Existing visual token compression methods often assume that shallow layers of MLLMs are critically important and should be preserved, limiting compression efficiency.
Current compression approaches lead to bottlenecks in memory usage and slow inference speeds, hindering practical deployment of MLLMs.
Method: The approach uses explainability methods (relevance propagation) to identify and quantify the semantic importance of each visual token, generating ground-truth relevance scores.
A lightweight, five-layer 1D convolutional network learns to predict these relevance scores from the first-layer attention map, enabling efficient, real-time compression.
The learned compressor compresses visual tokens at the input stage of the MLLM, retaining only the most relevant information before it enters the main LLM architecture.
Results: The method achieves over 98% of original performance on image tasks and over 99% on video tasks while retaining only 50% of visual tokens.
The learned compressor consistently outperformed FastV and other baselines across ten benchmarks for image and video tasks (e.g., MME, MMStar, MVBench), demonstrating superior efficiency gains.
Video tasks generally show better performance preservation after compression compared to image tasks, attributed to higher temporal redundancy in video content.
Takeaways: Aggressive visual token compression at the MLLM input stage can maintain high performance, challenging the assumption that shallow layers require all visual tokens.
Compressing tokens before LLM processing provides superior computational savings across all subsequent layers, including prefill and decode phases.
The learned compressor, based on a fully convolutional design, demonstrates strong generalization to visual inputs much larger than those seen during training.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.00513.Title: SSAM: Self-Supervised Association Modeling for Test-Time Adaption
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.00513.Summary: The SSAM framework introduces a self-supervised approach for Test-Time Adaptation in Vision-Language Models by dynamically refining the image encoder with lightweight adapters. This method consistently improves model robustness and generalization, outperforming existing TTA methods on cross-domain and out-of-distribution benchmarks by enhancing visual feature discriminability and visual-textual alignment.
Problem: Existing Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) methods for Vision-Language Models (VLMs) largely freeze the image encoder, neglecting its crucial role in handling visual distribution shifts.
Current TTA approaches primarily focus on text prompt tuning or cache-based adaptation, leaving the image encoder rigid in the face of dynamic visual inputs.
Image encoders must contend with substantial distribution shifts (domain, style, perturbations) during inference, unlike text encoders which operate on relatively fixed semantic concepts.
Method: A lightweight, architecture-agnostic adapter module is introduced to dynamically refine the image encoder during test-time, preserving pre-trained VLM knowledge.
Soft Prototype Estimation (SPE) establishes probabilistic associations between image features and category embeddings to derive robust, label-free visual prototypes.

Prototype-anchored Image Reconstruction (PIR) and a contrastive alignment loss provide self-supervised signals to optimize adapter parameters, guiding accurate categorical predictions and semantic consistency.
Results: SSAM achieved state-of-the-art average accuracy on cross-domain benchmarks, for instance, 64.43% for SSAM_DPE with ResNet-50 and 72.27% for SSAM_DMN-ZS with ViT-B/16, surpassing existing TTA methods.
It demonstrated superior performance on out-of-distribution benchmarks, with SSAM_DPE reaching 50.96% average accuracy on ResNet-50 and 66.26% on ViT-B/16, indicating enhanced robustness.

Ablation studies confirmed that both the Prototype-anchored Image Reconstruction loss (L_PIR) and the contrastive alignment loss (L_ca) contribute positively and synergistically to the overall performance improvements.
Takeaways: Actively adapting the image encoder is a critical yet overlooked component for effective Test-Time Adaptation in Vision-Language Models.
Self-supervised learning, specifically via prototype-anchored reconstruction and contrastive alignment, can effectively guide image encoder adaptation without explicit test-time labels.
The proposed method enhances visual feature discriminability and improves visual-textual feature alignment, leading to more robust and generalized representations for unseen data.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.00467.Title: SST: Self-training with Self-adaptive Thresholding for Semi-supervised Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.00467.Summary: The SST framework introduces an efficient and robust approach to semi-supervised learning that leverages Self-Adaptive Thresholding (SAT) for high-quality pseudo-label selection. This method achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on large-scale datasets like ImageNet-1K while dramatically reducing annotation costs and computational overhead.
Problem: The prohibitive cost and labor intensity of acquiring sufficient high-quality annotated data for deep learning models.
Limitations of fixed confidence thresholds in pseudo-labeling, which often lead to either too few useful pseudo-labels or the inclusion of too many inaccurate ones.

Existing dynamic thresholding methods (e.g., FlexMatch, FreeMatch) are computationally intensive due to frequent updates and can amplify confirmation bias by using non-converged models to generate pseudo-labels.
Method: SST employs an iterative self-training framework with a novel Self-Adaptive Thresholding (SAT) mechanism that generates class-specific thresholds.

SAT updates these thresholds sparingly (once per training cycle) using a well-trained, high-performance model from the previous cycle, drastically reducing computational cost and mitigating confirmation bias.
The framework is implemented as Super-SST (offline pseudo-labeling) and Semi-SST (combining offline SAT-filtered pseudo-labels with online EMA-Teacher pseudo-labeling, also filtered by SAT).
Results: Semi-SST-ViT-Huge achieved state-of-the-art Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K, reaching 80.7% with 1% labeled data and 84.9% with 10% labeled data.
Super-SST significantly reduces threshold updates (e.g., 3 cycles compared to over 1,000,000 for FlexMatch/FreeMatch) and demonstrates faster runtime (0.1s/iteration on ImageNet-1K).

Semi-SST-ViT-Huge with 10% labeled ImageNet-1K data achieved 84.9% Top-1 accuracy, surpassing the 84.8% of a fully-supervised DeiT-III-ViT-Huge model trained on 100% labeled data, indicating a tenfold reduction in annotation costs.
Takeaways: Updating pseudo-label selection thresholds infrequently with a converged, high-performance model is critical for reducing confirmation bias and computational overhead in semi-supervised learning.
Dynamically generated, class-specific thresholds (SAT) effectively balance the quantity and quality of pseudo-labels, adapting better to model learning progress than static thresholds.

Robust semi-supervised learning methods can achieve equivalent or superior performance to fully-supervised models with significantly less labeled data, leading to substantial reductions in annotation costs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.00318.Title: Chain-of-Frames: Advancing Video Understanding in Multimodal LLMs via Frame-Aware Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.00318.Summary: Chain-of-Frames (CoF) is a method that trains video Large Language Models to produce reasoning traces explicitly referencing specific video frames. This approach enhances interpretability and achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple video understanding benchmarks, including VSI-BENCH, VIDEO-MME, and MVBENCH.
Problem: Current video Chain-of-Thought (CoT) methods lack explicit temporal grounding, making reasoning steps difficult to verify.
Generating high-quality video reasoning datasets is costly and time-consuming due to complex multi-stage annotation processes.
Many advanced video reasoning techniques necessitate auxiliary networks or complex inference pipelines, increasing computational overhead.
Method: Develops Chain-of-Frames (CoF), a method where video LLMs explicitly reference specific video frames within their reasoning traces.
Leverages the natural video encoding format of modern multimodal LLMs, such as InternVL, which interleave frames with textual identifiers.
Fine-tunes these models using a newly constructed dataset, COF-DATA, which integrates both real-world video data and programmatically generated synthetic video data.
Results: CoF-enhanced models consistently improved performance by 3.4% to 16.0% across five video understanding benchmarks compared to their base models.
CoF-InternVL3-8B achieved state-of-the-art results on VSI-BENCH, VIDEO-MME, and MVBENCH, outperforming larger open-source and proprietary models like GPT-4o and Gemini 1.5 Pro on certain tasks.
Models trained with CoF demonstrated improved accuracy in quantitative reasoning and reduced hallucination, with the 8B model using frame references in 76.9% of its responses.
Takeaways: Explicitly grounding reasoning steps to specific video frames significantly enhances the interpretability and verifiability of a model's decision-making process.
A combined approach using both real-world and synthetically generated data is effective for creating large-scale, diverse, and high-quality training datasets for video reasoning.

Modern video LLMs' inherent video encoding formats (interleaving frames with textual identifiers) provide a natural foundation for integrating frame-aware reasoning without requiring additional architectural complexity.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.00123.Title: Visual Embodied Brain: Let Multimodal Large Language Models See, Think, and Control in Spaces
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.00123.Summary: Researchers from Shanghai AI Laboratory, Tsinghua University, and SenseTime Research developed VeBrain, a unified framework enabling Multimodal Large Language Models to integrate multimodal understanding, visual-spatial reasoning, and robotic control. This approach reformulates robot control tasks into 2D visual keypoint detection and embodied skill recognition, achieving up to +31.5% average performance gains against other frameworks across diverse benchmarks while preserving general multimodal understanding.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle to extend their intelligence from digital understanding to physical interaction, lacking inherent visual-spatial reasoning and direct physical control capabilities.

Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, while designed for robot control, often compromise their general multimodal understanding, creating a 'task gap' or 'knowledge forgetting' when attempting to unify MLLMs and VLAs.
There is a lack of high-quality, unified instruction datasets that seamlessly integrate and balance diverse capabilities like multimodal understanding, visual-spatial reasoning, and robot control.
Method: Reformulates robot control tasks into text-based MLLM objectives (2D keypoint detection and embodied skill recognition) within the 2D visual space of MLLMs.

Introduces a novel 'Robotic Adapter' component that translates the MLLM's 2D text-based predictions into real-world 3D robot motion policies, comprising a Point Tracker, Movement Controller, Skill Executor, and Dynamic Takeover module.
Developed VeBrain-600k, a diverse instruction dataset integrating multimodal understanding, visual-spatial reasoning, and robot control data, augmented with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) for training.
Results: VeBrain achieved the "best trade-off performance" across multimodal understanding, visual-spatial reasoning, and robot control tasks, yielding up to +31.5% average gains against other frameworks.

The model preserved strong general multimodal understanding capabilities (e.g., +5.6% on MMVet compared to Qwen2.5-VL) while remarkably outperforming specialized 2D models on 3D spatial reasoning benchmarks (e.g., +5.2 CIDEr on ScanQAval).

Demonstrated superior robot control performance on both legged robot and robotic arm tasks, achieving significantly higher success rates on complex, long-horizon scenarios (e.g., 50% gain on 'Complex Transport' compared to baselines).
Takeaways: Robot control tasks can be effectively reformulated as text-based Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) objectives (2D keypoint detection and embodied skill recognition), allowing MLLMs to leverage their strong understanding for physical control.

A specialized robotic adapter is crucial for robustly translating 2D visual predictions from MLLMs into precise 3D real-world robot actions, addressing challenges like ego-view changes and dynamic state awareness.

Training a unified embodied AI requires a comprehensive, high-quality instruction dataset that balances multimodal understanding, visual-spatial reasoning, and robot control, leveraging Chain-of-Thought for complex tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.00103.Title: Writing-Zero: Bridge the Gap Between Non-verifiable Tasks and Verifiable Rewards
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.00103.Summary: Researchers at Quark LLM, Alibaba Group, developed a method to apply Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) to non-verifiable tasks like creative writing. They introduced a pairwise Generative Reward Model (GenRM) and a novel algorithm, Bootstrapped Relative Policy Optimization (BRPO), enabling a 'Writing-Zero' model to achieve advanced writing proficiency directly from a pretrained base model and demonstrating enhanced resistance to reward hacking.
Problem: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) is highly effective for objective tasks (e.g., math, code) but struggles with non-verifiable, subjective tasks (e.g., creative writing) due to the absence of definitive ground truth.

Existing scalar reward models, typically used in RLHF for subjective tasks, suffer from limited generalization and vulnerability to reward hacking, such as over-explanation and length bias, which degrade true content quality.

Assessing quality in creative writing is inherently subjective and lacks a single definitive reference, making it difficult to design stable and scalable RL training processes using conventional methods.
Method: A Self-Principled Critique Pairwise Generative Reward Model (GenRM) is trained using filtered high-quality human preference data, which is then fine-tuned via RL using rule-based outcome rewards and a position bias weighting mechanism to provide robust, comparative scores for writing quality.

A novel Reinforcement Learning algorithm, Bootstrapped Relative Policy Optimization (BRPO), is introduced. For a given query, BRPO dynamically selects one policy-generated response as a temporary reference and compares all other responses against it using the pairwise GenRM.
The 'Writing-Zero' model is trained directly from a base pretrained LLM (Qwen3-32B-Base) without any supervised fine-tuning, using the proposed GenRM and BRPO framework.
Results: The Pairwise Writing Generative Reward Model outperformed Claude-3.5-Sonnet and other reward models on tested benchmarks (e.g., 87.4% accuracy on RewardBench), showing robust generalization even when trained solely on Chinese data.

Both Writing-Zero (Qwen3-32B-Base-GenRM-BRPO) and Writing-R1 (Writing-SFT-GenRM-BRPO) showed substantial improvements in writing capabilities over their base models and consistently outperformed scalar reward baselines on various writing test sets.

Models trained with the GenRM+BRPO approach demonstrated enhanced resistance to reward hacking, producing significantly shorter and less redundant responses compared to scalar-reward trained models, which exhibited severe over-explanation.
Takeaways: Generative Reward Models (GenRMs) can be effectively designed for inherently subjective tasks like creative writing, providing robust, comparative reward signals where objective ground truth is absent.

A bootstrapped relative policy optimization approach enables LLMs to improve continuously by comparing their own evolving outputs, eliminating the need for fixed external references for subjective evaluations.

It is feasible to achieve advanced writing capabilities in LLMs through pure reinforcement learning from a pretrained base model, bypassing the necessity for supervised fine-tuning, as demonstrated by the 'Writing-Zero' model.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.24864.Title: ProRL: Prolonged Reinforcement Learning Expands Reasoning Boundaries in Large Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.24864.Summary: NVIDIA researchers developed Prolonged Reinforcement Learning (ProRL) to expand large language models' reasoning capabilities beyond their initial pre-training. This method, featuring KL divergence control and reference policy resetting on diverse tasks, enables significant performance gains, including average pass@1 improvements of up to 54.8% on logic puzzles, and the discovery of novel solution pathways.
Problem: The community debates whether reinforcement learning genuinely expands a large language model's intrinsic reasoning capabilities or merely amplifies pre-existing knowledge.
Prior research, often focused on specialized domains like mathematics, suggested RL's impact was limited to refining existing solutions rather than discovering new ones.
Many existing RL experiments for LLMs utilized insufficient training steps, potentially hindering the full exploration of novel reasoning strategies.
Method: Develop Prolonged Reinforcement Learning (ProRL), an extended and stable RL training methodology for LLMs based on Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO).
Integrate key enhancements like a KL divergence penalty with periodic reference policy resetting to prevent policy drift and enable continuous exploration over long training durations.
Utilize a large and diverse training dataset spanning five distinct reasoning domains to promote generalization and the discovery of new strategies.
Results: The ProRL-trained 1.5B parameter model significantly outperforms its base model and even larger 7B models across diverse reasoning benchmarks, with average pass@1 improvements up to 54.8% on logic puzzles and +14.7% on math.

Prolonged RL training enabled the discovery of novel solution pathways, achieving 100% success on tasks where the base model had 0% pass@k, and demonstrated continued performance scaling with increased computational budget (over 2,000 training steps).
The model exhibits strong generalization capabilities, showing significant improvements on out-of-distribution tasks and maintaining higher accuracy on unseen, more difficult problem instances.
Takeaways: Reinforcement learning, when prolonged and carefully managed, can genuinely expand LLM reasoning capabilities and uncover novel solution pathways, refuting prior skepticism about its limitations.
Extended training duration, coupled with diverse task exposure, is crucial for fostering exploration, consolidating new strategies, and achieving significant performance gains.
The most substantial reasoning improvements from RL are observed in tasks where the base model initially performs poorly, indicating effective boundary expansion for challenging problems.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.24760.Title: REASONING GYM: Reasoning Environments for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.24760.Summary: Open-Thought developed REASONING GYM, a library of over 100 procedurally generated environments with verifiable rewards, enabling large language models (LLMs) to acquire transferable reasoning skills. This library addresses data scarcity for RLVR training, showing that models can improve on challenging tasks and achieve positive transfer to established external benchmarks like MATH and Big-Bench Hard.
Problem: The scarcity of high-quality, diverse, and robust training data limits the advancement of reasoning capabilities in Large Language Models (LLMs) using Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR).
Existing fixed datasets are prone to model memorization and do not allow for continuous challenging or precise evaluation of generalizable reasoning skills.
Traditional data sources, such as expensive human-curated datasets or noisy internet-scraped content, lack scalability and reliability for continuous RLVR training.
Method: Introduces REASONING GYM (RG), an open-source library comprising over 100 procedurally generated reasoning environments across eleven distinct categories.
Each RG task includes configurable parameters (difficulty, structural, stylistic) for fine-grained control over problem characteristics, enabling dynamic curriculum learning.
Integrates algorithmic 'verifiers' for every task, providing automatic, objective, and verifiable rewards crucial for efficient and robust RLVR training.
Results: Frontier LLMs exhibited low zero-shot performance and pronounced 'difficulty cliffs' on many challenging RG tasks, particularly in visual-spatial, algorithmic, and graph reasoning.
RLVR training on RG tasks resulted in consistent intra-domain performance improvements (e.g., Algebra +11.7%) and strong cross-domain transfer (e.g., algorithmic training boosted algebra by +29.1%).
Skills developed through RG training positively transferred to external benchmarks, with the RG-Math trained model achieving gains of +9.7% on MATH and +7.7% on Big-Bench Hard.
Takeaways: Procedural generation offers a scalable and verifiable alternative to traditional datasets, effectively addressing the data scarcity bottleneck for RLVR in LLMs.

Reasoning skills acquired through RG training demonstrate significant intra-domain transfer and surprising cross-domain transfer between different reasoning categories (e.g., algorithmic training improving algebra and geometry).
Curriculum learning, which adaptively increases task difficulty, consistently leads to superior performance across various difficulty levels compared to fixed-difficulty training.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.24726.Title: Reflect, Retry, Reward: Self-Improving LLMs via Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.24726.Summary: Writer, Inc. researchers develop a reinforcement learning framework that trains LLMs to generate more effective self-reflections by rewarding only the reflection tokens when a model's second attempt succeeds after initial failure, achieving substantial performance gains where trained 7B parameter models outperform vanilla 72B models on function calling (APIGen) and math equation tasks (Countdown) using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with binary success/failure feedback, while demonstrating minimal catastrophic forgetting (<1% degradation on MMLU-Pro, GSM8K benchmarks) and producing qualitatively superior reflections that are shorter, clearer, and more actionable compared to verbose vanilla model outputs.
Problem: LLMs exhibit unpredictable failures and inconsistent performance across similar tasks, creating reliability issues for real-world deployment
Direct retraining on failed tasks is often impractical due to data scarcity and inability of even large models to generate reliable synthetic training data
Existing self-reflection methods rely heavily on prompt quality and external supervision rather than learned capabilities
Method: Two-stage RL framework where models attempt a task, generate self-reflection upon failure, retry the task, and receive rewards only for reflection tokens when the retry succeeds
Uses Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with binary feedback to train models on "datasets of failures" extracted from initial unsuccessful attempts
Masks advantages for all non-reflection tokens to ensure learning focuses on reflection quality rather than task-specific answers
Results: Trained smaller models consistently outperform much larger vanilla models (Qwen2-7B beats Qwen2-72B on both tasks when given two attempts)
Average performance improvements of 4.7% on APIGen function calling and 8.6% on Countdown math after GRPO training with self-reflection
Minimal catastrophic forgetting with less than 1% degradation on general benchmarks while maintaining specialized self-correction abilities
Takeaways: Effective self-reflections are shorter and more focused rather than verbose, contradicting assumptions about chain-of-thought reasoning
Training on reflection process generalizes to improve first-attempt performance even when no explicit reflection is provided
Binary success/failure feedback is sufficient for meaningful self-improvement without requiring detailed human annotations or teacher models

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.24541.Title: Mixpert: Mitigating Multimodal Learning Conflicts with Efficient Mixture-of-Vision-Experts
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.24541.Summary: Mixpert applies the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) paradigm to the vision encoder of Multimodal Large Language Models, mitigating domain conflicts by using specialized experts for different visual tasks like charts, documents, or general images. This approach achieves consistent performance gains across diverse benchmarks while maintaining high computational efficiency during inference.
Problem: Single vision encoders in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) experience performance degradation due to conflicting optimization objectives when simultaneously handling diverse visual domains.
Using multiple independent vision encoders to address domain conflicts significantly increases computational costs, memory requirements, and deployment complexity.
A challenge existed in achieving the specialization benefits of multiple encoders while maintaining the efficiency and joint optimization advantages of a single, integrated system.
Method: Mixpert integrates a Mixture-of-Vision-Experts (MoE) paradigm into the MLLM's vision encoder, comprising a shared shallow component and multiple domain-specific experts (e.g., Document, Math, Chart, OCR, General, Versatile).
A lightweight two-layer MLP dynamic router analyzes features from the shared component and employs a "score-difference" strategy to determine which specialized expert receives the input.

A "Disentangled Vision Expert Tuning" strategy is used for training, where experts are initialized from a jointly trained MLLM and then fine-tuned on domain-specific data with frozen shared components and LLM parameters, followed by separate router training.
Results: Mixpert achieved consistent performance gains across diverse benchmarks, including +0.6% on ChartQA and DocVQA, +31 points on OCRBench, and +34 points on MME when integrated with LLaVA-OV.
The model demonstrates high efficiency, adding only 237.1M total parameters, activating just 1.3M additional parameters during inference, and incurring negligible FLOPs (0.001G) overhead.
The dynamic routing mechanism proved highly accurate in classifying visual inputs to specific domains, achieving, for example, 95.2% for OCR, 94.0% for Math, and 93.7% for General images.
Takeaways: Applying the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) paradigm to the vision encoder, specifically on deeper layers and the projector, can effectively mitigate domain conflicts in MLLMs without substantial computational overhead.

A training strategy that disentangles expert specialization (fine-tuning on domain-specific data with frozen shared components) from router training preserves joint learning benefits while enabling deep domain expertise.
A dynamic routing mechanism with a "score-difference" strategy effectively directs diverse visual inputs to the most appropriate specialized expert, providing robust handling for ambiguous cases.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.24257.Title: Out of Sight, Not Out of Context? Egocentric Spatial Reasoning in VLMs Across Disjoint Frames
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.24257.Summary: This research introduces DISJOINT-3DQA, a benchmark for evaluating Vision-Language Models' ability to perform spatial reasoning between objects that are never co-visible in an egocentric video sequence. Experiments reveal that current VLMs' primary limitation is their inability to construct accurate 3D representations from fragmented visual inputs, rather than a deficiency in spatial reasoning over existing 3D information.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) struggle with reasoning about spatial relationships between objects that are never simultaneously visible in input frames.
Existing VLMs lack the ability to integrate fragmented visual information across temporal sequences to construct and maintain coherent 3D spatial representations.
Embodied AI systems need to build persistent internal 3D maps from egocentric perspectives to enable sophisticated spatial reasoning.
Method: Researchers developed DISJOINT-3DQA, a comprehensive benchmark built on Aria Synthetic Environments (ASE) with a strict disjointness constraint for object visibility.
The benchmark includes 5,399 question-answer pairs across 5 spatial reasoning categories: Relative Direction, Distance, Size, Size and Fit, and Scene Description.
Evaluation systematically tests VLMs under varying levels of 3D contextual information: 2D-only, sparse 3D (textual trajectory, BEV), and full 3D (oracle ground truth).
Results: Human evaluators achieved 93.96% accuracy, while the best VLM (GPT-4o) reached 65.60% in the marked condition, showing a substantial performance gap.
Providing precise ground-truth 3D data (coordinates, metadata) to GPT-4o led to a dramatic 18% performance increase, reaching 83.2%, indicating the core bottleneck is 3D representation construction.
Model accuracy consistently declined with increasing 3D distance between object pairs, especially beyond 20 meters, suggesting limitations in long-range spatial context accumulation.
Takeaways: Current VLMs perform significantly below human levels on disjoint-frame spatial reasoning, with the best model reaching 65.60% compared to human 93.96%.

The primary limitation for VLMs in these tasks is not spatial reasoning ability itself, but their incapacity to construct accurate 3D scene representations from fragmented temporal visual observations.
Model performance degrades substantially as the 3D distance between objects increases, particularly beyond 20 meters, indicating difficulties with long-range spatial context accumulation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.24189.Title: Fine-Tune an SLM or Prompt an LLM? The Case of Generating Low-Code Workflows
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.24189.Summary: Research from ServiceNow found that fine-tuning a Small Language Model (SLM) on domain-specific data yields 10% higher quality outputs, measured by Flow Similarity, compared to prompting large language models for generating low-code workflows. This approach proved more effective for creating structured, precise outputs in complex enterprise automation tasks.
Problem: Generating precise, functional low-code workflows from natural language requirements within enterprise systems often leads to quality issues with general-purpose models.
Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently struggle with domain-specific knowledge, strict structural output rules, and are prone to hallucinations when creating complex, structured outputs.
Deploying LLMs for high-volume enterprise tasks faces practical challenges regarding inference costs, speed, and infrastructure requirements.
Method: A two-stage pipeline decomposes low-code workflow generation into outlining and populating step inputs, enhancing manageability.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is integrated to supply domain-specific steps and database artifacts, reducing hallucinations and grounding outputs.
A Small Language Model (Mistral-Nemo-12B-Base) is fine-tuned on custom enterprise workflow datasets and compared against carefully prompted state-of-the-art LLMs.
Results: The fine-tuned SLM achieved an average of 10% higher Flow Similarity (FlowSim) for complete workflow generation, with a 12.4% advantage on out-of-domain datasets.
Prompted LLMs like GPT-4o demonstrated significant structural error rates (e.g., 17.3% on the TEST set), compromising the usability and reliability of their generated workflows.
Fine-tuned SLMs excelled at handling enterprise-specific features and implicit actions, while LLMs showed some strength in complex structural logic like `FOREACH` or `PARALLEL`.
Takeaways: Fine-tuning an SLM on specialized data yields higher quality structured outputs for domain-specific tasks compared to prompting much larger, general-purpose LLMs.
Domain-specific training data is crucial for generating accurate and reliable enterprise workflows, outperforming even instruction-tuned SLMs without such specialization.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) primarily reduces hallucinations by providing valid entities, but the majority of errors stem from the model's intrinsic logical structuring and input population capabilities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.24034.Title: LlamaRL: A Distributed Asynchronous Reinforcement Learning Framework for Efficient Large-scale LLM Training
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.24034.Summary: Meta GenAI developed LlamaRL, a distributed asynchronous reinforcement learning framework that accelerates large-scale LLM post-training by up to 10.7x for 405B models, achieving efficient weight synchronization and maintaining model quality on downstream tasks.
Problem: Existing RL frameworks lack the flexibility to support the rapid evolution and diversity of new RL algorithms for LLMs.
Scaling RL training to increasingly massive LLMs (hundreds of billions of parameters) across thousands of GPUs is bottlenecked by computational and memory demands.
Synchronous RL execution leads to significant GPU underutilization due to idle bubbles and slow data/weight communication, prolonging training times.
Method: Introduced a fully-distributed, asynchronous architecture built on native PyTorch, decoupling generator, trainer, and reward model components for independent optimization.

Implemented Co-located Model Offloading for distributed model placement and allowing flexible, independent parallelism strategies (e.g., FSDP, Tensor Parallelism) and mixed-precision (quantization) for each component.

Developed Distributed Direct Memory Access (DDMA) for zero-copy, linearly scalable model weight synchronization between GPUs, bypassing CPU memory overheads, and integrated AIPO (Asynchronous Importance weighted Policy Optimization) for stable off-policy training.
Results: Achieved up to a 10.7x speedup for 405B-parameter models, 3.98x for 70B models, and 2.52x for 8B models compared to synchronous baselines.
Reduced model weight synchronization time to just 2.31 seconds for a 405B model and 1.15 seconds for a 70B model using DDMA, significantly outperforming prior methods.

Demonstrated comparable or slightly improved training quality on the MATH and GSM8K datasets against synchronous on-policy baselines, confirming that efficiency gains do not compromise model performance.
Takeaways: Decoupling RL components and running them asynchronously drastically improves GPU utilization and throughput, especially for very large LLMs, by eliminating idle times and allowing independent optimization of parallelism strategies.
Efficient, low-latency weight synchronization via direct memory access (DDMA) is a critical component for scaling distributed RL to terabyte-scale models across thousands of GPUs.

Asynchronous off-policy learning, when properly corrected with importance sampling (AIPO), can achieve significant efficiency gains without compromising the training stability or final quality of LLMs compared to synchronous on-policy methods.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.24025.Title: DINO-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in Vision Foundation Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.24025.Summary: DINO-R1 introduces Group Relative Query Optimization (GRQO), a reinforcement-style training strategy for vision foundation models, to enhance visual in-context reasoning for visual prompting. It achieves improved generalization and robustness in object detection across open-vocabulary and closed-set scenarios compared to supervised fine-tuning.
Problem: Current Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) primarily rely on supervised training, limiting their ability to generalize robustly to novel, ambiguous, or high-variance visual scenarios.

Existing visual prompting methods struggle with the high diversity and intra-class variation of visual exemplars, leading to unstable convergence and limited out-of-domain generalization with Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT).

While Reinforcement Learning (RL) has advanced reasoning in Large Language Models (LLMs), an equivalent RL-based training framework for pure vision foundation models, especially for dense prediction tasks like object detection, is largely unexplored.
Method: Developed VIS-G-DINO, an adaptation of Grounding DINO, which enables object detection conditioned on user-specified bounding boxes (visual prompts) over reference images instead of text.
Introduced Group Relative Query Optimization (GRQO), a novel reinforcement-style training strategy that includes a query-level relative reward and KL-divergence regularization.

GRQO calculates a group-normalized advantage for all decoder queries based on their minimum matching cost to ground-truth instances, providing dense supervision, and regularizes the objectness distribution against a reference model to prevent distributional drift.
Results: DINO-R1 models demonstrated improved generalization in out-of-domain detection, achieving a +4.1 mAP increase on COCO (DINO-R1-T) and a +3.4 AP_r improvement on LVIS rare categories (DINO-R1-B) over SFT baselines.
The framework showed enhanced visual reasoning in "in-the-wild" domains, outperforming SFT by +8.8 mAP on ODinW13 and +4.4 mAP on ODinW35, indicating better generalization across varied scenes.

Ablation studies confirmed that both query-level relative reward and KL-divergence regularization individually contribute to performance gains, with their combination in GRQO yielding the highest improvements of up to +4.7 mAP over SFT in fine-tune settings.
Takeaways: Reinforcement-style learning, adapted from LLM paradigms, can be successfully applied to pure vision foundation models for dense prediction tasks to incentivize visual in-context reasoning.

Normalizing rewards across a group of queries (group-relative reward) offers a more stable and discriminative learning signal compared to absolute rewards, effectively addressing high variance in visual prompts.

Combining group-relative rewards with KL-divergence regularization to a reference model is crucial for maintaining training stability and generalizable knowledge while adapting to diverse visual prompts.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23769.Title: TextRegion: Text-Aligned Region Tokens from Frozen Image-Text Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23769.Summary: Researchers at UIUC developed TextRegion, a training-free framework that combines frozen image-text models with frozen segmentation models to generate text-aligned region tokens. This method enables detailed visual understanding with open-vocabulary capabilities, demonstrating strong performance across open-world semantic segmentation, referring expression comprehension, and multiple object grounding tasks.
Problem: Large image-text models (e.g., CLIP) provide rich global semantic understanding but inherently lack fine-grained spatial localization for specific objects or regions.
Existing segmentation models (e.g., SAM) offer precise spatial boundaries but often struggle with broad open-vocabulary generalization or necessitate extensive training.
A gap exists in efficiently bridging global image-text understanding with precise region-level spatial localization without sacrificing open-vocabulary capabilities or requiring additional training.
Method: Leverages frozen image-text models and frozen SAM2 to create text-aligned region tokens without any further training.
Employs SAM2 to generate high-resolution soft masks for distinct regions, which are then downsampled to guide feature aggregation.

Adapts the image-text model's attention mechanism by performing mask-based attention pooling over the value features of patches from the final transformer layer, creating region-specific tokens compatible with text embeddings.
Refines region tokens by removing 'global patches' that interfere with localization and integrates multi-resolution features to improve representation of small objects.
Results: Achieved superior or competitive mIoU on open-world semantic segmentation across six benchmarks (e.g., 70.9 mIoU on VOC2012 with CLIP ViT-B/16), outperforming several training-free baselines.

Demonstrated strong zero-shot referring expression comprehension results on RefCOCO and RefCOCOg, with 56.4% on RefCOCO testA and 54.6% on RefCOCOg test (CLIP ViT-L/14@336), surpassing complex baselines like FGVP.

Obtained multiple object grounding performance comparable to training-based methods in a training-free setting, achieving 42.7 gIoU and 42.4 cIoU with LLaVA-interpreted queries, outperforming Trident and LISA.
Takeaways: The attention value features from the final layer of frozen image-text models are semantically rich and can be repurposed for fine-grained region-level understanding when appropriately aggregated.

A training-free combination of precise spatial masks from a segmentation model (SAM2) and semantic features from an image-text model effectively bridges the gap between global image-text understanding and local object localization.
Transforming dense segmentation problems into a more robust instance-level sparse prediction by classifying SAM2-generated regions using text-aligned tokens is highly effective.
Mitigating global token interference and incorporating multi-resolution feature encoding significantly enhances the quality and localization of region tokens, particularly for smaller objects.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23766.Title: Argus: Vision-Centric Reasoning with Grounded Chain-of-Thought
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23766.Summary: University of Illinois and NVIDIA researchers develop ARGUS, a multimodal large language model that incorporates explicit visual attention through grounded Chain-of-Thought reasoning, using predicted bounding boxes as intermediate visual reasoning steps and a Mixture-of-Vision-Experts architecture with three complementary encoders (CLIP, ConvNeXt, EVA-02), achieving state-of-the-art performance among open-source MLLMs on vision-centric benchmarks like V-Star (78.5) and CV-Bench while demonstrating competitive referring object grounding accuracy (87.45% on RefCOCO) through a re-sampling strategy that reuses cached visual embeddings for computational efficiency.
Problem: Current MLLMs struggle with vision-centric scenarios requiring precise visual focus, relying primarily on implicit self-attention mechanisms rather than explicit goal-directed visual engagement
Existing models lack conscious control over visual attention mechanisms and do not incorporate systematic strategies for extracting relevant visual tokens based on reasoning objectives
Method: Introduces grounded Chain-of-Thought framework where the model explicitly predicts bounding boxes as intermediate reasoning steps before generating final answers
Implements directed visual context re-engagement through either re-encoding cropped regions or re-sampling cached patch embeddings that overlap with predicted regions-of-interest
Results: Achieves leading performance among open-source MLLMs of comparable scale, surpassing proprietary models like GPT-4o on specific vision-centric tasks

Demonstrates competitive referring grounding performance (87.45% RefCOCO, 80.24% RefCOCO+, 76.54% RefCOCOg) while maintaining strong general multimodal reasoning capabilities across diverse benchmarks
Takeaways: Explicit visual attention mechanisms consistently outperform implicit approaches, with re-sampling strategy offering superior computational efficiency while preserving positional context
Integration of grounding datasets during training enhances both object localization accuracy and downstream reasoning performance, demonstrating synergy between perception and cognition
Non-shared MLP projectors for region-of-interest processing improve performance by optimizing for distinct visual distributions between full images and localized object-centric regions

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23764.Title: MMSI-Bench: A Benchmark for Multi-Image Spatial Intelligence
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23764.Summary: MMSI-Bench introduces a novel human-curated benchmark to evaluate multi-image spatial intelligence in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) across diverse real-world scenarios. The benchmark reveals a substantial gap, with top MLLMs achieving only 41.9% accuracy compared to humans' 97.2%, particularly struggling with scene reconstruction and multi-step reasoning tasks.
Problem: Existing MLLM evaluation benchmarks predominantly focus on single-image spatial understanding or simple relations, failing to capture the complexity of real-world multi-image spatial reasoning.

Current multi-image VQA benchmarks are often general, not specifically tailored for comprehensive spatial intelligence assessment, or rely on automated question generation, limiting diversity and difficulty.
A lack of benchmarks capable of providing diagnostic insights into MLLM failure modes for spatial reasoning hinders targeted research and development.
Method: Developed MMSI-Bench, a multiple-choice VQA benchmark with 1,000 human-curated questions (1,990 images) designed to require information integration across multiple real-world images.

Created a detailed taxonomy of 11 atomic spatial reasoning tasks, including camera, object, and region relationships, attributes, and motion, to guide free-form question generation by expert 3D vision researchers.
Integrated a novel automated error analysis pipeline, leveraging human-annotated step-by-step reasoning processes for each question, to diagnose specific failure categories in MLLMs.
Results: Human evaluators achieved 97.2% accuracy on MMSI-Bench, while the best proprietary MLLM (GPT-5) scored 41.9%, and the top open-source model (Qwen2.5-VL-72B) achieved 30.7%, indicating a considerable performance disparity.
Models showed particular weakness in Multi-Step Reasoning and camera motion tasks, performing near random chance on some of these challenging categories.
The automated error analysis confirmed that 'overlap-matching and scene-reconstruction errors' constitute the largest proportion of MLLM mistakes, providing specific targets for future research.
Takeaways: There is a vast and persistent gap between MLLM (highest 41.9% accuracy) and human (97.2% accuracy) performance in multi-image spatial intelligence, indicating significant foundational limitations in current models.
MLLMs primarily fail due to 'overlap-matching and scene-reconstruction errors,' struggling to identify corresponding elements across images and build coherent 3D scene representations.

Both model scaling and common prompting techniques (e.g., Chain-of-Thought, visual cues) yield only marginal or inconsistent improvements, suggesting the need for architectural innovations or richer spatial reasoning data rather than just scale.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23747.Title: Spatial-MLLM: Boosting MLLM Capabilities in Visual-based Spatial Intelligence
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23747.Summary: Tsinghua University researchers develop Spatial-MLLM, a framework that enhances multimodal large language models' spatial reasoning from 2D videos by combining a standard visual encoder with a spatial encoder initialized from a visual geometry foundation model (VGGT), achieving state-of-the-art performance on VSI-Bench and substantially outperforming existing video MLLMs on ScanQA and SQA3D through a dual-encoder architecture, space-aware frame sampling strategy, and reinforcement learning training on their new Spatial-MLLM-120k dataset covering diverse spatial understanding tasks.
Problem: Existing video MLLMs rely on CLIP-based visual encoders trained on image-text pairs, which capture semantic content but lack spatial awareness needed for 3D reasoning
Current 3D MLLMs require additional 3D or 2.5D data (point clouds, depth maps) that limit their applicability in scenarios with only 2D video available
MLLMs struggle with visual-based spatial intelligence tasks including object counting, distance estimation, and spatial relationship understanding from monocular video
Method: Dual-encoder architecture combining a 2D visual encoder for semantic features with a spatial encoder initialized from VGGT visual geometry foundation model for 3D structural information
Space-aware frame sampling strategy that reformulates frame selection as a maximum coverage problem over voxel grids to identify spatially informative frames under input length constraints

Two-stage training pipeline with supervised fine-tuning on Spatial-MLLM-120k dataset followed by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) reinforcement learning for enhanced chain-of-thought spatial reasoning
Results: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on VSI-Bench, surpassing both proprietary and open-source MLLMs including models with significantly larger parameter counts
Substantially outperforms video-input models on ScanQA and SQA3D benchmarks, even exceeding some task-specific models and approaches using 3D/2.5D input data
Ablation studies confirm effectiveness of dual-encoder architecture, space-aware frame sampling, and GRPO training components for spatial reasoning enhancement
Takeaways: Visual geometry foundation models pretrained on pixel-point pairs can effectively recover implicit 3D structural information from 2D video inputs when properly integrated with semantic encoders
Frame sampling based on spatial informativeness rather than temporal uniformity significantly improves performance by focusing computational resources on geometrically relevant content
Reinforcement learning with cold-start initialization and task-dependent reward modeling enhances long-chain spatial reasoning capabilities beyond supervised fine-tuning alone

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23745.Title: To Trust Or Not To Trust Your Vision-Language Model's Prediction
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23745.Summary: A framework named TrustVLM was developed to estimate the trustworthiness of Vision-Language Model predictions by combining image-to-text and image-to-image similarity scores. This training-free approach enhances misclassification detection, showing an average 20.69% reduction in AURC on fine-grained datasets and improving classification accuracy by up to 12.7% in its variants.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) frequently produce confident yet incorrect predictions, which poses risks in safety-critical applications.
Existing misclassification detection (MisD) methods for unimodal vision models do not adequately address the multimodal complexities or the inherent 'modality gap' in VLMs.
Despite significant research on VLM accuracy, the crucial task of reliably identifying when a prediction is untrustworthy (MisD) remains relatively underexplored in multimodal contexts.
Method: TrustVLM is introduced as a training-free framework that assesses VLM prediction trustworthiness by combining the standard image-to-text similarity with an additional image-to-image similarity score.
Visual prototypes for each class are pre-computed by averaging N-shot image embeddings using an auxiliary vision encoder.

The overall confidence score for an input is derived from the sum of the VLM's image-to-text prediction similarity and the image-to-image similarity between the input image and the visual prototype of the predicted class.
Results: TrustVLM-D (using DINOv2) achieved state-of-the-art misclassification detection, yielding average improvements of 20.69% lower AURC, 4.78% higher AUROC, and 15.63% lower FPR95 on fine-grained datasets.
TrustVLM* variants, which leverage visual prototypes for zero-shot classification, boosted accuracy by an average of 12.7% on fine-grained datasets, reducing the overall error rate.

The framework demonstrated robustness to distribution shifts, proved effective with few-shot samples (N=1) for prototypes, and consistently outperformed existing concept-based MisD methods like ORCA across various VLM architectures.
Takeaways: The inherent 'modality gap' in VLMs, where image and text embeddings occupy distinct regions, can be exploited to enhance trustworthiness assessment by leveraging the image embedding space's discriminative capacity.
Specialized misclassification detection methods are necessary for VLMs, as general out-of-distribution detection techniques often perform suboptimally for in-distribution misclassifications.
Combining confidence signals from both image-to-text and image-to-image similarity leads to a more robust and accurate assessment of VLM prediction trustworthiness.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23727.Title: PixelThink: Towards Efficient Chain-of-Pixel Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23727.Summary: Researchers from Zhejiang University, National University of Singapore, and Alibaba's AD Lab develop PIXELTHINK, an adaptive chain-of-pixel reasoning framework that addresses the "overthinking" problem in multimodal large language models for segmentation tasks by dynamically regulating reasoning length based on external task difficulty estimates and internal model uncertainty, achieving a 48% reduction in reasoning tokens (46.98 vs. 90.79) while simultaneously improving segmentation accuracy (63.81% vs. 61.63% gIoU) on their ReasonSeg-DIFF benchmark through reinforcement learning with adaptive token budgets and soft length penalties.
Problem: Existing reasoning segmentation models suffer from "overthinking," generating uniformly verbose reasoning chains regardless of task complexity, leading to elevated computational costs and reduced efficiency
Current reinforcement learning approaches for multimodal reasoning lack adaptive control mechanisms, producing redundant explanations that don't improve segmentation quality
No comprehensive evaluation framework exists to jointly assess reasoning quality, segmentation accuracy, and computational efficiency in vision-language tasks
Method: Develop an adaptive token budget allocation system that uses external task difficulty scores (scene complexity, segmentation challenge, linguistic ambiguity) and internal model uncertainty estimates to determine appropriate reasoning length

Implement a soft length penalty mechanism in reinforcement learning that modulates rewards based on whether token usage exceeds the difficulty-aware budget, encouraging concise yet sufficient reasoning
Create ReasonSeg-DIFF benchmark with difficulty annotations and introduce new metrics (SAT, RST, URSS) that evaluate reasoning efficiency alongside segmentation performance
Results: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on ReasonSeg with 60.2% gIoU using significantly fewer tokens, with the 3B model matching or exceeding prior 7B models
Demonstrates consistent improvements across difficulty levels on ReasonSeg-DIFF, maintaining superior accuracy while using substantially fewer reasoning tokens than baseline methods
Shows robust generalization on standard RefCOCO benchmarks while providing interpretable reasoning chains that are both concise and informative
Takeaways: Task difficulty and model uncertainty can be effectively combined to predict optimal reasoning length, with hard tasks requiring base budget plus uncertainty-driven tokens while easy tasks need minimal reasoning
Appropriate and concise reasoning consistently improves segmentation accuracy compared to no-reasoning approaches, but excessive verbosity offers no additional benefit
The reinforcement learning framework with Group-Relative Policy Optimization successfully balances reasoning adequacy with computational efficiency through adaptive reward design

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23725.Title: MuLoCo: Muon is a practical inner optimizer for DiLoCo
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23725.Summary: Mila researchers demonstrate that Muon optimizer significantly outperforms AdamW as the inner optimizer in DiLoCo distributed training frameworks, with MuLoCo achieving 8x communication reduction through 2-bit quantization and error feedback while maintaining faster convergence than standard DiLoCo on 220M parameter transformer pre-training, establishing that Muon updates are more resilient to aggressive compression and providing the first systematic evaluation of how inner optimizer choice affects communication efficiency in distributed large language model training.
Problem: Communication bottleneck in distributed LLM training creates major scalability limitations as networks require frequent synchronization of large parameter updates
Previous DiLoCo implementations used AdamW without systematic investigation of how inner optimizer choice affects compression effectiveness and communication efficiency
Lack of comprehensive evaluation of error feedback mechanisms combined with different optimizers in communication-constrained distributed training scenarios
Method: Replace AdamW with Muon optimizer in DiLoCo framework to create MuLoCo, leveraging Muon's superior optimization properties for distributed settings
Implement systematic compression schemes including quantization and top-k sparsification with error feedback to accumulate information lost during compression
Conduct thorough hyperparameter optimization and ablation studies across different compression levels and error feedback configurations
Results: MuLoCo with 2-bit quantization and error feedback achieves 8x communication reduction while converging faster than uncompressed DiLoCo with AdamW
MuLoCo without compression matches data-parallel baseline performance while providing substantial communication savings compared to traditional distributed training
Error feedback consistently improves performance across all compression schemes, with MuLoCo showing superior robustness to aggressive quantization levels
Takeaways: Muon optimizer produces updates that are inherently more compressible and resilient to quantization compared to AdamW updates
Error feedback mechanisms consistently improve convergence for both optimizers but provide greater benefits when combined with Muon
Communication efficiency and optimization performance are not mutually exclusive when proper optimizer-compression combinations are used

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23678.Title: Grounded Reinforcement Learning for Visual Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23678.Summary: ViGoRL introduces a method that enhances visual reasoning in Vision-Language Models by explicitly anchoring each reasoning step to specific image coordinates, leading to more structured problem-solving and improved performance across various fine-grained visual tasks. This approach enables models to dynamically refine visual attention, outperforming proprietary models on some benchmarks and fostering human-like cognitive behaviors.
Problem: Existing state-of-the-art Vision-Language Models (VLMs) often operate end-to-end, producing answers without exposing intermediate, interpretable reasoning steps or adapting their strategies to task specifics.
Standard Reinforcement Learning (RL) applications to VLMs frequently result in abstract, ungrounded reasoning, failing to effectively leverage fine-grained visual evidence.
Current prompt-based methods for VLM interpretability often rely on fixed, hand-crafted prompts, limiting their dynamic adaptability for complex visual reasoning tasks.
Method: ViGoRL models reasoning as explicit `⟨textual thought, (x, y) coordinate⟩` pairs, systematically anchoring abstract thoughts to concrete spatial evidence in the image.

A two-stage pipeline first warm-starts the VLM using Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to generate diverse, visually-grounded reasoning traces for Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), followed by Reinforcement Learning (GRPO) to refine these behaviors with task and grounding-specific rewards.

A novel multi-turn RL framework incorporates an 'interactive microscope,' allowing the model to dynamically request and process high-resolution crops of predicted coordinates for fine-grained visual information.
Results: ViGoRL achieved substantial accuracy gains on spatial reasoning tasks (e.g., 12.9 percentage points over vanilla GRPO on SAT-2) and competitive performance on web grounding benchmarks, even outperforming larger proprietary models on fine-grained visual search.

Ablation studies confirmed the critical necessity of Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), the MCTS-generated warm-start, and explicit visual grounding for performance improvements and for inducing desired reasoning behaviors.

Behavioral analysis showed ViGoRL amplified visual cognitive behaviors like region exploration, grounded subgoal setting, and uniquely enabled visual backtracking, leading to human-like interpretability with 72.8% accurate coordinate references.
Takeaways: Explicitly anchoring reasoning steps to image coordinates forces VLMs to engage in a more structured, human-aligned form of cognition, significantly enhancing both visual perception and reasoning capabilities.

Combining MCTS-driven warm-starting with RL can effectively induce complex visual cognitive behaviors in VLMs, such as region exploration, grounded subgoal setting, and visual backtracking, which are largely absent in ungrounded models.

Dynamic, multi-turn visual feedback, mimicking human visual exploration, provides a powerful mechanism for models to gather and utilize fine-grained visual information, leading to superior performance on detail-oriented tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23653.Title: How do Transformers Learn Implicit Reasoning?
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23653.Summary: Ye et al. from Tsinghua University, Peking University, and Siemens AG investigate how Transformers acquire implicit multi-hop reasoning by training them from scratch in a controlled symbolic environment. They identify a three-stage generalization trajectory, showing that successful reasoning correlates with the consistent cosine-space clustering of intermediate entity representations, while challenging the assumption that functional internal states must be explicitly decodable.
Problem: Understanding the internal processes by which Large Language Models (LLMs) acquire and perform implicit multi-hop reasoning.
Distinguishing genuine internal reasoning within LLMs from mere memorization or superficial shortcut learning.
Addressing the limitations of existing research, which either lack control in pre-trained LLMs or sufficient mechanistic granularity in symbolic datasets.
Method: Training decoder-only Transformers (like GPT-2) from scratch in a highly controlled symbolic environment, extended with fine-grained query-level control and targeted omissions.

Developing novel diagnostic tools: 'cross-query semantic patching' to causally identify semantically transferable intermediate representations, and a 'cosine-based representational lens' to analyze the structural consistency of internal representations.
Systematically tracking model performance across distinct training phases and various in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) query types, including 2-hop and 3-hop reasoning.
Results: Models achieve robust generalization for first-hop OOD queries (Test-OI), which is explained by OOD-derived representations aligning with ID-based clusters, but consistently fail for second-hop OOD queries (Test-IO, Test-OO) due to a lack of query-level compositional supervision.

Cross-query semantic patching successfully localized transferable intermediate entity representations primarily at the `r₁` token in middle layers of the Transformer, with patching success rates increasing as reasoning capabilities emerge.

Intermediate representations corresponding to the same entity coalesce into tight clusters in cosine space (high ID Cohesion) during in-distribution generalization, and OOD-derived representations align with these clusters (high OOD Alignment) during cross-distribution generalization, indicating a representational unification mechanism for generalization.
Takeaways: Implicit reasoning emerges through a consistent three-phase generalization trajectory: memorization, in-distribution generalization ('grokking'), and a newly identified cross-distribution generalization.
Successful reasoning, particularly generalization, is strongly correlated with the geometric regularity and consistent clustering of intermediate entity representations in cosine similarity space.

The explicit decodability of intermediate hidden states into tokens does not reliably indicate their functional role in reasoning; representations can be decodable even before reasoning capabilities emerge.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23590.Title: Jigsaw-R1: A Study of Rule-based Visual Reinforcement Learning with Jigsaw Puzzles
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23590.Summary: Researchers from KU Leuven and collaborators explored rule-based reinforcement learning (RL) for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) using jigsaw puzzles as a structured experimental framework. They found that MLLMs robustly generalize to various visual downstream tasks after training on jigsaw puzzles, with complex reasoning patterns being pre-existing and amplified rather than emerging, and demonstrated RL's superior generalization compared to Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT).
Problem: Extending successful rule-based RL paradigms from textual domains to complex multimodal MLLMs for perception-heavy tasks.
Investigating whether explicit, lengthy reasoning is beneficial or detrimental in perception-heavy visual tasks, unlike reasoning-intensive textual tasks.
Lack of structured, algorithmically verifiable visual benchmarks with inherent ground truth for generating rule-based rewards without expensive human annotation.
Method: Adapted jigsaw puzzles as a structured experimental framework, leveraging their inherent ground truth, adjustable difficulty (m x n grid), and demand for spatial reasoning.
Implemented a two-component rule-based reward system (accuracy and format) to guide MLLM training using an on-policy RL algorithm (GRPO).
Compared "thinking" (explicit reasoning chain) and "non-thinking" (direct answer) prompting strategies to analyze the role of explicit reasoning.
Results: MLLMs rapidly learn and generalize from simple 2x1 jigsaw puzzles to more complex 3x1 configurations after training, despite initial poor performance.
Models trained on jigsaw puzzles demonstrate improved performance across various downstream visual tasks (CV-Bench, MMVP, SAT, Super-CLEVR), indicating robust transfer capabilities.
Open-source MLLMs generally perform better with direct answers ("non-thinking") in perception tasks, and an SFT "cold start" can be detrimental to subsequent RL optimization.
Takeaways: Complex reasoning patterns in MLLMs are pre-existing and activated or amplified by structured tasks and increased difficulty, rather than suddenly emerging (the "aha moment" is not observed).
Rule-based RL training offers superior generalization to diverse downstream visual tasks compared to Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) for MLLMs.

The effectiveness of generalization depends on specific puzzle configurations, with 'pair' jigsaw puzzles often yielding better transfer and larger puzzle sizes improving generalization for non-thinking models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23585.Title: On-Policy RL with Optimal Reward Baseline
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23585.Summary: Microsoft Research introduces On-Policy RL with Optimal reward baseline (OPO), an algorithm that simplifies large language model alignment by eliminating auxiliary models and explicit regularization terms. OPO achieves superior performance on mathematical reasoning tasks while enhancing training stability and output diversity by adhering to exact on-policy training and a novel variance-reducing baseline.
Problem: Current RLHF algorithms for LLMs, such as PPO, require an auxiliary value model, leading to high computational and memory overhead.
PPO's loose on-policy constraint, where data is collected with an older policy, causes training instability, large policy shifts, and an 'alignment tax' where original model capabilities degrade.
Policy gradient methods suffer from high gradient variance, and while theoretical optimal baselines exist, their practical application for complex tasks like sequence generation has been elusive.
Method: OPO employs exact on-policy training, ensuring that all data used for gradient computation is freshly sampled from the very latest version of the policy.
It derives and applies a practically feasible optimal reward baseline for sequence generation, where the baseline is a length-weighted average of the reward from sampled responses.
The algorithm omits auxiliary value models and common regularization terms like KL divergence constraints or entropy bonuses, simplifying the objective function and training pipeline.
Results: OPO consistently outperforms off-policy and on-policy GRPO baselines on mathematical reasoning `pass@k` metrics, improving accuracy beyond the initial SFT baseline.
