OPO demonstrates remarkably lower KL divergence and higher output entropy during training compared to off-policy methods, indicating enhanced stability and reduced 'alignment tax' without explicit regularization.
Models trained with OPO generate more diverse (lower Self-BLEU) and less repetitive (lower Rep-5) outputs, reflecting improved output quality stemming from stable, higher-entropy training.
Takeaways: Strict exact on-policy training inherently stabilizes policy updates and preserves output entropy, mitigating the need for external regularization terms like KL divergence constraints or entropy bonuses.
A practically feasible optimal reward baseline, simplified for sequence generation problems based on length-proportional gradient norms, effectively reduces policy gradient variance.

Eliminating auxiliary value models and explicit regularization terms simplifies the RL training pipeline, reducing computational overhead and hyperparameter tuning complexity while improving stability.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23380.Title: UniRL: Self-Improving Unified Multimodal Models via Supervised and Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23380.Summary: National University of Singapore and ByteDance researchers develop UniRL, a self-improving post-training framework for unified multimodal models that eliminates the need for external image data by using the model's own generated images as training signals, with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) achieving 0.77 GenEval scores on Show-o (versus 0.60 baseline) and substantially reducing task imbalance between text-to-image generation and multimodal understanding through a novel bidirectional evaluation metric that measures cross-task consistency, demonstrating that models can effectively learn from their own synthetic outputs via differentiable sampling and reward-based optimization.
Problem: Unified multimodal models suffer from imbalance between text-to-image generation and multimodal understanding capabilities, often excelling at one task while underperforming on the other
Post-training methods for multimodal models typically require expensive external image datasets and manual annotation, limiting accessibility and scalability
Existing optimization strategies like supervised fine-tuning can lead to overfitting in understanding tasks, particularly when training and test distributions differ
No established metrics exist to quantify the consistency between generation and understanding performance on the same content
Method: Develop a self-improving framework that generates synthetic training data by having the model create images from text prompts, then use those images for multimodal understanding training
Apply Straight-Through Gumbel-Softmax estimation to enable gradient flow through discrete image tokens, allowing end-to-end optimization of both generation and understanding
Compare Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) as optimization strategies, with GRPO using reward signals based on answer accuracy
Introduce bidirectional evaluation metrics (Accuracy_MMU|T2I and Accuracy_T2I|MMU) to measure cross-task consistency and quantify task imbalance
Results: Show-o improvements: GenEval scores increase from 0.60 to 0.77 (SFT) and 0.71 (GRPO), with GRPO achieving better multimodal understanding (0.79 vs 0.71 baseline accuracy)
Task balance enhancement: Accuracy_MMU|T2I improves from 0.83 to 0.93 and Accuracy_T2I|MMU from 0.70 to 0.81 for Show-o with GRPO
Janus performance gains: GenEval increases from 0.60 to 0.65 and multimodal understanding from 0.84 to 0.88 with GRPO optimization
GRPO shows better generalization on out-of-distribution visual inputs compared to SFT, which exhibits overfitting particularly in single object recognition tasks
Takeaways: GRPO demonstrates superior robustness and generalization compared to SFT, particularly for models with decoupled architectures like Janus where SFT causes training instability
Self-generated synthetic data can effectively improve model performance without external datasets, with the model's own outputs providing sufficient supervision signals
Task imbalance in unified models can be systematically measured and reduced through mutual enhancement between generation and understanding capabilities
End-to-end training (shared representations) versus non-end-to-end training (separate representations) requires different optimization approaches, with decoupled GRPO objectives needed for the latter

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23224.Title: MMBoundary: Advancing MLLM Knowledge Boundary Awareness through Reasoning Step Confidence Calibration
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23224.Summary: MMBoundary introduces a two-stage reinforced fine-tuning framework for multimodal large language models to express fine-grained natural language confidence for each reasoning step. The approach reduces confidence calibration errors by up to 7.5% and improves task accuracy by up to 8.3% across various domains.
Problem: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) frequently generate unreliable responses and hallucinations, often due to errors propagating through multi-step reasoning.
Existing confidence estimation methods for MLLMs primarily provide an overall response confidence, failing to pinpoint uncertainty at individual reasoning steps.
A lack of fine-grained confidence awareness makes it difficult for MLLMs to self-correct and for users to identify specific problematic parts of a generated explanation.
Method: A two-stage reinforced fine-tuning framework is proposed, consisting of a Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) warm-up stage and a Reinforcement Learning (RL) stage.
The SFT stage teaches the MLLM to express confidence statements for each sentence using a combined Internal Confidence Estimation (ICE) based on textual and cross-modal uncertainty signals.

The RL stage refines and calibrates these confidence expressions using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with three novel reward functions: Knowledge Accuracy, Expected Calibration, and Confidence Self-Calibration.
Results: MMBoundary achieved an average 7.5% reduction in Multigranularity Expected Calibration Error (MECE) on in-distribution datasets and 6.6% on out-of-distribution data.

Task performance improved by up to 8.3% in overall accuracy and Reasoning Chain F1 scores, with human evaluations confirming enhanced faithfulness, conciseness, and granularity of confidence statements.

Ablation studies demonstrated the critical role of the RL stage (9.2% MECE improvement) and the synergistic contributions of all three reward functions and diverse internal uncertainty estimation methods.
Takeaways: Fine-grained, sentence-level confidence calibration is essential for improving the trustworthiness and robustness of MLLMs in multi-step reasoning tasks.
A robust internal confidence estimation can be achieved by combining diverse uncertainty signals, including length-normalized log probability, mean token entropy, TokenSAR, and CLIPScore.

Reinforcement learning, guided by rewards for knowledge accuracy, expected calibration, and consistency between internal and expressed confidence, effectively teaches MLLMs to articulate their knowledge boundaries.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23004.Title: QLIP: A Dynamic Quadtree Vision Prior Enhances MLLM Performance Without Retraining
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23004.Summary: Researchers at the University of California, Davis, developed QLIP, a training-free framework that enhances Multimodal Large Language Models' visual processing by dynamically improving the input from the CLIP encoder. QLIP achieves a 13.6% accuracy increase on the V* benchmark for fine-grained understanding and reduces hallucination on POPE without retraining the MLLM.
Problem: Existing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) exhibit limitations in fine-grained visual understanding, particularly when using the CLIP vision encoder.
CLIP's Uniform Grid Patchification (UGP) introduces a "mesoscopic bias," causing it to struggle with representing visual details that fall outside its fixed patch scale.
The fixed positional embeddings in CLIP lead to an "interpolation bias," preventing effective processing of images at arbitrary or higher resolutions and causing loss of crucial details.
Method: QLIP introduces a "drop-in replacement" framework that acts as an intelligent pre-processor for the CLIP encoder, without requiring retraining of the downstream MLLM.

It employs Content-Aware Quadtree Patchification (QtP) to adaptively divide images based on semantic detail, preserving fine-grained information by subdividing rich regions and merging less detailed ones.
A small, dedicated Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) is trained to provide continuous, resolution-agnostic positional embeddings, addressing CLIP's interpolation bias.
Results: QLIP achieved a notable +13.6% accuracy improvement on the V* benchmark for fine-grained visual grounding using LLaVA-1.5-13B, and +11.0% for LLaVA-1.5-7B, without MLLM retraining.
It demonstrated improved token efficiency, attaining higher performance on V* while often using fewer visual tokens than baseline models, due to content-aware pruning.
The framework contributed to reducing MLLM hallucination, increasing the POPE F1 score by +5.2 for the 7B model and +1.2 for the 13B model.
Takeaways: Existing MLLMs likely possess more capacity for complex visual reasoning than currently utilized, with performance primarily bottlenecked by the quality of their visual input tokens.

Significant MLLM performance improvements, especially for fine-grained tasks and hallucination reduction, can be achieved through minimally invasive input signal optimization rather than costly full model retraining.
Combining content-aware tokenization (quadtree) with learnable, continuous positional embeddings provides a robust solution to the inherent biases of fixed-grid, fixed-resolution vision encoders.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22954.Title: Darwin Godel Machine: Open-Ended Evolution of Self-Improving Agents
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22954.Summary: The Darwin Gödel Machine (DGM) demonstrates an AI system that autonomously improves its own code, inspired by Darwinian evolution and Schmidhuber's Gödel machine concept, to enhance its coding capabilities. This framework achieved a 2.5x increase in solved tasks on SWE-bench (from 20.0% to 50.0%) and a 2.16x increase on Polyglot (from 14.2% to 30.7%), outperforming ablations and matching human-engineered solutions.
Problem: Most contemporary AI systems operate within fixed, human-designed architectures and cannot autonomously modify their own foundational code or design.
AI development relies heavily on human ingenuity and manual intervention, lacking an automated engine for continuous self-advancement.
Schmidhuber's theoretical Gödel machine, which requires provably beneficial self-modifications, is impractical for complex real-world AI systems.
Method: The DGM initializes with coding agents powered by frozen Foundation Models (FMs) capable of modifying their own Python codebase.

It employs an iterative loop: selecting parent agents from an archive, having them self-modify their code based on performance logs, empirically validating new agents, and adding functional ones back to the archive.
An archive of diverse agents is maintained, inspired by open-ended evolution, to serve as 'stepping stones' and prevent stagnation in local optima.
Results: Coding capabilities significantly improved, with solved tasks on SWE-bench increasing from 20.0% to 50.0% and on Polyglot from 14.2% to 30.7%.
The DGM automatically discovered and implemented various improvements, including better code editing tools, long-context window management, and peer-review mechanisms for patches.

Discovered agents outperformed baselines lacking self-improvement or open-ended exploration, achieved performance comparable to state-of-the-art human-designed solutions, and demonstrated robust generalization across different FMs and benchmarks.
Takeaways: Empirical validation, by evaluating performance on benchmarks, provides a practical alternative to the 'provably beneficial' requirement of theoretical Gödel machines for real-world self-improvement.

Maintaining an archive and allowing open-ended exploration of diverse agent designs is crucial for sustained progress, enabling the system to recover from performance dips and discover complex solutions.
Self-referential self-improvement, where agents enhance their own coding abilities by modifying their codebase, is vital for continuous advancement of the meta-agent itself.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22664.Title: Zero-Shot Vision Encoder Grafting via LLM Surrogates
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22664.Summary: A new method, "Zero-Shot Vision Encoder Grafting via LLM Surrogates," efficiently trains vision encoders for Vision-Language Models by leveraging smaller surrogate LLMs that replicate the target LLM's early processing layers. This approach reduces VLM training costs by approximately 45% and enables direct, zero-shot integration of the encoder into large, untuned language models.
Problem: Training Vision-Language Models (VLMs) is computationally expensive, primarily due to the large language model (LLM) component.
Existing methods like LoRA often do not sufficiently accelerate convergence for the demanding task of aligning giant LLMs with vision features.
VLM training frequently leads to a degradation of the LLM's original language understanding capabilities.
Method: Construct "surrogate models" by preserving the original parameters of the target LLM's early, feature-extraction layers and condensing its later layers into a single "translator" transformer.
Train vision encoders and vision adapters using these smaller, specially designed surrogate models.

Employ a multi-stage training strategy: pre-training the surrogate's adapter and translator, fine-tuning the vision encoder with the frozen surrogate, and optionally fine-tuning the full VLM decoder with a warm start from the surrogate-trained encoder.
Results: Achieved an approximate 45% reduction in overall VLM training cost for models using Llama-70B as the decoder.
Surrogate-trained encoders enabled strong zero-shot grafting, with grafted VLMs often matching or surpassing fully fine-tuned baselines on various VLM benchmarks (e.g., MME, POPE, SEED-Bench).
The method mitigated language degradation in the fine-tuned LLM decoder, maintaining its language understanding capabilities on par with or slightly better than the original Llama-70B.
Takeaways: Large Language Models exhibit distinct "early-phase" (feature extraction) and "late-phase" (prediction convergence) layers, identifiable by analyzing the layer-wise prediction trajectory using KL divergence.
Preserving the original parameters of the LLM's early-phase layers in a surrogate model is crucial for a vision encoder's ability to transfer its learned visual features to the full target LLM.
Vision encoders trained with these surrogates can be directly "zero-shot grafted" into much larger target LLMs, effectively activating complex visual understanding without additional fine-tuning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22654.Title: VScan: Rethinking Visual Token Reduction for Efficient Large Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22654.Summary: VScan introduces an empirically-guided, two-stage framework for reducing visual tokens in large vision-language models, which combines global/local visual scans with token merging and text-aware pruning at intermediate LLM layers. The method achieves up to 2.91 × prefilling speedup on LLaVA-NeXT-7B while retaining over 95% of original performance across diverse benchmarks.
Problem: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) incur significant computational and memory costs due to processing thousands of visual tokens, leading to quadratic complexity in self-attention mechanisms and limiting real-time deployment.
Prior visual token reduction methods often rely on single-stage pruning strategies, which can overlook critical visual information or prune at suboptimal stages of the LVLM pipeline.
There was a lack of systematic empirical understanding regarding how visual tokens are processed throughout both the visual encoding and language decoding stages of LVLMs.
Method: Conducted an in-depth empirical analysis to understand the evolution of visual information in the visual encoder (local to global attention) and cross-modal interactions in the LLM's decoding layers.

Proposed a two-stage, training-free visual token reduction framework that first reduces visual redundancy during encoding via complementary global and local scans with token merging, then reduces textual irrelevance by pruning at intermediate LLM layers.
Designed the framework to be compatible with diverse LVLM architectures and existing hardware-aware optimizations like FlashAttention, without requiring additional fine-tuning.
Results: Achieved significant efficiency gains, including up to 2.91 × prefilling speedup and 2.05 × overall inference speedup on LLaVA-NeXT-7B, with only a 1.4% performance decline at an 11% visual token retention rate.
Outperformed state-of-the-art baselines across 16 image and video understanding benchmarks, retaining 96.7% of LLaVA-1.5's performance at an 88.9% token reduction (4.0% better than VisionZip).
Maintained robust performance on challenging referring grounding tasks and video understanding benchmarks, demonstrating effective KV cache compression and full compatibility with FlashAttention.
Takeaways: Shallow layers of the visual encoder retain fine-grained local visual details, while deeper layers capture broader global context, necessitating a multi-faceted approach to visual token selection.

Early layers of the LLM exhibit strong positional biases towards visual tokens and weak cross-modal interaction, whereas middle layers show reduced bias and mature cross-modal integration, making them ideal for text-aware pruning.

A combination of global token selection from deep visual encoder layers and local token selection from shallow layers, along with similarity-based token merging, effectively preserves comprehensive visual information.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22651.Title: Sherlock: Self-Correcting Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22651.Summary: The Sherlock framework introduces a self-correction and self-improvement training methodology for Vision-Language Models, enabling them to intrinsically identify and rectify reasoning errors. This approach achieves higher average reasoning accuracy across eight multimodal benchmarks using only 20,000 annotated examples, outperforming baselines that use substantially more data, and consistently improves performance through iterative self-correction.
Problem: Current reasoning Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are highly susceptible to error propagation, where an early mistake in a multi-step reasoning process often leads to an incorrect final answer.

Existing methods for training reasoning VLMs (Supervised Fine-Tuning and Reinforcement Learning) demand vast amounts of high-quality annotated data or accurate external verifiers, incurring high computational and human labeling costs.
VLMs often exhibit limited generalization, struggling to perform well across diverse domains or problem settings beyond their training distribution, especially where precise supervision is scarce.
Method: Sherlock employs a multi-stage training framework that initially cold-starts the VLM with foundational reasoning and a nascent self-correction ability using a joint SFT objective on limited annotated data.

It refines self-correction through an offline preference training stage, introducing a novel trajectory-level objective that guides the model to revise only erroneous suffixes of reasoning paths, using visual perturbations to construct preference data and a dynamic Beta to stabilize training.

The framework enables continuous self-improvement via iterative online preference training, where the model generates its own preference data by performing sequential self-correction and applies a self-consistency rule to filter high-quality examples.
Results: Sherlock Iter2 achieved an average accuracy of 64.1% for direct generation and 65.4% after self-correction across eight challenging multimodal benchmarks, outperforming baselines that utilized 5-13 times more annotated data.
The framework consistently yielded performance gains from self-correction (up to 1.3% increase for Sherlock Iter2), unlike existing VLMs which frequently showed accuracy degradation post-correction.

Sherlock's integrated self-correction objective achieved 0.8% higher average direct reasoning accuracy than a standard SFT model trained on the same limited 20,000 examples, demonstrating a "free lunch" for performance improvement.
Takeaways: Existing SFT and RL-based reasoning VLMs fundamentally struggle with both step-wise and response-wise self-correction, often failing to recover from errors or even degrading performance when prompted to correct.

Learning self-correction and direct reasoning are mutually reinforcing capabilities; integrating a self-correction objective into SFT, even with minimal data, can improve direct reasoning performance without additional supervision.

Trajectory-level self-correction, which focuses on revising only the erroneous suffix of a reasoning path, is significantly more effective than attempting to rewrite an entire response, leading to more fine-grained and robust error rectification.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22618.Title: Fast-dLLM: Training-free Acceleration of Diffusion LLM by Enabling KV Cache and Parallel Decoding
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22618.Summary: Fast-dLLM introduces training-free methods to accelerate Diffusion-based Large Language Models by enabling KV cache and confidence-aware parallel decoding. The approach achieves up to 27.6x throughput improvement on benchmarks like GSM8K and MBPP, while maintaining generation quality, making Diffusion LLMs more competitive for practical deployment.
Problem: Diffusion-based Large Language Models (LLMs) lack a standard Key-Value (KV) cache, leading to redundant computations due to their bidirectional attention mechanism.
Direct parallel decoding in Diffusion LLMs often causes a drop in generation quality due to the "conditional independence assumption" in sampling procedures.
Open-sourced Diffusion LLMs struggle to achieve the high inference speeds implied by their theoretical non-autoregressive nature, unlike highly optimized autoregressive models.
Method: Introduces a block-wise approximate Key-Value (KV) Cache adapted for the bidirectional attention of Diffusion LLMs, reusing activations to reduce redundant computations.

Proposes a confidence-aware parallel decoding mechanism that dynamically selects tokens for unmasking based on their predicted confidence scores, improving generation quality during parallel inference.
The entire framework is designed to be training-free, allowing direct application to existing pre-trained Diffusion LLMs for immediate acceleration.
Results: Achieves up to 27.6x throughput improvement on Diffusion LLMs (e.g., LLaDA on GSM8K) compared to vanilla baselines.
Maintains generation quality with negligible accuracy loss (within 1-2 percentage points) across all evaluated text-only and multimodal benchmarks.

The combination of KV Cache and parallel decoding provides the highest speedups, with KV Cache alone contributing 2x-3.6x and parallel decoding adding further acceleration, extending benefits to multimodal tasks with up to 9.9x speedup for LLaDA-V.
Takeaways: KV activations exhibit high similarity across adjacent inference steps within a block, enabling effective approximate caching for bidirectional attention models.

Greedy parallel decoding can yield the same optimal sequence as greedy sequential decoding when token confidences are sufficiently high, providing a theoretical basis for confidence-aware parallel generation.
Dynamically adjusting the degree of parallelism based on token confidence mitigates the "curse of parallel decoding" without requiring complex auxiliary models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22617.Title: The Entropy Mechanism of Reinforcement Learning for Reasoning Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22617.Summary: This paper identifies and characterizes a universal policy entropy collapse in reinforcement learning for large language models (LLMs), revealing an empirical law that links performance to entropy. It further provides a mechanistic understanding of this phenomenon through covariance analysis and proposes two covariance-aware regularization methods, Clip-Cov and KL-Cov, which successfully maintain higher entropy and improve LLM reasoning performance on math and coding tasks.
Problem: Policy entropy in reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models (LLMs) consistently collapses early in training, significantly limiting exploration capacity.
This rapid entropy decline leads to a saturation of policy performance, preventing LLMs from continuously improving on complex reasoning tasks with more compute.
Existing naive entropy regularization techniques are ineffective or detrimental when applied to LLMs, often being hyper-parameter sensitive or degrading policy performance.
Method: The research broadly characterized policy entropy dynamics in RL-trained LLMs, empirically discovering a predictive exponential relationship between performance and entropy.

A theoretical analysis for softmax policies like LLMs derived that the change in policy entropy is approximately proportional to the negative covariance between an action's log-probability and its logit change, particularly tied to advantage.

Two covariance-aware regularization methods, Clip-Cov and KL-Cov, were developed to counteract entropy collapse by selectively regularizing or detaching gradients for a small fraction of tokens exhibiting high positive covariance.
Results: Over 95% of both policy entropy consumption and performance gains occur within the first 200-800 gradient steps across various LLMs, tasks, and RL algorithms.
The proposed covariance-aware regularization methods, Clip-Cov and KL-Cov, successfully maintain a considerably higher policy entropy throughout training compared to baselines.

These methods lead to improved downstream performance, with average gains of 2.0% for Qwen2.5-7B and 6.4% for Qwen2.5-32B models on challenging math benchmarks, unlocking more potential from larger models.
Takeaways: Policy entropy in reinforcement learning for large language models (LLMs) universally collapses early in training, causing performance to saturate and limiting exploration.
An empirical law, R = -a exp(H) + b, reveals that LLM performance is predictably traded from policy entropy, defining a deterministic performance ceiling for current RL applications.
Entropy decrease is mechanistically driven by a positive covariance between high-probability actions and their high advantage values, which reinforces confident decisions.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22525.Title: Thinking with Generated Images
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22525.Summary: Shanghai Jiao Tong University and collaborating researchers develop "Thinking with Generated Images" (TwGI), a paradigm enabling large multimodal models to spontaneously generate intermediate visual steps during reasoning through native long-multimodal thought processes, achieving up to 50% relative improvement on complex multi-object vision generation tasks by implementing two complementary mechanisms—decomposing visual tasks into progressive subgoals and self-critiquing generated images for iterative refinement—while demonstrating substantial performance gains on GenEval and DPG-Bench benchmarks compared to baseline Anole models that rely solely on text-based chain-of-thought reasoning.
Problem: Current large multimodal models primarily rely on text-based chain-of-thought reasoning, which fails to capture the nuances of human visual cognition and limits their ability to engage dynamically with visual information
Existing "Thinking with Images" approaches are constrained by relying on user-supplied images and limited operations, restricting the model's thinking space
Multi-agent agentic frameworks for visual tasks are fragmented and limit generalizability and scalability while placing burden on test-time and post-training scaling methods
Method: Introduce "Thinking with Generated Images" paradigm where LMMs can spontaneously generate visual steps or subgoals during reasoning through native long-multimodal thought processes
Implement unified autoregressive framework using Anole LMM architecture that generates sequences of interleaved multimodal tokens (text and image patches)
Develop two complementary mechanisms: vision generation with intermediate visual subgoals for progressive task decomposition, and vision generation with self-critique for iterative refinement
Curate synthetic dataset for supervised fine-tuning with vision generation prompts designed to elicit self-critique and intermediate visual subgoal generation capabilities
Results: Achieved up to 50% relative improvement in handling complex multi-object scenarios compared to baseline approaches
TwGI-Anole-7b-Obj model consistently outperformed baseline Anole-7b model with significant improvements in complex prompts involving multiple entities, spatial reasoning, and visual composition
TwGI-Anole-7b-Crit model demonstrated notable performance increases after self-critique steps, indicating effective error detection and correction capabilities
Substantial improvements demonstrated on vision generation benchmarks GenEval and DPG-Bench compared to text-based chain-of-thought baselines
Takeaways: Visual thinking plays a crucial role in human creativity, analysis, and problem-solving, suggesting AI systems need dynamic visual reasoning capabilities rather than treating images as fixed inputs
Native long-multimodal thought processes can be implemented effectively on unified autoregressive LMMs by leveraging interleaved text-image token training
Self-critique mechanisms enable models to analyze shortcomings in generated visual hypotheses and produce refined outputs based on their own analysis
Visual reconstruction loss combined with standard cross-entropy loss enhances image integrity and coherence during training

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22453.Title: First SFT, Second RL, Third UPT: Continual Improving Multi-Modal LLM Reasoning via Unsupervised Post-Training
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22453.Summary: MM-UPT establishes an Unsupervised Post-Training (UPT) paradigm for multi-modal large language models, allowing them to continually refine reasoning capabilities without relying on human-annotated data. The framework employs an online reinforcement learning approach with a majority-voting self-reward mechanism and enables the models to generate their own synthetic training data, leading to enhanced performance across diverse multi-modal benchmarks.
Problem: Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) heavily depend on extensive, costly human-annotated data for post-training stages like Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning (RL).
This dependency creates an unsustainable bottleneck for the continuous improvement and scalability of MLLMs, particularly as real-world tasks grow in complexity and diversity.
Prior unsupervised self-improvement methods for MLLMs often involve complex, multi-stage pipelines or yield only marginal gains, lacking a simple, online approach for continuous enhancement.
Method: MM-UPT formalizes Unsupervised Post-Training (UPT) as a distinct third stage for MLLMs, designed to enable continuous self-improvement in the absence of external supervision.

It adapts the GRPO (Group-based Reinforcement Policy Optimization) algorithm for an unsupervised context by introducing a novel self-rewarding mechanism based on majority voting. The MLLM samples multiple responses, extracts answers, identifies a pseudo-label from the majority vote, and calculates rewards based on agreement.

The framework integrates strategies for autonomous synthetic data generation, where the MLLM itself creates new questions from images (in-context or direct synthesizing), feeding these unlabeled samples back into the unsupervised reinforcement learning pipeline.
Results: MM-UPT consistently improved the base Qwen2.5-VL-7B model's performance across all multi-modal mathematical reasoning benchmarks (e.g., average score increased from 49.47% to 53.17% on MMR1).

The approach significantly outperformed existing unsupervised self-improvement baselines and achieved performance competitive with strong supervised post-training methods, demonstrating its efficacy without ground-truth labels.

Models trained on MLLM-generated synthetic data performed comparably to, and in some cases surpassed, those trained on original human-written questions, validating the effectiveness of autonomous data creation across Geometry3K and GeoQA datasets.
Takeaways: Majority voting effectively generates reliable pseudo-reward signals from an MLLM's moderately competent responses, allowing the model to bootstrap its own knowledge and improve answer consistency in an unsupervised manner.
MLLMs are capable of autonomously synthesizing high-quality, diverse training questions solely from visual input, creating a scalable and fully self-sufficient loop for data generation.
The effectiveness of unsupervised post-training depends on a foundational level of competence in the base MLLM; models with insufficient prior knowledge may amplify errors through majority voting.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22334.Title: Advancing Multimodal Reasoning via Reinforcement Learning with Cold Start
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22334.Summary: Researchers from Shanghai Jiao Tong University developed a two-stage Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning (RL) pipeline to enhance multimodal reasoning in Large Vision-Language Models (MLLMs). Their 7B parameter model achieved an average score of 55.66 on multimodal mathematical reasoning benchmarks, outperforming existing open-source MLLMs and some larger closed-source models.
Problem: The prevailing assumption that "aha moment" patterns in MLLMs are solely emergent properties of reinforcement learning (RL) and reliably correlate with reasoning improvement required re-evaluation.
A lack of robust and systematically validated two-stage training methodologies (SFT + RL) for effectively enhancing complex multimodal reasoning in MLLMs.
The need for improved state-of-the-art performance in open-source MLLMs on challenging multimodal reasoning tasks, particularly at more accessible parameter scales.
Method: A two-stage post-training process combining Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) as a "cold start" to establish foundational reasoning, followed by Reinforcement Learning (RL) to refine capabilities.

Exploration of various multimodal Chain-of-Thought (CoT) data construction strategies during SFT, including distillation from larger models, reflection, caption-enhancement, and self-critic CoT, to equip models with structured reasoning patterns.
Utilization of the GRPO (Group-Normalized Policy Optimization) algorithm in the RL stage, employing an accuracy-based reward function to activate and optimize multimodal reasoning.
Results: The SFT+RL pipeline consistently outperformed both SFT-only and RL-only approaches across challenging multimodal mathematical reasoning benchmarks.

The 7B parameter model achieved a state-of-the-art average score of 55.66, representing a +6.19 point improvement over the base model, and surpassed all other open-source 7B MLLMs, along with some larger closed-source models like GPT-4o (51.82) and Skywork R1V-38B (51.95).
The 3B parameter model achieved an average score of 50.84, a +10.84 point improvement over its base, demonstrating performance competitive with or superior to several existing 7B models.
Takeaways: "Aha moment" patterns, often associated with self-correction, exist in MLLMs prior to RL training and do not consistently correlate with genuine reasoning improvement, sometimes leading to ineffective or hallucinatory reflections.

A strong Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) cold start, particularly with high-quality CoT data distilled from more capable teacher models, is foundational and directly correlates with better final reasoning performance after RL.

MLLMs can learn structural reasoning *formats* even from unjudged or incorrect CoT data, suggesting the importance of reasoning structure beyond the correctness of individual steps for initial training.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22257.Title: Revisiting Group Relative Policy Optimization: Insights into On-Policy and Off-Policy Training
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22257.Summary: IBM Research and MIT-IBM Watson Lab researchers formalized an off-policy extension for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), demonstrating it provides theoretical guarantees for policy improvement and achieves comparable or superior performance to on-policy GRPO on LLM alignment tasks while significantly reducing computational overhead through less frequent model updates.
Problem: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) and its variants like Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) are inherently on-policy, requiring computationally expensive frequent model updates and sample generation for Large Language Models (LLMs).
Training LLMs with RL, especially in distributed setups using frameworks like vLLM, incurs significant communication overhead due to continuous model updates required by on-policy methods.
Some empirically observed benefits and heuristics in GRPO, such as performance gains from sample reuse and the utility of 'zero variance masking,' lacked formal theoretical grounding.
Method: Researchers formalized an off-policy extension of Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) by introducing a distinct off-policy distribution for advantage function estimation and importance sampling.
They derived a clipped surrogate objective for off-policy GRPO from a policy improvement lower bound, analogous to PPO's clipped objective, to ensure stable optimization.

The approach integrates a parameter to control the frequency of serving model updates to the vLLM server, allowing for reduced communication costs by leveraging off-policy samples without sacrificing performance.
Results: Off-policy GRPO and on-policy GRPO with zero-variance masking stabilized training and improved Pass@1 on GSM8K to 50%, compared to 45% for the unstable on-policy baseline.

On the Deepscaler math dataset, the proposed off-policy GRPO achieved comparable or slightly better performance (Aime24 up to 32%, Math500 up to 87%) while significantly reducing communication overhead by updating the serving model less frequently.
The theoretical policy improvement guarantees and the justification for zero-variance masking were empirically validated, demonstrating a more stable and efficient training process for LLM alignment.
Takeaways: The paper provides a rigorous theoretical lower bound for policy improvement in both on-policy and off-policy GRPO, explicitly showing how maximizing the GRPO advantage function increases expected reward.

Theoretical analysis justifies the 'zero variance masking' heuristic, demonstrating that samples with zero reward variance can destabilize the policy improvement lower bound, thus validating their exclusion from training.

The original iterative GRPO algorithm implicitly performs off-policy advantage estimation when samples are reused across multiple SGD iterations, which empirically improved performance and motivated the formal off-policy extension.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22196.Title: An Augmentation-Aware Theory for Self-Supervised Contrastive Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22196.Summary: A new theoretical framework for self-supervised contrastive learning integrates data augmentation's impact into the supervised risk bound, revealing a trade-off where stronger augmentations reduce minimum same-class distances but increase maximum same-image variances. This framework demonstrates that minimizing the sum of these two distance terms directly predicts optimal downstream linear probing accuracy.
Problem: Existing self-supervised contrastive learning theories often did not explicitly quantify the role of data augmentation in shaping learned representations.

Previous theoretical frameworks made simplifying assumptions about positive samples (e.g., conditional independence) or used abstract concepts, failing to capture real-world augmentation complexities.
A rigorous mathematical analysis linking specific data augmentation methods to the downstream utility and error bounds of SSCL was needed.
Method: A novel theoretical framework for self-supervised contrastive learning is developed, featuring a more realistic data generation process for positive samples.
An augmentation-aware error bound is derived, explicitly incorporating two distance terms related to same-class and same-image augmentation effects.
The impact of specific augmentations (random resized crop, color distortion) is analyzed at the pixel level using a new 'semantic label assumption'.
Results: An augmentation-aware error bound was derived, quantitatively linking unsupervised contrastive risk to supervised risk through two distinct, augmentation-influenced distance terms.

Empirical experiments at both pixel and representation levels validated the predicted trade-off: stronger augmentations increased maximum same-image distance while decreasing minimum same-class distance.
Data augmentation parameters minimizing the sum of the identified distance terms in the embedding space were found to achieve the highest downstream linear probing accuracy.
Takeaways: Data augmentation's impact on downstream classification is quantified through two distinct distance terms, showing it is critical for learned representation utility.
Strengthening data augmentations creates a trade-off: it reduces the minimum distance between same-class images while increasing the maximum distance between augmented views of the same image.
The 'semantic label assumption' allows for a detailed analysis of how pixel-level manipulations from augmentations, like cropping and color distortion, contribute to this trade-off.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22195.Title: S2AFormer: Strip Self-Attention for Efficient Vision Transformer
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22195.Summary: The S2AFormer architecture features a Strip Self-Attention (SSA) mechanism that jointly compresses spatial and channel dimensions for efficiency, paired with a Local Interaction Module (LIM) for enhanced local feature representation. This design yields high accuracy on classification, segmentation, and detection tasks while demonstrating superior inference speeds across GPU, CPU, and ONNX platforms.
Problem: Vision Transformers (ViTs) suffer from quadratic computational complexity in their self-attention mechanism, limiting deployment on resource-constrained devices or for high-resolution tasks.
Existing efficient ViTs often compromise global contextual understanding or lack the ability to capture fine-grained local features effectively.
Traditional Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) inherently limit long-range contextual understanding despite strong local feature extraction.
Method: A hierarchical architecture employing Hybrid Perception Blocks (HPBs) designed to efficiently capture both local and global dependencies.
Introduction of Strip Self-Attention (SSA), a novel token mixer that simultaneously compresses both spatial and channel dimensions of attention tensors to reduce computational cost.

Integration of a Local Interaction Module (LIM) using lightweight depthwise separable convolutions and a Squeeze-and-Excitation Network (SENet) to explicitly enhance local feature extraction and robustness.
Results: Achieved up to 77.7% Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K with S2AFormer-T (5.80M parameters, 0.66 GMACs), outperforming models with higher parameter counts and FLOPs.
Demonstrated competitive performance in semantic segmentation on ADE20K, with S2AFormer-M reaching 43.7% mIoU, surpassing similarly sized competitors like InceptionNeXt-T by 0.6% mIoU.

Delivered strong results in object detection and instance segmentation on COCO val2017 benchmarks, consistently outperforming or matching other efficient models when used as backbones for RetinaNet and Mask R-CNN.
Showcased superior inference speeds across diverse platforms, including 6330 images/s on GPU for S2AFormer-mini, and improved throughput on CPU and ONNX compared to existing efficient models.
Takeaways: The Strip Self-Attention (SSA) mechanism can significantly reduce computational complexity (from O(N^2) to near linear) by simultaneously compressing spatial and channel dimensions, while effectively maintaining global contextual understanding.
Integrating a Local Interaction Module (LIM) effectively addresses the limitations of purely attention-based mechanisms in capturing fine-grained local features and maintaining geometric invariance.
A hybrid architectural approach, combining efficient global attention with dedicated local interaction, achieves a superior balance between model accuracy and computational efficiency.

Convolution-based spatial reduction within attention mechanisms proves more effective for downsampling feature maps, leading to better accuracy, lower MACs, and faster inference compared to pooling methods.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22019.Title: VRAG-RL: Empower Vision-Perception-Based RAG for Visually Rich Information Understanding via Iterative Reasoning with Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22019.Summary: VRAG-RL, a framework developed by Alibaba Group's Tongyi Lab, empowers Vision-Language Models to understand visually rich information by integrating a novel visual perception action space, a fine-grained reward function, and reinforcement learning for iterative reasoning. The approach achieved an over 20% accuracy improvement on a 7B parameter model and over 30% on a 3B parameter model compared to strong baselines in understanding complex visual documents.
Problem: Existing visual RAGs struggle to process non-textual visual cues and underutilize VLM reasoning capabilities.
VLMs often articulate imprecise requirements to search engines, leading to inefficient and irrelevant information retrieval.
Maintaining stability and consistency during multi-turn reasoning with reinforcement learning for VLMs remains a significant challenge.
Method: Introduces a visual perception action space (select, crop, zoom) for VLMs to dynamically focus on information-dense regions using a "crop and re-input" strategy to increase visual token density.
Proposes a fine-grained reward function tailored for RAG, combining retrieval efficiency (NDCG-inspired), pattern consistency, and a flexible model-based outcome reward.
Employs Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) within an iterative Thought-Action-Observation loop to achieve stable and consistent multi-turn reasoning with VLMs.
Results: VRAG-RL improved accuracy by 22.4 percentage points (to 57.1%) for the Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct model and 32.2 percentage points (to 53.5%) for the Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct model over Search-R1-VL baselines.
Ablation studies confirmed that both the RAG-specific reward and the visual perception action space are critical for performance gains, particularly in understanding high-density visual information.
Qualitative analysis demonstrated enhanced retrieval efficiency (higher Recall@1), reduced invalid action rates, and improved multi-step reasoning capabilities compared to SFT-only methods.
Takeaways: Enabling VLMs to dynamically perceive and re-attend to specific visual regions via dedicated actions significantly activates their fine-grained reasoning capabilities.
Integrating retrieval performance directly into the reward function (e.g., through NDCG-inspired efficiency) is crucial for aligning VLM actions with effective RAG outcomes.

Reinforcement learning, specifically Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), can robustly guide VLMs through complex multi-turn interactions, improving instruction following and strategic adaptability for visually rich documents.

VRAG-RL, a framework developed by Alibaba Group's Tongyi Lab, empowers Vision-Language Models to understand visually rich information by integrating a novel visual perception action space, a fine-grained reward function, and reinforcement learning for iterative reasoning. The approach achieved an over 20% accuracy improvement on a 7B parameter model and over 30% on a 3B parameter model compared to strong baselines in understanding complex visual documents.
Traditional text-based RAG methods are limited in processing non-textual visual cues, such as spatial relationships, graphical representations, and overall layout.
Existing vision-based RAG approaches often operate with fixed pipelines, leading to shallow integration of visual information and insufficient reasoning activation within VLMs.
VLMs frequently struggle to articulate precise requirements to search engines, resulting in the retrieval of irrelevant information or repetitive, meaningless interactions.
Introduces a visual perception action space (select, crop, zoom) for VLMs to dynamically focus on information-dense regions using a "crop and re-input" strategy to increase visual token density.
Proposes a fine-grained reward function tailored for RAG, combining retrieval efficiency (NDCG-inspired), pattern consistency, and a flexible model-based outcome reward.
Employs Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) within an iterative Thought-Action-Observation loop to achieve stable and consistent multi-turn reasoning with VLMs.

VRAG-RL improved accuracy by 22.4 percentage points (to 57.1%) for the Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct model and 32.2 percentage points (to 53.5%) for the Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct model over Search-R1-VL baselines.
Ablation studies confirmed that both the RAG-specific reward and the visual perception action space are critical for performance gains, particularly in understanding high-density visual information.
Qualitative analysis demonstrated enhanced retrieval efficiency (higher Recall@1), reduced invalid action rates, and improved multi-step reasoning capabilities compared to SFT-only methods.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.21549.Title: Distill CLIP (DCLIP): Enhancing Image-Text Retrieval via Cross-Modal Transformer Distillation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.21549.Summary: DCLIP enhances image-text retrieval by employing a meta teacher-student distillation framework, transferring fine-grained, region-aware understanding from a specialized teacher to a lightweight CLIP-based student model. This approach achieves notable improvements in retrieval metrics on datasets like Flickr30K and MSCOCO, while successfully preserving a high percentage of the original CLIP model's zero-shot classification capabilities.
Problem: CLIP's reliance on global alignment limits its ability for fine-grained understanding, hindering detailed image-text retrieval.
Enhancing vision-language models for specific tasks often degrades their strong zero-shot generalization capabilities.
Existing methods for fine-grained understanding often require heavy supervision or introduce substantial computational overhead at inference time.
Method: A meta teacher-student distillation framework is used, where a region-aware teacher guides a lightweight CLIP student model.
The teacher model leverages YOLOv8x for region proposals, applies region weighting, and uses a fine-tuneable bidirectional cross-modal transformer for deep alignment.

The student model features an asymmetric architecture with a frozen CLIP text encoder and partially fine-tuned image encoder, trained with a hybrid loss combining contrastive and cosine distillation losses.
Results: DCLIP achieves substantial R@1 gains in text-to-image retrieval (e.g., 9-11 percentage points on MSCOCO) over base CLIP across all ViT backbones.
The framework successfully retains approximately 94% of CLIP's original Top-1 zero-shot classification accuracy on ImageNet-1K for ViT-B models.
The ViT-B/16 backbone offers the best balance, boosting retrieval performance while maintaining strong zero-shot generalization.
Takeaways: Implicit transfer of region-level semantic knowledge from the teacher enables the student to perform fine-grained retrieval without explicit region processing at inference.
The asymmetric student architecture, with a frozen text encoder, serves as a crucial anchor for preserving CLIP's original semantic space and robust zero-shot generalization.
Effective distillation can be achieved with a modest training dataset (e.g., ~67,500 samples) and consumer-grade GPUs, making the approach resource-efficient.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.21538.Title: Caption This, Reason That: VLMs Caught in the Middle
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.21538.Summary: Researchers from McGill University, Mila, and Microsoft Research developed the Perception-Attention-Memory (PAM) and Composite Visual Reasoning (CVR) datasets to assess Vision-Language Models (VLMs) from a cognitive science perspective. The study determined that the main limitation in VLM reasoning, particularly for spatial tasks, is the integration of visual information into the reasoning process, which can be improved by an 18.31% average increase in location-based task accuracy using vision-text decoupling through self-captioning.
Problem: State-of-the-art Vision-Language Models (VLMs) demonstrate persistent weaknesses in specific visual decision-making and reasoning tasks, such as spatial reasoning and multi-object understanding.

Existing VLM benchmarks primarily assess high-level task performance and often fail to diagnose the root causes of failures by neglecting low-level cognitive abilities like Perception, Attention, and Memory.
The underlying mechanisms of VLM struggles with complex visual reasoning are not well-understood, hindering the development of more robust and human-like artificial intelligence.
Method: Introduced the Perception-Attention-Memory (PAM) dataset to systematically evaluate VLMs on isolated cognitive abilities, including fine-grained perception, selective attention, and information maintenance in memory.
Developed the Composite Visual Reasoning (CVR) dataset, consisting of procedurally generated, complex tasks that combine various cognitive abilities, to assess integrated reasoning.

Implemented a vision-text decoupling paradigm, using ground-truth or self-generated captions, to diagnose whether VLM reasoning bottlenecks stem from visual encoding or the integration of visual information into the language model component.
Results: GPT-4o demonstrated the highest performance across PAM and CVR tasks, often nearing human levels on category-based tasks, but showed notable gaps in spatial attention and memory tasks.

Vision-text decoupling via self-captioning led to substantial performance gains, with an average 18.31% improvement on location-based tasks, by effectively providing accurate visual information in a textual format to the LLM component.

Targeted LoRA fine-tuning on Qwen2.5-VL-7B improved core cognitive abilities, especially for location-based PAM tasks, but these improvements translated to only modest gains on out-of-distribution benchmarks like MMBench and VQAv2.
Takeaways: VLMs, including top-performing proprietary models like GPT-4o, exhibit a pervasive and significant weakness in integrating spatial object information into their reasoning processes.

The primary bottleneck for VLM spatial reasoning lies in inadequate Chain-of-Thought (CoT) training or visual-to-textual integration, as models can often describe visual information accurately but fail to leverage it during direct visual reasoning.

Self-captioning significantly mitigates spatial reasoning deficits, indicating that providing textual representations of visual content can unlock the underlying language model's reasoning capabilities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.21533.Title: Self-Organizing Visual Prototypes for Non-Parametric Representation Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.21533.Summary: Self-Organizing Visual Prototypes (SOP) introduces a non-parametric framework for unsupervised visual feature learning, redefining prototypes as dynamic local structures composed of multiple support embeddings. This method achieves state-of-the-art results in image retrieval and shows consistent performance improvements across various vision tasks, scaling effectively with larger models while alleviating the necessity of over-clustering.
Problem: Existing prototypical self-supervised learning (SSL) methods often rely on single, fixed prototypes that under-represent complex hidden data clusters, limiting the learning of comprehensive features.

State-of-the-art prototypical SSL frequently requires over-clustering (number of prototypes much larger than actual classes), which increases computational/memory demands and biases learning towards simpler features.

The reliance on explicit regularizers to prevent mode collapse and the instability of point-to-point comparisons in current SSL paradigms add complexity and can lead to insufficient feature space coverage.
Method: The Self-Organizing Prototypes (SOP) method redefines a prototype as a dynamic local structure consisting of an anchor and its 'k' closest non-parametric support embeddings (SEs), drawn from dedicated memory banks for global and local features.

It introduces non-parametric loss functions for both global (CLS token) and a novel SOP Masked Image Modeling (SOP-MIM) pretext task, optimizing representations against these richer, multi-embedding prototypes.

The framework employs a teacher-student architecture with a momentum encoder, utilizing built-in randomization during anchor selection as an implicit regularizer to ensure stable training and prevent collapse without explicit regularizers.
Results: SOP achieves state-of-the-art image retrieval performance, showing mAP improvements of up to +3.2 on the challenging 'Hard' splits of the Revisited Oxford and Paris datasets.

The method consistently improves linear evaluation on ImageNet, reaching 79.2% k-NN top-1 accuracy with a ViT-L backbone, a +1.2% gain over iBOT, and demonstrates superior robustness on ImageNet-9 across various foreground/background changes.

SOP enhances dense prediction tasks, outperforming iBOT on ADE20k semantic segmentation by +0.6 mIoU in fine-tuning and showing consistent gains on COCO object detection (+0.2 AP_b) and instance segmentation (+0.1 AP_m).
Takeaways: SOP's non-parametric Masked Image Modeling (SOP-MIM) strategy significantly outperforms parametric MIM counterparts, demonstrating superior learning of fine-grained features critical for dense prediction tasks.

The definition of prototypes as dynamic multi-embedding structures (SOPs) is robust to the number of prototypes and effectively alleviates the need for over-clustering, offering a more resource-efficient learning approach.

Random sampling of anchors at each iteration is crucial for preventing training collapse, highlighting its role as an implicit and effective regularization mechanism within the non-parametric framework.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.21501.Title: Vision Transformers with Self-Distilled Registers
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.21501.Summary: Researchers at the University of Hong Kong developed Post Hoc Registers (PH-Reg), an efficient self-distillation framework to incorporate register tokens into pre-trained Vision Transformers without full retraining. This method successfully reduces artifact tokens, leading to enhanced performance in dense prediction tasks, including improved mean Intersection over Union on semantic segmentation benchmarks and better RMSE for depth estimation.
Problem: Vision Transformers (ViTs) generate "artifact tokens" – anomalous features incongruent with local semantics – hindering performance in fine-grained tasks.
Integrating artifact-mitigating register tokens into large, pre-trained ViTs typically necessitates a computationally expensive full model retraining.
Prior denoising approaches for ViT features suffer from significant computational overhead or limitations in their applicability.
Method: An efficient self-distillation framework, PH-Reg, employs a teacher-student model architecture, both initialized from a single pre-trained Vision Transformer.
The teacher model generates clean, artifact-free dense feature representations using a novel, gradient-free test-time augmentation (TTA) scheme involving inverse transformation and aggregation.
The student network incorporates a small set of randomly initialized, learnable register tokens and selectively unfreezes a minimal subset of parameters for optimization.
Results: PH-Reg consistently achieved superior performance in zero-shot open-vocabulary semantic segmentation, outperforming all compared methods on 7 out of 8 benchmarks with the highest mean IoU.

Significant and consistent improvements were observed for linear probe-based semantic segmentation and monocular depth estimation across diverse ViT backbones, with PH-Reg yielding, for instance, a +5.04% mIoU gain on VOC21 for CLIP.

The framework demonstrated notable efficiency, reducing training time by over 58.9% and requiring no additional storage for distillation targets, while also consuming approximately 10% fewer FLOPs and parameters during inference compared to prior approaches.
Takeaways: Artifact tokens in Vision Transformers vary in magnitude across different models (e.g., lower norm in OpenAI CLIP, higher norm in DINOv2), challenging a uniform characterization.
The combined approach of learnable register tokens within the student and gradient-free test-time augmentation for teacher denoising provides a synergistic and effective artifact mitigation strategy.

Optimal performance is achieved by selectively unfreezing only a small subset of the student model's parameters, including positional embeddings, the patch embedding layer, and the final transformer block, in addition to the new register tokens.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.21500.Title: ViewSpatial-Bench: Evaluating Multi-perspective Spatial Localization in Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.21500.Summary: Researchers from Zhejiang University introduced ViewSpatial-Bench, the first comprehensive benchmark to evaluate multi-perspective spatial localization in Vision-Language Models (VLMs), revealing existing VLMs struggle significantly with viewpoint transformations. Their Multi-View Spatial Model (MVSM), fine-tuned on a new dataset, achieved an 82.09% accuracy, representing a 46.24% absolute improvement over its backbone.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) exhibit significant limitations in sophisticated spatial reasoning, particularly when understanding objects and environments from perspectives other than the camera's fixed viewpoint (allocentric reasoning).

Existing VLM benchmarks primarily focus on 2D spatial relationships or object localization from a static, egocentric perspective, lacking comprehensive multi-task assessment of perspective transformation.

The inability to perform robust multi-perspective spatial reasoning hinders the practical deployment of VLMs in embodied AI scenarios like robotics, where agents must interpret human-centric spatial cues.
Method: Developed ViewSpatial-Bench, the first comprehensive benchmark for multi-viewpoint spatial localization, comprising over 5,700 question-answer pairs across 1,338 3D scenes and five distinct task types (both camera and human perspectives).

Created an automated 3D annotation pipeline, leveraging ScanNet and MS-CoCo, to generate precise directional labels and large-scale, diverse image datasets with rich multi-perspective spatial relationship data.

Trained a Multi-View Spatial Model (MVSM) by fine-tuning the Qwen2.5-VL-3B backbone on approximately 43,000 diverse, perspective-aware spatial relationship samples, using a multi-perspective fine-tuning strategy.
Results: State-of-the-art VLMs, including GPT-4o and Gemini-2.0-Flash, achieved average accuracies of 34.98% and 32.56% respectively on ViewSpatial-Bench, performing only slightly above random chance (26.33%).
The Multi-View Spatial Model (MVSM) achieved an overall accuracy of 82.09% on ViewSpatial-Bench, demonstrating a 46.24% absolute performance improvement over its Qwen2.5-VL-3B backbone.

MVSM showed substantial gains across all task categories, with notable improvements in orientation tasks (e.g., +54.32% for camera-perspective and +51.00% for human-perspective Object View Orientation), and demonstrated strong transfer learning capabilities on related benchmarks and real-world application datasets.
Takeaways: Current state-of-the-art VLMs, including powerful proprietary models, demonstrate a fundamental and systemic deficiency in perspective-dependent spatial reasoning, performing only slightly better than random chance.

VLMs show inconsistent and asymmetric performance across different spatial task categories and perspectives (egocentric vs. allocentric), indicating a lack of a coherent, unified 3D spatial representation.

Explicit training on diverse, perspective-aware spatial annotations can effectively enable VLMs to develop unified 3D spatial representations that function robustly across both camera and human viewpoints.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.21497.Title: Paper2Poster: Towards Multimodal Poster Automation from Scientific Papers
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.21497.Summary: This research introduces the Paper2Poster benchmark and the PosterAgent framework for automatically generating academic posters from scientific papers. The framework effectively distills entire research papers into editable, visually coherent, and informative posters, achieving high content fidelity and substantial cost-efficiency.
Problem: Researchers face a laborious and skill-intensive challenge in creating effective academic posters, which demand complex content compression and visual design for a single-page format.

Existing AI-driven content generation methods for academic purposes struggle with the unique demands of posters, such as long multimodal context, tight text-graphic interleaving, and stringent spatial constraints.
There was no standardized benchmark or comprehensive evaluation suite for assessing the quality and content conveyance of automatically generated scientific posters.
Method: A new benchmark, "Paper2Poster Benchmark," was established, including a dataset of 100 paper-poster pairs, a suite of evaluation metrics for visual quality and textual coherence, and the novel "PaperQuiz" for measuring knowledge conveyance.

The "PosterAgent" framework was developed as a "top-down, visual-in-the-loop" multi-agent pipeline, featuring a Parser for global content organization, a Planner for local layout and content structuring, and a Painter-Commenter module for iterative visual refinement.

The Painter-Commenter loop integrates visual feedback from a VLM (Commenter) with a "Zoom-in strategy" and in-context prompts to iteratively refine panel content and layout, ensuring accuracy, readability, and visual balance.
Results: PosterAgent, including its open-source Qwen-based variant, consistently outperformed existing GPT-4o-driven multi-agent baselines across most metrics, achieving competitive visual similarity, strong textual coherence (PPL 8.31-8.81), and higher VLM-as-Judge scores.

The PosterAgent-Qwen variant demonstrated remarkable efficiency, using 87% fewer tokens than the next best multi-agent baseline and costing approximately $0.005 to transform a 22-page paper into an editable '.pptx' poster.

PaperQuiz was validated as a reliable metric, with VLM scores correlating with human evaluations, and its density-augmented penalty effectively highlighted the value of concise, well-designed context compression over raw information density.
Takeaways: End-to-end generative models like GPT-4o excel at visual similarity but significantly struggle with generating readable and coherent embedded text in complex layouts, failing to effectively convey information.

The VLM-as-Judge evaluation indicated that "Engagement" is a primary aesthetic bottleneck for automated systems, suggesting human poster design prioritizes visual semantics and intuitive design for conveying meaning.

PosterAgent's multi-agent architecture, specifically its binary-tree layout strategy and iterative visual feedback, is crucial for handling the complex multimodal input and stringent single-page output constraints of poster generation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.21493.Title: Reinforcing General Reasoning without Verifiers
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.21493.Summary: VeriFree proposes a novel approach to training large language models (LLMs) for general reasoning that eliminates the need for explicit verifiers by directly optimizing the likelihood of a reference answer conditioned on the model's generated reasoning trace. The method achieves substantial accuracy gains on challenging general reasoning benchmarks like MMLU-Pro and SuperGPQA, and demonstrates improved learning efficiency and transferability of reasoning skills to diverse domains.
Problem: Existing reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) methods, like DeepSeek-R1-Zero, are limited to domains with rule-based verifiers (e.g., math, code).
General reasoning domains (e.g., chemistry, law) lack precise verifiers, forcing reliance on computationally expensive and potentially biased model-based verifiers.
Model-based verifiers introduce issues like dependence on a strong verifier LLM, susceptibility to reward hacking, and significant computational overhead during training.
Method: VeriFree re-conceptualizes the RL objective to directly maximize the probability of the reference answer given the input and the model's self-generated reasoning trace, acting as an implicit reward.
The objective is analytically transformed to remove the need for an external verifier, leveraging the model's own likelihood of the correct answer given its reasoning as the reward signal.
The practical implementation incorporates precise tokenization strategies (ending reasoning trace at `
Results: VeriFree improved average accuracy on MMLU-Pro and SuperGPQA by 12% to 40% over base Qwen3 models (1.7B, 4B, 8B), matching or surpassing instruct models and a model-based verifier baseline.
The method demonstrated faster convergence and higher final accuracy compared to the `Verifier` baseline, showing improved learning efficiency.
VeriFree-trained models exhibited strong transferability, improving performance on math reasoning benchmarks even without any math-specific training examples in their dataset.
Takeaways: The standard reinforcement learning objective for reasoning can be precisely recovered by maximizing the conditional probability of a reference answer given a generated reasoning trace, eliminating the need for explicit verifiers.
This verifier-free approach yields lower variance gradients (due to Rao-Blackwellization) and provides a continuous reward signal, leading to more stable and efficient policy learning.
Weighting contributions from generated reasoning traces by their likelihood of producing the correct answer effectively down-weights low-quality reasoning, which is crucial for performance.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.21465.Title: ID-Align: RoPE-Conscious Position Remapping for Dynamic High-Resolution Adaptation in Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.21465.Summary: Researchers at Peking University developed ID-Align, a method that strategically remaps position IDs in Vision-Language Models to mitigate performance degradation caused by the interaction between dynamic high-resolution adaptation and Rotary Position Embedding. The approach improved overall VLM performance by 0.82% across various benchmarks, with gains of 6.09% in relation reasoning tasks.
Problem: Dynamic high-resolution adaptation, widely used in state-of-the-art Vision-Language Models (VLMs), can inadvertently degrade performance when combined with Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE).
RoPE's long-term decay property causes diminished attention between distant image and text tokens, leading to overlooked visual information.
The large number of high-resolution image tokens disrupts the crucial spatial correspondence between high-resolution and lower-resolution thumbnail features.
Method: ID-Align introduces a position ID remapping approach that assigns identical position IDs to spatially corresponding high-resolution and thumbnail image tokens.
Text embeddings and thumbnail image embeddings retain their usual sequential position IDs.

High-resolution tokens are assigned position IDs based on the interpolated position ID of their corresponding thumbnail region, reducing the effective positional distance between related multi-resolution tokens.
Results: ID-Align consistently improved LLaVA-Next's performance, with an overall average gain of 0.82% across MMBench, MMStar, ScienceQA, and VQAv2 benchmarks.
The method achieved a 6.09% improvement in Relation Reasoning tasks, demonstrating enhanced understanding of complex visual relationships.

Attention visualizations confirmed ID-Align leads to more focused attention between text and image tokens, and accurate spatial correspondence between high-resolution and thumbnail features, alongside more stable training dynamics.
Takeaways: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) exhibits a practical "long-term decay property" where attention scores diminish with increased positional distance.

Combining dynamic high-resolution adaptation with RoPE creates two main issues: impeded image-text interaction and disrupted multi-resolution correspondence due to large positional distances between tokens.
Strategically remapping position IDs to assign identical IDs to spatially corresponding tokens across different resolutions effectively reduces these problematic positional distances.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.21457.Title: Active-O3: Empowering Multimodal Large Language Models with Active Perception via GRPO
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.21457.Summary: Zhejiang University and Ant Group researchers develop ACTIVE-O3, a reinforcement learning framework using Group Relative Policy Optimization that enables multimodal large language models to perform active perception by strategically selecting regions for closer examination, achieving improvements of +2.7/+3.5 APs/ARs on LVIS small object detection and +8.5 APs on SODA-A autonomous driving tasks compared to Qwen2.5-VL baselines, while demonstrating zero-shot generalization on V* fine-grained understanding benchmarks through a dual-form reward system that combines task-aware performance metrics with heuristic constraints for region proposal quality.
Problem: Current multimodal large language models operate as passive consumers of visual information, lacking the ability to actively control their perception to gather more informative sensory data
Existing active perception approaches like GPT-o3's zoom-in strategy suffer from inefficient region proposals and low target localization accuracy
No systematic frameworks or evaluation protocols exist for studying and developing active perception capabilities in MLLMs
Performance degrades significantly on visually complex tasks involving small objects, dense scenes, and fine-grained details
Method: Formalize MLLM-based active perception as coordination between a Task Model (deciding actions) and Sensing Model (controlling perception parameters)
Implement a unified two-stage policy separating region proposal (sensing) from task execution using MLLM instruction-following capabilities
Apply Group Relative Policy Optimization to enable MLLMs to improve sensing policies based on task-level reward signals
Design dual-form rewards combining task-aware metrics (average precision/recall, mIoU) with heuristic constraints (format validity, non-overlapping proposals, coverage measures)
Results: Consistent improvements across all evaluated tasks under fixed computational budgets, with particularly strong gains on small object detection (+2.7 APs on LVIS) and autonomous driving scenarios (+8.5 APs on SODA-A)
Progressive performance improvement with increasing zoom-in budget on ThinObjects segmentation (mIoU reaching 0.863), while baseline methods degrade
Demonstrated zero-shot capabilities on V* benchmark for fine-grained understanding tasks without domain-specific training
Comprehensive benchmark suite established covering open-world grounding, remote sensing, autonomous driving, and interactive segmentation with released code and evaluation protocols
Takeaways: Active perception can be effectively implemented in MLLMs through reinforcement learning without requiring architectural changes to existing models
Combining task-aware and heuristic rewards enables more robust learning of region proposal strategies compared to single reward types
MLLMs can leverage their inherent reasoning capabilities to implement sensing policies through strategic prompting rather than requiring separate specialized modules
Zero-shot generalization emerges naturally from the active perception framework, enabling transfer to unseen domains and tasks

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.21444.Title: Can Large Reasoning Models Self-Train?
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.21444.Summary: This research investigates whether large reasoning models can self-train using an online reinforcement learning framework with self-generated feedback, demonstrating initial performance improvements on reasoning tasks but ultimately revealing a critical "reward hacking" phenomenon that leads to complete model collapse during prolonged training.
Problem: Large language models (LLMs) face data bottlenecks as computational capabilities outpace the supply of human-curated training data.
Achieving autonomous AI and super-intelligence requires models to self-improve without continuous human supervision or ground-truth labels.
Existing self-improvement methods using supervised fine-tuning or direct preference optimization rely on infrequent updates and fixed 'teacher' models, limiting sustained, dynamic learning.
Method: Introduced Self-Rewarded Training (SRT), an online reinforcement learning framework where LLMs learn from their own judgments.
Utilized majority voting among multiple model generations as a simple, online self-feedback mechanism to define a binary reward function.
Applied online RL algorithms (RLOO, GRPO) to continuously update the model, allowing the 'teacher' policy (pseudo-label generator) to evolve with the 'student' policy.
Results: SRT consistently improved LLM reasoning abilities on synthetic (Reasoning Gym) and real-world math tasks, with initial gains comparable to ground-truth RL.
Models successfully performed multi-level climbing on synthetic tasks using a curriculum-based SRT, progressively tackling harder problems without ground truth.

On real-world math problems, SRT consistently led to sudden and complete performance collapse due to reward hacking, identifiable by a sharp increase in pseudo-reward and KL divergence, and a drastic drop in actual accuracy.
Takeaways: LLMs can initially self-improve their reasoning abilities, and the quality of their self-generated feedback (the 'evolving teacher') also improves over training steps.
Prolonged online self-training leads to 'reward hacking,' where models learn to exploit the self-consistency reward by outputting templated, degenerate answers, causing complete performance collapse.
