The collapse mechanism is robust across different RL algorithms and hyperparameters, highlighting a fundamental challenge in designing robust self-supervision for continuous learning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20802.Title: Leaner Transformers: More Heads, Less Depth
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20802.Summary: This research demonstrates that many existing transformer models are unnecessarily large, proposing that depth can be traded for an increased number of attention heads to create more efficient architectures. The work establishes theoretically that multi-head attention improves optimization stability by enhancing conditioning and empirically shows up to 54% parameter reductions while maintaining or improving performance across various vision and language tasks.
Problem: The prevailing 'bigger is better' philosophy in transformer design leads to increasingly large and often oversized models, resulting in high computational costs and resource demands.
Lack of a clear understanding of the architectural components' impact on optimization stability and efficiency beyond simple scaling of depth and width.
Many existing transformer models consume excessive parameters and memory without a clear justification for their depth, contributing to sustainability concerns.
Method: The research proposes a 'more heads, less depth' design principle for transformers, suggesting that depth can be traded for additional attention heads to create more parameter-efficient models.
A theoretical framework is developed demonstrating that increasing the number of attention heads significantly improves the conditioning of attention blocks, thereby stabilizing optimization.

Systematic architectural modifications were applied to established transformer models, increasing attention heads while decreasing layers, and then empirically validated across diverse tasks and architectures.
Results: Modified ViT-B models with 8 layers and 12+ heads matched or surpassed the original 12-layer ViT-B's 80.1% ImageNet-1k accuracy while reducing parameters by 22-29%.
Extreme depth reduction to 4-layer ViT-B with 28 heads achieved 80.1% accuracy using only 42.5 million parameters, a 51% reduction from the original 86.6 million.

Across various vision (DeiT, XCiT, TNT, VOLO, DaViT) and language (BERT on GLUE, GPT-2 on TinyStories) models, the approach consistently yielded 21-54% parameter reductions and 22-43% memory savings while maintaining or improving performance.
Takeaways: Multi-head attention acts as an implicit conditioning mechanism, improving the optimization stability of transformer layers by reducing the condition number of attention matrices.

When multi-head attention matrices are composed of independent Gaussian random variables, increasing the number of heads approaches a condition number of 1, facilitating more stable gradient-based optimization.
Many current transformer architectures are unnecessarily oversized, and depth can be effectively traded for an increased number of attention heads without sacrificing performance.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20753.Title: Understand, Think, and Answer: Advancing Visual Reasoning with Large Multimodal Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20753.Summary: Researchers from CASIA and collaborators developed Griffon-R, an LMM incorporating a unified "understand-think-answer" mechanism for compositional visual reasoning. The model achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on benchmarks like CLEVR (63.7%), VSR (70.9%), and V-Star Spat. (77.6%), while demonstrating a 13x speedup over toolkit-based methods and reducing object hallucination to 89.3% accuracy on POPE.
Problem: Current Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) exhibit deficiencies in compositional visual reasoning, often resorting to "shortcut learning" that leads to unfaithful responses.
Existing Chain-of-Thought (CoT) methods are often task-specific and require multiple inference passes, reducing efficiency.
Toolkit-based approaches for visual reasoning introduce significant computational load and latency by relying on external expert models.
Method: A unified "Understand-Think-Answer" visual reasoning mechanism that enables LMMs to sequentially perform complex reasoning within a single forward pass.
A semi-automatic expert-supervised data engine to curate a large-scale (334K samples) visual reasoning dataset aligned with the "understand-think-answer" paradigm.
The Griffon-R model, built on a high-resolution single-branch architecture (Griffon v2 backbone with Gemma9B LLM), trained with the specialized data to intrinsically learn the reasoning process.
Results: Griffon-R achieved state-of-the-art accuracy on compositional visual reasoning benchmarks, including 63.7% on CLEVR, 70.9% on VSR, and 77.6% on V-Star Spat.
The model demonstrated comprehensive multimodal capabilities with a top score of 79.0 on MMBench and 87.0% on ScienceQA, while also reducing object hallucination to 89.3% on POPE.
The unified reasoning mechanism provided a 13x speedup over toolkit-based reasoning methods, with an inference time of 0.336s per sample.
Takeaways: LMMs can achieve human-like compositional visual reasoning intrinsically and efficiently in a single forward pass, without relying on external tools or multiple inference steps.
Training with a meticulously curated, mechanism-aligned dataset is essential for developing robust and accurate visual reasoning capabilities in LMMs.
Explicitly guiding LMMs through a structured "understand-think-answer" process significantly reduces object hallucination and leads to more faithful responses.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20686.Title: Accelerating RL for LLM Reasoning with Optimal Advantage Regression
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20686.Summary: Cornell University and Princeton University researchers develop A*-PO (Policy Optimization via Optimal Advantage Regression), a two-stage reinforcement learning framework that achieves up to 2× faster training and 30% lower memory usage compared to PPO and GRPO by eliminating explicit critic networks and requiring only single generations per prompt during online training, while maintaining competitive performance on mathematical reasoning benchmarks like GSM8K and MATH through offline optimal value function estimation followed by simplified advantage regression.
Problem: Current RL methods for LLM fine-tuning (PPO, GRPO, REBEL) require computationally expensive multiple generations per prompt or explicit critic networks during online training
High memory consumption from managing critic networks or concurrent generations limits scalability to larger models and longer contexts
Complex algorithmic designs with clipping mechanisms and normalization heuristics increase implementation difficulty and hyperparameter sensitivity
Method: Two-stage approach: offline estimation of optimal value function V* using reference policy samples, followed by online policy updates via advantage regression
Single generation per prompt during online training eliminates computational overhead of multiple concurrent generations
Direct optimal advantage approximation removes need for explicit critic networks while simplifying algorithm design
Optional filtering of unsolvable problems further reduces training time by focusing on learnable examples
Results: 2× faster training time than PPO/GRPO across Qwen2.5 models (1.5B, 3B, 7B) on GSM8K and MATH datasets while achieving competitive accuracy
Over 30% reduction in peak memory usage compared to baselines, with smallest KL divergence to reference policy indicating better knowledge preservation
Superior performance on long-context reasoning tasks (16,384 tokens) and strong generalization to out-of-domain benchmarks like OlympiadBench and AMC 2023
Ablation studies show performance plateaus at N=8 offline samples with optional problem filtering reducing training time by 28% while maintaining accuracy
Takeaways: Optimal value function can be accurately estimated offline using reference policy samples, decoupling expensive value estimation from online policy updates
Theoretical guarantees show near-optimal performance with polynomial sample complexity without requiring sophisticated exploration mechanisms
Bias in value function estimation is well-controlled and decreases with more offline samples, with 8 samples typically sufficient for good performance
Single-generation online updates combined with simplified regression loss achieve comparable or superior performance to complex multi-generation methods

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20612.Title: Roboflow100-VL: A Multi-Domain Object Detection Benchmark for Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20612.Summary: Researchers from Roboflow and Carnegie Mellon University introduce Roboflow100-VL (RF100-VL), a multi-domain object detection benchmark designed to evaluate Vision-Language Models' generalization to out-of-distribution concepts and diverse imaging modalities. The benchmark, which includes multi-modal annotation instructions, reveals that state-of-the-art VLMs exhibit significantly reduced performance, with zero-shot accuracy below 2% on some medical imaging datasets.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language Model (VLM) benchmarks primarily focus on common objects, failing to rigorously assess generalization to out-of-distribution (OOD) concepts, tasks, or imaging modalities found in real-world scenarios.

Many current VLM benchmarks emphasize visual question answering (VQA) or common sense reasoning rather than thoroughly evaluating fine-grained object detection capabilities in novel or specialized contexts.

Models trained on internet-scale data often struggle with rare concepts, scientific names, context-dependent classes, or non-standard imaging (e.g., X-rays, thermal), due to the long-tail distribution of pre-training data.
Method: Developed Roboflow100-VL, a large-scale benchmark of 100 object detection datasets (564 classes, 164,149 images, >1.3M annotations) from Roboflow Universe, specifically curated for novelty and OOD challenges across diverse domains like medical, industrial, and aerial.

Generated multi-modal annotation instructions for each dataset, comprising a few visual examples and rich textual descriptions per class, using GPT-4o with subsequent human refinement, to guide concept alignment for models.

Conducted comprehensive evaluations of state-of-the-art open-vocabulary detectors and multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) across zero-shot, few-shot, semi-supervised, and fully-supervised learning regimes.
Results: State-of-the-art models like GroundingDINO showed a considerable mAP reduction from 49.2 on ODinW-13 to 15.7 on RF100-VL, with medical imaging datasets yielding less than 2% zero-shot accuracy.
Specialized open-vocabulary detectors achieved higher performance than generalist MLLMs (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL 72B), which often performed worse than smaller specialist models in zero-shot settings.

Few-shot fine-tuning of GroundingDINO outperformed YOLO variants by over 10% mAP, and semi-supervised learning techniques achieved comparable or superior performance with only 10% of labeled data, demonstrating data efficiency.
Takeaways: Roboflow100-VL presents a substantially more challenging evaluation for VLM generalization than existing benchmarks, exposing significant performance drops for state-of-the-art models on OOD concepts.

Specialized open-vocabulary object detectors consistently outperform generalist Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) in object detection, as MLLMs struggle to effectively leverage the rich multi-modal annotation instructions provided.

Few-shot learning through fine-tuning, particularly for models like GroundingDINO, demonstrates greater efficiency in learning new concepts compared to in-context prompting, indicating that large-scale pre-training aids efficient adaptation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20561.Title: Beyond Markovian: Reflective Exploration via Bayes-Adaptive RL for LLM Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20561.Summary: Researchers from Northwestern University and Google DeepMind developed Bayes-Adaptive RL for LLM Reasoning (BARL), a framework that uses Bayesian reinforcement learning to enable principled reflective exploration in large language models. BARL achieved higher pass@1 accuracies on mathematical reasoning benchmarks while reducing token usage by up to 1.63x compared to progress baselines and 2x against GRPO.
Problem: Conventional Reinforcement Learning (RL) policies for Large Language Models (LLMs) are Markovian, which inherently prevents principled reflective exploration or adaptation based on past reasoning attempts.
The observed self-reflection behavior in RL-trained LLMs lacked a formal theoretical explanation for its emergence, consistency, or benefits within existing frameworks.
Standard RL approaches confine exploration to the training phase, failing to incentivize adaptive, information-gathering behaviors during test time.
Method: Introduced a Bayesian Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework that models epistemic uncertainty about the environment to formally ground reflective exploration in LLMs.
Developed Bayes-Adaptive RL for LLM Reasoning (BARL), an algorithm that optimizes for Bayes-expected return by maintaining a posterior distribution over candidate MDP hypotheses.
BARL provides explicit step-level guidance for LLMs to adapt strategies, using observed rewards to update beliefs and signal when to switch approaches through consistency-based penalties.
Results: BARL consistently surpassed conventional RL baselines (GRPO and progress-reward) with higher pass@1 accuracies across various LLMs and challenging mathematical reasoning tasks.
The method showed substantial token efficiency improvements, using up to 1.63x fewer tokens than progress baselines and 2x fewer than GRPO for superior performance.
BARL exhibited improved generalization capabilities on synthetic problems, adaptively discovering optimal strategies, unlike conventional RL which merely memorized training solutions.
Takeaways: Optimal policies derived from conventional Reinforcement Learning are Markovian, preventing principled reflective exploration and often leading to memorized solutions that generalize poorly.

Bayesian Reinforcement Learning naturally yields uncertainty-adaptive policies that are inherently incentivized to perform information-gathering actions, thereby inducing genuine reflective exploration.
Effective self-reflection in LLMs is tied to the quality and efficiency of token usage for exploration, rather than a mere high frequency of reflection-related phrases.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20444.Title: HoPE: Hybrid of Position Embedding for Long Context Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20444.Summary: Researchers from Carnegie Mellon University and Xiaohongshu Inc. developed HoPE, a hybrid position embedding approach for Vision-Language Models that theoretically and empirically improves long video understanding. HoPE integrates a theoretically-backed frequency allocation strategy and dynamic temporal scaling, achieving up to 22.23% higher accuracy on the V-NIAH benchmark compared to prior methods.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) experience performance degradation when processing long video contexts due to the difficulty of modeling intricate spatial-temporal dependencies across extended sequences.
Existing 1D Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE), designed for text, distorts spatial-temporal locality when directly applied to complex 3D visual data like flattened video patches.
Current multimodal RoPE extensions rely on heuristic frequency allocation strategies, lacking theoretical guarantees for reliably preserving semantic similarities over long contexts.
Method: Proposed a Hybrid Frequency Allocation (HFA) strategy that assigns higher frequencies to spatial components and critically sets the lowest frequencies for the temporal component to zero, maximizing the 'semantic preference' guarantee.
Introduced a Dynamic Temporal Scaling (DTS) mechanism that trains VLMs with a multi-scale set of temporal scaling factors to enhance robustness to varying video speeds and enable flexible inference.
Conducted a theoretical analysis demonstrating that setting temporal frequencies to zero within RoPE provides the strongest foundation for preserving semantic similarity over long temporal distances.
Results: HoPE consistently outperformed vanilla RoPE and other multimodal RoPE variants (M-RoPE, VideoRoPE) across long video understanding benchmarks, with improvements up to 4.05% for the 7B model at 32k context length.
Achieved superior extrapolation capabilities on the V-NIAH (Visual Needle-In-A-Haystack) benchmark, demonstrating a 22.23% higher accuracy (63.56% vs 52.00%) compared to the best baseline.
Ablation studies confirmed that both the Hybrid Frequency Allocation (HFA) and Dynamic Temporal Scaling (DTS) components individually contributed to HoPE's improved performance and robustness.
Takeaways: Directly applying 1D RoPE to flattened video tokens distorts their inherent 3D spatial-temporal locality.

Existing multimodal RoPE frequency allocation strategies are unreliable for maintaining 'semantic preference' over long contexts, as even low frequencies can cause arbitrary rotations that obscure semantic similarities.

Setting temporal frequencies to zero in a hybrid RoPE design maximizes the semantic preference guarantee, offering a theoretically sound method to preserve long-range semantic understanding in videos.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20289.Title: VisualToolAgent (VisTA): A Reinforcement Learning Framework for Visual Tool Selection
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20289.Summary: A research team from the University of Wisconsin-Madison and collaborators developed VisualToolAgent (VisTA), a reinforcement learning framework that enables visual agents to autonomously select and combine external tools to assist a frozen visual-language model. This method improved accuracy on visual reasoning benchmarks, notably achieving a 6.4-point gain on out-of-distribution ChartQA, and demonstrated the ability to transfer its tool-selection policy to stronger reasoning models like GPT-4o without requiring retraining.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are limited by static knowledge and cannot dynamically access external information or specialized computational resources.
Existing tool augmentation methods rely on static prompting or labor-intensive fine-tuning, struggling with diverse tool libraries or adapting to tools with unknown capabilities.
Current systems lack the ability to autonomously explore, select, or adapt tool choices based on query characteristics and empirical performance in complex visual reasoning tasks.
Method: VisTA introduces an end-to-end Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework that trains an autonomous agent (a VLM) to dynamically select sequences of external visual tools.
The agent's selected tool outputs are used to augment the input prompt for a *fixed, frozen* visual-language reasoner, allowing for modularity and transferability.

A novel task-specific reward function guides the RL optimization, penalizing tool selections that degrade performance while rewarding those that improve or maintain accuracy, even for redundant correct predictions.
Results: VisTA achieved substantial accuracy gains: 79.4% on ChartQA (3.0 points over baseline) and 73.2% on ChartQA-OoD (6.4 points over baseline) with QwenVL-7B as the reasoner.

The learned tool-selection policy demonstrated transferability to GPT-4o, improving performance to 88.9% on ChartQA and 76.8% on ChartQA-OoD (3.5 points over GPT-4o baselines in both cases) without additional training.

The agent's tool usage frequency significantly correlated with tool performance (Pearson correlation increased to over 0.8 during training), empirically demonstrating adaptive learning and preference for effective tools over less useful ones.
Takeaways: Reinforcement learning enables visual agents to empirically discover effective tool-selection policies, including synergistic combinations, without relying on extensive human supervision or detailed tool descriptions.
Decoupling the tool-selection policy from the core reasoning model allows the learned policy to be transferred zero-shot to more powerful, un-retrained reasoners (e.g., from QwenVL-7B to GPT-4o).

Strategic and adaptive tool selection, learned through RL feedback, consistently outperforms fixed integration of all available tools or random tool choices, as extraneous information can confuse the reasoning model.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20279.Title: VLM-3R: Vision-Language Models Augmented with Instruction-Aligned 3D Reconstruction
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20279.Summary: VLM-3R enhances Vision-Language Models' spatial and spatio-temporal reasoning by implicitly integrating 3D reconstruction directly from monocular video input. The framework achieves leading performance on static 3D spatial reasoning benchmarks and a newly introduced temporal 3D reasoning benchmark, VSTemporalI-Bench.
Problem: Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) primarily rely on 2D visual encodings, which leads to difficulties in tasks requiring deep 3D spatial reasoning and geometric understanding.

Prior 3D-aware LMMs either depend on specialized hardware (RGB-D sensors), limiting their scalability, or employ multi-stage explicit 3D reconstruction pipelines that are prone to errors and lack efficient 3D feature encoders.
Existing spatial reasoning datasets are often small-scale, limiting the comprehensive training and evaluation of robust spatial intelligence in LMMs.
Method: Introduces VLM-3R, a unified framework that leverages a pre-trained end-to-end 3D reconstruction model (CUT3R) to implicitly derive 3D feature and camera view tokens directly from monocular video.

Employs a Spatial-Visual-View Fusion mechanism to integrate these 3D tokens with 2D visual tokens and language instructions into the VLM's latent space, with only a few learnable layers efficiently fine-tuned.
Curates large-scale, automatically generated instruction-aligned 3D spatial (over 200K QA pairs) and spatio-temporal (VSTemporalI-Bench, ~138.6K QA pairs) datasets for training and evaluation.
Results: VLM-3R achieves state-of-the-art performance on the VSI-Bench for static spatial reasoning, outperforming open-source and proprietary models, particularly in tasks like Absolute Distance (49.4% MRA) and Object Size (69.2% MRA).

The framework demonstrates leading performance on the newly introduced VSTemporalI-Bench, excelling in temporal 3D reasoning tasks such as Camera Displacement (39.4% MRA) and Camera-Object Relative Distance (86.5% accuracy).
Ablation studies confirm the crucial role of both 3D geometry and camera tokens fusion, as their removal consistently degrades performance across various spatial reasoning tasks.
Takeaways: Implicit 3D reconstruction and latent 3D token integration from monocular video can effectively provide spatial context to VLMs without relying on external sensors or explicit, multi-stage pipelines.

Fusing 2D visual tokens with separate 3D geometric and camera view tokens through a cross-attention mechanism enables the VLM to learn a unified representation of visual appearance, camera perspective, and global 3D geometry.
Large-scale, automatically generated instruction-aligned QA datasets derived from 3D environments are critical for developing robust spatial and spatio-temporal reasoning in VLMs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20258.Title: ARM: Adaptive Reasoning Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20258.Summary: The Adaptive Reasoning Model (ARM) enables large reasoning models to adaptively select appropriate reasoning formats based on task difficulty, reducing token generation by an average of 30% and up to 70% on easy tasks while maintaining strong performance. This approach, using an adapted reinforcement learning algorithm, mitigates the "overthinking" problem and achieves a ~2x training speedup.
Problem: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) suffer from an "overthinking" problem, applying elaborate "Long Chain-of-Thought" (Long CoT) reasoning uniformly across all tasks regardless of difficulty.
This indiscriminate application leads to excessive token generation, substantial computational overhead, increased inference latency, and can sometimes degrade performance.
Existing solutions often rely on manual token budget estimations or require specialized, length-constrained model training, which are neither practical nor adaptively efficient.
Method: ARM employs a two-stage training framework: Supervised Fine-tuning (SFT) to understand four reasoning formats (Direct Answer, Short CoT, Code, Long CoT), followed by Reinforcement Learning (RL).

It introduces Adaptive Group Relative Policy Optimization (Ada-GRPO), an RL algorithm that overcomes "format collapse" by encouraging exploration of diverse reasoning formats through a format diversity scaling factor.
ARM supports three inference modes: Adaptive (autonomous selection), Instruction-Guided (user-specified format), and Consensus-Guided (efficient formats first, then Long CoT if disagreement).
Results: ARM reduces token cost by an average of ~30% and up to ~70% on easy tasks, while maintaining reasoning performance comparable to models that exclusively use Long CoT.

The model effectively learns to adapt its reasoning strategy, primarily using efficient formats for easy commonsense tasks and shifting to elaborate formats like Code and Long CoT for complex problems.
Ada-GRPO achieves approximately a ~2x speedup in training time compared to traditional GRPO by encouraging the generation of shorter, more efficient responses during the RL roll-out stage.
Takeaways: Large Reasoning Models can be trained to dynamically adjust their reasoning depth and token usage based on task complexity, moving beyond a uniform reasoning approach.

Reinforcement learning algorithms can be specifically adapted, via mechanisms like diversity scaling, to prevent 'format collapse' and encourage the balanced utilization of multiple problem-solving strategies.
Integrating and adaptively selecting from a palette of reasoning formats allows AI models to achieve an optimal balance between high accuracy and computational efficiency.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20229.Title: From What to How: Attributing CLIP's Latent Components Reveals Unexpected Semantic Reliance
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20229.Summary: The paper introduces a framework combining Sparse Autoencoders with attribution patching to explain how CLIP's latent components influence predictions. This method identifies unexpected semantic reliance and spurious correlations in CLIP, demonstrating its utility in debugging and improving model robustness, particularly in medical image analysis.
Problem: Existing methods for Vision-Language model interpretability primarily explain "what" concepts are encoded but lack instance-wise quantification of "how" these concepts influence specific model predictions.
There is a need for scalable frameworks that can uncover and attribute the influence of individual latent components in complex transformer-based models like CLIP.
Identifying unexpected semantic reliance, such as spurious correlations or reliance on unintended visual features, within CLIP's internal mechanisms remains a challenge.
Method: The paper introduces a framework that first extracts sparse, interpretable latent components from CLIP's final class token embedding using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs).
It then quantifies the instance-wise influence of individual SAE components on CLIP's predictions using an adapted attribution patching technique, specifically an Activation Gradient approach.

The framework identifies unexpected concept reliance by flagging components that are highly relevant to a prediction but have low semantic alignment, or by detecting components with unusually high relevance compared to a reference distribution.
Results: The proposed Act Grad attributions consistently demonstrated superior faithfulness in deletion and insertion experiments compared to other interpretability methods, accurately reflecting component influence.

Sparse Autoencoders extracted a large number of diverse and interpretable components (e.g., 17,455 for ViT-L/14), with hundreds found to encode unexpected or unintended semantic features not present in standard taxonomies.

The framework identified over 220 failure cases across four recurrent modes including polysemous prompts and visual typography, and in a melanoma detection case study, it revealed and helped mitigate a significant "red hue" spurious correlation, improving classifier robustness.
Takeaways: The framework successfully bridges the "what" (concept encoding) and "how" (predictive influence) gaps in CLIP interpretability by combining component extraction with instance-wise attribution.
CLIP's latent space contains a rich set of interpretable components, including many unexpected or unintended features like visual typography, dataset artifacts, and polysemous concepts.

Spurious correlations and semantic ambiguities can significantly impact CLIP's robustness, but the proposed framework can systematically identify and help mitigate these issues, especially in sensitive applications like medical diagnosis.

The research from Fraunhofer HHI and TU Berlin highlights that understanding specific component influences is crucial for developing robust and trustworthy AI systems, moving beyond global explanations to actionable insights for debugging foundation models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20164.Title: Thinking with Visual Abstract: Enhancing Multimodal Reasoning via Visual Abstraction
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20164.Summary: The research introduces Visual Abstract Thinking (VAT), a novel paradigm that transforms complex visual inputs into simplified visual abstracts (e.g., sketches) to enhance Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) reasoning. This approach achieves an average performance gain of 16.72% over the GPT-4o baseline and significantly reduces computational costs, requiring only 27.53% of the runtime and 10.00% of the tokens compared to tool-augmented methods.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle to effectively reason with the inherent richness and often redundant nature of visual inputs.
Existing reasoning paradigms, such as Chain-of-Thought (CoT) and tool-augmented methods, add more information, increasing computational complexity, potential for hallucination, and overall costs.
There is a lack of cognitively inspired paradigms that actively reduce redundant visual information, unlike how humans use abstract thinking to simplify complex inputs.
Method: The Visual Abstract Thinking (VAT) paradigm converts raw images into simplified visual abstracts (e.g., sketches, edge maps) using various methods, including pixel-based and deep learning-based techniques.
MLLMs are prompted with both the original image and its visual abstract, encouraging a more concentrated visual reasoning mechanism by directing models to focus on essential visual elements.
The methodology integrates the visual abstract into a simple prompt template alongside the original query, explicitly instructing the MLLM to leverage both inputs for optimal performance.
Results: VAT achieved an average performance gain of 16.72% over the GPT-4o baseline, outperforming Chain-of-Thought (CoT) by 3.56 percentage points on diverse multimodal reasoning benchmarks.
The approach significantly improved efficiency, requiring only 27.53% of the runtime and 10.00% of the token cost compared to tool-augmented methods like Visual Sketchpad.

OpenSketch style visual abstracts consistently yielded the highest overall improvements, effectively preserving essential geometric and semantic information while filtering noise for object-centric perception and relation reasoning tasks.
Takeaways: Abstract visual cues, derived from complex images, effectively enhance MLLM visual reasoning capabilities by filtering redundant information and highlighting salient features.
VAT offers substantial efficiency gains over existing methods, significantly reducing both runtime and token consumption by utilizing low-cost input tokens rather than expensive generated outputs.

The paradigm demonstrates generality across various MLLM architectures and scales, with larger models like GPT-4o showing more pronounced performance improvements, indicating an emergent capacity for abstract reasoning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20046.Title: REARANK: Reasoning Re-ranking Agent via Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20046.Summary: Mila - Quebec AI Institute and Fudan University researchers develop REARANK, a reasoning-based re-ranking agent that uses reinforcement learning to train a Qwen2.5-7B model for listwise passage reordering, achieving performance comparable to GPT-4 on TREC-DL and BEIR benchmarks despite training on only 179 annotated queries through a data augmentation pipeline that generates diverse candidate sets from BM25 retrievals, with GRPO optimization using NDCG-based rewards enabling the model to outperform GPT-4 on reasoning-intensive BRIGHT tasks while providing interpretable explanations for ranking decisions and demonstrating transferability to mathematical reasoning benchmarks.
Problem: Existing LLM-based re-ranking methods lack optimization for ranking objectives and suffer from data scarcity for supervised fine-tuning
Current approaches provide limited interpretable reasoning for ranking decisions and often depend on large, proprietary models
Retrieval-augmented generation systems require more accurate re-ranking to improve text generation quality
Computational costs and inference latency of large models create practical deployment challenges
Method: Formulate re-ranking as a Markov Decision Process and train using Grouped Policy Optimization with NDCG-based rewards
Implement listwise re-ranking strategy using sliding windows to capture order-based signals efficiently
Introduce Initial State Expansion data augmentation by sampling diverse candidate passage sets from BM25 top 100 results
Build reasoning capabilities into a compact Qwen2.5-7B model to provide interpretable explanations while maintaining efficiency
Results: Achieves performance comparable to GPT-4 on TREC-DL and BEIR benchmarks while using significantly fewer parameters
Outperforms GPT-4 on reasoning-intensive BRIGHT benchmark, demonstrating superior reasoning capabilities
Surpasses concurrent setwise RL approaches using the same base model architecture
Demonstrates successful transfer of reasoning abilities to mathematical reasoning tasks beyond information retrieval
Takeaways: Reinforcement learning enables effective training of reasoning-based re-ranking agents with limited annotated data
Listwise approaches provide richer ranking information and superior inference efficiency compared to setwise methods
Explicit reasoning processes enhance both ranking performance and interpretability without requiring massive model scale
Data augmentation through diverse candidate sampling can overcome training data scarcity for ranking tasks

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.19985.Title: Structured Initialization for Vision Transformers
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.19985.Summary: Researchers at the Australian Institute for Machine Learning (AIML) introduced a structured initialization method for Vision Transformers that embeds convolutional inductive biases into attention maps at initialization. This approach significantly enhances ViT performance on small and medium-scale datasets while preserving its capacity on large datasets, achieving faster convergence.
Problem: Vision Transformers (ViTs) exhibit poor performance on small-scale datasets compared to Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) due to their lack of inherent inductive biases.
Current effective ViT initialization strategies often necessitate access to large pre-trained models or modify the core architectural structure.
Bridging the performance gap between ViTs and CNNs on limited data without compromising ViT's architectural flexibility or relying on extensive pretraining.
Method: Introducing a "structured initialization" strategy that directly embeds convolutional inductive biases into ViT attention maps at initialization.
Approximating random impulse convolution kernels within the attention mechanism to provide a local spatial prior.
Utilizing positional encoding as a pseudo input in an SVD-based method to derive the initial Query and Key matrices for attention heads.
Results: Achieved substantial performance gains on small and medium-scale datasets, with improvements reaching up to 24.26% on Pets and 2-8% on other datasets.
Maintained comparable or slightly superior performance on large datasets such as ImageNet-1K, demonstrating 0.24% higher accuracy for ViT-Base*.
Showed faster early convergence and increased training robustness, while successfully generalizing to enhance performance in ViT variants like Swin Transformer and MLP-Mixer.
Takeaways: Deep network embeddings are often rank-deficient, implying that spatial mixing layers can achieve strong performance with fixed, adequately spanning spatial filters rather than learned ones.
Random impulse spatial convolution filters are theoretically shown to be as effective as trained filters for spatial mixing, justifying their use in initialization.
Imposing a structured, convolutional prior onto ViT attention maps at initialization can effectively address the lack of inductive biases without altering the model's architecture.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.19707.Title: MLLM-Guided VLM Fine-Tuning with Joint Inference for Zero-Shot Composed Image Retrieval
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.19707.Summary: The MVFT-JI framework introduces a method for Zero-Shot Composed Image Retrieval by directly fine-tuning a Vision-Language Model using synthetic supervision generated by a Multimodal Large Language Model. This approach eliminates the need for manual annotations while consistently outperforming state-of-the-art methods across FashionIQ, CIRCO, and CIRR benchmarks.
Problem: Traditional image retrieval methods struggle with nuanced queries combining a reference image with textual modifications (e.g., 'this shirt, but in blue').
Composed Image Retrieval (CIR) methods typically rely on expensive, manually annotated datasets of reference image, modifying text, and target image triplets.
Existing Zero-Shot CIR (ZS-CIR) approaches suffer from a deficiency in capturing rich visual semantics (often relying on pseudo-text tokens) and use indirect supervision paradigms.
Method: MVFT-JI generates synthetic training data for composed image retrieval using an MLLM (MiniCPM-V-2_6), creating target text retrieval triplets and text-to-image pairs from unlabeled images.
A Q-Former-based Vision-Language Model (VLM), initialized with BLIP2, is directly fine-tuned with dual InfoNCE losses for both target text retrieval and text-to-image retrieval tasks.

During inference, the framework employs a joint strategy that combines direct compositional matching from the fine-tuned VLM with an MLLM-augmented reasoning signal derived from MLLM-generated target descriptions.
Results: MVFT-JI achieved 34.84% R@10 on FashionIQ, an improvement of ~7-10% over the previous best (MLLM-I2W: 27.3%).
The framework attained 39.30% R@1 on CIRR, an 11% absolute gain over MCL (26.22%).
On CIRCO, MVFT-JI achieved 21.69% mAP@5, improving by 3.12% over CIReVL (18.57%).
Takeaways: A theoretical decomposition of the retrieval probability reveals two complementary tasks: text-to-image retrieval and target text retrieval, both addressed during training.
MLLM-generated synthetic supervision enables direct fine-tuning of a Vision-Language Model (VLM) for zero-shot composed image retrieval, eliminating the need for manual annotations.
The joint inference strategy, combining direct VLM compositional matching with MLLM-augmented reasoning (generating target descriptions), is crucial for achieving high retrieval performance.
The Target Text Retrieval task (optimizing alignment between composed queries and MLLM-generated target texts) is more critical for overall performance than the Text-to-Image Retrieval task.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.19702.Title: Point-RFT: Improving Multimodal Reasoning with Visually Grounded Reinforcement Finetuning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.19702.Summary: Point-RFT is a framework for multimodal reasoning that explicitly grounds Chain-of-Thought (CoT) steps to specific visual coordinates, enhancing reasoning accuracy and interpretability. This approach achieves 90.04% accuracy on the ChartQA dataset, outperforming previous methods and generalizing well to out-of-domain visual reasoning tasks.
Problem: Vision-language models often suffer from visual hallucinations and inadequate integration of visual information when generating reasoning chains in multimodal tasks.
Traditional text-only Chain-of-Thought (CoT) fails to leverage rich spatial and quantitative visual information, leading to factual inaccuracies in multimodal contexts.
There is a lack of mechanisms to verify if textual descriptions in reasoning chains accurately reflect visual content, complicating error diagnosis.
Method: Introduces Point-RFT, a two-stage training framework combining supervised format finetuning with reinforcement learning.

Develops the Point-CoT dataset, containing 71,000 diverse visual reasoning problems with step-by-step rationales explicitly grounded to visual coordinates using GPT-4o for reasoning and Molmo-7B for localization.

Utilizes Group-wise Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) for reinforcement finetuning, employing a dual reward system to optimize for both point-grounded CoT structure adherence and final answer accuracy.
Results: Achieved 90.04% accuracy on the ChartQA dataset, representing a 19.16 percentage point improvement over the format-finetuned baseline (70.88%) and 6.12 percentage points over text-only reinforcement learning (83.92%).
Demonstrated strong generalization capabilities by consistently outperforming alternative approaches on out-of-domain benchmarks including CharXiv, PlotQA, IconQA, and TabMWP.
Ablation studies confirmed that both visual grounding and reinforcement finetuning are crucial for optimal performance and interpretability, validating the complete Point-RFT framework design.
Takeaways: Explicitly grounding reasoning steps to visual coordinates significantly reduces visual hallucinations and improves factual accuracy in multimodal AI.
Connecting textual reasoning to precise visual elements enables better error diagnosis, distinguishing between perception and reasoning failures.
Reinforcement learning with dual rewards (format adherence and accuracy) can effectively optimize for both structural adherence (visual grounding) and correct logical reasoning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.19590.Title: Learning to Reason without External Rewards
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.19590.Summary: This research introduces Reinforcement Learning from Internal Feedback (RLIF) and its instantiation, INTUITOR, enabling large language models to enhance reasoning abilities using only intrinsic self-certainty as a reward. The approach achieves performance comparable to supervised methods on in-domain tasks while demonstrating superior generalization to out-of-domain problems like code generation.
Problem: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) is expensive, time-consuming, and prone to human biases due to its reliance on extensive human annotation.

Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) demands domain-specific verifiers and gold-standard solutions, limiting its applicability to tasks with objective correctness criteria and hindering generalization.

Current LLM training paradigms face scalability issues and struggle to enable truly autonomous self-improvement mechanisms for AI systems, particularly as models' capabilities grow beyond human evaluators.
Method: A novel paradigm, Reinforcement Learning from Internal Feedback (RLIF), is proposed, where LLMs learn from intrinsic, self-generated signals rather than external rewards or labeled data.

INTUITOR, an instantiation of RLIF, uses the model's own 'self-certainty' as the sole intrinsic reward, defined as the average KL divergence between a uniform distribution and the model's next-token distribution.

The self-certainty reward is integrated into the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) framework, where scores are normalized within sampled groups to update the policy, creating a self-reinforcing learning loop.
Results: INTUITOR achieved performance on mathematical reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH500) comparable to supervised GRPO, using only intrinsic rewards.
It demonstrated superior out-of-domain generalization, showing a 65% relative improvement on LiveCodeBench and a 76% gain on CRUXEval-O for code generation tasks compared to GRPO.

Models fine-tuned with INTUITOR exhibited enhanced instruction-following capabilities and improved self-assessment, consistently surpassing GRPO in Length Control Win Rate on AlpacaEval and showing stronger statistical separation between correct/incorrect answer self-certainty scores.
Takeaways: Optimizing for intrinsic self-certainty encourages LLMs to generate more structured, coherent, and long-form reasoning steps, leading to improved problem-solving processes.
Online self-certainty, where the reward signal evolves with the policy, effectively prevents 'reward hacking' and maintains stable training dynamics, unlike fixed offline reward functions.

Intrinsic feedback can effectively guide LLM learning, unlocking latent capabilities and fostering generalizable reasoning skills that transfer across diverse tasks without explicit external guidance.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.19255.Title: VTool-R1: VLMs Learn to Think with Images via Reinforcement Learning on Multimodal Tool Use
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.19255.Summary: VTool-R1 trains Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to generate multimodal chains of thought by dynamically interleaving textual and visual reasoning steps. This framework enables VLMs to strategically use visual editing tools through reinforcement learning, resulting in improved reasoning accuracy on visual question answering tasks involving tables and charts.
Problem: While LLMs have advanced in generating complex textual chains of thought and using external tools via RFT, VLMs lack a comparable capability for multimodal reasoning, typically producing only text-based outputs even for visual tasks.

Existing methods for incorporating visual steps (e.g., Visual Sketchpad) operate at inference time and rely on large, pre-trained models, without providing a mechanism for smaller VLMs to learn to generate and use these visual steps.

VLMs currently do not dynamically "think with images" as part of their reasoning process, limiting their ability to actively interact with and derive insights from visual elements in a human-like manner.
Method: VTool-R1 introduces a Reinforcement Learning Finetuning (RFT) framework that trains VLMs to generate multimodal chains of thought.
VLMs learn to strategically invoke external Python-based visual editing tools, with the modified image from tool execution fed back into the VLM for continued reasoning.
The training employs Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with an outcome-based reward function that assesses the correctness of the final answer.
Results: VTool-R1 significantly improves reasoning accuracy on challenging visual question answering tasks over tables and charts.
The Qwen-VL 3B model, for instance, increased its accuracy from approximately 24% to 57.9% on TableVQA and 64.0% on ChartQA with VTool-R1.
Models learn to generate and interpret multimodal chains of thought, dynamically incorporating visual edits like highlighting or masking into their reasoning processes.
Takeaways: Vision-Language Models can be explicitly trained to generate and integrate intermediate visual reasoning steps into their chains of thought using reinforcement learning.
An outcome-based reward function, focused solely on the correctness of the final answer, effectively guides VLMs to strategically utilize visual tools without leading to reward hacking.
Models learn to adaptively decide when to invoke visual tools and when to rely on direct reasoning, demonstrating a nuanced understanding of task requirements.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.19223.Title: LLaDA 1.5: Variance-Reduced Preference Optimization for Large Language Diffusion Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.19223.Summary: LLaDA 1.5 systematically improves the alignment of Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) with human preferences by introducing Variance-Reduced Preference Optimization (VRPO). This framework, developed by researchers from Renmin University of China and collaborators, effectively mitigates high variance in ELBO-based likelihood estimates, leading to consistent performance gains, including a +4.7 increase in GSM8K accuracy.
Problem: Systematic human preference alignment for Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) remained an underexplored area compared to autoregressive models.
MDMs rely on approximating log-likelihoods via Evidence Lower Bounds (ELBOs), which must be estimated using computationally intensive Monte Carlo methods.
These Monte Carlo ELBO estimates introduce high variance into preference optimization processes, hindering stable and effective alignment.
Method: Adapted Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) for MDMs by substituting exact log-likelihoods with Monte Carlo estimated Evidence Lower Bounds (ELBOs).
Proposed Variance-Reduced Preference Optimization (VRPO), a framework integrating three unbiased variance reduction strategies to mitigate high variance.
VRPO strategies include increasing the total sampling budget, optimally allocating the sampling budget across timesteps, and employing antithetic sampling for paired ELBOs.
Results: LLaDA 1.5, utilizing VRPO, consistently outperformed its LLaDA 8B Instruct (SFT-only) predecessor and a baseline LLaDA with naive DPO across diverse benchmarks.
Achieved notable quantitative improvements, including a +4.7 increase in GSM8K accuracy, +3.0 on HumanEval, and +4.0 on IFEval.
VRPO led to significantly smoother training loss curves and lower variability during optimization, demonstrating enhanced stability and efficiency in aligning MDMs with human preferences.
Takeaways: The bias and variance of the estimated DPO loss and its gradient are directly governed by the variance of the underlying preference score estimator.
For a fixed sampling budget, optimal allocation for ELBOs prioritizes sampling more distinct timesteps with fewer masked samples per timestep to minimize variance.
Antithetic sampling effectively reduces the variance of differences between correlated ELBO estimates without incurring additional computational cost, enhancing optimization stability.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.19094.Title: SATORI-R1: Incentivizing Multimodal Reasoning through Explicit Visual Anchoring
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.19094.Summary: The SATORI framework enhances Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) reasoning by explicitly integrating visual grounding into the reinforcement learning process. It achieves a 76.2% accuracy on the MathVista benchmark, outperforming existing open-source and some closed-source models, while also reducing training variance in reinforcement learning.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) applying free-form reasoning often experience visual attention diffusion, leading to a loss of precise visual grounding and inaccurate conclusions.

Unstructured reasoning paths in MLLMs result in sparse, unverifiable intermediate supervisory signals, which causes high policy-gradient variance and slow convergence during reinforcement learning training.
Method: SATORI introduces a "Glance-Focus-Think" paradigm, structuring multimodal reasoning into distinct stages: global captioning, identifying task-relevant bounding boxes, and synthesizing information for the final answer.

It employs Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO-zero) with dense, verifiable reward signals for each structured stage, including caption quality, bounding box accuracy, final answer correctness, and adherence to format.
A novel VQA-Verify dataset comprising 12,000 samples with integrated captions and bounding box annotations was developed to facilitate training with explicit visual anchoring.
Results: SATORI-7B achieved a 76.2% accuracy on the MathVista benchmark, establishing a new state-of-the-art among open-source models and surpassing leading closed-source systems like GPT-4o (63.8%).

The framework maintained higher Region Attention Density (0.2729 average) and reduced policy-gradient variance by 27% compared to free-form reasoning baselines, indicating sharper visual focus and more efficient training.

Ablation studies confirmed the efficacy of SATORI's individual components and its generalizability to other Vision LLM backbones, with the combined BBox and Caption rewards yielding the best performance.
Takeaways: Explicitly enforcing visual grounding through structured intermediate steps, such as captioning and bounding box identification, is crucial for maintaining MLLM visual attention and preventing attention diffusion.
Dense, verifiable intermediate rewards within an RL framework significantly reduce policy-gradient variance, leading to more stable and faster convergence in complex multimodal reasoning tasks.
The "Grounding-First" reasoning sequence (Glance → Focus → Think) demonstrates a causal link to improved accuracy, validating the design choice to establish visual context before logical deduction.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.19000.Title: VerIPO: Cultivating Long Reasoning in Video-LLMs via Verifier-Gudied Iterative Policy Optimization
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.19000.Summary: VerIPO cultivates deep, consistent, long-term reasoning in Video-LLMs by introducing a Verifier-guided Iterative Policy Optimization (VerIPO) algorithm. This approach uses a GRPO-Verifier-DPO training loop, leveraging a small LLM to dynamically curate high-quality preference data, resulting in improved accuracy and reasoning length on video reasoning benchmarks while reducing inconsistencies and repetitions.
Problem: High-quality, long Chain-of-Thought (Long-CoT) video datasets are scarce and costly, posing a data preparation bottleneck for Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RFT).
Existing online RL methods for Video-LLMs often produce shallow, inconsistent, or repetitive reasoning chains and show unstable performance, failing to cultivate deep, long-form reasoning.
Video-LLMs struggle to generate long, coherent, and contextually consistent step-by-step reasoning for complex video understanding tasks.
Method: Introduces VerIPO, a Verifier-guided Iterative Policy Optimization algorithm, structured around a GRPO-Verifier-DPO training loop.
Utilizes a "Rollout-Aware Verifier" (a small LLM) to critically assess the quality, consistency, and repetition of online generated reasoning chains.
The verifier dynamically constructs high-quality contrastive preference datasets, which are then used by DPO for efficient, targeted policy refinement.
Results: VerIPO consistently outperforms strong baselines, including instruction-tuned LMMs and other RL-trained thinking models, on various video reasoning benchmarks, such as a 5.6% improvement over Video-R1 on Video-MMMU.

The Verifier-guided DPO and iterative training significantly enhance "Acc-True" (correct answers with consistent reasoning) and increase average response length, while effectively reducing contextual inconsistencies and repetitive outputs.
An initial "Reasoning Activation" phase using text and image data proves more beneficial for generalizing to video tasks than cold-starting with video-specific Long-CoT data.
Takeaways: An iterative, verifier-guided reinforcement learning framework can effectively cultivate deep, long-term, and consistent reasoning in Video-LLMs without requiring large, pre-existing Long-CoT datasets.

Dynamically assessing and curating preference data from online model rollouts using a small LLM verifier is crucial for improving reasoning quality and addressing issues like inconsistency and repetition.
Combining the broad exploration capabilities of GRPO with the efficient, targeted refinement of DPO, guided by the verifier, leads to stable and superior performance gains in long reasoning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.18983.Title: AmorLIP: Efficient Language-Image Pretraining via Amortization
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.18983.Summary: A novel framework, AMORLIP, efficiently re-engineers Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP) by amortizing the intractable partition function using lightweight neural networks. This approach yields relative performance gains of up to 12.24% on diverse downstream tasks and accelerates training convergence by at least 30.3% compared to baselines, while requiring significantly fewer computational resources.
Problem: State-of-the-art CLIP models require extremely large batch sizes (tens of thousands) and extensive computational resources (hundreds/thousands of GPUs) for Noise Contrastive Estimation (NCE), creating high barriers to entry.
The `logsumexp` operation in CLIP's NCE objective introduces inter-sample dependencies, preventing efficient parallel computation.
Existing efficiency techniques often compromise downstream performance, prolong training duration, or struggle with scalability to web-scale datasets.
Method: The standard CLIP objective is reformulated as a Maximum Likelihood Estimation problem within an Energy-Based Model (EBM) framework, identifying the partition function as the core computational bottleneck.
Lightweight neural networks (MLPs) are introduced to learn and amortize the intractable partition function, replacing its direct computation with a continuously updated parametric estimate.

A modular two-stage training pipeline alternates between optimizing these amortization networks and updating the backbone image and text encoders, with stability enhanced by target networks and weighted combinations for the partition function estimate.
Results: AMORLIP consistently outperforms standard CLIP, achieving relative improvements of up to 12.24% on DataComp downstream tasks and 4.67% on ImageNet zero-shot classification.

It demonstrates significantly faster training convergence, reaching comparable performance at least 30.3% quicker (e.g., 10 epochs earlier) in large-scale settings with only 0.23% additional training time and 0.26% higher memory usage.
The `l2-log` amortization objective generally yields better performance and smoother training dynamics than `f-divergence`, attributed to its variance reduction properties despite theoretical bias.
Takeaways: CLIP's contrastive objective can be effectively and insightfully reformulated as an Energy-Based Model, highlighting the partition function as the key source of computational intractability.
The partition function is linearly representable by basis functions, theoretically justifying its efficient approximation using simple Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs).
Parametric amortization provides a more scalable and efficient alternative to memory-buffer-based methods for managing negative samples, crucial for training on web-scale datasets.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.18842.Title: v1: Learning to Point Visual Tokens for Multimodal Grounded Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.18842.Summary: Researchers from Yonsei University and Seoul National University developed `v1`, a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) that uses a "point-and-copy" mechanism to dynamically re-access specific visual information during reasoning, mitigating "visual grounding decay." The `v1` model achieves improved performance on multimodal mathematical reasoning benchmarks, outperforming comparable 7B-scale MLLMs and approaching the performance of larger 72B-scale models.
Problem: Current MLLMs experience "visual grounding decay," where attention to visual tokens weakens and focus on relevant regions declines during extended reasoning chains.
Existing MLLMs typically process an image once at the beginning of inference, relying on a static, cached visual representation for subsequent multi-step reasoning.
This limitation hinders performance on tasks requiring precise, iterative consultation of visual details, such as complex multimodal mathematical reasoning.
Method: Introduces `v1`, a lightweight MLLM architecture featuring a "point-and-copy" mechanism that augments the model's output space to allow direct referencing and copying of input visual patch embeddings.

Develops `v1g`, a large-scale dataset of 300K multimodal reasoning traces with fine-grained visual grounding annotations, constructed using an automated pipeline leveraging LLMs and MLLM cross-attention for robust object grounding.

The model learns to dynamically predict whether to generate a standard text token or a special "pointer token" that, when selected, injects the referenced continuous visual embedding into the subsequent decoding step.
Results: `v1` consistently outperformed comparable 7B-scale general-purpose and reasoning-specialized MLLMs across MathVista, MathVision, and MathVerse multimodal mathematical reasoning benchmarks.
Ablation studies confirmed the crucial role of the dynamic pointing mechanism, with `v1` achieving 34.5% accuracy on MathVision testmini compared to 23.6% for the base Qwen2.5-VL model.

The `v1g` dataset's attention-based grounding method achieved 83.3% correctness in human evaluations, and the trained `v1` model demonstrated high pointing accuracy (82.7% correct, 87.7% appropriate).
Takeaways: MLLMs demonstrably suffer from "visual grounding decay," an empirical finding showing declining overall visual attention and reduced focus on salient regions as inference chains lengthen.

A lightweight "point-and-copy" mechanism for dynamically re-accessing and incorporating visual information can significantly improve MLLM performance and interpretability for complex grounded reasoning tasks.

High-quality, fine-grained visual grounding datasets can be effectively generated through automated pipelines leveraging powerful LLMs for trace decomposition and MLLMs for attention-based region grounding.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.18600.Title: Chain-of-Zoom: Extreme Super-Resolution via Scale Autoregression and Preference Alignment
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.18600.Summary: The Chain-of-Zoom (CoZ) framework enables existing single-image super-resolution (SISR) models to achieve extreme magnifications up to 256x. It employs a scale autoregression strategy combined with multi-scale-aware textual prompts, generated by a Vision-Language Model (VLM) fine-tuned with Generalized Reward Policy Optimization (GRPO), to maintain high perceptual quality and fidelity.
Problem: Existing state-of-the-art SISR models are limited to fixed, relatively small upscaling factors (e.g., 4x) and collapse when pushed to extreme magnifications.
Training separate deep learning models for each extreme magnification factor (e.g., 16x, 32x) is computationally prohibitive due to memory and time constraints.

At very high magnifications, low-resolution inputs provide sparse visual cues, making it challenging for SR models to generate plausible and semantically coherent high-frequency details without hallucinating unreasonable outputs.
Method: The Chain-of-Zoom (CoZ) framework factorizes the super-resolution task into an autoregressive chain of intermediate scale-states, repeatedly applying any off-the-shelf SR backbone trained for a fixed, small upscaling factor.

Multi-scale-aware textual prompts, generated by a Vision-Language Model (VLM) conditioned on two previous image scales, guide the SR process at each zoom step, compensating for sparse visual information.

The prompt-extraction VLM is fine-tuned using Generalized Reward Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a composite reward function to align generated prompts with human preferences and reduce implausible hallucinations at extreme scales.
Results: CoZ achieves superior perceptual quality at extreme magnifications (up to 256x) compared to Nearest Neighbor interpolation and direct one-step SR, as evidenced by better no-reference quality scores (NIQE, MUSIQ, MANIQA-pipal, CLIPIQA).

GRPO fine-tuning effectively guides the VLM to produce prompts that reduce implausible hallucinations and yield statistically higher human preference scores for both image and text quality in user studies.
The framework demonstrates model-agnosticism and robustness, maintaining good performance when integrated with different existing SR backbones like an open-source OSEDiff model.
Takeaways: Extreme super-resolution can be effectively achieved by decomposing the task into an autoregressive sequence of smaller magnification steps, allowing a single SR backbone to be reused without retraining.

Semantic guidance from multi-scale-aware textual prompts, derived from Vision-Language Models, is critical for synthesizing coherent and plausible details when visual cues become highly sparse at high magnifications.

Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback, specifically GRPO, can successfully fine-tune VLM behavior to generate prompts that are more aligned with human aesthetic and semantic preferences, mitigating hallucinations in generative vision tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.18454.Title: Hybrid Latent Reasoning via Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.18454.Summary: Hybrid Latent Reasoning via Reinforcement Learning (HRPO) enables Large Language Models (LLMs) to integrate continuous latent representations with discrete token generation through a novel reinforcement learning framework. This approach allows compact Qwen2.5-1.5B and 3B models to achieve strong performance on knowledge and STEM benchmarks, surpassing larger RAG baselines and other RL methods without requiring Chain-of-Thought annotations.
Problem: Existing latent reasoning methods for LLMs often face incompatibility between continuous hidden representations and discrete token generation, leading to degraded output quality.
Many current LLM reasoning approaches heavily depend on resource-intensive explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) annotations for training, limiting scalability and broad applicability.
Prior attempts to leverage LLMs' intrinsic reasoning capabilities through latent states often incurred high training costs and did not fully exploit the potential of pre-trained models.
Method: Developed a Hybrid Reasoning with Gating mechanism that projects continuous hidden states into the embedding space using a differentiable mapping and blends them with discrete token embeddings via a learnable gate.

Introduced Hybrid Reasoning Policy Optimization (HRPO), an on-policy reinforcement learning framework that trains LLMs to autonomously develop hybrid reasoning based solely on outcome-based rewards, bypassing the need for CoT supervision.

Utilized LoRA for efficient fine-tuning and initialized the gating mechanism to prioritize discrete token embeddings, ensuring initial generative coherence while progressively incorporating more informative latent features.
Results: HRPO consistently achieved superior exact match scores on knowledge benchmarks, with the Qwen2.5-3B HRPO model outperforming the Qwen2.5-7B RAG baseline by 4.5% on average.

The method attained state-of-the-art results for smaller LLMs on reasoning-intensive STEM datasets, enabling the Qwen2.5-3B HRPO model to match the performance of several larger (≥ 7B) LLMs on four out of five datasets.

Analysis confirmed the efficacy of HRPO's hybrid design for stability and faster convergence, showing an increasing ratio of latent representations used during training, resulting in shorter completion lengths and exhibiting novel cross-lingual reasoning patterns.
Takeaways: A carefully designed gating mechanism effectively bridges the gap between continuous latent representations and discrete token generation, allowing for stable and coherent hybrid reasoning in LLMs.

Reinforcement learning provides an effective way for LLMs to intrinsically learn and leverage sophisticated internal reasoning patterns without explicit Chain-of-Thought supervision, promoting autonomous intelligence.

The dynamic and learnable integration of latent representations can lead to more concise and efficient reasoning trajectories, with emergent properties like cross-lingual reasoning observed in the generated outputs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.18129.Title: One RL to See Them All: Visual Triple Unified Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.18129.Summary: A Visual Triple Unified Reinforcement Learning system, V-Triune, enables Vision-Language Models to simultaneously improve across visual reasoning and perception tasks within a single training pipeline. Models trained using V-Triune, named Orsta, show performance gains of up to +14.1% on the MEGA-Bench Core, along with specific improvements like +7.81 mAP for COCO Detection and over 5% on the MathVista benchmark.
Problem: Reinforcement Learning (RL) applications for Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have primarily focused on visual reasoning tasks, neglecting perception-intensive tasks like object detection and grounding.

The absence of a unified RL framework makes it challenging to integrate diverse input formats, reward mechanisms, and evaluation metrics needed for jointly training VLMs on both reasoning and perception.
Current RL setups for VLMs lack specialized reward designs and stability measures for perception tasks, leading to issues such as reward ambiguity with fixed IoU thresholds or cold-start problems.
Method: Developed V-Triune, a unified RL system with a three-component architecture for Sample-Level Data Formatting, Verifier-Level Reward Computation via an asynchronous client-server, and Source-Level Metric Monitoring.

Introduced a Dynamic IoU reward mechanism for visual perception tasks, which adaptively adjusts the Intersection over Union threshold during training to facilitate stable learning towards high-precision outcomes.

Implemented a comprehensive training recipe featuring frozen Visual Transformer (ViT) parameters, filtering of spurious special tokens, a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompt pool, and optimized memory management to enhance training stability.
Results: Orsta models achieved up to a +14.1% performance increase on the MEGA-Bench Core benchmark compared to their Qwen2.5-VL backbones, with substantial improvements in mathematical and perception-related tasks.

Visual perception capabilities improved significantly, including +7.81 mAP for single-object detection and +3.77 mAP for multi-object detection on COCO, along with +5.3 mAP on OVDEval and new state-of-the-art results on CountBench.
Visual reasoning saw notable gains, with Orsta-7B improving by 4% on MMMU and all Orsta variants achieving over 5% gains on the MathVista benchmark.
Takeaways: Reinforcement Learning in VLMs primarily functions as an alignment strategy, refining decision-making and unlocking latent capabilities of pre-trained models rather than introducing entirely new knowledge.

Freezing the Visual Transformer (ViT) parameters and employing conservative learning rates are critical engineering optimizations for achieving stable and peak performance during VLM RL training, preventing instability.

Training VLMs on a combined corpus of reasoning and perception tasks leads to additive performance gains and transferable alignment signals, indicating synergy between these diverse learning objectives.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17812.Title: Seeing It or Not? Interpretable Vision-aware Latent Steering to Mitigate Object Hallucinations
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17812.Summary: Xi'an Jiaotong University researchers introduce VaLSe (Vision-aware Latent Steering), a framework that mitigates object hallucinations in Large Vision-Language Models by generating visual contribution maps to identify image regions influencing model predictions, then using these maps to construct steering samples that guide the model's latent representations toward semantically relevant objects, achieving effective hallucination reduction while maintaining general model capabilities and revealing limitations in existing evaluation metrics like CHAIR that incorrectly flag accurate descriptions due to incomplete ground-truth annotations.
Problem: Large Vision-Language Models frequently generate object hallucinations, producing content inconsistent with visual input that undermines reliability and safety for real-world deployment
Existing hallucination mitigation methods lack interpretability, making it difficult to understand why hallucinations occur and how visual inputs influence model decision-making processes
Current evaluation metrics for object hallucination assessment have limitations and may incorrectly assess model performance due to incomplete annotations
Method: Develop VaLSe framework with three components: visual-based token selection to identify visually-sensitive tokens, visual contribution map generation using attention mechanisms to highlight relevant image regions, and vision-aware latent steering using SVD to compute directional differences between positive and negative samples

Create positive steering samples by masking irrelevant image regions while preserving core objects, and negative samples using original images, then apply latent steering to adjust internal model representations
Implement artifact elimination techniques to improve interpretability of generated contribution maps and reduce neural network artifacts
Results: VaLSe achieves effective object hallucination mitigation comparable to or better than existing approaches while preserving general model capabilities on MME, GQA, and LLaVA-Bench benchmarks
Framework generates high-quality visual contribution maps that provide clear insights into model decision-making processes and enable identification of hallucination causes
Analysis reveals specific limitations in current evaluation methodologies, highlighting the need for more sophisticated and visually grounded assessment approaches for LVLM performance
Takeaways: Visual contribution maps reveal that models focus on wrong or irrelevant image regions when producing hallucinated content, providing clear interpretable evidence of decision-making flaws
Latent steering can effectively redirect model attention toward semantically relevant objects without requiring retraining or fine-tuning of the underlying architecture
Existing evaluation metrics like CHAIR contain systematic biases that incorrectly penalize accurate model descriptions due to incomplete ground-truth annotations

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17746.Title: Fast Quiet-STaR: Thinking Without Thought Tokens
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17746.Summary: Fast Quiet-STaR introduces a multi-stage training method for large language models to internalize token-level reasoning, achieving significant inference speedups while maintaining or improving accuracy. It enables models like Mistral 7B to show a 9% average accuracy increase on reasoning benchmarks at the same inference latency as standard pre-trained models.
Problem: The Quiet Self-Taught Reasoner (Quiet-STaR) paradigm, while effective for token-level reasoning, incurs substantial inference overhead and increased latency due to explicit thought trace generation for every predicted token.
The high computational cost of Quiet-STaR hinders its practical deployment in real-world, latency-sensitive applications.
Directly reducing the number of thought tokens in Quiet-STaR leads to a significant degradation in reasoning performance, creating a trade-off between efficiency and accuracy.
Method: A multi-stage curriculum learning strategy, called Fast Quiet-STaR, progressively reduces the number of thought tokens during training, starting with more and gradually moving to fewer, to compress explicit reasoning.
The final checkpoint from the curriculum learning is used to initialize a standard Next Token Prediction (NTP) model.

This NTP model is then fine-tuned using reinforcement learning (REINFORCE) to internalize the explicit thought process, enabling enhanced reasoning capabilities without generating explicit thought tokens during inference.
Results: Fast Quiet-STaR NTP improves average accuracy by 9% for Mistral 7B (from 32.0% to 41.0%) and 5.7% for Qwen2.5 7B (from 48.7% to 54.4%) on reasoning benchmarks, with identical inference latency to pre-trained baselines.

End-to-end generation latency is drastically reduced, with Fast Quiet-STaR NTP achieving only 6% of Quiet-STaR 16-8's generation time (3.2s vs. 52.7s for 128 tokens) by fully eliminating explicit thought tokens.

Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of the curriculum learning strategy and the importance of initializing the RL phase with a highly compressed thought-reasoner, showing that a 'hard-to-easy' progression or direct training performs worse.
Takeaways: A progressive curriculum learning approach, moving from 'easy' (more thought tokens) to 'hard' (fewer thought tokens), is crucial for effectively compressing and abstracting token-level reasoning into efficient patterns.

Reinforcement learning can successfully distill complex, explicit reasoning capabilities into implicit knowledge within a standard Next Token Prediction framework, eliminating the need for separate thought generation during inference.

The long-term inference cost savings from 'thinking without thought tokens' (Fast Quiet-STaR NTP) are substantial and quickly offset the initial training cost, making the approach economically viable for large-scale deployments.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17685.Title: FutureSightDrive: Thinking Visually with Spatio-Temporal CoT for Autonomous Driving
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17685.Summary: FutureSightDrive (FSDrive) introduces a framework for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models in autonomous driving that generates a visual spatio-temporal Chain-of-Thought (CoT) as a unified future image. This approach, which incorporates physically plausible future scenarios, improves trajectory planning accuracy and significantly reduces collision rates.
Problem: Existing MLLM-based autonomous driving systems rely on textual Chain-of-Thought (CoT), leading to lossy compression of visual information and a 'modality gap' between perception and action planning.
Textual CoT fails to adequately capture critical spatio-temporal relationships and fine-grained visual details essential for safe and anticipatory driving.
Activating visual generation capabilities in existing MLLMs for world modeling typically requires complex architectures, extensive training data, or sacrifices semantic understanding.
Method: The framework enables the VLA model to act as a world model, generating a unified visual future frame (spatio-temporal CoT) that includes predicted background and explicit physical priors like future lane dividers and 3D object bounding boxes.
The same VLA model then functions as an inverse dynamics model, planning a future trajectory autoregressively by conditioning on current observations and the generated visual CoT.

A unified pre-training paradigm expands the MLLM's vocabulary with VQ-VAE image tokens and combines Visual Question Answering (VQA) with progressive, 'easy-to-hard' future image generation to efficiently activate visual generation while preserving semantic understanding.
Results: FSDrive achieved state-of-the-art performance on the nuScenes dataset for end-to-end trajectory planning, with an average L2 displacement error of 0.28m and a collision rate of 0.10% using ST-P3 metrics.
