The framework generated future frames with a competitive Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) of 10.1 on nuScenes, performing comparably to specialized diffusion models despite utilizing a smaller 2B parameter model.

FSDrive scored 0.57 on the DriveLM GVQA benchmark for scene understanding, outperforming prior methods like Cube-LLM (0.50) and OmniDrive (0.56), validating its unified pre-training for both generation and understanding.
Takeaways: An image-based spatio-temporal CoT is more effective for autonomous driving reasoning than textual CoT, as it better preserves critical spatio-temporal relationships and fine-grained visual details, mimicking human cognitive processes.

Integrating explicit physical priors (lane dividers, 3D object boxes) directly into the generated visual future frames significantly enhances the physical plausibility and safety of the imagined scenarios.

Existing MLLMs can be efficiently empowered with visual generation capabilities for world modeling through minimal architectural changes, vocabulary expansion, and a unified, progressive pre-training strategy.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17508.Title: On the Design of KL-Regularized Policy Gradient Algorithms for LLM Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17508.Summary: A new theoretical framework, the Regularized Policy Gradient (RPG) view, unifies KL-regularized policy gradient algorithms for off-policy LLM training, providing exact gradient derivations for various KL divergences. This framework leads to RPG-REINFORCE with RPG-Style Clip, an algorithm that improves LLM reasoning accuracy by up to 6 absolute percentage points over DAPO on AIME24/25, achieving 52% on AIME25 for Qwen models at 8k context.
Problem: The design space for KL regularization in reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models (LLMs) lacks a unified theoretical understanding, especially concerning importance weighting in off-policy settings.
Existing KL-regularized policy gradient methods often suffer from high variance and instability when applied to LLM reasoning tasks, particularly with off-policy data collection.
Some current algorithms, such as GRPO, implement KL penalties with importance-weighting mismatches in off-policy settings, leading to biased gradients.
Method: The paper introduces the Regularized Policy Gradient (RPG) view, a unified theoretical framework that systematically derives exact policy gradients for various KL divergence types (forward/reverse, normalized/unnormalized) under off-policy sampling.
It proposes RPG-REINFORCE with RPG-Style Clip, a novel clipping mechanism for importance weights, combined with an iterative reference policy update to stabilize off-policy policy gradient training.
The methodology includes constructing gradient-equivalent surrogate loss functions and ensuring computational efficiency by allowing pre-computation of log probabilities for the old policy.
Results: RPG-REINFORCE, particularly with unnormalized reverse KL (URKL), enhances LLM reasoning accuracy by up to 6 absolute percentage points over DAPO on AIME24/25 benchmarks.
The method achieves 52% accuracy on AIME25 for Qwen3-4B at 8k context length, surpassing the official Qwen3-4B-Instruct model (47%) and outperforming other strong baselines.

RPG algorithms consistently demonstrate more stable training progressions, controlled policy entropy, and appropriate response lengths across various context lengths (2k, 4k, 8k) in mathematical reasoning tasks.
Takeaways: The widely used k3 estimator for regularization is formally equivalent to the unnormalized KL divergence (UKL), providing theoretical clarity to its empirical success.

Under off-policy sampling, precise importance weighting is critical for the surrogate objective to yield the exact gradient of the intended KL-regularized objective, correcting mismatches found in prior methods like GRPO.

RPG-Style Clip and the iterative reference policy update are crucial for maintaining stable training dynamics and achieving superior performance in off-policy LLM fine-tuning by managing variance and adapting the KL trust region.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17316.Title: Analyzing Fine-Grained Alignment and Enhancing Vision Understanding in Multimodal Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17316.Summary: Researchers at The Ohio State University developed "Patch-Aligned Training," a pretraining method for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) that explicitly enhances fine-grained vision-language alignment. This approach, which includes a novel patch-alignment loss and an automatically generated dataset, improved MLLM performance by up to 16% on referring expression comprehension and 4% on visual question answering.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) frequently exhibit limitations in fine-grained, region-specific visual understanding, often resulting in visual hallucination.
The vision-language projector, a critical component, struggles to precisely align individual visual patches with corresponding semantic word embeddings.
Existing MLLM training paradigms, primarily driven by captioning losses, do not adequately foster robust patch-level vision-language alignment.
Method: Conducted a two-tiered analysis of MLLM projectors, examining information compression via Von Neumann Entropy and patch-level alignment using IoU with ground-truth object masks.
Developed an automated annotation pipeline utilizing RAM, Grounding DINO, and SAM to create the Patch-Aligned Dataset (PAD) for fine-grained supervision.

Introduced "Patch-Aligned Training" by adding an L_patch loss during MLLM pretraining, which directly optimizes the cosine similarity between object-level vision embeddings and corresponding word embeddings.
Results: The P_Patch Aligned projector demonstrated superior information compression (entropy reduction from 3.8352 to 2.7991 for LLaVA) and significantly stronger patch-level alignment (mIoU of 0.279, compared to 0.142 for LLaVA).
Models trained with Patch-Aligned Training improved performance by approximately 16% on Referring Expression Comprehension across multiple benchmarks (RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, RefCOCOg).
The approach led to a 4% improvement on Visual Question Answering benchmarks and a 3% gain on modern instruction-following benchmarks.
Takeaways: MLLM projectors effectively compress visual information, reducing redundancy while preserving essential semantics, with MLP projectors showing better compression than linear ones.
Even in pretrained MLLMs like LLaVA, patch-level alignment between visual features and semantic word embeddings is weak and coarse, characterized by low IoU scores.
Direct supervision through the L_patch loss during pretraining enhances both information compression and the precision of patch-level vision-language alignment.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17083.Title: Scale-invariant Attention
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17083.Summary: A novel scale-invariant attention scheme, derived from first principles, enables large language models to generalize to context lengths 16 times longer than seen during training with minimal performance degradation. This method achieves uniformly lower validation loss across various context lengths and maintains high accuracy in long-context information retrieval tasks.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle with zero-shot length generalization, performing poorly on contexts significantly longer than those encountered during training.
Existing attention mechanisms often exhibit diffuse attention or an excessive prioritization of distant tokens over local context as the sequence length increases.
Current methods to improve long-context handling, such as continual pretraining or specific positional encodings, often incur high computational costs or have limitations in extreme extrapolation.
Method: A position-dependent logit transformation for attention was derived from formal definitions of 'scale-invariant total attention' and 'scale-invariant attention sparsity'.
The approach assumes attention logits are marginally Gaussian and solves for position-dependent scaling factors (variance) and additive biases (mean) to satisfy the scale-invariance desiderata.
The method was implemented and evaluated in GPT-2 style models, notably combined with p-RoPE positional embeddings, to balance local and global context attention.
Results: The scale-invariant p-RoPE method achieved uniformly lower validation loss across all tested context lengths (4k, 16k, 64k) compared to all other leading baseline methods.
Demonstrated unprecedented 16x zero-shot length extrapolation, maintaining a validation loss of 3.247 at 64k tokens when models were trained on only 4k tokens.
Maintained robust long-range information retrieval capabilities, achieving high validation accuracy of 0.969 at 64k context length in the Needle-in-a-Haystack task.
Takeaways: Attention mechanisms can be designed to be 'scale-invariant' by ensuring that total attention and attention sparsity remain consistent across exponentially increasing ranges of past tokens.
A theoretical derivation shows that a logarithmically increasing variance and logarithmically decreasing mean for attention logits achieves weak scale-invariant attention sparsity.

Empirical analysis confirmed that the marginal distribution of attention logits in existing LLMs closely approximates a Gaussian distribution, validating a key theoretical assumption for the derived transformation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17022.Title: GoT-R1: Unleashing Reasoning Capability of MLLM for Visual Generation with Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17022.Summary: Researchers from HKU MMLab, CUHK MMLab, Sensetime, and Beihang University develop GoT-R1, a framework that applies reinforcement learning to Generation Chain-of-Thought reasoning for visual generation, enabling multimodal large language models to autonomously discover effective reasoning strategies beyond predefined templates while achieving state-of-the-art performance on T2I-CompBench through a dual-stage training process that combines supervised fine-tuning with Group Relative Policy Optimization and a comprehensive multi-dimensional reward system evaluating both reasoning chains and generated images.
Problem: Existing Generation Chain-of-Thought (GoT) methods rely on supervised fine-tuning with human-defined templates, limiting models' ability to discover more effective reasoning strategies autonomously
Text-to-image models struggle with compositional fidelity when generating images from complex prompts requiring precise spatial relationships and attribute binding
Designing appropriate reward mechanisms for visual generation tasks that must assess semantic alignment, spatial accuracy, and visual quality simultaneously
Method: GoT-R1 framework combining Generation Chain-of-Thought with reinforcement learning using a unified MLLM architecture that jointly models text and image tokens
Dual-stage training process: supervised fine-tuning on annotated reasoning chains followed by reinforcement learning with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)
Multi-dimensional reward framework leveraging MLLMs as reward models to evaluate prompt-to-reasoning alignment, reasoning-to-image alignment, and overall compositional accuracy
Results: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on T2I-CompBench benchmark, surpassing existing methods including Stable Diffusion, DALLE·3, and LayoutGPT
Demonstrates significant improvements in compositional tasks involving precise spatial relationships and attribute binding
Shows that models can autonomously discover more effective reasoning strategies, leading to improved controllability and fidelity in text-to-image generation
Takeaways: Reinforcement learning enables visual generation models to discover reasoning strategies beyond predefined patterns, similar to advances seen in language model reasoning
MLLMs serve effectively as both generators and reward models due to their ability to make nuanced judgments about text-image correspondence
Comprehensive reward systems that evaluate both intermediate reasoning processes and final outputs are crucial for successful RL training in visual generation

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17018.Title: SophiaVL-R1: Reinforcing MLLMs Reasoning with Thinking Reward
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17018.Summary: SophiaVL-R1 improves multimodal reasoning by integrating a "thinking reward" that evaluates the quality of the model's reasoning process alongside traditional outcome-based rewards. This dual-reward approach allows smaller models, such as SophiaVL-R1-7B, to surpass larger models like LLaVA-OneVision-72B on benchmarks including MathVista and MMMU.
Problem: Current reinforcement learning approaches for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) rely solely on outcome-based rewards, neglecting the quality of the reasoning process.
Models can arrive at correct answers through flawed or unreliable reasoning strategies, which are not penalized by outcome-only rewards, potentially reinforcing non-generalizable patterns.
This limitation makes it difficult to ensure that MLLMs develop robust and trustworthy reasoning capabilities, especially in complex cross-modal understanding tasks.
Method: SophiaVL-R1 introduces a dual-reward system that evaluates both the final outcome and the quality of the intermediate reasoning steps (a "thinking reward").

A dedicated thinking reward model, initialized from Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct and trained on manually annotated reasoning examples, assesses reasoning quality based on logical soundness and error identification.

The Trust-GRPO algorithm dynamically adjusts the influence of thinking rewards using a trustworthiness weight (γ) and an annealing schedule to ensure reliable integration and prevent reward exploitation.
Results: SophiaVL-R1-7B outperforms LLaVA-OneVision-72B on the MathVista benchmark despite having significantly fewer parameters and achieves 4.5 points higher on MMMU.
Ablation studies confirm that the trained thinking reward model, trustworthiness weight (γ), and annealing strategy are all crucial components contributing to performance.
Training curves show that SophiaVL-R1 consistently achieves higher rewards and demonstrates faster improvement throughout training compared to baseline approaches.
Takeaways: Evaluating the quality of the reasoning process, in addition to the final outcome, is essential for developing robust and reliable Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs).
Model-generated rewards for reasoning quality can be effectively integrated into training through trustworthiness mechanisms, mitigating risks like reward hacking and ensuring stable learning.

Advanced training methodologies, such as dual-reward systems and trustworthy policy optimization, can enable smaller MLLMs to achieve performance competitive with or superior to significantly larger models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17015.Title: Multi-SpatialMLLM: Multi-Frame Spatial Understanding with Multi-Modal Large Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17015.Summary: Meta AI and CUHK researchers develop Multi-SpatialMLLM by creating the MultiSPA dataset—1.2 million multi-frame instruction-following samples from real-world 3D/4D datasets—to train language models for spatial reasoning across image pairs, achieving 36% performance gains over InternVL2 baseline on tasks including depth perception, visual correspondence, camera movement detection, and object tracking while demonstrating transferable spatial understanding on external benchmarks and showing potential as a multi-frame reward annotator for robotics applications.
Problem: Current multi-modal large language models lack robust spatial understanding capabilities, particularly across multiple frames
Existing MLLMs cannot effectively reason about depth, visual correspondence, or dynamic changes between images
Scarcity of large-scale training data specifically designed for multi-frame spatial reasoning tasks
Limited evaluation frameworks for assessing multi-frame spatial understanding in vision-language models
Method: Create MultiSPA dataset with 1.2 million instruction-following samples from Aria Digital Twin, Panoptic Studio, ScanNet, and TAPVid3D datasets
Develop data engine that samples image pairs with uniform overlap distribution and establishes pixel correspondences through backprojected point clouds
Design five core spatial reasoning tasks: depth perception, visual correspondence, camera movement, object movement, and object size perception
Fine-tune InternVL2 model using LoRA on MultiSPA dataset mixed with general instruction-following samples
Results: Multi-SpatialMLLM achieves 36% performance improvement over InternVL2 baseline on MultiSPA benchmark
Model outperforms proprietary systems including Claude-3.5, Gemini 2.0, and GPT-4o on multi-frame spatial tasks
Demonstrates good generalization on BLINK benchmark while maintaining standard VQA proficiency
Shows preliminary emergent behavior in challenging spatial tasks and potential for robotics reward annotation applications
Takeaways: Multi-task training on diverse spatial reasoning tasks provides synergistic benefits and improved generalization
Model performance scales with both training data size and model capacity, particularly for challenging vector prediction tasks
Rigid body segmentation for point cloud clustering enhances training data diversity and model robustness
Multi-frame spatial understanding transfers effectively to external benchmarks while preserving original VQA capabilities

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17012.Title: SpatialScore: Towards Comprehensive Evaluation for Spatial Intelligence
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17012.Summary: Researchers from Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Shanghai AI Laboratory introduce SpatialScore, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating multimodal large language models' (MLLMs) spatial intelligence, and propose SpatialCorpus for supervised fine-tuning and SpatialAgent for a training-free, tool-augmented enhancement. The work reveals significant performance gaps in MLLMs' 3D understanding, demonstrating that these methods can improve capabilities across various spatial reasoning tasks, with SpatialAgent achieving up to +8.33% accuracy on the benchmark.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) exhibit fragmented and limited capabilities in spatial intelligence, struggling with nuanced understanding of physical space.
Existing MLLM benchmarks for spatial reasoning are over-simplistic, focusing on superficial queries rather than rigorous visual geometry perception (e.g., camera pose, metric measurements).

Current evaluations have a narrow scope, relying on single-modality inputs or isolated skills, failing to provide a holistic assessment of spatial intelligence for real-world applications like embodied AI.
Method: Introduced SpatialScore, a comprehensive benchmark with 5,025 manually verified samples, covering 30 diverse spatial reasoning tasks across various data types, modalities, and question formats.
Developed SpatialCorpus, a large-scale training resource with 331K multimodal QA pairs for supervised fine-tuning of MLLMs, curated using automated 3D data repurposing and synthetic data generation.

Proposed SpatialAgent, a training-free, multi-agent framework that leverages an off-the-shelf MLLM core augmented with 12 specialized spatial perception tools, operating under Plan-Execute and ReAct paradigms.
Results: State-of-the-art proprietary MLLMs like Gemini-3-Pro achieved 60.12% on SpatialScore, while leading open-source models scored 56.63%, both substantially below human performance (86.60%).
Supervised fine-tuning of Qwen3-VL models on SpatialCorpus resulted in notable overall accuracy improvements, with the 4B model gaining +10.47% and the 8B model +9.23%.
SpatialAgent provided significant training-free enhancements, with the ReAct paradigm boosting Qwen3-VL 4B/8B by +7.78% and +8.33% respectively, showing consistent gains across most tasks.
Takeaways: A substantial gap persists between state-of-the-art MLLMs and human-level spatial intelligence, particularly in complex visual geometry and real-world 3D perception tasks.

Larger MLLMs generally exhibit stronger spatial reasoning, but existing spatial-specific fine-tuning datasets show limited efficacy, underscoring the need for more comprehensive evaluation and training data.

Both data-driven fine-tuning (SpatialCorpus) and training-free, tool-augmented agent-based approaches (SpatialAgent) are effective strategies for enhancing MLLMs' spatial intelligence, each with distinct advantages.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.16993.Title: Native Segmentation Vision Transformers
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.16993.Summary: NVIDIA researchers developed SeNaTra, a Vision Transformer that integrates content-aware spatial grouping directly into its backbone, enabling segmentation masks to emerge natively from the model's representations. This architecture demonstrates strong zero-shot segmentation performance and achieves competitive results on supervised benchmarks while being more parameter and FLOP efficient.
Problem: Traditional vision backbones rely on uniform spatial downsampling, leading to feature misalignment and requiring complex, separate segmentation decoder heads.
Existing image segmentation methods are often multi-component, with the backbone producing coarse features that decoders must refine and group.
Prior attempts at content-aware grouping in backbones (e.g., GroupViT) suffered from quadratic computational complexity, limiting scalability to high-resolution images.
Method: The Native Segmentation Vision Transformer (SeNaTra) integrates a content-aware spatial grouping layer that replaces traditional uniform downsampling.
A differentiable, iterative clustering process assigns input tokens to a reduced set of output tokens based on feature similarity, similar to Slot Attention.
Scalability is achieved by using local grouping in early stages (linear complexity) and dense grouping in the final stage, with custom CUDA-optimized kernels.
Results: SeNaTra significantly outperforms specialized state-of-the-art methods in zero-shot semantic segmentation across six benchmarks when pre-trained on image-text pairs.
As a drop-in backbone for Mask2Former, SeNaTra-T improves ADE20k semantic mIoU by +1.0 over Swin-T and +2.7 over NAT-T.

The "purely native" SeNaTra-T achieves 49.7 mIoU on ADE20k semantic segmentation and 49.2 PQ on COCO-Panoptic with 50% fewer parameters and 12% FLOPs compared to traditional backbones with heavy decoders.
Takeaways: Segmentation capabilities can emerge intrinsically from a backbone's representations if content-aware spatial grouping is integrated.
Efficient and scalable content-aware grouping layers, combining local and dense grouping, can replace uniform downsampling in hierarchical vision transformers.
Designing backbones with an inductive bias for pixel grouping can lead to improved zero-shot generalization and more efficient models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.16938.Title: InternAgent: When Agent Becomes the Scientist -- Building Closed-Loop System from Hypothesis to Verification
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.16938.Summary: The InternAgent framework establishes a unified closed-loop multi-agent system for autonomous scientific research, automating the entire cycle from hypothesis generation to experimental validation. It achieves substantial performance gains and cost-efficiency across 12 varied scientific and AI tasks, including handling complex repository-level codes.
Problem: Autonomous systems struggle to generate effective and novel research proposals that balance creativity with scientific rigor.
A major hurdle in ASR is the seamless, closed-loop integration of experiment design, execution, result analysis, and iterative hypothesis refinement across diverse domains.
Method: A unified closed-loop multi-agent framework is employed, featuring specialized agents for self-evolving idea generation with human-interactive feedback (Survey, Code Review, Idea Innovation, Assessment, Orchestration Agents).
A comprehensive idea-to-methodology construction process systematically bridges abstract research ideas to concrete, implementable methodologies (Methodology Development Agent).

An evolutionary experimental planning and execution capability utilizes an Exception-Guided Debugging Framework and Adaptive Evolution for converting theoretical concepts into functional, iteratively refined code.
Results: InternAgent consistently improved performance over baselines and existing auto-research systems across all 12 diverse scientific and AI tasks, achieving a maximum R² of 35.4% in Reaction Yield Prediction and 95.5% Overall Accuracy in 3D Point Cloud Classification.

It demonstrated cost-efficiency, with idea generation averaging around
0.6perideaandcomplexrepository−leveldebuggingapproximately1.2 per run, making it significantly more economical than some prior systems (e.g., one-sixth the cost of AI-Researcher for AutoRYP).

Human evaluators (Ph.D.s or candidates) consistently rated InternAgent-generated ideas higher than those from AI-Scientist-V2 in terms of soundness, contribution, and overall quality, confirming its ability to produce effective and novel research concepts.
Takeaways: A multi-agent architecture with specialized, collaborating roles can effectively automate the complex, iterative nature of scientific discovery, from literature review to experimental refinement.
Integrating human-interactive feedback and self-evolving idea generation mechanisms is crucial for fostering novelty and scientific validity in AI-generated hypotheses.

The ability to support repository-level code and an adaptive experimental evolution process is vital for enabling AI to tackle complex, real-world scientific problems beyond simple, single-file tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.16933.Title: LLaDA-V: Large Language Diffusion Models with Visual Instruction Tuning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.16933.Summary: LLaDA-V introduces a purely diffusion-based Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) capable of end-to-end training and sampling across modalities. It achieves competitive performance against and often surpasses autoregressive MLLMs like LLaMA3-V across various multimodal benchmarks, demonstrating enhanced data scalability in several key domains.
Problem: Most state-of-the-art Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are built upon autoregressive (AR) language models, limiting exploration of alternative probabilistic modeling approaches.
Previous attempts at purely diffusion-based MLLMs suffered from limited language modeling capacity, performing suboptimally compared to AR-based counterparts.
The potential of discrete language diffusion models, like LLaDA, to handle visual inputs and multimodal instruction following remained largely unexplored.
Method: LLaDA-V integrates a large language diffusion model (LLaDA-8B-Instruct) with a vision tower (SigLIP 2) via a two-layer MLP connector.
It employs a masked diffusion process for training, learning to predict masked tokens in responses given clean image features and prompts, differing from autoregressive next-token prediction.

Inference uses an iterative refinement process starting from a fully masked sequence, employing low-confidence re-masking, and is trained via a three-stage strategy for language-image alignment, visual instruction tuning, and multimodal reasoning enhancement.
Results: LLaDA-V achieved state-of-the-art performance among existing hybrid and pure diffusion MLLMs across 18 diverse multimodal tasks.
Outperformed LLaMA3-V on 11 of 18 tasks, particularly excelling in multidisciplinary knowledge, mathematical reasoning, multi-image, and video understanding benchmarks.
Demonstrated superior data scalability on MMMU and MMMU-Pro, with LLaDA-V trained on 1M samples outperforming LLaMA3-V with 9M samples on MMMU-Pro.
Takeaways: Purely diffusion-based MLLMs can achieve competitive performance against strong autoregressive MLLMs, challenging the dominant paradigm.
LLaDA-V demonstrates superior data scalability in certain domains like multidisciplinary knowledge and mathematical reasoning compared to its autoregressive counterpart, LLaMA3-V.
Fully bidirectional attention across all tokens in the diffusion process proved more effective for multimodal understanding than a dialogue causal mask.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.16854.Title: Think or Not? Selective Reasoning via Reinforcement Learning for Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.16854.Summary: A framework from researchers at The Chinese University of Hong Kong and the National University of Singapore enables Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to selectively engage in step-by-step reasoning, deciding when to generate explicit thoughts. This approach reduces output completion length by up to 90% while consistently matching or improving accuracy across diverse multimodal tasks.
Problem: Reinforcement Learning (RL) approaches for Vision-Language Models (VLMs) mandate comprehensive, step-by-step reasoning for all queries, leading to inefficient token generation and higher computational costs for simple tasks.
VLMs currently lack adaptive cognitive control, unable to selectively engage in deep reasoning based on perceived task difficulty, unlike human intelligence.
Existing methods primarily focus on compressing or truncating reasoning processes rather than enabling models to autonomously decide if explicit reasoning is required at all.
Method: Introduces TON, a two-stage training framework for selective reasoning in VLMs.

Employs Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) with a "thought dropout" mechanism, where reasoning traces are randomly replaced with empty delimiters to teach the model to skip thoughts, combined with a "reverse thinking" strategy for thought data generation.

Utilizes Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) in the second stage, leveraging the SFT-induced output diversity to learn an adaptive policy for deciding whether to generate explicit reasoning, guided by task-specific outcome rewards.
Results: Demonstrated significant reductions in completion length, decreasing token usage by up to 90% (e.g., GeoQA) and 70% (AITZ), leading to lower inference costs and faster response times.

Achieved comparable or superior accuracy across benchmarks, notably gaining up to 17% over GRPO on GeoQA and improving CLEVR accuracy from 93.5% to 98.5%, proving efficiency gains without performance compromise.

Showed strong generalizability across diverse tasks (counting, mathematical reasoning, agentic navigation) and modalities, with ablation studies confirming progressive learning of selective reasoning and robust out-of-distribution performance.
Takeaways: Models can achieve comparable or superior performance with significantly reduced reasoning steps, suggesting that "overthinking" might sometimes lead to less accurate outcomes.
Explicitly teaching the model to skip reasoning through Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) with "thought dropout" is crucial, as mere prompt engineering does not effectively enable selective thinking.

Reinforcement Learning, particularly GRPO, leverages the diversity introduced by "thought dropout" to enable models to progressively learn and adaptively decide when to generate or omit explicit reasoning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.16782.Title: Reasoning Beyond Language: A Comprehensive Survey on Latent Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.16782.Summary: A comprehensive survey by Chen et al. (2025) introduces the first unified taxonomy for latent Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, organizing a rapidly growing field into token-wise horizontal and layer-wise vertical approaches. It synthesizes current research, practical applications, and outlines critical challenges for future advancements in LLM efficiency and cognitive capabilities.
Problem: Existing explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning in LLMs suffers from expressive redundancy, leading to inflated token usage, slower inference, and potential overfitting to stylistic artifacts.
Explicit CoT faces a semantic bottleneck as discrete language struggles to fully capture abstract, continuous, or multi-conceptual thought processes, limiting reasoning depth.

The rapidly expanding and fragmented field of latent CoT reasoning lacked a comprehensive, structured overview and taxonomy, making it difficult to understand diverse methodologies and identify research gaps.
Method: The paper proposes the first unified taxonomy for latent CoT, categorizing methods into 'token-wise horizontal' (sequential generation of latent thoughts) and 'layer-wise vertical' (iterative refinement of hidden states across layers) approaches.
It provides an in-depth discussion of representative latent CoT works, analyzing their design principles, training strategies, architectural paradigms, and efficiency trade-offs.
The survey identifies critical open problems in latent CoT, such as unsupervised training and interpretability, and outlines promising future research directions to guide the field.
Results: The survey successfully established a unified taxonomy classifying latent CoT methods into token-wise horizontal and layer-wise vertical categories, clarifying the field's structural organization.
Latent CoT methods demonstrated practical utility across various domains, including textual reasoning, multimodal reasoning and generation, and information retrieval/recommendation systems.

Theoretical analyses and empirical findings suggest latent CoT can improve multi-step reasoning efficiency by solving structured problems with fewer steps and achieving reasoning depth through iterative computation.
Takeaways: Latent Chain-of-Thought reasoning offers advantages such as accelerated inference, richer and more compact cognitive representations, and the ability to explore multiple reasoning trajectories in parallel by decoupling reasoning from explicit linguistic tokens.
The proposed taxonomy effectively structures the diverse approaches in latent CoT, revealing fundamental differences in how latent thoughts are represented, optimized, and explored within LLMs.

Despite its potential, latent CoT faces significant challenges primarily due to the unobservable nature of its reasoning process, leading to difficulties in training stability, generalization to novel problems, and ensuring interpretability.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.16673.Title: R1-ShareVL: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability of Multimodal Large Language Models via Share-GRPO
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.16673.Summary: Researchers from Nanyang Technological University, ByteDance, and collaborating institutions develop Share-GRPO, a reinforcement learning framework for multimodal large language models that addresses sparse reward and advantage vanishing problems by expanding question spaces through semantic transformations and sharing reward information across question variants during training, with their R1-ShareVL model achieving substantial improvements on mathematical reasoning benchmarks including 4.2-point gains on MathVista and 3.8-point gains on MathVerse compared to baseline GRPO when applied to Qwen2.5-VL models.
Problem: Existing reinforcement learning methods like GRPO suffer from sparse rewards when training multimodal large language models, making it difficult to obtain positive feedback for complex reasoning tasks
Advantage vanishing occurs during training, where the model struggles to differentiate between different reasoning paths, limiting learning effectiveness
Method: Introduce Share-GRPO framework that expands question spaces using Semantically Consistent Transformation (SCT) through both offline textual rewrites and online multimodal transformations
Implement shared advantage estimation that aggregates reward information hierarchically across global and local levels to provide denser training signals
Apply shared policy optimization that leverages diverse reasoning trajectories from question variants to improve model learning
Results: R1-ShareVL achieves 4.2-point improvement on MathVista and 3.8-point improvement on MathVerse compared to GRPO baseline using Qwen2.5-VL-7B
Method scales effectively to larger models, with Qwen2.5-VL-32B showing consistent performance gains across mathematical and general reasoning benchmarks

Ablation studies confirm individual contributions of shared policy optimization and shared advantage estimation components, with the complete framework demonstrating complementarity with dynamic sampling techniques
Takeaways: Information sharing principles from multi-agent reinforcement learning can be effectively adapted to address fundamental challenges in multimodal language model training
Question space expansion through semantic transformations creates multiple learning opportunities from single training examples while maintaining task consistency
Hierarchical advantage estimation at both global and local levels provides more stable and informative gradients for policy optimization

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.16579.Title: Bridging the Dynamic Perception Gap: Training-Free Draft Chain-of-Thought for Dynamic Multimodal Spatial Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.16579.Summary: Researchers from Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Shanghai AI Lab developed a training-free framework, the Dynamic Draft Augmented Reasoning Framework (D2R), to enhance Multimodal Large Language Models' dynamic spatial reasoning. This approach, along with the novel Draft Chain-of-Thought method, improved MLLM performance on the new GRASSLAND benchmark, which systematically evaluates an AI's ability to reason about spatial relationships that change over time.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle with dynamic spatial reasoning tasks, where visual elements and spatial relationships change over time.
Existing MLLMs often fail to effectively integrate spatial and temporal information, particularly in scenarios requiring tracking moving objects or evolving relationships.
Traditional MLLM reasoning approaches primarily rely on textual input and lack sufficient mechanisms to visualize and verify reasoning steps in dynamic visual contexts.
Method: Introduced GRASSLAND, a specialized benchmark environment simulating dynamic maze scenarios to evaluate MLLMs' dynamic spatial reasoning capabilities.
Developed Draft Chain-of-Thought, a method that augments textual reasoning with corresponding visual drafts overlaid directly onto dynamic input images for models with image generation capabilities.

Created the Dynamic Draft Augmented Reasoning Framework (D2R), a training-free, three-phase framework (planning, iterative reasoning, answer generation) applicable to diverse MLLM architectures for enhancing dynamic spatial reasoning.
Results: Draft Chain-of-Thought achieved higher performance across most MLLM architectures on the GRASSLAND benchmark compared to baseline methods.
The Dynamic Draft Augmented Reasoning Framework (D2R) provided improvements for MLLMs, even those without image generation capabilities.
Ablation studies confirmed the crucial role of the visual component, demonstrating substantial performance drops when visual drafts were removed.
Takeaways: Effective dynamic spatial reasoning requires explicit tracking, visualization, and reasoning about changes over time, extending beyond static visual processing.
Augmenting textual reasoning steps with visual drafts significantly improves Multimodal Large Language Models' (MLLMs) spatial understanding and ability to track dynamic changes.
A training-free framework can substantially enhance MLLM capabilities for dynamic spatial reasoning, making it broadly applicable to existing models without fine-tuning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.16416.Title: Circle-RoPE: Cone-like Decoupled Rotary Positional Embedding for Large Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.16416.Summary: Researchers from Huawei Noah's Ark Lab and academic partners developed Circle-RoPE, a cone-like decoupled rotary positional embedding for Large Vision-Language Models that eliminates spurious cross-modal positional biases. The method improved average performance on multimodal benchmarks by +1.73 over baseline Qwen2.5-VL, achieving an average score of 61.13.
Problem: Existing RoPE implementations in Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) introduce spurious cross-modal positional biases, enforcing unnatural relative dependencies between text and image tokens.
Current methods either flatten 2D image data into 1D sequences, losing vital spatial information, or utilize 2D coordinates in ways that still cause cross-modal misalignment.
A lack of robust positional encoding fully decouples cross-modal dependencies while preserving rich intra-image spatial information, hindering accurate multimodal understanding.
Method: Introduces Circle-RoPE, a cone-like decoupled rotary positional embedding, which transforms 2D image token coordinates onto a 3D circular structure oriented perpendicularly to the text token index vector.
Applies Alternating Geometry Encoding (AGE), cyclically switching between Circle-RoPE and standard M-RoPE across different Transformer layers to leverage complementary positional information.
Extends encoding capabilities to multi-image sequences by translating each image's circular encoding center along a fixed global axis, preserving unique positional identifiers.
Results: Circle-RoPE achieved an average score of 61.13 on diverse multimodal benchmarks (e.g., MMMU, MathVista, MMStar), representing a +1.73 improvement over the Qwen2.5-VL baseline.
The method demonstrated notable performance gains on tasks requiring strong spatial reasoning, including MMStar (+4.07), AI2D (+3.66), and MathVista (+1.00).
Visual attention map analysis revealed enhanced focus on relevant image regions with fewer irrelevant allocations, indicating improved cross-modal alignment and more precise visual reasoning.
Takeaways: The Per-Token Distance (PTD) metric effectively quantifies cross-modal positional biases in existing RoPE variants, confirming the presence of biases (e.g., PTD of 2.22 for hard embedding and 0.64 for spatial embedding).
A novel geometric projection into a cone-like structure achieves complete cross-modal positional decoupling (PTD=0) while precisely retaining intra-image spatial relationships.

Cyclically applying different positional encoding types (Alternating Geometry Encoding) across Transformer layers optimally leverages their complementary strengths, enhancing overall multimodal representation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.16411.Title: Mitigating Hallucinations in Vision-Language Models through Image-Guided Head Suppression
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.16411.Summary: Researchers from USC and Intel Labs developed SPIN, an image-guided head suppression technique that dynamically deactivates image-inattentive attention heads in Vision-Language Models during inference. This training-free method achieves up to a 2.7x reduction in object hallucinations and 1.8x higher throughput without introducing additional computational overhead or latency.
Problem: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) frequently generate hallucinations—textual outputs factually inconsistent with visual input—hindering their reliability in critical applications.

Current hallucination mitigation strategies are either computationally expensive (training-based) or introduce significant inference latency (existing training-free methods), limiting practical deployment.
A lack of mechanistic understanding exists regarding how specific internal LVLM components, particularly attention heads, contribute to the generation of hallucinations.
Method: SPIN (SuPpressing image INattentive heads) introduces an attention-guided head suppression mechanism that dynamically masks specific attention heads during inference.
It identifies 'image-inattentive' heads, which allocate low cumulative attention to vision tokens for a given text query, and suppresses their output by a factor 'α'.

A three-stage hyperparameter tuning process systematically determines the optimal ratio of suppressed heads (r), suppression factor (α), and the specific layers for intervention to maximize hallucination reduction while preserving performance.
Results: SPIN achieved up to a 2.7x reduction in object hallucinations (C_s) and 2.2x reduction in C_i for LLaVA-1.5 (7B), and up to 3x lower CHAIR scores compared to existing training-free methods.
It consistently improved accuracy on POPE benchmarks (up to 3.4%) and F1 scores (up to 3.7%), and enhanced scores on MMHal-Bench, demonstrating broad efficacy across hallucination types.
The method provided the highest throughput among state-of-the-art mitigation techniques, up to 1.8x higher than alternatives, with no additional computational overhead or increased inference latency.
Takeaways: LVLM hallucinations often originate from 'image-inattentive' attention heads, especially in deeper layers, that insufficiently attend to visual input.
Dynamically suppressing these visually disconnected attention heads during inference can effectively reduce hallucinations without requiring model retraining or architectural changes.

The optimal configuration for head suppression (ratio, factor, and layers) varies across different LVLM architectures, necessitating a structured tuning approach to balance hallucination reduction with overall model performance.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.16192.Title: VLM-R$^3$: Region Recognition, Reasoning, and Refinement for Enhanced Multimodal Chain-of-Thought
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.16192.Summary: VLM-R³ introduces a framework that enhances Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by enabling dynamic visual region recognition, reasoning, and refinement within a chain-of-thought. This approach, supported by the new VLIR dataset and Region-Conditioned Reinforcement Policy Optimization (R-GRPO), achieved new state-of-the-art results across various multimodal reasoning benchmarks, including a 5.1% gain on MathVision and a 14.33% improvement on ScienceQA.
Problem: Existing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle with complex tasks requiring dynamic, iterative, and fine-grained interaction with visual regions because their visual input processing is largely static.

Current Chain-of-Thought (CoT) based MLLMs often suffer from 'attention decay,' where their focus on visual information diminishes as textual reasoning progresses, leading to incorrect inferences for tasks needing continuous visual grounding.
There was a lack of high-quality datasets specifically designed to train MLLMs for interleaved text-image CoT reasoning with explicit region-level interactions.
Method: VLM-R³ introduces a framework that enables MLLMs to dynamically recognize, reason about, and refine visual regions through an interactive inference pipeline.

A new dataset, Visuo-Lingual Interleaved Rationale (VLIR), was created, providing sequences of textual reasoning steps interspersed with explicit visual grounding actions and corresponding cropped visual evidence.

The model is trained using Region-Conditioned Reinforcement Policy Optimization (R-GRPO), which adapts a reinforcement learning framework to optimize the policy of deciding when and where to acquire visual information.
Results: VLM-R³ (7B parameters) achieved new state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks, including a 5.1% gain on MathVision (30.2%) and a 14.33% improvement on ScienceQA (87.90%) compared to its base model, Qwen2.5-VL 7B.

Ablation studies confirmed that interleaved visual evidence, VLIR fine-tuning, and R-GRPO are all essential for performance, with removing interleaved visual evidence causing significant drops (e.g., -12.5% on ScienceQA).
The model demonstrated improved reliability in avoiding visual hallucinations, scoring 62.0% on HallusionBench, which is an improvement over Mulberry's 54.1%.
Takeaways: Dynamic, interleaved visual evidence is crucial for complex multimodal reasoning tasks, outperforming static visual processing in MLLMs.

Training with an explicitly curated dataset (VLIR) that features interleaved text-image reasoning steps and region interactions is essential for enabling MLLMs to perform fine-grained visual grounding.
Reinforcement learning (R-GRPO) is effective for optimizing the policy of dynamically acquiring and integrating visual information, going beyond what supervised fine-tuning alone can achieve.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.16186.Title: SafeKey: Amplifying Aha-Moment Insights for Safety Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.16186.Summary: SafeKey, developed by researchers from UCSC, UCB, Yale, and Cisco Research, enhances safety for Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) by targeting the "safety aha-moment" within their internal reasoning process. It introduces training objectives that strengthen latent safety signals and amplify their influence on critical decision points, significantly improving LRM robustness against out-of-distribution harmful queries and jailbreak attacks while preserving general abilities.
Problem: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)-aligned Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) exhibit vulnerability to out-of-distribution harmful queries and evolving jailbreak attacks, struggling to generalize safety knowledge.
Current safety methods, like SFT, often fail to effectively leverage the LRM's internal recognition of harmful intent, even when such signals exist within the query understanding phase.
Existing approaches primarily focus on the input or final output, neglecting targeted interventions within the LRM's explicit intermediate reasoning steps.
Method: SafeKey proposes a framework with two complementary training objectives: Dual-Path Safety Head (DPSH) and Query-Mask Modeling (QMM), integrated into the LRM's SFT process.
DPSH introduces parallel binary safety prediction heads to strengthen safety signals in the LRM's internal hidden states, specifically for the input query (X) and query understanding (U).

QMM forces the LRM to generate the critical 'key sentence' (K) solely based on the query understanding (U) by masking input query tokens (X), thereby amplifying the influence of safety-laden U on K's generation.
Results: SafeKey consistently reduced the average harmfulness rate on out-of-distribution (OOD) and jailbreak datasets (WildChat, WildJailbreak, Multi-Turn, Pre-fill attacks) by 9.2% to 10.1% across various LRM sizes (7B, 8B, 14B) compared to SFT baselines.
The framework maintained comparable performance on general abilities benchmarks (e.g., Math500, HumanEval, MMLU-Pro), demonstrating that safety enhancements did not compromise overall utility.

Ablation studies confirmed that both DPSH and QMM individually contribute to safety improvements and achieve the highest average safety performance when combined, validating their complementary nature.
Takeaways: An LRM's internal reasoning process contains an identifiable 'safety aha-moment' – a 'key sentence' after query understanding – that is crucial for activating safety responses.
Even when successfully jailbroken, an LRM's internal 'query understanding' (U) often possesses sufficient information to detect the harmful nature of a prompt.
Targeting and amplifying the connection between latent safety signals in query understanding and the generation of this 'key sentence' can significantly improve LRM safety generalization.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.16151.Title: Training-Free Reasoning and Reflection in MLLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.16151.Summary: Researchers at Wuhan University developed FRANK, a training-free approach that integrates reasoning and reflection capabilities into Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by strategically merging a vision-pretrained MLLM with a reasoning-specialized LLM. This method, which uses a novel layer-wise fusion guided by observed functional specialization, achieves state-of-the-art performance on various multimodal reasoning benchmarks, including outperforming GPT-4o on MMMU (69.2 vs 69.1) while preserving visual perception.
Problem: Endowing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) with sophisticated, multi-step reasoning capabilities, similar to advanced text-only LLMs.
The prohibitive computational costs and the scarcity of high-quality, verifiable multimodal reasoning datasets required for retraining or fine-tuning MLLMs for reasoning tasks.
Existing MLLMs, despite strong perceptual abilities, often lack complex logical inference for tasks like visual math or interpreting diagrams.
Method: FRANK, a training-free approach, merges a visual-pretrained MLLM with a reasoning-specialized LLM by combining their task vectors.
It employs a novel layer-wise fusion mechanism that leverages the observed functional specialization within MLLM decoders (shallow for perception, deep for reasoning).

An attention-guided exponential decay function is used to derive modality priors, enabling an optimal closed-form solution for per-layer fusion weights that balance visual grounding and symbolic reasoning without additional training or data.
Results: FRANK-38B achieves state-of-the-art results on multimodal reasoning benchmarks, scoring 69.2 on MMMU (outperforming GPT-4o at 69.1), 56.8 on MMMU-Pro (+8.8 vs. InternVL2.5-38B), and significant gains on MathVision (+7.5) and WeMath (+8.7).
The method successfully preserves fundamental visual perception capabilities, with only slight drops on the MME benchmark while sometimes enhancing commonsense reasoning.

Ablation studies confirm the necessity of layer-wise fusion and the attention-guided modality prior for optimal performance, and qualitative analysis reveals intrinsic self-correction and adaptive reasoning depth through generated reflection tokens.
Takeaways: MLLMs exhibit layer-wise functional specialization, with shallow decoder layers primarily handling visual perception and deeper layers focusing on textual semantics and higher-level reasoning.

Capabilities from different fine-tuned models (e.g., vision-specific and reasoning-specific) can be effectively integrated via homologous model merging, viewing them as task vector additions from a common base.

Optimal per-layer fusion weights for combining visual and reasoning task vectors can be derived in a closed-form solution using Taylor approximation and by leveraging the empirical orthogonality of task vectors, eliminating the need for additional data or training.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.16149.Title: When VLMs Meet Image Classification: Test Sets Renovation via Missing Label Identification
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.16149.Summary: REVEAL, a new framework, renovates image classification test sets by identifying and correcting both noisy and missing labels using an ensemble of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and other curation methods. This approach generates soft-labeled outputs with likelihoods, demonstrating high alignment with human annotations, such as a 0.976 agreement rate on CIFAR-10.
Problem: Image classification benchmark datasets are compromised by pervasive noisy labels and, critically, overlooked missing labels, leading to misleading model evaluations.

Existing label cleaning methods primarily focus on correcting incorrectly assigned labels (noisy labels), largely neglecting instances where an image contains multiple valid classes but is only partially annotated.
These label errors, particularly within test sets, result in unfair comparisons and an unreliable assessment of model performance.
Method: The REVEAL framework integrates diverse Vision-Language Models (BLIP, Janus, Qwen, LLaVA) with established label curation methods (Cleanlab, Docta) to identify label errors.
It employs a weighted aggregation strategy that estimates the expertise of each method against a pseudo ground-truth to build a robust consensus.
A post-aggregation filtering and softmax normalization step generates soft-labeled outputs with likelihoods, providing a comprehensive and probabilistic representation of image content.
Results: REVEAL identified substantial label errors across datasets; for instance, CIFAR-100 contained 552 noisy labels and 6083 missing labels in its test set.
The framework demonstrated high alignment with human annotations, achieving agreement rates of 0.976 on CIFAR-10, 0.880 on CIFAR-100, and 0.946 on Caltech256.
The findings provide a systematic analysis of VLM capabilities for data curation, highlighting their distinct failure modes and biases while demonstrating their utility when combined intelligently.
Takeaways: Missing labels are a pervasive and often more extensive problem than noisy labels in benchmark test sets, challenging the assumption of single-label ground truth.

While powerful, individual VLMs exhibit specific limitations, including struggles with fine-grained class prediction, repetitive label generation, hallucinations, refusal of null responses, and class-specific biases.
REVEAL's ensembling and refinement strategy effectively mitigates the limitations of individual VLMs, consistently achieving superior alignment with human judgments compared to any single VLM.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15970.Title: Analyzing Hierarchical Structure in Vision Models with Sparse Autoencoders
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15970.Summary: This research investigates whether the DINOv2 vision foundation model implicitly learns hierarchical visual concepts by applying Sparse Autoencoders to its class token representations. The study reveals a progressive development of taxonomic features across model layers, with late layers forming rich, spatially grounded hierarchical representations.
Problem: Deep learning models, especially large vision models, operate as 'black boxes,' making their internal decision-making processes opaque.
A lack of understanding exists regarding whether vision models implicitly learn hierarchical structures that mirror human cognitive organization.
There was a need to investigate if state-of-the-art unsupervised vision foundation models spontaneously organize visual concepts in taxonomic hierarchies without explicit supervision.
Method: The research employs Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), adapted from Large Language Model interpretability techniques, to extract and analyze hierarchical features from DINOv2.
Forty separate SAEs are trained, one for each intermediate layer of DINOv2's class token, allowing for a granular analysis of representation evolution through the network.
Two novel metrics, Lowest Common Hypernym (LCH) Height and Ontological Coverage, are introduced to quantify how well SAE-extracted features align with ImageNet's hierarchical structure.
Results: Early layers of DINOv2's class token show very low reconstruction error and poor classification performance, indicating minimal class-specific information.

Layer 36 of DINOv2's class token demonstrates remarkable hierarchical organization, with 90 Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) heads achieving perfect ontological coverage for broad categories such as 'elasmobranch', 'whales', and 'woodwind instruments'.

Relevancy maps confirmed that SAE-extracted hierarchical features are spatially grounded, consistently activating on semantically relevant regions across different images (e.g., a 'whale' concept activating on whale-like forms).
Takeaways: DINOv2's class token exhibits late information emergence, with early layers containing minimal class-specific data and semantic information gradually accumulating.

A clear progression in hierarchical feature development occurs, with features evolving from single-class or dissimilar activations in early layers (e.g., Layer 24) to broad, high-level taxonomic concepts in later layers (e.g., Layer 36).

Extracted hierarchical features are spatially grounded, consistently activating on relevant image regions for specific concepts (e.g., a 'whale' concept activating on whale-like shapes across different species).

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15966.Title: Pixel Reasoner: Incentivizing Pixel-Space Reasoning with Curiosity-Driven Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15966.Summary: Researchers from the University of Waterloo, HKUST, and Vector Institute developed Pixel Reasoner, a system that enables Vision-Language Models to perform reasoning directly in pixel space using visual operations like zoom-in and select-frame. This approach achieved state-of-the-art accuracy on four multimodal benchmarks, surpassing larger open-source and several proprietary models.
Problem: Current Vision-Language Models (VLMs) struggle to capture fine-grained visual details due to their reasoning process being confined exclusively to textual space.
Existing VLMs lack the ability to directly interact with visual inputs (e.g., zoom, select frames) during complex reasoning, limiting their capacity for deep visual inference.
The 'textual reasoning bottleneck' leads to potential loss of crucial visual information when translating visual observations into text tokens for intermediate steps.
Method: Introduces pixel-space reasoning, where the VLM policy generates sequences of either textual thinking or visual operations (`zoom-in`, `select-frame`) to directly manipulate visual inputs.
Employs a two-phase post-training approach: warm-start instruction tuning for foundational understanding and error-induced self-correction capabilities.

Utilizes curiosity-driven reinforcement learning with a dynamic reward scheme to overcome the 'learning trap' by incentivizing exploration and mastery of pixel-space operations when usage is historically low.
Results: Pixel-Reasoner, a 7B parameter model, achieved state-of-the-art accuracy across four multimodal benchmarks: 84.3% on V* Bench, 73.8% on TallyQA-Complex, 67.8% on MVBench, and 84.0% (ANLS) on InfographicsVQA.

The model outperformed larger open-source models (e.g., 27B Gemma3) and demonstrated performance comparable to or superior to leading proprietary models, including a 5.1 percentage point lead over Gemini-2.5-Pro on V* Bench.

Reinforcement learning, particularly with the curiosity bonus, was essential for cultivating robust pixel-space reasoning, as instruction tuning alone initially led to a decrease in performance on several benchmarks.
Takeaways: The 'textual reasoning bottleneck' prevents current VLMs from fully exploiting rich visual information, hindering performance on visually intensive tasks.
A 'learning trap' exists where nascent skills like pixel-space reasoning are overlooked by models favoring established, stronger textual reasoning, requiring specific incentives for cultivation.

Combining warm-start instruction tuning, including self-correction trajectories, with curiosity-driven reinforcement learning is critical for developing robust and effective interactive visual reasoning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15879.Title: GRIT: Teaching MLLMs to Think with Images
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15879.Summary: GRIT enables Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) from UC Santa Cruz and eBay to generate visually grounded reasoning chains by interleaving natural language with explicit bounding box coordinates. This method teaches MLLMs to "think with images" using a lightweight reinforcement learning approach on a dataset of only 20 image-question-answer triplets, achieving strong performance on various visual reasoning tasks without dense human annotations.
Problem: Existing open-source visual reasoning models primarily generate reasoning content using pure natural language, often lacking explicit integration of visual information, making their reasoning opaque and difficult to verify.

MLLMs face technical challenges in directly generating visual elements like bounding box coordinates within a textual reasoning chain and maintaining context across sequences interleaving numerous visual elements.
Obtaining human-annotated data that explicitly incorporates visual evidence in each reasoning step is exceptionally scarce and expensive, hindering the training of truly visually grounded models.
Method: Introduces a 'grounded reasoning paradigm' where MLLMs generate reasoning chains that seamlessly interleave natural language text with explicit bounding box coordinates, acting as pointers to specific image regions.

Employs GRPO-GR, a novel reinforcement learning algorithm, to train MLLMs to adhere to this paradigm, utilizing a composite reward system that incentivizes correct answers and proper formatting of interleaved text and bounding boxes.

Achieves high data efficiency by training models with as few as 20 unique image-query-answer triplets from existing datasets, eliminating the need for expensive human annotations of intermediate reasoning steps or bounding box labels.
Results: GRIT-trained models consistently outperformed all baselines in both GPT-as-judge answer accuracy and grounding IoU across diverse in-domain and out-of-domain visual reasoning datasets (e.g., VSR, TallyQA, GQA, MathVista-mini, MME), despite training on only 20 image-query-answer triplets.

Qualitative analysis demonstrated GRIT models exhibit flexible reasoning strategies, dynamically grounding critical image regions when necessary and correctly avoiding groundings for non-existent entities.

GRIT models achieved significantly higher Vision-Language Reasoning Cross-Modal Correlation, indicating strong semantic alignment between generated text and image regions, and analysis showed generated bounding boxes actively increased visual attention in subsequent reasoning steps.
Takeaways: Reinforcement learning, specifically GRPO-GR, effectively teaches Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to unify visual grounding and textual reasoning into a single generative process without requiring dense, step-by-step annotations.

The act of generating bounding boxes actively enhances the model's attention to relevant visual input in subsequent reasoning segments, leading to more visually consistent and coherent thought processes.

Interleaved visual-textual reasoning, where models 'think with images' by dynamically mixing bounding boxes and natural language, can be achieved in an open-source MLLM via lightweight RL, democratizing a capability previously seen in proprietary systems.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15809.Title: MMaDA: Multimodal Large Diffusion Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15809.Summary: MMaDA introduces a unified diffusion architecture that simultaneously handles textual reasoning, multimodal understanding, and text-to-image generation through a modality-agnostic design. It leverages novel post-training methods, including Mixed Long Chain-of-Thought fine-tuning and a Unified Reinforcement Learning algorithm (UniGRPO), to achieve competitive performance across these diverse tasks, notably improving reasoning and factual consistency.
Problem: Existing multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often rely on modality-specific components or hybrid autoregressive/diffusion architectures, leading to architectural complexity and inconsistencies.
There is a critical gap in exploring effective post-training methodologies for non-autoregressive, unified multimodal diffusion models, particularly concerning complex reasoning capabilities.
Many current unified models primarily focus on generic understanding and generation, often lacking explicit mechanisms for knowledge-intensive reasoning and maintaining factual consistency.
Method: Developed a unified diffusion architecture that employs a shared probabilistic formulation and modality-agnostic tokenization (using LLaDA for text, MAGVIT-v2 for images) for both text and visual data.
Introduced Mixed Long Chain-of-Thought (CoT) fine-tuning, curating a high-quality dataset of unified CoT trajectories to enhance textual and multimodal reasoning abilities.

Pioneered Unified Reinforcement Learning (UniGRPO), a policy-gradient-based RL algorithm specifically adapted for diffusion foundation models to improve performance on knowledge-intensive tasks and complex generation scenarios.
Results: MMaDA-8B achieved comparable or superior performance against dedicated understanding-only models (e.g., LLaVA-v1.5) and consistently outperformed other unified models across various multimodal understanding benchmarks.

Attained the highest CLIP Score and ImageReward among both generation-only models (e.g., SDXL) and other unified models for text-to-image generation, demonstrating superior compositionality and world knowledge-aware generation.

Showcased strong textual reasoning, outperforming the diffusion-based LLaDA-8B on mathematical reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH) and achieving performance comparable to strong autoregressive baselines (e.g., Qwen2-7B, LLaMA3-8B) on general language tasks.
Takeaways: A truly unified diffusion architecture can effectively serve as a general-purpose foundation model for multimodal intelligence, challenging the prevailing reliance on autoregressive or hybrid approaches.

Sophisticated post-training strategies, such as Cold Start Long-CoT fine-tuning and a diffusion-adapted RL algorithm (UniGRPO), are critical for boosting reasoning, factual consistency, and overall performance in non-autoregressive multimodal models.

Diffusion models' inherent parallelism and masked token prediction objective provide significant efficiency advantages and architectural flexibility, naturally supporting tasks like inpainting and extrapolation across modalities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15804.Title: STAR-R1: Spatial TrAnsformation Reasoning by Reinforcing Multimodal LLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15804.Summary: STAR-R1 enhances multimodal large language models' (MLLMs) spatial reasoning by achieving state-of-the-art performance on the Transformation-Driven Visual Reasoning (TVR) task, surpassing models like GPT-4o by 37.9% and Gemini-1.5-Pro by 45.5% in Total Accuracy using a single-stage Reinforcement Learning approach with a dense, fine-grained reward function.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle with complex spatial reasoning, particularly the Transformation-Driven Visual Reasoning (TVR) task which requires identifying and describing object transformations across images, often under varying viewpoints.

Traditional Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) methods fail to adequately capture the multi-step Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning required for TVR, especially in cross-view scenarios where object correspondence is ambiguous.

Existing Reinforcement Learning (RL) applications for multimodal reasoning often rely on two-stage training paradigms and sparse reward signals, leading to inefficient exploration and slow convergence for multi-component answers like those in TVR.
Method: The proposed framework, STAR-R1, employs a novel single-stage, pure Reinforcement Learning (RL) paradigm based on Group Reinforcement Policy Optimization (GRPO).

It features a sophisticated, dense reward function comprising a binary format reward and a multi-component accuracy reward. The accuracy reward provides positive feedback for partial correctness (matching object index, attribute, and value) and specific punishments for mistaken predictions and under-predictions.
The model is trained end-to-end on a cleaned version of the TRANCE dataset, without any supervised fine-tuning (SFT) as a prerequisite, using Qwen2.5-VL-7B as the base MLLM.
Results: STAR-R1 achieves state-of-the-art performance across all eleven TVR evaluation metrics, surpassing GPT-4o by 37.9% and Gemini-1.5-Pro by 45.5% in Total Accuracy.
The pure RL approach of STAR-R1 yields approximately a 13% gain in Total Accuracy compared to SFT methods under the same training settings.

STAR-R1 demonstrates robust generalization in challenging Out-of-Domain (cross-view) scenarios, performing full object comparisons in 81% of OOD cases and showing a substantial performance advantage over SFT-based approaches.
Takeaways: STAR-R1's pure Reinforcement Learning approach fosters an "anthropomorphic behavior" for systematic object comparison across views, leading to a 23% Total Accuracy advantage over Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) in Out-of-Domain (OOD) scenarios.

The model's response length exhibits a non-linear dynamic during RL training, initially decreasing for conciseness, then gradually increasing as the model learns to systematically explore all objects for comprehensive analysis.

Ablation studies confirm that all components of the dense reward function (object, attribute, under-prediction, and wrong-answer punishments) are essential for efficient exploration and robust performance, significantly outperforming naive GRPO.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15612.Title: Learn to Reason Efficiently with Adaptive Length-based Reward Shaping
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15612.Summary: This paper presents LASER methods (LASER, LASER-D, LASER-DE), which utilize adaptive length-based reward shaping within a reinforcement learning framework to enhance the efficiency of Large Reasoning Models. These methods improve the balance between reasoning accuracy and token usage, achieving substantial reductions in token consumption while maintaining or increasing accuracy on challenging mathematical benchmarks.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) employing Chain-of-Thought (CoT) often 'overthink', generating verbose and redundant reasoning steps.
This overthinking leads to inefficiency, increasing computational costs and hindering the practical deployment of these Large Reasoning Models (LRMs).
Existing methods for improving reasoning efficiency often face a steep trade-off, where token reduction comes at the cost of reasoning accuracy.
Method: Introduces a unified reinforcement learning framework that formulates efficient reasoning as an optimization problem incorporating correctness and length-based rewards.
Proposes LASER (Length-bAsed StEp Reward), a method that applies a step function reward to penalize reasoning chains exceeding a target length.
Develops LASER-D (Dynamic and Difficulty-aware) which adaptively adjusts the target reasoning length throughout training based on problem difficulty and current model accuracy.
Introduces LASER-DE (with additional Exploration), a variant of LASER-D that encourages further exploration on incorrect responses to discover better reasoning paths.
Results: The LASER methods achieve an improved Pareto-optimal balance between reasoning accuracy and token efficiency compared to prior approaches.
On the AIME2024 benchmark, LASER-D and LASER-DE improved accuracy by 6.1 percentage points while reducing token usage by 63%.
The proposed methods demonstrate robust generalization across out-of-domain benchmarks, including MATH500, AMC2023, and OlympiadBench.
Takeaways: A unified framework for length-based reward shaping provides a systematic approach to mitigating overthinking in large reasoning models.
Reinforcement learning with length-based reward shaping leads to more concise reasoning chains, eliminating redundant steps and reducing unnecessary self-reflection.
Dynamic adjustment of target reasoning length based on problem difficulty allows for adaptive 'fast' and 'slow' thinking, optimizing efficiency without sacrificing accuracy.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15510.Title: Visual Thoughts: A Unified Perspective of Understanding Multimodal Chain-of-Thought
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15510.Summary: This research introduces "visual thoughts" as a unified concept to explain the effectiveness of Multimodal Chain-of-Thought (MCoT) reasoning in Large Vision-Language Models. The study defines and analyzes four distinct expressions of visual thoughts, demonstrating that their clarity and conciseness are critical for MCoT performance and that they function as a cache, facilitating deeper visual information flow within the models.
Problem: The precise mechanisms and underlying reasons for Multimodal Chain-of-Thought (MCoT) effectiveness in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) remain largely unclear.
A lack of unified theoretical framework exists to explain why different MCoT paradigms (Textual-MCoT vs. Interleaved-MCoT) enhance LVLMs in distinct ways.
There is an absence of systematic understanding regarding the optimal MCoT paradigm for various tasks or how to derive generalizable insights across diverse applications.
Method: Proposed "visual thoughts" as intermediate, logic-driven cross-modal representations that act as a cache for distilled visual information, bridging raw pixels and linguistic rationales.

Categorized visual thoughts into four distinct strategies based on expression modality: Natural Language (N-LANG), Structured Language (S-LANG) for Textual-MCoT, and Edited Image (E-IMG), Generative Image (G-IMG) for Interleaved-MCoT.

Conducted extensive experiments across four state-of-the-art LVLMs and various multimodal benchmarks, coupled with detailed internal attention and information flow analysis to verify the concept and mechanisms.
Results: All four distinct visual thought expressions consistently enhanced LVLM performance, with image-form VTs outperforming text-form VTs in complex tasks, showing up to a 47.83% improvement on CoMT-Selection.
Textual-MCoT is more effective for coarse-grained perception tasks, while Interleaved-MCoT excels in scenarios requiring fine-grained visual operations and complex manipulations.

Internal analysis revealed that models shift attention significantly to visual thoughts, which then convey visual information more deeply into transformer layers and are primarily queried by input questions, optimizing visual data for reasoning.
Takeaways: Visual thoughts are essential for MCoT's effectiveness, functioning as a distilled visual information cache rather than a direct replica of the original image.
The clarity and conciseness of visual thought expressions are strongly and positively correlated with reasoning accuracy, enabling more effective information retrieval and utilization.

Visual thoughts facilitate deeper and more sustained visual information propagation into transformer layers compared to direct image input, acting as a vital intermediary for sophisticated cross-modal interaction.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15506.Title: Prompt Tuning Vision Language Models with Margin Regularizer for Few-Shot Learning under Distribution Shifts
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15506.Summary: PromptMargin, developed by researchers at the Indian Institute of Science, introduces a prompt-tuning framework for adapting pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) like CLIP to few-shot learning scenarios with distribution shifts, without relying on source-domain data. The method integrates selective augmentation and a multimodal margin regularizer, demonstrating improved performance over baselines on 15 diverse datasets, including substantial accuracy gains of up to 10.79% on challenging domains.
Problem: Pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) often experience performance degradation when adapted to target datasets with limited labeled data (few-shot learning) and significant distribution shifts from their pre-training data.

Traditional fine-tuning of large VLMs on few samples is prone to overfitting and catastrophic forgetting, while many few-shot adaptation methods require access to source-domain meta-training data, which is frequently unavailable in real-world applications.
Effectively adapting VLMs in a 'completely source-free' manner, using only a few target samples and potentially unfamiliar class names, remains a significant challenge.
Method: A prompt-tuning framework called PromptMargin is introduced, which builds upon the MaPLe baseline by only fine-tuning learnable multimodal prompts (text and visual) while keeping the VLM backbone frozen.

Selective Augmentation is employed to mitigate overfitting in few-shot settings by dynamically filtering generated augmented images, retaining only those whose embeddings are sufficiently close to their corresponding class text embeddings.
