A Multimodal Margin Regularizer (MMReg) is proposed, which enforces uniform separation not only for class text embeddings but also for class-wise image prototypes in the joint feature space, enhancing inter-class discrimination and multimodal consistency.
Results: PromptMargin achieved average accuracies of 72.00% (1-shot) and 82.76% (5-shot) across 15 datasets, outperforming the MaPLe baseline on 11 and 12 datasets, respectively.

The method demonstrated substantial accuracy improvements, with gains up to 10.79% on challenging datasets where class names were non-descriptive or unavailable (e.g., Plantae, Traffic Signs, ISIC with pseudo-classnames).

An initial analysis revealed a strong negative Pearson correlation of -0.713 between the proposed `diff_D_target` metric and zero-shot CLIP performance, indicating the utility of the metric for identifying adaptation opportunities.
Takeaways: A quantifiable metric (`diff_D_target`) can estimate the semantic and distribution difference between a target dataset and CLIP's pre-training data, reliably predicting zero-shot performance and the potential for improvement via fine-tuning.

Filtering 'bad' or unhelpful augmentations through a selective process can reduce training time by approximately 40% and consistently improve or maintain classification accuracy in data-scarce few-shot learning.

Explicitly regularizing both text and image feature separation (multimodal margin) is critical for robust class discrimination and consistent performance gains, particularly in domains with weak or ambiguous class names.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15436.Title: Adaptive Chain-of-Focus Reasoning via Dynamic Visual Search and Zooming for Efficient VLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15436.Summary: Researchers from Beijing Institute of Technology and BIGAI developed Adaptive Chain-of-Focus (Adaptive-CoF), a framework enabling Vision-Language Models to perform efficient multimodal reasoning by adaptively deciding when and where to zoom into image regions. This approach reduces unnecessary zoom-in operations by 75% and visual token consumption by 50% for equivalent accuracy, while establishing new state-of-the-art results on high-resolution and complex reasoning benchmarks.
Problem: Existing "think-with-image" Vision-Language Models (VLMs) incur substantial computational costs due to proactive and frequent visual zooming, leading to excessive token generation.
Current methods struggle to balance the need for fine-grained visual detail, crucial for complex tasks, with the computational efficiency required for practical VLM deployment.
Interactive VLMs often lack an adaptive mechanism to dynamically determine whether and where to focus attention on image regions based on the specific query and current context.
Method: An Adaptive Chain-of-Focus (Adaptive-CoF) framework allows the VLM to iteratively refine visual understanding by selectively invoking "zoom-in" operations on key regions only when assessed as necessary.
The model is trained using a two-stage pipeline: initial Supervised Fine-tuning (SFT) on a custom MM-Adaptive-CoF dataset, which includes fine-grained reasoning trajectories.

Reinforcement Learning (RL) with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and a novel Adaptive Group-Aware Reward (AGAR) is then applied to optimize the model for both accuracy and efficient, adaptive visual interaction.
Results: Adaptive-CoF achieved state-of-the-art performance on high-resolution benchmarks like V⋆ Bench (90.1) and HR-Bench 4K, and the MME-RealWorld-Lite comprehensive reasoning benchmark, surpassing larger models.
The framework demonstrated exceptional computational efficiency, reducing zoom-in operations by 75% and visual token usage by 50% to achieve comparable peak accuracy against existing baselines.

Adaptive-CoF exhibited intelligent behavior by inversely correlating zoom-in operations with input image resolution, performing significantly fewer calls at higher resolutions when sufficient detail was already present.
Takeaways: Vision-Language Models can be trained to adaptively allocate visual processing resources, dynamically deciding whether to zoom or respond, leading to substantial efficiency gains over proactive approaches.

A meticulously constructed dataset, incorporating diverse zoom-in requirements and step-by-step reasoning trajectories, is essential for effectively supervising and shaping adaptive visual search behaviors in VLMs.

The design of an adaptive, group-aware reward mechanism in reinforcement learning is crucial for guiding the model to balance accuracy with computational efficiency by explicitly penalizing superfluous visual explorations.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15134.Title: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Entropy Minimization in LLM Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15134.Summary: This research from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign explores entropy minimization as a standalone, unsupervised objective to enhance Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning. The study demonstrates that minimizing uncertainty in LLM generations, across fine-tuning and inference stages, significantly improves performance on challenging math, coding, and scientific reasoning tasks, often outperforming supervised methods and achieving competitive results with advanced proprietary models while being more computationally efficient.
Problem: Adapting large language models (LLMs) for complex reasoning tasks often requires extensive supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), which are data-intensive and computationally expensive.
Existing unsupervised LLM improvement methods, like self-consistency, often rely on answer extraction, limiting their applicability to tasks like code generation.
Many current scaling methods for LLMs at inference time incur high computational overhead.
Method: EM-FT, an unsupervised fine-tuning method, directly minimizes the empirical token-level entropy of model-generated outputs via gradient descent, making token predictions more deterministic.
EM-RL frames entropy minimization as a reinforcement learning objective, maximizing negative token-level or sequence-level entropy as a pseudo-reward signal using policy gradients.

EM-INF applies entropy minimization at inference time by treating output logits as free parameters and optimizing them to minimize the induced probability distribution's entropy before token sampling, without updating model parameters.
Results: EM-FT (unsupervised finetuning) improved performance by 8% on average across math and coding, achieving comparable or better results than strong RL baselines trained on 60K labeled examples.
EM-RL (unsupervised RL) improved base model performance by 11% on average, outperforming output-verified RL baselines on multiple math and coding tasks.

EM-INF (inference-time logit optimization) consistently improved base model performance by ~3% on average, was 3x more computationally efficient than self-consistency, and enabled a 32B model to match or exceed proprietary models like GPT-4o on the SciCode benchmark.
Takeaways: Minimizing internal uncertainty (entropy) within an LLM's generations can effectively elicit and reinforce latent reasoning abilities acquired during pre-training, without requiring external labeled data.
The effectiveness of entropy minimization depends on the base model's inherent capability, as it amplifies existing reasoning strengths but does not create entirely new ones.
Confidence from entropy minimization correlates with correctness on objective reasoning tasks but may not be reliable for subjective tasks requiring human value alignment.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15045.Title: Diffusion vs. Autoregressive Language Models: A Text Embedding Perspective
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15045.Summary: Researchers from Nanyang Technological University, Yale University, and NYU Shanghai demonstrate that diffusion language models outperform autoregressive LLMs for text embedding tasks, with their DIFFEMBED approach achieving 20% improvement on long-document retrieval and 8% improvement on reasoning-intensive retrieval by leveraging the inherent bidirectional attention architecture of diffusion models, while also introducing REASONAUG, a new training dataset for logical reasoning tasks.
Problem: Autoregressive language models have unidirectional attention that limits their ability to capture global context in text embedding tasks
Existing LLM-based embedding models struggle with long documents and reasoning-intensive retrieval scenarios
Current training datasets lack sufficient reasoning-intensive examples for developing specialized embedding capabilities
Method: Propose DIFFEMBED, which uses diffusion language models (DREAM-7B) as the backbone for text embeddings instead of autoregressive LLMs
Leverage the bidirectional attention inherent in diffusion models to better capture global document context
Create REASONAUG dataset with logically related question-solution pairs and hard negatives for training reasoning capabilities
Apply contrastive learning to fine-tune the diffusion model for embedding tasks
Results: 20% improvement over LLM-based models on LONGEMBED long-document retrieval benchmark
8% improvement on BRIGHT reasoning-intensive retrieval, with 16.4% improvement on TheoremQA specifically when using REASONAUG training
Competitive performance on instruction-following retrieval and traditional MTEB text embedding benchmarks
Ablation studies confirm bidirectional attention's importance for global context understanding
Takeaways: Bidirectional attention is crucial for encoding long and complex documents, with reverse attention having greater impact than in LLM-based models
Generalist embedding models underperform on reasoning tasks because they aren't trained to recognize theorems or use them as clustering signals
Diffusion models' architecture naturally suits text embedding tasks better than the unidirectional nature of autoregressive models

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.14970.Title: Self-Evolving Curriculum for LLM Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.14970.Summary: Researchers at Mila, ServiceNow AI Research, and other institutions developed the Self-Evolving Curriculum (SEC), an automated framework that fine-tunes Large Language Models by dynamically selecting training problems to maximize learning gain. This method improves LLM reasoning, particularly generalization to out-of-distribution problems, achieving up to 33% relative accuracy gains on specific challenging math benchmarks.
Problem: Reinforcement Learning (RL) fine-tuning for Large Language Models (LLMs) is highly dependent on the quality and sequencing of training data, often limited by suboptimal curricula.
Existing curriculum strategies are either manually designed (labor-intensive, non-adaptive), random (suboptimal), or rely on computationally expensive online filtering methods.
Poor curriculum design hinders learning efficiency, limits generalization to novel problems, and prevents the emergence of complex reasoning behaviors in LLMs.
Method: Formulates curriculum selection as a non-stationary Multi-Armed Bandit (MAB) problem, where problem categories are arms whose expected learning gains evolve over time.

Introduces the 'absolute advantage' from policy gradient methods as an efficient, locally measurable proxy reward for immediate learning gain, which prioritizes problems in the model's Zone of Proximal Development.

Implements an interleaved training process that updates the LLM policy using sampled problems and simultaneously updates the curriculum policy using TD(0) and Boltzmann exploration to adapt problem selection.
Results: Achieved consistent performance improvements across various reasoning domains (planning, inductive reasoning, mathematics), with up to 33% relative gain on challenging AIME24 mathematics problems (OOD) for the Qwen2.5-3B model.
Demonstrated adaptive curriculum adjustment, progressively introducing more challenging problems as the model's capabilities improved and adapting to different model capacities.

Maintained stable and robust performance in multi-task learning settings (SEC-2D variant), preventing performance collapse, and showed broad compatibility with alternative RL algorithms (PPO, RLOO) and automatically inferred curriculum categories.
Takeaways: Maximizing the batch-wise expectation of the absolute advantage inherently guides the curriculum to prioritize problems with an approximate 0.5 success rate, optimizing learning efficiency.
An automatic and computationally efficient curriculum can be achieved by framing it as a non-stationary MAB, eliminating the need for manual design or expensive online filtering.

Dynamically adapting the training curriculum based on the model's evolving capabilities is crucial for enhancing LLM generalization to out-of-distribution problems and maintaining stable performance in multi-task learning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.14683.Title: Emerging Properties in Unified Multimodal Pretraining
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.14683.Summary: ByteDance Seed introduced BAGEL, an open-source unified multimodal foundation model trained on trillions of interleaved text, image, and video tokens. This model demonstrates emergent reasoning abilities and achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-source alternatives, narrowing the capability gap with leading proprietary systems.
Problem: A significant performance gap existed between cutting-edge proprietary multimodal systems and publicly available academic/open-source models, often due to undisclosed techniques and data scaling strategies.

Previous open-source efforts were often limited by data diversity, relying predominantly on image-text paired data, and architectural bottlenecks that hindered seamless multimodal understanding and generation.
The research community lacked an open-source foundation model capable of unified multimodal understanding and generation with advanced complex reasoning capabilities across various modalities.
Method: BAGEL was developed with a unified, decoder-only Mixture-of-Transformer-Experts (MoT) architecture, featuring shared self-attention operations for bottleneck-free interaction between understanding and generation modules.

The model was pretrained on 'trillions of tokens' sourced from a diverse, meticulously curated, and interleaved dataset including text, image-text pairs, and especially video and web data for rich context.

A multi-stage training strategy was implemented, dynamically adjusting data mixtures and resolutions, and incorporating reasoning-augmented Chain-of-Thought (CoT) data for enhanced multimodal reasoning.
Specialized visual encoders (ViT for understanding and VAE for generation) were integrated, alongside a generalized causal attention mechanism and rectified flow for visual token prediction.
Results: BAGEL achieved state-of-the-art performance among open-source unified models on various image understanding benchmarks (e.g., MME, MMBench, MMMU, MM-Vet, MathVista, MMVP) and text-to-image generation benchmarks (88% on GenEval and 0.52 WISE score).
On the novel IntelligentBench for complex reasoning, BAGEL scored 44.9, significantly outperforming specialist models like Step1X-Edit (14.9), and further increased to 55.3 with Chain-of-Thought.

Incorporating Chain-of-Thought reasoning improved BAGEL's WISE score from 0.52 to 0.70 and its IntelligentBench score from 44.9 to 55.3, demonstrating enhanced world knowledge integration and instruction following.

The model showcased robust world modeling capabilities through fine-tuning, including free-form visual manipulation, future frame prediction, 3D manipulation, and dynamic world navigation, generalizing across diverse domains.
Takeaways: Complex compositional reasoning and 'intelligent editing' capabilities emerge non-linearly and significantly later during large-scale pretraining (beyond 2.6T tokens) compared to basic understanding and generation.

The unified Mixture-of-Transformer-Experts architecture with shared self-attention effectively supports both multimodal understanding and generation without introducing heuristic bottlenecks, outperforming dense and standard MoE designs.
The inclusion of visual-semantic reasoning provided by ViT tokens is critical for complex, intelligence-demanding tasks like 'Intelligent Editing,' while having less impact on basic editing.

Explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, integrated into both generative and understanding tasks, substantially boosts the model's ability to leverage world knowledge and follow complex instructions, improving scores by up to 0.18 points on WISE.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.14677.Title: Visionary-R1: Mitigating Shortcuts in Visual Reasoning with Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.14677.Summary: The VISIONARY-R1 framework trains visual language models for complex reasoning using reinforcement learning and CoT-free question-answer pairs, outperforming leading proprietary models like GPT-4o on benchmarks such as MathVista. It effectively mitigates shortcut learning in VLMs by enforcing a structured caption-reason-answer output and employing an AI-feedback-based caption reward.
Problem: Existing visual reasoning models are computationally expensive, often relying on multi-stage training pipelines or large volumes of human-annotated Chain-of-Thought (CoT) data.

Directly applying reinforcement learning (RL) techniques from text-only models to Visual Language Models (VLMs) leads to 'shortcut learning,' where models exploit non-visual cues instead of performing genuine visual reasoning.
These models exhibit poor generalization performance on diverse visual reasoning tasks due to their reliance on superficial patterns rather than deep visual understanding.
Method: The framework utilizes the Qwen2.5-VL-3B model and adapts the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) algorithm for visual reasoning tasks.
It enforces a structured output format, `.........`, which mandates a detailed image caption prior to reasoning and providing an answer.

A novel AI-feedback-based caption reward (`r_c`) is introduced, which uses the policy's own LLM component to evaluate if the generated caption is sufficient to answer the original question, promoting informative visual descriptions.
Results: Visionary-R1 achieved substantial performance gains, including +7.9% on MathVista and +5.6% on MathVision, over base models, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and GRPO baselines.
The 3B-parameter Visionary-R1 model surpassed leading proprietary models such as GPT-4o, Claude3.5-Sonnet, and Gemini-1.5-Pro on challenging benchmarks like MathVista and MMBench.

Ablation studies confirmed the critical impact of both the caption output format and the AI-feedback-based caption reward, with the caption reward alone contributing significant accuracy gains (e.g., +2.1% on MMBench over GRPO+Caption).
Takeaways: Shortcut learning is a critical failure mode in VLMs when applying RL, resulting in minimal, uninformative reasoning for easy training examples and poor generalization on harder test data.
Explicitly forcing visual interpretation through a structured captioning step before reasoning is crucial for robust visual grounding and effectively mitigating shortcut learning in VLMs.
The quality and informativeness of visual descriptions, measured by their sufficiency for reasoning, are more impactful than mere presence or length in achieving strong visual reasoning performance.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.14674.Title: Reward Reasoning Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.14674.Summary: Reward Reasoning Models (RRMs) introduce explicit chain-of-thought reasoning before generating a reward, allowing for adaptive utilization of test-time compute. This approach achieves competitive accuracy on reward modeling benchmarks and improves best-of-N inference for large language models.
Problem: Current reward models apply a nearly uniform computational budget across all inputs, leading to suboptimal performance on complex queries and inefficiency for simple ones.
Existing reward models often lack an inherent reasoning mechanism to accurately assess the quality of responses for intricate tasks, where the correct reward is not immediately apparent.
There is an ineffective utilization of test-time compute to enhance reward model performance, preventing adaptive effort proportional to query complexity.
Method: Proposes Reward Reasoning Models (RRMs) which utilize a Transformer-decoder backbone to autoregressively generate a chain-of-thought reasoning process followed by a final reward.

Develops a self-evolving reinforcement learning framework, using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), that trains RRMs to acquire reasoning capabilities based on a simple rule-based reward function (correct vs. incorrect judgment), without explicit human-annotated reasoning traces.

Implements multi-response rewarding strategies, including ELO rating systems and knockout tournaments, to apply pairwise-trained RRMs to scenarios with multiple candidate responses, leveraging majority voting for enhanced robustness.
Results: Reward Reasoning Models (RRMs) achieved 98.6% accuracy in the 'Reasoning' category of RewardBench, consistently outperforming 'DirectJudge' models.
RRM-32B (voting@5) reached 83.0% on MMLU-Pro, 91.8% on MATH, and 64.3% on GPQA for best-of-N inference, surpassing baseline models.

RRMs successfully guided LLM post-training via reinforcement learning on unlabeled data and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) with RRM-annotated preferences, improving downstream performance on benchmarks like Arena-Hard.
Takeaways: Explicit chain-of-thought reasoning within reward models enhances their performance, particularly on complex evaluation tasks.
Reward models can self-evolve sophisticated reasoning capabilities through a simple rule-based reinforcement learning signal, without requiring human-annotated reasoning traces.
Adaptive utilization of test-time compute (both parallel and sequential scaling) in reward models directly translates to improved accuracy and efficiency.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.14631.Title: Think Only When You Need with Large Hybrid-Reasoning Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.14631.Summary: Large Hybrid-Reasoning Models (LHRMs) from Microsoft Research and Peking University adaptively determine whether to engage in extended reasoning or provide a direct answer, addressing the "overthinking" issue in current large reasoning models. Trained with a two-stage pipeline, LHRMs reduce token consumption and latency while achieving strong reasoning capabilities, notably improving Hybrid Accuracy by over 90% compared to alternative methods at 7B scale.
Problem: Current Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) "overthink," generating lengthy reasoning traces even for simple queries.
This overthinking leads to excessive token consumption, increased latency, and wasted computational resources.
Existing models struggle to balance robust reasoning for complex tasks with efficient, direct responses for simple queries.
Method: Introduces Large Hybrid-Reasoning Models (LHRMs) capable of adaptively selecting between "Thinking" and "No-Thinking" modes.
Employs a two-stage training pipeline: Hybrid Fine-Tuning (HFT) to establish distinct modes and Hybrid Group Policy Optimization (HGPO) for adaptive mode selection.
HGPO uses an online reinforcement learning approach with inter-group and intra-group rewards to teach optimal mode choice for diverse queries.
Results: LHRMs consistently outperformed baselines, achieving average performance gains of 9.2% (1.5B) and 7.1% (7B) over HFT-DPO on various benchmarks.
Demonstrated superior adaptive behavior, with LHRM-7B achieving over 90% higher Hybrid Accuracy than HFT-DPO, correctly selecting reasoning modes.
Showed strong reasoning capabilities, improving 10.3% (1.5B) and 13.6% (7B) on AIME24 over HFT-DPO, while reducing thinking ratios for simpler queries.
Takeaways: Adaptive mode selection, mimicking human System 1/System 2 thinking, significantly improves efficiency and user experience in large language models.
A specialized reinforcement learning algorithm like Hybrid Group Policy Optimization (HGPO) is effective in training models to dynamically choose optimal reasoning paths.
The new Hybrid Accuracy (H_Acc) metric is crucial for evaluating a model's ability to correctly select the appropriate reasoning mode for varied queries.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.14404.Title: ViC-Bench: Benchmarking Visual-Interleaved Chain-of-Thought Capability in MLLMs with Free-Style Intermediate State Representations
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.14404.Summary: ViC-Bench introduces a new benchmark for evaluating Multi-modal Large Language Models' (MLLMs) Visual-Interleaved Chain-of-Thought (VI-CoT) capabilities, featuring free-style intermediate visual state representations across four diverse tasks. The comprehensive evaluation strategy uncovers MLLMs' strengths and weaknesses in dynamically utilizing visual feedback for complex reasoning, revealing substantial performance gaps and areas for improvement.
Problem: Existing Visual-Interleaved Chain-of-Thought (VI-CoT) benchmarks provide models with fixed Intermediate Visual States (IVS), potentially misrepresenting their true reasoning abilities.
There is a lack of systematic exploration into how various IVS representations (positive, negative, or neutral) influence Multi-modal Large Language Model (MLLM) reasoning performance.
Current evaluation methods often fail to capture MLLMs' intrinsic capacity for dynamic visual thinking, which is crucial for human-like complex problem-solving.
Method: ViC-Bench is introduced, featuring four diverse tasks (maze navigation, jigsaw puzzle, embodied planning, complex counting) that inherently demand dynamic interaction with visual contexts.
Dedicated data construction pipelines enable free-style Intermediate Visual State (IVS) generation, allowing models to interact with adaptive visual feedback via function calls.

A progressive three-stage evaluation strategy with novel metrics, including ThinkGain, systematically assesses Visual-Interleaved Chain-of-Thought (VI-CoT) performance and the gains from free-style IVS.
Results: Commercial proprietary MLLMs consistently outperform open-source models, particularly in complex reasoning and leveraging free-style Intermediate Visual States (IVS).

A significant performance drop is observed from multiple-choice to open-ended question answering, especially in embodied planning (e.g., GPT-4o's ACC dropped from 57.2% to 0.04%), indicating a struggle with autonomous, unguided reasoning.

Free-style IVS yields substantial 'ThinkGain' in tasks requiring sequential verification (e.g., maze navigation, embodied planning), yet surprisingly leads to negative ThinkGain for jigsaw puzzles, suggesting potential distraction or misinterpretation of visual feedback.
Takeaways: Free-style Intermediate Visual States (IVS) act as crucial visual anchors, significantly enhancing reasoning in sequential tasks like maze navigation and embodied planning, but can sometimes distract or lead to irrational decisions in tasks requiring fine-grained semantic understanding.
There is a notable performance disparity between commercial proprietary MLLMs and open-source models, especially in their ability to leverage complex reasoning and free-style IVS.

Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) face considerable challenges in open-ended reasoning without explicit options, often exhibiting 'embodied hallucinations' and a lack of grounded physical world understanding.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.14362.Title: DeepEyes: Incentivizing "Thinking with Images" via Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.14362.Summary: DeepEyes enables Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to perform 'thinking with images' by dynamically integrating visual re-perception into their reasoning process through end-to-end reinforcement learning. This approach, developed by researchers from Xiaohongshu Inc. and Xi'an Jiaotong University, achieves notable performance improvements, including an 18.9% accuracy gain on V* Bench and a 1.8% reduction in hallucinations on POPE compared to baselines.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language Models (VLMs) primarily rely on text-based Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, treating visual input as static and limiting dynamic visual re-evaluation.
Prior methods for integrating visual tools often use rigid, pre-defined workflows or require separate, specialized models, leading to sub-optimal performance and poor generalization.
Lack of a native mechanism for iterative visual reasoning within VLMs, unlike human cognition which seamlessly integrates visual perception and re-evaluation during thought.
Method: Introduces Interleaved Multimodal Chain-of-Thought (iMCoT), allowing the VLM to autonomously invoke an image zoom-in tool to crop and re-incorporate specific visual regions during reasoning.

Utilizes an agentic Reinforcement Learning framework with a composite reward design, including a conditional tool usage bonus, to incentivize effective visual tool utilization without cold-start supervised fine-tuning.

Employs a tool-use-oriented data selection mechanism that prioritizes samples where visual tool use provides significant information gain, drawing from diverse fine-grained, chart, and reasoning datasets.
Results: DeepEyes achieved 90.1% accuracy on V* Bench, an 18.9% gain over the baseline Qwen2.5-VL 7B, and improved HR-Bench 4K by 6.3% and HR-Bench 8K by 7.3%.
It demonstrated improved visual grounding and reduced hallucinations, achieving 87.7% accuracy on POPE (a 1.8% increase) by enabling the model to zoom in and verify object presence.
Qualitative analysis revealed emergent human-like reasoning patterns, including visual search, comparison, and confirmation, and distinct stages of tool-use learning during RL.
Takeaways: The ability for Vision-Language Models to perform dynamic visual re-perception (thinking with images) can emerge natively through end-to-end reinforcement learning.
A conditional tool usage reward, given only when a tool is used and the final answer is correct, effectively incentivizes efficient and purposeful tool exploitation during RL training.
The model's tool-calling behavior evolves through distinct stages during RL, from exploration to high-frequency usage, culminating in efficient and selective tool utilization.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.14246.Title: Visual Agentic Reinforcement Fine-Tuning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.14246.Summary: Researchers from Shanghai AI Lab and collaborating institutions develop Visual-ARFT, a reinforcement fine-tuning framework that enables Large Vision-Language Models to use web search and code execution tools for complex visual reasoning tasks, achieving up to 18.6% improvement in F1 scores over baselines while surpassing GPT-4o performance on image manipulation tasks.
Problem: Current Large Vision-Language Models lack effective multimodal agentic capabilities for combining visual and textual reasoning
Existing supervised fine-tuning approaches for enabling tool use are costly and difficult to generalize
Method: Visual Agentic Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (Visual-ARFT) framework using verifiable rewards
Group Relative Policy Optimization to maintain training stability
New Multi-modal Agentic Tool Bench (MAT) for standardized evaluation
Results: 18.6% F1 score improvement on MAT-Coding benchmark over baseline models
10.3% F1 score improvement on MAT-Search tasks
29.3% F1 score gains on existing multi-hop QA benchmarks like 2Wiki and HotpotQA
Surpassed GPT-4o performance on image manipulation tasks while using open-source models
Takeaways: Verifiable rewards based on format compliance and answer accuracy provide better training signals than learned reward models
Combining web search and code execution capabilities enables more complex visual reasoning tasks
Reinforcement fine-tuning can be effectively adapted for multimodal tool use

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.14231.Title: UniVG-R1: Reasoning Guided Universal Visual Grounding with Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.14231.Summary: UniVG-R1 introduces a reasoning-guided multimodal large language model for universal visual grounding, employing a two-stage training approach combining Chain-of-Thought supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning with a difficulty-aware weighting strategy. The model achieves state-of-the-art performance on multi-image grounding benchmarks while demonstrating strong zero-shot generalization across diverse reasoning tasks.
Problem: Existing visual grounding methods struggle with implicit and complex instructions, particularly when information is spread across multiple images.
Current multimodal large language models (MLLMs) lack explicit reasoning processes tailored for deep multimodal grounding challenges in multi-image settings.

Reinforcement learning for MLLMs faces a 'cold-start' problem, struggling to generate correct reasoning without initial guidance, and can suffer from a 'difficulty bias' where training over-emphasizes easier samples.
Method: UniVG-R1 employs a two-stage training protocol built on Qwen2-VL, starting with Chain-of-Thought Supervised Fine-tuning (CoT-SFT) using a 90k curated dataset of reasoning chains to address the RL 'cold-start' problem.

The second stage refines reasoning capabilities through rule-based Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), which uses accuracy and format rewards to guide the model towards correct reasoning and bounding box predictions.

A difficulty-aware weight adjustment strategy is introduced into the GRPO objective function to mitigate the 'difficulty bias,' dynamically increasing the influence of harder samples during training based on their mean Intersection over Union (IoU).
Results: UniVG-R1 achieves state-of-the-art performance on the MIG-Bench for multi-image grounding, surpassing the previous best model by 9.1% average accuracy while using considerably less data (approx. 8.3% of the data size).

It demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization, achieving an average improvement of 23.4% across four diverse reasoning-guided grounding benchmarks (LISA-Grounding, LLMSeg-Grounding, ReasonVOS-Grounding, ReVOS-Grounding).

Ablation studies confirm that both the Chain-of-Thought Supervised Fine-tuning stage and the difficulty-aware Group Relative Policy Optimization stage contribute to performance gains, with the latter providing an additional 2.0% improvement and showing greater benefit for smaller models.
Takeaways: A supervised 'cold-start' with high-quality reasoning chains is necessary to effectively initiate reinforcement learning for complex multi-image reasoning tasks.
Explicitly training models to generate and follow Chain-of-Thought processes significantly enhances performance on reasoning-heavy visual grounding tasks.
Addressing difficulty bias in reinforcement learning through dynamic weighting improves model learning, particularly for challenging samples.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.14204.Title: Beginning with You: Perceptual-Initialization Improves Vision-Language Representation and Alignment
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.14204.Summary: Researchers at Vanderbilt University propose a new paradigm for training vision-language models, called perceptual-initialization, which involves first training the vision encoder on human perceptual similarity data before standard web-scale pretraining. This approach led to improvements in zero-shot classification performance by up to 4.0 percentage points and demonstrated superior scaling laws, allowing for more compute-efficient training.
Problem: Current vision-language models (VLMs) like CLIP rely heavily on noisy, web-scraped image-caption data, which may not accurately reflect human perception.
Random initialization of deep neural networks creates arbitrary starting points that can hinder alignment with human perceptual space and amplify early training biases.

Traditional post-hoc alignment methods, such as fine-tuning, are computationally expensive and can distort the VLM's pre-trained representation space, failing to adequately align with human perception.
Method: A two-stage training paradigm begins by initializing the vision encoder with knowledge derived from human perceptual similarity judgments using the NIGHTS dataset and a triplet contrastive loss.
Only the vision encoder's parameters are updated during the first stage, establishing a human-aligned initial representation space.
The second stage proceeds with standard contrastive vision-language pretraining on web-scale data (YFCC15M), using the perceptually-initialized vision encoder and a randomly initialized text encoder.
Results: The perceptually-initialized model improved zero-shot classification accuracy by +3.8 percentage points on ImageNet and +3.5 percentage points on ImageNet OOD compared to baselines.
Achieved superior zero-shot retrieval performance across MS-COCO and Flickr30k datasets, with higher recall scores for both image-to-text and text-to-image tasks.
Demonstrated higher scaling exponents (e.g., ImageNet: β = 0.681 vs. 0.511 for baseline), indicating more efficient learning and faster performance gains as training data increases.
Takeaways: Initializing vision encoders with human perceptual data leads to more human-aligned representations and superior performance compared to random initialization.
Perceptual initialization results in more favorable scaling laws, indicating faster performance improvements with increasing data and greater compute efficiency.

Attempting post-hoc alignment through fine-tuning on perceptual data can disrupt learned representations and degrade zero-shot performance, emphasizing the importance of early integration of human perceptual structure.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13975.Title: DRP: Distilled Reasoning Pruning with Skill-aware Step Decomposition for Efficient Large Reasoning Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13975.Summary: The DRP framework enables small-scale Large Reasoning Models to achieve efficient and accurate reasoning by using a powerful teacher model to prune and refine the student's own verbose reasoning trajectories, notably reducing token usage by 64% while improving GSM8K accuracy from 91.7% to 94.1%. This process is enhanced by skill-aware step decomposition, which creates precise, functionally aligned reasoning units for more effective distillation.
Problem: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) tend to "overthink," producing excessively verbose and often redundant reasoning steps, leading to high inference overhead and computational costs.
Existing inference-time pruning methods often risk prematurely halting reasoning, causing a degradation in accuracy for complex tasks.

Traditional distillation methods face a "learnability gap" when attempting to transfer concise reasoning from a teacher to a student model that naturally generates verbose explanations, hindering effective knowledge transfer.
Method: The Distilled Reasoning Pruning (DRP) framework is introduced, employing a three-stage process to refine student model reasoning: Skill-Based Step Decomposition, Step-Level Pruning, and Supervised Fine-Tuning.
A powerful teacher model (e.g., GPT-4o) is used to segment the student's initial verbose reasoning into fine-grained, skill-labeled steps, ensuring semantic coherence.

The teacher then performs step-level revision actions (keep, delete, rewrite, merge) on these decomposed steps to create a concise, refined reasoning trace, which is used to fine-tune the student model.
Results: DRP achieved substantial token reductions, such as a 64% decrease on GSM8K (from 917 to 328 tokens), while consistently maintaining or improving Pass@1 accuracy across various benchmarks, including an increase from 91.7% to 94.1% on GSM8K.

The framework significantly outperformed prior methods like TALE and CoT-Valve in both compression and accuracy, particularly on out-of-domain tasks, and showed competitive performance with RL-based ThinkPrune with higher accuracy improvements.

Ablation studies confirmed the superiority of skill-based decomposition for robust generalization and demonstrated DRP's effectiveness is consistent across different teacher models, with greater impact on smaller student models (e.g., 12.7% accuracy increase for 1.5B model on GSM8K).
Takeaways: Effective reasoning distillation requires supervision that is not merely short but also informative and structurally consistent with the student's natural reasoning style to bridge the learnability gap.
Skill-based step decomposition provides a more stable and effective basis for pruning and revision than simple sentence splitting, enhancing both fine-grained signal and out-of-domain generalization.

Teacher-guided structural pruning of a student model's own verbose Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning is more effective than direct distillation of a teacher's concise CoT, leading to simultaneous improvements in efficiency and accuracy.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13934.Title: RLVR-World: Training World Models with Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13934.Summary: The Tsinghua University Machine Learning Group developed RLVR-World, a framework that fine-tunes pre-trained language and video world models using reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. This approach directly optimizes for task-specific prediction metrics, leading to improved accuracy by up to 44.8% in text game state prediction, a 30.3% F1 score increase for web page state prediction, and a 9.2% LPIPS improvement in robot video prediction, all while significantly reducing training steps and mitigating generative artifacts like repetition.
Problem: Traditional Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) for world models often leads to a misalignment between training objectives and desired task-specific prediction goals.
MLE can result in artifacts like blurry video predictions or repetition in generated sequences and does not directly optimize for metrics like accuracy or perceptual quality.
A unified, efficient post-training method for diverse world models (language, video) to directly improve their utility for downstream tasks was lacking.
Method: A unified framework transforms language and video world modeling into an autoregressive token sequence generation task using decoder-only Transformers, initially pre-trained with MLE.

Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) is applied post-training, where the model generates multiple candidate predictions, and modality-specific decoders convert them back to the original form.

Rule-based, verifiable rewards are computed by directly comparing predictions against ground truth, and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is used to fine-tune the model without a separate value function.
Results: For language world models, RLVR-World improved text game state prediction accuracy by up to 44.8% and web page state prediction F1-score by 30.3% over supervised fine-tuning baselines, also boosting web agent success rates by 18.4%.
Video world models showed substantial gains on robot manipulation tasks, including a 9.2% relative LPIPS improvement and a 26.1% relative MSE improvement for multi-step prediction.

RLVR fine-tuning achieved these performance boosts with only a few hundred gradient steps, drastically more efficiently than the hundreds of thousands of steps for MLE pre-training, and reduced video repetition rates from 48.6% to 9.9%.
Takeaways: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) provides a highly efficient and effective post-training paradigm to align world models directly with task-specific metrics across diverse modalities.
Formulating world modeling tasks as a unified token-based autoregressive sequence generation problem enables the broad application of RLVR to both language and video.
Direct optimization with verifiable rewards can significantly reduce common generative model artifacts, such as repetition, and improve overall prediction quality with minimal training steps.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13840.Title: EfficientLLM: Efficiency in Large Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13840.Summary: A comprehensive empirical evaluation framework assesses efficiency techniques for Large Language Models across architecture pretraining, fine-tuning, and quantization dimensions, revealing key trade-offs between memory usage, compute utilization, latency, throughput and energy consumption while demonstrating effective transfer of findings to vision and multimodal models.
Problem: LLMs' escalating resource demands (compute, memory, energy) limit widespread adoption
Lack of systematic comparison of efficiency techniques across model scales and tasks
Method: Novel benchmark (EfficientLLM) with fine-grained efficiency metrics
Systematic evaluation of state-of-the-art techniques on production hardware
Open-source datasets, evaluation pipelines and leaderboards
Results: MQA achieves best memory-latency trade-off for resource-constrained scenarios
RSLoRA outperforms LoRA for models >14B parameters in both loss and latency
Int4 quantization significantly reduces memory/energy with moderate accuracy impact
Efficiency findings demonstrate consistent patterns across modalities (LLM, LVM, VLM)
Takeaways: No universally optimal efficiency method - each improves some metrics while regressing others
Optimal techniques depend heavily on model scale and specific task requirements
Efficiency techniques validated on LLMs transfer effectively to vision/multimodal models

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13584.Title: Self-Supervised Learning for Image Segmentation: A Comprehensive Survey
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13584.Summary: Thangarajah Akilan and colleagues systematically review over 150 recent publications on self-supervised learning for image segmentation, organizing SSL approaches into three categories (predictive, generative, and contrastive pretext tasks) while compiling benchmark datasets and identifying key challenges including sensitivity to hyperparameters, difficulty capturing complex spatial relationships, and limited interpretability of learned representations.
Problem: Supervised deep learning for image segmentation requires large, precisely labeled datasets that are expensive and time-consuming to create
Lack of comprehensive surveys specifically focused on self-supervised learning approaches for image segmentation tasks
Researchers need structured guidance to select appropriate SSL methods for their specific segmentation applications
Method: Systematic literature review of SSL methodologies across multiple academic databases using specific selection criteria
Categorization of pretext tasks into predictive (jigsaw puzzles, rotation prediction), generative (colorization, denoising, inpainting), and contrastive (SimCLR, MoCo, BYOL) approaches
Compilation of benchmark datasets with detailed characteristics and comparative analysis of existing SSL methods
Results: Comprehensive categorization and analysis of SSL approaches spanning predictive, generative, and contrastive methodologies
Curated resource of commonly used benchmark datasets with image resolution, sample counts, and class information
Identification of key research gaps and proposed future directions including few-shot learning integration and real-time optimization strategies
Takeaways: Different SSL pretext task categories exhibit distinct strengths and weaknesses for segmentation applications
Current SSL methods face challenges in defining meaningful objectives that translate effectively to pixel-level segmentation tasks
Integration of semantic information and domain adaptation techniques represent promising directions for improving SSL effectiveness

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13445.Title: Trust, But Verify: A Self-Verification Approach to Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13445.Summary: Researchers from Tencent and CUHK-Shenzhen introduce RISE, a reinforcement learning framework that trains language models to simultaneously improve reasoning and self-verification capabilities through online verification, demonstrating enhanced performance across mathematical reasoning benchmarks while maintaining strong verification abilities across multiple model sizes (1.5B-7B parameters).
Problem: Existing LLMs often exhibit superficial self-reflection and struggle with robust self-assessment
Current approaches tend to decouple problem-solving from verification, lacking direct feedback for verification skills
Method: Unified RL framework combining problem-solving and self-verification training
Online verification system where models verify their own on-policy generated solutions
Integration of verification-weighted majority voting for enhanced test-time performance
Results: Consistent outperformance of Zero-RL baseline in both reasoning and self-verification accuracy
Significant improvements over standard SFT and base models across different model sizes
Enhanced test-time scaling through improved consistency with verification-weighted majority voting
Demonstrated scalability across different model sizes while maintaining verification capabilities
Takeaways: Online verification of self-generated solutions is crucial for developing robust verification capabilities
Unified training of both solving and verification skills leads to better overall performance
Model performance continues to scale with increased training compute

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13438.Title: Optimizing Anytime Reasoning via Budget Relative Policy Optimization
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13438.Summary: Researchers from Sea AI Lab and the National University of Singapore developed AnytimeReasoner, a framework that optimizes Large Language Models for reasoning under varying computational budgets. This approach, using verifiable dense rewards and Budget Relative Policy Optimization (BRPO), consistently improves "anytime" accuracy and final performance across mathematical reasoning benchmarks while enhancing token efficiency.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) typically optimize reasoning for a single, fixed, and often large token budget, leading to high computational costs and limited serving capacity for online services.

Existing LLM reasoning methods lack inherent "anytime" capability, meaning they cannot gracefully provide improving solutions or optimal performance under variable or interrupted computational budgets.

Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) in LLMs suffers from sparse, end-of-trace rewards, which hinder effective credit assignment for long reasoning chains and often lead to unstable training.
Method: The AnytimeReasoner framework decouples the thinking process (Chain-of-Thought) from the answer summarization, allowing for a valid summary even when the thinking process is incomplete or truncated.

It optimizes for anytime reasoning by sampling varying thinking budgets and generating verifiable dense rewards at multiple truncation points within a reasoning chain, providing richer training signals.

A novel variance reduction technique, Budget Relative Policy Optimization (BRPO), is introduced, combining intra-trajectory progress and group average baselines to stabilize and improve the efficiency of RL training for the thinking policy.
Results: AnytimeReasoner variants consistently outperformed the GRPO baseline across all evaluated mathematical reasoning benchmarks and thinking budget prior distributions, showing superior "anytime" and final accuracy.

Models trained with the framework achieved significantly shorter "Average Thinking Length" under maximum budgets, indicating improved token efficiency and more concise reasoning without compromising accuracy.

Ablation studies confirmed that verifiable dense rewards, decoupled policy optimization, and Budget Relative Policy Optimization (BRPO) each independently contribute to improved reasoning performance and training stability.
The framework maintained its clear performance advantages, showing up to 5 absolute percentage points improvement in "anytime" reasoning accuracy, when scaled to larger 7B parameter LLMs.
Takeaways: Dense, verifiable rewards generated at various budget points throughout a reasoning trace significantly improve credit assignment and learning stability for LLMs compared to traditional sparse end-of-trace rewards.

Decoupling the thinking and summary policies, and specifically training the summary policy with a uniform budget distribution, is crucial for robustly extracting optimal answers from incomplete reasoning processes.
Budget Relative Policy Optimization (BRPO) effectively reduces variance in RL training for LLM generation, enhancing stability and performance, especially for optimizing long reasoning sequences.
Optimizing LLMs for "anytime" reasoning, which maximizes performance across all computational budgets, also inherently leads to improvements in final accuracy under maximum budget conditions.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13379.Title: Thinkless: LLM Learns When to Think
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13379.Summary: Researchers at the National University of Singapore developed "Thinkless," an RL-based framework that enables large language models to autonomously decide whether to employ concise or detailed reasoning for a given query. This adaptivity reduces token generation by 50-90% while maintaining performance across various mathematical benchmarks.
Problem: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning in large language models (LLMs) is computationally inefficient, applying extensive reasoning steps to every query regardless of its complexity.

Existing hybrid reasoning approaches, which attempt to switch between concise and detailed responses, rely on manually designed heuristics or separate router models that lack adaptability and generalizability.
This 'overthinking' leads to redundant token generation, increased memory consumption, and substantially higher inference costs for LLMs.
Method: Introduced two special control tokens, `` and ``, generated as the first token of an LLM's output to signal whether to produce a concise or detailed reasoning response.

Implemented a two-stage training process: an initial distillation phase (Supervised Fine-Tuning) warms up the model to generate both short and long-form responses, followed by a reinforcement learning phase.

Developed Decoupled Group Relative Policy Optimization (DeGRPO), a novel RL algorithm that independently normalizes and balances gradient signals for mode selection and content generation, mitigating 'mode collapse' during training.
Results: "Thinkless" reduced the usage of long-chain thinking by 50% to 90% across various benchmarks (e.g., Minerva Algebra, MATH-500, GSM8K), leading to significant token reduction and computational savings.
The framework maintained or improved task performance, achieving efficiency gains with minimal to no degradation in accuracy (e.g., within 1% on Minerva Algebra).
It outperformed heuristic-based length-compressing techniques and router-based approaches by providing a truly adaptive and confidence-informed reasoning dispatch without manual tuning.
Takeaways: LLMs can learn to autonomously adapt their reasoning depth based on task complexity and their own capabilities, moving beyond reliance on manual heuristics.

Decoupling the reinforcement learning objective for mode selection and content generation is critical for stable training, effectively preventing 'mode collapse' that hinders learning in standard optimization methods.

The 'U-shaped learning curve' observed in Decoupled GRPO indicates a complex learning process where the model initially favors longer reasoning for accuracy, then optimizes by shifting simpler tasks to efficient short responses.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13317.Title: Unlabeled Data vs. Pre-trained Knowledge: Rethinking SSL in the Era of Large Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13317.Summary: Nanjing University researchers introduce "Few-shot SSL," a unified framework for comparing semi-supervised learning (SSL) and pretrain-finetuning with Vision-Language Models (VLMs). Their comparative analysis indicates that VLMs generally achieve superior performance and efficiency across diverse low-labeled-data scenarios, while SSL remains more effective for low-resolution inputs or semantically coarse tasks.
Problem: Deep learning applications face a significant bottleneck due to the high cost and laboriousness of acquiring large, meticulously labeled datasets.
Practitioners and researchers lack clear guidance on whether to leverage additional unlabeled data (SSL) or pre-trained knowledge (VLMs) when labeled data is scarce.
A systematic and fair comparison framework was missing to evaluate the comparative efficacy and optimal application scenarios of SSL and pretrain-finetuning paradigms.
Method: Proposed "Few-shot SSL," a unified evaluation framework designed for a fair comparison between SSL methods and pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) under various limited labeled data conditions.
Conducted extensive comparative experiments across four semi-supervised settings: standard, open-set, open-world, and long-tailed, to investigate the performance of both paradigms.
Utilized prominent SSL methods (e.g., FixMatch, DWD) and VLM fine-tuning techniques (e.g., CLIP, CoOp, PromptSRC) as representative baselines.
Results: VLMs generally outperformed SSL methods across most semi-supervised settings (e.g., over 73% accuracy on ImageNet with 2% labeled data vs. FixMatch with 10% labels), particularly on datasets with resolutions higher than 32x32 pixels.
SSL methods demonstrated better performance on lower-resolution datasets like CIFAR-10/100, where VLM performance was degraded by upsampling distortions.

VLMs exhibited strong robustness against out-of-distribution unlabeled data and effectively handled long-tailed distributions, showing balanced performance across known and unseen classes in open-world settings on high-resolution data.
Takeaways: Pre-trained VLMs generally exhibit stronger generalization capabilities and data efficiency compared to SSL, especially when dealing with higher image resolutions and clear semantic categories.
SSL methods maintain a performance advantage in specific niches, particularly with low-resolution inputs or when semantic structures are ambiguous among categories.

The presence of out-of-distribution (OOD) data in the unlabeled pool and severe class imbalance in long-tailed distributions disproportionately affect SSL performance, making VLMs a more robust alternative in these cases.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13308.Title: Seek in the Dark: Reasoning via Test-Time Instance-Level Policy Gradient in Latent Space
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13308.Summary: Researchers from NLCo Lab at BIGAI and collaborators developed LATENTSEEK, a framework enhancing LLM reasoning by applying test-time policy gradient optimization in the continuous latent space. It achieves average gains of 15.23 points over Best-of-N on GSM8K and demonstrates a novel axis for test-time scaling without parameter updates.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle with tasks requiring structured, meticulous, step-by-step reasoning.
Existing methods for enhancing LLM reasoning are either limited in expressiveness (e.g., prompt engineering) or are computationally expensive and data-intensive (e.g., training-based RL).
A need exists for efficient test-time scaling methods that extend beyond discrete token generation to explore continuous latent spaces for more effective and adaptive reasoning.
Method: LATENTSEEK proposes optimizing initial latent representations in the LLM's continuous latent space using the REINFORCE policy gradient method at test time, without updating model parameters.
It employs self-generated reward signals from the LLM itself to guide iterative updates of a fraction of initial latent representations.
The framework performs instance-level adaptation by decoding optimized latents into reasoning sequences and iteratively refines them for a problem-specific solution.
Results: LATENTSEEK consistently outperforms all tested baselines, achieving average gains of 15.23 points over Best-of-N on GSM8K and improving over Self-Reflection on MATH-500 and Chain-of-Thought on AIME2024.
The method demonstrates robustness across various LLM architectures (Qwen2, Qwen2.5, LLaMA3.1) and sizes (from 1.5B to 14B parameters).

Under a Perfect Sparse Reward Model, a small Qwen2.5-1.5B model achieves significant performance, surpassing GPT-4o on AIME2024 by 14 points and nearing o1-preview on MATH-500, indicating high latent space expressivity.
Takeaways: Active, gradient-guided optimization in the LLM's continuous latent space at test time offers a powerful, lightweight alternative for enhancing reasoning capabilities.
The optimal reasoning paths for LLMs in latent space may not always align with human-interpretable linguistic coherence, suggesting a distinct mode of effective AI reasoning.

The concept of 'test-time scaling' can be extended beyond searching in discrete token space to iterative optimization within latent representations, showing performance gains with increased iterations.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13138.Title: Neurosymbolic Diffusion Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13138.Summary: This research introduces Neurosymbolic Diffusion Models (NESYDMS), a framework that integrates masked diffusion models with symbolic programs to learn expressive distributions over symbolic concepts and task outputs. The approach achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on high-dimensional reasoning tasks like visual path planning (97.40% on 30x30 grids) and demonstrates improved concept calibration for better reasoning shortcut awareness.
Problem: Standard probabilistic neurosymbolic predictors rely on a conditional independence assumption between extracted symbolic concepts, limiting their ability to model complex interactions and quantify uncertainty.

This conditional independence leads to 'reasoning shortcuts' (RSs), where models achieve high output accuracy with incorrect underlying concepts, resulting in overconfident predictions and poor generalization to out-of-distribution data.

Existing methods to overcome the independence assumption often face scalability issues, requiring exponential time or a large number of additional parameters, making them impractical for complex reasoning tasks.
Method: The authors introduce Neurosymbolic Diffusion Models (NESYDMS), which leverage masked diffusion models (MDMs) as neural concept extractors to explicitly model dependencies between symbolic concepts.

A novel continuous-time variational lower bound (NELBO) is derived, enabling scalable training by incorporating symbolic programs and decomposing the loss into concept unmasking, output unmasking (via Weighted Model Counts), and variational entropy terms.

A sampling-based approach using the REINFORCE Leave-One-Out (RLOO) gradient estimator is employed to approximate gradients for intractable components like WMC, coupled with self-normalised importance sampling for latent concept inference.
Results:
NESYDMS achieved state-of-the-art accuracy on high-dimensional visual path planning tasks, reaching 97.40% ± 1.23 on challenging 30x30 grids with a
5
900
combinatorial space.

The model demonstrated significantly improved concept accuracy and calibration (lower ECE) on reasoning shortcut (RS) benchmarks like RSBench, with an ECE
c,ID
of 4.18% for MNIST Half compared to 36.81% for prior state-of-the-art BEARS.

On the real-world BDD-OIA (autonomous driving) task, NESYDMS showed better predictive performance (MF1
y
of 62.63%) and improved concept calibration (ECE
c
of 21.72%) compared to independence-assuming baselines.
Takeaways: Masked diffusion models can effectively capture global dependencies between symbolic concepts while maintaining local tractability, allowing for scalable integration into neurosymbolic frameworks.
Explicitly modeling concept dependencies and incorporating entropy regularization in the loss function significantly improves reasoning shortcut awareness and the calibration of concept predictions.

A principled continuous-time variational lower bound can be formulated for neurosymbolic diffusion, providing a robust theoretical foundation for learning expressive, non-factorized distributions under hard symbolic constraints.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13031.Title: MindOmni: Unleashing Reasoning Generation in Vision Language Models with RGPO
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13031.Summary: MindOmni, a unified multimodal large language model, enhances reasoning generation in vision-language tasks by integrating Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning with a novel Reinforcement Learning (RGPO) algorithm. The model produces explicit logical steps before image generation and achieves a 0.71 score on the WISE benchmark for reasoning-aware image generation, while maintaining strong performance in general image generation and vision understanding.
Problem: Current Text-to-Image (T2I) systems lack multimodal input capabilities and explicit reasoning, failing on complex prompts requiring world knowledge or logic.
Existing unified Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) primarily function as semantic feature extractors, often underperforming on tasks requiring deep reasoning.
Prior Chain-of-Thought (CoT) approaches for image synthesis are often constrained to specific domains, rely on inflexible templates, or lack generalizable complex reasoning.
Method: MindOmni employs a unified architecture based on Qwen2.5-VL and an OmniGen diffusion decoder, connected by a lightweight two-layer connector.
A three-phase training strategy includes supervised pre-training for unified capabilities, supervised fine-tuning with coarse-to-fine Chain-of-Thought instruction data, and reinforcement learning.

A novel Reasoning Generation Policy Optimization (RGPO) algorithm enhances explicit reasoning generation using format and consistency rewards, alongside dual KL regularizers (text and image) for training stability.
Results: MindOmni achieved an overall score of 0.71 on the WISE benchmark for reasoning-aware image generation, outperforming all other methods, including leading generative-only and unified models.
The model achieved an 83% overall score on GenEval, representing state-of-the-art performance for unified MLLMs in general text-to-image generation.
MindOmni maintained strong vision understanding performance, showing a negligible 0.1% average difference from its Qwen2.5-VL backbone and improving 10.6% on MMMU over Janus-Pro.
Takeaways: Reinforcement learning, specifically the RGPO algorithm, can successfully foster explicit, step-by-step reasoning (Chain-of-Thought) in generative multimodal models.
Integrating explicit reasoning generation improves the accuracy and contextual appropriateness of visual outputs for complex, logically demanding prompts.

A multi-stage training strategy, including supervised fine-tuning with Chain-of-Thought instruction data and reinforcement learning, is effective for achieving superior performance in reasoning-aware image generation while maintaining strong general capabilities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.12514.Title: Reasoning by Superposition: A Theoretical Perspective on Chain of Continuous Thought
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.12514.Summary: Researchers from UC Berkeley, UCSD, and Meta AI theoretically demonstrate that Chain-of-Continuous-Thought allows Large Language Models to solve directed graph reachability in significantly fewer steps (D steps vs. O(n^2) for discrete CoT) by forming "superposition states" that encode multiple search frontiers simultaneously. This efficiency and the emergent parallel search behavior were confirmed empirically with a lightweight transformer achieving near-perfect accuracy.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) with traditional discrete Chain-of-Thought (CoT) exhibit limitations in scalability and efficiency for complex reasoning tasks, often requiring numerous sequential steps.
Solving fundamental graph reasoning problems, such as directed graph reachability, using constant-depth transformers with discrete CoT is known to require O(n^2) decoding steps.

A formal theoretical understanding of the mechanisms behind the observed empirical performance gains of continuous Chain-of-Thought (COCONUT) and its ability to store "superposition states" was lacking.
Method: The authors constructed a rigorous theoretical proof-by-construction, designing a minimal two-layer autoregressive transformer capable of solving directed graph reachability using continuous thought vectors.

A key element of the construction involves an "attention chooser" mechanism enabling attention heads to selectively process specific relative positions, facilitating flexible, length-independent information flow.

Experimental validation was conducted by training a 2-layer GPT-2 style decoder on graph reasoning tasks from the ProsQA dataset and empirically analyzing its internal attention patterns and continuous thought representations.
Results: A two-layer transformer with D steps of continuous CoT (where D is graph diameter) was theoretically proven to solve directed graph reachability, offering a drastic improvement over the O(n^2) steps required for discrete CoT.

Empirical evaluations demonstrated that a lightweight 2-layer COCONUT model achieved near-perfect accuracy on the ProsQA graph reachability task, outperforming both 2-layer and larger 12-layer discrete CoT models.

Analysis of attention maps and latent space similarity confirmed that continuous thought vectors effectively encode reachable, frontier, and optimal nodes in superposition, aligning with theoretical predictions.
Takeaways: Continuous thought vectors within transformers can function as "superposition states," simultaneously encoding multiple candidate search frontiers, enabling parallel exploration in reasoning tasks.
This parallel processing mechanism allows for a substantial reduction in the number of reasoning steps needed for tasks like graph reachability, significantly improving efficiency over discrete CoT.
The superpositional representations and parallel search strategy can emerge automatically during gradient-based training, even with intermediate supervision focused solely on optimal paths.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.12477.Title: Joint Embedding vs Reconstruction: Provable Benefits of Latent Space Prediction for Self Supervised Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.12477.Summary: Researchers introduced a theoretical framework to compare reconstruction-based and joint-embedding self-supervised learning (SSL) methods, demonstrating how data augmentation's alignment with irrelevant features dictates their optimal performance. The findings reveal that joint-embedding methods are more robust in high-noise environments, explaining their empirical success in computer vision, while reconstruction excels when irrelevant noise is low.
Problem: A lack of clear theoretical guidance on when to choose between reconstruction-based and joint-embedding self-supervised learning methods.
The precise impact of data augmentation on learned representations in different SSL paradigms remained poorly understood from a rigorous statistical standpoint.
Discrepancies in empirical performance, where joint-embedding methods often outperform reconstruction in vision while reconstruction excels in NLP, lacked a fundamental theoretical explanation.
Method: Developed a theoretical framework using simplified linear models to derive novel closed-form solutions for both reconstruction-based and joint-embedding SSL, explicitly incorporating data augmentation parameters.

Introduced a controlled data model where samples consist of signal and irrelevant noise components, along with an augmentation model parameterized by its alignment (α) with these irrelevant noise features.

Performed asymptotic analysis on these closed-form solutions to determine conditions for optimal performance and validated findings empirically using linear models and deep neural networks (DINO, BYOL, MAE) on various datasets and corruption levels.
Results: Derived novel closed-form solutions for linear reconstruction-based SSL (Theorem 3.1) and linear joint-embedding SSL (Theorem 3.2), directly parameterizing them by data augmentation structure.

Theoretically established that joint-embedding SSL requires a strictly weaker augmentation-noise alignment (`α_JE < α_RC`) to achieve optimal performance in high-noise scenarios, while reconstruction is more robust with arbitrary augmentations in low-noise settings (Corollary 4.5).

Empirically validated with deep networks on ImageNet-C corruptions that joint-embedding methods (DINO, BYOL) are considerably more robust to severe data corruptions (e.g., 10.5-12.4% accuracy drop from severity 1 to 5) than reconstruction-based MAE (25.1% accuracy drop).
Takeaways: Self-supervised learning paradigms, unlike supervised learning, require a minimal alignment between data augmentations and irrelevant noise features to achieve optimal performance, even with infinite sample sizes.
Reconstruction-based SSL performs better in scenarios with low-magnitude irrelevant noise, where the augmentation alignment with noise is less stringent.

Joint-embedding SSL demonstrates greater robustness and requires a weaker augmentation-noise alignment condition when irrelevant features have high magnitude, aligning with its observed successes in computer vision.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.12448.Title: SSR: Enhancing Depth Perception in Vision-Language Models via Rationale-Guided Spatial Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.12448.Summary: The SSR framework enhances Vision-Language Models' depth perception by transforming raw depth data into structured textual rationales, then encoding them into compact latent embeddings. This method improves spatial reasoning accuracy by up to 13.6% and significantly reduces inference time by integrating depth inferentially.
Problem: Visual-Language Models (VLMs) relying on 2D RGB inputs inherently lack precise spatial information, limiting their understanding of 3D relationships crucial for real-world applications.
Existing methods for integrating depth information often treat it superficially, failing to leverage its inferential value for higher-order spatial reasoning in VLMs.
This deficiency restricts VLM performance in applications requiring robust spatial understanding, such as robotics and autonomous navigation.
Method: Introduces the Spatial Sense and Reasoning (SSR) framework, which transforms monocular depth maps into structured textual rationales via a Mamba-based Image-Depth Interpreter (MIDI).
Employs knowledge distillation to encode these rationales into compact, plug-and-play latent embeddings for efficient integration into existing VLM architectures.
Curates SSR-COT, a million-scale dataset with depth-aware visual-language reasoning annotations, and SSRBENCH, a comprehensive multi-task benchmark for spatial understanding.
Results: Achieved up to 13.6% average and 6.77% overall accuracy improvement on spatial reasoning benchmarks like SpatialBench and SSRBENCH, outperforming proprietary models such as GPT-4o-mini.
Demonstrated a substantial reduction in inference time per sample (e.g., from 23.16s to 0.32s on SpatialBench) by dramatically decreasing the required Chain-of-Thought tokens.
Showed enhanced generalization capabilities across various out-of-domain and general Visual Question Answering benchmarks, indicating broader benefits beyond specialized spatial tasks.
Takeaways: Transforming raw depth data into textual rationales and distilling them into latent embeddings effectively bridges low-level depth perception with high-level linguistic reasoning.
A modular, two-stage training paradigm allows for efficient integration of spatial enhancements into existing VLM architectures without extensive retraining.
Explicitly guiding VLMs with depth-aware spatial reasoning, rather than merely appending depth, yields superior and more generalized multi-modal understanding.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.12434.Title: VideoRFT: Incentivizing Video Reasoning Capability in MLLMs via Reinforced Fine-Tuning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.12434.Summary: A framework named VIDEORFT, developed by researchers from Beijing Institute of Technology and Shenzhen University, enables multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to perform human-like, visually grounded video reasoning through reinforcement fine-tuning. The approach leverages a novel data curation pipeline and a specialized semantic-consistency reward, achieving state-of-the-art performance and outperforming proprietary models like GPT-4o on several video reasoning benchmarks.
Problem: Current video MLLMs are predominantly "answer-driven," providing outputs without explicitly revealing their internal reasoning processes, limiting transparency and interpretability.
Applying Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RFT) to video reasoning is hampered by a scarcity of high-quality Chain-of-Thought (CoT) datasets with complex temporal, causal, and logical structures.
A major challenge in cross-modal video reasoning is ensuring that generated reasoning steps are faithfully aligned with and supported by visual evidence, preventing hallucinations.
Method: A multi-expert-driven, cognition-inspired pipeline automatically curates large-scale, high-quality video Chain-of-Thought (CoT) annotations, resulting in the VideoRFT-CoT-102K and VideoRFT-RL-310K datasets.
A novel rule-based reward system for Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RFT) is introduced, comprising format, accuracy, and a unique semantic-consistency reward.

The semantic-consistency reward explicitly guides MLLMs to produce visually grounded reasoning by measuring cosine similarity between video description tokens and visual features, activated only for factually correct answers.
Results: VIDEORFT achieved state-of-the-art performance on six challenging video reasoning benchmarks, surpassing its base model (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) by up to +7.2% and outperforming GPT-4o on VSI-Bench by +2.8%.

Diagnostic experiments confirmed that the cross-modal CoT refinement stage effectively mitigates visual hallucinations, and the full two-stage SFT and RL training paradigm, including the semantic-consistency reward, significantly improved performance over individual components.

The generated VideoRFT-CoT-102K dataset exhibits more elaborate and video-centric reasoning processes, with broader distribution and longer average token lengths compared to existing video Chain-of-Thought datasets.
Takeaways: High-quality, cognitively-inspired Chain-of-Thought (CoT) data, curated through cross-modal refinement, is essential for training MLLMs to perform robust video reasoning and mitigate visual hallucinations.
Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RFT) with a carefully designed reward system can effectively incentivize MLLMs to generate explicit, visually grounded reasoning steps for complex video content.

A conditional semantic-consistency reward, activated only when an answer is factually correct, is crucial for promoting visually faithful reasoning while preventing the reinforcement of visually plausible but incorrect explanations.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.12363.Title: Towards Visuospatial Cognition via Hierarchical Fusion of Visual Experts
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.12363.Summary: Kyoto University introduces ViCA2, a multimodal large language model that significantly advances visuospatial cognition by integrating a dual vision encoder and specialized training on the ViCA-322K dataset. The model achieves state-of-the-art average performance of 56.8 on the VSI-Bench, outperforming larger open-source and proprietary MLLMs.
