Problem: Existing MLLMs struggle with robust visuospatial cognition, including fine-grained understanding of object layouts, spatial relations, and geometric attributes, despite strong performance on general vision-language tasks.
Current MLLM architectures primarily rely on single semantic vision encoders, which often lack the high-resolution spatial details necessary for precise spatial reasoning.
There is a scarcity of specialized, large-scale training datasets specifically designed for fine-grained spatial reasoning tasks in MLLMs.
Method: ViCA2 integrates a novel dual vision encoder architecture, combining SigLIP for global semantics and Hiera for fine-grained spatial features, with an efficient token ratio control mechanism.
A new large-scale, spatially grounded dataset, ViCA-322K, was developed, comprising over 322,000 question-answer pairs covering diverse spatial reasoning tasks.
A three-stage training strategy is employed, including Hiera projector calibration, full multimodal capability restoration, and targeted spatial reasoning fine-tuning using ViCA-322K.
Results: ViCA2-7B achieves an average score of 56.8 on the VSI-Bench benchmark, outperforming leading open-source models (e.g., LLaVA-NeXT-Video-72B at 40.9) and proprietary models (e.g., Gemini-1.5 Pro at 45.4).
The model demonstrates consistent performance gains across most spatial tasks, with notable improvements of +20.1 in 'Absolute Distance' and +17.0 in 'Room Size' compared to the next best models.

Experiments show ViCA2-7B's accuracy continuously improves with increasing training data size from ViCA-322K, indicating its architecture's capacity is not yet saturated and can benefit from even larger datasets.
Takeaways: Hierarchical fusion of specialized visual experts (semantic and spatial) effectively addresses the limitations of single encoders, enabling comprehensive visuospatial understanding.
Targeted instruction tuning with a curated, large-scale dataset like ViCA-322K is crucial for instilling and enhancing specific cognitive abilities like spatial reasoning in MLLMs.

Even compact models (7B parameters) can achieve state-of-the-art performance by combining intelligent architectural design with specialized data, potentially outperforming much larger and proprietary systems.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.12312.Title: Visuospatial Cognitive Assistant
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.12312.Summary: Kyoto University's ViCA introduces a 322K-pair dataset and a 7B-parameter model, ViCA-7B, for video-based spatial cognition, achieving leading performance on the VSI-Bench benchmark over larger models. The research also presents ViCA-7B-Thinking, which generates explicit reasoning chains for enhanced interpretability.
Problem: Existing Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) lack sophisticated video-based spatial cognition, struggling with fine-grained 3D relationships, geometric changes, and precise estimations from video.
There is a scarcity of large-scale, diverse datasets providing targeted supervision for intricate spatial skills, particularly those with precise 3D ground truth from real-world videos.
Current VLM reasoning processes are often opaque, limiting interpretability and trust for critical applications requiring spatial decision-making.
Method: A large-scale dataset, ViCA-322K, was created from real-world indoor videos with 3D metadata-grounded and complex spatial reasoning queries.
ViCA-7B, a 7B-parameter VLM, was developed by fine-tuning LLaVA-Video-7B-Qwen2 on the ViCA-322K dataset for enhanced spatial cognition.
ViCA-Thinking-2.68K, a dataset with explicit reasoning chains, was used to fine-tune ViCA-7B into ViCA-7B-Thinking for improved model interpretability.
Results: ViCA-7B established new state-of-the-art performance on the VSI-Bench benchmark, surpassing larger open-source models and several proprietary systems.
The Complex Spatial Reasoning (CSR) portion of the ViCA-322K dataset contributed a 5.17 average score improvement on VSI-Bench.
ViCA-7B-Thinking provided transparent, step-by-step reasoning processes, though this came with an average 22.1-point decrease in VSI-Bench accuracy.
Takeaways: Targeted fine-tuning on diverse, 3D-grounded spatial reasoning data significantly boosts VLM performance, enabling smaller models to outperform larger generalist models.
Explicit temporal instructions or simply increasing input frames do not improve spatial reasoning, indicating architectural limitations in effectively leveraging structured temporal cues.
Achieving explicit, human-like reasoning chains in VLMs currently incurs a trade-off with raw predictive accuracy, particularly for numerical tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.12082.Title: Model Merging in Pre-training of Large Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.12082.Summary: Pre-trained Model Average (PMA), developed by researchers at ByteDance Seed, Peking University, and The University of Hong Kong, consistently improves performance across large language models up to 200 billion parameters by merging checkpoints during pre-training. This method can predict final annealing performance from constant learning rate phases and enhances training stability, notably by recovering training from otherwise irrecoverable loss spikes.
Problem: Large Language Model (LLM) pre-training faces immense computational costs, unpredictable performance scaling, and inherent training instability.
While model merging is applied in post-training, its potential during the pre-training phase, especially for very large models, remains largely unexplored and undocumented publicly.
Independent researchers find it practically difficult to evaluate pre-training merging due to limited access to intermediate checkpoints from extensive training runs.
Method: Proposed Pre-trained Model Average (PMA), a novel model-level weight merging strategy, specifically designed for the LLM pre-training phase.
Conducted extensive experiments on independently trained dense and Mixture-of-Experts LLMs ranging from 411 million to 200 billion parameters.
Evaluated different merging variants (SMA, EMA, WMA) and performed ablation studies on key hyperparameters like merging interval and the number of models.
Results: Pre-trained Model Average yielded consistent performance improvements across a wide range of LLMs, from 411 million to 200 billion parameters.
PMA-init enhanced training stability, leading to reduced loss spikes and successful recovery from otherwise irrecoverable training collapses.

Optimal merging intervals showed a scaling relationship with model size (e.g., ~8B tokens for 1.3B models), and merging a larger number of models consistently improved performance in later training stages.
Takeaways: Pre-training with a constant learning rate combined with PMA can effectively match the performance of an annealed model, potentially eliminating the need for a separate learning rate annealing phase.
PMA-merged models ("PMA-init") can serve as robust initialization weights for continual training and supervised fine-tuning, requiring less learning rate tuning.
Model merging is effective when individual checkpoints have explored complementary regions in the loss landscape, allowing the average to find a better optimum.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.12081.Title: VisionReasoner: Unified Reasoning-Integrated Visual Perception via Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.12081.Summary: Researchers from the Chinese University of Hong Kong and SmartMore developed VisionReasoner, a unified framework for visual perception that integrates a large vision-language model with reinforcement learning. This system handles diverse tasks including detection, segmentation, and counting through a shared reasoning process, demonstrating improved performance across these benchmarks and generating interpretable thought traces without explicit reasoning training.
Problem: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) often require task-specific modules or fine-tuning for visual perception, limiting their true unified potential and scalability across diverse tasks.
Reinforcement learning applications in visual perception have predominantly used task-specific reward functions, hindering generalizability across multiple tasks within LVLMs.
Traditional vision models excel at simple categorical queries but struggle with complex, compositional, or reasoning-intensive instructions due to a lack of inherent language understanding.
Method: VisionReasoner unifies diverse visual perception tasks (detection, segmentation, counting) into a single framework, leveraging an LVLM initialized with Qwen2.5-VL and SAM2.

It integrates reinforcement learning with a novel unified reward mechanism for group relative policy optimization (GRPO) that guides learning across multiple tasks using both format and accuracy rewards.

An efficient multi-object cognition strategy, employing batch computation and the Hungarian algorithm for optimal prediction-to-ground-truth matching, is incorporated to handle multi-object scenarios effectively.
Results: VisionReasoner-7B achieved strong performance across ten diverse tasks, including a 29.1% relative gain on COCO-val (detection), 22.1% on ReasonSeg-test (segmentation), and 15.3% on CountBench-test (counting) compared to Qwen2.5VL-7B.
The model retained robust Visual Question Answering (VQA) capabilities, performing comparably or better than baselines across various VQA benchmarks despite not being explicitly trained on VQA data.

Human evaluation confirmed the faithfulness of the generated reasoning traces, with 97.0% image consistency and 90.5% answer consistency, and ablation studies validated the 4x speedup from multi-object matching and the positive impact of reasoning rewards.
Takeaways: Diverse visual perception tasks, despite apparent differences, share a common underlying multi-object cognition structure, making them amenable to a unified framework.
A single, unified reward mechanism can effectively guide reinforcement learning for LVLMs across multiple visual perception tasks, promoting generalizability beyond task-specific approaches.

Explicitly generating an interpretable reasoning process improves model transparency and trustworthiness, and this capability can be learned through reward signals without requiring human-annotated reasoning data.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11907.Title: Are Multimodal Large Language Models Ready for Omnidirectional Spatial Reasoning?
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11907.Summary: Researchers introduce OSR-Bench, the first benchmark to evaluate multimodal large language models' spatial reasoning in 360-degree panoramic images. Evaluation of eight state-of-the-art MLLMs revealed limited capabilities in omnidirectional spatial understanding and high sensitivity to hallucination.
Problem: Most existing MLLMs are trained and evaluated primarily on traditional 2D pinhole camera images, which only capture a limited field of view.
There was no comprehensive benchmark to systematically evaluate MLLMs' spatial reasoning capabilities in 360-degree omnidirectional (panoramic) environments.
Understanding spatial relationships in full 360-degree contexts is crucial for applications in embodied AI, augmented/virtual reality, and robotics.
Method: Introduced OSR-Bench (Omnidirectional Spatial Reasoning Benchmark), the first comprehensive benchmark specifically designed to evaluate MLLMs' spatial reasoning in panoramic images.
Constructed the dataset from ReplicaPano and DeepPanoContext, comprising 1,526 panoramic scenes across 65 object categories.
Defined three spatial reasoning categories: object counting, relative distance, and relative direction, supported by omni-cognitive maps and a negative sampling strategy for robustness.
Developed a two-stage evaluation framework assessing cognitive map generation via Hungarian matching and spatial reasoning tasks using rule-based and LLM-based evaluators.
Results: All eight state-of-the-art MLLMs evaluated achieved only modest success rates, indicating limited omnidirectional spatial understanding.
Proprietary models (GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Pro) consistently outperformed open-source models across most tasks, showing a performance gap.
Models frequently hallucinate, providing answers about non-existent objects when distractor objects are present, indicating limited robustness in visual verification.
Structured reasoning prompts ("think mode") generally improved performance across tasks, with the most significant gains observed in relative direction reasoning.
Takeaways: Current multimodal large language models (MLLMs) demonstrate limited spatial reasoning capabilities when processing panoramic images.
Proprietary models consistently outperform open-source alternatives in omnidirectional spatial understanding tasks, particularly in instruction following and cognitive map generation.
All evaluated models show significant vulnerability to hallucination, frequently generating responses about non-existent objects in panoramic scenes.
Utilizing chain-of-thought reasoning ("think mode") generally improves MLLM performance, especially for complex relative direction tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11896.Title: AdaCoT: Pareto-Optimal Adaptive Chain-of-Thought Triggering via Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11896.Summary: ByteDance Seed developed AdaCoT, a framework enabling large language models (LLMs) to adaptively decide whether to invoke Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning based on query complexity. This approach achieved up to a 70.6% reduction in average response tokens and significantly lowered CoT triggering rates (e.g., 3.18% on mobile) while maintaining performance comparable to always-on CoT models.
Problem: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) indiscriminately generates verbose reasoning steps for all queries, regardless of complexity, leading to increased computational overhead, higher latency, and amplified inference costs.
Existing CoT methods lack adaptability, treating all queries uniformly and failing to discern when detailed reasoning is genuinely necessary versus when a direct answer suffices.

There is an inherent tension in practical LLM deployment between achieving high performance (accuracy and reasoning quality) and minimizing deployment costs (token usage, latency), which prior approaches often struggled to balance systematically.
Method: AdaCoT frames adaptive reasoning as a Pareto optimization problem, seeking to simultaneously maximize model performance and minimize CoT usage, guided by adjustable penalty coefficients in the reward function.

It employs a two-phase training pipeline: an SFT warm-up phase uses principle-guided annotated data to teach the LLM initial CoT triggering distinctions, followed by multi-stage Reinforcement Learning (RL) using PPO.

The RL stage uses a customized reward function that penalizes both reasoning omission and reasoning overuse, while the novel Selective Loss Masking (SLM) addresses decision boundary collapse by selectively masking the loss contribution of the CoT decision token.
Results: AdaCoT models achieved up to a 64.4% average score with only 67.7% CoT usage, forming an improved Pareto frontier that significantly reduces CoT invocation compared to full CoT baselines (65.0% score at 100% CoT).

On production traffic testsets, AdaCoT dramatically reduced CoT triggering rates to as low as 3.18% on mobile devices and 12.50% on PCs, translating to 69.1% and 70.6% reductions in average response tokens, respectively.

The Selective Loss Masking (SLM) technique effectively prevented decision boundary collapse during RL training, maintaining high adaptive triggering precision (0.938) and accuracy (0.813) where models without SLM failed.
Takeaways: Adaptive CoT triggering, where the LLM decides *if* to invoke CoT, is crucial for efficiency beyond just reducing CoT *length*.
Framing the efficiency-performance trade-off as a Pareto optimization problem allows for systematic and principled management of competing objectives.
Multi-stage Reinforcement Learning combined with techniques like Selective Loss Masking is effective in training stable adaptive reasoning policies in LLMs, preventing 'decision boundary collapse'.
Efficient LLM performance does not require sacrificing peak reasoning capability, as AdaCoT models can achieve high performance when explicitly prompted to reason.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11820.Title: Chain-of-Model Learning for Language Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11820.Summary: A new learning paradigm called Chain-of-Model (CoM) enables large language models to scale incrementally and adapt elastically during inference. Implemented as CoLM and CoLM-Air, this approach integrates multiple sub-models within a single structure, demonstrating comparable performance to traditional models while significantly accelerating prefilling for long contexts.
Problem: Current LLM scaling policies require training new models from scratch, leading to high computational costs and inefficient knowledge acquisition.
Existing LLM architectures operate at a fixed capacity, lacking dynamic adaptability for flexible deployment across diverse computational environments.
The high computational cost of prefilling (generating key-value caches for long prompts) and the inability to seamlessly switch between different LLM scales pose practical deployment challenges.
Method: Introduces the Chain-of-Model (CoM) paradigm, built upon Chain-of-Representation (CoR) and Chain-of-Layer (CoL), to integrate multiple sub-models of varying capacities within a unified structure.

Instantiates CoM into Chain-of-Language-Model (CoLM) for Transformer architectures, reformulating linear layers, attention, and feed-forward networks with causal dependencies across distinct 'chains' of representation.
Develops CoLM-Air, a specialized variant that implements a key-value (KV) sharing mechanism to accelerate prefilling and facilitate seamless switching between different LLM scales and capabilities.
Results: CoLM models achieve competitive average accuracy on commonsense reasoning tasks, performing comparably to or slightly better than standard Transformer baselines of similar parameter counts.

Chain expansion allows for incremental model growth, with experiments showing that adding a new chain to pre-trained models can lead to performance improvements (e.g., TinyLLaMA-v1.1 gained 0.92% average accuracy).

CoLM-Air demonstrates up to 3.0x faster prefilling for 1M tokens (and an impressive 27x faster when combined with MInference) compared to standard LLaMa models, highlighting a major efficiency gain for long-context processing.
Takeaways: Formulating hidden states as causally dependent sub-representations (CoR) allows for inherent multi-scale encoding, enabling incremental model scaling and elastic inference within a single architecture.

The Chain-of-Layer (CoL) property, when applied to Transformer components, ensures that information flows progressively across chains, allowing a unified model to contain multiple distinct sub-models.
Sharing key and value caches across different chains in CoLM-Air significantly reduces computational overhead for prefilling long sequences and supports dynamic, runtime adaptation of model scale.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11815.Title: UniMoCo: Unified Modality Completion for Robust Multi-Modal Embeddings
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11815.Summary: UniMoCo introduces a framework for robust multi-modal embeddings by integrating a lightweight modality-completion module within a Large Vision-Language Model backbone, specifically designed to handle diverse and incomplete modality combinations. The model achieved an overall average score of 63.2 on the Massive Multi-modal Embedding Benchmark (MMEB), demonstrating superior performance and consistent robustness across varying input modalities.
Problem: Existing multi-modal embedding models struggle with diverse and incomplete modality combinations in real-world scenarios, like text-only inputs or missing images.
An "inherent bias" in current models causes performance degradation on modality combinations that are less represented in training data.
Conventional dual-encoder architectures are not robust to fine-grained cross-modal reasoning or when one modality is absent during inference.
Method: It introduces UniMoCo, an architecture built on a Large Vision-Language Model (LVLM) backbone, incorporating a lightweight modality-completion module.

The modality-completion module generates pseudo visual embeddings directly from text, leveraging a compact language model and an auxiliary vision encoder to ensure consistent representations when visual input is absent.
A unique training strategy combines contrastive learning with an auxiliary loss, which explicitly aligns embeddings from complete inputs and their modality-completed pseudo versions.
Results: UniMoCo achieved an overall average score of 63.2 on the MMEB, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines by a margin of up to 7.8 points in classification tasks.
The model demonstrated robust and consistent performance across diverse and incomplete modality combinations, effectively mitigating the "modality combination bias" seen in traditional architectures.

Ablation studies confirmed that both the padding strategy and the additional vision encoder in the modality-completion module, along with the auxiliary loss, were crucial for the observed performance gains and robustness.
Takeaways: Traditional multi-modal embedding models exhibit a quantifiable "modality combination bias," leading to performance drops on less common input configurations.
Generating lightweight "pseudo visual embeddings" from text is an effective and efficient method to achieve modality completeness without the computational cost of full image generation.
Explicitly aligning embeddings from original and modality-completed inputs through an auxiliary loss is critical for developing robust and bias-mitigated multi-modal systems.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11711.Title: Reinforcement Learning Finetunes Small Subnetworks in Large Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11711.Summary: This research from UIUC reveals that reinforcement learning (RL) finetuning of large language models (LLMs) consistently updates only a small, sparse subnetwork (5-30% of parameters) across diverse models and algorithms. Finetuning solely this subnetwork achieves performance equivalent to or better than full finetuning, converging to nearly identical parameter values, and this sparsity is primarily driven by training on in-distribution data rather than explicit regularization.
Problem: The high computational cost and resource demands associated with finetuning large language models, particularly with reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF).
A lack of mechanistic understanding of how RL finetuning modifies LLMs, specifically whether significant behavioral changes necessitate updates across the entire parameter space.
The prevailing assumption that achieving sophisticated aligned behaviors in LLMs requires extensive, dense modifications throughout the network, leading to full finetuning practices.
Method: Empirically measuring parameter update sparsity across a wide array of 10 LLMs and 7 RL algorithms (e.g., PPO, DPO, PRIME) to quantify the extent and location of modifications.

Developing a method to identify the active subnetwork during full RL finetuning and then performing 'masked finetuning' on a fresh model, updating only these parameters, to test if it recovers full model performance and parameter values.

Analyzing the consistency of the identified subnetworks under varying training conditions (seeds, data, algorithms) and investigating factors (regularization, prior SFT, data distribution) that contribute to the observed sparsity.
Results: RL finetuning consistently updates only 5% to 30% of LLM parameters, exhibiting 68.5% to 96.0% sparsity across diverse models and algorithms, in contrast to SFT's much lower 6% to 15% sparsity.

Finetuning only the identified sparse subnetwork recovers or even slightly improves performance (e.g., +1.6% for DPO, +2.4% for PRIME) compared to full finetuning, and leads to nearly identical final parameter values (90.5-94.0% identical with bfloat16 precision).

RL-updated subnetworks show substantial consistency, with significantly higher overlap than random chance across different random seeds (~60.5%), training data (~67.1%), and even different RL algorithms (up to ~59.1% across multiple changes).
Takeaways: Reinforcement learning naturally induces strong parameter update sparsity (68.5% to 96.0%) in LLMs, a pervasive phenomenon distinct from the dense updates seen in supervised finetuning.

The active subnetwork is distributed across nearly all transformer layers and parameter matrices, making sparse yet almost always full-rank modifications, not confined to low-rank subspaces like LoRA.

Training on 'in-distribution' data—where the input data is close to the model's current policy distribution—is the primary driver for RL-induced sparsity, while traditional regularization techniques have limited impact.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11614.Title: Using Reinforcement Learning to Train Large Language Models to Explain Human Decisions
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11614.Summary: Researchers from Princeton University and Georgia Institute of Technology trained Large Language Models using reinforcement learning to generate natural language explanations for human risky choices, while maintaining predictive accuracy comparable to supervised methods. The resulting Chains-of-Thought reveal dominant cognitive mechanisms, such as expected value computation and risk aversion, that the model leverages to explain human decisions.
Problem: Computational cognitive models, especially complex neural networks, often lack interpretability, functioning as "black boxes" despite high predictive accuracy.
Large Language Models (LLMs) can predict human behavior but typically do not provide transparent, natural language reasoning for their decisions.
Cognitive science aims for deep theoretical understanding of human behavior, which opaque models hinder, leading to an "interpretability dilemma."
Method: Applied Reinforcement Learning, specifically the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) algorithm, to fine-tune a Large Language Model (Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct) to generate step-by-step reasoning (Chains-of-Thought) alongside predictions.

Designed an outcome-based reward function that incentivized both accurate prediction of human choices and structured, well-formatted reasoning explanations, also incorporating a format reward to guide output structure.
Compared the efficacy of RL training against standard Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and a Centaur-style SFT variant on a large-scale human risky-choice dataset (choices13k).
Results: Reinforcement Learning (RL) trained LLMs achieved predictive accuracy on human risky choices comparable to supervised fine-tuning methods (e.g., MSE around 0.0148).
RL models generated more elaborate and psychologically grounded explanations, with human evaluators perceiving RL-generated CoTs as more reasonable in 61.5% of cases compared to backbone models.
Analysis of the CoTs revealed that "expected value computation" and "risk aversion" were the two most frequently used cognitive mechanisms (29-36% of thoughts), alongside other psychological factors.
Takeaways: Reinforcement Learning can effectively guide LLMs to produce psychologically grounded and interpretable natural language explanations for human decisions.
The quality of the generated Chain-of-Thought (CoT) is causally linked to prediction accuracy, suggesting that the reasoning process itself contributes to better behavioral fit.
The success of RL in eliciting meaningful CoT and accurate predictions is dependent on the underlying backbone LLM's inherent capabilities and pre-trained knowledge.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11484.Title: SoftCoT++: Test-Time Scaling with Soft Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11484.Summary: SoftCoT++ introduces the first framework for scalable test-time reasoning in continuous latent space, leveraging specialized initial tokens and a contrastive learning loss to generate diverse soft thoughts. This approach consistently boosts performance across various reasoning tasks and LLM architectures, outperforming prior methods and demonstrating complementarity with discrete-space scaling.
Problem: No established methods existed for applying Test-Time Scaling (TTS) to continuous-space Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, preventing these approaches from fully realizing their potential.

The deterministic nature of continuous latent representations makes it non-trivial to sample diverse reasoning paths or multiple hypotheses, which is a core mechanism for improving performance in discrete CoT TTS methods.
The challenge was to enable scalable test-time reasoning in continuous latent space to enhance LLM performance on complex tasks.
Method: SoftCoT++ introduces multiple specialized initial tokens to prompt the assistant model to generate diverse continuous latent soft thought representations for the same input query.

It incorporates a contrastive learning loss to maximize the distance and variance among these diverse soft thought representations in the latent space, encouraging a broader exploration of the solution space.
The approach optimizes a lightweight projection module while keeping the main LLM and assistant model frozen, maintaining efficiency benefits during inference.
Results: SoftCoT++ consistently outperforms all established baselines, including its predecessor SoftCoT-SC, across five diverse reasoning benchmarks (e.g., GSM8K, StrategyQA) and two LLM architectures (LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B).
Ablation studies confirm that the contrastive learning objective is critical for maximizing diversity among soft thoughts, significantly contributing to the performance gains.
Combining SoftCoT++ (thinking-stage scaling) with Self-Consistency (reasoning-stage scaling) yields further additive performance improvements, demonstrating their synergistic effect.
Takeaways: Test-time scaling can be effectively applied to continuous latent space, which was previously a challenge for continuous-space reasoning methods.
Explicitly promoting diversity among continuous latent thoughts via a contrastive learning objective is crucial for realizing performance gains from test-time scaling.
Scaling in the continuous "thinking" stage is complementary and synergistic with scaling in the discrete "reasoning" stage, allowing for additive performance gains.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11409.Title: Visual Planning: Let's Think Only with Images
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11409.Summary: A new paradigm, Visual Planning, enables AI models to perform multi-step reasoning solely through sequences of images, eliminating the need for textual mediation. The Visual Planning via Reinforcement Learning (VPRL) framework, applied to vision-first navigation tasks, achieved an 80.6% average Exact Match rate and 84.9% Progress Rate, outperforming text-based reasoning methods by 27%.
Problem: Current multimodal large language models (MLLMs) predominantly rely on text as the medium for reasoning, even with visual inputs, creating a 'modality gap'.
Translating rich visual information into textual descriptions for reasoning often fails to accurately capture intricate visual features and dynamic state transitions in 'vision-first' tasks.
Existing multimodal reasoning paradigms, even those incorporating visual aids, remain fundamentally text-driven, constraining AI's ability to genuinely 'think' visually.
Method: The paper proposes a 'Visual Planning' paradigm where reasoning is defined as the generation of a sequence of intermediate images, without any textual mediation, using a generative vision model.

They introduce Visual Planning via Reinforcement Learning (VPRL), a two-stage framework leveraging Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to train a Large Vision Model (LVM-7B) exclusively on visual data.

VPRL incorporates a reward function with a rule-based dynamics interpreter and a progress estimator to guide optimal visual state transitions, penalizing invalid actions and encouraging goal progression.
Results: VPRL achieved an average Exact Match rate of 80.6% and a Progress Rate of 84.9% across three grid-based navigation tasks, demonstrating a 27% higher average EM rate compared to the best text-based reasoning methods.

Language-based planning methods, including proprietary MLLMs (Gemini 2.5 Pro) and fine-tuned open-source models, consistently underperformed, with proprietary models yielding average EM below 50%, supporting the 'modality gap' hypothesis.

VPRL exhibited superior robustness and generalization, maintaining higher accuracy on larger, unseen grids (e.g., 82.4% EM on 6x6 FROZENLAKE compared to 38.8% for Gemini 2.5 Pro) and reducing the invalid-failure ratio by at least 24% across tasks.
Takeaways: Purely visual reasoning offers a more intuitive and effective approach for 'vision-first' tasks, overcoming the limitations imposed by language-mediated reasoning's 'modality gap'.

A two-stage reinforcement learning process, involving policy initialization through random trajectories followed by goal-aligned optimization, is critical for developing robust visual planning capabilities in large vision models.

Directly planning with image sequences allows for improved generalization, particularly in out-of-distribution scenarios and with increased task complexity, as models learn underlying visual strategies rather than relying on textual translations.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11221.Title: Sample Efficient Reinforcement Learning via Large Vision Language Model Distillation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11221.Summary: A framework called LVLM2P distills knowledge from large vision-language models (LVLMs) into compact reinforcement learning (RL) agents, enhancing sample efficiency by an average of 2.56 times for PPO and 2.86 times for A2C. This approach enables faster learning for RL agents in decision-making tasks without the computational overhead of deploying large foundation models directly.
Problem: Reinforcement Learning (RL) suffers from high sample inefficiency, requiring vast numbers of interactions with an environment, which is costly and impractical for real-world applications.
Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) possess powerful reasoning capabilities but are computationally expensive and too large for efficient real-time deployment on resource-constrained systems.
Prior approaches leveraging LLMs/LVLMs in RL often require labor-intensive, hand-engineered textual descriptions of environmental states.
Method: LVLM2P employs a knowledge distillation framework where a pre-trained LVLM acts as a "teacher" for a smaller "student" RL agent during training.

The LVLM teacher uses a two-stage prompting mechanism (Analysis and Action Inference) to generate soft probability distributions over actions directly from raw visual observations, eliminating manual textual descriptions.

The student RL agent is trained with a combined objective function that balances traditional RL rewards with a Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence loss to imitate the teacher's soft action probabilities.
Results: LVLM2P consistently enhanced the sample efficiency of both PPO and A2C algorithms across four MiniGrid environments, achieving an average improvement of 2.56 times for PPO and 2.86 times for A2C.
The LVLM teacher policy, Gemini-1.5-Flash, demonstrated strong decision-making, achieving an average success rate of approximately 0.96 across tasks, validating its effectiveness as a guide.

Ablation studies confirmed that using soft probability distributions for distillation yielded better performance than hard targets, and an optimal "lambda"=0.01 was identified for balancing RL and distillation objectives.
Takeaways: The broad, generalized knowledge within LVLMs can be effectively transferred to compact RL agents to accelerate learning, even for tasks the LVLM hasn't been explicitly trained on as a policy.

Distilling soft probability distributions from the teacher LVLM provides richer information to the student, leading to more robust policies and improved sample efficiency compared to using hard (one-hot) action targets.

A balanced objective, combining environmental feedback with teacher guidance (controlled by hyperparameter "lambda"), is crucial for the student to leverage teacher knowledge for efficient exploration while adapting to the specific task.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11192.Title: FALCON: False-Negative Aware Learning of Contrastive Negatives in Vision-Language Alignment
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11192.Summary: Researchers at Korea University developed FALCON, a learning-based approach to dynamically schedule negative samples during Vision-Language Pretraining (VLP) by balancing hard and false negatives. This method consistently achieves superior performance across image-text retrieval, VQA, and NLVR2 tasks, for example, attaining R@1 of 62.28 for Text Retrieval on MSCOCO, and proves robust across various VLP frameworks and noisy datasets.
Problem: Hard negative sampling, crucial for robust representations in Vision-Language Pretraining (VLP), significantly increases the risk of encountering "false negatives."
False negatives (semantically related pairs mistakenly treated as negatives) degrade representation quality by forcing the model to separate embeddings that should be close.

Existing solutions rely on static heuristics, fixed pretrained models, or predefined thresholds, which fail to adapt to dynamic, anchor-specific negative hardness and evolving embedding spaces during training.
Method: FALCON introduces a trainable "negative mining scheduler" (πϕ) implemented as a lightweight residual MLP, which dynamically determines an appropriate negative hardness level (quantile value) for each anchor.
The scheduler is trained to maximize the reduction in masked language modeling (MLM) loss after a VLP model update, serving as a proxy signal for improved cross-modal alignment.
Mini-batches are constructed by iteratively selecting samples based on the scheduler's predicted quantile, enabling adaptive balancing of hard and false negatives during VLP.
Results: FALCON consistently achieved the best performance on image-text retrieval, VQA, and NLVR2 tasks, e.g., R@1 of 62.28 for Text Retrieval on MSCOCO, outperforming heuristic baselines.

The method demonstrates adaptive scheduling behavior, initially sampling harder negatives and then lowering the target quantile as training progresses, leading to better performance across all training stages and improved wall-clock time efficiency.
FALCON proved robust across various VLP architectures (ALBEF, BLIP-2, SigLIP-2) and datasets, including noisy web-crawled data, with performance gains being more pronounced on cleaner datasets.
Takeaways: The optimal balance between hard and false negatives is not static but is anchor-specific and dynamically evolves throughout the VLP training process.
Using the reduction in masked language modeling (MLM) loss serves as an effective, robust, and non-exploitable proxy signal for guiding a negative mining scheduler, outperforming contrastive losses.

An instance-level, adaptive negative sampling strategy, guided by a learned scheduler, is crucial for mitigating false negatives and improving cross-modal representation quality in diverse VLP datasets.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11129.Title: PhiNet v2: A Mask-Free Brain-Inspired Vision Foundation Model from Video
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11129.Summary: PhiNet v2 introduces a mask-free, brain-inspired vision foundation model for video, utilizing a Transformer architecture and a probabilistically derived objective based on temporal prediction. This model learns robust visual representations from sequential data without relying on strong data augmentation or pixel-level reconstruction, achieving competitive performance on video understanding benchmarks like DAVIS with a J&Fm score of 60.1.
Problem: Existing self-supervised learning (SSL) methods for video often rely on pixel-level masking or reconstruction tasks and heavy data augmentation, limiting their generalizability and biological plausibility.
Prior brain-inspired models (e.g., PhiNet v1) primarily used convolutional backbones and were designed for static images, not continuous video streams, also depending on strong augmentations.
A lack of computationally practical and biologically aligned vision foundation models that learn robust representations from sequential visual input without relying on complex data transformations.
Method: Developed PhiNet v2, a brain-inspired vision foundation model that adapts the Complementary Learning Systems theory and temporal prediction hypothesis to a Transformer-based architecture for video.
Formulated a probabilistic learning objective via variational inference, resulting in two main loss terms (Sim-1 and Sim-2) that model rapid hippocampal learning and slow neocortical learning.
Employed a mask-free and augmentation-light approach by using Exponential Moving Average (EMA) for slow encoder updates and strategic stop-gradient operations for training stability.
Results: PhiNet v2 achieves competitive performance on video label propagation, with a J&Fm score of 60.1 on the DAVIS dataset, outperforming mask-based and augmentation-heavy baselines like RSP (59.9) and CropMAE (57.0).
The model demonstrates its mask-free advantage by achieving strong results without an auxiliary Masked Autoencoder (MAE) module, which RSP required for its top performance.
Ablation studies confirm the necessity of key components like Exponential Moving Average (EMA) for preventing collapse and the beneficial contributions of symmetric loss and a linear predictor.
Takeaways: A brain-inspired architecture combining Entorhinal Cortex, Hippocampus, and Neocortex components with a Transformer backbone can learn robust video representations.
Exponential Moving Average (EMA) and precisely placed stop-gradients are critical for stabilizing the training of this mask-free, augmentation-light model and preventing representational collapse.
A symmetric loss function and a simple linear predictor in the hippocampal (CA3) component enhance performance and contribute to the model's effectiveness.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11081.Title: ShiQ: Bringing back Bellman to LLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11081.Summary: Cohere researchers introduce ShiQ, an off-policy Q-learning framework for fine-tuning Large Language Models that enables token-wise learning from existing data, achieving competitive performance on UltraFeedback and BFCL-V3 benchmarks while maintaining low divergence from reference policies through theoretically-grounded Bellman equations.
Problem: Current RLHF methods rely on computationally expensive sampling and on-policy learning
Existing approaches struggle with token-wise reward signals and multi-turn interactions
Direct application of Q-learning to LLMs faces challenges with model size and initialization
Method: Developed ShiQ algorithm based on modified Bellman equations specific to LLM characteristics
Leveraged reference policy for improved initialization and multi-step reward propagation
Implemented token-wise learning capability while maintaining off-policy training
Results: Achieved competitive performance on UltraFeedback while maintaining reasonable KL divergence
Outperformed existing methods on multi-turn function-calling tasks in BFCL-V3
Demonstrated ability to learn from fine-grained reward structures in synthetic experiments
Enabled sample-efficient learning from existing data without requiring new samples
Takeaways: LLMs can be effectively modeled as regularized Markov Decision Processes
Careful modification of Bellman equations enables practical Q-learning for LLMs
Multi-step extensions help handle sparse rewards common in LLM tasks

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.10559.Title: Neural Thermodynamic Laws for Large Language Model Training
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.10559.Summary: This research formulates Neural Thermodynamic Laws (NTL) to provide a mechanistic understanding of large language model (LLM) training dynamics. The work demonstrates that the learning rate functions as an effective temperature and derives an optimal 1/(t+t_h) decay schedule, linking training phenomena to classical thermodynamic principles such as the Equipartition Theorem and the Laws of Thermodynamics.
Problem: Existing neural scaling laws for LLMs are empirical and do not explain the underlying mechanistic dynamics of training.
Understanding the complex, high-dimensional loss landscapes of LLMs and how optimizers navigate them remains a challenge.
Current learning rate schedules (e.g., warmup-stable-decay) are largely empirically derived, lacking a deep scientific or theoretical basis.
Method: The paper proposes the Neural Thermodynamic Laws (NTL) framework, drawing analogies between LLM training dynamics and classical thermodynamics.
A fast-slow decomposition of the loss function is introduced, mapping slow loss to work and fast loss to heat, following the First Law of Thermodynamics.
A simplified 2D 'river-valley' toy model is developed and analytically solved to derive properties like the learning rate's role as temperature, optimal decay schedules, and entropic forces.
Results:
Empirical tests on GPT-2-small confirmed the linear relationship between final validation loss and the final learning rate, supporting the
ℓ
f
∝η relation.
Synthetic experiments on quadratic loss landscapes validated the derived optimal 1/t decay schedule for annealing, demonstrating its effectiveness.
Entropic forces, while theoretically derived, were found to be largely negligible in early GPT-2 training, suggesting slow loss primarily depends on the cumulative learning rate sum.
Takeaways: The total loss in LLM training can be conceptually decomposed into "slow loss" (analogous to thermodynamic work) and "fast loss" (analogous to heat).
The learning rate acts as an effective "temperature," with the averaged fast/thermal loss being directly proportional to it, analogous to the Equipartition Theorem in classical thermodynamics.
An optimal learning rate decay schedule for minimizing thermal loss during training follows a 1/(t+t_h) functional form, which is slower than commonly used schedules.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.10557.Title: MathCoder-VL: Bridging Vision and Code for Enhanced Multimodal Mathematical Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.10557.Summary: Researchers from CUHK introduce MathCoder-VL, a multimodal large language model that leverages code supervision and synthesized data to enhance mathematical reasoning capabilities, achieving state-of-the-art performance across mathematical benchmarks while outperforming GPT-4V on geometry tasks through a novel two-stage training approach combining image-to-code training and mathematical instruction fine-tuning.
Problem: Large multimodal models struggle with mathematical reasoning tasks that require integrating visual and textual information
Existing datasets lack high-quality, math-specific cross-modal data needed for effective training
Method: Developed ImgCode-8.6M dataset using model-in-the-loop approach to translate math images into executable code
Created MM-MathInstruct-3M dataset combining collected K12 problems with synthetically generated figures and solutions
Implemented two-stage training process with image-to-code mid-training followed by mathematical instruction fine-tuning
Results: Outperformed GPT-4o on plane geometry tasks by a significant margin
Achieved superior performance on multi-step problems compared to GPT-4o
Demonstrated competitive results against closed-source models like GPT-4-turbo and Claude3.5-Sonnet
Successfully generated diverse new math figures and problems through the FigCodifier pipeline
Takeaways: Code supervision provides precise alignment between visual and textual modalities
Combining real and synthetic data with verified solutions improves model performance
Two-stage training approach enables effective learning of both visual-code relationships and mathematical reasoning

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.10526.Title: MASSV: Multimodal Adaptation and Self-Data Distillation for Speculative Decoding of Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.10526.Summary: Cerebras Systems researchers developed MASSV, a framework that accelerates Vision-Language Model (VLM) inference through speculative decoding by adapting existing smaller language models into multimodal drafters. This approach, leveraging a two-phase training with self-data distillation, achieves end-to-end speedups up to 1.46x and generalizes to larger VLM variants without additional training.
Problem: High computational cost and latency of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) during inference due to their autoregressive nature.
Applying speculative decoding to VLMs is challenging due to architectural incompatibility (small drafters lack vision components) and distribution mismatch between unimodal drafters and VLM outputs.
Prior methods either neglect crucial visual context or require computationally expensive training of multimodal drafters from scratch.
Method: MASSV employs a two-phase training strategy to convert a small language model (SLM) into an efficient multimodal drafter for LLaVA-style VLMs.
Phase 1: Multimodal Projector Pretraining trains a lightweight projector to map visual features from a shared, frozen vision encoder into the SLM's embedding space.

Phase 2: Self-Distilled Visual Instruction Tuning (SDViT) fine-tunes the entire drafter (projector and SLM) using responses generated by the target VLM with diverse sampling, meticulously aligning the drafter's token prediction distribution to the target's visually-grounded outputs.
Results: MASSV achieved overall end-to-end inference speedups of up to 1.28x for Qwen2.5-VL 7B Instruct and 1.18x for Gemma3-12B IT, with peak speedups reaching 1.46x on visually-intensive tasks like COCO Captioning.
The Mean Accepted Length (MAL) increased by 30.1% overall for Qwen2.5-VL 7B and by 47.5% for visually-intensive tasks compared to text-only drafting baselines.
The method demonstrated generalization to larger models, providing 1.17x speedup for Qwen2.5-VL 32B and 1.14x for Gemma3-27B, even without direct SDViT alignment on these larger variants.
Takeaways: Effective VLM speculative decoding requires both architectural adaptation (multimodal projector) and precise alignment of token prediction distributions via self-data distillation.

Self-Distilled Visual Instruction Tuning (SDViT) is crucial for maximizing token acceptance rates by ensuring the drafter's output closely matches the target VLM's distribution, especially for visually-conditioned generation.
Leveraging smaller language models from the same family as the target VLM facilitates compatibility and allows for generalization of learned acceleration benefits to larger models within that family.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.10468.Title: AI Agents vs. Agentic AI: A Conceptual Taxonomy, Applications and Challenges
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.10468.Summary: This work from Cornell University and the University of the Peloponnese establishes a conceptual taxonomy to differentiate between AI Agents and Agentic AI within the post-ChatGPT era. It clarifies their distinct architectures, capabilities, and application domains, while also mapping out associated opportunities and challenges for the developing field.
Problem: The rapid evolution of AI, particularly after the rise of large-scale generative models, led to ambiguous and interchangeable use of terms like "AI Agents" and "Agentic AI."
This conceptual ambiguity caused challenges in system design, inconsistent evaluation, and inefficient deployment of autonomous AI systems.
A lack of structured understanding hindered researchers and practitioners in aligning AI capabilities with specific task complexities.
Method: The researchers developed a structured, multi-stage methodology involving a comprehensive literature review across academic databases and AI-powered tools.
They created a formal conceptual taxonomy that systematically categorizes Generative AI, AI Agents, and Agentic AI based on dimensions like autonomy, coordination, interaction, and reasoning scope.
The approach included comparative analysis of architectural evolution, mapping of application domains, and a detailed examination of inherent limitations and potential solutions.
Results: A formal taxonomy was established, clearly differentiating Generative AI, AI Agents, and Agentic AI, and detailing their architectural and operational characteristics.

Application domains for both AI Agents (e.g., customer support, email filtering) and Agentic AI (e.g., multi-agent research assistants, intelligent robotics coordination) were mapped, illustrating their distinct practical utilities.

The paper outlined a roadmap for future development, including technical solutions like Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and causal modeling, and governance-aware architectures to address identified challenges in explainability, safety, and ethics.
Takeaways: Generative AI serves as a reactive, input-driven precursor, while AI Agents are autonomous, tool-augmented entities designed for specific goal-directed tasks within bounded environments.

Agentic AI represents a paradigm shift towards collaborative, multi-agent ecosystems capable of complex, high-level objectives through goal decomposition, inter-agent communication, and persistent memory.

Key challenges for AI Agents include inherited LLM limitations (e.g., hallucinations, prompt brittleness) and limited long-horizon planning, while Agentic AI faces amplified issues like communication bottlenecks, emergent behavior, scalability, and ethical governance concerns.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.10425.Title: Learning to Think: Information-Theoretic Reinforcement Fine-Tuning for LLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.10425.Summary: The Learning to Think (L2T) framework fine-unes large language models to achieve higher reasoning accuracy with significantly fewer tokens. It introduces a universal, information-theoretic dense process reward that guides models to adaptively optimize reasoning depth.
Problem: Existing LLMs fine-tuned with outcome-based rewards tend to generate excessively long Chain-of-Thought (CoT) sequences, leading to wasted computational resources and reduced efficiency.

Reinforcement learning approaches for LLMs primarily rely on sparse, final-outcome rewards, which fail to provide specific, dense feedback on the quality or efficiency of intermediate reasoning steps.
Prior attempts at process-based rewards often require task-specific evaluators or expensive human annotations, limiting their generalizability and scalability across diverse tasks.
Method: Reformulates LLM fine-tuning as a hierarchical, episodic reinforcement learning problem, segmenting the reasoning process into multiple discrete episodes.

Introduces a novel information-theoretic dense process reward for each episode, which quantifies the fitting information gain (reduction in answer uncertainty) and includes a parameter compression penalty to discourage redundant information.
Employs efficient approximation techniques, such as low-rank parameter proxies and Fisher Information Matrix estimation, to make the computation of the dense reward feasible for large-scale LLMs.
Results: Achieved an average accuracy gain of approximately 3.7% in mathematical reasoning tasks (AIME, AMC, MATH500, MinervaMATH) compared to outcome-reward-based methods.

Improved token efficiency by roughly 2x compared to outcome-reward approaches and approximately 1.3x compared to other process-reward baselines, using fewer tokens to reach comparable or higher performance.
Demonstrated consistent performance improvements across various base models (1.5B to 7B parameters) and diverse task types, including mathematical reasoning and code generation.
Takeaways: Integrating a dense, internally derived information-theoretic reward enables LLMs to learn both effective and efficient reasoning, balancing accuracy with token consumption.
Quantifying the information gain in model parameters and penalizing redundant parameter updates at each step effectively guides the model to learn parsimonious and relevant reasoning.
Decomposing complex reasoning into a sequence of episodic decisions provides granular control and feedback, allowing LLMs to adapt their reasoning depth dynamically to task requirements.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.10320.Title: J1: Incentivizing Thinking in LLM-as-a-Judge via Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.10320.Summary: FAIR at Meta developed J1, an online reinforcement learning framework that explicitly optimizes chain-of-thought reasoning in LLMs acting as judges for other LLM responses. J1 models achieve state-of-the-art performance across five diverse benchmarks using only synthetic data, demonstrating robust generalizability and effectively mitigating positional bias.
Problem: Traditional LLM evaluation methods struggle with the complexity and diversity of LLM outputs, creating a bottleneck in AI development.
Existing LLM-as-a-Judge methods primarily rely on prompting or offline fine-tuning, which do not directly optimize the reasoning process and often depend on costly human preference data.
Challenges include data scarcity, the need for generalizability across verifiable and subjective tasks, and issues like positional bias in pairwise evaluations.
Method: J1 introduces an online Reinforcement Learning approach using GRPO to directly optimize the chain-of-thought reasoning process for LLM judges, incentivizing detailed thinking.
It converts all judgment tasks into a unified, verifiable format by generating synthetic preference data, eliminating the need for human annotation.

The framework employs multitask training, combining pairwise comparisons and pointwise scoring (where pointwise judges are trained via distant supervision from pairwise data), and integrates consistency-based rewards to mitigate positional bias.
Results: J1 models, particularly J1-Qwen-32B-MultiTask, achieved state-of-the-art performance across all five evaluated benchmarks (PPE, RewardBench, JudgeBench, RM-Bench, FollowBenchEval).

J1-Qwen-32B-MultiTask outperformed strong generative reward models like EvalPlanner (+6.8%) and DeepSeek-GRM-27B (+17%), and even surpassed the 671B DeepSeek-R1 and closed models like OpenAI's o1-mini and o3 on some benchmarks.

Ablation studies confirmed that including both response orderings in training and applying verdict consistency rewards significantly improved position-consistent accuracy and reduced verdict flips in pairwise evaluations, while the multitask formulation offered superior performance.
Takeaways: Directly optimizing chain-of-thought reasoning in LLM judges via online RL with verifiable rewards substantially improves evaluation quality and robustness.
High-performing, generalist LLM judges can be trained solely on large-scale synthetic preference data, significantly reducing reliance on expensive human annotations.
A multitask approach, synergistically combining pairwise and pointwise evaluation paradigms and addressing positional bias through consistency rewards, yields superior and more reliable performance.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.10088.Title: MMRL++: Parameter-Efficient and Interaction-Aware Representation Learning for Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.10088.Summary: MMRL++ is a parameter-efficient method for adapting Vision-Language Models to downstream tasks, achieving state-of-the-art base-to-novel generalization with 85.53% base and 78.32% novel accuracy while reducing parameters by over 80% compared to its predecessor. It achieves this by fostering balanced multimodal interactions through a shared representation space and a decoupled inference strategy.
Problem: Adapting pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to downstream tasks, especially in few-shot settings, is challenging.
Existing adaptation methods often suffer from shallow-layer prompt concatenation, which can modify general concepts and hinder generalization.
Many VLM adaptation approaches are text-centric, leading to imbalanced multimodal interactions, limited visual adaptation, and inefficient parameter usage.
Method: Introduces a shared, modality-agnostic representation space with learnable tokens integrated into higher layers of both image and text encoders.
Employs a Shared-Residual Representation Aligner (SRRA) to significantly reduce trainable parameters via low-rank residual components and enhance cross-layer gradient interaction.
Utilizes Progressive Representation Composition (PRC) to enable deep representation tokens to assimilate instance-level information across different layers.
Applies a decoupled inference strategy, combining class and representation features for base classes while relying solely on class features for novel tasks.
Results: Achieves 85.53% accuracy on base classes and 78.32% on novel classes for base-to-novel generalization, outperforming MaPLe by over 3% in both categories.
Reduces the number of trainable parameters by over 80% (from 4.992M to 0.813M) compared to its predecessor, MMRL, while simultaneously improving performance.

Consistently outperforms other methods in few-shot learning across 11 datasets and demonstrates improved cross-dataset generalization, with feature visualizations showing more discriminative class boundaries.
Takeaways: A shared, modality-agnostic representation space facilitates balanced cross-modal interactions, improving Vision-Language Model adaptation.
Integrating learnable tokens into higher encoder layers allows preservation of general pre-trained knowledge while enabling specific adaptation.
A decoupled inference strategy is crucial for balancing task-specific adaptation for base classes with robust generalization for novel classes.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.09651.Title: Unlocking Location Intelligence: A Survey from Deep Learning to The LLM Era
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.09651.Summary: This survey paper provides a comprehensive review of geospatial representation learning, covering advancements from deep learning to large language models (LLMs). It introduces a novel three-dimensional taxonomy to systematically organize research and highlights the evolving landscape of Location Intelligence.
Problem: The rapidly evolving field of Location Intelligence (LI) lacked a systematic and up-to-date review that encompasses both deep learning and emerging Large Language Model (LLM) paradigms.

Existing surveys often had limited scope, focusing on specific data types or methodologies, and failed to adequately integrate multimodal approaches or recent breakthroughs like Transformers and LLMs.
There was no clear, structured taxonomy to categorize and compare the diverse research approaches in geospatial representation learning, hindering a holistic understanding of the field's progress.
Method: The authors conducted a comprehensive literature review of geospatial representation learning, tracing its evolution through the deep learning and LLM eras.
A novel three-dimensional taxonomy was introduced to categorize representative works based on methodology (single, dual, multiple view), modality, and downstream tasks.
The survey framed geospatial representation learning within a complete pipeline, analyzing it from data, methodological (location/region representation learning), and application perspectives.
Results: Identified spatial data (POIs, satellite imagery) as the most prevalent data modality (67%) in geospatial representation learning, followed by mobility data (18%).
Showcased a clear progression from single-view to dual-view and multi-view multimodal integration methods, significantly enhancing representation learning for various geospatial tasks.
Demonstrated an expanding application landscape for learned representations in predicting socioeconomic indicators, managing regions and POIs, and advanced location sensing.
Takeaways: Location Intelligence has experienced two transformative phases: first driven by deep neural networks for structured data, and now by LLMs for cross-modal reasoning and unstructured geo-textual data.
The field is increasingly moving towards multimodal integration, with contrastive learning and Graph Neural Networks being key techniques for combining diverse geospatial data modalities.
While LLMs are emerging enhancers, the GeoAI domain currently lacks dedicated foundation models, unified benchmarks, and large-scale, comprehensive multimodal geospatial datasets.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.09568.Title: BLIP3-o: A Family of Fully Open Unified Multimodal Models-Architecture, Training and Dataset
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.09568.Summary: Salesforce Research and collaborators introduce BLIP3-o, a family of unified multimodal models excelling in both image understanding and generation, by systematically investigating hybrid autoregressive-diffusion architectures. The models achieve superior performance on image understanding benchmarks, such as 83.1 on VQAv2 and 83.5 on MMBench, and demonstrate high visual quality and prompt alignment in human evaluations for image generation.
Problem: Historically, image understanding and image generation tasks have often been handled by separate models or pipelines.

The underlying architectural and training principles for unifying image understanding and generation within a single multimodal model, especially using hybrid autoregressive and diffusion architectures, remained underexplored.
A systematic understanding was needed to determine optimal design choices for unified models regarding image representations, modeling objectives, and training strategies.
Method: Salesforce Research and collaborators developed BLIP3-o, a family of unified multimodal models based on a hybrid autoregressive and diffusion architecture.

They systematically investigated optimal design choices, including image representations (comparing VAE vs. CLIP), modeling objectives for latent representations (Mean Squared Error vs. Flow Matching), and training strategies (joint vs. sequential).

BLIP3-o models were trained using a two-stage sequential approach: initial multimodal understanding pretraining with a frozen backbone, followed by dedicated image generation training leveraging CLIP features and Flow Matching for the diffusion component.
Results: BLIP3-o 8B achieved superior performance across major image understanding benchmarks, including 83.1 on VQAv2, 83.5 on MMBench, and 77.5 on SEED.
Human evaluations indicated BLIP3-o 8B's generated images were preferred over Janus Pro 7B in visual quality (50.4% wins) and prompt alignment (51.5% wins), with high statistical confidence.

The instruction-tuning dataset BLIP3o-60k, curated with AI-generated prompts, yielded immediate and significant gains in prompt alignment and visual aesthetics, demonstrating rapid adaptation to AI-generated data styles.
Takeaways: CLIP image features provide more compact and semantically richer representations than VAE features, leading to faster training and higher image generation quality.
Flow Matching is more effective than Mean Squared Error (MSE) for modeling continuous image distributions, resulting in greater sample diversity and enhanced visual quality.
Sequential training effectively preserves the model's image understanding capabilities while developing strong image generation ability, avoiding negative inter-task interference.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.09343.Title: Insights into DeepSeek-V3: Scaling Challenges and Reflections on Hardware for AI Architectures
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.09343.Summary: DeepSeek-V3 showcases how a hardware-software co-design strategy can achieve state-of-the-art large language model performance using a comparatively modest cluster of 2,048 NVIDIA H800 GPUs. The paper highlights innovations like Multi-head Latent Attention, DeepSeekMoE, FP8 mixed-precision training, and a Multi-Plane Fat-Tree network, which collectively reduce memory consumption, lower training costs, and accelerate inference.
Problem: The escalating computational and memory demands of large language models (LLMs) lead to prohibitive training and inference costs, posing an "AI memory wall" challenge.
Current hardware architectures struggle with memory capacity, computational efficiency, and interconnection bandwidth, making further LLM scaling unsustainable without architectural innovation.
Developing and deploying state-of-the-art LLMs typically requires immense, specialized infrastructure, creating barriers to broader research and development.
Method: DeepSeek-V3 integrates Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) to reduce KV cache memory and a DeepSeekMoE architecture for cost-effective scaling by activating only a subset of parameters per token.
It employs Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) to accelerate inference and utilizes FP8 mixed-precision training across the MoE model to decrease memory consumption and computational costs.

The infrastructure incorporates a Multi-Plane Fat-Tree (MPFT) network topology and hardware-aware parallelism (e.g., Node-Limited Routing, enhanced Pipeline Parallelism) optimized for the specific H800 GPU cluster.
Results: DeepSeek-V3 achieved state-of-the-art performance with 2,048 NVIDIA H800 GPUs, demonstrating cost-effective scaling for large models.
Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) reduced KV cache memory consumption to 70.272 KB per token, 4.66x less than Qwen-2.5 72B and 7.28x less than LLaMA-3.1 405B.

The DeepSeekMoE architecture (671B parameters, 37B active) resulted in a training cost of approximately 250 GFLOPS/token, while Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) boosted inference speed by 1.8x with 80-90% acceptance rates.
Takeaways: Effective hardware-software co-design can enable state-of-the-art LLM performance with significantly reduced computational and financial resources, moving beyond simple hardware scaling.
Architectural innovations like MLA effectively mitigate the KV cache memory bottleneck, making long-context processing more feasible for large models.

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures, combined with low-precision training and optimized network topologies, offer a practical pathway to scale models in total parameter count while maintaining manageable active computation and cost.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.08971.Title: Prioritizing Image-Related Tokens Enhances Vision-Language Pre-Training
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.08971.Summary: A novel training approach called PRIOR enhances vision-language pre-training by intelligently weighting image-related tokens during model optimization, achieving 19% relative improvement for heterogeneous LVLMs and 8% for unified LVLMs across standard benchmarks while reducing hallucination risks through better visual grounding.
Problem: Standard vision-language pre-training treats all caption tokens equally, wasting compute on irrelevant tokens
Models tend to overfit to caption noise and generate hallucinations not grounded in visual content
Method: Use a text-only LLM to identify and prioritize image-related tokens during training
Implement reweighted next-token prediction loss based on token importance scores
Apply framework to both heterogeneous and unified LVLM architectures
Results: 19% relative improvement for heterogeneous LVLMs across vision-language benchmarks
8% improvement for unified LVLMs with better training stability
Superior scaling properties with higher scaling coefficients compared to baseline
Reduced performance fluctuations and prevention of significant drops during training
Takeaways: Tokens that are difficult for text-only LLMs to predict tend to be more visually relevant
Importance sampling provides theoretical foundation for token reweighting approach
Method maintains strong performance on both image-related and unrelated tokens

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.08617.Title: OpenThinkIMG: Learning to Think with Images via Visual Tool Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.08617.Summary: Researchers from Soochow University, Microsoft, and other institutions developed OPENTHINKIMG, an open-source framework, and V-TOOLRL, a reinforcement learning method, enabling Large Vision-Language Models to adaptively use visual tools for complex reasoning tasks. This approach improved accuracy on chart reasoning by 29.83 points over baseline models and outperformed GPT-4.1, teaching agents to efficiently invoke tools with visual feedback.
Problem: Current Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) predominantly rely on textual reasoning, even for visual tasks, contrasting with human-like active manipulation of visual information.

Existing tool-augmented multimodal reasoning approaches suffer from heterogeneous tool definitions, high costs in generating tool-use trajectories, and limited policy generalization from static supervised fine-tuning.
The absence of a unified framework complicates the integration of diverse visual tools and hinders systematic development and reproducibility.
Method: Introduces OPENTHINKIMG, a comprehensive open-source framework with a unified registry for seamlessly integrating diverse vision tools (e.g., GROUNDINGDINO, SAM, OCR) and LVLM backbones.

Proposes V-TOOLRL, a novel reinforcement learning paradigm that combines a supervised fine-tuning cold-start with Group-wise Proximal Policy Optimization (GRPO) to learn adaptive tool-usage policies using visual feedback.

Develops a scalable three-stage pipeline for constructing high-quality vision tool-use trajectories, leveraging GPT-4o for planning, batch tool invocation, and multi-stage filtering with rule-based validation.
Results: V-TOOLRL achieved 59.39% accuracy on the CHARTGEMMA test set, outperforming open-source baselines like TACO-8B (30.50%) and COGCOM-13B (15.07%), and closed-source GPT-4.1 (50.71%).

The full V-TOOLRL framework provided a +29.83 point accuracy improvement over the Qwen2-VL-2B base model and a +7.76 point gain over a text-based RL approach, highlighting the impact of visual feedback.

During V-TOOLRL training, the average number of tool calls per sample decreased from approximately 0.63 to 0.10-0.12, while the average output length increased from ~66 tokens to 83-86 tokens, indicating greater efficiency and reasoning depth.
Takeaways: Direct integration of visual tool outputs as feedback into the reinforcement learning process (V-TOOLRL) is crucial for maximizing performance on visually grounded tasks, significantly outperforming text-only RL.

Reinforcement learning enables LVLMs to learn highly efficient and parsimonious tool invocation strategies, substantially reducing the number of unnecessary tool calls over time while increasing reasoning complexity.
The framework and RL approach equip LVLMs with adaptive behaviors for dynamic tool invocation, moving beyond static demonstrations to foster human-like interactive visual cognition.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.07956.Title: Symbolic Regression with Multimodal Large Language Models and Kolmogorov Arnold Networks
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.07956.Summary: A novel symbolic regression framework combines multimodal large language models with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks to infer mathematical expressions from data plots, achieving higher success rates than Mathematica's FindFormula on randomly generated functions while demonstrating effectiveness with both commercial and open-source LLMs.
Problem: Traditional symbolic regression methods often require manual specification of basis functions and struggle with complex expressions
Existing approaches lack the human-like intuition for inferring functional forms from visual data representations
Method: LLM-LEx algorithm uses vision-capable LLMs to propose ansatze based on function plots
KAN-LEx extension leverages Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks to handle multivariate functions through decomposition into univariate components
Results: Higher success rate than Mathematica's FindFormula in identifying exact expressions for random functions
Demonstrated resilience to moderate noise levels while maintaining accuracy
Successfully extended to multivariate functions through KAN decomposition
Achieved comparable performance using open-source models, making the approach widely accessible
Takeaways: LLMs can effectively emulate human intuition in suggesting appropriate functional forms from visual data
Combining genetic algorithms with LLM-guided proposals enables efficient exploration of the solution space
Open-source models like codestral can perform comparably to GPT-4 for this task

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.07675.Title: Simple yet Effective Semi-supervised Knowledge Distillation from Vision-Language Models via Dual-Head Optimization
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.07675.Summary: A framework named Dual-Head Optimization (DHO) addresses gradient conflicts in semi-supervised knowledge distillation from Vision-Language Models (VLMs) by employing separate heads for supervised and distillation losses. This method, developed by researchers from VUNO Inc. and KAIST, achieves new state-of-the-art results on ImageNet semi-supervised benchmarks and allows for efficient post-training hyperparameter tuning.
Problem: Gradient conflicts arise in conventional single-head knowledge distillation when combining strong VLM teacher signals with weaker, scarce labeled data, leading to suboptimal feature learning.
Traditional semi-supervised learning (SSL) methods struggle to fully exploit the powerful generalized representations learned by large Vision-Language Models.
Large VLMs are computationally expensive and impractical for direct deployment in many real-world, task-specific applications, necessitating efficient knowledge transfer.
Method: Introduces Dual-Head Optimization (DHO), which employs two distinct prediction heads on a shared feature extractor: one for supervised cross-entropy loss and another for VLM teacher distillation loss.
Optimizes each head independently, resolving gradient conflicts and enabling improved feature representation learning within the shared encoder.
Utilizes a linear interpolation of the outputs from both heads at inference time, allowing for flexible post-training adjustment of balancing hyperparameters without costly retraining.
Results: Consistently outperforms conventional single-head knowledge distillation baselines across 15 diverse datasets, including ImageNet and various fine-grained recognition tasks.
Achieves new state-of-the-art performance on ImageNet in low-shot semi-supervised settings, surpassing previous methods by up to 3.0% with fewer parameters.
DHO-trained student models, despite being smaller, frequently outperform their larger VLM teachers on specific tasks, demonstrating improved task-specific adaptation and up to 4.4% higher accuracy.
Takeaways: Explicitly decoupling the optimization paths for supervised and distillation signals effectively mitigates destructive gradient conflicts, a fundamental limitation in multi-objective learning.
Resolving these conflicts leads to learning enhanced, more discriminative feature representations in the student model's shared encoder.
The ability to tune the contributions of each head during inference provides significant flexibility and efficiency for adapting the model to specific tasks or data characteristics after training.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.07538.Title: Selftok: Discrete Visual Tokens of Autoregression, by Diffusion, and for Reasoning
