https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.07538.Summary: Huawei's Media Technology Institute developed Selftok, a discrete visual tokenizer that represents images as autoregressive tokens derived from the reverse diffusion process. This approach facilitates purely discrete Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and enables effective visual Reinforcement Learning (RL), achieving state-of-the-art visual generation and reasoning capabilities.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language Models (VLMs) struggle with incompatible continuous autoregressive (cAR) methods for images or use conventional spatial discrete tokens that are not truly autoregressive.
Non-autoregressive visual representations, particularly spatial tokens, violate the policy improvement optimality required for effective Reinforcement Learning (RL) in visual generation tasks.
Large Language Models (LLMs) are facing data saturation with text, and there is a need for robust methods to integrate non-language modalities like images and videos into unified AI frameworks.
Method: Selftok, a self-consistency tokenizer, encodes images into discrete, non-spatial, autoregressive tokens by leveraging the recursive nature of the reverse diffusion process in its ODE form.

A purely discrete autoregressive VLM is constructed by initializing from a Llama3-8B LLM, expanding its vocabulary with Selftok's visual words, and training it using standard language modeling objectives.

Visual Reinforcement Learning (RL) is applied by framing visual generation as a finite Markov Decision Process, validated by Selftok's AR structure that satisfies the Bellman equation, using both program-based and QA-based reward models for optimization.
Results: The Selftok tokenizer achieves superior image reconstruction quality on ImageNet-1k, reaching a PSNR of 26.30 and an LPIPS of 0.063 with 1024 tokens, outperforming established spatial and diffusion-based tokenizers.

The Selftok-Zero model, optimized with visual RL, attains a GenEval score of 95 (surpassing SD3-Medium's 74) and a DPG-Bench score of 85.57, demonstrating substantial performance improvements (+21 on GenEval, +3.77 on DPG-Bench) in text-to-image generation and reasoning tasks.

Selftok-based VLMs exhibit positive synergy between visual generation and comprehension and effectively mitigate hallucination issues, accurately generating rare object combinations that supervised models struggle with due to training data biases.
Takeaways: The reverse diffusion process exhibits an inherent recursive structure that can be directly mapped to an autoregressive causal graph, enabling the learning of naturally autoregressive visual tokens.

Autoregressive discrete visual tokens, unlike conventional spatial tokens, adhere to the Bellman equation, which is foundational for enabling optimal policy improvement in Reinforcement Learning for visual generation.

Discarding the spatial prior in visual tokenization and adopting an autoregressive structure allows for a minimalist, unified LLM-centric architecture for multimodal AI, simplifying integration and training.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.07291.Title: INTELLECT-2: A Reasoning Model Trained Through Globally Decentralized Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.07291.Summary: A decentralized reinforcement learning framework enables training of a 32-billion parameter language model across distributed compute nodes, demonstrating improved performance on mathematics and coding tasks while reducing reliance on centralized infrastructure through novel asynchronous training methods and verifiable inference protocols.
Problem: Traditional LLM training requires massive centralized computing resources, limiting access to well-funded organizations
Existing distributed training approaches face challenges with trust, verification, and efficient resource utilization
Method: Custom infrastructure (PRIME-RL, SHARDCAST) for decentralized RL training across untrusted nodes
Modified GRPO training with two-sided clipping and TOPLOC verification for stable distributed learning
Asynchronous training pipeline optimizing compute-communication overlap
Results: Successfully trained 32B parameter model with improved mathematics and coding performance vs QwQ-32B baseline
Achieved efficient resource utilization with high ratio of inference to training compute
Released open-source implementation enabling wider access to LLM training infrastructure
Demonstrated stable training across heterogeneous computing environments through modified GRPO objective
Takeaways: Reinforcement learning is naturally suited for decentralized training due to its asynchronous nature
Separating trusted training nodes from untrusted inference nodes enables scalable distributed compute
Test-time compute scaling represents a new axis for improving LLM capabilities

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.07062.Title: Seed1.5-VL Technical Report
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.07062.Summary: An advanced vision-language model from ByteDance Seed achieves state-of-the-art performance on 38 out of 60 public benchmarks through a three-stage pre-training pipeline and novel data synthesis approaches, demonstrating particularly strong capabilities in GUI control, document understanding, and video comprehension while maintaining a relatively compact architecture.
Problem: Vision-language models suffer from data scarcity compared to text-only models
Existing VLMs struggle with 3D spatial understanding, object counting, and interactive gameplay
Balancing model capabilities across diverse multimodal tasks while maintaining efficiency
Method: Three-stage pre-training pipeline combining masked image modeling, contrastive learning, and omni-modal training
Custom data synthesis pipelines for generating high-quality training data across multiple domains
Hybrid parallelism and workload balancing techniques for efficient large-scale training
Results: State-of-the-art performance on 38/60 public benchmarks
Superior performance in GUI agent tasks compared to existing foundation VLMs
Strong capabilities in document understanding, grounding, counting, and video comprehension
Successful deployment in real-world applications through Doubao chatbot and Volcano Engine API
Takeaways: Training loss on specific data categories predicts performance on related downstream tasks
Rejection sampling combined with online reinforcement learning enables progressive model enhancement
Balance between model size and computational efficiency is crucial for practical deployment

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06890.Title: Image Classification Using a Diffusion Model as a Pre-Training Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06890.Summary: A new self-supervised learning framework, the Representation-Conditioned Latent Diffusion Transformer (RCLDT), utilizes diffusion models with a joint representation-conditioning mechanism to achieve high image classification accuracy for hematoma detection in brain CT scans. The approach surpassed the DINOv2 baseline by 6.15% in accuracy, leveraging minimal labeled data.
Problem: Traditional self-supervised contrastive learning methods often struggle with fine-grained local details and are sensitive to viewpoint variations or occlusions.
Existing diffusion model applications for self-supervised representation learning lack specific optimization for downstream recognition and integrated latent-level conditioning mechanisms.
Medical imaging domains, such as hematoma detection, face significant challenges due to high data annotation costs and scarcity of labeled datasets.
Method: A Representation-Conditioned Latent Diffusion Transformer (RCLDT) is proposed, extending DiT by integrating high-level representations from a Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder as conditioning signals.
The ViT encoder and the diffusion model's denoising network are jointly trained to optimize the learned representations for the noise prediction task.
A two-stage self-supervised learning framework involves pre-training RCLDT on large unlabeled datasets, followed by fine-tuning on minimal labeled data for downstream classification.
Results: The Representation-Conditioned Latent Diffusion Transformer (RCLDT) achieved a classification accuracy of 0.9497 and an F1-score of 0.8235 for hematoma detection.
RCLDT improved accuracy by +6.15% and F1-score by +13.60% over the DINOv2 baseline on the hematoma classification task.
The model demonstrated superior image generation quality with an FID score of 10.00, along with a pre-training loss two orders of magnitude lower than the unconditional baseline.
Takeaways: Generative reconstruction-based self-supervised learning, when properly conditioned, can yield representations superior to contrastive learning for image classification, particularly in detailed tasks.
Jointly training a representation encoder with a diffusion model optimizes the representations specifically for the denoising process, enhancing their utility for feature extraction.
Integrating explicit latent-level representation conditioning enables the diffusion model to predict latent images with greater accuracy and at earlier denoising steps, improving fine-detail capture.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06710.Title: SimMIL: A Universal Weakly Supervised Pre-Training Framework for Multi-Instance Learning in Whole Slide Pathology Images
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06710.Summary: The SimMIL framework from Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Fudan University introduces a weakly supervised pre-training method for Multi-Instance Learning (MIL) in whole slide pathology images, enhancing feature extractors by propagating bag-level labels to instances. This approach improves performance across various classification and survival prediction tasks, demonstrating competitive results against existing methods and scalability on merged datasets.
Problem: Current Multi-Instance Learning (MIL) methods for Whole Slide Images (WSIs) primarily focus on feature aggregators, often overlooking the quality of instance-level representations from the feature extractor itself.

Off-the-shelf feature extractors (e.g., ImageNet pre-trained) suffer from a domain gap with histopathology, while self-supervised learning (SSL) on WSIs is task-agnostic, making learned features suboptimal for specific MIL objectives.
Standard instance-level representation quality metrics do not reliably predict performance in bag-level MIL tasks, indicating a need for MIL-specific feature learning.
Method: SimMIL proposes a weakly-supervised pre-training framework that propagates bag-level labels directly to all instances within a bag, encoding standard MIL assumptions into the feature learning process.

The framework employs strong data augmentation, a non-linear prediction head, and robust loss functions (Symmetric Cross Entropy for classification, ranking loss for survival prediction) to mitigate the impact of noisy labels.
Evaluation of feature extractors is conducted using MIL-specific protocols such as Linear MIL Probing and Two-Stage Bag MIL, rather than traditional instance-level metrics.
Results: SimMIL consistently outperformed ImageNet pre-training and general SSL approaches on Camelyon16, TCGA-NSCLC, and TCGA-BRCA for classification and subtyping, often achieving superior or competitive results compared to models with stronger WSI-specific backbones.
The framework obtained the best C-index scores for survival prediction on TCGA-LUAD, TCGA-BLCA, and TCGA-LUSC datasets.

Pre-training SimMIL on merged datasets improved performance on individual test sets, and fine-tuning existing SSL models with SimMIL efficiently boosted their downstream MIL performance within 1-5 epochs.
Takeaways: Standard instance-level representation quality metrics do not correlate with bag-level MIL performance, highlighting the necessity of pre-training schemes specifically tailored for MIL objectives.
Weakly supervised propagation of bag-level labels to instances, combined with noise-robust components, can effectively train feature extractors optimized for MIL tasks in computational pathology.
SimMIL can efficiently enhance existing state-of-the-art WSI-specific self-supervised learning models by rapidly injecting task-specific knowledge with minimal fine-tuning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.05626.Title: Perceiving Beyond Language Priors: Enhancing Visual Comprehension and Attention in Multimodal Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.05626.Summary: PERCEPTLLM, a multimodal large language model, integrates architectural disentanglement, auxiliary visual supervision, and input masking to enhance visual grounding and reduce reliance on language priors. This approach achieves superior performance on spatial reasoning benchmarks, outperforming larger models while maintaining inference efficiency.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) exhibit weak visual grounding, frequently generating plausible but factually incorrect responses by over-relying on linguistic patterns.
Existing MLLMs struggle with fine-grained visual details, precise spatial reasoning, and object attribute identification due to sparse visual training signals and strong language priors.
A single Transformer backbone faces a tension between optimizing for causal language modeling and rich spatial representation learning, hindering robust multimodal integration.
Method: Introduced VISUALLOSS, an auxiliary loss leveraging powerful self-supervised vision encoders (I-JEPA/AIM-v2) to compel the LLM backbone to build rich, disentangled visual representations.
Implemented BLANKTOKENS, a strategy that masks portions of input text during training, forcing the model to initiate and sustain responses based primarily on visual information.

Developed a disentangled architecture with independent weights for vision and text pathways within the LLM backbone, optimizing each modality's processing without incurring additional inference overhead.
Generated a specialized synthetic dataset featuring programmatically arranged objects and spatially-focused questions to explicitly train for precise visual parsing and spatial reasoning.
Results: PERCEPTLLM demonstrated consistent reductions in next-token prediction loss on visually-dependent datasets, with the disentangled architecture alone contributing a notable drop from 3.48 to 3.20.
On the SpatialEval benchmark, the full PERCEPTLLM model achieved an average normalized accuracy improvement of 1.52 compared to the baseline, outperforming the larger Llama 3.2 11B model.

The combination of all proposed techniques, including the advanced AIM-v2 encoder, yielded superior performance while maintaining a smaller model size (8B vs 11B) and lower input resolution (224x224 vs 560x560).
Takeaways: MLLMs inherently develop a preliminary capability to associate semantic labels with image patches, indicating a foundation for enhanced visual understanding that can be explicitly guided.

Decoupling visual and textual processing with independent weights within the LLM backbone resolves the conflict between non-autoregressive spatial representation and autoregressive language generation, improving overall performance and efficiency.

Targeted, explicit visual supervision and the systematic weakening of language priors during training are crucial for MLLMs to move beyond superficial visual processing toward truly visually faithful reasoning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.05522.Title: Continuous Thought Machines
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.05522.Summary: Researchers at Sakana AI introduce Continuous Thought Machines (CTM), a neural network architecture that leverages neuron-level temporal dynamics and neural synchronization as fundamental computational principles. The model demonstrates native adaptive computation, complex sequential reasoning for maze navigation, and the ability to learn interpretable algorithms, achieving competitive performance on ImageNet-1K while forming internal world models.
Problem: Modern artificial neural networks abstract away complex, time-dependent neural dynamics seen in biological brains for computational efficiency, limiting their flexibility and generalization.

Dominant AI paradigms struggle with efficient open-world learning and common sense reasoning due to their reliance on static representations and a lack of rich internal temporal processing at the neuron level.
Method: The architecture introduces 'Neuron-Level Models' (NLMs), where each neuron possesses private, learnable parameters to process its unique history of incoming signals over an internal, decoupled time dimension.
Neural synchronization, defined as the inner product of neuron activity histories, is explicitly used as the primary latent representation for both observation and prediction.

A novel adaptive loss function optimizes for both minimum prediction loss and maximum certainty across internal processing steps, enabling the model to dynamically adjust its computational effort for varying task difficulties.
Results: The CTM significantly outperformed baselines in 2D maze navigation, demonstrating robust sequential reasoning, generalization to larger mazes, and the emergence of internal world models or 'cognitive maps' without positional encodings.

On ImageNet-1K, the CTM achieved competitive accuracy (e.g., 72.47% Top-1) and exhibited native adaptive computation, dynamically allocating processing time based on prediction certainty, along with strong model calibration.

The model developed interpretable, sequential problem-solving strategies for tasks like parity computation, consistently improving with more internal ticks and achieving perfect accuracy in some runs, demonstrating algorithmic thinking.
Takeaways: Reintroducing biologically inspired temporal dynamics at the neuron level and treating synchronization as a core computational primitive can unlock capabilities like adaptive compute and complex sequential reasoning in AI systems.
By allowing individual neurons to have unique temporal processing models, the CTM fosters the emergence of rich, interpretable internal strategies for problem-solving.
Designing an architecture around an internal, self-generated 'thought sequence' enables iterative refinement of representations and the formation of internal world models, even for static inputs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.05472.Title: Mogao: An Omni Foundation Model for Interleaved Multi-Modal Generation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.05472.Summary: Mogao, an omni foundation model from ByteDance Seed, enables the causal, multi-turn generation of interleaved text and images by seamlessly integrating autoregressive and diffusion models. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across multimodal understanding and text-to-image generation benchmarks, while also demonstrating emergent capabilities like zero-shot image editing.
Problem: Integrating text-based autoregressive models with image-based diffusion models effectively without architectural misalignment or compromising individual strengths.
The challenge of creating unified visual representations that are optimal for both high-fidelity image generation and robust semantic understanding.
Enabling truly interleaved multi-turn generation of both text and images, where any previous output can condition subsequent outputs across modalities.
Method: A hybrid architecture that causally models sequential distributions of modalities, using next token prediction for text and rectified flow matching for images.
Employs a dual visual encoder (ViT for understanding, VAE for generation) and a deep-fusion architecture with modality-specific MLPs and projectors to mitigate task interference.
Introduces Interleaved Rotary Position Embedding (IL-RoPE) for improved 3D positional encoding and Efficient Complete Teacher Forcing (ECTF) for efficient training on interleaved data.
Results: Mogao-7B achieved an overall score of 0.89 on the GenEval benchmark, outperforming Janus-Pro-7B (0.80) and SD3-Medium (0.74) in text-to-image generation.
It obtained the highest average score of 57.4 across six diverse multimodal understanding benchmarks (POPE, MME-P, MMBench, SEEDBench, GQA, MMMU), surpassing other unified models.
The model demonstrated emergent zero-shot image editing capabilities, including adding, removing, and modifying elements, and applying style transfers through interleaved multi-turn interactions.
Takeaways: High-quality multimodal understanding and generation can be harmonized within a single foundation model by carefully designing architectural components, such as dual encoders and deep-fusion with modality-specific paths, to mitigate task interference.
Training on diverse, large-scale interleaved multimodal data enables emergent capabilities like zero-shot image editing and compositional generation, even without explicit task-specific fine-tuning.

Efficient training strategies, including Efficient Complete Teacher Forcing (ECTF) and optimized positional embeddings (IL-RoPE), are crucial for scaling and practically realizing interleaved multimodal generation models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.05470.Title: Flow-GRPO: Training Flow Matching Models via Online RL
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.05470.Summary: Researchers from MMLab, Tsinghua University, Kuaishou Technology, and Shanghai AI Lab developed Flow-GRPO, a framework that integrates online policy gradient reinforcement learning into flow matching models. This method significantly enhances capabilities in compositional image generation, visual text rendering, and human preference alignment, achieving up to 95% GenEval accuracy on SD3.5-M by addressing challenges of determinism and sampling efficiency through an ODE-to-SDE conversion and denoising reduction.
Problem: Flow matching generative models struggle with composing complex scenes involving multiple objects and attributes, as well as accurately rendering text within images.
Applying online reinforcement learning (RL) to these models is challenging due to their deterministic ODE-based generation process, which conflicts with RL's need for stochastic exploration.
The high computational cost of generating numerous high-quality samples for online RL training makes the process prohibitively slow for large flow models.
Method: The iterative denoising process of flow matching models is formulated as a Markov Decision Process (MDP), and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is applied for its memory efficiency.

The deterministic Flow-ODE is converted into an equivalent Stochastic Differential Equation (SDE) to enable stochastic sampling for RL exploration, preserving the original model's marginal probability density function.

A 'Denoising Reduction' strategy uses significantly fewer denoising steps during training sample collection (e.g., 10 steps) to accelerate online RL, while retaining full steps (e.g., 40 steps) for high-quality inference.
Results: Flow-GRPO-tuned Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium (SD3.5-M) improved GenEval accuracy from 63% to 95% for compositional generation, surpassing GPT-4o's 84% performance.
Visual text rendering accuracy for SD3.5-M increased from 59% to 92%, and the framework demonstrated strong generalization to unseen compositional elements and different flow-matching backbones.

The Denoising Reduction strategy achieved over a 4x speedup in training sample collection, and KL regularization effectively mitigated reward hacking, preserving image quality and diversity during optimization.
Takeaways: Online policy gradient RL, when properly integrated, can effectively enhance compositional reasoning and text rendering abilities of flow matching models.
Injecting stochasticity into deterministic flow models via an ODE-to-SDE conversion provides the necessary exploration for online RL without sacrificing the original model's probabilistic properties.
Informative reward signals for online RL can be derived from lower-quality, few-step generated samples, allowing for drastic improvements in training efficiency for large generative models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.05464.Title: Bring Reason to Vision: Understanding Perception and Reasoning through Model Merging
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.05464.Summary: This research from City University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, National University of Singapore, and Northwestern University enhances vision-language models' reasoning abilities by merging their language components with reasoning-specialized large language models, a training-free process that yielded up to a 3.6-point absolute improvement on MathVista and a 30% relative increase on MathVerse's Text-Dominant mode. It also leverages model merging as an interpretability tool to localize perception in early layers and reasoning in middle-to-late layers of VLMs.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) often exhibit limitations in complex multimodal reasoning tasks, such as visual math problems, despite their strong perceptual abilities.
The scarcity of high-quality multimodal reasoning data makes it challenging to train VLMs for advanced reasoning through traditional fine-tuning methods.
A lack of understanding exists regarding where perception and reasoning capabilities are specifically encoded and interact within the architectural layers of VLMs.
Method: The authors propose a novel cross-modal model merging strategy that combines the language model component of a VLM with task vectors from reasoning-specialized Large Language Models (LLMs).
They utilize linear merging (θ' = θ_base + λτ_vlm + (1-λ)τ_reason) as the primary training-free method, applied to VLMs like LLaVA-Next and InternVL2.

An interpretability methodology, involving 'masking out' specific VLM layers or modules with base model parameters or uniform noise, is used to analyze the internal localization of perception and reasoning.
Results: Model merging consistently improved VLM reasoning capabilities, achieving a 3.6-point absolute improvement on MathVista's math subset and a 30% relative increase (6-point absolute) on MathVerse's Text-Dominant tasks for LLaVA-Next-LLaMA3-8B.

Merged models exhibited significantly longer and more detailed reasoning processes during inference, with prediction lengths for chain-of-thought intensive tasks sometimes exceeding 250% of the original answer length.

Interpretability analysis demonstrated that reasoning capabilities contribute across nearly all layers after merging, while perception abilities remained largely stable, confirming a targeted enhancement of reasoning with minimal disruption to perceptual foundations.
Takeaways: Complex reasoning abilities from text-focused LLMs can be effectively transferred to VLMs through cross-modal model merging, providing a training-free and efficient method for capability enhancement.

Within VLMs, visual perception abilities and general world knowledge are primarily localized in the early layers, while mathematical and chain-of-thought reasoning skills are concentrated in the middle-to-late layers.
Model merging serves as an effective interpretability tool, revealing how different capabilities are distributed across a model's layers and how they are affected by the merging process.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.05456.Title: SITE: towards Spatial Intelligence Thorough Evaluation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.05456.Summary: This research introduces SITE (Spatial Intelligence Thorough Evaluation), a benchmark dataset designed to rigorously assess the visuospatial abilities of large vision-language models (VLMs). Evaluation with SITE reveals a substantial performance gap between current VLMs and humans, particularly in novel view-taking and dynamic scene understanding, and demonstrates a strong correlation between VLM spatial intelligence proficiency and success in robot manipulation tasks.
Problem: Existing vision-language model (VLM) benchmarks lack comprehensive and systematic evaluation of fine-grained spatial intelligence (SI).
Current benchmarks are often limited to static scenes, single viewpoints, or treat spatial reasoning as a minor component among many tasks.
Key aspects of human spatial cognition, such as view-taking (perspective transformation) and reasoning in dynamic contexts, are largely unaddressed in VLM evaluation.
Method: Developed SITE, a novel benchmark, by combining a bottom-up survey of existing datasets with a top-down, cognitive science-inspired taxonomy to identify evaluation gaps.
Designed new tasks, including Ego-exo View Association and Shuffled Frames Reordering, using the Ego-Exo4D dataset to cover underrepresented areas like view-taking and dynamic scenes.
Standardized tasks into a multiple-choice visual question answering (VQA) format and used Chance-Adjusted Accuracy (CAA) for robust and fair evaluation of various state-of-the-art VLMs.
Results: GPT-4o, the best-performing VLM, achieved an overall Chance-Adjusted Accuracy (CAA) of 37.8% on SITE, trailing human performance (67.5% on a tiny subset) by approximately 32%.

VLMs struggled significantly with Ego-exo View Association tasks, with GPT-4o scoring only 28.20% CAA compared to human perfect accuracy (100%), and with Shuffled Frames Reordering tasks, where human performance remained high (96-98%).
A strong positive Pearson correlation coefficient (0.902) was found between a VLM's overall SITE CAA score and its success rate in robot manipulation tasks on the LIBERO-Spatial dataset.
Takeaways: VLMs exhibit a significant spatial intelligence gap compared to humans, performing especially poorly in tasks requiring perspective transformation and reasoning in dynamic, multi-view contexts.
Integrating cognitive science classification systems helps identify critical gaps in AI's spatial understanding and enables the creation of more targeted and comprehensive benchmarks.
Stronger spatial intelligence in VLMs, as measured by SITE, correlates directly with improved performance in embodied AI tasks, specifically robot manipulation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.05422.Title: TokLIP: Marry Visual Tokens to CLIP for Multimodal Comprehension and Generation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.05422.Summary: TokLIP presents a novel method for integrating multimodal comprehension and generation by semanticizing low-level VQ tokens with high-level CLIP understanding. This approach enables a unified autoregressive model to achieve competitive performance in comprehension tasks like zero-shot classification and multimodal question answering, alongside improved image generation quality, all with reduced data and computational requirements.
Problem: Existing unified autoregressive models struggle with limited multimodal comprehension performance due to VQ tokens lacking high-level semantic understanding.
Prior attempts to discretize high-level semantic features for unified models face conflicting objectives between low-level reconstruction and semantic alignment, leading to "semantic degradation."

Achieving both high-fidelity image generation and robust multimodal comprehension within a single, end-to-end autoregressive framework remains a challenge, often requiring prohibitive computational resources.
Method: TokLIP introduces a "discrete-to-continuous" visual tokenizer that enriches low-level VQ tokens with high-level CLIP semantics, rather than discretizing continuous CLIP features.
It utilizes an off-the-shelf, frozen VQGAN encoder for low-level image features and a separate ViT-based causal token encoder, initialized with pre-trained CLIP weights, for semantic learning.

The causal token encoder is trained using contrastive and distillation losses to align its outputs with CLIP representations, then integrated into an autoregressive Transformer alongside text tokens for unified learning across modalities.
Results: TokLIP demonstrates exceptional data efficiency, achieving comparable multimodal comprehension with less than 20% of the pretraining data required by VILA-U and only 5% of SynerGen-VL's data.

The model significantly enhances multimodal comprehension, with TokLIP-L (Qwen2.5-7B, 384 resolution) matching or surpassing LLaVA-v1.5 across various benchmarks, and TokLIP-XL (512 resolution) achieving state-of-the-art results on AI2D, MME, SEED-Bench, and MMB.

In class-conditional image generation, TokLIP-enhanced models achieved lower FID scores (e.g., 7.64 FID for GPT-B with TokLIP vs. 9.70 for VQGAN alone), indicating improved generation quality by combining high-level semantics with low-level codes.
Takeaways: Disentangling the training objectives for low-level generation fidelity (via VQGAN) and high-level semantic comprehension (via CLIP-aligned causal encoder) avoids performance conflicts.
Semanticizing existing VQ tokens is a more data-efficient and effective strategy for multimodal comprehension than attempting to discretize continuous high-level features.
Leveraging pre-trained CLIP vision encoder weights for initialization and distillation is crucial for transferring rich semantic knowledge into the causal token encoder.
Causal attention in the token encoder is vital for maintaining the end-to-end autoregressive nature required for unified next-token prediction, enabling both comprehension and generation tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.05177.Title: MARK: Memory Augmented Refinement of Knowledge
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.05177.Summary: A memory-augmented framework called MARK enables continuous learning and knowledge refinement in Large Language Models through specialized agents managing domain insights, user interactions, and response refinement, achieving improved accuracy and reduced hallucinations while maintaining coherence across multi-turn conversations without requiring model fine-tuning.
Problem: Traditional LLMs struggle with incorporating evolving domain knowledge and adapting to user-specific contexts
Current approaches like RAG rely on fixed knowledge sources requiring manual updates
LLMs face challenges with hallucination and maintaining consistency over multiple interactions
Method: Introduces specialized memory agents for managing domain insights, user questions, and LLM responses
Implements Memory Builder Service (MBS) and Memory Search Service (MSS) for knowledge extraction and retrieval
Uses Memory Relevance Scoring to prioritize information based on recall count, recency, and feedback
Results: Demonstrated reduction in hallucinations through memory-based refinements
Achieved improved efficiency with lower average token count per response
Maintained response coherence and knowledge adaptation across multi-turn, multi-user interactions
Successfully integrated domain expert knowledge and user feedback into the system's responses
Takeaways: Memory augmentation significantly improves response accuracy while reducing token usage
Dynamic memory refinement enables continuous learning without model fine-tuning
Structured memory architecture helps maintain coherence across multiple conversation turns

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.05062.Title: ULFine: Unbiased Lightweight Fine-tuning for Foundation-Model-Assisted Long-Tailed Semi-Supervised Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.05062.Summary: A framework for long-tailed semi-supervised learning leverages foundation models through prototype adaptive fitting and dual logit fusion, achieving state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmark datasets while effectively mitigating minority bottleneck and majority overconfidence issues common in imbalanced data scenarios.
Problem: Traditional long-tailed semi-supervised learning methods struggle with class imbalance and limited labeled data
Direct application of foundation models leads to "minority bottleneck" and "majority overconfidence" issues that hurt performance on tail classes
Method: Prototype Adaptive Fitting (PAF) adjusts textual prototypes based on confidence-aware pseudo-labeling
Dual Logit Fusion (DLF) combines unbiased textual prototypes with linear probing to reduce classifier bias
Lightweight fine-tuning strategy preserves foundation model's knowledge while enabling task-specific adaptation
Results: Outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on CIFAR10-LT, CIFAR100-LT, STL10-LT and ImageNet-127 benchmarks
Achieves more balanced performance across head and tail classes compared to baseline approaches
Reduces training costs significantly compared to training from scratch while maintaining superior accuracy
Ablation studies confirm the importance of both PAF and DLF components
Takeaways: Full fine-tuning of foundation models can degrade performance by disrupting intra-class distance distributions
Confidence-aware prototype adaptation helps address majority class overconfidence
Combining multiple prediction sources (textual + linear) improves tail class performance

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.04921.Title: Perception, Reason, Think, and Plan: A Survey on Large Multimodal Reasoning Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.04921.Summary: Researchers from Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen, surveyed Large Multimodal Reasoning Models (LMRMs), tracing their evolution through four stages from perception-driven modularity to language-centric reasoning. The survey highlights current limitations of state-of-the-art models in omni-modal and agentic benchmarks, and proposes Native Large Multimodal Reasoning Models (N-LMRMs) as a future paradigm for inherently multimodal and integrated AI systems.
Problem: AI systems require robust and adaptive reasoning for complex, open, and multimodal environments.
Existing surveys on multimodal models lacked comprehensive analysis of reinforcement learning-enhanced reasoning and future technical prospects for large multimodal reasoning models (LMRMs).
Current large multimodal models (LMMs) show limitations in omni-modal generalization, reasoning depth, and agentic behavior.
Method: The authors from Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen, conducted a comprehensive, structured survey organized around a four-stage developmental roadmap for multimodal reasoning models.

The survey analyzes the evolution from perception-driven modularity to language-centric short and long reasoning, and proposes the future concept of Native Large Multimodal Reasoning Models (N-LMRMs).
It provides empirical insights into the capabilities and limitations of state-of-the-art models, including preliminary studies on OpenAI O3 and O4-mini, and updates existing datasets and benchmarks.
Results: The survey identifies a clear four-stage evolution of multimodal reasoning models, progressing from perception-driven modularity to language-centric "System-1" and "System-2" reasoning paradigms.
State-of-the-art LMRMs show limited omni-modal generalization (e.g., GPT-4o and Gemini-1.5-Pro achieving below 20% on OmniMMI) and struggle with agentic tasks (e.g., GPT-4o at 0.6% on BrowseComp).

Preliminary studies with OpenAI O3 revealed strong multi-modal Chain-of-Thought capabilities, but also limitations such as language knowledge interference, input file handling issues, and the fabrication of reasoning rationales.
Takeaways: Multimodal reasoning models are evolving from modular, perception-driven designs to more unified, language-centric frameworks, with a future vision for native omni-modal integration.

Current state-of-the-art Large Multimodal Reasoning Models (LMRMs) exhibit limitations in omni-modal generalization, reasoning depth, and agentic behavior, failing to achieve human-level reliability in complex tasks.

Preliminary studies on models like OpenAI O3 suggest potential issues such as language knowledge interference over visual input, difficulties with file handling and multimedia generation, and the fabrication of reasoning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.04601.Title: OpenVision: A Fully-Open, Cost-Effective Family of Advanced Vision Encoders for Multimodal Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.04601.Summary: OpenVision introduces a family of fully open vision encoders that match or exceed OpenAI's CLIP performance on multimodal benchmarks while providing multiple parameter scales and resolution options, achieved through systematic analysis of training efficiency factors and progressive resolution training using open datasets and frameworks.
Problem: Existing multimodal systems heavily depend on proprietary vision encoders like CLIP, limiting transparency and reproducibility
Current open-source vision encoders lag behind proprietary models in performance and parameter scale flexibility
Known weaknesses exist in spatial understanding and object counting with current encoders
Method: Developed fully open vision encoders by leveraging enhanced CLIP training and Recap-DataComp-1B dataset
Implemented three-stage progressive resolution training with auxiliary text decoder
Created multiple encoder variants optimized for different input resolutions and computational budgets
Results: OpenVision-B/16 and L/14 outperform CLIP counterparts on most multimodal benchmarks
OpenVision-H/14 shows substantial gains in high-resolution VQA, OCR and retrieval tasks
Successfully scales from lightweight to high-capacity models while maintaining performance
Full transparency with released training data, code and checkpoints enables reproducibility
Takeaways: High-quality synthetic captions and auxiliary text decoder are crucial for strong multimodal performance
Balanced allocation across resolutions during training improves efficiency and capabilities
Progressive resolution training enables both computational efficiency and high performance

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.04588.Title: ZeroSearch: Incentivize the Search Capability of LLMs without Searching
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.04588.Summary: A framework called ZEROSEARCH enables training large language models (LLMs) to leverage search capabilities by replacing costly real-world search engine APIs with a simulated LLM environment. This approach from Alibaba Group's Tongyi Lab achieves superior performance while substantially reducing training costs.
Problem: Training large language models (LLMs) to effectively use real-world search engines via reinforcement learning (RL) incurs prohibitively high API costs.
Real search engines provide uncontrolled document quality, which can lead to unstable and inefficient RL training for search-augmented LLMs.
LLMs inherently have static knowledge, leading to issues like hallucination and an inability to access real-time information without external tools.
Method: Introduces an RL framework that replaces real search engine interactions with a lightweight fine-tuned LLM acting as a 'simulation search engine' during training.

Employs a curriculum learning-based rollout mechanism that dynamically controls the probability of generating 'noisy' documents, progressing from easier (more useful) to harder (more noisy) training scenarios.
Utilizes a rule-based F1 score for reward calculation and applies loss masking for document tokens to ensure stable and effective reinforcement learning.
Results: ZEROSEARCH consistently outperforms all baseline methods, including models trained with real search engines like Search-R1, achieving higher average Exact Match (EM) scores across diverse question answering datasets.

The framework significantly reduces training costs, cutting expenses by over 85% compared to using commercial search APIs (e.g., ~
70.8vs. 586.7 for 64,000 search requests over 12 hours of training).

It demonstrates strong generalizability across different LLM sizes (3B to 7B) and model families, with performance improving as the simulation LLM size increases, and benefits from curriculum rollout for enhanced stability.
Takeaways: Large language models (LLMs) can effectively simulate real-world search engines, providing a controllable and cost-efficient environment for training search-augmented LLMs.
Training LLMs with a simulated search environment yields superior performance compared to using real search engines, largely due to enhanced training stability and controlled document quality.
A curriculum learning strategy that gradually increases the proportion of noisy documents during training improves the robustness and reasoning capabilities of search-augmented LLMs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.04410.Title: DeCLIP: Decoupled Learning for Open-Vocabulary Dense Perception
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.04410.Summary: A decoupled learning framework enhances CLIP's capabilities for open-vocabulary dense perception tasks by separately optimizing content and context features through unsupervised fine-tuning, achieving state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks including object detection and semantic segmentation while maintaining CLIP's open-vocabulary capabilities.
Problem: CLIP's image tokens fail to effectively aggregate information from spatially or semantically related regions
Direct application of vision-language models to dense prediction tasks leads to suboptimal performance due to poor local discriminability and spatial consistency
Method: Decouple CLIP's self-attention module into separate content and context components
Use Vision Foundation Models to guide learning of spatial relationships while maintaining visual-language alignment through self-distillation
Results: Achieved state-of-the-art performance on open-vocabulary object detection benchmarks (OV-COCO, OV-LVIS)
Demonstrated superior performance on semantic segmentation tasks (ADE20K, Pascal VOC, Pascal Context)
Successfully maintained CLIP's ability to generalize to unseen categories while improving dense prediction capabilities
DINOv2 proved most effective among tested Vision Foundation Models for balancing region classification and segmentation
Takeaways: There is an inherent trade-off between optimizing for spatial correlations versus visual-language alignment
The "proxy token" phenomenon in CLIP's attention maps hinders information aggregation from related regions
Unsupervised fine-tuning can improve dense prediction without requiring labeled data

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.03981.Title: X-Reasoner: Towards Generalizable Reasoning Across Modalities and Domains
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.03981.Summary: A framework combining supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning enables vision-language models to develop generalizable reasoning capabilities through text-only training, achieving state-of-the-art performance on multimodal benchmarks like MMMU and MathVista while demonstrating successful transfer to specialized domains like medicine.
Problem: Existing multimodal models require expensive task-specific datasets and training
Limited understanding of whether reasoning skills can generalize across modalities and domains
Method: Two-stage post-training approach using text-only data on vision-language models
Combines supervised fine-tuning using distilled long chain-of-thoughts with reinforcement learning using verifiable rewards
Results: Outperformed existing state-of-the-art models on multiple multimodal benchmarks (MMMU, MMMU-Pro, MathVista)
Achieved new state-of-the-art results on medical benchmarks after domain-specific fine-tuning
Ablation studies confirmed genuine multimodal reasoning rather than relying on text-based shortcuts
Takeaways: Mathematical reasoning trained on text serves as an effective "anchor domain" for developing generalizable reasoning capabilities
Text-only training can improve multimodal reasoning without requiring multimodal training data
Domain-specific fine-tuning further enhances performance in specialized areas like medicine

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.03703.Title: Fill the Gap: Quantifying and Reducing the Modality Gap in Image-Text Representation Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.03703.Summary: A model-agnostic framework introduces spectral and optimal transport techniques to reduce the separation between image and text embeddings in vision-language models, achieving improved cross-modal retrieval performance while introducing new metrics to quantify embedding alignment quality across different model architectures.
Problem: Vision-language models exhibit a "modality gap" where image and text embeddings remain separated in shared representation space
Existing solutions are model-specific and lack direct ways to measure embedding alignment quality
Method: Post-processing techniques using spectral embedding and optimal transport to align embeddings
New evaluation metrics including Image-Text Ratio and distribution-based measures to quantify alignment
Model-agnostic approach that works with pre-trained models without architectural changes
Results: Significant reduction in modality bias metrics (ITR and TIR values)
Lower Text Mean Rank (TMR) and Image Mean Rank (IMR) indicating better cross-modal retrieval
Improved Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) scores showing closer embedding distributions
Maintained semantic relevance between corresponding image-text pairs
Takeaways: Spectral-based methods outperform other approaches for reducing modality bias
Simply reducing dimensionality without considering semantic similarity doesn't improve retrieval
Post-processing can effectively align embeddings while preserving semantic relationships

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.03335.Title: Absolute Zero: Reinforced Self-play Reasoning with Zero Data
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.03335.Summary: The 'Absolute Zero' paradigm introduces a self-supervised learning framework where a language model autonomously proposes tasks and improves its reasoning using verifiable environmental feedback, entirely without human-curated data. This method achieved state-of-the-art performance on coding and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, demonstrating robust cross-domain generalization.
Problem: Current LLMs heavily rely on large, human-curated datasets, leading to unsustainable scaling bottlenecks and data scarcity.
Existing Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) methods, even 'zero' variants, still require expertly curated distributions of reasoning tasks.
Human-defined tasks can constrain the learning potential of future AI systems that might surpass human intellect.
Method: Introduced the 'Absolute Zero' paradigm, where a single language model acts as both a task proposer and a solver in a continuous self-improvement loop.
Employed a code executor as an open-ended, verifiable environment, allowing the model to learn deduction, abduction, and induction through code-based reasoning tasks.
Designed a difficulty-aware proposer reward and a binary solver reward, optimizing jointly using Task-Relative REINFORCE++ (TRR++) with separate baselines for each task role.
Results: The Absolute Zero Reasoner (AZR)-Coder-7B achieved state-of-the-art overall performance on diverse reasoning benchmarks, surpassing prior models by 1.8 percentage points in overall average and 0.3 points in coding average without using external human-curated data.
AZR models demonstrated strong cross-domain generalization, with AZR-Coder-7B improving mathematical reasoning accuracy by 15.2 percentage points despite being trained exclusively on code tasks.
Performance scaled positively with model size, and the system exhibited emergent cognitive behaviors such as intermediate planning and diverse task proposals during self-play.
Takeaways: State-of-the-art reasoning capabilities can emerge in LLMs without any human-curated, domain-targeted data, challenging current data-hungry AI development.
Autonomous curriculum generation within a verifiable environment fosters strong cross-domain generalization, as evidenced by code-trained models improving mathematical reasoning.
Complex cognitive behaviors, such as ReAct-style planning and distinct task-specific reasoning strategies, naturally emerge from the self-play training process.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.03318.Title: Unified Multimodal Chain-of-Thought Reward Model through Reinforcement Fine-Tuning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.03318.Summary: Researchers from Fudan University, Shanghai AI Lab, and Tencent's Hunyuan developed UNIFIEDREWARD-THINK, the first unified multimodal Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reward model that integrates multi-dimensional, step-by-step reasoning. The model consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art reward models across image and video understanding and generation tasks, providing enhanced accuracy and interpretability.
Problem: Existing multimodal reward models often lack interpretability and provide shallow justifications, leading to inaccuracies in complex visual scenarios.
There is a scarcity of large-scale, high-quality Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reward data, making it challenging to train models with explicit reasoning via traditional supervised methods.
Visual-language models (VLMs) possess latent reasoning capabilities, but current training methodologies struggle to effectively elicit and refine these for reward modeling.
Method: A three-stage exploration-driven reinforcement fine-tuning pipeline (Cold Start, Rejection Sampling, Group Relative Policy Optimization - GRPO) is introduced to activate and refine CoT reasoning.

The model leverages a small amount of GPT-4o distilled CoT data for an initial 'cold start' to learn reasoning formats, followed by rejection sampling and GRPO to generalize and enhance reasoning for challenging cases.

A novel multidimensional CoT reward scoring strategy is embedded, prompting the model to evaluate candidates along multiple task-relevant dimensions, ensuring alignment between reasoning steps and final judgments.
Results: UNIFIEDREWARD-THINK consistently outperforms state-of-the-art multimodal reward models, including strong baselines like GPT-4o and Gemini-1.5-Pro, across image and video understanding and generation benchmarks.

Ablation studies confirm that each stage of the training pipeline, particularly the GRPO reinforcement fine-tuning, contributes substantial performance gains, with GRPO yielding the most significant improvements for challenging samples.
The methodology demonstrates robustness by achieving consistent improvements when trained on different base models (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL-7B), showcasing its generalizability.
Takeaways: Integrating explicit long Chains-of-Thought substantially enhances the reliability and robustness of multimodal reward models across diverse visual tasks.
Training with explicit CoT reasoning also improves the model's accuracy in providing direct, implicit reward signals, demonstrating a deeper internalization of logical thinking.

An exploration-driven reinforcement fine-tuning approach, specifically GRPO, effectively elicits and refines complex CoT reasoning even with limited initial CoT data by focusing on challenging samples.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.03181.Title: VLM Q-Learning: Aligning Vision-Language Models for Interactive Decision-Making
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.03181.Summary: A reinforcement learning framework called AFSFT (Advantage Filtered SFT) enables vision-language models to learn interactive decision-making from both successful and unsuccessful demonstrations through off-policy learning, achieving improved performance across Gym Cards, BabyAI, and MiniWoB benchmarks while maintaining the stability of supervised fine-tuning approaches.
Problem: Vision-language models (VLMs) struggle with strict output syntax requirements and long-context prompting in interactive tasks
Current approaches rely heavily on high-quality supervised demonstrations, limiting performance to the best strategy in training data
Method: Combines supervised fine-tuning with off-policy reinforcement learning through token-level advantage filtering
Uses actor-critic architecture where VLM acts as policy and separate critic head estimates token values
Enables offline-to-online learning where agent initially learns from fixed dataset before collecting new interactions
Results: Matches or exceeds performance of previous RL methods on Gym Cards tasks
Successfully enables online learning and policy refinement in BabyAI environment
Demonstrates ability to recover effective policies from noisy datasets in MiniWoB benchmark
Retains performance while requiring minimal parameter overhead through LoRA adaptation
Takeaways: Token-based action space allows treating each word in agent's reply as separate action for standard RL formulation
Filtering out suboptimal tokens from training data enables self-improvement beyond demonstration quality
Combining SFT stability with RL exploration capabilities produces more robust agents

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.03176.Title: seq-JEPA: Autoregressive Predictive Learning of Invariant-Equivariant World Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.03176.Summary: From the Université de Montréal and Mila - Quebec AI Institute, `seq-JEPA` introduces an autoregressive predictive learning framework for world models, processing sequences of action-observation pairs to simultaneously learn invariant and equivariant visual representations. This approach disentangles these properties through architectural inductive biases, demonstrating improved performance on both classification and transformation prediction tasks across various benchmarks.
Problem: Existing self-supervised learning methods often struggle with a fundamental trade-off, either excelling at learning invariant representations (for classification) or equivariant representations (for fine-grained tasks), but rarely both simultaneously.

The prevalent 'two-view paradigm' in self-supervised learning inherently limits the flexibility of learned representations, often forcing models to discard or preserve transformation-specific information.
Many current equivariant self-supervised methods rely on explicit equivariance loss terms, dual predictors, or complex contrastive strategies, which can make them less elegant or generalizable.
Method: `seq-JEPA` integrates sequential processing and action-conditioned predictive learning into Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) to learn distinct invariant and equivariant representations.
A transformer-based sequence aggregator integrates information from multiple observations and their corresponding relative transformations (actions), generating an invariant aggregate representation.

A predictor head, conditioned on the upcoming action, forecasts the latent representation of the next observation, compelling the online encoder to learn equivariant features without additional loss terms.
Results: `seq-JEPA` effectively resolves the invariance-equivariance trade-off, matching or surpassing leading equivariant baselines in transformation prediction (e.g., R² of 0.71 on 3DIEBench rotation) while significantly outperforming them in classification (86.14% vs. 80.40%).

Qualitative UMAP analysis shows encoder representations exhibiting clear equivariance (smooth gradients across transformations) and aggregate representations forming compact, invariant class clusters, confirming architectural disentanglement.

The framework excels at biologically inspired tasks like Predictive Learning Across Saccades (PLS) with 83.44% accuracy on STL-10 and demonstrates robust path integration, with performance scaling positively with longer training and inference sequence lengths.
Takeaways: Architectural inductive biases, specifically action conditioning and sequence aggregation, can naturally disentangle invariant and equivariant properties within a single self-supervised model.

Biologically inspired sequential processing of action-observation pairs provides a powerful and generalizable learning signal, allowing models to learn from dynamic interactions rather than static image pairs.
Non-generative world models predicting latent representations conditioned on actions can effectively learn the dynamics of transformations and support complex tasks like path integration.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.03113.Title: Image Recognition with Online Lightweight Vision Transformer: A Survey
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.03113.Summary: This survey systematically reviews online lightweighting techniques for Vision Transformers, categorizing methods like efficient component design, dynamic networks, and knowledge distillation. It comprehensively analyzes their trade-offs between performance and efficiency, demonstrating how these advancements enable high accuracy with reduced computational cost for practical deployment.
Problem: Vision Transformers (ViTs) achieve high performance in image recognition but incur significant computational and memory overheads, limiting their deployment in resource-constrained environments.
Traditional lightweighting techniques are often applied offline (post-training), potentially leading to performance degradation or requiring specialized hardware.
A structured understanding of online lightweighting methods, which optimize models during training, was lacking for ViTs.
Method: The paper provides a comprehensive survey of online lightweighting techniques for ViTs, categorizing them into Efficient Component Design, Dynamic Network, and Knowledge Distillation.
It presents a systematic analysis of the trade-offs between precision (Top-1 Accuracy), model parameters, computational cost (FLOPs), and throughput for various methods on the ImageNet-1K benchmark.
The survey identifies current limitations and proposes future research directions to guide the development of more efficient and deployable ViT models.
Results: Efficient Component Design methods, such as CrossViT variants, demonstrate accuracy improvements (e.g., 73.9% to 77.1%) with competitive FLOPs by integrating local feature extraction.
Dynamic Network approaches like DynamicViT significantly increase throughput (e.g., 36.6%) and reduce FLOPs (27.5%) through token pruning and merging, with minimal accuracy drops.

Knowledge Distillation techniques effectively transfer complex token relation knowledge, allowing lightweight ViT models to achieve high accuracy comparable to larger teacher models, exemplified by TinyMIM's performance through unique token relation distillation.
Takeaways: Online lightweighting strategies are highly effective in reducing computational and memory demands for ViTs while maintaining, and sometimes improving, accuracy.
Exploiting locality (e.g., in patch embedding, self-attention) and implementing dynamic adaptation (e.g., dynamic token pruning/merging, early exit) are crucial for achieving efficiency gains.
Knowledge Distillation, particularly transferring unique ViT token relation knowledge, offers a powerful mechanism to train smaller, efficient student models without significant performance loss.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.02831.Title: No Other Representation Component Is Needed: Diffusion Transformers Can Provide Representation Guidance by Themselves
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.02831.Summary: Self-Representation Alignment (SRA) introduces a method for diffusion transformers to leverage their own internal representations for guidance, eliminating the need for external components to accelerate training and improve generation quality. The approach consistently improves FID scores and training convergence, outperforming or matching methods that use external guidance.
Problem: Existing methods for representation guidance in diffusion transformers rely on auxiliary external tasks or large pre-trained representation encoders, increasing computational overhead and external dependencies.
The reliance on external components limits the applicability and resource efficiency of training advanced diffusion models, especially for modalities lacking robust external encoders.
A key challenge is enhancing generative model training convergence and output quality without introducing additional complex external supervisory signals.
Method: Self-Representation Alignment (SRA) employs a self-distillation mechanism where a diffusion transformer guides its own representation learning via a student-teacher setup with an EMA-updated teacher model.

It aligns 'weaker' latent representations from the student's earlier layers/higher noise levels with 'better' representations from the teacher's later layers/lower noise levels, using a lightweight projection head and a patch-wise smooth-ℓ1 loss.
The self-alignment loss is combined with the standard generative loss, allowing the model to learn enhanced representations intrinsically during the training process without external models or tasks.
Results: SRA consistently improves generation quality, achieving lower FID and higher IS scores across various DiT and SiT models (B/2, L/2, XL/2) on ImageNet and COCO2014 datasets.
The method substantially accelerates training convergence, with SRA-equipped SiT-XL/2 outperforming the original SiT-XL model with 1000 fewer epochs on ImageNet 256x256 while achieving FID 1.58.
SRA achieves performance comparable to or superior to state-of-the-art methods relying on external pre-trained encoders (e.g., REPA) while eliminating all external representation components.
Takeaways: Diffusion transformers inherently learn a 'bad-to-good' discriminative hierarchy of latent representations, with features becoming more refined and discriminative in later layers and at lower noise levels.
This intrinsic representation progression can be effectively harnessed for self-supervision, providing valuable guidance internally without the need for external components or pre-trained models.
The EMA-updated teacher model consistently maintains a higher quality of representation, ensuring stable and effective guidance to the student model throughout the training process.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.02665.Title: A Survey of Slow Thinking-based Reasoning LLMs using Reinforced Learning and Inference-time Scaling Law
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.02665.Summary: A survey details recent progress in Large Language Models designed for "slow thinking" (System 2 cognition) by analyzing over 160 studies across test-time scaling, reinforced learning, and dedicated slow thinking frameworks. The work synthesizes how these methods enhance deliberative reasoning, consistently showing improved performance on benchmarks like MATH, MMLU, and GPQA.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) often lack robust, deliberate reasoning capabilities for complex problems, failing to fully emulate human "System 2" slow thinking.

The current research landscape for reasoning LLMs is fragmented, lacking a comprehensive survey that integrates cognitive inspiration (slow thinking) with key technical solutions (RL and inference-time scaling).
LLMs require enhanced deliberative processes to reliably tackle challenging tasks in fields like mathematics, multi-agent planning, and medical diagnosis.
Method: The survey systematically reviews over 160 studies, classifying slow-thinking LLM methodologies into three core categories: Test-Time Scaling, Reinforced Learning, and Slow Thinking Frameworks.
It details solutions involving dynamic inference-time scaling, such as advanced search, sampling, and verification mechanisms, to adjust computational resources based on task complexity.
It analyzes methods leveraging Reinforcement Learning for iterative reasoning refinement, including policy network optimization, diverse reward design, and self-evolution strategies.
Results: LLMs incorporating slow-thinking principles, RL, and inference-time scaling demonstrate consistent performance improvements across diverse reasoning benchmarks.
Specific models like DeepSeek-R1 achieved 79.8 on MATH and 90.8 on MMLU, while Kimi k1.5 scored 77.5 on MATH and 87.4 on MMLU.
Test-time scaling methods, including advanced search algorithms and dynamic verification, enhance output quality and reasoning efficiency without altering core model parameters.
Takeaways: "Slow thinking" from cognitive science offers a potent conceptual framework for advancing LLMs beyond heuristic responses to deliberate reasoning.
Reinforcement Learning (RL) and Inference-time Scaling are identified as crucial, synergistic technical drivers for equipping LLMs with System 2-like reasoning capabilities.
Future LLM development should focus on hybrid architectures that balance fast and slow thinking, robust RL reward mechanisms, and self-improving learning paradigms.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.02567.Title: Unified Multimodal Understanding and Generation Models: Advances, Challenges, and Opportunities
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.02567.Summary: Researchers from Alibaba Group and affiliated universities provide a comprehensive survey and taxonomy of unified multimodal understanding and generation models, detailing their architectural approaches, data strategies, and evaluation methodologies. The paper categorizes existing models into Diffusion, Autoregressive, and Fused Autoregressive and Diffusion paradigms, while also outlining challenges and opportunities for future research.
Problem: Multimodal understanding and generation models have historically developed independently, leading to divergent architectural paradigms (autoregressive vs. diffusion).
The burgeoning field of unified multimodal AI lacked a systematic overview and consolidated resource to guide researchers through diverse approaches and emerging complexities.
Significant architectural challenges exist in merging these distinct paradigms, including effective tokenization, cross-modal attention, and data management for integrated systems.
Method: The authors conducted a systematic review, categorization, and critical analysis of existing literature on unified multimodal understanding and generation models.
A clear taxonomy was established, classifying models into Diffusion, Autoregressive (further sub-categorized by image tokenization), and Fused Autoregressive and Diffusion architectures.
Comprehensive compilations of relevant datasets and benchmarks were provided to support training and evaluation across understanding, generation, and interleaved tasks.
Results: The paper delivered a comprehensive taxonomy of unified multimodal models, detailing their architectural designs and visual encoding strategies, which serves as a foundational reference for the field.

An extensive compilation of relevant datasets was provided, categorized for multimodal understanding, text-to-image generation, image editing, and interleaved image-text tasks, highlighting the increasing use of synthetic data.

A structured overview of benchmarks for evaluating understanding (perception, reasoning), image generation (fidelity, compositionality), and interleaved generation tasks was presented, along with identified future research opportunities.
Takeaways: Unified multimodal models are broadly categorized into three architectural paradigms: Diffusion models (leveraging denoising), Autoregressive models (using LLM backbones), and Fused approaches (combining AR for text and diffusion for images).
Visual encoding strategies, such as pixel-based, semantic, learnable query, and hybrid methods, are critical for the performance and efficiency of autoregressive multimodal models.

Key challenges include managing high-dimensionality multimodal data, optimizing cross-modal attention mechanisms, addressing dataset noise and bias, and developing adequate evaluation protocols for integrated tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.02406.Title: Token Coordinated Prompt Attention is Needed for Visual Prompting
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.02406.Summary: A Token Coordinated Prompt Attention (TCPA) module is proposed to enhance visual prompting for Vision Transformers by assigning specific, coordinated prompts to different token types and individual image tokens. This approach leads to the extraction of more discriminative and diverse features, resulting in consistent performance improvements across a wide range of visual classification benchmarks.
Problem: Existing token-level visual prompting methods apply uniform prompts to all tokens, disregarding the distinct functionalities of CLS (classification) and image tokens.
This indiscriminate application leads to redundant attention patterns and "indistinguishable and biased prompt-extracted features" due to the low-rank nature of self-attention.
The uniform approach limits the Vision Transformer's representational capacity and its ability to capture comprehensive and diverse discriminative information for downstream tasks.
Method: Introduces Token Coordinated Prompt Attention (TCPA), a plug-and-play module that disentangles prompts based on token functionalities for attention-based interactions.
Employs Coordinated Prompt Attention of CLS and Image Tokens (R-TCPA) to use separate, exclusive prompt sets for CLS and image tokens.

Utilizes Coordinated Prompt Attention of Different Image Tokens (T-TCPA) by employing prompt pools and a matching function to assign appropriate prompts to individual tokens, then modifies the attention mechanism with a binarized mask to enforce these token-specific interactions.
Results: TCPA improved average accuracy by 1.2% to 2.0% when integrated with existing visual prompting methods (VP, VPT, DAMVP, AutoVP, VFPT) across various datasets in the HTA benchmark.
Consistent performance gains of 0.9% to 2.1% were observed across all categories of the VTAB benchmark (Natural, Specialized, Structured) for various base prompting methods.

Ablation studies confirmed that both disentangling CLS/image prompts (R-TCPA) and coordinating individual image token prompts (T-TCPA) contributed to performance improvements with minimal additional computational cost (e.g., 0.05-0.13 seconds per epoch).
Takeaways: The distinct roles of CLS and image tokens, as well as varying information in different image tokens, necessitate token-specific prompt interactions for effective visual prompting.
Existing methods' uniform prompt application leads to redundant attention and limits the discriminative power of extracted features.
Disentangling prompts and coordinating their interaction with specific tokens can significantly enhance feature diversity and classification performance while maintaining computational efficiency.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.02387.Title: RM-R1: Reward Modeling as Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.02387.Summary: Researchers from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and collaborators present RM-R1, a new class of Reasoning Reward Models (REASRMS) that integrate deep, interpretable reasoning into the reward assignment process. This approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on three major reward model benchmarks by employing a two-stage training pipeline (reasoning distillation and reinforcement learning) and a structured "Chain-of-Rubrics" mechanism, providing transparent and coherent rationales for judgments.
Problem: Scalar-based Reward Models (ScalarRMs) are opaque, lacking interpretability or explicit reasoning steps, limiting their utility in complex, reasoning-intensive tasks.
Generative Reward Models (GenRMs) offer free-form textual judgments but often provide superficial, unstructured, and less reliable reasoning, leading to suboptimal performance compared to ScalarRMs.

Accurate human preference judgments in real-world scenarios require deep cognitive processes like criteria inference, trade-off analysis, and consequence simulation, which existing reward models do not fully embody.
Method: Introduces Reasoning Reward Models (REASRMS), a new class of generative reward models designed to integrate deep, interpretable reasoning into the reward assignment process.

Proposes a two-stage training pipeline: an initial Reasoning Distillation stage to bootstrap the model's ability to generate structured reasoning traces, followed by Reinforcement Learning (RL) using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to refine generalization and critical thinking.

Develops a Chain-of-Rubrics (CoR) rollout mechanism via a sophisticated system prompt that guides the model to adapt its reasoning strategy based on task type (e.g., self-solve for reasoning tasks, generate tailored criteria for chat tasks) prior to making a judgment.
Results: RM-R1 models achieve state-of-the-art performance across RewardBench, RM-Bench, and RMB benchmarks, outperforming larger open-weight models and even proprietary models by up to 4.9%.
On the reasoning-intensive RM-Bench, RM-R1-DeepSeek-Distilled-Qwen-32B sets new state-of-the-art accuracy with 91.8% in math and 74.1% in code.

Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of the two-stage training (distillation + RL), Chain-of-Rubrics prompting, and explicit query categorization, demonstrating that these components are crucial for superior performance and interpretability, and that performance scales with model size and inference-time compute.
Takeaways: Integrating robust, structured reasoning capabilities into reward modeling significantly enhances both RM's interpretability and its performance, particularly in complex scenarios.

A two-stage training pipeline combining reasoning distillation with subsequent reinforcement learning is highly effective for training high-performing Reasoning Reward Models (REASRMS), allowing for data efficiency and generalization.

Structured prompting mechanisms like Chain-of-Rubrics and explicit task categorization are crucial for enabling models to proactively generate effective reasoning traces and adapt evaluation strategies.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.02278.Title: Compositional Image-Text Matching and Retrieval by Grounding Entities
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.02278.Summary: Researchers from George Mason University developed Grounding CLIP (GCLIP), a training-free method to enhance the compositional understanding of existing vision-language models. GCLIP explicitly grounds textual entities and relationships to image regions, improving image-text matching by leveraging fine-grained visual-linguistic alignments. The approach improved Recall@1 by 12% over CLIP on the Flickr30K dataset and outperformed other baselines.
Problem: Current vision-language models like CLIP struggle with compositional understanding, failing to grasp how different objects relate to each other in an image based on text descriptions.
These models treat images and captions as holistic units, often unable to ground specific textual elements to corresponding visual regions.
Limitations include poor fine-grained matching and confusion regarding relationships between subjects and objects.
Method: Proposing Grounding CLIP (GCLIP), a training-free approach that enhances compositional image-text matching and retrieval.
The method decomposes input text into entities and relationships using a large language model (GPT-3.5), then localizes these entities in the image with an open-vocabulary detector (Grounding DINO).
It computes component-level similarity scores between sub-images and textual descriptions, combining them with global similarity to refine the overall image-text match.
Results: Grounding CLIP (GCLIP) improved Recall@1 by 12% over CLIP on Flickr30K, achieving 66.5% compared to CLIP's 54.4%, demonstrating enhanced compositional understanding.
GCLIP consistently outperformed both CLIP and ComCLIP across evaluated metrics and datasets, including compositional benchmarks like ComVG and SVO Probes.
On MS-COCO, GCLIP showed Recall@1 of 20.4%, a modest improvement over CLIP's 19.4%.
Takeaways: Explicitly identifying and grounding textual entities (objects, attributes, relationships) to visual regions significantly improves compositional understanding in vision-language models.
Large language models (GPT-3.5) can effectively decompose text into its constituent entities and relationships for fine-grained analysis.
Open-vocabulary object detectors (Grounding DINO) are crucial for localizing diverse textual entities within images without prior training.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.02222.Title: Practical Efficiency of Muon for Pretraining
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.02222.Summary: Essential AI demonstrates that Muon, a second-order optimizer, offers superior practical efficiency over AdamW for large language model pretraining, expanding the compute-time Pareto frontier and requiring 10-15% fewer tokens to reach target losses.
