They also introduce a "telescoping algorithm" for efficient hyperparameter tuning with Muon, validating its compatibility with Maximal Update Parameterization (muP) to achieve substantial compute savings for hyperparameter search.
Problem: AdamW has been the de facto optimizer for LLMs, but second-order methods theoretically offer better convergence, yet were deemed impractical due to high computational and memory costs.
Hyperparameter optimization (HPO) for massive LLMs is prohibitively expensive, and the compatibility of principled scaling methods like muP with novel optimizers like Muon was unconfirmed.

Traditional optimizer comparisons often fail to capture the complex interplay between compute resources, training time, and data efficiency, especially at large batch sizes common in distributed training.
Method: The paper proposes Muon as a simple, memory-efficient second-order optimizer and validates its practical advantages over AdamW for LLM pretraining.
It introduces the 'compute-time Pareto frontier' and 'token ratio' as comprehensive metrics for evaluating optimizer performance across varying compute configurations and batch sizes.

A 'telescoping algorithm' is developed for efficient hyperparameter tuning with Muon, leveraging Maximal Update Parameterization (muP) to transfer hyperparameters from smaller to larger models while controlling errors.
Results: Muon consistently expanded the compute-time Pareto frontier compared to AdamW, allowing for a target loss to be achieved either faster or with fewer compute resources.
Muon required 10-15% fewer tokens than AdamW to reach an identical target loss, with the absolute token savings largely agnostic to model size (e.g., ~2 billion fewer tokens to reach 3.2 nats).
The 'telescoping algorithm' for hyperparameter tuning provided over 50% compute savings compared to brute-force search, successfully tracking optimal hyperparameters and reducing errors.
Takeaways: Muon, a second-order optimizer, practically outperforms AdamW by offering a more favorable compute-time tradeoff for large language model pretraining.
Muon maintains superior relative data efficiency even at very large batch sizes, where AdamW typically shows diminishing returns.
The Maximal Update Parameterization (muP) framework is compatible with Muon, and the proposed 'telescoping algorithm' efficiently enables principled hyperparameter transfer across model scales.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.02056.Title: Handling Imbalanced Pseudolabels for Vision-Language Models with Concept Alignment and Confusion-Aware Calibrated Margin
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.02056.Summary: A framework for improving vision-language model adaptation combines concept alignment through LLM-enhanced text descriptions with confusion-aware calibrated margins to address pseudo-label imbalance, achieving state-of-the-art results across six image classification benchmarks while reducing reliance on manually labeled data.
Problem: Vision-language models generate imbalanced pseudo-labels when adapting to downstream tasks
Concept mismatch and confusion between classes leads to unreliable self-training
Method: Iterative clustering identifies concept-mismatched classes and uses LLM to generate enhanced descriptions
Confusion-aware calibrated margin adjusts loss function based on class similarities
Separate adapters for reliable and dynamically generated pseudo-labels reduce confirmation bias
Results: Outperforms existing methods on six benchmark datasets across three learning paradigms
Achieves higher pseudo-label accuracy compared to standard top-k strategies
Reduces Expected Calibration Error in concept-confused groups
Demonstrates effectiveness in both unsupervised and semi-supervised settings
Takeaways: Addressing underlying causes of pseudo-label imbalance (concept mismatch and confusion) more effective than enforcing artificial balance
LLM-enhanced text descriptions can significantly improve pseudo-label accuracy
Calibrated margins based on class similarity help distinguish confused concepts

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.01996.Title: Always Skip Attention
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.01996.Summary: Researchers at Adelaide University and CSIRO found that the self-attention mechanism in Vision Transformers requires skip connections to prevent catastrophic training failure, attributing this to its intrinsic ill-conditioning. They introduced Token Graying, a pre-conditioning method that improved ViT accuracy on ImageNet-1K by up to 0.3% with minimal computational cost.
Problem: Vision Transformers (ViTs) catastrophically fail to train if skip connections are removed from the self-attention block, an observation not shared by other network components or CNNs.
A lack of theoretical understanding explaining why the self-attention mechanism, unlike other layers, is uniquely dependent on skip connections for stable training.
The ongoing need to develop effective methods for improving the conditioning of input tokens in ViTs to enhance performance and stability.
Method: Empirically demonstrated that removing skip connections from the self-attention block in ViTs leads to catastrophic training failure, while removal from Feedforward Networks (FFNs) results in only a modest performance drop.

Developed a theoretical framework showing that the condition number of a linear self-attention output embedding (without skip connections) is bounded by the cube of the input condition number, and proved that skip connections regularize this ill-conditioning.
Proposed Token Graying (TG) methods, SVDTG and the computationally efficient DCTTG, to pre-condition input tokens by adjusting singular values or Discrete Cosine Transform coefficients.
Results: Removing skip connections from the self-attention block resulted in a catastrophic 22% accuracy loss on CIFAR-10 for ViT-Tiny and complete training failure on Tiny-ImageNet, whereas FFNs experienced only a modest 2% drop.

The computationally efficient DCT Token Graying (DCTTG) consistently improved Top-1 accuracy by 0.2-0.3% across various ViT architectures (e.g., ViT-Base to 81.3% from 81.0%) in supervised and self-supervised settings on ImageNet-1K.
DCTTG achieved these performance improvements with negligible computational overhead, adding less than 1% to the training time, making it practical for real-world application.
Takeaways: The self-attention mechanism is intrinsically ill-conditioned, with its output embedding's condition number bounded by the cube of the input's, making it uniquely reliant on skip connections for stable optimization.
Skip connections serve as fundamental regularizers for self-attention, critically stabilizing gradient flow and signal propagation, rather than merely offering a performance benefit.
Pre-conditioning input tokens through methods like DCT Token Graying can further improve ViT performance and conditioning, complementing the role of skip connections.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.01812.Title: $\textit{New News}$: System-2 Fine-tuning for Robust Integration of New Knowledge
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.01812.Summary: Researchers from Harvard University and NTT Research developed the New News dataset and System-2 Fine-tuning (Sys2-FT) protocols to enable Large Language Models to robustly internalize new, plausible information into their model weights. This approach significantly bridges the gap between naive fine-tuning and in-context learning, with the Self-QA protocol achieving near in-context learning performance in quantitative domains while preserving general model capabilities.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle to internalize new information into their permanent weights, exhibiting a substantial "fine-tuning to in-context learning gap" (FT-ICL gap).
Existing knowledge editing methods often focus on isolated factual corrections and can introduce unintended "ripple effects," lacking a holistic approach for complex, plausible knowledge updates.
The absence of robust in-weight knowledge integration limits LLMs' adaptability and continuous learning capabilities in dynamic environments.
Method: Introduced the "New News" dataset, comprising 75 manually curated, hypothetical yet plausible news items across five diverse domains, each with five downstream evaluation questions.

Developed System-2 Fine-tuning (Sys2-FT) protocols (Paraphrase, Implication, Self-QA) which leverage the LLM's own in-context learning ability to generate diverse "replay elements" (synthetic data) from the news.

Fine-tuned models using LoRA on these generated conversation-formatted replay elements, where the Self-QA protocol involves the model generating questions and then answering them based on the provided news.
Results: Sys2-FT protocols, especially the Self-QA method, significantly improved models' ability to internalize new knowledge, often achieving near-ICL performance in quantitative domains like mathematics and coding.
Sys2-FT largely preserved the models' general capabilities (MMLU-Pro), mathematical reasoning (GSM8K), and instruction-following abilities (IFEval), with only minor degradation in specific cases.
The study quantitatively confirmed a substantial "FT-ICL gap," showing that naive fine-tuning performed poorly compared to in-context learning for integrating new information.
Takeaways: A "Contextual Shadowing Effect" was discovered, where explicitly including the original news during Sys2-FT data generation catastrophically degrades the learning signal for in-weight integration.
The "Curse of Overexposure" suggests that excessive fine-tuning on new information can sometimes degrade the model's in-context learning ability for that same knowledge.
Preliminary evidence indicates a compute-dependent scaling law for Sys2-FT, where larger models are more sample-efficient learners, requiring less effective data to achieve comparable performance.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.01441.Title: Agentic Reasoning and Tool Integration for LLMs via Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.01441.Summary: The ARTIST framework from Microsoft Research unifies agentic reasoning, dynamic tool integration, and reinforcement learning within large language models, allowing them to autonomously learn when and how to use external tools. This approach achieves superior performance on complex mathematical reasoning and multi-turn function calling tasks, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines and even larger frontier models while exhibiting emergent self-correction capabilities.
Problem: Large language models (LLMs) primarily rely on static pre-trained knowledge and text-only reasoning, leading to inaccuracies or limitations in handling dynamic, time-sensitive, or knowledge-intensive tasks.

Existing tool integration methods often depend on labor-intensive hand-crafted prompts or extensive supervised fine-tuning, limiting their scalability, generalization, and robustness in complex, multi-turn scenarios.

Current reinforcement learning (RL) approaches for LLMs largely focus on refining internal reasoning or output style, without explicitly integrating dynamic external tool use as a first-class operation within the RL loop.
Method: ARTIST (Agentic Reasoning and Tool Integration in Self-Improving Transformers) is a unified framework that interleaves the LLM's text-based thinking, structured tool queries, and processing of tool outputs within a dynamic reasoning trajectory.
It employs Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), an RL algorithm, adapted with a loss masking strategy to focus optimization on the agent's decision-making and reasoning for tool invocation.

A composite reward system guides the learning process, providing feedback based on final answer correctness, adherence to prompt format, and the fraction of successful tool calls, eliminating the need for step-level supervision.
Results: ARTIST achieves the highest Pass@1 accuracy across challenging math benchmarks, with Qwen2.5-14B-ARTIST showing up to +22.0% absolute improvement over base models on AMC and outperforming GPT-4o on all math benchmarks (e.g., +8.9% on Olympiad, +7.6% on AIME).
On multi-turn function calling benchmarks (τ-bench, BFCL v3), ARTIST substantially improves performance, more than doubling the base model's accuracy on τ-bench Airline (0.260 vs. 0.120).

ARTIST exhibits emergent agentic behaviors such as self-refinement, self-correction (diagnosing and recovering from tool errors), and self-reflection, leading to more interpretable and robust problem-solving strategies without explicit supervision.
Takeaways: Unifying agentic reasoning, dynamic tool integration, and outcome-based reinforcement learning allows large language models to autonomously learn when, how, and which tools to use.

Applying a loss masking strategy during RL training, focusing gradients only on agent-generated tokens (thinking and tool calls), is crucial for learning effective tool invocation strategies, rather than just imitating outputs.

A composite reward mechanism, incorporating answer correctness, adherence to structured prompt templates, and successful tool execution, enables the model to develop robust, context-aware, and self-correcting behaviors.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.01109.Title: Self-Supervision Enhances Instance-based Multiple Instance Learning Methods in Digital Pathology: A Benchmark Study
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.01109.Summary: A comprehensive benchmark study reveals that simple instance-based Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) methods combined with self-supervised learning achieve comparable or superior performance to complex embedding-based approaches in digital pathology, establishing new state-of-the-art results on the BRACS and Camelyon16 datasets while providing better interpretability through patch-level predictions.
Problem: Whole Slide Images (WSIs) are extremely large and lack patch-level annotations, making direct application of deep learning challenging
Conventional wisdom suggests embedding-based MIL methods are superior, but they lack interpretability and are computationally expensive
Method: Evaluate 10 MIL methods (both instance and embedding-based) with 6 self-supervised learning strategies across 4 datasets
Introduce 4 novel instance-based MIL methods adapted from sound event detection
Compare performance using different backbones and foundation models
Results: New state-of-the-art results achieved on BRACS and Camelyon16 benchmarks
Instance-based methods provide better interpretability through patch-level predictions
Findings are robust across different datasets, backbones, and SSL methods
Foundation models perform well but highlight importance of domain-specific data
Takeaways: Simple instance-based MIL methods with strong SSL features perform as well or better than complex embedding approaches
MOCOv3, DINO and Barlow Twins provide the most stable SSL performance
Domain-specific pre-training consistently outperforms ImageNet pre-training

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.01064.Title: Efficient Vocabulary-Free Fine-Grained Visual Recognition in the Age of Multimodal LLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.01064.Summary: A novel framework called NeaR enables efficient vocabulary-free fine-grained visual recognition by combining MLLM-generated labels with nearest-neighbor refinement and CLIP model fine-tuning, achieving comparable or better performance than direct MLLM inference while significantly reducing computational costs and inference time across multiple benchmark datasets.
Problem: Direct use of MLLMs for fine-grained visual recognition is computationally expensive and time-consuming
Traditional FGVR methods require large expertly annotated datasets which are often unavailable
Existing approaches struggle with vocabulary-free settings where categories aren't predefined
Method: Generate initial labels using MLLMs on a small training set
Refine labels using K-nearest neighbors in CLIP embedding space and GMM-based noise detection
Fine-tune CLIP model using refined labels for efficient inference
Implement label filtering to reduce complexity at inference time
Results: Outperforms direct MLLM inference and baseline methods across multiple datasets
Shows robustness across different MLLMs including GPT-4V, GeminiPro, and open-source models
Achieves significant reduction in computational costs compared to direct MLLM queries
Demonstrates effectiveness with limited training data and imbalanced class distributions
Takeaways: Similar images likely share similar labels (manifold assumption)
MLLM-generated labels can be effectively refined using neighbor information
Knowledge can be distilled from expensive MLLMs to more efficient CLIP models
Label filtering helps manage vocabulary size while maintaining performance

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.00949.Title: Llama-Nemotron: Efficient Reasoning Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.00949.Summary: NVIDIA's Llama-Nemotron introduces a family of open-source language models designed for advanced reasoning, achieving state-of-the-art performance on complex tasks while delivering superior inference efficiency. The models integrate a dynamic reasoning toggle and surpass benchmarks like GPQA-Diamond with significantly higher throughput compared to existing models.
Problem: Existing state-of-the-art reasoning models are computationally expensive, leading to high inference costs and longer response times, hindering practical deployment.
Users lack dynamic control over the verbosity and depth of reasoning, leading to inefficient resource allocation for simpler queries and suboptimal user experience.
A need exists for commercially permissive open-source models that combine advanced reasoning capabilities with practical inference efficiency.
Method: Developed a family of heterogeneous reasoning models (Nano, Super, Ultra) based on Llama 3.1/3.3, featuring a dynamic reasoning toggle to control output verbosity.
Implemented a multi-stage training pipeline encompassing Neural Architecture Search (NAS), FFN Fusion for efficiency, knowledge distillation, continued pretraining, and supervised fine-tuning.

Utilized large-scale, curriculum-driven Reinforcement Learning (GRPO, RLOO) and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) to enhance reasoning capabilities, alignment, and surpass teacher model performance.
Results: LN-Ultra (253B) achieves state-of-the-art open-source performance on GPQA-Diamond (76.0% accuracy), surpassing DeepSeek-R1 (71.5%) and demonstrating significantly higher inference throughput (e.g., 4x-1.9x speedup).
LN-Super (49B) delivers a 5x throughput speedup over Llama 3.3-70B-Instruct on a single H100 GPU at batch size 256 (TP1) while maintaining competitive reasoning performance.

The models successfully support a dynamic reasoning toggle, effectively modulating response styles based on user prompts, and exhibit strong generalization on out-of-distribution tasks like LLM-as-a-Judge.
Takeaways: A comprehensive multi-stage training methodology, integrating architectural optimization (NAS), distillation, SFT, and large-scale RL, is crucial for achieving both state-of-the-art reasoning and high inference efficiency.
Large-scale, curriculum-driven Reinforcement Learning is essential for models to surpass their teacher's reasoning capabilities on challenging tasks, overcoming a performance ceiling.
Implementing a dynamic reasoning toggle provides users with effective control over response style and computational resources, enhancing model versatility and practicality.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.00703.Title: T2I-R1: Reinforcing Image Generation with Collaborative Semantic-level and Token-level CoT
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.00703.Summary: T2I-R1 introduces a text-to-image generation model that integrates a bi-level Chain-of-Thought process, combining semantic-level planning and token-level generation. Through Reinforcement Learning, the model improves image quality and prompt adherence, particularly for complex and reasoning-intensive prompts, achieving significant gains on T2I-CompBench and the WISE benchmark over its baseline and state-of-the-art diffusion models.
Problem: Existing Chain-of-Thought (CoT) applications are largely explored for text or visual understanding tasks, with limited exploration in visual generation.
Unified Large Multimodal Models (ULMs) often decouple understanding and generation capabilities, preventing understanding prowess from directly benefiting image generation.
Mainstream text-to-image (T2I) models lack explicit high-level semantic planning and struggle with compositional or reasoning-intensive prompts, leading to failures in complex scenarios.
Method: T2I-R1 introduces a bi-level Chain-of-Thought (CoT): a semantic-level textual reasoning phase for high-level planning and a token-level CoT for autoregressive image token generation.
The model is trained using BiCoT-GRPO (Bi-level CoT Group Relative Policy Optimization), a Reinforcement Learning framework, on a Unified Large Multimodal Model (Janus-Pro).
An ensemble of diverse vision experts (Human Preference Model, Object Detector, VQA Model, Output Reward Model) provides a multi-faceted reward for comprehensive image evaluation and optimization.
Results: T2I-R1 improves performance by 13% on T2I-CompBench and 19% on the WISE benchmark compared to its Janus-Pro-7B baseline.

The model outperforms state-of-the-art diffusion models like FLUX.1 on challenging benchmarks, leading in five out of six subtasks on T2I-CompBench and achieving the highest overall score on WISE by 4%.
Qualitative analysis shows T2I-R1 generates images that are more aligned with human intentions for complex and abstract prompts, demonstrating enhanced reasoning and robustness in unusual scenarios.
Takeaways: A bi-level Chain-of-Thought (CoT) process, encompassing semantic-level planning and token-level generation, is effective for improving text-to-image synthesis.
Reinforcement Learning, specifically BiCoT-GRPO, can effectively train a Unified Large Multimodal Model to fuse its understanding and generation capabilities for enhanced reasoning in T2I.
An ensemble of diverse vision experts as reward models is crucial for robustly evaluating and optimizing image generation, overcoming the challenges of subjective quality assessment.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.00551.Title: 100 Days After DeepSeek-R1: A Survey on Replication Studies and More Directions for Reasoning Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.00551.Summary: This survey by MiroMind and affiliated universities synthesizes open-source replication studies of DeepSeek-R1, detailing methodologies for reasoning language models (RLMs) through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR). It highlights the critical role of high-quality data and adapted RL algorithms in achieving strong reasoning capabilities, also identifying emerging research directions and challenges.
Problem: The emergence of powerful Reasoning Language Models (RLMs) like DeepSeek-R1, which demonstrate advanced step-by-step reasoning capabilities.
DeepSeek-R1's proprietary nature and lack of full open-sourcing (training data, configurations) created a knowledge gap for the open-source community.
A fragmented landscape of uncoordinated open-source replication efforts made it difficult for researchers to stay updated and identify best practices for RLM development.
Method: The paper provides a comprehensive survey of open-source replication studies related to DeepSeek-R1's reasoning capabilities.
It systematically categorizes and analyzes training methodologies, focusing on Supervised Fine-tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR).
The survey synthesizes findings regarding data curation, algorithm adaptations, and training configurations, providing a structured overview and identifying future research directions.
Results: SFT replication studies primarily concentrate on math and coding datasets, emphasizing rigorous data cleaning, verification, and often benefiting from fine-tuning already capable instruction-tuned models.
RLVR success relies on large, diverse datasets of moderately difficult problems, with numerous algorithm modifications (e.g., DAPO, Dr. GRPO, VC-PPO) proposed to enhance stability and efficiency.
The role of KL loss in RLVR is debated among studies, and increased context lengths (up to 32k tokens) and curriculum learning are effective strategies for improving performance.
Takeaways: High-quality, verified Chain-of-Thought (CoT) data is essential for effective Supervised Fine-tuning (SFT) of reasoning language models (RLMs).
Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), particularly with rule-based outcome rewards and adapted algorithms, is crucial for refining and enhancing RLM reasoning.
RL-trained models demonstrate improved out-of-domain generalization across tasks and modalities, though safety concerns like reward hacking and overthinking are emerging.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.00315.Title: Mixture of Sparse Attention: Content-Based Learnable Sparse Attention via Expert-Choice Routing
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.00315.Summary: A novel sparse attention mechanism called MoSA (Mixture of Sparse Attention) enables more efficient transformer models by dynamically selecting relevant tokens for each attention head, achieving 27% better perplexity than dense attention baselines while reducing computational costs and KV-cache size.
Problem: Traditional self-attention in transformers has quadratic computational and memory complexity
Existing sparse attention methods often fail to match dense attention performance in practice
Method: Expert-choice routing allows each attention head to dynamically select the most relevant tokens
Hybrid architecture combines sparse MoSA heads with dense attention heads for stability
Sparse computation only on selected tokens reduces resource requirements
Results: 27% better perplexity compared to dense baselines with equal compute budget
Significant reductions in wall-clock time, training memory, and KV-cache size
Only sparse attention method tested that outperforms dense baseline in IsoFLOP setting
Maintains effectiveness across varying sequence lengths
Takeaways: Dynamic content-based token selection outperforms static sparse patterns
Hybridization with dense heads is crucial for optimal performance
Performance advantage increases with longer sequence lengths

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.00147.Title: AdaptMI: Adaptive Skill-based In-context Math Instruction for Small Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.00147.Summary: Researchers at Princeton Language and Intelligence developed AdaptMI and AdaptMI+, adaptive methods that enhance Small Language Models' in-context learning for mathematical reasoning by dynamically selecting skill-based examples to prevent cognitive overload. The approach improves accuracy by up to 6% on math benchmarks compared to non-adaptive skill-based strategies.
Problem: Small Language Models (SLMs) exhibit a significant performance gap in in-context learning (ICL) compared to larger models, particularly in complex reasoning tasks like mathematics.
Skill-based prompting, effective for Large Language Models (LLMs), often yields minimal or even negative impacts on SLM performance due to "cognitive overload" on simpler problems.
SLMs frequently produce unnecessarily long and erroneous responses when presented with inappropriate or excessive skill-based instructions for questions they could otherwise solve easily.
Method: A two-stage adaptive framework, AdaptMI, classifies questions as "easy" or "difficult" for a specific SLM using a process reward model (PRM) to analyze step-by-step reasoning.
For "difficult" questions, AdaptMI applies skill-based in-context examples, while for "easy" questions, it reverts to fixed, simpler examples.

AdaptMI+ further refines this by using a large LLM to analyze initial failed responses on difficult questions, identifying specific *missing* skills, and then selecting in-context examples only for those targeted skills.
Results: AdaptMI and AdaptMI+ consistently surpassed non-adaptive baselines, with AdaptMI+ achieving accuracy improvements of up to 6% over naive skill-based strategies on math benchmarks.
Performance gains were most pronounced for smaller models (e.g., Qwen2.5-1.5B, Llama-3.2-1B), highlighting the methods' effectiveness in enhancing resource-constrained SLMs.
An iterative version of AdaptMI+ demonstrated continuous accuracy improvements, boosting performance by up to 7.2% for the Qwen2.5-1.5B model on the MATH dataset.
Takeaways: Small Language Models (SLMs) experience "cognitive overload," where providing excessive or inappropriate skill-based information for easy problems degrades performance, leading to longer and erroneous responses.
Adaptive selection of in-context examples, rather than uniform application, is critical for optimizing SLM performance, mirroring principles from human adaptive teaching.
Process reward models, which evaluate step-by-step reasoning, are more effective than outcome reward models for accurately identifying reasoning flaws and classifying question difficulty for SLMs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.00024.Title: Nemotron-Research-Tool-N1: Exploring Tool-Using Language Models with Reinforced Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.00024.Summary: NVIDIA, Pennsylvania State University, and the University of Washington introduce Nemotron-Research-Tool-N1, which applies rule-based reinforcement learning (R1-style RL) to train large language models for tool-calling. This approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on various tool-use benchmarks, outperforming models like GPT-4o, and demonstrates that pure RL training can be more effective than traditional supervised fine-tuning or SFT-then-RL pipelines.
Problem: Existing tool-augmented Large Language Models primarily rely on supervised fine-tuning (SFT), which often leads to imitative reasoning rather than robust, generalized understanding.
SFT-trained models frequently struggle to generalize to novel or out-of-distribution tool-use scenarios due to a lack of explicit reasoning supervision.
SFT's rigid next-token prediction penalizes semantically equivalent but syntactically different tool-call outputs, limiting the model's flexibility.
Method: The paper applies a rule-based (R1-style) reinforcement learning paradigm using the GRPO algorithm to train LLMs for general-purpose tool-calling.

A simple binary reward function is employed, granting a reward of 1 only if the output adheres to a specified structured format and the predicted tool call(s) exactly match the ground-truth functionally.
A lightweight 'thinking template' guides the LLM to produce internal reasoning within XML tags followed by tool invocations as JSON, ensuring structured output while allowing flexible reasoning.
Results: Nemotron-Research-Tool-N1 models achieved state-of-the-art performance on tool-calling benchmarks, with Tool-N1-14B improving approximately 2% over GPT-4o on BFCL and surpassing GPT-4o by 5.03% on APIBank.
Pure R1-style RL consistently outperformed both Reason-SFT and No-Reason SFT under equal data budgets, demonstrating the efficacy of the RL-centric approach.
The training method scaled effectively with model size (7B and 14B models showing significant gains) and generalized well across different LLM backbones like Qwen2.5-Instruct and LLaMA series.
Takeaways: The commonly adopted SFT-then-RL paradigm does not necessarily outperform pure RL for tool-calling tasks under equal data budgets, challenging established RLHF assumptions.

A simple binary reward scheme (all-or-nothing for format and tool-call correctness) is more effective than fine-grained partial rewards, preventing 'reward hacking' and encouraging full functional accuracy.
Explicitly guiding the model to output structured reasoning within specific tags, even without supervising the reasoning content, is crucial for performance.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.21850.Title: COMPACT: COMPositional Atomic-to-Complex Visual Capability Tuning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.21850.Summary: COMPACT introduces a method for generating compositionally complex visual instruction tuning data, enabling MLLMs to achieve 100.2% relative performance compared to a full LLaVA-665K baseline while using only 10% of its data. This approach significantly improves performance on complex benchmarks like MM-Vet (+8.6%) and MMStar (+2.9%) by increasing the information density per training sample.
Problem: Existing Visual Instruction Tuning (VIT) datasets often contain simplistic questions that under-utilize the rich visual information in images, leading to data inefficiency.
The prevailing "quantity over quality" paradigm in MLLM training prioritizes dataset scale without explicitly designing questions for compositional reasoning.
MLLMs frequently struggle with complex visual reasoning tasks requiring the combination of multiple fundamental visual capabilities due to inadequate learning during training.
Method: COMPACT develops a four-step data recipe to generate high-quality, compositionally complex visual instruction tuning data by synthesizing questions that integrate multiple "atomic visual capabilities."
It establishes a taxonomy of 10 atomic visual capabilities and introduces a "k-value" to formally quantify the compositional complexity of questions.

The method employs Gemini-2.0-Flash with strict prompt engineering and multi-stage quality verification to ensure the generated question-answer pairs naturally integrate the sampled capabilities and maintain high data quality.
Results: COMPACT achieves an average relative performance of 100.2% compared to the full LLaVA-665K baseline, utilizing only 10% (65K samples) of its data, significantly outperforming other data reduction methods.

The approach demonstrates substantial performance gains on complex benchmarks, including +8.6% on MM-Vet, +2.9% on MMStar, and +13.8% on InfoVQA compared to models trained on the full LLaVA-665K dataset.
The generated compositional data exhibits a higher mean k-value of 2.89 (compared to 1.95 in LLaVA-665K) and is more token-efficient, using 46.88% fewer total tokens per entry.
Takeaways: Scaling data *complexity* through compositional tuning is more data-efficient and effective for MLLM training than merely scaling data *volume*.
Explicitly training models on tasks requiring the integration of multiple atomic visual capabilities leads to superior performance on complex, multi-modal reasoning benchmarks.

A small, carefully selected subset (approximately 5%) of conventional VIT data is sufficient for MLLMs to acquire general instruction-following and response formatting, separate from core visual reasoning capabilities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.21801.Title: DeepSeek-Prover-V2: Advancing Formal Mathematical Reasoning via Reinforcement Learning for Subgoal Decomposition
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.21801.Summary: DeepSeek-Prover-V2 improves formal theorem proving in Lean 4 by employing a recursive proof search with subgoal decomposition and a novel synthetic data generation pipeline. It achieves state-of-the-art results on benchmarks like MiniF2F and ProofNet, demonstrating a narrowed gap between informal LLM reasoning and formal proof generation.
Problem: Bridging the gap between the informal reasoning of Large Language Models (LLMs) and the rigorous demands of formal theorem proving.
Addressing the scarcity of high-quality formal proof data for training automated provers.
Improving the efficiency of proof search in formal verification systems.
Method: A recursive proof search pipeline that decomposes complex theorems into subgoals using a large LLM (DeepSeek-V3) and resolves them with a smaller 7B prover model.
A novel "cold-start" synthetic data generation strategy that unifies informal natural language proof sketches with formal Lean 4 proof construction.
Reinforcement learning, specifically Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a consistency reward, to guide the model towards accurate and structured formal proofs.
Results: Achieves a new state-of-the-art on MiniF2F-test, with the 671B CoT model reaching an 88.9% pass ratio (Pass@8192).
Demonstrates strong generalization, solving 37.1% of problems on ProofNet-test and 47 problems on PutnamBench with its 671B CoT variant.
Successfully solves 6 out of 15 AIME problems on the newly introduced ProverBench, substantially narrowing the performance gap between informal LLM mathematical reasoning and formal theorem proving.
Takeaways: Hierarchical subgoal decomposition, mirroring human mathematical problem-solving, is effective for formal theorem proving.
Generating synthetic "cold-start" data by combining informal LLM reasoning with formal proof verification can overcome data sparsity for training provers.
Explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning consistently and substantially improves formal proof generation accuracy over direct, non-CoT methods.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.21776.Title: WebThinker: Empowering Large Reasoning Models with Deep Research Capability
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.21776.Summary: The WebThinker framework, developed by researchers from Renmin University of China and collaborators, equips Large Reasoning Models with autonomous deep web exploration and an interleaved think-search-and-draft strategy for comprehensive report generation. It achieved state-of-the-art performance among 32B models on challenging reasoning benchmarks like GAIA and Humanity's Last Exam, and produced more complete and thorough scientific reports than existing methods.
Problem: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) are limited by reliance on static, internal knowledge, making them suboptimal for complex, knowledge-intensive tasks requiring up-to-date external information.
Existing open-source Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) agents often use predefined workflows, restricting LRMs' ability to deeply explore the web and dynamically interact with search results.
There is a need for systems that can conduct in-depth web information retrieval, mining, and integration beyond shallow search to generate comprehensive and accurate reports.
Method: WebThinker introduces a 'Deep Web Explorer' module, allowing LRMs to autonomously search, navigate web pages (via link-clicking), and extract information to address knowledge gaps.

An 'Autonomous Think-Search-and-Draft' strategy enables LRMs to seamlessly interleave reasoning, information gathering, and report writing, using specialized tools for drafting, checking, and editing content.
The framework employs iterative online Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to refine the LRM's ability to perceive information needs, reason, and effectively utilize research tools.
Results: WebThinker-32B-RL achieved State-of-the-Art (SOTA) performance among 32B models on complex reasoning benchmarks, including a +21.5% gain over its base version on Humanity's Last Exam (HLE) and surpassing stronger proprietary models like o3-mini (High) on HLE.

On scientific report generation tasks from Glaive, WebThinker-32B (RL version) achieved the highest overall average score (8.1), outperforming RAG baselines and advanced non-proprietary systems like Grok3 DeeperSearch.

Ablation studies confirmed the critical contributions of the Deep Web Explorer, especially its link-clicking capability, and the 'Autonomous Report Draft' component, with RL training being vital for complex problem-solving performance.
Takeaways: Interleaving reasoning with dynamic information gathering and iterative report refinement is crucial for tackling complex, knowledge-intensive tasks, surpassing static RAG workflows.
Empowering LRMs with hierarchical web exploration capabilities, including deep navigation beyond initial search results, is vital for comprehensive information acquisition.
Reinforcement learning, specifically iterative online DPO, effectively optimizes an LRM's strategic use of research tools, leading to significant performance gains in complex problem-solving.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.21559.Title: Black-Box Visual Prompt Engineering for Mitigating Object Hallucination in Large Vision Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.21559.Summary: Black-Box Visual Prompt Engineering (BBVPE) mitigates object hallucination in Large Vision Language Models (LVLMs) by strategically applying visual cues to input images, without requiring access to model internals. This approach improved accuracy on the POPE Random benchmark by up to 1.77% for LLaVA 1.5 and 1.50% for GPT-4o.
Problem: Large Vision Language Models (LVLMs) frequently hallucinate objects, incorrectly claiming to perceive objects not present in images.
This object hallucination reduces the reliability and utility of LVLMs in sensitive applications.
Current mitigation techniques often require access to internal model parameters, preventing their use with black-box proprietary LVLMs like GPT-4o.
Method: The Black-Box Visual Prompt Engineering (BBVPE) framework modifies input images with visual cues to guide LVLMs toward accurate visual understanding.
It leverages an object segmentation model to identify objects, then applies various visual prompt types (e.g., bounding boxes, reverse blur, crop).
A trained Visual Prompt Router selects the most effective visual prompt for each image-query pair to minimize hallucination.
Results: BBVPE consistently improved LVLM accuracy on the POPE and CHAIR hallucination benchmarks, outperforming baselines across all tested models.
On the POPE Random benchmark, BBVPE increased accuracy by 1.77% for LLaVA 1.5, 1.50% for GPT-4o, and 0.91% for Claude 3.0-Sonnet.
The visual prompt router, trained on COCO, demonstrated effective generalization by improving performance on unseen datasets like GQA.
Takeaways: Object hallucination in LVLMs often arises from imperfect alignment between vision and language components, compounded by pre-training data biases.
The optimal type of visual prompt for reducing hallucination varies significantly across different LVLMs (e.g., GPT-4o vs. LLaVA) and datasets.
Dynamically selecting the most effective visual prompt for a given image and query, rather than using a fixed prompt, yields better hallucination mitigation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.21447.Title: Multimodal Language Models See Better When They Look Shallower
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.21447.Summary: Researchers systematically analyzed visual layer selection in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), demonstrating that integrating features from shallow, middle, and deep Vision Transformer layers via a simple concatenation fusion outperforms conventional deep-layer reliance and more complex fusion strategies.
Problem: Current MLLMs primarily extract visual features from the final or penultimate layers of Vision Transformers (ViTs), a practice lacking systematic justification and potentially suboptimal.
The direct impact of hierarchical information across different ViT layers on downstream MLLM performance, particularly for fine-grained visual tasks, has been largely underexplored.
Existing multi-layer fusion methods often rely on heuristics or complex architectures without a principled understanding of optimal layer contributions for MLLM tasks.
Method: The authors systematically explored the impact of each of the 24 CLIP-ViT layers by individually connecting them to an MLLM and evaluating performance across 10 diverse benchmarks.
They partitioned ViT layers into semantically coherent shallow, middle, and deep groups based on Layer-wise Representation Similarity (LRS) analysis.
A lightweight fusion strategy was proposed, concatenating features from selected shallow, middle, and deep layers (e.g., layers 23, 18, 3) and passing them through a single-layer MLP connector.
Results: Layer 23 consistently outperformed Layer 24 across nearly all benchmarks, especially on general tasks, OCR, and hallucination evaluation, validating its superiority among deep layers.

Shallow and middle layers significantly improved performance on approximately one-third of fine-grained visual sub-tasks, with Layer 18 showing a 20% improvement over the penultimate layer on MME 'position' tasks.

The proposed simple linear fusion strategy, combining features from layers 23, 18, and 3, consistently achieved substantial performance gains over both single-layer baselines and state-of-the-art fusion methods across multiple benchmarks.
Takeaways: The absolute final ViT layer (Layer 24) is suboptimal for MLLMs due to CLIP's contrastive training, with the penultimate layer (Layer 23) providing a better balance for general tasks.

Shallow and middle ViT layers contain rich, underutilized fine-grained visual information crucial for tasks requiring precise localization, counting, and fine-grained perception, often outperforming deep layers in these areas.

A simple concatenation of features from strategically chosen shallow, middle, and deep layers can achieve superior performance over both single-layer baselines and more complex, specialized fusion architectures, suggesting 'less is more' in fusion complexity.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.21356.Title: Nexus-Gen: Unified Image Understanding, Generation, and Editing via Prefilled Autoregression in Shared Embedding Space
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.21356.Summary: Nexus-Gen, developed by Zhejiang University and Alibaba Group, unifies image understanding, generation, and editing within a single 7B-parameter framework, introducing a "prefilled autoregression" strategy to mitigate error accumulation in continuous embedding prediction. The model achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse benchmarks and releases a new high-quality instruction-guided image editing dataset.
Problem: Unified multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often achieve lower image synthesis quality compared to specialized diffusion models.
Autoregressive generation of continuous image embeddings in MLLMs using diffusion decoders suffers from severe error accumulation, leading to degraded image quality.
Many existing unified models lack robust and validated capabilities for complex downstream tasks, particularly high-fidelity fine-grained image editing.
Method: Nexus-Gen proposes a unified architecture integrating a vision encoder (from Qwen2.5-VL), a 7B autoregressive model, and a diffusion-based vision decoder operating within a shared continuous image embedding space.

It introduces a novel "prefilled autoregression" strategy that initializes and pre-fills input sequences with learned image embeddings during inference, preventing error propagation and aligning training with inference.

A dedicated dual-conditioning editing decoder is developed, combining 81-token semantic embeddings from the autoregressive model with 324-token fine-grained embeddings from the input image for robust detail preservation during editing.
Results: Achieves leading scores across multimodal understanding benchmarks (MME, SEED-Bench, MMMU, TextVQA) with its 7B autoregressive component, without additional parameters or performance loss.

Attains a state-of-the-art overall score of 0.81 on the GenEval benchmark for image generation after instruction tuning, showing particular strength in compositional understanding (e.g., "Two Object," "Counting").
Demonstrates superior performance on the ImagePulse benchmark for image editing, with a CLIP-T score of 0.324 and strong fidelity preservation (L1 0.134, CLIP-O 0.909, DINO-O 0.834).
Takeaways: The "prefilled autoregression" strategy effectively mitigates error accumulation during the autoregressive prediction of continuous embeddings, resulting in significantly lower MSE loss compared to naive autoregression.
A specialized dual-conditioning editing decoder is critical for high-fidelity image editing, substantially improving the preservation of non-edited regions compared to a general generation decoder.

An optimal token quantity (81 tokens) for autoregressive generation balances semantic coverage and ease of prediction, while a higher token count (324 tokens) from the input image is beneficial for detail preservation in editing tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.21318.Title: Phi-4-reasoning Technical Report
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.21318.Summary: Microsoft researchers develop a 14B parameter language model specialized in reasoning through careful data curation and a combination of supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, achieving performance competitive with much larger models while maintaining efficiency through targeted training on complex reasoning tasks.
Problem: Existing reasoning-focused language models require massive parameter counts, limiting their practical deployment
Difficult to maintain strong reasoning capabilities while reducing model size and computational requirements
Method: Carefully curated dataset combining web-sourced and synthetic reasoning problems with high-quality responses
Two-stage training approach using supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning for math reasoning
Specialized architecture modifications including longer context and reasoning block tokens
Results: Outperforms significantly larger open-weight models like DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B on reasoning benchmarks
Shows strong generalization to algorithmic problem solving and planning tasks
Maintains high performance on general-purpose skills like instruction following and long-context QA
Offers flexible accuracy vs token length tradeoffs between base and plus versions
Takeaways: High-quality data curation and targeted training can enable smaller models to match larger ones' reasoning ability
Combining supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning provides complementary benefits
Models exhibit strong generalization to unseen reasoning tasks not directly targeted in training

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.21277.Title: Reinforced MLLM: A Survey on RL-Based Reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.21277.Summary: The paper provides the first comprehensive survey on the application of Reinforcement Learning to enhance reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models. It systematically reviews current algorithmic designs, reward mechanisms, and applications, highlighting how RL enables more robust and adaptive reasoning while identifying key challenges such as text-centric biases in multimodal reasoning paths and the need for more sophisticated reward designs.
Problem: Existing surveys on MLLM reasoning or RL in LLMs did not specifically address the rapidly growing intersection of RL and reasoning in multimodal contexts.
MLLMs struggled to achieve robust and sophisticated reasoning across diverse modalities (vision, audio, video) due to text-centric biases and limited, simple rule-based reward functions.
Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) methods for MLLMs exhibited limitations in generalization to out-of-distribution (OOD) data and could suffer from catastrophic forgetting.
Method: The paper provides a comprehensive and systematic review of the field of RL-based reasoning in MLLMs, categorizing algorithmic designs, reward mechanisms, and applications.
It analyzes core RL algorithmic designs in LLMs/MLLMs, classifying them into value-model-free and value-model-based methods and discussing their respective strengths and weaknesses.
The survey examines algorithmic frameworks and reward function designs for multimodal perception, detailing strategies for integrating multiple modalities and surveying relevant benchmark datasets.
Results: The survey found that RL effectively activates powerful reasoning capabilities in MLLMs, evidenced by the successful transfer of the 'R1 training paradigm' to multimodal tasks.

Value-model-free RL methods like GRPO dominate current RL-based MLLM reasoning approaches due to their simplicity and robustness, while value-model-based methods are gaining traction with new optimizations.

Current reward mechanisms are largely outcome-supervised, with a growing trend towards cross-modal interaction and process-supervised rewards, yet significant challenges remain in addressing sparse rewards and promoting truly multimodal reasoning trajectories.
Takeaways: Reinforcement Learning (RL) is crucial for cultivating abstract, adaptive, and robust reasoning capabilities in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), complementing Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) which primarily imbues specific knowledge.
The 'R1 training paradigm', originating from LLMs, has become a foundational approach for enhancing reasoning in MLLMs, primarily relying on verifiable outcome-based rewards.

Current RL-based MLLM reasoning methods largely generate text-only Chain-of-Thought (CoT) and struggle with sparse rewards, leading to inefficient reasoning trajectories and underutilization of true cross-modal interactions.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.21233.Title: Phi-4-Mini-Reasoning: Exploring the Limits of Small Reasoning Language Models in Math
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.21233.Summary: Microsoft researchers demonstrate that a carefully designed multi-stage training recipe combining synthetic data distillation, supervised fine-tuning, preference optimization, and reinforcement learning enables a 3.8B parameter language model (Phi-4-Mini) to outperform reasoning models nearly twice its size, achieving a 3.2-point improvement over DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B on Math-500.
Problem: Small language models (SLMs) struggle to match the reasoning capabilities of larger models
Existing approaches for improving SLM reasoning lack a comprehensive, systematic training methodology
Method: Four-stage training recipe combining distillation, fine-tuning, preference learning, and reinforcement learning
Novel implementation techniques including packing mode for efficiency and temperature annealing for stable RL
Results: Outperforms 7B-8B parameter models on math reasoning benchmarks despite using only 3.8B parameters
Exceeds DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B by 3.2 points on Math-500
Demonstrates stable learning curves and consistent improvements across multiple evaluation metrics
Successfully maintains reasoning capabilities while reducing model size and computational requirements
Takeaways: High-quality Chain-of-Thought data is crucial for developing reasoning capabilities in small models
Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards provides more stable improvements than direct preference optimization
Each stage of the training recipe contributes measurably to overall performance gains

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.20996.Title: X-Fusion: Introducing New Modality to Frozen Large Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.20996.Summary: A dual-tower architecture enables integration of visual capabilities into frozen Large Language Models by introducing separate modality-specific weights, achieving strong performance on both image-to-text and text-to-image tasks while preserving the LLM's original language capabilities through parameter isolation.
Problem: Existing approaches to adding visual capabilities to LLMs either require expensive training from scratch or risk degrading language abilities through fine-tuning
Cross-modal reasoning and error accumulation challenges in current hybrid approaches combining LLMs with image generation models
Method: Dual-tower architecture with frozen LLM "text tower" and trainable "vision tower" with modality-specific weights
Feature alignment at intermediate processing levels between towers while maintaining parameter isolation
Optional X-Fuse operation to combine text features from both towers
Results: Outperforms alternative architectures on both image-to-text and text-to-image tasks while preserving language capabilities
Successfully handles multiple downstream tasks including visual QA and image editing without task-specific weights
Demonstrates practical efficiency advantages over training from scratch or fine-tuning approaches
Takeaways: Incorporating understanding-focused data (image-to-text) improves generation quality (text-to-image)
Reducing image data noise in image-to-text samples enhances overall performance
Feature alignment with pre-trained vision features accelerates convergence for smaller models but has minimal impact on larger ones

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.20966.Title: Softpick: No Attention Sink, No Massive Activations with Rectified Softmax
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.20966.Summary: Researchers at MBZUAI developed Softpick, a rectified, non-sum-to-one normalization function for transformer attention, which eliminates attention sink and massive activations. This new function results in functionally sparse attention maps (over 95% sparsity) and substantially enhances quantization performance at lower bit precisions, outperforming softmax in 2-bit and 3-bit settings.
Problem: The standard softmax function in transformer attention leads to "attention sink," where irrelevant tokens (like BOS) receive disproportionately high attention scores.
Softmax also contributes to "massive activations" in hidden states, presenting extreme outlier values that significantly hinder model quantization and low-precision training.
Existing solutions for these issues often introduce complexity, additional parameters, or require custom optimizers, lacking a straightforward, universally applicable replacement for softmax.
Method: Softpick is introduced as a rectified, non-sum-to-one attention normalization function, defined by applying ReLU to (exp(x) - 1) in the numerator and normalizing by the sum of absolute values of (exp(x) - 1) in the denominator.
The function's asymmetric design (ReLU in numerator, absolute value in denominator) allows for zero-valued attention scores and enables gradient flow for negative inputs, preventing 'dying heads'.
Softpick is designed as a drop-in replacement for softmax, maintaining compatibility with optimized kernels like FlashAttention-2, and requiring no extra parameters or specialized optimizers.
Results: Softpick successfully eliminated attention sink, achieving a 0% sink rate across all tested models and thresholds, compared to significant rates (e.g., 68.28%) for softmax models.
Massive activations were entirely mitigated, with kurtosis in hidden states drastically reduced (e.g., from 33510 to 340 in 340M models) and activation magnitudes reduced by an order of magnitude.
Attention maps generated by Softpick exhibited high functional sparsity (99.34% for 340M, 95.63% for 1.8B models), allowing for direct opportunities for sparsity-based optimizations.

Quantized Softpick models consistently outperformed softmax across various bit precisions and quantization techniques (HQQ, GPTQ, BNB), with particularly large gains at 2-bit and 3-bit, indicating enhanced robustness to quantization errors.
Takeaways: The rectification (ReLU in numerator) allows for genuine sparsity in attention maps, producing many exact zero scores, while the absolute value in the denominator ensures stable gradient flow even for inputs that would otherwise result in zero attention.
Eliminating massive activations directly addresses a core challenge for efficient model quantization, enabling models to retain more accuracy at very low bit precisions (e.g., 2-bit).
The inherent sparsity in Softpick's attention mechanisms offers potential for significant computational savings through sparse matrix operations and improved model interpretability.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.20648.Title: SpaRE: Enhancing Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models with Synthetic Data
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.20648.Summary: Researchers from the University of Waterloo develop a synthetic data generation pipeline that leverages hyper-detailed image descriptions to enhance spatial reasoning in Vision-Language Models (VLMs), achieving up to 49% performance gains on spatial reasoning benchmarks while maintaining general capabilities across standard VLM tasks.
Problem: VLMs struggle with spatial reasoning despite strong performance in general vision-language tasks
Existing datasets lack sufficient examples of diverse spatial relationships, particularly less common ones
Current synthetic datasets use simplified geometric shapes that don't generalize well to real-world scenarios
Method: Generated synthetic QA pairs from hyper-detailed image descriptions using LLM-based extraction
Implemented comprehensive quality assurance measures including consistency checks and human evaluation
Fine-tuned VLMs on the resulting high-quality spatial reasoning dataset
Results: Up to 49% performance improvement on the What's Up spatial reasoning benchmark
Maintained performance on general benchmarks like MMMU, MMBench, and TextVQA
Successfully demonstrated generalization to real-world spatial reasoning scenarios
Showed improved accuracy on VSR, 3DSRBench, and RealWorldQA benchmarks
Takeaways: Hyper-detailed image descriptions provide rich spatial information that can be leveraged for synthetic data generation
Quality assurance measures are crucial for ensuring reliable synthetic data
Spatial reasoning can be improved without compromising general VLM capabilities

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.20595.Title: ReasonIR: Training Retrievers for Reasoning Tasks
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.20595.Summary: Researchers from Meta FAIR and multiple universities introduce ReasonIR, a retrieval system trained on synthetically generated reasoning-intensive queries that achieves state-of-the-art performance on the BRIGHT benchmark while demonstrating superior scaling with query length and improved RAG performance on MMLU and GPQA tasks.
Problem: Existing retrievers struggle with reasoning-intensive tasks due to training primarily on short, factual queries
Limited availability of high-quality training data for complex reasoning queries
Method: REASONIR-SYNTHESIZER pipeline generates synthetic training data including varied-length queries and hard negatives
Fine-tuned LLAMA3.1-8B model with modified bi-directional attention for improved reasoning capabilities
Integration of query rewriting and LLM reranking for enhanced retrieval performance
Results: State-of-the-art performance on BRIGHT benchmark for reasoning-intensive retrieval
Consistent performance improvements with longer rewritten queries while other retrievers plateau
Superior recall when combined with LLM reranking compared to existing retrievers
Improved RAG performance on MMLU and GPQA benchmarks
Takeaways: Synthetic data generation covering longer queries (300-2000 words) crucial for extending effective context length
Multi-turn approach for hard negative generation improves discrimination between relevant and irrelevant documents
Combination of varied-length and hard query data provides synergistic benefits

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.20571.Title: Reinforcement Learning for Reasoning in Large Language Models with One Training Example
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.20571.Summary: Researchers at the University of Washington and Microsoft introduced 1-shot Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Reward (1-shot RLVR), demonstrating that training Large Language Models (LLMs) with a single example can achieve mathematical reasoning performance comparable to training with thousands of examples. This approach boosted mathematical reasoning accuracy on benchmarks like MATH500 by over 8% and improved average performance across six mathematical benchmarks from 17.6% to 35.7% on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B.
Problem: Large Language Model (LLM) fine-tuning via Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Reward (RLVR) conventionally assumes the necessity of extensive datasets, leading to high computational and data curation costs.
The data-centric aspects of RLVR, specifically the minimum data quantity required for effective reasoning enhancement, remained largely unexplored despite advancements in RL algorithms.
A clear understanding of whether RLVR primarily teaches new skills or unlocks existing latent capabilities within LLMs, particularly when trained with sparse data, was lacking.
Method: The core solution involves 1-shot Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Reward (1-shot RLVR), which fine-tunes LLMs using just one or a few carefully selected examples, rather than large datasets.
The methodology employs GRPO (Group-normalized Proximal Policy Optimization) as the default RL algorithm, utilizing a binary (0-1) outcome reward for mathematical problems.

A Historical Variance Score (HVS) was proposed to select high-impact single or few-shot examples for training, and the approach was validated through extensive experiments on multiple LLMs and evaluation benchmarks.
Results: 1-shot RLVR with a single example on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B boosted MATH500 accuracy from a base of 36.0% to 73.6% and improved average performance across six mathematical benchmarks from 17.6% to 35.7%.

This performance was comparable to, or even slightly exceeded, results obtained using much larger datasets (e.g., a 1.2k DeepScaleR subset or the 7.5k MATH train set), demonstrating remarkable data efficiency.

The improvements generalized across different mathematical categories and were robust across various base LLMs (including Qwen2.5-Math-7B, Llama3.2-3B-Instruct) and different RL algorithms (GRPO and PPO).
Takeaways: LLMs possess significant latent reasoning capabilities that 1-shot RLVR can effectively activate with extremely sparse data, suggesting RLVR primarily acts as a catalyst for existing skills rather than teaching entirely new ones.

The phenomenon of "post-saturation generalization" was identified, where test performance continues to improve long after training accuracy saturates and even when the model overfits, distinguishing it from traditional "grokking."
Policy gradient loss is the primary driver of reasoning improvements, while entropy loss plays a critical role in promoting diverse exploration and enhancing sustained generalization across tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.20364.Title: Exploring internal representation of self-supervised networks: few-shot learning abilities and comparison with human semantics and recognition of objects
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.20364.Summary: Deep neural networks trained with self-supervised learning develop internal representations that closely align with human semantic organization and recognition patterns. These human-like representational structures emerge in earlier layers of self-supervised networks compared to those trained with supervised learning.
Problem: Understanding how deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) internally represent information, especially when trained with self-supervised learning (SSL).
Investigating how the categorical organization within SSL DCNNs relates to human perception and semantic cognition.
Exploring the emergence of meaningful visual representations in neural networks without explicit category labels.
Method: Pre-trained DCNNs (modified ResNet-18) using self-supervised contrastive learning (SimCLR, SimSiam) and supervised object classification on CIFAR-100.
Evaluated the pre-trained networks on their few-shot learning capabilities for novel categories by freezing network weights and classifying based on prototype similarity.
Compared the networks' internal representations, including category cluster structures and error patterns, to human semantic organization and recognition data from CIFAR-10H.
Results: Self-supervised DCNNs accurately perform few-shot classification of novel object categories.
Internal representations of self-supervised networks show high alignment with human semantic organization, with this alignment appearing in earlier network layers than in supervised networks.
Self-supervised networks' recognition error patterns strongly correlate with human recognition errors, achieving high similarity in earlier layers compared to supervised networks.
Takeaways: Self-supervised networks achieve optimal few-shot learning performance and human-like semantic organization in earlier convolutional layers (conv2-conv3).
Supervised networks require deeper layers (fc1-fc3) to attain comparable levels of few-shot performance and alignment with human semantics and recognition patterns.
Self-supervised learning may lead to more efficient and distributed representations that align with human-like perceptual and cognitive structures earlier in the processing hierarchy.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.20199.Title: Weaving Context Across Images: Improving Vision-Language Models through Focus-Centric Visual Chains
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.20199.Summary: This paper introduces the Focus-Centric Visual Chain (FCVC) paradigm and the Focus-Centric Data Synthesis (FCDS) framework to improve Vision-Language Models' (VLMs) ability to reason across multiple images. Fine-tuning VLMs with the resulting VISC-150K dataset led to an average accuracy increase of 3.16% on multi-image benchmarks for LLaVA-OneVision, establishing new state-of-the-art results on four benchmarks while preserving general VLM capabilities.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) demonstrate significant performance degradation when processing and reasoning across multiple images, despite their capabilities with single images.
VLMs struggle with cross-image correlations and visual discontinuity, making it difficult to grasp intricate relationships and integrate information scattered across multiple visual inputs.
There is a scarcity of high-quality, scalable, and cost-effective multi-image reasoning data, hindering the development of robust multi-image VLMs.
Method: Proposing the Focus-Centric Visual Chain (FCVC), a multi-step reasoning paradigm that breaks down complex multi-image queries into a sequence of sub-questions with dynamic visual foci.
Developing Focus-Centric Data Synthesis (FCDS), a bottom-up framework that uses open-source models (Extractor, Connector, Annotator, Questioner) to generate structured multi-image reasoning data.
Constructing VISC-150K, a large-scale dataset of 150,000 high-quality multi-image reasoning samples following the FCVC format, to train and evaluate VLMs.
Results: Fine-tuning with VISC-150K led to an average accuracy increase of 3.16% for LLaVA-OneVision and 2.24% for Qwen2-VL across seven diverse multi-image benchmarks.
The method established new state-of-the-art results on four benchmarks: MMIU, MIRB, BLINK, and NLVR2, and showed measurable gains on the video benchmark MVBench.

A quality assessment on synthesized data yielded a 97.5% overall accuracy, validating the reliability of the FCDS framework, and general VLM abilities were maintained or slightly improved on single-image benchmarks.
Takeaways: The Focus-Centric Visual Chain (FCVC) paradigm enables VLMs to perform multi-step 'slow thinking' by dynamically focusing on relevant visual subsets and decomposing complex tasks into sequential sub-questions.

The Focus-Centric Data Synthesis (FCDS) framework can generate high-quality, reliable, and cost-effective multi-image reasoning data using open-source models, overcoming data scarcity and cost issues.
Fine-tuning VLMs with a large-scale, structured dataset like VISC-150K significantly enhances multi-image reasoning capabilities without compromising general vision-language understanding.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.20073.Title: RAGEN: Understanding Self-Evolution in LLM Agents via Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.20073.Summary: Researchers from Northwestern University, Stanford, NYU, and Microsoft developed StarPO, a reinforcement learning framework, and RAGEN, a modular system, to train self-evolving large language model agents in multi-turn environments. The work identifies a new instability called the "Echo Trap" and proposes StarPO-S, which uses uncertainty-based filtering and gradient shaping to achieve more robust training and higher success rates across various interactive tasks.
Problem: Current LLM training and single-turn RL methods are insufficient for multi-turn, interactive, and stochastic environments requiring sequential decision-making and continuous self-improvement.
LLM agents face significant training instability, including managing complex reward signals and achieving generalization across diverse environments.
Understanding how to enable LLM agents to learn effectively and stably in self-evolutionary settings, especially concerning internal reasoning processes, is an open challenge.
Method: Introduce StarPO (State-Thinking-Actions-Reward Policy Optimization), a trajectory-level reinforcement learning framework that optimizes entire multi-turn interaction histories, including an agent's internal reasoning.
Develop RAGEN, a modular system built on StarPO, serving as a comprehensive platform for training and evaluating LLM agents in controlled, multi-turn, stochastic environments.

Implement StarPO-S, a stabilized variant, utilizing uncertainty-based trajectory filtering and asymmetric gradient clipping to address training instabilities observed in multi-turn LLM agent learning.
Results: Vanilla reinforcement learning methods like PPO and GRPO consistently lead to performance collapse in multi-turn LLM agent environments, often due to the "Echo Trap" phenomenon.

The proposed StarPO-S variant significantly enhances training stability and achieves higher final success rates across diverse environments by employing uncertainty-based filtering and gradient shaping techniques.
Factors such as increased task diversity, moderate interaction granularity, and frequent rollout updates demonstrably improve generalization capabilities of LLM agents.

While reasoning can enhance performance in simple single-turn tasks, its utility in complex multi-turn tasks is limited and prone to degradation, highlighting the necessity of fine-grained, reasoning-aware reward signals to maintain coherent thought processes.
Takeaways: Multi-turn LLM agent training with standard RL methods introduces a new instability, termed the "Echo Trap," characterized by agents overfitting to repetitive reasoning patterns and collapsing behavioral diversity.
Training stability can be significantly improved by filtering training data based on reward uncertainty and using asymmetric gradient shaping (StarPO-S).

Explicit reasoning in LLM agents does not consistently improve generalization in complex multi-turn tasks and can even degrade or become "hallucinated" if reward signals are not fine-grained and reasoning-aware.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.19627.Title: VCM: Vision Concept Modeling Based on Implicit Contrastive Learning with Vision-Language Instruction Fine-Tuning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.19627.Summary: The VCM framework introduces a self-supervised approach to vision concept modeling, enabling Large Vision-Language Models to adaptively compress visual tokens based on task instructions. It achieves up to 85% FLOPs reduction and improves average accuracy on VQA benchmarks by 1.3% while enhancing dense perception capabilities across various vision-language tasks.
Problem: Existing Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) process entire images at a low-level token granularity, leading to substantial computational costs and inefficiency, particularly for high-resolution inputs and video sequences.

Prior vision token reduction methods often lack semantic grounding, fail to preserve crucial spatial relationships, or cannot precisely control the number of retained tokens, limiting their applicability.

Current LVLM approaches do not effectively mimic human cognition's selective focus on high-level vision concepts, restricting their scalability and versatility in real-world scenarios requiring fine-grained understanding.
Method: VCM proposes a self-supervised framework that leverages correlations between vision tokens and text priors (keyword counts in instructions/responses) to dynamically estimate the optimal vision concept length for a given task.
A semantic alignment module, pre-trained with a semantic alignment loss, adaptively extracts task-relevant keywords from instructions and responses, guiding the vision concept extraction process.

A novel dynamic programming-based forward-backward algorithm efficiently selects vision tokens with adaptive length and spatial alignment, further optimized by a parallelized segment merging operation that significantly speeds up feature processing.
Results: VCM achieved a computational cost reduction of up to 85% in FLOPs for LLaVA-1.5-7B and improved average accuracy by 1.3% over the vanilla model on 11 VQA benchmarks (e.g., +4.9% on VizWiz, +5.7% on SEED, +2.5% on MMStar) with 75% fewer vision tokens.

The framework enhanced dense perception capabilities, demonstrating improved performance in region-level VQA (RefCOCO), zero-shot image classification (CLIP ViT on COCO), open-vocabulary object detection (F-VLM on OV-COCO), and semantic segmentation (CatSeg on ADE-150/847).

A crucial parallelized segment merging operation, integral to concept extraction, delivered a 100x speedup, effectively eliminating a significant computational bottleneck for variable-length feature processing.
Takeaways: The required number of vision tokens for a task correlates with image-related keyword counts in the associated text, providing a viable pseudo-label for self-supervised learning of vision concept length.

Dynamically extracting and compressing only task-relevant vision concepts based on instruction fine-tuning significantly reduces computational costs while simultaneously enhancing the dense perception capabilities of LVLMs.

Implicit contrastive sampling through random keyword masking in instructions proves effective for robust vision concept modeling, enhancing learning and offering control over vision token length during inference.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.19599.Title: GVPO: Group Variance Policy Optimization for Large Language Model Post-Training
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.19599.Summary: Group Variance Policy Optimization (GVPO) introduces a method for Large Language Model post-training that guarantees convergence to a unique optimal solution for KL-constrained reward maximization. It empirically demonstrates superior performance on math reasoning benchmarks, achieving 20.72 on AIME2024 compared to GRPO's 14.79, and shows increased stability and efficiency for off-policy training.
Problem: Existing group-based policy optimization methods, like GRPO, often suffer from training instability and sensitivity to hyperparameters.
Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) may not converge to the true optimal policy for KL-constrained reward maximization due to limitations in its underlying model.
Directly applying closed-form optimal policies is hindered by the computationally intractable partition function Z(x).
Off-policy training in LLM post-training struggles with sample efficiency or stability issues (e.g., gradient explosion) when using importance sampling.
Method: GVPO formulates its policy optimization by designing gradient weights that sum to zero within a prompt group, thus circumventing the need to compute the intractable partition function Z(x).
The method's loss gradient is derived as the mean squared error between the central distances of implicit rewards (from the current policy) and actual rewards.
Its objective implicitly incorporates regularization through covariance and variance terms, promoting stable updates and balancing exploration without sensitive hyperparameter tuning.
Results: GVPO consistently achieved superior performance on math reasoning benchmarks, notably scoring 20.72 on AIME2024 against GRPO's 14.79 and 62.65 on AMC against GRPO's 55.42.

It demonstrated high robustness to hyperparameter variations (e.g., beta), different sampling distributions, and across multiple random seeds and foundation models (Qwen2.5-Math-7B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct).
