Ablation studies confirmed that the inherent variance and covariance regularization terms are essential for training stability, leading to model failure if removed, and outperform standard entropy regularization.
Takeaways: LLM post-training algorithms share a unified mathematical structure, allowing for direct design of preference-encoding weights based on loss gradients.
The intractable partition function in KL-constrained reward maximization can be circumvented if the sum of assigned response weights for a prompt group is zero.
The GVPO loss inherently provides regularization through covariance and variance terms, promoting stable policy updates and balanced exploration without requiring sensitive hyperparameter tuning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.19475.Title: Prisma: An Open Source Toolkit for Mechanistic Interpretability in Vision and Video
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.19475.Summary: Prisma is an open-source toolkit that adapts mechanistic interpretability methods from language models to vision and video transformers, providing a unified interface and pre-trained sparse autoencoders. The toolkit enables researchers to analyze the internal workings of vision models and has been used to observe that vision sparse autoencoders exhibit lower sparsity than their language counterparts and that sparse autoencoder reconstructions can sometimes improve model loss.
Problem: Progress in mechanistic interpretability (MI) for vision and video models lagged significantly behind that for language models due to a lack of accessible frameworks and pre-trained interpretability artifacts.

Existing MI tools for language models were not directly transferable to vision/video domains due to architectural and data-specific differences (e.g., continuous visual input, patch tokenization, self-supervised objectives).
Researchers lacked unified toolkits to easily access activations, train sparse coders, and perform circuit analysis on a wide range of vision and video transformer architectures.
Method: Prisma provides a unified, open-source Python toolkit featuring a `HookedViT` class for easy access to activations and weights across over 75 vision and video transformer models.

The toolkit offers comprehensive support for training and evaluating sparse coder architectures, including Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), transcoders, and crosscoders, with configurable training parameters.

The project releases over 80 pre-trained SAEs for CLIP-B and DINO-B ViTs, along with tutorial notebooks and toy vision transformers, to lower the computational burden and entry barriers for vision mechanistic interpretability research.
Results: Vision Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) exhibit substantially higher activation density (lower sparsity) than language SAEs, with L0 values often exceeding 500 active features per patch in models like CLIP-B/32.

Reconstructions from SAEs can sometimes decrease the original model's cross-entropy loss when reinjected into the forward pass, particularly in deeper layers of certain CLIP and DINO models, suggesting a potential denoising effect.
Sparsity patterns and feature utilization in vision SAEs vary significantly between spatial patches and the CLS token, with the CLS token showing higher L0, especially in deeper layers.
Takeaways: Successful mechanistic interpretability paradigms from language models, such as 'hooked' architectures and sparse autoencoders, can be adapted to vision and video transformers despite modality differences.

Providing comprehensive open-source tooling, pre-trained interpretability artifacts, and educational resources is crucial for accelerating and democratizing research in emerging AI interpretability subfields.

Preliminary analyses using newly developed tools can reveal fundamental and surprising properties about how vision models represent information, such as distinct sparsity patterns compared to language models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.19254.Title: Uncertainty Quantification for Language Models: A Suite of Black-Box, White-Box, LLM Judge, and Ensemble Scorers
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.19254.Summary: Researchers from CVS Health developed a framework and an open-source toolkit (`uqlm`) to quantify uncertainty in Large Language Models (LLMs) for real-time, closed-book hallucination detection. The framework standardizes various black-box, white-box, and LLM-as-a-Judge techniques into comparable confidence scores, featuring a tunable ensemble method that consistently outperforms individual scorers.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently generate factual errors (hallucinations), posing significant reliability and safety risks in high-stakes applications like healthcare.
Current hallucination detection methods, such as ground truth comparison or source content verification, are often not viable for real-time, closed-book inference scenarios.
A unified and adaptable framework is needed to easily implement, compare, and optimize diverse uncertainty quantification (UQ) techniques for specific LLM deployment contexts.
Method: A comprehensive framework integrates and standardizes various UQ methods, including black-box, white-box, and LLM-as-a-Judge approaches, to produce 0-1 confidence scores for real-time, closed-book hallucination detection.

A tunable ensemble scorer is introduced, allowing any combination of individual UQ methods to be weighted and optimized using a small set of user-provided graded responses, adapting to specific use cases.
An accompanying open-source Python toolkit, `uqlm`, provides ready-to-use implementations of all presented UQ scorers and the ensemble method, facilitating practical adoption.
Results: The tunable ensemble scorer achieved superior performance over individual scorers in 20 out of 24 AUROC scenarios and 17 out of 24 F1-score scenarios, with top AUROC values reaching 0.986.
NLI-based black-box methods (NCP, NSN) showed the strongest performance among black-box scorers, leading in AUROC for 13 out of 24 scenarios and F1-score for 18 out of 24 black-box scenarios.

Applying confidence thresholds to filter low-confidence responses monotonically increased the accuracy of the remaining LLM outputs, demonstrating practical utility (e.g., Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite accuracy on PopQA improved from 0.35 to 0.61 at τ=0.6).
Takeaways: The tunable ensemble scorer consistently delivers superior hallucination detection performance compared to individual UQ methods, highlighting the benefit of combining multiple uncertainty signals.
Individual UQ scorer performance varies significantly across different LLMs and datasets, indicating that optimal detection strategies require use-case-specific customization.

Natural Language Inference (NLI)-based black-box methods (e.g., Non-Contradiction Probability) and LLM-as-a-Judge scorers (when the judge LLM is proficient in the task) are frequently among the top-performing individual techniques.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.18397.Title: Unsupervised Visual Chain-of-Thought Reasoning via Preference Optimization
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.18397.Summary: A framework for Unsupervised Visual Chain-of-Thought (UV-CoT) reasoning enables Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to perform image-level reasoning by automatically generating preference data and using a novel Score-DPO, surpassing supervised methods and demonstrating robust generalization across diverse visual tasks.
Problem: Existing text-level Chain-of-Thought (CoT) in MLLMs suffers from information loss and struggles with fine-grained visual comprehension due to fixed-granularity image processing.
Prior image-level Visual CoT methods rely heavily on supervised fine-tuning with expensive, human-labeled bounding box data, limiting scalability and generalization.
Traditional preference optimization methods often rank responses without quantifying the intensity of preference, which is insufficient for nuanced visual reasoning.
Method: An automatic, two-step pipeline uses MLLMs to generate diverse bounding box proposals and evaluate their quality by considering both immediate and future reasoning chain utility.
A novel Score-DPO (sDPO) algorithm optimizes the target MLLM by incorporating the degree of preference between visual reasoning steps, explicitly differentiating key visual regions.
An iterative learning approach dynamically refines the target MLLM by generating fresh preference data with its evolving policy, enhancing training robustness and scalability.
Results: UV-CoT, using 10% of supervised labels for initialization, outperforms fully supervised Visual-CoT-7B by an average of 2.1% across various VQA datasets, demonstrating superior data efficiency.

The framework exhibits robust zero-shot generalization, surpassing all baselines by an average of 2.5% on unseen datasets and achieving over 50% gains on high-resolution OCR tasks compared to non-CoT baselines.
Ablation studies confirm the necessity of image-level CoT, Score-DPO (naïve DPO yields 1.9% average drop), and iterative learning (omission causes 3.5% average drop) for overall performance.
Takeaways: Explicit image-level visual CoT is crucial for complex multimodal reasoning, consistently outperforming text-only CoT approaches by dynamically integrating visual cues.
Unsupervised generation of visual preference data, combined with a refined preference optimization technique (sDPO), can match or exceed the performance of supervised visual CoT methods.
Evaluating visual regions based on their cumulative impact on the entire reasoning chain, not just immediate relevance, is vital for training MLLMs to construct effective visual CoT.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.18158.Title: E-InMeMo: Enhanced Prompting for Visual In-Context Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.18158.Summary: E-InMeMo enhances visual in-context learning by introducing learnable, pixel-level perturbations to in-context pairs, refining guidance for frozen large-scale vision models. This approach achieved state-of-the-art results on foreground segmentation and single object detection, showing up to 17.04 mIoU improvement over baselines, and extended effectiveness to medical imaging datasets.
Problem: Existing Visual In-Context Learning (VICL) heavily relies on the quality and semantic relevance of retrieved in-context examples, leading to suboptimal performance when examples are not ideal.
A mismatch often occurs between the content of static in-context prompts and the latent knowledge embedded within large-scale vision models.
Traditional VICL methods lack a mechanism to actively refine or transform visual prompts to provide more effective guidance to frozen foundation models.
Method: Introduces E-InMeMo, a framework that incorporates a "Prompt Enhancer" to apply learnable, pixel-level perturbations to in-context images and their labels.
Employs a Feature-Map-Level Retrieval (FMLR) strategy using DINOv2 features to select high-quality in-context pairs.
Trains only the lightweight Prompt Enhancer module (27,540 parameters) using cross-entropy loss, keeping the large-scale vision backbone frozen.
Results: Achieved state-of-the-art performance on foreground segmentation (7.99 mIoU improvement on Pascal-5i) and single object detection (17.04 mIoU improvement on PASCAL VOC 2012) compared to baselines.
Demonstrated strong robustness to domain shifts and generalizability, achieving state-of-the-art results on medical imaging datasets (Kvasir-SEG and ISIC for segmentation).
Ablation studies confirmed optimal prompt placement on both in-context image and label, and demonstrated E-InMeMo's data efficiency, outperforming baselines with significantly less retrieval data.
Takeaways: Learnable, pixel-level perturbations applied directly to in-context image-label pairs can effectively refine prompts and inject task-specific information into the frozen model.
By optimizing these small, input-agnostic perturbations, the latent space distributions of enhanced prompts can be aligned with ground truth, leading to improved predictions.

Significant performance improvements in Visual In-Context Learning can be achieved through highly parameter-efficient training, without altering the millions of parameters of a large pre-trained vision model.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.18053.Title: DREAM: Disentangling Risks to Enhance Safety Alignment in Multimodal Large Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.18053.Summary: DREAM, developed by Alibaba Group, Zhejiang University, and partners, introduces a two-stage training framework to enhance Multimodal Large Language Models' (MLLMs) safety alignment by enabling them to disentangle complex multimodal risks. This approach significantly reduces both attack success rates on unsafe inputs and over-refusal rates on benign content, achieving up to a 16.17% improvement in "safe & effective" scores compared to GPT-4V.
Problem: MLLMs face complex safety challenges due to the intricate interplay between visual and textual data, creating new attack surfaces and subtle risk combinations.
Existing safety alignment methods often result in either 'unsafety' (failing to block harmful content) or 'oversafety' (erroneously refusing benign queries, also known as 'alignment tax').
Prior approaches generally lack explicit, step-by-step reasoning about multimodal risk combinations, assuming MLLMs inherently possess the ability to identify them.
Method: DREAM utilizes Multimodal Risk Disentanglement (MRD) to systematically analyze multimodal inputs by breaking them into constituent parts and identifying specific risk categories, forming the foundation for training.

The first stage, Risk-aware Fine-tuning, employs a powerful 'teacher' model to generate detailed, disentangled risk observations and corresponding safe, helpful responses for supervised fine-tuning of a student model.

The second stage, Risk-aware Preference Optimization, refines the student model's safety alignment through iterative Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback (RLAIF) using teacher-generated observation-wise and global scores to guide Direct Preference Optimization (DPO).
Results: The preliminary Multimodal Risk Disentanglement (MRD) strategy, even as an inference-time method, outperformed existing baselines by achieving a substantially lower average Attack Success Rate (ASR) / Refusal Rate (RR) score (e.g., 9.37% for InternVL2-26B vs. 33.34% vanilla).

DREAM demonstrated superior robustness to oversafety, maintaining very low refusal rates on benign benchmarks (e.g., 0% for InternVL2-8B), in contrast to 100% oversafety rates exhibited by some previous training-time methods like VLGuard.

DREAM achieved a significant 16.17% improvement in the 'safe & effective' score on the SIUO benchmark compared to GPT-4V (InternVL2-26B at 39.52% vs. GPT-4V at 23.35%), while effectively maintaining the model's general helpfulness and utility.
Takeaways: Explicit, step-by-step disentanglement of multimodal risks significantly improves MLLMs' risk awareness, leading to better detection of unsafety and mitigation of oversafety.

Internalizing this risk disentanglement capability through a two-stage training process (fine-tuning and iterative preference optimization) allows MLLMs to inherently understand and respond to complex safety challenges without explicit prompting.

Combining fine-grained, observation-wise feedback with global safety and helpfulness scores during preference optimization effectively balances safety alignment with the model's general utility and helpfulness.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.17432.Title: Breaking the Modality Barrier: Universal Embedding Learning with Multimodal LLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.17432.Summary: The UniME framework introduces a two-stage approach that enables Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to learn universal, discriminative representations for diverse vision-language tasks. This method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the MMEB benchmark, showing significant improvements over previous models in short and long caption retrieval, and compositional cross-modal retrieval by overcoming limitations of traditional frameworks like CLIP.
Problem: Existing multimodal models like CLIP suffer from text token truncation, isolated image-text processing, and poor compositional understanding.
Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are primarily designed for generative tasks, limiting their capacity to learn transferable, discriminative representations.
Current MLLM-based embedding methods struggle with data diversity, causal attention constraints, and false negative contamination in contrastive learning.
Method: A two-stage framework, UniME, is introduced to enable Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to learn universal, discriminative embeddings.

Stage 1 employs textual discriminative knowledge distillation, transferring strong textual embedding capabilities from a powerful LLM teacher (NV-Embed V2) to the MLLM's language component using KL divergence.

Stage 2 refines the embeddings through hard negative enhanced instruction tuning, which mitigates false negative contamination and strategically samples truly challenging negative pairs for robust contrastive learning.
Results: UniME achieves state-of-the-art results on the Massive Multimodal Embedding Benchmark (MMEB), with the LLaVA-OneVision backbone reaching an impressive 70.7% overall average score.
The framework demonstrates superior performance in long caption cross-modal retrieval, surpassing EVA-CLIP(8B) by 14.8%-18.1% on the Urban1K dataset due to its ability to handle extended text inputs.

UniME consistently outperforms baselines on the SugarCrepe compositional benchmark, showing improvements of 3.9%, 4.2%, and 9.1% over VLM2Vec in relation replacement, object swapping, and attribute addition tasks, respectively.
Takeaways: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), despite their autoregressive nature, can be effectively transformed into powerful discriminative embedding models.
Textual discriminative knowledge distillation is a successful method for injecting robust embedding capabilities into the LLM component of an MLLM, overcoming causal attention limitations.
Strategic mitigation of false negatives and selection of hard negative samples are crucial for refining cross-modal alignment and enhancing discriminative power in multimodal contrastive learning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.17379.Title: A Spatially-Aware Multiple Instance Learning Framework for Digital Pathology
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.17379.Summary: Researchers from Eindhoven University of Technology introduce Global ABMIL (GABMIL), an extension of Attention-Based Deep Multiple Instance Learning, which enhances whole slide image classification by integrating spatial information into patch features using computationally efficient MLP-based modules. The framework demonstrates improved accuracy for tumor subtyping while maintaining ABMIL's efficiency, often matching or surpassing the performance of more complex Transformer-based models.
Problem: Traditional Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) methods for Whole Slide Image (WSI) analysis often overlook the spatial relationships between tissue patches, missing crucial diagnostic context pathologists rely on.

Existing spatially-aware MIL approaches, such as Transformer-based models, incur high computational costs due to their self-attention mechanisms, limiting their practical applicability to gigapixel WSIs.
It was unclear if an MLP-based MIL framework could effectively integrate spatial context to improve performance without a complete architectural redesign or prohibitive computational overhead.
Method: The proposed Global ABMIL (GABMIL) framework enhances the standard ABMIL by incorporating a Spatial Information Mixing Module (SIMM) to enrich patch feature embeddings with spatial context.
SIMM explicitly reconfigures 1D patch features into their original 2D spatial grid and applies MLP-based BLOCK and GRID attention modules to capture both local and global spatial dependencies.
Spatially contextualized patch features are then fed into the conventional ABMIL attention mechanism for weighted aggregation and subsequent slide-level classification.
Results: GABMIL consistently improved classification performance across TCGA Breast Invasive Carcinoma and Lung Cancer datasets, achieving up to a 2 percentage point increase in AUC and a 7 percentage point increase in AUPRC on BRCA over baseline ABMIL.

The framework maintained computational efficiency, demonstrating similar FLOPs (approximately 94M) to ABMIL, which is substantially lower than TransMIL (614M FLOPs), while achieving comparable or superior accuracy.
Qualitative analysis confirmed that the SIMM effectively refines slide-level feature maps by integrating spatial information, leading to more discriminative representations.
Takeaways: Explicitly modeling spatial interactions among patches is vital for enhancing the accuracy of weakly supervised WSI classification in digital pathology.

Computationally efficient MLP-based mechanisms, inspired by architectures like MaxViT and MLP-Mixer, can effectively capture these spatial dependencies without relying on the higher computational burden of Transformer's self-attention.

The BLOCK attention module, which captures local spatial relationships within defined windows, proved particularly effective and robust in refining patch representations across different datasets and feature types.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.17207.Title: Perspective-Aware Reasoning in Vision-Language Models via Mental Imagery Simulation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.17207.Summary: KAIST and Stanford researchers develop an Abstract Perspective Change framework that enables vision-language models to reason about spatial relationships from different viewpoints by simulating mental imagery through scene abstraction and perspective transformation, demonstrating improved performance on both synthetic and real-image benchmarks while maintaining accuracy across varying angular offsets.
Problem: Current vision-language models are limited to egocentric reasoning (from camera viewpoint only)
VLMs struggle with allocentric spatial reasoning needed for real-world navigation and interaction
Method: Abstract Perspective Change (APC) framework that converts allocentric problems to egocentric ones
Three-stage pipeline: scene abstraction, perspective change, and perspective prompting using visual/numerical formats
Results: Significant performance improvements over baseline VLMs on COMFORT++ and 3DSR-Bench datasets
Consistent accuracy maintained across different angular offsets between camera and reference viewpoints
Framework generalizes well across various spatial reasoning tasks without task-specific fine-tuning
Outperforms previous spatial reasoning models and novel-view-synthesis approaches
Takeaways: Emulating human mental imagery through abstract scene representations improves spatial reasoning
Converting allocentric questions to egocentric format leverages existing VLM strengths
Visual prompts often outperform numerical ones for perspective-aware reasoning tasks

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.17192.Title: Paper2Code: Automating Code Generation from Scientific Papers in Machine Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.17192.Summary: Researchers at KAIST developed PaperCoder, a multi-agent Large Language Model (LLM) framework that generates functional, repository-level code directly from machine learning scientific papers. This approach significantly outperforms existing LLM-based code generation methods, achieving an average score of 3.74 out of 5 on the Paper2CodeBench and requiring only 0.81% of code line modifications for successful execution.
Problem: A pervasive reproducibility crisis in machine learning, where only 19.5% of top-tier papers provide code, making validation and extension difficult.
The process of manually reverse-engineering methods and experimental setups from textual paper descriptions is time-consuming and labor-intensive for researchers.

Existing LLM-based code generation tools often rely on pre-existing implementations, partial code snippets, or defined APIs, failing to address the "cold start" problem of generating code solely from papers.
Method: PaperCoder employs a multi-agent, multi-stage LLM-powered framework that mimics human software development workflows, decomposing the process into Planning, Analysis, and Coding stages.

The Planning stage generates structured abstractions like overall plans, architectural designs (file lists, class/sequence diagrams), logic designs (ordered file lists, fine-grained specifications), and configuration files.

The Analysis stage then iteratively processes each file to create detailed implementation guidelines, followed by the Coding stage that generates the repository code sequentially using all accumulated context.
Results: PaperCoder consistently outperformed all baselines (ChatDev, MetaGPT, Abstract, Paper) on the Paper2CodeBench, achieving an average score of 3.74 (out of 5) compared to ChatDev's 2.97 and MetaGPT's 2.73.
On the PaperBench Code-Dev benchmark, PaperCoder achieved the highest replication score (45.14% with o3-mini-high), substantially outperforming existing agentic baselines (e.g., BasicAgent at 5.1%).

Generated repositories were near-executable, requiring an average of only 0.81% of code lines to be modified for successful execution, and 92% of human judges found the repositories "helpful" for reproduction.
Takeaways: A structured, multi-stage pipeline effectively reduces the cognitive load on LLMs, enabling them to tackle complex, repository-level code generation tasks from scientific papers with higher accuracy.
Emulating human development practices, such as explicit planning for architecture and logic design, is crucial for producing cohesive and dependency-aware multi-file codebases.
The quality of code generation is highly dependent on the precision and detail within the paper's methodology section, underscoring the importance of comprehensive scientific descriptions.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.17040.Title: DyMU: Dynamic Merging and Virtual Unmerging for Efficient VLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.17040.Summary: DYMU presents a training-free framework for Vision-Language Models (VLMs) that dynamically reduces visual token counts based on image complexity, overcoming the inefficiency of fixed-length token representations. It achieves up to an 85% reduction in visual tokens while maintaining over 96% of baseline performance across various VLM architectures and benchmarks by employing dynamic merging and virtual unmerging techniques.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) generate a fixed, excessively large number of visual tokens from images, regardless of image content, leading to high computational costs during inference.
Existing token reduction methods often apply a fixed compression ratio, failing to adapt to the varying complexity of input images, leading to inefficiencies or performance degradation.
Improving VLM efficiency typically requires costly and resource-intensive retraining or fine-tuning, which is often infeasible due to closed-source training recipes.
Method: DYMU introduces Dynamic Token Merging (DToMe) that adaptively reduces visual token embeddings from the Vision Transformer (ViT) based on image content complexity and learnable layer-wise thresholds.

It employs Virtual Token Unmerging (VTU) to make the dynamically reduced visual token sequence compatible with pre-trained Large Language Models (LLMs) without explicit expansion, by virtually reconstructing attention dynamics.
The entire framework is training-free and can be seamlessly integrated into existing pre-trained VLMs that use ViT-based visual encoders and RoPE-based LLMs.
Results: DYMU-low reduced the average visual token count by 84.5% (from 576 to 89±27 tokens) for LLaVA 1.5, while retaining 97.5% of the original baseline performance across nine benchmarks.

The framework demonstrated compatibility and efficiency with different visual encoders (SigLIP) and state-of-the-art any-resolution VLMs (LLaVA-OneVision), achieving ~96.5% of baseline performance with ~14% of tokens on image benchmarks.
Ablation studies confirmed Virtual Token Unmerging (VTU) is critical for performance preservation; omitting VTU led to significant performance drops across benchmarks.
Takeaways: Image content complexity varies significantly, making a fixed number of visual tokens for all images inefficient and wasteful.
Pre-trained Large Language Models (LLMs) within VLMs are typically fine-tuned to expect a fixed number of visual tokens, making direct reduction of visual tokens problematic for performance.
Computational efficiency in VLMs can be substantially improved without requiring expensive retraining or fine-tuning, by intelligently managing visual tokens.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16929.Title: I-Con: A Unifying Framework for Representation Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16929.Summary: Researchers at MIT, Google, and Microsoft developed I-Con, an information-theoretic framework that unifies over 23 diverse machine learning loss functions, including those for dimensionality reduction, contrastive learning, and supervised learning, under a single KL-divergence objective. This unified perspective enabled the creation of new debiasing strategies and a novel unsupervised clustering method, "Debiased InfoNCE Clustering," which achieved state-of-the-art performance on ImageNet-1K with gains of up to 7.8% in Hungarian accuracy.
Problem: The field of representation learning suffers from a fragmented landscape with a proliferation of diverse loss functions, making it challenging to understand their relationships and select optimal objectives.
Prior attempts to connect different representation learning methods have generally been limited to isolated pairs or small subsets, lacking a comprehensive unifying framework.
Developing new, improved algorithms often relies on empirical trial-and-error rather than a principled method for combining insights across traditionally separate research silos.
Method:
I-Con introduces a unifying information-theoretic loss function based on the minimization of the average Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between a "supervisory" conditional probability distribution (
p
θ
(j∣i)) and a "learned" conditional probability distribution (
q
ϕ
(j∣i)).

It demonstrates that a wide array of existing machine learning loss functions can be recovered as special cases by making specific choices for the supervisory distribution (e.g., ground truth labels, k-NN graphs) and the learned distribution (e.g., softmax over embeddings, Gaussian affinities).

The framework serves as a generative tool to derive new algorithms and debiasing methods by systematically exploring and combining different choices for
p
θ
and
q
ϕ
components.
Results: The I-Con framework successfully unifies over 23 distinct representation learning methods, including dimensionality reduction, contrastive learning, supervised learning, and clustering, under a single information-theoretic objective.

A new method, "Debiased InfoNCE Clustering," derived from I-Con, achieved state-of-the-art unsupervised image classification on ImageNet-1K, outperforming TEMI by +4.5% (ViT-B/14) and +7.8% (ViT-L/14) in Hungarian accuracy.

Novel debiasing strategies, like Uniform Debiasing (alpha-debiasing) and Neighbor Propagation (k-NN walks), were derived and empirically validated, showing improvements in accuracy (e.g., +8% on ImageNet-1K for uniform debiasing) and better-calibrated probability distributions.
Takeaways: I-Con provides a "periodic table" for machine learning losses, revealing a shared information geometry underlying diverse algorithms by showing they minimize the same core objective.

The framework enables the systematic derivation of new loss functions and debiasing strategies by combining components (choices of supervisory and learned distributions) from across different domains.
A unified theoretical understanding of loss functions can directly lead to practical performance improvements and simplified algorithm design by guiding principled modifications.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16828.Title: Process Reward Models That Think
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16828.Summary: This research introduces THINKPRM, a generative process reward model that enables large language models to provide verbalized, long Chain-of-Thought (CoT) verification for their reasoning steps. The model, developed by a collaboration including University of Michigan and LG AI Research, achieves high performance with orders of magnitude less step-level supervision than traditional discriminative models, while significantly improving reliability and generalizability.
Problem: Existing discriminative process reward models (PRMs) require immense volumes of costly step-level human annotations, making them difficult to scale and adapt.

Generative verifiers (like LLM-as-a-Judge) are often unreliable, prone to errors such as overthinking, infinite looping, or generating unparseable outputs, and have limited ability to leverage long Chain-of-Thought for verification.
The inability to efficiently scale verification compute and lack of interpretable reasoning pose challenges for robust LLM reasoning.
Method: The authors fine-tuned open-weight reasoning models (LRMs) into generative PRMs by framing verification as a language generation task that produces comprehensive 'verification CoTs'.

They created a small (1K verification CoTs, 8K step labels) yet high-quality synthetic dataset by prompting a powerful LRM and rigorously filtering outputs to ensure format adherence, agreement with gold step labels, and appropriate CoT length.

The trained THINKPRM models utilize this lightweight fine-tuning to provide interpretable, step-by-step verification, capable of effective test-time scaling through both parallel and sequential (deeper thinking) compute utilization.
Results: THINKPRM-14B, fine-tuned on 8K process labels, outperformed discriminative PRMs (DiscPRM-14B) trained on ~700K labels on the ProcessBench benchmark.
The model substantially improved verification F1-score (e.g., >70 F1 points for R1-Qwen-1.5B) and significantly reduced invalid judgment rates compared to LLM-as-a-Judge baselines.

THINKPRM demonstrated superior reasoning accuracy in Best-of-N selection and verifier-guided search across MATH-500 and AIME '24 benchmarks, and showed strong out-of-domain generalization on GPQA-Diamond and LiveCodeBench.
Takeaways: High-quality generative process reward models can be trained with orders of magnitude less step-level supervision than discriminative PRMs, achieving comparable or superior performance.
Rigorous, process-based filtering of synthetically generated verification Chain-of-Thoughts is crucial for mitigating issues like invalid outputs and overthinking in generative verifiers.

Fine-tuning large reasoning models on even a small, high-quality synthetic dataset dramatically enhances their reliability, reduces undesirable inference behaviors, and improves F1-score for process-level verification.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16801.Title: Decoupled Global-Local Alignment for Improving Compositional Understanding
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16801.Summary: A new framework, Decoupled Global-Local Alignment (DeGLA), enhances compositional understanding in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) by leveraging LLM-driven hard negative samples and a self-distillation mechanism. This approach improves compositional reasoning on benchmarks like SugarCrepe by up to 6.9% over prior state-of-the-art, while preserving general capabilities with only a minor reduction in zero-shot classification accuracy compared to original CLIP and outperforming CE-CLIP by 13.0%.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) like CLIP, relying on global contrastive learning, struggle to interpret compositional concepts (e.g., relations, attributes, element order) in image-text pairs.
Prior methods to improve compositional understanding often cause catastrophic forgetting, leading to a significant degradation of the model's general capabilities.
There is a critical trade-off between achieving fine-grained compositional reasoning and maintaining broad general comprehension in VLMs.
Method: DeGLA introduces an LLM-driven pipeline to generate diverse, high-quality hard negative captions for fine-grained compositional training, categorized by intra-sentence reshuffling and semantic substitution.

A decoupled alignment strategy combines a global hard negative-aware contrastive loss with local Image-Grounded Contrast (IGC) and Text-Grounded Contrast (TGC) losses, enhancing specific compositional understanding.

A self-distillation mechanism, using an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) teacher, regularizes the student model's training to preserve foundational pre-trained knowledge and mitigate catastrophic forgetting.
Results: DeGLA achieved state-of-the-art compositional performance on VALSE, SugarCrepe (e.g., 6.9% improvement on SugarCrepe Swap over CE-CLIP), and ARO benchmarks.
The framework successfully preserved general capabilities, with zero-shot classification accuracy of 58.7% (compared to CLIP's 61.0%), marking a 13.0% improvement over CE-CLIP.
DeGLA outperformed other compositional methods in zero-shot image-text retrieval tasks on MSCOCO and Flickr30k datasets, indicating no compromise on general retrieval accuracy.
Takeaways: Large Language Models are effective for generating high-quality and diverse hard negative samples that are crucial for learning fine-grained compositional distinctions.
Achieving a balance between compositional understanding and general capabilities requires a decoupled approach that combines global and local alignment with a self-distillation mechanism.

The use of a frozen EMA teacher embedding in a text-grounded contrastive loss helps enhance the text encoder's discriminative power against compositional negatives while maintaining overall semantic alignment.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16656.Title: Skywork R1V2: Multimodal Hybrid Reinforcement Learning for Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16656.Summary: Skywork R1V2, developed by Skywork AI, introduces a multimodal hybrid reinforcement learning approach to enhance reasoning capabilities, achieving state-of-the-art results among open-source models on diverse reasoning benchmarks while effectively mitigating visual hallucinations. This 38B-parameter model demonstrates competitive performance against larger proprietary systems by directly acquiring reasoning skills through a novel training paradigm that combines Mixed Preference Optimization and Group Relative Policy Optimization, supported by a Selective Sample Buffer.
Problem: Existing multimodal models often struggle with deep, 'slow-thinking' reasoning tasks, primarily focusing on rapid generation rather than complex problem-solving.
Models optimized for specialized reasoning frequently experience a trade-off, leading to performance degradation on general perception tasks.
Visual hallucinations are a common issue in vision-language models, compromising factual accuracy and reliability.
Method: A modular architecture decouples visual-language alignment from reasoning, using a lightweight MLP adapter to connect a frozen InternViT-6B vision encoder with a QwQ-32B language model, eliminating the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) stage.

A hybrid reinforcement learning paradigm combines Mixed Preference Optimization (MPO) for foundational alignment and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) for fine-tuning reasoning, integrating reward model guidance with rule-based constraints.

The Selective Sample Buffer (SSB) mechanism caches and re-introduces high-quality, informative training examples to address the 'vanishing advantages' problem, enhancing GRPO training efficiency and stability.
Results: Skywork R1V2 achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-source models across diverse benchmarks, including 73.6% on MMMU, 74.0% on MathVista, and 62.6% on OlympiadBench.

The model significantly outperforms its predecessor, Skywork-R1V1, with improvements such as 6.9 percentage points on AIME24 and 18.6 points on LiveBench, demonstrating the effectiveness of the hybrid RL approach.
Hybrid MPO+GRPO leads to the best overall performance, notably on OlympiadBench, while reducing hallucination rates to 9.1%, compared to 18.4% with standard supervised fine-tuning.
Takeaways: A direct reinforcement learning approach using Mixed Preference Optimization (MPO) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) can acquire complex reasoning skills in multimodal models without supervised fine-tuning or teacher model distillation.
The 'adapter-only' training strategy effectively facilitates cross-modal alignment, with capabilities showing high transferability between text and vision modalities.

The Selective Sample Buffer (SSB) mechanism effectively addresses the 'vanishing advantages' dilemma in GRPO, maintaining over 60% effective training samples and improving optimization stability and performance.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16591.Title: JEPA for RL: Investigating Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures for Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16591.Summary: University of Bielefeld researchers develop an adapted Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) framework for reinforcement learning from images, combining vision transformers with predictive modeling to learn low-dimensional state representations while addressing model collapse through gradient propagation and regularization techniques.
Problem: Learning directly from high-dimensional image inputs in reinforcement learning is computationally expensive and sample-inefficient
Traditional JEPA architectures are prone to model collapse when applied to reinforcement learning tasks
Method: Adapt JEPA architecture using separate context and target networks with vision transformers as encoders
Combine JEPA loss with actor-critic gradient propagation and regularization to prevent model collapse
Use learnable classification tokens to generate lower-dimensional representations
Results: Successfully learned effective state representations from pixel observations in Cart Pole task
Combined JEPA-RL approach achieved faster learning and better overall performance
Proposed collapse prevention techniques enabled stable training with informative embeddings
Framework demonstrated potential for learning transferable representations for RL tasks
Takeaways: Training with both JEPA and RL losses produces better performance than using either alone
Backpropagating actor-critic gradients through the encoder helps prevent model collapse
Adding regularization enables learning useful representations even without RL gradients

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16129.Title: MARFT: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Fine-Tuning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16129.Summary: A framework called Multi-Agent Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (MARFT) is introduced to optimize Large Language Model-based Multi-Agent Systems (LaMAS) using reinforcement learning techniques. It leverages a Flexible Markov Game formulation and achieves performance improvements on agentic tasks like mathematical problem-solving and coding, with MARFT-A increasing episodic return by approximately 18.45% on the MATH dataset and 14.75% in coding benchmarks.
Problem: LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems (LaMAS) lack principled methods for optimization and fine-tuning using foundational reinforcement learning (RL) techniques.

Conventional Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) methods are not directly applicable to LaMAS due to their unique characteristics, such as asynchronous interactions, agent heterogeneity, and dynamic organizational structures.
Existing LaMAS optimization approaches are primarily tuning-free or rely on ad-hoc parameter fine-tuning without strong theoretical grounding in RL.
Method: Introduces Multi-Agent Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (MARFT) as a novel paradigm that reframes LaMAS optimization as a sequential decision-making process for effective reinforcement fine-tuning.
Proposes the Flexible Markov Game (Flex-MG) formulation, which includes a dynamic dependency function to model asynchronous and dependency-driven interactions inherent in LaMAS workflows.
Develops two main instantiations, MARFT-A (action-level optimization) and MARFT-T (token-level optimization), utilizing LoRA fine-tuning and a modified PPO objective with agent-by-agent updates.
Results: MARFT-A on a Duo system improved Episodic Return by approximately 8 percentage points (~18.45%) on mathematical problem-solving tasks (MATH) and achieved stable score increases of ~14.75% in coding tasks.
MARFT-A-tuned LaMAS demonstrated improved generalization, effectively enhancing performance in both in-domain and out-of-domain settings for mathematical problems.

Multi-agent systems, particularly the Duo setup, significantly outperformed solo agents on complex tasks (e.g., 7.5 p.p. better on MATH500), while MARFT improved even initially sub-optimal multi-agent configurations.
Takeaways: The Flexible Markov Game (Flex-MG) provides a suitable theoretical foundation for LaMAS by explicitly modeling dynamic inter-agent dependencies and asynchronous execution.
Optimizing agent policies at the action-level (MARFT-A) generally yields more stable and faster performance improvements compared to token-level optimization (MARFT-T) for end-task objectives.
Integrating explicit agent profiles into the joint observation space and using PPO's clipping mechanism helps preserve base LLM language capabilities while enhancing task-specific skills.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16084.Title: TTRL: Test-Time Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16084.Summary: TTRL is a framework enabling Large Language Models to self-improve through Reinforcement Learning on unlabeled test data, using self-generated rewards derived from majority voting. This approach substantially boosts performance on complex reasoning tasks, with one model achieving a 211% improvement on AIME 2024, by fostering a self-reinforcing learning loop.
Problem: Applying Reinforcement Learning to Large Language Models for reasoning tasks is bottlenecked by the high cost and scarcity of human-annotated ground-truth labels for reward estimation.
Existing RL methods for LLMs heavily rely on supervised reward signals, making continuous self-improvement difficult on newly encountered or unlabeled test data.
The inability to obtain explicit reward signals at inference time limits the ability of LLMs to adapt and enhance generalization to new distributions without human intervention.
Method: Introduces Test-Time Reinforcement Learning (TTRL), a framework that enables LLMs to update their parameters and enhance generalization at test time using RL.
Generates reward signals without explicit ground-truth labels by using repeated sampling of model outputs and deriving a 'consensus output' via majority voting.

Calculates binary rule-based rewards for individual sampled outputs based on their match with the majority-voted pseudo-label, which are then used to optimize the model's policy via an RL algorithm like GRPO.
Results: TTRL consistently improved performance across various LLMs and reasoning benchmarks; for instance, Qwen-2.5-Math-7B achieved an approximate 211% improvement in pass@1 performance on AIME 2024 (from 12.9% to 40.2%).
The method proved effective even on highly capable Large Reasoning Models, yielding approximately 10-point improvements on models like Skywork-OR1-Math-7B and Qwen3-8B.

TTRL demonstrated a sustainable self-evolution, consistently surpassing the initial majority accuracy (maj@n) of the model, and closely approached the performance of models trained with ground-truth labels (RL with leakage).
Takeaways: Repeated sampling combined with majority voting can reliably generate pseudo-rewards for test-time reinforcement learning, even without ground-truth labels.
Large Language Models can self-evolve by dynamically improving their own self-supervision signals, leading to a self-reinforcing learning loop that surpasses initial accuracy.
Test-time adaptation through Reinforcement Learning on unlabeled data yields generalizable improvements in reasoning capabilities, rather than just overfitting to specific test sets.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16072.Title: Describe Anything: Detailed Localized Image and Video Captioning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16072.Summary: NVIDIA and UC Berkeley researchers introduce DAM (Describe Anything Model), a vision-language architecture that generates detailed captions for specific regions in images and videos through a focal prompt mechanism and localized vision backbone, achieving state-of-the-art performance across 7 benchmarks while addressing data scarcity through a semi-supervised learning pipeline.
Problem: Existing vision-language models struggle to generate detailed, accurate captions for specific regions within images and videos
Limited availability of high-quality datasets for training detailed localized captioning models
Current evaluation metrics rely on reference captions that often lack comprehensive details
Method: Developed DAM architecture with focal prompt and localized vision backbone for multi-granular regional captioning
Created SSL-based Data Pipeline (DLC-SDP) leveraging segmentation datasets and unlabeled web images
Introduced DLC-Bench for evaluating detailed localized captioning without reference captions
Results: Achieved state-of-the-art performance on 7 benchmarks spanning keyword, phrase, and detailed captioning tasks
Demonstrated superior performance on challenging tasks like PACO benchmark for distinguishing objects and parts
Generated more detailed and accurate descriptions compared to existing methods based on qualitative analysis
Successfully applied the approach to both image and video captioning tasks
Takeaways: Focal prompt encoding preserves both local detail and global context by using varying token densities
Semi-supervised learning can effectively expand limited human annotations into diverse training data
Evaluation methods based on predefined attributes rather than reference captions enable more accurate assessment

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.15777.Title: Tina: Tiny Reasoning Models via LoRA
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.15777.Summary: Tina, a research initiative from the University of Southern California, demonstrates a highly cost-effective approach to instill strong reasoning abilities in language models. It shows that combining a tiny 1.5B base model with LoRA-based reinforcement learning can match or surpass the reasoning performance of state-of-the-art RL models built on the same base, achieving this at post-training costs as low as $9 USD for a single model.
Problem: Achieving robust, multi-step reasoning in large language models remains a significant challenge.
Current methods for enhancing LLM reasoning, such as supervised fine-tuning or reinforcement learning, are resource-intensive and often require substantial computational power and large models.
The high cost and complexity of RL pipelines limit accessibility and widespread research into RL-based reasoning for language models.
Method: Leverage a small 1.5 billion parameter base model, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, known for its initial reasoning aptitude.
Apply Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) for parameter-efficient reinforcement learning using a GRPO-style algorithm, updating only a small fraction of model parameters.
Utilize a minimalist training setup on two NVIDIA L40S GPUs and publicly available reasoning datasets to ensure cost-efficiency and direct comparability with existing models.
Results: Tina models achieved an average performance of 50.60% across six challenging reasoning benchmarks, surpassing SOTA RL models built on the same 1.5B base model (e.g., Open-RS2 at 41.60%).

The best Tina model obtained a >20% reasoning performance increase and 43.33% Pass@1 accuracy on AIME24, with a post-training and evaluation cost of approximately $9 USD, representing a ~260x cost reduction.

Ablation studies demonstrated that concise, high-quality datasets (7k examples) yielded superior performance compared to significantly larger ones, and low LoRA ranks (e.g., 16 or 32) proved highly effective.
Takeaways: LoRA primarily adapts models to the structural format of reasoning (e.g., step-by-step thinking) rewarded by RL, while largely preserving the base model Hovering around 50%, an impressive gain that could be achieved with minimal resources.

A "less compute can yield more performance" phenomenon indicates that increasing training FLOPs with LoRA can sometimes inversely affect reasoning performance, suggesting efficiency in format adaptation.
A distinct "phase transition" point in format-related metrics during training correlates with the best-performing checkpoints, implying an optimal stopping point for LoRA-based RL.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.15619.Title: AdaViP: Aligning Multi-modal LLMs via Adaptive Vision-enhanced Preference Optimization
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.15619.Summary: Researchers from USTC develop AdaViP, a preference optimization framework that reduces hallucinations in multimodal language models by incorporating vision-based preference pairs and adaptive optimization, achieving state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks including Object HalBench and AMBER while surpassing GPT-4V on certain trustworthiness metrics.
Problem: Existing preference learning methods for MLLMs focus primarily on language preferences while neglecting visual context
MLLMs frequently generate responses that contradict or ignore important visual information (hallucinations)
Method: Vision-based preference pair construction using cascade of visual foundation models to create modified images
Adaptive optimization strategy that dynamically balances vision and language-based preferences during training
Results: Outperforms existing DPO methods and hallucination-specific baselines across multiple benchmarks
Achieves superior trustworthiness compared to proprietary models like GPT-4V on certain metrics
Ablation studies confirm both vision-based pairs and adaptive optimization contribute to improvements
Analysis shows successful transition from visual-heavy to balanced preference integration during training
Takeaways: Removing key visual elements from images creates effective preference pairs for training
Adaptive weighting between visual and language preferences improves optimization
Models initially rely more on visual preferences before achieving balanced integration

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.15280.Title: Seeing from Another Perspective: Evaluating Multi-View Understanding in MLLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.15280.Summary: Researchers from UC Berkeley, TranscEngram, and collaborating institutions introduced All-Angles Bench, a new comprehensive benchmark to evaluate multi-view understanding in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). The study demonstrated that current MLLMs exhibit a substantial performance gap and high inconsistency compared to human performance in tasks requiring 3D geometric reasoning across multiple camera perspectives.
Problem: While MLLMs show promise for embodied AI, their ability to interpret and reconcile visual information across multiple, disparate viewpoints for robust 3D scene understanding remains underexplored.
Existing MLLM benchmarks primarily focus on single-view, egocentric, or temporal reasoning, failing to rigorously assess cross-view correspondence and geometric consistency.

The lack of robust multi-view understanding prevents MLLMs from achieving human-level proficiency in real-world tasks like navigation and object manipulation, where a coherent 3D mental model is crucial.
Method: Developed All-Angles Bench, the first comprehensive benchmark designed specifically to evaluate multi-view understanding in MLLMs using 90 diverse multi-view scenes from real-world datasets.

Designed six distinct task categories (e.g., Counting, Attribute Identification, Camera Pose Estimation) and generated over 2,100 human-annotated multiple-choice questions, including 'paired questions' to assess consistency.
Evaluated 27 representative MLLMs, including leading closed- and open-source models, and conducted in-depth qualitative analysis of failure modes.
Results: Human annotators achieved an average accuracy of 82.0% across tasks, while top MLLMs significantly lagged, with differences exceeding 50% in tasks like Camera Pose Estimation.
Certain open-source models (e.g., Ovis2-34B, Qwen2.5-VL-72B) unexpectedly outperformed leading closed-source models in orientation-sensitive tasks like Object Manipulation.

GPT-4o showed approximately 70% inconsistency on Relative Distance tasks, and all models struggled with Relative Direction, exhibiting over 40% inconsistency, highlighting a widespread lack of robust multi-view consistency.
Takeaways: Current state-of-the-art MLLMs demonstrate a significant performance gap compared to human-level multi-view understanding, particularly in geometric and spatial reasoning tasks.
MLLMs exhibit high inconsistency on semantically equivalent 'paired questions,' indicating a lack of stable and genuine understanding across varying perspectives rather than deep comprehension.
Failure modes primarily stem from the inability to establish multi-view correspondence for partially occluded objects and a fundamental lack of accurate coarse camera pose estimation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.15279.Title: VisuLogic: A Benchmark for Evaluating Visual Reasoning in Multi-modal Large Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.15279.Summary: A new benchmark called VisuLogic evaluates true visual reasoning capabilities in multimodal language models through carefully designed tasks that prevent language-based shortcuts, revealing that current MLLMs achieve only 30% accuracy compared to 51.4% human performance while demonstrating how reinforcement learning can help bridge this gap.
Problem: Existing benchmarks allow MLLMs to solve visual tasks using language shortcuts rather than true visual reasoning
Current evaluation metrics overestimate MLLMs' visual reasoning abilities by conflating them with basic perception or language-based solutions
Method: Created VisuLogic benchmark with tasks that inherently require vision-centric reasoning and cannot be solved through text alone
Implemented reinforcement learning fine-tuning approach to improve visual reasoning capabilities
Results: Current MLLMs achieve only 30% accuracy on VisuLogic compared to 51.4% human performance
Models struggle most with spatial reasoning (LLMs) and stylistic reasoning (MLLMs)
Reinforcement learning fine-tuning significantly improves performance by enabling iterative hypothesis revision
Hint prompts boost performance but models still struggle to construct coherent reasoning chains
Takeaways: Most MLLMs perform only slightly above random chance (25%) on genuine visual reasoning tasks
Text-only LLMs with detailed image descriptions barely exceed random baseline, confirming the necessity of true visual reasoning
Chain-of-thought prompting shows minimal benefit for visual reasoning tasks

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.15271.Title: Eagle 2.5: Boosting Long-Context Post-Training for Frontier Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.15271.Summary: NVIDIA researchers develop an efficient long-context vision-language model capable of processing extended video sequences and high-resolution images through novel training strategies like information-first sampling and progressive mixed post-training, achieving 72.4% accuracy on Video-MME with 512 input frames while using only 8B parameters compared to larger 72B+ models.
Problem: Existing vision-language models struggle with processing and integrating information from long visual contexts like videos
Current approaches either use computationally expensive compression modules or suffer from degraded performance with increased visual input
Method: Information-first sampling strategy preserves essential visual/semantic content through image area preservation and automatic degradation sampling
Progressive mixed post-training incrementally expands context length during training
New Eagle-Video-110K dataset with both story-level and clip-level annotations for improved video understanding
Results: Matches performance of 72B+ parameter models while using only 8B parameters
Achieves 72.4% accuracy on Video-MME benchmark with 512 input frames
Strong performance across document understanding, chart interpretation and video analysis tasks
Information-first sampling improves results particularly on high-resolution images and fine-grained video tasks
Takeaways: Preserving image area and balancing visual-textual inputs is critical for long-context performance
Incrementally increasing context length during training is more effective than fixed long-context training
Dual-level video annotations (story + clip) enable better understanding of temporal relationships

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.15037.Title: Scaling and Beyond: Advancing Spatial Reasoning in MLLMs Requires New Recipes
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.15037.Summary: This position paper argues that multimodal large language models (MLLMs) exhibit critical limitations in spatial reasoning and that simply scaling existing architectures will not resolve this. It proposes a framework for spatial reasoning and identifies specific deficiencies across training data, model architecture, training objectives, and evaluation, advocating for targeted methodological innovations.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) consistently struggle with spatial reasoning, a capability essential for understanding and interacting with the physical world.

Current MLLM development, often focused on scaling, does not adequately address the qualitative challenges of spatial understanding, limiting their potential in real-world applications like embodied AI and autonomous driving.
A lack of a precise, comprehensive framework and systematic analysis hinders progress in diagnosing and overcoming MLLMs' spatial reasoning deficiencies.
Method: The paper establishes a comprehensive framework for spatial reasoning, decomposing it into 'Relational Reasoning' (static relationships) and 'Transformation Reasoning' (dynamic manipulations).

It advocates for 'new recipes' across the MLLM pipeline, including specifically designed training data with explicit spatial annotations, architecturally aware components (e.g., advanced positional encodings, spatially-preserving connectors), and spatially-explicit training objectives.
The work calls for improved evaluation benchmarks that better correlate with real-world performance and the development of more sophisticated multimodal reasoning methods.
Results: Analysis of widely used pre-training datasets (e.g., LAION-2B, CC-3M) revealed extremely low frequencies of explicit spatial prepositions (e.g., 0.22%-1.44%), indicating a foundational data gap.

A case study comparing Qwen2-VL and LLaVA 1.5 demonstrated that current MLLMs primarily focus on object-level semantic information rather than forming a holistic understanding of spatial layouts, consistently failing at complex path planning.

The paper systematically identified that current MLLM recipes, across data, architecture, training, and evaluation, are fundamentally constrained, concluding that scaling alone is insufficient to achieve human-like spatial intelligence.
Takeaways: Spatial reasoning in MLLMs is fundamentally limited by the scarcity of explicit spatial annotations in pre-training data and the inadequacy of current textual representations for complex spatial configurations.
Architectural choices like flattening 2D visual information into 1D sequences for LLM backbones and compression in connectors inherently compromise the retention of crucial spatial structure.

Existing training objectives and evaluation benchmarks fail to adequately foster and assess robust spatial reasoning, with common techniques like Chain-of-Thought sometimes proving ineffective or even detrimental for spatial tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.14988.Title: Benchmarking Large Vision-Language Models on Fine-Grained Image Tasks: A Comprehensive Evaluation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.14988.Summary: The paper introduces FG-BMK, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) on fine-grained image tasks, demonstrating that current LVLMs exhibit struggles with subtle distinctions, pronounced knowledge biases due to training data imbalance, and generally underperform specialized fine-grained models.
Problem: A critical gap exists in systematically evaluating Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) on fine-grained image tasks, which demand distinguishing subtle visual cues between subordinate categories.
Existing holistic and specialized benchmarks do not adequately assess LVLMs' ability to perform at this granular level.
The true capabilities and limitations of LVLMs in fine-grained domains, crucial for applications like biodiversity monitoring or product retrieval, remained largely unexplored.
Method: Introduces FG-BMK, a comprehensive fine-grained evaluation benchmark comprising 1.01 million questions and 0.33 million images sourced from 12 established fine-grained datasets.

Employs a human-oriented evaluation paradigm to assess conversational understanding and knowledge recall through attribute recognition, knowledge bias estimation, and hierarchical granularity recognition tasks.
Utilizes a machine-oriented evaluation paradigm to directly assess the quality of visual feature representations using image retrieval and classification tasks within and across meta-categories.
Results: LVLMs' accuracy declines significantly as the granularity of recognition questions increases, showing struggles with excessively fine-grained categories (e.g., species vs. class level distinctions).
LVLMs exhibit pronounced knowledge biases across fine-grained categories, primarily attributed to uneven representation in their vast, general training data.

Current LVLMs consistently underperform state-of-the-art specialized fine-grained models on classification tasks and show significantly higher susceptibility to adversarial perturbations in fine-grained settings.
Takeaways: The granularity mismatch between fine-grained visual content and coarse-grained textual descriptions in alignment data can impair the fine-grained discriminability of visual features.
Models trained with contrastive loss exhibit superior fine-grained discriminability compared to those using generative or reconstruction-based paradigms.
Data quality and effective training paradigms are more important than sheer data quantity or vision encoder size for achieving robust fine-grained capabilities in LVLMs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.14945.Title: Learning to Reason under Off-Policy Guidance
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.14945.Summary: LUFFY introduces a framework that enhances Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) by integrating off-policy guidance into Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR). This approach enables LRMs to acquire new reasoning capabilities from stronger external policies, achieving state-of-the-art performance on math benchmarks, superior generalization on out-of-distribution tasks, and successfully training weaker foundation models where on-policy methods fail.
Problem: Existing Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) for Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) operates in an "on-policy" manner, limiting models to learning from their own self-generated outputs.
This on-policy constraint restricts LRMs from acquiring genuinely new cognitive capacities or reasoning strategies that lie beyond their initial exploration capabilities.
Models trained with on-policy RLVR often reach performance plateaus, unable to progress further due to a lack of foundational behaviors for advancement.
Method: LUFFY extends Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) by integrating off-policy reasoning traces generated by stronger external models into the training process.

It employs "Mixed-Policy GRPO" which incorporates both on-policy and off-policy rollouts for advantage computation, adaptively weighting the influence of external demonstrations based on the trained model's performance.

"Policy Shaping via Regularized Importance Sampling" re-weights gradients for off-policy distributions, encouraging the model to learn from low-probability tokens and maintaining exploration to prevent "entropy collapse".
Results: LUFFY achieved an average gain of +6.4 points across six challenging math reasoning benchmarks and showed a +6.2 points advantage on average over baselines for out-of-distribution tasks.
It successfully trained weaker foundation models, such as LLaMA-3.1-8B, in scenarios where on-policy RLVR methods completely failed to make progress.

Training dynamics revealed LUFFY maintains higher generation entropy throughout training, indicating continuous exploration, and dynamically balances imitation of off-policy traces with self-driven exploration.
Takeaways: Off-policy guidance allows Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) to transcend their initial cognitive boundaries by internalizing complex reasoning patterns from more capable external models.
Dynamically balancing imitation of external guidance with self-exploration is crucial for acquiring new skills and preventing models from becoming overly deterministic.
Off-policy learning enables the successful training of weaker foundation models that on-policy Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) methods cannot effectively optimize.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.14920.Title: DyFo: A Training-Free Dynamic Focus Visual Search for Enhancing LMMs in Fine-Grained Visual Understanding
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.14920.Summary: DyFo, developed by researchers at Peking University and Tencent, is a training-free dynamic focus visual search method designed to enhance Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) in fine-grained visual understanding and reduce visual hallucinations. It achieves this by orchestrating a bidirectional interaction between LMMs and visual experts via a Monte Carlo Tree Search, demonstrating improved performance on benchmarks such as POPE and V* Bench by enabling LMMs to effectively filter irrelevant visual content.
Problem: Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) struggle with fine-grained visual understanding, especially in high-resolution or cluttered images, due to fixed-resolution encoders that lose details during downsampling.
Dynamic-resolution LMMs, while processing more data, can be overwhelmed by irrelevant visual information, which paradoxically exacerbates hallucination issues by increasing noise.

Existing solutions for fine-grained understanding often require significant architectural modifications, extensive data collection, or costly fine-tuning, limiting their generalizability and practicality.
Method: Researchers at Peking University and Tencent developed DyFo (Dynamic Focus), a training-free visual search method that enables LMMs to dynamically focus on crucial visual regions.

DyFo orchestrates a bidirectional interaction between an LMM (for text refinement) and an off-the-shelf visual expert (for image region updates) using a compact action space (semantic focus and semantic scatter).

A Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) algorithm guides this dynamic focusing process, exploring potential focus regions and leveraging a reward mechanism based on consistency and conciseness to efficiently identify the most relevant visual information.
Results: DyFo consistently improved LMM performance on the POPE benchmark, reducing visual hallucinations; for example, it boosted Qwen2-VL's F1 Score on POPE-COCO (random) from 89.22 to 91.71.

On the V* Bench, designed for fine-grained understanding in high-resolution images, DyFo-Q (Qwen2-VL with DyFo) achieved an overall accuracy of 81.15%, surpassing fine-tuned methods like SEAL (75.39%).

Ablation studies confirmed the effectiveness of the combined semantic focus and scatter actions, and demonstrated that Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) was the most efficient search algorithm, requiring fewer steps (3.20 on V* Bench) compared to alternatives.
Takeaways: A training-free method can effectively integrate off-the-shelf visual experts with LMMs, providing an "out-of-the-box" solution that avoids costly fine-tuning or architectural changes.

Orchestrating a bidirectional interaction between LMMs (for semantic understanding) and visual experts (for precise localization) through a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) algorithm enhances fine-grained understanding and reduces visual hallucinations.

A human-inspired dynamic focus mechanism, utilizing actions like semantic focus and semantic scatter, efficiently guides the visual search, allowing LMMs to filter irrelevant content and concentrate on critical details.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.14200.Title: Enhancing Multimodal In-Context Learning for Image Classification through Coreset Optimization
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.14200.Summary: Key-based Coreset Optimization (KeCO) introduces a framework to refine a compact set of in-context learning examples for Large Vision-Language Models by iteratively updating their visual features using information from larger, 'untapped' datasets. Its diversity-based variant, KeCO-DS, improves average performance by over 20% for OpenFlamingo-3B and 10% for IDEFICS-8B compared to using an unrefined coreset, and notably surpasses methods using the entire, larger support set by approximately 10% and 4% respectively.
Problem: Existing in-context learning (ICL) methods for Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) incur high computational and memory costs due to storing and processing entire support sets for demonstration selection.
Traditional coreset selection techniques are often ineffective for multimodal (image) data, struggling to adequately represent diverse visual features within a small, fixed subset.
Conventional coreset strategies lead to information loss by discarding the majority of the support set, leaving valuable 'untapped' samples unused in downstream inference.
Method: Introduces Key-based Coreset Optimization (KeCO), an iterative framework that refines a compact coreset of image features by leveraging 'untapped' data from the larger support set.
Employs a feature-level update mechanism where visual 'keys' of coreset samples are adjusted towards averaged features of related untapped samples using linear interpolation.

Investigates three target sample selection strategies (Random, Similarity-based, Diversity-based) to determine which coreset samples should be updated by incoming untapped data, and extends this to simulated online scenarios.
Results: KeCO-DS achieved average performance improvements exceeding 20% for OpenFlamingo-3B and 10% for IDEFICS-8B over unrefined coresets of the same size.
KeCO-DS consistently surpassed methods using the entire, five-times larger support set, demonstrating approximately 10% improvement for OpenFlamingo-3B and 4% for IDEFICS-8B on average.

The framework demonstrated robust and stable performance in simulated online scenarios, maintaining superior results compared to baselines when data arrives sequentially, with KeCO-DS achieving approximately 5% improvement on CUB-200 for Qwen2-VL.
Takeaways: Dynamically refining coreset representations with 'untapped' data significantly enhances ICL performance, often outperforming methods using the full, unoptimized support set.

Diversity-based target sample selection (KeCO-DS), which updates coreset samples with *least similar* query samples of the same class, is most effective for filtering out category-irrelevant attributes.

KeCO brings larger performance gains to fine-grained image classification tasks, suggesting its utility in improving LVLM understanding of subtle visual distinctions often overlooked by models pre-trained on coarse-grained data.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.14117.Title: PEFT A2Z: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning Survey for Large Language and Vision Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.14117.Summary: This survey provides a structured overview of Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) techniques, examining their mechanisms, trade-offs, and applications across language, vision, and multimodal domains. It details how PEFT methods, such as LoRA and various adapter designs, enable the efficient adaptation of large models by updating only a small fraction of parameters, thereby addressing the resource and storage challenges of full fine-tuning.
Problem: Traditional fine-tuning of large language and vision models demands substantial computational resources, memory, and storage, making it inaccessible for many researchers and organizations.
Full fine-tuning often leads to overfitting on small datasets, catastrophic forgetting of previously learned knowledge, and parameter inefficiency due to redundancy.
Storing and deploying multiple fully fine-tuned models for various tasks results in significant storage requirements and practical deployment challenges.
Method: The paper surveys Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) techniques that adapt large pre-trained models by updating only a fraction of their parameters or introducing a limited number of new ones.
PEFT methods are classified into additive (e.g., adapters, prompt tuning), reparameterized (e.g., LoRA), selective (e.g., BitFit), hybrid, and unified approaches.
These methods enable efficient model adaptation by reducing memory, computational overhead, and storage requirements while aiming to maintain performance comparable to full fine-tuning.
Results: PEFT techniques have been successfully applied across language, vision, and multimodal domains, enabling efficient adaptation of large models to specialized tasks like fine-grained classification, object detection, and cross-modal understanding.

Specific PEFT methods, such as adapters and prompt tuning, have shown effectiveness in language tasks, while LoRA significantly reduces the number of trainable parameters in large models without sacrificing performance.
The survey highlights the practical impact of PEFT in broadening the adoption of powerful AI models by making fine-tuning more accessible and resource-efficient.
Takeaways: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods can be systematically categorized into five main families: additive, reparameterized, selective, hybrid, and unified approaches, each with distinct mechanisms and trade-offs.
Reparameterized methods like LoRA leverage low-rank decomposition to reduce trainable parameters by over 99% for models like GPT-3 while maintaining performance comparable to full fine-tuning.

The choice of PEFT method depends on specific task requirements, computational resources, and desired performance characteristics, with different methods being more effective for knowledge-intensive, structural, or generative tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13958.Title: ToolRL: Reward is All Tool Learning Needs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13958.Summary: This research presents ToolRL, a novel reinforcement learning framework that utilizes a meticulously designed reward mechanism to enhance tool-use capabilities in Large Language Models. The approach achieves up to a 17% performance improvement over raw base models and 15% over Supervised Fine-Tuning models on the Berkeley Function Call Leaderboard, while also demonstrating strong generalization to unseen scenarios and fostering emergent agentic behaviors.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) inherently possess limitations such as outdated knowledge, calculation inaccuracies, and shallow reasoning, which external tools can help address.
