Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), the prevalent method for training LLMs in Tool-Integrated Reasoning (TIR), struggles with generalization to complex or unseen scenarios and lacks exploratory capabilities, often leading to superficial imitation.
Designing effective and generalizable reward signals for multi-step, multi-tool invocation tasks within a Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework for TIR has been largely unexplored.
Method: Introduces ToolRL, a novel Reinforcement Learning (RL) approach for Tool-Integrated Reasoning (TIR) in LLMs, centered on a principled, rule-based reward design.
Deploys a fine-grained correctness reward that assesses tool invocation accuracy across tool names, parameter names, and parameter content, providing dense intermediate feedback.

Utilizes Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) for stable training, with a custom advantage normalization and an omission of the KL penalty to encourage adaptation to the structured reward signals.
Results: ToolRL, using GRPO with cold start, consistently outperformed raw base models by approximately 17% and SFT models by 15% on the BFCL benchmark (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct improved from 41.97% to 58.38% on BFCL).
GRPO-trained models demonstrated strong generalization performance on unfamiliar programming languages and novel task objectives like detecting irrelevant tools.

Models exhibited emergent proactiveness (e.g., clarifying ambiguous intent) and metacognitive reasoning (e.g., opting to answer directly when tools are irrelevant), enhancing efficiency and reducing hallucinations.
Takeaways: Longer reasoning (measured by the length of the field) is not consistently beneficial for tool-use tasks and can sometimes degrade performance.
Fine-grained reward decomposition, which separately evaluates tool name, parameter names, and parameter values, provides richer and more effective learning signals than coarser granularities.
Training GRPO from a 'cold start' (raw instruct model) often outperforms models initialized with Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), suggesting SFT can hinder generalization by promoting memorization.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13828.Title: Generative AI Act II: Test Time Scaling Drives Cognition Engineering
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13828.Summary: Researchers from Shanghai Jiao Tong University, SII, and the Generative AI Research Lab delineate "Cognition Engineering" as the new paradigm for generative AI's "Act II," emphasizing test-time scaling methods to advance Large Language Models beyond knowledge retrieval towards deep reasoning. The work introduces a framework for understanding and implementing techniques such as parallel sampling, tree search, multi-turn correction, and long Chain-of-Thought, demonstrating their role in cultivating AI's cognitive abilities, particularly when enhanced by reinforcement learning.
Problem: Existing Large Language Models (LLMs) from the "Act I" era exhibited limitations in deep reasoning, struggling with complex, multi-step problems and novel concepts.
These models primarily functioned as knowledge retrieval systems, lacking the capacity for human-like depth of thought or generating truly novel insights.
Traditional scaling methods (increasing parameters and training data) were insufficient to bridge this observed "wisdom gap" in AI capabilities.
Method: Introduces "Cognition Engineering" as a new systematic methodology to develop and optimize AI's thinking capabilities, moving models from the knowledge level to the wisdom level.
Proposes "test-time scaling" as the core mechanism, categorizing and detailing methods like Parallel Sampling, Tree Search, Multi-turn Correction, and Long Chain-of-Thought (CoT).

Explores how training strategies, especially Reinforcement Learning (RL) with verifiable rewards and Supervised Fine-tuning (SFT) on high-quality CoT data, elicit and enhance these advanced cognitive behaviors.
Results: Test-time scaling methods, particularly RL-driven Long Chain-of-Thought, achieved human-competitive performance in complex domains, exemplified by DeepSeek-R1's 79.8 score on AIME and OpenAI's o1 series excelling on coding benchmarks.

Parallel sampling consistently increased `Pass@N` metrics, while tree search and multi-turn correction (with reliable external feedback) significantly enhanced deliberate planning and iterative response refinement.

The "RL scaling phenomenon" demonstrated that online Reinforcement Learning with carefully designed rewards enabled LLMs to learn and master advanced, complex long-CoT behaviors, often surpassing outcomes achieved through supervised learning alone.
Takeaways: Generative AI is transitioning into "Act II," driven by "test-time scaling" which enables Large Language Models to move from superficial knowledge retrieval to deep reasoning and thought construction.

Online Reinforcement Learning (RL) with verifiable, rule-based rewards can unlock significant, autonomous reasoning capabilities in LLMs, demonstrating an "RL scaling phenomenon" for complex long Chain-of-Thought behaviors.

Long Chain-of-Thought (CoT) methods, incorporating patterns like reflection and backtracking, facilitate the most human-like cognitive behaviors and achieve the highest performance for complex problems.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13818.Title: Not All Rollouts are Useful: Down-Sampling Rollouts in LLM Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13818.Summary: Researchers at Carnegie Mellon University developed PODS (Policy Optimization with Down-Sampling), a framework that addresses the computational imbalance in large language model reinforcement learning by strategically selecting informative rollouts. This method allows for up to 3.0x faster training convergence and often achieves higher peak accuracy on mathematical reasoning tasks like GSM8K and MATH, utilizing diverse model architectures and hardware configurations.
Problem: Large language model (LLM) reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) suffers from computational asymmetry between fast, parallelizable rollout generation and slow, memory-intensive policy updates.
Policy updates scale poorly with batch size due to memory constraints and communication overhead, leading to hardware underutilization or increased latency.
Not all generated rollouts equally contribute to model improvement, leading to redundant computation in the policy update phase.
Method: PODS decouples the inference and policy-update phases by first generating a large batch of 'n' rollouts and then applying a principled down-sampling rule.
A max-variance down-sampling rule selects a smaller, more informative subset of 'm' rollouts (where m < n), which prioritizes examples at the extremes of the reward distribution.
Policy updates are performed exclusively on this selected 'm' subset, significantly reducing the memory and computational burden on the policy update phase.
Results: GRPO-PODS consistently achieved faster convergence, reaching baseline peak accuracies at least 1.7x faster and up to 3.0x faster across various benchmarks, models (Qwen, Llama), and hardware setups.
The max-variance down-sampling rule consistently outperformed trivial baselines like random sampling and max-reward sampling, demonstrating its effectiveness in enhancing the learning signal.

PODS showed robust performance across a wide range of down-sampling ratios, with typical ratios of 2 to 4 (e.g., updating with 16 rollouts from 32 or 64 generated) offering an effective balance between efficiency and accuracy.
Takeaways: Maximizing the empirical reward variance within a subset of rollouts provides a stronger contrastive signal for policy learning, effectively distinguishing between highly successful and unsuccessful reasoning paths.
For a sorted list of rewards, the variance-maximizing subset of any given size always consists of the highest and lowest rewarded rollouts.
Intelligently down-sampling rollouts within each prompt can leverage efficient inference capabilities while mitigating the high costs of policy updates, thereby accelerating LLM RLVR training.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13469.Title: HMPE:HeatMap Embedding for Efficient Transformer-Based Small Object Detection
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13469.Summary: The HeatMap Embedding (HMPE) framework enhances Transformer-based models for small object detection by dynamically aligning positional encoding with object detection semantics through heatmap-guided adaptive learning. This approach improves detection accuracy by 1.9% mAP on NWPU VHR-10 and reduces computational overhead by decreasing decoder layers.
Problem: Transformer-based models struggle with small object detection due to insufficient utilization of positional and semantic information during query generation.
Existing models often generate low-quality queries and are susceptible to background noise, leading to reduced detection accuracy.
Decoder redundancy in current Transformer architectures results in slow inference speeds and high computational costs, particularly challenging for real-time applications.
Method: The HeatMap Embedding (HMPE) framework enhances Transformer-based models by embedding heatmap information that dynamically aligns positional encoding with object detection semantics.
The Multi-Scale ObjectBox-Heatmap Fusion Encoder (MOHFE) integrates class and bounding box semantics into the encoder via heatmap embeddings for multi-scale feature fusion.
The HeatMap Induced High-Quality Queries for Decoder (HIDQ) transforms mixed heatmap features into high-quality queries, reducing decoder redundancy and accelerating inference.
Results: The HMPE framework achieved a 1.9% increase in mean average precision (mAP) on the NWPU VHR-10 dataset for small object detection.
It demonstrated enhanced performance on general datasets with a 1.2% increase in mAP on the PASCAL VOC dataset.
HMPE reduced computational overhead by decreasing the required decoder layers from eight to a minimum of three, leading to faster inference and lower training costs.
Takeaways: Heatmap-guided adaptive learning dynamically aligns positional encoding with object detection semantics, improving the utilization of crucial information.
The MOHFE module uses a mask filter to decouple relevant (hot) and irrelevant (cold) regions, allowing focused attention on potential object locations.

Linear-Snake Convolution (LSConv) extracts discriminative features from sparse small objects using a dual-path design that combines flexible snake-like receptive fields with stable linear convolution.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13292.Title: Let Me Grok for You: Accelerating Grokking via Embedding Transfer from a Weaker Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13292.Summary: A method called GrokTransfer accelerates the "grokking" phenomenon in neural networks by transferring embeddings from smaller, weaker models to larger target models, eliminating delayed generalization while maintaining performance across algorithmic tasks like modular arithmetic and sparse parity.
Problem: Neural networks often exhibit "grokking" where generalization is significantly delayed after memorization, making training unpredictable and inefficient
Existing approaches don't address the root cause of delayed generalization or provide principled solutions for accelerating grokking
Method: Train a smaller "weak" model until it achieves basic generalization
Extract and linearly map the weak model's learned embeddings to initialize the target model
Use the transferred embeddings to enable direct generalization without delay
Results: Eliminates delayed generalization in synthetic XOR tasks through theoretically proven direct generalization
Successfully transfers embeddings between different architectures (FNNs to Transformers)
Reduces computational costs compared to training large models from scratch
Works across multiple algorithmic tasks while maintaining target model performance
Takeaways: Input embeddings play a crucial role in determining training dynamics and generalization
Even very small weak models (e.g., 3 neurons) can provide sufficient embedding information
The weak model must achieve some level of generalization for effective transfer

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13181.Title: Perception Encoder: The best visual embeddings are not at the output of the network
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13181.Summary: Perception Encoder introduces a family of vision models that achieve state-of-the-art performance across diverse vision and vision-language tasks, demonstrating that general, high-quality visual features can be extracted from the intermediate layers of a single, contrastively-trained network. It provides specific alignment tuning methods to make these features accessible for tasks ranging from zero-shot classification to dense spatial prediction and multimodal language understanding.
Problem: Computer vision has relied on specialized large-scale pretrained encoders for different tasks, leading to fragmentation and complexity.
Combining diverse pretraining techniques (e.g., contrastive, captioning, self-supervised spatial) results in complex, difficult-to-scale multi-objective schemes.
There is a need for a single, simple, and scalable pretraining technique that can learn state-of-the-art features for all downstream vision and vision-language tasks.
Method: Developed PE_core, a unified image-and-video encoder, through robust, multi-stage contrastive training using a refined image-text recipe and a novel video data engine.
Designed "alignment tuning" methods to extract and align potent features residing in PE_core's intermediate layers for different task families.

PE_lang adapts PE_core for MLLMs by projecting from optimal intermediate layers, while PE_spatial uses self-distillation and SAM mask logit distillation to enhance spatial coherence for dense prediction.
Results: PE_core_G achieved an 86.6% average zero-shot ImageNet robustness and 76.9% zero-shot Kinetics-400 accuracy, outperforming specialized models in image and video classification/retrieval.

PE_lang_G, by aligning intermediate features, individually outperformed other vision encoders for MLLMs, achieving leading results on OCR (94.6% DocVQA), VQA, and video understanding (82.7% PerceptionTest) benchmarks.
PE_spatial_G achieved state-of-the-art performance on dense prediction tasks, including 61.5% J&F on zero-shot tracking and a new COCO state-of-the-art of 66.0 box mAP for detection.
Takeaways: Robust global vision-language contrastive learning alone can produce strong, general embeddings for a wide variety of downstream tasks.

Powerful, task-agnostic visual features are often learned and reside within the intermediate layers of contrastively trained vision transformers, even when the final output layer does not adequately express them.

Novel "alignment tuning" methods can effectively extract and align these hidden intermediate features to the network's output, making them readily usable for diverse applications without retraining the entire model.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13180.Title: PerceptionLM: Open-Access Data and Models for Detailed Visual Understanding
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13180.Summary: The PerceptionLM project introduces open-access Vision-Language Models, comprehensive datasets, and a benchmark for detailed image and video understanding, developed collaboratively by Meta FAIR and academic partners. This initiative provides a fully reproducible framework, achieving competitive performance without relying on proprietary models, and notably excels in fine-grained spatio-temporal video reasoning.
Problem: The Vision-Language Model (VLM) research landscape is dominated by high-performing, closed-source models from proprietary entities, hindering scientific understanding, reproducibility, and open innovation.
Existing synthetic data and benchmarks fall short in fostering detailed video understanding, especially for fine-grained spatio-temporal reasoning, often relying on 'image-centric' approaches.
The reliance on 'distillation from black-box models' further entrenches dependence on opaque systems, impeding fundamental knowledge about VLM training from scratch.
Method: Developed PerceptionLM, an open-access VLM framework leveraging Llama 3 as the language decoder and a pre-trained Perception Encoder, trained through a three-stage process including projector warm-up, large-scale synthetic data training, and supervised fine-tuning.
Created an open-source data engine to generate a vast synthetic dataset (66.1M samples) for general VLM capabilities across images and videos, enabling scaling law analysis.

Introduced two novel, large-scale, human-annotated datasets: PLM–FGQA (2.4M fine-grained QA pairs) and PLM–STC (476.2K spatio-temporal captions), specifically designed to enhance detailed video understanding, alongside the new PLM–VideoBench for evaluation.
Results: PerceptionLM-8B achieved strong and competitive performance across a wide range of 40 image and video benchmarks, often matching or exceeding other open-access models and, in specific cases, proprietary models.

PLM-8B demonstrated substantial outperformance on the newly introduced PLM–VideoBench, notably excelling in spatio-temporal tasks like RDCap (52.8 SODA† compared to GPT-4o's 20.9), largely closing the gap with human performance.

Ablation studies confirmed that the custom human-annotated data (PLM-STC and PLM-FGQA) provided significant performance boosts specifically for spatio-temporal tasks (+27.4 points) and fine-grained activity understanding (+13.1 points), addressing limitations of synthetic data.
Takeaways: A fully open and reproducible VLM development paradigm can achieve competitive performance against state-of-the-art open-weight models without relying on proprietary model distillation.

While synthetic data scales effectively for established VLM tasks like OCR and general QA, its efficacy significantly diminishes for 'challenging' video tasks requiring fine-grained spatio-temporal understanding.

Targeted, high-quality human-annotated datasets are crucial for bridging the performance gap in complex video reasoning, enabling models to grasp nuanced spatio-temporal dynamics beyond what synthetic data provides.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13173.Title: It's All Connected: A Journey Through Test-Time Memorization, Attentional Bias, Retention, and Online Optimization
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13173.Summary: A unified framework from Google Research introduces "Miras" for sequence modeling that reinterprets attention mechanisms and forgetting gates as forms of memory optimization, leading to three new architectures (Moneta, Yaad, and Memora) that demonstrate improved performance on language modeling and recall-intensive tasks while providing theoretical insights into existing models.
Problem: Existing sequence models like Transformers face limitations with long sequences due to quadratic complexity
Lack of unified understanding of how different sequence modeling architectures relate to each other theoretically
Method: Developed Miras framework that unifies different sequence models through associative memory and attentional bias concepts
Created new architectures with alternative attention mechanisms and retention gates based on framework insights
Results: Three new architectures outperform state-of-the-art baselines on various sequence modeling tasks
Models demonstrate better scaling with context length and model size
Framework successfully unifies understanding of existing architectures like Transformers and linear RNNs
Moneta variant shows improved robustness to noise through p-norm objectives
Takeaways: Forgetting mechanisms in sequence models can be reinterpreted as retention regularization
Different sequence models share underlying principles in how they manage memory and attention
Novel attention configurations and retention gates can improve model performance

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13161.Title: Nemotron-CLIMB: CLustering-based Iterative Data Mixture Bootstrapping for Language Model Pre-training
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13161.Summary: Nemotron-CLIMB, developed by NVIDIA and Georgia Institute of Technology, introduces an automated framework for discovering semantic domains in unstructured web data and iteratively optimizing data mixtures for large language model pre-training. This approach achieved a 2.0% average performance improvement over Llama-3.2 1.2B on general reasoning benchmarks with a 950M parameter model and released two new datasets, NEMOTRON-CLIMBLAB and NEMOTRON-CLIMBMIX.
Problem: Vast, heterogeneous web datasets for LLM pre-training lack explicit domain labels, making optimal data mixture selection challenging.
Existing data mixing methods often rely on predefined domains or labor-intensive manual curation, limiting scalability and adaptability.
The complex, non-linear relationship between data composition and LLM performance makes brute-force optimal mixture search computationally prohibitive.
Method: An unsupervised clustering method, utilizing text embeddings and pruning/merging, automatically identifies semantically coherent domains within large-scale web data.
An iterative bootstrapping framework, employing smaller 'proxy models' and a regression 'predictor', efficiently searches for optimal data mixture weights.
A coordinate descent approach refines the sampling strategy and predictor simultaneously, focusing the search on promising configurations to reduce computational cost.
Results: CLIMB's optimal data mixture consistently outperformed state-of-the-art baselines (Random, DoReMi, RegMix) by achieving up to 60.41% average accuracy for 1B models on 40B tokens.
A 950M CLIMB model, trained on 400B tokens with the optimized mixture, surpassed Llama-3.2 1.2B by 2.0% on average across general reasoning benchmarks.

The research contributed two new high-quality datasets: NEMOTRON-CLIMBLAB (a 1.2-trillion-token clustered corpus) and NEMOTRON-CLIMBMIX (a 400-billion-token optimized dataset for efficient pre-training).
Takeaways: Automated domain discovery from unstructured data, rather than reliance on predefined labels, enables more effective data mixture optimization for LLM pre-training.
An iterative search strategy, leveraging proxy models and a predictor, significantly reduces the computational overhead of identifying high-performing data compositions.
Optimal data mixtures not only contain content relevant to downstream tasks but also exhibit crucial diversity among selected clusters to enhance model generalization.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13055.Title: NoisyRollout: Reinforcing Visual Reasoning with Data Augmentation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13055.Summary: NoisyRollout introduces a data augmentation method for training Vision-Language Models (VLMs) using Reinforcement Learning, applying controlled visual noise during RL rollouts to enhance reasoning capabilities. This approach improves robustness and generalization, achieving superior performance on five out-of-domain benchmarks and demonstrating exceptional sample efficiency compared to existing methods.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) leveraging Reinforcement Learning (RL) for reasoning struggle with effective policy exploration, as methods like increasing decoding temperature often lead to superficial diversity.
VLMs possess inherent limitations in visual perception, such as hallucinations, which can propagate and hinder subsequent reasoning steps during RL training.
Existing RL adaptations, often directly borrowed from Language Models, do not specifically address the unique visual-centric challenges faced by multimodal reasoning agents.
Method: A hybrid rollout strategy is implemented where the old policy generates responses from both clean and moderately distorted images for each training sample.

All rollouts (from both clean and noisy inputs) are combined into a single group to compute a unified baseline reward and normalized advantages, using reward discrepancies as implicit contrastive signals.
A noise annealing schedule gradually reduces the distortion strength of visual noise over training steps, ensuring stability while maintaining diverse exploration signals.
Results: NoisyRollout achieved state-of-the-art out-of-domain generalization, outperforming vanilla GRPO and other leading RL-tuned models across five benchmarks, including MathVerse (53.2%), MathVision (28.5%), and HallusionBench (72.1%).

The method demonstrated exceptional sample efficiency, achieving strong performance with only 2.1K training samples from Geometry3K, requiring significantly less data than comparable state-of-the-art models.

It exhibited robust and scalable performance, consistently improving over vanilla GRPO for both 7B and 32B parameter models, and maintaining gains across different training datasets and varying data scales.
Takeaways: Injecting controlled visual noise during RL rollouts creates targeted perceptual diversity, leading to more robust reasoning paths and improved generalization.
Reward differences between clean and noisy rollouts provide implicit contrastive signals, which help refine the model's visual perception by reducing negative exploration space.
An annealing schedule for noise strength is critical for stable training, enabling a smooth transition from broad exploration early on to more 'on-policy' learning as the VLM's capabilities improve.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.12717.Title: Post-pre-training for Modality Alignment in Vision-Language Foundation Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.12717.Summary: A post-pre-training framework improves alignment between image and text features in CLIP models through Random Feature Alignment (RaFA) and Hybrid Contrastive-Distillation (HyCD), achieving enhanced zero-shot performance across classification and retrieval tasks while maintaining computational efficiency compared to full pre-training approaches.
Problem: CLIP and other vision-language models suffer from modality gap where image and text features are not perfectly aligned
Existing solutions either require expensive pre-training modifications or sacrifice zero-shot performance through task-specific fine-tuning
Method: Random Feature Alignment (RaFA) aligns features to a shared prior distribution
Hybrid Contrastive-Distillation (HyCD) updates the model while preserving knowledge from pre-trained CLIP
Post-pre-training approach that operates between pre-training and fine-tuning phases
Results: Improved zero-shot performance on classification and cross-modal retrieval tasks
Enhanced robustness demonstrated on test sets while maintaining computational efficiency
Benefits extend to downstream fine-tuning tasks while preserving zero-shot capabilities
Takeaways: Quality of image-text pairs used for post-pre-training significantly impacts performance
Combining RaFA with HyCD improves feature space uniformity while reducing modality gap
Method generalizes across different pre-trained CLIP model variants

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.12680.Title: Embodied-R: Collaborative Framework for Activating Embodied Spatial Reasoning in Foundation Models via Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.12680.Summary: A collaborative framework from Tsinghua University enables foundation models to perform embodied spatial reasoning by combining large vision-language models for perception with reinforcement learning-trained small language models for reasoning, achieving comparable performance to state-of-the-art multimodal models while reducing computational costs through key frame extraction and logical consistency rewards.
Problem: Current foundation models lack human-like spatial cognition abilities needed for embodied reasoning in physical environments
Existing multimodal models face limitations with input token limits, frame redundancy, and poor generalization for embodied video understanding
Method: Collaborative framework combining large VLMs for perception with small LMs for reasoning
RL training with novel logical consistency reward to improve reasoning quality
Key frame extractor to reduce computational costs by eliminating redundant frames
Three-stage training schedule optimizing RL performance
Results: Achieved comparable or better performance than proprietary models like OpenAI-o1 and Gemini-2.5-Pro
Demonstrated strong generalization on out-of-distribution datasets like EgoSchema and MVBench
Reduced computational costs while maintaining accuracy through key frame selection
RL training improved reasoning quality and mitigated reward hacking through logical consistency
Takeaways: Small LMs can match large model performance when trained with RL and logical consistency rewards
Frame extraction and collaborative approach enable efficient processing of embodied video
RL training leads to better out-of-distribution generalization compared to supervised fine-tuning

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.12328.Title: A Comprehensive Survey of Reward Models: Taxonomy, Applications, Challenges, and Future
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.12328.Summary: A comprehensive survey consolidates research on Reward Models (RMs) in the Large Language Model (LLM) era, introducing an elaborate taxonomy for their lifecycle components. It details RM types and granularities, explores diverse applications, and identifies challenges alongside future research directions.
Problem: Despite the critical role of Reward Models (RMs) in aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) with human values and safety guidelines via RLHF, a comprehensive and dedicated survey specifically focused on RMs in the LLM era was lacking.
The rapidly expanding and diverse research on RMs lacked systematic organization and an in-depth analysis, making it challenging for both newcomers and experienced researchers to navigate.

Existing literature touched upon RMs as part of broader discussions on LLM alignment or RLHF limitations, but did not provide the focused, structured overview necessary to address the complexities of RM development and deployment.
Method: The paper introduces the first comprehensive survey specifically focused on parameterized Reward Models (RMs) in the Large Language Model (LLM) era, which are used to reflect human preferences.

An elaborate taxonomy is developed that systematically reviews RMs across three main dimensions: how preference data is collected (Human Preference vs. AI Preference), the mechanisms of reward modeling (Type Level: Discriminative, Generative, Implicit; Granularity Level: Outcome-level, Process-level), and their various usage scenarios in the LLM lifecycle.

The survey analyzes the current application landscape of RMs, discusses existing benchmarking and evaluation methodologies, and identifies key challenges and open problems while proposing future research directions to facilitate further advancement in the field.
Results: The survey confirms the established role of RMs in LLM alignment and identifies that preference data for training RMs can originate from both human annotation and increasingly from AI models, demonstrating high consistency with human judgment.

A comprehensive RM taxonomy is presented, categorizing models by type (discriminative, generative, implicit) and granularity (outcome-level vs. process-level), and their diverse applications across the LLM lifecycle (data selection, policy training, inference) are mapped.

Significant evaluation challenges are identified, including the lack of general and standardized benchmarks, high cost, and sensitivity to input variations; key challenges like data quality, overoptimization (reward hacking), and evaluation biases are highlighted with proposed future directions.
Takeaways: Reward Models (RMs) are indispensable for aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) with human preferences, acting as crucial proxies for human judgment in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF).

Preference data for RMs can be sourced from both human annotations (with ongoing research to improve efficiency and quality) and increasingly from capable AI models, which offer scalability for superhuman tasks.

A multi-faceted taxonomy is critical for understanding RMs, classifying them by underlying model type (discriminative, generative, implicit) and the granularity of their feedback (outcome-level vs. process-level), each with distinct advantages and challenges.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.12216.Title: d1: Scaling Reasoning in Diffusion Large Language Models via Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.12216.Summary: This paper presents `d1`, a two-stage post-training framework that applies reinforcement learning to discrete diffusion large language models (dLLMs) to enhance their reasoning abilities. The work introduces `diffu-GRPO`, a novel policy gradient algorithm for masked dLLMs, which demonstrates consistent performance improvements on mathematical, planning, and coding benchmarks, such as a +26.2% gain on Countdown for the LLaDA-8B-Instruct model.
Problem: Large language models (LLMs) based on the autoregressive (AR) paradigm have substantially improved their reasoning abilities through reinforcement learning (RL) post-training, but this approach has not been explored for discrete diffusion LLMs (dLLMs).

Adapting existing RL algorithms like Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) or Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to dLLMs is challenging because their non-sequential generation process makes efficient computation of token-level and sequence-level log-probabilities difficult.
It was unclear if dLLMs, with their iterative denoising generation, could effectively integrate and benefit from RL signals to enhance their reasoning capabilities beyond basic language modeling.
Method: The paper introduces `d1`, a two-stage post-training framework for masked dLLMs that combines masked Supervised Finetuning (SFT) with a novel reinforcement learning algorithm.
It proposes `diffu-GRPO`, a policy gradient method specifically tailored for masked dLLMs, which utilizes an efficient one-step, prompt-masked log-probability estimation to enable online RL training.

Random prompt masking is incorporated during `diffu-GRPO`'s inner gradient updates, serving as a regularization technique that allows for more frequent updates per batch, reducing costly online generations and accelerating convergence.
Results: `diffu-GRPO` consistently outperforms the base LLaDA-8B-Instruct model across all evaluated math and planning benchmarks, showing improvements in all 12 tested setups.

The combined `d1` framework (Supervised Finetuning + `diffu-GRPO`) consistently yields the highest gains, outperforming the `diffu-GRPO`-only approach in 11 out of 12 setups, demonstrating synergistic benefits.
`d1` achieves improvements of +26.2% on Countdown and +10.0% on Sudoku, and the approach generalizes effectively to multi-task settings and coding benchmarks like HumanEval and MBPP.
Takeaways: Policy gradient-based reinforcement learning, specifically `diffu-GRPO`, can be effectively applied to large discrete diffusion language models (dLLMs) for complex reasoning tasks, challenging prior assumptions about autoregressive models' unique suitability for RL-based reasoning.

A novel one-step, prompt-masked log-probability estimation technique enables efficient online RL training for dLLMs by circumventing the computational challenges of their non-sequential generation process.

Randomized prompt masking during gradient updates acts as a strong regularization, allowing for significantly more inner optimization steps per batch and reducing the need for costly online generations, thereby improving training efficiency and stability.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.12104.Title: Logits DeConfusion with CLIP for Few-Shot Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.12104.Summary: A framework for few-shot learning enhances CLIP's performance by modeling and eliminating inter-class confusion in logits through Multi-level Adapter Fusion and Inter-Class Deconfusion modules, demonstrating improved classification accuracy across 11 benchmark datasets while maintaining CLIP's rich feature representations.
Problem: CLIP exhibits significant inter-class confusion in logits during few-shot learning tasks, limiting its ability to distinguish between similar categories
Standard few-shot learning approaches fail to fully leverage CLIP's pre-trained features while adapting to new tasks with limited data
Method: Multi-level Adapter Fusion (MAF) module combines features from different levels of CLIP's image encoder
Inter-Class Deconfusion (ICD) module learns and removes confusion patterns using visual features as prior guidance
Adaptive Logits Fusion combines MAF and ICD outputs to preserve useful features while reducing confusion
Results: Significant performance improvements on 11 benchmark datasets, particularly EuroSAT, FGVCAircraft, StanfordCars, and UCF101
Ablation studies confirm ICD module contributes most to accuracy gains
Method shows robustness on ImageNet-V2 but indicates room for improvement on tasks with large domain shifts
Takeaways: Inter-class confusion can be modeled as a learnable noise term that can be identified and removed
Combining multiple feature levels helps capture both low-level details and high-level semantics
Visual features provide effective prior guidance for identifying confusion patterns

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.11536.Title: ReTool: Reinforcement Learning for Strategic Tool Use in LLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.11536.Summary: ReTool, developed by ByteDance Seed, introduces a reinforcement learning framework that enables Large Language Models to strategically use code interpreters for complex problem-solving. It achieved 67.0% accuracy on the AIME 2024 benchmark, significantly improving performance over text-based reasoning and demonstrating emergent self-correction capabilities in code generation.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) often struggle with tasks requiring high precision, complex numerical computation, or symbolic manipulation (e.g., advanced mathematics) due to the inherent 'fuzziness' of textual reasoning.

Existing tool-integrated reasoning (TIR) methods, primarily based on supervised fine-tuning (SFT), train LLMs to imitate pre-defined tool invocation patterns, limiting their ability to adaptively decide when and how to strategically use tools.
Pure text-based reasoning can lead to compounding errors and lack of verifiable accuracy in domains requiring exact solutions.
Method: ReTool employs a two-stage training framework: an initial cold-start supervised fine-tuning (SFT) phase, followed by a reinforcement learning (RL) phase using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO).
The SFT phase utilizes automatically constructed code-integrated data (`D_CI`) to teach foundational tool invocation and output interpretation.

The core RL phase features dynamic, interleaved code execution, where the LLM generates code that is immediately run in an external sandbox, and the interpreter's output (success or error) is fed back to the model, guiding subsequent reasoning based on a simple accuracy reward.
Results: ReTool achieved 67.0% accuracy on AIME 2024 using Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, significantly outperforming the text-based RL baseline (40.0%) and other competitive baselines.
The approach demonstrated high training efficiency, reaching superior performance in only 400 training steps, compared to over 1000 steps for the text-based RL baseline.

Cognitive analysis revealed a 40% reduction in average response length (from 10k to 6k tokens), a near fivefold increase in code lines per response, and a high code pass rate (approaching 100%) in correct responses after RL training.
Takeaways: Reinforcement learning enables LLMs to develop strategic tool-use behaviors, such as increasing code invocation frequency and learning to invoke tools earlier in the reasoning process.
The model exhibits emergent meta-cognitive abilities, including autonomously self-correcting non-executable code based on real-time interpreter error feedback.
RL training promotes more diverse code utilization, moving beyond basic calculations to encompass a wider range of problem-solving purposes.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.11468.Title: SFT or RL? An Early Investigation into Training R1-Like Reasoning Large Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.11468.Summary: A comparative study examines the effectiveness of Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) versus Reinforcement Learning (RL) for training reasoning-capable vision-language models, revealing that SFT can impede subsequent RL performance by inducing superficial reasoning patterns, while direct RL training through Group Relative Policy Optimization achieves state-of-the-art performance on multimodal reasoning benchmarks.
Problem: Traditional "SFT then RL" training paradigm's effectiveness for vision-language models remains unexamined
Lack of understanding about how SFT and RL distinctly contribute to multimodal reasoning capabilities
Method: Created VLAA-Thinking dataset with carefully curated SFT and RL splits based on presence of self-reflective reasoning
Implemented mixed reward GRPO framework combining rule-based and open-ended rewards
Conducted systematic comparison of SFT, RL, and combined approaches across multiple model scales
Results: VLAA-Thinker-Qwen2.5VL-3B achieves top performance among 4B-scale models on Open LMM Reasoning Leaderboard
Models trained directly with GRPO show emergence of authentic self-reflective reasoning
SFT followed by GRPO performs worse than GRPO alone, challenging the conventional training paradigm
Takeaways: SFT can induce "pseudo reasoning paths" that hinder genuine reasoning development
Increasing SFT data volume or model size does not mitigate adverse effects
Direct RL training through GRPO consistently outperforms SFT-based approaches

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.11343.Title: A Minimalist Approach to LLM Reasoning: from Rejection Sampling to Reinforce
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.11343.Summary: The paper empirically investigates reinforcement learning algorithms for fine-tuning Large Language Models on mathematical reasoning, demonstrating that simple rejection sampling methods perform comparably to complex RL algorithms like GRPO, whose effectiveness is primarily attributed to implicit data filtering rather than its reward normalization.
Problem: Complex Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms like PPO introduce significant computational overhead and algorithmic complexity for LLM fine-tuning.
The empirical success of Gradient Regularized Policy Optimization (GRPO) in LLM training, particularly for mathematical reasoning, lacked a clear understanding of its underlying mechanisms.

Uncertainty existed regarding whether simpler, positive-only RL approaches like Reward-ranked Fine-tuning (RAFT) could effectively compete with or outperform more complex RL methods that utilize negative feedback.
Method: The authors formally analyzed and compared existing RL algorithms (RAFT, Reinforce, GRPO) and proposed RAFT++, an improved rejection sampling method.
They performed systematic ablation studies to disentangle the contributions of GRPO's components, specifically focusing on reward normalization and sample filtering.
Based on these insights, a new lightweight algorithm, Reinforce-Rej, was developed, which incorporates targeted data filtering for improved stability and performance.
Results: RAFT++ achieved 56.1% average accuracy on mathematical reasoning benchmarks for Qwen2.5-Math-7B-base, closely matching GRPO's 56.3% and outperforming iterative DPO (48.8%).

Ablation studies revealed that filtering prompts with entirely incorrect responses was the most impactful component of GRPO, leading to significant performance gains, while reward normalization had minimal effect.

The proposed Reinforce-Rej method, which filters both all-correct and all-incorrect samples, demonstrated comparable final performance to GRPO with improved KL efficiency and controlled entropy behavior.
Takeaways: Simple, positive-only fine-tuning methods (like RAFT and RAFT++) can achieve performance comparable to or better than more complex RL algorithms, challenging the necessity of negative signals.

The primary driver of GRPO's effectiveness is its implicit filtering of problematic samples (specifically, those where all generated responses are incorrect), rather than its sophisticated reward normalization.
Training on prompts where all sampled responses are incorrect ("harmful prompts") can actively degrade model performance, highlighting the importance of intelligent sample selection.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.10903.Title: Efficient Reasoning Models: A Survey
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.10903.Summary: Researchers at the National University of Singapore present a comprehensive survey that categorizes and analyzes methods to improve the computational efficiency of large language models for reasoning tasks, focusing on generating shorter reasoning chains, building smaller models, and enabling faster decoding.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) employing "slow-thinking" paradigms for complex reasoning incur substantial computational costs and memory demands.
These models often "overthink," generating unnecessarily long or redundant reasoning chains, which wastes resources and can accumulate errors.
The significant size of current reasoning models limits their practical deployment in resource-constrained environments and hinders real-time applications due to high latency.
Method: The authors introduce a goal-driven taxonomy, categorizing methods into "Shorter" for compressing lengthy reasoning chains.
Another category, "Smaller," focuses on developing compact language models that retain strong reasoning capabilities.
The "Faster" category investigates strategies for designing efficient decoding mechanisms to accelerate the inference of reasoning models.
Results: Methods for "shorter" reasoning successfully reduce Chain-of-Thought length, with latent reasoning offering high speedups and prompt engineering providing cost-effective gains.
Approaches for "smaller" models demonstrate that distillation effectively transfers reasoning capabilities, and high-bit quantization reduces memory footprint with minimal performance impact.
"Faster" decoding is achieved by optimizing Test-Time Scaling strategies and implementing adaptive compute allocation, often without requiring additional model training.
Takeaways: Diverse efficiency approaches, including reinforcement learning, supervised fine-tuning, prompt-driven strategies, and latent reasoning, are used to reduce reasoning chain length.
Knowledge distillation is a highly effective method for transferring complex reasoning abilities from large models to smaller ones, enabling more compact solutions.
A critical challenge in the field is the need for holistic evaluation metrics that can jointly capture the trade-off between reasoning performance and computational efficiency.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.10479.Title: InternVL3: Exploring Advanced Training and Test-Time Recipes for Open-Source Multimodal Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.10479.Summary: InternVL3 establishes a new native multimodal pre-training paradigm for MLLMs, allowing the model to jointly acquire visual and linguistic capabilities from the outset. This approach achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-source models, reaching 72.2 on the MMMU benchmark, and demonstrates strong competitiveness with leading proprietary models across a wide range of multimodal tasks.
Problem: Conventional Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) use a 'post-hoc' adaptation approach, adding vision to pre-trained text LLMs, which is resource-intensive and prone to alignment issues.
Existing MLLM training paradigms struggle with efficient scalability for extended multimodal contexts and balancing computational load across modalities.
Bridging the performance gap between open-source and proprietary MLLMs while maintaining strong linguistic capabilities is a challenge.
Method: Introduces a native multimodal pre-training paradigm that simultaneously acquires multimodal and linguistic capabilities from diverse data and pure-text corpora in a single, unified stage.

Integrates Variable Visual Position Encoding (V2PE) to support extended multimodal contexts and employs a two-stage post-training strategy with Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Mixed Preference Optimization (MPO).
Utilizes an optimized InternEVO training infrastructure for efficient scaling to thousands of GPUs, incorporating dynamic workload balancing for visual and textual modules.
Results: InternVL3-78B achieved a new open-source state-of-the-art score of 72.2 on the MMMU benchmark, demonstrating competitiveness with leading proprietary models like ChatGPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet.
The models showed significant improvements across diverse benchmarks, including a 7.3-point increase on MathVista (79.6%) and a 52-point increase on OCRBench (906) compared to InternVL2.5.
InternVL3 maintained and often surpassed the pure-language proficiency of text-only LLMs on benchmarks like MMLU and C-Eval, indicating that joint training does not compromise linguistic abilities.
Takeaways: Native multimodal pre-training, which jointly optimizes vision and language from scratch, is effective and comparable to or better than traditional multi-stage adaptation.
Variable Visual Position Encoding (V2PE) enhances performance across multimodal tasks by efficiently managing varied visual token densities and supporting extended contexts.
Mixed Preference Optimization (MPO) significantly improves reasoning performance by explicitly addressing the train-inference discrepancy in Chain-of-Thought reasoning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.10462.Title: The Scalability of Simplicity: Empirical Analysis of Vision-Language Learning with a Single Transformer
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.10462.Summary: A unified transformer architecture from ByteDance Seed demonstrates competitive performance with modular vision-language models while enabling more efficient scaling, achieving comparable results to ViT-22B on semantic segmentation tasks through end-to-end training without a separate vision encoder.
Problem: Current multimodal models rely on separate pre-trained vision encoders and language models, leading to fragmented processing and deployment complexity
Limited understanding of fundamental properties and scalability of single-transformer approaches for vision-language tasks
Method: Developed SAIL, a single transformer architecture based on Mistral-7B that processes both image patches and text directly
Implemented mixed attention mechanisms and two-stage pretraining to enable effective visual knowledge acquisition
Conducted comprehensive empirical analysis of scaling behavior and cross-modal information flow
Results: Achieved performance comparable to modular MLLMs on vision-language benchmarks
Matched ViT-22B performance on semantic segmentation without requiring a separate vision encoder
Demonstrated more direct vision-centric processing through higher attention scores on image tokens
Showed strong scaling potential with increased data and model size
Takeaways: Single transformers show steeper performance gains with data scaling compared to modular approaches
Mixed attention mechanism with bidirectional processing of image patches significantly improves visual representation learning
Interleaving pure text data during pretraining is crucial for maintaining language capabilities

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.10449.Title: M1: Towards Scalable Test-Time Compute with Mamba Reasoning Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.10449.Summary: M1 introduces a hybrid linear RNN reasoning model based on the Mamba architecture, addressing the scalability limitations of Transformers for complex reasoning tasks. It achieves competitive reasoning performance, demonstrates over 3x faster inference throughput than similarly sized Transformers, and effectively translates this speed into higher accuracy on mathematical benchmarks when leveraging test-time compute strategies like self-consistency.
Problem: Transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) suffer from quadratic computational complexity and linear memory requirements, hindering scalable reasoning tasks.
These limitations restrict the efficient handling of long Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning sequences and large batch sizes during inference.
There was a need to evaluate if alternative architectures, specifically Mamba, could maintain strong performance on specialized reasoning tasks compared to Transformers.
Method: A hybrid linear RNN reasoning model, M1, was developed using the Mamba architecture with 6 interleaved attention layers among its 28 total layers.

A three-stage training process was implemented: distillation from a Transformer using reverse KL divergence, followed by multi-round supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on general math and reasoning-specific datasets.
The model underwent a final reinforcement learning (RL) phase using the GRPO loss function, with adaptations to remove the KL penalty and add an entropy bonus for policy refinement.
Results: M1-3B achieved competitive reasoning scores, for instance, scoring 23.5% on AIME25 and 47.3% on OlympiadBench, often matching or slightly exceeding state-of-the-art distilled Transformer reasoning models.
The model demonstrated over a 3x speedup in inference throughput compared to a Llama-3.2-3B Transformer at large batch sizes and was at least 2x faster for long sequence generation.

Under a fixed time budget, M1 achieved comparable or higher reasoning accuracy than Transformer models by enabling a greater number of samples for self-consistency, effectively converting speed into enhanced performance.
Takeaways: Hybrid Mamba architectures can achieve reasoning performance comparable to or slightly surpassing specialized distilled Transformer models on complex mathematical benchmarks.
Mamba's memory efficiency enables significant inference speedups (over 3x at large batch sizes and 2x for long sequence generation) compared to similarly-sized Transformer models.

The increased inference throughput of Mamba models can be directly leveraged to enhance reasoning accuracy by allowing more extensive test-time compute (e.g., self-consistency voting) within the same time budget.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.10428.Title: Learning with Positive and Imperfect Unlabeled Data
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.10428.Summary: A framework from Yale University enables learning binary classifiers using positive and imperfect unlabeled data through an iterative constrained optimization approach, demonstrating polynomial-time algorithms for handling distribution shifts and corrupted data while providing theoretical guarantees based on VC-dimension bounds.
Problem: Classical Positive-Unlabeled (PU) learning assumes perfect alignment between positive and unlabeled data distributions, which is unrealistic in practice
Existing approaches fail when unlabeled data is corrupted or exhibits distribution shift
Method: Introduces Positive and Imperfect Unlabeled (PIU) Learning model that handles misaligned distributions
Develops efficient approximation algorithm using constrained L1-regression and list-decoding techniques
Solves multiple instances of Pessimistic-ERM optimization iteratively
Results: Achieves misclassification error of ε with polynomial runtime and sample complexity
Enables learning from smooth distributions using only positive samples
Provides first algorithm for detecting truncation in non-product distributions
Demonstrates applications in parameter estimation for exponential family distributions
Takeaways: Sample complexity is characterized by the VC-dimension of the hypothesis class
Distribution shifts can be handled by focusing on regions where previous iterations performed poorly
Connection to truncated statistics enables parameter estimation under unknown censoring

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.09848.Title: A Survey of Large Language Model-Powered Spatial Intelligence Across Scales: Advances in Embodied Agents, Smart Cities, and Earth Science
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.09848.Summary: A comprehensive survey from Tsinghua University examines how large language models enable spatial intelligence across three scales - embodied agents, smart cities, and Earth science applications - while establishing connections between cognitive science principles and practical implementations through a unified analytical framework.
Problem: Research on LLM-powered spatial intelligence is fragmented across different domains and scales
Lack of unified framework connecting cognitive foundations with practical applications
Need for better understanding of LLMs' capabilities and limitations in spatial tasks
Method: Developed taxonomy categorizing spatial intelligence into foundational capabilities and real-world applications
Created analytical framework connecting cognitive science principles to LLM implementations
Synthesized findings across embodied AI, urban intelligence, and Earth science domains
Results: Mapped relationships between human spatial cognition and LLM capabilities
Identified key challenges including topological reasoning errors and lack of true spatial cognition
Outlined future research directions emphasizing need for robust evaluation frameworks
Demonstrated applications across robotics, urban planning, and environmental monitoring
Takeaways: LLMs show promise in spatial memory and reasoning but still face challenges like hallucination
Interdisciplinary integration between cognitive science and AI is crucial for advancement
Current evaluation metrics are insufficient for assessing spatial intelligence holistically

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.09828.Title: FATE: A Prompt-Tuning-Based Semi-Supervised Learning Framework for Extremely Limited Labeled Data
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.09828.Summary: The FATE framework addresses semi-supervised learning with extremely limited labeled data by introducing a two-stage prompt-tuning approach for pre-trained models. It achieves an average accuracy improvement of 33.74% over state-of-the-art SSL methods, performing robustly even with just one labeled sample per class.
Problem: Existing semi-supervised learning (SSL) methods underperform when labeled data is extremely limited (e.g., 1-4 samples per class) due to insufficient discriminative features.
Generating reliable pseudo-labels for unlabeled data is difficult in label-scarce scenarios, hindering the effectiveness of traditional SSL algorithms.
Balancing pre-trained knowledge with task-specific adaptations is challenging when only a handful of labeled examples are available, leading to poor generalization or overfitting.
Method: FATE (Firstly Adapt, Then catEgorize) introduces a two-stage semi-supervised learning framework built on pre-trained models and parameter-efficient prompt tuning.
The first stage uses unsupervised learning with Distribution-adaptive Prompts (DP) to adapt the pre-trained model to the downstream data's feature distribution.
The second stage refines the model with limited labeled data using Classification Prompts (CP) and an adapted SSL method like FixMatch, keeping the pre-trained model parameters frozen.
Results: FATE achieved an average accuracy improvement of 33.74% across seven visual classification benchmarks compared to state-of-the-art SSL methods.
The framework maintained considerable accuracy with just one labeled sample per class, a scenario where other methods failed significantly.
FATE consistently outperformed CLIP's zero-shot baseline and few-shot learning methods across diverse datasets, demonstrating robust performance with varying numbers of labeled samples.
Takeaways: The two-stage prompt tuning approach, with separate adaptation (DP) and classification (CP) prompts, effectively leverages pre-trained models and unlabeled data in extremely label-scarce settings.
Parameter-efficient prompt tuning prevents overfitting to very limited labeled data while allowing the model to adapt to the downstream task's feature distribution.

Unsupervised adaptation in the first stage helps the model to better understand the feature space of the downstream task, significantly improving performance when classification prompts are introduced in the second stage.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.09819.Title: Density-based Object Detection in Crowded Scenes
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.09819.Summary: This paper from the City University of Hong Kong presents a unified framework for object detection in crowded scenes that incorporates object density information into both the training and inference processes. The approach improves anchor assignment using an unbalanced optimal transport framework and enhances post-processing with density-guided non-maximum suppression, leading to gains of up to 4.2% AP on the CrowdHuman dataset.
Problem: Heavy occlusion among objects in crowded scenes makes accurate feature extraction difficult.
Traditional anchor assignment strategies struggle to correctly associate anchors with ground truth objects when significant overlap occurs.
Standard Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) often suppresses legitimate detections in crowded areas by misclassifying them as duplicates.
Method: Introduces Density-Guided Anchors (DGA) which use a predicted multi-level density map to guide anchor assignment during training.
Develops an Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT) framework for anchor assignment, treating it as a mass distribution problem to dynamically select positive anchors.
Proposes Density-Guided NMS (DG-NMS) that adaptively adjusts the suppression threshold based on the predicted density, preserving detections in crowded regions.
Results: Achieved 91.2% AP with an FCOS backbone on the CrowdHuman dataset, representing a 3.5% improvement over the baseline.
Showed consistent performance gains on the CityPersons dataset, confirming effectiveness across different crowding levels.
Ablation studies validated the individual contributions of the Unbalanced Optimal Transport framework, the overlap-aware transport cost, and Density-Guided NMS.
Takeaways: Object density information can be effectively leveraged during both training (anchor assignment) and inference (NMS) to improve detection in crowded scenes.
Formulating anchor assignment as an Unbalanced Optimal Transport problem allows for dynamic and context-aware positive anchor selection, especially for overlapping objects.
An overlap-aware transport cost function helps distinguish an anchor's relevance to its target object amidst nearby overlapping objects.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.09130.Title: VisuoThink: Empowering LVLM Reasoning with Multimodal Tree Search
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.09130.Summary: VisuoThink introduces a framework that enhances Large Vision-Language Model reasoning by dynamically interleaving visual and textual information within a multimodal tree search, achieving up to a 21.8% accuracy improvement on geometry problem-solving benchmarks without requiring model fine-tuning.
Problem: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) struggle with complex reasoning tasks that require both visual aids and step-by-step thinking.
Existing Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting methods primarily focus on textual reasoning and do not effectively leverage visual information dynamically.
Current vision-aided reasoning approaches typically incorporate visual information in a single step, failing to capture the intricate, interleaved nature of human visual-verbal reasoning.
Method: Introduces Vision-Text Interleaved Reasoning, an iterative cycle of "Thought," "Action," and "Observation" that combines textual reasoning with dynamic visual information generated via external tools.

Implements Predictive Rollout Search, a multimodal tree search algorithm that explores multiple reasoning paths, simulates their complete outcomes, and selects the most promising one using a self-voting mechanism.
The framework operates at test-time, enhancing LVLM capabilities on complex tasks without requiring model fine-tuning.
Results: VisuoThink achieved up to 48.5% accuracy on the Geomverse-109 benchmark, demonstrating a 21.8% accuracy improvement over the state-of-the-art baseline.
Performance generally increased with longer reasoning chains (up to 40 steps), indicating the benefits of extended, interleaved reasoning.
Ablation studies confirmed that both Vision-Text Interleaved Reasoning and Predictive Rollout Search components contribute to the overall performance gains.
Takeaways: Dynamically integrating visual and textual information throughout the reasoning process, rather than in isolation or single steps, is crucial for complex multimodal reasoning.

Mimicking human "slow thinking" through a predictive rollout search enables exploring diverse reasoning paths and identifying optimal solutions, extending test-time scaling methods to visual reasoning.

There exists an optimal balance for exploration during tree search, as increasing the number of explored paths (tree width) beyond a certain point can lead to diminishing returns or performance decline.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.09037.Title: A Survey of Frontiers in LLM Reasoning: Inference Scaling, Learning to Reason, and Agentic Systems
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.09037.Summary: Researchers from Salesforce AI Research, National University of Singapore, Nanyang Technological University, and A*STAR present a comprehensive survey that introduces an orthogonal categorization framework for LLM reasoning research. The survey identifies a shift towards learning-to-reason methods and agentic systems, highlighting major trends and algorithms from Chain-of-Thought prompting to advanced training paradigms.
Problem: The rapidly accelerating and fragmented landscape of LLM reasoning research, especially since the advent of Chain-of-Thought prompting, lacks a systematic and unified understanding.
A need exists to categorize diverse reasoning methodologies and identify overarching trends to provide clarity for future research directions.
The evolving nature of LLM capabilities requires a structured review to consolidate knowledge on inference scaling, learning to reason, and agentic systems.
Method: The paper introduces a novel two-dimensional, orthogonal categorization framework that classifies LLM reasoning approaches by 'Regimes' (Inference Scaling vs. Learning to Reason) and 'Architectures' (Standalone LLM vs. Agentic Systems).
Each dimension is further examined through 'Input Level' and 'Output Level' perspectives, providing a fine-grained analysis of techniques across different reasoning paradigms.

The survey formalizes LLM reasoning within a Markov Decision Process (MDP) framework, defining key components like Reasoner, Verifier, and Refiner, and outlining common architectural patterns for agentic systems.
Results: The framework systematically maps techniques, revealing that many inference-scaling methods for trajectory collection can be repurposed for learning-to-reason, as seen in milestones like DeepSeek-R1.

The analysis details the increasing adoption of agentic systems that leverage external environments, tools, and inter-agent communication to refine perceptions and actions, thereby improving reasoning accuracy and autonomy.

The survey synthesizes the application and evolution of key learning algorithms (e.g., SFT, PPO, DPO, GRPO) and sophisticated verifier training methodologies (e.g., ORM, PRM, Generative Verifiers) as crucial for developing robust reasoning abilities and enabling cost-aware training.
Takeaways: There is an observed shift in LLM reasoning research from solely relying on inference-time prompting (inference scaling) towards dedicated training-time approaches (learning to reason) to enhance intrinsic capabilities.

Reasoning capabilities are increasingly evolving from single, static LLM operations to dynamic, interactive 'agentic systems,' encompassing both single-agent (tool-augmented) and multi-agent (collaborative) setups.
A growing trend focuses on developing highly capable, domain-specific reasoners for areas such as mathematical problem-solving, code generation, and tabular data analysis.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.08837.Title: VL-Rethinker: Incentivizing Self-Reflection of Vision-Language Models with Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.08837.Summary: VL-Rethinker enhances the multimodal reasoning capabilities of Vision-Language Models through a direct reinforcement learning approach. The work introduces Selective Sample Replay to stabilize RL training and Forced Rethinking to incentivize adaptive self-reflection, resulting in new state-of-the-art performance on various multimodal benchmarks, including MathVista and MathVerse.
Problem: Text-only 'slow-thinking' LLMs excel in complex reasoning tasks (e.g., math), but this capability does not readily transfer to multimodal reasoning in VLMs, leaving a performance gap.

Existing methods for multimodal reasoning often depend on resource-intensive, multi-stage pipelines involving supervised fine-tuning on detailed reasoning traces, often distilled from powerful teacher models.
Standard reinforcement learning for VLMs, especially with binary rewards, faces training instability due to 'vanishing advantages,' which hinders the emergence of deep, explicit reasoning patterns.
Method: The VL-Rethinker project employs a two-stage reinforcement learning methodology using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on a base instruction-tuned VLM.

Selective Sample Replay (SSR) is introduced to address the 'vanishing advantages' problem in GRPO by maintaining a replay buffer that only stores and prioritizes samples with non-zero advantage signals.

A 'Forced Rethinking' mechanism compels the model to generate self-reflection steps (e.g., 'Wait, does it seem right?'), and successful rethinking trajectories are reinforced with an additional Supervised Fine-tuning loss.
Results: VL-Rethinker-72B achieved new state-of-the-art results on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, scoring 80.4% on MathVista and 63.5% on MathVerse, outperforming OpenAI-o1 and other open-source models.
The model also set new open-source state-of-the-art on multi-disciplinary benchmarks like MMMU-Pro (55.9%) and EMMA (38.5%), narrowing the gap with proprietary models.

Ablation studies confirmed that Selective Sample Replay (SSR) effectively mitigates vanishing advantages, stabilizing training, while Forced Rethinking cultivates adaptive self-reflection, leading to a higher Pass@1 than passive prompting.
Takeaways: Vision-language models possess latent self-correction capabilities that can be activated and enhanced through targeted training.

Reinforcement learning, when properly stabilized with techniques like Selective Sample Replay, can directly incentivize complex reasoning and self-reflection in VLMs without relying on distillation from larger models or pre-generated reasoning traces.

Forcing a VLM to rethink during training, coupled with an SFT loss on successful attempts, enables the model to learn adaptive metacognitive behaviors, strategically engaging in self-correction only when necessary.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.08672.Title: Genius: A Generalizable and Purely Unsupervised Self-Training Framework For Advanced Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.08672.Summary: Genius is a purely unsupervised self-training framework designed to enhance Large Language Model reasoning without external supervision, achieving over 7% average performance improvement across seven diverse reasoning benchmarks and outperforming supervised and semi-supervised baselines by more than 2%.
Problem: Existing methods for improving LLM reasoning, such as Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) with external feedback, are limited by the high cost and scalability issues of human-annotated data or ground-truth answers.
Training external reward models for feedback is expensive and can introduce issues like "reward hacking" and difficulties in generalization.
There is a need for a framework that can enhance LLM reasoning capabilities using purely unsupervised data to address scalability bottlenecks.
Method: Introduces a purely unsupervised self-training framework with two iterative phases: response synthesis/rewarding and LLM optimization.
Employs "Stepwise Foresight Re-Sampling" which uses simulated future steps to calculate "foresight scores" for step-level self-rewarding and leverages re-sampling for exploration and exploitation.

Proposes an "Advantage-Calibrated Optimization (ACO) Loss" that adaptively scales penalties for negative self-generated examples based on their relative advantage, enhancing robustness to noisy self-supervision.
Results: Demonstrates over 7% average performance improvement on 7 diverse reasoning benchmarks, outperforming strong baselines by more than 2% using only 25K unsupervised queries.
Generalizes effectively across different LLM backbones (e.g., LLaMA3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-Instruct 3B/7B), consistently yielding superior gains.
Achieves a 6.67% performance boost on the competition-level AIME 2024 math benchmark, with ablation studies validating the core components (foresight, re-sampling, ACO loss).
Takeaways: Purely unsupervised self-training is feasible for advancing LLM reasoning, removing the reliance on expensive human annotations or explicit ground truths.

LLMs can self-evaluate intermediate reasoning steps by simulating future outcomes ("foresight"), overcoming the short-sightedness of autoregressive generation and providing more globally-aware feedback.
Robust optimization strategies, such as Advantage-Calibrated Optimization, are crucial for learning effectively from inherently noisy self-generated supervision signals.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.07951.Title: Scaling Laws for Native Multimodal Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.07951.Summary: Researchers at Apple conducted a comprehensive study on scaling laws for native multimodal models, demonstrating that early-fusion architectures trained from scratch can achieve comparable performance to late-fusion approaches while offering superior training efficiency and lower deployment costs. Integrating Mixture of Experts into these early-fusion designs further enhances performance and enables implicit specialization to different modalities.
Problem: The dominant paradigm for multimodal AI relies on 'late-fusion' architectures, integrating separately pre-trained unimodal components, whose inherent optimality for general multimodal perception is questioned.

A lack of comprehensive scaling laws for Native Multimodal Models (NMMs) limits understanding of their performance scaling with compute, parameters, and data, unlike well-established laws for unimodal LLMs.
Current late-fusion approaches involve managing multiple complex components, which can hinder overall scaling efficiency, memory usage, and practical deployment.
Method: Conducted an extensive empirical study involving 457 trained models to systematically compare 'early-fusion' and 'late-fusion' Native Multimodal Models (NMMs) trained entirely from scratch on diverse image-text data.

Extended and applied the scaling laws framework to NMMs, analyzing how validation loss scales with computational resources (FLOPs), model parameters, and training tokens across different architectural designs.

Integrated sparse Mixture of Experts (MoEs) into early-fusion NMMs, exploring both modality-agnostic and modality-aware routing to investigate their impact on performance, efficiency, and implicit modality specialization.
Results: Early-fusion NMMs consistently matched late-fusion NMMs in validation loss curves, exhibiting nearly identical compute scaling exponents (e.g., c = -0.0492 vs. c = -0.0494), but with better efficiency, especially at lower compute budgets.
Native multimodal models follow scaling laws similar to LLMs, with compute-optimal scaling achieved by roughly balancing increases in parameters and training tokens (N* ∝ C^0.526, D* ∝ C^0.473).

Sparse MoE early-fusion NMMs significantly outperformed dense models on validation loss and downstream tasks, with modality-agnostic routing proving more effective than modality-aware routing, and observed emergent modality specialization in network layers.
Takeaways: Early-fusion architectures trained from scratch yield similar validation loss scaling exponents compared to late-fusion architectures, suggesting no inherent performance advantage for late-fusion in a from-scratch training regime.

Native Multimodal Models, particularly early-fusion variants, demonstrate superior training efficiency (faster training, less memory) and more favorable parameter-to-data trade-offs for compute-optimal scaling, leading to lower inference costs.

Mixture of Experts (MoEs) significantly improve the performance of early-fusion NMMs at the same inference cost, and their experts implicitly learn to specialize in different modalities (image vs. text) without explicit modality-aware routing.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.07934.Title: SoTA with Less: MCTS-Guided Sample Selection for Data-Efficient Visual Reasoning Self-Improvement
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.07934.Summary: This research introduces ThinkLite-VL, a family of visual reasoning models that achieve state-of-the-art performance using an order of magnitude fewer training samples by leveraging Monte Carlo Tree Search for data-efficient sample selection. The models achieve 75.1% on MathVista with only 11k samples (7B model) and 79.7% with 7.5k samples (72B model), demonstrating that data quality over quantity can drive VLM self-improvement.
Problem: Existing reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) methods for vision-language models (VLMs) in reasoning tasks are often ineffective or rely on cumbersome pipelines involving knowledge distillation from larger models.
Achieving strong VLM reasoning performance typically requires very large datasets (e.g., 60k to 260k samples), which are resource-intensive and computationally expensive.
Reliably and scalably quantifying sample difficulty to identify high-quality, challenging training data for VLMs is non-trivial.
Method: The ThinkLite-VL framework re-purposes Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) as a mechanism to estimate the difficulty of visual reasoning tasks, defined by the number of MCTS iterations a VLM requires to solve them.
A small, high-quality training dataset is created by filtering 70,000 open-source samples to select those requiring more than 5 MCTS iterations or remaining unsolved after 50 iterations.

The curated, small subsets of data are used for Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RFT) with the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) loss function on base Qwen2.5-VL models, without prior supervised fine-tuning or knowledge distillation.
Results: ThinkLite-VL-7B achieved a new state-of-the-art score of 75.1% on MathVista and outperformed existing 7B-level models across six of eight visual reasoning benchmarks.
ThinkLite-VL-72B established new state-of-the-art with 79.7% on MathVista and 64.3% on MathVerse, outperforming all existing open-source VLMs across six benchmarks.
The models achieved these results using significantly fewer training samples (11k for 7B, 7.5k for 72B), an order of magnitude less than prior models, without relying on knowledge distillation.
Takeaways: Sample difficulty, specifically measured by MCTS iterations, critically influences the effectiveness of reinforcement fine-tuning for visual reasoning.
A carefully curated mix of 'unsolved' (most difficult) and 'medium-difficulty' samples, requiring more than 5 MCTS iterations, is optimal for driving VLM self-improvement.

Optimal challenging samples are model-specific; training a model with data curated for a different-sized model significantly reduces performance gains, highlighting the need for tailored data curation.
