https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.07745.Title: SF2T: Self-supervised Fragment Finetuning of Video-LLMs for Fine-Grained Understanding
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.07745.Summary: Researchers introduce Self-supervised Fragment Fine-Tuning (SF2T), a method to improve fine-grained video understanding in Video-LLMs by leveraging self-supervised tasks on video fragments, eliminating the need for manual annotations. This approach consistently boosted the performance of various Video-LLMs on fine-grained tasks, with MiniCPM-V 2.6 showing a notable improvement from 51.71% to 81.76%, and also contributes FineVidBench, a new benchmark for assessing detailed video comprehension.
Problem: Video-Language Large Language Models (Video-LLMs) struggle with fine-grained video understanding, missing subtle temporal dynamics, object interactions, and spatial changes.
Existing Video-LLMs often use sparse frame sampling, losing fine-grained temporal information, and detailed temporal annotations are resource-intensive.
Current benchmarks primarily evaluate high-level understanding, lacking specific metrics for assessing detailed spatiotemporal reasoning.
Method: Introduces Self-supervised Fragment Fine-Tuning (SF2T), which automatically generates training tasks at the video fragment level without human annotations.
SF2T utilizes five self-supervised tasks: Counting, Consistency Verification, Localization, Disorder Detection, and Rearrangement, to teach models temporal and spatial relationships.
Developed FineVidBench, a new benchmark with fragment-level and scene-level tests categorized by action types and incorporating diverse video sources and data augmentation techniques.
Results: SF2T consistently improved performance across all tested state-of-the-art Video-LLMs (LLaVA-NeXT-Video, MiniCPM-V 2.6, VideoLLaMA 2.1, Qwen2-VL), with MiniCPM-V 2.6 showing the highest gain (from 51.71% to 81.76%).
Models fine-tuned with SF2T particularly excelled in differentiating between video speeds, indicating enhanced fine-grained temporal understanding.
Ablation studies confirmed that combining long-range and short-range temporal information and using motion-salient area sampling were crucial for optimal performance.
Takeaways: Self-supervised Fragment Fine-Tuning (SF2T) effectively enhances fine-grained video understanding in Video-LLMs without requiring human annotations, leveraging automatically generated fragment-level tasks.
SF2T improves models' attention mechanisms, leading to a stronger focus on action execution areas, interacting objects, and enabling better temporal prediction.
Optimal performance relies on balancing both short-range and long-range temporal information, and using motion-salient area sampling to focus on dynamic regions.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.07615.Title: VLM-R1: A Stable and Generalizable R1-style Large Vision-Language Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.07615.Summary: VLM-R1 introduces an open-source framework that applies rule-based reinforcement learning to Vision-Language Models (VLMs), enhancing their visual reasoning and generalization abilities on tasks like Referring Expression Comprehension and Open-Vocabulary Object Detection. The approach demonstrates improved out-of-domain performance compared to supervised fine-tuning and showcases emergent reasoning behaviors.
Problem: Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) often struggle with generalization and precise visual reasoning, despite their size, frequently underperforming specialized vision models on tasks like Referring Expression Comprehension (REC) and Open-Vocabulary Object Detection (OVD).
Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) of VLMs frequently leads to memorization of training data rather than true generalization of reasoning capabilities to novel visual scenarios.
The nascent field of applying reinforcement learning (RL) to VLMs lacked a dedicated, flexible, and comprehensive framework for experimentation and in-depth analysis.
Method: Introduces VLM-R1, an open-source framework extending DeepSeek R1's rule-based reinforcement learning approach to Vision-Language Models, built for modularity and scalability.

Employs the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) algorithm with custom, rule-based reward functions designed for precise visual tasks like Referring Expression Comprehension (REC) and Open-Vocabulary Object Detection (OVD).
Developed an 'odLength' reward for OVD, which penalizes redundant predictions to counteract reward hacking and encourage precise object localization and quantity prediction.
Results: VLM-R1 achieved substantial generalization improvements on out-of-domain REC tasks (e.g., 63.14% accuracy on LISA-Grounding for the 3B model, surpassing SFT's 54.82%).

The RL model significantly outperformed SFT on OVD benchmarks (e.g., 21.1% mAP on COCO_filtered and 31.01 nms-AP on OVDEval for the 3B model), showing gains in complex categories like Position and Relationship detection.
The introduced 'odLength' reward effectively prevented reward hacking in OVD, leading to more precise outputs and an emergent 'OD aha moment' where the model explicitly plans its detections.
Takeaways: R1-style reinforcement learning enhances VLM generalization to out-of-domain visual reasoning tasks, moving beyond supervised fine-tuning's tendency for memorization.
Careful reward engineering, exemplified by the 'odLength' reward, is crucial to mitigate 'reward hacking' and align model behavior with true task objectives in visual RL.
RL can foster emergent reasoning behaviors, such as the 'OD aha moment' where the VLM spontaneously adopts a two-step thinking process for complex object detection.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.07491.Title: Kimi-VL Technical Report
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.07491.Summary: Kimi-VL is an efficient open-source Mixture-of-Experts vision-language model that achieves competitive performance across diverse multimodal tasks, often matching or exceeding larger proprietary and open-source models with only 2.8 billion activated parameters. Its "Thinking" variants enhance reasoning, while the architecture supports 128K extended context and native-resolution visual inputs.
Problem: Open-source multimodal models trail proprietary ones in scalability, computational efficiency, and advanced reasoning capabilities.
Existing open-source vision-language models often rely on computationally intensive dense architectures.
Current open-source solutions lack comprehensive support for long-context understanding and sophisticated multi-step chain-of-thought reasoning.
Method: Employ an efficient Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture for the language model, Moonlight, with only 2.8B activated parameters.
Integrate a native-resolution vision encoder, MoonViT, capable of processing diverse image resolutions up to 3.2 million pixels.
Utilize a multi-stage pre-training and post-training pipeline, including specialized long-context activation and reinforcement learning for enhanced reasoning.
Results: Kimi-VL-A3B achieves 83.1% on MMBench-EN-v1.1 and 68.7% on MathVista, often matching or surpassing larger proprietary models like GPT-4o with only 2.8 billion activated parameters.

The model demonstrates strong performance in specific domains, scoring 86.7% on OCRBench, 92.0% on ScreenSpot-V2 for agent grounding, and competitive results on long-context benchmarks like MMLongBench-Doc.
Kimi-VL-Thinking variants exhibit significant reasoning improvements, with gains such as +15.4% on MathVision, and achieve a 65.2% score on VideoMMMU, setting a new open-source state-of-the-art.
Takeaways: High performance in vision-language models is achievable with an efficient Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, significantly reducing activated parameters.
Combining native-resolution vision encoding with an extended context window (128K) is crucial for comprehensive understanding of high-detail and long-form multimodal content.
Long Chain-of-Thought (CoT) supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning effectively imbue models with robust multi-step reasoning and agent capabilities in multimodal settings.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.07213.Title: Evolutionary Machine Learning meets Self-Supervised Learning: a comprehensive survey
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.07213.Summary: This survey paper systematically reviews the growing body of literature combining Evolutionary Machine Learning (EML) and Self-Supervised Learning (SSL), formally proposing 'Evolutionary Self-Supervised Learning (E-SSL)' as a distinct sub-area. It introduces a novel taxonomy for E-SSL based on 72 identified works, highlighting the prevalence of autoencoder models in applications where EC enhances SSL and vice-versa.
Problem: A growing number of studies combine Evolutionary Machine Learning (EML) and Self-Supervised Learning (SSL), but a comprehensive review and systematization of this intersection was absent.
The complementary strengths of EML (automating design, robustness) and SSL (learning from unlabeled data) were not fully explored or formalized in a unified framework.
The lack of a structured taxonomy made it difficult to understand the diverse ways these two fields interact and to guide future research.
Method: Conducted a systematic literature review across major academic databases, using combined keywords for Evolutionary Computation and Self-Supervised Learning to identify relevant papers.
Formalized "Evolutionary Self-Supervised Learning (E-SSL)" as a new research area to provide a cohesive identity to the combined efforts of EML and SSL.
Developed a novel, structured taxonomy for E-SSL, categorizing existing works based on how evolutionary algorithms and self-supervised learning interact and the specific components they target.
Results: Identified 72 relevant papers published since 2014, demonstrating the increasing interest in combining EML and SSL.

Proposed a novel taxonomy for Evolutionary Self-Supervised Learning (E-SSL), categorizing works into two main branches: "EC for SSL" (e.g., optimizing pretext tasks, topology, learning) and "SSL for EC" (e.g., enhancing evolutionary representation, operators, fitness evaluation).

Revealed the predominance of autoencoder models in both EC for SSL (e.g., evolving AE/VAE topologies) and SSL for EC (e.g., using DAEs for evolutionary representation or mutation operators) applications.
Takeaways: Evolutionary Self-Supervised Learning (E-SSL) emerges as a distinct and rapidly growing interdisciplinary field, providing a structured approach to combining two powerful AI paradigms.
The combination offers mutual benefits: EML can automate and enhance SSL processes, while SSL can provide robust representations to improve evolutionary algorithms.
A key challenge lies in automating pretext task design and developing standardized, efficient fitness metrics that balance speed and fidelity in E-SSL evaluations.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.06608.Title: A Cross-Domain Few-Shot Learning Method Based on Domain Knowledge Mapping
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.06608.Summary: A cross-domain few-shot learning method based on domain knowledge mapping is introduced, which dynamically adjusts knowledge transfer according to domain similarity. This approach outperforms established meta-learning and cross-domain few-shot learning methods on six diverse datasets, demonstrating strong performance, especially on tasks with high domain transfer difficulty like CUB and Plantae, and showing effectiveness in industrial defect detection.
Problem: Traditional few-shot learning methods assume training and testing tasks are from the same domain (i.i.d.), which is unrealistic for cross-domain applications.
Pre-trained features from a source domain often do not align well with target domain features, hindering generalization.
Models can overfit to source domain characteristics during meta-knowledge transfer, limiting adaptability to new domains.
Method: A three-phase framework (pre-training, training, testing) is employed for structured adaptation.
A maximum mutual information-based hybrid-supervised learning approach is used in pre-training to improve feature extraction and prevent mode collapse.
A domain knowledge mapping layer and a domain classifier are introduced to dynamically adjust knowledge transfer based on domain similarity.
Results: The method consistently surpasses traditional meta-learning and existing cross-domain few-shot learning methods across various few-shot settings (5-way/2-way 1-shot and 5-shot).
It shows stronger performance on datasets with high domain transfer difficulty, such as CUB and Plantae.

Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of each component: hybrid-supervised pre-training enhances fine-grained feature extraction, domain knowledge mapping separates task-relevant features, and dynamic weighting optimizes knowledge transfer.
Takeaways: Maximizing mutual information during pre-training helps generate robust features, preventing category mode collapse and improving fine-grained feature extraction for cross-domain generalization.
Dynamically adjusting knowledge transfer based on domain similarity allows the model to efficiently leverage source domain information while adapting to new target domains.
Generating a pseudo-unseen domain and training a domain classifier enables the model to estimate domain similarity and guide the knowledge mapping process effectively.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.06389.Title: SemiDAViL: Semi-supervised Domain Adaptation with Vision-Language Guidance for Semantic Segmentation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.06389.Summary: Researchers at Stony Brook University developed SemiDAViL, the first language-guided semi-supervised domain adaptation framework for semantic segmentation. It leverages Vision-Language Models for rich semantic priors and introduces a dynamic class-balancing loss, achieving up to 71.1% mIoU on GTA5→Cityscapes with minimal target labels and improving minority class segmentation.
Problem: Semantic segmentation faces high annotation costs for dense pixel-wise labels and experiences significant performance degradation when models encounter domain shifts.

Existing semi-supervised domain adaptation (SSDA) methods for semantic segmentation struggle with class confusion due to limited target supervision and over-prioritize source features, leading to noisy pseudo-labels.
Real-world datasets for semantic segmentation exhibit severe class imbalance, resulting in poor performance for underrepresented minority classes.
Method: Initializes student-teacher segmentation encoders with pre-trained vision encoders from Vision-Language Models (VLMs) like CLIP to transfer rich semantic priors.
Introduces a Dense Language Guidance (DLG) module that fuses visual and language embeddings through a balanced attention mechanism, providing pixel-level language guidance.
Employs a Dynamic Cross-Entropy (DyCE) loss that reweights minority classes based on real-time batch statistics, ensuring equitable learning across all classes and addressing class imbalance.
Results: Achieved 71.1% mIoU on GTA5→Cityscapes with only 100 labeled target samples, surpassing previous state-of-the-art by 1.6%.
Showed consistent improvements across SYNTHIA→Cityscapes and a 5% mIoU gain in a zero-shot domain adaptation setting (67.7% mIoU) without any target labels.

Demonstrated significant mIoU improvements for minority classes through the DyCE loss (+8.8% over consistency training) and VLM pre-training (+11.1% mIoU), improving segmentation quality for rare objects like 'Rider' and 'Motorcycle'.
Takeaways: Leveraging Vision-Language Models (VLMs) like CLIP can provide rich semantic priors that significantly improve feature extraction and semantic differentiation for ambiguous classes, even at a pixel-level.

Balanced fusion of visual and language features via a Dense Language Guidance (DLG) module is crucial for robust multimodal understanding in dense prediction tasks, preventing single-modality dominance.

Dynamically reweighting loss for minority classes based on real-time batch statistics (Dynamic Cross-Entropy loss) can effectively mitigate the severe class imbalance problem common in real-world semantic segmentation datasets.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.06256.Title: Transfer between Modalities with MetaQueries
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.06256.Summary: Meta and NYU researchers introduce MetaQueries, a framework that bridges frozen multimodal language models (MLLMs) with diffusion models using learnable query tokens, enabling high-quality image generation while preserving the MLLMs' understanding capabilities and requiring only image-caption paired data for training.
Problem: Existing unified multimodal models require complex training procedures and often compromise between understanding and generation capabilities
Difficulty in leveraging pre-trained MLLMs' knowledge and reasoning abilities for image generation without extensive fine-tuning
Method: Introduced MetaQueries as learnable query tokens that extract multimodal conditions from frozen MLLMs
Developed a trainable connector to align MLLM's latent space with diffusion model's input space
Created a novel data curation pipeline for instruction-tuning using naturally occurring image pairs
Results: Achieved state-of-the-art performance in both multimodal understanding and generation tasks
Successfully demonstrated complex image manipulation including reconstruction, editing, and subject-driven generation
Enabled advanced multimodal generation without sacrificing MLLM's understanding capabilities
Showed effective knowledge transfer through complex prompt handling requiring real-world understanding
Takeaways: Freezing the MLLM preserves its pre-trained understanding capabilities while enabling strong generative performance
MetaQueries can effectively transfer MLLM's reasoning and knowledge to image generation tasks
Simple image-caption paired data and standard diffusion objectives are sufficient for training

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.06120.Title: Hyperbolic Category Discovery
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.06120.Summary: The Hyperbolic Category Discovery (HypCD) framework from the Visual AI Lab at the University of Hong Kong addresses generalized category discovery by embedding image features into hyperbolic space. This approach, which is compatible with existing parametric and non-parametric methods, improves classification accuracy and better transfers knowledge to novel categories by naturally representing hierarchical relationships in data.
Problem: Classifying images in datasets that contain both labeled data from known categories and unlabeled data which may include both known and novel categories (Generalized Category Discovery, GCD).
Traditional GCD methods operating in Euclidean or spherical spaces are limited in their ability to effectively represent and leverage hierarchical relationships between object categories.
Existing approaches often exhibit a significant performance gap in classifying known versus novel categories, indicating challenges in transferring knowledge to unseen classes.
Method: Introduces the Hyperbolic Category Discovery (HypCD) framework, which maps image features from a pre-trained encoder into hyperbolic space (Poincaré ball model) using exponential mapping.
Implements hyperbolic representation learning via contrastive loss functions that combine hyperbolic distance-based and angle-based terms to encourage distinct clustering.

Integrates a Hyperbolic Feed-Forward Network for parametric classification or utilizes semi-supervised k-means clustering in hyperbolic space for non-parametric category discovery, making the framework compatible with various GCD methods.
Results: Achieved consistent improvements in overall classification accuracy across standard GCD benchmarks including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet-100, and the Semi-Supervised Benchmark (SSB) when integrated with existing baseline methods.
Reduced the accuracy gap between known and unknown categories, demonstrating better knowledge transfer and improved performance on novel classes.
Produced more distinct and tightly clustered groups for categories in t-SNE visualizations compared to Euclidean approaches, indicating more effective feature separation.
Takeaways: Hyperbolic spaces, due to their exponential volume growth, are naturally well-suited for embedding hierarchical data structures like those found in object categories and their parts.

Representing image features in hyperbolic space enables more effective capture of hierarchical relationships, which in turn facilitates better knowledge transfer from known to unknown categories in Generalized Category Discovery (GCD).

Utilizing a combination of hyperbolic distance-based and angle-based losses within a contrastive learning framework enhances the learning of discriminative and clustered features in hyperbolic geometry.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.05786.Title: How to Enable LLM with 3D Capacity? A Survey of Spatial Reasoning in LLM
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.05786.Summary: Researchers from Tsinghua University and HKUST-GZ present a comprehensive survey of methods for enabling spatial reasoning in Large Language Models (LLMs), organizing approaches into image-based, point cloud-based, and hybrid modalities while analyzing current limitations and future directions for integrating 3D understanding capabilities.
Problem: LLMs lack inherent ability to understand and reason about 3D spatial information
Fundamental mismatch between sequential text processing and continuous 3D spatial structures
Scarcity of high-quality 3D datasets compared to text corpora
Method: Systematic categorization of approaches based on input modality (image, point cloud, hybrid)
Analysis of different alignment strategies for connecting language and 3D data
Review of architectural modifications and training strategies for spatial reasoning
Results: Comprehensive taxonomy for understanding diverse approaches to 3D-capable LLMs
Identification of key technical challenges across different modalities
Analysis of current limitations in dataset quality, computation, and cross-scene generalization
Roadmap of future research directions in perception, fusion, and real-world applications
Takeaways: Image-based methods offer data availability advantages but struggle with depth perception
Point cloud approaches provide better geometric fidelity but face computational challenges
Hybrid methods can leverage complementary strengths through careful architectural design
Three main alignment strategies emerge: direct, step-by-step, and task-specific

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.05520.Title: Efficient Reinforcement Finetuning via Adaptive Curriculum Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.05520.Summary: Researchers at USC and the University of Maryland developed ADARFT, a method that uses adaptive curriculum learning to improve the efficiency and accuracy of Reinforcement Finetuning (RFT) for Large Language Models (LLMs) in mathematical reasoning tasks. The system dynamically adjusts problem difficulty based on the model's performance, leading to up to 2x faster training convergence and consistent final accuracy improvements across various models and data distributions.
Problem: Reinforcement Finetuning (RFT) for LLMs is sample-inefficient and computationally expensive, requiring extensive resources and training time.
Existing RFT methods struggle with non-uniform or imbalanced data distributions, leading to suboptimal learning when problems are too easy or too hard.
Current curriculum learning approaches for RFT are either manually staged and lack adaptivity or incur significant online rollout overhead for data filtering.
Method: ADARFT employs a dynamic curriculum learning strategy that adjusts training problem difficulty based on the model's recent reward signals, sampling problems closest to a 'target difficulty'.
It theoretically justifies setting the target success rate (beta) at 0.5, maximizing the learning signal by focusing on problems where the model experiences a productive struggle.

Difficulty scores are estimated using rollout-based empirical methods, pre-existing labels (AoPS), or lightweight LLM-judged assessments, making it flexible and generalizable as a 'plug-and-play' extension for various RFT algorithms.
Results: ADARFT reduced training steps by up to 2x (e.g., Qwen 2.5 Math 1.5B in `skew-difficult` setting, requiring 71.7% fewer steps than standard PPO to reach comparable performance).
It consistently achieved higher final accuracy, with gains up to 3.91 percentage points (e.g., Qwen 2.5 Math 1.5B in `uniform` setting, from 37.20% to 41.11%).
The approach maintained effectiveness even when using lightweight LLM-judged difficulty scores, demonstrating practicality without requiring extensive rollouts for difficulty estimation.
Takeaways: Training on problems where the model has approximately a 50% chance of success (target reward β=0.5) maximizes the learning signal, leading to the strongest policy updates and highest accuracy.

A dynamically adjusted curriculum, as opposed to static or online filtering methods, significantly improves both training efficiency and final model performance, especially in imbalanced data scenarios.
ADARFT's lightweight and algorithm-agnostic design allows it to seamlessly integrate with and enhance existing RFT algorithms (e.g., PPO, REINFORCE++, GRPO) without specific modifications.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.05299.Title: SmolVLM: Redefining small and efficient multimodal models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.05299.Summary: Hugging Face and Stanford researchers develop SmolVLM, a family of compact multimodal models that process both images and videos while requiring less than 1GB of GPU memory for the smallest 256M parameter variant, achieving competitive performance through optimized architecture design and training strategies that specifically target resource-constrained environments.
Problem: Large vision-language models (VLMs) require significant computational resources, limiting their deployment on mobile and edge devices
Simply scaling down existing architectures leads to inefficient small models with degraded performance
Method: Systematically explore architectural choices and training strategies optimized for compact models
Balance parameter allocation between vision encoder and language model components
Employ aggressive visual token compression and learned positional tokens
Optimize context length and training data composition for small-scale models
Results: SmolVLM-256M achieves competitive performance while using <1GB GPU memory
SmolVLM-2.2B rivals state-of-the-art VLMs with significantly lower resource usage
Models demonstrate strong generalization to video tasks without architecture modifications
Successful deployment on consumer hardware enables practical on-device applications
Takeaways: Smaller language models benefit less from larger vision encoders while larger models gain more from powerful encoders
Image splitting enhances performance for vision tasks but video frame averaging degrades results
System prompts and media tokens significantly improve compact VLM performance
Excessive chain-of-thought data harms compact model performance

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.05118.Title: VAPO: Efficient and Reliable Reinforcement Learning for Advanced Reasoning Tasks
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.05118.Summary: VAPO introduces a value-model-based reinforcement learning framework that reliably enhances large language model performance on advanced Chain-of-Thought reasoning tasks. The framework achieves a new state-of-the-art score of 60.4 on the AIME 2024 dataset using Qwen2.5-32B, outperforming previous value-model-free methods by over 10 points while demonstrating exceptional training efficiency.
Problem: Value models for long Chain-of-Thought (CoT) sequences suffer from positive bias due to objective mismatch and exponential decay of reward signals for earlier tokens.
Heterogeneous sequence lengths in reasoning tasks lead to suboptimal fixed lambda parameters in GAE, causing high variance in short sequences and high bias in long sequences.
Verifier-based reward models provide sparse, end-of-sequence feedback, creating difficult exploration-exploitation dilemmas and reducing the efficiency of positive sample utilization.
Method: Mitigates value model bias over long sequences through Value-Pretraining and Decoupled-GAE, using a lambda of 1.0 for value updates for unbiased gradient descent.

Manages heterogeneous sequence lengths by introducing Length-Adaptive GAE that dynamically adjusts the policy's lambda based on sequence length, and uses Token-Level Policy Gradient Loss for uniform token weighting.

Addresses reward signal sparsity via Clip-Higher (modifying PPO clipping range), Positive Example LM Loss (imitating successful trajectories), and Group-Sampling (generating richer contrastive signals).
Results: Achieved a state-of-the-art score of 60.4 on the AIME 2024 dataset with Qwen2.5-32B, outperforming DeepSeek-R1-Zero-Qwen-32B (47 points) by over 13 points and DAPO (50 points) by over 10 points.
Demonstrated exceptional training efficiency, reaching state-of-the-art performance within 5,000 steps, matching DAPO's performance using only 60% of its training steps.

Exhibited high training reliability with no observed training crashes and consistently similar peak scores (60-61) across multiple independent runs, a notable improvement over vanilla PPO which collapsed.
Takeaways: Value-model-based reinforcement learning can outperform value-model-free methods in complex, long Chain-of-Thought reasoning tasks by systematically addressing biases, variance, and sparse reward challenges.

A robust RL system for large language models benefits from the synergistic integration of multiple technical modifications, with components like proper value initialization and adaptive credit assignment being crucial for stability and performance.
Significant training efficiency and reliability improvements are achievable in large-scale RL for LLMs, leading to reduced computational costs and more predictable experimental outcomes.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.04736.Title: Synthetic Data Generation & Multi-Step RL for Reasoning & Tool Use
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.04736.Summary: SWiRL is an offline multi-step reinforcement learning methodology designed to enhance Large Language Models' reasoning and tool-use capabilities. It generates and utilizes synthetic data, applying process-based filtering for step-wise optimization, which leads to substantial performance gains and strong cross-domain generalization in complex tasks.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) often struggle with complex queries requiring multi-step reasoning and strategic interaction with external tools.
Traditional reinforcement learning (RL) methods for LLMs provide sparse, single-step reward signals, which are insufficient for training models on long, sequential reasoning tasks.
Existing multi-step optimization approaches for LLMs frequently lack integrated tool use or rely on outcome-based filtering of data, limiting their ability to learn robust intermediate processes.
Method: SWiRL (Step-Wise Reinforcement Learning) introduces an offline multi-step optimization technique that leverages synthetic data generation with iterative tool execution.

The methodology employs a generative reward model to provide a granular, step-wise reward signal, evaluating the quality and reasonableness of each individual action within its specific sub-trajectory context.
It explores and prioritizes process-based filtering of synthetic trajectories, retaining data based on the soundness of intermediate steps rather than solely on the correctness of the final outcome.
Results: SWiRL achieved significant relative accuracy improvements of 21.5% on GSM8K, 12.3% on HotPotQA, 14.8% on CofCA, 11.1% on MuSiQue, and 15.3% on BeerQA.
Training SWiRL on HotPotQA improved zero-shot GSM8K performance by a relative 16.9%, while GSM8K training improved HotPotQA by 9.2%, demonstrating strong cross-domain and cross-tool transferability.

SWiRL-finetuned Gemma-2-27b models outperformed their base counterparts and, in several cases, even the stronger Gemini 1.5 Pro reward model on out-of-distribution benchmarks, indicating active learning beyond distillation.
Takeaways: Process-based filtering of synthetic data, which evaluates the reasonableness of each intermediate step, is more effective for multi-step reinforcement learning than filtering based on the final outcome.

SWiRL demonstrates robust generalization capabilities, improving performance across different multi-step tasks (e.g., question answering to mathematical reasoning) and tool types (e.g., search to calculator) even when trained on a single domain.

The method can effectively learn from trajectories with logically sound intermediate steps, even if the final answer is incorrect, showcasing a deeper learning of reasoning processes compared to Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT).

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.03151.Title: Why Reasoning Matters? A Survey of Advancements in Multimodal Reasoning (v1)
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.03151.Summary: A survey from the University of Rochester and collaborating institutions organizes and analyzes current advancements in reasoning for both textual and multimodal large language models. It presents a systematic framework for understanding and enhancing reasoning capabilities, categorizing methods into post-training optimizations and test-time inference strategies, and integrating insights from cognitive science.
Problem: Extending advanced reasoning capabilities from text-based LLMs to multimodal contexts introduces new complexities for integrating diverse information.
Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle with coherently integrating diverse inputs, resolving ambiguities, handling inconsistencies, and filling information gaps between modalities.

Developing robust reasoning is essential for MLLMs to achieve compositional understanding, error correction, hallucination reduction, and hypothetical scenario analysis, which are crucial for human-like AI.
Method: The survey systematically categorizes reasoning techniques for LLMs and MLLMs into 'post-training improvements' (optimizing model policy) and 'test-time compute' (improving inference with a fixed policy).
It provides a comprehensive review of existing methodologies, including architectural innovations, search strategies, adaptive inference, and reward/feedback mechanisms.

The work also reviews relevant datasets and benchmarks, and uniquely draws connections between Chain-of-Thought reasoning and established cognitive science theories to provide deeper theoretical grounding.
Results: The analysis reveals that while textual reasoning in LLMs has progressed, the multimodal domain presents unique complexities and limitations, especially in tasks requiring temporal, spatial, and counterfactual understanding.

The survey identifies specific research gaps and opportunities, such as the need for more vision-focused reward signals and verifiers, and improved benchmarks that challenge MLLMs in areas where they currently show significant performance disparities compared to humans.

It establishes that AI reasoning strategies like Chain-of-Thought align with established cognitive science theories, providing a theoretical foundation for developing more interpretable, reliable, and human-like AI systems.
Takeaways: Reasoning in MLLMs is moving towards structured, step-by-step processes, often using iterative refinement and self-correction, as enumerating all possible reasoning paths is intractable.
Policy optimization via reinforcement learning and imitation learning, coupled with fine-grained reward alignment, is crucial for developing human-like reasoning processes in MLLMs.

Effective multimodal reasoning benefits from architectural innovations that improve visual attention and computational efficiency, dynamic spatial-temporal modeling, and adaptive inference strategies during test time.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.02495.Title: Inference-Time Scaling for Generalist Reward Modeling
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.02495.Summary: DeepSeek-AI and Tsinghua University developed Self-Principled Critique Tuning (SPCT) and DeepSeek-GRM models, a pointwise generative reward modeling approach that achieves state-of-the-art performance in generalist reward benchmarks. This method demonstrates effective inference-time scalability, allowing smaller models to match or exceed the performance of much larger models by leveraging increased compute during inference, thereby improving LLM alignment.
Problem: Existing Reward Models (RMs) often lack generalizability and flexibility, struggling with diverse "general queries" where reward criteria are complex and lack explicit references.
There is limited potential for RMs to improve quality by scaling inference-time compute (e.g., through multiple samplings), particularly for scalar RMs which lack diverse outputs.
Traditional RM approaches, like pairwise scoring, restrict input flexibility, making it challenging to uniformly evaluate single, paired, or multiple responses.
Method: Developed Pointwise Generative Reward Modeling (GRM) to output textual critiques and numerical scores, ensuring input flexibility for single, paired, or multiple responses.
Introduced Self-Principled Critique Tuning (SPCT), a two-phase learning method (Rejective Fine-Tuning and Rule-Based Online RL) that trains GRMs to generate adaptive principles and critiques.

Implemented inference-time scaling strategies, including Voting with Parallel Sampling and Meta Reward Model Guided Voting, to leverage increased compute for finer-grained and more robust reward signals.
Results: DeepSeek-GRM-27B, trained with SPCT, achieves leading performance on various RM benchmarks, often outperforming or matching larger, state-of-the-art models like Nemotron-4-340B-Reward and GPT-4o.

The DeepSeek-GRM models show a substantial performance increase (e.g., highest gain over greedy decoding with 8 samples) and significantly reduced domain biases through inference-time scaling with parallel sampling.

Meta Reward Modeling further enhances accuracy by filtering low-quality sampled critiques, enabling DeepSeek-GRM-27B with MetaRM-guided voting to achieve results better than a 671B MoE model (DeepSeek-V3) on specific benchmarks.
Takeaways: Proper learning methods, such as SPCT, can instill "scalable behaviors" in RMs, enabling them to consistently generate higher-quality reward signals with increased inference compute.
Pointwise generative reward modeling inherently allows for input flexibility and diverse outputs, crucial for effective sampling-based inference-time scaling across general domains.

Inference-time scaling with a well-trained GRM can achieve performance comparable to or better than traditional training-time scaling (larger model sizes), offering a more compute-efficient path to high-quality RMs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.01990.Title: Advances and Challenges in Foundation Agents: From Brain-Inspired Intelligence to Evolutionary, Collaborative, and Safe Systems
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.01990.Summary: A comprehensive, brain-inspired framework integrates diverse research areas of LLM-based intelligent agents, encompassing individual architecture, collaborative systems, and safety. The framework formally conceptualizes agent components, maps AI capabilities to human cognition to identify research gaps, and outlines a roadmap for developing autonomous, adaptive, and safe AI.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) provide powerful 'engines' for AI, but integrating them into truly intelligent, autonomous agents with human-like cognitive functions remains a complex challenge.
A lack of comprehensive, brain-inspired frameworks existed to holistically conceptualize LLM-based agents, which should include modular architectures for memory, planning, and safe interaction.

The long-standing quest for 'truly intelligent' systems that can learn, plan, reason, sense, communicate, act, remember, and demonstrate various human-like abilities highlights an unfulfilled need for a unified approach.
Method: Proposed a 'Foundation Agent' framework formalizing autonomous, adaptive systems capable of multimodal perception, cognitive adaptation, reasoning, action, and collaboration.

Established a modular 'Perception–Cognition–Action' loop, deeply decomposing cognition into interconnected modules like memory, world model, emotional state, goals, and reward, inspired by human brain functions.

Systematically reviewed and synthesized existing research across individual agent architecture, self-enhancement, multi-agent collaboration, and safety, using a detailed taxonomy and a brain-AI comparison.
Results: Established a formal 'Foundation Agent' definition and a 'Foundation MAS Loop,' providing a structured knowledge base for understanding LLM-based agents and their collective intelligence.

Identified and categorized critical research gaps by mapping AI agent capabilities to human brain functions, designating areas like general working memory and intrinsic motivation as 'underexplored (L3)'.
Detailed intrinsic and extrinsic safety threats for AI agents and proposed superalignment, a 'Safety Scaling Law,' and the 'AI-45° Rule' for developing beneficial and trustworthy AI systems.
Takeaways: Current LLM-based agents possess strengths in specific perceptual and language tasks but exhibit significant gaps in robust working memory, cognitive flexibility, episodic memory, and intrinsic motivation compared to human cognition.

The development of truly intelligent, autonomous, and safe agents necessitates a deep integration of cognitive principles with advanced computational architectures, spanning individual, collaborative, and ethical dimensions.
A critical challenge for agent learning is the lack of sophisticated internal reward systems that drive active, exploratory learning and continuous adaptation, mirroring human intrinsic motivation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.01805.Title: SpaceR: Reinforcing MLLMs in Video Spatial Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.01805.Summary: SpaceR introduces a framework for improving Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) in video spatial reasoning, achieving state-of-the-art performance on benchmarks such as VSI-Bench by surpassing GPT-4o by 11.6% accuracy. This advancement is facilitated by a novel, large-scale dataset, SpaceR-151k, and a training approach called Spatially-Guided Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Reward (SG-RLVR), which includes a map imagination mechanism.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle with inferring and reconstructing underlying 3D spatial layouts and relationships from sequences of 2D video frames.
There is a scarcity of high-quality, verifiable training datasets specifically designed to foster and evaluate spatial reasoning in MLLMs.
Current training strategies, primarily Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), are often insufficient for cultivating deep, abstract reasoning capabilities in MLLMs.
Method: Created `SpaceR-151k`, a novel large-scale dataset (151,310 samples) tailored for video spatial reasoning, including 91k verifiable spatial reasoning QA pairs derived from 3D scene data and 60k general video understanding samples.
Developed `Spatially-Guided Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Reward (SG-RLVR)`, which extends the GRPO algorithm with specialized mechanisms and reward functions for spatial reasoning.

Introduced a `map imagination mechanism` that guides the MLLM to explicitly generate a cognitive map of object distributions and positions, and a `Map Reward` to quantitatively evaluate its accuracy, encouraging spatial thinking.
Results: SpaceR achieves state-of-the-art performance on spatial reasoning benchmarks, scoring 45.6% accuracy on VSI-Bench and surpassing GPT-4o by 11.6% accuracy.

The SG-RLVR training paradigm consistently improves performance across all evaluated spatial reasoning and general video understanding benchmarks (VSI-Bench, STI-Bench, SPAR-Bench, Video-MME, TempCompass, LongVideoBench), demonstrating superior generalizability compared to SFT.

Ablation studies confirm the critical contribution of the `SpaceR-151k` dataset, particularly its spatial reasoning component, and the `map imagination mechanism` for enhancing spatial reasoning and overall video understanding.
Takeaways: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Reward (SG-RLVR) significantly outperforms Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) in fostering generalizable reasoning capabilities in MLLMs, especially for complex tasks like spatial understanding.

Explicitly guiding MLLMs to generate cognitive maps during their reasoning process, coupled with a reward for map accuracy, effectively enhances their ability to infer and represent 3D spatial layouts from video.

The creation of a large-scale, high-quality dataset specifically designed for spatial reasoning, derived from 3D scene reconstructions, is crucial for training MLLMs in this advanced cognitive ability.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.01017.Title: Scaling Language-Free Visual Representation Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.01017.Summary: Meta AI and academic researchers demonstrate that scaled self-supervised visual learning achieves comparable performance to language-supervised methods like CLIP across multimodal tasks, training models up to 7B parameters on 2 billion images while matching or exceeding CLIP's capabilities in visual question answering and OCR tasks without requiring text supervision.
Problem: Language-supervised models like CLIP dominate multimodal tasks, with an assumption that language supervision is necessary for strong performance
Previous visual self-supervised learning methods showed limitations in tasks requiring language understanding like OCR and chart interpretation
Method: Train large-scale self-supervised visual models (Web-SSL) on the same dataset used for CLIP training
Scale both model size (up to 7B parameters) and training data (2B images) while using DINOv2 and MAE architectures
Results: Web-SSL models match or exceed CLIP performance on 16 VQA tasks spanning general, knowledge, OCR, and vision-centric categories
Models maintain strong performance on traditional computer vision benchmarks while improving at language-related tasks
Higher resolution training (518x518) enables Web-DINO to bridge performance gaps with high-resolution CLIP variants
Natural alignment develops between vision models and LLMs as scale increases, without explicit language supervision
Takeaways: Visual self-supervised learning can naturally develop text-sensitive features and align with language models without explicit language supervision
Model and data scaling enables SSL to match CLIP's performance across general vision and language-heavy tasks
Training data composition, particularly the ratio of text-containing images, significantly impacts OCR capabilities

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.00883.Title: Improved Visual-Spatial Reasoning via R1-Zero-Like Training
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.00883.Summary: Researchers at Shanghai Jiao Tong University and OPPO AI Center developed an R1-Zero-like training approach using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to enhance video-based visual-spatial reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models. Their 2B parameter model, trained with just 120 GPU hours, surpassed GPT-4o's performance on the VSI-bench, demonstrating improved efficiency and efficacy in this domain.
Problem: Small- to medium-sized Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) exhibit limited visual-spatial reasoning, especially for video-based understanding.
Standard Chain of Thought (CoT) prompting strategies fail to activate reasoning capabilities in these MLLMs.
There is a scarcity of high-quality, large-scale training data specifically designed for visual-spatial question answering.
Method: Created VSI-100k, a large-scale video-based visual-spatial question-answering dataset derived from ScanNet's 3D annotations.
Applied Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), a critic-free reinforcement learning technique, to fine-tune MLLMs for visual-spatial reasoning.
Utilized a carefully designed reward mechanism within GRPO, incorporating both format and accuracy rewards to guide the training process.
Results: GRPO-trained models achieved substantial improvements in visual-spatial reasoning, with vsGRPO-2B outperforming GPT-4o on VSI-bench and vsGRPO-7B rivalling LLaVA-NeXT-Video-72B.
GRPO training successfully enabled and improved Chain of Thought (CoT) capabilities in MLLMs where prompting alone was previously ineffective.
The trained models demonstrated improved performance and some inter-task generalization on held-out visual-spatial reasoning topics like Route Planning.
Takeaways: Chain of Thought prompting alone is insufficient to activate visual-spatial reasoning in smaller MLLMs, indicating a need for direct training.
For visual-spatial reasoning, a vanilla-mode (direct answering) GRPO training approach can be more effective than explicit CoT-based training for the tested model sizes.
A small KL penalty term is essential for stabilizing Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) training and preventing model collapse.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.00595.Title: Open-Qwen2VL: Compute-Efficient Pre-Training of Fully-Open Multimodal LLMs on Academic Resources
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.00595.Summary: Open-Qwen2VL presents a 2B-parameter multimodal LLM pre-trained using 220 A100-40G GPU hours, which outperforms Qwen2-VL-2B on several benchmarks. The project provides a fully open-source training pipeline, data filtering techniques, and pre-training data to promote reproducibility and accessibility.
Problem: State-of-the-art Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) developed by major tech companies are often only partially open, with critical training details (data filtering, mixture strategies, codebases) remaining undisclosed, hindering reproducibility.
Pre-training SOTA MLLMs requires vast computational resources, creating a significant barrier for academic institutions and smaller research groups with limited GPU access.
The lack of transparency in MLLM pre-training pipelines makes it difficult for the community to understand underlying mechanisms or build upon advancements effectively.
Method: Developed a 2B-parameter MLLM (Open-Qwen2VL) using a Qwen2.5-1.5B LLM backbone and a SigLIP-SO-400M vision encoder, employing a low-to-high dynamic image resolution strategy for efficiency.

Employed a rigorous data strategy including MLLM-based data filtering (MLM-Filter) to curate high-quality multimodal caption data and multimodal sequence packing to maximize context window utilization.
Released a fully open-source training codebase, detailed data filtering techniques, and all pre-training and supervised fine-tuning data to ensure full reproducibility and community access.
Results: Open-Qwen2VL was pre-trained using only 220 A100-40G GPU hours, representing 0.36% of the multimodal pre-training tokens used by Qwen2-VL.
The instruction-tuned Open-Qwen2VL outperforms Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct on several multimodal benchmarks, including MMBench, SEEDBench-img, MMStar, and MathVista.
Multimodal sequence packing significantly improved few-shot multimodal in-context learning, yielding +3% to +12% performance improvements on VQA datasets compared to 0-shot reasoning.
Takeaways: MLLM-based data filtering (MLM-Filter) introduces beneficial, diverse data distributions that complement conventional CLIP-filtered data, leading to improved performance.
Low-to-high dynamic image resolution and multimodal sequence packing significantly enhance pre-training efficiency and improve multi-image in-context learning capabilities.
Achieving competitive MLLM pre-training and performance is feasible with academic-level computing resources (e.g., 8x A100-40G GPUs) when employing compute-efficient methodologies.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.00557.Title: Efficient LLaMA-3.2-Vision by Trimming Cross-attended Visual Features
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.00557.Summary: Nota Inc. researchers introduce Trimmed Llama, a training-free method that reduces inference costs in cross-attention vision-language models by identifying and pruning redundant visual features, achieving equivalent performance while using only 50% of image features and significantly reducing KV cache memory requirements, especially at larger batch sizes.
Problem: Cross-attention based vision-language models face computational bottlenecks due to large key-value caches from visual tokens
Existing optimization approaches focus mainly on self-attention architectures, leaving cross-attention efficiency relatively unexplored
Method: Analyze cross-attention patterns to identify consistently important visual features across attention heads
Develop training-free pruning method that selectively keeps top-k salient features based on attention scores
Adaptively allocate pruning ratios based on task requirements
Results: Maintains model performance while using only 50% of image features
Reduces KV cache memory requirements, with benefits scaling with batch size
Successfully preserves task-critical visual information like text cues and key objects
Demonstrates effectiveness across multiple benchmarks including MMVP, MME, and SEED-Bench
Takeaways: Cross-attention mechanisms show structured patterns with early convergence and selective focus
Different vision-language tasks require varying levels of visual feature preservation
Attention-based feature selection outperforms random and spatial sampling approaches

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.24290.Title: Open-Reasoner-Zero: An Open Source Approach to Scaling Up Reinforcement Learning on the Base Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.24290.Summary: This research from StepFun and Tsinghua University presents Open-Reasoner-Zero (ORZ), the first comprehensive open-source implementation for scaling reinforcement learning directly on base large language models for reasoning tasks. ORZ demonstrates that a minimalist PPO setup, utilizing specific GAE parameters and no KL regularization, can achieve state-of-the-art reasoning performance while requiring significantly fewer training steps than comparable methods.
Problem: Previous work demonstrated a 'scaling phenomenon' in RL training for LLMs on reasoning tasks, where performance consistently improved with more computation, but the precise methodologies and open-source implementations were lacking.

Most RLHF pipelines for LLMs begin with instruction-tuned models, leaving an open question about the feasibility and effectiveness of directly applying large-scale RL to base models for diverse reasoning skills.

The complexity and instability often associated with large-scale reinforcement learning, particularly the tuning of regularization terms like KL divergence, posed a challenge for broader accessibility and research.
Method: Introduces Open-Reasoner-Zero (ORZ), the first fully open-source implementation of large-scale reasoning-oriented RL training applied directly to base LLMs, bypassing supervised fine-tuning.

Employs a vanilla Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm with specific Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE) parameters (lambda=1, gamma=1) and a minimalist, binary (0 or 1) rule-based reward function.

Critically, all KL-based regularization techniques (KL shaped rewards, KL loss) are explicitly removed, demonstrating that a simpler, unregularized setup can be highly effective and stable for scaling reasoning capabilities.
Results: Open-Reasoner-Zero (ORZ)-32B surpasses DeepSeek-R1-Zero-Qwen-32B on challenging benchmarks like AIME2024 (48.1% vs 47.0%), MATH500 (92.2% vs 91.6%), and GPQA Diamond (55.5% vs 55.0%), achieving this with only 1/10 of the training steps.

The methodology consistently replicates the scaling phenomenon across various model sizes (0.5B to 32B), showing steady growth in training reward and response length, validating the robustness of the minimalist approach.

Ablation studies confirm PPO's superior stability over GRPO and validate the benefits of specific GAE parameters (lambda=1, gamma=1) and the complete removal of KL regularization for optimal training stability, performance, and efficiency.
Takeaways: A minimalist PPO setup with a learned critic is surprisingly effective and stable for large-scale RL on base LLMs, especially when designed without KL regularization, simplifying training and improving efficiency.
Specific GAE parameters (lambda=1, gamma=1) are optimal for reasoning tasks, simplifying advantage calculation and stabilizing training by valuing long-term rewards and minimizing bias.

The learned critic in PPO plays a crucial role in assigning accurate token-level credit, effectively identifying and penalizing undesirable patterns like repetition, which contributes to superior training stability over GRPO.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.24235.Title: A Survey on Test-Time Scaling in Large Language Models: What, How, Where, and How Well?
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.24235.Summary: A comprehensive survey introduces a unified, four-axis taxonomy to systematically organize the rapidly growing field of Test-Time Scaling (TTS) in Large Language Models (LLMs). This work provides a structured framework for classifying methods, offers practical guidelines for deployment, and identifies critical open challenges for future research in enhancing LLM performance during inference.
Problem: Traditional pre-training scaling of Large Language Models (LLMs) faces diminishing returns due to prohibitive resource intensity and finite high-quality data.
Existing LLMs possess latent reasoning capabilities that are not fully elicited or utilized during standard inference.
The burgeoning research into Test-Time Scaling (TTS) for LLMs lacked a unified, multi-dimensional framework to systematically organize and compare diverse methods.
Method: Introduced a novel four-axis taxonomy ("what to scale," "how to scale," "where to scale," and "how well to scale") to provide a structured framework for Test-Time Scaling (TTS) methods.
Systematically organized and analyzed a vast body of existing TTS literature by mapping methods to this multi-dimensional taxonomy.
Distilled practical guidelines for researchers and practitioners on deploying TTS, including task applicability, implementation pathways, and efficiency improvements.
Results: Identified a clear evolutionary trajectory for Test-Time Scaling (TTS), progressing from structured inference (e.g., CoT prompting) to advanced autonomous reasoning through techniques like Process Reward Models and Reinforcement Learning.

Provided hands-on guidelines for practical TTS deployment, emphasizing its utility across a wide range of tasks, particularly complex reasoning, and outlining key considerations for efficiency and method integration.

Articulated critical open challenges and future research opportunities, focusing on advancing the limits of different scaling types, enhancing theoretical understanding, optimizing for efficiency beyond raw accuracy, and generalizing TTS methods across diverse domains.
Takeaways: Test-Time Scaling (TTS) is an emerging paradigm for enhancing LLM capabilities by allocating additional computation during inference, similar to System 2 thinking.
Different TTS techniques (e.g., parallel, sequential, hybrid, internal scaling) are often complementary, with frontier strategies involving integrated pipelines of methods.
The distinction between tuning-based and inference-based TTS is becoming less clear, as high-quality data generated from inference strategies is increasingly used for model fine-tuning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.24067.Title: TransMamba: A Sequence-Level Hybrid Transformer-Mamba Language Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.24067.Summary: A sequence-level hybrid Transformer-Mamba language model, TransMamba, unifies these architectures through shared parameters and dynamic switching, achieving improved performance on various NLP and long-text tasks while reducing training time by up to 25%.
Problem: Transformers face quadratic computational complexity (O(T^2)) with sequence length, leading to high costs for very long sequences in both training and inference.
Initial Mamba models, while efficient with linear complexity, exhibit unstable contextual learning and suboptimal multitask generalization compared to Transformers.
Existing layer-level hybrid models suffer from rigid structural restrictions and often fail to dynamically adapt to varying sequence lengths and contextual demands.
Method: Unifies Transformer and Mamba architectures through shared parameter matrices, allowing a single set of core parameters to serve as both QKV for Attention and CBx for SSM.
Introduces a sequence-level dynamic switching mechanism via a "TransPoint" within each layer, allowing the model to process different parts of the input sequence with either Attention or SSM.
Employs a lossless Memory Converter to seamlessly and without additional parameters transfer contextual information from the Attention mechanism to the initial hidden state of the Mamba SSM.
Results: TransMamba consistently outperforms pure Transformer, pure Mamba2, and naive Hybrid models across general English tasks and long-context benchmarks like LongBench-v2 (e.g., 38.76 for TransMamba-1.5B vs. 31.61 for Transformer).
Achieves up to a 25% reduction in average training time compared to Transformer models, demonstrating significant efficiency improvements consistent with theoretical FLOPs analysis.
Effective TransPoint scheduling, particularly layer-specific, broad-range, and fine-grained approaches, yields the best validation loss (2.898) and perplexity (1.813).
Takeaways: A deeper consistency exists between Transformer's attention and Mamba's state space model, enabling them to share core parameter matrices within a unified architecture.
Dynamic, sequence-level adaptation between different mechanisms (Attention and SSM) using principled scheduling can effectively balance computational efficiency and robust contextual learning.
Lossless information transfer between distinct architectural components, facilitated by a Memory Converter, is critical for effective integration in hybrid models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.23829.Title: Crossing the Reward Bridge: Expanding RL with Verifiable Rewards Across Diverse Domains
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.23829.Summary: Tencent AI Lab and Soochow University developed an approach to extend Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) to diverse, unstructured domains by employing a generative, model-based soft reward mechanism. Their method successfully trains a compact 7B reward model that achieves performance competitive with a much larger 72B model, enabling RL to enhance LLM reasoning on complex, free-form tasks where traditional verification is challenging.
Problem: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has been limited to highly structured tasks (e.g., math, code) due to its reliance on rule-based or programmatic binary feedback.
Real-world domains (e.g., medicine, economics) often involve free-form, unstructured answers that lack easily verifiable objective ground truth, making traditional RLVR difficult to apply.

Obtaining reliable reward signals for complex, nuanced, and open-ended LLM responses traditionally requires extensive domain-specific human annotation or computationally expensive large LLMs as judges.
Method: The authors propose using a generative Large Language Model as a verifier to produce both binary and novel soft rewards, where soft rewards are derived from the probability of the verifier's judgment tokens (e.g., '1' for correct, '0' for incorrect).

A compact (7B parameter) cross-domain reward model (RM-7B) is trained by distilling binary judgments from a larger, fixed generative teacher model (Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct) on responses generated during RL exploration.

The approach is validated on large-scale datasets featuring free-form, unstructured reference answers from diverse domains, including mathematics (773k QA pairs) and multi-subject college-level exams (638k QA pairs spanning 48 subjects).
Results: Reinforcement Learning consistently outperformed Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) across mathematics and multi-subject tasks, with model-based RL achieving 63.0% accuracy on math tasks compared to SFT's 45.7%.
A distilled 7B reward model (RM-7B) achieved competitive or superior performance compared to a 72B teacher model, demonstrating the efficacy of compact cross-domain generative reward verifiers.

Soft rewards demonstrated a clear advantage over binary rewards in multi-subject tasks (e.g., 31.2% vs. 27.3% accuracy for REINFORCE with RM-7B), and learned reward models exhibited superior scalability and out-of-distribution generalization compared to rule-based methods.
Takeaways: Binary correctness judgments on broad, nuanced tasks show high agreement across powerful LLMs when high-quality expert-written reference answers are provided, simplifying ground-truth signal acquisition.
It is feasible and effective to distill multi-domain generative verifier models from relatively compact LLMs (as small as 7B) without extensive, costly domain-specific human annotation.

Soft reward functions, leveraging the probability of a generative verifier's judgment tokens, can better accommodate the inherent uncertainty and ambiguity of open-domain evaluation compared to binary rewards.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.23765.Title: STI-Bench: Are MLLMs Ready for Precise Spatial-Temporal World Understanding?
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.23765.Summary: STI-Bench introduces a novel benchmark to evaluate Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) for precise spatial-temporal understanding in real-world scenarios, revealing that current models achieve only modest accuracy, with the best performing model, Gemini-2.5-Pro, scoring 41.4%. The benchmark highlights MLLMs' significant limitations in quantitative spatial and temporal reasoning, crucial for embodied AI and autonomous driving applications.
Problem: MLLMs are increasingly used for embodied AI and autonomous driving, but their precise and quantitative spatial-temporal understanding remains largely unevaluated.
Existing video benchmarks for MLLMs primarily focus on high-level semantic understanding or 2D visual reasoning, neglecting 3D spatial measurements and dynamic properties.
There is uncertainty regarding MLLMs' readiness for real-world physical interactions due to a lack of rigorous, task-specific evaluation in precise spatial-temporal intelligence.
Method: Developed STI-Bench, a novel benchmark comprising over 300 real-world videos and more than 2,000 carefully curated Question-Answering pairs, spanning desktop, indoor, and outdoor scenarios.

Designed eight distinct tasks covering both static (dimensional measurement, spatial relation, 3D video grounding) and dynamic (displacement, speed, ego-centric orientation, trajectory description, pose estimation) understanding.

Utilized a robust construction pipeline involving ground truth computation from detailed 3D annotations, automatic QA generation with MLLMs, and rigorous human quality control with fine-grained distractors to ensure precision and challenge.
Results: The best-performing MLLM, Gemini-2.5-Pro, achieved an average accuracy of only 41.4% on STI-Bench, closely followed by the open-source Qwen2.5-VL-72B at 40.7%, indicating substantial room for improvement.

Models performed weakest on tasks requiring precise numerical estimation of physical quantities (e.g., Dimensional Measurement 38.7%, Displacement & Path Length 33.9%, Speed & Acceleration 33.1% for Gemini-2.5-Pro).

MLLMs showed relatively stronger capabilities in tasks involving relative understanding or object state estimation, such as Pose Estimation (Claude-3.7-Sonnet 62.7%) and Spatial Relation (Gemini-2.5-Pro 53.8%).
Takeaways: Current state-of-the-art MLLMs exhibit significant limitations in precise spatial-temporal understanding, especially for quantitative tasks, despite their advancements in general visual comprehension.

MLLMs struggle with accurate spatial quantification, often failing to precisely estimate static properties like object dimensions and distances due to difficulties in inferring metric scale and depth from 2D pixel data.

Models demonstrate flawed temporal dynamics understanding, struggling to integrate information across sparse video frames and to accurately interpret motion, including differentiating ego-motion from object motion.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.23508.Title: Re-Aligning Language to Visual Objects with an Agentic Workflow
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.23508.Summary: Real-LOD is an agentic workflow that systematically refines language descriptions to improve their alignment with visual objects for language-based object detection. Training an LOD model on the refined Real-Data dataset led to performance improvements of approximately 50% over existing methods on standard benchmarks, highlighting the impact of data quality over quantity.
Problem: Vision-language models (VLMs) often generate training data for language-based object detection (LOD) that contains "hallucinations," or inaccurate descriptions of visual objects.
This misalignment between language descriptions and visual objects, primarily due to category and attribute errors, significantly impairs the performance of LOD models.
Traditional approaches often focus on increasing data quantity, which does not address the underlying quality issues of VLM-generated descriptions.
Method: Introduced Real-LOD, an agentic workflow that uses a large language model (LLM) as an intelligent agent to identify and correct misalignments between language descriptions and visual objects.
The workflow operates in an iterative cycle of Planning, Tool Use, and Reflection, allowing the agent to systematically refine descriptions.
It leverages an LLM (Vicuna) for reasoning and rewriting, and a VLM (LLaVA) with various image processing tools (object crops, extended crops, highlights) for visual perception and analysis.
Results: The Language-based Object Detection (LOD) model trained on the Real-Data dataset substantially outperformed existing LOD methods, achieving approximately 50% higher performance on standard benchmarks.

The Real-LOD agent demonstrated high effectiveness in correcting various error types, achieving 100% correction rates for location and accessory errors, and nearly 90% for category and attribute errors.
The study indicated that focusing on data quality through iterative refinement, rather than just data quantity, leads to more effective and reliable vision-language models.
Takeaways: Improving the quality of language-object alignment in training data can lead to substantial performance gains for LOD models, even with smaller datasets.
Large language models can effectively function as intelligent agents for reasoning about and correcting multimodal information, specifically misalignments between language and vision.
The iterative refinement process demonstrates diminishing returns, with most error corrections occurring within the first few iterations, indicating the efficiency of the agentic workflow.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.23383.Title: ToRL: Scaling Tool-Integrated RL
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.23383.Summary: The paper "TORL: Scaling Tool-Integrated RL" introduces a framework for training large language models (LLMs) to autonomously use computational tools by scaling reinforcement learning directly from base models. The TORL framework consistently improves mathematical reasoning across benchmarks, achieving up to a 14.7% absolute accuracy gain for a 7B model compared to SFT-based baselines, and enables emergent behaviors like self-correction and reflection.
Problem: Large language models (LLMs) struggle with precise computation and symbolic manipulation, necessitating external tools despite their advanced natural language reasoning.
Existing Tool-Integrated Reasoning (TIR) approaches rely on supervised fine-tuning (SFT), which limits the model's exploration and ability to discover optimal or novel tool usage strategies.
The implementation transparency of some prior reinforcement learning (RL) applications to tool use has been limited, hindering community understanding and reproducibility.
Method: The paper introduces TORL, a framework that integrates a code interpreter directly into a reinforcement learning environment, enabling LLMs to learn tool utilization from base models without prior supervised fine-tuning.

It utilizes a high-quality mathematical dataset constructed through reinforcement learning data distillation (LIMR) and adopts an iterative Tool-Integrated Reasoning (TIR) paradigm for problem-solving.
The framework employs the GRPO algorithm within the veRL framework, uses Qwen-2.5-Math models as foundational LLMs, and feeds code execution error messages back to the LLM to enhance code generation.
Results: TORL-1.5B achieved an average accuracy of 48.5% on mathematical benchmarks, marking an absolute 7.2% improvement over the SFT-based TIR baseline (Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct-TIR).
TORL-7B attained an impressive 62.1% average accuracy, outperforming other open-source models on the same base by 14.7% absolute, and reached 43.3% on AIME24, comparable to some 32B models.

The model demonstrated emergent cognitive behaviors, including self-regulation (correcting code based on error messages) and reflection (cross-validating analytical reasoning with tool outputs and making corrections).
Takeaways: Sophisticated tool-augmented reasoning capabilities, including strategic tool invocation and error recovery, can emerge in LLMs purely through reward-driven learning from base models, without prior supervised fine-tuning.
The model autonomously learns to generate code more frequently, correctly, and effectively over training, demonstrating an increased pass ratio and purposeful code use.

While increasing the maximum number of allowed tool calls per problem can enhance performance, it substantially reduces training efficiency due to increased GPU idle time, highlighting an important trade-off.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.23077.Title: Efficient Inference for Large Reasoning Models: A Survey
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.23077.Summary: Researchers from National University of Singapore and collaborators provide the first comprehensive survey on efficient inference for Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), establishing a taxonomy of methods that reduce token consumption and improve inference time while maintaining reasoning quality. The work categorizes approaches into explicit compact Chain-of-Thought and implicit latent Chain-of-Thought, identifying current limitations and future research avenues.
Problem: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) generate extensive intermediate reasoning steps, leading to high token consumption and increased inference time.
The deliberative nature of LRMs results in significant memory overhead, making their deployment costly and resource-intensive.
Traditional efficiency techniques for Large Language Models (LLMs) do not specifically target the token inefficiency inherent in LRMs' verbose reasoning chains.
Method: The authors conduct a systematic review, proposing a hierarchical taxonomy for efficient LRM inference methods focused on token efficiency.
The taxonomy classifies methods into "explicit compact Chain-of-Thought" (reducing visible tokens) and "implicit latent Chain-of-Thought" (encoding reasoning in hidden states).
The survey provides empirical analyses of existing methods, detailing their performance across reasoning scenarios, objective functions, and efficiency metrics like accuracy and token costs.
Results: The survey established a comprehensive hierarchical taxonomy for efficient LRM inference, categorizing methods based on their approach to compacting reasoning steps.
Empirical analyses on datasets like GSM8K demonstrated a clear trade-off between reasoning accuracy and token cost, highlighting the practical utility of distilled models.

The work identified four key open challenges: achieving user-centric controllable reasoning, balancing interpretability with efficiency, ensuring the safety of efficient LRMs, and expanding application domains beyond math and code.
Takeaways: Efficient LRM inference approaches primarily diverge into explicit compact CoT, which maintains visible reasoning steps, and implicit latent CoT, which embeds reasoning in hidden representations for greater token efficiency.
Research on LRM inference efficiency is predominantly focused on mathematical reasoning benchmarks due to their structured nature, simplifying objective function design.

An inherent trade-off exists between achieving high reasoning accuracy and minimizing token consumption, with model distillation presenting a viable path to retaining performance while reducing resource use.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.22020.Title: CoT-VLA: Visual Chain-of-Thought Reasoning for Vision-Language-Action Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.22020.Summary: CoT-VLA integrates visual chain-of-thought reasoning into Vision-Language-Action models by having them predict subgoal images before generating actions. This approach leverages large-scale action-less video data for training, enabling the model to outperform state-of-the-art VLA models by 17% in real-world manipulation and 6% in simulation benchmarks.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models primarily use direct end-to-end mapping from observations to actions, lacking explicit intermediate reasoning steps crucial for complex, multi-stage manipulation tasks.
Current VLA models struggle with effective temporal planning and foresight, limiting their performance on tasks requiring a sequence of sub-goals.
Abundant, action-less video data from the internet remains largely underutilized by robot learning models, which often rely exclusively on expensive action-annotated robot demonstrations.
Method: Introduces visual chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning where the VLA model first predicts a future image frame as a visual subgoal, then generates a sequence of actions conditioned on this subgoal.
Leverages a 7B-parameter unified multimodal foundation model, VILA-U, for both understanding visual observations and generating image and action tokens.

Employs a two-stage training approach, using robot demonstrations for both visual and action prediction, and large-scale action-less video datasets (e.g., EPIC-KITCHENS) specifically for training visual subgoal generation.
Results: CoT-VLA surpasses state-of-the-art VLA models, achieving a 17% improvement in real-world manipulation tasks and a 6% improvement in simulation benchmarks.

The model demonstrates superior instruction following on the LIBERO benchmark and robust adaptation to novel environments in Franka-Tabletop experiments, especially for complex multi-instruction tasks.
Ablation studies confirm the individual and combined effectiveness of visual chain-of-thought, action chunking, and a novel hybrid attention mechanism in boosting task performance.
Takeaways: Explicit visual chain-of-thought reasoning, using predicted subgoal images, significantly enhances the reasoning and generalization capabilities of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models.

Large-scale action-less video datasets can effectively be leveraged for pre-training the visual reasoning component of robot policies, reducing reliance on costly action-annotated robot demonstrations.
Improvements in the visual reasoning capabilities of VLA models directly translate to higher robotic task success rates, particularly for challenging out-of-distribution and long-horizon tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.21776.Title: Video-R1: Reinforcing Video Reasoning in MLLMs
