https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.21776.Summary: Researchers introduced Video-R1, the first framework to apply a rule-based reinforcement learning paradigm for enhancing temporal reasoning capabilities in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) for video. Video-R1, leveraging a new temporal-aware RL algorithm and dedicated video reasoning datasets, consistently outperforms previous state-of-the-art models, achieving 37.1% accuracy on VSI-Bench, surpassing GPT-4o's 34.0%.
Problem: Existing MLLMs primarily excel at video perception tasks but lack robust, explicit temporal reasoning abilities to understand dynamic events and relationships over time.
Current reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms for reasoning, designed for text, do not inherently provide reward signals that encourage temporal understanding in videos.
A scarcity of high-quality, complex video reasoning datasets hinders the effective training and generalization of MLLMs for sophisticated video-based reasoning tasks.
Method: Constructed two comprehensive datasets, Video-R1-CoT-165k (for SFT) and Video-R1-260k (for RL), incorporating a hybrid of high-quality image and video reasoning data to build foundational and temporal reasoning skills.

Introduced Temporal Group Relative Policy Optimization (T-GRPO), an RL algorithm that explicitly incentivizes temporal reasoning using a contrastive reward mechanism based on comparing responses to ordered versus randomly shuffled video frames.

Implemented a two-stage training strategy: an initial Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) cold start on Video-R1-CoT-165k, followed by RL training with T-GRPO on Video-R1-260k, enhanced with a length-based reward for response coherence.
Results: Video-R1 consistently and significantly outperformed previous state-of-the-art MLLMs across six challenging video benchmarks, with Video-R1-7B (64 frames) achieving 37.1% accuracy on VSI-Bench, surpassing GPT-4o (34.0%).
Reinforcement learning, even after only 1k steps, yielded significant performance improvements, demonstrating its effectiveness in generalizing video reasoning capabilities beyond SFT.

Ablation studies confirmed the critical role of both the hybrid image-video data for general reasoning and the T-GRPO algorithm for explicit temporal understanding, as removing either component led to noticeable performance drops.
Takeaways: Reinforcement Learning (RL) with a temporal-aware algorithm (T-GRPO) is crucial for unlocking generalized and robust video reasoning in MLLMs, offering performance improvements over SFT-only approaches.

The explicit incentivization of temporal understanding through a contrastive reward mechanism effectively guides the MLLM to leverage correct temporal order, leading to deeper temporal reasoning rather than relying on superficial cues.
Combining image-based reasoning data with video data during training provides a robust foundation of general reasoning skills that significantly boosts performance on complex video reasoning tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.21614.Title: A Survey of Efficient Reasoning for Large Reasoning Models: Language, Multimodality, and Beyond
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.21614.Summary: A collaborative survey by researchers from Shanghai AI Laboratory and other institutions maps current techniques for enhancing reasoning efficiency in Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) across their lifecycle. It systematically categorizes approaches to mitigate verbose and computationally expensive reasoning traces, aiming to optimize "intelligence per token" for practical LRM deployment.
Problem: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) generate excessively long, often redundant, and inefficient reasoning traces (Chain-of-Thought), leading to high computational costs for training and inference.
Existing surveys on LRMs have not specifically addressed the growing challenge of reasoning efficiency, leaving a gap in synthesized knowledge for this critical area.
The inherent verbosity of LRMs creates a "token economy" problem, impacting memory consumption, inference latency, and overall computational expenses, thus hindering real-world applicability.
Method: The survey formally defines reasoning efficiency and identifies common patterns of LRM inefficiency (e.g., redundant content, overthinking) along with unique challenges.

It systematically categorizes and details methods for improving reasoning efficiency across the entire LRM lifecycle: during inference, with supervised fine-tuning (SFT), through reinforcement learning (RL), and during pre-training.
The authors provide a comprehensive taxonomy of techniques within each stage and maintain a real-time GitHub repository to serve as a dynamic community resource.
Results: Efficient inference techniques include length budgeting, dynamic switching between models or systems, and parallel search strategies to prune suboptimal reasoning paths.
Supervised fine-tuning methods enable reasoning chain compression through data engineering or facilitate latent-space reasoning where explicit token generation is minimized.
Reinforcement learning approaches utilize explicit length penalties or implicit biases from preference modeling to guide models toward generating optimal and concise reasoning chains.

Pre-training strategies focus on inherent efficiency through latent space reasoning or by adopting subquadratic attention mechanisms and linear recurrent structures to overcome Transformer limitations.
Takeaways: Reasoning efficiency, defined as the ratio of solution quality to computational cost, is crucial for maximizing "intelligence per token" in LRMs.
Inefficiency in LRMs manifests as redundant content, overthinking simple questions, and incoherent or suboptimal reasoning paths, requiring targeted interventions.

Achieving efficient reasoning necessitates addressing challenges such as quantifying the utility of individual reasoning steps, controlling thinking length dynamically, and overcoming architectural bottlenecks of Transformers.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.20783.Title: Understanding R1-Zero-Like Training: A Critical Perspective
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.20783.Summary: Researchers from Sea AI Lab and partner universities critically analyze R1-Zero-like training for large language models, revealing inherent biases in the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) algorithm and pre-existing self-reflection behaviors in base models. The study introduces an unbiased optimization method, Dr. GRPO, and a minimalist recipe that achieves 43.3% accuracy on AIME 2024 with a 7B model, setting a new state-of-the-art efficiently.
Problem: The mechanisms behind the reported success of R1-Zero training, including the emergence of 'Aha moments' and reasoning improvements without supervised fine-tuning (SFT), were not fully understood.
The influence of diverse base model characteristics (e.g., pretraining data, template responsiveness) on subsequent reinforcement learning (RL) performance lacked systematic investigation.
Potential optimization biases within the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) algorithm, particularly concerning response length and training efficiency, remained unexamined.
Method: Conducted a comprehensive analysis of various open-source base models to assess their inherent reasoning capabilities, template dependencies, and pre-existing self-reflection behaviors.
Performed theoretical derivations and empirical experiments to identify and correct optimization biases in GRPO, leading to the development of 'Dr. GRPO' as an unbiased alternative.

Developed and validated a 'minimalist R1-Zero recipe' by studying the interaction of templates, question sets, and domain-specific pretraining to create an efficient and reproducible training approach.
Results: Dr. GRPO effectively mitigates the length bias in GRPO, preventing uncontrolled growth of response length during training and reducing the length of incorrect responses during evaluation without sacrificing accuracy.
The developed minimalist R1-Zero recipe, using RL-tuned Qwen2.5-Math-7B with Dr. GRPO, achieved 43.3% accuracy on AIME 2024, establishing a new state-of-the-art for a 7B model.

The study demonstrated that even smaller, out-of-distribution question sets can effectively induce strong reasoning ability through RL when paired with suitable base models and templates, suggesting RL reinforces existing capabilities.
Takeaways: Self-reflection ('Aha moment') is largely a pre-existing characteristic of many base models, including DeepSeek-V3-Base, rather than a solely emergent property of pure RL training.

Standard GRPO exhibits a response-level length bias that disproportionately penalizes shorter correct responses and artificially increases the length of incorrect responses, a bias also found in many open-source PPO implementations.

Specific base models, like Qwen2.5-Math, demonstrate peak reasoning performance without explicit prompt templates, suggesting their pretraining implicitly creates SFT-like capabilities that impact RL.
Domain-specific continual pretraining significantly elevates the performance ceiling for subsequent RL, enhancing the reasoning capabilities of even inherently weaker base models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.20752.Title: Reason-RFT: Reinforcement Fine-Tuning for Visual Reasoning of Vision Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.20752.Summary: Reason-RFT introduces a two-stage reinforcement fine-tuning framework to enhance the visual reasoning and generalization capabilities of Vision-Language Models. The method achieves state-of-the-art or highly competitive performance across various visual reasoning tasks, particularly demonstrating strong generalization under domain shifts while maintaining data efficiency.
Problem: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) for Vision-Language Models often leads to cognitive rigidity and poor generalization to domain-shifted visual reasoning tasks due to over-reliance on extensive Chain-of-Thought (CoT) data.
Pure reinforcement learning (RL) methods, while dynamic, may lack robustness to visual domain shifts and struggle with initial acquisition of complex reasoning skills.
Current visual reasoning approaches are often data-intensive, requiring meticulously annotated CoT data that can be costly and difficult to scale.
Method: A two-stage framework, Reason-RFT, is proposed, starting with SFT-based Visual Reasoning Activation to establish foundational task-specific priors using CoT data.
The second stage employs Reinforcement Learning using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to dynamically refine the model and enhance generalization.
Task-specific reward functions are designed for diverse visual reasoning types (discrete, mathematical, function-based), combining format adherence and accuracy, with configurable partial credit.
Results: Reason-RFT achieved state-of-the-art or highly competitive performance across visual counting, structural perception, and spatial transformation tasks, outperforming models like GPT-4o and Gemini-1.5-Pro.
Demonstrated superior generalization under domain shift conditions, with the 2B Reason-RFT model surpassing GPT-4o by 31.7% in spatial transformation under perspective shifts.
Exhibited high data efficiency, achieving 70% of the peak performance with only 3% of the training data for spatial transformation tasks in the 2B model, and over 92% for the 7B model.
Takeaways: The synergistic combination of SFT for initial skill activation and RL for dynamic refinement effectively overcomes the generalization limitations of purely supervised methods in visual reasoning.
SFT provides crucial inductive biases, especially for smaller models and tasks with complex output structures, enabling more effective RL adaptation.

Stricter 'hard rewards' that penalize partial matches in RL can improve generalization under domain shifts more effectively than allowing partial credit, indicating a better signal for robust serialized reasoning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.20680.Title: Vision as LoRA
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.20680.Summary: Vision as LoRA (VoRA), developed by ByteDance, proposes an encoder-free architecture for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by internalizing vision capabilities directly into LLMs using mergeable LoRA layers. This approach achieves performance comparable to encoder-based models with near-zero additional inference cost and supports arbitrary image resolutions, all while demonstrating stable and data-efficient training through block-wise distillation and bi-directional attention for vision.
Problem: Existing encoder-based Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) suffer from high computational and memory overhead due to separate vision encoders, along with fixed-resolution constraints and sequential processing.

Prior encoder-free MLLMs struggle with modality conflicts and catastrophic forgetting when trying to learn both language and vision within a single LLM, often requiring parameter expansion that doubles model size during inference.
Teaching an LLM to understand vision from scratch is data-intensive and slow, and traditional attention mechanisms in LLMs (causal masks) are not optimal for global visual context understanding.
Method: Introduces "Vision as LoRA" (VoRA), integrating LoRA layers into the first N_vit blocks of an LLM to decouple vision-specific parameters, which are then merged into the base LLM weights post-training for inference efficiency.

Employs a block-wise distillation paradigm to transfer visual knowledge from a pre-trained Vision Transformer (ViT) to the LLM by aligning intermediate representations of each LLM block with corresponding ViT features.
Adapts the LLM's attention mechanism by using bi-directional attention masks for visual tokens to enable comprehensive spatial context understanding, while retaining causal masks for text tokens.
Results: VoRA achieved performance comparable to official and reproduced LLaVA-1.5 baselines (encoder-based models) across a wide range of standard benchmarks, including VQAv2, SQA-I, TextVQA, and MMBench, demonstrating an LLM can acquire native multimodal capabilities without an external vision model.

Ablation studies confirmed that LoRA-based parameter decoupling successfully stabilized training, and the combination of bi-directional attention masks and block-wise distillation significantly improved data efficiency, requiring only 64.5% of the training steps to reach a comparable loss compared to a vanilla LoRA baseline.
The LoRA parameters are mergeable into the base LLM weights post-training, eliminating additional computational cost and memory overhead during inference, making VoRA highly efficient for deployment.
Takeaways: LoRA-based parameter decoupling within an LLM effectively stabilizes training and prevents catastrophic forgetting when introducing visual modalities, critically, without incurring additional inference-time overhead.
Block-wise knowledge distillation from a pre-trained Vision Transformer significantly accelerates visual learning in the LLM and improves data efficiency by transferring fine-grained visual priors.
Employing bi-directional attention masks for visual tokens within the LLM enhances the model's ability to capture comprehensive spatial and contextual relationships in images, improving performance.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.19903.Title: Scaling Vision Pre-Training to 4K Resolution
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.19903.Summary: Researchers from UC Berkeley and NVIDIA developed PS3 (Pre-training with Scale-Selective Scaling), a framework enabling efficient CLIP-style vision pre-training at 4K resolution through localized contrastive learning and intelligent patch selection. This approach reduces pre-training compute by 79x and powers VILA-HD, an MLLM that achieved state-of-the-art results on newly introduced 4K-specific benchmarks, outperforming models like GPT-4o by 16.1%.
Problem: Most modern vision models are pre-trained at low resolutions (e.g., 378x378 pixels), leading to a fundamental inability to perceive fine visual details required by many real-world applications.
Scaling vision pre-training to high resolutions incurs a prohibitive computational cost, increasing quadratically for CNNs and quartically for Vision Transformers (ViTs).

Existing methods for high-resolution MLLMs are suboptimal, either adapting low-resolution models post-training or incurring significant latency and memory overhead by processing entire high-resolution images.
Method: Developed PS3, a scale-selective pre-training framework that learns detailed visual representations by focusing on local regions rather than global processing.
Created a new pre-training dataset of 75M high-resolution images paired with automated local captions and bounding boxes for salient regions and documents.

Designed a three-stage vision encoder for PS3 that extracts low-resolution global features, performs text-aware or saliency-based multi-scale patch selection, and processes high-resolution patches using a low-resolution KV cache for global context.
Integrated PS3 into MLLMs (VILA-HD) with specific fine-tuning strategies to align high-resolution features and enable prompt-aware patch selection.
Results: Achieved a 79x reduction in pre-training compute compared to global contrastive learning approaches like SigLIP when scaling to 4K resolution.
VILA-HD-4K, powered by PS3, significantly surpassed state-of-the-art MLLMs on the new 4KPro benchmark, showing a 16.1% improvement over GPT-4o and 7.5% over Qwen2.5-VL with 1.67x speedup.

PS3 demonstrated superior efficiency and performance over token pruning methods, consistently providing lower ViT latency and better accuracy while being the only method capable of efficiently handling 4K resolution without out-of-memory errors.
Takeaways: Efficient 4K vision pre-training is achievable with a near-constant computational cost by combining localized contrastive learning with intelligent, selective patch processing.

Leveraging high-resolution pre-training data fundamentally improves visual feature quality for MLLMs, leading to superior perception compared to training-free adaptations or post-encoding token pruning.
Existing benchmarks often do not genuinely require ultra-high-resolution perception, necessitating dedicated datasets like 4KPro to evaluate models on tasks demanding true 4K understanding.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.19707.Title: Mind the Gap: Benchmarking Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.19707.Summary: University of Edinburgh researchers develop a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating spatial reasoning capabilities in vision-language models (VLMs), revealing that current state-of-the-art models perform near random chance across multiple spatial reasoning tasks while demonstrating particular weakness in mental rotation abilities.
Problem: Existing VLM benchmarks don't effectively isolate or assess spatial reasoning abilities
Lack of standardized evaluation methods for comparing spatial reasoning capabilities across different VLM architectures
Method: Created a multi-component benchmark combining synthetic, GenAI-generated, and real-world images
Developed specific tests for spatial relations, orientation, navigation, and mental rotation
Evaluated 13 state-of-the-art VLMs using the new benchmark framework
Results: Average accuracy across 13 tested VLMs was close to random chance
Mental rotation tasks proved particularly challenging for all models
Models demonstrated inconsistent performance across different spatial reasoning components
Ablation studies showed limitations persist even with different image generation approaches
Takeaways: VLMs show relatively strong performance on basic spatial relations but struggle with complex transformations
Success in one spatial reasoning component doesn't translate to robust performance across others
Using GenAI-generated images doesn't significantly improve model performance

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.19612.Title: RL-finetuning LLMs from on- and off-policy data with a single algorithm
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.19612.Summary: Researchers from Meta GenAI and Meta FAIR present the Any-Generation Reward Optimization (AGRO) algorithm, a unified reinforcement learning approach for fine-tuning large language models using both on-policy and off-policy data. AGRO achieves a +7% performance increase on the MATH dataset with Llama 3 8B, demonstrating superior data efficiency and improved robustness in offline learning compared to traditional methods.
Problem: Existing RLHF algorithms for LLMs are largely compartmentalized into either computationally intensive online methods or static, often sub-optimal, offline methods.
This dichotomy prevents the seamless integration of diverse data sources, such as iteratively collected online feedback and large, pre-collected offline datasets.
Naive adaptations of on-policy KL-regularized policy gradient algorithms to off-policy settings do not reliably converge to the optimal target policy.
Method: AGRO introduces the theoretical concept of "generation consistency," stating that at optimality, the KL-regularized reward is invariant across any generation for a given prompt.
The algorithm derives unified loss functions for both on-policy and off-policy settings, which minimize the variance of this regularized reward to converge to the optimal policy.
AGRO employs sample-based gradient estimates, and for scenarios with multiple generations per prompt (n>1), it directly estimates variance, eliminating the need for an auxiliary value function.
Results: On-policy AGRO achieved a +7% performance improvement on the challenging MATH dataset compared to the supervised fine-tuned Llama 3 8B reference model.

In on-policy settings, AGRO demonstrated superior data efficiency, making faster progress in training reward for the same number of learning iterations than standard regularized policy gradient methods.
Off-policy AGRO consistently showed better overall performance and stability than adapted KL-regularized policy gradients in extreme offline learning scenarios, confirming its theoretical advantages.
Takeaways: The core insight is that the optimal policy in a regularized RLHF problem ensures the quantity `r(x, y) - beta log(pi(y|x)/pi_ref(y|x))` is constant across all generated responses `y` for a given prompt `x`.

By minimizing the variance of this generation-consistent regularized reward, AGRO provides a single, theoretically grounded framework capable of learning from any mix of on-policy and off-policy data.
On-policy AGRO leverages both pathwise-derivative and likelihood ratio gradient estimates, leading to more efficient learning dynamics and faster training progress.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.19470.Title: ReSearch: Learning to Reason with Search for LLMs via Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.19470.Summary: The ReSearch framework enables Large Language Models to integrate multi-step reasoning with external search, learning interactively via reinforcement learning without supervised intermediate steps. It yields substantial performance gains on complex multi-hop question answering benchmarks and reveals emergent self-correction capabilities.
Problem: Existing multi-step Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) approaches for LLMs rely on labor-intensive, manually designed prompts or fixed heuristics for external search, limiting scalability and adaptability.
Training LLMs to reason with external tools traditionally requires costly supervised datasets that meticulously detail intermediate reasoning steps and search actions.

LLMs often struggle with factual accuracy and exhibit hallucinations when addressing complex, knowledge-intensive questions, underscoring a need for more robust integration with up-to-date external information.
Method: ReSearch trains LLMs to dynamically incorporate internal thought processes, search query formulation, and integration of retrieved information into a structured reasoning chain using specific tags.

The framework employs Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), a reinforcement learning algorithm, to optimize the LLM's policy for search operations, guided by a simple F1-score-based reward function.
Retrieval results from the external search environment are masked during loss calculation, directing the LLM's learning focus specifically to its generated reasoning steps and search queries.
Results: ReSearch models achieved average improvements ranging from 14.82% to 15.81% in Exact Match (EM) and 15.46% to 17.56% in LLM-as-a-Judge (LJ) compared to the strongest baselines across four multi-hop QA benchmarks.
The framework demonstrated strong generalization ability, performing effectively on diverse multi-hop datasets despite being trained exclusively on the MuSiQue training set.

Analysis of training progression showed models increasing their response length and the average number of search operations per rollout, indicating a learned ability to engage in more extensive and iterative reasoning.
Takeaways: Reinforcement learning, driven by straightforward outcome-based rewards, can effectively teach LLMs to autonomously perform interactive, multi-step reasoning by leveraging external search tools.
Structuring search operations within the LLM's thought process using explicit tags fosters a robust and dynamic interaction with external knowledge sources.

Advanced reasoning capabilities, such as self-elicited reflection and self-correction of search queries, can naturally emerge from the reinforcement learning process without explicit design or training for these behaviors.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.19355.Title: ST-VLM: Kinematic Instruction Tuning for Spatio-Temporal Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.19355.Summary: ST-VLM, a Vision-Language Model, is developed using a kinematic instruction tuning framework to enable precise spatio-temporal reasoning about moving objects in dynamic videos. The model, trained on the new STKit dataset and evaluated on STKit-Bench, demonstrates superior performance in quantifying object kinematics compared to existing VLMs, including proprietary models.
Problem: Current Vision-Language Models (VLMs) struggle to perform precise, quantitative kinematic analysis of moving objects in dynamic videos (e.g., calculating distance, speed, or direction).
A significant data scarcity exists for large-scale, video-based instruction tuning datasets focused explicitly on kinematic understanding.
VLMs lack the ability to integrate visual kinematic perception with linguistic knowledge, logical inference, and arithmetic for complex multi-step reasoning in dynamic contexts.
Method: A novel kinematic instruction tuning framework is introduced, defining seven fundamental spatio-temporal tasks for quantifying object motion.
A new dataset, STKit, is constructed from 3D-annotated videos and expanded using a scalable 4D reconstruction-based pseudo-labeling pipeline for unlabeled videos.
ST-VLM is developed by fine-tuning LLaVA-OneVision on the blended STKit and other VLM datasets to endow it with specialized kinematic understanding, and STKit-Bench is created for evaluation.
Results: ST-VLM achieved an average accuracy of 59.8% on the STKit-Bench, significantly outperforming GPT-4V (28.5%) and other leading VLMs by more than 30 percentage points in kinematic reasoning tasks.

Ablation studies confirmed that both 3D-annotated video data and pseudo-labeled data from the 4D reconstruction pipeline are essential, contributing to an average accuracy improvement from 27.9% to 51.1% and then to 59.8%, respectively.

The model also demonstrated improved performance on various general video understanding and physical reasoning benchmarks (e.g., PerceptionTest, MVBench), indicating a broader enhancement of video comprehension.
Takeaways: Dedicated kinematic instruction tuning, particularly with precise 3D-annotated video data, significantly enhances a VLM's ability to perform quantitative spatio-temporal reasoning.
A scalable pseudo-labeling pipeline leveraging 4D reconstruction effectively addresses data scarcity by generating high-quality kinematic labels from unlabeled videos.
Acquiring robust kinematic understanding not only improves specialized tasks but also generalizes to enhance overall video comprehension and physical reasoning in VLMs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.19263.Title: DWIM: Towards Tool-aware Visual Reasoning via Discrepancy-aware Workflow Generation & Instruct-Masking Tuning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.19263.Summary: DWIM enables Large Language Model (LLM) agents to perform tool-aware visual reasoning by addressing the challenges of noisy perception tools and data scarcity. The framework achieves state-of-the-art performance with an average absolute improvement of over 9.73% on various visual reasoning datasets and demonstrates a 10% lower failure rate due to tool errors in human evaluation compared to frozen LLMs.
Problem: Existing compositional visual reasoning methods rely on frozen LLMs that lack deep understanding of specific visual tools' capabilities and limitations, hindering optimal workflow generation.
Fine-tuning LLMs for visual reasoning is challenging due to data scarcity and the inherent inaccuracies of perception tools, which lead to noisy training data unsuitable for standard fine-tuning.
Current approaches inefficiently utilize training data by discarding workflows that fail due to tool errors, preventing models from learning how to recover from imperfections.
Method: An "Auto-Exploring Agentic Framework" that, during training workflow generation, leverages ground truth to enable the LLM to identify factual discrepancies from tool feedback and generate "Rethink" actions to explore alternative tool usages.

A "Discrepancy-aware Training Workflow Generation" method that dynamically refines actions when tool errors are detected, increasing the success rate of workflows and generating a larger, more effective dataset.

"Instruct-Masking Fine-tuning," a semantic masking strategy that flags actions as effective or ineffective; it masks effective actions for reproduction while unmasking ineffective actions and "Rethink" descriptions to explicitly teach the model error recovery.
Results: Achieved state-of-the-art performance with an average absolute improvement of over 9.73% across six diverse visual reasoning datasets (e.g., GQA, SugarCREPE, RefCOCO) and exhibited strong zero-shot cross-dataset generalization with a 4.8% improvement over baselines.

Reduced average tool utilization per successful sample to 1.74, significantly lower than baselines (2.49-3.26), indicating more precise and effective tool usage, and showed improved performance across various open-source LLM backbones (>12.4% absolute gain).

Ablation studies confirmed that Discrepancy-aware Workflow Generation boosted data utilization by ~17% and Instruct-Masking Fine-tuning yielded up to 16.3% absolute performance gain over naive SFT, validating the efficacy of both core components.
Takeaways: LLMs can be trained to intelligently assess the effectiveness of visual perception tools, detect discrepancies in their outputs, and self-correct through iterative reasoning, rather than merely chaining tools.
Generating training data that explicitly accounts for tool imperfections and recovery mechanisms significantly improves an LLM's robustness and tool awareness in complex visual environments.

A fine-tuning approach that selectively reinforces successful actions while also exposing the model to failures and recovery strategies (via instruct-masking) leads to more resilient and efficient tool utilization.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.19108.Title: Your ViT is Secretly an Image Segmentation Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.19108.Summary: Research across three European universities demonstrates that standard Vision Transformers (ViTs) can perform image segmentation tasks without complex task-specific components when leveraging large-scale pre-trained models, achieving competitive performance while reducing computational overhead through an Encoder-only Mask Transformer architecture.
Problem: Current state-of-the-art ViT-based segmentation models rely on complex, computationally expensive task-specific components
These additional architectural elements limit the models' ability to benefit from advances in ViT architectures and hardware acceleration
Method: Development of Encoder-only Mask Transformer (EoMT) that repurposes standard ViT architecture for segmentation
Introduction of mask annealing training strategy to eliminate masked attention during inference
Leveraging large-scale pre-trained Vision Foundation Models like DINOv2
Results: Achieved competitive performance with state-of-the-art models while being significantly faster
Successfully demonstrated compatibility with token merging techniques for additional efficiency gains
Maintained strong out-of-distribution generalization capabilities through Vision Foundation Model integration
Reduced architectural complexity while preserving segmentation accuracy across multiple benchmarks
Takeaways: Task-specific components become less important as model size and pre-training scale increases
Standard ViT architectures contain sufficient representational power for segmentation tasks
Masked attention can be eliminated during inference through careful training strategies

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.18866.Title: Reasoning to Learn from Latent Thoughts
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.18866.Summary: Researchers at Stanford University, the University of Toronto, and the Vector Institute introduced "Reasoning to Learn," a framework that enhances large language model data efficiency by explicitly modeling and leveraging latent thought processes during pretraining. Their Bootstrapping Latent Thought (BoLT) algorithm allows models to iteratively improve their ability to generate and learn from high-quality latent thoughts, achieving 25.38% on MATH and outperforming strong baselines by a large margin.
Problem: Data scarcity and the data bottleneck threaten to limit the continued scaling and advancement of large language models.
Existing synthetic data generation techniques often fail to explicitly capture the underlying human reasoning processes crucial for efficient learning.
LMs need mechanisms to improve their learning efficiency from observed data without relying on extensive external supervision or task-specific rewards.
Method: Developed "Reasoning to Learn," a latent variable approach that trains LMs to decompress observed text (X) by inferring natural language latent thoughts (Z), modeling the joint distribution p(Z, X).

Introduced the Bootstrapping Latent Thought (BoLT) algorithm, an Expectation-Maximization (EM) based iterative self-improvement loop. In the E-step, the model generates improved latent thoughts, and in the M-step, it trains on these bootstrapped (X, Z) pairs.

Utilized a frontier model (GPT-4o-mini) for warmstarting latent thought generation, then allowed the model to self-improve, generating latent thoughts in a dedicated 'latent space' using special tokens during next-token prediction training.
Results: Training with GPT-4o-mini-synthesized latent thoughts achieved 25.38% on MATH, significantly outperforming baselines like Raw-Repeat (5.74%) and WRAP-CoT (19.36%) while using 3.3x fewer raw data epochs.
The BoLT algorithm demonstrated monotonic self-improvement over several iterations on fixed data, consistently increasing both the ELBO and downstream MATH accuracy.

Models trained with BoLT using increased Monte Carlo samples (K) for latent generation showed improved ELBO and MATH accuracy, affirming the link between inference compute investment and latent quality.
Takeaways: Explicitly modeling latent thoughts in a separate, dedicated space is crucial for data-efficient learning, outperforming methods that intersperse reasoning directly within the raw text.
Language models can iteratively bootstrap their own ability to infer and utilize high-quality latent thoughts through an EM-like self-improvement process, moving beyond initial external supervision.

Increased inference compute during the E-step (latent generation) directly correlates with higher-quality synthetic latents and improved downstream model performance, offering a new avenue for scaling data efficiency.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.17352.Title: OpenVLThinker: Complex Vision-Language Reasoning via Iterative SFT-RL Cycles
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.17352.Summary: Researchers at UCLA developed OpenVLThinker, an open-source large vision-language model, leveraging an iterative supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning cycle to achieve complex, multi-step reasoning. This model demonstrates competitive performance with proprietary LVLMs and surpasses other open-source models on challenging benchmarks, showing data efficiency with 10x less data.
Problem: Open-source Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) typically lack the sophisticated multi-step reasoning capabilities (e.g., planning, reflection, verification) observed in proprietary multimodal models or text-only R1 models.
Distilling reasoning directly from text-only R1 models into LVLMs through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) often leads to performance degradation due to imprecise visual grounding.

Applying pure reinforcement learning (RL) from scratch to smaller LVLMs (e.g., 7B parameters) for reasoning is inefficient due to the prohibitively large search space for reflective behaviors to emerge.
Method: An iterative self-improvement framework alternates between Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning (RL) using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO).
SFT datasets are curated by using the base LVLM for captioning, feeding captions to a text-based R1 model for CoT generation, and then self-generating higher-quality CoTs in subsequent iterations.
A two-stage, source-based curriculum RL strategy trains the model first on medium-difficulty data and then on hard-difficulty data to optimize learning efficiency and maximize performance.
Results: OpenVLThinker-7B achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-source LVLMs across six challenging benchmarks, with average accuracy of 47.9% and specific improvements such as 3.8% on MathVista and 2.4% on EMMA.
The model performs competitively with larger proprietary models like GPT-4o (47.3% average) and Claude-3.5-Sonnet (48.4% average) on Math and Perception tasks.

Empirical analysis validates that while initial SFT might cause a temporary performance drop, the iterative SFT-RL cycle consistently yields significant gains, confirming the efficacy of the proposed self-improvement paradigm.
Takeaways: The iterative SFT-RL cycle synergistically fosters complex reasoning, where initial SFT acts as an 'action highlighting' mechanism to surface reasoning behaviors and narrow the RL search space.

RL refines these reasoning actions and improves generalization from the SFT-provided foundation, playing a crucial role in enhancing overall accuracy and generating better SFT data for subsequent iterations.

Robust complex reasoning can be instilled in LVLMs with significantly less training data (using only 12K examples per iteration) compared to concurrent single-iteration methods that require 10x more data.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.16660.Title: When Less is Enough: Adaptive Token Reduction for Efficient Image Representation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.16660.Summary: A token reduction framework enables efficient processing of high-resolution images in multimodal AI systems by selecting only the most informative visual features through an autoencoder-based approach, allowing up to 50-90% token reduction while maintaining performance across multiple vision-language benchmarks and achieving significant memory savings without requiring model fine-tuning.
Problem: Vision Transformers in multimodal models suffer from quadratic computational costs due to long sequences of visual tokens
Existing token reduction methods are often task-specific and require model fine-tuning, limiting their practical applicability
Method: Autoencoder architecture with Gumbel-Softmax selection mechanism identifies essential visual tokens
Feature Selector and Reconstructor work together to learn which tokens can be safely discarded while maintaining information
Integration with existing models without requiring additional training
Results: Achieved 50-90% token reduction while maintaining performance across multiple benchmarks
Demonstrated superior performance compared to random selection, especially for detail-intensive tasks
Enabled significant memory savings and faster inference without compromising model capabilities
Provided interpretable results showing which visual elements are most important for different tasks
Takeaways: Most visual tokens are redundant for downstream tasks, with up to 90% being dispensable for certain applications
Token selection effectiveness varies by task type - more critical for detail-oriented tasks like OCR than general reasoning
Random selection performs surprisingly well for reasoning tasks, suggesting alternative reduction strategies may be viable

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.16434.Title: Interactive Sketchpad: A Multimodal Tutoring System for Collaborative, Visual Problem-Solving
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.16434.Summary: MIT researchers developed Interactive Sketchpad, a multimodal tutoring system utilizing GPT-4o and code execution to provide dynamic, interactive visualizations and hint-based guidance for visual problem-solving. The system significantly improved accuracy on graph algorithms and mathematical functions (e.g., 100% on Maxflow from IsoBench dataset) and received high user satisfaction for enhancing conceptual understanding in various math problems.
Problem: Existing intelligent tutoring systems are predominantly text-based, struggling to support tasks requiring visual or spatial reasoning.
Text-only feedback often falls short in subjects like geometry or calculus where diagrams and sketches are critical for comprehension and problem-solving.
Traditional AI tutors can hinder active learning by providing direct answers, rather than fostering deeper conceptual understanding through interactive engagement.
Method: Interactive Sketchpad uses a pre-trained Large Multimodal Model (LMM), GPT-4o, enhanced with code execution via OpenAI Code Interpreter to generate precise and dynamic visualizations.
The system provides step-by-step textual hints, fine-tuned on human demonstrations, alongside interactive visual aids displayed on a shared whiteboard.
Students can input text queries and interact directly with the whiteboard using sketches and annotations, which the LMM processes to provide context-aware feedback.
Results: Interactive Sketchpad achieved 100% accuracy on 'Maxflow' and significantly higher scores across other categories of the IsoBench dataset, outperforming GPT-4o (25.0% on Maxflow) and Visual Sketchpad (66.3% on Maxflow).
User studies showed high satisfaction with an average Likert score of 4.71/5 for Interface Intuitiveness and Accuracy of Visuals, and 4.57/5 for Effectiveness of Hints.
Qualitative feedback indicated that generated visualizations and the hint-based, iterative guidance significantly improved conceptual understanding and problem-solving engagement for students.
Takeaways: Leveraging LMMs with external code execution for visualization generation dramatically improves accuracy and robustness in visual problem-solving compared to relying solely on internal model reasoning.
A multimodal approach combining subtle, hint-based textual guidance with dynamic, interactive visual aids fosters deeper conceptual understanding and active learning.
An interactive whiteboard serves as a natural shared workspace, facilitating seamless human-AI collaboration for solving visually complex problems.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.16419.Title: Stop Overthinking: A Survey on Efficient Reasoning for Large Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.16419.Summary: Researchers from Rice University and the University of Houston present the first structured survey on efficient reasoning for Large Language Models, classifying methodologies that address the "overthinking phenomenon" by optimizing the length and necessity of generated reasoning sequences. This survey provides a comprehensive taxonomy and critical insights to guide the development of more practical and cost-effective LLM applications.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) often exhibit an "overthinking phenomenon," generating verbose and redundant reasoning sequences for complex tasks.
This verbosity leads to substantial computational overhead, increased inference costs, and higher latency, hindering practical deployment in real-world, computation-sensitive applications.
The inefficiency limits the application of powerful reasoning models in latency-sensitive or resource-constrained environments.
Method: The survey systematically categorizes current research on efficient reasoning into three primary mechanisms: model-based, reasoning output-based, and input prompts-based approaches.

It analyzes techniques for intrinsic model modifications, such as reinforcement learning with length rewards and supervised fine-tuning with variable-length Chain-of-Thought (CoT) data, to produce concise reasoning.

It explores methods that dynamically compress or guide reasoning during inference (e.g., latent representations, confidence-based pruning) and strategies leveraging prompt attributes (e.g., token budgeting, complexity-driven routing).
Results: The survey identifies three main categories of efficient reasoning: model-based (e.g., RL with length rewards, SFT with variable-length CoT data), reasoning output-based (e.g., latent representation compression, dynamic inference paradigms), and input prompt-based (e.g., explicit token budgeting, complexity-driven routing).
It details how techniques like integrating length penalties in RL or constructing concise CoT datasets in SFT can fine-tune models for intrinsic conciseness.

The analysis shows that approaches leveraging latent representations or dynamic inference paradigms, guided by confidence or rewards, can significantly reduce explicit reasoning steps during inference.
Takeaways: Efficient reasoning is emerging as a crucial subfield for the widespread and sustainable adoption of advanced LLMs, moving beyond marginal optimization.
Current LLM training paradigms often implicitly encourage verbosity, necessitating dedicated research to achieve efficiency in reasoning.
A fundamental trade-off exists between reasoning efficiency and model safety, which requires careful consideration in future research endeavors.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.16416.Title: Survey on Evaluation of LLM-based Agents
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.16416.Summary: A survey provides the first comprehensive mapping of evaluation methodologies for LLM-based agents, categorizing benchmarks across fundamental capabilities and application-specific domains. It highlights the field's shift towards more realistic and live evaluation, while identifying critical needs for granular metrics, cost efficiency, scalable automation, and robust safety assessments.
Problem: Traditional Large Language Models (LLMs) are limited to static, single-turn text-to-text interactions, lacking the dynamic capabilities of agents.
The emergence of LLM-based agents, capable of multi-step reasoning, tool use, and memory in dynamic environments, necessitates new and robust evaluation methodologies.
The existing evaluation landscape for these agents was fragmented, lacking a comprehensive and systematic overview.
Method: Provides the first comprehensive survey of evaluation methodologies specifically for LLM-based agents.
Systematically analyzes existing benchmarks and frameworks, categorizing them by fundamental agent capabilities and application-specific domains.
Synthesizes findings to identify current trends and highlight critical gaps in agent evaluation practices.
Results: Identified a clear trend towards more realistic, challenging, and live benchmarks, moving beyond static environments to dynamic, real-world scenarios.
Revealed significant gaps in current evaluation practices, including a lack of granular, fine-grained metrics for diagnosing specific agent failures.
Highlighted the insufficient focus on cost, efficiency, scalability, automation, and critical safety and compliance aspects in existing evaluation paradigms.
Takeaways: Evaluating LLM-based agents requires new methodologies focusing on multi-step behavior, dynamic interaction, and decision-making processes, distinct from traditional LLM evaluation.
The lack of a comprehensive evaluation framework prior to this work hindered standardization and identification of research directions in a rapidly evolving field.
Current evaluation trends show a shift towards more realistic and continuously updated benchmarks for agent assessment.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.16219.Title: Reinforcement Learning for Reasoning in Small LLMs: What Works and What Doesn't
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.16219.Summary: Knovel Engineering Lab and VNU University of Science developed a reinforcement learning approach to enhance mathematical reasoning in 1.5-billion-parameter language models. The method achieved competitive performance against larger, more expensive models, including outperforming OpenAI's o1-preview on AIME24, with an estimated training cost of only $42 using a curated dataset and rule-based rewards.
Problem: Advanced reasoning capabilities are typically tied to massive LLMs with immense computational demands, limiting accessibility for most researchers and organizations.
Existing RL-based fine-tuning methods for smaller LLMs often still incur high computational costs or require extensive datasets, hindering practical deployment.
There is a need for resource-efficient approaches to elevate reasoning performance in small LLMs (1-10 billion parameters) to democratize access to advanced AI capabilities.
Method: A 1.5-billion-parameter model (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B) was fine-tuned using the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) algorithm under strict constraints (4 NVIDIA A40 GPUs, 24-hour training, 1 epoch).
A compact, high-quality mathematical reasoning dataset of 39,659 examples was meticulously curated from existing sources to maximize learning efficiency.
A rule-based reward system, comprising accuracy, cosine, and format rewards, was implemented to guide RL optimization without the need for a resource-intensive neural critic model.
Results: The fine-tuned models (Open-RS1, Open-RS2, Open-RS3) achieved average zero-shot pass@1 scores of 53.0% to 56.3% on math benchmarks, competing with and in some cases exceeding other 1.5B and even some 7B models.
Open-RS3 achieved a 46.7% AIME24 score, surpassing OpenAI's o1-preview (44.6%) and DeepScaleR-1.5B-Preview (43.1%) on this specific benchmark.

The approach demonstrated significant cost and data efficiency, using only 7,000 samples and an estimated training cost of $42, a substantial reduction compared to baseline models costing thousands of dollars.
Takeaways: Small LLMs can achieve rapid reasoning improvements (within 50-100 steps) with limited high-quality data, but prolonged training under fixed length constraints can lead to performance degradation and output instability.
Incorporating a balanced mix of easy and hard problems stabilizes initial reasoning performance, though long-term issues like language drift in multilingual base models persist.

Cosine rewards are effective for stabilizing output lengths, but extending length limits is crucial for handling extremely complex reasoning tasks, especially with multilingual base models prone to language drift.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.16188.Title: Think or Not Think: A Study of Explicit Thinking in Rule-Based Visual Reinforcement Fine-Tuning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.16188.Summary: A study of thinking in rule-based visual reinforcement fine-tuning for multi-modal large language models reveals that explicit reasoning processes are not always necessary and can even be detrimental, especially for visual perception tasks. For 2B models, a "no-thinking" strategy achieved a 3.14% higher average accuracy in image classification and offered significant computational efficiency over thinking-based methods.
Problem: Conventional rule-based reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) for large language models (LLMs) heavily relies on explicit "thinking" processes like Chain-of-Thought, assuming this translates universally to Multi-modal LLMs (MLLMs).
Thinking-based RFT introduces significant computational overhead, including longer fine-tuning times and higher GPU memory requirements, due to generating lengthy reasoning responses.
The necessity and specific impact of explicit thinking during MLLM RFT were largely unexplored, especially considering observations of "overthinking" phenomena during LLM/MLLM inference.
Method: Introduced "No-Thinking-RFT" where models are strictly prompted to output direct answers without explicit reasoning, utilizing an equality-based accuracy reward to penalize extraneous text.

Proposed "Think-After-Answer" and "Adaptive-Thinking" variants to investigate the timing and strategic adoption of thinking, all implemented within the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) framework.

Conducted systematic comparative studies across diverse MLLM models (Qwen2-VL-2B/7B, InternVL2.5) and a wide range of visual and multi-modal tasks, including image classification and various reasoning benchmarks.
Results: No-Thinking-RFT consistently outperformed Thinking-RFT for visual perception tasks, achieving an average of 3.14% higher accuracy for 2B models in image classification.
No-Thinking-RFT demonstrated substantial computational efficiency, with significantly faster fine-tuning and inference times, and quicker reward convergence compared to Thinking-RFT.
Thinking-RFT responses frequently showed inconsistencies between the generated reasoning and the final answer, particularly in mid-sized models on reasoning tasks, impacting overall accuracy.
Takeaways: The optimal "thinking" strategy in MLLM RFT is highly dependent on both the model's inherent capability and the specific task complexity; smaller models and visual perception tasks often do not benefit from explicit thinking.
Explicit thinking processes that occur *before* verifiable answers can hinder reward convergence during fine-tuning, suggesting a "fine-tuning overthinking" phenomenon.
MLLMs can adaptively learn to decide *when* to engage in a thinking process during RFT, converging to strategies that align with their capabilities and task requirements.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.15621.Title: LLaVA-MORE: A Comparative Study of LLMs and Visual Backbones for Enhanced Visual Instruction Tuning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.15621.Summary: LLaVA-MORE introduces a systematic comparative study of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), investigating the impact of various Large Language Models and visual backbones under a unified training and evaluation protocol. This empirical analysis provides insights into component contributions and architectural trade-offs, establishing new performance baselines for MLLMs.
Problem: Most state-of-the-art MLLMs converge on a narrow technical approach, largely relying on LLaMA-derived LLMs and CLIP-based visual encoders, limiting architectural exploration.
Inconsistent training data, datasets, and evaluation protocols across rapidly introduced MLLM models hinder fair comparisons and a clear understanding of optimal design choices.
There is a need to systematically understand the trade-offs between MLLM component size, architecture, and performance, rather than just pursuing parameter scaling.
Method: LLaVA-MORE systematically pairs diverse small-to-medium scale LLMs (e.g., Gemma, Phi, LLaMA, DeepSeek) with various visual backbones (e.g., CLIP, DINOv2, SigLIP, SigLIP2) under a unified framework.
A consistent two-stage training protocol (visual-linguistic alignment and instruction tuning) and a comprehensive set of evaluation benchmarks are applied to all model configurations.
Results: LLaVA-MORE models consistently surpassed existing LLaVA baselines across both small and medium scales, with Gemma-2-9B emerging as a top performer, particularly in VQA benchmarks.
SigLIP-based visual backbones demonstrated substantial improvements over CLIP, establishing a new performance frontier due to their larger-scale image-text pre-training.
Qualitative results showed LLaVA-MORE models generated more detailed and accurate image descriptions while significantly reducing object hallucinations compared to the LLaVA-1.5-7B baseline.
Takeaways: Architectural choices and fine-tuning strategies can enable smaller LLMs (e.g., Phi-4-3.8B) to outperform larger baselines on specific benchmarks, challenging the assumption that only larger models perform better.

Visual backbones pre-trained with image-text data (e.g., SigLIP family) consistently outperform self-supervised backbones (DINOv2), suggesting that inherent text alignment simplifies multimodal integration.
Optimal MLLM configurations are highly task-dependent, with the benefits of increased image resolution and specific pre-training datasets varying based on model scale and the visual task at hand.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.15485.Title: TULIP: Towards Unified Language-Image Pretraining
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.15485.Summary: TULIP introduces a unified language-image pretraining framework that integrates global semantic understanding with fine-grained visual perception. It establishes new state-of-the-art performance across various vision-language and vision-centric benchmarks, including zero-shot classification, image retrieval, and fine-grained recognition.
Problem: Existing Contrastive Image-Text (CIT) models like CLIP excel at high-level vision-language tasks but often struggle with fine-grained visual understanding (e.g., counting, spatial reasoning) due to over-optimization for global semantic alignment.

Vision-centric self-supervised learning models (e.g., DINOv2) capture intricate visual details effectively but inherently lack language grounding, limiting their applicability in language-driven multimodal systems.
There is a trade-off in current multimodal models between achieving strong global semantic alignment and retaining high-fidelity, fine-grained visual information.
Method: TULIP unifies image-text, image-image, and text-text contrastive learning by extending the SigLIP loss function and using a DINOv2-style image encoder with an EMA teacher, and a T5-based text encoder.

Introduces GeCo (GEnerative COntrastive view augmentation), a novel strategy that employs large language models (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) and diffusion models (InstructPix2Pix) to generate diverse positive and challenging 'hard negative' samples for both image and text modalities.
Incorporates a pixel-level reconstruction regularization objective for both image (masked autoencoder-style) and text (causal decoder) to encourage the model to retain high-frequency local details.
Results: Achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot classification performance on ImageNet-1K (e.g., 85.0% for So/14, 384px), surpassing SigLIP 2.

Demonstrates superior performance in fine-grained classification (e.g., 9.8% on RxRx1, nearly 2x over SigLIP) and compositional reasoning (e.g., up to 30% improvement on Winoground compared to existing CIT models).

Functions as a strong visual encoder for multimodal large language models, significantly improving performance on vision-centric benchmarks like MMVP (20.3% vs. SigLIP 5.9%) while maintaining strong language-centric performance.
Takeaways: Combining diverse contrastive views (image-text, image-image, text-text) with generative augmentation enables learning both global semantics and fine-grained details within a unified framework.
Leveraging large generative models to create 'hard negatives' forces the model to learn more precise semantic distinctions across image and text modalities.
Incorporating a reconstruction regularization objective counteracts the loss of high-frequency visual details that can occur in purely contrastive training, ensuring richer visual representations.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14858.Title: 1000 Layer Networks for Self-Supervised RL: Scaling Depth Can Enable New Goal-Reaching Capabilities
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14858.Summary: This research investigates scaling network depth in self-supervised reinforcement learning (RL) using Contrastive RL (CRL), showing that increasing depth up to 1000 layers leads to substantial performance gains. The approach enables the emergence of complex, qualitatively distinct behaviors across diverse locomotion, navigation, and manipulation tasks.
Problem: Reinforcement learning (RL) models typically remain shallow (2-5 layers), in contrast to the hundreds or thousands of layers used in other AI domains like NLP and CV.
Prior attempts to increase network depth in RL often yielded only marginal benefits, instability, or even negative impacts.
The lack of clear 'scaling laws' in RL limits the development of more general and powerful learning agents.
Method: Utilized Contrastive Reinforcement Learning (CRL), an actor-critic method, for goal-conditioned learning without explicit rewards, employing an InfoNCE objective for the critic.
Designed and trained very deep networks (up to 1024 layers) for both actor and critic, incorporating residual connections, Layer Normalization, and Swish activations to stabilize training.
Conducted experiments on a diverse suite of 10 simulated environments using the GPU-accelerated JaxGCRL framework to facilitate high-throughput data collection and training.
Results: Achieved performance improvements ranging from 2x to over 50x by increasing network depth from 4 to 64 layers, with continued gains observed up to 1024 layers.
Unlocked qualitatively new capabilities and behaviors, such as a depth-256 Humanoid agent performing 'vaulting walls' or 'worming its way' over obstacles.
Demonstrated that scaling network depth is more effective than scaling width, that joint actor and critic scaling is beneficial, and that deeper networks effectively leverage larger batch sizes.
Takeaways: Self-supervised learning, particularly CRL, is essential for enabling stable and effective depth scaling in RL, unlike other standard TD-based RL methods.
Deeper networks learn richer, more topological representations of the environment, moving beyond naive distance metrics and strategically allocating representational capacity.
The benefits of depth scaling stem from a synergistic enhancement of both exploration capabilities (collecting better data) and model expressivity (learning more effectively from that data).

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14476.Title: DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14476.Summary: Researchers from ByteDance Seed, Tsinghua University, and The University of Hong Kong developed DAPO, an open-source reinforcement learning system for large language models. The system achieved 50 points on the AIME 2024 dataset with a Qwen2.5-32B model, surpassing the prior 47-point score of DeepSeek-R1-Zero-Qwen-32B while requiring 50% fewer training steps.
Problem: There is a lack of transparency and reproducibility in state-of-the-art LLM reinforcement learning (RL) systems, as key technical details are often concealed by leading research groups.
Large-scale LLM RL training for complex, long Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning tasks faces significant practical challenges, including entropy collapse, reward noise, and training instability.
Eliciting and enhancing sophisticated reasoning capabilities in LLMs requires specialized RL approaches beyond standard alignment techniques.
Method: DAPO, an open-source LLM reinforcement learning system, builds on Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a rule-based reward model and without a KL divergence penalty.

It introduces four core techniques: Clip-Higher for mitigating entropy collapse, Dynamic Sampling for improving sample efficiency by filtering zero-gradient samples, Token-Level Policy Gradient Loss for balanced gradient contribution, and Soft Overlong Punishment for refined length-aware reward shaping.
A carefully curated dataset, DAPO-Math-17K, was created with integer-transformed answers to enable precise, verifiable rule-based reward signals for mathematical reasoning.
Results: DAPO trained a Qwen2.5-32B base model to achieve 50 points on the AIME 2024 dataset, outperforming the previous state-of-the-art DeepSeek-R1-Zero-Qwen-32B which scored 47 points.
The system demonstrated enhanced training efficiency, achieving its performance with 50% fewer training steps compared to the prior method.

Ablation studies confirmed that Dynamic Sampling was the most impactful component, contributing 8 points to the final score, while Clip-Higher, Soft Overlong Punishment, and Token-level Loss also provided cumulative improvements.
Takeaways: The combination of specific algorithmic refinements (Clip-Higher, Dynamic Sampling, Token-level loss, Overlong Reward Shaping) is critical for stable and efficient large-scale LLM RL training, especially for long Chain-of-Thought reasoning.
Maintaining a healthy level of policy entropy and ensuring consistent, effective gradients by filtering out zero-gradient samples are crucial for improving performance and accelerating convergence.
Reinforcement learning can foster the emergence of new, complex reasoning behaviors in LLMs, such as self-reflection and error correction, which were not explicitly present in the base model.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13551.Title: Towards Hierarchical Multi-Step Reward Models for Enhanced Reasoning in Large Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13551.Summary: Hierarchical Reward Models (HRM) and Hierarchical Node Compression (HNC) were developed to enhance the reliability and scalability of reward models for multi-step mathematical reasoning in LLMs. HRM combats reward hacking by evaluating reasoning at both individual and consecutive multi-step levels, leading to more stable and generalizable reasoning, while HNC efficiently augments training data for improved robustness.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently struggle with detecting and correcting intermediate errors in complex multi-step reasoning, leading to error propagation.
Outcome Reward Models (ORMs) suffer from delayed feedback, credit assignment issues, and susceptibility to spurious reasoning.
Process Reward Models (PRMs) are vulnerable to reward hacking and incur high computational and human annotation costs for training data generation.
Method: Introduced a Hierarchical Reward Model (HRM) that evaluates reasoning at both fine-grained (individual steps) and coarse-grained (merged consecutive steps) levels, promoting coherence and self-correction.

Developed Hierarchical Node Compression (HNC), a data augmentation strategy that merges consecutive nodes in MCTS-generated trees to enhance data diversity and robustness with minimal computational overhead.
Applied a self-training strategy for policy models, fine-tuning them on high-quality reasoning data identified by HRM and regularized with KL divergence to maintain generalization capabilities.
Results: HRM achieved 80% accuracy on the PRM800K test set, demonstrating stable performance and consistently outperforming traditional ORM and PRM which showed fluctuations.
HRM, when trained with HNC-augmented data, consistently showed greater robustness and stability across various policy models, with HNC requiring only 30 minutes of CPU for augmentation.
Policy models fine-tuned using HRM-identified high-quality reasoning data achieved higher maximum accuracy (e.g., 80% vs. 74.4% for PRM-trained models on PRM800K) and improved robustness.
HRM demonstrated superior generalization, achieving 74.2% accuracy on the out-of-domain MATH500 dataset compared to PRM's 65.6% at N=64.
Takeaways: Evaluating reasoning hierarchically, by considering both individual steps and multi-step coherence, effectively combats reward hacking and fosters more reliable LLM reasoning.
An efficient data augmentation method like HNC can significantly improve the diversity and robustness of autonomously generated training data for reward models without substantial computational cost.
Careful regularization with KL divergence is critical during policy model self-training to prevent catastrophic forgetting of general capabilities when fine-tuned on task-specific, high-quality data.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13436.Title: Unified Autoregressive Visual Generation and Understanding with Continuous Tokens
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13436.Summary: Google DeepMind's UniFluid unifies visual generation and understanding within a single autoregressive framework by leveraging continuous visual tokens and a pre-trained Gemma large language model backbone. The model demonstrates that joint training on both tasks improves image generation quality and achieves competitive performance across diverse visual understanding and editing applications.
Problem: Existing multimodal AI models often specialize in either visual generation or understanding, lacking a unified framework that can perform both tasks seamlessly.
Many autoregressive image generation models rely on discrete visual tokens, which can lead to information loss and quantization artifacts.
The challenge of integrating visual and textual modalities into a single, consistent autoregressive framework while overcoming the limitations of discrete tokenization for images.
Method: UniFluid develops a unified autoregressive framework that processes both discrete text tokens and continuous visual tokens within a single decoder-only transformer backbone.

It employs a continuous Variational Autoencoder (VAE) for image tokenization during generation and a pre-trained SigLIP encoder for understanding, with task-specific prediction heads for text (classification) and images (diffusion).

The framework uses a unified loss function combining cross-entropy for text and a diffusion loss for continuous visual tokens, along with dynamic random-order generation for image tokens during training.
Results: UniFluid, trained with a unified objective, achieved better image generation quality (e.g., FID 7.20 for 2B models) compared to a model trained solely for text-to-image (FID 7.88).

The hyperparameter lambda (λ) effectively controls the trade-off between generation and understanding performance; a smaller λ (e.g., 0.005) yields high-fidelity generation while retaining significant understanding ability.

The model demonstrated strong transferability to various downstream tasks, achieving competitive results on 4 image captioning benchmarks and 20 visual question answering tasks, and successfully performing image editing.
Takeaways: Unified training on both generation and understanding tasks can mutually benefit each other, leading to improved image generation quality compared to generation-only models.
A stronger pre-trained large language model backbone significantly enhances performance across both visual generation and understanding tasks within the unified framework.
Random-order image generation during training is crucial for achieving high-quality image synthesis, while raster-order processing may slightly benefit understanding tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.12811.Title: A Multi-Power Law for Loss Curve Prediction Across Learning Rate Schedules
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.12811.Summary: Researchers from Tsinghua University and partners derive a Multi-Power Law (MPL) that accurately predicts the training loss curves of large language models under different learning rate schedules, enabling optimization of training efficiency while reducing the computational cost of hyperparameter tuning through theoretical analysis and empirical validation across multiple model architectures.
Problem: Existing scaling laws don't account for learning rate schedules, limiting their practical utility
Hyperparameter tuning for large language models is extremely resource-intensive
Understanding the relationship between learning rate schedules and training loss evolution
Method: Developed Multi-Power Law combining learning rate sum matching with decay-induced loss reduction
Created a theoretical framework explaining power-law behavior in optimization landscapes
Implemented schedule optimization based on loss predictions
Results: MPL accurately predicts loss curves for unseen schedules and longer training horizons
Discovered learning rate schedules that outperform standard cosine decay
Provided theoretical justification through analysis of quadratic loss functions
Demonstrated applicability across different model sizes and architectures
Takeaways: Training runs with same cumulative learning rate tend to have similar losses
Loss reduction exhibits power-law relationship with learning rate decay
Optimized schedules naturally resemble Warmup-Stable-Decay pattern

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.12799.Title: Grounded Chain-of-Thought for Multimodal Large Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.12799.Summary: Researchers at Xiamen University introduce Grounded Chain-of-Thought (GCoT), a framework that integrates explicit visual-spatial grounding into MLLM reasoning steps to mitigate visual hallucination. They construct the MM-GCoT dataset and show that fine-tuning models with GCoT significantly boosts answer-grounding consistency, indicating more reliable visual reasoning.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) suffer from visual hallucination, specifically 'language bias' where they provide correct answers without genuinely relying on visual evidence.
Existing Chain-of-Thought methods for MLLMs primarily focus on textual reasoning or external knowledge without explicitly grounding each reasoning step to specific visual regions.
Current benchmarks often overlook this subtle form of hallucination, focusing on explicit visual failures rather than the trustworthiness of the reasoning process.
Method: Introduces Grounded Chain-of-Thought (GCoT), a novel task requiring MLLMs to generate step-by-step reasoning where each step includes both textual reasoning and associated visual bounding box coordinates.
Constructs MM-GCoT, a large-scale supervised fine-tuning dataset with 23,028 examples, designed with multi-step reasoning chains linked to precise spatial grounding for diverse task types.
Proposes a comprehensive evaluation system including Answer Accuracy (A-Acc), Grounding Accuracy (G-Acc), and a key metric, Answer-Grounding Consistency (Consist.), to quantify reliable reasoning.
Results: State-of-the-art MLLMs exhibit a large gap between answer accuracy (e.g., 75.7% A-Acc for LLaVA-OneVision-72B) and answer-grounding consistency (e.g., 11.1% Consist. for same model).
Training with MM-GCoT data dramatically improves consistency; LLaVA-7B GCoT achieved a 55.7% boost in consistency (from 10.1% to 65.8%) and a 4.5% increase in answer accuracy.
GCoT-trained models demonstrated improved visual understanding and reliable reasoning, with qualitative analyses showing successful generalization of grounded reasoning to unseen tasks.
Takeaways: Visual hallucination, particularly language bias (correct answers without visual grounding), is pervasive in current MLLMs, with many exhibiting low answer-grounding consistency (e.g., as low as 11.1%).
Simply scaling up MLLM parameters does not necessarily alleviate visual hallucination; some larger models show worse consistency compared to smaller variants, suggesting data overfitting.

Explicit GCoT training effectively cultivates reliable visual reasoning, significantly improving consistency and enabling generalization to other multimodal tasks like open-world QA and Referring Expression Comprehension.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.12797.Title: DeepPerception: Advancing R1-like Cognitive Visual Perception in MLLMs for Knowledge-Intensive Visual Grounding
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.12797.Summary: DeepPerception introduces an MLLM-based framework to advance R1-like cognitive visual perception for knowledge-intensive visual grounding through a two-stage training process. The framework achieves an average accuracy of 62.20% on the new KVG-Bench, an 8.08% improvement over direct fine-tuning, and establishes new state-of-the-art results on fine-grained visual recognition tasks.
Problem: Current MLLMs lack fine-grained visual discrimination when tasks require deep domain-specific knowledge and structured cognitive reasoning.
Existing MLLMs tend to provide direct answers without integrating their vast knowledge bases with perceptual features through a step-by-step cognitive analysis.
There is a scarcity of high-quality, knowledge-aligned training data suitable for developing advanced cognitive visual perception in MLLMs.
Method: Defined the Knowledge-Intensive Visual Grounding (KVG) task and introduced KVG-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating cognitive visual perception.

Developed DeepPerception, an MLLM-based framework with a two-stage cognitive training process combining Chain-of-Thought Supervised Fine-Tuning (CoT-SFT) and Perception-oriented Reinforcement Learning (GRPO).
Implemented an automated data synthesis pipeline to generate knowledge-aligned training samples, including composite images, to overcome data scarcity for KVG.
Results: DeepPerception achieved 62.20% average accuracy on KVG-Bench, an 8.08% increase over direct fine-tuning, and surpassed 70B-scale MLLMs using a 7B-scale base model.

The framework demonstrated strong cross-domain generalization with 60.85% accuracy on unseen categories and established state-of-the-art performance on standard Fine-Grained Visual Recognition tasks (83.21% average accuracy).
General multimodal understanding and reasoning abilities were preserved, as shown by comparable performance to the base model on benchmarks like MMBench and MMMU.
Takeaways: Explicitly integrating cognitive reasoning processes (planning, analysis, comparison, conclusion) into MLLM training significantly enhances their ability to perform fine-grained visual discrimination.
A two-stage framework, combining CoT-SFT for establishing cognitive chains and GRPO for refining perceptual accuracy, effectively optimizes the synergy between MLLM perception and cognition.

Automated data synthesis, especially through composite image generation with visually similar entities, is an effective strategy to create data for knowledge-intensive visual tasks, reducing reliance on manual annotation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.12605.Title: Multimodal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning: A Comprehensive Survey
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.12605.Summary: This paper offers the first comprehensive survey of Multimodal Chain-of-Thought (MCoT) reasoning, analyzing its evolution, diverse methodologies, and applications across various modalities. It consolidates scattered research, providing a systematic taxonomy, elucidating foundational concepts, and identifying future research directions to foster innovation in multimodal AI.
Problem: The rapid growth and scattered nature of Multimodal Chain-of-Thought (MCoT) research lacked a comprehensive, systematic, and up-to-date review.
Researchers faced difficulty grasping foundational concepts, diverse methodologies, and future trajectories of MCoT due to the absence of consolidated knowledge.
A clear framework was needed to categorize and analyze MCoT methodologies across various modalities and application scenarios.
Method: The authors conducted the first systematic survey solely dedicated to Multimodal Chain-of-Thought (MCoT) reasoning.
