Proposes a 'Region Selection Token' mechanism that enables the MLLM to identify and re-encode specific image regions using grid-based coordinates, effectively increasing resolution for relevant areas.

Develops a 'Vision Re-Encoding Token' that prompts the MLLM to re-encode the entire image with an additional, specialized vision encoder, with the token's hidden state acting as a control signal to a dedicated projector for feature integration.
Results: A 2B parameter MLLM equipped with Visual Perception Tokens (2B+VPT) achieved an average performance score of 0.749, a 30.9% improvement over the base 2B model and outperforming a larger 7B base model by 20.0%.

VPT substantially improved performance on fine-grained VQA (0.207 improvement over 7B baseline) and visual reasoning tasks, demonstrating enhanced capability in handling complex visual relationships and minute details.
The approach maintained or surpassed the performance of larger models in zero-shot settings and across different image resolutions (224 and 512), indicating robust generalization and adaptability.
Takeaways: Introducing Visual Perception Tokens allows MLLMs to autonomously control their visual perception, shifting from passive processing to active, iterative visual information extraction.
The use of grid-based Region Selection Tokens provides a robust and learnable method for MLLMs to focus on specific image regions, outperforming direct pixel-level bounding box generation.

Leveraging the hidden state of a 'Re-Encoding Control' token enables fine-grained influence over how enriched visual features from specialized encoders are integrated, enhancing feature utility for the LLM.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.17422.Title: MLLMs Know Where to Look: Training-free Perception of Small Visual Details with Multimodal LLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.17422.Summary: A comprehensive analysis from USC and VU Amsterdam researchers reveals fundamental limitations in multimodal language models' ability to process small visual details, while introducing novel training-free cropping methods that significantly improve perception without compromising overall performance.
Problem: MLLMs struggle to accurately perceive and process small visual details in images
This limitation poses risks for critical applications like healthcare and autonomous driving
Unclear whether issues stem from localization or perception problems
Method: Developed systematic evaluation framework using TextVQA dataset with annotated bounding boxes
Created three automatic visual cropping methods leveraging model internal states
Implemented intervention studies to isolate perception vs localization issues
Results: Successfully established causal relationship between visual subject size and MLLM performance
Demonstrated effectiveness of training-free solutions for improving visual perception
Provided practical guidelines for safer deployment of MLLMs in critical applications
Created new metrics and evaluation methods for analyzing MLLM attention patterns
Takeaways: Performance consistently degrades as visual subjects become smaller
Issues primarily stem from perception rather than localization - models can find but not properly interpret small details
Training-free approaches can significantly improve small detail perception without compromising other capabilities

https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.17416.Title: Reasoning with Latent Thoughts: On the Power of Looped Transformers
https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.17416.Summary: Google Research investigators reveal that deep but parameter-efficient looped transformers can match or exceed the reasoning capabilities of much larger models, achieving comparable performance with up to 75% fewer parameters while providing new theoretical insights into how neural networks implement chain-of-thought reasoning.
Problem: Language models typically require massive parameter counts to achieve strong reasoning capabilities
The relationship between model architecture, parameter efficiency, and reasoning ability is poorly understood
Unclear whether reasoning requires large parameter counts or if architectural choices like depth are more important
Method: Introduce looped transformer architectures that reuse layers multiple times
Systematically study performance on synthetic reasoning tasks and language modeling
Develop theoretical framework connecting looped architectures to chain-of-thought reasoning
Results: Looped models match performance of larger non-looped models with 75% parameter reduction
Strong performance on synthetic reasoning tasks like n-ary addition and p-hop induction
Comparable downstream task performance to larger models despite worse perplexity
Theoretical guarantees for simulating chain-of-thought reasoning in certain settings
Takeaways: Many reasoning tasks require depth but not necessarily large parameter counts
Looped models can achieve strong reasoning performance despite worse language modeling metrics
Architecture choices focused on depth may be more important than raw parameter count
Looped transformers can effectively simulate chain-of-thought reasoning processes

https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.17159.Title: RobustMerge: Parameter-Efficient Model Merging for MLLMs with Direction Robustness
https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.17159.Summary: Researchers developed RobustMerge, a training-free, data-free, and storage-free model merging method specifically for parameter-efficient tuning (PEFT) modules in Multimodal Large Language Models. This approach significantly enhances knowledge consolidation, leading to a 3.4% average performance improvement on seen generative tasks and a 4.5% gain on unseen tasks on a new multimodal benchmark compared to previous merging techniques.
Problem: Existing model merging methods, primarily designed for full fine-tuning, perform poorly when directly applied to parameter-efficient tuning (PEFT) modules.
Advanced model merging techniques often rely on validation data or test-time adaptation, limiting their generalization to unseen tasks and practical applicability in data-agnostic scenarios.
Efficiently consolidating knowledge from multiple task-specific PEFT-tuned MLLMs into a single model without extensive retraining or data access remains a challenge.
Method: Introduced a method combining magnitude-based parameter pruning with complementary parameter scaling for LoRA matrices to preserve critical directions and reduce interference.
Developed a cross-task normalization mechanism for scaling coefficients to balance the influence of different tasks and improve generalization across diverse domains.
The final merged PEFT module is formed by adaptively summing these pruned and scaled low-rank matrices, requiring no training, additional data, or extra storage.
Results: Achieved an average performance of 57.33% on eight seen multimodal generative tasks and 37.99% on four unseen tasks on the MM-MergeBench, representing a 3.4% and 4.5% average improvement respectively over adapted baseline methods.

Demonstrated superior performance on general MLLM benchmarks (POPE, MME, MMBench) and for vision tasks using CLIP-ViT-B-32 and CLIP-ViT-L-14, with up to a 4.4% average accuracy increase over previous merging techniques.

Ablation studies confirmed that both parameter pruning with complementary scaling and cross-task normalization are vital components, significantly contributing to direction robustness and overall performance gains.
Takeaways: Parameter-efficient tuning (PEFT) modules, such as LoRA, exhibit distinct singular value distributions and wider parameter ranges compared to full fine-tuning, rendering existing merging methods unsuitable.

Maintaining "direction robustness" by preserving the singular vector directions, particularly for smaller singular values, is essential for minimizing task interference and effective merging of PEFT modules.

Compensating for significant singular value gaps through adaptive inter-parameter scaling, combined with cross-task normalization, enhances stability and generalization to unseen tasks without explicit singular value decomposition.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.16982.Title: Muon is Scalable for LLM Training
https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.16982.Summary: Moonshot AI researchers demonstrate a breakthrough in large language model training efficiency with the Muon optimizer, achieving 2x faster convergence than AdamW while successfully scaling to 16B parameter models and maintaining superior performance across key benchmarks like MMLU and GSM8K.
Problem: Traditional optimizers like AdamW face efficiency challenges in large-scale LLM training
Scaling promising optimization techniques to massive models remains technically challenging
Distributed training implementations often introduce additional complexity and instability
Method: Enhanced Muon optimizer with weight decay and careful parameter update scaling
Developed efficient distributed implementation compatible with ZeRO-1 optimization
Built comprehensive training framework demonstrated on 3B/16B parameter MoE models
Results: Achieved 2x computational efficiency improvement compared to AdamW
Successfully trained 3B/16B parameter models with improved benchmark performance
Demonstrated better weight matrix properties through improved singular value distribution
Provided open-source implementation and model checkpoints for reproducibility
Takeaways: Matrix orthogonalization techniques can significantly improve training efficiency
Proper scaling and implementation choices are crucial for optimizer performance
Stable training without loss spikes can be achieved through careful parameter updates

https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.16025.Title: FeatSharp: Your Vision Model Features, Sharper
https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.16025.Summary: NVIDIA researchers developed FeatSharp, a method to generate sharper, more detailed high-resolution features from low-resolution vision encoders by combining joint bilateral upsampling with tile-guided attentional refinement. The approach achieves state-of-the-art multi-view consistency fidelity, improves semantic segmentation mIoU on ADE20k by +1.66%, and boosts object detection AP on COCO 2017, while maintaining computational efficiency.
Problem: State-of-the-art vision encoders, particularly Vision Transformers, operate at low resolutions, leading to a loss of fine-grained details critical for many perception tasks.
Running these encoders at genuinely high resolutions is computationally prohibitive due to the quadratic scaling of self-attention mechanisms.

Many Vision Transformers are inflexible to resolution changes, with learned position embeddings degrading feature quality if input resolution is simply increased without specific design or finetuning.
Method: FeatSharp combines an extended Joint Bilateral Upsampling (JBU) stack with a novel tile-guided attentional refinement module to upsample features and reintroduce fine-grained details.

It processes overlapping image tiles with the original low-resolution vision encoder to generate a 'tiled mosaic' of local features, which is then fused with global JBU-upsampled features using a 2D local attention transformer block.
A learnable de-bias buffer and PHI-S normalization are incorporated to reduce inherent encoder noise and standardize feature distributions, ensuring consistent and coherent output features.
Results: FeatSharp consistently achieved the highest multi-view consistency fidelity across all tested foundation models, demonstrating superior robustness and semantic coherence of its upsampled features.

It delivered substantial performance improvements on downstream tasks, including an mIoU gain of +1.66% on ADE20k for semantic segmentation and higher Average Precision (AP) on COCO 2017 for object detection, particularly for small objects.

When used to provide high-resolution teacher targets for agglomerative models like RADIO, FeatSharp-enhanced teachers led to an average Multi-Task Learning Gain of +0.39% across diverse benchmarks, improving student model performance.
Takeaways: Tiling strategies, common in Vision-Language Models for high-resolution input, can be effectively leveraged to re-evaluate low-resolution encoders on local patches, thereby recovering lost fine-grained details.

Local attention within a transformer block is sufficient and computationally efficient for coherently fusing global context with detailed local information from tiled features, avoiding the quadratic cost of full high-resolution inference.

Feature normalization (PHI-S) and the removal of systematic biases (learned de-bias module) are crucial for maintaining the fidelity, multi-view consistency, and overall quality of upsampled features.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.14819.Title: Learning from Reward-Free Offline Data: A Case for Planning with Latent Dynamics Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.14819.Summary: Researchers at NYU and Meta FAIR developed Planning with Latent Dynamics Models (PLDM), a method leveraging reconstruction-free Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPA) to learn environment dynamics from unannotated offline data. This approach demonstrated strong generalization to new tasks and previously unseen environments in various navigation domains, outperforming existing model-free reinforcement learning techniques.
Problem: Traditional Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents require extensive, costly, and often dangerous online interactions, and crafting precise reward functions for complex real-world tasks is challenging.

A vast amount of passively collected, reward-free trajectory data exists, but effectively learning generalizable skills for autonomous agents from such unlabeled and potentially suboptimal offline data remains an unsolved problem.

There was a lack of systematic comparative analysis between model-free (RL-based) and model-based (control-based) approaches in the reward-free offline setting, especially concerning how different data characteristics influence their generalization abilities.
Method: Introduced Planning with Latent Dynamics Models (PLDM), a model-based optimal control method that learns an explicit dynamics model of the environment in a latent space directly from reward-free offline data.

PLDM employs a Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) for reconstruction-free self-supervised learning of latent dynamics, incorporating VICReg-inspired regularization, inverse dynamics modeling, and temporal smoothness objectives to learn robust representations.

Utilizes Model Predictive Control (MPC) with MPPI at test time to plan actions by minimizing a cost function in the latent space, allowing for flexible adaptation to diverse tasks (e.g., goal-reaching, state-avoidance) by simply modifying the cost.
Results: PLDM consistently outperformed all model-free RL methods in generalizing to unseen maze layouts and showed strong zero-shot adaptation to new tasks like state avoidance, simply by inverting the planning objective.

PLDM and GCIQL exhibited superior sample efficiency, achieving nearly 80% success with only a few thousand transitions, and PLDM, HILP, and GCIQL proved most robust to low-quality data generated by random policies.

Ablation studies confirmed the necessity of PLDM's reconstruction-free JEPA objective components for learning effective representations, with direct comparisons showing it significantly outperformed reconstruction-based approaches like DreamerV3 and TD-MPC2 in the reward-free offline setting.
Takeaways: Model-based planning with latent dynamics (PLDM) provides superior generalization to unseen environment layouts and novel tasks when learning from reward-free offline data compared to state-of-the-art model-free methods.

Reconstruction-free self-supervised learning, as implemented in JEPA, is crucial for learning effective and generalizable latent dynamics models from passive, unannotated data, outperforming reconstruction-based world models in this context.

The robustness and data efficiency of different learning paradigms for reward-free offline data vary significantly based on data quality, quantity, and diversity, with PLDM showing strong performance across varying data conditions.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.14786.Title: SigLIP 2: Multilingual Vision-Language Encoders with Improved Semantic Understanding, Localization, and Dense Features
https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.14786.Summary: Google DeepMind's SigLIP 2 introduces a family of multilingual vision-language encoders, integrating decoder-based pretraining, self-supervised losses, and active data curation to enhance semantic understanding, localization, and dense features. It consistently outperforms previous SigLIP models and other open-source baselines across zero-shot classification, retrieval, dense prediction, and localization tasks, while also reducing representation bias.
Problem: Traditional contrastive vision-language models often lacked strong fine-grained spatial understanding for dense prediction and localization tasks.

Existing open-source vision-language model efforts had not yet unified the broad range of recent advancements (e.g., decoder-based pretraining, self-supervised learning, data curation) into a single, high-performing model family.
There was a need for vision-language encoders with robust multilingual capabilities and reduced societal biases for broader real-world applicability.
Method: Extends the original SigLIP training recipe by integrating decoder-based pretraining for auxiliary tasks like image captioning and referring expression prediction.
Incorporates self-supervised losses, including local-to-global consistency and masked prediction, during the later stages of training to enhance dense feature representations.

Leverages the WebLI multilingual dataset with fairness-mitigation filtering and employs active data curation to boost the performance of smaller models, alongside introducing 'NaFlex' variants for variable resolution and native aspect ratio support.
Results: SigLIP 2 consistently outperforms SigLIP and other open-weight baselines across zero-shot classification, image-text retrieval (including multilingual XM3600), and serves as a stronger vision encoder for Vision-Language Models.

It shows substantial improvements on dense prediction tasks (e.g., semantic segmentation, depth estimation) and localization tasks (e.g., referring expression comprehension, open-vocabulary detection), attributed to integrated self-supervised and decoder-based losses.

The models exhibit improved cultural diversity understanding and significantly reduced representation bias (e.g., a reduction from 35.5% bias to 7.3% for the L/16 model), while NaFlex variants achieve better performance on aspect-sensitive document and OCR benchmarks.
Takeaways: A unified training recipe combining diverse advanced techniques, such as decoder-based pretraining, self-supervised losses, and active data curation, can yield compounded performance improvements in vision-language models.
Integrating auxiliary decoder tasks and self-supervised losses during pretraining effectively enhances models' capabilities for dense prediction and fine-grained localization.
Fairness mitigation techniques applied during training can substantially reduce representation biases in vision-language models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.14214.Title: Asymmetric Co-Training for Source-Free Few-Shot Domain Adaptation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.14214.Summary: Researchers from Jilin University introduce Asymmetric Co-Training (ACT), a method for Source-Free Few-Shot Domain Adaptation (SFFSDA) that adapts pre-trained models to new target domains using only a small labeled support set without access to source data. ACT consistently outperforms state-of-the-art SFUDA and few-shot transfer learning approaches, achieving 52.56% accuracy at 1-shot on TerraIncognita compared to 31.01% for the leading SFUDA baseline.
Problem: Deep Neural Networks suffer significant performance degradation due to domain shift when trained on a source domain and applied to a target domain.
Traditional Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) methods require simultaneous access to both source and target data, which is often unfeasible due to privacy or computational constraints.

Source-Free Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (SFUDA) methods remove the need for source data but still depend on large volumes of unlabeled target data, which can be scarce or difficult to acquire in many real-world scenarios.
Method: The paper proposes Asymmetric Co-Training (ACT), a novel method for the Source-Free Few-Shot Domain Adaptation (SFFSDA) setting, which leverages a two-branch network architecture.
ACT employs a strong-weak data augmentation strategy, including AutoAugment, to artificially increase data diversity and prevent overfitting in limited few-shot target support sets.

The approach utilizes a two-step iterative optimization process combining various loss functions (Label Smoothing Cross-Entropy, Entropy Minimization, Reverse Cross-Entropy, Classifier Determinacy Disparity) and Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) optimization.
Results: ACT consistently outperformed state-of-the-art SFUDA methods across all few-shot settings on benchmarks like Office31, OfficeHome, VisDA-C, and TerraIncognita, showing a 52.56% accuracy at 1-shot on TerraIncognita compared to 31.01% for the best SFUDA baseline.
The proposed method demonstrated superior performance against existing few-shot transfer learning and SFFSDA techniques, particularly on label-imbalanced datasets, further confirming its robustness.

An ablation study confirmed that all proposed components, including strong-weak augmentation, SAM optimization, and the specific loss functions, contribute positively and significantly to ACT's overall performance and robustness.
Takeaways: Adapting models with only a small labeled support set from the target domain (SFFSDA) is a practical and efficient solution for domain adaptation when source data is unavailable and large unlabeled target datasets are scarce.

The strategic combination of strong-weak data augmentation with an asymmetric co-training framework effectively mitigates overfitting and enhances model generalization in data-limited, few-shot environments.

Integrating diverse loss functions for discriminative learning, source knowledge retention, and enforcing consistent, confident predictions across multiple classifiers is critical for robust and high-performing domain adaptation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.14010.Title: Which Attention Heads Matter for In-Context Learning?
https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.14010.Summary: This research from UC Berkeley demonstrates that Function Vector (FV) attention heads are the primary drivers of in-context learning in large language models, rather than induction heads. The study resolves discrepancies in prior work by emphasizing the importance of specific evaluation metrics and controlling for functional correlations between different attention head types, showing that many induction heads develop FV capabilities during training.
Problem: Understanding the internal mechanisms enabling in-context learning (ICL) in large language models (LLMs).
Resolving conflicting hypotheses about whether induction mechanisms or function vector representations are more crucial for ICL.
Identifying which specific attention heads within transformer models are most responsible for ICL capabilities.
Method: Analyzed 12 decoder-only transformer models (70M to 7B parameters) from Pythia, GPT-2, and Llama 2 suites.
Identified induction heads using an 'induction score' and Function Vector (FV) heads using causal mediation analysis.

Conducted comprehensive ablation studies (mean ablation and ablation with exclusion) to measure the impact of different head types on ICL accuracy and token-loss difference, while also analyzing training dynamics.
Results: Ablating Function Vector (FV) heads consistently led to the largest degradation in ICL accuracy across various model sizes, affirming their primary role.
When controlling for correlations, induction heads showed a significantly smaller impact on ICL performance compared to FV heads.
Analysis of training dynamics revealed that many induction heads acquire FV functionality over time, and the relative importance of FV heads increases with model scale.
Takeaways: Function Vector (FV) heads are the primary drivers of in-context learning, consistently causing the largest performance drops when ablated.
Induction heads play a secondary role in ICL, especially when controlling for correlations with FV functionality.

Many attention heads that initially function as induction heads evolve to develop FV functionality during training, suggesting a developmental trajectory from simpler pattern matching to more sophisticated task representation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.13130.Title: Magma: A Foundation Model for Multimodal AI Agents
https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.13130.Summary: Microsoft Research and academic partners introduce Magma, a breakthrough foundation model that unifies multimodal understanding with action capabilities across both digital and physical domains, achieving state-of-the-art performance in UI navigation and robotic tasks through novel Set-of-Mark and Trace-of-Mark techniques that bridge verbal and spatial intelligence.
Problem: Existing AI systems struggle to combine language understanding with physical action execution
Traditional approaches require separate specialized models for different domains and tasks
Difficulty in creating scalable methods for learning actions from diverse data sources
Method: Unified architecture combining ConvNeXt vision encoder with LLaMA-3-8B language model
Novel Set-of-Mark (SoM) technique for grounding actions in images across domains
Trace-of-Mark (ToM) approach for learning action trajectories from video data
Results: Outperforms specialized models on both UI navigation and robotic manipulation tasks
Demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization capabilities across domains
Successfully combines multimodal understanding with action execution in a single model
Shows effective few-shot learning abilities in new task contexts
Takeaways: Verbal and spatial intelligence can be effectively combined through joint training
Numerical markers provide a universal representation for action grounding
Video data can be leveraged efficiently for action learning using temporal marking

https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.11859.Title: Defining and Evaluating Visual Language Models' Basic Spatial Abilities: A Perspective from Psychometrics
https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.11859.Summary: Researchers from Tsinghua University established a psychometric framework to define and evaluate Visual Language Models' fundamental spatial abilities, revealing that current VLMs achieve an average overall score of 24.95 compared to humans' 68.38 and suffer from constraints in dynamic simulation and precise metric encoding.
Problem: Existing research into AI spatial abilities is fragmented, often focusing on isolated tasks without a comprehensive theoretical foundation.
Prior VLM evaluations lack clear benchmarks against human performance, making it difficult to systematically compare capabilities or align them with human cognitive frameworks.
A systematic, psychometrically-grounded approach was needed to understand how VLMs' spatial intelligence is structured and where fundamental limitations lie.
Method: The study adopted a psychometric framework from human spatial intelligence, defining five Basic Spatial Abilities (BSAs) for VLMs: Spatial Perception, Spatial Relation, Spatial Orientation, Mental Rotation, and Spatial Visualization.
Nine classic psychometric tests (e.g., Mental Rotation Test, Santa Barbara Solids Test) were selected and converted into image-based questions to evaluate these BSAs across 13 mainstream VLMs.
Intervention strategies, including Chain-of-Thought prompting and example-based few-shot learning, were applied to assess their impact on VLM spatial reasoning.
Results: VLMs achieved an average overall spatial ability score of 24.95, markedly lower than the human average of 68.38 across all psychometric tests.

The Qwen series demonstrated superior performance (average 30.82) compared to models from Google, OpenAI, and InternVL2, while smaller models often outperformed their larger counterparts within the same series.

VLMs exhibited fundamental constraints including weak metric encoding, lack of dynamic simulation, poor cross-modal grounding, and over-reliance on static pre-training patterns, with limited improvements from Chain-of-Thought or few-shot prompting.
Takeaways: Despite a significant performance gap, VLMs paradoxically mirror human performance hierarchies across spatial tasks, excelling in 2D orientation while struggling with 3D mental manipulation.
The weak correlation between different Basic Spatial Abilities in VLMs validates their independence, supporting the chosen psychometric decomposition.

Model size does not positively correlate with spatial ability, suggesting that architectural optimization and training methodologies are more critical than parameter count for spatial reasoning tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.10694.Title: Simulations of Common Unsupervised Domain Adaptation Algorithms for Image Classification
https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.10694.Summary: This study conducts extensive empirical simulations of several common Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) algorithms for image classification, evaluating their performance across diverse natural and medical imaging datasets. It provides practical insights into the strengths and weaknesses of different techniques under varying conditions, including neural network backbones and data quality.
Problem: Machine learning models often degrade when applied to data from a different distribution than their training data, a phenomenon known as domain shift.
Acquiring large volumes of labeled data for every new target domain is costly, time-consuming, or restricted by privacy concerns, especially in fields like medical imaging.
Practitioners lack a comprehensive, comparative empirical evaluation of existing UDA algorithms under diverse real-world conditions to guide method selection.
Method: Systematically classified UDA methods into traditional and deep learning-based approaches, distinguishing between adversarial and non-adversarial deep learning techniques.
Simulated and compared seven prevalent UDA algorithms (Deep Coral, DANN, DAN, DSAN, BNM, DCAN, SSRT) using various neural network backbones (AlexNet, ResNet, ViT).

Evaluated algorithm performance on diverse public benchmarks, including natural image datasets (Office-31, Office-Home, Modern Office-31) and medical imaging datasets (ChestXray17, Brain Tumor, Skin Cancer), under conditions of cross-dataset generalization and varying data quality (Gaussian noise).
Results: SSRT achieved the highest accuracy on Office-31 (91.6% for SSRT-S) but showed a notable performance drop on Office-Home with limited batch sizes, demonstrating its sensitivity.
DANN exhibited improved performance in the simulations (e.g., +2.8% average on Office-31) and demonstrated the best gain on the Modern Office-31 dataset (+9.4% compared to ResNet50 alone).
MMD-based techniques, particularly DSAN, showed strong efficacy on medical imaging datasets like ChestXray17, outperforming other DA methods and non-DA CNNs.
Some DA methods (Deep Coral, BNM) exhibited 'negative adaptation' when source data was noisy, performing worse than models without DA, indicating limitations when source data quality is poor.
Takeaways: Advanced UDA algorithms, while high-performing, can be sensitive to hyperparameters like batch size and require substantial computational resources for optimal results.

Meticulous hyperparameter tuning and efficient training strategies can significantly enhance the performance of even established UDA methods, such as DANN, sometimes exceeding original reported results.

The effectiveness of UDA algorithms is highly context-dependent, varying significantly with the chosen neural network backbone, the nature of the domain shift, and the specific data domain (e.g., natural vs. medical images).

https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.10385.Title: Simplifying DINO via Coding Rate Regularization
https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.10385.Summary: UC Berkeley and Microsoft Research teams introduce SimDINO, a dramatically simplified version of the DINO self-supervised learning framework that achieves superior performance through principled coding rate regularization, eliminating complex collapse prevention mechanisms while improving robustness and computational efficiency.
Problem: DINO/DINOv2 frameworks rely on complex, empirically-motivated design choices and ad-hoc mechanisms
Current approaches require large batch sizes and are sensitive to hyperparameter tuning
Method: Replace complex collapse prevention mechanisms with explicit coding rate regularization
Eliminate dimension-increasing layers and complex post-processing while maintaining core self-distillation
Results: Achieves better performance than original DINO/DINOv2 on multiple benchmarks
Demonstrates greater robustness to hyperparameter choices and architectural variations
Requires less computational resources while maintaining state-of-the-art performance
Shows improved transfer learning capabilities on downstream tasks
Takeaways: Principled theoretical approaches can replace empirically-derived heuristics while improving performance
Explicit regularization enables more robust training with smaller batch sizes
Complex architectural components often mask underlying principles that can be expressed more simply

https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.09992.Title: Large Language Diffusion Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.09992.Summary: LLaDA introduces a novel 8-billion parameter diffusion model trained from scratch, demonstrating that diffusion models can achieve performance competitive with state-of-the-art autoregressive models in large-scale language modeling. This work challenges the assumption that LLM capabilities inherently rely on autoregressive architectures and provides a solution to the 'reversal curse'.
Problem: The prevailing belief that large language model capabilities (scalability, in-context learning) are exclusive to autoregressive architectures.
Limitations of autoregressive models, such as the 'reversal curse' where models struggle with tasks requiring bidirectional or inverse reasoning.
Lack of large-scale diffusion models for language that could rival multi-billion parameter autoregressive models in performance.
Method: Developed LLaDA, a masked diffusion model (MDM) for discrete token sequences, utilizing a Transformer backbone without a causal mask.
Trained an 8-billion parameter LLaDA model from scratch on a 2.3 trillion token dataset, optimizing a principled cross-entropy loss that upper bounds the negative log-likelihood.
Implemented flexible iterative sampling strategies for inference, including a low-confidence remasking technique to balance generation quality and speed.
Results: LLaDA 8B Base shows strong in-context learning, outperforming LLaMA2 7B Base and performing comparably to LLaMA3 8B Base on 15 zero/few-shot tasks, particularly in math and Chinese.
LLaDA 8B Instruct, after supervised fine-tuning, demonstrates competitive instruction-following capabilities, comparable to LLaMA3 8B Instruct, despite lacking reinforcement learning alignment.

The model effectively mitigates the 'reversal curse', achieving 45.6% accuracy on a poem reversal task, outperforming GPT-4o (34.3%) and showing consistent zero-shot performance in both forward and reversal directions.
Takeaways: Generative modeling principles, rather than the autoregressive formulation, are the core drivers of large language model capabilities and scalability.
Diffusion models can natively support intrinsic bidirectional reasoning, offering a principled solution to the 'reversal curse' observed in autoregressive models.

A principled probabilistic formulation and standard LLM training pipeline enable masked diffusion models to achieve comparable performance to state-of-the-art autoregressive models at an unprecedented scale.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.08922.Title: Self-Consistency of the Internal Reward Models Improves Self-Rewarding Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.08922.Summary: The Self-Consistent Internal Rewards (SCIR) framework improves Large Language Model alignment by enforcing consistency between the model's generative and implicit reward mechanisms. This approach leads to more reliable preference judgments and demonstrates superior performance, including a 14% improvement in length-controlled win rate on AlpacaEval 2.0 and higher MT-Bench scores.
Problem: Ensuring LLM outputs align with human preferences traditionally requires expensive, time-consuming human-annotated preference data.
Self-Rewarding Language Models (SRLMs) mitigate this by using the model itself to generate preference judgments, but different internal reward models often produce inconsistent evaluations.
This internal inconsistency leads to unreliable self-generated training data, hindering the overall alignment performance of SRLMs.
Method: The Self-Consistent Internal Rewards (SCIR) framework enforces consistency between an LLM's generative and implicit internal reward models.

It employs "Consistency Training" to penalize disagreements between these internal models and "Dynamic Consistency Preference Optimization (DCPO)" to select only consistently judged preference data for training.
The iterative process refines the model by generating response pairs, evaluating them, and optimizing with a combination of consistency and preference optimization losses.
Results: SCIR significantly increases the consistency rates between internal reward models compared to standard SRLM approaches, improving across training iterations.
The framework improves the model's reward modeling accuracy on benchmarks like RewardBench and demonstrates superior overall performance on alignment benchmarks.
Achieved a 14% improvement in length-controlled win rate on AlpacaEval 2.0 and higher MT-Bench scores, consistently outperforming various baseline methods.
Takeaways: A fundamental limitation in Self-Rewarding Language Models (SRLMs) is the inconsistency between different internal reward mechanisms (e.g., explicit LLM-as-a-Judge and implicit DPO-derived rewards).
Improving the self-consistency of these internal reward models directly translates to more reliable self-generated preference data for training.

Explicitly encouraging consistency through training and dynamically selecting highly consistent preference pairs can significantly enhance LLM alignment with human preferences without reliance on new human annotations.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.07503.Title: Recursive Inference Scaling: A Winning Path to Scalable Inference in Language and Multimodal Systems
https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.07503.Summary: Recursive Inference Scaling (RINS) is an architectural approach from Google DeepMind that enhances the performance of language and multimodal models by intelligently applying recursion during inference. It achieves superior results by repeatedly applying an early portion of the network, outperforming other parameter-sharing methods under equivalent training compute, and is validated across language modeling and vision-language tasks.
Problem: Traditional neural scaling laws primarily focus on training performance, with less emphasis on efficient and effective ways to scale models at inference time.
Prior recursive and parameter-sharing architectures often lacked conclusive evidence of superior scaling exponents or were not rigorously compared under compute-matched training conditions.
There was a need to intrinsically leverage the inherent properties of data, such as the hypothesized fractal nature of language, within model architectures to enhance performance.
Method: Introduces Recursive INference Scaling (RINS), a novel architectural paradigm defined by a degree 1 and A^rB signature, where an initial block (A) is recursively applied to its own output 'r' times before passing to a final block (B).
Employs a rigorous compute-matched training regime, ensuring that recursive models are trained on fewer examples to equalize total training FLOPs with non-recursive baselines for fair comparison.

Develops stochastic RINS with lightweight linear adapters to enable flexibility in inference-time compute and establish a "no-regret" pretraining strategy, where training with RINS improves performance even at baseline inference costs.
Results: RINS consistently outperforms over 55 other parameter-sharing variants, including RAO and latent recurrent thinking, in language modeling tasks under compute-matched training, with the performance gap widening at higher training compute budgets.

The approach successfully generalizes to multimodal systems (SigLIP-B/16), improving zero-shot classification accuracy (e.g., ImageNet 0-shot from 73.4% to 74.1%) and retrieval performance, and pushing state-of-the-art in overtraining regimes.

Stochastic RINS, combined with linear adapters, provides a "no-regret" pretraining strategy, enhancing baseline performance even when recursive inference is not utilized, and improves both asymptotic performance limits and scaling exponents for language modeling.
Takeaways: Language exhibits a self-similar or fractal nature, which can be effectively exploited by recursive decoding mechanisms to improve model performance.

Intelligent architectural design focusing on inference-time compute, such as RINS, can yield greater performance gains and more efficient scaling laws compared to simply increasing model size, data, or training compute.
Rigorous compute-matched training comparisons are essential to accurately attribute performance improvements to architectural innovation rather than merely increased training resources.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.06772.Title: ReasonFlux: Hierarchical LLM Reasoning via Scaling Thought Templates
https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.06772.Summary: ReasonFlux presents a hierarchical framework for Large Language Model reasoning that leverages a structured thought template library and hierarchical reinforcement learning to plan optimal reasoning paths. The approach achieved 91.2% accuracy on the MATH benchmark, outperforming OpenAI o1-preview by 6.7%, and 56.7% accuracy on AIME 2024, surpassing o1-preview by 27%, while demonstrating cost-efficient training with 8 GPUs.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle with complex multi-step reasoning tasks like mathematical Olympiads, requiring fine-grained search and overcoming token sampling randomness.
Existing deliberate search (e.g., Tree of Thoughts) and reward-model-guided methods are computationally expensive, lack generalizability, and face exploration-exploitation trade-offs.
Current template-based reasoning methods struggle to integrate multiple knowledge pieces effectively and face scalability issues with large template libraries due to simple retrieval mechanisms.
Method: A structured and compact thought template library of approximately 500 high-level mathematical reasoning strategies was constructed, meticulously organized with metadata for precise retrieval.
Hierarchical reinforcement learning was employed to train a "navigator" LLM to plan optimal, generalizable sequences of thought templates (trajectories) based on problem analysis.

An adaptive inference scaling system was designed, allowing for multi-round, iterative interaction between the navigator and an inference LLM to dynamically select and instantiate templates, refining reasoning steps based on feedback.
Results: ReasonFlux-32B achieved 91.2% accuracy on the MATH benchmark, outperforming OpenAI o1-preview by 6.7%, and 56.7% accuracy on AIME 2024, surpassing o1-preview by 27%.

The framework demonstrated strong generalization across diverse mathematical benchmarks, including OlympiadBench and Chinese College Entrance Mathematics Exam, consistently outperforming comparable models.
ReasonFlux-32B was trained efficiently using only 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs and generates interpretable reasoning structures via its planned template trajectories.
Takeaways: Structuring a knowledge base into high-level thought templates with detailed metadata allows for more precise and scalable retrieval, improving reasoning efficiency.
Hierarchical reinforcement learning can effectively train LLMs to plan optimal sequences of abstract reasoning steps (template trajectories), guiding the problem-solving process.

Dynamically adapting the depth and breadth of reasoning (e.g., number of templates, interaction rounds) based on problem complexity leads to a superior exploration-exploitation trade-off during inference.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.05234.Title: Optimizing Temperature for Language Models with Multi-Sample Inference
https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.05234.Summary: A method called TURN is introduced to automatically identify the near-optimal sampling temperature for large language models when using multi-sample aggregation, eliminating the need for labeled validation data. This approach leverages an intrinsic "entropy turning point" (EntP) to predict effective temperatures, achieving performance within 0.32% to 0.59% of grid-search optimum on math problem-solving and code generation tasks.
Problem: Optimizing the temperature hyperparameter for multi-sample Large Language Model (LLM) inference is challenging, often relying on suboptimal fixed values or costly empirical tuning.
Current methods for temperature selection require extensive labeled validation data, which is frequently scarce or impractical to obtain for diverse tasks and models.
Suboptimal temperature settings hinder the full potential of multi-sample aggregation strategies (e.g., majority voting, best-of-N) in achieving high accuracy and reliability.
Method: The researchers developed TURN (Turning Point Temperature Selection), an automated, data-agnostic algorithm to identify the near-optimal temperature for LLM multi-sample inference.
TURN utilizes the "entropy turning point" (EntP), an intrinsic characteristic of an LLM's token-level entropy curve, which signals a rapid decline in sample quality beyond this temperature.
The algorithm computes the EntP by finding where the second derivative of the log-entropy curve transitions from negative to positive, then applies a small aggregation-specific adaptation factor.
Results: The TURN method accurately predicted optimal temperatures, achieving a Hit Rate of 12/13 models on MATH and 11/13 on MBPP within the "epsilon"-optimal range.
TURN incurred a minimal performance drop compared to exhaustive grid search, averaging only 0.32% on MATH and 0.59% on MBPP, while consistently outperforming fixed-temperature baselines.
The EntP showed a high correlation with the best empirically found temperature (0.9998 for MATH, 0.9913 for MBPP), demonstrating its reliability as an intrinsic signal.
Takeaways: The optimal sampling temperature for multi-sample LLM inference varies considerably based on model architecture, training, and task, with fine-tuned models performing best at higher temperatures.
An "entropy turning point" (EntP) exists in the log-scale token-level entropy curve, strongly correlating with the empirically determined optimal temperature for achieving peak accuracy.

A simplified stochastic process model can reproduce the observed entropy spike, providing a theoretical explanation that EntP marks a rapid increase in "improper" tokens, signifying a collapse in sample quality.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.05171.Title: Scaling up Test-Time Compute with Latent Reasoning: A Recurrent Depth Approach
https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.05171.Summary: Researchers from ELLIS Institute Tübingen, University of Maryland, and Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory introduce a recurrent depth transformer architecture that scales reasoning abilities by implicitly processing information in a continuous latent space. The 3.5 billion parameter model, Huginn-0125, trained on the Frontier supercomputer, demonstrates significant performance gains on reasoning benchmarks with increased test-time iterations, sometimes matching or exceeding larger models without requiring specialized Chain-of-Thought training data.
Problem: Traditional LLM scaling relies on increasing model parameters, leading to immense computational and memory demands during training and inference.
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning requires specialized training data, consumes significant context window memory, and is limited to reasoning types that can be explicitly verbalized.
Existing LLM architectures may prioritize memorization over learning generalizable algorithms, limiting deeper reasoning abilities.
Method: Introduces a recurrent depth transformer architecture with a Prelude, an iteratively applied Core Recurrent Block, and a Coda, enabling arbitrary scaling of effective depth at test-time.
Trains the model using randomized unrolling of recurrent iterations with a heavy-tailed log-normal Poisson distribution and truncated backpropagation to manage memory and encourage extrapolation.

Employs large-scale training on the Oak Ridge National Laboratory’s Frontier supercomputer, utilizing 4096 AMD MI250X GPUs, with careful parameter initialization and a custom distributed data parallel implementation.
Results: The 3.5B parameter Huginn-0125 model shows dramatic performance improvements on reasoning benchmarks with increased test-time recurrent iterations, sometimes matching or exceeding 50B parameter open-source models.
It achieves strong performance on mathematical and coding benchmarks (e.g., surpassing most compared models on GSM8K and MATH), demonstrating an inclination towards reasoning over general knowledge.

Analysis reveals complex emergent computational patterns in the latent space, such as context-dependent convergence, 'orbits,' and 'sliders,' suggesting sophisticated non-linear information processing.
Takeaways: Test-time recurrent depth offers a "third axis" for scaling LLM performance, complementary to increasing parameter count and explicit Chain-of-Thought methods.
Implicit, latent reasoning within the model's continuous high-dimensional space can capture complex thought processes not easily verbalized and does not require specialized CoT training data.

The recurrent architecture naturally enables zero-shot capabilities like adaptive compute, KV-cache sharing, continuous latent CoT, and self-speculative decoding, simplifying advanced LLM functionalities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.03714.Title: Universal Sparse Autoencoders: Interpretable Cross-Model Concept Alignment
https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.03714.Summary: This paper presents Universal Sparse Autoencoders (USAEs), a method for jointly learning a shared, interpretable concept space across multiple distinct deep neural networks. It demonstrates the ability to discover a range of universal concepts, from low-level features to high-level abstractions, and shows effective cross-model activation reconstruction with positive R² scores, revealing a strong correlation between a concept's importance and its universality across different models.
Problem: Traditional interpretability methods primarily focus on single models, lacking scalability and efficiency for analyzing the growing number of deep neural networks.
Existing techniques for identifying shared concepts across models are often post-hoc and computationally expensive, hindering direct concept translation or interaction.
The absence of a shared conceptual space complicates multi-model applications and a unified understanding of diverse AI systems.
Method: Introduces Universal Sparse Autoencoders (USAEs), which jointly learn a single, overcomplete sparse autoencoder to reconstruct and interpret the internal activations of multiple pretrained deep neural networks simultaneously.

The architecture uses model-specific encoders to map individual model activations to a shared sparse code representing the universal concept space, from which model-specific decoders can reconstruct activations.

A universal training process is employed where, in each mini-batch, one model's activations are encoded into the shared code, and this same code is then used to reconstruct feature representations for all models, with loss aggregated across all reconstructions.
Results: Qualitatively, Universal Sparse Autoencoders (USAEs) discover a broad range of semantically coherent and interpretable concepts (e.g., 'yellow', 'dog face', 'keypads') that activate consistently across diverse vision models like DinoV2, SigLIP, and ViT.

Quantitative evaluation using R² scores demonstrates USAEs effectively reconstruct internal activations across models, with positive off-diagonal R² values confirming the shared latent space captures universal features.

Analysis of firing entropy and co-fire proportion reveals a strong positive correlation between a concept's importance (reconstruction energy) and its universality (co-firing frequency), indicating the most important concepts are also highly universal.
Takeaways: Deep neural networks, even when trained for diverse tasks, converge on a range of semantically coherent and interpretable universal concepts, from low-level features to high-level abstractions.
The most important concepts, measured by their contribution to reconstruction energy, are also the most universal, consistently activating across different model architectures.
The universal training objective of USAEs can uncover shared representations that do not emerge when sparse autoencoders are trained on individual models in isolation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.03387.Title: LIMO: Less is More for Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.03387.Summary: The LIMO (Less is More for Reasoning) research from Shanghai Jiao Tong University and SII-GAIR develops a supervised fine-tuning method for large language models, demonstrating that advanced mathematical reasoning can be achieved with a minimal dataset of 800 carefully curated examples. This approach yields an average performance of 78.1% across various benchmarks, outperforming models like OpenAI-o1-preview (61.1%) and QwQ-32B-Preview (66.9%) that were fine-tuned on significantly larger datasets.
Problem: The prevailing assumption that complex reasoning in large language models necessitates vast quantities of training data.
High computational costs and resource demands associated with collecting and training on massive datasets.
Limited generalization and potential memorization in models trained on large, uncurated reasoning datasets.
Method: A data-efficient supervised fine-tuning (SFT) approach, named LIMO, which utilizes a minimal dataset.
A highly curated dataset of 800 mathematical reasoning problems, constructed through multi-stage filtering for question difficulty and detailed rule-based scoring for reasoning chain quality.
The training process enables the base model to integrate meta-reasoning tasks into cohesive chains, leveraging its pre-trained knowledge.
Results: LIMO achieved an average performance of 78.1% across all benchmarks, outperforming state-of-the-art LLMs like OpenAI-o1-preview (61.1%) and QwQ-32B-Preview (66.9%).
The model exhibited strong out-of-distribution generalization, successfully tackling diverse mathematical and multilingual benchmarks, including novel Chinese-language exams.
Ablation studies confirmed that high-quality reasoning chains and training on challenging problems significantly enhance performance, with diminishing returns observed for data beyond 800 samples.
Takeaways: Complex reasoning in LLMs can emerge from minimal, high-quality data if foundation models possess comprehensive pre-trained domain knowledge.
The quality of reasoning chains and the difficulty of training problems are critical factors in fostering robust and generalized reasoning abilities.
A rich pre-trained knowledge base in the foundation model is essential for efficient elicitation of reasoning capabilities through fine-tuning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.03275.Title: Token Assorted: Mixing Latent and Text Tokens for Improved Language Model Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.03275.Summary: Researchers at Meta AI and collaborators developed Token Assorted, a method that combines discrete latent tokens with text tokens for Large Language Model reasoning. This approach enhances reasoning accuracy on synthetic and mathematical benchmarks while reducing reasoning trace length by an average of 17%.
Problem: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning in LLMs significantly improves accuracy but generates lengthy textual traces, leading to high computational costs during training and inference.
Much of the textual content in CoT traces serves for linguistic coherence rather than conveying core reasoning information, resulting in inefficiency.
Existing efforts to compress or internalize reasoning traces often involve complex multi-stage training, incur high computational costs, or lead to performance degradation.
Method: A two-stage approach uses a Vector-Quantized Variational Autoencoder (VQ-VAE) to abstract initial Chain-of-Thought (CoT) steps into discrete latent tokens, with a compression rate of 16:1.
Pre-trained LLMs are fine-tuned using a hybrid representation where the beginning of CoT traces is replaced with these discrete latent tokens, while the rest remains explicit text.

A randomized, left-to-right replacement strategy during fine-tuning allows the LLM to quickly adapt to the new latent tokens by stochastically mixing varying degrees of abstraction in training samples, avoiding complex curriculum learning.
Results: The method consistently outperformed baselines (Sol-Only, CoT, iCoT, Pause Token) across synthetic and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, achieving an average accuracy improvement of 2.9 to 4.5 percentage points on Llama models (1B, 3B, 8B).
It reduced reasoning trace length by an average of 17% compared to the full CoT baseline across all mathematical benchmarks, while simultaneously achieving higher accuracy.
On synthetic benchmarks, the approach yielded substantial accuracy gains, for instance, +19.8% on Keys-Finding Maze and +18.7% on ProsQA, with significantly shorter reasoning traces.
Takeaways: Mixing abstract discrete latent tokens with explicit text tokens creates a 'bridge' that allows LLMs to leverage both high-level summaries and detailed textual information for more effective reasoning.
The randomized partial replacement strategy during fine-tuning facilitates robust and efficient adaptation to an extended vocabulary including novel latent tokens in a single training stage.

Compressing verbose textual CoT allows the model to focus attention more effectively on crucial tokens (e.g., numerical values, mathematical operations), leading to improved internal reasoning efficiency.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.03214.Title: iVISPAR -- An Interactive Visual-Spatial Reasoning Benchmark for VLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.03214.Summary: The iVISPAR benchmark evaluates interactive visual-spatial reasoning in Vision-Language Models (VLMs), revealing that even state-of-the-art models significantly underperform humans in 3D environments due to struggles with precise object localization and complex planning. Closed-source models achieved higher success rates, with 2D visual inputs generally yielding better performance than 3D or text.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) consistently demonstrate weaknesses in spatial reasoning and visual alignment, which are critical for real-world physical agent tasks.
Existing VLM benchmarks primarily rely on static 2D inputs, failing to capture the dynamic, interactive, and multi-step complexity of real-world 3D spatial problems.
This lack of appropriate evaluation hinders the development of VLMs capable of effective visuomotor reasoning and spatial decision-making in grounded contexts.
Method: Researchers introduced iVISPAR, an interactive multimodal benchmark based on a 3D sliding geometric puzzle (SGP), enabling VLMs to act as agents in dynamic environments.
Models interact via a natural language prompt-based API, executing commands and receiving updated board states in an iterative action-perception loop across 3D vision, 2D vision, or text modalities.
The benchmark utilizes procedural generation for scalable complexity and includes human, optimal, and random agent baselines for comprehensive performance comparison.
Results: Closed-source models (e.g., Sonnet-3.5) dramatically outperformed open-source models, with Sonnet-3.5 achieving an 89.7% success rate in the 2D visual modality.
Performance consistently degraded with increasing task complexity (number of objects, shortest path length), with 3D vision showing a steeper decline.
An auxiliary board state inference task showed models correctly identified an average of 4.2 objects in 2D images but only 1.4 in 3D images, primarily due to coordinate prediction errors in 3D.
Takeaways: VLMs consistently fall short of human-level spatial reasoning and performance, especially in complex 3D scenarios, indicating a substantial gap in cognitive capabilities.
Models exhibit a strong bias towards 2D visual inputs, achieving their best performance with 2D vision and worst with 3D vision, potentially due to training data characteristics.
The primary cause for VLM failure in 3D environments is an inability to precisely localize objects, leading to frequent coordinate prediction errors and ineffective moves during problem-solving.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.02339.Title: AStar: Boosting Multimodal Reasoning with Automated Structured Thinking
https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.02339.Summary: The AStar framework from Tsinghua University and Chinese Academy of Sciences introduces a training-free, automated structured thinking paradigm to enhance multimodal reasoning in Large Language Models. It achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing GPT-4o on benchmarks like MathVerse (53.9% vs. 50.2%) and MathVision (32.7% vs. 30.4%), while reducing data requirements by 520-fold and eliminating training time.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle with complex visual reasoning tasks that require sophisticated, 'System 2' problem-solving strategies due to a scarcity of high-quality, long-chain reasoning data.
Existing explicit search methods (e.g., MCTS) are computationally inefficient due to extensive exploration of solution spaces during inference.

Post-training methods (e.g., SFT, RL) demand massive datasets and computational resources, often face training instability, and exhibit limited generalization beyond their training distribution, with reliance on proprietary models for data synthesis creating accessibility barriers.
Method: AStar implements a training-free, inference-time framework for 'Automated Structured thinking' to boost multimodal reasoning by dynamically leveraging external reasoning guidelines.

It constructs abstract 'thought cards'—high-level reasoning patterns derived from only 500 prior samples—using Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to acquire optimal paths and a VOC-inspired metric to distill these paths.

During inference, AStar adaptively retrieves the most relevant thought cards for a new query based on problem complexity and semantics, generating candidate solutions that are then verified using unified self-consistency checks and text-domain outcome reward models.
Results: AStar (with Qwen2.5-7B) achieved state-of-the-art accuracy, surpassing GPT-4o on MathVerse (53.9% vs. 50.2%) and MathVision (32.7% vs. 30.4%), and consistently outperformed other open-source MLLMs.

The framework demonstrated extreme efficiency, requiring only 0.5K prior samples and 50 minutes for thought card generation, representing a 520-fold reduction in data compared to search-based methods and eliminating training time.

AStar showed strong transferability and flexibility, enhancing GPT-4o on benchmarks like MMMU (73.2% vs. 70.3%) and GAOKAO-MM (52.2% vs. 47.8%), and boosting smaller models (e.g., AStar+Qwen2-VL-2B outperformed Qwen2-VL-7B).
Takeaways: Abstract, high-level reasoning patterns, when systematically distilled into 'thought cards,' can effectively guide MLLMs for complex tasks without requiring extensive post-training or large datasets.
Integrating explicit external reasoning guidelines with an MLLM's internal implicit knowledge through adaptive retrieval at inference time leads to superior performance and computational efficiency.

The training-free nature of AStar, combined with its compact 'thought card' library, enables significant reductions in data and training time while providing robust cross-domain generalization capabilities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.02316.Title: DIME:Diffusion-Based Maximum Entropy Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.02316.Summary: Researchers developed DIME, an algorithm that integrates diffusion policies into Maximum Entropy Reinforcement Learning by deriving a tractable lower bound on their marginal entropy. This approach achieves superior performance over other diffusion-based methods and competes with leading Gaussian policy-based algorithms on complex continuous control tasks, demonstrating improved computational efficiency.
Problem: Traditional Maximum Entropy Reinforcement Learning (MaxEnt-RL) policies, typically using Gaussian distributions, lack the representational capacity to model complex, multi-modal action distributions necessary for intricate high-dimensional control tasks.
A major challenge in combining MaxEnt-RL with expressive diffusion models is the intractability of computing the marginal entropy of diffusion policies, a critical component of the MaxEnt objective.

Existing diffusion-based RL methods often rely on ad-hoc or artificial noise for exploration, rather than leveraging principled, entropy-guided exploration inherent to MaxEnt-RL, thus failing to fully utilize diffusion models' potential.
Method: DIME reformulates the MaxEnt-RL objective for diffusion policies as an approximate inference problem, deriving a tractable lower bound on the marginal entropy by discretizing the diffusion process.

A policy iteration scheme with provable convergence guarantees is introduced, adapting traditional policy iteration to the context of diffusion policies and leveraging the derived entropy lower bound.

The practical algorithm employs parameterized neural networks for the Q-function and policy, incorporates techniques like distributional Q-learning, and includes adaptive tuning for both the MaxEnt temperature and the diffusion coefficient.
Results: DIME consistently and significantly outperforms all other diffusion-based RL methods across 13 evaluated continuous control environments, establishing a new state-of-the-art for this category.

The algorithm demonstrates strong competitiveness with and often surpasses leading Gaussian policy-based methods like CrossQ and BRO, particularly on challenging high-dimensional tasks such as Humanoid and Myo Suite environments.

DIME achieves comparable or superior performance with improved computational efficiency, requiring fewer algorithmic design choices and less training time (e.g., 4.5 hours vs. 8.5 hours for BRO on humanoid-run).
Takeaways: The intractable marginal entropy of diffusion policies can be effectively approximated by deriving a tractable lower bound, enabling their principled integration into the Maximum Entropy Reinforcement Learning framework.
Leveraging the inherent stochasticity and expressiveness of diffusion models for entropy-guided exploration leads to more diverse and effective learning than methods relying on artificial noise.
Treating the diffusion coefficient as a learnable parameter allows the diffusion process to adapt during training, reducing hyperparameter sensitivity and potentially enhancing performance.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.02202.Title: Multi-level Supervised Contrastive Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.02202.Summary: The Multi-level Supervised Contrastive Learning (MLCL) framework enhances supervised contrastive learning by incorporating multiple projection heads with adaptive temperatures to capture multi-level similarity for multi-label and hierarchical classification. It achieves improved performance, notably up to 10% higher accuracy than SupCon with limited training data, and converges four times faster.
Problem: Standard supervised contrastive learning methods (like SupCon) define similarity based on a single, atomic label, which oversimplifies complex relationships in real-world data.
Existing SCL approaches are inadequate for datasets with multi-label or hierarchical structures, often requiring specialized, disjointed solutions.
A lack of a unified framework to simultaneously leverage various levels of similarity for robust representation learning in complex classification tasks.
Method: Introduces Multi-level Supervised Contrastive Learning (MLCL) which employs multiple distinct projection heads, each dedicated to capturing a specific aspect or level of similarity.

Each projection head is trained with its own supervised contrastive loss and a unique temperature hyperparameter, allowing for adaptive learning based on the granularity of similarity (e.g., lower temperature for subclasses, higher for superclasses).
For multi-label tasks, MLCL uses label-specific heads and an additional global projection head that incorporates Jaccard similarity to capture overall semantic relationships.
Results: MLCL achieved approximately 1% accuracy improvement over SupCon on full CIFAR-100 and DeepFashion datasets, and significantly outperformed baselines under limited data conditions (e.g., 9-10% higher accuracy on CIFAR-100 with 1,000 samples).
Demonstrated superior training efficiency by converging four times faster than SupCon (250 vs. 1,000 epochs) on CIFAR-100.
Outperformed BERT with cross-entropy loss on multi-label text classification benchmarks (TripAdvisor, BeerAdvocate), showing improved accuracy across various limited training sample sizes.
Takeaways: Explicitly modeling different levels of similarity (e.g., subclass and superclass) through separate projection heads leads to richer, more structured, and semantically meaningful representations.

Optimizing temperature parameters independently for each projection head is crucial, with lower temperatures effectively distinguishing fine-grained similarities and higher temperatures suitable for broader categories.
A global projection head, particularly in multi-label scenarios, can regularize the learning process, capturing overall semantic relatedness and improving robustness to label noise.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.02133.Title: Synthesis of Model Predictive Control and Reinforcement Learning: Survey and Classification
https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.02133.Summary: A comprehensive survey establishes a systematic classification of methods synthesizing Model Predictive Control (MPC) and Reinforcement Learning (RL), categorizing approaches based on MPC's role as an expert actor, within a deployed policy, or as a critic. It details their complementary strengths, theoretical foundations, and practical implementation challenges, offering a structured roadmap for interdisciplinary research.
Problem: MPC and RL, despite solving similar control problems, possess orthogonal strengths and weaknesses, making their direct integration complex without a unifying framework.
MPC traditionally requires accurate mathematical models and can be computationally expensive, while RL often lacks safety guarantees, constraint satisfaction, and sample efficiency.
The burgeoning field of MPC-RL combinations lacked a systematic classification and detailed comparative analysis, hindering interdisciplinary understanding and targeted research.
Method: The authors systematically review, synthesize, and classify existing literature on MPC-RL combinations into a novel framework centered around the actor-critic RL paradigm.
They provide a detailed comparative analysis of MPC and RL, highlighting their distinct characteristics, shared principles, and inherent advantages and disadvantages.

The work identifies and defines four architectural archetypes for integrating neural networks with MPC, such as Integrated, Hierarchical, Parallel, and Parameterized MPC, to support the classification.
Results: The survey produced a novel, actor-critic-centric classification scheme for MPC-RL combinations, categorizing approaches into MPC as an expert actor, within the deployed policy, or as a critic, detailed across nine sub-categories.

Four distinct architectural archetypes for integrating neural networks with MPC (Integrated, Hierarchical, Parallel, Parameterized) were identified, providing a meta-framework for structural understanding.

Key practical challenges such as the need for differentiable optimization solvers and the computational overhead of repeated optimization were detailed, alongside emerging software tools designed to bridge the gap between ML frameworks and MPC.
Takeaways: MPC and RL possess fundamentally complementary strengths, with MPC excelling in constraint handling and stability and RL in data-driven adaptation and complex environments, justifying their synergistic combination.

MPC can be systematically integrated into the actor-critic reinforcement learning framework in three primary roles: as an expert actor, as an integral component of the deployed policy, or as a critic for value estimation.

Theoretical analysis reveals that appropriately formulated Economic NMPC can approximate optimal value functions and policies for discounted Markov Decision Processes, providing a strong basis for their integration.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.02013.Title: Layer by Layer: Uncovering Hidden Representations in Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.02013.Summary: Intermediate layers in large language models often provide superior representations for downstream tasks compared to final layers, yielding 2-16% performance improvements on average across 32 text embedding tasks. This work introduces a unified framework based on matrix-based entropy to explain this phenomenon and enable unsupervised identification of optimal layers.
Problem: The common assumption that the final layer of large language models provides the most effective representations for downstream tasks may be suboptimal.
There is a lack of comprehensive understanding regarding how information is processed and transformed within the intermediate layers of LLMs.
Existing methods for analyzing neural network representation quality are diverse and lack a unified theoretical framework.
Method: Proposed a unified theoretical framework based on matrix-based entropy to quantify and compare representation quality across neural network layers.
Utilized seven specific metrics, derived from the framework, covering information-theoretic, geometric, and augmentation-invariance properties of representations.
Conducted extensive empirical validation across a wide range of language models (transformers, state-space models) and vision models, on diverse downstream tasks.
Results: Intermediate layers achieved 2% to 16% average performance improvements over final layers across 32 MTEB text embedding tasks.
Unsupervised layer selection using the proposed metrics (e.g., DiME) led to a 3% average MTEB score boost for Pythia-410M models.

Autoregressive models (e.g., Pythia, Llama3, AIM) exhibit a pronounced mid-layer 'compression valley' in prompt entropy, while masked/bidirectional models (e.g., BERT) show more uniform entropy across layers.
Takeaways: Intermediate layers in autoregressive models consistently yield superior representations for downstream tasks, challenging the reliance on final layers.
The proposed matrix-based entropy metrics effectively correlate with downstream performance, enabling unsupervised selection of optimal layers.
The training objective, particularly autoregression, significantly influences the layer-wise information compression and representation dynamics, observed across both language and vision models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.01962.Title: Memory Efficient Transformer Adapter for Dense Predictions
https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.01962.Summary: META (Memory Efficient Transformer Adapter) enhances Vision Transformer performance for dense prediction tasks by explicitly minimizing memory access operations, leading to notable improvements in inference speed and memory efficiency. The method achieves state-of-the-art accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across object detection, instance segmentation, and semantic segmentation benchmarks.
Problem: Existing Vision Transformer (ViT) adapters, despite reducing parameter counts, implicitly hinder inference speed due to inefficient memory access operations like standard normalization and frequent tensor reshaping.
Deploying large pre-trained ViT models for dense prediction tasks requires substantial memory and computational resources, limiting their use in real-time or resource-constrained environments.
Pure ViT architectures often exhibit weak local inductive biases, which are empirically beneficial and often necessary for high performance in fine-grained dense prediction tasks.
Method: Developed META, a Vision Transformer adapter featuring a Memory Efficient Adapter (MEA) block integrated into a cascaded injector-extractor architecture.
The MEA block minimizes memory access bottlenecks by utilizing a single shared layer normalization for its Attention (Attn) and Feed-Forward Network (FFN) branches.
Incorporates Cross-Shaped Self-Attention (CSA) to reduce frequent tensor reshaping and a lightweight convolutional branch to introduce local inductive biases beneficial for dense prediction tasks.
Results: META achieved state-of-the-art accuracy-efficiency trade-offs, consistently outperforming existing ViT adapter methods on MS-COCO for object detection and instance segmentation, and on ADE20K for semantic segmentation.

The method significantly reduced memory consumption (e.g., META-L used 62% of LoSA-L's memory), leading to higher Frames Per Second (FPS) and faster inference speeds across various ViT backbones and tasks.

Ablation studies validated the efficacy of shared layer normalization for efficiency gains, the convolutional branch for introducing local inductive biases and improving accuracy, and the cascaded architecture for enhancing feature diversity.
Takeaways: True efficiency in Vision Transformer adapters necessitates explicitly addressing memory access operations, such as normalization and tensor reshaping, as these are critical, often overlooked, bottlenecks for practical inference speed.

A hybrid adapter block that carefully combines shared layer normalization, cross-shaped self-attention, and a lightweight convolutional branch can synergistically reduce memory access inefficiencies while simultaneously improving feature representation.

The effective fusion of global semantic features from the ViT backbone with task-specific local inductive biases introduced by the adapter enriches information entropy, leading to superior generalization and adaptability for dense prediction tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.19393.Title: s1: Simple test-time scaling
https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.19393.Summary: Researchers at Stanford, UW, and AI2 developed `s1-32B`, an open-source model that achieves state-of-the-art reasoning performance and clear test-time scaling on challenging benchmarks by fine-tuning on only 1,000 high-quality reasoning samples and employing a simple 'budget forcing' inference technique.
