Integrating robust uncertainty quantification into VLM-based few-shot learning, particularly with computationally efficient methods, remains a challenge.
Method: The Adaptive Prompt Tuning (APT) framework introduces a learnable cross-attention module that dynamically tunes initial text prompts based on real-time visual input from the frozen CLIP image encoder.

Dropout layers are strategically placed within the cross-attention module and kept active during inference to implement Monte-Carlo Dropout (MCD), enabling the quantification of predictive uncertainty.
The final classification is performed by computing cosine similarity between the image's `[CLS]` token feature and the dynamically tuned text features, followed by a softmax function.
Results: APT consistently achieved superior accuracy on fine-grained datasets, notably on FGVC Aircraft (e.g., 47% at 16 shots, outperforming Zero-shot 17%) and CUBirds (77% at 16 shots), surpassing state-of-the-art prompt tuning methods.

The framework demonstrated improved generalization capabilities to new, unseen classes, achieving the highest F1-Mean scores on FGVC Aircraft (36.46) and Oxford Flowers (83.23) in base-to-new evaluation setups.

Integration of Monte-Carlo Dropout successfully quantified uncertainty, with Expected Calibration Error (ECE) decreasing with more training data, and the model exhibited high uncertainty for out-of-distribution inputs.
Takeaways: Dynamically adjusting text prompts with visual information via a cross-attention mechanism allows for better adaptation to subtle visual cues, crucial for fine-grained few-shot learning tasks.
Monte-Carlo Dropout offers an efficient and scalable approach to provide well-calibrated confidence estimates and quantify uncertainty in large pre-trained Vision-Language Models like CLIP.

Models equipped with effective uncertainty quantification can distinguish between in-distribution and out-of-distribution data, expressing higher uncertainty for unfamiliar inputs, thereby increasing system reliability.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.14171.Title: Thinking in Space: How Multimodal Large Language Models See, Remember, and Recall Spaces
https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.14171.Summary: Researchers from New York University, Yale University, and Stanford University introduced VSI-Bench, a video-based benchmark, to assess the visual-spatial intelligence of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). The study found a substantial performance gap between MLLMs and human capabilities in spatial reasoning, identifying relational reasoning and egocentric-allocentric transformation as key limitations, while demonstrating that explicit cognitive map generation can enhance spatial distance understanding.
Problem: Most existing multimodal large language model (MLLM) benchmarks primarily focus on content-level understanding or temporal reasoning from video, neglecting 3D spatial relationships.
MLLMs lack the intuitive human ability to perceive, remember, and reason about spaces from sequential visual observations, such as building an implicit "cognitive map."
There was a need to diagnose the strengths and limitations of MLLMs in visual-spatial intelligence and understand how they process spatial information.
Method: The researchers developed VSI-Bench, a novel video-based benchmark with over 5,000 question-answer pairs derived from real indoor 3D scene datasets (ScanNet, ARKitScenes), designed to evaluate MLLMs' understanding of spatial relationships.
They evaluated 15 diverse MLLMs in zero-shot settings using metrics like Accuracy and a new Mean Relative Accuracy (MRA) for quantitative tasks, comparing performance against human baselines.
They probed MLLMs' spatial thinking by analyzing linguistic self-explanations for errors and by prompting models to generate explicit cognitive maps of observed scenes.
Results: Human evaluators achieved 79.2% accuracy on VSI-Bench, significantly outperforming the best MLLM (Gemini-1.5 Pro) which scored 48.8%.
Manual error analysis of MLLM self-explanations revealed that approximately 71% of errors were due to faulty spatial reasoning capabilities.
Explicitly generating and using cognitive maps improved MLLMs' relative distance reasoning accuracy by 10% on VSI-Bench, highlighting the potential of integrating explicit spatial world models.
Takeaways: Spatial reasoning, specifically relational reasoning and egocentric-allocentric transformation, is identified as the primary bottleneck for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) in visual-spatial tasks.

Linguistic prompting techniques like Chain-of-Thought surprisingly led to performance degradation in MLLMs on spatial reasoning tasks, indicating these methods do not inherently solve visual-spatial challenges.
MLLMs tend to form localized, rather than globally consistent, cognitive maps from video observations, showing strong local spatial awareness but poor global understanding.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.14164.Title: MetaMorph: Multimodal Understanding and Generation via Instruction Tuning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.14164.Summary: This paper introduces a method to enable Large Language Models to both understand and generate visual content through a simple instruction tuning approach
Problem: Existing multimodal models often treat visual understanding and generation as separate capabilities requiring complex architectures and extensive training
Current unified models need substantial architectural changes and large-scale pretraining to handle both tasks
Unclear how visual understanding and generation abilities relate and influence each other
Method: Proposes Visual-Predictive Instruction Tuning (VPiT) that extends standard instruction tuning to predict both text and visual tokens
Uses a pretrained LLM with separate heads for text and vision prediction, trained jointly on understanding and generation tasks
Leverages a diffusion model to visualize the predicted visual tokens
Results: Model achieves competitive performance on both visual understanding and generation benchmarks
Visual generation can be unlocked with as little as 200k samples when jointly trained with understanding data
Model demonstrates ability to leverage LLM knowledge for generation and perform implicit visual reasoning
Shows that unified models can be developed effectively from pretrained LLMs without extensive architectural changes
Takeaways: Visual generation ability emerges naturally from improved visual understanding with minimal additional training data
Understanding and generation capabilities are mutually beneficial but asymmetric - understanding data contributes more to both abilities
LLMs appear to have inherent visual capabilities that can be efficiently unlocked through instruction tuning
Joint training with diverse data types improves performance compared to training on generation data alone

https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.13871.Title: LLaVA-UHD v2: an MLLM Integrating High-Resolution Semantic Pyramid via Hierarchical Window Transformer
https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.13871.Summary: LLaVA-UHD v2 integrates a Hierarchical Window (Hiwin) Transformer into Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), constructing a high-resolution semantic pyramid to enrich CLIP-ViT features with fine-grained details. This system achieves an average accuracy improvement of 3.7% across 14 MLLM benchmarks, including a 9.3% increase on DocVQA, while maintaining computational efficiency for high-resolution image processing.
Problem: Existing MLLMs, particularly those relying on CLIP-ViT, perform poorly on tasks requiring fine-grained visual details like OCR or precise visual grounding.

Incorporating hierarchical visual features into MLLMs faces challenges: replacing CLIP-ViT disrupts its image-text alignment, and naive compression of multi-level features leads to significant detail loss.
Efficiently processing high-resolution images in MLLMs without prohibitive computational costs remains a significant hurdle.
Method: A Hierarchical Window (Hiwin) Transformer is introduced as a vision-language projector, featuring a Visual Detail Injection Module (VDIM) and a Hierarchical Window Attention module.

The VDIM constructs an Inverse Semantic Pyramid (ISP) by progressively injecting low-level visual details from image priors into high-level CLIP-ViT features, guided by a Multi-level Reconstruction (MLR) loss to preserve vision-language alignment.

The Hierarchical Window Attention module efficiently compresses these multi-level ISP features into a compact, spatially consistent set of visual tokens for the LLM, utilizing cross-scale window querying and learnable local queries.
Results: LLaVA-UHD v2 establishes new state-of-the-art performance, with an average 3.7% accuracy increase across 14 diverse benchmarks and a notable 9.3% improvement on DocVQA and 5.7% on RefCOCOs.

The model supports higher input resolutions (e.g., 1008x672) with competitive or lower computational costs (e.g., 14.3T FLOPs for Qwen2-7B) compared to previous MLLMs, while also requiring less training data and time.

Ablation studies confirm that the VDIM contributes an average of 2.2% improvement, the Hiwin attention adds another 1.3%, and spatially consistent token organization further enhances performance, particularly on detail-intensive and spatial reasoning tasks.
Takeaways: Low-level visual details can be effectively injected into high-level, language-aligned CLIP-ViT features to form a rich inverse semantic pyramid without compromising pre-existing semantic alignment.

Intelligent, cross-scale window-based attention mechanisms provide an efficient way to compress multi-resolution visual features into a manageable token count for LLMs, preserving critical spatial relationships and fine-grained information.
Explicit multi-level reconstruction loss during feature pyramid construction is crucial for maintaining robust vision-language alignment while simultaneously enhancing visual granularity.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.13810.Title: CAD-Assistant: Tool-Augmented VLLMs as Generic CAD Task Solvers
https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.13810.Summary: CAD-Assistant presents a tool-augmented Vision and Large Language Model (VLLM) framework that integrates GPT-4o with specialized CAD tools and the FreeCAD software to enable generic CAD task solving. This framework demonstrates robust performance across diverse multimodal inputs, achieving superior results compared to baselines in tasks like autoconstraining and hand-drawn sketch parameterization.
Problem: Existing CAD automation solutions are primarily task-specific, focusing on fixed workflows and lacking the generality to support the entire iterative design process.
Vision and Large Language Models (VLLMs) inherently struggle with precise geometric reasoning, mathematical accuracy, and understanding the complex effects of CAD commands.
There is a need for adaptable CAD agents capable of processing diverse multimodal inputs and interacting dynamically with evolving design states to provide comprehensive AI assistance.
Method: A tool-augmented VLLM framework, CAD-Assistant, was developed using GPT-4o as a high-level planner to generate natural language plans and corresponding Python code actions.

The framework integrates a comprehensive set of CAD-specific tools, including a hand-drawn image parameterizer, sketch/3D solid recognizers, and a constraint checker, along with direct FreeCAD API access.
An iterative plan-action-execution-feedback loop allows the VLLM to dynamically refine its strategy based on textual feedback and visual renderings from the CAD environment.
Results: CAD-Assistant achieved 0.979 Primitive F1 (PF1) and 0.484 Constraint F1 (CF1) on the SketchGraphs benchmark for autoconstraining, outperforming raw GPT-4o (0.693 PF1, 0.274 CF1) and supervised methods like Vitruvion.
It demonstrated strong performance in CAD Question Answering (CQA), with 0.791 Accuracy (2D) and 0.857 Accuracy (3D), representing substantial gains over raw VLLM baselines.

The system successfully performed real-world tasks such as 3D reverse engineering from scans, visual interpretation of hand-drawn commands, and 3D solid generation from sketches, with an average cost per user request ranging from
0.0299to0.0887.
Takeaways: Tool-augmentation effectively overcomes the geometric reasoning shortcomings of VLLMs, enabling them to achieve high precision in complex CAD tasks by offloading specific operations to dedicated tools.
Multimodal input, specifically precise 2D renderings of sketches and over-parameterized JSON representations, significantly improves the VLLM's understanding and reasoning about CAD geometry.
The training-free nature and reliance on docstrings for tool integration make the framework highly extensible and adaptable to a wide array of CAD commands without requiring extensive retraining.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.13303.Title: FastVLM: Efficient Vision Encoding for Vision Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.13303.Summary: FastVLM, an efficient Vision Language Model developed by Apple, employs a novel FastViTHD vision encoder designed for rapid high-resolution image processing. This approach achieves over 2.5 points higher average performance on VLM benchmarks while being up to 3 times faster on an M1 MacBook Pro, significantly improving on-device VLM efficiency.
Problem: Vision Language Models (VLMs) suffer from high latency (Time-To-First-Token) at high image resolutions, particularly for text-rich content, due to the large number of visual tokens generated.
Existing VLM vision encoders, often ViT-based, are computationally expensive and inefficient for deployment on resource-constrained edge devices.
Many VLM pipelines rely on complex, separate token pruning or sampling modules to manage visual token count, adding complexity and overhead.
Method: Developed FastViTHD, a novel 5-stage hybrid convolutional-transformer vision encoder with an increased 64x downsampling factor to inherently reduce the number of visual tokens.
Integrated multi-scale features through depth-wise convolutions within the FastViTHD architecture to enhance feature granularity and information capture.
Employed a systematic multi-stage LLaVA-1.5-like training pipeline to adapt FastViTHD with various LLMs and input resolutions, optimizing the accuracy-latency trade-off.
Results: FastVLM achieves over 2.5 points higher average performance on key VLM benchmarks (Avg-5) for a given runtime budget compared to prior efficient VLMs.

FastVLM reaches target VLM performance up to 3 times faster and demonstrates up to 85 times faster Time-To-First-Token (TTFT) on an M1 MacBook Pro compared to larger, less efficient models like LLaVA-OneVision.

FastViTHD, FastVLM's vision encoder, inherently produces fewer visual tokens and outperforms models that use multiple encoders or explicit token pruning, such as MM1 and MiniGemini-HD, on various benchmarks.
Takeaways: An efficiency-first architectural design for the vision encoder, specifically a hierarchical hybrid convolutional-transformer, can inherently reduce visual tokens and latency more effectively than post-hoc pruning.
The vision encoder's latency becomes the dominant bottleneck in VLM performance at high resolutions, necessitating optimized vision backbone design.
Directly setting static input resolution for the VLM model generally offers a better accuracy-latency trade-off compared to dynamic tiling strategies.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.13171.Title: Compressed Chain of Thought: Efficient Reasoning Through Dense Representations
https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.13171.Summary: The Compressed Chain of Thought (CCoT) framework enables large language models to perform complex reasoning efficiently by learning to generate compact, continuous representations of reasoning steps. This method achieves up to a 9 percentage point increase in accuracy on the GSM8K dataset while incurring only a 0.45-second latency increase compared to a direct answer baseline.
Problem: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning significantly boosts Large Language Model (LLM) performance on complex tasks but incurs high generation latency due to explicitly decoding verbose reasoning steps.
Existing methods that provide LLMs with extra computation during inference often rely on non-contentful or discrete 'contemplation tokens', which may not be effective for all types of reasoning.
There is a need for an efficient alternative to explicit CoT that can perform 'additional reasoning over dense contentful representations' without the full generation cost.
Method: Introduces Compressed Chain of Thought (CCoT), a two-phase LoRA finetuning framework for decoder-only LLMs (LLAMA2-7B-CHAT).

Trains models to generate 'contentful' and 'continuous' contemplation tokens autoregressively by matching their intermediate hidden states (e.g., at layer 15) to gold hidden states from a full CoT trace using scaled Mean Squared Error (MSE).

A separate module is finetuned to decode the final answer conditioned on the initial query and the generated contemplation tokens, with an additional classifier to predict the optimal number of contemplation tokens at inference.
Results: CCoT with a 10x compression ratio achieved 17.9% accuracy on GSM8K with a 0.78-second decode time, representing a 9 percentage point accuracy improvement over the 8.9% baseline (0.33s).
CCoT significantly outperformed non-contentful PAUSE tokens, which showed only marginal accuracy improvements (0.3-1.0 percentage points) at comparable decode times.
The framework demonstrated an adaptive trade-off between reasoning accuracy and generation speed, allowing for dynamic control over computational effort by adjusting the compression ratio.
Takeaways: Complex reasoning tasks, such as those in GSM8K, benefit more from sequential, 'depth-bottlenecked' computation provided by autoregressive continuous contemplation tokens rather than purely parallel methods.
Intermediate hidden states (e.g., at layer 15 for LLAMA2-7B) are optimal for encoding and passing information across autoregressive contemplation steps.
An adaptive control over reasoning depth, achieved by varying the compression ratio of contemplation tokens, allows for a flexible trade-off between accuracy and inference efficiency.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.11974.Title: Emma-X: An Embodied Multimodal Action Model with Grounded Chain of Thought and Look-ahead Spatial Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.11974.Summary: Researchers at the Singapore University of Technology and Design developed EMMA-X, an embodied multimodal action model that enhances robot policies with visually grounded chain-of-thought and look-ahead spatial reasoning. This approach leads to a 24.17% increase in task success rate over the OpenVLA baseline on real-world robot manipulation tasks, particularly improving performance in scenarios requiring complex spatial understanding and generalization to new instructions.
Problem: Current Visual-Language-Action (VLA) models often lack long-horizon spatial reasoning, exhibiting "muscle memory" without foresight for multi-step movements or future states.
Task planning in VLAs, particularly with chain-of-thought reasoning, frequently suffers from hallucination due to insufficient visual grounding, leading to incoherent or physically impossible plans.
Existing robotic control policies, including traditional reinforcement learning and prior VLA models, struggle with generalization to diverse environments, unseen objects, or varied instructions.
Method: EMMA-X constructs a hierarchical embodiment dataset by auto-annotating existing robot trajectories with grounded task reasoning and look-ahead spatial guidance.
It employs a novel trajectory segmentation strategy using HDBSCAN with a custom distance metric and gripper state changes to define coherent action segments.
The model integrates future 2D gripper position prediction, natural language 3D movement plans, and visually grounded chain-of-thought reasoning into a fine-tuned 7B-parameter OpenVLA model.
Results: EMMA-X achieved a 24.17% increase in task success rate and a 26.25% increase in half-success rate compared to OpenVLA across 12 real-world WidowX-250 robot manipulation tasks.

The model showed the most pronounced improvements (35% over OpenVLA in half-success rate) on tasks requiring complex spatial relations and demonstrated substantial gains on out-of-domain instruction tasks.

Ablation studies confirmed the critical contribution of each core component, with removing grounded chain-of-thought reasoning leading to a 43%-55% performance drop, and removing spatial reasoning components causing 25%-45% declines.
Takeaways: Visually grounding chain-of-thought reasoning with segmented image sequences significantly mitigates hallucination and enhances the coherence of task planning in VLA models.
Integrating explicit look-ahead predictions of future 2D gripper positions and high-level 3D movement plans enables robots to achieve superior long-horizon spatial reasoning and more precise actions.
A novel trajectory segmentation strategy, combining motion clustering and gripper state changes, is crucial for constructing high-quality hierarchical training data necessary for embodied reasoning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.10439.Title: CogNav: Cognitive Process Modeling for Object Goal Navigation with LLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.10439.Summary: CogNav introduces an LLM-driven framework for Object Goal Navigation that models fine-grained human-like cognitive processes, dynamically managing search strategies across five states (e.g., Broad Search, Candidate Verification) using a heterogeneous cognitive map. The framework achieves state-of-the-art success rates, improving by 10.5% on HM3D, 6.4% on MP3D, and 7.1% on RoboTHOR, and demonstrates real-world applicability on physical robots.
Problem: Existing Object Goal Navigation (ObjectNav) methods struggle with the 'cognitive aspect' (reasoning, planning, decision-making) despite advancements in visual perception.

Prior cognitive modeling approaches rely on either implicit learning (poor generality, high computational cost) or coarse heuristic rules (oversimplify human cognitive processes, lack fine-grained reasoning).
Integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) into embodied AI for navigation has largely been limited to high-level scene understanding or static reasoning, not dynamic cognitive process management.
Method: CogNav constructs a dynamic, heterogeneous cognitive map (scene graph, occupancy map, landmark graph) using foundation models (OpenSEED, GPT-4v) to ground LLM reasoning with real-time environmental information.

It defines five fine-grained cognitive states (Broad Search, Contextual Search, Observe Target, Candidate Verification, Target Confirmation) inspired by neuroscientific findings of human object search.

An LLM (GPT-3) acts as a dynamic scheduler for adaptive state transitions and a planner for strategic landmark selection within each state, utilizing natural language prompts derived from the cognitive map.
Results: Achieved state-of-the-art success rates (SR) in zero-shot, open-vocabulary ObjectNav, with absolute improvements of 10.5% on HM3D (72.5% SR), 6.4% on MP3D (46.6% SR), and 7.1% on RoboTHOR (54.6% SR) over previous baselines.

Ablation studies confirmed the criticality of each fine-grained cognitive state for optimal performance, with 'Candidate Verification' leading to higher success rates by improving robustness and reducing misidentifications.

Successfully deployed and validated on real-world robot platforms (a custom mobile robot and a Unitree quadruped), demonstrating the practical effectiveness and generalizability of the framework beyond simulation environments.
Takeaways: Modeling fine-grained human-like cognitive states, particularly the 'Candidate Verification' stage, significantly enhances navigation robustness and success by enabling adaptive error recovery and observation from multiple viewpoints.

LLMs can effectively serve as dynamic cognitive schedulers and planners for embodied agents, leveraging their commonsense knowledge for adaptive decision-making without requiring extensive task-specific policy training.

A dynamically updated 'heterogeneous cognitive map' is crucial for grounding abstract LLM reasoning with concrete, real-time spatial and semantic environmental information, bridging the gap between symbolic AI and physical world interactions.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.09544.Title: Sail into the Headwind: Alignment via Robust Rewards and Dynamic Labels against Reward Hacking
https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.09544.Summary: Researchers at Meta AI's FAIR group developed POWER-DL, a framework designed to identify and address two types of reward hacking in preference-based learning for AI alignment. The method leverages robust reward estimation and dynamic preference labels to improve alignment performance and maintain initial model capabilities across instruction-following, conversational, and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods like DPO.
Problem: AI alignment via Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) is vulnerable to 'reward hacking', where AI exploits flaws in the reward signal instead of genuinely aligning with human values.
Reward hacking occurs in two ways: Type I (suboptimal choices appear favorable due to noisy data) and Type II (high-quality choices are underrepresented, leading to performance degradation).
Current preference optimization methods like DPO and its variants lack mechanisms to robustly handle the statistical uncertainty and distribution shift inherent in human preference datasets.
Method: Introduces POWER (Preference Optimization via Weighted Entropy Robust Rewards), which addresses Type I reward hacking by integrating Guiaşu's Weighted Entropy with robust reward maximization to account for uncertainty.

Proposes Dynamic Labels, a technique to mitigate Type II reward hacking by adaptively adjusting the influence of preference pairs during training based on their consistency with current reward estimates.
Combines these two techniques into POWER-DL, an integrated framework for robust preference optimization with theoretical guarantees for finite-sample performance under general function approximation.
Results: POWER-DL consistently outperformed DPO and SimPO on AlpacaEval 2.0, achieving up to 13.0% higher win rates with Helpsteer2 and 4.8% with Zephyr.
The method showed gains of up to 11.5% on Arena-Hard and maintained or improved mathematical reasoning capabilities on GSM8K, unlike baselines that often degraded performance.
Experiments demonstrated that POWER-DL is less prone to the degradation effects of Type II reward hacking, consistently maintaining or improving performance over the initial model.
Takeaways: Reward hacking in preference optimization manifests as two distinct types: Type I (statistical fluctuations causing overestimation) and Type II (underrepresentation of good behaviors leading to degradation).

Existing preference optimization methods like DPO are theoretically vulnerable to both types of reward hacking due to insufficient accounting for statistical uncertainty and inadequate regularization.

Integrating pessimistic reward estimation (via weighted entropy and robust reward maximization) and adaptive preference weighting (dynamic labels) can effectively mitigate both forms of reward hacking.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.09413.Title: Imitate, Explore, and Self-Improve: A Reproduction Report on Slow-thinking Reasoning Systems
https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.09413.Summary: Researchers at Renmin University of China introduce STILL-2, an open-source framework that reproduces o1-like "slow-thinking" reasoning in LLMs through an "imitate, explore, and self-improve" approach. The system achieves performance closely approaching leading proprietary systems on complex reasoning tasks, with 90.2% accuracy on MATH-OAI and 46.7% on AIME, suggesting that fine-tuning with high-quality, long-form thought data can elicit strong reasoning without explicit tree search.
Problem: Proprietary "slow-thinking" LLMs (like OpenAI's o1) exhibit advanced, multi-step reasoning capabilities but operate as "black boxes," hindering academic understanding, reproduction, and open research.
Previous academic attempts to replicate such systems were often limited to specific domains, used weaker base models, or failed to achieve performance comparable to industrial counterparts.
The authors' prior framework (STILL-1) faced challenges with domain-specific reward models, high inference costs due to tree search, and a lack of train-time scaling.
Method: Introduces the STILL-2 framework, employing an "imitate, explore, and self-improve" (IES) three-phase training approach for developing LLM-based slow-thinking reasoning.

Shifts away from complex reward models and explicit tree search during inference, opting for a single-pass text generation process that produces both internal reasoning (thought) and the final solution in a unified output.

Constructs high-quality, long-form thought datasets by distilling trajectories from open o1-like systems (DeepSeek-R1-Lite-Preview, QwQ-32B-preview), with meticulous data cleaning, format unification, and mixing across diverse, challenging domains.
Results: The STILL-2 distillation variant, trained on 3.9k instances, achieved 90.2% accuracy on MATH-OAI and an impressive 46.7% on AIME, demonstrating a +251.1% gain over the Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct backbone model on AIME.

Exploration and self-improvement strategies (SFT or DPO) further improved performance over the baseline fine-tuned model (e.g., AIME scores improved from 33.3% to 40.0% or 46.7%), though constrained by current limitations in the number of rollouts.

Training on hard mathematical problems was found to be crucial for developing long-form thinking capabilities, which then generalize effectively across different reasoning domains (e.g., math and science).
Takeaways: Fine-tuning with a limited amount of carefully curated, high-quality long-form thought data, especially from challenging problems, is highly effective for eliciting advanced LLM reasoning, with performance approaching industry-leading systems.

The ability to perform long-form reasoning, once instilled through focused training, demonstrates strong cross-domain transferability, generalizing across mathematical, coding, and scientific reasoning tasks.

Complex reward models or explicit tree search during inference may not be strictly necessary; a finely tuned, single-pass generation of interwoven thought and solution can achieve robust "slow-thinking" capabilities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.08635.Title: Multimodal Latent Language Modeling with Next-Token Diffusion
https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.08635.Summary: This paper introduces a unified framework called LatentLM for handling both discrete and continuous data using causal Transformers with next-token diffusion
Problem: Existing multimodal models struggle to handle both discrete data (text, code) and continuous data (images, audio, video) in a unified way
Previous approaches rely on pipelines or quantization which creates information bottlenecks
Different objectives and architectures for discrete vs continuous data make joint training challenging
Method: Represents continuous data as latent vectors using σ-VAE with fixed variance
Introduces next-token diffusion to autoregressively generate latent vectors one by one
Uses shared causal Transformer backbone with unified language modeling objective
Integrates both diffusion head for continuous data and softmax head for discrete data
Results: Outperforms DiT in image generation when scaling up model size
Better performance than Transfusion and VQ models on multimodal language tasks
10x fewer decoding steps than VALL-E 2 on text-to-speech while maintaining quality
Strong scalability properties across different model sizes and batch sizes
Higher compression ratios enable more efficient training and inference
Takeaways: Higher compression ratio than vector quantization while maintaining quality
Unified architecture enables better information sharing between modalities
σ-VAE with fixed variance helps prevent collapse and improves autoregressive generation
Simpler implementation by reusing existing language model infrastructure
Allows end-to-end training across modalities

https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.07755.Title: SAT: Dynamic Spatial Aptitude Training for Multimodal Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.07755.Summary: Researchers from Boston University, University of Washington, Allen Institute for AI, Microsoft Research, and NYU introduced Spatial Aptitude Training (SAT), a framework utilizing 3D simulators to generate a large, perfectly annotated spatial question-answer dataset. This training improved multimodal language models' static and dynamic spatial reasoning capabilities on real-world images and videos, showing gains on benchmarks like CVBench and a custom dynamic test set.
Problem: Current large multimodal language models (MLMs) exhibit critical weaknesses in spatial reasoning, especially when dealing with dynamic relationships and understanding motion.
The scarcity of high-quality, scalable spatial annotations, particularly for complex 3D movements and their causal effects, limits MLMs' ability to learn these skills.
Manual annotation of dynamic spatial relationships in real-world data is prohibitively expensive and prone to errors.
Method: Developed Spatial Aptitude Training (SAT), a data generation framework that leverages 3D simulators to procedurally create a large-scale dataset of perfectly annotated static and dynamic spatial question-answer pairs.
The SAT dataset includes five categories of dynamic spatial reasoning tasks: egocentric movement, object movement, allocentric perspective, goal aiming, and action consequence prediction.

Instruction-tuned existing multimodal language models (LLaVA-1.5-13B and LLaVA-Video-7B) with the SAT data, incorporating a portion of their original training data to maintain general vision-language capabilities.
Results: SAT training improved LLaVA-1.5-13B's static spatial reasoning on CVBench and BLINK by an average of 23.9%, achieving 75.6% accuracy and often matching or surpassing proprietary models.
Models fine-tuned with SAT data demonstrated sim-to-real transfer, with LLaVA-1.5-13B improving dynamic spatial reasoning on the real-image SAT test set by 13.3% to 54.9%.

SAT-trained LLaVA-Video-7B showed enhanced video spatial reasoning, including a 5.2% gain in route planning on VSI-Bench and a 4% average improvement on out-of-domain outdoor videos from MME-RealWorld-Lite.
Takeaways: Perfectly annotated synthetic data from 3D simulators proves more effective for imparting spatial reasoning to MLMs than noisy pseudo-annotated real-image data.
Training with dynamic spatial tasks facilitates robust sim-to-real transfer, enabling models to apply learned spatial intelligence to real-world images and out-of-domain videos.
Procedural generation of spatial QA data offers a scalable and cost-effective approach to overcome the limitations of manual annotation for complex spatial reasoning tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.07679.Title: RADIOv2.5: Improved Baselines for Agglomerative Vision Foundation Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.07679.Summary: RADIOv2.5 from NVIDIA Research establishes new baselines for agglomerative vision foundation models by addressing multi-resolution inconsistencies and computational inefficiencies, achieving state-of-the-art performance across dense visual tasks and Vision-Language Model benchmarks. It demonstrates improved robustness by eliminating resolution-dependent mode switching and enhances efficiency through novel token compression techniques.
Problem: Existing agglomerative vision foundation models exhibit "mode switching" behavior, where feature distributions change dramatically with input resolution, leading to inconsistent performance.
Teacher models have varying activation magnitudes and feature distributions, causing unbalanced learning in multi-teacher distillation.
High-resolution visual encoders produce excessive output tokens, which significantly bottleneck the efficiency and performance of Vision-Language Models due to quadratic attention complexity.
Method: Implemented a Multi-Resolution Training (MRT) schedule, augmented with Mosaic Augmentation, allowing the student model to learn consistently from all teachers across multiple resolutions.
Applied PCA-Hadamard Isotropic Standardization (PHI-S) to balance teacher contributions by normalizing activation magnitudes and distributions, improving training stability.
Integrated a token merging technique inspired by ToMeSD, which uses bipartite soft matching to efficiently compress visual tokens while preserving essential information for Vision-Language Models.
Results: Multi-resolution training eliminated "mode switching," resulting in consistent accuracy across input resolutions, with specific improvements such as +2.8 mIoU on ADE20k and +3.4 average VLM score.
Outperformed prior agglomerative models (e.g., SAM-CLIP, Theia, UNIC) on dense tasks, with RADIOv2.5-B exceeding DINOv2-g-reg's ADE20k performance despite being significantly smaller.

Achieved state-of-the-art VLM performance, with configurations showing a 6.7-point average VLM score increase by using SigLIP as a teacher and a 5.9-point average increase from efficient token merging.
Takeaways: Simultaneously training across multiple resolutions with adaptive teacher handling (like mosaic augmentation for SAM) effectively mitigates resolution-dependent "mode switching" and improves model robustness.
Properly balancing teacher contributions via methods like PHI-S is crucial for stable training and allows seemingly challenging teachers, like SAM, to become genuinely beneficial for diverse tasks.

Token merging strategies, when applied judiciously, can drastically reduce the token count from high-resolution vision encoders while retaining sufficient information for significant performance gains in Vision-Language Models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.07012.Title: ProVision: Programmatically Scaling Vision-centric Instruction Data for Multimodal Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.07012.Summary: Researchers from the University of Washington and Salesforce Research developed PROVISION, a programmatic system for generating over 10 million high-quality, vision-centric instruction data points for multimodal language models. This data significantly improved MLM performance on various vision-centric benchmarks, showing up to an 8% increase in specific tasks.
Problem: Multimodal Language Models (MLMs) lack sufficient high-quality, vision-centric instruction data for effective training.
Existing data generation methods using Large Language Models (LLMs) or MLMs are prone to hallucinations, lack interpretability, are expensive, and may have licensing issues.
MLMs often struggle with fine-grained visual reasoning tasks like object counting, spatial relations, and depth estimation.
Method: PROVISION introduces a programmatic pipeline that leverages augmented scene graphs—structured symbolic representations of images including objects, attributes, relations, segmentation, and depth.
Human-written instruction generators, comprising 24 single-image and 14 multi-image types with hundreds of templates, systematically synthesize diverse question-answer pairs from these scene graphs.

An automated pipeline integrates state-of-the-art models (e.g., YOLO-world, SAM-2, LLaVA-1.5-13B, Osprey, Depth Anything V2) to generate augmented scene graphs for images lacking manual annotations, enabling large-scale data creation.
Results: Instruction tuning LLaVA-1.5-7B with single-image PROVISION data showed up to a 7% improvement on CVBench's 2D split and 8% on its 3D split, along with a 3% increase on QBench2, RealWorldQA, and MMMU.
Multi-image PROVISION data led to an 8% improvement in LLaVA-1.5-7B performance on the Mantis-Eval benchmark.
Incorporating PROVISION data into both pre-training and instruction tuning stages of xGen-MM-4B models resulted in the best overall performance, averaging a 1.6% improvement across 11 benchmarks.
Takeaways: Programmatic data generation offers enhanced interpretability, factual accuracy, scalability, and cost-effectiveness compared to purely generative model-based approaches.
While data derived from human-annotated scene graphs generally performs better, large quantities of model-generated scene graph data can achieve comparable performance for single-image tasks.

Optimal MLM performance is achieved through a synergistic approach, incorporating PROVISION data in both pre-training and instruction tuning stages, and utilizing a mix of multiple-choice and short-answer formats.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.06769.Title: Training Large Language Models to Reason in a Continuous Latent Space
https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.06769.Summary: Researchers from FAIR at Meta introduced Coconut, a paradigm training Large Language Models to perform reasoning in a continuous latent space by iteratively feeding hidden states. This approach demonstrates emergent breadth-first search capabilities, achieving higher accuracy on logical tasks like ProsQA with significantly greater token efficiency compared to traditional language-based Chain-of-Thought methods.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) relying on Chain-of-Thought (CoT) are constrained by natural language, which is often suboptimal and inefficient for complex reasoning.
CoT generates many 'fluency tokens' that contribute little to core reasoning, wasting computational resources.
Autoregressive language generation forces LLMs to commit prematurely to a single reasoning path, hindering complex planning and exploration of alternatives.
Method: The Coconut (Chain of Continuous Thought) paradigm utilizes the LLM's last hidden state as a continuous representation of 'thought,' feeding it back as the next input embedding instead of generating word tokens.
A multi-stage training curriculum gradually replaces initial language reasoning steps from existing CoT data with continuous thoughts, guiding the model to learn latent reasoning.
The model operates in distinct 'language mode' for textual output and 'latent mode' for internal continuous thought processing, enabling end-to-end optimization.
Results: Coconut significantly outperforms language-based CoT on logical reasoning tasks like ProntoQA and the novel ProsQA dataset, achieving 97.0% accuracy on ProsQA compared to CoT's 77.5%.
The method demonstrates a superior accuracy-efficiency trade-off, achieving comparable or better accuracy on tasks like GSM8k while generating substantially fewer tokens during inference.

Analysis revealed that Coconut's latent space maintains diverse high-probability candidate paths at early reasoning stages, progressively converging to the most promising solution, showcasing a non-greedy search strategy.
Takeaways: Reasoning in a continuous latent space allows LLMs to encode and explore multiple alternative reasoning steps simultaneously, leading to emergent breadth-first search (BFS) behavior.
The multi-stage training curriculum is crucial for LLMs to effectively learn and leverage continuous latent thoughts for sophisticated reasoning.
Continuous thoughts implicitly encode intermediate variables or concepts, serving as efficient, compact representations for problem-solving steps.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.05479.Title: LATTE: Learning to Think with Vision Specialists
https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.05479.Summary: The LATTE framework trains open-source vision-language models to perform complex multimodal reasoning by integrating and orchestrating 15 specialized vision tools. This approach yields 4-5% average accuracy improvements across diverse benchmarks and up to 10-20% gains on complex reasoning tasks like MMVet, outperforming models that do not explicitly leverage external vision specialists.
Problem: Open-source vision-language models (VLMs) demonstrate a performance gap compared to proprietary, large-scale models when handling complex multimodal reasoning tasks.
Smaller VLMs often exhibit generalized perception limitations, underperforming dedicated computer vision specialist models in specific perceptual tasks.
A lack of large-scale, high-quality training data exists for teaching VLMs to effectively perform multi-step reasoning by interacting with external tools.
Method: Develops a novel 'learning to reason with vision specialists' paradigm, where VLMs generate explicit thoughts and actions to call specialized vision tools for perceptual information.
Introduces `LATTE-trace`, a `(thought, action, observation)` data format, used to train models on how to utilize 15 diverse vision specialists (e.g., OCR, object detection, depth estimation).

Generates a large-scale dataset of 293K `LATTE-traces` using a dual approach: a GPT-4o-based engine for diverse scenarios and a programmatic engine for specific capabilities, both with rigorous filtering for correctness.
Results: LATTE consistently achieves 4-5% average accuracy gains over vanilla instruction-tuned baselines across six diverse benchmarks, with improvements up to 10-20% on reasoning-heavy benchmarks like MMVet.
The method demonstrates superior performance compared to other distillation baselines (e.g., VPD, LLaVa-CoT), which aim to distill both perception and reasoning from larger generalist models.

Careful data filtering to include only 'LATTE-useful' traces (where specialists lead to correct answers) proves more beneficial than simply increasing data volume, and poor-quality traces can degrade performance.
Takeaways: Decoupling perception from reasoning by delegating perceptual tasks to specialized vision tools is an effective strategy for significantly enhancing the reasoning abilities of open-source VLMs.

The quality of reasoning traces, particularly the correctness of tool usage and alignment with ground truth, is more critical for training effective multimodal reasoners than the sheer quantity of data.
The accuracy of individual vision specialists (e.g., OCR) directly impacts the overall performance of the VLM, highlighting the importance of high-quality tools within the framework.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.05265.Title: Reinforcement Learning: An Overview
https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.05265.Summary: Kevin P. Murphy's overview synthesizes the expansive and rapidly evolving field of Reinforcement Learning, providing a structured exposition of its foundational concepts, core algorithmic paradigms, and advanced topics. It clarifies the interconnections between diverse methodologies, offering a comprehensive reference for understanding and applying RL. The work details the advancements from classic dynamic programming to contemporary deep RL, multi-agent systems, and the integration with Large Language Models.
Problem: The rapid growth and complexity of Reinforcement Learning (RL) have created a fragmented landscape, making it challenging for researchers and practitioners to gain a unified understanding.
A structured resource is needed to consolidate foundational theories, diverse algorithmic approaches, and emerging research frontiers in RL.
Connecting disparate RL methods and understanding their underlying assumptions, trade-offs, and practical implications poses a significant challenge.
Method: A systematic and hierarchical exposition of RL is presented, moving from fundamental principles (e.g., MDPs) to specialized techniques.
Algorithms are categorized into value-based, policy-based, and model-based paradigms, with detailed discussions on their evolution, strengths, and interconnections.
Dedicated chapters cover advanced topics, including Multi-agent RL (MARL) and the symbiotic relationship between Large Language Models (LLMs) and RL, alongside practical insights.
Results: A comprehensive intellectual map of Reinforcement Learning is established, clarifying major concepts, methodologies, and challenges from foundational theories to cutting-edge applications.
The paper categorizes and details the evolution of RL algorithms, including the progression from tabular Q-learning to Deep Q-Networks and advanced multi-agent strategies like self-play.
A structured understanding of the symbiotic relationship between LLMs and RL is provided, outlining how each field benefits from the other and highlighting future research directions in AI.
Takeaways: Reinforcement Learning provides a universal framework for sequential decision-making, applicable across various problem formulations from simple bandits to complex multi-agent environments.
RL algorithms can be systematically organized into three core paradigms—value-based, policy-based, and model-based—each addressing distinct aspects of learning and control.
The integration of RL with Large Language Models represents a critical frontier, with RL fine-tuning LLMs for alignment and reasoning, and LLMs serving as powerful components within RL systems.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.04468.Title: NVILA: Efficient Frontier Visual Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.04468.Summary: NVILA, developed by a collaboration including NVIDIA and MIT, introduces a family of open Visual Language Models that achieve state-of-the-art accuracy on diverse image and video benchmarks while drastically improving efficiency across training, fine-tuning, and deployment. The models demonstrate training cost reductions of 1.9-5.1x and inference speedups of up to 2.8x, enabling practical deployment on resource-constrained devices and democratizing VLM development.
Problem: Current state-of-the-art Visual Language Models (VLMs) incur prohibitively high training costs, requiring hundreds of GPU days.
Fine-tuning VLMs for domain-specific applications is memory-intensive, often exceeding 64GB, which limits accessibility on standard hardware.
Deploying VLMs on resource-constrained edge devices or in real-time applications faces significant computational and memory challenges due to their large size.
Method: Introduces a "Scale-Then-Compress" architectural paradigm with Dynamic-S2 for images and temporal averaging for videos to efficiently handle high-resolution and long-context visual inputs.
Employs efficient training techniques including unsupervised dataset pruning (DeltaLoss) to reduce data redundancy and FP8 mixed precision training for higher throughput.

Proposes optimized fine-tuning strategies with differentiated learning rates and efficient Layer Normalization (LN) tuning for the vision encoder, along with specialized inference engine optimizations including W8A8 and W4A16 quantization.
Results: NVILA matches or surpasses the accuracy of many leading open-source models and performs competitively with powerful proprietary models across diverse image and video benchmarks.
The models reduce VLM training costs by 1.9x to 5.1x and accelerate inference by 1.6x to 2.8x compared to baselines through quantization and optimized kernels.
NVILA enables VLM fine-tuning under 24 GB of GPU memory, making adaptation accessible on consumer-grade GPUs, and demonstrates real-time robotic navigation on a single laptop GPU.
Takeaways: A "scale-then-compress" paradigm, combining adaptive scaling with aggressive token reduction, effectively balances visual information capture and computational efficiency for high-resolution images and long videos.
Holistic optimization across the entire VLM lifecycle, from data selection and training to fine-tuning and deployment, is crucial for achieving substantial efficiency gains.
Fine-tuning specific sub-components (e.g., Layer Normalization layers of the vision encoder) can make VLM adaptation memory-efficient and accessible without sacrificing accuracy.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.04073.Title: TransAdapter: Vision Transformer for Feature-Centric Unsupervised Domain Adaptation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.04073.Summary: TransAdapter, a new Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) framework developed at Ozyegin University, enhances Vision Transformers for feature-centric domain alignment through specialized modules. The framework achieves new state-of-the-art average accuracies of 89.4% on Office-Home, 91.2% on VisDA-2017, 95.5% on Office-31, and 53.7% on DomainNet.
Problem: Traditional CNN-based UDA methods struggle with capturing complex domain relationships and long-range dependencies, limiting generalization across significant domain gaps.

Vision Transformers (ViTs) like the Swin Transformer, while powerful, face challenges in UDA due to their localized attention and reliance on extensive pretraining with fixed partitioning, hindering adaptation to fine-grained domain shifts.
Existing UDA approaches often require task-specific alignment modules and struggle to achieve deep, multi-granularity feature alignment between source and target domains.
Method: The TransAdapter framework leverages a Swin Transformer backbone, augmented with three novel modules: Graph Domain Discriminator (GDD), Adaptive Double Attention (ADA), and Cross-Feature Transform (CFT).

A Graph Domain Discriminator (GDD) uses Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) and cosine similarity-based adjacency matrices to capture non-Euclidean inter-pixel correlations and enable hierarchical, adversarial domain alignment.

An Adaptive Double Attention (ADA) module integrates dual attention (window and shifted window) with entropy-guided reweighting to align both local and long-range dependencies, while a Cross-Feature Transform (CFT) dynamically mixes features bidirectionally between domains for enhanced transferability.
Results: TransAdapter-B established new state-of-the-art average accuracies on Office-Home (89.4%), VisDA-2017 (91.2%), Office-31 (95.5%), and DomainNet (53.7%), outperforming leading transformer-based UDA methods.
Ablation studies confirmed the effectiveness of each proposed module, with the GDD contributing up to +3.6% and the ADA module up to +5.6% improvement on specific datasets like VisDA-2017.

t-SNE visualizations demonstrated that the sequential integration of GDD, Pixelwise Transform, CFT, and ADA progressively improved the alignment and clustering of source and target features, indicating enhanced domain-invariant representation learning.
Takeaways: Modeling inter-pixel relationships through graph convolutional networks (GDD) provides a more nuanced understanding of domain shifts, leading to improved domain-invariant feature learning compared to standard discriminators.

Dynamically reweighting combined local and long-range attention using an entropy-guided mechanism (ADA) effectively unifies diverse feature dependencies and prioritizes transferable information for robust adaptation.

A dynamic, bidirectional cross-feature transformation (CFT) strategy fosters more adaptive and generalized knowledge transfer, significantly bridging domain gaps by implicitly mixing and optimizing features.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.03548.Title: Perception Tokens Enhance Visual Reasoning in Multimodal Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.03548.Summary: This work by researchers from the University of Washington and Google Research introduces "Perception Tokens" to enable Multimodal Language Models (MLMs) to internally generate and reason about intrinsic visual representations like depth maps and bounding boxes. This approach improves performance on visual reasoning tasks, achieving a 6.4 percentage point boost in relative depth estimation on BLINK and substantial gains in object counting over fine-tuned baselines, even surpassing tool-augmented closed-source models in some cases.
Problem: Current Multimodal Language Models (MLMs) struggle with fundamental visual perception tasks that require detailed understanding of intrinsic image properties, such as 3D structure (e.g., relative depth) or 2D object instances (e.g., precise counting).
Existing solutions like direct finetuning offer marginal improvements, and tool-using MLMs are computationally inefficient and prone to error propagation from external modules.
While some advanced models can generate visual outputs (e.g., segmentation masks), they typically lack the ability to internally reason over their own generated outputs for subsequent tasks.
Method: Introduces 'Perception Tokens,' which are intrinsic image representations (e.g., depth maps, bounding boxes) transformed into a tokenized format that MLMs can process and generate.
Proposes AURORA, a training framework that integrates these perception tokens into the MLM's chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning process, allowing the model to use them as intermediate steps.

Employs a specialist-to-generalist distillation strategy to train the MLM to predict these tokens, alongside a curriculum learning approach that progresses from atomic token generation to multi-step visual reasoning tasks.
Results: LLaVA-AURORA improves relative depth estimation by 6.4 percentage points on the BLINK dataset compared to fine-tuned LLaVA and surpasses GPT-4 Turbo + Tool, with performance gains increasing on more complex datasets like HardBLINK.

The model achieves substantial gains in object counting, with improvements of +10.8% on BLINK, +11.3% on CVBench, and +8.3% on SEED-Bench over fine-tuned LLaVA models, also outperforming GPT-4 Turbo + Tool.

The system can decode its learned depth tokens back into coherent depth maps that qualitatively resemble ground truth and quantitatively outperform other methods in relative depth estimation when using its own generated maps, demonstrating the interpretability of its intermediate visual reasoning.
Takeaways: Multimodal Language Models (MLMs) can be augmented to internally generate and reason over intrinsic visual representations, such as depth maps and bounding boxes, akin to how language models perform chain-of-thought reasoning.
Integrating these 'Perception Tokens' enables MLMs to perform deeper visual reasoning, addressing tasks requiring precise spatial or instance-level understanding beyond high-level feature extraction.

A training framework combining specialist-to-generalist distillation and curriculum learning is effective for teaching MLMs to predict and utilize these novel visual tokens within their reasoning process.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.03069.Title: TokenFlow: Unified Image Tokenizer for Multimodal Understanding and Generation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.03069.Summary: ByteDance researchers developed TokenFlow, a unified image tokenizer featuring a dual-codebook architecture that enables discrete visual inputs to achieve state-of-the-art performance in both multimodal understanding and visual generation. The system surpasses continuous input baselines in understanding tasks and significantly reduces inference steps for high-quality autoregressive image generation.
Problem: The fundamental divide between multimodal understanding (perception) and visual generation paradigms, requiring distinct architectures and visual representations.
Existing discrete image tokenizers (VQ encoders), often optimized for pixel reconstruction, compromise on capturing rich semantic features needed for complex understanding tasks.
Discrete visual inputs have historically lagged continuous visual inputs in multimodal understanding benchmarks, limiting the effectiveness of truly unified models.
Method: A novel dual-codebook architecture, employing separate codebooks for semantic and pixel-level features but sharing a single set of indices through a weighted distance minimization for token selection.
A dual-encoder and dual-decoder training framework that distills high-level semantic priors from a pre-trained teacher model while also ensuring high-fidelity pixel reconstruction.
A multi-step sampling strategy for autoregressive text-to-image generation that iteratively refines the sampling space, significantly enhancing generation quality and coherence.
Results: TokenFlow-XL, using discrete visual input, surpassed LLaVA-1.5 13B (a strong continuous-input baseline) by an average of 7.2% across a comprehensive suite of multimodal understanding benchmarks.
Achieved state-of-the-art performance in autoregressive text-to-image generation with a GenEval score of 0.55, comparable to SDXL, while reducing inference steps to only 25.
Demonstrated exceptional codebook utilization exceeding 95% for codebook sizes up to 131,072 entries, alongside strong image reconstruction fidelity with an rFID of 0.63 at 384x384 resolution.
Takeaways: A single discrete token can effectively encode both fine-grained pixel details and high-level semantic information by judiciously decoupling and aligning their learning processes within a dual-codebook structure.

Careful initialization and multi-task optimization for the tokenizer allow discrete visual representations to surpass continuous counterparts in multimodal understanding benchmarks for the first time.
Autoregressive image generation can achieve state-of-the-art quality with dramatically fewer inference steps by introducing a progressive multi-step sampling method.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.01951.Title: Self-Improvement in Language Models: The Sharpening Mechanism
https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.01951.Summary: This research introduces "sharpening" as a theoretical framework to explain and formalize self-improvement in language models by leveraging their superior ability to verify response quality compared to generating them. The work provides theoretical guarantees for self-improvement algorithms using the model's own log-probabilities as self-reward, demonstrating that performance gains observed at inference time can be effectively amortized into a fine-tuned model for efficient deployment.
Problem: Understanding why large language models (LLMs) can improve their performance through self-refinement processes (e.g., self-play, self-critique) without external human feedback, which appears to contradict the data-processing inequality.
Identifying the source of "hidden knowledge" within LLMs that allows for such improvements, despite the difficulty in efficiently accessing or generating it.
Amortizing the computational cost of inference-time self-improvement techniques (e.g., Best-of-N sampling) into a more efficient post-training phase.
Method: Formalizing self-improvement as "sharpening," where the model's probability mass is tilted towards high-quality, high-certainty sequences that represent its "hidden knowledge."
Introducing a rigorous "sample-and-evaluate" statistical framework to analyze the sample complexity and derive fundamental limits for self-improvement algorithms.

Analyzing and proposing algorithms, including SFT-Sharpening and RLHF-Sharpening (leveraging DPO-like objectives with maximum-likelihood self-reward), to efficiently amortize the cost of finding high-likelihood responses into a training phase.
Results: Best-of-N sampling using the model's own sequence-level log-probability consistently improved accuracy across various LLMs and reasoning tasks (e.g., up to 28.6% lift on MATH for Phi3-Medium) compared to greedy decoding.

The theoretical framework established a lower bound on sample complexity for sharpening algorithms, demonstrating its dependence on the base model's "coverage coefficient," while SFT-Sharpening was shown to be minimax optimal under sufficient coverage.
Empirical application of SFT-Sharpening via fine-tuning successfully amortized inference-time performance gains into fine-tuned models, allowing for comparable quality with efficient greedy decoding.
Takeaways: Self-improvement in language models operates as a "sharpening mechanism," extracting latent knowledge by leveraging the model's superior capability to verify response quality (assign high likelihood) compared to generating optimal responses directly.
The model's own sequence-level log-probability (`log(π_base(y|x))`) serves as a concrete and effective self-reward signal for identifying high-quality outputs.

Reinforcement Learning-based sharpening algorithms that employ active online exploration can achieve exponentially better sample complexity compared to methods relying solely on sampling from the base model, particularly when the base model's coverage of optimal responses is low.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.01282.Title: Align-KD: Distilling Cross-Modal Alignment Knowledge for Mobile Vision-Language Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.01282.Summary: This research from Peking University and Huawei Noah’s Ark Lab introduces Align-KD, a knowledge distillation strategy that specifically transfers cross-modal alignment knowledge from larger Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to smaller mobile VLMs. The approach significantly boosts the performance of a MobileVLM V2 1.7B model by up to 2.0 average points across six benchmarks, enabling more capable VLM deployment on edge devices.
Problem: Modern Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are excessively large and computationally intensive, restricting their deployment on resource-constrained edge devices like mobile phones.
Scaling down VLM architectures often leads to a severe trade-off, where performance significantly degrades as model size is reduced further.
Existing knowledge distillation (KD) techniques for large models primarily focus on single-modal LLMs or neglect the crucial aspect of cross-modal alignment specific to VLMs.
Method: The method identifies the first layer of the VLM's LLM component as the key location for cross-modal alignment by analyzing feature transformations.

It proposes distilling cross-modal alignment knowledge through three specific loss components: first-layer text-query-vision attention, vision enhancement based on text's focusing, and Reverse Kullback-Leibler Divergence for output distribution.
Align-KD integrates these novel distillation losses with a standard supervised learning loss, training a smaller student model (MobileVLM V2 1.7B) from a larger teacher (MobileVLM V2 7B).
Results: Align-KD improved the MobileVLM V2 1.7B model's average performance by 1.4 points on the 'Long' dataset and 2.0 points on the 'Short' dataset across six VLM benchmarks.

Ablation studies confirmed that distilling the first layer's text-query-vision attention (
L
A
1,t−v
) was the most impactful component, outperforming other attention distillation strategies.
The proposed method maintains acceptable computational overhead, requiring 296-676 GPU hours and 22.3-30.7 GB/device memory, making it feasible for practical training.
Takeaways: Cross-modal alignment, crucial for Vision-Language Models (VLMs), primarily occurs at the first layer of the Large Language Model (LLM) component.
Explicitly distilling the first layer's text-query-vision attention is highly effective and efficient for transferring critical cross-modal alignment knowledge to smaller VLM students.

Targeted knowledge distillation can significantly mitigate performance degradation in resource-limited training scenarios, allowing smaller VLMs to achieve comparable or superior performance to larger baselines.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.00420.Title: TAROT: Targeted Data Selection via Optimal Transport
https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.00420.Summary: TAROT introduces a targeted data selection framework that leverages Whitened Feature Distance (WFD) and Optimal Transport (OT) to identify data subsets that optimally enhance model performance on specific target tasks. The method consistently achieved superior results in semantic segmentation, motion prediction, and LLM instruction tuning, often using significantly less data than full datasets or prior methods.
Problem: Existing targeted data selection methods, often relying on influence estimation and greedy heuristics, struggle with complex, multimodal data distributions.
Influence estimation in high-dimensional data is susceptible to bias from dominant feature components, leading to inaccurate data selection.
Prior greedy selection strategies often assume a restrictive linear additive impact of training samples, which fails to capture non-linear interactions within data.
Method: TAROT frames targeted data selection as an Optimal Transport (OT) problem, aiming to select a subset of candidate data that minimizes the OT distance to the target distribution.
It introduces Whitened Feature Distance (WFD) as a novel pairwise cost metric, based on whitened and normalized model loss gradients, to robustly measure data similarity and influence.

A greedy algorithm, utilizing the sparsity of gradient features and optionally incorporating data weighting via OT potentials, iteratively selects the most relevant data points to minimize the OT distance.
Results: TAROT's Whitened Feature Distance (WFD) consistently outperformed state-of-the-art data attribution methods (e.g., TRAK) in terms of Linear Data Modeling Score (LDS) across various tasks like image classification and motion prediction.

On semantic segmentation (GTA5 to Cityscapes), TAROT's Optimal Transport Minimization (OTM) scheme automatically selected ~24% of the data, achieving higher mIoU than models trained on the full dataset or other baselines.

For motion prediction (multi-source to nuScenes) and LLM instruction tuning, TAROT achieved state-of-the-art performance using significantly reduced data subsets (e.g., <0.5% for LLMs), demonstrating high data efficiency and transferability across different model architectures.
Takeaways: Optimal Transport offers a principled framework for targeted data selection by directly minimizing the distributional discrepancy between selected candidate data and a target domain.

Whitened Feature Distance (WFD), derived from whitened and normalized model gradients, provides more accurate and robust influence estimates compared to prior methods, especially in high-dimensional and correlated feature spaces.

Selecting data based on its distributional alignment with the target task, rather than just individual influence scores, enables models to achieve higher performance with significantly smaller, carefully curated datasets.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.19488.Title: Interleaved-Modal Chain-of-Thought
https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.19488.Summary: This work introduces Interleaved-modal Chain-of-Thought (ICoT), a method for Vision-Language Models that integrates relevant image patches directly into reasoning steps. Leveraging an Attention-driven Selection (ADS) mechanism, ICoT enhances fine-grained association between visual and textual information, leading to improved performance and interpretability on complex multimodal reasoning tasks.
Problem: Existing multimodal Chain-of-Thought (CoT) for Vision-Language Models (VLMs) generates text-only rationales, leading to a lack of fine-grained association with visual details.
Textual descriptions in CoT often suffer from ambiguity, potential for misunderstanding, overgeneralization, or hallucination without explicit visual grounding.
Current VLM architectures are not inherently designed to generate fine-grained interleaved visual and textual content as part of their reasoning process.
Method: The paper introduces Interleaved-modal Chain-of-Thought (ICoT), which generates sequential reasoning steps composed of paired visual (image patches) and textual rationales.
Attention-driven Selection (ADS) is proposed as a training-free, plug-and-play mechanism to enable ICoT on existing VLMs by selecting relevant image patches from the input based on attention scores.

ADS works by caching visual tokens, triggering selection upon a signal token, and then concatenating selected visual tokens with text for subsequent VLM generation, effectively grounding textual rationales visually.
Results: ICoT consistently outperformed all tested baselines (No-CoT, Multimodal CoT, CCoT, DDCoT, SCAFFOLD) across M3CoT, ScienceQA, and LLaVA-W benchmarks.
The method achieved up to a 14% ROUGE-L score improvement on the LLaVA-W benchmark, demonstrating its ability to capture and utilize fine-grained visual information for complex reasoning.
Qualitative analyses showed ICoT's interleaved rationales resolved issues of misunderstanding, overgeneralization, and hallucination observed in text-only CoT, enhancing interpretability.
Takeaways: Interleaving visual patches with textual rationales directly addresses issues like misunderstanding, overgeneralization, and hallucination in VLM reasoning, making the process more interpretable.

The Attention-driven Selection (ADS) mechanism effectively leverages existing VLM attention to select relevant visual regions for reasoning without requiring additional training or architectural changes.

The quality of fine-grained visual information in demonstrations is crucial for guiding VLMs to adopt the interleaved reasoning format, with human-crafted examples outperforming automatically generated ones.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.19331.Title: Talking to DINO: Bridging Self-Supervised Vision Backbones with Language for Open-Vocabulary Segmentation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.19331.Summary: Talk2DINO, developed by researchers at UNIMORE and ISTI-CNR, combines the fine-grained visual features of DINOv2 with the rich semantic understanding of CLIP for open-vocabulary segmentation. The approach uses a lightweight, learned projection to bridge their embedding spaces, reaching an average mIoU of 46.3 on eight unsupervised OVS benchmarks with significantly fewer trained parameters than existing methods.
Problem: Open-Vocabulary Segmentation (OVS) aims to segment arbitrary visual concepts from natural language queries, requiring both broad semantic understanding and precise spatial localization.
Vision-language models like CLIP excel at global semantic alignment but lack the fine-grained spatial understanding necessary for accurate pixel-level segmentation.
Self-supervised vision backbones such as DINOv2 provide excellent fine-grained visual features and attention maps but lack inherent alignment with natural language concepts.
Method: A lightweight, non-linear projection function (ψ) is introduced to map CLIP's textual embeddings directly into DINOv2's visual embedding space, keeping both DINOv2 and CLIP backbones frozen.

During training, the ψ function is learned using an InfoNCE loss, maximizing similarity between projected text embeddings and dynamically selected region-specific visual embeddings derived from DINOv2 attention maps.
A novel background cleaning procedure leverages DINOv2's attention maps to reshape similarity maps, improving foreground-background distinction during inference.
Results: Achieved state-of-the-art performance in unsupervised OVS, with an average mIoU of 46.3 across eight standard benchmarks (e.g., Pascal VOC-20, COCO Stuff), surpassing prior methods like ProxyCLIP (42.5 mIoU).

Demonstrated high computational efficiency by freezing large DINOv2 and CLIP backbones, training only a small projection function, leading to fewer trainable parameters and FLOPS than many competitors.

The novel background cleaning procedure significantly improved mIoU by +1.6 on Pascal VOC-21 and +3.9 on COCO Object for ViT-Base models, enhancing the distinction between foreground objects and background.
Takeaways: Effective open-vocabulary segmentation can be achieved by efficiently bridging self-supervised visual features (DINOv2) with vision-language semantics (CLIP) through a minimal-parameter, learned projection function.
DINOv2's attention maps, particularly when utilizing models with 'registers,' provide crucial and clean spatial information necessary for robust language-guided segmentation.
Dynamically selecting the most relevant DINOv2 attention head for a given text query, based on maximum similarity with the projected text embedding, enhances alignment and segmentation accuracy.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.17673.Title: SketchAgent: Language-Driven Sequential Sketch Generation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.17673.Summary: SketchAgent introduces a method for language-driven, sequential sketch generation that leverages off-the-shelf multimodal large language models without additional training. The system generates sketches stroke-by-stroke, enabling real-time interactive collaboration and achieving human-like drawing aesthetics with high recognition rates.
Problem: Traditional sketch generation methods are limited by training data, lack generalizability, and often produce static or non-sequential output.
Existing vision-language model (VLM)-based approaches are slow, generate sketches in a single step (lacking interpretable intermediates), and often produce mechanical-looking vector graphics.
Multimodal Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle with fine-grained spatial reasoning, which is crucial for creating and editing visual content like sketches.
Method: Leverages off-the-shelf, frozen multimodal LLMs (e.g., Claude3.5-Sonnet) to generate sequential sketches, without requiring additional training or fine-tuning.
Introduces a structured 50x50 grid-based canvas and a precise "sketching language" (specifying points and t-values) to enhance the LLM's spatial reasoning abilities.
Employs a cubic Bezier curve fitting process to convert LLM-specified points into smooth, freehand-like strokes, ensuring a natural, human-like appearance.

Uses a comprehensive prompting strategy, including a system prompt, Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, and in-context learning (ICL) examples, to guide the LLM's sequential generation and support interactive editing.
Results: Achieved a Top-1 CLIP accuracy of 0.23 and Top-5 accuracy of 0.44 on 50 QuickDraw categories, approaching human-level recognition rates (human sketches 0.27 Top-1, 0.49 Top-5).
User studies showed SketchAgent's drawings were perceived as more human-like (74.90% preference over direct prompting) and achieved 45.32% human-likeness when compared to actual human drawings.
Generated sketches in approximately 20 seconds, enabling real-time interactive editing with 92% accuracy for instructions and effective human-agent collaborative sketching with high recognizability.
Takeaways: It is possible to achieve language-driven, sequential sketch generation using off-the-shelf multimodal LLMs without any specific training or fine-tuning, by carefully structuring prompts and outputs.
Augmenting LLMs with a structured "sketching language" and a grid-based canvas can significantly improve their spatial reasoning for visual creation tasks.

The stroke-by-stroke generation process of SketchAgent allows for meaningful intermediate steps, real-time interaction, and effective human-AI collaborative sketching, mimicking human creative workflows.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.16044.Title: ZoomEye: Enhancing Multimodal LLMs with Human-Like Zooming Capabilities through Tree-Based Image Exploration
https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.16044.Summary: ZoomEye, a training-free and model-agnostic framework, enhances Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) with human-like zooming capabilities through tree-based image exploration. This approach substantially improves MLLM performance on high-resolution visual tasks, enabling smaller models (3B-8B parameters) to surpass larger commercial models like GPT-4o on specific detail-oriented benchmarks.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle to effectively process and reason about high-resolution images rich in fine-grained details.
Current MLLMs rely on static visual input (fixed resolution or block division), leading to information loss and a 'perception gap' where subtle visual cues are missed.
MLLM reasoning is predominantly 'text-level,' lacking dynamic visual interaction or exploration capabilities akin to human visual cognition.
Method: ZoomEye introduces a training-free and model-agnostic tree search algorithm that enables MLLMs to perform vision-level reasoning by dynamically zooming into specific regions of interest.
