An image is represented as a hierarchical tree of patches, allowing MLLMs to navigate and explore sub-regions based on a ranking function that leverages both existing and latent confidence for visual cues.
The search employs a dynamic stopping criterion, where the MLLM assesses its confidence in answering a question for a given patch, adapting to varying search depths.
Results: ZoomEye consistently and substantially improved performance across various MLLMs, with InternVL2.5-8B showing increases of 15.71% on V*Bench and 16.25% on HR-Bench 8K.
Smaller MLLMs (e.g., Qwen2.5VL-3B with ZoomEye) outperformed GPT-4o on high-resolution benchmarks, achieving an overall score of 68.38% on HR-Bench 8K compared to GPT-4o's 55.5%.
ZoomEye demonstrated superior performance compared to existing high-resolution MLLM processing techniques (DC², VisCrop, Pixel Reasoner) without requiring specialized training or additional encoders.
Takeaways: The research identified a novel 'vision-level test-time scaling' phenomenon, demonstrating that MLLM performance consistently improves with an increased number of visual exploration steps.
The dynamic 'zoom' operation is critical for MLLM accuracy, with substantial performance gains observed when ZoomEye successfully localizes target objects.

By incorporating vision-level reasoning, smaller MLLMs (3B-8B parameters) can achieve performance comparable to, or even surpass, much larger closed-source models on complex, detail-oriented visual tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.15869.Title: Self-Calibrated CLIP for Training-Free Open-Vocabulary Segmentation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.15869.Summary: A training-free method named Self-Calibrated CLIP (SC-CLIP) improves open-vocabulary segmentation by resolving "anomaly tokens" and leveraging CLIP's intermediate features for enhanced semantic coherence. It achieves 43.9% mIoU on CLIP ViT-B/16, surpassing prior state-of-the-art by 9.5% without additional parameters or backbones.
Problem: CLIP's image-level pre-training emphasizes global context, causing it to neglect fine-grained local details crucial for dense prediction tasks like segmentation.
The emergence of "anomaly tokens" during CLIP's forward pass leads to uniform attention activations and feature homogenization, which degrades local spatial awareness.
Directly applying vanilla CLIP to open-vocabulary segmentation results in noisy outputs and significantly low performance, such as 14.4% mIoU on ViT-B/16.
Method: Identify and resolve "anomaly tokens" using the Local Outlier Factor (LOF) algorithm, replacing them with interpolated values from neighboring patches to regularize attention.

Implement a self-adjusting strategy that aggregates deep features using similarity maps derived from coherent mid-level features and enhances the last layer's attention with mid-level semantic consistency.
Apply a two-pass multi-level feature fusion strategy, processing summed multi-level features through the last layer's parameters to maintain compatibility and integrity without additional training.
Results: SC-CLIP achieved an average mIoU of 43.9% on CLIP ViT-B/16, surpassing previous state-of-the-art methods by 9.5%, and 45.2% mIoU on ViT-L/14, an improvement of 3.5%.
The method boosted vanilla CLIP's performance by threefold on ViT-B/16 and 6.8 times on ViT-L/14, significantly enhancing its latent potential for dense prediction tasks.
SC-CLIP reduced computational cost to 17.5G FLOPs and increased inference speed to 6.5 FPS, demonstrating superior efficiency compared to approaches using auxiliary backbones like DINO.
Takeaways: CLIP's image-level pre-training leads to the formation of "anomaly tokens" that hinder local spatial awareness by causing uniform attention distribution across features.

Despite poor last-layer spatial coherence, CLIP's mid-level features retain strong semantic consistency, comparable to specialized models like DINO, offering a reliable source for internal calibration.
Effective training-free multi-level feature fusion requires aligning features with the final layer's parameter space and preserving the integrity of the last layer's representation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.15594.Title: A Survey on LLM-as-a-Judge
https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.15594.Summary: Researchers present a comprehensive survey of the "LLM-as-a-Judge" paradigm, providing formal definitions, a unified framework, and an empirical meta-evaluation to assess the reliability of large language models in evaluative roles. The work identifies effective strategies and highlights persistent biases and the need for advanced benchmarks.
Problem: Traditional AI evaluation methods are either costly and inconsistent (human experts) or scalable but superficial (automatic metrics), struggling to balance depth, consistency, and scalability.
The emerging field of "LLM-as-a-Judge" lacks formal definitions, a unified understanding, and standardized practices, leading to fragmented research.

Concerns exist regarding the reliability of LLM evaluations, including inherent biases, susceptibility to adversarial attacks, and inconsistencies, which hinder their trustworthiness and widespread adoption.
Method: The paper establishes formal and contextualized definitions of LLM-as-a-Judge, including a specific definition for reliability, and presents a unified conceptual framework for the field.
Existing literature is systematically reorganized into a coherent framework addressing key questions (what it is, how to use, improve, and evaluate), with reliability as the central unifying theme.

An empirical meta-evaluation is conducted to compare the performance of various LLMs and improvement strategies on human alignment and different biases, alongside proposing a novel meta-evaluation benchmark.
Results: GPT-4-turbo generally outperforms other models across meta-evaluation dimensions (human alignment, various biases), though it still shows degradation in specific biases like Empty Reference and Nested Instruction Bias.
Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct emerges as a strong open-source alternative, often outperforming GPT-3.5-turbo in most metrics, highlighting its potential for robust LLM-as-a-Judge applications.

Multi-round majority voting (e.g., majority@5) significantly improves LLM-as-a-Judge performance and bias mitigation, whereas other aggregation methods like mean scoring or strategies like self-validation often yield minimal or negative effects.
Takeaways: Reliability is identified as the paramount challenge for LLM-as-a-Judge adoption, requiring deliberate design to ensure consistency, bias mitigation, and robustness.
GPT-4-turbo consistently exhibits superior performance in human alignment and demonstrates fewer biases compared to other models, positioning it as a current leading model for evaluation tasks.

The effectiveness of improvement strategies varies; multi-round majority voting significantly enhances reliability and mitigates biases, while 'providing evaluations with explanations' and 'self-validation' show limited or even negative impacts.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.14405.Title: Marco-o1: Towards Open Reasoning Models for Open-Ended Solutions
https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.14405.Summary: The Marco-o1 project from Alibaba International Digital Commerce explores a hybrid approach for Large Reasoning Models to address open-ended problem-solving. It demonstrates improved mathematical reasoning on MGSM datasets through a combination of Supervised Fine-Tuning, Monte Carlo Tree Search, and a reflection mechanism, and shows enhanced ability to translate nuanced colloquial language.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle to generalize advanced reasoning capabilities, exemplified by models like o1, from well-defined problems (e.g., math, coding with clear answers) to complex, open-ended real-world scenarios.
Developing robust Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) for tasks where clear standards are absent and rewards are challenging to quantify presents an unclear technical roadmap.
Existing machine translation tools often lack the ability to accurately translate colloquial expressions and slang, which require deeper contextual and cultural understanding.
Method: The base model, Qwen2-7B-Instruct, is fine-tuned using Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) with a curated dataset including filtered Open-O1 CoT, synthetically generated Marco-o1 CoT via MCTS, and instruction-following data.

Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) is integrated with the LLM, where nodes represent reasoning states and actions are LLM outputs; paths are evaluated by a confidence score based on token log probabilities.
A reflection mechanism is incorporated by prompting the model to self-critique and re-evaluate its reasoning, along with exploring different action granularities (step vs. mini-step) within the MCTS.
Results: Marco-o1-MCTS (step) achieved 90.40% accuracy on MGSM-En, a 6.4% improvement over Marco-o1-CoT, and Marco-o1-MCTS (mini-step) reached 82.40% on MGSM-Zh, an 11.2% improvement over Marco-o1-CoT.
The reflection mechanism helped solve about half of the difficult problems that the model initially failed, demonstrating its effectiveness in self-correction.

A qualitative case study showed Marco-o1 provided more accurate and natural translations of Chinese colloquialisms into English compared to Google Translate, excelling in understanding context and nuances.
Takeaways: Integrating Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) with Large Language Models effectively expands the solution space, increasing the probability of finding correct answers, particularly evident in improved Test@1 scores.
A self-reflection mechanism, which prompts the model to re-evaluate its reasoning, helps solve approximately half of previously failed challenging problems.

Applying Large Reasoning Models to machine translation, especially for colloquialisms and slang, shows promise in handling nuanced linguistic and cultural contexts, an area where traditional systems struggle.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.14402.Title: Multimodal Autoregressive Pre-training of Large Vision Encoders
https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.14402.Summary: Apple's AIMV2 introduces a pre-training method for large-scale vision encoders, combining autoregressive modeling with multimodal learning. This approach enables the model to achieve 89.5% ImageNet-1k accuracy with a frozen trunk and consistently outperforms state-of-the-art contrastive models like CLIP and SigLIP on multimodal understanding tasks.
Problem: Traditional discriminative vision pre-training methods, like contrastive learning, can be challenging to scale and implement effectively.
Generative pre-training methods, such as Masked Autoencoders, are simpler but often require larger models to achieve comparable performance.

There was a need for a pre-training approach that combined the scalability and simplicity of generative methods with the parameter efficiency of discriminative ones, while also supporting multimodal understanding for modern AI systems.
Method: AIMV2 utilizes a Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder with prefix attention, allowing bidirectional attention during inference without additional tuning.
A multimodal decoder generates both image patches and text tokens autoregressively, with the image always prepended to the text to achieve stronger conditioning on visual features.
The model is trained using a joint loss function, combining pixel-level regression for image patches and cross-entropy for text tokens, on a dataset of 12 billion image-text pairs.
Results: Achieved 89.5% accuracy on ImageNet-1k with a frozen trunk for image recognition.
Consistently outperformed state-of-the-art contrastive models like CLIP and SigLIP on multimodal image understanding tasks.
Surpassed DINOv2 on open-vocabulary object detection tasks and demonstrated strong performance in referring expression comprehension.
Takeaways: Combining autoregressive generation with multimodal learning allows AIMV2 to capture both visual and visual-linguistic representations effectively.
The use of prefix attention in the vision encoder enhances its ability to capture complex visual relationships and supports bidirectional attention during inference.

The image-level objective within the multimodal autoregressive pre-training consistently improves performance compared to captioning-only models, highlighting its importance for robust vision encoders.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.14251.Title: Natural Language Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.14251.Summary: The paper introduces Natural Language Reinforcement Learning (NLRL), a framework that redefines core reinforcement learning components like value functions and policies in natural language using large language models. This approach enables agents to gain a deeper, interpretable understanding of their experiences, demonstrating superior performance and more stable learning on multi-step tasks like maze navigation and board games compared to traditional and LLM-based baselines.
Problem: Traditional Reinforcement Learning (RL) relies on scalar value functions, which limit agents' deep, structural understanding of "why" certain actions are beneficial, only indicating "what" is good.
RL agents primarily learn passively through extensive environmental sampling, struggling to proactively adjust strategies via deliberative reasoning.
Applying traditional scalar reward optimization to Large Language Models (LLMs) can degrade their Chain-of-Thought reasoning capabilities.
Method: Introduces Natural Language Reinforcement Learning (NLRL), re-conceptualizing core RL components (value functions, policy, Bellman equation) directly in natural language.
Defines a Language Value Function (LVF) as an interpretable linguistic narrative explaining the rationale behind an evaluation, implemented by training Large Language Models (LLMs).

Leverages LLMs as language policy, language Monte Carlo/Temporal Difference operators for value estimation, and policy improvement operators for deliberative learning, all through unsupervised environment interaction and fine-tuning.
Results: Language Temporal Difference (TD) estimates produced better performance in maze navigation compared to prompt-based language value functions.
A trained Language Value Function (LVF) achieved over 0.85 evaluation accuracy in a 5x5 Breakthrough game, significantly outperforming prompting-based LLMs (~0.61) and demonstrating scalability.

Natural Language Actor-Critic learning achieved a ~0.9 win rate in Tic-tac-toe and showed superior performance and stability over prior LLM agent frameworks (e.g., RAGEN) in FrozenLake, while maintaining rigorous Chain-of-Thought reasoning.
Takeaways: Replacing scalar value functions with linguistic narratives enables agents to develop deeper, interpretable understanding and provide transparent reasoning for their decisions.
By verbalizing core RL components, agents can engage in active, deliberative learning, analyzing "root causes of success or failure" rather than relying solely on passive sampling.
Large Language Models can serve as effective foundational components for a language-native reinforcement learning system, facilitating both policy execution and value evaluation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.12591.Title: Thinking Before Looking: Improving Multimodal LLM Reasoning via Mitigating Visual Hallucination
https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.12591.Summary: This research introduces the Visual Inference Chain (VIC) framework, a "thinking before looking" paradigm for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) designed to mitigate visual hallucination. The VIC framework consistently improves zero-shot performance across various vision-related tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness in refining MLLM reasoning capabilities, with average hallucination reduction of 15.62% on MMVP and general capability improvements of 9.13% on MME.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are prone to visual hallucination (generating non-existent objects, misinterpreting visual information) during complex reasoning tasks.

Current multimodal Chain-of-Thought (MMCoT) approaches, operating under a "thinking while looking" paradigm, foster cross-modal biases and stereotypical reasoning due to simultaneous visual and textual processing.
Hallucinations undermine the reliability and accuracy of MLLM reasoning, hindering their practical application in critical scenarios.
Method: The Visual Inference Chain (VIC) framework introduces a "thinking before looking" paradigm, decoupling visual and textual inputs through a three-stage process.
VIC Generation involves a language model creating a sequence of "visual inference steps" (a reasoning chain) solely from the textual question before any image is processed.

VIC Rationale Extraction uses an MLLM to interact with the image, but its attention is guided by the pre-generated inference steps to extract relevant visual rationales; Answer Inference then synthesizes information with a reflection prompt to ensure coherence and correctness.
Results: VIC consistently improved performance on hallucination detection benchmarks, reducing hallucinations by an average of 15.62% on MMVP and showing notable gains on HallusionBench and POPE adversarial samples.
The framework enhanced general multimodal capabilities, improving MME performance by an average of 9.13% and SEED-Bench scores across most subtasks, particularly for complex reasoning.

VIC demonstrated strong effectiveness with closed-source models (GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Pro/Flash) but showed performance declines with open-source models like Qwen-VL Plus, indicating current limitations of open-source models in handling multi-modal long-context processing.
Takeaways: Decoupling reasoning from immediate visual input, as in the "thinking before looking" paradigm, reduces cross-modal biases and stereotypical reasoning in MLLMs.
A multi-stage process involving preliminary textual reasoning, guided visual rationale extraction, and a final reflective inference significantly mitigates visual hallucination.
Including a reflection step in the final answer generation helps MLLMs reconsider and re-evaluate extracted rationales, leading to more robust and accurate responses.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.11930.Title: AtomThink: Multimodal Slow Thinking with Atomic Step Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.11930.Summary: AtomThink introduces a framework for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) that employs Self-structured Chain-of-Thought (SCoT) reasoning, enabling adaptive adjustment of reasoning depth and structure based on problem complexity. This approach yields an average accuracy improvement exceeding 10% on mathematical reasoning benchmarks and reduces inference time by 85.3% compared to baselines.
Problem: Existing Chain-of-Thought (CoT) methods for MLLMs are either too rigid with fixed templates (structured CoT) or inefficient and prone to 'overthinking' (unstructured CoT).
Structured CoT approaches limit reasoning diversity and generalization across varied multimodal tasks due to predefined structures.
Unstructured CoT often consumes excessive tokens and computational resources by generating unnecessarily long reasoning chains for simpler problems.
Method: A Self-structured Chain-of-Thought (SCoT) paradigm that decomposes complex reasoning into minimal 'atomic steps', allowing MLLMs to dynamically generate and adapt the length and structure of reasoning paths.
Development of the AMATH data engine, a high-quality multimodal long CoT dataset, generated through dynamic prompting and rigorous filtering, to supervise granular, step-by-step reasoning.

Implementation of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) for atomic step learning and policy-guided inference with a Process Reward Model (PRM) to search for optimal reasoning paths during multi-turn inference.
Results: AtomThink achieved an average accuracy improvement of over 10% (up to 16.6% with PRM) on mathematical reasoning benchmarks and outperformed GPT-4V by 8.5% on MathVista and 3.2% on WeMath.
The framework demonstrated strong cross-domain generalization, showing gains of +25.3% on ChartQA, +12.2% on TextVQA, and +20.2% on ScienceQA, despite its mathematical-centric training.
AtomThink significantly improved resource efficiency, with 5 times higher data utilization and reductions of 87.8% in output tokens and 85.3% in inference time per sample in SCoT mode.
Takeaways: Decomposing reasoning into 'atomic steps' enables MLLMs to dynamically scale their 'slow thinking' depth according to problem difficulty, leading to both efficiency and higher accuracy.

Training on a high-quality, fine-grained multimodal CoT dataset, even if primarily mathematical, fosters robust reasoning skills that generalize effectively to diverse domains like scientific and general visual question answering.
Policy-guided search mechanisms, such as beam search, can further refine the generated reasoning paths, enhancing performance while maintaining significant improvements in inference efficiency.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.10442.Title: Enhancing the Reasoning Ability of Multimodal Large Language Models via Mixed Preference Optimization
https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.10442.Summary: Researchers introduced Mixed Preference Optimization (MPO) and a scalable automated pipeline for constructing multimodal reasoning preference data (MMPR) to improve the complex reasoning abilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). The approach enabled InternVL2-8B-MPO to achieve 67.0% accuracy on MathVista, an 8.7-point gain, making its performance comparable to a 10 times larger model, and established new state-of-the-art results on MathVision.
Problem: Current open-source Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) exhibit substantial limitations in complex multimodal reasoning tasks, especially with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting.
The supervised fine-tuning (SFT) paradigm for MLLMs suffers from a "distribution shift" during CoT inference, often leading to performance degradation compared to direct answers.
A critical scarcity exists in high-quality, large-scale multimodal reasoning preference datasets, which are essential for advanced alignment techniques like Preference Optimization.
Method: Developed Mixed Preference Optimization (MPO), an algorithm that combines DPO (preference), BCO (quality), and SFT (generation) losses to effectively train MLLMs for enhanced reasoning.

Created a scalable automated pipeline for constructing the MultiModal PReference dataset (MMPR), comprising approximately 3 million samples, including a novel Dropout Next-Token Prediction (DropoutNTP) method for efficient negative sample generation.

Integrated specialized Chain-of-Thought (CoT) methods, such as background knowledge-based or visual content-based CoT, directly into the data generation process to ensure effective multimodal input integration into reasoning.
Results: MPO-trained InternVL2-8B-MPO achieved 67.0% accuracy on MathVista, an 8.7-point improvement over its baseline, demonstrating performance comparable to the 10 times larger InternVL2-76B.
InternVL2-76B-MPO set a new state-of-the-art on the MathVision benchmark with 30.6% accuracy and showed substantial gains across various other multimodal reasoning benchmarks.

The MPO approach consistently and significantly outperformed standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) for reasoning tasks, effectively mitigating the detrimental CoT performance degradation observed in SFT-only models.
Takeaways: Preference Optimization (PO) techniques, when thoughtfully adapted, can fundamentally strengthen multimodal reasoning and Chain-of-Thought capabilities in MLLMs beyond just mitigating hallucinations.

An automated and efficient data generation pipeline like DropoutNTP can overcome the significant bottleneck of scarce multimodal reasoning preference data, making advanced MLLM alignment more feasible and cost-effective.

A mixed objective function, MPO, which strategically combines preference, quality, and generative losses, is crucial for simultaneously achieving accurate reasoning alignment and maintaining generative fluency in MLLMs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.10440.Title: LLaVA-CoT: Let Vision Language Models Reason Step-by-Step
https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.10440.Summary: LLaVA-CoT, from a collaboration including Peking University and Tsinghua University, introduces a Vision-Language Model capable of autonomous multistage reasoning, enhanced by a novel test-time self-correction mechanism named Stage-wise Retracing Search (SWIRES). It improves reasoning-intensive tasks by 5.8% over its base model and demonstrates competitive performance against larger multimodal models.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) struggle with systematic and structured reasoning for complex visual question-answering (VQA) tasks, unlike Large Language Models (LLMs).

Existing VLM Chain-of-Thought (CoT) implementations frequently produce errors, inconsistencies, or hallucinations because their reasoning processes are often not sufficiently systematic or structured.
VLMs tend to initiate responses without proper problem organization, deviate from logical paths, or prematurely state conclusions, leading to flawed reasoning trajectories.
Method: The model employs an autonomous multistage reasoning approach, decomposing answer generation into four distinct, explicitly tagged stages: Summary, Caption, Reasoning, and Conclusion.

A specialized LLaVA-CoT-100k dataset was created using GPT-4o to generate detailed, structured reasoning annotations for a diverse set of VQA pairs, then used for supervised fine-tuning of the Llama-3.2-11B-Vision-Instruct model.

Stage-wise Retracing Search (SWIRES), a novel test-time scaling method, dynamically assesses the quality of intermediate reasoning steps and can "retrace" to earlier stages to regenerate better outputs, enhancing self-correction during inference.
Results: LLaVA-CoT achieved a 5.8% average benchmark score increase over its Llama-3.2-11B-Vision-Instruct base model across six multimodal reasoning benchmarks.

Ablation studies confirmed that both the multistage format and explicit structured tags within the LLaVA-CoT-100k dataset are essential for the observed performance gains in reasoning-intensive tasks.

SWIRES consistently outperformed other test-time scaling strategies, exhibiting a stronger scaling effect with increased computation and enabling the 11B LLaVA-CoT to achieve competitive performance against larger and closed-source state-of-the-art multimodal models.
Takeaways: Explicitly structured reasoning, guided by distinct stages and tags, is crucial for imbuing VLMs with systematic, in-depth thinking abilities.
A high-quality, multistage reasoning dataset (LLaVA-CoT-100k) is essential for training VLMs to adopt and effectively utilize structured thought processes.

Dynamic, stage-aligned self-correction during inference, as implemented by SWIRES, significantly improves VLM robustness and accuracy by recovering from suboptimal intermediate steps, outperforming traditional test-time scaling methods.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.10231.Title: A Low-Resolution Image is Worth 1x1 Words: Enabling Fine Image Super-Resolution with Transformers and TaylorShift
https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.10231.Summary: Researchers from DFKI and the University of Kaiserslautern-Landau developed TaylorIR, an approach for transformer-based image super-resolution that combines 1x1 pixel-wise patch embeddings with the efficient TaylorShift attention mechanism. This method enables fine-grained image enhancement while reducing memory consumption by up to 60% compared to existing state-of-the-art transformer models, achieving competitive or superior reconstruction quality.
Problem: Transformer-based image super-resolution models achieve high performance but suffer from high computational costs and substantial memory requirements due to the quadratic complexity of self-attention.
Existing workarounds like restricted window sizes or larger patch sizes (e.g., 4x4) compromise the model's ability to capture fine details and long-range dependencies.
The prohibitive memory and computational demands limit the practical application and deployment of advanced transformer-based SR models, especially on resource-constrained devices.
Method: Introduces TaylorIR, a novel approach for transformer-based image super-resolution that enables pixel-level processing and reduces computational load.
Utilizes 1x1 pixel-wise patch embeddings to treat each pixel as an independent entity, allowing for precise, individualized feature extraction across the entire image.

Implements TaylorShift, an efficient attention mechanism based on Taylor series expansion, which approximates full self-attention with linear computational complexity, significantly reducing memory requirements.
Results: TaylorSwinIR achieves competitive or superior PSNR and SSIM scores compared to the original SwinIR across multiple scaling factors (x2, x3, x4) on benchmark datasets.
The method reduces memory consumption by up to 60% (e.g., from 11.7 GB to 4.87 GB) compared to standard SwinIR with similar performance, making it more practical for deployment.
Qualitative comparisons indicate TaylorSwinIR produces sharper and more detailed results, particularly in areas with complex textures and fine structures, due to pixel-level processing.
Takeaways: Approximating self-attention using Taylor series expansion (TaylorShift) reduces computational complexity from quadratic to linear, enabling processing of longer sequences efficiently.
Using 1 A pixel-wise (1x1) patch embedding allows for fine-grained feature extraction, which is crucial for recovering intricate image details in super-resolution.

Combining linear-complexity attention with pixel-wise embeddings enables the use of significantly larger contextual windows (e.g., 48x48) without prohibitive memory costs, improving the model's ability to capture long-range dependencies.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.09691.Title: Advancing Fine-Grained Visual Understanding with Multi-Scale Alignment in Multi-Modal Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.09691.Summary: TinyGroundingGPT introduces a series of compact Multi-Modal Large Language Models that enhance fine-grained visual understanding by implementing a comprehensive multi-scale alignment method and a specialized data synthesis pipeline. These models achieve competitive performance on grounding benchmarks and reduce object hallucination while maintaining a small parameter footprint.
Problem: Existing Multi-Modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle with fine-grained visual understanding, specifically precisely comprehending and aligning local details within images.
MLLMs often handle only a subset of possible modality alignments (coordinates, text, images), leading to incomplete visual information integration.
Challenges include effectively integrating different modalities, capturing precise local visual details, and mitigating object hallucination.
Method: Introduces TinyGroundingGPT, a series of compact MLLMs (1.5B and 3B parameters) built on Qwen2.5 with multi-scale vision encoders.

Implements a three-stage training methodology that progressively builds fine-grained visual understanding through object and relation perception, multi-scale local knowledge alignment across all modality pairs, and detailed global knowledge alignment.

Develops a multi-scale fine-grained enhancement data synthesis pipeline to generate over 300,000 high-quality training samples, including object recognition, grounding, relationship extraction, and QA generation.
Results: TinyGroundingGPT models achieve strong performance on standard grounding benchmarks, with the 3B parameter model reaching state-of-the-art results among models of comparable size.
The models exhibit a reduced tendency toward object hallucination and maintain competitive performance on general image understanding benchmarks.
Attention map visualizations confirm more precise attention distributions on relevant regions, and coordinate-enhanced queries lead to higher confidence predictions.
Takeaways: Comprehensive alignment of all six modality pairs (coordinates-to-text, coordinates-to-image, text-to-coordinates, text-to-image, image-to-text, image-to-coordinates) is essential for robust fine-grained visual understanding.
A systematic data synthesis pipeline can generate high-quality, multi-scale fine-grained training data, which is critical for learning precise visual grounding.

Compact Multi-Modal Large Language Models (1.5B-3B parameters) can achieve competitive performance with much larger models by focusing on improved alignment methods and targeted data rather than just increasing model scale.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.04997.Title: LLM2CLIP: Powerful Language Model Unlocks Richer Visual Representation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.04997.Summary: The LLM2CLIP framework integrates large language models (LLMs) with pre-trained CLIP models, employing a two-stage post-training strategy to unlock richer visual representations. This approach achieves superior performance in zero-shot English and cross-lingual text-image retrieval, yielding gains of up to +15.8 points over EVA02 on long-text benchmarks and enhancing multimodal large language models.
Problem: CLIP's text encoder is limited in processing long, complex, or dense image captions, hindering its ability to fully leverage advanced language understanding for visual representation.

Large Language Models (LLMs), despite their superior language comprehension and open-world knowledge, do not naturally produce discriminative text embeddings suitable for CLIP's contrastive learning objectives.
Existing multimodal frameworks struggle to effectively translate LLMs' advanced linguistic capabilities into corresponding improvements for visual representation learning.
Method: A two-stage post-training strategy is introduced: first, LLM Caption Contrastive (CC) fine-tuning to make LLMs discriminative encoders, and second, LLM2CLIP post fine-tuning.
Stage 1 modifies LLMs with bidirectional attention and LoRA, fine-tuning them via textual contrastive learning (Supervised SimCSE) on augmented caption datasets to improve feature separability.
Stage 2 integrates the discriminative LLM (with a linear adaptor and frozen gradients for efficiency) as a rich supervisor to post-train the CLIP visual encoder, leveraging dense captions.
Results: The Caption Contrastive fine-tuning increased LLama 3 8B's caption-to-caption retrieval accuracy from 5.2% to 29.5%, confirming its role in enabling discriminative text encoding.

LLM2CLIP achieved superior zero-shot text-image retrieval performance, demonstrating gains of up to +15.8 points over EVA02 on long-text benchmarks and consistent improvements over SigLip2 on both English and cross-lingual datasets.
Integration into the Llava 1.5 framework enhanced multimodal model performance on over 87.5% of VQA and other multimodal benchmarks, indicating improved visual features for complex reasoning.
Takeaways: Large Language Models (LLMs) inherently lack discriminative feature separability for contrastive learning, but targeted Caption Contrastive fine-tuning can overcome this limitation, transforming them into effective text encoders for multimodal tasks.
Efficiently integrating a discriminative LLM as a supervisor allows CLIP's visual encoder to learn richer, more semantically nuanced visual representations from complex and dense captions.

Strategic gradient freezing, adaptor utilization, and offline feature precomputation during post-training enable a highly efficient integration of LLMs, drastically reducing computational demands for enhancing existing vision-language models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.04983.Title: DINO-WM: World Models on Pre-trained Visual Features enable Zero-shot Planning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.04983.Summary: Researchers at NYU and Meta AI introduce DINO-WM, a task-agnostic world model that leverages frozen DINOv2 pre-trained visual features to enable zero-shot planning. The model demonstrates high-quality future state predictions and superior planning success rates across diverse robotic manipulation and navigation tasks from offline data.
Problem: Current robotics and embodied AI systems struggle with generalization, as feed-forward policies often require extensive prior exposure to diverse scenarios and lack runtime adaptability.

Existing world models are either online, requiring continuous interaction and retraining, or offline but reliant on strong auxiliary information (rewards, expert demonstrations) which limits their generality.
Developing a world model that can be trained efficiently on offline data and support flexible, task-agnostic behavior optimization at test time remains a challenge.
Method: DINO-WM utilizes a frozen, pre-trained DINOv2 model as its observation encoder, converting raw RGB images into compact, spatially rich patch embeddings.

A Vision Transformer (ViT) acts as a transition model, predicting future DINOv2 latent states based on past latent states and actions, trained with a latent consistency loss without pixel reconstruction.

Zero-shot planning is performed at test time using Model Predictive Control (MPC) with the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) to optimize action sequences that minimize the distance between predicted and goal latent states.
Results: DINO-WM produces superior future world predictions, showing up to a 56% improvement in LPIPS scores (e.g., 0.007 on PushT) compared to prior state-of-the-art models.

It achieves high success rates for zero-shot planning in diverse environments, outperforming prior work in manipulation tasks by an average of 45% (e.g., 0.90 success rate on PushT vs. 0.32 for IRIS).

The model demonstrates promising generalization to novel environment configurations within task families (e.g., 0.82 SR in WallRandom, 0.63 Chamfer Distance in GranularRandom), indicating learned general concepts.
Takeaways: Pre-trained, general-purpose visual features (like DINOv2 patch embeddings) are essential for building robust and consistent world models, especially in complex manipulation tasks.

Decoupling the world model's dynamics learning from pixel-level reconstruction via latent space prediction improves performance and computational efficiency, while still enabling high-fidelity rollouts for planning.
A truly task-agnostic world model trained on offline data can enable effective zero-shot planning for arbitrary visual goals, without needing task-specific rewards or expert demonstrations.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.04109.Title: Self-Consistency Preference Optimization
https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.04109.Summary: Self-Consistency Preference Optimization (SCPO) is an iterative, unsupervised method that enhances large language models' performance on complex reasoning tasks by creating preference data from consistent model-generated answers. This approach achieves results comparable to supervised training and empowers smaller models, like Llama-3 8B, to surpass larger counterparts on challenging benchmarks such as ZebraLogic.
Problem: Large language model (LLM) training for complex reasoning tasks heavily relies on costly and time-consuming human annotation for ground truth and preference data.
Existing self-training methods often struggle with reliably evaluating the correctness of complex reasoning outputs generated by LLMs themselves.
External reward models can suffer from limitations when encountering out-of-distribution problems or requiring specialized training for specific reasoning tasks.
Method: SCPO iteratively trains LLMs by generating diverse responses for problems and constructing preference pairs based on a "vote function" that measures the consistency of final answers across samples.

It introduces a novel weighted loss function that incorporates the "vote margin" between chosen (most consistent) and rejected (least consistent) responses, emphasizing more confident preference signals.
The method includes a problem generation step, where the model itself creates new reasoning problems to scale the training data, filtered for answerability by self-consistency.
Results: Unsupervised SCPO significantly outperforms other unsupervised baselines on GSM8K (22.74% greedy gain over seed) and MATH (5.26% gain), achieving performance nearly on par with gold-label supervised methods.
A SCPO-trained Llama-3 8B model achieves higher accuracy on the complex ZebraLogic benchmark than Llama-3 Instruct 70B, Gemma-2 27B, and Claude-3 Haiku by up to 3.8%.
Semi-supervised SCPO, combining self-generated preferences with available human-labeled data, further boosts performance beyond purely supervised approaches on both GSM8K and MATH.
Takeaways: Self-consistency, traditionally an inference-time technique, serves as a robust and scalable unsupervised signal for correctness that effectively guides LLM training for reasoning tasks.
Iterative application of SCPO consistently improves the model's accuracy and internal consistency, indicating that models learn to produce more reliable single-sample outputs.
The instance-level weighting of the SCPO loss, based on the confidence derived from vote margins, is critical for effectively learning from self-generated preference data.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.21676.Title: How Does Critical Batch Size Scale in Pre-training?
https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.21676.Summary: This study establishes that the critical batch size (CBS) in large language model pre-training scales primarily with the total training data size, not the model's parameter count. It introduces and validates Exponential Weight Averaging (EWA) for efficient, target-loss-driven training and offers theoretical explanations for the observed scaling behaviors.
Problem: The precise scaling behavior of the critical batch size (CBS) in large language model pre-training, specifically its relationship with model and data sizes, was not fully understood.
Previous scaling law studies often scaled model and data sizes jointly, making it difficult to ascertain their independent impact on optimization efficiency.
Traditional fixed-duration training protocols limit flexibility and efficient exploration of optimal training strategies, especially when aiming for a target performance level.
Method: Researchers precisely defined CBS as the batch size incurring 20% overhead in steps to reach a target validation loss relative to linear scaling from an optimal small batch size.
Controlled experiments systematically decoupled the effects of model size and data size on CBS, by holding one constant while varying the other.
Exponential Weight Averaging (EWA) was proposed and evaluated as a training strategy to flexibly reach target validation losses without predefined training durations or learning rate schedules.
Results: Empirically, CBS scaled as approximately D^0.47 with data size (D) when model size was fixed, but only as N^0.087 with model size (N) when data size was fixed, demonstrating its primary dependence on data.
The 'Constant+EWA' strategy matched or exceeded the performance of cosine learning rate scheduling, providing comparable or improved training efficiency across various batch sizes.

Theoretical analysis, leveraging infinite-width neural network limits and mini-batch SGD in linear regression, substantiated the empirical findings that CBS grows with data size but is invariant to model size in certain regimes.
Takeaways: The critical batch size primarily scales with the amount of training data, showing a weak dependence on model size when data is held constant.

Exponential Weight Averaging (EWA) is an effective and flexible alternative to traditional learning rate schedules, particularly beneficial for large-batch and long-duration training by enabling target-loss-driven convergence.
Optimal Adam optimizer hyper-parameters (e.g., beta_2) are highly sensitive to training duration and batch size, requiring careful tuning beyond default values for peak efficiency.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.20722.Title: Interpretable Image Classification with Adaptive Prototype-based Vision Transformers
https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.20722.Summary: ProtoViT, developed by researchers from Dartmouth College, Duke University, and the University of Maine, integrates Vision Transformers with prototype-based reasoning to create an interpretable image classification model. It achieves superior classification accuracy while providing transparent, human-understandable explanations for its decisions by showing which parts of an input image are similar to learned prototypes.
Problem: Existing interpretable models, particularly prototype-based ones, often relied on less powerful CNN backbones, limiting their performance compared to modern Vision Transformers (ViTs).

Many prototype models suffered from limitations like spatially rigid prototypes, lack of semantic coherence in learned features, or failing to provide truly interpretable explanations when combined with ViTs.
The need for AI systems in high-stakes domains to not only be accurate but also to clearly explain their decision-making process in human-understandable terms.
Method: ProtoViT integrates a pre-trained Vision Transformer as a feature encoder with a novel Greedy Matching Layer and an Evidence Layer for classification.

The Greedy Matching Layer incorporates a greedy matching algorithm with adjacency masking to ensure contiguous and non-redundant sub-prototypes, and an adaptive slots mechanism for flexible prototype complexity.
A four-stage training process optimizes for classification accuracy, prototype coherence, and sparsity, critically including prototype projection to real training image patches for interpretability.
Results: ProtoViT achieved 86.5% accuracy on the CUB-200-2011 dataset, outperforming previous prototype-based models like ProtoPNet (84.8%) and other ViT-based approaches.
The model demonstrated at least equivalent robustness to CNN-based prototype models against adversarial attacks in the Location Misalignment Benchmark.

A user study indicated that ProtoViT provided clearer explanations and more coherent prototypical features compared to ProtoPNet and Deformable ProtoPNet, with participants rating its explanations as more understandable.
Takeaways: Combining Vision Transformers with prototype-based reasoning can yield models that are both high-performing and inherently interpretable.

Enforcing geometric coherence and allowing adaptive prototype complexity through techniques like greedy matching with adjacency masking and adaptive slots leads to more semantically meaningful and understandable prototypes.
A multi-stage training process, including prototype projection to real image patches, is crucial for ensuring that learned prototypes are directly human-inspectable and meaningful.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.19925.Title: Improving Multimodal Large Language Models Using Continual Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.19925.Summary: A study from the University of Rochester and Rochester Institute of Technology systematically quantified linguistic forgetting in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) during their adaptation and sequential acquisition of vision-language tasks. The work demonstrated that integrating continual learning techniques, such as Soft Targets and mSGM with Rehearsal, effectively preserves unimodal language abilities while sustaining or improving multimodal performance.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) often experience catastrophic forgetting of their core natural language understanding (NLU) and generation (NLG) capabilities when adapted to multimodal contexts.
The degradation of linguistic abilities is particularly pronounced in smaller MLLMs, with NLG tasks being more susceptible to forgetting than NLU tasks.
Current MLLM training paradigms frequently force a trade-off between acquiring multimodal skills and retaining fundamental linguistic knowledge, hindering their versatility.
Method: The researchers systematically analyzed linguistic forgetting across 9 diverse LLMs (including Pythia, Phi2, LLaMA 2 variants) adapted into the LLaVA 1.5 multimodal architecture.
Five established continual learning (CL) methods (LoRA, Soft Targets, Rehearsal, mSGM, mSGM + Rehearsal) were evaluated against naive fine-tuning to mitigate linguistic forgetting.

Experiments were conducted in two settings: reducing forgetting during initial LLaVA 1.5 adaptation and enabling sequential learning of multiple vision-language tasks without sacrificing prior knowledge.
Results: Soft Targets emerged as the most effective method for smaller models (e.g., Pythia 160M), achieving high vision-language accuracy with minimal linguistic forgetting and occasionally positive backward transfer.

In sequential multimodal learning scenarios, mSGM + Rehearsal consistently achieved the least linguistic forgetting, preserving NLU/NLG performance while maintaining or exceeding naive fine-tuning's multimodal performance across model scales.

While naive fine-tuning led to a consistent and severe drop in NLU/NLG performance when scaled, mSGM + Rehearsal showed little to no NLU/NLG forgetting, even achieving positive backward transfer for the Pythia 1B model.
Takeaways: Linguistic forgetting is significantly more severe for Natural Language Generation (NLG) tasks compared to Natural Language Understanding (NLU) tasks in MLLMs, especially for smaller models.

Instruction-tuned LLMs demonstrate increased resilience to linguistic forgetting during multimodal adaptation, potentially due to the distributional alignment between text-only and visual-instruction tuning.

Continual learning methods, notably Soft Targets and mSGM combined with Rehearsal, effectively prevent linguistic forgetting and can even induce positive backward transfer, enhancing language skills during multimodal training.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.19878.Title: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning in Large Models: A Survey of Methodologies
https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.19878.Summary: This survey paper from Zhejiang Laboratory systematically classifies over 100 Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methodologies, expanding the taxonomy to six categories beyond traditional NLP to include computer vision, multimodal, and diffusion models. It details how these methods significantly reduce computational costs and parameter counts for adapting large models while maintaining performance.
Problem: Large language models (LLMs) and other large models have billions to trillions of parameters, requiring immense computational resources and memory for fine-tuning.
The high resource intensity of full fine-tuning creates barriers to entry for many researchers and practitioners and limits rapid experimentation.
Existing PEFT surveys often focus predominantly on NLP applications or use limited classification systems, making it challenging to navigate the rapidly evolving landscape across diverse AI domains.
Method: The survey introduces a comprehensive and unified taxonomy for PEFT methods, categorizing them into six types: Additive, Reparameterized, Selective, Hybrid, Quantization, and Multi-task PEFT.
It provides detailed explanations of core principles and mathematical formulations for over 100 PEFT algorithms, enhancing understanding and accessibility.
The work broadens the scope of PEFT applications beyond NLP, extensively covering its use in computer vision, diffusion models, and multimodal fusion.
Results: The survey presents a unified classification system for PEFT methods, including new categories like Hybrid, Quantization, and Multi-task PEFT, and details representative algorithms for each.
It provides a comprehensive overview of PEFT applications in vision models, diffusion models, and multimodal large language models, showcasing their practical advantages.
The work identifies seven promising future research directions, including PEFT for multi-objective tasks, multimodal learning, automated PEFT design, and integration of differential privacy.
Takeaways: PEFT methods effectively reduce trainable parameters to less than 1-2% of the total, drastically cutting computational and memory costs for adapting large models.
The utility of PEFT extends across diverse AI modalities, enabling efficient fine-tuning for tasks in computer vision, diffusion model generation, and multimodal learning.
Hybrid PEFT and Quantization PEFT represent emerging trends, combining different efficiency techniques to further enhance performance or reduce resource requirements.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17517.Title: The Hive Mind is a Single Reinforcement Learning Agent
https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17517.Summary: This research introduces a theoretical framework that formally equates collective decision-making in biological and social systems, specifically honey bee swarms, with single-agent reinforcement learning. It presents Maynard-Cross Learning (MCL) as a new multi-armed bandit algorithm whose dynamics match the collective behavior of a "hive mind," demonstrating how groups achieve efficient learning through simple imitation rules.
Problem: Lack of a formal, mathematical framework to precisely describe the phenomenon of "emergence" in swarm intelligence and collective decision-making.
Understanding how simple individual behaviors in natural collective systems can lead to sophisticated and optimal group-level intelligence.
Bridging the theoretical gap between individual-centric reinforcement learning algorithms and population-level dynamics found in evolutionary game theory and swarm intelligence.
Method: The authors establish a formal equivalence between established models of "imitation of success" from Evolutionary Game Theory (EGT) and existing Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms like Cross Learning (CL).

They introduce Maynard-Cross Learning (MCL), a new multi-armed bandit RL algorithm, and formally prove its mathematical equivalence to the "weighted voter model" that describes honey bee collective decision-making.

Computational simulations are employed to validate the theoretical derivations, explore the efficiency of parallel collective learning, and investigate the evolutionary rationale behind simple imitation rules.
Results: The paper formally demonstrated that "imitation of success" dynamics (EGT) are equivalent to Cross Learning (RL) and that the "weighted voter model" (e.g., honey bees) is equivalent to a new RL algorithm, Maynard-Cross Learning (MCL).

Simulations showed that the collective R_wvoter (MCL) mechanism converges significantly faster to optimal decisions compared to individual learning, with populations of around 500 individuals closely following theoretical dynamics.

The "promoting" aspect of the weighted voter model (R_wvoter) was found to offer a speed advantage over simple "imitation of success" (R_success), especially for low or middle reward qualities, confirming its efficiency in collective exploration.
Takeaways: Collective decision-making through imitation can be formally reinterpreted as the behavior of a single, abstract reinforcement learning agent operating at the group level.
Natural collective systems inherently provide a highly efficient form of parallel RL, where each individual acts as an independent action sample for the group's macro-agent, accelerating learning.

Evolution may favor seemingly simple and "blind" imitation rules, like the weighted voter model, because they achieve robust collective reinforcement learning with minimal individual cognitive demands, trading some convergence speed for simplicity and robustness.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17385.Title: Do Vision-Language Models Represent Space and How? Evaluating Spatial Frame of Reference Under Ambiguities
https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17385.Summary: A new evaluation protocol assesses Vision-Language Models' spatial understanding, revealing that current models predominantly rely on English-centric egocentric perspectives for spatial reasoning and lack robustness and flexibility in adopting alternative Frames of Reference.
Problem: Existing VLM benchmarks for spatial reasoning largely overlook the inherent ambiguities in spatial expressions related to Frames of Reference (FoR).
Current evaluations lack measures for spatial continuity, robustness, and consistency, treating spatial relations as fixed ground truths.
VLMs need to align with the nuanced, ambiguous, and culturally diverse nature of human spatial cognition to truly exhibit human-like intelligence.
Method: The COMFORT (COnsistent Multilingual F rame O f Reference Test) protocol uses synthetic 3D scenes with controllable spatial relations and perspectives to simulate continuous spatial environments.
It employs binary questions with explicit or implicit perspective prompts, translated into 109 languages, to test different Frames of Reference (FoR) and cross-lingual understanding.

Novel metrics are introduced, including Region Parsing Error (ε), Robustness (Standard Deviation, Prediction Noise), and Consistency (Spatial Symmetric, Spatial Opposite), to evaluate fine-grained VLM behavior.
Results: Most evaluated VLMs exhibit a preference for the reflected coordinate transformation and an egocentric relative Frame of Reference, aligning with English linguistic conventions.

VLMs significantly struggle to adopt alternative Frames of Reference (intrinsic, addressee-centered) when explicitly prompted, often performing near chance levels, indicating inflexibility in perspective-taking.

Models generally show a lack of robustness and consistency in their spatial representations, with high variability under minor visual changes and poor adherence to geometric principles; cross-lingual evaluation also indicates an English-centric bias.
Takeaways: Spatial language in situated communication is inherently ambiguous, with meanings varying based on the adopted Frame of Reference (FoR) and cultural conventions.
Current VLM evaluations often overlook these fundamental ambiguities, focusing on fixed spatial relations rather than the flexibility and consistency required for human-like spatial cognition.
Cross-cultural analysis is essential as human conventions for resolving spatial ambiguities are not uniform across languages, potentially revealing biases in multilingual VLMs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.16512.Title: TIPS: Text-Image Pretraining with Spatial awareness
https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.16512.Summary: Google DeepMind's TIPS model creates general-purpose image representations by unifying image-text and self-supervised learning, producing features competitive with DINOv2 for dense understanding while maintaining strong performance on global and multimodal vision-language tasks. This is achieved through a dual embedding mechanism for both synthetic and noisy captions, combined with self-distillation and masked image modeling.
Problem: Current weakly-supervised image-text models (e.g., CLIP) excel at global semantic understanding but lack fine-grained spatial awareness for dense pixel-level tasks.
Self-supervised image-only models (e.g., DINOv2) produce strong spatially coherent features but are limited to vision-only applications as they cannot directly interpret text.
Noisy web-scraped image captions, typically used for weak supervision, often lack the detailed spatial and background information needed for learning rich, spatially-aware representations.
Method: Leverages an off-the-shelf multimodal generative model (PaliGemma) to create high-quality, spatially rich synthetic captions to augment or replace noisy web captions.
Introduces a dual embedding mechanism in the Vision Transformer (ViT) image encoder, training one global embedding with noisy web captions and a second with synthetic captions via InfoNCE losses.

Integrates self-distillation, by aligning local student crop embeddings with a global teacher embedding, and Masked Image Modeling (MIM), by reconstructing masked patch tokens, into the image-text pre-training objective.
Results: TIPS-g/14 achieves competitive performance with DINOv2-g/14 on various dense prediction tasks (e.g., 49.9 mIoU on ADE20k segmentation, 0.353 RMSE on NYUv2 depth), notably surpassing other image-text models.
The model maintains strong or competitive performance across multimodal retrieval (e.g., 93.0% R@1 for I→T retrieval on Flickr) and zero-shot image classification benchmarks.

TIPS features improve performance in downstream applications such as single-image to 3D reconstruction, leading to higher novel view synthesis quality (21.75 PSNR) compared to DINO-B/16 features (21.13 PSNR).
Takeaways: Enriching noisy web captions with high-quality, synthetically generated descriptions significantly improves a model's spatial awareness without compromising global understanding.
A dual embedding mechanism for image-text models effectively leverages both object-centric, discriminative information from noisy captions and detailed spatial information from synthetic captions.

The combination of self-distillation and Masked Image Modeling (MIM) within an image-text pre-training framework synergistically boosts the spatial coherence and robustness of learned visual features.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.16400.Title: VipAct: Visual-Perception Enhancement via Specialized VLM Agent Collaboration and Tool-use
https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.16400.Summary: The VipAct framework enhances fine-grained visual perception in large multimodal models (VLMs) by orchestrating specialized VLM agents and integrating high-precision vision expert models. This approach achieved state-of-the-art accuracy, such as 73.79% on the Blink benchmark with GPT-4o, consistently outperforming traditional prompting and visual programming methods on challenging tasks.
Problem: State-of-the-art Vision-Language Models (VLMs) struggle with fine-grained visual perception tasks requiring detailed pixel-level analysis.
Prior visual programming methods for VLMs often lack generalizability, depend solely on text queries for code generation, and employ rigid tool selection.
Text-based prompting strategies frequently lead to ungrounded reasoning or hallucinations in visual tasks, and visual prompting can adversely affect VLM perception by cluttering images.
Method: VipAct introduces an autonomous VLM-based agent framework featuring an orchestrator agent that receives direct image input for comprehensive task analysis and planning.
The framework incorporates three specialized VLM-based agents for focused image captioning, visual prompt description, and focused image comparison to provide targeted visual analysis.

It integrates a suite of vision expert models (e.g., depth estimation, object detection, segmentation) that return both textual and processed image data directly into the VLM's reasoning workflow for pixel-level precision.
Results: VipAct achieved state-of-the-art performance on all sub-tasks in the Blink and MMVP benchmarks, obtaining an average accuracy of 73.79% on Blink with GPT-4o, significantly surpassing baseline methods.

Ablation studies confirmed that multi-agent collaboration, direct visual input to the orchestrator, and the inclusion of specialized VLM agents and vision expert models are indispensable for the framework's performance.

Closed-source VLMs like GPT-4o demonstrated robust performance with VipAct, while open-source models exhibited instruction-following limitations, highlighting the importance of strong VLM capabilities for agentic frameworks.
Takeaways: Multi-agent collaboration is crucial for eliciting comprehensive System-2 reasoning in VLMs, enabling significantly more detailed image analysis compared to direct prompting.
Providing direct image input to the orchestrator agent is essential for grounding task planning and precise parameter selection for tools, leading to more accurate visual understanding.
Traditional text-based prompting and visual prompting methods do not consistently improve fine-grained visual perception with VLMs; they can lead to ungrounded reasoning or impaired perception.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.15639.Title: Can Large Language Models Invent Algorithms to Improve Themselves?: Algorithm Discovery for Recursive Self-Improvement through Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.15639.Summary: A framework called Self-Developing enables Large Language Models to autonomously discover and refine algorithms for their own improvement, specifically focusing on model merging. This approach allowed an LLM to invent algorithms that outperformed human-designed methods, achieving a 6% accuracy improvement over the seed model on GSM8k and demonstrating strong transferability to out-of-domain models with a 7.4% gain over human-optimized baselines.
Problem: Large Language Model (LLM) improvement is largely constrained by human experts manually designing and testing new architectures, training methodologies, and fine-tuning strategies.
Existing LLM self-improvement methods, such as self-generated data or iterative refinement, do not enable the LLM to invent the underlying improvement algorithms themselves.
Many current LLM self-improvement techniques depend on more powerful external models (e.g., GPT-4) to guide the improvement process, limiting autonomous development.
Method: The NEC Corporation team developed Self-Developing, an iterative, reinforcement learning-based framework where an 'algorithm factory' LLM (initialized from the seed model) generates model-improving algorithms.
Algorithms are produced as executable Python code for a specific task (model merging) and evaluated on performance metrics to generate preference data.
The algorithm factory LLM is continuously refined using Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) based on the performance of its generated algorithms, creating a recursive self-improvement loop.
Results: LLM-discovered algorithms consistently outperformed the seed model, achieving a 6% accuracy improvement on GSM8k and an 8% improvement on MATH, using only the seed model's capabilities.
The best LLM-discovered algorithm for GSM8k surpassed human-designed methods like Task Arithmetic and TIES Merging by over 4% (e.g., 76.1% vs 71.9%).
Discovered algorithms showed strong transferability to out-of-domain models, yielding 78.8% accuracy on GSM8k with new models, outperforming a human-optimized baseline by 7.4% (71.4%).
Takeaways: Large Language Models (LLMs) can autonomously invent and refine complex algorithms, even surpassing human-designed methods for specific tasks like model merging.
Iterative refinement of the algorithm-generating LLM using Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) significantly enhances the quality and performance of the discovered algorithms over time.
Algorithms discovered by the framework demonstrate strong generalization capabilities, maintaining high performance even when applied to out-of-domain models not used during their generation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13848.Title: Janus: Decoupling Visual Encoding for Unified Multimodal Understanding and Generation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13848.Summary: Janus introduces a unified multimodal AI model that resolves the inherent granularity conflict between visual understanding and image generation tasks by employing separate visual encoders for each. This decoupled encoding strategy enables the model to achieve improved performance across both multimodal understanding benchmarks, such as a 41% improvement on MME, and high-quality image generation.
Problem: Unified multimodal AI models typically use a single visual encoder, which struggles to simultaneously meet the distinct visual granularity requirements of understanding and generation tasks.
Multimodal understanding requires high-level semantic information, while image generation necessitates fine-grained spatial and textural details.
This inherent conflict leads to suboptimal performance, where unified models often excel at one task at the expense of the other.
Method: Janus employs dual visual encoders: a SigLIP encoder for high-level semantic understanding and a VQ tokenizer for fine-grained visual generation.
Specialized adaptors map features from these distinct encoders into the input space of a single, unified Large Language Model.
A three-stage training process, including adaptor training, unified pretraining, and supervised fine-tuning, integrates the components and optimizes performance across tasks.
Results: Janus achieved a 41% improvement on the MME dataset and a 30% improvement on the GQA dataset for multimodal understanding.
For visual generation, the model obtained FIDs of 8.53 on COCO-30K and 10.10 on MJHQ-30K, demonstrating high-quality image output.
Ablation studies confirmed that the decoupled encoding approach prevents the significant performance trade-offs observed when a single visual encoder is used for both understanding and generation.
Takeaways: Decoupling visual encoding for distinct tasks (understanding vs. generation) is crucial for overcoming performance trade-offs in unified multimodal models.
A single Large Language Model can effectively manage both multimodal understanding and image generation when provided with appropriately encoded visual features.
A multi-stage training methodology allows for the effective integration and optimization of specialized visual encoders and a unified LLM within a multimodal framework.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13842.Title: D-FINE: Redefine Regression Task in DETRs as Fine-grained Distribution Refinement
https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13842.Summary: D-FINE redefines bounding box regression in DETR models by transforming fixed coordinate predictions into a fine-grained distribution refinement process. It achieves a superior balance of accuracy and real-time performance, with D-FINE-X reaching 55.8% AP at 78 FPS on COCO, and up to 59.3% AP with pretraining.
Problem: Traditional object detectors using fixed coordinate regression (Dirac delta distributions) struggle to account for localization uncertainty, making optimization difficult in complex scenes.
Existing knowledge distillation techniques are often inefficient at transferring localization knowledge from deeper to shallower layers within Detection Transformer (DETR) models.
Balancing high detection accuracy with real-time performance remains a challenge, with many models excelling in one aspect at the expense of the other.
Method: Introduces Fine-grained Distribution Refinement (FDR), which redefines bounding box regression as an iterative refinement of probability distributions, using a non-uniform weighting function for precise adjustments.

Implements Global Optimal Localization Self-Distillation (GO-LSD), a novel self-distillation strategy that leverages unified Hungarian matching across all layers to optimize both matched and unmatched predictions.

Employs a Fine-Grained Localization (FGL) Loss and a Decoupled Distillation Focal (DDF) Loss to align predicted distributions with ground truth and facilitate effective knowledge transfer across decoder layers.
Results: D-FINE-L achieved 54.0% AP at 124 FPS on the COCO dataset, while D-FINE-X reached 55.8% AP at 78 FPS.
When pretrained on Objects365, D-FINE-L and D-FINE-X boosted their performance to 57.1% AP and 59.3% AP respectively.
The method enhances a range of DETR models by up to 5.3% AP with minimal additional parameters and training costs, demonstrating an improved accuracy-speed balance among real-time detectors.
Takeaways: Modeling localization uncertainty through fine-grained probability distributions allows for more precise bounding box regression.
Iterative refinement of these probability distributions across decoder layers progressively enhances detection accuracy.
A global optimal localization self-distillation strategy effectively transfers localization knowledge across layers, improving training efficiency and stability.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13733.Title: Improving Multi-modal Large Language Model through Boosting Vision Capabilities
https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13733.Summary: Arcana improves the visual perception of Multi-Modal Large Language Models by introducing the Query Ladder Adapter for enhanced visual feature extraction and Multimodal LoRA for modality-specific learning in the decoder. This approach achieves competitive performance on general VQA and LVLM benchmarks, outperforming many existing MLLMs on OKVQA, ScienceQA, and AI2D, all while maintaining computational efficiency.
Problem: Current Multi-Modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) exhibit limitations in low-level visual perception (e.g., color recognition, counting) and high-level visual understanding (e.g., small object detection, accurate localization).
Existing MLLMs often use CLIP as a visual encoder, which is not optimized for detailed visual understanding, leading to insufficient visual feature representation.
Language-driven decoders in MLLMs suffer from modality interference, where language processing can dominate and hinder effective visual information processing.
Method: Arcana introduces the Query Ladder Adapter (QLadder), a lightweight module that enhances visual feature extraction from a frozen CLIP encoder using learnable query tokens and progressive refinement.
It integrates Multimodal LoRA (MM-LoRA) into the language model decoder, utilizing distinct parameter sets for visual and textual information to mitigate modality interference.
The model is trained in a two-stage process, beginning with pre-training for vision-language alignment, followed by multimodal instruction fine-tuning on diverse datasets.
Results: Arcana achieves competitive performance across six general VQA benchmarks, notably outperforming most existing MLLMs on OKVQA, ScienceQA, and AI2D.

The model demonstrates robust reasoning and generalization capabilities on five LVLM benchmarks, including MMBench and SEED-Bench, while maintaining competitive performance on pure language understanding tasks.

Ablation studies confirm that MM-LoRA significantly outperforms traditional LoRA by separating visual and language learning spaces, and QLadder effectively enhances visual representation, achieving strong results with computational efficiency.
Takeaways: Enhancing visual perception in MLLMs can be achieved efficiently through lightweight architectural innovations without requiring extensive computational resources.
Separating learning spaces for different modalities within the decoder, as demonstrated by MM-LoRA, effectively reduces interference and improves multimodal understanding.
Augmenting existing visual encoders with adaptable modules, like the Query Ladder Adapter, is an effective strategy for learning complementary and detailed visual representations.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.12735.Title: CREAM: Consistency Regularized Self-Rewarding Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.12735.Summary: CREAM, a consistency-regularized self-rewarding language model, introduces a mechanism that mitigates bias and overconfident preference labeling in iterative LLM alignment by adapting the DPO loss based on ranking consistency between current and previous model iterations. This approach enables sustained self-improvement and achieves performance competitive with oracle models, particularly for 7B Llama-3, without external human feedback or reward models.
Problem: Existing Self-Rewarding Language Models (SRLMs) suffer from unreliable and inaccurate self-generated rewards, especially for smaller LLMs.
The same LLM acting as both generator and judge can accumulate biases and generate noisy, overconfident preference labels, particularly for responses of similar quality.
This accumulated bias often leads to diminished returns or performance degradation after a few self-training iterations, limiting SRLMs' scalability and effectiveness.
Method: CREAM introduces a consistency regularization term to the Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) loss, effectively transforming it into a soft-labeled DPO objective.
It estimates the confidence in a self-generated preference label by measuring the consistency of reward rankings between the current model iteration and the previous iteration using Kendall's Tau.
This consistency score adaptively weights the DPO loss, enabling the model to down-weight unreliable or inconsistent preference pairs and mitigate overconfidence and bias accumulation.
Results: CREAM significantly outperforms standard SRLM for Llama-2 and Llama-3 models, achieving substantial performance gains and demonstrating consistent iterative improvement across benchmarks.
For Llama-3, CREAM M3 achieved an average accuracy of 83.37%, competitively matching or slightly surpassing Oracle M3 (82.12%) without relying on external reward models.
CREAM maintains significantly higher rewarding consistency and achieves higher pairwise ranking accuracy on both self-generated and external datasets compared to standard SRLM.
Takeaways: Blindly trusting self-generated preferences in SRLMs leads to overconfident mistakes and the accumulation of biases, particularly when distinguishing between responses of similar quality.
A generalized iterative preference fine-tuning framework can formally represent SRLMs, helping to identify the source of rewarding bias as overconfident preference labeling.

The consistency of reward rankings across successive model iterations provides an intrinsic, self-contained signal for assessing the reliability of self-generated preferences without external supervision.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.10855.Title: Core Knowledge Deficits in Multi-Modal Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.10855.Summary: A new study by researchers from UCSD, JHU, and CMU, among others, evaluates Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) for fundamental cognitive abilities, revealing consistent deficits in core knowledge and a reliance on shortcut learning even in state-of-the-art models.
Problem: Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) demonstrate strong performance on complex reasoning tasks but struggle with basic, intuitive human cognitive abilities, a phenomenon known as Moravec's Paradox.
Current MLLMs lack robustness, generalization, and are susceptible to shortcut learning, raising questions about their genuine conceptual understanding.
Existing benchmarks primarily assess high-level reasoning, failing to evaluate the foundational "core knowledge" that underpins human intelligence from early development.
Method: A new large-scale benchmark, CoreCognition, was developed, featuring 1,503 multi-modal samples across 12 core knowledge concepts derived from human cognitive development theory.
230 diverse Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) were evaluated using robust inference infrastructure and various prompting strategies, including a "circular evaluation" method to mitigate bias.
A novel "Concept Hacking" methodology was introduced, comparing model performance on control vs. causally manipulated stimuli to distinguish genuine understanding from shortcut learning.
Results: MLLMs consistently underperformed on low-level cognitive abilities (Sensorimotor and Concrete Operational stages), trailing human performance by 15-22% on average, while showing better but still deficient performance on higher-level abilities.
Concept Hacking experiments demonstrated that MLLMs, even as they scale, primarily exhibit core deficits or rely on shortcut learning, with few models displaying genuine, robust core knowledge.
Scaling models, reasoning-augmented approaches, and most prompting techniques did not resolve these deficits, although a specific "cognitive instruction" prompt improved accuracy by over 6%.
Takeaways: Unlike human cognition, MLLMs do not exhibit coherent, hierarchically structured competencies for core knowledge, with weak correlations between foundational and advanced abilities.
