Core knowledge abilities in MLLMs do not scale with increasing model parameters; performance on low-level tasks shows limited or no improvement, and in some cases, even degradation (e.g., inverse scaling for perspective-taking).
Stronger performance on CoreCognition abilities generally predicts better performance on most external high-level MLLM benchmarks, despite the models' internal deficits.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.08202.Title: Mono-InternVL: Pushing the Boundaries of Monolithic Multimodal Large Language Models with Endogenous Visual Pre-training
https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.08202.Summary: Mono-InternVL introduces a monolithic multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) that achieves competitive performance against leading modular MLLMs. The model demonstrates substantial improvements in deployment efficiency and effectively addresses catastrophic forgetting through its unique architecture and training strategy.
Problem: Monolithic MLLMs have historically underperformed modular counterparts due to visual processing constraints and complex training.
Existing methods for integrating visual capabilities into pre-trained LLMs often lead to catastrophic forgetting of learned linguistic knowledge.
Modular MLLMs, while performant, incur deployment inefficiencies like higher first-token latency and increased memory usage due to their two-component architecture.
Method: Integrates visual encoding and language decoding into a single LLM using a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts (MMoE) structure with modality-specific FFNs and static routing.

Employs an Endogenous Visual Pre-training (EViP) strategy, a three-stage progressive learning process that utilizes delta tuning to optimize only visual parameters, preserving the LLM's core language abilities.
Incorporates a visual tokenizer for direct image patchification, supporting high-resolution inputs and integrating a "thumbnail" for global context within the monolithic architecture.
Results: Mono-InternVL-2B surpasses all existing monolithic MLLMs across 16 benchmarks and achieves comparable or superior multimodal performance to leading modular MLLMs, including its counterpart InternVL-1.5-2B.
The model reduces first token latency by up to 67% and increases overall throughput by up to 31% compared to modular MLLMs, validating its architectural efficiency.
NLP capabilities are retained, with Mono-InternVL-2B performing similarly to its base LLM, demonstrating effective mitigation of catastrophic forgetting.
Takeaways: Delta tuning, which freezes the pre-trained LLM parameters while optimizing visual experts, is critical for integrating visual knowledge without catastrophic forgetting.
The multimodal Mixture-of-Experts (MMoE) architecture allows for efficient, modality-specific processing and capacity expansion within a unified model.
Progressive endogenous visual pre-training effectively guides the model to learn from low-level concepts to high-level semantics, leading to robust multimodal capabilities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.08146.Title: Rewarding Progress: Scaling Automated Process Verifiers for LLM Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.08146.Summary: A new approach, Process Advantage Verifiers (PAVs), is introduced to measure step-level progress in multi-step reasoning traces of large language models. This method leads to improved accuracy and efficiency in tasks like mathematical problem-solving during both test-time search and online reinforcement learning.
Problem: Large language models (LLMs) often struggle with complex multi-step reasoning tasks, making errors that are difficult to pinpoint within a long reasoning trace.
Traditional outcome-only feedback (Outcome Reward Models) provides a sparse signal, hindering effective identification of helpful or harmful intermediate steps.

Existing process reward models face challenges such as the high cost of human annotation, limited effectiveness of automatically generated labels, and an unclear definition of what constitutes a "good" intermediate step.
Method: Introduces Process Advantage Verifiers (PAVs), models trained to predict "progress" at each step of a reasoning trace.
Progress is defined as the difference in the probability of a prover policy completing a trace correctly before and after a given step.
PAVs are trained via supervised learning, using empirically estimated progress derived from completing partial traces with a designated "prover policy" and calculating success rate differences.
Results: Using PAVs for test-time beam search yielded 1.5-5x compute efficiency and 8-10% accuracy improvements across different LLM sizes (Gemma-2B, 9B, 27B).
When integrated into online reinforcement learning as dense rewards, PAVs achieved 6x sample efficiency and 6-7% accuracy improvements on mathematical reasoning tasks.
PAVs consistently outperformed traditional outcome reward models and other automated process reward baselines across various experimental settings.
Takeaways: Process rewards are defined as "progress," representing the increase in the likelihood of a correct solution after a step, mathematically formulated as a step-level advantage based on a prover policy's Q-values.

Optimal "prover policies" for estimating progress are not necessarily the most capable, but rather those that are "complementary" to the base policy, meaning they can effectively distinguish between good and bad steps it generates.
The approach enables scalable process supervision by automating the generation of progress labels, circumventing the need for expensive human annotation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.08021.Title: OneRef: Unified One-tower Expression Grounding and Segmentation with Mask Referring Modeling
https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.08021.Summary: OneRef introduces a minimalist, one-tower Transformer for unified visual grounding and segmentation, leveraging a novel Mask Referring Modeling (MRefM) pre-training paradigm to achieve state-of-the-art performance with significantly reduced computational complexity. The framework demonstrates superior accuracy across referring expression comprehension and segmentation tasks, while being substantially more parameter- and inference-efficient than prior methods.
Problem: Existing visual grounding and referring segmentation methods rely on complex architectures with separate vision and language encoders, bulky fusion modules, and many parameters.
Generic Mask Vision Language Modeling (MVLM) pre-training often fails to capture the intricate, fine-grained referential relationships critical for regression-like referring tasks.
Current grounding and segmentation models frequently depend on special grounding tokens or multiple query anchors, adding architectural complexity and potentially disrupting pre-trained backbones.
Method: OneRef employs a unified, modality-shared one-tower Transformer to integrate visual and linguistic feature spaces from the outset, simplifying the overall architecture.

Introduced Mask Referring Modeling (MRefM), comprising Referring-aware Mask Image Modeling (MIM) and Referring-aware Mask Language Modeling (MLM), to explicitly pre-train for referential understanding.

Implemented a referring-aware dynamic image masking strategy and reconstructed visual/semantic target-relation scores to embed precise spatial and semantic referential information directly into backbone features.
Results: Achieved new state-of-the-art performance across various Visual Grounding (REC/PG) and Referring Expression Segmentation (RES) benchmarks, outperforming larger and more complex models like Grounding-DINO and LION.
Demonstrated significant computational efficiency, utilizing 34.9% fewer FLOPs than Grounding-DINO, 25.2% fewer than MDETR, and up to 10x faster inference speed.

Ablation studies confirmed the efficacy of MRefM components, with combined elements yielding a 6.21% performance gain on RefCOCOg-test, and the referring-aware dynamic masking outperforming fixed masking strategies.
Takeaways: Explicitly modeling fine-grained referential relationships during pre-training through MRefM allows a unified one-tower Transformer to achieve high performance with a simplified architecture.
A minimalist design with lightweight task heads can outperform complex multi-encoder/decoder models when the backbone's features are inherently rich in referring information.
The dynamic masking strategy, which assigns higher mask ratios to referred regions, is crucial for effectively embedding specific referential understanding into the visual features.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.02742.Title: Grounding Large Language Models In Embodied Environment With Imperfect World Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.02742.Summary: The GLIMO framework, developed by researchers at UCSD, enables large language models (LLMs) to effectively learn and generalize for embodied tasks by fine-tuning them with experiences generated from imperfect world models. This approach allows open-source LLMs like LLaMA-3 to achieve significant performance gains, including up to 2.04x task completion improvement and outperforming GPT-4 in specific embodied environments.
Problem: Large language models (LLMs) lack direct physical world experience, leading to difficulties in basic physical reasoning and execution of embodied tasks.
Existing methods for physically grounding LLMs often rely on the costly and unsafe assumption of access to perfect world models or simulators.
Generating diverse and high-quality instruction datasets for fine-tuning LLMs is a labor-intensive, unscalable process that limits generalizability to new robotics tasks.
Method: GLIMO introduces a framework to fine-tune LLMs using embodied experiences sampled from readily available, low-cost, and interactive 'imperfect world models' (simulators).
An automated LLM agent-based data generator autonomously navigates imperfect environments, interprets experiences, and transforms them into diverse, high-quality instruction tuning datasets.
A two-stage fine-tuning approach with LoRA is employed to specialize LLMs on these grounded embodied experiences while mitigating catastrophic forgetting and enhancing generalization.
Results: Fine-tuned open-source LLMs (e.g., LLaMA-3) achieved significant task completion improvements of 2.04x, 1.54x, and 1.82x across Agent World, Urban Driving, and Multi-Agent benchmarks, respectively.
The fine-tuned LLaMA-3 models demonstrated competitive performance against or surpassed GPT-4, outperforming it by 51.7% in Agent World and 84.5% in Urban Driving task completion percentage.

The approach enhanced zero-shot generalization capabilities in out-of-distribution QA accuracy and improved environment understanding, with fine-tuned models largely preserving general language modeling capabilities.
Takeaways: LLMs can effectively learn useful, domain-invariant knowledge from imperfect world models that transfers to more complex, real-world environments, challenging the necessity of perfect simulators.

Automated LLM agents can generate high-quality, diverse instruction data through self-guided sampling, iterative refining, and specific QA formats (rationale, counterfactual, episodic memory), significantly reducing manual effort.

Training with data predominantly from imperfect world models can act as an effective regularization technique, improving LLM generalization and robustness, particularly in out-of-distribution scenarios.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.02735.Title: OOD-Chameleon: Is Algorithm Selection for OOD Generalization Learnable?
https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.02735.Summary: OOD-Chameleon introduces a meta-learning framework for predicting the most suitable out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization algorithm for a given dataset based on measurable characteristics, achieving up to 90.9% 0-1 accuracy in algorithm selection across diverse tasks without requiring target model training.
Problem: No single OOD generalization algorithm consistently performs optimally across all types of distribution shifts, leaving practitioners with a manual, inefficient selection process.
Real-world distribution shifts are complex and often involve interacting types (covariate, label, spurious correlations), making theoretical analysis and a priori algorithm selection challenging.
The lack of OOD evaluation data in real-world scenarios hinders empirical trial-and-error approaches for algorithm selection.
Method: The OOD-Chameleon framework formulates OOD algorithm selection as a multi-label classification task, predicting algorithm suitability based on dataset characteristics.
A meta-dataset is constructed by generating tasks with quantifiable distribution shifts and recording the worst-group error of a "zoo" of five established OOD algorithms.
A non-linear selector (e.g., MLP, Decision Tree) is trained on measurable dataset descriptors to predict the best OOD algorithm *a priori*, before any target model training.
Results: OOD-Chameleon significantly reduced worst-group test error and achieved high 0-1 accuracy (up to 90.9% on NLP, 80.6% on vision tasks) in algorithm selection compared to baselines like random or global best selection.
The approach effectively generalizes from meta-training on specific datasets (e.g., CelebA) to selecting algorithms for entirely different, unseen datasets (e.g., MetaShift, OfficeHome, MultiNLI).
The selector maintained accurate predictions even when dataset descriptors were estimated rather than provided as ground truth, demonstrating robustness for practical scenarios.
Takeaways: Algorithm selection for OOD generalization is demonstrably learnable, with OOD-Chameleon achieving high accuracy in identifying suitable methods.
The learned selector exhibits strong generalizability, effectively transferring knowledge from meta-training datasets to unseen tasks and entirely different datasets.

The optimal algorithm selection relies on complex, non-linear interactions between dataset characteristics and algorithm performance, as evidenced by the superior performance of non-linear predictors.
Analysis of the learned decision rules offers valuable, interpretable insights into the specific applicability conditions of different OOD algorithms.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.02355.Title: AlphaEdit: Null-Space Constrained Knowledge Editing for Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.02355.Summary: AlphaEdit proposes a null-space constrained knowledge editing method for large language models, preventing catastrophic forgetting during sequential updates by projecting parameter perturbations to ensure preserved knowledge remains undisturbed. This approach leads to an average 36.7% improvement in editing capabilities while maintaining the model's general knowledge and fluency.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) can produce outdated or incorrect information and are computationally expensive to fully fine-tune for updates.
Current parameter-modifying model editing methods struggle with sequential updates, often disrupting previously stored knowledge.
This leads to catastrophic forgetting, a distribution shift in hidden representations, and degradation of general capabilities during multiple edits.
Method: AlphaEdit proposes projecting parameter perturbations onto the null space of the preserved knowledge's key matrix.

This mathematical projection guarantees that previous knowledge (key-value associations) remains undisturbed while new information is embedded, by removing the preservation term from the optimization objective.
The method efficiently computes a projection matrix once using Singular Value Decomposition, which is then applied to perturbations, ensuring negligible additional runtime overhead.
Results: Achieved an average 12.54% improvement in Efficacy and 16.78% in Generalization during sequential editing across LLaMA3, GPT-J, and GPT2-XL, with even higher gains on LLaMA3 (32.85% Efficacy, 30.60% Generalization).
Maintained original model performance on GLUE benchmarks after extensive sequential editing, unlike baselines that experienced significant degradation in general capabilities.

Demonstrated stable hidden representation distributions post-editing, empirically validating the null-space projection's ability to prevent distributional shifts, and significantly boosted the performance of existing editing methods (e.g., MEMIT, PRUNE) by an average of 28.24% in editing capability and 42.65% in general capability when integrated.
Takeaways: The inherent trade-off in model editing between updating new knowledge and preserving old knowledge can be resolved by projecting perturbations into a null space that decouples these objectives.
Maintaining the stability of hidden representations is crucial for preventing catastrophic forgetting and preserving general model capabilities during sequential knowledge updates.
Simple, mathematically grounded projection techniques can be integrated into existing model editing methods to significantly boost their performance across various metrics.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.01735.Title: LASeR: Learning to Adaptively Select Reward Models with Multi-Armed Bandits
https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.01735.Summary: LASeR (Learning to Adaptively Select Reward models) introduces a framework that uses Multi-Armed Bandits to dynamically select the most suitable reward model for each batch during iterative LLM training. This adaptive approach improved LLM alignment, achieving higher accuracy on reasoning tasks, better instruction-following capabilities, and up to 3x faster training compared to single-RM and ensemble baselines.
Problem: Single, fixed Reward Models (RMs) often lack generalization across diverse tasks, are prone to 'reward hacking,' and can provide unreliable feedback during LLM alignment.
Ensemble-based RM approaches are computationally prohibitive due to the need to run multiple large models simultaneously and can suffer from conflicting preference signals.
Manually selecting optimal RMs or designing effective aggregation strategies for ensembles is a labor-intensive and inefficient process.
Method: LASeR frames the problem of selecting an RM from a pool of candidates as a contextual Multi-Armed Bandit (MAB) problem, primarily utilizing the LinUCB algorithm.
It dynamically selects a single RM for each mini-batch during iterative LLM fine-tuning (e.g., DPO) and uses its feedback to update the LLM.
The MAB's reward signal is defined as the negative normalized training loss of the LLM from that batch, enabling it to learn which RMs provide the most informative guidance for different contexts.
Results: LASeR achieved an absolute average accuracy of 76.32% on reasoning benchmarks (StrategyQA, GSM8K, MMLU) with Llama-3-8B, outperforming the 'Best RM' baseline by 1.45% and the 'RM Score Ensemble' by 2.67%.
It demonstrated superior AlpacaEval win rates on instruction-following tasks (WildChat dataset), significantly beating 'Random RM Selection' (78.33%) and 'RM Score Ensemble' (72.69%) baselines.

The method provided a 2x to 3x speedup in wall-clock training time compared to ensemble and sequential baselines while delivering higher performance, and also consistently improved reranking for long-context tasks.
Takeaways: Dynamically selecting a single, context-appropriate RM per batch mitigates the computational overhead and conflicting signals inherent in traditional ensemble methods.
The MAB effectively balances exploration of different RMs with exploitation of those performing well, adapting its selection strategy as the LLM policy evolves.
Using the downstream LLM's training loss as the MAB's reward provides a robust and direct signal for assessing the quality and utility of a selected RM in a given context.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.01679.Title: VinePPO: Refining Credit Assignment in RL Training of LLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.01679.Summary: VinePPO refines credit assignment in reinforcement learning for large language models by replacing PPO's learned value network with unbiased Monte Carlo estimations, leveraging the inherent ability to reset to intermediate states in language environments. This approach consistently outperforms standard PPO and other baselines on mathematical reasoning tasks, achieving higher accuracy in less wall-clock time and demonstrating improved generalization.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) face challenges with accurate credit assignment in multi-step reasoning tasks due to sparse and delayed rewards, making it difficult to attribute success or failure to individual intermediate steps.

Standard Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), a common method for RL finetuning of LLMs, often relies on a value network whose practical efficacy for fine-grained credit assignment in complex reasoning tasks is questionable.
Recent simplified RL-free or PPO variants have achieved strong results without explicit fine-grained credit assignment, raising doubts about the necessity of complex value networks.
Method: Replaces PPO's learned value network with unbiased Monte Carlo (MC) estimations of state values for credit assignment.

Leverages the deterministic nature of language environments, which allows for exact 'resets' to any intermediate state by re-feeding partial context, making MC rollouts for value estimation computationally feasible.

Computes state values by generating K auxiliary rollouts from each state using the current policy and uses the empirical mean of their returns to calculate advantages for the standard PPO policy update.
Results: VinePPO consistently outperforms standard PPO and other baselines (RLOO, GRPO, DPO+, RestEM) on mathematical reasoning datasets (MATH, GSM8K) for different model sizes.
It achieves higher peak performance in less wall-clock time, reaching PPO's peak accuracy up to 3.0x faster for 1.1B models and 1.51x faster for 7B models on the MATH dataset.

The method demonstrates a steeper generalization slope, yielding higher test accuracy for a given training accuracy and enabling more efficient learning from limited high-quality reasoning data. Analysis confirms VinePPO's Monte Carlo estimates are unbiased and significantly more accurate than PPO's value network predictions.
Takeaways: Language environments, when modeled as Markov Decision Processes, allow for exact 'resets' to intermediate states, enabling unbiased Monte Carlo estimation of state values, a technique generally difficult in other RL settings.

Standard PPO's value networks are often ineffective for LLM reasoning tasks, producing inaccurate and biased value predictions that struggle to identify optimal next actions and degrade as reasoning chains progress.

Accurate and unbiased credit assignment is crucial for effective reinforcement learning in LLMs, particularly for complex reasoning, challenging the notion that simplified methods are always sufficient.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.18869.Title: Emu3: Next-Token Prediction is All You Need
https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.18869.Summary: The Emu3 model from BAAI demonstrates that next-token prediction, a method typically used for language models, can effectively handle multiple modalities, including text, images, and video. It achieves competitive performance in tasks such as image and video generation and vision-language understanding through a unified transformer decoder architecture and a dedicated vision tokenizer.
Problem: Multimodal AI historically relies on fragmented architectures, with separate models dominating different domains (e.g., diffusion models for image generation, transformers for text, compositional approaches for multimodal understanding).
Applying the next-token prediction paradigm to non-textual modalities like images and video has been challenging, often requiring hybrid approaches or multiple training objectives.
Previous multimodal systems often suffer from architectural complexity due to the need to combine disparate components for different modalities.
Method: Emu3 employs a single transformer decoder architecture, similar to Llama-2, adapted with an expanded embedding layer and an extended context length (up to 131,072 tokens).
A dedicated vision tokenizer (based on SBER-MoVQGAN) converts images and videos into discrete tokens, allowing them to be processed alongside text tokens in the unified framework.

The model is trained in two stages using a comprehensive dataset of high-quality text, image, and video data, followed by post-training refinements like Quality Fine-Tuning and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO).
Results: Emu3 achieves competitive performance in text-to-image generation, outperforming SDXL and achieving comparable results to DALL-E 3 and Midjourney v5.2 in human evaluations.
The model demonstrates strong video capabilities, including text-to-video generation and future prediction, scoring 81.0 on the VBench benchmark compared to OpenSora 1.2's 79.8.
Emu3 performs competitively across 12 vision-language benchmarks, averaging 62.1, which is comparable to LLaVA-1.6's 61.8, using a unified next-token prediction approach.
Takeaways: Next-token prediction, the paradigm powering large language models, can be effectively extended to handle multiple modalities including text, images, and video.

By converting images and videos into discrete tokens, a single transformer decoder architecture can achieve competitive performance across diverse tasks without specialized components or multiple training objectives.
The unified token-based approach offers architectural simplicity, improved scaling properties, and potential for emergent cross-modal capabilities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.17146.Title: Molmo and PixMo: Open Weights and Open Data for State-of-the-Art Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.17146.Summary: This work introduces Molmo, a family of state-of-the-art open-weight Vision-Language Models (VLMs), and PixMo, a comprehensive suite of VLM-independent training datasets. Molmo-72B achieves leading performance on academic benchmarks and human preference evaluations, demonstrating that high-performing VLMs can be built entirely from truly open data and models without relying on proprietary systems for data generation.
Problem: Many open-weight Vision-Language Models (VLMs) rely heavily on synthetic data generated by proprietary VLMs, hindering true scientific understanding and reproducibility of VLM development.
Collecting large-scale, high-quality multimodal training data is expensive and difficult, often leading to reliance on less transparent or less effective methods.
Lack of truly open, foundational VLM resources creates barriers to independent research and development outside of large tech companies.
Method: Develops Molmo, a family of state-of-the-art open-weight VLMs with a streamlined architecture featuring a pre-trained vision encoder, an LLM, and an optimized connector using overlapping multi-crop vision input.

Introduces PixMo, a novel suite of seven multimodal datasets collected entirely without relying on proprietary or other external VLMs, utilizing innovative methods like oral descriptions for dense captions and interactive human-in-the-loop editing for Q&A.

Employs a simplified two-stage training pipeline (pre-training on dense captions, fine-tuning on a mix of all PixMo and academic datasets) with specific optimizations like text-only dropout and efficient multi-annotation processing.
Results: Molmo-72B achieves state-of-the-art academic benchmark scores among all tested models and ranks second in human preference (Elo score) just behind GPT-4o.
Molmo models significantly outperform other VLMs, including proprietary ones, on counting tasks (e.g., CountBenchQA) and an in-the-wild clock reading benchmark.
The most efficient model, MolmoE-1B, based on a 1B-7B mixture-of-experts LLM, approaches the performance of GPT-4V on academic benchmarks and human preference.
Takeaways: High-quality human-annotated data, collected without reliance on proprietary VLMs, performs comparably to data generated by powerful commercial models for VLM training.
Architectural choices like overlapping multi-crops for vision input and text-only dropout during pre-training significantly improve VLM performance.
Targeted, VLM-independent synthetic data can effectively imbue models with robust, specialized skills, as demonstrated by leading performance in clock reading and counting.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.15310.Title: Visual Prompting in Multimodal Large Language Models: A Survey
https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.15310.Summary: This survey paper by Junda Wu and colleagues systematically categorizes and examines visual prompting techniques for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). It outlines how visual cues, such as bounding boxes and pixel-level masks, enhance MLLMs' abilities in visual grounding, object referring, and compositional reasoning by providing direct control over model attention.
Problem: Text-only instructions often struggle to precisely describe visual elements, leading to ambiguity and a lack of fine-grained control over Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs).
MLLMs can suffer from visual hallucinations and language bias when solely relying on textual prompts for interpreting visual content.
There was a lack of a comprehensive overview of visual prompting techniques specifically for MLLMs, distinguishing it from textual prompting for LLMs or visual prompting for pure vision models.
Method: The survey categorizes visual prompts into four main types: bounding boxes for spatial localization, marker prompts for specific locations, pixel-level prompts for detailed outlines, and soft prompts operating in the model's feature space.
Visual prompt generation methods include manual engineering, automatic generation via segmentation models like SAM, or object detection models to create precise cues.
MLLMs are trained to interpret visual prompts through pre-training with prompt-augmented datasets, fine-tuning on smaller prompt-specific data, or via in-context learning through demonstrations.
Results: Visual prompts demonstrably improve MLLMs' visual grounding by connecting language expressions to specific visual elements, reducing misidentification.
The use of visual prompts enables more precise object referring, clarifying ambiguous references in complex scenes with multiple similar objects.
Models show enhanced compositional reasoning by processing relationships between highlighted elements, and improved navigation/planning in embodied AI by marking spatial cues.
Takeaways: Visual prompts enhance MLLM capabilities in visual grounding, object referring, compositional reasoning, and navigation/planning by providing direct spatial and semantic guidance.
Effective visual prompts can be generated through engineering, segmentation-based, or detection-based approaches, with hybrid methods offering increased robustness.
Successfully integrating visual prompts requires specific learning strategies, including pre-training, fine-tuning, or in-context learning, along with careful alignment to human intent.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.14401.Title: Investigating the Impact of Hard Samples on Accuracy Reveals In-class Data Imbalance
https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.14401.Summary: Pukowski and Lu introduce the concept of "in-class data imbalance," revealing that datasets contain disproportionate amounts of "easy" and "hard" samples within each class, challenging the sole reliance on test accuracy. The research demonstrates that models trained on easy samples perform poorly on hard samples, suggesting that hard samples are crucial for robust generalization.
Problem: Machine learning models are primarily evaluated using aggregate test accuracy, which can obscure poor performance on specific types of data samples.
The conventional understanding of data imbalance focuses on class distribution, overlooking varying complexities within a single class.
Current evaluation methods do not sufficiently account for the intrinsic complexity of individual data samples and their differential impact on model learning.
Method: The paper introduces the concept of 'in-class data imbalance,' distinguishing between 'easy' and 'hard' samples based on their intrinsic complexity and contribution to model learning.
It adapts the 'straggler' concept, rooted in the manifold hypothesis, to identify hard samples as those consistently misclassified at the 'inversion point' of class manifold radii.
A systematic experimental design manipulated the proportion of easy and hard samples in training sets to evaluate their differential impact on model performance on separate easy and hard test sets.
Results: Models trained exclusively on easy samples achieved 95-97% accuracy on easy test samples but only 20-25% accuracy on hard test samples.
Training solely on hard samples resulted in moderate accuracy on easy samples, indicating hard samples contain more generalizable information.

The straggler-based method for identifying hard samples showed a greater performance gap between easy and hard samples, outperforming confidence-based and energy-based methods in distinguishing sample hardness.
Takeaways: Easy and hard data samples contribute differently to model learning and generalization, with hard samples containing more generalizable information.
Hard samples are not merely anomalies but represent legitimate, complex features essential for robust generalization.
The geometric 'straggler-based' method for identifying hard samples is more effective than confidence-based or energy-based approaches.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.04429.Title: VILA-U: a Unified Foundation Model Integrating Visual Understanding and Generation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.04429.Summary: Researchers from Tsinghua, MIT, NVIDIA, UC Berkeley, and UC San Diego developed VILA-U, a unified foundation model that integrates visual understanding and generation using a single autoregressive framework. The model achieves competitive performance across image and video understanding and generation tasks, demonstrating that an end-to-end discrete token-based approach can bridge the gap between semantic understanding and high-fidelity visual synthesis without external diffusion models.
Problem: Existing unified multi-modal models using VQGAN-based discrete tokens suffer from poor visual understanding due to a lack of semantic information in their visual tokens.
Unified models that leverage semantically rich CLIP features for understanding require external diffusion models for generation, adding architectural complexity and infrastructure overhead.
Traditional visual language models often rely on separate modules for understanding and generation, leading to complex architectures and potential misalignment between components.
Method: VILA-U introduces a unified foundation vision tower that learns text-aligned discrete visual tokens by simultaneously optimizing for VQ-based image reconstruction and text-image contrastive loss.
It employs a unified multi-modal generative pre-training procedure that concatenates discrete visual tokens and text tokens into a single sequence for end-to-end autoregressive next-token prediction.
A "depth transformer" within the LLM predicts multiple residual tokens for each visual position, enabling finer visual detail generation while maintaining the efficiency of autoregressive processing.
Results: VILA-U achieves significantly better image reconstruction (rFID 1.80 for 256x256) than VQ-GAN and strong text alignment (Top-1 ImageNet accuracy of 78.0% for 384 resolution).
On image-language benchmarks, VILA-U (384 resolution) obtains competitive scores (e.g., 79.4 on VQAv2, 60.8 on GQA), approaching leading VLMs despite using discrete visual tokens.

For image generation, VILA-U (384 resolution) yields an FID of 7.69, outperforming other autoregressive methods and demonstrating performance comparable to some diffusion models on less data; it also shows strong video generation (74.01 on VBench).
Takeaways: A unified vision tower trained with both image reconstruction and text-image contrastive losses can create discrete visual tokens rich in both appearance and semantic information.

End-to-end autoregressive next-token prediction can achieve competitive performance in both visual understanding and generation, challenging the necessity of external diffusion models for high-quality synthesis.

Balancing the conflicting objectives of visual understanding (requiring semantic richness) and generation (requiring reconstruction fidelity) within a unified token space presents a key trade-off that requires careful architectural and training considerations.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.17059.Title: A Survey of the Self Supervised Learning Mechanisms for Vision Transformers
https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.17059.Summary: A comprehensive survey details self-supervised learning mechanisms tailored for Vision Transformers, presenting a new taxonomy and consolidating performance benchmarks. It highlights key advancements, open challenges, and future research directions to facilitate learning robust features with reduced labeled data requirements.
Problem: Vision Transformers (ViTs) often require vast amounts of labeled data for optimal performance, creating high costs and practical limitations for deployment.
A structured understanding and systematic overview of self-supervised learning (SSL) techniques specifically adapted for ViTs was lacking in the scientific literature.
Researchers needed a comprehensive resource to navigate the diverse landscape of SSL methods for ViTs and identify effective strategies.
Method: The survey systematically reviewed and synthesized existing self-supervised learning (SSL) techniques and their adaptation for Vision Transformers (ViTs).
It proposed a comprehensive taxonomy, classifying SSL methods for ViTs into five main categories: Contrastive, Generative, Clustering, Knowledge Distillation, and Hybrid approaches.
The paper conducted a comparative analysis of state-of-the-art SSL methods, evaluating their performance across various computer vision tasks and benchmarks like ImageNet, COCO, and ADE20K.
Results: SSL-pre-trained ViTs achieved over 82.0% Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K with end-to-end fine-tuning, with methods like MSG-MAE reaching 85.3%.
For dense prediction tasks on COCO, top SSL methods yielded object detection AP_box up to 54.6 and instance segmentation AP_mask up to 48.8 using Mask R-CNN.
SSL methods demonstrated strong transferability, with ViTs pre-trained using SSL achieving high accuracies on smaller datasets, for instance, Deit-III reaching 99.3% on CIFAR-10.
Takeaways: SSL pre-training enables ViTs to achieve state-of-the-art performance across image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation, significantly reducing their dependency on extensive labeled data.
Diverse SSL methods inherently integrate regularization principles (e.g., consistency, momentum encoding, redundancy reduction), contributing to model stability and generalization.

Despite advancements, challenges persist in designing robust data augmentation strategies, effectively incorporating spatial information, improving sample efficiency, and enhancing interpretability for SSL-ViTs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.15240.Title: Generative Verifiers: Reward Modeling as Next-Token Prediction
https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.15240.Summary: Generative Verifiers (GenRM), developed by Google DeepMind, reframes reward modeling for Large Language Models as a next-token prediction task, enabling models to leverage their generative capabilities for verification. This approach, particularly with Chain-of-Thought reasoning and synthetic rationales, substantially improves performance on complex algorithmic and mathematical reasoning tasks, outperforming traditional discriminative verifiers.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) often generate logically or factually incorrect information ("hallucinations"), particularly in complex reasoning tasks like mathematics.

Traditional discriminative verifiers, used in "Best-of-N" strategies to mitigate hallucinations, fail to fully leverage the generative capabilities (e.g., Chain-of-Thought reasoning, instruction tuning) inherent in pre-trained LLMs.
Existing methods like "LLM-as-a-Judge" or DPO have limitations in performance or task-specific fine-tuning for robust verification.
Method: Introduces Generative Verifiers (GenRM) that reframe reward modeling as a next-token prediction task, fine-tuned using standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT).
Develops GenRM-CoT, which incorporates Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning by training the model to generate an explicit critique before outputting a correctness judgment.
Utilizes purely synthetic, reference-guided rationales to train GenRM-CoT, reducing reliance on expensive human annotations.
Results: GenRM-CoT consistently and substantially outperforms discriminative reward models, DPO, and LLM-as-a-Judge across algorithmic and mathematical reasoning tasks.
On GSM8K, using a Gemma2-9B GenRM-CoT verifier on Gemini 1.0 Pro solutions, the problem-solving rate increased from 73% to 93.4%.
The approach demonstrates strong easy-to-hard generalization, improving performance on the challenging MATH dataset from 28% to 44.6% (Best-of-32) when trained on GSM8K.
Takeaways: Realigning reward modeling with the native next-token prediction objective of LLMs allows verifiers to leverage their full generative capabilities, improving accuracy.

Incorporating Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning within the verifier, particularly with inference-time majority voting, leads to substantial performance gains and strong generalization to harder problems.
High-quality verifiers can be effectively trained using purely synthetic, LLM-generated verification rationales, significantly reducing annotation costs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.14371.Title: SelEx: Self-Expertise in Fine-Grained Generalized Category Discovery
https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.14371.Summary: SelEx introduces a Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) method for fine-grained classification by fostering 'self-expertise' through hierarchical representation learning and refined contrastive strategies. The approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on fine-grained datasets, demonstrating 87.4% overall accuracy on CUB-200 and competitive results across other benchmarks.
Problem: Existing Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) methods often struggle with fine-grained distinctions, leading to fragmented clustering and high false negative rates.
Traditional contrastive learning, a common foundation for GCD, faces limitations in distinguishing subtly different categories due to its general positive/negative pairing mechanism.
The challenge lies in simultaneously classifying known categories and discovering novel ones with high accuracy, particularly when subtle visual differences are crucial.
Method: SelEx develops 'self-expertise' for fine-grained GCD using a combination of Hierarchical Pseudo-Label Extraction, Unsupervised Self-Expertise, and Supervised Self-Expertise.
A Balanced Semi-Supervised K-means (BSSK) and Hierarchical Semi-Supervised K-means (HSSK) generate multi-level pseudo-labels to provide hierarchical supervisory signals.

Unsupervised Self-Expertise (L_USE) refines contrastive learning by emphasizing hierarchical 'hard negatives', while Supervised Self-Expertise (L_SSE) leverages abstract pseudo-labels with segmented latent dimensions to accelerate learning.
Results: SelEx consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance on fine-grained datasets including CUB-200 (87.4% overall accuracy), FGVC-Aircraft, Stanford-Cars, and Oxford-IIIT Pet, outperforming prior methods.
The method demonstrates robustness to various conditions, including varying ratios of labeled data, estimated numbers of categories, and adaptability to long-tailed datasets.

Ablation studies confirm the individual contribution of each component, with Hierarchical Semi-Supervised K-means (HSSK) providing the most significant improvement, increasing overall accuracy on CUB-200 from 46.1% to 62.6%.
Takeaways: A theoretical framework based on KL divergence shows that a hierarchical approach reduces the upper bound on estimation error in both supervised and unsupervised contrastive learning, enabling finer granularity.
Segmenting the latent embedding dimension across hierarchical levels forces the model to learn progressively finer-grained distinctions, building 'self-expertise' from coarse to fine.

Refining negative sample treatment with hierarchical pseudo-labels and label smoothing allows the model to differentiate subtly similar instances more effectively without indiscriminately repelling semantically related samples.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.13296.Title: The Ultimate Guide to Fine-Tuning LLMs from Basics to Breakthroughs: An Exhaustive Review of Technologies, Research, Best Practices, Applied Research Challenges and Opportunities
https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.13296.Summary: This report from CeADAR: Ireland’s Centre for AI, located at University College Dublin, offers an exhaustive review of Large Language Model (LLM) fine-tuning. It structures the process into a seven-stage pipeline, detailing methodologies, best practices, and challenges from data preparation to model deployment and maintenance, consolidating a broad spectrum of existing knowledge.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) need adaptation to specific tasks and domains to achieve optimal utility, as pre-trained models are general-purpose.
The process of fine-tuning LLMs is complex, involving diverse methodologies, significant resource constraints, and a rapidly evolving landscape.
There is a need for a consolidated, comprehensive guide that integrates theoretical insights with practical applications and best practices for LLM fine-tuning.
Method: The paper conducts a comprehensive analysis of LLM fine-tuning techniques, covering theoretical foundations, practical strategies, and challenges.
A structured, seven-stage fine-tuning pipeline is introduced to guide users through the entire lifecycle of adapting LLMs.
Detailed comparisons of various fine-tuning methods, evaluation techniques, deployment strategies, and industrial platforms are presented.
Results: A seven-stage fine-tuning pipeline was developed, providing a systematic roadmap from dataset preparation to ongoing monitoring and maintenance.

The review consolidated knowledge on key fine-tuning techniques, including a thorough examination of Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods and advanced alignment approaches like DPO and ORPO.

An extensive overview of industrial fine-tuning platforms and frameworks was provided, along with an identification of open challenges such as scalability, ethical considerations, and future research directions.
Takeaways: High-quality and well-prepared data are foundational for effective fine-tuning, impacting subsequent model performance.
Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods like LoRA, QLoRA, and DoRA are crucial for adapting LLMs efficiently, overcoming computational constraints while often maintaining performance.
Beyond traditional metrics, comprehensive evaluation of fine-tuned LLMs requires considering factuality, context relevance, and critical safety benchmarks to ensure trustworthy deployment.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.12528.Title: Show-o: One Single Transformer to Unify Multimodal Understanding and Generation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.12528.Summary: Show-o, developed by Show Lab at NUS and ByteDance, presents a single transformer capable of unifying multimodal understanding and generation by adaptively combining autoregressive modeling for text and discrete diffusion for images. The model achieves competitive performance across various vision-language benchmarks with only 1.3 billion parameters and significantly improves image generation efficiency with fewer sampling steps.
Problem: Existing unified multimodal models typically rely on fragmented architectures with multiple specialized 'expert' components, leading to increased complexity and redundancy.

Prior single-transformer approaches for multimodal unification, like Chameleon, suffered from inefficient image generation due to fully autoregressive modeling requiring a prohibitively large number of sampling steps.

There was a need for a truly unified foundational model that could intelligently adapt its modeling approach (e.g., sequential for text, parallel denoising for images) to different modalities within a single coherent architecture.
Method: Show-o is built upon a single pre-trained Large Language Model (LLM) backbone, expanded with unified discrete tokenization for both text and images, allowing for a shared vocabulary.

An innovative 'Omni-Attention' mechanism dynamically switches between causal attention for text tokens and full attention for image tokens, enabling adaptive processing within the unified transformer.

The model integrates two distinct training objectives: Next Token Prediction (NTP) for autoregressive text tasks and Mask Token Prediction (MTP) for discrete diffusion-based image generation, combining them into a single training pipeline.
Results: Achieved comparable multimodal understanding performance to dedicated understanding-only models (e.g., LLaVA-v1.5-Phi-1.5) and outperformed or matched larger unified models across various benchmarks (POPE, MME, VQAv2, GQA) with only 1.3B parameters.
Demonstrated superior text-to-image generation quality, achieving a FID-30K of 9.24 on MSCOCO and an overall GenEval score of 0.68, outperforming several larger generation-only and unified models.

Natively supports novel mixed-modality applications like text-guided image inpainting, extrapolation, and interleaved video keyframe generation without specific fine-tuning, showcasing its versatility.
Takeaways: A single transformer can effectively unify multimodal understanding and generation by adaptively applying different optimal modeling paradigms (autoregressive for text, discrete diffusion for images).
This adaptive, unified architecture significantly enhances efficiency in image generation, requiring approximately 20 times fewer sampling steps compared to fully autoregressive models.
By leveraging a pre-trained LLM as its foundation, the model can inherently encode text conditional information and maintain strong language capabilities while learning robust cross-modal alignment.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.11039.Title: Transfusion: Predict the Next Token and Diffuse Images with One Multi-Modal Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.11039.Summary: Transfusion introduces a unified AI model capable of both text generation and high-quality image synthesis by directly processing continuous image representations alongside text tokens. The framework eliminates the information loss associated with quantizing continuous data, outperforming quantization-based multi-modal models in scaling efficiency and achieving image quality comparable to specialized diffusion models like DALL-E 2 and Stable Diffusion XL.
Problem: Current AI systems excel at single modalities (e.g., LMs for text, diffusion models for images) but struggle to integrate both discrete and continuous data types within a unified framework.
Existing multi-modal approaches either quantize continuous data, leading to information loss and quality degradation, or rely on complex tool integration of separate, specialized models.
The challenge lies in reconciling the distinct processing paradigms for discrete (next token prediction) and continuous (denoising) data within a single, coherent architecture.
Method: Transfusion introduces a mixed-modal representation where text is tokenized into discrete tokens and images are encoded into continuous latent patches, delimited by special tokens.
A single transformer backbone processes these mixed-modal sequences, employing dual processing modes: standard language modeling for text and diffusion modeling for image regions.

The architecture uses shared transformer core with modality-specific components (embeddings for text, U-Net components for images) and mixed attention patterns (causal for text, bidirectional for images).
Results: Transfusion models demonstrate superior scaling behavior and achieve text perplexity parity with less computational resources compared to quantization-based models like Chameleon.
The 7B parameter Transfusion model generates images comparable in quality to specialized diffusion models such as DALL-E 2 and Stable Diffusion XL, while simultaneously performing text generation.
The model exhibits capabilities in both text-to-image generation and various image editing tasks (e.g., object removal, replacement, style transfer) after fine-tuning.
Takeaways: Avoiding quantization for continuous data (images) within a unified model preserves information and leads to higher quality image generation.

A single transformer architecture can effectively process both discrete text tokens (with causal attention) and continuous image patches (with bidirectional attention for images) by employing a combined loss function.
U-Net components, when integrated around the transformer, and bidirectional attention within image regions are crucial for achieving high-quality image generation performance.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.10787.Title: Lightweight Modular Parameter-Efficient Tuning for Open-Vocabulary Object Detection
https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.10787.Summary: UniProj-Det presents a lightweight modular framework for Open-Vocabulary Object Detection training, utilizing a small, shared Universal Projection module and learnable modality tokens while freezing large vision and language backbones. This approach achieves competitive or superior accuracy across phrase grounding, referring expression comprehension, and segmentation tasks, while reducing trainable parameters by over an order of magnitude (e.g., from 231.1M to 15.2M) and substantially lowering training GPU memory consumption.
Problem: State-of-the-art Open-Vocabulary Object Detection (OVD) models incur prohibitive computational costs (GPU hours, memory) due to fine-tuning all parameters of large vision-language backbones.
Existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods for OVD often suffer from sensitivity to layer selection for adaptation and can introduce non-trivial inference overhead.
A need for more accessible, scalable, and environmentally friendly OVD solutions that do not compromise on performance for resource-constrained environments.
Method: UniProj-Det fully freezes pretrained visual and text encoders, introducing a small, trainable Universal Projection (UP) module that adapts features for OVD tasks.
Learnable modality tokens are integrated with encoder outputs before the UP module, enabling a single shared projection to effectively process both visual and textual features.
UniProj-Detv2, an enhanced variant, incorporates a lightweight cross-fusion stage (linear projection and few-head cross-attention) before the UP module to facilitate early cross-modal interactions.
Results: UniProj-Detv2 achieved 57.1% Pr@0.5 and 53.9% mIoU on PhraseCut referring expression segmentation, outperforming fully fine-tuned baselines like MDETR (53.1% mIoU) and GLIP (52.8% mIoU).
The framework drastically reduced trainable parameters from 231.1M (full fine-tuning) to 15.2M for UniProj-Det and 15.6M for UniProj-Detv2, representing over an order of magnitude reduction.
Peak GPU memory during training was significantly reduced (e.g., from 23.4GB for MDETR to 17.5GB for UniProj-Det), with only marginal increases in FLOPs and competitive inference latency.
Takeaways: Completely freezing large pretrained backbones and relying on a minimal Universal Projection module with modality-aware tokens can achieve strong OVD performance with significantly reduced training costs.
Learnable modality tokens are critical for a shared, modality-agnostic projection module to effectively differentiate and process inputs from different modalities (vision and language).
A moderately deep (e.g., 4-layer) Universal Projection module provides an optimal balance between accuracy and computational efficiency, with simple additive feature fusion proving highly effective.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.07666.Title: Model Merging in LLMs, MLLMs, and Beyond: Methods, Theories, Applications and Opportunities
https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.07666.Summary: A comprehensive survey of model merging techniques provides a novel two-phase taxonomy for classification and extensively reviews existing methods, their applications across large language models, multimodal models, and other machine learning subfields, alongside theoretical insights and future research directions.
Problem: The absence of a systematic and comprehensive review of model merging, despite its rapid evolution and increasing adoption across various ML fields.
The need for efficient, often data-free, knowledge integration from multiple pre-trained machine learning models to avoid prohibitive computational costs and data requirements.
Challenges in effectively combining the strengths of an increasing number of specialized, open-source model checkpoints.
Method: A systematic and comprehensive survey offering a novel, two-phase taxonomic framework to classify model merging methods into "Pre-Merging" and "During-Merging" strategies.

Extensive review of methodologies, including merger-friendly fine-tuning, architecture transformation, weight alignment, basic averaging, weighted merging, subspace methods, optimization-based techniques, routing-based approaches, and post-calibration.
A detailed analysis of model merging's applications across foundation models (LLMs, MLLMs, visual generative models) and over ten diverse machine learning subfields.
Results: The establishment of a novel, two-phase taxonomic framework successfully categorizes and clarifies diverse model merging techniques.

Model merging is shown to be widely applicable, enhancing capabilities like human value alignment in LLMs, multimodal fusion in MLLMs, and style mixing in visual generative models, while also mitigating catastrophic forgetting in continual learning.

Empirical results indicate that advanced merging techniques significantly outperform basic methods, but a performance gap often remains when compared to individually fine-tuned expert models, especially for complex scenarios or numerous tasks.
Takeaways: Model merging methods can be systematically categorized into two phases: "Pre-Merging" techniques that prepare models for combination, and "During-Merging" strategies for parameter aggregation.

Model merging acts as a versatile and efficient knowledge integration paradigm, applicable to foundation models (LLMs, MLLMs, visual generative models) and various ML subfields to enhance capabilities or address specific challenges.
Despite empirical advancements, the theoretical understanding of model merging remains constrained, lacking a unified framework, especially for heterogeneous cross-task merging.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.05674.Title: PS-TTL: Prototype-based Soft-labels and Test-Time Learning for Few-shot Object Detection
https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.05674.Summary: PS-TTL enhances few-shot object detection by enabling detectors to adapt to novel classes during the testing phase without additional human annotation. The framework leverages a test-time learning module for pseudo-labeling and a prototype-based soft-label strategy for utilizing low-confidence predictions, achieving state-of-the-art results on PASCAL VOC and MS COCO benchmarks.
Problem: Few-shot object detection (FSOD) struggles to accurately model the data distribution of novel classes due to extremely limited labeled examples.
Current fine-tuning based FSOD methods often overfit due to insufficient novel class samples, leading to poor generalization.
Existing approaches either generate synthetic data that differs from real distributions or rely on unrealistic assumptions about novel instances in base data.
Method: Introduces PS-TTL, a framework that employs Test-Time Learning (TTL) using a mean-teacher network to generate pseudo-labels for unlabeled test data.
Implements a Prototype-based Soft-labels (PS) strategy that leverages low-confidence detector predictions by assigning soft-labels based on cosine similarity to category prototypes.
Continuously adapts the detector to novel class distributions during the testing phase by training a student network on both few-shot labeled data and pseudo-labeled test data.
Results: PS-TTL achieves state-of-the-art performance on the PASCAL VOC dataset across various few-shot settings (1, 2, 3, 5, and 10 shots).
The framework outperforms existing methods on the more challenging MS COCO dataset, demonstrating its effectiveness.
Performance consistently improves with increasing training iterations, showing particular gains in extremely low-shot scenarios (1-shot and 2-shot).
Takeaways: Adapting the object detector during the testing phase using unlabeled test data can effectively address the data scarcity challenge for novel classes.
Leveraging low-confidence predictions by assigning them soft-labels based on similarity to category prototypes improves learning from limited data.
Dynamically updating category prototypes during test-time learning allows the model to better capture evolving understandings of novel classes.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21311.Title: EUDA: An Efficient Unsupervised Domain Adaptation via Self-Supervised Vision Transformer
https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21311.Summary: A framework for efficient unsupervised domain adaptation, EUDA, leverages a frozen self-supervised DINOv2 Vision Transformer and a simplified bottleneck with a synergistic domain alignment loss. This approach delivers competitive classification accuracy across multiple benchmarks while reducing trainable parameters by up to 99.7% compared to other ViT-based state-of-the-art models.
Problem: Deep learning models struggle with performance degradation when applied to new target domains due to discrepancies in data distribution (domain shift).
Current state-of-the-art UDA methods, especially those based on Vision Transformers, are computationally intensive and possess a large number of trainable parameters.
This high complexity restricts their practical deployment in resource-constrained environments and on edge devices.
Method: Developed EUDA, an Unsupervised Domain Adaptation framework, by employing a pre-trained DINOv2 Vision Transformer as a frozen feature extractor.
Designed a simplified and adjustable bottleneck of fully connected layers to refine features and minimize trainable parameters.
Utilized a Synergistic Domain Alignment Loss (SDAL) that combines Cross-Entropy for source classification and Maximum Mean Discrepancy for robust domain feature alignment.
Results: EUDA consistently surpassed ResNet-based UDA models and achieved competitive performance with state-of-the-art ViT-based methods across four major benchmarks.
Demonstrated a substantial reduction in trainable parameters, ranging from 42% to 99.7% fewer than other ViT-based SOTA UDA models.
The Synergistic Domain Alignment Loss improved performance by up to 8.1% on VisDA-2017 compared to source-only baselines, validating the MMD component.
Takeaways: Freezing a self-supervised Vision Transformer (DINOv2) allows leveraging robust, generalized features while significantly reducing trainable parameters in UDA.
A simplified bottleneck layer combined with a synergistic loss function can effectively align features and achieve competitive domain adaptation performance.
Explicitly balancing classification accuracy on the source domain with maximum mean discrepancy for feature alignment is key to effective unsupervised domain transfer.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.19666.Title: Take A Step Back: Rethinking the Two Stages in Visual Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.19666.Summary: Researchers from Shanghai Jiao Tong University propose a two-stage framework for visual reasoning, disentangling task-specific symbolization from a shared, generalizable reasoner. This approach allows a simple MLP reasoner to achieve performance comparable to state-of-the-art ad-hoc models across diverse visual reasoning benchmarks, demonstrating improved generalization on out-of-domain tasks when trained multi-domain.
Problem: Current end-to-end visual reasoning models entangle recognition and reasoning, leading to poor generalization and susceptibility to data biases.
Existing methods struggle with efficiency and often remain confined to specific datasets, failing to achieve broad cross-domain generalization.
Multi-Modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) perform well on text but still struggle with complex visual reasoning tasks requiring precise logical operations.
Method: A two-stage framework is proposed, explicitly separating task-specific symbolization (via dedicated encoders) from a shared logical reasoning component.
The framework uses separate encoders for different data modalities and tasks, feeding their symbolic outputs into a single, unified reasoner.
Comprehensive experiments systematically evaluate optimal symbolization depth, suitable reasoner architectures, and the generalization capabilities of the shared reasoner via multi-domain training.
Results: The proposed "Shared-Reasoner-Only" architecture consistently outperformed other design paradigms, validating the core hypothesis of separating symbolization and sharing reasoning.

A simple Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) reasoner, when combined with task-specific symbol encoders, achieved performance comparable to or surpassing "lite" ad-hoc state-of-the-art models across various visual reasoning benchmarks.
Training the shared reasoner on an increasing number of diverse datasets consistently improved its generalization performance on unseen, out-of-domain tasks, confirming the "approximation principle."
While powerful, MiniGPT-4 struggled with precise logical reasoning in complex visual puzzles compared to the MLP reasoner, highlighting limitations of current MLLMs in this specific area.
Takeaways: Disentangling symbolization (perception) from logical reasoning leads to superior generalization capabilities in visual reasoning systems.
The optimal depth and design for the symbolization stage vary significantly across different visual tasks, necessitating task-specific encoders.
Surprisingly, a simple Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) can serve as an effective and efficient shared reasoner when provided with well-formed symbolic inputs.
Training a shared reasoner on diverse, cross-domain datasets significantly enhances its ability to generalize to unseen, out-of-domain tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.15173.Title: Rethinking Domain Adaptation and Generalization in the Era of CLIP
https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.15173.Summary: A framework rethinks domain adaptation and generalization for CLIP models by leveraging domain-specific prompts, pseudo-labeling on target data, and parameter-efficient tuning to reduce reliance on labeled source data. It demonstrates improved zero-shot recognition and enhanced generalization across various domains.
Problem: Performance degradation of computer vision models when encountering data distributions different from their training data (domain shift).
Traditional domain adaptation methods often rely heavily on labeled source domain data to learn transferable features.
The assumptions underlying existing domain adaptation and generalization paradigms needed re-evaluation in the context of CLIP's strong pre-trained capabilities.
Method: Enhance CLIP's zero-shot recognition by incorporating domain-specific knowledge into text prompts, such as 'a sketch of a [class]'.

Adapt CLIP through pseudo-labeling based self-training on unlabeled target domain data, reducing reliance on source data, combined with parameter-efficient Task Residual Learning (TaskRes) for tuning.

Introduce a label-free multi-source domain generalization framework that disentangles task residuals into domain-shared and domain-specific components during training, using only the shared component for inference on unseen domains.
Results: Domain-aware prompts improved CLIP's zero-shot recognition accuracy by several percentage points across various domains, including Office-Home and DomainNet.
Pseudo-labeling based self-training achieved competitive or superior performance compared to traditional unsupervised domain adaptation methods, especially with limited source data.
The label-free multi-source domain generalization framework demonstrated superior performance against baseline methods, effectively leveraging multiple unlabeled domains to enhance generalization.
Takeaways: CLIP's extensive pre-training provides inherently domain-robust representations, shifting the focus of domain adaptation from learning invariant features to efficient adaptation strategies.
Incorporating domain-specific knowledge into text prompts significantly enhances CLIP's zero-shot recognition by providing crucial contextual guidance.
Effective adaptation of CLIP can prioritize the utilization of unlabeled target domain data over a heavy reliance on labeled source domain data.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.14414.Title: System-1.x: Learning to Balance Fast and Slow Planning with Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.14414.Summary: A framework is introduced that allows large language models to dynamically balance between fast, intuitive System-1 planning and deliberate, explicit System-2 planning for complex tasks. This method achieves improved planning success rates and better generalization, especially under constrained computational budgets, compared to isolated planning approaches.
Problem: Existing LLM planners struggle with long-horizon tasks due to a lack of explicit search, leading to poor accuracy and robustness.
Current approaches are either fast but inaccurate (System-1) or accurate but computationally expensive (System-2), lacking a flexible balance between the two.
There is no systematic way for users to control the trade-off between computational cost and planning accuracy in LLM-based systems.
Method: A framework named System-1.x is introduced, comprising a Controller, a System-1 Planner, and a System-2 Planner, all fine-tuned on a single LLM.
The Controller decomposes planning problems into sub-goals and classifies each as "easy" or "hard," directing them to the System-1 or System-2 planner respectively.
Training data is automatically generated from gold search traces, incorporating a user-defined "hybridization factor" (x) that controls the balance between fast and slow planning during training.
Results: System-1.x achieved 70.4% valid plans in Maze Navigation, outperforming System-1 (48.7%) and truncated System-2 (37.2%) at matched computational budgets.
The framework demonstrated improved out-of-distribution generalization in Blocksworld, achieving 25% validity at low budgets where other methods neared 0%.

The "hybridization factor" allowed for controllable trade-offs, with a System-1.75 model achieving 75.7% validity compared to System-1.5's 70.4%, demonstrating adaptability to user-defined preferences for accuracy over compute.
Takeaways: Human-like dual-process cognition (fast intuition and slow deliberation) can be effectively applied to LLM-based planning by dynamically switching between planning modes.
Intelligent decomposition of complex problems into easier and harder sub-goals, coupled with dynamic resource allocation, improves planning efficiency and accuracy.
Controllability through a "hybridization factor" allows users to systematically balance the trade-off between computational cost and planning performance at both training and test time.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.13771.Title: Training-Free Model Merging for Multi-target Domain Adaptation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.13771.Summary: This paper introduces a training-free model merging technique for multi-target domain adaptation in semantic segmentation, overcoming the need for simultaneous access to all target domain data. The method leverages linear mode connectivity between domain-adapted models and proposes a principled approach to merge batch normalization statistics, achieving performance comparable to models trained with combined datasets.
Problem: Existing multi-target domain adaptation (MTDA) methods for semantic segmentation often require simultaneous access to data from all target domains during training.
This requirement is impractical due to data privacy concerns, large data transfer costs, and computational scalability issues for numerous domains.

Semantic segmentation models deployed in new environments experience significant performance degradation due to domain shift, posing challenges in safety-critical applications like autonomous driving.
Method: A two-stage pipeline is proposed: first, separate models are trained for each target domain using existing single-target domain adaptation (STDA) methods.
Second, these independently trained models are merged into a single unified model without accessing any original training data.
Model merging involves averaging the trainable layer parameters and merging the running statistics of batch normalization layers using a method based on Gaussian distribution assumptions.
Results: The merged model achieves performance comparable to models trained by combining all target datasets, despite not requiring simultaneous access to domain data during training.
The approach significantly outperforms previous MTDA methods that rely on explicit consistency training and provides better qualitative semantic segmentation outputs.
Both parameter merging and the proposed batch normalization buffer merging are essential components, with the method scaling effectively with an increasing number of target domains.
Takeaways: Domain-adapted models derived from the same pretrained weights exhibit linear mode connectivity, allowing for simple averaging of parameters without significant performance loss.
Batch normalization running statistics, which capture domain-specific characteristics, require a specialized merging approach based on Gaussian distribution assumptions for optimal performance.
Sharing identical pretrained weights is crucial for establishing the common optimization landscape that enables successful model merging.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.11464.Title: Crowd-SAM: SAM as a Smart Annotator for Object Detection in Crowded Scenes
https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.11464.Summary: Crowd-SAM introduces a framework that adapts the Segment Anything Model (SAM) and DINOv2 to serve as a smart annotator for object detection in crowded scenes, achieving performance comparable to fully-supervised methods using as few as 10 labeled images. This approach effectively resolves geometric ambiguities and efficiently generates high-quality object masks by integrating lightweight, learnable modules.
Problem: High annotation costs for object detection, particularly in 'crowded scenes' with numerous, often occluded objects, where manual labeling is time-consuming and expensive.
Existing object detectors and even foundation models like SAM struggle with accuracy and efficiency in highly occluded and dense environments, often producing part-level segments or false positives.
Traditional label-efficient methods often introduce complexity or do not specifically address the unique challenges of crowded scenes while requiring significant labeled data.
Method: Crowd-SAM integrates frozen SAM and DINOv2 foundation models with specialized, lightweight, and learnable modules to act as a smart annotator.
It generates class-specific prompts using a DINOv2-based semantic heatmap, trained with refined pseudo-labels derived from SAM with ground truth bounding box centers.

An Efficient Prompt Sampler (EPS) prunes redundant prompts for computational efficiency, while a Part-Whole Discrimination Network (PWD-Net) selects the best mask and distinguishes whole objects from parts or background noise in occluded scenarios.
Results: Crowd-SAM achieves 78.4% AP on the CrowdHuman dataset with only 10 labeled images, demonstrating performance comparable to state-of-the-art fully-supervised detectors.
On the OccHuman dataset for occluded pedestrian detection, it obtains 31.4% AP, outperforming the fully-supervised Pose2Seg by 9.2% AP.
Ablation studies confirm that the Part-Whole Discrimination Network is critical, contributing a 40% AP increase, and the DINOv2-based foreground location module improves AP by 7.4%.
Takeaways: Powerful pre-trained foundation models like SAM and DINOv2 can be effectively adapted for challenging downstream tasks with minimal task-specific training and few learnable parameters.
A dedicated discrimination network (PWD-Net) is indispensable for accurate mask selection in crowded scenes, crucial for addressing occlusion and part-whole ambiguity.
Efficient prompt sampling and semantic-guided prompt generation are essential for managing computational costs and improving recall in dense object environments.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.10490.Title: Learning Dynamics of LLM Finetuning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.10490.Summary: The paper presents a learning dynamics framework to analyze LLM fine-tuning, explaining phenomena like hallucination and text degeneration through a "squeezing effect" where negative gradients on unlikely tokens disproportionately boost already confident ones. A proposed "extend" SFT method, which trains on both preferred and rejected examples, mitigates this effect and improves alignment performance.
Problem: Understanding the step-wise evolution of LLM predictions during fine-tuning (SFT, DPO) beyond just end-state analysis.
Explaining counter-intuitive behaviors like hallucination, text degeneration, and confidence decay observed during Direct Preference Optimization (DPO).
Identifying underlying mechanisms behind the success or failure of different LLM alignment algorithms.
Method: Extends the "learning dynamics" framework to LLMs, decomposing gradient updates into Activation, empirical Neural Tangent Kernel (eNTK), and a loss-derived residual term.
Applies this framework to SFT and DPO, deriving specific update rules for each algorithm to analyze their impact on output probabilities.

Identifies and formally characterizes the "squeezing effect" to explain how negative gradients on low-probability tokens lead to probability mass being disproportionately pushed to the already most confident token.
Results: Empirical analyses confirm that SFT increases confidence in target responses and unrelated preferred responses, while DPO causes a general confidence decay, validating the proposed dynamics.
The "squeezing effect" is shown to be a key mechanism explaining text degeneration and the observed confidence dynamics in DPO.

A proposed "extend" SFT method, which includes training on rejected responses during SFT, effectively mitigates the squeezing effect and leads to demonstrably higher win rates in LLM evaluations, improving alignment.
Takeaways: SFT typically pulls up preferred response confidence but also indirectly increases confidence in preferred responses from *other* training examples, explaining a form of hallucination.

Off-policy DPO leads to a general *decrease* in confidence across most responses due to the "squeezing effect," where large negative gradients on unlikely tokens disproportionately boost already confident ones.
On-policy DPO variants perform better because their rejected responses are sampled from the current model, residing in higher probability regions and thus mitigating the extreme squeezing effect.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.06135.Title: ANOLE: An Open, Autoregressive, Native Large Multimodal Models for Interleaved Image-Text Generation
