https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.06135.Summary: ANOLE is an open, autoregressive, native large multimodal model that enables interleaved image and text generation by efficiently facilitating these capabilities from Meta AI’s open-source Chameleon. It required fine-tuning fewer than 40 million parameters on approximately 6,000 images in just 30 minutes, producing high-quality and coherent multimodal outputs.
Problem: Many open-source LMMs lacked native integration, relying on adapters or external components for multimodal understanding and generation.
Existing open-source LMMs capable of generation were often limited to single-modal outputs or relied on complex external diffusion models for visual generation.
Meta AI's open-source Chameleon, a promising token-based model, did not support image or general multimodal generation despite its architecture
Method: Adopted Chameleon's early-fusion, token-based, autoregressive architecture, processing both image and text as discrete tokens in a unified transformer.
Employed a data and parameter-efficient fine-tuning strategy, freezing most of the base model and only fine-tuning image token logits in the output head.
Achieved high efficiency by using a minimal dataset (~6,000 images) for fine-tuning, completed in around 30 minutes on 8 A100 GPUs
Results: Demonstrated high-quality text-to-image generation, accurately reflecting prompts and showcasing versatility across diverse scenes.
Produced coherent interleaved image-text sequences with seamless integration between visual and textual elements, enhancing information conveyance.
Achieved these generative capabilities by fine-tuning fewer than 40 million parameters on approximately 6,000 images in about 30 minutes
Takeaways: Complex multimodal generation capabilities can be efficiently unlocked from pre-trained LMMs with minimal data and parameter fine-tuning.
Purely token-based, autoregressive architectures are effective for unified multimodal modeling and interleaved image-text generation without external diffusion models.
Open-sourcing models and training frameworks significantly democratizes access to advanced multimodal AI, fostering broader research and development.
The efficiency of fine-tuning indicates a latent potential within large pre-trained models to acquire complex functionalities with surprisingly low resource requirements

https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01400.Title: GalLoP: Learning Global and Local Prompts for Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01400.Summary: GalLoP introduces a prompt learning method for Vision-Language Models that integrates global and local visual features to achieve superior performance. The approach consistently improves few-shot classification accuracy by an average of +1.5 percentage points while simultaneously enhancing robustness for domain generalization and out-of-distribution detection.
Problem: Existing prompt learning methods for Vision-Language Models often face a trade-off between classification accuracy and robustness, requiring a compromise in performance.

Local visual features from pre-trained VLMs (e.g., CLIP) are underutilized and suboptimal for fine-grained tasks due to global pre-training and a lack of specific text-vision alignment for local regions.
Ensembling multiple prompts frequently suffers from a lack of diversity, leading to redundant information and limited improvements in combined predictive power.
Method:
GalLoP learns specialized global and local prompts, incorporating a sparse local similarity (top-
k) mechanism and a learned linear projection to make local features more discriminative and aligned with text.
It enforces diversity among global prompts through 'prompt dropout,' selecting a random subset of prompts for each training batch to encourage learning complementary aspects.

Local prompts are diversified via 'multiscale training,' where each prompt specializes in a different number of top-
k relevant visual regions, capturing varied granularities of information.
Results: GalLoP achieved an average of +1.5 percentage points higher Top-1 accuracy over 11 diverse datasets compared to previous state-of-the-art prompt learning methods.

The method demonstrated improved robustness, outperforming specialized domain generalization methods by +0.5pt on average and dedicated OOD detection methods by up to -2.9pt FPR95, while maintaining higher in-distribution accuracy.

Ablation studies validated that sparse local feature selection (up to +18.4pt accuracy gain), linear projection for local alignment (+10pt accuracy gain), prompt dropout, and multiscale training are critical for GalLoP's superior performance.
Takeaways: Effective integration of local visual features in VLM prompt learning requires both sparsity (selecting relevant regions) and explicit realignment with textual semantics to overcome limitations of global pre-training.
Enhancing diversity across an ensemble of global and local prompts is crucial for achieving high performance in both accuracy and robustness simultaneously.
Simple regularization techniques, such as prompt dropout and multiscale training, can effectively induce prompt diversity without needing complex architectures or explicit diversity losses.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.19934.Title: From the Least to the Most: Building a Plug-and-Play Visual Reasoner via Data Synthesis
https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.19934.Summary: This paper presents a method for generating high-quality, multi-step visual reasoning data using a 'least-to-most' synthesis approach, primarily leveraging open-source models. The synthesized data then trains a plug-and-play visual reasoner, which consistently enhances the reasoning capabilities of existing Vision-Language Models across diverse visual question answering benchmarks.
Problem: Current Vision-Language Models (VLMs) struggle with multi-step visual reasoning due to the scarcity of training data that explicitly outlines sequential reasoning paths (similar to Chain-of-Thought for LLMs).
VLMs lack the ability to dynamically manipulate or focus on specific visual regions and objects during intermediate reasoning steps, hindering complex visual deduction.

Existing methods for enhancing VLM reasoning often rely on expensive, proprietary Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) for top-down data generation, leading to issues with cost, reproducibility, and data quality.
Method: Introduces a 'Least-to-Most Visual Reasoning' paradigm where a visual reasoner decomposes complex visual questions into simpler sub-questions and iteratively invokes specialized tools (Grounding, Highlight, OCR, Answer) to resolve them.

Proposes a 'Least-to-Most Synthesis' pipeline, a bottom-up data generation method that automatically constructs multi-step visual reasoning data by identifying entities, building multi-level nodes (single-entity, entity-group, whole-image), and synthesizing questions and reasoning paths using fine-tuned open-source LLMs.

Constructs the large-scale VIsual REasOning (VIREO) dataset (50K examples, with a 500K version released) using the synthesis method and fine-tunes an LLaVA-1.5-7B model on it to serve as a general-purpose, plug-and-play visual reasoner.
Results: The Reasoner consistently improved performance for four representative VLMs (BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, LLaVA) across various VQA benchmarks, with absolute gains up to 38.96% on TallyQA-C.

A human study confirmed the high quality of the synthesized VIREO dataset, with all 200 sampled examples rated as correct across sub-question fidelity, tool argument accuracy, and main question coherence.

Ablation studies demonstrated that the removal of any specialized tool (OCR, Highlight, Grounding) negatively impacted performance, affirming the necessity of multi-tool integration for robust visual reasoning.
Takeaways: A bottom-up, open-source-reliant data synthesis approach can effectively generate high-quality, multi-step visual reasoning data (VIREO dataset), validated by human evaluation.
Complex visual reasoning tasks benefit significantly from the synergistic application of modular, specialized tools (Grounding, Highlight, OCR) integrated into a reasoning framework.
A fine-tuned visual reasoner can act as a 'plug-and-play' module, universally enhancing the reasoning capabilities of diverse existing Vision-Language Models without requiring their re-training.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.18925.Title: Selective Vision is the Challenge for Visual Reasoning: A Benchmark for Visual Argument Understanding
https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.18925.Summary: Researchers from Yonsei University and collaborators introduced VisArgs, a new dataset and benchmark to evaluate AI's capacity for visual argument understanding. Experiments on VisArgs show that current multimodal AI models struggle with "selective vision," identifying argumentatively relevant visual cues (e.g., GPT-4-O at 79.50% accuracy compared to human 98.00% for premise identification), while basic visual grounding is more robust.
Problem: Current AI models struggle to move beyond factual recognition to genuinely interpret complex, persuasive visual arguments.
Existing multimodal benchmarks primarily focus on descriptive tasks or simple factual reasoning, lacking a resource for visual argument understanding.
AI systems lack the ability to discern contextually relevant visual information within an image, often failing to identify implicit knowledge or persuasive intent.
Method: Developed VisArgs, a novel dataset of 1,611 images (ads and cartoons), providing structured annotations including visual premises with bounding boxes, commonsense premises, conclusions, and argumentation trees.
Employed a hybrid human-AI annotation strategy, leveraging GPT-4-O for initial premise and structure generation, followed by extensive human review and visual grounding.
Proposed three diagnostic tasks—Premise Localization, Premise Identification, and Conclusion Deduction—to systematically evaluate different facets of visual argument understanding.
Results: AI models achieve reasonable performance on basic visual grounding (e.g., 86.43% accuracy on closed-set premise localization), but struggle with generating bounding boxes for semantically complex premise regions (e.g., 54.98% IoU accuracy for open-set).

A substantial performance gap exists in premise identification, particularly with semantic negative samples, where top models like GPT-4-O achieve 79.50% accuracy compared to 98.00% for human performance.
Incrementally providing ground-truth visual premises significantly boosts conclusion deduction performance across models, with LLaVA-1.5 showing a 17.8% BERTScore gain when visual premises are added.
Takeaways: "Selective vision" – the ability to identify and focus on argumentatively relevant visual cues – is the primary bottleneck for AI in understanding visual arguments.
True comprehension of visual arguments necessitates discerning the contextual relevance of visual stimuli, rather than mere perceptual recognition.
Current AI models often rely on common word associations rather than sophisticated reasoning about visual object relevance in an argumentative context.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.18505.Title: Mental Modeling of Reinforcement Learning Agents by Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.18505.Summary: An empirical study investigates the capability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to construct "mental models" of reinforcement learning (RL) agents by inferring agent policies and environmental dynamics from interaction history. Findings indicate LLMs can partially model simpler tasks, such as predicting agent actions in MountainCar with 86.18% accuracy, but performance degrades with increasing task complexity and requires careful context provisioning, with explicit dynamics principles significantly improving understanding.
Problem: While Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate advanced linguistic reasoning, their inherent capacity to interpret and model decision-making agents operating in dynamic, physical or simulated environments remains underexplored.

Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents often operate as black boxes, making their behavior difficult for humans to understand, trust, and debug, posing a significant challenge for Explainable Reinforcement Learning (XRL).
There is a lack of empirical investigation into whether off-the-shelf LLMs can inherently construct "mental models" of an agent's policy and environmental dynamics solely from interaction history.
Method: The LLM-Xavier evaluation framework is introduced, assessing LLMs' agent mental modelling capabilities within Markov Decision Process (MDP) contexts using in-context learning.

Prompts are meticulously constructed with a system-level description of the RL task, a subset of the agent's interaction history (state-action-reward tuples), and specific evaluation questions, employing Chain-of-Thought (CoT) for step-by-step reasoning.

Evaluation metrics are defined for both "Actions Understanding" (agent's policy) and "Dynamics Understanding" (environment's transition function), covering prediction and deduction tasks for discrete and continuous spaces.
Results: LLMs demonstrated the ability to predict agent behaviors in simpler tasks with accuracies significantly above baseline, such as Llama3-70b achieving 86.18% for next action prediction in MountainCar.
Agent mental modeling capabilities consistently declined with increasing task complexity, particularly for environments with larger state and action spaces like Acrobot and Fetch tasks.

The optimal interaction history length for in-context learning exhibited a saturation point, with excessively long histories sometimes degrading performance, especially for dynamics predictions, and qualitative analysis revealed recurring errors in task understanding, logical reasoning, and physical/mathematical comprehension.
Takeaways: Large Language Models can establish partial mental models for simpler reinforcement learning tasks by leveraging common-sense knowledge and inferring from interaction history.

The processing of interaction history for in-context learning is non-linear, with benefits saturating and sometimes degrading with excessive length, and LLMs surprisingly predict absolute continuous actions better than binned categories.

Providing explicit "dynamics principles" (e.g., equations) in the system prompt significantly enhances LLMs' ability to understand both agent behavior and environmental transitions, indicating their capacity to integrate structured physical knowledge.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.17639.Title: Mitigate the Gap: Investigating Approaches for Improving Cross-Modal Alignment in CLIP
https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.17639.Summary: AlignCLIP improves the cross-modal alignment in CLIP by addressing the modality gap, where image and text embeddings for the same concept remain distant. It achieves better alignment through shared encoder parameters and a novel semantically-regularized intra-modality separation loss, leading to enhanced performance across zero-shot classification, robustness benchmarks, and multi-modal retrieval tasks.
Problem: The Contrastive Language–Image Pre-training (CLIP) model exhibits a "modality gap," where image and text embeddings for the same semantic concept do not perfectly align, populating distinct sub-regions of the embedding space.
This modality gap results in a sparse and disconnected embedding space, hindering effective cross-modal understanding and potentially limiting downstream task performance.
Existing solutions often involve altering training data or using naive isomorphic translations that may distort semantic structure, rather than intrinsically improving the representation space.
Method: Introduced SharedCLIP, an architectural modification where the transformer encoder and projection layer are shared between vision and language modalities to compel a more unified mapping function.
Developed an Intra-Modality Separation (IMSep) objective, a vision-to-vision contrastive loss, to explicitly regularize distances within the image modality.
Integrated semantic regularization into IMSep using a pre-trained sentence encoder to prevent the erroneous separation of semantically similar images, thus preserving the embedding space's integrity.
Results: AlignCLIP achieved the best cross-modal alignment scores (0.62-0.67), reducing the average angle between paired multi-modal samples to 47 degrees, a substantial improvement over CLIP's 61-68 degrees.

Consistently outperformed original CLIP in zero-shot image classification, showing up to 8% (Top-1) improvement on CIFAR-10 and about 8% (Top-1) on CIFAR-100, and also improved performance with linear probing.

Demonstrated enhanced robustness to natural distribution shifts, achieving 1-2% improvements in Top1 and Top5 accuracy across ImageNetV2, ImageNet-R, ImageNet-A, and ImageNetSketch datasets compared to CLIP.
Takeaways: Sharing parameters between vision and language encoders (SharedCLIP) significantly reduces the modality gap, suggesting that a unified architectural backbone naturally fosters better multi-modal alignment.

Explicitly enforcing intra-modality separation for image embeddings, combined with semantic regularization (AlignCLIP's IMSep), is crucial for creating a more coherent and globally meaningful embedding space.
The cross-modal objective provides sufficient supervision for text embeddings, as explicitly enforcing intra-modality separation on text embeddings can be detrimental to performance.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.14852.Title: Is A Picture Worth A Thousand Words? Delving Into Spatial Reasoning for Vision Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.14852.Summary: Researchers from the University of Wisconsin–Madison, Salesforce AI Research, and Microsoft Research introduced SpatialEval, a benchmark designed to assess spatial reasoning in Vision-Language Models (VLMs). The study found that current VLMs often struggle with spatial reasoning from visual inputs alone, frequently relying more on textual information even when images are present, and sometimes perform better without visual input or with noisy images.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) demonstrate limited and inadequately explored proficiency in spatial understanding and reasoning.
Existing benchmarks for LLMs and multi-modal models predominantly focus on textual or relational reasoning, lacking systematic evaluation of diverse spatial reasoning aspects.

There is a need to systematically investigate the assumption that providing visual input inherently improves VLM performance across all types of tasks, especially those requiring detailed visual spatial understanding.
Method: Researchers developed SpatialEval, a novel and comprehensive benchmark comprising four diverse tasks (Spatial-Map, Maze-Nav, Spatial-Grid, Spatial-Real) to assess spatial reasoning abilities.

SpatialEval is designed to support three distinct input modalities for each problem: Text-only (TQA), Vision-only (VQA), and redundant Vision-text (VTQA), enabling systematic study of modality impact.
A wide range of state-of-the-art open-source and proprietary LLMs and VLMs were systematically evaluated on SpatialEval to analyze their performance and identify limitations.
Results: Most VLMs, when provided with Vision-only (VQA) input for synthetic spatial tasks, performed at levels similar to or below random guessing.

VLMs with Vision-only (VQA) input often underperformed their LLM counterparts (TQA format) with the same language backbone; for example, LLaVA-v1.6-Mistral-7B (VQA) was 15% worse than Mistral-7B (TQA) on Spatial-Grid.

VLM performance on spatial reasoning tasks often improved when the original image was entirely removed (TQA for VLM) or replaced with Gaussian noise/random mismatched images, particularly when textual information was sufficient.
Takeaways: Current VLMs often struggle with complex spatial reasoning when relying solely on visual information, sometimes performing at or below random chance.
VLMs tend to prioritize textual information for spatial reasoning, with performance sometimes improving when images are removed or replaced with noise, particularly if sufficient text is provided.
The current paradigm of "translating" visual input into a language space is insufficient for robust spatial reasoning, suggesting a need for fundamentally new architectures.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.14830.Title: CLIP-Decoder : ZeroShot Multilabel Classification using Multimodal CLIP Aligned Representation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.14830.Summary: The CLIP-Decoder integrates CLIP-aligned representations into a transformer-decoder architecture, achieving state-of-the-art performance in multi-label zero-shot and generalized zero-shot classification. It improved mean Average Precision by 2.3% and 3.9% on the NUS-WIDE dataset for ZSL and GZSL respectively, compared to previous best methods.
Problem: Existing multi-label classification methods struggle to classify images into categories for which no training data has been provided (Zero-Shot Learning, ZSL).
A significant 'semantic gap' exists between visual features and textual label descriptions, hindering effective generalization to unseen classes.
Obtaining exhaustive labeled training data for every possible category in real-world multi-label classification is often impractical or impossible.
Method: A novel CLIP-Decoder architecture is proposed, combining a TResNet image encoder, a CLIP text encoder, and a transformer-decoder head.
The method leverages CLIP's multimodal representations by projecting image and text embeddings into a shared semantic dimension, guided by prompt engineering for class labels.
A multi-scale weighted joint loss function is employed to optimize both classification accuracy and the alignment of vision-language representations.
Results: The CLIP-Decoder achieved an mAP of 33.4 in Zero-Shot Learning (ZSL) on NUS-WIDE, an absolute increase of 2.3% over the previous best method (ML-Decoder).
In Generalized Zero-Shot Learning (GZSL), it attained an mAP of 23.8 on NUS-WIDE, marking an absolute increase of 3.9% compared to the previous state-of-the-art (ML-Decoder).
Ablation studies confirmed that both the use of CLIP embeddings and the combined vision-language alignment loss incrementally contributed to improved mean Average Precision and F1 scores.
Takeaways: Pre-trained vision-language models like CLIP can effectively bridge the semantic gap in zero-shot multi-label classification by providing robust, aligned multimodal representations.
Explicitly optimizing for both classification and multimodal alignment via a weighted joint loss function significantly enhances performance in ZSL and GZSL settings.

Integrating CLIP-aligned text embeddings as queries into a transformer-decoder structure (building on ML-Decoder) allows for improved contextual and visual understanding, leading to better generalization.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.10973.Title: ExPLoRA: Parameter-Efficient Extended Pre-Training to Adapt Vision Transformers under Domain Shifts
https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.10973.Summary: ExPLoRA introduces a parameter-efficient extended pre-training methodology that effectively adapts Vision Transformers to new visual domains. This approach substantially reduces computational costs by 8-10x and uses significantly fewer trainable parameters, while achieving state-of-the-art or highly competitive performance across a diverse range of benchmarks.
Problem: Pre-training Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) from scratch on new, domain-specific datasets is computationally expensive, requiring vast GPU resources and time.
VFMs pre-trained on natural images often experience significant performance degradation when applied directly to visually distinct domains like satellite or medical imagery.

Existing Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods primarily adapt models for *supervised* downstream tasks, rather than addressing the fundamental domain shift during unsupervised pre-training itself.
Method: ExPLoRA employs a two-stage process: parameter-efficient extended unsupervised pre-training on unlabeled target domain data, followed by parameter-efficient supervised fine-tuning for downstream tasks.

During extended pre-training, a hybrid strategy is used: a small, specific subset of deep Vision Transformer blocks are completely unfrozen and fully updated, while Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is applied to other blocks.
Crucially, layer normalization parameters across all blocks are unfrozen and updated, and the original self-supervised objective (e.g., MAE, DinoV2) is maintained for consistent learning signals.
Results: Achieved 77.48% top-1 linear probing accuracy on fMoW-RGB (satellite imagery), an over 8.2% improvement compared to prior state-of-the-art methods, and 79.28% with LoRA fine-tuning.
Reduced pre-training compute by 8-10x (e.g., 100 GPU hours versus 900-960+ for full pre-training) and utilized only 6% of the original ViT encoder parameters.

Demonstrated robust performance across diverse and challenging datasets including multi-spectral satellite imagery (fMoW-Sentinel), medical images (Camelyon17), and wildlife (iWildcam), often matching or outperforming fully pre-trained domain-specific models.
Takeaways: Knowledge transfer from existing natural-image VFMs through extended pre-training is more efficient and effective for domain adaptation than pre-training from scratch on a new domain.
A strategic combination of full-rank updates (selectively unfrozen deep blocks) and low-rank updates (LoRA) allows for robust domain adaptation while maintaining high parameter efficiency.
Unfreezing deeper ViT layers and layer normalization parameters is critical for capturing global semantic information and adapting to new data distributions under significant domain shifts.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.09403.Title: Visual Sketchpad: Sketching as a Visual Chain of Thought for Multimodal Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.09403.Summary: VisualSKETCHPAD equips multimodal language models with the ability to generate and utilize intermediate visual sketches as a dynamic reasoning aid. The University of Washington and Allen Institute for AI framework significantly improves performance across various math and computer vision benchmarks, setting new state-of-the-art results by enabling LMMs to create and observe their own visual 'thoughts'.
Problem: Current multimodal language models (LMMs) struggle with tasks requiring deep visuo-spatial understanding or symbolic grounding where intermediate visual aids are crucial, unlike humans who use sketching for problem-solving.
Existing Chain-of-Thought (CoT) and tool-use paradigms for LMMs primarily rely on text-based intermediate steps, overlooking the powerful role of visual representation in many reasoning processes.
Prior tool-use models often follow predefined plans and lack the flexibility for LMs to dynamically adjust their approach based on intermediate visual feedback, limiting their adaptiveness.
Method: The VisualSKETCHPAD framework employs an iterative Thought-Action-Observation loop where an LMM agent plans a visual action, generates Python code to execute it, and observes the resulting visual sketch.

Visual sketches are generated dynamically through code generation, utilizing `matplotlib` for mathematical plotting (geometry, functions, graphs) and specialized, off-the-shelf vision models (e.g., Grounding-DINO for detection, SegmentAnything for segmentation) wrapped as Python functions.
The framework provides utility functions for image manipulation like zooming and overlaying images, allowing the LMM to interactively process and refine visual information as part of its reasoning.
Results: SKETCHPAD improved GPT-4o's average accuracy on math tasks by 11.2% (GPT-4 Turbo by 23.4%), with significant gains on Graph Algorithms (e.g., 41.3% on Max Flow) and Mathematical Functions (over 88% accuracy).

The framework achieved new state-of-the-art results on all seven evaluated computer vision tasks from V*Bench, MMVP, and BLINK, with GPT-4o showing average absolute gains of 14.3% on V*Bench and 9.0% on BLINK tasks.
Human evaluations indicated high alignment, with LMs generating geometry plans similar to human-created ones 80% of the time and 92.8% of GPT-4o's vision plans being rated as valid by human subjects.
Takeaways: Visual sketches serve as an effective 'visual chain of thought', allowing multimodal language models to externalize and iterate on their reasoning in a visually interpretable manner.
Enabling dynamic, feedback-driven generation and observation of visual artifacts (sketches) significantly enhances LMMs' ability to solve complex visuo-spatial and mathematical problems.

Integrating off-the-shelf specialist vision models and plotting libraries as 'sketching tools' via code generation allows LMMs to dynamically leverage powerful perceptual capabilities within their reasoning loop.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.09308.Title: Transformers meet Neural Algorithmic Reasoners
https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.09308.Summary: Google DeepMind introduces TransNAR, a model that integrates large language models with graph neural network-based Neural Algorithmic Reasoners to enhance algorithmic reasoning. The approach leads to significant improvements in out-of-distribution generalization on algorithmic tasks, allowing new reasoning capabilities to emerge.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate fragility and struggle with precise, robust algorithmic reasoning, especially regarding out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization.

Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based Neural Algorithmic Reasoners (NARs) achieve robust OOD generalization but require rigidly structured inputs, preventing their direct use with natural language problems.
A gap exists between AI systems capable of high-level, fuzzy language understanding and those that master precise, low-level algorithmic computation.
Method: A novel hybrid architecture called TransNAR combines a decoder-only Transformer with a pre-trained, frozen GNN-based Neural Algorithmic Reasoner (NAR).
Gated cross-attention layers allow the Transformer's token embeddings to be conditioned by the NAR's node and edge embeddings, enabling information flow from the graph-based reasoning module.

A two-phase training procedure involves pre-training the NAR on graph inputs to ensure algorithmic robustness, followed by fine-tuning TransNAR on a textual algorithmic benchmark (CLRS-Text) while keeping NAR parameters frozen.
Results: TransNAR consistently and significantly outperformed Transformer baselines, achieving over 20% absolute improvement in average execution accuracy on OOD examples for several algorithm classes.

The model demonstrated the emergence of reasoning capabilities on tasks where baseline Transformers exhibited near-zero performance, indicating the acquisition of entirely new problem-solving capacities.
TransNAR substantially alleviated shape mismatch issues in OOD scenarios, significantly increasing the proportion of correctly structured outputs compared to baseline Transformers.
Takeaways: Integrating a GNN-based NAR as an 'internal tool' allows Transformers to acquire new, robust algorithmic reasoning capabilities, overcoming their inherent fragility in such tasks.
Cross-attention serves as an effective mechanism for tightly integrating structured algorithmic knowledge from an external neural module into the Transformer's internal representations.
Freezing the pre-trained NAR's parameters is crucial for preserving its algorithmic precision and out-of-distribution generalization, preventing degradation from Transformer gradients.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.09294.Title: You Don't Need Domain-Specific Data Augmentations When Scaling Self-Supervised Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.09294.Summary: Researchers at FAIR at Meta demonstrated that joint-embedding self-supervised learning models like DINOv2 can achieve state-of-the-art performance with minimal data augmentations, such as simple cropping and masking, when trained with large datasets and sufficient compute. This finding challenges the conventional belief that aggressive, hand-crafted augmentations are essential for preventing model collapse and enforcing invariances, instead suggesting that data scale is the primary driver.
Problem: The reliance on strong, hand-crafted data augmentations in Joint-Embedding Architectures (JEAs) limits their applicability to non-image modalities where such transformations are not easily defined.

A discrepancy exists in augmentation requirements between JEAs (historically needing strong augmentations) and other self-supervised learning (SSL) paradigms like generative models (using minimal augmentations).
It was unclear whether augmentations primarily enforce invariances or artificially increase dataset diversity and sample count, especially at large training scales.
Method: Conducted a systematic experimental study using DINOv2, a robust Joint-Embedding Architecture, as the base model to investigate the role of data augmentations.

Varied data augmentation strategies (from full photometric augmentations to minimal cropping) across different dataset scales (ImageNet-1k, ImageNet-22k, LVD-142M), model capacities, and training durations.

Evaluated learned representations using linear probing on a wide range of downstream tasks (classification, segmentation, depth estimation) and quantitatively measured learned invariance to transformations.
Results: When trained on the LVD-142M dataset for 500 epochs, the 'Crop' setting (minimal augmentations) achieved performance comparable to, and often surpassing, the 'Original' full-augmentation setup across diverse downstream tasks.
Models trained with reduced or minimal augmentations often outperformed heavily augmented setups on novel, out-of-domain tasks (e.g., medical imaging), indicating better generalization.

The model trained with minimal 'Crop' augmentations on ImageNet-22k achieved state-of-the-art results, surpassing other SSL methods that previously claimed to use 'less augmentations' but still incorporated `RandomResizedCrop`.
Takeaways: The primary role of data augmentations, especially on smaller datasets, is to increase effective sample count and diversity rather than solely enforcing specific invariances.

At sufficient scale (large datasets and long training schedules), explicit, hand-crafted photometric augmentations become largely unnecessary for JEAs, and can even hinder generalization to out-of-domain tasks.
Research conclusions regarding the necessity of data augmentations are highly sensitive to compute budgets and hyperparameter optimization, highlighting the context-dependent nature of scaling laws.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.06592.Title: Improve Mathematical Reasoning in Language Models by Automated Process Supervision
https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.06592.Summary: Luo et al. introduce OmegaPRM, a Monte Carlo Tree Search algorithm, to automate the generation of over 1.5 million per-step process supervision annotations for large language models. This method efficiently creates data for training Process Reward Models, leading to substantial improvements in LLM mathematical reasoning on benchmarks like MATH500 and GSM8K.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle with complex, multi-step reasoning tasks like mathematics, where intermediate errors can propagate unnoticed.
Process Reward Models (PRMs), which provide granular step-by-step feedback, require extensive and costly human-annotated process supervision data.
Existing automated Monte Carlo methods for generating process supervision data are inefficient due to their brute-force approach of evaluating every intermediate step.
Method: Introduces OmegaPRM, a divide-and-conquer Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) algorithm designed to automate and efficiently generate process supervision data.
Utilizes a binary-search-based Monte Carlo estimation within rollouts to pinpoint the first error in a reasoning chain, significantly reducing the complexity of correctness evaluation.
Constructs a state-action tree similar to MCTS to effectively reuse generated rollouts and strategically select valuable examples (supposed-to-be-correct wrong-answer rollouts) for PRM training.
Results: OmegaPRM successfully generated over 1.5 million per-step process supervision annotations without human intervention.
The algorithm demonstrated a 75-times efficiency improvement over brute-force Monte Carlo methods for data generation, yielding 1.5 million data points versus 200K for the same computational budget.
PRMs trained with OmegaPRM data boosted Gemini Pro's success rate on MATH500 from 51% to 69.4% and on GSM8K from 86.4% to 93.6%, with similar gains for Gemma2 27B.
Takeaways: Automated process supervision data generation using an MCTS-inspired algorithm, OmegaPRM, is highly efficient and scalable, enabling the creation of large datasets without human intervention.
Training Process Reward Models (PRMs) with these automatically generated, high-quality process supervision datasets substantially enhances large language models' mathematical reasoning abilities.

The pointwise soft label objective, which uses direct Monte Carlo estimation as the correctness score, proves effective for PRM training, yielding better classification accuracy than hard or pairwise labels.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.03816.Title: ReST-MCTS*: LLM Self-Training via Process Reward Guided Tree Search
https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.03816.Summary: ReST-MCTS*, developed by researchers at Tsinghua University and Caltech, enhances large language model self-training by iteratively improving both the generator and a process reward model, leveraging a modified Monte Carlo Tree Search guided by automatically inferred per-step quality values. The method achieves improved LLM performance on complex reasoning benchmarks by producing higher-quality reasoning traces.
Problem: Existing LLM self-training methods suffer from 'false positives,' where correct final answers might derive from flawed intermediate reasoning, leading to low-quality fine-tuning data.
Training reliable per-step process reward models (PRMs) traditionally requires costly and labor-intensive human annotation for each intermediate step.
Integrating tree-search algorithms with LLMs often relies on sparse outcome rewards, lacking fine-grained guidance for intermediate reasoning steps.
Method: Introduces ReST-MCTS*, a reinforced self-training framework that employs a modified Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS*) guided by a trained per-step process reward model (PRM).
Automatically infers per-step reward labels (quality value 'v_k' and weighted reward 'w_s_k') from rollouts and verified traces, circumventing the need for manual annotation to train the PRM.
Employs a 'MuZero-style learning' paradigm to iteratively and mutually improve both the LLM policy (generator) and the process reward model (verifier) based on self-generated, high-quality data.
Results: ReST-MCTS* consistently improved LLM performance on complex reasoning benchmarks (MATH, GSM8K, SciBench) across multiple models and iterations, outperforming other self-training methods.

The autonomously trained process reward model achieved higher accuracy compared to state-of-the-art PRM training techniques (e.g., MATH-SHEPHERD) on GSM8K (87.5% vs 87.1%) and MATH500 (39.0% vs 37.3%) datasets.

The MCTS* policy demonstrated superior accuracy over baselines (e.g., Self-Consistency, Tree-of-Thought) for the same search budget on challenging reasoning tasks like MATH and SciBench, achieving up to 48.5% on MATH.
Takeaways: Novel definitions for quality value and weighted reward enable automated inference of per-step process rewards from oracle final answers, bypassing manual annotation.
A synergistic, iterative self-training loop between the LLM policy and the process reward model allows for continuous, mutual improvement of both components.
Guiding a modified Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS*) with a fine-grained, learned process reward model effectively explores and selects higher-quality reasoning paths.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.03303.Title: Learning Visual Prompts for Guiding the Attention of Vision Transformers
https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.03303.Summary: Researchers from Technical University of Munich, Volkswagen AG, and University of Oxford developed a self-supervised framework to learn visual prompts that effectively guide the attention of pre-trained Vision Transformers to specific image regions. These learned prompts consistently achieved higher attention gain and improved performance on downstream tasks compared to traditional manually designed prompts.
Problem: Traditional visual prompts are manually designed (e.g., red circles), relying on human intuition and often suboptimal for specific Vision Transformer (ViT) architectures.
Existing prompts do not account for architectural differences between ViTs or adapt to specific tasks and data distributions.
There was a lack of a data-driven, self-supervised method to learn effective visual cues for guiding ViT attention.
Method: A self-supervised optimization framework uses a U-Net as a 'neural prior' to generate visual prompts, avoiding direct pixel optimization.
During training, prompts are randomly placed on input images, and the attention weights of the frozen ViT's CLS token are extracted.
A Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence loss minimizes the difference between the extracted attention weights and a target Gaussian distribution centered at the prompt location.
Results: Learned prompts consistently achieved higher relative attention gain, particularly in higher transformer layers, compared to manually designed prompts across various ViT models (e.g., CLIP-B, DeiT).
Different ViT architectures (e.g., DeiT, DINOv2, SigLIP) exhibited unique responses and developed distinct optimal visual prompt patterns.
The learned prompts improved performance on downstream tasks, including keypoint naming on CUB, referring expression recognition on RefCOCO, and enhancing multimodal large language model accuracy.
Takeaways: Optimal visual prompts are model-specific, with different Vision Transformer architectures responding distinctly to learned patterns.
A self-supervised framework can effectively learn complex, data-driven visual prompts without requiring labeled data.
Guiding attention through learned visual prompts can enhance model interpretability and performance, facilitating adaptation of pre-trained models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.02537.Title: TopViewRS: Vision-Language Models as Top-View Spatial Reasoners
https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.02537.Summary: Researchers at the University of Cambridge introduce TOPVIEWRS, a novel multi-scale benchmark and dataset for evaluating Vision-Language Models' top-view spatial reasoning, revealing that current state-of-the-art models perform unsatisfactorily and show a substantial gap compared to human performance across various spatial tasks.
Problem: State-of-the-art Vision-Language Models (VLMs) lack comprehensive and fine-grained evaluation of their spatial reasoning capabilities, particularly from a top-view perspective.
Prior spatial reasoning evaluations primarily use first-person views, which introduce occlusions and perspective distortions, making it difficult to disentangle specific spatial abilities.
There was no standardized, fine-grained benchmark specifically designed for top-view spatial reasoning that differentiates between basic perception and complex reasoning tasks.
Method: Developed a hierarchical taxonomy of nine top-view spatial reasoning tasks, ranging from basic recognition and localization to complex static and dynamic relational reasoning.
Created TOPVIEWRS, a dataset of 11,384 multiple-choice questions featuring both photo-realistic and abstract semantic top-view maps of indoor scenes from the Matterport3D dataset.
Evaluated 10 state-of-the-art open- and closed-source Vision-Language Models (VLMs) using this benchmark, establishing human performance baselines and investigating Chain-of-Thought prompting.
Results: State-of-the-art VLMs, including large closed-source models, achieved average Exact Match scores below 50% across the benchmark, performing best on recognition and localization tasks but struggling with complex static and dynamic reasoning.
A substantial performance gap exists between VLMs and human annotators, with humans achieving over 90% accuracy and top VLMs lagging by more than 50% on average in spatial awareness.
Chain-of-Thought prompting improved performance for GPT-4V and Gemini on Static Spatial Reasoning tasks by an average of 5.82% (6.50% on realistic maps, 5.14% on semantic maps).
Takeaways: Increasing VLM model size does not consistently improve top-view spatial reasoning, challenging traditional scaling laws observed in other VLM capabilities.

VLMs struggle to effectively leverage abstract semantic maps for complex tasks, despite their simplified visual information, potentially due to out-of-distribution training data or difficulty integrating explicit symbolic cues.
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting significantly boosts VLM performance on complex static spatial reasoning tasks, suggesting that explicit step-by-step reasoning can unlock latent spatial abilities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.01920.Title: CODE: Contrasting Self-generated Description to Combat Hallucination in Large Multi-modal Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.01920.Summary: CODE, developed by researchers at KAIST's Integrated Vision and Language Lab, introduces a training-free decoding method that combats cross-modal hallucination in Large Multi-modal Models by contrasting responses against the model's own self-generated visual descriptions. This approach consistently improves performance on hallucination benchmarks like POPE and MMHal-Bench, demonstrating enhanced factual consistency across various state-of-the-art LMMs.
Problem: Large Multi-modal Models (LMMs) frequently generate "hallucinations," meaning responses that are factually incorrect or inconsistent with the provided visual content.
This cross-modal inconsistency undermines the reliability and trustworthiness of LMMs.
The persistent issue of hallucination limits the practical deployment of LMMs in real-world applications requiring high factual accuracy.
Method: Introduces COuntering DEscription Contrastive Decoding (CODE), a training-free method, to mitigate hallucination during LMM inference.
Utilizes the LMM's own self-generated, comprehensive visual descriptions as a contrasting "amateur" reference for next-token prediction.
Implements Dynamic Restriction (DR) via "α_t" and Adaptive Information Constraint (AIC) via "β_t" to dynamically control information flow and candidate token selection based on prediction divergence.
Results: CODE consistently achieved the highest accuracy and F1 scores on discriminative hallucination benchmarks like POPE, e.g., reaching 86.93 Acc and 87.53 F1 with InternVL 1.5.

It demonstrated notable improvements on generative benchmarks, including a "remarkable gain" in average score on MMVP and an improved overall score (e.g., 95.3 for LLaVA-NeXT 34B) and reduced hallucination ratio (e.g., 25.00 for IXC2-VL) on MMHal-Bench.
Ablation studies confirmed the necessity of both Dynamic Restriction ("α_t") and Adaptive Information Constraint ("β_t") for CODE's superior performance across models and benchmarks.
Takeaways: LMMs' self-generated descriptions, despite being comprehensive, are inherently less informative or partially incorrect compared to direct visual input, making them ideal for contrastive decoding.
By recursively referring to these self-generated descriptions, the model can identify and restrict inconsistent information during response generation, enabling a self-correction mechanism.

Dynamically controlling the contrastive influence and adaptively constraining the candidate token search space based on prediction divergence is essential for enhancing visual grounding and coherence.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.01584.Title: SpatialRGPT: Grounded Spatial Reasoning in Vision Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.01584.Summary: SpatialRGPT, developed by UC San Diego and NVIDIA, enhances Vision-Language Models' grounded spatial reasoning by creating a scalable data pipeline to generate 3D scene graphs from single 2D images and integrating a flexible depth information plugin. It surpasses existing baselines on the SpatialRGPT-Bench for spatial understanding and shows utility as a region-aware reward annotator for robotics.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) lack robust and accurate grounded spatial reasoning capabilities, struggling with both qualitative and quantitative 3D relationships.
Existing VLMs lack precise region-level parsing and the ability to reason about specific object instances in complex spatial contexts.
Current VLM architectures do not effectively integrate 3D information, such as depth, from 2D images, which is crucial for true spatial understanding.
Method: A scalable data pipeline automatically generates 3D scene graphs from single 2D images, creating the Open Spatial Dataset (OSD) with diverse region-aware spatial QA pairs.
A novel "plugin" module flexibly integrates relative-depth information into the visual encoder of existing VLMs without requiring depth for all inputs.
A multimodal VLM architecture, SpatialRGPT, combines a visual encoder, region-feature extractor, multi-modal connectors, and a language model, trained on the OSD and general VLM datasets.
Results: SpatialRGPT significantly outperforms other VLMs and LLMs on the new SpatialRGPT-Bench, achieving over 90% success rates for qualitative spatial reasoning and substantially lower error rates for quantitative measurements.

The model achieves state-of-the-art performance on the BLINK Relative Depth Benchmark, improving accuracy by over 20% compared to previous models, while maintaining comparable performance on general VLM benchmarks.

SpatialRGPT demonstrates practical utility as a region-aware dense reward annotator for robotic tasks, enabling precise distance-based feedback for control, and is capable of complex multi-hop spatial reasoning.
Takeaways: Integrating flexible depth information into VLM architectures significantly improves 3D spatial reasoning, especially for depth-sensitive relationships like "behind/front" and metric distances.

Large-scale, automatically generated 3D scene graphs derived from 2D images can effectively teach complex, grounded spatial understanding to VLMs, overcoming limitations of manual annotation or multi-view data.
VLMs can develop robust generalization capabilities for novel spatial tasks and multi-hop reasoning when trained with precise region-aware and depth-informed data.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.19783.Title: Instruction-Guided Visual Masking
https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.19783.Summary: Instruction-guided Visual Masking (IVM) introduces a versatile visual grounding model that automatically masks instruction-irrelevant image regions, allowing large multimodal models (LMMs) to focus on task-relevant visual content. The approach, leveraging a 1-million-sample dataset and a novel training framework, improved GPT4-V's accuracy on V*Bench by 26.2% and enhanced robotic control generalization.
Problem: Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) struggle with precise visual grounding, leading to misalignment between textual instructions and relevant image regions.
LMMs are susceptible to distractions from instruction-irrelevant visual content, resulting in issues like 'hallucinations' and factually incorrect responses.
Existing visual grounding methods are often limited to predefined categories or simple instructions, lacking the versatility for diverse, complex real-world scenarios.
Method: Developed Instruction-guided Visual Masking (IVM), a plug-and-play visual grounding model that generates masks for instruction-irrelevant image regions, to explicitly guide LMM focus.

Constructed IVM-Mix-1M, a 1-million-sample dataset of image-instruction pairs with pixel-level mask annotations, using an LLM-empowered Mixture of Expert visual grounding pipeline and a small human-annotated subset.
Introduced Discriminator-Weighted Supervised Learning (DWSL) to train IVM, effectively leveraging the mixed-quality auto-generated and human-annotated data by prioritizing high-quality samples.
Results: IVM boosted GPT4-V's accuracy on the challenging V*Bench benchmark by 26.2%, from 55.0% to 81.2%, establishing a new state-of-the-art.
Improved LLaVA-7B performance across several benchmarks, including +3.4% on EgoThink, +1.3% on POPE, and +58 points on MME.

Enhanced the generalization and robustness of Language-Conditioned Behavior Cloning (LCBC) robot agents in real-world manipulation tasks, allowing successful performance even under strong visual distractions.
Takeaways: Explicitly masking instruction-irrelevant visual regions significantly enhances LMMs' ability to align with complex instructions and reduces errors caused by visual noise.
A sophisticated data generation pipeline, combining LLMs with an ensemble of visual grounding models, can efficiently create large-scale, high-quality, fine-grained visual grounding datasets.
The DWSL framework effectively addresses the challenge of mixed-quality training data by weighting samples based on discriminator-assessed quality, leading to more robust model training.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.19334.Title: LLMs Meet Multimodal Generation and Editing: A Survey
https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.19334.Summary: This survey systematically reviews how Large Language Models (LLMs) are integrated into multimodal generation and editing across images, videos, 3D content, and audio. It categorizes existing approaches, details the diverse roles LLMs play in these processes, and outlines critical safety considerations and future research directions.
Problem: Prior surveys on Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) largely concentrated on multimodal understanding, neglecting the rapidly evolving areas of generation and editing.
The explosive growth of LLMs created a need for a systematic framework to understand their application in generating and modifying diverse non-textual content.
Researchers lacked a unified overview of how LLMs enhance multimodal content creation across modalities like images, videos, 3D, and audio.
Method: The authors conducted a systematic review, categorizing methods into pre-LLM (CLIP/T5-based) and LLM-based approaches for multimodal generation and editing across various modalities.
They detailed the diverse roles LLMs assume in these generative pipelines, such as layout planners, prompt synthesizers, backbones, or orchestrators for external tools.
The survey also examined key technical components, relevant datasets, and dedicated sections to tool-augmented multimodal agents and generative AI safety.
Results: The survey documented a clear paradigm shift from CLIP/T5-based methods to LLM-dominant approaches, which enable more controllable and interactive multimodal content creation.
It elucidated how LLMs fulfill diverse, specialized roles (e.g., planners, synthesizers, backbones) that enhance generation and editing across images, videos, 3D, and audio.

The research highlighted the critical emergence of LLM-orchestrated multimodal agents and underscored the increasing importance of generative AI safety concerns, including bias, copyright, and fabricated content.
Takeaways: Large Language Models (LLMs) are fundamentally shifting multimodal generation and editing from basic conditioning to advanced prompt understanding, reasoning, and interactive capabilities.

LLMs adopt diverse and specialized roles across modalities, acting as layout planners for images, temporal prompt generators for videos, semantic guides for 3D content, and coordinated backbones for audio.
The rise of LLMs as orchestrators for tool-augmented multimodal agents represents a new paradigm for complex, interactive content creation, further extending their utility beyond text.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.18392.Title: Scaling Laws and Compute-Optimal Training Beyond Fixed Training Durations
https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.18392.Summary: Constant learning rates with a short cooldown or Stochastic Weight Averaging can match the performance of cosine schedules in large language model training while reducing the compute needed for scaling law experiments by a factor of two or more. This work provides flexible and efficient alternatives to the prevailing fixed-duration training paradigm for LLMs.
Problem: The standard cosine learning rate schedule necessitates knowing the full training duration in advance, making LLM training inflexible and costly for iterative experimentation or continual learning.
Deriving scaling laws traditionally requires training numerous models from scratch for each target duration, leading to high computational expense (GPU hours and FLOPs).
The rigidity of existing training recipes hinders the broader accessibility of LLM research and slows down the refinement of scaling laws for new architectures and data mixtures.
Method: Proposes a simpler learning rate strategy: a constant learning rate for most of training, followed by a short, aggressive decay phase (cooldown).
Investigates various functional forms for the cooldown, identifying a (1-sqrt) decay as optimal, and determines efficient cooldown lengths (e.g., 5-20% of total steps).
Explores Stochastic Weight Averaging (SWA) and Schedule-Free Optimizers (SFO) as alternative methods to achieve robust performance without explicit long-term learning rate decay.
Results: The constant learning rate with a short cooldown strategy achieves perplexity values comparable to or better than a well-tuned cosine schedule across different training durations and model sizes (up to 8B parameters).

Stochastic Weight Averaging significantly improves the performance of models trained with a constant learning rate, closing much of the gap to explicit cooldowns, and enhances generalization for cosine-trained models.
The proposed constant LR + cooldown method reduces the total compute and GPU hours for scaling law experiments by a factor of two or more compared to traditional cosine-based approaches.
Takeaways: A constant learning rate combined with a brief cooldown phase can achieve performance equivalent to the cosine learning rate schedule for LLMs.
Stochastic Weight Averaging (SWA) provides strong intermediate models and improves generalization, offering a method to obtain robust checkpoints throughout training.
The (1-sqrt) functional form for the cooldown phase consistently outperforms standard linear decay and often surpasses untuned cosine schedules.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.17104.Title: LLM-Optic: Unveiling the Capabilities of Large Language Models for Universal Visual Grounding
https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.17104.Summary: The LLM-Optic framework integrates large language models (LLMs) and large multimodal models (LMMs) with visual grounding systems to enable universal visual grounding without additional training. This approach significantly improves comprehension of complex natural language queries, demonstrating a 22% increase in Accuracy@0.5 over Grounding DINO on RefCOCOg and outperforming fine-tuned models like UNINEXT on the D3 dataset.
Problem: Current visual grounding models face limitations in comprehending complex natural language queries, including intricate sentence structures and subtle semantic relationships.
Challenges exist in accurately localizing multiple objects or interpreting precise spatial relationships described in human language.
Large Multimodal Models (LMMs), while strong in language understanding, lack inherent precision for bounding box generation and require substantial training for visual grounding tasks.
Method: An innovative, modular, and training-free framework, LLM-Optic, integrates an LLM-based Text Grounder, a Candidate Positioning and Setting Marks module, and an LMM-based Visual Grounder.
The Text Grounder leverages an LLM to parse complex user queries, extract the primary subject, and simplify the request for visual processing.
A "Setting Marks" mechanism annotates candidate bounding boxes generated by an open-vocabulary detector with numerical identifiers, bridging visual and linguistic information for the LMM.
Results: LLM-Optic achieved state-of-the-art zero-shot visual grounding, notably improving Accuracy@0.5 by 22% over Grounding DINO on RefCOCOg and surpassing fine-tuned UNINEXT by 20% on the D3 dataset.
The framework robustly handles diverse query types, including complex multi-object descriptions and scenarios where the described object is absent, enabling "Universal Visual Grounding."
Direct application of LMMs like GPT-4V for visual grounding yielded poor results (mIoU of 0-0.227), validating the necessity of LLM-Optic's hybrid approach for precise bounding box generation.
Takeaways: Decomposing complex visual grounding into semantic interpretation, candidate generation, and contextual reasoning allows for effective zero-shot integration of specialized foundation models.
Large Language Models can effectively interpret and simplify intricate natural language queries, providing a refined textual input for visual detectors.
Explicitly linking visual candidates with numerical marks through "Set-of-Mark Visual Prompting" enhances LMMs' ability to perform precise visual reasoning and reduces hallucination.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.16417.Title: CRoFT: Robust Fine-Tuning with Concurrent Optimization for OOD Generalization and Open-Set OOD Detection
https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.16417.Summary: Researchers from Shanghai Jiao Tong University introduced CRoFT, a fine-tuning framework for Vision-Language Pre-trained Models that concurrently optimizes for out-of-distribution generalization and open-set OOD detection. This approach, which theoretically links OOD detection to generalization via Hessian matrices, achieved improved performance in both areas, including a 25.3% reduction in FPR95 for OOD detection in one setting and a 4.3% boost in OOD generalization accuracy.
Problem: Fine-tuning Vision-Language Pre-trained Models (VL-PTMs) for specific tasks often degrades their ability to generalize to out-of-distribution (OOD) data and detect novel, unseen classes.

Real-world AI applications encounter both covariate shifts (requiring OOD generalization for known classes) and semantic shifts (requiring open-set OOD detection for unknown classes), challenges typically addressed independently.
Current fine-tuning strategies for VL-PTMs lack a unified approach to simultaneously enhance robustness to distribution shifts and reliably identify novel categories.
Method: A lightweight adapter-tuning strategy is applied to Vision-Language Pre-trained Models (VL-PTMs) to efficiently adapt them to downstream tasks.
An Energy Distribution Reshaping (EDR) loss is introduced to optimize open-set Out-of-Distribution (OOD) detection by reshaping energy distributions, making unknown classes more distinguishable.
Adversarial learning is employed to generate worst-case covariate-shifted OOD features, which are then used to minimize a novel Hessian-based OOD generalization bound.
Results: The framework achieved state-of-the-art performance in both Out-of-Distribution (OOD) generalization and open-set OOD detection across multiple benchmarks.
CRoFT reduced the False Positive Rate at 95% True Positive Rate (FPR95) by up to 25.3% for OOD detection and improved OOD generalization accuracy by 4.3% compared to baselines in various settings.

Ablation studies confirmed the individual contributions of the EDR loss and adversarial loss, and visualizations showed improved separation of feature and energy distributions for different data types.
Takeaways: A theoretical connection exists between open-set Out-of-Distribution (OOD) detection and OOD generalization, demonstrating that optimizing for one can benefit the other through domain-consistent Hessians.
Minimizing the gradient magnitude of energy scores on in-distribution data effectively reshapes energy distributions, improving the discriminability of open-set OOD data.
Adversarial generation of worst-case covariate-shifted features during training helps the model learn more robust adapters for improved generalization to various data styles.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14838.Title: From Explicit CoT to Implicit CoT: Learning to Internalize CoT Step by Step
https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14838.Summary: The Allen Institute for AI, University of Waterloo, University of Washington, and Harvard University introduce Stepwise Internalization, a training method that enables language models to solve complex reasoning tasks like multi-digit multiplication and grade-school math problems without generating explicit intermediate steps. This approach internalizes reasoning, achieving high accuracy with improved computational efficiency and offering a configurable balance between speed and performance.
Problem: Explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, while effective for complex tasks, introduces significant computational overhead due to increased sequence length and slower inference times.
Existing approaches for implicit CoT, such as knowledge distillation, can be complex and may not fully capture the reasoning capabilities of the original models.
The computational cost of explicit CoT limits its practical use in resource-constrained environments or real-time applications.
Method: The paper introduces Stepwise Internalization (SI), a curriculum-based training method that gradually removes explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) tokens from training data.
Models are initially trained with full CoT, then continuously fine-tuned as intermediate steps are progressively removed until only the input and final output remain.
The approach incorporates techniques such as a linear removal schedule, optimizer resetting, and removal smoothing to ensure stable training dynamics as steps are internalized.
Results: A GPT-2 Small model trained with Stepwise Internalization achieved near-perfect accuracy on 9x9 multi-digit multiplication without explicit steps, outperforming standard training.

The Mistral-7B model using Stepwise Internalization reached over 50% accuracy on GSM8K math problems without generating intermediate steps, matching or exceeding prior knowledge distillation methods for implicit reasoning.
The method demonstrates a clear accuracy-speed tradeoff, allowing models to achieve explicit CoT-level accuracy with improved speed or maximize speed by internalizing more steps.
Takeaways: Language models can be systematically trained to internalize complex reasoning steps, transitioning from explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) to implicit problem-solving.
Gradual and structured removal of intermediate steps, combined with specific training adjustments (like optimizer resets), is crucial for successful internalization.
The approach allows for a flexible balance between computational speed and reasoning accuracy, enabling deployment across diverse application requirements.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.13872.Title: Image-of-Thought Prompting for Visual Reasoning Refinement in Multimodal Large Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.13872.Summary: Researchers at Westlake University, City University of Hong Kong, and Johns Hopkins University developed Image-of-Thought (IoT) prompting, a method that allows Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to autonomously generate and utilize both visual and textual rationales for complex reasoning. This approach improved MLLM performance in visual question-answering tasks across benchmarks like MMBench, MME, and MMVet, particularly enhancing cognitive reasoning capabilities without requiring model fine-tuning.
Problem: Existing Chain-of-Thought (CoT) methods for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) suffer from 'superficial integration' of visual data, often relying predominantly on textual rationales.

MLLMs struggle with hallucination and lack genuine visual grounding in their reasoning processes, as their internal thinking remains largely language-centric rather than deeply engaging with visual information.
Current multimodal reasoning approaches often require pre-dictated external tools or fixed templates, preventing MLLMs from achieving true automatic, step-by-step multimodal thinking.
Method: Image-of-Thought (IoT) prompting enables Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to generate and leverage both visual and textual rationales in a step-by-step manner.

The method empowers MLLMs to autonomously select and apply external image processing tools (e.g., FastSAM, GroundingDINO, PIL-based functions) to extract visual rationales (e.g., segmented objects, zoomed areas).

A two-stage process involves 'Chain-of-Multimodal-Rationales Generation' where MLLMs break down problems into sub-goals and create multimodal rationales, followed by 'Hybrid-Rationale-based Answer Refining' to produce the final answer.
Results: Image-of-Thought (IoT) prompting consistently improved the performance of GPT-4o and Gemini-Pro-1.5 across MMBench, MME, and MMVet benchmarks, with GPT-4o seeing an increase from 86.2% to 87.6% on MMBench (dev).

Notable performance gains were observed in higher-level cognitive tasks, such as 'Cognition' on MME (+5.6% for GPT-4o, +23.9% for Gemini-Pro-1.5) and categories requiring precise spatial understanding like 'Physical Relation' (+20.98%) on MMBench.

An ablation study confirmed the necessity of visual rationales, showing performance declines without them, while analysis of action statistics revealed MLLMs predominantly use 'Object Detection', 'Segmentation', and 'Zoom-in' to process visual information.
Takeaways: Human-like multimodal reasoning benefits from direct visual engagement, which Image-of-Thought (IoT) prompting emulates by enabling MLLMs to autonomously design and execute visual processing operations.

Integrating visual rationales (processed images) with textual rationales is crucial for grounding MLLM reasoning, mitigating issues like hallucination, and enhancing performance in complex visual tasks.
The 'training-free' nature of IoT makes it an efficient and highly adaptable method for improving MLLM interpretability and performance without the need for extensive fine-tuning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.13532.Title: What Makes Good Few-shot Examples for Vision-Language Models?
https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.13532.Summary: The research demonstrates that few-shot learning with Vision-Language models is highly sensitive to the chosen examples, often exhibiting significant performance variability with random sampling. Researchers from Fudan University, Bytedance, and Sensetime introduce two example selection methods, Montecarlo and Representativeness, which consistently outperform random sampling and active learning strategies across various datasets and few-shot frameworks.
Problem: Few-shot learning performance of pre-trained Vision-Language (VL) models shows high variability due to the specific choice of training examples.
Standard practice of random sampling for few-shot examples leads to suboptimal and inconsistent results.
Existing instance selection methods designed for single-modality tasks do not effectively address the unique challenges of multi-modal VL settings.
Method: Propose Gaussian Monte Carlo (Montecarlo) to select examples that are "unfamiliar" to the pre-trained VL model, based on robustness to Gaussian noise perturbation in embedding space.
Propose Representativeness (REPRE) to select examples closest to their class centroid, aiming for highly characteristic data points.
Evaluate both proposed and existing Active Learning methods (Entropy, Margin) across 11 diverse image recognition datasets and three few-shot VL frameworks (Linear Probe CLIP, CoOp, MaPLe).
Results: The proposed Montecarlo and Representativeness methods consistently achieve better accuracy compared to random sampling and Active Learning strategies across all tested datasets and few-shot learners.
Montecarlo notably outperformed other methods when integrated with CoOp, while Representativeness showed superior performance with MaPLe and Linear Probe.
Active Learning methods (Entropy, Margin) frequently underperformed random selection, indicating their limitations in few-shot Vision-Language contexts.
Takeaways: The choice of few-shot examples significantly impacts Vision-Language model performance, challenging assumptions that random sampling is sufficient.
Traditional Active Learning methods based on uncertainty are generally ineffective in low-shot Vision-Language settings due to unreliable initial model predictions.

Effective few-shot examples for Vision-Language models are characterized by either their "unfamiliarity" to the pre-trained model or their "representativeness" of a class, rather than just model uncertainty.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.10739.Title: Efficient Multimodal Large Language Models: A Survey
https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.10739.Summary: A collaborative team from Tencent Youtu Lab, SJTU, BAAI, and ECNU presents a comprehensive survey categorizing and analyzing methods for developing efficient Multimodal Large Language Models. The survey demonstrates how diverse architectural and training strategies enable models with reduced computational costs to achieve performance competitive with, or sometimes exceeding, much larger general MLLMs across 14 visual-language benchmarks.
Problem: Contemporary Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) achieve high performance due to scaling laws, but incur immense computational and memory costs for both training and inference.
The extensive resource demands restrict MLLM access to a few dominant corporations, raising concerns about the democratization of AI and user privacy.
Deploying powerful MLLMs on resource-constrained edge devices remains a significant challenge, hindering widespread adoption and real-world application.
Method: The authors conducted a systematic literature review, synthesizing and organizing existing research on efficient MLLMs.
A six-primary category taxonomy was developed to classify diverse research efforts: Architecture, Efficient Vision, Efficient LLMs, Training, Data and Benchmarks, and Application.
A detailed comparative analysis was performed on 22 efficient MLLMs and 13 larger MLLMs across 14 established visual-language benchmarks, providing empirical context and a public GitHub repository.
Results: Architectural advancements, including compact vision encoders, efficient vision-language projectors (e.g., Mamba-based), and Small Language Models (SLMs) under 3 billion parameters, are fundamental to constructing efficient MLLMs.
Vision token compression methods, such as multi-view input and specialized token processing modules, effectively manage the computational burden of high-resolution images and long video sequences.

Empirical comparisons show that many efficient MLLMs achieve performance comparable to, and occasionally surpass, much larger general MLLMs on 14 established visual-language benchmarks, enabling their practical use in resource-sensitive applications like biomedical analysis and document understanding.
Takeaways: Efficiency in MLLMs is achieved through a multi-faceted approach, combining architectural innovations, optimized training methodologies, and strategic data utilization, rather than solely relying on smaller base models.

Techniques like vision token compression, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE), and Mamba architectures are crucial for effectively processing high-resolution inputs and improving inference speed while maintaining scalability.

High-quality pre-training and instruction-tuning data, coupled with parameter-efficient transfer learning techniques, are essential for adapting MLLMs to specific tasks with reduced resource expenditure and preserving pre-trained knowledge.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.10292.Title: Fine-Tuning Large Vision-Language Models as Decision-Making Agents via Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.10292.Summary: A framework is introduced for directly fine-tuning Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) using reinforcement learning (RL) to enhance their interactive decision-making capabilities. The method, integrating Chain-of-Thought reasoning, enables a 7B VLM to outperform larger commercial models like GPT-4V and Gemini on multi-step visual-language tasks.
Problem: Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) trained via supervised instruction-tuning struggle with dynamic, multi-step, goal-directed tasks requiring continuous environmental interaction.
Applying reinforcement learning (RL) end-to-end to fine-tune VLMs for complex multimodal decision-making tasks has been largely unexplored.
Understanding how Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning can be leveraged and integrated into the active learning process of VLMs via RL.
Method: The framework directly fine-tunes the entire VLM (vision encoder, LLM backbone) using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) for goal-directed tasks.
VLMs are prompted to generate structured outputs including Chain-of-Thought reasoning and a text-based action, which is then parsed for environmental execution.
A novel scaling factor "λ" is introduced to correctly estimate action probabilities by balancing the influence of CoT and action log-likelihoods during policy gradient updates.
Results: The RL fine-tuned 7B LLaVA model ("Ours") achieved 45.5% average success on gym_cards and 21.7% on ALFWorld, surpassing GPT-4V (25.4%, 19.4%) and Gemini (28.6%, 13.5%) respectively.
Ablation studies showed that removing Chain-of-Thought reasoning significantly reduced performance, for instance, a 21.2% drop on gym_cards tasks.
Empirical tuning of the "λ" scaling factor revealed that moderate values (0.3-0.5) were crucial for optimal performance during RL fine-tuning.
Takeaways: Direct reinforcement learning fine-tuning is an effective paradigm for enhancing the decision-making abilities of VLMs beyond static instruction following.
Chain-of-Thought reasoning is a crucial component for efficient exploration and improved performance when VLMs are actively learning through RL, rather than just a prompting technique.
Careful weighting of Chain-of-Thought tokens versus action tokens (via the "λ" factor) is essential for stable and effective RL training of VLMs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.09818.Title: Chameleon: Mixed-Modal Early-Fusion Foundation Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.09818.Summary: FAIR at Meta introduces Chameleon, an early-fusion, token-based mixed-modal foundation model designed to unify understanding and generation across images, text, and code. The 34 billion parameter model outperforms Llama-2 on text-only tasks, achieves state-of-the-art performance on image captioning, and demonstrates superior human preference for long-form, interleaved mixed-modal generation compared to augmented GPT-4V and Gemini Pro.
Problem: Existing multimodal models often employ 'late-fusion' approaches, limiting deep integration and seamless generation of complex, interleaved text and image content.
Scaling early-fusion token-based multimodal models historically presented significant technical challenges related to optimization stability and training at large scales.
A lack of truly unified models capable of understanding and generating arbitrary, interleaved sequences of images and text within a single architecture.
Method: Develops a family of early-fusion, token-based mixed-modal Transformer models (up to 34 billion parameters) that project all modalities (images, text, code) into a single, shared token space.
