Introduces architectural modifications such as Query-Key Normalization (QK-Norm) and revised Layer Norm placement, along with Z-loss regularization, to ensure training stability at scale.

Pre-trains the model on 9.2 trillion tokens across two stages, leveraging diverse text-only, text-image, and interleaved text/image datasets, followed by a supervised fine-tuning stage with carefully curated high-quality and safety data.
Results: Chameleon-34B outperforms Llama-2-70B on 5 out of 8 text-only reasoning and comprehension benchmarks and is competitive with models like Mixtral 8x7B and Gemini Pro.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance on MS-COCO image captioning and is a leading performer on Flickr30k, outperforming larger late-fusion models like Flamingo and IDEFICS.
In human evaluations for long-form mixed-modal generation, Chameleon-34B was preferred over augmented GPT-4V+ in 51.6% of comparisons and over augmented Gemini+ in 60.4% of comparisons.
Takeaways: Early-fusion, token-based architectures can be successfully scaled to large foundation models by introducing specific architectural innovations and training stability techniques.
A single, unified model can achieve competitive or state-of-the-art performance across diverse unimodal (text) and multimodal (image-to-text, mixed-modal generation) tasks simultaneously.
Human evaluations are critical for assessing novel, open-ended mixed-modal reasoning and generation capabilities, as current benchmarks do not fully capture these complex interactions.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.08593.Title: Open-Vocabulary Object Detection via Neighboring Region Attention Alignment
https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.08593.Summary: The Neighboring Region Attention Alignment (NRAA) framework improves open-vocabulary object detection by explicitly modeling relationships between neighboring image regions through an attention mechanism, achieving 39.8% APnovel50 on OV-COCO and 22.1% mask APr on OV-LVIS.
Problem: Object detectors are typically limited to recognizing objects from predefined, trained categories, hindering their application in dynamic real-world scenarios.
Real-world applications often encounter novel object types beyond a model's training vocabulary, requiring open-vocabulary capabilities.

Previous open-vocabulary object detection methods, particularly distillation-based ones, often neglect the contextual relationships between different regions within an image, losing valuable information.
Method: Introduces Neighboring Region Sampling to identify spatially related regions around each object proposal.
Develops a Neighboring Region Attention (NRA) mechanism that uses self-attention to facilitate interaction and contextual understanding between a proposal region and its sampled neighbors.
Aligns the context-aware features produced by the NRA module with a pre-trained Vision-Language Model (CLIP) using a contrastive loss for open-vocabulary knowledge transfer.
Results: NRAA achieved 39.8% APnovel50 on the OV-COCO dataset, outperforming the prior method BARON by 5.6%.
On the OV-LVIS dataset, the method attained 22.1% mask APr, which is a 1.7% improvement over RegionCLIP.

Ablation studies confirm the efficacy of the Neighboring Region Attention module, with visualizations showing it learns more discriminative features and meaningful inter-regional attention patterns, especially for novel categories.
Takeaways: Contextual information derived from relationships between neighboring image regions is crucial for improving open-vocabulary object detection.
An attention mechanism can effectively model and integrate features from a primary region and its spatial neighbors.
Aligning these contextually enriched features with Vision-Language Models enables better generalization to novel object categories.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.02797.Title: Adapting to Distribution Shift by Visual Domain Prompt Generation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.02797.Summary: VDPG introduces a method for Few-Shot Test-Time Domain Adaptation (FSTT-DA) by generating domain-specific visual prompts to guide frozen CLIP features. This approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on WILDS benchmarks, demonstrating an 8.2% Macro F1 improvement on iWildCam over baselines, and outperforms existing methods on DomainNet by reaching 59.8% average accuracy, all while maintaining computational efficiency.
Problem: Machine learning models often suffer significant performance degradation under distribution shift when test data distributions differ from training data.

Existing Few-Shot Test-Time Domain Adaptation (FSTT-DA) methods are often inefficient, struggle to effectively leverage powerful foundation models like CLIP, or fail to extract truly transferable domain knowledge from limited target data.
Directly finetuning large foundation models with few-shot target data can compromise their inherent robustness, is computationally expensive, and often restricted in black-box scenarios.
Method: VDPG utilizes a frozen CLIP image encoder to preserve its robust generalized features, preventing performance degradation that can result from finetuning with limited data.
A learnable Knowledge Bank and a Conditional Domain Prompt Generator (G) synthesize domain-specific visual prompts for a target domain using a few unlabeled samples and cross-attention.

A Domain Guidance Module (GM) integrates the generated prompt into CLIP's visual features for all images in the target domain, and an episodic meta-learning strategy, with domain-aware contrastive and correlation losses, trains the system to adapt effectively.
Results: VDPG achieved state-of-the-art performance on three out of four WILDS benchmarks (iWildCam, Camelyon17, FMoW), for example, improving Macro F1 on iWildCam by 8.2% and achieving 96.0% accuracy on FMoW.
The method surpassed all compared approaches on DomainNet, reaching an average accuracy of 59.8% across its six domains, demonstrating superior adaptation capabilities.

VDPG is computationally efficient at test-time, requiring only 19.7T FLOPS for inference on 512 images (using ViT/B-16) and avoids costly backbone finetuning, making it suitable for resource-constrained deployment.
Takeaways: Generating and applying domain-specific visual prompts to guide frozen foundation model features provides an effective and efficient FSTT-DA strategy without compromising the model's intrinsic robustness.
Episodic meta-learning, combined with a transferable knowledge bank and a domain-aware contrastive loss, enables the distillation of pure domain-level characteristics from limited unlabeled data.
The generated prompts are critically important and truly domain-specific, exhibiting strong intra-domain similarity and inter-domain discrepancy, which is essential for effective adaptation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.17202.Title: Self-supervised visual learning in the low-data regime: a comparative evaluation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.17202.Summary: A comparative evaluation reveals how Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) methods perform in low-data regimes (50,000-300,000 images), demonstrating that in-domain low-data SSL, particularly DINO, can surpass large-scale generic pretraining for specialized domains like medical or security imaging, while identifying an effectiveness threshold between 50,000 and 65,000 images.
Problem: State-of-the-art Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) methods typically require massive unlabeled datasets (millions of images) and significant computational resources for pretraining.
Specialized real-world applications (e.g., medical imaging, security imaging) often lack the ability to collect millions of relevant unlabeled images, making large-scale SSL impractical.
A lack of systematic understanding existed regarding the behavior and effectiveness of different SSL categories and architectures when pretraining data is limited.
Method: Defined a "low-data regime" as pretraining datasets ranging from 50,000 to 300,000 images based on empirical observations of SSL effectiveness thresholds.

Conducted a comprehensive comparative evaluation of four representative SSL methods (MAE, SimCLR, DINO, DeepClusterV2) and architectures (ResNet-50, ViT-L/16) across classification and object detection tasks.
Evaluated the methods on diverse settings including single-dataset, transfer learning, semi-supervised, robustness benchmarks, and crucially, multiple highly distinct domain-specific visual datasets.
Results: SimCLR (ResNet-50) consistently achieved the highest accuracy in low-data single-dataset classification scenarios, sometimes outperforming ViT-based DINO.
MAE and DINO (ViT-L/16) were the most robust low-data SSL approaches across various corruptions, imbalances, and cross-domain shifts.

In-domain low-data DINO pretraining significantly surpassed DINOv2 and large-scale supervised baselines in medical imaging (ChestX-Det), security imaging (SIXRay-10), and UAV-captured infrared footage (HIT-UAV object detection).
Takeaways: For highly specialized visual domains (e.g., medical X-rays, security scans, thermal infrared), in-domain low-data SSL pretraining (especially DINO) outperforms large-scale generic pretraining and even DINOv2.
A practical lower bound for SSL effectiveness was identified to be between 50,000 and 65,000 images for single-dataset scenarios, below which pretraining offers minimal benefits.

Vision Transformers (ViTs) generally exhibit higher data-hunger than CNNs in very low-data single-dataset settings, but DINO (ViT-based) shows strong generalization in semi-supervised and transfer learning contexts.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16710.Title: LayerSkip: Enabling Early Exit Inference and Self-Speculative Decoding
https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16710.Summary: Meta's LayerSkip accelerates Large Language Model (LLM) inference by enabling accurate early exit and self-speculative decoding within a single model. It introduces a training recipe with non-uniform layer dropout and early exit loss, allowing the model to produce accurate predictions from intermediate layers and to efficiently verify tokens drafted by its own early layers. This approach achieves 1.34x to 2.16x inference speedups across various LLM sizes and tasks with no degradation in final output accuracy.
Problem: High computational and memory costs of Large Language Model (LLM) inference limit widespread deployment and increase operational expenses.

Existing LLM acceleration techniques often involve accuracy trade-offs or require complex multi-model setups (e.g., separate draft models for speculative decoding), increasing memory footprint and implementation complexity.

Standard LLM training does not incentivize earlier layers to produce accurate predictions, leading to redundant computation as models process all layers even for 'easy' tokens, and a lack of robust early exit capability.
Method: A novel training recipe combines non-uniform layer dropout, which progressively increases dropout rates for later layers, with an early exit loss that directly supervises intermediate layer outputs.
Utilizes a single, shared Language Model (LM) head across all transformer layers during training and inference, avoiding auxiliary modules and reducing memory footprint.

Introduces self-speculative decoding where the model uses its early layers to generate draft tokens and then verifies them using its remaining layers, seamlessly reusing KV and 'exit query' caches for efficiency.
Results: Achieves inference speedups ranging from 1.34x to 2.16x across various LLM sizes (1.5B to 13B) and tasks (summarization, code generation, semantic parsing) with lossless accuracy compared to autoregressive baselines.

Significantly improves the accuracy of predictions from earlier layers (e.g., Llama2 7B on NaturalQuestions baseline 0.0554% to LayerSkip 4.07%), enabling effective early exit inference for speed-accuracy trade-offs.
Demonstrates competitive performance against other self-speculative decoding methods, and shows a near 2x speedup on CPU inference, highlighting its efficiency and broad applicability.
Takeaways: Large Language Models can be made robust to early exits and support self-speculative decoding through a novel training recipe that combines non-uniform layer dropout and early exit loss.

A single LLM can efficiently perform self-speculative decoding by using its early layers for drafting and later layers for verification, significantly benefiting from shared KV and exit query cache reuse.

Standard LLM pretraining can cause intermediate layers to diverge in perplexity, making them less suitable for early exit; LayerSkip's training counteracts this, improving the accuracy of earlier layers while maintaining final layer performance.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.15817.Title: Vision Transformer-based Adversarial Domain Adaptation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.15817.Summary: Research from Jilin University introduces Vision Transformer-based Adversarial Domain Adaptation (VT-ADA), integrating Vision Transformers as feature extractors into existing UDA frameworks. This approach demonstrated enhanced performance across three benchmark datasets, notably boosting accuracy on the challenging Office-Home dataset by 15.2% for VT-ADA(CDAN) compared to its CNN-based counterpart, while also achieving faster convergence.
Problem: Deep Neural Networks experience significant performance degradation when training (source) and test (target) data domains have different distributions, requiring costly target domain data annotation.

Existing Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) methods, especially adversarial ones, primarily utilize Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) as feature extractors, which may limit their ability to capture global context.

The efficacy of Vision Transformers (ViTs) in learning domain-invariant features within adversarial domain adaptation frameworks remained largely unexplored despite their success in other computer vision tasks.
Method: Introduce Vision Transformer-based Adversarial Domain Adaptation (VT-ADA) by replacing the traditional CNN feature extractor with a Vision Transformer (ViT).
Integrate a pre-trained ViT-B/16 into established adversarial UDA frameworks, specifically DANN and CDAN, as a "plug-and-play" module.
The ViT acts as the feature extractor, learning domain-invariant representations that simultaneously aid in classification and confuse a domain discriminator.
Results: VT-ADA achieved substantial performance improvements, with VT-ADA(CDAN) boosting average accuracy on Office-Home by 15.2% (to 79.0%) over the original CDAN, and surpassing the best comparative method by 4.3%.
The Vision Transformer-based approach demonstrated faster convergence speed during training compared to conventional CNN-based adversarial domain adaptation methods.
t-SNE visualizations indicated markedly superior feature alignment and indistinguishability between source and target domain features in the latent space for VT-ADA(CDAN).
Takeaways: Vision Transformers, with their global context modeling capabilities, are more effective than CNNs in learning robust and transferable domain-invariant features for UDA.

Directly replacing CNN feature extractors with ViTs in adversarial UDA frameworks acts as an effective "plug-and-play" module, leading to significant performance gains without extensive architectural redesign.
The use of ViTs in ADA facilitates superior feature alignment and separability between source and target domains in the latent space, as visually confirmed by t-SNE.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.14396.Title: SEED-X: Multimodal Models with Unified Multi-granularity Comprehension and Generation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.14396.Summary: Tencent AI Lab researchers introduce SEED-X, a multimodal large language model that unifies multi-granularity comprehension and generation by processing arbitrary-sized images and enabling precise image manipulation. It achieved an overall 51% accuracy on compositional image generation tasks like GenEval and competitive performance across various multimodal comprehension benchmarks, often surpassing or matching specialized models.
Problem: Existing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggled to effectively interpret and respond to diverse real-world user instructions.
Prior MLLMs typically required fixed-resolution inputs, leading to information loss when processing images of arbitrary sizes and aspect ratios.
A gap existed in unifying high-level instructional image generation with precise, low-level image manipulation and editing within a single model.
Method: Developed SEED-X, a unified foundation model built on Llama2-chat-13B, enhanced with a pre-trained Vision Transformer for visual tokenization and a two-stage de-tokenizer for image generation.

Implemented a dynamic resolution image encoding strategy that divides images into sub-images processed by the visual encoder, augmented with extrapolatable 2D positional embeddings for spatial awareness.

Employed a comprehensive multimodal pre-training regimen (including image-caption, grounded, interleaved data) followed by instruction tuning (LoRA) on diverse tasks to enable multi-granularity comprehension and generation.
Results: The instruction-tuned SEED-X-I achieved competitive performance on established multimodal comprehension benchmarks (e.g., POPE, MME-P, VQAv2), often matching or exceeding specialized models.
On the GenEval benchmark, SEED-X demonstrated an overall accuracy of 51% for compositional image generation, showcasing strong instruction-following capabilities.

SEED-X-Edit exhibited superior high-precision image manipulation, accurately performing specific edits while meticulously preserving low-level details of input images, outperforming existing models like Emu2-Gen and MGIE.
Takeaways: A unified ViT-based visual tokenizer and a specialized two-stage de-tokenizer training process, which optimizes specific parts of an SD-XL U-Net, can effectively achieve both semantic consistency and fine-grained detail retention in image generation.

Processing arbitrary-sized images by dividing them into a grid of sub-images and incorporating dynamic 2D positional embeddings allows MLLMs to comprehend diverse visual inputs without fixed-resolution constraints.

Extensive multimodal pre-training and instruction tuning enable a single MLLM to function as a versatile AI assistant, proficient in tasks ranging from fine-grained object detection and reasoning to creative text-to-image generation and high-precision image editing.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.13013.Title: Groma: Localized Visual Tokenization for Grounding Multimodal Large Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.13013.Summary: Groma enhances Multimodal Large Language Models with robust visual grounding by introducing a localized visual tokenization approach. This method efficiently embeds precise region-level understanding directly into the image tokenization process, achieving superior performance on referring expression comprehension and localization benchmarks, including the newly introduced LVIS-Ground benchmark.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle with precise region-level comprehension, limiting their utility in applications requiring detailed visual analysis.
Existing localization methods for MLLMs are either computationally inefficient (LLM directly predicts coordinates) or introduce latency (relying on external modules like SAM).
Current MLLMs often treat localization and recognition as a single task, hindering specialized development for each.
Method: Groma introduces localized visual tokenization, which identifies semantic regions within images and represents them as unique tokens with associated location information.

The architecture decouples localization and recognition, using an Image Encoder (DINOv2) and a Region Proposer (Deformable DETR) to generate region tokens that are then processed by a Large Language Model (Vicuna).

A three-stage training pipeline is employed: detection pretraining for the region proposer, alignment pretraining of vision and language features, and instruction finetuning on high-quality datasets including the new Groma Instruct dataset.
Results: Groma outperforms comparable MLLMs on standard referring expression comprehension benchmarks (RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, RefCOCOg).
It achieves superior performance on the new LVIS-Ground benchmark, demonstrating robust and precise localization for 1,203 diverse object categories.
The model maintains strong general image understanding abilities on benchmarks like LLaVA Bench (COCO) and shows comparable or improved performance on region captioning.
Takeaways: Decoupling localization from recognition, by embedding localization capabilities directly into the image tokenization process, enhances MLLM performance.
Representing semantic regions as unique tokens with associated location information allows for better semantic alignment and a unified framework for referring expressions and grounding.
Pretraining a region proposer on diverse detection datasets, followed by alignment and instruction finetuning, effectively enables robust visual grounding.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.09216.Title: DetCLIPv3: Towards Versatile Generative Open-vocabulary Object Detection
https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.09216.Summary: DetCLIPv3 advances open-vocabulary object detection by enabling models to not only identify objects beyond predefined categories but also generate hierarchical descriptions for them. This model achieves 47.0 AP on the LVIS minival benchmark and demonstrates robust dense captioning capabilities, providing multi-granular understanding of visual content.
Problem: Current open-vocabulary object detection (OVD) models are restricted to predefined categories, limiting their effectiveness for novel objects.
Existing OVD models lack the ability to understand objects at multiple levels of granularity, unlike human perception.
The reliance on fixed categories makes it challenging to adapt OVD models to new domains or specialized applications.
Method: DetCLIPv3 introduces a dual-path architecture combining an Open Vocabulary Detector for object identification and an Object Captioner for generative hierarchical description.

The Object Captioner, built on a transformer-based architecture, produces three levels of description: detailed phrase, category, and parent category, treating description as a sequence generation task.

A custom data annotation pipeline generates GranuCap50M, a dataset of 50 million image-text pairs with hierarchical labels, using VLLMs for recaptioning and LLMs for entity extraction and instruction tuning.
Results: DetCLIPv3 achieves 47.0 AP on the LVIS minival benchmark with a Swin-T backbone, outperforming previous open-vocabulary detection methods.
The model demonstrates strong dense captioning capabilities, achieving 19.7 AP on the Visual Genome dataset.
DetCLIPv3 shows enhanced performance on rare object categories and improved robustness to distribution shifts, indicating broad concept recognition.
Takeaways: Human cognition's hierarchical understanding of objects inspired the model's ability to generate multi-granular descriptions (phrase, category, parent category).

A novel data annotation pipeline leverages Visual Large Language Models (VLLMs) and LLMs (InstructBLIP, GPT-4, LLaVA) to create the GranuCap50M dataset with hierarchical annotations, overcoming the data scarcity for such a task.
A multi-stage training strategy efficiently combines detection and language modeling objectives, enabling the model to learn from diverse, large-scale data.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.07664.Title: Finding Dino: A Plug-and-Play Framework for Zero-Shot Detection of Out-of-Distribution Objects Using Prototypes
https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.07664.Summary: Researchers from Fraunhofer IKS and Technical University of Munich developed PROWL, a plug-and-play framework for zero-shot, unsupervised detection and segmentation of Out-of-Distribution (OOD) objects. The system, leveraging frozen DINOv2 features and prototype matching, achieved state-of-the-art or comparable performance on road driving OOD benchmarks and generalized effectively to rail (83.29 IoU) and maritime (73.30 IoU) domains without retraining.
Problem: Autonomous systems operating in open-world environments (e.g., vehicles, trains) require the ability to detect Out-of-Distribution (OOD) objects not encountered during training for safety reasons.
Current supervised anomaly segmentation methods necessitate extensive annotations or auxiliary OOD samples, which is impractical and often impossible for truly novel unknowns.
Existing Open-World Object Detection (OWOD) approaches frequently struggle to differentiate relevant unknown objects from generic background clutter, leading to noisy or imprecise detections.
Method: The PROWL framework utilizes a frozen, self-supervised pre-trained foundation model (DINOv2) as a robust feature extractor.
It establishes a "prototype feature bank" for known object classes by extracting features from a minimal set of segmented instances in an offline, one-time process.

During inference, OOD objects are identified by calculating the Inverse Normalised Cosine Similarity (INCS) of test image pixels to all known prototypes, classifying pixels with low similarity as OOD.

An optional refinement module integrates unsupervised foreground masks from models like CutLER to aggregate pixel-level OOD detections into coherent object instances, improving segmentation precision.
Results: PROWL + CutLER achieved state-of-the-art or comparable performance on road driving OOD benchmarks (RoadObstacle, RoadAnomaly, FS Static) against supervised methods trained without auxiliary OOD data.
The framework successfully generalized to new domains, achieving an IoU of 83.29 and F1 of 90.38 on an in-house rail dataset, and IoU of 73.30 and F1 of 84.08 on the maritime MODD dataset.

It significantly outperformed a supervised baseline (Maskomaly) in binary OOD segmentation, demonstrating an IoU of 75.22 and F1 of 85.25 on RoadAnomaly compared to Maskomaly's 46.86 IoU and 56.76 F1.
Takeaways: Self-supervised pre-trained foundation models like DINOv2 learn highly generalizable visual features that are effective for differentiating known objects from Out-of-Distribution (OOD) elements without explicit OOD training.
Zero-shot OOD object detection and segmentation can be achieved through an inference-only prototype matching approach, eliminating the need for domain-specific training or auxiliary OOD data.
Integrating unsupervised instance-level foreground masks significantly refines pixel-wise OOD predictions, leading to more precise, coherent, and less noisy OOD object segmentations.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.04452.Title: Vision transformers in domain adaptation and domain generalization: a study of robustness
https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.04452.Summary: This review systematically categorizes and analyzes existing research on Vision Transformers (ViTs) in Domain Adaptation and Domain Generalization. It establishes that ViTs exhibit superior robustness to distribution shifts compared to CNNs, applying effectively across diverse tasks like semantic segmentation, action recognition, face analysis, and medical imaging.
Problem: Traditional Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) often exhibit limited generalization and performance degradation when encountering shifts in data distribution between training and deployment environments.
Deploying deep learning models reliably in real-world scenarios, especially safety-critical ones, requires effective strategies to mitigate the ubiquitous challenge of distribution shifts.
A consolidated understanding of how Vision Transformers (ViTs) address these domain adaptation and generalization challenges was absent despite their rising prominence.
Method: A comprehensive scientific literature review was conducted to explore existing research on Vision Transformers (ViTs) in Domain Adaptation (DA) and Domain Generalization (DG).
The research systematically categorized DA methods for ViTs into feature-level, instance-level, model-level, and hybrid approaches.
Similarly, DG methods for ViTs were categorized into multi-domain learning, meta-learning, regularization techniques, and data augmentation strategies.
Results: Vision Transformers demonstrate superior capability in managing distribution shifts compared to conventional CNN architectures across diverse evaluations.
The review successfully established a structured landscape of Domain Adaptation (DA) and Domain Generalization (DG) strategies for ViTs, categorizing research into distinct methodological groups.
ViTs are effectively applied beyond image classification, showing utility in tasks such as semantic segmentation, action recognition, face analysis, and various medical imaging applications.
Takeaways: Vision Transformers (ViTs) leverage dynamic weight computation and multi-head self-attention to capture global features, offering superior robustness to distribution shifts compared to CNNs.
ViTs exhibit a reduced texture bias, favoring shape recognition, which contributes to their enhanced generalization capabilities across varied domains.
Existing research often employs hybrid methods, combining multiple adaptation and generalization strategies to achieve more robust performance.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.03622.Title: Mind's Eye of LLMs: Visualization-of-Thought Elicits Spatial Reasoning in Large Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.03622.Summary: A study from Microsoft Research introduces Visualization-of-Thought (VoT) prompting, a method that enables large language models to generate and manipulate internal text-based mental images for spatial reasoning tasks. This approach allows LLMs to outperform multimodal models on certain visual challenges, demonstrating an emergent 'mind's eye' capability.
Problem: Large language models (LLMs) often demonstrate underdeveloped spatial reasoning abilities, frequently relying on superficial linguistic cues rather than a deep, grounded understanding of space.
Despite advancements in other reasoning domains, LLMs lack a genuine spatial awareness or a mechanism analogous to human mental imagery for simulating spatial interactions.
Previous approaches in NLP for spatial reasoning improved performance on benchmarks but did not necessarily equip LLMs with a grounded understanding of spatial relationships.
Method: The researchers propose Visualization-of-Thought (VoT) prompting, which explicitly prompts LLMs to 'Visualize the state after each reasoning step.'
This strategy forces LLMs to generate an interleaved sequence of textual reasoning steps and text-based 2D grid visualizations, simulating a 'visuospatial sketchpad.'
The approach was evaluated on three multi-hop spatial reasoning tasks: Natural Language Navigation, Visual Navigation (Route Planning, Next Step Prediction), and Visual Tiling.
Results: GPT-4 with Visualization-of-Thought (VoT) prompting consistently outperformed all other settings, including GPT-4 CoT, GPT-4 w/o Viz, and GPT-4 Vision, across multi-hop spatial reasoning tasks.

VoT led to a 23.5% accuracy improvement for GPT-4 in Natural Language Navigation (59.00% vs 35.50% for CoT) and allowed GPT-4 to outperform GPT-4 Vision by over 14% (63.94% vs 49.62%) in Visual Navigation's next step prediction.

The method significantly increased LLMs' 'visual state tracking' behavior (e.g., 96.2% complete tracking rate for Visual Navigation-Route Planning), and when internal state visualizations were accurate, correct decisions were made in 65-77% of cases.
Takeaways: Large language models (LLMs), primarily trained on text, can exhibit an emergent capability akin to the human 'mind's eye' by generating and manipulating internal text-based spatial representations.

For certain abstract spatial reasoning tasks, internal spatial representation and manipulation via Visualization-of-Thought (VoT) in LLMs can be more effective than direct pixel-level perception in multimodal large language models (MLLMs).
The emergent visual state tracking ability in LLMs may stem from pre-training exposure to structured data such as tabular formats, city grids, or ASCII art in code comments.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.19103.Title: Automated Black-box Prompt Engineering for Personalized Text-to-Image Generation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.19103.Summary: PRISM introduces an iterative VLM-driven algorithm that automatically generates human-interpretable and transferable text prompts for black-box text-to-image (T2I) models. The system achieves superior generalizability and visual accuracy across various T2I generators, including DALL-E and Midjourney, while producing prompts that are easily understandable and editable by users.
Problem: Controlling text-to-image models requires labor-intensive manual prompt engineering, which is sensitive to phrasing and demands significant human expertise.
Existing automated prompt generation methods often lack transferability across different T2I models or necessitate white-box access to proprietary models.
Many automated approaches produce non-interpretable 'soft tokens' or embeddings, hindering human understanding, refinement, or creative editing of the generated prompts.
Method: PRISM employs an iterative, Vision-Language Model (VLM)-driven approach, using a 'Prompt Engineer Assistant' (GPT-4V) to propose and refine textual prompts by analyzing feedback.

A VLM-based 'Judge Model' (GPT-4V) evaluates visual similarity between generated and reference images with nuanced, flexible criteria, guiding the prompt refinement process without needing white-box access.

The algorithm refines a distribution of candidate prompts in parallel streams, leveraging the VLM's in-context learning and reasoning abilities to improve prompt quality and interpretability over iterations.
Results: PRISM demonstrated superior performance and generalizability across closed-source T2I models (DALL-E 2, DALL-E 3, Midjourney) compared to baselines that often require white-box access.
The method produced fully human-readable and editable prompts, achieving low mean negative log-likelihood scores and enabling intuitive user modifications for creative applications.

PRISM maintained high visual accuracy (CLIP-I and DINO scores) in generated images for personalized T2I and image inversion tasks, while also significantly reducing unsafe prompt generation (0.1-6.9% failure rate on DALL-E safeguards).
Takeaways: Vision-Language Models can effectively function as iterative optimizers and reasoning engines for complex, black-box creative tasks like prompt engineering, mimicking human problem-solving strategies.

An iterative feedback loop between a T2I generator, a VLM-based prompt refiner, and a VLM-based judge enables the generation of highly transferable and human-interpretable prompts for black-box models.
Refining a distribution of candidate prompts over multiple parallel streams allows for broader exploration of the solution space and enhanced robustness compared to optimizing a single prompt.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.18361.Title: ViTAR: Vision Transformer with Any Resolution
https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.18361.Summary: ViTAR introduces a Vision Transformer architecture capable of efficiently processing images of arbitrary resolution by integrating an Adaptive Token Merger (ATM) for computational reduction and Fuzzy Positional Encoding (FPE) for robust positional awareness. The model achieves high accuracy across various vision tasks while drastically reducing computational overhead, and is fully compatible with self-supervised learning frameworks like MAE.
Problem: Traditional Vision Transformers (ViTs) suffer significant performance degradation and encounter Out-of-Memory (OOM) errors when processing input images at resolutions different from or higher than their training resolution.

Previous multi-resolution training methods, like ResFormer, have a limited effective resolution range and incur substantial computational costs when scaling, making them impractical for very high-resolution inputs.

Existing resolution-robust positional encoding methods often introduce fixed spatial inductive biases (e.g., convolution-based) that are incompatible with powerful self-supervised learning (SSL) frameworks like Masked Autoencoders (MAE).
Method: The Adaptive Token Merger (ATM) module iteratively processes and merges input tokens into a fixed, manageable number of "grid tokens" using a shared-weight GridAttention mechanism, drastically reducing computational complexity at high resolutions.

Fuzzy Positional Encoding (FPE) introduces controlled positional perturbations (random uniform offsets) during training to build robust positional awareness and generalization across resolutions, without using fixed spatial inductive biases.
ViTAR employs a simplified multi-resolution training strategy, leveraging ATM's efficiency to train on a broader range of resolutions with consistent batch resolution and standard cross-entropy loss.
Results: ViTAR achieves up to 80.4% ImageNet-1K accuracy at 4032x4032 resolution, outperforming all baselines and operating successfully where others fail due to OOM errors (e.g., 17x FLOPs reduction at 1120x1120, 49G FLOPs vs. 863G FLOPs).

It demonstrates strong performance across diverse tasks, achieving 48.3 AP_b on COCO2017 for object detection and 49.0 mIoU on ADE20K for semantic segmentation, outperforming ResFormer by 0.6 points in both cases.

ViTAR integrates seamlessly with MAE self-supervised pre-training, maintaining high accuracy (82.0% at 4032x4032) and resolution robustness, which standard ViT+MAE models fail to achieve (e.g., 13.4% at 1792x1792 and OOMs above 2240x2240).
Takeaways: Iterative and adaptive token merging through modules like ATM can significantly reduce the quadratic computational complexity of ViTs for high-resolution inputs, making them practical for real-world scenarios.

Introducing 'fuzziness' or controlled perturbation to positional encodings during training (FPE) is an effective strategy to improve resolution generalization and prevent overfitting to specific resolutions at inference time.
To maintain compatibility with powerful self-supervised learning techniques like MAE, resolution-robust positional encoding methods must avoid introducing fixed spatial inductive biases.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.18293.Title: Efficient Test-Time Adaptation of Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.18293.Summary: The Training-Free Dynamic Adapter (TDA) enables efficient test-time adaptation for Vision-Language Models (VLMs) by eliminating the need for backpropagation. This method uses a dynamic dual-cache system to adapt to new data distributions, improving CLIP's accuracy on ImageNet from 59.81% to 61.35% while processing data significantly faster than prior adaptation techniques.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) like CLIP experience performance degradation when deployed on data with distribution shifts, differing from their training data.
Existing Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) methods for VLMs, such as Test-time Prompt Tuning (TPT), are computationally expensive and time-consuming due to requiring backpropagation during inference.
Current TTA approaches often rely on potentially noisy pseudo labels, which can propagate errors and limit adaptation effectiveness.
Method: Introduces the Training-Free Dynamic Adapter (TDA), a lightweight, non-parametric adaptation mechanism that operates without backpropagation.
Employs dynamic key-value caches: a positive cache stores high-confidence image features and their pseudo labels, while a negative cache captures what classes an image does not belong to.
Adapts predictions by combining the original CLIP output with information retrieved from both positive and negative caches, which are updated on-the-fly based on prediction confidence.
Results: The Training-Free Dynamic Adapter (TDA) processes the ImageNet validation set in approximately 16 minutes, a substantial improvement compared to 12+ hours for Test-time Prompt Tuning (TPT) methods.
TDA improved CLIP with a ResNet-50 backbone accuracy on ImageNet from a baseline of 59.81% to 61.35%, outperforming TPT and DiffTPT while being orders of magnitude faster.

TDA consistently outperforms or matches state-of-the-art TTA methods across various datasets, including ImageNet variants and cross-domain benchmarks, demonstrating superior efficiency and comparable accuracy.
Takeaways: Test-time adaptation for Vision-Language Models can be achieved efficiently without computationally intensive backpropagation by utilizing dynamic key-value caches.
A dual-cache system, comprising both positive and negative caches, enhances robustness against distribution shifts and mitigates the impact of noisy pseudo labels.
Negative pseudo-labeling, which identifies classes an image does not belong to, provides valuable complementary information to positive associations, improving overall adaptation performance.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.16999.Title: Visual CoT: Advancing Multi-Modal Language Models with a Comprehensive Dataset and Benchmark for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.16999.Summary: This work introduces a Visual Chain-of-Thought (CoT) framework to enhance the interpretability and reasoning capabilities of Multi-Modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by enabling them to dynamically focus on specific visual regions. It includes a large-scale dataset with bounding box annotations and textual reasoning steps, demonstrating improved performance in tasks requiring fine-grained visual attention and competitive results on general MLLM benchmarks.
Problem: Current Multi-Modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) often lack interpretability, operating as "black boxes" without revealing their reasoning steps.
MLLMs struggle with complex visual inputs, particularly high-resolution images or small, crucial regions, due to fixed-grain processing.
The application of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting for visual understanding in MLLMs remains largely underexplored, with existing approaches focusing mainly on text-level reasoning.
Method: A comprehensive Visual CoT dataset was created with 438,000 question-answer pairs, each annotated with a bounding box highlighting the key image region, and 98,000 with detailed textual reasoning steps, spanning diverse domains (Text/Doc, Charts, Fine-Grained, General VQA, Relation Reasoning).

A multi-turn processing pipeline called VisCoT was developed, which first prompts the MLLM to predict a bounding box for the most informative region, then extracts localized image features from that region, and finally integrates both global and local visual information for precise answer generation.

The VisCoT framework leverages pre-trained vision encoders (ViT-L/14) and LLMs (Vicuna-7B/13B) and is fine-tuned in a two-stage process using the Visual CoT dataset alongside other multimodal datasets to enhance its ability to identify and understand specific locations.
Results: VisCoT consistently outperforms existing MLLMs like LLaVA-1.5 and SPHINX-13B on the Visual CoT benchmark, achieving up to an 8x performance increase in doc/text-related tasks (e.g., SROIE dataset).

Ablation studies confirm that using model-predicted bounding boxes significantly improves performance compared to baselines, and careful visual sampler design (expanded/centered cropping) further enhances accuracy.

VisCoT demonstrates improved token efficiency, achieving higher accuracy at lower resolutions (e.g., 224x224 using double visual tokens) than standard pipelines at higher resolutions (e.g., 448x448), and shows competitive performance on general MLLM and visual grounding benchmarks.
Takeaways: Explicit intermediate visual grounding through bounding box prediction enables MLLMs to dynamically focus on relevant image regions, mimicking human visual processing.
A multi-turn processing pipeline integrating both original and localized image features allows for more precise and contextually aware reasoning.
The benefits of Visual CoT are particularly pronounced for tasks requiring fine-grained attention to small objects or text, an area where standard MLLMs often struggle.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.14608.Title: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Large Models: A Comprehensive Survey
https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.14608.Summary: This comprehensive survey by Han et al. (2024) systematically reviews Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods for large models, classifying algorithms into four types and detailing their application across various deep neural networks including LLMs, ViTs, and Diffusion models. It also addresses crucial system-level challenges and solutions for deploying and training PEFT-enabled models.
Problem: Fine-tuning large models for specific tasks is computationally intensive, memory-demanding, and time-consuming due to their vast number of parameters.
The high resource requirements limit the accessibility and practical deployment of state-of-the-art large models for many users and organizations.
The rapid growth of Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods created a need for a consolidated, systematic overview of algorithmic, application, and system-level challenges.
Method: The survey provides a comprehensive review and systematic classification of existing Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) algorithms.
It analyzes techniques used to enhance computational efficiency during PEFT, such as KV-cache management, pruning, and quantization.

The work extends its scope to cover the application of PEFT across diverse deep learning architectures, including Vision Transformers and Diffusion models, and addresses critical system-level design challenges for practical PEFT deployment.
Results: A systematic taxonomy of PEFT methods is established, categorizing them into additive, selective, reparameterized, and hybrid approaches with detailed examples.
Critical efficiency techniques are highlighted, including KV-cache management, pruning, and quantization, which further reduce computational and memory overheads of PEFT itself.
The survey demonstrates the broad applicability of PEFT across diverse DNN architectures, including Vision Transformers, Vision-Language Alignment models, and Diffusion models, alongside LLMs.

Key system-level challenges for PEFT deployment are identified, encompassing centralized query serving, distributed training, and multi-PEFT training, along with existing solutions and evaluation metrics.
Takeaways: A comprehensive taxonomy categorizes PEFT methods into additive, selective, reparameterized, and hybrid types, detailing their mechanisms and efficiency.
Beyond parameter reduction, computational efficiency in PEFT relies on critical techniques like KV-cache management, pruning, and quantization.
PEFT is broadly applicable across various deep neural networks, including Vision Transformers, Vision-Language Alignment models, and Diffusion models, beyond just Large Language Models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.13298.Title: Rotary Position Embedding for Vision Transformer
https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.13298.Summary: This paper from NAVER AI Lab systematically investigates the application of Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) to Vision Transformers, addressing the challenge of performance degradation when input image resolutions vary. It introduces RoPE-Mixed, a novel 2D adaptation that uses learnable mixed frequencies to capture diagonal relationships, demonstrating superior performance in resolution extrapolation and notable improvements across image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation tasks with minimal computational overhead.
Problem: Existing positional embeddings (Absolute Positional Embedding, Relative Position Bias) in Vision Transformers struggle to maintain performance when inference image resolution significantly differs from training resolution.
Standard Vision Transformers face an 'extrapolation' problem in real-world applications (e.g., high-resolution object detection) that require processing images at scales unseen during training.
Prior solutions for multi-resolution inference in ViTs often require specialized training recipes (e.g., continuous augmentation, self-distillation), complicating their integration and use.
Method: The research adapts Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE), originally from language models, for use in Vision Transformers.

A novel 2D RoPE variant, 'RoPE-Mixed,' is introduced, which defines a rotation matrix with learnable mixed frequencies for both x and y positions to effectively encode 2D relative spatial information, including diagonal relationships.
The solution is integrated and evaluated across standard ViT and Swin Transformer architectures as a direct replacement or in combination with existing positional embeddings (APE, RPB).
Results: 2D RoPE, particularly RoPE-Mixed, significantly improves multi-resolution image classification performance on ImageNet-1k, outperforming APE and RPB at extrapolated resolutions.
RoPE-Mixed improves object detection on MS-COCO, achieving up to +1.8 percentage points in bounding box AP for DINO-ViTDet models compared to APE, and similar gains for DINO-Swin.

Semantic segmentation on ADE20k also shows improvements, with RoPE-Mixed+APE yielding up to +2.5 mIoU for ViT-UperNet, and RoPE similarly benefiting Swin-Mask2Former, all with negligible computational overhead.
Takeaways: The proposed RoPE-Mixed formulation, which employs learnable mixed frequencies for both x and y axes, effectively captures diagonal relationships in 2D image data, outperforming simpler axial adaptations.
RoPE encourages longer-range and more diverse attention interactions in Vision Transformers, especially at varying input resolutions, contributing to its improved extrapolation capabilities.

RoPE can synergistically combine with existing positional embeddings like APE for ViT, enhancing interpolation performance while maintaining extrapolation benefits, but can largely replace RPB in Swin Transformers.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.13257.Title: Arcee's MergeKit: A Toolkit for Merging Large Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.13257.Summary: Arcee's MergeKit provides an open-source, efficient, and user-friendly toolkit that facilitates the merging of Large Language Models (LLMs) from diverse architectures into a single, unified model. The toolkit has been widely adopted, enabling the creation of thousands of powerful open-source checkpoints and demonstrating improved performance in specialized domains like medicine while maintaining generalization.
Problem: Training Large Language Models from scratch is computationally expensive and beyond the reach of many researchers and organizations.
Fine-tuning LLMs for specific tasks often leads to catastrophic forgetting of general capabilities, and managing numerous specialized models is inefficient.
Combining knowledge from independently trained models or creating versatile, multi-task AI systems without retraining is challenging.
Method: MergeKit offers a unified, open-source library supporting a wide array of existing and novel model merging techniques via an intuitive YAML configuration or a graphical user interface.
It employs an out-of-core approach with Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) scheduling to efficiently handle large models across diverse hardware, from GPUs to memory-constrained CPUs.
The toolkit is designed for modularity and extensibility, allowing for easy integration of new merging methods and fostering community contributions.
Results: MergeKit has facilitated the merging of thousands of models, contributing to powerful open-source checkpoints, demonstrating significant real-world adoption and utility.

Merged models consistently outperformed base models in an empirical study, with merged Meditron-7B/Llama2-7B models showing improved performance across medical benchmarks (e.g., USMLE, MedMCQA, PubMedQA) and enhanced generalization in common LLM benchmarks.

The toolkit enables the creation of novel model architectures like Franken-MoE and has been used to build models such as Goliath-120b, showcasing its capability to go beyond simple merging to create new model structures.
Takeaways: Abstracting complex merge operations into a user-friendly YAML configuration lowers the barrier to entry, democratizing advanced LLM development.
Efficient out-of-core processing and DAG scheduling enable large-scale model merging on commodity hardware, making the process accessible and scalable.
Supporting a diverse set of established and novel merging methods (like FrankenMerging and Franken-MoE) within an extensible framework accelerates research and practical application of model merging.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.13187.Title: Evolutionary Optimization of Model Merging Recipes
https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.13187.Summary: Sakana AI researchers developed Evolutionary Model Merge, an automated framework utilizing evolutionary algorithms to optimize the combination of pre-trained large language and vision-language models. This method produced EvoLLM-JP, achieving 55.2% on Japanese math reasoning and outperforming 70B-parameter models on general Japanese benchmarks, alongside EvoVLM-JP, which improved culturally-aware visual question answering for Japanese.
Problem: Current model merging techniques heavily rely on human intuition and trial-and-error, making recipe discovery unsystematic and limiting scalability.
Training large foundation models from scratch is prohibitively expensive and resource-intensive.
Systematically combining knowledge from models trained on disparate domains to achieve novel, emergent capabilities is challenging.
Method: Utilizes evolutionary algorithms, specifically CMA-ES, to automate the discovery of optimal model merging "recipes."
Explores the Parameter Space (PS) to optimize layer-wise weight merging coefficients using an enhanced TIES-Merging with DARE.
Navigates the Data Flow Space (DFS) by evolving sequences of layers from different models, incorporating a learnable scaling matrix to manage distribution shifts.
Allows for hybrid approaches combining both parameter and data flow space optimizations.
Results: EvoLLM-JP achieved 55.2% accuracy on MGSM-JA (Japanese Math), a substantial improvement over source models (below 30%) and surpassed a 70B-parameter model on general Japanese benchmarks (70.5% vs 68.3%).

EvoVLM-JP demonstrated enhanced cultural awareness and improved performance on Japanese visual question answering, achieving 51.2% ROUGE-L on a new culturally-specific benchmark, compared to 41.1% for the baseline.
The evolutionary approach consistently outperformed unoptimized merging methods and specialized LoRA fine-tuning, avoiding catastrophic forgetting while achieving higher task-specific performance.
Takeaways: Evolutionary algorithms effectively automate the search for optimal model merging recipes across vast configuration spaces.
Optimizing for a specific cross-domain task can lead to surprising generalization and performance improvements on unrelated, broader benchmarks.
A learnable scaling matrix is critical in Data Flow Space merging to mitigate distribution shifts between layers from different base models.
Evolutionary merging can integrate disparate knowledge domains, leading to emergent capabilities that are difficult to achieve with conventional methods.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.13043.Title: When Do We Not Need Larger Vision Models?
https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.13043.Summary: Researchers from UC Berkeley and Microsoft Research developed 'Scaling on Scales (S²)', a parameter-free method that enables smaller, pre-trained vision models to achieve performance comparable to or exceeding much larger models. This approach processes images across multiple scales, resulting in significantly fewer parameters and lower computational costs for similar performance, notably achieving state-of-the-art visual detail understanding with a LLaVA-1.5 model on the V* benchmark.
Problem: The prevailing 'scaling law' paradigm in AI relies on continuously increasing model size (parameters, depth, width) to achieve better performance, leading to high computational costs, energy consumption, and accessibility barriers.
Training and deploying large vision models demand immense computational power, resulting in substantial carbon footprints and financial barriers that limit research and application access.

Existing multi-scale methods in computer vision often require specialized architectures, extensive re-training, or are primarily used as test-time augmentations, not as general parameter-free scaling approaches.
Method: The paper introduces 'Scaling on Scales (S²)', a parameter-free scaling approach that allows any pre-trained and frozen smaller vision model to process images at multiple scales.
S² employs an 'S²-Wrapper' that interpolates input images to various scales, splits larger scales into sub-images, and feeds each individually into the same frozen model.

Features extracted from different scales are then merged and concatenated to create a unified multi-scale representation with a consistent output token count, suitable for downstream tasks like classification or integration with large language models.
Results: S²-enhanced smaller vision models (e.g., ViT-B) achieved comparable or superior performance to significantly larger models (e.g., ViT-H, ViT-G) across diverse perception tasks (image classification, semantic segmentation, depth estimation) using remarkably fewer parameters (0.28x to 0.07x).
Scaling an OpenCLIP vision backbone with S² enabled LLaVA-1.5 to achieve state-of-the-art visual detail understanding on the V* benchmark, surpassing commercial models like Gemini Pro and GPT-4V.

When pre-trained with S², smaller models matched or exceeded the performance of larger models, demonstrating that their generalization capabilities are not inherently limited but benefit from multi-scale training.
Takeaways: The features learned by larger vision models can be effectively approximated by those of multi-scale smaller models through a simple linear transform, suggesting comparable representational capacity.
Smaller models' generalizability limitations are often not inherent but stem from single-scale pre-training; multi-scale pre-training can close performance gaps with larger models.
Splitting large images into sub-images and processing them independently is crucial for efficiency and performance in multi-scale processing, preventing quadratic complexity issues.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.12966.Title: Chain-of-Spot: Interactive Reasoning Improves Large Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.12966.Summary: Chain-of-Spot (CoS), developed by researchers from Tsinghua University and Tencent, introduces an interactive reasoning paradigm for Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) that guides the model to first identify a relevant Region of Interest (ROI) in an image before generating a response. This method significantly improved LLaVA-1.5's performance, achieving new state-of-the-art results across 11 multimodal benchmarks, including a 4.4% accuracy increase on VizWiz, while efficiently processing visual details.
Problem: Existing LVLMs often use lower-resolution images due to computational cost, limiting access to fine-grained visual details.
Visual encoders in LVLMs extract global image features, which can be inefficient and lead to hallucinations as they struggle to prioritize salient regions pertinent to a query.
LVLMs lack a structured, deeper visual reasoning capability comparable to Chain-of-Thought in Large Language Models (LLMs).
Method: Introduces Chain-of-Spot (CoS), a two-stage interactive reasoning pipeline: first predicting a Region of Interest (ROI), then generating the final answer using both global and ROI features.
Develops a novel ROI annotation method for training data based on relevance propagation through attention mechanisms from a Faster R-CNN visual encoder.
Fine-tunes LLaVA-1.5 models with specific instruction prompts, guiding them to identify the ROI in the first step and then use it for a more detailed answer generation in the second.
Results: LLaVA-1.5+CoS/13B achieved new state-of-the-art results on VQA-v2 (+1.8%), GQA (+1.5%), VizWiz (+4.4% to 58.0%), and OKVQA (+2.0%).
Consistently outperformed baselines across five multimodal benchmarks, including SEEDBench (+0.7%), MMBench (+0.5%), and MM-Vet (+2.2%), establishing new state-of-the-art.
Qualitative analyses show CoS accurately identifies relevant ROIs and corrects errors made by baseline LLaVA-1.5, enhancing interpretability and refined reasoning.
Takeaways: Explicitly guiding Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) to identify question-tailored Regions of Interest (ROIs) enhances visual reasoning and understanding.
Accessing fine-grained visual details via selective cropping and re-scaling of ROIs is computationally more efficient than processing full high-resolution images or patches.
An interactive, multi-step visual reasoning process, analogous to Chain-of-Thought, significantly improves LVLM performance across diverse multimodal tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.12884.Title: HYDRA: A Hyper Agent for Dynamic Compositional Visual Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.12884.Summary: HYDRA, a new multi-stage framework for dynamic compositional visual reasoning, integrates an RL agent as a cognitive controller, a feedback loop, and incremental reasoning with LLMs and VFMs. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across various visual reasoning tasks, demonstrating superior generalization and robustness compared to prior end-to-end and compositional models.
Problem: Monolithic end-to-end Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) suffer from high training costs, limited generalization, and a lack of interpretability.

Existing compositional visual reasoning approaches face issues with Large Language Models (LLMs) generating unverified or erroneous outputs, lack real-time visual feedback for dynamic planning, and often restart planning without utilizing historical information.
Prior compositional models heavily rely on LLM commonsense knowledge without adequate visual verification, leading to potential inaccuracies and inefficiencies.
Method: HYDRA introduces a multi-stage framework featuring a Planner (LLM), a Cognitive Controller (Reinforcement Learning agent), and a Reasoner (LLM-based code generator interacting with Visual Foundation Models).

A Reinforcement Learning (RL) agent acts as a cognitive controller, dynamically selecting optimal instructions from multiple samples generated by the planner and providing a feedback loop for validation.
An incremental reasoning mechanism is implemented via a State Memory Bank, which stores historical information to enable the system to build upon previous steps and refine its understanding.
Results: Achieved state-of-the-art performance across diverse visual reasoning tasks, including 48.6% accuracy on OK-VQA, 61.7% IoU on RefCOCO, and 47.9% accuracy on GQA, surpassing leading end-to-end VLMs and prior compositional methods.

Demonstrated superior cross-dataset generalization, with the RL agent maintaining competitive or better performance on unseen datasets without retraining, significantly outperforming baselines like ViLT (32.13% vs. 48.17% on OK-VQA).

Ablation studies confirmed the critical contributions of its components: the RL-Agent improved accuracy by 4.71%, Incremental Reasoning by 3.87%, and Sampling by 2.70%, validating their synergistic benefits within the HYDRA framework.
Takeaways: Integrating an RL agent as a cognitive controller effectively validates LLM outputs and makes high-level decisions, significantly improving the reliability and adaptiveness of compositional visual reasoning.
Dynamic visual feedback and historical state information are crucial for achieving robust generalization and efficiency, allowing the system to adjust actions based on continuous perceptual results.

Generating multiple instruction samples with confidence probabilities from the planner offers a richer decision space for the RL controller, enhancing the robustness and adaptability of the planning phase.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.12488.Title: DetToolChain: A New Prompting Paradigm to Unleash Detection Ability of MLLM
https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.12488.Summary: This paper presents DetToolChain, a novel prompting paradigm that enables powerful Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) like GPT-4V and Gemini to perform zero-shot object detection with enhanced precision. The method combines a detection-specific Chain-of-Thought with a toolkit of visual processing and reasoning prompts, resulting in significant performance improvements across open vocabulary, described, referring expression, and oriented object detection benchmarks, often surpassing prior state-of-the-art zero-shot approaches.
Problem: Existing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle with precise object detection, particularly for challenging instances like occluded, small, or rotational objects, despite their advanced visual intelligence.
Finetuning MLLMs for detection is computationally expensive, requires vast manual data preparation, and is impractical for state-of-the-art closed-source MLLMs like GPT-4V.
Prior prompting methods for MLLMs often rely on pre-extracted bounding boxes from external detectors, rather than truly unleashing the MLLM's inherent detection ability.
Method: DetToolChain introduces a novel prompting paradigm combining a 'detection prompting toolkit' with a 'multimodal detection Chain-of-Thought (Det-CoT)' to guide MLLMs in object detection.
Det-CoT orchestrates an iterative, step-by-step process where the MLLM generates a 'thought' to conclude or engage a tool, then constructs and appends an appropriate prompt to the message history.

The 'detection prompting toolkit' comprises Visual Processing Prompts (e.g., Ruler Marker, Image Split, Box Marker) that preprocess images with visual aids, and Detection Reasoning Prompts (e.g., Problem Insight Guider, Self-Verification Promoter) that guide MLLM internal reasoning for refinement.
Results: DetToolChain improved baseline GPT-4V and Gemini performance by 20% to 50% across various detection metrics, significantly outperforming prior zero-shot methods.

On Open Vocabulary Object Detection (MS COCO), zero-shot GPT-4V+DetToolChain surpassed CORA by +22.7% AP50 on Novel classes and achieved better AP50 (+6.4%) than supervised Faster R-CNN-R50 on COCO val2017.

For Described Object Detection (D-cube dataset), GPT-4V+DetToolChain improved upon the best prior method FIBER-B by +14.5% AP on FULL settings, demonstrating enhanced ability to comprehend complex descriptions for localization.
Takeaways: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) like GPT-4V and Gemini possess an inherent, yet untapped, zero-shot object detection capability that can be effectively unlocked through strategic prompting.

Integrating visual processing prompts (e.g., ruler markers, image splits) directly into the image input, combined with reasoning prompts, provides MLLMs with the necessary 'prior knowledge' and 'reasoning capabilities' to perform precise localization.

An iterative Chain-of-Thought (CoT) paradigm tailored for detection (Det-CoT) enables MLLMs to decompose complex detection tasks, dynamically apply specialized tools, and progressively refine bounding box predictions.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.11999.Title: HIRI-ViT: Scaling Vision Transformer with High Resolution Inputs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.11999.Summary: HIRI-ViT, a five-stage Vision Transformer architecture from HiDream.ai, introduces a principled approach to efficiently process high-resolution images. This architecture integrates specialized CNN-based operations with transformer blocks and a mixed normalization strategy, enabling it to achieve state-of-the-art performance on image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation benchmarks while maintaining manageable computational costs.
Problem: Traditional Vision Transformers face quadratic computational complexity with increasing input image resolutions due to the self-attention mechanism, making high-resolution processing prohibitively expensive.
Standard ViT architectures often lose fine-grained details when downsampling high-resolution images, which are critical for dense prediction tasks like detection and segmentation.
Achieving an efficient balance between performance and computational cost when scaling ViTs to very high resolutions remains a challenge for existing hierarchical or hybrid approaches.
There was a need for a principled way to scale CNN+ViT hybrid backbones for high-resolution inputs while maintaining comparable computational overheads to lower-resolution models.
Method: HIRI-ViT introduces a five-stage Vision Transformer architecture that processes high-resolution inputs through progressive stages, with the first three stages focusing on high-resolution CNN-based operations and the last two on transformer blocks.

A novel High-Resolution Stem (HR-stem) and High-Resolution Block (HR-block) are designed with a two-branch structure (high-resolution and low-resolution paths) to efficiently process fine details and fuse results.

The model incorporates Inverted Residual Downsampling (IRDS) between stages to better preserve information during resolution reduction by creating parallel paths that maintain different aspects of input features.

It employs a mixed normalization strategy, utilizing Batch Normalization in the initial high-resolution stages and Layer Normalization in the later low-resolution stages to optimize training stability and inference efficiency.
Results: Achieves 84.3% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K with 448 448 inputs at approximately 5.0 GFLOPs, outperforming competing models and reaching 86.1% at 768 768 resolution.
Consistently outperforms other backbones on COCO object detection and instance segmentation, with HIRI-ViT-L attaining 49.1% box AP and 44.0% mask AP.
Demonstrates superior performance on ADE20K semantic segmentation, with HIRI-ViT-L achieving 51.3% mIoU.

Establishes a new efficiency frontier for high-resolution vision models across GFLOPs, parameter count, and inference time, offering higher accuracy at comparable computational costs compared to state-of-the-art models like Swin and DaViT.
Takeaways: A five-stage CNN+ViT hybrid architecture effectively scales Vision Transformers to high-resolution inputs by gradually reducing spatial dimensions while increasing feature dimensions.

Specialized two-branch processing within the High-Resolution Stem (HR-stem) and High-Resolution Block (HR-block) efficiently preserves fine-grained details and expands receptive fields at lower computational cost.
A mixed normalization strategy, using Batch Normalization for high-resolution stages and Layer Normalization for low-resolution stages, optimizes both training stability and inference efficiency.
Sophisticated downsampling through Inverted Residual Downsampling (IRDS) further contributes to preserving rich feature representations during resolution transitions between stages.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.10191.Title: Generative Region-Language Pretraining for Open-Ended Object Detection
https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.10191.Summary: GenerateU is a framework for open-ended object detection that can detect objects and generate their names in natural language without relying on predefined categories during inference. This approach achieves performance comparable to Open-Vocabulary Object Detection methods on zero-shot LVIS while offering greater flexibility for unknown object categories.
Problem: Traditional object detection systems are limited to recognizing only predefined categories and fail to generalize to novel objects.
Existing Open-Vocabulary Object Detection (OVOD) methods still require predefined category names during inference, limiting true open-world applicability.
The challenge exists to detect objects and generate their descriptive names in a free-form manner without any category constraints or specific text prompts at inference.
Addressing the long-tail distribution of object categories, where rare objects are often poorly detected, remains a challenge for existing methods.
Method: Introduces GenerateU, a framework that combines an open-world, class-agnostic object detector (Deformable DETR) with a generative language model.
Employs an end-to-end generative region-language pretraining strategy to jointly optimize both the object detector and the language model components.
Incorporates a region-word alignment loss to strengthen the association between visual regions and their corresponding textual descriptions.
Leverages a diverse training data strategy, combining human-annotated data with pseudo-labeled large-scale image-text pairs to expand vocabulary and improve generalization.
Utilizes beam search decoding during inference to enhance the generation of names for rare object categories.
Results: GenerateU achieves performance comparable to existing Open-Vocabulary Object Detection methods on zero-shot LVIS, even without access to category names during inference.
The model demonstrates substantial improvements in Average Precision (AP) metrics across rare, common, and frequent categories, particularly enhancing performance on rare categories.
End-to-end training of GenerateU outperforms transfer learning from frozen MLLMs, indicating better adaptation to the object detection domain.
The framework exhibits good transferability to other datasets such as COCO and Objects365, indicating robust generalization capabilities.
The region-word alignment loss contributes to improved performance by enhancing the model's ability to distinguish between different object categories.
Takeaways: End-to-end training of the object detector and language model proves more effective than transferring from frozen Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) due to better domain adaptation.
A region-word alignment loss significantly improves the model's ability to distinguish between different object categories and their corresponding textual descriptions.
Beam search decoding during inference enhances performance, particularly for rare categories, effectively addressing the long-tail problem in object detection datasets.
The combination of diverse human-annotated data and pseudo-labeled large-scale image-text pairs helps scale vocabulary and improve generalization capabilities of the model.
Generative open-ended object detection is a practical problem that can be effectively addressed by linking class-agnostic object detection with language generation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07392.Title: ViT-CoMer: Vision Transformer with Convolutional Multi-scale Feature Interaction for Dense Predictions
https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07392.Summary: ViT-CoMer introduces a Vision Transformer backbone that integrates convolutional multi-scale feature interaction for dense prediction tasks. It leverages existing ViT pre-trained weights while achieving state-of-the-art performance, with ViT-CoMer-L reaching 64.3% AP on COCO val2017 for object detection when using DINOv2 pre-training.
Problem: Plain Vision Transformers (ViTs) lack inner-patch information interaction, leading to a loss of fine-grained local details necessary for dense prediction tasks.
ViTs typically produce single-scale features, limiting their ability to handle objects at diverse scales and contexts in dense prediction.
Adapting ViTs for dense prediction often requires costly re-pre-training of modified architectures, hindering research and application development.
Method: ViT-CoMer employs a two-branch architecture combining a plain ViT with a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) stream, facilitating bidirectional feature interaction across multiple stages.
A Multi-Receptive Field Feature Pyramid (MRFP) module enhances the CNN branch by providing rich multi-scale spatial information and expanded receptive fields.

A CNN-Transformer Bidirectional Fusion Interaction (CTI) module integrates and unifies features from both branches through multi-scale self-attention and bidirectional injection, without altering the core ViT structure or requiring re-pre-training of the ViT component.
Results: Achieved 64.3% AP on COCO val2017 for object detection with ViT-CoMer-L using DINOv2 pre-training, setting a new record without extra detection-specific training data.
Outperformed plain ViT-S by +5.6% APb and +3.4% APm on COCO val2017, and surpassed many existing vision-specific and adapted backbones of comparable size.
Demonstrated competitive results on semantic segmentation, with ViT-CoMer-L achieving 55.6% MS mIoU on ADE20K, a 2.1% improvement over Swin-L.
Takeaways: Bidirectional interaction between CNN (local, multi-scale) and Transformer (global context) features effectively combines their strengths, enhancing ViTs with local and multi-scale perception.
Directly utilizing powerful, open-source ViT pre-trained weights while only randomly initializing new CNN-based components significantly reduces computational costs and accelerates development.
The MRFP module, by generating diverse receptive fields within the CNN stream, is crucial for improving plain ViT's performance in dense prediction tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.01753.Title: Training-Free Pretrained Model Merging
https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.01753.Summary: Merging under Dual-Space Constraints (MuDSC) is a training-free framework that combines multiple pre-trained neural networks into a single multi-talent model. It achieves this by iteratively optimizing unit matching using similarity measures from both weight and activation spaces, demonstrating consistent performance improvements over baselines across homogeneous and heterogeneous tasks.
Problem: Existing training-free model merging methods, like Task Arithmetic, require all models to be fine-tuned from the same pre-trained initialization, limiting their real-world applicability.
Prior unit matching algorithms for merging often rely on unit similarity in either weight space or activation space, which frequently exhibit inconsistencies, leading to suboptimal merged models.

The proliferation of specialized deep neural networks creates challenges in model storage and computational overhead, necessitating efficient consolidation into multi-functional entities without additional training.
Method: MuDSC proposes an iterative algorithm that optimizes unit matching by considering a weighted linear combination of similarity measures from both the activation space and the weight space.

The method iteratively refines permutation matrices for each layer, updating weight-space representations based on adjacent layers' permutations and combining with static activation-space similarities until convergence.

It includes adaptations for neural network architectures with group structures (e.g., Group Normalization, Multi-Head Attention) through group alignment and group zip strategies to ensure broad compatibility.
Results: MuDSC consistently outperforms state-of-the-art training-free merging baselines across various homogeneous tasks (e.g., CIFAR-100, ImageNet) for models trained from scratch or fine-tuned from different pre-trained backbones.

The framework shows significant scaled performance improvements in heterogeneous task merging on the Taskonomy dataset, with `MuDSC_Align` maintaining or surpassing SOTA in 83% of tasks (e.g., +5.12% in 'Segment Semantic') and `MuDSC_Zip` in 75% of tasks (e.g., +11.42% in 'Segment Semantic').

Loss landscape visualizations demonstrate that MuDSC places the merged model directly at the lowest point of the multi-task loss basin, achieving a unified lower loss for each task, indicating better generalization and robustness.
