Takeaways: Unit similarity in the weight space and activation space often do not align, with many units showing high similarity in one space but low in the other, which empirically motivates a dual-space approach for effective merging.

Considering both weight and activation space similarities during unit matching allows the merged model to reside in a more favorable multi-task loss landscape, achieving lower, overlapping loss basins for individual tasks.

The iterative refinement of permutations across layers is crucial for effectively integrating information from both dual spaces, as the optimal weight-space representation for a layer depends on the permutations of adjacent layers.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.01299.Title: A Photonic Physically Unclonable Function's Resilience to Multiple-Valued Machine Learning Attacks
https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.01299.Summary: A study from Southern Methodist University and Anametric, Inc. assessed a photonic Physically Unclonable Function's resistance to machine learning attacks using multiple-valued logic representations. Results indicate that approximately 1,000 Challenge-Response Pairs are required for models to achieve above-chance prediction accuracy, with higher non-power-of-two radices further impeding attack success.
Problem: Many electronic Physically Unclonable Functions (PUFs) are vulnerable to machine learning (ML) attacks capable of predicting responses from known Challenge-Response Pairs (CRPs).
There is a need for new PUF architectures, such as photonic PUFs, that can inherently resist sophisticated ML modeling attacks.
The specific resilience of photonic PUFs, particularly when their outputs are represented using Multiple-Valued Logic (MVL), against ML attacks had not been thoroughly quantified.
Method: A computational model of a 24-cell photonic PUF was developed to efficiently generate large datasets of Challenge-Response Pairs (CRPs) for ML attack training and testing.

A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) neural network was designed and trained as an ML attack model, evaluating its performance across various Multiple-Valued Logic (MVL) radices for both challenges and responses.

The methodology involved training 6,600 models, systematically evaluating resilience across diverse CRP training set sizes (10 to 100,000) and numerous radix combinations using 5-fold cross-validation.
Results: Approximately 1,000 Challenge-Response Pairs (CRPs) were needed for ML models to achieve an average prediction accuracy above 50% (random chance) across individual response bits.
Even with 10,000 CRPs, ML models rarely surpassed 60% average prediction accuracy in 31 out of 33 radix combinations, indicating strong overall resilience.

ML attack models demonstrated the lowest prediction accuracies for radix-3 challenges (R_c=3) and higher non-power-of-two response radices, while binary responses (R_r=2) were the most susceptible to prediction.
Takeaways: Photonic PUFs demonstrate inherent resilience against ML attacks, demanding a substantial number of CRPs to achieve prediction accuracy significantly better than random chance.
The choice of radix for representing challenges and responses in Multiple-Valued Logic (MVL) plays a critical role in determining the effectiveness of an ML attack.
Lower radices and those that are powers of two generally allow for more predictable PUF responses, whereas higher, non-power-of-two radices enhance the PUF's security by reducing attack efficacy.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.15116.Title: Large Multimodal Agents: A Survey
https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.15116.Summary: A survey systematically reviews Large Multimodal Agents (LMAs), structuring the field by deconstructing their core components and proposing a four-type taxonomy. The work consolidates existing evaluation methodologies and identifies future research directions, providing a unified framework for understanding and advancing multimodal AI.
Problem: The rapidly expanding field of Large Multimodal Agents (LMAs) suffered from fragmented understanding, inconsistent terminology, and a lack of standardized evaluation methods.
Existing LLM-powered agents were limited to text-based interactions, unable to effectively interpret and respond to diverse real-world multimodal information (e.g., visual, audio).
Research on LMAs was often conducted in isolation, hindering effective comparison and cumulative progress across different systems.
Method: The authors conducted a systematic and comprehensive review of LLM-driven multimodal agents, consolidating scattered knowledge and proposing a coherent taxonomy.
The survey deconstructed LMAs into fundamental building blocks: perception, planning, action, and memory, providing a granular understanding of their architecture and evolution.
It compiled and analyzed diverse evaluation methodologies and highlighted frameworks for multi-agent collaboration, while also delineating future research directions.
Results: A novel four-type taxonomy for LMAs was proposed, categorizing agents based on their planner type (closed-source vs. fine-tuned open-source LLM) and long-term memory integration (none, indirect, native).

Detailed analysis of LMA core components (perception, planning, action, memory) revealed the evolution from simple modality conversion to sophisticated multimodal processing and native multimodal memory systems.
A comprehensive overview of LMA applications across domains like GUI automation, robotics, autonomous driving, video understanding, and complex visual reasoning was provided.
Takeaways: LMAs are complex systems requiring sophisticated perception (multimodal data interpretation), planning (reasoning, plan formulation), action (tool use, embodied actions), and memory (multimodal long-term storage).

LMA development has progressed through four types, from early agents leveraging closed-source LLMs without memory to advanced agents with native multimodal long-term memory, enabling enhanced generalization.
Evaluating LMAs remains challenging due to diverse methods, necessitating standardized objective benchmarks and consideration of subjective metrics like versatility, scalability, and safety.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.15109.Title: Remaining-data-free Machine Unlearning by Suppressing Sample Contribution
https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.15109.Summary: MU-Mis introduces a machine unlearning method that efficiently removes data influence from deep neural networks without requiring access to remaining training data. It minimizes the input sensitivity gap between target and irrelevant class logits for forgotten samples, outperforming previous remaining-data-free methods and rivaling data-dependent state-of-the-art approaches while being up to 30 times faster for large models.
Problem: Deep neural networks often memorize training data, leading to privacy risks and making compliance with "right to be forgotten" regulations computationally prohibitive due to expensive retraining.
Existing approximate machine unlearning (MU) methods suffer from limitations like computational expense,
catastrophe unlearning
or critically, requiring access to remaining training data, which is often unavailable or introduces additional privacy concerns.
Current remaining-data-free MU methods generally exhibit a significant performance gap compared to state-of-the-art methods that utilize remaining data.
Method: Proposes MU-Mis (Machine Unlearning by Minimizing Input Sensitivity), a remaining-data-free method that reconceptualizes unlearning as withdrawing a sample's contribution to the learning process.

The method directly suppresses the learned model's input sensitivity for forgotten data by minimizing a novel loss function that reduces the magnitude gap between target and irrelevant class logit sensitivities.

MU-Mis fine-tunes the pre-trained model using only the forgetting data, employing a pragmatic, remaining-data-free stopping guideline and freezing batch normalization layers to preserve utility on remaining data.
Results: MU-Mis significantly outperforms all four existing remaining-data-free unlearning methods and is the first remaining-data-free method to rival or surpass data-dependent state-of-the-art approaches, achieving the lowest Average Gap to the retrained model on datasets like CIFAR-100 and PinsFaceRecognition.

The method achieves strong privacy protection with Membership Inference Attack success rates near 0% and provides substantial efficiency gains, reducing unlearning time by up to 30x for large models like ViT on Tiny ImageNet.

MU-Mis demonstrates superior resilience and stability in sequential unlearning tasks, maintaining low utility and resilience gaps while avoiding issues like performance recovery, knowledge residue, and utility breakdown observed in other state-of-the-art methods.
Takeaways: A sample's contribution to the dynamic learning process in deep neural networks reflects in the learned model's static *sensitivity to its input*, which can be precisely quantified and targeted for unlearning.

During training, models significantly amplify the input sensitivity of the target class logit and suppress that of irrelevant class logits for training data, creating a discernible "magnitude gap" encoding the sample's contribution.

Unlearning can be effectively achieved by minimizing this sensitivity magnitude gap for the forgetting data, thereby reversing the impact of their original contribution without requiring access to any remaining training data.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.12479.Title: In value-based deep reinforcement learning, a pruned network is a good network
https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.12479.Summary: Researchers from Google DeepMind, Mila, and Université de Montréal demonstrate that gradual magnitude pruning dramatically enhances deep reinforcement learning agent performance, achieving up to 60% improvement on Atari, and enables robust scaling of network architectures by improving learning stability and plasticity.
Problem: Deep reinforcement learning networks often struggle with training instabilities, parameter under-utilization, and diminishing returns or degradation as network size increases.
Existing deep RL networks commonly suffer from pathologies like dormant neurons, loss of plasticity, and a tendency to overfit early experiences.
Scaling neural network parameters in deep RL does not reliably lead to performance gains, contrasting with 'scaling laws' observed in supervised learning.
Method: The authors systematically applied gradual magnitude pruning (GMP), a technique that progressively removes low-magnitude parameters during training, to various deep RL agents.
They investigated GMP across diverse value-based agents (DQN, Rainbow, IQN), offline RL settings (CQL), and actor-critic methods (SAC, PPO), primarily using an Impala-based ResNet architecture.
Experiments were conducted on the Arcade Learning Environment, Atari 100k, and MuJoCo, varying network widths, sparsity levels, and other hyperparameters to assess generality and scalability.
Results: Gradual magnitude pruning achieved up to a 60% performance improvement for DQN and 50% for Rainbow over dense baselines on Atari, consistently using only 5% of the original network parameters.
Pruned networks exhibited monotonically increasing performance with increased network width, effectively mitigating the performance degradation typically observed in larger dense RL models.
The technique consistently outperformed alternative regularization methods, plasticity injection techniques, and other sparse training approaches like RigL across various RL algorithms and regimes.
Takeaways: Gradual magnitude pruning acts as a potent regularization mechanism, reducing Q-value variance, average parameter norms, and the fraction of dormant neurons within the network.
Pruning enhances network plasticity by increasing the effective rank of network parameters and significantly reducing gradient correlation and interference during training.
The benefits of pruning extend beyond simple compression, actively shaping learning dynamics to enable robust performance scaling with larger initial network architectures.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.10093.Title: MIM-Refiner: A Contrastive Learning Boost from Intermediate Pre-Trained Representations
https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.10093.Summary: MIM-Refiner enhances pre-trained Masked Image Modeling (MIM) vision models by applying a short, efficient contrastive learning refinement to intermediate encoder blocks, which were found to contain peak representation quality. This method achieves new state-of-the-art results on ImageNet-1K linear probing with 84.7% accuracy and significantly improves low-shot classification and clustering performance using only 20-30 epochs of additional training.
Problem: Masked Image Modeling (MIM) models often have peak representation quality in intermediate encoder blocks, with feature degradation in later layers due to their lightweight decoders delegating reconstruction tasks to the final encoder blocks.

MIM models, while efficient for pre-training and excellent for fine-tuning with abundant labels, typically perform less optimally in low-shot classification or semantic clustering tasks compared to instance discrimination methods.

Existing combined MIM and instance discrimination (ID) approaches are either computationally intensive with end-to-end joint training or focus only on refining the final encoder block, not fully leveraging the potential of intermediate representations.
Method: Introduces MIM-Refiner as a sequential, short refinement stage (20-30 epochs) applied to a fully pre-trained MIM encoder, leveraging the same pre-training dataset.
Utilizes an ensemble of Instance Discrimination (ID) heads strategically attached to multiple intermediate and later blocks of the MIM encoder, rather than just the final layer.

Employs a Nearest Neighbor Alignment (NNA) objective, which performs nearest neighbor alignment for positive samples (from a FIFO queue) but applies direct repulsion from negative batch samples without an NN-swap, stabilizing training for large models.
Results: Achieves new state-of-the-art (SOTA) on ImageNet-1K linear probing, with a refined ViT-H/14 model achieving 84.7% accuracy, outperforming prior SOTA and competing with models trained on significantly larger datasets.
Demonstrates drastic improvements in low-shot classification, reaching 64.2% for 1-shot ImageNet-1K with a refined data2vec 2.0 H model, surpassing models pre-trained on datasets 2000 times larger.
Significantly enhances clustering performance, achieving 67.4% k-means cluster accuracy on ImageNet-1K, surpassing previous SOTA and models like DINOv2-g (47.7%) trained on 100x more data.
Takeaways: Representation quality within MIM encoders peaks at intermediate blocks and degrades towards the final layers due to the asymmetric encoder-decoder architecture, where later encoder blocks are co-opted for pixel-level reconstruction.

A targeted, efficient refinement using an instance discrimination objective, specifically applied to these high-quality intermediate and later blocks, can significantly boost the semantic utility of pre-trained MIM features.

The Nearest Neighbor Alignment (NNA) objective, with a specific design choice to omit nearest-neighbor swapping for negative samples, is critical for stabilizing contrastive learning and improving performance when refining large MIM models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.04236.Title: CogCoM: A Visual Language Model with Chain-of-Manipulations Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.04236.Summary: CogCoM, a visual language model developed by Tsinghua University and Zhipu AI, introduces Chain of Manipulations (CoM) to enable intrinsic visual operations for multi-step reasoning, leading to improved performance on detailed visual question answering and visual grounding benchmarks while enhancing interpretability.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language Models (VLMs) often provide "conclusive responses" without revealing essential intermediate visual reasoning steps.
This limitation causes VLMs to struggle with tasks requiring subtle visual details or multi-step analysis, leading to unfaithful responses and hallucinations.
The black-box nature of current VLM outputs hinders interpretability and error diagnosis.
Method: Introduces Chain of Manipulations (CoM), a sequence of intrinsic visual operations (e.g., OCR, Grounding, CropZoomIn) designed to mimic human cognitive problem-solving.
Develops an automated data generation pipeline that leverages large language models and visual foundational models to produce 70K CoM reasoning chains for training.
Extends the CogVLM architecture with a memory-based system to handle multi-turn interactions and integrate sequentially processed original and manipulated images.
Results: CogCoM achieves state-of-the-art performance on detailed Visual Question Answering (VQA) benchmarks, including up to a 9.0 percentage point improvement on TextVQA over its CogVLM baseline.
It demonstrates superior visual grounding capabilities, achieving top performance across RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, and RefCOCOg datasets, comparable to specialist models.

The model improves general multimodal abilities on MM-Vet and shows enhanced performance in reducing hallucinations on POPE, while ablation studies confirm the benefits of Chain of Manipulations training data.
Takeaways: Explicitly modeling visual manipulations allows Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to perform step-by-step, evidential reasoning, mimicking human cognitive processes.
Training an end-to-end VLM to intrinsically perform visual manipulations, rather than relying on external tools, enables deeper integration of visual reasoning.

An automated data generation pipeline, combining large language models for linguistic annotation and visual foundational models for visual annotation, can efficiently create high-quality, complex multimodal reasoning data.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.02242.Title: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Pre-Trained Vision Models: A Survey and Benchmark
https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.02242.Summary: Researchers from Shanghai Jiao Tong University and collaborators introduce a comprehensive survey and the V-PEFT Bench, a unified benchmark for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) in vision models. The work demonstrates that PEFT methods often outperform full fine-tuning on limited data across diverse vision tasks, achieving comparable performance with as little as 0.05% of the trainable parameters.
Problem: Full fine-tuning large Pre-trained Vision Models (PVMs) demands prohibitive computational resources, memory, and storage for each new task.
Traditional full fine-tuning often leads to overfitting and reduced generalization performance when adapting PVMs to smaller downstream datasets.
The visual domain lacked a systematic survey and a standardized benchmarking framework for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods.
Method: A systematic survey categorizes visual PEFT methods into four main types: addition-based, partial-based, unified-based, and multi-task tuning.
The V-PEFT Bench, a unified benchmark, evaluates 25 representative PEFT algorithms across various vision tasks including image recognition, video action recognition, and dense prediction.
A novel Performance-Parameter Trade-off (PPT) metric is introduced to holistically assess PEFT methods based on both performance and parameter efficiency.
Results: PEFT algorithms consistently outperformed full fine-tuning across 19 VTAB-1k image recognition datasets, demonstrating superior generalization on limited data, with DTL showing the best performance-parameter trade-off (PPT=0.75).
On video action recognition tasks, PEFTs strongly surpassed full fine-tuning on data-scarce HMDB51, and methods like BAPAT achieved leading results on both large and small video datasets.
For dense prediction, PEFTs outperformed full fine-tuning on smaller datasets such as PASCAL VOC, and select methods like Mona even exceeded full fine-tuning on the large MS-COCO dataset.
Takeaways: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning methods consistently outperform full fine-tuning when adapting large vision models to tasks with limited data by preventing overfitting.
Different PEFT approaches present distinct trade-offs in terms of added modules, structural changes, and efficiency during inference and memory usage.
The effectiveness of PEFT is influenced by factors like the pre-training strategy of the base vision model and the data abundance of the downstream task.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.00253.Title: A Survey on Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.00253.Summary: A survey from Huawei Technologies comprehensively defines and categorizes hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs), synthesizing current evaluation methods, root causes, and mitigation strategies to provide a structured overview of this critical issue. The work maps hallucination types, identifies its origins across the LVLM pipeline components, and reviews diverse solutions being developed.
Problem: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) like MiniGPT-4 and LLaVA exhibit 'hallucination,' a critical issue where generated text factually misaligns with the visual content of an image.
LVLM hallucinations extend beyond simple object presence to include incorrect attributes and relationships, significantly impeding their reliability and trustworthiness for practical applications.

The rapidly evolving field lacked a comprehensive, structured overview defining this complex problem, categorizing its symptoms, consolidating evaluation methods, analyzing root causes, and reviewing mitigation strategies.
Method: The authors from Huawei Technologies conducted a comprehensive survey to systematically define and categorize LVLM hallucination, developing a taxonomy for its symptoms.
They structured a review of existing evaluation methodologies and benchmarks for LVLM hallucination, distinguishing between generative and discriminative approaches.

The survey provides a pipeline-centric analysis of the root causes of hallucinations in LVLMs and systematically reviews and categorizes existing mitigation strategies, linking them to their corresponding causes.
Results: The survey formally defines LVLM hallucination as a 'disagreement between factual visual content and corresponding textual generation,' distinguishing its multifaceted symptoms including cognitive and semantic errors.

It identifies two main evaluation approaches (non-hallucinatory generation and hallucination discrimination) and categorizes current benchmarks, noting trends towards generative benchmarks covering broader hallucination types.

Four primary root causes for LVLM hallucination are detailed: issues from training data (bias, irrelevance), vision encoder limitations (resolution, fine-grained semantics), modality aligning module simplicity (connection, token constraints), and inherited LLM issues (context attention, stochastic sampling, capability misalignment).
Takeaways: Hallucination in LVLMs is a multifaceted phenomenon manifesting as cognitive errors (judgment, descriptive inaccuracies) and semantic errors concerning objects, attributes, and relations, distinct from purely linguistic model issues.

The root causes of LVLM hallucinations are traceable to specific components of the model pipeline, including data biases, vision encoder limitations, simple modality alignment modules, and inherited issues from the large language model component.

Current mitigation strategies directly correspond to these identified root causes, targeting improvements in data quality, vision encoding, modality alignment training, LLM decoding, and post-processing techniques.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.17981.Title: From Training-Free to Adaptive: Empirical Insights into MLLMs' Understanding of Detection Information
https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.17981.Summary: This paper empirically investigates how different training strategies influence Multimodal Large Language Models' (MLLMs) comprehension of infused textual detection information from object detection and OCR models. It demonstrates that fine-tuning a pre-trained MLLM for a single epoch effectively enables it to utilize this information, outperforming training-free methods and full retraining, leading to improved performance across various multimodal benchmarks.
Problem: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) frequently struggle with fine-grained visual details, leading to issues like object hallucination, miscounting, and inaccurate text identification within images.
Integrating the capabilities of specialized vision detection models (object detection and OCR) into MLLMs is challenging, particularly optimizing the fusion of their textualized outputs.
Prior work largely relied on 'training-free' strategies for textual detection information infusion, lacking systematic investigation into the effects of adaptive training on MLLM comprehension.
Method: Developed a systematic experimental framework to compare three distinct strategies for infusing textual detection information into MLLMs: Training-free Infusion (TFI), Retraining Based Infusion (RBI), and Fine-tuning Based Infusion (FTBI).

Transformed outputs from DINO (object detection) and PaddleOCRv2 (OCR) into compressed textual formats, using central coordinates and instruction sentences, which are then supplied as supplementary input to the MLLM's language backbone.
Evaluated LLaVA-1.5 across 10 diverse multimodal benchmarks, covering comprehensive VQA, perceptual reasoning, text recognition, and fine-grained detail understanding.
Results: Training-free infusion (TFI) of detection information yielded inconsistent improvements and sometimes led to performance degradation on MLLMs like LLaVA-1.5.

Retraining-based infusion (RBI) improved performance on specific benchmarks with detection information but notably degraded the MLLM's general image comprehension when detection data was not provided.

Fine-tuning based infusion (FTBI) consistently outperformed LLaVA-1.5, TFI, and RBI across nearly all 10 evaluated benchmarks, achieving performance increases up to 3.99% for 7B models and up to 6.71% for 13B models over training-free methods, while also demonstrating robustness to changes in underlying detectors.
Takeaways: Training-free infusion of raw textual detection information often introduces noise and can degrade Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) performance.
Retraining MLLMs from scratch with continuous detection information infusion negatively impacts their ability to interpret original image encoder features.

Fine-tuning a pre-trained MLLM for a single epoch provides a balanced approach, preserving original image understanding while effectively utilizing new detection information and adapting to varying detector qualities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.13987.Title: Cross-Domain Few-Shot Learning via Adaptive Transformer Networks
https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.13987.Summary: ADAPTER (Adaptive Transformer Networks) introduces a method for cross-domain few-shot learning by integrating Transformer architectures with self-supervised learning and label smoothing. This approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the BSCD-FSL benchmark, showing improvements of 1-9% across various scenarios, particularly on challenging medical imaging domains.
Problem: Deep learning models struggle to generalize to new visual domains when only a few labeled examples are available, due to substantial domain shifts.
The "domain gap" between source and target datasets (e.g., natural images to medical scans) degrades performance in cross-domain few-shot learning (CD-FSL).
Traditional supervised training on base domains can lead to "supervision collapse," where learned features are not transferable to diverse target domains.
Method: Employs ADAPTER, a Transformer-based architecture built upon the Compact Convolutional Transformer (CCT) backbone.
Utilizes a "quadruple transformer block" with bidirectional cross-attention to process base, target, and cross-domain features simultaneously, enabling implicit domain alignment.
Implements a two-phase learning strategy: self-supervised representation learning via DINO followed by few-shot adaptation using label propagation for smoothing.
Results: Outperformed nine state-of-the-art methods on the BSCD-FSL benchmark, achieving 1-9% higher accuracy across most scenarios.
Demonstrated particularly strong performance on challenging medical image datasets (ISIC, ChestX), showing improvements up to 9%.
Ablation studies confirmed that self-supervised DINO pre-training, bidirectional cross-attention, and label smoothing via propagation are all crucial components for the observed performance gains.
Takeaways: The bidirectional cross-attention mechanism within Transformer blocks effectively achieves implicit domain alignment, eliminating the need for explicit alignment methods.
Self-supervised pre-training using DINO, applied across all feature combinations, fosters transferable representations and outperforms supervised base training for cross-domain generalization.
Label propagation provides an effective label smoothing mechanism, improving prediction robustness and consistency in scenarios with extremely limited labeled data.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.12168.Title: SpatialVLM: Endowing Vision-Language Models with Spatial Reasoning Capabilities
https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.12168.Summary: SpatialVLM, from Google DeepMind and Google Research, equips Vision-Language Models with quantitative spatial reasoning abilities, such as estimating distances and object sizes. This is achieved through an automated data synthesis pipeline that generates 2 billion spatial reasoning question-answer pairs, enabling the model to accurately reason about physical space and support applications in robotics.
Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) frequently struggle with quantitative spatial reasoning tasks, such as understanding distances, object sizes, and precise relative positions in 3D space.
Existing VLMs primarily process 2D image information and lack inherent 3D depth, making it challenging to ground their understanding in physical metric dimensions.
Training datasets for VLMs typically lack sufficient examples with accurate distance and size information, and spatial references within questions can be ambiguous without clear referents.
Method: Developed an automated data synthesis pipeline to generate a large-scale dataset of 10 million images with 2 billion spatial reasoning question-answer pairs, incorporating 3D context from 2D images via metric depth estimation.

The pipeline includes stages for semantic filtering, 2D context extraction (region captioning, depth, segmentation), conversion to 3D context, ambiguity resolution, and human-aligned question-answer synthesis.

Trained a VLM based on a modified PaLM-E architecture (using PaLM 2-S and a ViT-L/14 vision encoder), mixing general VQA data with the newly generated spatial reasoning dataset, and found unfreezing the ViT encoder optimal.
Results: SpatialVLM demonstrated improved accuracy in both qualitative (e.g., relative positions) and quantitative (e.g., distances in meters, object sizes) spatial reasoning compared to models like GPT-4V, PaLI, and PaLM-E.
The model successfully learned to estimate distances between objects in meters and measure object sizes, performing consistently well across a range of distances.

SpatialVLM was applied to robotics tasks, providing accurate reward annotation for robot learning and enabling enhanced embodied planning by predicting precise gripper-to-object distances for grasping and navigation.
Takeaways: Large-scale synthetic data generation, leveraging existing computer vision tools for depth and segmentation, can effectively imbue Vision-Language Models with quantitative spatial reasoning skills.
Despite reliance on noisy monocular depth estimations in training data, SpatialVLM learned generalizable quantitative spatial understanding that transfers to real-world scenarios.
Combining SpatialVLM with a Large Language Model via chain-of-thought prompting enables complex, multi-step spatial reasoning problems to be solved.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.10020.Title: Self-Rewarding Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.10020.Summary: Self-Rewarding Language Models introduces an iterative training method where a single language model learns to both generate and evaluate its own responses, leading to improvements in instruction following and self-assessment capabilities. This approach enables models to outperform leading open-source models on instruction-following benchmarks like AlpacaEval 2.0 and MT-Bench.
Problem: Current LLM alignment methods like RLHF and DPO are limited by the scalability and quality of human-annotated preference data.
Reliance on human preferences caps LLMs' ability to surpass human-level performance, as they cannot receive 'superhuman feedback'.
Separate reward models used in RLHF are typically frozen and cannot adapt or improve alongside the evolving capabilities of the LLM.
Method: An iterative Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) framework where a single language model acts as both an instruction follower and its own judge.

The process begins by fine-tuning a base LLM (
M
0
) on human instruction and evaluation (LLM-as-a-Judge) seed data to create an initial self-rewarding model (
M
1
).

In subsequent iterations, the current model generates new prompts, creates multiple candidate responses, and then evaluates these responses using its internal judge capability to form DPO preference pairs for training the next model version.
Results:
The iterative self-rewarding process progressively improved instruction-following, with the final model (
M
3
) achieving a 20.44% win rate against GPT-4 Turbo on AlpacaEval 2.0 and scoring 7.25 on MT-Bench.

The model's reward modeling ability also improved iteratively, with pairwise accuracy aligning with human rankings increasing from 78.7% (
M
1
) to 81.7% (
M
3
).
The self-rewarding models maintained performance on traditional NLP benchmarks, indicating that the alignment process did not incur a significant 'alignment tax' on general capabilities.
Takeaways: Large language models (LLMs) can simultaneously improve their instruction-following ability and their capacity to evaluate responses through an iterative self-training process.
This self-alignment mechanism allows LLMs to generate their own high-quality feedback, moving beyond the limitations of static human or fixed AI feedback sources.
Explicitly training the LLM to act as a judge with a custom, additive scoring prompt is crucial for developing its evaluation capabilities, which then further enhances its instruction-following.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.09865.Title: Improving fine-grained understanding in image-text pre-training
https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.09865.Summary: Google DeepMind researchers introduce SPARse Fine-grained Contrastive Alignment (SPARC), a pre-training approach that enhances vision-language models by efficiently capturing fine-grained relationships between image regions and text tokens. SPARC achieves improved visual localization and downstream task performance, such as 72.4% on zero-shot ImageNet and better object detection, while maintaining computational efficiency similar to CLIP.
Problem: Current vision-language models struggle with fine-grained understanding, lacking the ability to connect specific image regions with particular text phrases.
Existing fine-grained alignment methods often incur prohibitive computational costs and may suffer from training instability.
Many approaches assume rigid one-to-one mappings between text tokens and image patches, failing to capture the natural one-to-many relationships in visual language.
Method: SPARC uses sparse similarity matrices by computing similarities between image patches and text tokens, then retaining only the strongest connections through a thresholding approach.
It introduces language-grouped vision embeddings, where each text token's visual representation is a weighted average of relevant image patch embeddings, allowing one-to-many mappings.

The method combines a standard global contrastive loss for whole image-text alignment with a novel sequence-wise fine-grained contrastive loss to align language-grouped vision embeddings with text tokens.
Results: SPARC achieves 72.4% accuracy on zero-shot ImageNet classification, comparable to CLIP's 71.5%, and outperforms CLIP on COCO and Flickr30K image-text retrieval benchmarks.
It demonstrates significantly enhanced object detection and segmentation capabilities when fine-tuned, and shows improved visual localization on semantic segmentation benchmarks without fine-tuning.
SPARC maintains computational efficiency similar to CLIP, with substantially lower TFLOPS and peak memory usage compared to other fine-grained methods, particularly at larger batch sizes.
Takeaways: Fine-grained understanding can be efficiently integrated into vision-language models without sacrificing global context or incurring prohibitive computational costs.
Sparsifying the patch-token similarity matrix and grouping visual embeddings by language tokens effectively captures one-to-many visual-textual relationships.
Combining global and fine-grained contrastive objectives leads to improved performance across diverse downstream tasks, including localization and generative applications.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.08541.Title: Scalable Pre-training of Large Autoregressive Image Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.08541.Summary: Researchers at Apple developed Autoregressive Image Models (AIM), a scalable pre-training approach for large vision models that predicts image patches sequentially. AIM demonstrates strong scaling properties with increased model size and training data, achieving competitive performance on 15 image recognition benchmarks, including 84.0% ImageNet-1k accuracy with a frozen backbone.
Problem: Traditional self-supervised learning methods in vision (contrastive, masked autoencoding) have limitations like computational intensity, reliance on complex techniques to avoid trivial solutions, or hyperparameter sensitivity.
Existing vision models had not fully explored the effectiveness of autoregressive objectives, which are highly successful in NLP, for large-scale pre-training.
There was a need to investigate if similar scaling properties observed in large language models could be replicated in the visual domain without manual annotations.
Method: Introduces Autoregressive Image Models (AIM) that treat images as sequences of patches and predict each patch based on preceding ones, mirroring language model training.
Employs a Vision Transformer (ViT) backbone with a novel prefix attention mechanism that allows bidirectional attention for an initial set of patches while maintaining causal attention for the rest.
Utilizes heavily parameterized token-level prediction heads (MLP blocks) for predicting patches and prioritizes increasing model width over depth when scaling up.
Results: AIM models consistently improved performance with increased model size (from 0.6B to 7B parameters) and training data (up to 2 billion images), showing no saturation in performance.
The largest model, AIM-7B, achieved 84.0% accuracy on ImageNet-1k with a frozen backbone and attained competitive performance across 15 diverse image recognition benchmarks.

AIM's approach proved competitive with or outperformed state-of-the-art self-supervised methods like DINO and MAE on various benchmarks, particularly with larger model sizes, while being simpler and more stable.
Takeaways: Autoregressive objectives successfully apply to vision tasks and exhibit strong scaling properties similar to language models across model size, training data, and compute budget.
The choice of patch ordering significantly impacts performance, with raster (row-major) order outperforming other patterns due to maintaining consistent prediction difficulty throughout the sequence.
Prefix attention and heavily parameterized MLP prediction heads contribute to the effectiveness and scalability of the autoregressive vision model.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.08190.Title: MARIO: MAth Reasoning with code Interpreter Output -- A Reproducible Pipeline
https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.08190.Summary: Researchers at Alibaba Group developed MARIO, a reproducible pipeline that enhances Large Language Models' mathematical reasoning through a hybrid approach combining textual analysis with code execution. This framework achieves state-of-the-art results on challenging math benchmarks like MATH and improves solution accuracy by integrating an Outcome Value Model for verification.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle with precise mathematical reasoning, often due to their probabilistic nature which is ill-suited for exact calculations.
Existing tool-augmented LLMs, while good at computation, sometimes lack common sense or contextual understanding for math word problems, leading to illogical answers.
There is a need for high-quality, reproducible, and cost-effective protocols for fine-tuning math-specific LLMs and curating suitable datasets.
Method: A reproducible pipeline for mathematical reasoning, MARIO, constructs a rich dataset by combining human-reviewed solutions from GSM8K/MATH with self-trained data and MetaMath augmentation, re-formatted into an HTML-like structure.

A three-stage fine-tuning protocol is used: starting with a math-oriented foundation model (Llemma), followed by Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on correct solutions, and then multi-task LoRA fine-tuning to train an Outcome Value Model (OVM) for solution evaluation.
During inference, the SFT LLM generates multiple candidate solutions, and the OVM re-ranks them using an outlier-free selection algorithm to identify the most accurate answer.
Results: MARIO-7B achieved a 47.0% accuracy on the MATH dataset, establishing a new state-of-the-art for 7B-parameter models, and showed strong generalization on challenging out-of-domain datasets (OCWCourses: 21.7%, GaoKao2023-Math-En: 38.2%).
The outlier-free OVM selection algorithm improved MARIO-7B's GSM8K accuracy by +12.8% (to 82.9%) and MATH accuracy by +12.1% (to 59.1%) over its base SFT performance.
Converting training data to an HTML-like format resulted in a 20% reduction in training loss during initial iterations compared to a key-value (REACT) format.
Takeaways: Integrating textual analysis with code execution enhances mathematical reasoning by providing common sense checks and problem decomposition, leading to more robust solutions than purely code-centric methods.
Re-formatting training data to an HTML-like structure can significantly reduce initial training loss, suggesting better alignment with LLM pre-training corpora.

An Outcome Value Model (OVM) trained with a multi-task approach and an outlier-free selection algorithm effectively improves solution accuracy by re-ranking generated outputs, outperforming simple majority voting.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.07629.Title: Fine-Grained Prototypes Distillation for Few-Shot Object Detection
https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.07629.Summary: FPD introduces a method for few-shot object detection that distills fine-grained prototypes from mid-level features and enhances high-level feature fusion. It achieved state-of-the-art results on PASCAL VOC, notably improving performance by up to 4.0 percentage points AP50 on some novel sets, and competitive scores on MS COCO.
Problem: Meta-learning-based Few-Shot Object Detection (FSOD) methods often rely on coarse, class-level prototypes lacking fine-grained local context for precise object identification.
Previous attempts at detailed feature matching were computationally inefficient and struggled to identify critical details or integrate information from multiple support shots.
Existing high-level feature fusion strategies in FSOD use simplistic aggregation or element-wise multiplication, which may not effectively capture complex inter-class relationships.
Method: Introduces a Fine-Grained Feature Aggregation (FFA) module that distills mid-level support features into distinct fine-grained prototypes using class-exclusive feature queries and assigns them to query features via cross-attention.
Develops a Balanced Class-Agnostic Sampling (B-CAS) strategy to select both positive and negative class prototypes, enhancing inter-class relationship modeling for high-level feature aggregation.
Proposes a Non-Linear Fusion (NLF) module that employs a sophisticated non-linear network to combine RoI features and class prototypes, preserving original RoI information for improved localization.
Results: FPD achieved state-of-the-art performance on the PASCAL VOC benchmark, notably surpassing previous methods by up to 4.0 AP50 percentage points for 10-shot detection on Novel Set 3.
The method demonstrated competitive results on the challenging MS COCO dataset, improving upon the prior best meta-learning approach (VFA) by 1.2 AP percentage points for 30-shot scenarios.
Ablation studies confirmed that all proposed modules (FFA, B-CAS, NLF) incrementally contribute to performance gains, with FFA consistently outperforming direct dense feature matching strategies.
Takeaways: Leveraging fine-grained prototypes, distilled from mid-level features, is crucial for capturing subtle local context and improving object detection accuracy in few-shot scenarios.
Distilling representative features with learnable queries offers a more efficient and robust alternative to direct dense feature matching for modeling detailed relationships.
A balanced approach to high-level feature aggregation, incorporating both positive and negative class samples through non-linear fusion, enhances the model's ability to discriminate between classes.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.05946.Title: Learning Cognitive Maps from Transformer Representations for Efficient Planning in Partially Observed Environments
https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.05946.Summary: Researchers at Google DeepMind developed the Transformer with Discrete Bottleneck (TDB) architecture, which enables transformers to learn explicit, interpretable cognitive maps from sequence data. This allows for near-perfect, exponentially faster planning and navigation in perceptually aliased and novel partially observed environments compared to vanilla transformer models.
Problem: Vanilla transformers, despite their predictive power, do not learn explicit, interpretable world models amenable to efficient, goal-directed planning.
Planning and navigation in partially observed environments (POEs) is challenging due to perceptual aliasing, where identical observations correspond to different true states.
Traditional transformer-based planning relies on computationally expensive forward rollouts, which are inefficient and often fail in aliased settings.
Method: The Transformer with Discrete Bottleneck (TDB) integrates a Vector Quantization (VQ) layer into a causal transformer to compress intermediate representations into discrete latent codes.

TDB employs augmented training objectives, such as multi-step observation prediction or next encoding prediction (with a teacher network), to force the discrete bottleneck to learn robust, disambiguated latent representations.
A cognitive map (latent graph) is explicitly constructed from the sequence of learned bottleneck indices, which an external solver then uses for efficient path planning.
Results: TDB achieved near-perfect planning accuracy (99% success rate with optimal path lengths) in aliased 2D and 3D environments, demonstrating an exponential speed-up over vanilla sequence models.
The model successfully learned accurate cognitive maps, nearly isomorphic to ground truth environment dynamics (NormGED ~0.005-0.12), enabling robust planning even under perceptual aliasing.

TDB generalized to novel, unseen partially observed environments at inference time, performing near-perfect in-context prediction and planning, and also successfully extracted interpretable structures from abstract text data (GINC dataset).
Takeaways: Augmented training objectives (multi-step prediction, next encoding prediction) are crucial for compelling the discrete bottleneck to learn disambiguated latent states, effectively resolving perceptual aliasing.
The TDB architecture can achieve emergent in-context learning, inferring and utilizing accurate cognitive maps for efficient planning in entirely novel, unseen partially observed environments.

Extracting an explicit, queryable cognitive map from latent representations allows for planning that is exponentially more efficient than forward rollouts and provides interpretability into the agent's world understanding.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.17686.Title: Multiscale Vision Transformers meet Bipartite Matching for efficient single-stage Action Localization
https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.17686.Summary: Researchers from Queen Mary University of London and Samsung AI Center Cambridge developed BMViT, an encoder-only Multiscale Vision Transformer architecture that applies bipartite matching directly to output tokens for efficient single-stage action localization. The method achieves 30.0 mAP on AVA 2.2, outperforming two-stage MViTv2-S (26.8 mAP) while requiring fewer computational resources, and demonstrates competitive performance against other single-stage approaches.
Problem: Existing two-stage action localization methods are computationally inefficient and slow, making them unsuitable for real-time applications due to separate detection and classification stages.
Current single-stage methods, often based on DETR, introduce significant architectural complexity with encoder-decoder designs and learnable queries, making them challenging to train.
The task of spatio-temporal action localization itself is complex, requiring sophisticated reasoning beyond static object detection to simultaneously detect bounding boxes and classify actions.
Method: The BMViT framework employs a standard Multi-scale Vision Transformer (MViTv2-S) as an encoder-only backbone, directly utilizing its output tokens as prediction slots.

It eliminates the need for external person detectors or complex encoder-decoder structures by feeding output tokens into simple MLP heads for bounding box, actor likelihood, and action class predictions.
Training involves a direct bipartite matching loss (Hungarian Algorithm) applied to these output tokens, enabling end-to-end optimization for simultaneous detection and classification.
Results: BMViT achieved 30.0 mAP on AVA 2.2 using MViTv2-S, surpassing the two-stage MViTv2-S (26.8 mAP) while requiring significantly fewer FLOPs (121.2 GFLOPs vs. 311 GFLOPs including external detector).

The method demonstrated competitive or superior performance against leading single-stage methods on AVA 2.2, such as outperforming TubeR (29.2 mAP) and STMixer (27.8 mAP) with its simpler architecture.
BMViT generalized well across datasets, achieving 85.6 mAP on UCF101-24 and 80.7 mAP on JHMDB51-21 with MViTv2-S, with further improvements when scaling to a ViT-B backbone (90.7 mAP on UCF101-24).
Takeaways: A streamlined, encoder-only Vision Transformer architecture, combined with direct bipartite matching, can effectively perform single-stage action localization, challenging the need for complex decoder structures or external detectors.
Increasing the spatial resolution of the Vision Transformer's output tokens and employing a strategic selection method for detection and classification tasks significantly improves performance.
Training with fixed input aspect ratios enhances model stability and performance by providing a consistent structure for output tokens, which are directly matched to ground truth.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.14135.Title: V*: Guided Visual Search as a Core Mechanism in Multimodal LLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.14135.Summary: This research introduces V*, an LLM-guided visual search mechanism, to address the visual information bottleneck in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), enabling them to actively process and reason about high-resolution visual details. The proposed SEAL framework allows MLLMs to identify missing visual information and dynamically search for it, leading to a 20%+ improvement in accuracy over commercial MLLMs like GPT-4V on fine-grained visual reasoning tasks and reduced hallucinations.
Problem: Existing end-to-end MLLMs suffer from a 'visual information bottleneck' due to processing low-resolution images, leading to significant loss of fine-grained detail.
Current MLLMs lack an intrinsic mechanism to actively identify missing visual information or proactively seek it out in complex, high-resolution scenes.
LLM-tool-using systems rely on text-only processing of visual information, leading to potential data loss and cascaded errors from imperfect vision experts.
Method: Introduces SEAL (Show, SEArch, and TelL), a meta-architecture that integrates an LLM-guided visual search mechanism (V*) into existing MLLMs.
The V* visual search model enables MLLMs to actively query for missing visual details and utilize their internal world knowledge and common sense to guide efficient, hierarchical search.
A Visual Working Memory (VWM) is constructed to store and integrate global image, question, and dynamically searched target information for the VQA LLM to generate more informed responses.
Results: The SEAL framework, incorporating V*, achieved 75.39% accuracy on the V*Bench benchmark for fine-grained visual grounding, outperforming GPT-4V (54.97%) and Gemini Pro (48.16%).

V* significantly reduced the average 'search length' to 4.65 steps per target, demonstrating an informed search strategy that is more efficient than baseline methods and comparable to human eye fixations.

The integration of V* maintained the base model's general multimodal capabilities and improved performance on the POPE hallucination benchmark (from 76.5% to 82.4%), indicating reduced object hallucination.
Takeaways: Active visual search, inspired by human cognition, is crucial for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to achieve precise visual grounding on high-resolution, visually crowded images.
Large Language Models (LLMs) can effectively guide visual search using common sense and world knowledge, enhancing efficiency and accuracy beyond generic object detectors.
Training MLLMs to identify missing information and incorporate dynamically retrieved visual details into a visual working memory improves reasoning and reduces visual hallucinations.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.13286.Title: Generative Multimodal Models are In-Context Learners
https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.13286.Summary: Emu2, a 37-billion-parameter generative multimodal model developed by the Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence (BAAI), demonstrates robust in-context learning capabilities by predicting the next multimodal element in a sequence. The model achieves state-of-the-art performance in few-shot settings across a wide range of multimodal understanding and generation tasks, including visual question answering, referring expression comprehension, text-to-image generation, and subject-driven image editing.
Problem: Multimodal AI systems often require task-specific architectures and extensive supervised datasets for each new task, which is difficult to scale and adapt to diverse, novel challenges.
Existing multimodal models lack human-like in-context learning abilities, struggling to adapt to new tasks with minimal demonstrations or simple instructions.
Inefficiency in AI development due to the repeated need to design and train new models for each distinct multimodal task.
Method: Introduces Emu2, a 37-billion-parameter generative multimodal model from BAAI, trained with a unified autoregressive objective to predict the next multimodal element.

Employs a three-component architecture: a Visual Encoder (EVA-02-CLIP-E-plus), a Multimodal Modeling component (LLaMA-33B Transformer decoder), and a Visual Decoder (SDXL-based for images, adapted 3D U-Net for video).

Undergoes extensive pretraining on large-scale, diverse multimodal sequences (image-text, video-text, interleaved, grounded) followed by specialized instruction tuning to create Emu2-Chat and Emu2-Gen models.
Results: Emu2 (37B parameters) demonstrates superior few-shot in-context learning on VQAv2, VizWiz, and TextVQA, outperforming larger models like Flamingo-80B and IDEFICS-80B.

Emu2-Chat achieves state-of-the-art performance on image and video question answering benchmarks (e.g., VQAv2, OKVQA, MSVD-QA) and sets new records on complex LMM benchmarks (SEED-Bench, MM-Vet, MMMU).
Emu2-Gen reaches state-of-the-art zero-shot text-to-image generation on MS-COCO (highest CLIP-I and CLIP-T scores) and excels in subject fidelity on DreamBench for subject-driven generation.
Takeaways: Scaling a generative multimodal model with a unified autoregressive objective (predicting the next multimodal element) significantly enhances in-context learning capabilities.
A single, versatile base model can adapt to a broad spectrum of multimodal tasks with few demonstrations or instructions, mirroring human cognitive flexibility.

Sophisticated emergent abilities like visual prompting and object-grounded generation appear through large-scale generative pretraining, and Emu2 achieves competitive results with fewer parameters than some larger models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.12148.Title: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning Methods for Pretrained Language Models: A Critical Review and Assessment
https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.12148.Summary: This paper provides a comprehensive review and assessment of Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods for pretrained language models, systematically categorizing existing techniques. An extensive empirical evaluation demonstrates that PEFT methods significantly reduce computational costs and memory requirements while achieving performance comparable to or better than full fine-tuning across various benchmarks.
Problem: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) requires substantial computational resources and GPU memory, making adaptation impractical for many researchers and organizations.
High memory usage and slow training/inference times limit the accessibility and practical application of LLMs.
Full fine-tuning can lead to catastrophic forgetting of pretrained knowledge in low-resource scenarios.
Method: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) adapts large pretrained models by updating only a small subset of existing parameters or introducing a limited number of new trainable parameters.
PEFT methods are systematically categorized into five main types: Additive, Partial, Reparameterized, Hybrid, and Unified Fine-Tuning.
Specific techniques include Adapter-based methods (e.g., (IA)³), Prompt-based methods (e.g., Prefix Tuning), and low-rank adaptation (e.g., LoRA, QLoRA).
Results: PEFT methods reduced memory usage on LLaMA-13B-Alpaca, with (IA)³ by 33.55%, LoRA by 39.46%, and QLoRA by 76.86% compared to full fine-tuning.
Most PEFT methods achieved performance comparable to or better than full fine-tuning on various benchmarks, despite updating significantly fewer parameters.

On the GLUE benchmark, ProPELT demonstrated the best average performance with relatively few trainable parameters, while Prompt Tuning, though requiring the fewest parameters, yielded lower performance.
Takeaways: PEFT methods significantly reduce computational and memory requirements compared to full fine-tuning, making large language models more accessible.
Many PEFT techniques achieve comparable or even improved performance relative to full fine-tuning on various benchmarks while using a fraction of the trainable parameters.
The effectiveness of PEFT in reducing memory usage becomes more pronounced as model size increases, highlighting their value for very large models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.10439.Title: Simple Image-level Classification Improves Open-vocabulary Object Detection
https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.10439.Summary: A method for Open-Vocabulary Object Detection (OVOD), SIC-CADS, integrates global scene understanding from Vision-Language Models (VLMs) by training a multi-label recognition module to generate image-level contextual scores that refine instance-level detection scores. This approach leads to 1.4-3.9 points improvement in AP_r on OV-LVIS and 1.7-3.2 points in AP_novel on OV-COCO, while also improving cross-dataset generalization.
Problem: Existing Open-Vocabulary Object Detection (OVOD) methods insufficiently utilize the global scene understanding capabilities of Vision-Language Models (VLMs).
OVOD models struggle to accurately detect "hard objects" (small, blurred, occluded, ambiguous) as these rely heavily on surrounding contextual information, which regional features often miss.
There is a performance gap in detecting novel object categories, particularly for challenging instances, due to the lack of explicit contextual feature learning for these classes.
Method: SIC-CADS introduces a Multi-modal Multi-Label Recognition (MLR) module that leverages CLIP's global image encoder to predict image-level scores for object categories.
The MLR module combines a Text MLR branch, aligning learned image embeddings with CLIP text embeddings, and a Visual MLR branch, distilling knowledge from the CLIP image encoder.
Instance-level detection scores from existing OVOD models are refined by fusing them with the MLR module's image-level contextual scores using a weighted geometric mean during inference.
Results: SIC-CADS consistently improved novel category detection by 1.4-3.9 AP_r points on OV-LVIS and 1.7-3.2 AP_novel points on OV-COCO across various base models.
The method enhanced cross-dataset generalization, showing 1.9-2.1 mAP_50 points gain on Objects365 and 1.5-3.9 mAP_50 points gain on OpenImages.
Achieved these gains with minimal additional computational cost (8.3-12.5% increase in GFLOPs) and only a marginal decrease in inference speed (FPS).
Takeaways: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) possess rich global scene understanding, including object co-occurrence patterns, that is underexploited by region-focused Open-Vocabulary Object Detection (OVOD) models.
Explicitly leveraging image-level global contextual information from VLMs can substantially improve the detection of challenging objects (small, occluded, ambiguous), especially for novel categories.
A lightweight, independently trained multi-label recognition module can serve as a general and efficient plug-and-play mechanism to boost the performance of diverse OVOD architectures.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.08762.Title: Multi-modal Latent Space Learning for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.08762.Summary: A new method called DPMM-CoT enhances multi-modal reasoning by using diffusion models to learn a latent space that aligns visual and textual information more effectively. This approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on benchmarks like ScienceQA, outperforming prior multi-modal Chain-of-Thought methods by up to 6.06%.
Problem: Current multi-modal Chain-of-Thought (CoT) approaches rely on fixed image features from pre-trained vision models that are not optimized for reasoning tasks.
Extracted image features often poorly align with the language reasoning process, creating a semantic gap between visual and textual information.
Existing methods struggle with effectively combining visual and textual information, particularly for complex reasoning requiring deep semantic understanding of visual elements.
Method: Introduces Diffusion Process enhanced Multi-Modal CoT (DPMM-CoT), a novel approach using diffusion models to learn a text-image aligned latent space for multi-modal reasoning.

Leverages a diffusion process to learn a shared latent representation that captures deep semantic information from images and aligns it with textual information, rather than using fixed image features.
Incorporates a gated mechanism to effectively combine the learned visual features with textual representations and uses a Text Decoder to generate reasoning rationales and final answers.
Results: DPMM-CoT achieved state-of-the-art performance on ScienceQA, outperforming existing methods like MM-CoT (DETR) by 6.06% for the Base version and 1.67% for the Large version.

The method demonstrated stronger results on questions requiring reasoning based on images, indicating the effectiveness of the multi-modal latent space learning, and generated higher-quality reasoning chains (ROUGE-L score).
DPMM-CoT achieved better results than ChatGPT with less than 1/100th of the parameters and showed improved generalization on multi-modal machine translation tasks.
Takeaways: Diffusion models can effectively learn deep semantic representations from images that better support reasoning tasks by capturing nuanced relationships.
Aligning visual and textual information in a shared latent space via a diffusion process bridges the semantic gap inherent in multi-modal reasoning.
Optimizing image features specifically for reasoning tasks, rather than using fixed pre-trained features, significantly improves multi-modal understanding and rationale generation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06709.Title: AM-RADIO: Agglomerative Vision Foundation Model -- Reduce All Domains Into One
https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06709.Summary: The AM-RADIO framework unifies diverse Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) like CLIP, DINOv2, and SAM into a single student model, achieving superior performance across various visual understanding tasks. It also introduces E-RADIO, a hardware-efficient architecture that delivers comparable quality while offering at least 6x faster inference speeds.
Problem: Current Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) are specialized (e.g., CLIP for language, SAM for segmentation, DINOv2 for dense features), leading to a fragmented ecosystem.
Using multiple distinct VFMs for comprehensive visual intelligence is computationally inefficient and complex.
Large Foundation Models (FMs) have prohibitive computational and memory demands for many real-world applications.
Method: A multi-teacher knowledge distillation framework, AM-RADIO, trains a student model from scratch using CLIP, DINOv2, and SAM as teachers.
The approach distills both summary and spatial feature representations from teachers via adaptor heads, primarily using cosine similarity loss.
A novel, hardware-efficient hybrid CNN-Transformer architecture called E-RADIO is developed to optimize throughput and performance during distillation.
Results: The flagship RADIO-ViT-H/16 model surpasses its individual teacher models, achieving the best metrics on 6 out of 9 evaluated tasks, including ImageNet-1K k-NN (86.06%) and ADE20k semantic segmentation (51.34%).
The E-RADIO-L architecture achieves comparable quality to larger models while demonstrating at least 6x faster inference speeds compared to teachers at matched resolutions.
RADIO effectively retains the specialized functionalities of its teachers, serving as a drop-in replacement for SAM's vision encoder with comparable COCO mIOU.
Probing revealed that RADIO's 3D awareness is on par with larger DINOv2 models for tasks like monocular depth estimation.
Takeaways: Distilling both summary and spatial feature representations from teachers is essential, leading to an 18% relative improvement on dense tasks like ADE20K.
DINOv2's spatial features are particularly effective for dense image understanding, outperforming SAM in this regard for linear probing.
Simple, equally-weighted loss balancing performed comparably to more complex automatic methods, indicating robustness of the feature matching approach.
Cropped Position Embedding (CPE) effectively enables ViTs to generalize to arbitrary input resolutions, enhancing performance on semantic segmentation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.04684.Title: LaRS: Latent Reasoning Skills for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.04684.Summary: LaRS introduces an unsupervised method that discovers and leverages latent reasoning skills from Chain-of-Thought rationales using a Conditional Variational Autoencoder. This approach consistently improves LLM performance on complex reasoning tasks, achieving up to 4x faster pre-processing and significantly enhanced robustness to noisy example banks compared to prior skill-based selection methods.
Problem: Existing Chain-of-Thought (CoT) demonstration selection methods, based on question similarity, often lead to 'skill mismatches' as similar questions may require different reasoning processes.

Prior skill-based CoT selection methods, like Skill-KNN, rely on expensive LLM inferences to generate explicit textual skill descriptions, leading to high computational costs, poor scalability, and subjective skill representations.
The quality and consistency of CoT prompting can be severely degraded by suboptimal examples, highlighting a need for more robust selection strategies.
Method: LaRS proposes a 'latent skill model' that formulates rationale generation as conditioned on both the question and a latent reasoning skill, providing a theoretical framework for skill-based CoT.

It implements this model using a Conditional Variational Autoencoder (CVAE) with lightweight MLPs and pre-trained embedding models to unsupervisedly discover latent reasoning skills from question-rationale pairs.

Demonstration selection for a new query involves inferring its desired latent skill, computing demonstrated skills for examples in the bank, and selecting top-k examples based on cosine similarity in the latent skill space.
Results: LaRS consistently outperformed the state-of-the-art `Skill-KNN-zero` in 18 out of 20 experiments across four reasoning benchmarks (TabMWP, GSM8K, Spider, COGS), and matched oracle performance in nearly half of the experiments.
It achieved a 4x faster pre-processing time for example banks and eliminated LLM inference costs for skill discovery, saving approximately $30 per 1k examples compared to `Skill-KNN-zero`.

The method demonstrated superior robustness to sub-optimal example banks, showing minimal performance degradation (0.1% to 1.9%) with 30% random rationales, whereas `Skill-KNN-zero` experienced drops up to 11.7%.
Takeaways: Reasoning rationales are not solely dependent on the question but are also governed by underlying 'latent reasoning skills' that can be automatically discovered without explicit textual descriptions.
Unsupervised learning with a CVAE can effectively capture abstract reasoning concepts in a continuous latent space, which aligns with human understanding of distinct skills.

Representing skills as continuous latent variables and using lightweight models for inference dramatically improves computational efficiency and scalability compared to methods relying on LLM-generated skill descriptions.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.13601.Title: Visual In-Context Prompting
https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.13601.Summary: DINOv is a unified visual segmentation framework that extends in-context prompting to generic vision tasks using purely visual cues, demonstrating strong open-set generalization and competitive performance across various benchmarks. It unifies referring and generic segmentation within a single architecture, leveraging diverse data effectively.
Problem: Existing visual prompting models primarily address referring segmentation, lacking robust capabilities for generic vision tasks like open-set object detection or panoptic segmentation.
Visual prompts, often represented as dense masks, hinder generalization to entirely novel concepts and struggle with identifying multiple instances of the same semantic concept.
Bridging the gap between LLM-style in-context learning and pixel-level vision tasks, as current vision models have limited adaptability to new tasks via visual examples alone.
Method: DINOv introduces a unified encoder-decoder architecture, building on MaskDINO principles, with a specialized PromptEncoder that reuses the internal vision encoder to process diverse visual prompts (masks, boxes, points).
It formulates generic segmentation by aggregating in-context examples across a batch to form category representatives and referring segmentation via a "self-referring" strategy.

The model employs dual decoder queries P-generic queries for object proposals and interactive point queries for specific instance segmentation P-and is jointly trained on semantically labeled (COCO) and pixel-annotated (SA-1B) datasets.
Results: DINOv-L achieves 57.7 PQ on COCO 2017 panoptic segmentation, nearly matching the text-prompted MaskDINO-L baseline and significantly surpassing other visual-prompted models like SegGPT-L (43.4 PQ).
For out-of-domain open-set segmentation, DINOv demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization on ADE20K with 23.2 PQ, outperforming or matching previous text-prompted open-set models.
In zero-shot video object segmentation, DINOv-T achieves 73.3 J&F on DAVIS2017, outperforming SEEM-T (60.4 J&F) and other non-video-trained models.
Takeaways: Visual in-context prompting can be successfully extended to generic vision tasks, enabling strong open-set generalization without relying on explicit text labels or large-scale vision-language models for semantic knowledge.

A dedicated prompt encoder that reuses the vision encoder and focuses on fine-grained appearance features is critical for effective visual in-context learning, outperforming external pre-trained vision-language encoders.
Joint training on both semantically labeled and pixel-level annotated datasets, combined with a dual-query decoder, yields synergistic improvements for both generic and referring segmentation tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.12424.Title: Looped Transformers are Better at Learning Learning Algorithms
https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.12424.Summary: A looped transformer architecture from the University of Wisconsin, Madison, efficiently emulates iterative learning algorithms, achieving comparable or superior in-context learning performance with over 90% fewer parameters than standard transformers. The model demonstrates stable convergence to fixed-point solutions and exhibits enhanced sample efficiency and a
Problem: Standard feed-forward transformer architectures lack an inherent iterative structure, making them inefficient for emulating step-by-step algorithms like gradient descent.
Direct solutions for some problems (e.g., linear regression) are computationally complex for transformers to learn in a single forward pass, potentially requiring many layers.
The high parameter count of deep standard transformers for in-context learning poses efficiency challenges and limits deployment in resource-constrained environments.
Method: A single-layer GPT-2 decoder model is repeatedly applied in a loop, with the original input additively injected at each iteration to imbue the architecture with iterative processing capabilities.
The looped transformer significantly reduces parameter count (0.79M) compared to a standard 12-layer transformer (9.48M) by reusing a single computational block.

A specialized training methodology minimizes expected loss over a range of loop iterations with a truncated loss window, encouraging performance improvement, convergence, and indefinite stability for fixed-point solutions.
Results: The looped transformer achieved comparable or superior in-context learning performance using 0.79 million parameters, a >90% reduction compared to a standard 12-layer transformer (9.48 million parameters).
Successfully emulated iterative algorithms by converging to stable fixed-point solutions over many inference iterations, with the

Demonstrated superior sample efficiency during training and consistent or improved performance across linear, sparse linear, decision tree, and 2-layer ReLU NN function classes, outperforming traditional Lasso regression in certain sparse settings.
Takeaways: Looped transformers can effectively emulate iterative algorithms, achieving stable fixed-point solutions that do not degrade even when run for more iterations than trained for.
This recurrent architecture enables significant parameter efficiency (over 90% reduction) while maintaining or improving in-context learning performance compared to deeper standard transformers.
The model exhibits a

https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.09191.Title: Domain Aligned CLIP for Few-shot Classification
https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.09191.Summary: The Domain Aligned CLIP (DAC) framework enhances few-shot image classification by adapting large vision-language models through explicit optimization of both intra-modal (image-to-image) and inter-modal (image-to-text) alignment on target distributions. The method consistently outperforms competitive baselines across 11 diverse datasets, showing improved robustness to distribution shifts.
Problem: Large vision-language models like CLIP perform sub-optimally on specific downstream tasks due to domain gaps between pre-training and target data distributions.
Existing few-shot adaptation methods for CLIP often neglect comprehensive alignment, focusing on only one modality or type of alignment.
Full fine-tuning of CLIP for adaptation requires significant computational resources and can reduce out-of-distribution robustness.
Method: A two-stage Domain Aligned CLIP (DAC) framework is proposed, comprising DAC-V for visual domain adaptation and DAC-VT for textual domain adaptation.
DAC-V employs intra-modal contrastive learning with a lightweight adapter to improve visual feature alignment and create an adapted visual cache for better class separation.
DAC-VT directly fine-tunes the text embeddings of class labels to enhance inter-modal alignment with the adapted visual features from the first stage.
Results: The Domain Aligned CLIP (DAC-VT) framework consistently outperforms competitive baselines, including Tip-Adapter, across 11 diverse image classification benchmarks in few-shot settings.
DAC-VT demonstrates enhanced robustness to distribution shifts, making fewer classification errors compared to vanilla CLIP across various datasets.
Performance improvements from the DAC framework scale positively with the number of training examples, showing more pronounced gains as the shot number increases.
Takeaways: Explicitly optimizing both intra-modal (image-to-image) and inter-modal (image-to-text) alignment for the target domain is crucial for superior few-shot adaptation of vision-language models.
Intra-modal contrastive learning with a lightweight adapter effectively creates better-separated visual feature representations for different classes.
Directly adapting textual embeddings of class labels significantly improves inter-modal alignment, particularly for domain-specific vocabularies.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.05437.Title: LLaVA-Plus: Learning to Use Tools for Creating Multimodal Agents
https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.05437.Summary: LLaVA-Plus, developed by researchers from Tsinghua University and Microsoft Research, introduces an approach that trains a Large Multimodal Model (LMM) to intelligently leverage external vision and vision-language tools from a skill repository. It establishes new state-of-the-art performance on benchmarks like VisiT-Bench and LLaVA-Bench (Tools), demonstrating improved visual understanding, content generation, and interactive capabilities.
Problem: End-to-end Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) struggle to seamlessly integrate a wide range of specialized vision and vision-language skills like precise segmentation or advanced image generation.
Existing tool-chaining methods, while flexible, heavily rely on brittle prompt engineering for tool selection and composition, lacking robustness and adaptability in dynamic real-world scenarios.
