Prior tool-augmented LLMs often lose active visual grounding during the interaction, only engaging the image when a specific multimodal tool is activated, which limits their planning and reasoning.
Method: Extends existing LMMs (like LLaVA) by training them with visual instruction tuning to act as planners that leverage a diverse 'skill repository' of specialized vision models.
Implements a four-step dialogue flow (Human Input, LMM Planning, Tool Execution, LMM Aggregation & Response) where the LMM continuously considers the raw image query while planning tool usage.

Constructs a novel, comprehensive multimodal instruction-following dataset for tool use via a self-instruct method, using GPT-4 to generate diverse human-AI interaction sessions and skill composition scenarios.
Results: LLaVA-Plus variants consistently outperform LLaVA on LLaVA-Bench, SEED-Bench (e.g., LLaVA-Plus (All Tools) achieves 83.9 on LLaVA-Bench COCO vs. LLaVA's 81.2), and MMVet, demonstrating improved existing capabilities, especially in OCR and spatial categories.
Achieves a new State-of-the-Art Elo rating of 1203 on VisiT-Bench, surpassing LLaVA (1095) and other leading methods, showcasing its practical effectiveness in real-world use cases.

Exhibits emergent capabilities such as precise object detection and contextual reasoning, semantic segmentation with mask-based conditional image generation, and multimodal social media post creation, while also reducing false positives from individual tools like Grounding DINO (from 90 to 20 instances in a test set).
Takeaways: An end-to-end trained Large Multimodal Model (LMM) can effectively learn to select, activate, and compose diverse external tools, offering greater robustness and adaptability than prompt-engineered methods.

Maintaining active visual grounding throughout the entire human-AI interaction significantly improves the LMM's ability to understand complex visual instructions and generate coherent, visually grounded responses.
A high-quality, large-scale multimodal instruction-following dataset, particularly curated with advanced LLMs like GPT-4, is critical for teaching LMMs to intelligently utilize external tools.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.04157.Title: A Simple Interpretable Transformer for Fine-Grained Image Classification and Analysis
https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.04157.Summary: The INTR model introduces a simple, inherently interpretable Transformer for fine-grained image classification by having each class actively search for itself within an image. This approach provides built-in, attribute-level visual explanations directly from cross-attention maps, outperforming other interpretable models in identifying distinctive traits across various biological and object datasets.
Problem: Deep learning models for image classification often act as "black boxes," lacking transparency in their decision-making processes.
Existing post-hoc interpretability methods can suffer from low resolution, computational cost, and potential unfaithfulness to the model's true reasoning.
Prior self-interpretable models often require complex, custom architectures or multi-stage training, limiting their generalizability and ease of use.
Fine-grained classification tasks necessitate identifying subtle, discriminative attributes, which current explanation methods struggle to pinpoint accurately and consistently.
Method: INTR adapts a standard Transformer encoder-decoder architecture, replacing generic object queries with learnable, class-specific query vectors for the decoder.
A cross-attention mechanism within the decoder allows each class-specific query to directly attend to and aggregate relevant image features, forming class-specific feature representations.
The model uses a single learnable class-agnostic presence vector to classify based on these class-specific features, and is trained end-to-end with standard cross-entropy loss.
Results: INTR consistently provides faithful, built-in, attribute-level interpretations across eight diverse fine-grained datasets (e.g., birds, fish, butterflies), demonstrating its robust generalizability.
A human study showed INTR achieved 74.7% attribute identification accuracy on the CUB dataset, significantly outperforming ProtoPFormer's 42.2%.

The model exhibits high sensitivity to subtle attribute manipulations in images, directly altering cross-attention maps and often leading to changes in classification, affirming that predictions are driven by localized attributes.
INTR achieves classification accuracy comparable to a fine-tuned ResNet-50 on most datasets, with a 9.2% improvement on the Fish dataset, while offering inherent interpretability.
Takeaways: By designing each class to "search for itself" via dedicated query vectors and cross-attention, the model intrinsically generates faithful, attribute-level visual explanations without additional post-hoc steps.
The multi-head attention mechanism naturally learns to localize multiple, distinct attributes for each class, aiding fine-grained differentiation.

The mathematical formulation demonstrates that INTR's cross-attention maps are directly tied to prediction logits, providing a strong theoretical basis for their interpretability and addressing the "attention is not explanation" debate.
Self-attention among class queries in the decoder allows for contextual reasoning, enabling the model to focus on finer distinguishing attributes when comparing visually similar classes.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.03099.Title: Language Models are Super Mario: Absorbing Abilities from Homologous Models as a Free Lunch
https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.03099.Summary: This paper unveils extreme redundancy in Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) delta parameters of large language models, proposing DARE (Drop And REscale) to eliminate up to 99% of these parameters without retraining. Applying DARE significantly enhances model merging performance, enabling the creation of multi-competent models that can even surpass individual specialized source models.
Problem: High computational costs and resource demands for developing and deploying diverse capabilities in large language models (LLMs).
The implicit redundancy within parameters modified by Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT).
Parameter interference issues encountered when attempting to merge multiple task-specific LLMs into a single, versatile model.
Method: Defining SFT delta parameters as the difference between fine-tuned and pre-trained weights, focusing on the specific changes introduced by fine-tuning.
Introducing DARE (Drop And REscale), a two-step technique to randomly drop a proportion of delta parameters and then rescale the remaining ones, operating solely on CPUs without requiring retraining.
Integrating DARE as a pre-processing step for existing model merging frameworks to mitigate parameter interference and enhance the performance of composite models.
Results: DARE effectively removes up to 99% of SFT delta parameters from large language models with negligible performance degradation, demonstrating extreme redundancy.

Application of DARE consistently improves various model merging methods, with merged models showing potential to surpass the performance of individual source models (e.g., up to 19.57% improvement on MBPP over the code-specific model).
A 7B parameter merged model, 'supermario v2', created using DARE, achieved the top ranking on the Open LLM Leaderboard for its size class as of January 2024.
Takeaways: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) delta parameters exhibit extreme redundancy, allowing for 90-99% removal with minimal performance impact.
The rescale operation in DARE is critical for preserving model performance by maintaining original embedding approximations after parameters are dropped.
SFT primarily unlocks pre-existing capabilities within LLMs rather than introducing entirely new knowledge, as evidenced by catastrophic performance loss when fine-tuned parameters are removed.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.00530.Title: Advances in Embodied Navigation Using Large Language Models: A Survey
https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.00530.Summary: A survey by researchers at multiple Chinese institutions comprehensively reviews the application of Large Language Models (LLMs) in embodied navigation. It categorizes LLMs' roles, compares LLM-based and non-LLM models, analyzes relevant datasets, and identifies persistent challenges and future research directions.
Problem: Integrating diverse multimodal sensor data (text, images, real-time inputs) into robust navigation systems presents a significant challenge.
High latency and substantial computational demands of Large Language Models (LLMs) hinder their real-time application in dynamic navigation scenarios.
A need exists for a structured understanding of how LLMs can enhance embodied navigation, considering their language understanding and planning capabilities.
Method: The paper systematically reviews existing LLM-based navigation models, categorizing LLMs' roles into grounded language understanding and few-shot planning.
It comparatively analyzes LLM-based models against traditional Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) models, outlining their respective advantages and limitations.
A thorough analysis of commonly used datasets relevant to embodied navigation is presented, discussing their applicability, issues, and limitations.
Results: LLM-based models like NavGPT and SayNav show capabilities in complex planning, sub-goal decomposition, landmark recognition, and dynamic instruction generation.
The survey highlights that LLM-based models often excel in natural language understanding and few-shot learning but are computationally demanding and can struggle with fine-grained spatial reasoning.
Identified challenges include data diversity for granular navigation, improving spatial reasoning, addressing computational efficiency, and ensuring privacy in embodied AI systems.
Takeaways: LLMs primarily function in embodied navigation either by providing grounded language understanding for exploration policies or by directly generating actions as few-shot planners.
LLM-based agents demonstrate strong capabilities in path planning, environmental understanding, and human-agent interaction due to their natural language processing strengths.

While offering superior language understanding, LLMs face challenges in fine-grained spatial reasoning, integration of diverse real-time sensor data, and computational efficiency for navigation tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.18969.Title: Analyzing Vision Transformers for Image Classification in Class Embedding Space
https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.18969.Summary: Researchers at Goethe University Frankfurt developed a framework for Vision Transformers (ViTs) that projects internal representations onto a learned class embedding space, revealing how class-specific information is built across layers. This method provides an efficient and task-relevant tool for mechanistic interpretability and explainability, offering insights into the distinct contributions of self-attention and MLP layers.
Problem: Deep neural networks, particularly Vision Transformers, often operate as 'black boxes', making it challenging to mechanistically understand why they make specific predictions.
Existing interpretability methods for ViTs, such as linear probing, suffer from limitations in computational efficiency and direct relevance to the model's actual decision-making process.
The internal representational dynamics of ViTs are less understood compared to traditional CNNs or NLP transformers, hindering trust, debugging, and targeted improvements.
Method: The framework projects hidden states of image and `[CLS]` tokens, as well as parameter matrices (e.g., MLP `W_out`), onto the learned class embedding space to quantify 'class identifiability'.
It utilizes a gradient-based method to generate fine-grained, block- and attention-head-specific feature importance maps, identifying image regions critical for class representation.

The approach draws on NLP interpretability by treating transformer layers as key-value memory systems, analyzing how self-attention and MLP layers contribute to categorical updates via their value vectors.
Results: Class identifiability scores consistently increased across ViT blocks for both image and `[CLS]` tokens in all 7 tested ViT variants.
MLP layers promoted stronger categorical updates, with their value vectors manually inspected to cluster semantically similar concepts like 'racket, tennis ball, ping-pong ball'.

The gradient-based explainability tool generates global relevancy maps comparable in quality to established methods while being significantly more time-efficient, requiring only a single forward pass over validation images.
Takeaways: Image tokens progressively encode class-specific information across ViT layers, not solely relying on the `[CLS]` token, with distinct patterns for class-labeled versus context-labeled regions.

Self-attention layers provide weaker, more compositional, and broadly distributed categorical updates, primarily in earlier blocks, while MLP layers yield stronger, more direct, and semantically clustered updates, peaking in penultimate blocks.

The proposed method offers a more task-relevant and efficient measure of feature importance compared to linear probing, which often fails to predict actual token relevance to the network's classification decision.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.15308.Title: SAM-CLIP: Merging Vision Foundation Models towards Semantic and Spatial Understanding
https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.15308.Summary: SAM-CLIP unifies the vision encoders of SAM and CLIP into a single model, enabling state-of-the-art zero-shot semantic segmentation by combining semantic and spatial understanding. This merged architecture largely retains the individual capabilities of its constituent models while significantly reducing inference costs for edge device deployment.
Problem: Deploying separate Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) like CLIP and SAM is inefficient, leading to high memory and computational resource demands for inference, particularly on edge devices.
Specialized VFMs (e.g., CLIP for semantics, SAM for spatial segmentation) lack a unified representation for tasks requiring both types of understanding.
Training multi-task VFMs from scratch is prohibitively expensive in terms of data and computation, and simple model merging often results in catastrophic forgetting of original capabilities.
Method: A two-stage rehearsal-based multi-task distillation process merges SAM's vision encoder with a lightweight CLIP head into a single backbone, keeping other VFM components frozen.

Uses a combined loss function (CLIP teacher distillation and SAM self-distillation) with differentiated learning rates for different model parts to balance knowledge transfer and prevent catastrophic forgetting.
Leverages limited subsets of the original pre-training datasets for efficient 'memory replay' during the merging process.
Results: Achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot semantic segmentation, outperforming previous models by +6.8% mean IoU on Pascal-VOC (60.6%) and +5.9% on COCO-Stuff (31.5%).
Largely retains the zero-shot classification capabilities of CLIP (e.g., 72.4% accuracy on ImageNet) and the instance segmentation performance of SAM (e.g., 40.9 mAP on COCO) with minimal forgetting.
Reduces the computational cost and data requirements for merging to less than 10% of the original pre-training, making it efficient for deployment on edge devices.
Takeaways: Intelligently merging specialized VFMs can create a unified model with richer, more holistic visual representations that combine high-frequency localization and low-frequency semantic information.
Emergent capabilities, such as state-of-the-art zero-shot semantic segmentation, can arise from the synergistic combination of distinct VFM expertise within a single architecture.

Efficient continual learning and knowledge distillation techniques are effective for transferring knowledge and preserving original model strengths for large VFMs, without requiring full multi-task pre-training.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.11441.Title: Set-of-Mark Prompting Unleashes Extraordinary Visual Grounding in GPT-4V
https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.11441.Summary: Set-of-Mark prompting enhances GPT-4V's fine-grained visual grounding by augmenting images with unique alphanumeric marks, enabling the model to precisely refer to and output specific image regions. This approach allows GPT-4V to achieve performance on tasks like referring segmentation that often surpasses fine-tuned specialist models in a zero-shot setting.
Problem: State-of-the-art large multimodal models (LMMs) like GPT-4V exhibit weak fine-grained visual grounding, struggling to precisely pinpoint or refer to specific objects or regions within an image.
LMMs cannot easily produce accurate spatial outputs such as coordinates for specific objects or parts within an image.
Existing visual prompting methods often struggle with referring to multiple objects or are not 'speakable' by LLMs, limiting their utility for true multimodal grounding.
Method: The proposed Set-of-Mark (SoM) Prompting technique augments input images with unique, speakable alphanumeric marks generated for semantically meaningful regions.
Image regions are automatically partitioned using a suite of state-of-the-art open-vocabulary segmentation models, including MaskDINO, SEEM, and SAM, which provide rich granularity.

A clever mark allocation algorithm ensures unique mark placement within each region, minimizing overlaps, and these marked images are then used with either plain or interleaved text prompts to enable precise human-AI interaction.
Results: Set-of-Mark (SoM) prompting dramatically improves GPT-4V's performance on Referring Expression Comprehension (REC) from 25.7 ACC@0.5 to 86.4 ACC@0.5 on RefCOCOg.

GPT-4V + SoM achieves 75.6 mIoU for Referring Expression Segmentation (RES) on RefCOCOg, outperforming state-of-the-art fine-tuned specialist models like PolyFormer (67.2 mIoU) in a zero-shot setting.

The method demonstrates strong performance across various tasks, including phrase grounding (89.2 Recall@1 on Flickr30K) and video object segmentation (78.8 J&F on DAVIS2017), consistently outperforming other open-source LMMs.
Takeaways: Powerful LMMs like GPT-4V possess latent fine-grained visual grounding abilities that can be unlocked by simple, speakable visual prompting techniques.
Set-of-Mark bridging visual and language prompting by making visual cues 'speakable' allows for seamless, symbolic integration of visual and textual information in prompts and responses.

The quality of initial image partitioning using off-the-shelf segmentation models serves as a bottleneck, indicating that GPT-4V's grounding capability is even stronger when provided with more precise regions.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.05916.Title: Interpreting CLIP's Image Representation via Text-Based Decomposition
https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.05916.Summary: Researchers from UC Berkeley developed a systematic method to interpret CLIP's image representations by decomposing its internal components and grounding them in natural language. This approach revealed that specific attention heads specialize in semantic properties like shape and color, and enabled improving model robustness on the Waterbirds dataset by 25.2% and achieving state-of-the-art zero-shot image segmentation.
Problem: Limited understanding of the internal information encoded within large-scale vision-language models like CLIP, hindering debugging and improvement.
The 'black-box' nature of deep learning models makes it difficult to ascertain why specific decisions are made, particularly at the level of individual internal components.
Models like CLIP can learn spurious correlations from training data, leading to poor generalization and robustness on out-of-distribution examples.
Method: Decomposing CLIP-ViT's image representation into contributions from individual layers, attention heads, and image tokens, leveraging its residual connections and attention mechanism.
Introducing TEXTSPAN, an algorithm that identifies a sparse, interpretable text basis to semantically label the output space of individual attention heads.

Applying mean-ablation to quantify the direct effect of model components and generating heatmaps to visualize the contributions of image patches to specific text directions for zero-shot segmentation.
Results: Improved worst-group accuracy on the Waterbirds dataset from 47.7% to 72.9% for ViT-L by manually ablating 'geolocation' and 'image-location' attention heads.
Achieved state-of-the-art zero-shot image segmentation on the ImageNet-segmentation dataset, with 75.21% Pixel Accuracy, outperforming previous methods.
Discovered and quantitatively validated that a small set of text descriptions can capture over 95% of the variance in individual attention head outputs, allowing for property-based image retrieval.
Takeaways: The direct effects on CLIP's final image representation are concentrated in the last four Multi-Head Self-Attention (MSA) layers, with MLP layers having negligible direct contribution.
Individual attention heads within CLIP-ViT specialize in encoding distinct semantic properties, such as shapes, colors, object counts, and geo-locations, interpretable via text.
CLIP exhibits an emergent spatial localization capability, where image patches contribute to the representation's alignment with specific text concepts.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.04406.Title: Language Agent Tree Search Unifies Reasoning Acting and Planning in Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.04406.Summary: Language Agent Tree Search (LATS) unifies reasoning, acting, and planning capabilities in language models by adapting Monte Carlo Tree Search to incorporate external environmental feedback and LM-powered self-reflection. The framework achieves competitive or state-of-the-art results across diverse tasks, including reaching 92.7% Pass@1 accuracy on HumanEval and improving performance on interactive question answering and web navigation.
Problem: Existing LM-based reasoning methods (e.g., CoT, ToT) primarily rely on internal knowledge, often leading to factual hallucinations, error propagation, and an inability to incorporate real-time external feedback.

Current LM acting methods (e.g., ReAct, Reflexion) are 'reflexive', exploring only a single trajectory at a time and lacking deliberate multi-path planning or deep lookahead in combinatorial action spaces.

There was no single general framework that effectively unified reasoning, acting, and sophisticated planning while robustly incorporating continuous external feedback and self-reflection in language models.
Method: Language Agent Tree Search (LATS) unifies reasoning, acting, and planning by framing problem-solving as a tree search, where each node represents a state with a history of actions and observations.

It adapts Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) with six core operations: Selection (using UCT), Expansion (sampling multiple LM actions and executing them in the environment), Simulation, and Backpropagation.

LATS introduces a novel LM-powered value function that combines an LM's self-generated correctness score with a self-consistency score, and incorporates LM-generated self-reflection for strategy refinement based on failures.
Results: Achieved 0.71 Exact Match (EM) on HotPotQA using GPT-3.5, outperforming strong baselines like ReAct (0.32 EM) and Reflexion (0.51 EM) by unifying CoT and ReAct prompting.
Attained 92.7% Pass@1 accuracy on HumanEval with GPT-4 and 83.8% with GPT-3.5, surpassing Reflexion (91.0% and 68.1% respectively) and demonstrating the value of external test suite feedback.

Secured an average score of 75.9 and a 38.0% success rate on WebShop with GPT-3.5, outperforming prompting-based methods (ReAct: 53.8 score, 28.0 SR) and achieving competitive performance against fine-tuning approaches without additional model training.
Takeaways: Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) can be effectively adapted for language agents because many LM tasks allow convenient reversion to earlier states, bypassing a common challenge for model-free MCTS.

Pre-trained Large Language Models (LMs) can function not only as decision-makers but also as sophisticated heuristic state evaluators and self-reflection generators within a search framework, providing a 'semantic gradient signal'.

Unifying reasoning, acting, and planning with continuous external feedback and self-correction allows LMs to engage in deliberate, multi-path exploration, moving beyond greedy, reflexive problem-solving.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.03744.Title: Improved Baselines with Visual Instruction Tuning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.03744.Summary: LLaVA-1.5 presents an enhanced Large Multimodal Model from UW-Madison and Microsoft Research that achieves state-of-the-art performance across 11 diverse visual benchmarks. This work establishes a strong, reproducible open-source baseline by demonstrating that a simple architectural update and careful instruction tuning can yield robust generalization with significantly less training data and computational resources than comparable models.
Problem: Ambiguity exists regarding the optimal design and training strategies for developing truly general-purpose Large Multimodal Models (LMMs).
Many LMMs struggle with balancing performance on academic, short-form VQA benchmarks and general, long-form conversational responses.
The lack of systematic, controlled studies and accessible, reproducible open-source baselines hinders broader research and comparison in LMM development.
Method: Enhances the LLaVA framework with a two-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) for the vision-language connector, replacing the original linear projection.
Introduces response format prompting and full Large Language Model (LLM) fine-tuning to effectively balance short-form VQA answers with long-form conversational responses.
Integrates additional publicly available academic-task-oriented datasets, including VQA, OCR, and region-level data, to broaden specialized visual capabilities.
Develops a novel grid-splitting and feature-merging approach with global context (LLaVA-1.5-HD) to efficiently scale to higher input resolutions without expensive pre-training.
Results: LLaVA-1.5 achieves state-of-the-art performance across 11 diverse visual understanding and instruction-following benchmarks, including VQAv2, GQA, and LLaVA-Bench.
It demonstrates remarkable data and computational efficiency, training on only 1.2 million publicly available data points in approximately 1 day on a single 8-A100 node.
LLaVA-1.5-HD, with increased input resolution (448x448), further improves performance, particularly on fine-grained perception tasks, and reduces hallucination.

The model exhibits emergent properties such as generalization to novel response formats (e.g., JSON output) and multilingual multimodal capabilities (e.g., in Chinese and Spanish) despite English-only visual instruction tuning.
Takeaways: Simple architectural improvements, such as a two-layer MLP connector and precise response formatting prompts, are highly effective in boosting LMM performance across diverse tasks.

High-quality visual instruction tuning with strong pre-trained components can achieve state-of-the-art results with significantly less training data and computational resources than previously thought necessary.

Insufficient input resolution can contribute to model hallucination, and scaling to higher visual inputs can mitigate this, suggesting a direct link between visual information quality and model reliability.
LLaVA-1.5 exhibits compositional capabilities, such as emergent multilingual multimodal understanding derived from text-only multilingual data combined with English visual instruction tuning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.02239.Title: MiniGPT-5: Interleaved Vision-and-Language Generation via Generative Vokens
https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.02239.Summary: MiniGPT-5 introduces a framework for interleaved vision-and-language generation by integrating "generative vokens" to bridge large language models with diffusion models. This method supports description-free training, achieves robust multimodal coherence, and demonstrates improved generation quality on VIST and MMDialog benchmarks.
Problem: Existing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) excel at understanding but lack robust, simultaneous generation of interleaved text and images.
Prior multimodal generation approaches often require extensive full-model retraining or rely on labor-intensive, detailed image descriptions for training.
Text-to-image models typically operate as separate modules, not inherently integrated into an LLM's generative flow for coherent multimodal outputs.
Method: MiniGPT-5 utilizes "generative vokens" as a bridge, allowing an LLM to directly command a text-to-image diffusion model for visual generation within its autoregressive output.
A two-stage training strategy (pretraining on CC3M, fine-tuning on VIST/MMDialog) enables description-free multimodal generation without relying on detailed image descriptions.

The framework employs parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) techniques like LoRA and prefix tuning on pretrained backbones (MiniGPT-4, Stable Diffusion 2.1) and integrates classifier-free guidance for enhanced coherence.
Results: MiniGPT-5 achieved best-in-class CLIP-I (0.66) and FID (366.62) for image generation on VIST, outperforming baselines like Fine-tuned SD 2.1 and GILL.
The model demonstrated superior multimodal coherence (MM-Relevance: 0.67) and strong textual response generation (BLEU-1: 0.3369) in multimodal dialogs on MMDialog.
Human evaluations on VIST confirmed MiniGPT-5's superiority in language continuity (55.22%), image quality (52.43%), and multimodal coherence (56.90%) compared to a two-stage baseline.
Takeaways: Generative vokens provide an effective mechanism for LLMs to transition from understanding multimodal inputs to actively generating them, serving as direct commands for image synthesis.
The modular design, leveraging existing powerful pretrained models and PEFT, makes the approach parameter-efficient and scalable compared to full-model retraining.
A dual-loss strategy and classifier-free guidance are critical for ensuring high-quality and coherent alignment between generated text and images in complex interleaved sequences.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.00754.Title: Analyzing and Mitigating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.00754.Summary: Researchers from UNC-Chapel Hill, Rutgers, Columbia, and Stanford analyze object hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs), attributing it to co-occurrence, uncertainty, and object position. They introduce LURE, a lightweight, post-hoc revisor that significantly reduces hallucination across six LVLMs, for instance, lowering CHAIR_S on MiniGPT-4 from 26.8 to 19.7 and CHAIR_I from 7.3 to 4.9.
Problem: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) frequently generate descriptions that include objects not present in the image or misrepresent existing ones, termed object hallucination, which undermines their reliability.
Existing hallucination mitigation methods for smaller models are often incompatible with the auto-regressive architectures and scale of modern LVLMs.
Current LVLM-specific solutions primarily rely on improving training dataset quality, which is a prohibitively resource-intensive and labor-intensive process.
Method: The research conducts a rigorous statistical and theoretical analysis, identifying object co-occurrence, generation uncertainty, and object position as key contributing factors to hallucination in LVLMs.
It introduces LURE (LVLM Hallucination Revisor), a lightweight, post-hoc rectification method that leverages a separate LVLM fine-tuned for denoising.

LURE trains a revisor by curating a synthetic dataset where 'hallucinatory' descriptions are created by adding co-occurring objects or replacing uncertain/late-appearing objects with a special placeholder, forcing the revisor to correct these errors.
Results: LURE significantly reduces object hallucination across six open-source LVLMs; for MiniGPT-4, it lowers CHAIR_S from 26.8 to 19.7 and CHAIR_I from 7.3 to 4.9.
Both human and GPT-3.5 evaluations consistently rank LURE's rectified descriptions as having the fewest hallucinations compared to strong baselines.
LURE demonstrates robustness and generalizability, consistently reducing hallucination across diverse LVLM backbones, various new datasets like ImageNet, and benchmarks such as POPE and MME.
Takeaways: Object hallucination in LVLMs is strongly linked to spurious co-occurrence patterns learned from training data, quantified by a 'CoScore'.
Objects generated with higher uncertainty (lower confidence) during auto-regressive decoding are more prone to being hallucinatory, indicated by a 'UnScore'.
Hallucinations tend to appear more frequently in the latter parts of generated descriptions, attributed to the accumulation of misinterpretations and uncertainties as generation progresses.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.00632.Title: Win-Win: Training High-Resolution Vision Transformers from Two Windows
https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.00632.Summary: Naver Labs Europe introduces WIN-WIN, a training strategy for high-resolution Vision Transformers that utilizes structured token masking during training. This approach reduces training time by 3 to 4 times and memory usage by half while enabling direct, single-pass high-resolution inference without artifacts, achieving state-of-the-art optical flow performance on the Full-HD Spring benchmark with 0.475 EPE.
Problem: High-resolution Vision Transformers (ViTs) for dense prediction tasks incur prohibitive computational costs due to the quadratic complexity of global self-attention.
ViTs often exhibit poor generalization when tested at resolutions significantly different from those used during training, leading to performance degradation.
Existing solutions like architectural modifications alter the vanilla ViT structure, while training on low-resolution crops necessitates slow and artifact-prone test-time tiling strategies.
Method: The WIN-WIN method trains vanilla ViTs by feeding a structured subset of input tokens derived from N (typically N=2) non-overlapping rectangular windows randomly sampled from the high-resolution image.
It leverages Relative Positional Embeddings (RoPE) for improved generalization and is compatible with standard convolutional heads for dense prediction tasks.

At inference, the masking scheme is removed, allowing the model to process the full high-resolution image in a single forward pass, eliminating the need for slow tiling strategies, and uses a softmax temperature factor to compensate for token distribution changes.
Results: Achieves 3 to 4 times faster training and half the memory usage compared to full-resolution ViT training, while yielding comparable or superior performance.

Outperforms or matches existing methods on semantic segmentation (63.6% mIoU on BDD100k) and sets a new state-of-the-art on the Full-HD Spring optical flow benchmark with 0.475 EPE, demonstrating over an order of magnitude faster inference than tiling methods.
Demonstrates superior robustness to varying test resolutions and produces smooth, artifact-free high-resolution dense predictions, unlike tiling-based approaches.
Takeaways: Structured masking with just two non-overlapping windows ("Win-Win") effectively allows the ViT to learn both local and global interactions with a significantly reduced token budget during training.
Relative positional embeddings (RoPE) are critical for Vision Transformers to generalize robustly to varying resolutions and maintain translation equivariance in dense prediction tasks.
Direct, high-resolution inference with a trained masked-input ViT is viable, provided that potential shifts in self-attention distributions due to varying token counts are appropriately managed.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.16797.Title: Promptbreeder: Self-Referential Self-Improvement Via Prompt Evolution
https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.16797.Summary: PromptBreeder from Google DeepMind automates prompt engineering for Large Language Models by employing a self-improving evolutionary algorithm that evolves both task prompts and the meta-level mutation prompts. This system autonomously discovers effective reasoning strategies, achieving improved performance on various reasoning tasks compared to baseline and some human-crafted prompts.
Problem: Crafting effective prompts for Large Language Models (LLMs) requires substantial human expertise and extensive experimentation.
The performance of LLMs is highly dependent on the quality of the prompts provided.
Prompt engineering is typically a manual and iterative process, limiting the accessibility and efficiency of LLM utilization.
Method: Google DeepMind developed PromptBreeder, a system that automates prompt engineering using a self-improving evolutionary algorithm.
The system employs a dual-layered evolutionary process where both task prompts (for specific problems) and mutation prompts (meta-instructions for prompt modification) evolve concurrently.
PromptBreeder iteratively generates, evaluates, and selects prompts using various mutation operators and a fitness function measuring LLM performance on target tasks.
Results: PromptBreeder demonstrated improved performance on a variety of reasoning tasks, including arithmetic and commonsense reasoning problems.
The system, without human guidance, generated prompts that outperformed baseline prompts and, in some cases, human-crafted prompts like Chain-of-Thought and Plan-and-Solve.
Ablation studies showed that removing self-referential components led to significant performance drops (e.g., 39% to 80% decrease in prompts outperforming baseline), confirming their essential role.
Takeaways: The self-referential evolution of both task prompts and mutation prompts is critical for PromptBreeder's effectiveness, enabling the system to improve how it generates new prompts.
Automating prompt evolution allows the discovery of sophisticated reasoning strategies and prompt structures that might not be obvious to human prompt engineers.
The research demonstrates that language can serve as a substrate for AI self-improvement, offering an alternative to traditional gradient-based parameter updates.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.15129.Title: Evaluating Cognitive Maps and Planning in Large Language Models with CogEval
https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.15129.Summary: Microsoft Research introduced CogEval, a cognitive science-inspired protocol, to systematically evaluate large language models' (LLMs) cognitive mapping and planning abilities. The study found that current LLMs, including GPT-4, display "apparent competence" in simpler tasks but consistently fail on complex planning problems requiring the inference of latent relational structures, exhibiting common issues like hallucinating invalid paths and generating suboptimal routes.
Problem: Claims about emergent cognitive abilities in large language models (LLMs) often lack rigorous, controlled evaluation and may be susceptible to data contamination.
Existing AI evaluation methods can conflate linguistic fluency with deeper, functional cognitive capacities like planning or causal inference.
There is a need for unbiased assessment of whether LLMs can genuinely grasp and utilize latent relational structures for planning, rather than simply retrieving memorized patterns.
Method: Introduced CogEval, a cognitive science-inspired protocol for systematic evaluation of LLM cognitive abilities, adhering to practices like latent construct operationalization and using non-linguistic human experiment paradigms.

Systematically evaluated eight state-of-the-art LLMs across diverse graph structures, domains, and planning task conditions (e.g., reward revaluation, shortcuts) to assess cognitive maps and planning.
Investigated the effect of Chain of Thought instructions on GPT-4's performance and conducted supplementary experiments on systematic graph explorations.
Results: LLM version, graph structure, task condition, and domain all significantly contributed to performance variations (all p-values < 0.001) in planning tasks.
LLMs, including GPT-4, showed apparent competence in simpler tasks but significantly failed on tasks requiring genuine understanding of latent relational structures, particularly in community graphs.

Chain of Thought instructions resulted in only marginal and inconsistent performance improvements, and common failure modes included hallucinating invalid edges, getting trapped in loops, and generating suboptimally long routes.
Takeaways: LLMs' planning capabilities are highly sensitive to graph structure, task condition, and domain, but the temperature parameter had no significant effect on overall performance in broad tasks.
Apparent competence in simpler planning tasks stems from "route memorization" of explicitly provided information rather than a genuine understanding of latent relational structures.

CogEval provides a robust, cognitive science-inspired framework for assessing LLMs' cognitive capacities, challenging claims of emergent intelligence by demonstrating systematic failure modes under controlled conditions.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.14322.Title: Small-scale proxies for large-scale Transformer training instabilities
https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.14322.Summary: Researchers at Google DeepMind successfully reproduce and investigate large-scale Transformer training instabilities, such as attention logit growth and output logit divergence, using much smaller models. This approach enables the study of these issues without vast computational resources and identifies new insights like the impact of AdamW's epsilon on very large models' training.
Problem: Training instabilities (e.g., sudden loss spikes, divergence) in large Transformer models are prohibitively expensive and resource-intensive to investigate, hindering understanding and mitigation.
These instabilities often manifest uniquely or are more pronounced at very large scales, making it difficult to study them without vast computational resources.
Existing research primarily focused on performance scaling, leaving a gap in systematic study of stability and failure modes at scale.
Method: The authors developed a methodology to reproduce and study large-scale Transformer training instabilities using small, decoder-only Transformer models (2.4M to 1.2B parameters) at high learning rates.
They introduced 'learning rate sensitivity' as a quantitative metric to characterize training stability and systematically analyzed the impact of various architectural and optimizer interventions.
Internal model characteristics, such as activation and gradient norms, were monitored to identify scaling trends and serve as potential predictors for instability.
Results: Qk-layernorm successfully mitigated attention logit growth, and z-loss regularization or independent weight decay addressed output logit divergence in small models, mirroring their effectiveness at large scales.
Longer warm-up periods and independent weight decay consistently reduced learning rate sensitivity, improving training robustness across model scales.

Extrapolating maximum attention logits from smaller models accurately predicted instability for a 4.8 billion parameter model at a 1e-2 learning rate, and decreasing AdamW's epsilon to 1e-15 improved training for large models at high learning rates.
Takeaways: Large-scale Transformer training instabilities, such as attention logit growth and output logit divergence, can be reliably reproduced and investigated using much smaller models.
Monitoring internal model characteristics like attention logits and gradient norms provides early warning signals for impending instabilities, allowing for proactive adjustments.
A novel instability was identified where very low gradient RMS values in large models can cause AdamW updates to stall if the default epsilon (1e-8) is relatively too large.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.11069.Title: Dynamic Tiling: A Model-Agnostic, Adaptive, Scalable, and Inference-Data-Centric Approach for Efficient and Accurate Small Object Detection
https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.11069.Summary: Dynamic Tiling introduces a model-agnostic and inference-data-centric approach for small object detection, adaptively processing image tiles based on initial detection results. This method improves detection accuracy, particularly for small objects, while simultaneously reducing computational overhead compared to uniform tiling techniques.
Problem: Small objects have limited pixel representation, making them difficult for detection models to identify accurately.
Traditional object detection models struggle with extreme scale differences, and small objects at tile boundaries are often fragmented or missed.
Detecting small objects in high-resolution images demands significant computational resources, hindering real-time applications.
Method: Divides the input image into initial non-overlapping tiles for object detection and identifies objects near tile boundaries as potentially fragmented.
Generates dynamic, overlapping patches selectively around identified potential fragmentations, creating varying degrees of overlap only where needed.
Aggregates these dynamic patches into composite images using a Tile Minimizer to reduce the total number of neural network forward passes, maintaining efficiency.
Results: Dynamic Tiling outperformed existing model-agnostic uniform cropping methods, such as DarkHelp and SAHI, in mean Average Precision (mAP) on the VisDrone 2019 dataset.
The approach reduced computational overhead by selectively applying overlapping patches and aggregating them with a Tile Minimizer, decreasing the number of neural network forward passes.
It demonstrated strong adaptability across different operational environments without requiring laborious recalibration, providing a practical solution for real-world deployment.
Takeaways: Applying overlapping patches selectively only where potential object fragmentations are identified significantly reduces computational overhead compared to uniform tiling.
Optimizing the inference stage by adaptively analyzing and processing image tiles can achieve accuracy and efficiency gains without requiring model architecture modifications or retraining.
Combining tile-based detection for small objects with full-image inference for larger objects provides a comprehensive approach to handle diverse object scales efficiently.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.08912.Title: Delving into Multimodal Prompting for Fine-grained Visual Classification
https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.08912.Summary: MP-FGVC introduces a multimodal prompting and adaptation framework to effectively leverage pre-trained vision-language models like CLIP for close-set Fine-Grained Visual Classification. This approach achieved state-of-the-art Top-1 Accuracy across four datasets, demonstrating improvements up to 0.9% on Food101 while enhancing sensitivity to subcategory-specific visual and linguistic cues.
Problem: Fine-grained Visual Classification (FGVC) is challenging due to subtle inter-class differences and large intra-class variations.
Existing visual-only methods struggle to capture minute discriminative features, while pre-trained vision-language models like CLIP lack fine-grained sensitivity for subcategory-level classification.
Standard FGVC datasets typically provide only subcategory labels, hindering the direct application and full exploitation of rich textual knowledge from vision-language models.
Method: A Multimodal Prompting for Fine-grained Visual Classification (MP-FGVC) framework, built on pre-trained CLIP, employs a two-stage optimization strategy.

It introduces a Subcategory-specific Vision Prompt (SSVP) to identify discriminative visual regions and a Discrepancy-aware Text Prompt (DATP) with learnable tokens for fine-grained textual descriptions.
A Vision-Language Fusion Module (VLFM) uses cross-modal attention to align and integrate visual and textual embeddings, forming a more discriminative feature for classification.
Results: MP-FGVC achieved state-of-the-art Top-1 Accuracy on four fine-grained datasets (CUB-200-2011, Stanford Dogs, NABirds, Food101).
The method demonstrated improvements of up to 0.9% on Food101 and 0.4% to 1.8% over other ViT-based methods across datasets.
Ablation studies confirmed that all proposed components, including SSVP, DATP, and VLFM, individually contribute to the overall performance gains.
Takeaways: Effectively adapting pre-trained vision-language models for fine-grained tasks requires explicitly engineering prompts to capture subcategory-specific visual and linguistic discrepancies.
A two-stage optimization strategy is crucial for successfully adapting large pre-trained models, allowing initial prompt refinement before full multimodal adaptation.
Learnable text tokens with supercategory labels can generate effective discrepancy-aware text descriptions, overcoming the lack of detailed annotations in FGVC datasets.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.05858.Title: Uncovering mesa-optimization algorithms in Transformers
https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.05858.Summary: Researchers at Google's Paradigms of Intelligence Team and ETH Zürich provide a mechanistic explanation for emergent in-context learning in Transformers, demonstrating that standard next-token prediction training leads to the spontaneous development of internal, gradient-based "mesa-optimization" algorithms. These emergent optimizers efficiently solve problems like linear regression in-context and account for observed LLM behaviors such as "early ascent" and prompt tuning effectiveness.
Problem: The mechanistic origins of emergent in-context learning (ICL) in Transformers, trained with standard self-supervision, remained poorly understood.
A theoretical gap existed between Transformers explicitly trained as meta-learners and the spontaneously arising ICL observed in large language models.
Understanding the specific algorithms Transformers learn internally to adapt to new tasks from context was an open question.
Method: The authors hypothesized that in-context learning arises from "mesa-optimization," where the Transformer's training process instills internal, gradient-based learning algorithms in its forward pass.
Synthetic sequence prediction tasks, including linear and non-linear systems with varying parameters per sequence, were used to provide a controlled environment for studying emergent ICL.

A multi-faceted approach combined theoretical proofs for how attention layers can implement optimization, the design of a novel "mesa-layer," and extensive empirical analysis (probing, attention maps, distillation) of trained Transformers.
Results: Trained linear attention models precisely implemented theoretical gradient-based optimization algorithms, learning optimal parameters and showing preconditioning behavior consistent with mesa-optimization.

Full Transformer models, trained on synthetic tasks, spontaneously exhibited emergent few-shot and continual learning, reproducing phenomena such as "early ascent" and the efficacy of prompt tuning observed in large language models.

A novel "mesa-layer," explicitly designed for least-squares in-context learning, achieved superior performance compared to standard Transformer layers, often matching or outperforming deeper conventional architectures.
Takeaways: Transformers trained on next-token prediction develop a "token binding" mechanism in early layers, aggregating multi-time-step observations into composite internal representations for in-context training.

Linear attention layers can be trained to implement one-step or multi-step gradient descent algorithms for quadratic loss functions in-context, including learning optimal learning rates and preconditioning.

Softmax attention, particularly in deeper layers, operates in an approximately linear regime during inference for ICL, which enables the observed efficient, principled optimization and avoids the curse of dimensionality.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.05519.Title: NExT-GPT: Any-to-Any Multimodal LLM
https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.05519.Summary: NExT-GPT, from researchers at the National University of Singapore's NExT++ Research Center, introduces an end-to-end, general-purpose multimodal large language model capable of perceiving inputs and generating content across text, image, video, and audio modalities. The model leverages an LLM core for reasoning and achieves efficient training by fine-tuning only approximately 1% of total parameters, demonstrating enhanced performance in both multimodal understanding and generation tasks.
Problem: Most existing Multimodal Large Language Models (MM-LLMs) primarily focus on input-side multimodal understanding, lacking the ability to generate content in modalities other than text.

Prior 'any-to-any' approaches often relied on pipeline-based systems (LLM combined with external tools), which suffer from information transfer noise, limited semantic understanding due to non-end-to-end training, and reliance on inference-only tools.
There was a lack of an end-to-end, general-purpose MM-LLM that leverages an LLM's core reasoning capabilities while supporting arbitrary multimodal generation to mimic human-like interaction.
Method: A three-tier architecture is proposed, comprising a multimodal encoding stage (using ImageBind and a multi-stage grouping projection), an LLM core (Vicuna) for understanding and reasoning, and a multimodal generation stage (output projection layers and diffusion decoders like Stable Diffusion, Zeroscope, and AudioLDM).

A lightweight multimodal alignment learning strategy is employed, fine-tuning only the input and output projection layers and a small subset of LLM parameters (approximately 1% of total parameters), while freezing pre-trained encoders and decoders.

Modality-switching Instruction Tuning (MosIT) is introduced, utilizing a manually curated, high-quality 5,000-sample multi-turn dataset to train the model for complex cross-modal reasoning and dynamic modality switching in both input and output.
Results: NExT-GPT achieved competitive or superior performance in multimodal perception tasks, including image captioning, image question answering (e.g., 0.534 SPIDEr on AudioCaps), and video/audio comprehension.

The model demonstrated superior performance in multimodal generation, with a FID score of 10.07 for text-to-image on MS COCO, a FAD score of 1.68 for text-to-audio on AudioCaps, and a CLIPSIM score of 31.97 for text-to-video on MSRVTT.

Human evaluations rated NExT-GPT significantly higher in "Instruction Following," "Rationality," and "Quality" compared to pipeline-based systems like Visual-ChatGPT and HuggingGPT, validating the benefits of end-to-end training.
Takeaways: The use of 'modality signal' tokens within the LLM's output effectively enables implicit, continuous communication and instruction to multimodal decoders, overcoming the limitations of discrete textual intermediaries in pipeline systems.

Lightweight fine-tuning, involving only approximately 1% of total parameters, is highly effective for aligning diverse pre-trained multimodal components with an LLM, making the approach computationally efficient and easily extensible.

The multi-stage grouping mechanism for input projection significantly improves the alignment between multimodal features and the LLM's semantic understanding, enhancing the model's perceptual capabilities across modalities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.02031.Title: A survey on efficient vision transformers: algorithms, techniques, and performance benchmarking
https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.02031.Summary: Researchers from Sapienza University of Rome and The University of Sydney present a comprehensive survey of efficient Vision Transformer (ViT) strategies, classifying them into four distinct categories and introducing a new "Efficient Error Rate" (EER) metric for normalized evaluation. The work benchmarks various models, identifying TinyViT-21M (Knowledge Distillation) as highly efficient with 83.1% Top-1 accuracy and 43.5% EER_all, and Castling-MViTv2-T (Compact Architecture) as providing a balanced trade-off with 84.1% Top-1 accuracy and 45.6% EER_all.
Problem: Vision Transformers (ViTs) achieve high performance in computer vision tasks but suffer from significant computational and memory demands, largely due to the quadratic scaling of their self-attention mechanism.
The high resource consumption of large ViT models hinders their practical deployment on resource-constrained devices like embedded systems, mobile platforms, and edge AI applications.

Existing surveys offered limited focus specifically on the architectural and algorithmic efficiency of ViTs for inference, lacking a comprehensive categorization and comparative evaluation of these methods.
Method: Systematically categorized efficient Vision Transformer (ViT) strategies into four main groups: Compact Architecture, Pruning, Knowledge Distillation, and Quantization.
Provided mathematical formulations and detailed reviews of state-of-the-art methodologies within each efficiency category, illustrating their evolution and mechanisms.

Introduced a novel "Efficient Error Rate (EER)" metric to offer a normalized and holistic benchmarking tool, accounting for multiple hardware-affecting features like parameters, FLOPs, bits, and model size during inference.
Results: Castling-MViTv2-T (Compact Architecture) demonstrated the best Paretian optimality, balancing 84.1% Top-1 accuracy with an EER_all of 45.6% across various hardware-affecting metrics.
TinyViT-21M (Knowledge Distillation) was identified as the most overall efficient, achieving 83.1% Top-1 accuracy with the lowest EER_all of 43.5%.

NoisyQuant-PTQ4ViT-Swin-B (Quantization) delivered the highest Top-1 accuracy at 84.7% and smallest model size (66.0MB) among the top candidates, offering a strong option where memory footprint is a primary concern.
Takeaways: The four identified efficiency strategies offer distinct trade-offs between estimation performance and resource consumption, which the EER metric effectively unifies for comparison.

Compact Architecture (CA) models and Knowledge Distillation (KD) strategies generally achieve the most balanced trade-offs between high accuracy and overall efficiency for general-purpose applications.

Quantization (Q) provides the most drastic reductions in memory footprint and inference speed but its efficacy depends on the ViT architecture's robustness and often requires specialized hardware support for optimal gains.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.12216.Title: SG-Former: Self-guided Transformer with Evolving Token Reallocation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.12216.Summary: SG-Former introduces a hierarchical Vision Transformer that employs self-guided, evolving token reallocation to achieve efficient global self-attention with adaptive fine granularity. This architecture yields higher accuracy on ImageNet-1K classification, COCO object detection, and ADE20K semantic segmentation compared to prior Vision Transformers, frequently with reduced computational cost.
Problem: Vision Transformers incur quadratic computational and memory costs with input size, limiting their application to high-resolution images.
Existing efficient Vision Transformers either sacrifice global context for local detail or lose fine-grained information for global context.
Static token reduction methods fail to adaptively allocate computational resources based on the varying semantic importance of image regions.
Method: A hierarchical Transformer architecture is developed, featuring Self-guided Attention (SG-Attention) and Hybrid-scale Attention modules.
SG-Attention dynamically reallocates Key and Value tokens based on a learned significance map, assigning more tokens to salient regions for fine-grained analysis.
Hybrid-scale Attention extracts multi-granularity information simultaneously and generates the significance map that guides token reallocation in SG-Attention.
Results: Achieved 84.7% Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K (224x224) with SG-Former-B, surpassing Swin-B by +1.3% and CSWin-B by +0.4%.
Demonstrated 51.3 mAP and 45.2 mIoU on COCO object detection and instance segmentation, outperforming Swin-B by +2.8 mAP.
Attained 52.7 mIoU on ADE20K semantic segmentation using UperNet, exceeding Swin-B by +3 mIoU, often with competitive or reduced parameter and FLOP counts.
Takeaways: Computational resources in Vision Transformers can be optimized by adaptively allocating more attention to semantically important image regions and less to less important ones.
A model's understanding of regional significance can be learned and dynamically refined, enabling self-guided and evolving token reallocation strategies.

Integrating hybrid-scale attention within a single layer effectively extracts both fine-grained local and coarse-grained global information while simultaneously generating a reliable significance map for adaptive processing.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.10677.Title: Visual Crowd Analysis: Open Research Problems
https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.10677.Summary: Researchers from the Qatar Mobility Innovations Center and Qatar University present a comprehensive survey categorizing and evaluating the field of visual crowd analysis, highlighting deep learning advancements and crucial unresolved challenges across six key application areas. The review maps the current state-of-the-art and identifies persistent issues like severe occlusions, semantic gap in behavior recognition, and data scarcity in anomaly detection and crowd prediction.
Problem: Ensuring public safety in increasingly dense urban environments necessitates efficient and automated crowd analysis, as manual methods are tedious and inefficient.

Despite advancements in deep learning, automated visual crowd analysis still faces significant challenges due to inherent scene complexities such as severe occlusions, drastic scale variations, and unpredictable crowd behaviors.
A need exists for an updated and intuitively categorized comprehensive review of the visual crowd analysis field to guide future research and understanding for a broad audience.
Method: Conducted a systematic and critical literature review, thoroughly investigating works on visual crowd analysis, primarily focusing on deep learning approaches.

Proposed and applied a novel, intuitive categorization of the field into six distinct areas: crowd counting, object detection and tracking, motion analysis, behavior recognition, anomaly detection, and crowd prediction.
Analyzed each area by outlining its definition, state-of-the-art methods, and critically identified crucial unresolved challenges and open problems.
Results: Found that deep learning has led to substantial advancements in crowd counting (e.g., improved MAE with CNNs and Transformers) and object detection (with robust models like YOLO), though limitations remain in dense, complex crowd scenarios.

Identified that higher-level tasks like motion analysis, behavior recognition, anomaly detection, and crowd prediction are significantly hampered by the semantic gap, lack of standardized definitions for events/behaviors, and the severe scarcity of realistic and diverse datasets.

Highlighted common unresolved issues across tasks, including effectively handling severe occlusions, drastic scale variations, illumination changes, and the computational demands for real-time edge deployment.
Takeaways: Deep learning has significantly improved performance in fundamental crowd analysis tasks like counting and object detection, yet challenges persist with extreme conditions and real-time edge deployment.

Higher-level analytical tasks such as behavior recognition, anomaly detection, and crowd prediction are severely constrained by the semantic gap between visual features and high-level concepts, as well as a lack of universal definitions and diverse datasets.

Current methods struggle with the inherent complexities of crowd scenes, including severe occlusions, drastic scale variations, and unpredictable collective behaviors, underscoring the need for more context-aware and robust models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.05659.Title: AD-CLIP: Adapting Domains in Prompt Space Using CLIP
https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.05659.Summary: AD-CLIP proposes a data-driven prompt learning framework within CLIP's prompt space, addressing unsupervised domain adaptation by learning domain-invariant and class-generalizable prompts. The method establishes new performance benchmarks on Office-Home, VisDA-2017, and Mini-DomainNet, with average accuracy improvements up to 2.2% over previous state-of-the-art.
Problem: Deep learning models struggle with the "domain-shift problem" where training and test data distributions diverge, limiting generalization in real-world applications.

Traditional Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) methods, often relying on CNNs, lack "semantic richness" to capture deeper conceptual relationships for robust generalization across visually diverse domains.
Prior attempts to apply CLIP to UDA used ad-hoc prompting or neglected intrinsic visual distributions, leading to suboptimal performance or overfitting.
Method: Utilizes frozen CLIP vision and text backbones, integrating only a minimal set of learnable projector networks for style and content features.
Develops a novel prompt learning scheme that dynamically combines a Domain-Agnostic Token (DAT) and image-specific context tokens derived from multi-scale visual features.
Introduces a Target-to-Source Style Mapping Network to approximate source domain style characteristics from target data, enabling robust inference without explicit source access.
Results: Achieved state-of-the-art average accuracy across UDA benchmarks: 90.5% on Office-Home, 92.7% on VisDA-2017, and 91.4% on Mini-DomainNet (with ViT-L/14 backbone).
Outperformed previous state-of-the-art methods by an average of 1.8% on Office-Home, 2.2% on VisDA-2017, and 1.6% on Mini-DomainNet.
t-SNE visualizations confirm that AD-CLIP successfully achieves both domain invariance and class discriminativeness in the learned text embeddings, validating its core objective.
Takeaways: Leveraging multi-scale visual features for content extraction consistently improves performance, indicating the importance of nuanced visual information for prompts.

The Domain-Agnostic Token is critical for learning domain-invariant representations, while the Target-to-Source Style Mapping Network prevents overfitting and maintains performance during target-only inference.

Both Entropy Minimization and KL Divergence Loss terms are indispensable for promoting discriminative alignment within the target domain and ensuring distributional similarity between source and target prompt embeddings.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.00692.Title: LISA: Reasoning Segmentation via Large Language Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.00692.Summary: A new model, LISA, introduces "reasoning segmentation," enabling multimodal large language models to generate precise segmentation masks from complex, implicit natural language queries. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on a new benchmark, outperforming baselines by over 15 gIoU points in zero-shot settings while maintaining strong performance on standard referring segmentation tasks.
Problem: Existing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are limited to generating text outputs, lacking the ability to produce fine-grained visual outputs like segmentation masks.

Current image segmentation models typically require explicit prompts (e.g., bounding boxes, points, or predefined categories) and struggle to interpret complex, implicit human instructions that necessitate reasoning or world knowledge.
There was a gap in AI systems' ability to translate high-level language understanding and reasoning into precise, pixel-level visual actions based on nuanced user intent.
Method: LISA introduces the "embedding-as-mask" paradigm, enabling MLLMs to generate segmentation masks by integrating a special `` token whose hidden embedding is projected to a mask via a trainable decoder.
The architecture leverages a frozen vision backbone (e.g., ViT-H from SAM) for dense visual features and an MLLM (e.g., LLaVA) fine-tuned efficiently using LoRA, for end-to-end training.

Training involves a composite loss function for both text generation and segmentation, using diverse datasets including semantic segmentation, vanilla referring segmentation, and VQA data, to preserve language and visual capabilities.
Results: LISA significantly outperforms existing methods on the new ReasonSeg benchmark, achieving over 15 gIoU points higher than the best baseline (OVSeg) in zero-shot settings.

The model demonstrates robust zero-shot reasoning, with fine-tuning on a small set of reasoning data (239 samples) leading to substantial performance gains, e.g., LISA-13B improving from 48.9 to 56.2 gIoU.
LISA also achieves state-of-the-art results on standard referring segmentation benchmarks (refCOCO, refCOCO+, refCOCOg), such as 79.1 cIoU on refCOCO testA.
Takeaways: Multimodal LLMs can be effectively extended to produce fine-grained pixel-level outputs like segmentation masks by projecting an LLM's internal embedding.
Strong zero-shot reasoning capabilities for complex visual queries can emerge from training on general, reasoning-free semantic and referring segmentation datasets.
Efficient adaptation to novel reasoning tasks is possible with minimal fine-tuning data, leveraging the inherent reasoning of the LLM and rich features from pre-trained vision models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.12813.Title: Described Object Detection: Liberating Object Detection with Flexible Expressions
https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.12813.Summary: Researchers introduce Described Object Detection (DOD), a new task that unifies open-vocabulary and referring expression object detection by enabling detection with flexible language, existence verification, and multi-target support. A new benchmark, D³, is established, and an OFA-DOD baseline method is proposed, demonstrating improved performance over existing approaches on the challenging DOD task.
Problem: Open-Vocabulary Object Detection (OVD) is limited to short category names, unable to handle complex attributes or relationships in natural language descriptions.
Referring Expression Comprehension (REC) assumes the target object always exists, leading to false positives in real-world scenarios where the object might be absent.
Existing bi-functional models often maintain separate training and inference for OVD and REC, leading to compromises and inheriting individual limitations rather than a truly unified solution.
Method: Introduces Described Object Detection (DOD), a new task unifying OVD and REC by allowing flexible language expressions, explicit existence verification, and multi-target detection.
Constructs the Description Detection Dataset (D³), featuring complete instance annotations, unrestricted language (including 'absence expressions'), and multi-instance support to benchmark DOD.

Proposes OFA-DOD, an adapted baseline model leveraging Granularity Decomposition, Reconstructed Data, and Task Decomposition to improve localization, multi-target handling, and negative instance rejection.
Results: OFA-DOD significantly outperforms all existing baseline methods on the D³ dataset, achieving 21.6% intra-scenario mAP and 5.7% inter-scenario mAP.

Ablation studies confirm that Granularity Decomposition, Reconstructed Data, and Task Decomposition progressively improve OFA-DOD's mAP from 3.4% to 21.6%, with Task Decomposition being crucial for false positive rejection.

Existing REC and bi-functional methods show high 'False Positives Per Category' on 'no-instance' images and struggle with multi-instance detection, while OVD methods degrade rapidly with longer descriptions.
Takeaways: Current state-of-the-art OVD, REC, and bi-functional methods are insufficient for Described Object Detection, particularly struggling with absence expressions, multi-instance detection, and rejecting non-existent targets.

Referring Expression Comprehension (REC) methods poorly distinguish between true and false positives due to their 'always positive' grounding formulation, leading to many false positives when the object is absent.

The ability to explicitly verify object existence and reject negative instances is a critical, unmet challenge for language-guided object detection, with most existing methods failing to achieve this effectively.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.09220.Title: A Survey on Open-Vocabulary Detection and Segmentation: Past, Present, and Future
https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.09220.Summary: A survey from The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology offers a novel taxonomy to comprehensively review Open-Vocabulary Detection and Segmentation, detailing the paradigm shift driven by Vision-Language Models and weak supervision, and outlining current challenges and future research directions.
Problem: Traditional object detection and segmentation models are constrained by a 'closed vocabulary,' limiting them to recognizing pre-defined categories.
The high cost and labor intensity of manual annotation restrict the scalability and real-world applicability of these models to novel, unseen objects.
Current AI systems lack the ability to classify and segment arbitrary visual concepts, a core human perception capability.
Method: Developed a comprehensive taxonomy that categorizes Open-Vocabulary Detection and Segmentation methods based on their use of weak supervision signals.
Systematically analyzed diverse methodologies, including visual-semantic space mapping, pseudo-labeling, knowledge distillation, and transfer learning.
Distinguished between 'Zero-Shot' (without weak supervision) and 'Open-Vocabulary' (with weak supervision) settings across various vision tasks.
Results: The survey consolidates diverse research into a structured framework, demonstrating a 'huge performance leap' in open-vocabulary capabilities over traditional zero-shot methods.
It highlights the central role of Vision-Language Models in achieving state-of-the-art results across detection and segmentation tasks.
The work identifies critical challenges and outlines future research directions, aiming to guide the development of more generalizable and adaptable AI perception systems for real-world applications.
Takeaways: A significant performance improvement in OVD/OVS is directly linked to the adoption of weak supervision signals and large pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs).
VLMs are foundational for state-of-the-art approaches, utilizing their text encoders as generalized classifiers and image encoders for feature extraction or knowledge distillation.
Effective methodologies include region-aware training, pseudo-labeling, knowledge distillation, and transfer learning from VLMs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.09120.Title: Light-Weight Vision Transformer with Parallel Local and Global Self-Attention
https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.09120.Summary: This paper introduces Light-Weight PLG-ViT, an efficient vision transformer architecture designed for resource-constrained hardware. It achieves competitive accuracy on vision benchmarks while significantly reducing computational requirements, making ViTs viable for deployment on edge devices in applications such as autonomous driving.
Problem: Vision Transformers (ViTs) possess high computational intensity, including large parameter counts and memory requirements.
The significant floating-point operations (FLOPs) and latency of standard ViTs limit their deployment on resource-constrained edge devices.
Real-time applications, such as autonomous driving, are impractical with conventional ViTs due to their computational demands.
Method: Introduced Light-Weight PLG-ViT, an efficient vision transformer architecture based on the Parallel Local-Global Vision Transformer (PLG-ViT).
Implemented strategic modifications including optimized downsampling using strided convolutions, an enhanced global attention branch, and careful balancing of model width and depth.
Developed an optimized Feed-Forward Network (CCF-FFN+) incorporating SiLU activation, Gated Residual Networks, and a reduced expansion factor to improve efficiency.
Results: Achieved 79.5% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet with LW PLG-ViT-A (5M parameters) and 77.8% with LW PLG-ViT-R, maintaining competitive performance for their size.
Reduced parameters by a factor of 5 compared to the original PLG-ViT, requiring 25-40% fewer operations than comparable models for typical input sizes.
Demonstrated robust object detection performance across diverse autonomous driving datasets (BDD100k, GERALD, SVIRO, NuScenes), confirming real-time viability on edge hardware.
Takeaways: Strategic architectural modifications, including optimized downsampling and an enhanced FFN design, enable significant reduction in computational cost while preserving accuracy.
Light-Weight PLG-ViT variants exhibit favorable computational complexity scaling with increasing input dimensions compared to other vision models.
Careful balancing of model width and depth, combined with adjusted regularization, can effectively reduce parameters for efficient ViT deployment on edge devices.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.06304.Title: Patch n' Pack: NaViT, a Vision Transformer for any Aspect Ratio and Resolution
https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.06304.Summary: NaViT, developed by Google DeepMind, is a Vision Transformer that processes images at their native resolutions and aspect ratios, eliminating the need for fixed-size input preprocessing. This approach enables NaViT to train 4-5 times faster than traditional ViTs for comparable performance while also improving out-of-distribution robustness and fairness metrics.
Problem: Traditional Vision Transformers (ViTs) require images to be resized to a fixed square resolution, which distorts original proportions and potentially removes valuable visual information.
Preprocessing methods for ViTs often introduce padding to accommodate rectangular images, leading to computational inefficiencies by processing unnecessary tokens.
Most modern visual datasets contain a high percentage of non-square images (e.g., 85.9% in ImageNet), creating a mismatch between real-world data and square-input models.
Method: Google DeepMind developed NaViT (Native-resolution Vision Transformer), which processes images at their native resolutions and aspect ratios, eliminating the need for fixed-size input preprocessing.
The core innovation is "Patch n' Pack," a technique that preserves original image aspect ratios, packs multiple images into a single sequence batch, and uses masks to prevent cross-image attention.

NaViT incorporates architectural adaptations, including masked self-attention and factorized positional embeddings with fractional coordinates, to handle variable resolutions and aspect ratios efficiently.
Results: NaViT trains 4-5 times faster than traditional ViTs for comparable accuracy, allowing it to process up to twice as many training examples with the same computational budget.

A single NaViT model demonstrates high performance across a wide range of input resolutions and enables flexible compute-performance trade-offs at inference time, achieving 5-6x sequence length reductions with less than a 1% accuracy drop.
The model shows improved out-of-distribution robustness (e.g., ImageNet-A accuracy of 63.8% vs. ViT's 45.9%) and enhanced fairness across demographic attributes compared to fixed-resolution ViTs.
