Takeaways: Processing images at their native resolutions and aspect ratios significantly improves training efficiency and model performance.
Packing multiple variable-sized image token sequences into a single batch, combined with masked attention, allows for efficient batch processing without requiring uniform input dimensions.

Dynamically adjusting the token dropping rate during training, particularly with a decreasing schedule, enhances efficiency while maintaining or improving accuracy, allowing the model to see more diverse examples earlier in training and more complete examples later on.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03601.Title: GPT4RoI: Instruction Tuning Large Language Model on Region-of-Interest
https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03601.Summary: GPT4RoI introduces an end-to-end vision-language model instruction-tuned for fine-grained region-of-interest understanding. The model achieves superior performance in interactive visual reasoning and region recognition, attaining near human-level accuracy on the Visual Commonsense Reasoning benchmark.
Problem: Existing vision-language models primarily operate on image-level understanding, limiting their ability to comprehend and respond to queries about specific objects or localized events.
User interaction with multimodal AI systems lacks precision, as there is no direct mechanism for referring to specific visual regions through explicit spatial cues like bounding boxes.

Non-end-to-end architectures that leverage external vision models for region understanding suffer from architectural complexity, potential latency, and reduced integration between vision and language components.
Method: An end-to-end architecture is proposed, integrating a pre-trained CLIP vision encoder, an image-level feature projector, a dedicated region feature extractor (using multi-level feature pyramids and RoIAlign), and an instruction-tuned Large Language Model (Vicuna).

A "spatial instruction tuning" approach is developed, using special `` tokens to embed bounding box-derived region features directly into the LLM's input sequence, enabling explicit region referencing.

A two-stage training process is employed: first, pre-training for simple region-text alignment using object detection and referring expression datasets, followed by end-to-end fine-tuning on complex reasoning, captioning, and conversational data.
Results: GPT4RoI-7B achieved an overall score of 35.1 on the ViP-Bench, outperforming concurrent models like Kosmos-2 (26.9) and Shikra-7B (33.7) in comprehensive region understanding.
The model demonstrated superior open-vocabulary region recognition across Cityscapes and ADE20K datasets, surpassing Kosmos-2 and Shikra-7B in panoptic, instance, and semantic segmentation metrics.
GPT4RoI-13B reached 81.6% accuracy on the Visual Commonsense Reasoning (VCR) Q→AR task, exceeding all existing models by over 6 points and approaching human-level performance of 85.0%.
Takeaways: Integrating a dedicated region feature extractor with multi-level image features and RoIAlign within an end-to-end LLM framework allows for effective fine-grained visual grounding.
Spatial instruction tuning enables LLMs to process and reason about user-specified visual regions directly, significantly enhancing interactive and conversational capabilities at a granular level.

Progressive training, starting with basic region-text alignment and moving to complex reasoning tasks, effectively aligns region features with language embeddings and unlocks powerful visual common sense in LLMs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.15880.Title: Towards Open Vocabulary Learning: A Survey
https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.15880.Summary: This survey provides the first exhaustive review of open vocabulary learning, a paradigm enabling AI systems to recognize categories beyond their training data, by consolidating methodologies across tasks like object detection and segmentation. The work categorizes over 50 models, highlighting the foundational role of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and identifying key trends, benchmarks, and future challenges in the field.
Problem: Conventional computer vision models operate under a 'close-set assumption,' limiting them to recognizing only categories seen during training, which is impractical for dynamic real-world applications.
The inability to generalize to novel, unseen categories without costly re-annotation and retraining poses a significant bottleneck for deploying adaptable AI systems.
A lack of a unified, comprehensive literature review exists specifically for open vocabulary learning, hindering systematic understanding and progression in this rapidly evolving field.
Method: The survey systematically defines open vocabulary learning, distinguishing it from related concepts like zero-shot learning and open-set recognition.

It provides a structured, task-wise categorization of methodologies across object detection, segmentation, video understanding, and 3D scene understanding, analyzing how VLMs and language data are leveraged.
The paper offers a comparative analysis of representative methods on standard benchmarks and datasets, accompanied by a discussion of challenges and future research directions.
Results: The survey found that two-stage detectors consistently outperform one-stage detectors in open vocabulary object detection, particularly with large backbones and sophisticated distillation/alignment techniques.
For open vocabulary segmentation, models leveraging extensive VLM pre-training and large-scale caption data achieve the highest mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) scores.

The work identifies base class overfitting, high training costs, and the absence of unified benchmarks as persistent challenges, suggesting future work in temporal information, advanced 3D understanding, and LLM integration.
Takeaways: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) like CLIP are foundational, enabling open vocabulary capabilities by transferring knowledge and aligning visual and linguistic features.
Auxiliary language data, such as image captions, serves as a cost-effective weak supervision signal, providing an expansive vocabulary for models to generalize to novel classes.
Generating pseudo-labels for novel categories and adapting existing close-set architectures with VLM-derived text embeddings are common and effective strategies across various tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.15195.Title: Shikra: Unleashing Multimodal LLM's Referential Dialogue Magic
https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.15195.Summary: Shikra introduces a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) that integrates natural referential dialogue by processing and generating precise spatial coordinates directly within natural language. This model achieved state-of-the-art performance on PointQA tasks and demonstrated improved reasoning and reduced visual hallucinations through the use of grounded Chain of Thoughts.
Problem: Current MLLMs cannot engage in precise referential dialogue, lacking the ability to understand or generate responses tied to specific spatial regions within an image.
Existing vision-language positioning tasks are fragmented, typically handling either input or output of positional information but not both flexibly and simultaneously within a natural dialogue.
Prior MLLMs inherently lack precise spatial awareness, performing at random chance (25.96% accuracy) on tasks requiring absolute spatial localization, as shown by the 'chessboard test'.
Method: Shikra employs a simple, unified three-component architecture consisting of a frozen CLIP ViT-L/14 visual encoder, a single fully connected alignment layer, and a fine-tuned Vicuna-7B or Vicuna-13B LLM.

Spatial coordinates (bounding boxes or points) are represented as normalized numerical values (e.g., `[0.123, 0.456, ...]`) directly integrated into natural language sequences without requiring special tokens or architectural modifications.

The model is trained on a comprehensive instruction dataset, which includes reorganized public vision-language datasets and new, high-quality referential dialogue data generated by GPT-4, utilizing a two-stage tuning process.
Results: Achieved state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on PointQA tasks, including Visual-7W and LookTwice-QA, demonstrating effective comprehension and utilization of positional inputs.

Showed competitive performance on Referring Expression Comprehension (REC) tasks across RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, and RefCOCOg, as well as on general VQA and Image Captioning benchmarks (VQAv2, OK-VQA, COCO, Flickr30k).
Demonstrated competitive performance in reducing object hallucination on the POPE evaluation pipeline, comparable to InstructBLIP and surpassing several other popular MLLMs like MiniGPT-4 and LLaVA.
Takeaways: Integrating numerical positional annotations into Chain of Thoughts (Grounding CoT) significantly improves reasoning and reduces visual hallucinations, yielding a 5.9-point performance increase on the CLEVR dataset compared to direct answering.

Representing coordinates as natural language numerical values is more effective and flexible than using extra vocabulary tokens, offering greater precision control and eliminating the need for vocabulary modification.
Existing general MLLMs, despite coarse-grained vision-language alignment, do not inherently capture precise spatial positions, validating the need for direct referential dialogue capabilities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.14824.Title: Kosmos-2: Grounding Multimodal Large Language Models to the World
https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.14824.Summary: Microsoft Research developed KOSMOS-2, a multimodal large language model that integrates grounding capabilities, allowing it to perceive object descriptions (bounding boxes) and precisely link text to the visual world. The model achieved strong zero-shot performance on phrase grounding (78.7% R@1 on Flickr30k Entities) and referring expression generation (CIDEr 60.3 on RefCOCOg), while largely preserving its existing vision-language and language-only capabilities.
Problem: Existing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) often lack robust grounding capabilities, making them unable to precisely pinpoint or refer to specific objects or regions within an image.
Human-AI interaction was limited to high-level textual descriptions, lacking the intuitive "pointing" and "showing" fundamental to human communication about the physical world.
MLLMs struggled to provide visual answers (e.g., bounding boxes) or to visually resolve coreference ambiguity for objects in an image.
Method: Introduced KOSMOS-2, a Transformer-based multimodal large language model that integrates grounding and referring capabilities by representing continuous bounding box coordinates as discrete location tokens.

Constructed GRIT, a large-scale (91 million images, 115 million text spans, 137 million bounding boxes) grounded image-text dataset, by automatically extracting noun-chunk-bounding-box and referring-expression-bounding-box pairs from existing web-scale datasets.

Employed a novel "hyperlink" data format to explicitly link text spans with their associated location tokens, enabling the model to learn the association between language and visual regions during training.
Utilized instruction tuning with newly constructed grounded instruction data to align KOSMOS-2's capabilities with human instructions for tasks requiring visual grounding.
Results: KOSMOS-2 achieved 78.7% R@1 zero-shot performance on Flickr30k Entities for phrase grounding, significantly outperforming a previous zero-shot model, GRILL (18.9% R@1).
It demonstrated strong zero-shot referring expression generation with a CIDEr score of 60.3 on RefCOCOg, surprisingly outperforming a finetuned listener-speaker model.

The model maintained or slightly improved performance on perception-language tasks (e.g., Flickr30k Image Captioning CIDEr 66.7, up from KOSMOS-1's 65.2) and largely preserved language-only task proficiency.
Takeaways: Explicitly encoding bounding box information as discrete location tokens within the text stream allows a causal language model to learn grounding generatively.
Creating a massive, automatically constructed grounded image-text dataset (GRIT) is crucial for training effective grounding capabilities in multimodal large language models.
A "hyperlink" format for associating text spans with bounding boxes provides a clear signal for the model to learn multimodal grounding.
Grounding capabilities can be integrated into multimodal large language models without significantly degrading their general perception-language or language-only abilities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.13643.Title: LightGlue: Local Feature Matching at Light Speed
https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.13643.Summary: LightGlue presents an adaptive deep feature matching approach that achieves comparable or superior accuracy to SuperGlue while being up to 10x faster. It integrates adaptive computation mechanisms, such as early stopping and feature pruning, to dynamically adjust computational effort based on task complexity.
Problem: State-of-the-art deep feature matching methods, like SuperGlue, are computationally expensive, hindering real-time applications and deployment on resource-constrained devices.
SuperGlue processes all features with a fixed computational budget and relies on a complex Sinkhorn layer, leading to high inference and training costs.
The significant resource requirements limit the practical adoption of advanced feature matching in critical computer vision applications.
Method: Implements relative positional encoding and a lightweight prediction head to reduce computational complexity compared to prior methods.
Introduces adaptive computation mechanisms, including early stopping and progressive point pruning, to dynamically adjust the network's depth and width based on matching task difficulty.
Develops a simplified two-stage training pipeline that converges faster and requires fewer computational resources.
Results: Achieves up to 10x faster inference speeds compared to SuperGlue, with lower memory requirements and improved scaling with increasing keypoint counts.
Demonstrates comparable or superior accuracy to SuperGlue on standard benchmarks, including state-of-the-art performance on relative pose estimation tasks.
Exhibits robust performance across various feature detectors (e.g., SIFT, SuperPoint, DISK) and diverse scene types, including outdoor and indoor environments.
Takeaways: Dynamically adjusting computational effort, through adaptive depth and width, in feature matching networks can yield substantial efficiency gains while preserving accuracy.
Replacing complex optimal transport layers with more efficient prediction heads and utilizing relative positional encoding improves model performance and reduces overhead.
A streamlined two-stage training process enables faster convergence and reduces the computational resources required for deep feature matching model development.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.13549.Title: A Survey on Multimodal Large Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.13549.Summary: This survey provides a comprehensive synthesis of the rapidly evolving field of Multimodal Large Language Models, detailing their common architectures, multi-stage training paradigms, and diverse evaluation methodologies. It highlights the importance of data quality for instruction tuning and addresses key challenges, including the pervasive issue of multimodal hallucination.
Problem: The rapid and uncoordinated progress in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) has created a fragmented research landscape, making it difficult for researchers to keep pace with developments.
There was a lack of a comprehensive and structured overview that synthesizes the state-of-the-art, core components, and emerging trends in the nascent MLLM field.
Researchers needed a unified resource to understand MLLM architectures, training strategies, data considerations, evaluation methodologies, and prevalent challenges like multimodal hallucination.
Method: The survey deconstructs MLLMs into fundamental architectural components (modality encoders, LLMs, modality interfaces) and analyzes their typical lifecycle-based training paradigms (pre-training, instruction-tuning, alignment tuning).
It provides a categorical framework for MLLM evaluation, distinguishing between closed-set and open-set assessment methods.

The paper systematically discusses key challenges such as multimodal hallucination, outlining its types, evaluation methods, and mitigation strategies, and details advanced techniques like M-ICL, M-CoT, and LLM-Aided Visual Reasoning.
Results: MLLMs show improved performance and emergent zero-shot capabilities with increased LLM parameter size and higher input resolutions, with MoE architectures showing promise for scaling.
Evaluation methodologies for MLLMs are evolving from traditional closed-set benchmarks to more comprehensive open-ended assessments, often relying on human or AI-based scoring.
MLLMs are expanding their capabilities to finer granularities (region/pixel-level), diverse modalities (3D, audio, video), multiple languages, and specialized real-world scenarios.
Takeaways: MLLMs typically follow a three-module architecture: a pre-trained modality encoder, a pre-trained Large Language Model, and a learnable modality interface.
A multi-stage training paradigm involving pre-training, instruction-tuning, and alignment tuning is common, with data quality being more critical than quantity, especially for instruction tuning.
Multimodal hallucination remains a persistent and critical challenge, with ongoing efforts in data engineering, architectural fixes, and post-correction strategies.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.09683.Title: Scaling Open-Vocabulary Object Detection
https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.09683.Summary: Google DeepMind's OWLv2 framework achieves state-of-the-art open-vocabulary object detection by successfully scaling self-training on over a billion weakly supervised image-text pairs. The approach yielded a 43% relative improvement, reaching 44.6% AP on LVIS rare classes for the L/14 architecture, and up to 47.2% mAP_rare with a larger ViT-G/14 model.
Problem: Open-vocabulary object detection (OV-OD) is hampered by the scarcity of high-quality human-annotated bounding box data, making it challenging to generalize to unseen concepts.
Existing self-training methods for OV-OD have not fully exploited the potential of Web-scale weak supervision, operating at relatively smaller scales.
Challenges persist in defining effective label spaces for pseudo-annotations, developing filtering strategies for noisy data, and ensuring training efficiency at massive scales.
Method: A three-step OWL-ST self-training recipe leverages WebLI, a dataset of 10 billion image-text pairs, to generate pseudo-annotations using an OWL-ViT teacher model.

The approach utilizes a machine-generated N-gram label space from alt-text for diverse queries and applies weak confidence filtering to pseudo-annotations, prioritizing data volume over strict label precision.
The OWLv2 architecture integrates training efficiency optimizations, including token dropping, instance selection, and mosaics, reducing training FLOPS by 50% and doubling throughput.
Results: The OWLv2 L/14 model, self-trained on N-gram pseudo-annotations and fine-tuned on LVIS_base, achieved 44.6% AP on LVIS rare classes, marking a 43% relative improvement over previous state-of-the-art.
The largest model (ViT-G/14 backbone with SigLIP encoder) further improved performance to 47.2% LVIS mAP_rare, demonstrating continued gains with increased scale.
OWLv2's architectural optimizations collectively reduced training FLOPS by approximately 50% and doubled training throughput, making Web-scale self-training on billions of examples feasible.
Takeaways: Detection performance scales monotonically with training compute and data, confirming classic scaling laws in the context of open-vocabulary object detection.
A diverse, machine-generated N-gram label space is critical for strong open-vocabulary generalization, outperforming human-curated vocabularies for 'in the wild' tasks.
Weak pseudo-annotation filtering, coupled with massive data volume, effectively compensates for individual label noise and improves overall detection performance at Web-scale.
Weight ensembling offers an effective strategy to mitigate the trade-off between improving performance on specific fine-tuned classes and retaining broad open-world generalization.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.08543.Title: MiniLLM: Knowledge Distillation of Large Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.08543.Summary: MiniLLM introduces a knowledge distillation method for generative large language models, leveraging reverse Kullback-Leibler Divergence and on-policy optimization to compress white-box teacher models. Student models distilled with MiniLLM achieve superior performance, higher precision in generated text, and improved calibration across various instruction-following tasks, facilitating more efficient and reliable LLM deployment.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) incur substantial computational and memory costs, impeding their broad deployment and fine-tuning, especially in resource-constrained settings.

Standard Knowledge Distillation (KD) methods, particularly those based on forward Kullback-Leibler Divergence (KLD), prove ineffective for compressing generative LLMs, often leading student models to produce low-quality or inaccurate text.
Forward KLD encourages student models to cover all modes of a complex teacher distribution, potentially causing them to assign excessive probability to less probable or 'void' output regions.
Method: The methodology replaces standard forward KLD with reverse KLD (KL[q||p]) to encourage mode-seeking behavior, thereby focusing the student model on the major, high-quality modes of the teacher's distribution.

An on-policy optimization strategy, similar to Reinforcement Learning, is implemented to train the student model by sampling from its own distribution and deriving gradients using the Policy Gradient Theorem.

The approach incorporates specific techniques to stabilize on-policy training, including single-step decomposition for variance reduction, teacher-mixed sampling to prevent 'reward hacking', and length normalization to mitigate bias towards shorter sentences.
Results: MINILLM consistently outperforms all tested baselines (SFT w/o KD, KD, SeqKD) across diverse evaluation datasets and model families (GPT-2, OPT, LLaMA), demonstrating superior overall generation quality and generalizability.

The approach achieves higher precision and quality in generated responses, as evidenced by improved Rouge-L scores and higher GPT-4 feedback scores, with some student models even surpassing teacher models on Rouge-L for specific tasks.

Student models distilled with MINILLM exhibit reduced exposure bias and better calibration compared to other KD methods, particularly for long-text generation and classification tasks, enhancing model reliability and trustworthiness.
Takeaways: Reverse Kullback-Leibler Divergence (KL[q||p]) is inherently more suitable for generative Knowledge Distillation than forward KLD (KL[p||q]), as it guides smaller student models to prioritize high-quality, major modes of the teacher's distribution.

On-policy optimization effectively addresses the challenges of training generative student models by allowing them to learn from their own generated samples, which significantly mitigates exposure bias.

Specific algorithmic improvements, such as single-step decomposition for gradient calculation, teacher-mixed sampling during generation, and length normalization, are crucial for robustly applying policy gradient methods to generative Knowledge Distillation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.06189.Title: FasterViT: Fast Vision Transformers with Hierarchical Attention
https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.06189.Summary: Researchers at NVIDIA developed FasterViT, a new family of vision models that combine convolutional layers and a novel Hierarchical Attention mechanism to significantly improve the accuracy-throughput trade-off. These models achieve a new state-of-the-art Pareto front in image classification and demonstrate superior performance-throughput balance across object detection and semantic segmentation tasks.
Problem: Vision Transformers (ViTs) suffer from high computational and memory complexity due to the quadratic scaling of self-attention with image resolution, limiting their inference speed (throughput) for high-resolution images.
Pure ViTs lack inherent inductive biases like locality and translation equivariance, requiring vast amounts of data for effective training compared to Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs).

Existing efficient ViTs or hybrid models often struggle to achieve an optimal balance between high accuracy and high image throughput, especially for dense prediction tasks and high-resolution inputs.
Method: Developed FasterViT, a family of neural networks with a multi-stage, hybrid CNN-ViT architecture that leverages efficient convolutional layers in early stages and Transformer blocks in later stages.

Introduced Hierarchical Attention (HAT), a novel attention mechanism where 'carrier tokens' summarize local windows, enabling efficient global information exchange through global carrier attention and local window-carrier attention.

Optimized the architecture for hardware efficiency by minimizing memory-bound operations in early stages and strategically placing more expressive (but potentially more compute-intensive) HAT-based Transformer operations in later, compute-bound stages.
Results: FasterViT models establish a new state-of-the-art Pareto front for ImageNet-1K classification, demonstrating higher accuracy at comparable or better throughput compared to ConvNeXt and Swin Transformer families (e.g., FasterViT-2 achieves 84.2% Top-1 accuracy at 3161 img/sec vs. ConvNeXt-S at 83.1% Top-1 and 2008 img/sec).

On MS COCO object detection, FasterViT backbones lead to better accuracy-throughput trade-offs, outperforming ConvNeXt-B and Swin-B in both box AP and mask AP while achieving 15-30% higher throughput.
For ADE20K semantic segmentation, FasterViT-4 with UPerNet achieves 49.1 mIoU, surpassing comparable Swin and ConvNeXt models while maintaining higher inference speeds.
Takeaways: A hybrid architecture combining efficient CNNs in early, high-resolution stages and Transformer blocks in later, lower-resolution stages effectively balances inductive bias, global context modeling, and hardware efficiency.

The Hierarchical Attention (HAT) mechanism, using learnable 'carrier tokens' for cross-window communication, provides an efficient way to capture long-range dependencies without the quadratic complexity of global self-attention.

Hardware-aware design, preferring dense convolutions in memory-bound early layers and expressive Transformer operations in compute-bound later layers, is crucial for optimizing throughput on modern GPUs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.03514.Title: Recognize Anything: A Strong Image Tagging Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.03514.Summary: The Recognize Anything Model (RAM) presents an image tagging foundation model that leverages large-scale, annotation-free web data and a refined data engine to achieve open-vocabulary recognition. It shows high accuracy on common categories, outperforming existing vision-language models like CLIP and BLIP, and obtaining a higher mAP (86.0) on OpenImages-common than ML-Decoder (85.8).
Problem: Existing image tagging models often have limited category scope, suffer from suboptimal accuracy, or produce redundant tags, hindering comprehensive open-vocabulary recognition.
The collection of large-scale, high-quality, universal annotation data for image tagging is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming.
A critical gap exists for a foundational model capable of comprehensive semantic recognition in images, akin to SAM's prowess in localization but with added semantic understanding.
Method: Employs an annotation-free paradigm, using automatic text semantic parsing on large-scale web image-text pairs to acquire initial tags.
Introduces a data engine to automatically generate missing tags and clean noisy labels through region localization with Grounding-Dino and consistency filtering.
Designs an open-vocabulary model architecture utilizing textual label queries derived from a CLIP text encoder and CLIP image feature distillation for robust zero-shot generalization.
Results: Achieves superior zero-shot performance, outperforming vision-language models like CLIP and BLIP by over 20% on most evaluated multi-label classification, detection, and segmentation benchmarks.
RAM-4M, trained on annotation-free data, attains a higher mAP (86.0) on the OpenImages-common dataset compared to the fully supervised ML-Decoder (85.8).
The data engine's generation and cleaning processes increase tag count from 12.0M to 41.7M and enhance label quality, leading to consistent performance improvements across various test sets.
Takeaways: High-quality visual recognition models can be built from large-scale, noisy, and annotation-free web data, potentially surpassing fully supervised approaches.
The joint training of image captioning and tagging tasks within a unified architecture effectively promotes stronger tagging abilities.
Open-vocabulary recognition is greatly enhanced by using semantically rich textual label queries for categories, enabling generalization beyond explicitly seen tags.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.01708.Title: TIES-Merging: Resolving Interference When Merging Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.01708.Summary: TIES-MERGING introduces a three-step approach to combine multiple fine-tuned models into a single multitask model by explicitly resolving parameter interference stemming from redundant changes and sign disagreements. This method consistently outperforms existing merging techniques across NLP and vision tasks, demonstrating average performance improvements up to 3.6% on T5-large models and superior out-of-domain generalization.
Problem: Existing model merging methods often suffer from performance degradation due to parameter interference between different fine-tuned models.
Redundant, low-magnitude parameter changes introduced during fine-tuning interfere with more influential changes from other models when merged.
Parameter values often have conflicting signs across different fine-tuned models, leading to cancellation or shrinkage when simply averaged.
Method: TIES-MERGING (TRIM, ELECT, MERGE) is a three-step method that operates on "task vectors," which are the differences between fine-tuned and initial pre-trained model parameters.
TRIM removes redundant parameter changes by setting low-magnitude values in each task vector to zero, retaining only the top-k% influential parameters.

ELECT resolves sign disagreements for each parameter by electing a dominant sign based on the greater total magnitude (positive or negative sum) across all trimmed task vectors, and DISJOINT MERGE then averages only the parameter values whose signs align with the elected sign.
Results: TIES-MERGING consistently outperformed baselines like Simple Averaging and Task Arithmetic across NLP (T5) and Vision (ViT) modalities, model sizes, and fine-tuning settings, with average improvements up to 3.6% on T5-large and 2.5% on PEFT models.
It demonstrated superior out-of-domain generalization, outperforming the strongest baseline by 1.0% (T5-base) and 4.4% (T5-Large) on held-out tasks.

The method exhibited more graceful performance degradation when merging a larger number of tasks, served as a better initialization strategy for subsequent fine-tuning, and improved robustness when merging multiple checkpoints from the same task.
Takeaways: Parameter interference in model merging primarily stems from redundant low-magnitude changes and sign disagreements across task-specific fine-tuned models.
Explicitly trimming redundant parameters and resolving sign conflicts can significantly improve merged model performance by preserving influential parameter magnitudes.

The correct sign direction for a parameter is crucial, as demonstrated by catastrophic performance drops when signs are flipped for high-magnitude parameters, and accurately estimating the optimal sign vector is key to bridging the performance gap with full multitask training.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.17216.Title: Generating Images with Multimodal Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.17216.Summary: GILL (Generating Images with Large Language Models) introduces a multimodal language model that generates novel images, retrieves existing images, and produces text, all conditioned on interleaved image and text inputs. The model leverages frozen foundation models and lightweight mapping networks to improve image generation coherence in complex contexts like visual storytelling and dialogue, outperforming baselines in various metrics.
Problem: Existing multimodal language models could process diverse inputs and generate text, but none could synthesize novel images within a dynamic, conversational context.
State-of-the-art text-to-image models struggle with longer, more nuanced, or conversational language inputs, lacking the deep contextual understanding of Large Language Models (LLMs).
Training large multimodal models from scratch is computationally expensive, necessitating efficient adaptation methods that combine existing powerful models.
Method: GILL efficiently adapts frozen LLMs (OPT-6.7B), visual encoders (CLIP ViT-L), and text-to-image generators (Stable Diffusion v1.5) by learning lightweight mapping networks (~50M trainable parameters).

A novel GILLMapper (4-layer Transformer) is introduced to translate LLM's high-level visual intent from special output tokens into the Stable Diffusion text encoder's embedding space for novel image generation.

A multi-task loss function combines objectives for image captioning, predicting image output tokens, novel image generation, and image retrieval, alongside a separate decision module to choose between generation and retrieval.
Results: GILL demonstrates superior contextual image generation, with CLIP Similarity improving from 0.581 to 0.641 on the VIST dataset when moving from single-caption to full multimodal context, outperforming Stable Diffusion (0.598 with 5 captions).

On the VisDial dataset, GILL's image generation performance consistently improves with increased dialogue rounds, achieving a CLIP Similarity of 0.645 at 10 rounds, surpassing Stable Diffusion (0.622).

GILL maintains strong performance on other multimodal tasks, performing comparably or better than similar-sized models on VQA (0.3178 zero-shot accuracy) and image captioning (0.1059 BLEU-4), while also matching or exceeding FROMAGe in image retrieval (20.3 Recall@1 on VIST).
Takeaways: Leveraging the long-range contextual understanding of frozen LLMs significantly enhances the relevance and coherence of generated images in multi-turn dialogues and visual storytelling scenarios.

An efficient modular architecture, by freezing large foundation models and training only small connecting components, enables powerful multimodal capabilities with substantially reduced computational training costs.

A dedicated mapping module (GILLMapper) is crucial for effectively bridging the semantic gap between LLM representations and the specific input requirements of a pre-trained text-to-image diffusion model.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14992.Title: Reasoning with Language Model is Planning with World Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14992.Summary: The Reasoning via Planning (RAP) framework from UC San Diego and University of Florida integrates Large Language Models (LLMs) with an internal world model and Monte Carlo Tree Search to enable deliberate, multi-step reasoning. This approach allows LLaMA-33B to outperform GPT-4 on plan generation and achieves higher accuracy on math and logical reasoning tasks compared to existing LLM reasoning methods.
Problem: Current Large Language Models (LLMs) often lack an explicit internal 'world model' to simulate the consequences of actions or anticipate future states in complex reasoning tasks.

Existing LLM reasoning paradigms, such as Chain-of-Thought, generate steps autoregressively without explicit feedback mechanisms to evaluate intermediate steps or balance exploration versus exploitation in reasoning paths.
LLMs struggle with problems requiring deliberate planning and foresight, leading to high error rates in tasks like multi-step plan generation or complex logical deduction.
Method: The Reasoning via Planning (RAP) framework repurposes LLMs to serve dual roles: as a reasoning agent to generate actions and as a world model to predict subsequent states.

Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) is employed as the core planning algorithm to strategically explore the reasoning space, enabling the LLM to balance exploring novel paths and exploiting promising options.

A flexible reward mechanism is introduced, incorporating action likelihood, state confidence, LLM self-evaluation, and task-specific heuristics, to quantitatively assess and guide the quality of each reasoning step.
Results: On Blocksworld plan generation, LLaMA-33B with RAP achieved an average success rate of 64%, surpassing GPT-4 with Chain-of-Thought by 33% relative improvement.
For GSM8K math reasoning, RAP achieved 48.6% accuracy, with RAP-Aggregation further boosting it to 51.6%, outperforming strong baselines like Chain-of-Thought with Self-Consistency.
In PrOntoQA logical reasoning, RAP achieved 94.2% prediction accuracy and 78.8% proof accuracy, demonstrating improved performance over Chain-of-Thought and its self-consistency variants.
Takeaways: LLMs can be effectively repurposed to function as internal 'world models,' simulating environmental dynamics for planning and predicting state transitions.
Integrating principled search algorithms like Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) with LLMs enables more deliberate and robust multi-step reasoning beyond autoregressive generation.
Explicitly modeling world states and incorporating diverse reward signals are crucial for enhancing LLM performance on complex planning tasks, allowing for guided exploration and evaluation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14676.Title: GRILL: Grounded Vision-language Pre-training via Aligning Text and Image Regions
https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14676.Summary: GRILL introduces a pre-training approach that explicitly connects textual references to visual elements through novel hybrid sequences and object-word alignments. The model achieves strong zero- and few-shot generalization across diverse vision-language tasks, particularly excelling in grounding capabilities on benchmarks like Visual Question Answering and Flickr30k-entities.
Problem: Existing vision-language models often struggle with grounding tasks that require precise localization of objects or regions based on textual descriptions.
Current methods either require task-specific fine-tuning for region/object representations or are few-shot learners that generalize across tasks but lack strong grounding abilities.

A need exists for a unified pre-training approach that can generalize to diverse vision-language tasks and perform well on grounding tasks without relying on external object detectors or extensive fine-tuning.
Method: GRILL employs a generative sequence-to-sequence transformer model with a Swin transformer as its vision encoder to process image patches as visual tokens.
A key innovation is the use of 'hybrid sequences' during pre-training, where referring words in captions are replaced with corresponding visual patches from the image.
The model is pre-trained with three complementary objectives: Prefix Language Modeling, Masked Language Modeling, and a Discriminative Objective to align vision and language.
Results: GRILL consistently outperforms state-of-the-art few-shot methods across diverse vision-language tasks in zero-shot and few-shot settings.
In zero-shot Visual Question Answering (VQA), GRILL achieved 49.6% accuracy, compared to 39.7% for baseline models.
The model showed particularly effective performance on grounding tasks like Flickr30k-entities, demonstrating significant improvements over baseline models.
Takeaways: Using hybrid sequences during pre-training significantly enhances the model's grounding capabilities by explicitly linking textual references to image regions.
The combination of language modeling and discriminative objectives in pre-training leads to improved overall performance across tasks.
GRILL demonstrates strong zero-shot performance across multiple vision-language tasks, indicating effective general understanding without extensive fine-tuning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13689.Title: Know Your Self-supervised Learning: A Survey on Image-based Generative and Discriminative Training
https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13689.Summary: This comprehensive survey outlines the evolution and current landscape of image-based self-supervised learning, dissecting its methodologies into generative and discriminative paradigms. It elucidates core technical concepts and evaluates modern SSL frameworks, highlighting their ability to learn powerful representations competitive with supervised methods, often using Vision Transformers.
Problem: Traditional supervised learning requires vast amounts of manually labeled data, which is often expensive and time-consuming to obtain, limiting scalability and application in data-scarce domains.
Supervised learning approaches, despite strong performance on benchmarks, are approaching performance plateaus and face inherent limitations due to their dependence on explicit labels.
The challenge of effectively leveraging abundant unlabeled data for learning robust and generalizable visual representations.
Method: The survey examines self-supervised learning as a paradigm that generates supervisory signals from unlabeled data itself, allowing models to learn meaningful representations.

It categorizes existing image-based SSL approaches into two main groups: discriminative SSL (e.g., contrastive learning, non-contrastive methods, clustering) and generative SSL (e.g., masked image modeling, denoising).
It details the technical concepts and architectural components common across SSL frameworks, such as Siamese networks, stop-gradient operations, momentum encoders, and various loss functions.
Results: Both discriminative and generative SSL methods have achieved performance levels comparable to or exceeding supervised learning benchmarks on various computer vision tasks.
Vision Transformers (ViTs) have emerged as the dominant architecture, particularly for generative SSL methods like Masked Image Modeling, demonstrating improved performance with increased model size.
Discriminative SSL methods often yield strong results with linear evaluation on frozen features, while generative methods typically show superior performance when fine-tuned on downstream tasks.
Takeaways: Self-supervised learning (SSL) has evolved from diverse pretext tasks (e.g., colorization, inpainting) to sophisticated frameworks like contrastive learning and masked image modeling.
SSL methods can be broadly categorized into discriminative approaches, which learn to distinguish instances, and generative approaches, which focus on reconstructing or generating data.

Key technical concepts such as Siamese networks, stop-gradient, momentum encoders, and projection heads are fundamental to modern SSL framework design, particularly for preventing representation collapse and improving feature quality.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.09880.Title: A survey of the Vision Transformers and their CNN-Transformer based Variants
https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.09880.Summary: This survey paper provides a comprehensive review and systematic taxonomy of Vision Transformers (ViTs) and particularly emphasizes Hybrid Vision Transformers (HVTs), which combine Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Transformers. It classifies HVTs into seven distinct integration patterns, outlining their design rationales, performance trends, and widespread applicability across diverse computer vision tasks.
Problem: Pure Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) excel at local feature extraction but often struggle to capture long-range dependencies and global contextual information in images.
Traditional Vision Transformers (ViTs) effectively model global relationships but typically require vast amounts of training data due to weaker inductive biases and can be computationally expensive.
The rapid proliferation of hybrid CNN-Transformer architectures necessitated a structured overview to understand their diverse designs and integration strategies.
Method: The authors conducted a systematic review, establishing a foundational understanding of ViT components and general ViT architectures.

A detailed and novel taxonomy was developed for Hybrid Vision Transformers (HVTs), classifying them into seven distinct categories based on how CNN operations integrate with self-attention mechanisms.

The paper provides empirical comparisons, discussing the strengths, weaknesses, and performance metrics of various models, alongside an overview of their applications, challenges, and future directions.
Results: The survey presents a comprehensive taxonomy of general ViT architectures into five main categories (e.g., patch-based, knowledge transfer-based, shifted window-based).
A detailed taxonomy for HVTs is established, classifying them into seven integration patterns with illustrative examples (e.g., DETR for early-layer, CoAtNet for sequential, MaxViT for hierarchical).

It demonstrates the widespread applicability of both ViTs and HVTs across almost all major computer vision domains, including image recognition, segmentation, generation, and medical image analysis, documenting their successful deployment in these areas.
Takeaways: Hybrid Vision Transformers (HVTs) offer a powerful solution by combining CNNs' inductive biases for local feature extraction with Transformers' capacity for global, long-range dependency modeling.

The integration of CNNs and Transformers can occur in diverse ways, including early-layer, lateral-layer, sequential, parallel, hierarchical, attention-based, and channel boosting-based methods, each with distinct architectural implications and performance characteristics.
HVTs generally aim for improved state-of-the-art performance, better efficiency, reduced data requirements, and enhanced generalization across benchmarks compared to pure CNNs or ViTs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.07011.Title: Region-Aware Pretraining for Open-Vocabulary Object Detection with Vision Transformers
https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.07011.Summary: Google Research introduces Region-aware Open-vocabulary Vision Transformers (RO-ViT), a novel pretraining approach for Vision Transformers that specifically enhances their ability for open-vocabulary object detection. This method achieves a new state-of-the-art of 34.1 APr on the LVIS benchmark and surprisingly improves image-text retrieval performance on MS COCO and Flickr30K.
Problem: Traditional object detectors are limited by their reliance on expensive, manually annotated bounding boxes and class labels, restricting their vocabulary size.
Vision-Language Models (VLMs) pre-trained for image-level tasks do not optimally capture region-level information, creating a gap for precise object localization in detection tasks.
Common object proposal generation methods struggle to identify novel or unlabeled objects, often misclassifying them as background.
Method: A region-aware image-text pretraining recipe for Vision Transformers, featuring Cropped Positional Embeddings (CPE) to make PEs robust to partial views.
Integration of Focal Loss into the contrastive learning objective to focus training on hard negative examples and improve discriminative power.
Refinements in downstream finetuning, including localization quality-based object proposals and normalized output layers for improved generalization on novel categories.
Results: Achieved a new state-of-the-art of 34.1 APr on the LVIS open-vocabulary object detection benchmark, an improvement of +7.8 APr over the previous best method.
Secured state-of-the-art performance on 9 out of 12 metrics for image-text retrieval on MS COCO and Flickr30K, surpassing larger models like CoCa.
Demonstrated strong zero-shot transfer capabilities, reaching 17.1 AP on Objects365, outperforming ViLD and DetPro by more than 5 AP.
Takeaways: Pretraining Vision-Language Models with explicit region-aware mechanisms, rather than solely adapting image-level VLMs, significantly enhances their suitability for object detection.
Simple modifications like Cropped Positional Embeddings and Focal Loss during the core pretraining phase can lead to substantial performance gains without increasing model complexity.
Optimizing for region-level understanding during pretraining can synergistically improve global image representations, leading to better performance in both object detection and image-text retrieval.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.06500.Title: InstructBLIP: Towards General-purpose Vision-Language Models with Instruction Tuning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.06500.Summary: InstructBLIP advances general-purpose vision-language models by systematically applying instruction tuning, building on the BLIP-2 architecture. This work introduces an instruction-aware visual feature extraction mechanism and leverages a diverse, instruction-formatted dataset, leading to state-of-the-art zero-shot performance across various unseen vision-language tasks and achieving significant generalization improvements.
Problem: Existing vision-language models (VLMs) struggle to generalize broadly to diverse, unseen tasks and instructions, unlike instruction-tuned large language models (LLMs) in NLP.
Previous VLM approaches often use instruction-agnostic visual feature extraction, which limits their ability to adapt visual understanding to specific task instructions.
Training VLMs on image caption data is too limited for broad generalization, while existing multitask learning approaches for VL tasks often fail to yield strong zero-shot performance.
Method: The model systematically applies instruction tuning to vision-language tasks by finetuning only the Query Transformer (Q-Former) component of the BLIP-2 architecture, keeping the image encoder and LLM frozen.

It introduces an "instruction-aware" Q-Former that integrates textual instructions to guide visual feature extraction, allowing the model to dynamically adapt its visual understanding based on the task.

InstructBLIP curates 26 diverse vision-language datasets into an instruction-tuning format, using 10-15 distinct natural language templates per task and employing a balanced sampling strategy during training.
Results: InstructBLIP achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot performance across 13 held-out datasets, outperforming its BLIP-2 backbone by an average relative improvement of 15.0% (FlanT5-XL).

It demonstrates strong generalization to entirely unseen task categories, such as video question answering, showing up to a 47.1% relative improvement on MSRVTT-QA despite no prior temporal video training.

The smallest InstructBLIP FlanT5-XL model (4 billion parameters) outperforms the significantly larger Flamingo-80B model across all six shared evaluation datasets by an average of 24.8% relative improvement.
Takeaways: Instruction-aware visual feature extraction, where the Q-Former adapts its visual understanding based on the textual instruction, is crucial for improving model performance and generalization, especially for tasks requiring fine-grained reasoning.

A balanced sampling strategy during instruction tuning is essential for effective and stable training across diverse vision-language datasets, preventing overfitting to smaller datasets and underfitting to larger ones.

Instruction tuning, rather than just multitask learning with unified formatting, is the primary driver for enhancing a vision-language model's zero-shot generalization capabilities to unseen tasks and categories.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.05665.Title: ImageBind: One Embedding Space To Bind Them All
https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.05665.Summary: ImageBind, developed by FAIR, Meta AI, establishes a single, unified embedding space across six distinct modalities (images, text, audio, depth, thermal, and IMU) by uniquely leveraging images as a central anchor for alignment. This approach enables emergent zero-shot capabilities between modalities never directly paired during training, allowing for state-of-the-art performance on various classification and retrieval tasks and unlocking novel applications like audio-driven image generation.
Problem: Existing multimodal models often create fragmented, task-specific embedding spaces, limiting their versatility and requiring complex bridging mechanisms for new cross-modal tasks.
Acquiring massive datasets where a multitude of modalities are simultaneously present and perfectly aligned is practically infeasible.
Prior multimodal approaches are inherently constrained to the specific modality pairs they were explicitly trained on, preventing generalization to other cross-modal interactions.
There was no generalized method to leverage the inherent semantic connections between various sensory inputs and transfer knowledge across them without direct explicit pairing during training.
Method: Learns a single, unified joint embedding space across six modalities (images, text, audio, depth, thermal, IMU) by exclusively aligning each non-image modality to images using paired data.
Employs individual Transformer-based encoders for each modality, where image and text encoders are initialized from strong pre-trained models (like OpenCLIP) and often kept frozen.
Utilizes a contrastive learning objective (InfoNCE loss) to pull aligned image-modality pairs closer in the embedding space while pushing unrelated examples apart.
Avoids the need for datasets where all modalities co-occur, instead leveraging distinct datasets for each image-modality pair (e.g., Image-Text, Video-Audio, Image-Depth).
Results: Achieves state-of-the-art or highly competitive emergent zero-shot classification performance on audio, depth, thermal, and IMU datasets, often matching or outperforming specialist models trained with direct supervision.
Demonstrates strong cross-modal retrieval capabilities, significantly outperforming prior methods on text-to-audio retrieval and showing competitive performance on text-to-video retrieval.

Enables novel emergent applications like audio-to-image generation and audio-based object detection by directly leveraging ImageBind embeddings with existing generative and recognition models, without requiring retraining.
Exhibits strong label-efficiency for few-shot classification, outperforming other multimodal models across various few-shot settings on audio and depth benchmarks.

Qualitatively demonstrates the ability to perform multimodal embedding space arithmetic, allowing for the composition of concepts across different modalities (e.g., image + audio to retrieve combined concepts).
Takeaways: Images can serve as a universal "binder" for diverse sensory modalities, even without direct simultaneous pairing of all modalities.
Aligning individual modalities to a strong visual representation enables emergent alignment between non-image modalities (e.g., audio and text).

Contrastive learning with image-paired data can efficiently transfer semantic understanding from visual-textual space to other sensory inputs, circumventing the need for all-modality co-occurrence datasets.

The strength of the image encoder is critical; scaling it up significantly improves emergent performance across all other modalities, underscoring the importance of robust visual representations for binding diverse senses.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.00104.Title: MMViT: Multiscale Multiview Vision Transformers
https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.00104.Summary: MMViT introduces a novel Transformer architecture that merges multiscale feature hierarchies with parallel multiview encoding and cross-attention for robust representation learning. The model achieves state-of-the-art performance on AudioSet (43.0% mAP) and ImageNet1K (83.2% Top-1 accuracy) while also featuring an effective audio-specific CutMix augmentation.
Problem: Existing Transformer architectures like Multiscale Vision Transformers (MViT) and Multiview Transformers (MTV) typically focus on either hierarchical scaling or parallel view processing, but not a unified combination.
The need for a versatile and general-purpose backbone model that can achieve state-of-the-art performance across diverse modalities, such as audio and image classification.
Transformer-based audio models are often susceptible to overfitting, particularly when fine-tuning from models pre-trained on large image datasets.
Method: MMViT introduces a novel Transformer architecture that seamlessly integrates multiscale feature hierarchies with parallel multiview encoding, processing distinct views of the input at varying resolutions.
The model employs strategically placed cross-attention blocks within its multiscale stages to fuse information between different views, enhancing global contextual understanding.
It utilizes an 'audio-specific CutMix' data augmentation technique that performs cuts only along the temporal axis to improve regularization and prevent overfitting in audio classification tasks.
Results: Achieved state-of-the-art performance on AudioSet with 32.2% mAP on AudioSet Balanced and 43.0% mAP on AudioSet Full, outperforming AST (37.2% mAP) and MViTv2 (42.4% mAP).
Secured state-of-the-art results on ImageNet1K image classification with a Top-1 accuracy of 83.2%, surpassing the MViTv2 baseline (82.7%).

Ablation studies demonstrated that the audio-specific CutMix improved AudioSet mAP from 39% to 43%, and that using two views was optimal, as three views led to a performance decrease to 82.3% on ImageNet1K.
Takeaways: Combining multiscale feature hierarchies with parallel multiview encoding and cross-attention provides a more comprehensive and robust approach to representation learning than either strategy alone.

Overlapping patchification and a specialized 'audio-specific CutMix' augmentation are critical for preventing overfitting and enhancing performance, especially when transferring knowledge from image pre-training to audio tasks.

The synergistic integration of these architectural elements enables a versatile Transformer backbone capable of achieving state-of-the-art results across distinct modalities like image and audio classification.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.07193.Title: DINOv2: Learning Robust Visual Features without Supervision
https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.07193.Summary: Meta AI's DINOv2 learns robust, general-purpose visual features without supervision, achieving state-of-the-art 'out-of-the-box' performance across a wide range of computer vision tasks by scaling self-supervised learning on a newly curated 142-million image dataset and optimizing training for billion-parameter models. This approach demonstrates that existing discriminative self-supervised methods can produce broadly applicable visual features when scaled appropriately with high-quality data.
Problem: Bridging the gap between the success of foundation models in NLP (e.g., LLMs providing versatile text features) and the development of analogous general-purpose vision features.

Limitations of existing vision pre-training approaches: text-guided models (e.g., CLIP) are constrained by caption information density and dataset availability, while traditional self-supervised learning struggled to scale beyond small, curated datasets to 'in-the-wild' data.
The need for robust, 'out-of-the-box' visual features that require minimal or no fine-tuning for diverse downstream tasks, currently lacking in many self-supervised vision models.
Method: Refined discriminative self-supervised pre-training by enhancing DINO and iBOT with untied head weights, Sinkhorn-Knopp centering, a KoLeo regularizer for feature diversity, and resolution adaptation.

Developed an automatic data curation pipeline (LVD-142M, 142 million images) that uses self-supervised image retrieval to augment curated seed datasets with visually similar, deduplicated images from a large uncurated web pool.

Implemented significant engineering optimizations for large-scale training, including FlashAttention, sequence packing, efficient stochastic depth, and PyTorch's Fully-Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) to train models up to 1 billion parameters efficiently.
Results: DINOv2 ViT-g/14 achieved 86.5% top-1 accuracy with a linear probe on ImageNet-1k, outperforming previous SSL models by +4.2% and matching leading weakly-supervised models like OpenCLIP-G/14.

Demonstrated exceptional 'out-of-the-box' performance on instance retrieval tasks, improving by +34% mAP on Oxford-Hard compared to OpenCLIP, and showing strong results on dense prediction tasks like depth estimation and semantic segmentation.
Exhibited improved generalization (e.g., +1.1% on ImageNet-V2 vs. EVA-CLIP) and significantly enhanced robustness on ImageNet-A, R, and Sketch benchmarks compared to other self-supervised methods.
Takeaways: Discriminative self-supervised learning, when scaled with sufficient data curation and model size, can yield general-purpose visual features that are competitive with or surpass text-guided and weakly-supervised models.

Automated, content-based data curation pipelines are crucial for building high-quality, diverse datasets at scale, enabling the training of powerful vision foundation models without manual annotation.

Self-supervised pre-training at scale can lead to emergent properties like unsupervised foreground/background detection, semantic part matching, and implicit scene geometry understanding, indicating a rich visual semantic learning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.06712.Title: What does CLIP know about a red circle? Visual prompt engineering for VLMs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.06712.Summary: Researchers from the Visual Geometry Group (VGG) at the University of Oxford explore "visual prompt engineering" for Vision-Language Models (VLMs), demonstrating that simple red circles can effectively steer a model's attention while preserving global context. This method achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot performance in referring expression comprehension tasks and, critically, reveals how such visual prompts can trigger latent biases within VLMs.
Problem: Adapting frozen Vision-Language Models (VLMs) like CLIP for fine-grained localization tasks (e.g., referring expression comprehension, keypoint localization) without requiring extensive fine-tuning.
Traditional image transformation methods like cropping often remove valuable contextual information, which can be suboptimal for VLMs that benefit from holistic scene understanding.
Understanding the emergent properties and potential biases embedded within large-scale VLMs trained on vast, uncurated internet data.
Method: Introduces "visual prompt engineering" as an alternative to image cropping, where graphical annotations (e.g., red circles) are directly overlaid onto image pixels.
Frames various computer vision problems as a question-answering task, where the VLM scores transformed image inputs (with marks) against textual queries.
Empirically determined that a red circle is the most effective visual marker for directing VLM attention across different tasks and VLM backbones.
Results: Red circle visual prompting nearly doubled the accuracy of cropping-based methods in the "Naming Keypoints" task.
The approach achieved state-of-the-art zero-shot performance in referring expression comprehension on most RefCOCO benchmarks, without task-specific fine-tuning.
Applying red circles to human images increased the probability of VLMs classifying individuals into negative or criminal categories by 17% to over 32%.
Takeaways: Visual marking, especially simple red circles, effectively directs VLM attention for localization tasks, outperforming traditional image cropping by preserving global context.
This capability is an emergent property, implicitly learned from rare but consistent visual cues in vast training datasets, and its effectiveness scales with VLM model capacity.
Visual prompts can inadvertently trigger or amplify undesirable biases within VLMs, revealing problematic latent associations linked to sensitive categories like criminal classifications.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.06250.Title: RSIR Transformer: Hierarchical Vision Transformer using Random Sampling Windows and Important Region Windows
https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.06250.Summary: The RSIR Transformer, developed at Southwest Jiaotong University, introduces Random Sampling Windows (RS-Win) and Important Region Windows (IR-Win) to create an efficient hierarchical Vision Transformer. This architecture achieved 83.9% Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K with its tiny variant, outperforming MaxViT-T by 0.3%, and demonstrated superior performance across object detection and semantic segmentation tasks.
Problem: Existing Vision Transformers suffered from high computational costs due to global self-attention, hindering practical application for high-resolution images.
Local window-based self-attention in hierarchical ViTs restricted receptive fields, leading to insufficient global context modeling and reduced model capacity.
Previous methods for inter-window communication often resulted in complex architectures, fixed patterns, or slow growth of the effective receptive field.
Method: A hierarchical Vision Transformer that integrates two parallel self-attention modules: Random Sampling Windows (RS-Win) and Important Region Windows (IR-Win) within each block.
RS-Win uses randomized token sampling across the entire image to introduce flexible global context modeling with linear computational complexity.
IR-Win employs data-dependent attention, grouping patches based on an inferred importance map to deterministically focus on salient regions for local interaction.
Results: Achieved 83.9% Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K with RSIR-T (outperforming MaxViT-T by 0.3%) and 85.1% with RSIR-B (outperforming MaxViT-B by 0.2%), demonstrating state-of-the-art performance at competitive GFLOPs.
Showcased improved data efficiency on small datasets like Caltech-256 and Mini-ImageNet, consistently surpassing MaxViT variants.
Set new benchmarks on COCO object detection (e.g., RSIR-T achieved 47.6 box mAP, +0.7 over MaxViT-T) and ADE20K semantic segmentation (e.g., RSIR-T 49.9% SS mIoU, +0.4 over MaxViT-T).
Takeaways: Combining randomized global context exploration (RS-Win) with deterministic data-dependent local focusing (IR-Win) effectively balances efficiency and rich feature learning.
Parallel execution of distinct attention mechanisms within a single block allows for simultaneous incorporation of global and intelligently guided local information, optimizing computational cost.
The proposed attention mechanism significantly improves data efficiency and robustness of hierarchical Vision Transformers, making them more suitable for smaller datasets.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.04514.Title: DetCLIPv2: Scalable Open-Vocabulary Object Detection Pre-training via Word-Region Alignment
https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.04514.Summary: DetCLIPv2 introduces an end-to-end pre-training framework for open-vocabulary object detection that directly learns fine-grained word-region alignment from large-scale image-text pairs. The framework achieved 40.4% zero-shot AP on LVIS and efficiently utilized 13x more image-text pairs than its predecessor in similar training time.
Problem: Traditional object detection models are limited to recognizing a predefined, closed set of object categories.
Real-world applications require detecting arbitrary object categories, including those not seen during training.
Existing open-vocabulary detection methods face challenges like domain gaps when transferring knowledge from vision-language models or limitations due to the quality of pseudo-labels.
Method: Developed DetCLIPv2, a scalable end-to-end pre-training framework for open-vocabulary object detection.
Directly learns from large-scale image-text pairs by performing fine-grained word-region alignment.
Implements an efficient alternating training scheme and processes image-text pairs at lower resolution to enhance efficiency.
Results: Achieved 40.4% zero-shot AP on LVIS using a Swin-T backbone, surpassing previous methods like GLIP and DetCLIP.
Demonstrated balanced detection performance across frequent, common, and rare object categories on LVIS.
Showed improved training efficiency, processing 13x more image-text pairs than its predecessor (DetCLIP) within comparable training durations.
Takeaways: Directly aligning individual textual words with visual regions in image-text pairs is effective for open-vocabulary object detection, circumventing limitations of knowledge distillation or pseudo-labeling.
A unified triplet data formulation allows for effective training with heterogeneous supervisions from detection, grounding, and image-text sources.
Efficient training strategies, including alternating training and low-resolution processing of image-text pairs, are crucial for scaling OVD pre-training with large datasets.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.03977.Title: EMP-SSL: Towards Self-Supervised Learning in One Training Epoch
https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.03977.Summary: EMP-SSL introduces an approach to dramatically accelerate self-supervised learning by processing numerous overlapping image patches to efficiently learn co-occurrence statistics. This method achieves competitive performance, such as 85.1% accuracy on CIFAR-10, in a single training epoch, significantly reducing computational requirements compared to traditional SSL.
Problem: Current self-supervised learning (SSL) methods are computationally inefficient, typically requiring hundreds of training epochs to converge.
This inefficiency creates substantial computational barriers, limiting the broad application of SSL approaches.
Traditional SSL relies on a small number of augmented views per image, necessitating many passes through the dataset to accumulate sufficient statistics.
Method: EMP-SSL processes a large number of random, overlapping patches (20-200) from each input image, instead of relying on a small number of augmented views.

The architecture consists of a standard encoder network (ResNet-18) and a two-part objective function: Total Coding Rate (TCR) to prevent collapse and an Invariance Loss to enforce consistency among patch representations.
The approach avoids complex components like momentum encoders, prediction networks, or non-differentiable operators, resulting in a clean and efficient implementation.
Results: EMP-SSL achieved impressive accuracies in a single training epoch: 85.1% on CIFAR-10, 58.5% on CIFAR-100, 38.1% on Tiny ImageNet, and 58.5% on ImageNet-100.
The method significantly outperformed traditional SSL methods (BYOL, VICReg, SwAV, SimCLR) when all were limited to few training epochs, showing a strong performance gap in early stages.
EMP-SSL attained over 90% accuracy on CIFAR-10 in fewer than 10 epochs, reaching competitive results in 10-30 epochs, compared to hundreds required by conventional methods.
Representations learned by EMP-SSL showed clearer class separation in t-SNE visualizations and exhibited better transferability to out-of-domain datasets than baseline SSL methods.
Takeaways: Self-supervised learning methods fundamentally learn the co-occurrence statistics of image patches.
Processing a large number of overlapping patches from a single image allows for efficient capture of co-occurrence statistics in a single training pass.
A balanced loss function combining invariance objectives with total coding rate regularization prevents representation collapse while encouraging meaningful feature learning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.14240.Title: Adaptive Base-class Suppression and Prior Guidance Network for One-Shot Object Detection
https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.14240.Summary: The Base-class Suppression and Prior Guidance (BSPG) network improves one-shot object detection by mitigating base-class bias and providing semantic guidance. This framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on the PASCAL VOC and MS COCO benchmarks, demonstrating particular gains on the challenging MS COCO dataset.
Problem: Most conventional object detection models require large amounts of annotated data for each object category, limiting their applicability to novel classes.
Existing one-shot object detection (OSOD) methods overlook the issue of base-class bias, where models trained on abundant base data struggle with novel categories.
This base-class bias leads to misclassification of novel objects as base classes, failure to detect novel objects, and lower confidence for novel detections.
Method: A novel Base-class Suppression and Prior Guidance (BSPG) network is introduced to directly address base-class bias in one-shot object detection.
The Base-class Suppression (BcS) module adaptively eliminates base-class detections by comparing similarity between query and proposal features, preventing misclassification.
The Prior Guidance (PG) module generates class-agnostic semantic prior maps from high-level features to guide the novel-class predictor toward potential novel object regions.
Results: The BSPG network consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art OSOD methods on both PASCAL VOC and MS COCO datasets, showing significant improvements on the more challenging COCO dataset.

Ablation studies confirm that both the Base-class Suppression (BcS) module and the Prior Guidance (PG) module contribute to performance improvements, with the full BSPG framework achieving the best results.
The BSPG framework extends effectively to few-shot detection scenarios, demonstrating superior performance, especially in the 5-shot setting, by leveraging additional query examples.
Takeaways: One-shot object detection models trained on base classes develop a strong bias toward these categories, leading to poor performance on novel classes.
Explicitly addressing base-class bias through adaptive suppression is crucial for improving novel object detection accuracy.
Generating and utilizing high-level, class-agnostic semantic prior maps can effectively guide object detection models to novel object regions.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.13434.Title: Patch-Mix Transformer for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation: A Game Perspective
https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.13434.Summary: PMTrans introduces a Patch-Mix Transformer that constructs an intermediate domain to bridge source and target in Unsupervised Domain Adaptation, framed as a min-max Cross-Entropy game. This approach demonstrates superior performance, achieving 89.0% average accuracy on Office-Home and a 52.4% average accuracy on the challenging DomainNet dataset, outperforming prior ViT-based methods by 7.2% on DomainNet.
Problem: Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) struggles with significant distribution shifts between labeled source and unlabeled target domains.
Existing Vision Transformer (ViT)-based UDA methods are highly sensitive to the quality of pseudo-labels, which are often unreliable under large domain gaps.
Direct alignment strategies between vastly different source and target domains often prove ineffective for robust knowledge transfer.
Method: Introduces an intermediate domain to smoothly bridge the source and target distributions, avoiding direct alignment.
Formulates Unsupervised Domain Adaptation as a three-player min-max Cross-Entropy game involving a feature extractor, classifier, and a novel PatchMix module.
Develops PatchMix, a module that learns adaptive patch-level mixing proportions via a learnable Beta distribution and re-weights mixed labels using attention maps.
Results: Achieves 89.0% average accuracy on Office-Home, 95.3% on Office-31, and 88.0% on VisDA-2017, outperforming prior state-of-the-art methods.
Demonstrates robust performance on the challenging DomainNet dataset with 52.4% average accuracy, a 7.2% improvement over previous ViT-based UDA methods across all 30 sub-tasks.
Ablation studies confirm that learnable mixup parameters and the combination of feature and label space mixup losses are crucial for performance gains.
Takeaways: Bridging the domain gap indirectly via an adaptively constructed intermediate domain is more effective than direct alignment, especially for large domain shifts.

Framing Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) as a min-max game among a feature extractor, classifier, and mixing module can lead to more stable and robust domain alignment by achieving Nash Equilibria.
Adaptive patch-level mixing, guided by learnable distributions and attention mechanisms, improves the quality of mixed samples and leads to more domain-discriminative features in Vision Transformers.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.13076.Title: CORA: Adapting CLIP for Open-Vocabulary Detection with Region Prompting and Anchor Pre-Matching
https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.13076.Summary: CORA, a DETR-style framework, adapts CLIP for open-vocabulary object detection using region prompting and anchor pre-matching to address distribution mismatch and improve generalization. It achieved 41.7 AP50 on novel classes on COCO OVD, outperforming prior methods by 2.4 AP50 without extra training data, and 22.2 APr on rare classes on LVIS OVD.
Problem: Traditional object detection is limited to predefined categories, hindering real-world applicability for novel objects.
Adapting Vision-Language Pre-trained Models (VLPMs) like CLIP for region-level detection faces a distribution mismatch between whole-image training and region-level inference.
Existing open-vocabulary detection (OVD) approaches often require additional image-text data, multiple inference passes, or struggle with generalization to novel classes.
Method: Introduces CORA, a DETR-style framework that adapts CLIP for Open-Vocabulary Detection through two main innovations.
Employs "Region Prompting" to bridge the distribution gap between CLIP's whole-image training and region-level feature extraction by augmenting features with learnable prompts.
Utilizes "Anchor Pre-Matching" to associate object queries with dynamic anchor boxes and pre-match them with categories, enabling efficient single-pass, class-aware regression for novel classes.
Results: Achieved 41.7 AP50 on novel classes on the COCO OVD benchmark, surpassing previous state-of-the-art by 2.4 AP50 without additional training data.
Obtained 22.2 APr on rare classes on the LVIS OVD benchmark (without extra data) and 28.1 APr (with extra data), outperforming existing methods.
Ablation studies demonstrated Region Prompting improved novel class classification performance from 63.9% to 74.1%, and Anchor Pre-Matching enhanced localization across diverse domains.
Takeaways: Directly applying whole-image pre-trained features (like CLIP's) to region-level object detection leads to a distribution mismatch that can be mitigated through adaptive region prompting.
Class-aware object localization for open-vocabulary detection can be achieved efficiently in a single inference pass by pre-matching object queries with target categories.
Strategic training techniques, such as class dropout and CLIP-aligned labeling, are important for enhancing generalization to novel and rare object categories.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.11381.Title: MM-REACT: Prompting ChatGPT for Multimodal Reasoning and Action
