https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.11381.Summary: MM-REACT, a framework developed by Microsoft Azure AI, enables large language models like ChatGPT to understand and reason about visual content by integrating specialized vision models through a prompting mechanism. This approach allows the system to perform complex visual reasoning tasks by decomposing them into a series of steps, all without requiring extensive multimodal training. The system demonstrates capabilities in multi-hop reasoning, multi-image analysis, spatial understanding, and video summarization.
Problem: Developing artificial intelligence systems that can comprehensively understand and reason across different types of information, such as images, text, and video, remains challenging.
Traditional vision-language models often require extensive, costly joint training on vast multimodal datasets.
Existing models frequently struggle with compositional reasoning that requires multiple sequential steps of analysis and information integration.
Method: Microsoft Azure AI developed MM-REACT, a framework that integrates specialized vision models with large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT through a prompting mechanism.

The framework operates on a thought-action-observation loop where the LLM decides which vision 'expert' to call, processes the textualized output from the expert, and iteratively refines its understanding.

Visual inputs are represented as file paths in prompts, allowing the LLM to reference images and videos without directly processing visual data, while expert outputs are converted into text for LLM comprehension.
Results: The system successfully performs multi-hop reasoning by chaining vision experts for tasks like celebrity identification and information retrieval, and demonstrates multi-image reasoning for comparative analysis of documents (e.g., receipt analysis).
It exhibits spatial understanding by reasoning about the relative positions of objects within images and solves visual mathematics problems presented in images.

MM-REACT provides video summarization into step-by-step instructions with timestamps and identifies open-world concepts by combining visual recognition with external knowledge, achieving comparable performance to PaLM-E on certain tasks without requiring joint training.
Takeaways: A modular architecture allows complex visual tasks to be decomposed and solved by specialized vision models.
Prompt engineering effectively instructs the large language model (LLM) on how to utilize various vision experts and interpret their textualized outputs.
The system supports multi-round reasoning, enabling iterative calls to vision experts and multi-hop reasoning chains based on intermediate results.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.11331.Title: EVA-02: A Visual Representation for Neon Genesis
https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.11331.Summary: EVA-02 introduces a Transformer-based visual representation that achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse computer vision tasks while using moderate model sizes and exclusively publicly available training data. The model reached 90.0% ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy with 304M parameters, and EVA-02-CLIP-L achieved 80.4% zero-shot ImageNet-1K accuracy, outperforming larger open-sourced models.
Problem: The growing disparity between state-of-the-art large-scale models and their accessibility to the wider research community due to immense computational resources and reliance on private data.
The high cost and limited transparency associated with training and fine-tuning multi-billion parameter models, hindering widespread experimentation and verification.
The underestimated potential of smaller-sized plain Vision Transformers in achieving top-tier performance on diverse computer vision tasks.
Method: Developed a next-generation Transformer-based visual representation by incorporating architectural refinements from language models (e.g., SwiGLU FFN, Sub-Layer Normalization, 2D Rotary Position Embedding) into plain Vision Transformers.

Utilized a Masked Image Modeling (MIM) pre-training strategy where models reconstruct strong, language-aligned vision features from a publicly accessible giant EVA-CLIP vision encoder, rather than raw pixels.
Conducted extensive pre-training exclusively on publicly accessible datasets, such as ImageNet-21K and Merged-38M (a composite of IN-21K, CC12M, COCO, etc.), across various model scales.
Results: EVA-02-L (304M parameters) achieved 90.0% fine-tuning top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K, surpassing several larger and more resource-intensive models.

EVA-02-CLIP-L reached 80.4% zero-shot top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K, outperforming the previous largest open-sourced CLIP model (OpenCLIP-Giant, ~1.8B parameters) with approximately 1/6th of the parameters and training data.

Demonstrated superior transfer learning by achieving competitive and often state-of-the-art results on downstream tasks like object detection (COCO, LVIS) and semantic segmentation (COCO-Stuff-164K, ADE20K), including new SOTA on LVIS (65.2 APbox & 57.3 APmask).
Takeaways: Moderate-sized Vision Transformers, when robustly optimized, can achieve state-of-the-art performance with significantly fewer parameters and compute, challenging the 'bigger is always better' paradigm.

Architectural advancements originally explored in large language models, such as SwiGLU FFN and Rotary Position Embeddings, effectively transfer to vision Transformers, yielding performance improvements.

Pre-training via Masked Image Modeling (MIM) by regressing features from a strong, publicly accessible giant CLIP encoder is an effective strategy for learning highly transferable visual representations.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.08128.Title: ViperGPT: Visual Inference via Python Execution for Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.08128.Summary: ViperGPT, developed by researchers at Columbia University, enables visual reasoning by having a large language model generate Python programs that orchestrate calls to specialized vision and language modules. The system achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot performance across various visual reasoning benchmarks, including compositional image Q&A and knowledge-dependent Q&A.
Problem: End-to-end deep learning models for visual reasoning often lack interpretability and provide opaque decision-making processes.
These models struggle with systematic generalization to novel compositions and complex multi-step reasoning tasks.
Training specialized models for every unique visual task or adapting them to new capabilities can be inflexible and resource-intensive.
Method: ViperGPT utilizes a large language model (Codex) to generate Python programs from natural language queries that solve visual reasoning tasks.
The generated code orchestrates a set of predefined, specialized vision and language API modules (e.g., object detection, depth estimation, property verification) that act as building blocks.
A Python interpreter executes the generated program on visual inputs, enabling complex reasoning through control flow, mathematical operations, and logical conditions.
Results: Achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot accuracy on compositional image question answering (GQA) and knowledge-dependent question answering (OK-VQA) benchmarks.
Outperforms other zero-shot methods in visual grounding tasks (RefCOCO/RefCOCO+).
Performs comparably to supervised models on video reasoning tasks (NExT-QA) despite not being specifically trained for video processing.
Takeaways: Leveraging large language models' code generation capabilities allows for explicit, interpretable reasoning steps in visual tasks.
Decomposing complex visual queries into sub-problems solvable by modular, pre-trained vision components enhances flexibility and adaptability.
Using Python's native programming constructs (control flow, loops, conditionals) provides a robust framework for implementing multi-step and conditional visual reasoning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.05499.Title: Grounding DINO: Marrying DINO with Grounded Pre-Training for Open-Set Object Detection
https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.05499.Summary: Grounding DINO develops an open-set object detector by integrating deep language-vision fusion into a Transformer-based DINO architecture, leveraging large-scale grounded pre-training. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on zero-shot object detection benchmarks, including 52.5 AP on COCO minival and 26.1 AP on ODinW.
Problem: Traditional object detectors are limited to detecting objects from a pre-defined set of categories and cannot identify novel objects.
Previous open-set detectors often lacked deep, multi-stage integration of vision and language information, limiting their generalization capabilities.
Concatenating multiple unrelated category names for text prompts could lead to interference during multi-modal training in prior grounding models.
Method: A dual-encoder, single-decoder architecture based on DINO is employed, featuring a Swin Transformer visual backbone and a BERT text backbone.
Achieves 'tight modality fusion' through a Feature Enhancer (neck), Language-Guided Query Selection (query initialization), and a Cross-Modality Decoder (head).
Utilizes a 'sub-sentence level text feature' technique that applies attention masks to prevent interaction between unrelated categories in text prompts during pre-training.
Results: Grounding DINO achieved 52.5 AP on the COCO minival benchmark for zero-shot object detection, surpassing previous models like GLIP-L (49.8 AP).
It established a new state-of-the-art with a mean 26.1 AP on the ODinW benchmark, outperforming models including Florence and GLIP-T.

Ablation studies demonstrated that each proposed component—encoder fusion, language-guided query selection, text cross-attention, and sub-sentence level text prompts—individually contributed to the model's performance improvements.
Takeaways: Deeply integrating language information into multiple stages of a Transformer-based detector pipeline enhances alignment and generalization for open-set detection.
Reforming object detection as a phrase grounding task, combined with large-scale pre-training on diverse data, is an effective strategy for zero-shot transfer.
Applying attention masks to create 'sub-sentence level' text features improves prompt processing by preventing interactions between unrelated concepts in concatenated category lists.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.04671.Title: Visual ChatGPT: Talking, Drawing and Editing with Visual Foundation Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.04671.Summary: Visual ChatGPT, developed by Microsoft Research Asia, integrates large language models like ChatGPT with various visual foundation models to enable conversational interaction with visual content. The system performs complex image generation, editing, and understanding tasks by orchestrating specialized visual models through a novel Prompt Manager and adapting Chain of Thought reasoning.
Problem: Integrating the conversational abilities of large language models with the image processing and generation capabilities of visual models.
Enabling complex, multi-step visual operations (e.g., image generation, editing, and style transfer) within a natural conversational flow.
Developing a system that can leverage diverse, specialized visual models without requiring a single, monolithic, end-to-end trained multimodal model.
Method: A modular architecture combining ChatGPT, a collection of Visual Foundation Models (VFMs), and a novel 'Prompt Manager' as an intermediary.
The Prompt Manager facilitates communication by providing ChatGPT with VFM documentation, managing dialogue history, and structuring reasoning steps.
An adaptation of Chain of Thought reasoning is implemented to enable ChatGPT to orchestrate multiple VFMs for complex, multi-step visual tasks.
Results: Visual ChatGPT demonstrates the ability to perform complex visual operations, such as generating an image based on depth information and then applying a cartoon style, all within a single conversational turn.
The system successfully supports multimodal conversation, allowing users to interact with and modify images iteratively through natural language commands.
It showcases capabilities like visual question answering and chain of visual reasoning, breaking down requests into logical steps and explaining the process to users.
Takeaways: A modular system that leverages existing large language models (LLMs) and visual foundation models (VFMs) can achieve multimodal capabilities without extensive end-to-end retraining.
The Prompt Manager mechanism effectively bridges the gap between the textual understanding of LLMs and the structured inputs required by VFMs, enabling complex visual task orchestration.
Adapting Chain of Thought reasoning allows the system to break down intricate visual tasks into a series of manageable steps, improving task execution and explainability.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.01906.Title: Generalized Semantic Segmentation by Self-Supervised Source Domain Projection and Multi-Level Contrastive Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.01906.Summary: The Domain Projection and Contrastive Learning (DPCL) framework enables generalized semantic segmentation by projecting target images into the source domain's appearance space and learning discriminative features through a multi-level contrastive approach. This method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art techniques on synthetic-to-real segmentation benchmarks without requiring target domain data during training.
Problem: Deep learning models for semantic segmentation suffer significant performance degradation when deployed in environments (target domains) that differ from their training data (source domain), a phenomenon known as domain shift.
Domain shift manifests as differences in appearance (e.g., lighting, weather) or content (e.g., object layouts), leading to inaccurate dense pixel predictions.
Existing domain generalization methods often struggle with severe domain shifts and may require complex training procedures or additional data.
Method: The Domain Projection and Contrastive Learning (DPCL) framework is introduced, combining Self-Supervised Source Domain Projection (SSDP) and Multi-Level Contrastive Learning (MLCL).
SSDP learns to project images from any domain into the appearance space of the source domain through a self-supervised reconstruction task, trained using augmented source images.

MLCL employs three complementary contrastive learning objectives (pixel-to-pixel, pixel-to-class, and instance-to-class) to learn discriminative and generalizable features at multiple levels of granularity.
Results: The DPCL framework consistently outperformed state-of-the-art domain generalization methods on synthetic-to-real semantic segmentation tasks, specifically when trained on GTAV and tested on Cityscapes, BDD100K, and Mapillary.
Qualitative results demonstrate improved segmentation quality, producing more accurate and refined boundaries compared to baseline methods.

Ablation studies confirmed that both SSDP and each component of MLCL contribute to the overall performance, with SSDP alone providing significant improvements and the full MLCL yielding the best results.
Takeaways: Self-Supervised Source Domain Projection (SSDP) effectively reduces the domain gap by transforming target domain images to match the appearance of the source domain while preserving semantic content.

Multi-Level Contrastive Learning (MLCL) with pixel-to-pixel, pixel-to-class, and instance-to-class objectives learns discriminative and generalizable features crucial for accurate segmentation across domains.

The combination of appearance projection (SSDP) and feature discrimination (MLCL) is essential for achieving superior generalization performance in semantic segmentation across diverse unseen domains.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.08242.Title: Tuning computer vision models with task rewards
https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.08242.Summary: Researchers from Google Research Brain Team in Zürich introduce a reward tuning framework that applies reinforcement learning techniques to fine-tune pretrained computer vision models, directly optimizing for task-specific metrics like mAP or Panoptic Quality. The approach demonstrates consistent performance gains across diverse tasks, including increasing object detection mAP by 15.1% and panoptic segmentation PQ by 3.0%.
Problem: Computer vision models trained with standard loss functions often misalign with desired real-world task performance metrics.
Traditional training objectives (e.g., cross-entropy) do not directly optimize for complex, non-differentiable evaluation metrics like mean Average Precision (mAP) or Panoptic Quality (PQ).
Existing solutions often involve specialized architectures, complex loss functions, or post-processing, which are not easily transferable across tasks.
Method: A two-step framework is proposed: first, a base computer vision model is pretrained using standard Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) objectives.
Second, the pretrained model is fine-tuned using the REINFORCE algorithm to maximize a reward function that directly measures task performance.
The REINFORCE algorithm enables optimizing non-differentiable reward functions by sampling model outputs, computing rewards, and updating parameters to favor high-reward outputs.
Results: Object detection models tuned for mAP showed an increase from 39.2% to 54.3%, and AR@100 improved from 54.4% to 68.4%.
Panoptic segmentation models improved Panoptic Quality (PQ) from 43.1% to 46.1%, with visually better handling of small objects.
Image colorization models produced significantly more vivid colors, increasing the vivid color fraction from 0.46 to 0.97 and hue entropy from 1.03 to 1.84.
Takeaways: Reinforcement learning, specifically REINFORCE, can effectively bridge the gap between standard training objectives and true task-specific evaluation metrics in computer vision.
Directly optimizing for non-differentiable task metrics like mAP, Panoptic Quality, or subjective qualities (e.g., colorfulness) leads to substantial performance improvements.
The proposed reward tuning framework provides a general and transferable approach applicable across diverse vision tasks without requiring specialized architectures or task-specific heuristics.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.05442.Title: Scaling Vision Transformers to 22 Billion Parameters
https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.05442.Summary: A Vision Transformer with 22 billion parameters, ViT-22B, was successfully trained, establishing the feasibility of scaling visual models to the size range of large language models. This model achieves 89.5% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet and demonstrates enhanced few-shot learning, fairness, robustness, and human alignment, properties previously observed in large language models.
Problem: Vision models have historically lagged behind Large Language Models (LLMs) in terms of parameter scale, limiting their potential.
The standard Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture becomes numerically unstable and difficult to train when scaled to extreme parameter counts.
Method: Introduced architectural modifications including parallel Attention-MLP blocks for efficiency and Query/Key (QK) Normalization for training stability.
Eliminated bias terms from QKV projections and LayerNorms to optimize accelerator utilization.
Employed model parallelism and asynchronous linear operations, training on an extended JFT dataset of approximately 4 billion images using TPUv4 accelerators.
Results: Achieved 89.5% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet classification and demonstrated strong performance across various vision tasks including transfer learning, semantic segmentation, and depth estimation.
Exhibited enhanced few-shot learning capabilities, improved fairness metrics, and increased robustness to distribution shifts.

Demonstrated a shape bias of 87% (approaching human perception) and improved reliability metrics such as calibration and consistency, with its knowledge successfully distilled into smaller, more efficient models.
Takeaways: Scaling Vision Transformers to 22 billion parameters is feasible, bridging the gap between language and vision model scales.
Query/Key (QK) normalization is critical for ensuring training stability and preventing numerical issues in extremely large ViT models.

Extreme scaling of vision models unlocks emergent properties, including improved few-shot learning, enhanced fairness, robustness to distribution shifts, and stronger alignment with human visual perception.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.01107.Title: A Survey on Efficient Training of Transformers
https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.01107.Summary: Researchers systematically categorize techniques for efficient Transformer training, offering the first comprehensive overview of methods that reduce computational cost, memory footprint, and optimize for hardware co-design. The work compiles strategies such as sparse training, various parallelism approaches, and low-precision computation to mitigate the substantial resource demands of large-scale models.
Problem: Large Transformer models incur immense computational costs, leading to high energy consumption and making cutting-edge AI inaccessible to many.
Training these models demands an exponentially growing memory footprint, posing significant hardware and scaling challenges.
A lack of systematic overview existed for the diverse efficient training techniques developed to mitigate these Transformer efficiency issues.
Method: A systematic review and organization of existing literature on efficient Transformer training methods is presented.
Techniques are categorized into three main themes: computation efficiency, memory efficiency, and hardware/algorithm co-design.
Methods are analyzed and compared based on their mechanisms for reducing computational load and memory footprint during training.
Results: The survey consolidates and explains diverse methods for computation efficiency, including advanced optimizers (e.g., Lion, SAM), effective initialization (e.g., Fixup, ReZero), sparse training, large batch training, incremental learning, and data selection.

It details memory efficiency techniques such as various parallelism strategies (Data, Model, Tensor, Pipeline), quantized training (e.g., AMP, FP8), rematerialization, offloading (e.g., ZeRO-Offload), and parameter-efficient tuning (e.g., LoRA).

Hardware/algorithm co-design approaches are highlighted, covering sparse matrix multiplication, hardware-aware low-precision computations (e.g., 4-bit queries), and optimized attention mechanisms (e.g., FlashAttention).
Takeaways: Efficient Transformer training necessitates a holistic strategy, integrating algorithmic optimizations for computation and memory with hardware/algorithm co-design principles.
Diverse techniques, ranging from advanced optimizers and sparse training to various parallelism strategies and parameter-efficient tuning, contribute to making large models more manageable.
Further advancements require a focus on joint training and deployment optimization, on-device training, and the establishment of a standardized benchmarking framework.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.00923.Title: Multimodal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.00923.Summary: A Multimodal Chain-of-Thought (Multimodal-CoT) framework for language models under 1 billion parameters is developed to integrate language and vision, mitigating hallucinated rationales in smaller models. The framework achieves 90.45% accuracy on the ScienceQA benchmark, outperforming prior state-of-the-art for models of its scale.
Problem: Existing Chain-of-Thought (CoT) methods primarily focus on text-only inputs, limiting their applicability to real-world problems that involve multiple modalities.
Smaller language models (under 1 billion parameters) often generate hallucinated rationales that mislead answer inference when attempting CoT.
Converting visual inputs to text captions for multimodal large language models leads to significant information loss and lacks synergistic representation.
Method: A two-stage Multimodal Chain-of-Thought (Multimodal-CoT) framework is introduced, explicitly separating rationale generation and answer inference.
The model integrates language and vision features through a Transformer-based encoder-decoder architecture, utilizing a language encoder and a vision extractor.
A gated fusion mechanism dynamically combines cross-attended vision features with language representations to create a fused multimodal input for the decoder.
Results: The Multimodal-CoT model (738M parameters) achieved 90.45% accuracy on the ScienceQA benchmark, establishing a new state-of-the-art for models under 1 billion parameters.
Ablation studies confirmed that the two-stage framework and the inclusion of vision features are crucial, with vision features correcting 60.7% of previous hallucination errors.
The framework demonstrates effectiveness on the A-OKVQA benchmark and proves adaptable by leveraging machine-generated rationales for training, showing comparable performance to human annotations.
Takeaways: Unlike very large language models, smaller models trained for Chain-of-Thought reasoning often produce hallucinated rationales that degrade overall performance.
Integrating multimodal (vision and language) context during rationale generation is essential to mitigate hallucination and improve reasoning accuracy in smaller models.
A two-stage approach, separating rationale generation from answer inference, is more effective for smaller models than a single-stage Chain-of-Thought due to the hallucination issue.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.00674.Title: Improving Few-Shot Generalization by Exploring and Exploiting Auxiliary Data
https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.00674.Summary: A method for Few-shot Learning with Auxiliary Data (FLAD) that models dataset selection as a Multi-Armed Bandit (MAB) problem enables adaptive auxiliary data utilization. This approach boosts a 3 billion parameter model's performance by 5.6-9.2% over baselines, allowing it to surpass a 175 billion parameter GPT-3 on few-shot benchmarks.
Problem: Few-shot learning (FSL) struggles to generalize effectively from very limited labeled examples, hindering real-world applications.
Previous Few-shot Learning with Auxiliary Data (FLAD) methods face severe scalability issues, typically only handling 1-3 auxiliary datasets due to increasing computational complexity.
Manually selecting useful auxiliary data or designing training curricula for a large pool of datasets is combinatorially complex and often leads to sub-optimal results.
Method: The authors reformulate FLAD as a Multi-Armed Bandit (MAB) problem, treating each auxiliary dataset as an 'arm' to be explored and exploited.
They design efficient gradient-based reward functions (Gradient Alignment, Gradient Magnitude Similarity, Aggregate Reward) computed solely on language modeling head parameters to minimize overhead.
Two MAB algorithms, EXP3-FLAD and UCB1-FLAD, are adapted to dynamically select auxiliary datasets for model updates, balancing exploration of new data with exploitation of known beneficial data.
Results: EXP3-FLAD and UCB1-FLAD consistently outperformed all baselines, achieving absolute performance gains of 5.6% to 9.2% over Target-Only fine-tuning.
A 3 billion parameter T0-3B model, when utilizing MAB-FLAD with the P3 dataset, demonstrated superior performance to the 175 billion parameter GPT-3 on the evaluated few-shot benchmarks.

MAB-based methods exhibited robust scalability, improving performance with a larger number of auxiliary datasets (from 35 to 260) while maintaining computational efficiency with modest increases in time-to-convergence.
Takeaways: Prioritized, adaptive sampling of auxiliary data via MAB methods is more effective than static mixing or loss-scaling approaches, especially with numerous auxiliary datasets.
An intelligent balance between exploring diverse auxiliary data and exploiting beneficial subsets is critical for improved few-shot generalization.

Effective data interaction strategies can enable smaller models (3 billion parameters) to achieve or exceed the few-shot performance of significantly larger models (175 billion parameters) by leveraging auxiliary data.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.11915.Title: Understanding Self-Supervised Pretraining with Part-Aware Representation Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.11915.Summary: Researchers investigated the capability of self-supervised pretraining methods to learn part-aware representations, finding that contrastive learning and Context AutoEncoder (CAE) effectively capture fine-grained semantic parts, often surpassing supervised baselines on part-level tasks. A combination of these paradigms, as seen in iBOT, yielded robust representations across both object and part levels.
Problem: Prior research on understanding self-supervised learning (SSL) primarily focused on augmentation strategies, loss functions, or scaling laws, lacking a deep, quantitative insight into the semantic granularity of learned representations.

It was unclear if SSL methods, particularly contrastive learning (CL) and masked image modeling (MIM), implicitly or explicitly learn robust part-aware features, despite qualitative observations from Vision Transformers (ViTs) suggesting such capabilities.

A comprehensive empirical framework was needed to compare and understand the part-awareness capabilities of various state-of-the-art SSL models against fully-supervised baselines across diverse tasks.
Method: Proposed and empirically validated two hypotheses: contrastive learning operates as a 'part-to-whole' task where encoders learn part information and projectors infer whole objects, while masked image modeling acts as a 'part-to-part' task focusing on contextual inter-part relationships.

Developed a comprehensive empirical evaluation framework using a diverse suite of object-level (e.g., image classification, object retrieval) and part-level recognition tasks (e.g., patch retrieval, part classification, part segmentation).
Compared representative self-supervised models (MoCo v3, DINO, BEiT, MAE, CAE, iBOT) against a fully-supervised DeiT baseline, all utilizing a frozen ViT-B encoder architecture for evaluation.
Results: Self-supervised methods, especially modern CL and CAE, significantly outperformed the supervised DeiT model on part-level recognition tasks (e.g., patch retrieval, part classification, part segmentation).

The iBOT model, combining contrastive learning and masked image modeling, achieved top or near-top performance across almost all object-level and part-level tasks, even surpassing DeiT in some object-level benchmarks like ADE20K object segmentation.

Contrastive learning's encoded features yielded higher performance on part retrieval, while its projected features showed better object-level retrieval, quantitatively supporting the 'part-to-whole' operational mechanism.
Takeaways: Self-supervised pretraining methods consistently learn strong part-aware representations, often outperforming supervised models on fine-grained part-level tasks, demonstrating a unique strength in capturing local semantics.
Contrastive learning's encoder learns rich part information which its projector then generalizes to a more holistic, object-level representation, supporting the 'part-to-whole' hypothesis.

Masked image modeling, particularly CAE, excels in learning part-aware features through 'part-to-part' prediction, and the choice of reconstruction target in MIM (e.g., RGB vs. discrete tokens) significantly influences the level of features learned.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.08243.Title: Self-Supervised Learning from Images with a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture
https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.08243.Summary: I-JEPA presents a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) for self-supervised image learning that predicts abstract representations of masked image blocks. This approach achieves competitive performance on ImageNet-1K linear evaluation and dense prediction tasks while significantly reducing pretraining computational costs by over 10x compared to prior methods like MAE.
Problem: Invariance-based self-supervised learning methods rely on hand-crafted data augmentations, which introduce strong biases and limit generalizability across tasks or modalities.

Generative self-supervised learning methods (e.g., masked autoencoders) learn lower-level features because they reconstruct fine-grained pixel details, leading to sub-optimal performance on semantic tasks in linear probing.
Both existing self-supervised learning paradigms can be computationally intensive, requiring significant resources for large-scale pretraining.
Method: Introduces I-JEPA, an instantiation of a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA), that predicts abstract representations of masked target blocks from a single context block.
Utilizes an asymmetric Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture comprising a learned context encoder, an EMA-updated target encoder, and a lightweight predictor network.
Employs a multi-block masking strategy where context and target regions are distinct, and the loss is computed between predicted and actual abstract representations of the target blocks.
Results: Achieves 81.1% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K linear probing with a ViT-H/16, matching view-invariance methods without relying on hand-crafted augmentations.
Demonstrates superior performance on local and dense prediction tasks, such as object counting and depth prediction (e.g., 72.4% on Clevr/Dist) compared to augmentation-based methods.
Reduces pretraining computational cost significantly, requiring less than 1200 GPU hours for a ViT-H/14, which is over 10x faster than MAE and 2.5x faster than iBOT for comparable model sizes.
Takeaways: Predicting abstract representations in embedding space, rather than pixel space, is crucial for learning semantic features.
A multi-block masking strategy with an informative context, where targets are derived from the target encoder's output, effectively guides the model to learn semantic understanding.
An asymmetric architecture, using an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) for the target encoder weights and a separate, lightweight predictor, prevents representation collapse.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.08028.Title: A Tutorial on Meta-Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.08028.Summary: This tutorial comprehensively structures the field of Meta-Reinforcement Learning, categorizing diverse algorithms and problem settings, elucidating core challenges like meta-gradient computation and meta-learned exploration, and formalizing the problem via POMDPs. It provides a systematic overview to help overcome the data inefficiency and limited generality of traditional deep reinforcement learning.
Problem: Traditional deep reinforcement learning (RL) suffers from poor data efficiency, requiring immense amounts of interaction data to train policies.
Policies learned with traditional RL often have limited generality, struggling to adapt quickly and efficiently to new, unseen tasks or environments.
Humans currently meticulously design and tune RL algorithms for every new task, which is a time-consuming and often suboptimal process.
Method: Meta-RL casts the development of better reinforcement learning algorithms as a machine learning problem itself, aiming to learn an RL algorithm or its components from data.
The approach is formalized as a bi-level optimization problem, comprising an inner-loop (adaptation to a specific task) and an outer-loop (meta-training across a distribution of tasks).

Meta-RL can be understood as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) where the hidden state includes the identity of the sampled task, necessitating policies conditioned on interaction history to infer task parameters.
Results: The tutorial provides a comprehensive categorization of Meta-RL algorithms, distinguishing between few-shot and many-shot as well as multi-task and single-task problem settings.
It clarifies core challenges unique to Meta-RL, such as the complexities of bi-level optimization and the specific demands for meta-learned exploration strategies.

The work offers unified theoretical perspectives by formalizing Meta-RL as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) and connecting it to Bayes-Adaptive Optimality for principled exploration.
Takeaways: Meta-RL methods can be broadly categorized into Parameterized Policy Gradient, Black Box, and Task Inference approaches, each with distinct strengths and weaknesses regarding generalization and specialization.
Effective exploration is a unique and fundamental challenge in Meta-RL, requiring meta-learned exploration strategies for efficient adaptation within novel environments.
The bi-level optimization structure of Meta-RL introduces complexities in meta-gradient estimation, often leading to bias-variance trade-offs in different algorithmic approaches.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.05226.Title: See, Think, Confirm: Interactive Prompting Between Vision and Language Models for Knowledge-based Visual Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.05226.Summary: Researchers from MIT-IBM Watson AI Lab introduce the Interactive Prompting Visual Reasoner (IPVR) framework, which leverages iterative interaction between pre-trained vision and language models for few-shot knowledge-based visual reasoning. The framework achieves superior performance on A-OKVQA (46.0%) and OK-VQA while providing step-by-step transparent reasoning traces and higher quality rationales compared to baseline methods.
Problem: Knowledge-based visual question answering (KB-VQA) requires complex reasoning that integrates both visual understanding and external world knowledge.
Existing fine-tuning methods for large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are computationally intensive and lack transparency in their reasoning processes.

Prior prompt-based visual reasoning approaches often generate generic image descriptions, failing to provide question-specific visual grounding, and offer limited insight into the LLM's decision-making.
Method: The Interactive Prompting Visual Reasoner (IPVR) framework mimics human "See, Think, Confirm" reasoning through an iterative process utilizing existing large pre-trained vision and language models in a few-shot setup.

A "See" module extracts visual information via object detection and global captioning, while a "Think" module adaptively attends to question-relevant visual concepts, generates regional descriptions, and predicts answers using an LLM.

A "Confirm" module generates supporting rationales, verifies their visual consistency against the image using CLIP, and iteratively self-corrects the reasoning until a stable answer or maximum iterations are met.
Results: IPVR consistently outperforms strong few-shot baselines like PICa and Chain-of-Thought on KB-VQA datasets, achieving 46.0% accuracy on the A-OKVQA test set with OPT-66B and 57.5% with GPT-3, surpassing some fully-supervised methods.
The framework provides enhanced transparency by generating complete reasoning traces and produces higher quality rationales (BLEU score of 14.34) compared to Chain-of-Thought baselines.

Ablation studies confirm that all IPVR modules, particularly the adaptive "attend" module, contribute positively to overall performance and demonstrate the computational efficiency of the interactive prompting approach.
Takeaways: The interactive "See, Think, Confirm" paradigm enables total transparency by generating explicit, step-by-step reasoning traces and supporting rationales, addressing the "black-box" problem in multimodal AI.
Adaptive, question-specific visual grounding, combined with iterative rationale generation and verification, significantly enhances both the accuracy and consistency of answers in few-shot KB-VQA.

The framework's transparency provides clear diagnostic capabilities, allowing researchers to pinpoint whether reasoning failures originate from visual perception limitations or language model reasoning/knowledge recall.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.02419.Title: Exploring Efficient Few-shot Adaptation for Vision Transformers
https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.02419.Summary: Researchers from Fudan University and Tencent developed an efficient Transformer Tuning (eTT) method for few-shot learning with Vision Transformers, which addresses inefficiency and overfitting by using Attentive Prefix Tuning and Domain Residual Adapters. The method achieves an average rank of 1.6 on the Meta-Dataset benchmark, outperforming prior state-of-the-art while modifying only about 9% of the model's parameters during adaptation.
Problem: Inefficiency and high computational cost associated with finetuning large Vision Transformers (ViTs) for each new few-shot task.
Severe overfitting of high-capacity ViT models when attempting to adapt to novel categories with only a handful of labeled examples.
The challenge of effectively leveraging ViTs' global feature extraction capabilities for Few-shot Learning (FSL) without incurring prohibitive resource demands or poor generalization.
Method: Proposed efficient Transformer Tuning (eTT), a pretrain-finetune pipeline that adapts ViTs for few-shot learning while maintaining efficiency.

Introduced Attentive Prefix Tuning (APT) to inject task-specific information using small learnable prefixes, initialized with attentive prototypes, to influence attention mechanisms across all layers.
Integrated a lightweight Domain Residual Adapter (DRA) with learnable offset vectors to effectively bridge domain shifts between base and novel categories.
Utilized a novel prototypical regularization loss to ensure consistency between learned task-specific information and initial prototypes, thereby mitigating overfitting.
Results: eTT, leveraging a ViT-small backbone, achieved an average rank of 1.6 across 10 diverse datasets on the Meta-Dataset benchmark, outperforming existing ResNet-based state-of-the-art and naive ViT finetuning methods.
The method demonstrates high efficiency by tuning only approximately 9% of the total ViT model parameters during adaptation, making it suitable for resource-constrained environments.

eTT significantly mitigates overfitting in low-shot episodes, maintaining superior performance on query sets compared to naive finetuning, even when presented with extremely limited support examples (e.g., 1-2 shots).

Ablation studies confirmed the individual contributions of DINO pretraining, Attentive Prefix Tuning, Domain Residual Adapters, attentive prototypical initialization, and the prototypical regularization term to the method's overall performance and efficiency.
Takeaways: Self-supervised pre-training, specifically DINO on the meta-train split, is critical for enabling robust cross-domain generalization of ViTs in few-shot learning.

Highly efficient adaptation of ViTs for FSL can be achieved by introducing minimal, strategically placed learnable parameters like APT prefixes and DRA offsets, enabling comprehensive task-specific adaptation.
Data-driven initialization of prefixes using 'attentive prototypes' extracted from support sets provides valuable object-centric prior knowledge, leading to a substantial performance boost.

A dedicated prototypical regularization term effectively stabilizes training and prevents overfitting by maintaining consistency between the adapted model's representations and the initial task-specific prototypes.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.08013.Title: FlexiViT: One Model for All Patch Sizes
https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.08013.Summary: FlexiViT, developed by Google Research, introduces a method to train a single Vision Transformer model capable of effective performance across a wide range of patch sizes, eliminating the need for retraining for different speed/accuracy trade-offs. The model achieves this flexibility while often matching or exceeding the performance of fixed-patch-size ViTs on various computer vision tasks.
Problem: Standard Vision Transformers (ViTs) are typically trained and optimized for a single, fixed patch size, making them inflexible for deployment under varying computational budgets.
The choice of patch size in ViTs introduces a rigid trade-off between model speed (computational cost) and accuracy, requiring costly re-training for each desired operating point.
Current ViT deployment strategies necessitate maintaining multiple specialized models for different computational constraints, increasing development and management overhead.
Method: The model is trained by uniformly sampling patch sizes randomly from a predefined set during each training step.
A novel 'PI-resize' method is introduced for adaptively resizing patch embedding weights on-the-fly, along with bilinear interpolation for position embeddings, to maintain embedding integrity.
Knowledge distillation, coupled with initializing the student FlexiViT with a pre-trained fixed-patch-size teacher, is used to boost performance, especially at larger patch sizes.
Results: FlexiViT models achieve robust performance across patch sizes (e.g., 8x8 to 48x48), matching or outperforming standard ViTs trained for specific fixed patch sizes.

The method enables resource-efficient transfer learning, allowing models to be fine-tuned cheaply with large patches and deployed with small patches for higher performance without additional training.
FlexiViT models perform comparably to, and often slightly better than, fixed-patch ViTs across a diverse set of downstream tasks including classification, object detection, and segmentation.
Takeaways: Randomizing patch sizes during training, combined with principled embedding resizing, enables a single ViT model to learn robust representations adaptable to diverse patch granularities.
The PI-resize method effectively preserves the magnitude and meaning of patch embeddings across different scales, which is crucial for generalized performance.
FlexiViT models learn consistent internal representations across varying patch sizes, indicating a shared understanding of visual features regardless of input granularity.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.07143.Title: Reproducible scaling laws for contrastive language-image learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.07143.Summary: Researchers systematically investigated scaling laws for contrastive language-image models using public LAION datasets, revealing how performance scales with model size, data quantity, and training samples, and crucially, how pre-training data distribution influences task-specific scaling behaviors. This open-source study provides a reproducible framework for understanding large-scale multimodal AI, indicating that gains continue with scale, but the optimal scaling strategy depends on the underlying dataset.
Problem: Prior research on scaling laws primarily focused on uni-modal models (language or vision) and often relied on private datasets and proprietary models.

The influential CLIP model demonstrated strong multimodal capabilities, but its training dataset (WIT-400M) was private, hindering systematic, reproducible investigations of scaling trends in this domain.
A lack of open and reproducible large-scale studies made it difficult for the broader research community to understand and verify fundamental scaling properties of multimodal AI models.
Method: The authors conducted a systematic empirical study of scaling laws for contrastive language-image learning using OpenCLIP models (ViT-B/32 to ViT-g/14) and publicly available LAION datasets (LAION-80M, LAION-400M, LAION-2B).
Models were trained using an open-source framework on supercomputing infrastructure, varying model size, data size, and total samples seen (up to 34 billion) to explore scaling dimensions.

Performance was evaluated comprehensively across diverse downstream tasks, including zero-shot classification, image/text retrieval, linear probing, and full fine-tuning, to identify generalizable scaling trends.
Results: Performance across zero-shot classification, retrieval, linear probing, and fine-tuning consistently follows power-law relationships with increased scale, confirming scaling laws for multimodal models.

OpenCLIP models (LAION-trained) demonstrate stronger scaling for zero-shot image retrieval tasks compared to OpenAI's CLIP, while OpenAI's CLIP shows stronger scaling for zero-shot classification (e.g., OpenCLIP
α=−0.11 vs. CLIP
α=−0.16 on ImageNet).

Derived power laws enable predictions for larger scales, estimating that a ViT-G/14 CLIP model trained on 68 billion samples could achieve 81.9% zero-shot ImageNet accuracy and 76.99% Recall@5 on MS-COCO.
Takeaways: Scaling laws observed in unimodal learning extend to contrastive language-image models, with consistent power-law improvements across diverse downstream tasks as model size, data size, and samples seen increase.

The specific pre-training data distribution critically influences scaling behavior and task-specific performance; for instance, models trained on LAION datasets show stronger scaling for retrieval tasks, while OpenAI's CLIP (trained on private WIT-400M) exhibits stronger scaling for zero-shot classification.

Performance improvements plateau if one scaling dimension (model size, data quantity, or training steps) is fixed while others are increased, highlighting the necessity of balanced scaling across all dimensions.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.12588.Title: Program of Thoughts Prompting: Disentangling Computation from Reasoning for Numerical Reasoning Tasks
https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.12588.Summary: Program of Thoughts (PoT) prompting enables Large Language Models (LLMs) to enhance their numerical reasoning capabilities by generating executable programs (e.g., Python code) for computation, which are then processed by an external interpreter. This method consistently improves performance on mathematical word problems and financial question-answering tasks, yielding gains of approximately 8% on MWP datasets and 15% on financial datasets in few-shot settings compared to Chain-of-Thought.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) are prone to arithmetic errors and struggle with complex mathematical expressions when performing calculations directly within their natural language Chain-of-Thought (CoT).
CoT prompting is inefficient and error-prone for numerical problems involving repetitive calculations or complex iterations.
The inherent computational weaknesses of LLMs limit their reliability and accuracy in quantitative reasoning tasks, even when their high-level reasoning is conceptually sound.
Method: The method prompts Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate formal programs (e.g., Python code) that encapsulate the reasoning steps for numerical problems.
An external, precise program interpreter (e.g., Python 3.8 with SymPy) executes the generated code to perform all calculations and obtain the final answer.

This approach allows LLMs to leverage their strengths in language understanding and high-level logical structuring while offloading computationally intensive or precise operations to a specialized, deterministic system.
Results: PoT consistently outperformed Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, showing an average accuracy gain of approximately 8% on Math Word Problem (MWP) datasets and 15% on financial datasets in few-shot settings.
Zero-shot PoT often surpassed the performance of few-shot CoT, highlighting the method's strong generalization capabilities without needing task-specific examples.

When combined with Self-Consistency (PoT+SC), the method achieved the best-known results on all evaluated MWP datasets (pre-GPT-4), and `gpt-3.5-turbo` emerged as a top-performing LLM backend for PoT.
Takeaways: Disentangling reasoning (handled by the LLM) from precise computation (delegated to an external interpreter) is critical for achieving robust numerical problem-solving with LLMs.
Prompting LLMs to generate executable code, rather than natural language rationales, enables them to leverage external, exact computational tools effectively.
Using semantically meaningful variable names and encouraging multi-step program generation significantly aids LLMs in structuring their reasoning for complex numerical problems.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.11559.Title: Visual Programming: Compositional visual reasoning without training
https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.11559.Summary: VISPROG, developed by the PRIOR team at Allen Institute for AI, introduces a neuro-symbolic approach that generates executable programs for visual reasoning tasks using large language models and in-context learning. The system enables adaptable visual reasoning without task-specific training and produces predictions along with visual rationales explaining the reasoning process.
Problem: Traditional end-to-end trainable models for visual reasoning tasks often require large datasets for each specific task.
Such approaches frequently struggle with compositional generalization and fail to handle the long tail of diverse real-world visual tasks.
Method: The system leverages an LLM (GPT-3) as a Program Generator to translate natural language instructions into executable Python-like programs using in-context learning.

A Program Interpreter executes these generated programs by invoking specialized Visual Modules that perform specific visual processing (e.g., object detection, image manipulation) and knowledge retrieval tasks.
This approach operates at a higher level of abstraction, composing state-of-the-art vision models and non-neural subroutines without requiring any task-specific fine-tuning.
Results: VISPROG achieved a 2.7-point accuracy gain over a baseline VQA model on a subset of the GQA dataset for compositional visual question answering.
It demonstrated a strong zero-shot accuracy of 62.4% on the NLVR2 benchmark, indicating its ability to generalize to new tasks without image pair training.

The system successfully performs diverse language-guided image editing operations and achieves a 63.7% tagging F1 score for factual knowledge object tagging, along with generating interpretable visual rationales for its reasoning.
Takeaways: Large language models can effectively generate complex, executable programs for visual tasks through in-context learning with only a few examples.
Decomposing complex visual reasoning tasks into sequences of operations performed by modular, specialized visual components enhances interpretability and adaptability.
Combining the symbolic reasoning capabilities of LLMs with powerful pre-trained vision models enables robust visual reasoning without task-specific training.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.10435.Title: PAL: Program-aided Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.10435.Summary: Program-aided Language Models (PAL) from Carnegie Mellon University enhance Large Language Models' reasoning by prompting them to generate Python programs, which are then executed by an external interpreter. This approach achieves state-of-the-art few-shot accuracy across 13 mathematical, symbolic, and algorithmic datasets, significantly improving robustness to numerical complexity compared to existing methods like Chain-of-Thought.
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at decomposing complex problems into logical steps (e.g., via Chain-of-Thought prompting) but frequently make errors during the execution or calculation phase.
LLMs, being pattern matchers, are not inherently reliable for precise arithmetic, symbolic, or logical computation, especially with complex numbers or intricate manipulations.
This limitation leads to situations where an LLM's reasoning chain might be conceptually correct, but its final numerical or logical answer is erroneous due to calculation mistakes.
Method: PAL introduces a novel prompting strategy where the Large Language Model generates an interleaved sequence of natural language comments and executable Python code as intermediate reasoning steps.
Instead of the LLM performing internal calculations, the generated Python program is passed to and executed by a standard, external Python interpreter.
The final solution is derived directly from the interpreter's output, effectively decoupling the LLM's problem decomposition capabilities from the precise execution of computational steps.
Results: PAL achieved state-of-the-art few-shot accuracy across all 13 evaluated mathematical, symbolic, and algorithmic reasoning datasets, outperforming larger models like PaLM-540B and Minerva-540B using Chain-of-Thought.

On GSM8K, PAL reached 72.0% accuracy, surpassing CoT with Codex (65.6%); on the harder GSM-HARD dataset, PAL maintained 61.2% accuracy, demonstrating superior robustness compared to CoT's drop to 23.1%.

PAL showed substantial gains across BIG-Bench Hard symbolic and algorithmic tasks, with improvements ranging from 8.8% to 23.7% over Chain-of-Thought on datasets such as COLORED OBJECTS, PENGUINS, OBJECT COUNTING, and REPEAT COPY.
Takeaways: Integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) with external symbolic interpreters, such as a Python interpreter, is an effective strategy for achieving accurate and robust reasoning.

The primary benefit of PAL comes from offloading precise computation to a deterministic external interpreter, rather than solely from prompting LLMs to generate structured code for internal execution.
The inclusion of natural language comments and meaningful variable names within the Python code prompts is crucial for the LLM's performance and its ability to generate correct and grounded programs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.10277.Title: Task Residual for Tuning Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.10277.Summary: Task Residual Tuning (TaskRes) introduces a method for efficiently adapting Vision-Language Models by explicitly decoupling the preservation of pre-trained knowledge from the acquisition of new, task-specific information. This approach sets new performance benchmarks across 11 diverse datasets in few-shot settings and improves domain generalization, while significantly reducing training time and tunable parameters.
Problem: Prompt tuning methods for Vision-Language Models (VLMs) often discard or damage the VLM's valuable pre-trained classifier knowledge.
Adapter-style tuning methods for VLMs are excessively biased towards prior knowledge, limiting the flexibility to explore genuinely new task-specific information.

Existing efficient transfer learning (ETL) approaches for large VLMs struggle to balance preserving foundational knowledge with acquiring specialized task knowledge, particularly in data-scarce environments.
Method: TaskRes freezes the VLM's pre-trained text-based classifier to explicitly guarantee the preservation of prior knowledge.
It introduces a set of prior-independent, tunable "task residual" parameters that are additively combined with the fixed base classifier to form a new classifier.
Only the task residual parameters are updated during training, ensuring high efficiency, minimal tunable parameters, and low computational overhead.
Results: TaskRes consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance across 11 benchmark datasets in few-shot settings (1 to 16 shots), surpassing Zero-shot CLIP and leading ETL methods like CoOp and CLIP-Adapter.
It demonstrates superior domain generalization capabilities to unseen ImageNet variant datasets (ImageNet-V2, -Sketch, -A, -R), indicating more robust and transferable task-specific adjustments.
The method offers high training efficiency, for example, requiring only 11 minutes for 4-shot ImageNet compared to 121 minutes for prompt tuning, due to its minimal parameters and optimized design.
Takeaways: Explicitly decoupling the preservation of prior VLM knowledge from the flexible exploration of new task-specific knowledge is crucial for optimal VLM adaptation.
The magnitude of the learned task residual positively correlates with the relative transfer difficulty of a task, indicating adaptive knowledge acquisition.
Applying the task residual to the text branch of the VLM is more effective than to the image branch or both, providing stable task-level information and reducing overfitting.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.09699.Title: PromptCap: Prompt-Guided Task-Aware Image Captioning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.09699.Summary: PROMPTCAP introduces an image captioning model that generates question-aware captions, tailoring visual descriptions for black-box Large Language Models. This approach achieved 60.4% accuracy on OK-VQA and 73.1% on A-OKVQA, outperforming prior methods by providing task-relevant visual context.
Problem: Black-box Large Language Models (LLMs) require visual information to be converted into text, but generic image captions often lack task-specific details.
Generic image captions, used as context for LLMs in Visual Question Answering (VQA), often omit crucial visual information needed to answer specific questions.
Developing datasets of task-aware captions typically requires costly and time-consuming human annotation.
Method: Introduces PROMPTCAP, an image captioning model based on a pre-trained OFA encoder-decoder Transformer, which generates captions conditioned on both an image and a natural language prompt (question).
Develops an innovative data synthesis pipeline leveraging GPT-3 with few-shot in-context learning to create question-aware caption training data from existing VQA datasets.
Implements a two-stage filtering process for synthesized captions, using VQA accuracy and CIDEr scores to ensure quality.
Results: PROMPTCAP + GPT-3 achieved 60.4% accuracy on OK-VQA and 73.1% on A-OKVQA (multiple-choice), outperforming prior methods on knowledge-based VQA benchmarks.
Ablation studies showed PROMPTCAP provided an absolute accuracy gain of 3.8% on OK-VQA, 5.3% on A-OKVQA, and 9.2% on VQAv2 compared to generic captioning.
The system demonstrated strong generalization, outperforming supervised baselines on the WebQA benchmark without specific training.
Takeaways: Providing Large Language Models with prompt-guided, task-aware image captions substantially improves their performance on knowledge-based Visual Question Answering tasks.
High-quality training data for specific visual-linguistic tasks can be synthesized cost-effectively using powerful black-box LLMs and few-shot in-context learning.
The selection of in-context examples using similarity metrics is crucial for maximizing the performance of black-box LLMs in multimodal inference.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.03876.Title: CoNMix for Source-free Single and Multi-target Domain Adaptation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.03876.Summary: CoNMix, developed by researchers at the Indian Institute of Science, introduces a three-stage framework for source-free single and multi-target domain adaptation, leveraging Vision Transformers and MixUp knowledge distillation. The method establishes new state-of-the-art performance for source-free single-target domain adaptation and provides the first comprehensive baselines for the novel source-free multi-target domain adaptation task, demonstrating robust generalization across various datasets.
Problem: Deep learning models trained on a source domain perform poorly when data distribution shifts in a target domain (domain shift).
Traditional domain adaptation methods require access to labeled source data during adaptation, posing challenges due to privacy concerns and resource constraints on edge devices.

Existing research lacked a robust solution for adapting a model from a single source to multiple diverse target domains simultaneously without source data (Source-Free Multi-Target Domain Adaptation).
Method: The CoNMix framework consists of three stages: source training with Vision Transformers, source-free single-target domain adaptation (SF-STDA) for individual target domains, and source-free multi-target domain adaptation (SF-MTDA) to consolidate knowledge.

For SF-STDA, the method employs Nuclear-Norm Maximization to improve class-discriminability and prediction-diversity, combined with pseudo-label refinement and a consistency loss using data augmentations.

For SF-MTDA, a novel MixUp Knowledge Distillation technique is used to distil knowledge from multiple target-specific "expert teacher" models (generated in SF-STDA) into a single student network capable of generalizing across all target domains.
Results: Achieved state-of-the-art results in Source-Free Single-Target Domain Adaptation (SF-STDA), improving average accuracy on Office-Home to 76.0% and showing a 6.0% improvement over existing SOTA on DomainNet.

Established the first comprehensive baselines for Source-Free Multi-Target Domain Adaptation (SF-MTDA), outperforming existing non-source-free MTDA methods like D-CGCT by 5.6% on Office-Home (75.4% average accuracy).
CoNMix achieved a new SOTA for MTDA on Office-Caltech at 96.9% and provided the first SF-MTDA results for the large-scale DomainNet dataset, achieving an average accuracy of 33.7%.
Takeaways: Vision Transformers (VTs) are empirically shown to provide superior feature representations for domain adaptation compared to CNNs, exhibiting better domain transferability and class-discriminative features.

Nuclear-Norm Maximization is a critical component for effective source-free adaptation, enhancing both class-discriminability and prediction diversity on unlabeled target data, especially when combined with pseudo-label refinement.

MixUp Knowledge Distillation effectively enables a single student model to generalize across multiple diverse target domains in a source-free setting by leveraging mixed inputs and pseudo-labels from domain-specific teacher models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.05639.Title: Discovered Policy Optimisation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.05639.Summary: Researchers at FLAIR Oxford, UC Berkeley, and Google Brain discovered a new reinforcement learning algorithm, Discovered Policy Optimisation (DPO), by meta-learning a key component within the theoretically-sound Mirror Learning framework. DPO consistently outperforms PPO across various continuous control tasks, generalizes to unseen environments, and is a simple, analytically derived algorithm with provable guarantees.
Problem: Traditional reinforcement learning algorithms are hand-designed, leading to methods that can be brittle to hyperparameters, lack robustness, and struggle to generalize.

Existing algorithm discovery methods often produce black-box solutions without theoretical guarantees, frequently fail to consistently outperform handcrafted algorithms, and struggle with generalization beyond training distributions.
A lack of interpretability in meta-learned algorithms hinders understanding and systematic improvement of policy optimization principles.
Method: Utilize the Mirror Learning framework, which guarantees monotonic policy improvement and convergence, to define a space of theoretically sound algorithms.
Parameterize the 'drift function' within Mirror Learning using a neural network, imposing architectural constraints to ensure theoretical validity.

Meta-train the drift function's parameters using Evolution Strategies (ES) to optimize the final return of the inner-loop RL agent, allowing for learning from scratch (LPO-Zero) or fine-tuning from PPO (LPO).
Analyze the behavior of the learned LPO drift function to derive a novel, interpretable, closed-form analytical expression for Discovered Policy Optimisation (DPO).
Results: The meta-learned LPO algorithm consistently outperformed PPO across most Brax continuous control environments and demonstrated strong generalization to unseen environments and varied hyperparameter settings.
Analysis of the learned LPO drift function led to the formulation of Discovered Policy Optimisation (DPO), a novel, closed-form algorithm that is theoretically sound and easily implementable.
DPO matched LPO's state-of-the-art performance, consistently outperforming PPO on both Brax and Minatar tasks, showcasing its transferability and practical utility.
Takeaways: Effective policy optimization benefits from a 'rollback' mechanism for actions with negative advantages and decreased probabilities, and 'cautious optimism' for actions with positive advantages and increased probabilities.
The learned drift function implicitly encourages higher policy entropy throughout training without an explicit entropy bonus, promoting robust exploration.
Sophisticated, asymmetric update rules, learned by the meta-algorithm, can lead to superior performance and generalization compared to symmetric clipping methods like PPO.
Meta-learning within a principled, theoretically-sound framework enables the discovery of high-performing, interpretable algorithms with provable guarantees.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629.Title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629.Summary: Researchers from Princeton University and Google Research introduced ReAct, a paradigm that enables large language models to synergize reasoning and acting by interleaving internal thoughts with external actions. This approach achieved an impressive 71% success rate on the ALFWorld benchmark and 40% on WebShop, significantly outperforming prior methods while notably reducing hallucination errors in knowledge-intensive tasks.
Problem: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit factual hallucination and error propagation in multi-step reasoning (e.g., Chain-of-Thought) due to a lack of grounding in external information.
LLMs used for planning and acting in interactive environments typically lack abstract reasoning or a dynamic working memory for complex, long-horizon tasks, leading to purely reactive behaviors.
The capabilities of reasoning and acting in LLMs have primarily been studied and implemented in isolation, limiting their robustness and adaptability in real-world scenarios.
Method: The ReAct paradigm expands the language model's action space to include a 'language space' for generating explicit thoughts, which are interleaved with task-specific actions.
Leveraging few-shot in-context learning with large language models like PaLM-540B, the system generates sequences of thoughts, actions, and observations to navigate and solve tasks.

The approach tailors domain-specific action spaces (e.g., Wikipedia API for QA, text-based actions for ALFWorld) and adapts thought generation density based on task characteristics (dense for reasoning, sparse for decision-making).
Results: ReAct achieved a 71% average success rate on ALFWorld and 40% on WebShop with just one or two few-shot examples, outperforming imitation learning and RL methods requiring 10^3 to 10^5 training instances.

On knowledge-intensive tasks, ReAct significantly reduced hallucination compared to Chain-of-Thought (6% vs. 14% false positives on HotpotQA), demonstrating superior grounding through external interaction.

Finetuning smaller PaLM models (8B/62B) with ReAct trajectories drastically improved performance, with finetuned PaLM-62B ReAct surpassing all 540B prompting methods, indicating a more generalizable skill learning.
Takeaways: Interleaving internal reasoning ('thoughts') with external actions creates a dynamic feedback loop, where reasoning guides actions and observations from actions refine subsequent reasoning.
Explicit thought processes in language models enhance interpretability, allowing humans to diagnose failures and understand decision-making, which also facilitates human-in-the-loop control.
Interacting with external tools (e.g., APIs) allows LLMs to retrieve up-to-date information, significantly reducing hallucination compared to internal-only reasoning and improving fact-groundedness.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.15639.Title: F-VLM: Open-Vocabulary Object Detection upon Frozen Vision and Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.15639.Summary: A new open-vocabulary object detection framework, F-VLM, leverages frozen Vision and Language Models with a minimal trainable detector head to achieve state-of-the-art results on LVIS and COCO benchmarks. This approach significantly reduces training computational costs, offering up to 226x compute savings over prior methods.
Problem: Object detection traditionally struggles with fixed, limited vocabularies due to the high cost of bounding box annotation for novel categories.
Prior open-vocabulary object detection (OVD) methods relied on computationally intensive multi-stage training pipelines like knowledge distillation or extensive VLM finetuning.
Effectively transferring the image-level open-vocabulary capabilities of Vision and Language Models (VLMs) to granular object-level detection remained a complex challenge.
Method: F-VLM utilizes a completely frozen, pre-trained Vision and Language Model (VLM) backbone as the feature extractor.
A minimal, randomly initialized, and trainable detector head (Mask R-CNN with FPN) is attached to the frozen VLM for class-agnostic object localization.
During inference, a geometric mean combines localization scores from the detector head with open-vocabulary classification scores derived from the frozen VLM's region embeddings and text embeddings.
Results: The largest F-VLM model achieved 32.8 mask APr on LVIS rare categories, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art (ViLD-EN-B7) by 6.5 mask APr.
F-VLM demonstrated a significant reduction in training resources, achieving comparable or better performance with up to 226x less compute and 57x faster wall clock time than prior methods.
The method exhibited strong cross-dataset transfer capabilities, outperforming existing approaches by 5.9 AP on COCO and 3.2 AP on Objects365 when trained solely on LVIS base categories.
Takeaways: Frozen Vision and Language Model (VLM) backbones inherently possess locality-sensitive features capable of delineating object shapes and boundaries.
Features extracted from a frozen VLM are robust enough for accurate region classification, demonstrating strong transferable semantic understanding without finetuning.
The geometric mean proves effective for fusing detection scores from the trainable head with VLM's classification scores, ensuring both localization and semantic quality.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.09407.Title: DetCLIP: Dictionary-Enriched Visual-Concept Paralleled Pre-training for Open-world Detection
https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.09407.Summary: DetCLIP, developed by researchers from HKUST, Huawei Noah’s Ark Lab, and Sun Yat-Sen University, proposes a pre-training framework for open-world object detection that significantly improves efficiency and performance. It leverages a novel paralleled concept formulation and a dictionary-enriched concept space, achieving state-of-the-art zero-shot detection on LVIS minival with a 9.9% mAP gain over GLIP and a 5x reduction in training time.
Problem: Traditional object detectors are limited to a fixed set of categories, requiring costly manual annotation for expansion and struggling with generalization to unseen objects.

Prior vision-language pre-training methods for detection, like GLIP, suffered from inefficient sequential processing of category names, limiting the number of concepts and increasing computational burden.
Integrating diverse data sources (e.g., detection, grounding, image-text pairs) and incorporating external semantic knowledge effectively for open-world detection remained challenging.
Method: Introduces a 'paralleled concept formulation' where each concept (category name or noun phrase) is processed individually and in parallel by the text encoder, avoiding unnecessary attention interactions.
Develops a large-scale 'concept dictionary' of approximately 14,000 concepts with WordNet definitions to unify the concept space and provide rich prior knowledge for concept enrichment.

Integrates hybrid supervision from detection, grounding, and image-text pair data, employing the concept dictionary for robust negative sampling and 'label completion' during pseudo-labeling of image-text data.
Results: DetCLIP-T achieved 35.9% mAP on LVIS minival, outperforming GLIP-T by 9.9% mAP and a fully-supervised ATSS model by 2.3% mAP, with a 12.4% higher APr for rare categories compared to GLIP-T.
DetCLIP-T demonstrated remarkable efficiency, training over 5 times faster (2.0K vs. 10.7K GPU hours) and achieving nearly 19 times faster inference (2.3 FPS vs. 0.12 FPS) than GLIP-T.

Ablation studies confirmed the effectiveness of the paralleled concept formulation (+4.1% mAP), concept enrichment with definitions, a large concept dictionary, and label completion for pseudo-labeling.
Takeaways: Processing concepts in parallel eliminates unnecessary interactions between unrelated categories, significantly improving training and inference efficiency.
Enriching concepts with external semantic knowledge from a comprehensive dictionary unifies diverse concept spaces and enhances the model's understanding of relationships between categories.
Leveraging a concept dictionary enables effective negative sampling and 'label completion' during pseudo-labeling of weakly-supervised data, maximizing the utility of heterogeneous datasets.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.13050.Title: Efficient High-Resolution Deep Learning: A Survey
https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.13050.Summary: Researchers from Aarhus University provide the first comprehensive survey on efficient high-resolution deep learning, categorizing existing methods into five groups and outlining their applications and datasets. The work offers a structured overview of techniques designed to address the significant computational and memory challenges presented by high-resolution visual data.
Problem: High-resolution input data causes substantial increases in computational cost, memory consumption, and inference latency for deep learning models, particularly Vision Transformers.
Naive approaches like uniform downsampling or cutting images into patches compromise accuracy by losing crucial details or destroying global context, respectively.
A systematic overview and categorization of existing methods to efficiently process high-resolution visual data was absent from the literature.
Method: Conducted a systematic literature review to identify and classify efficient high-resolution deep learning methods into five distinct categories.
Empirically demonstrated the limitations of naive baselines, such as uniform downsampling and cutting into patches, on a crowd counting task.
Compiled a comprehensive list of high-resolution datasets and described real-world applications where these methods are critical.
Results: The survey established a new taxonomy, categorizing efficient high-resolution deep learning methods into Non-Uniform Downsampling, Selective Zooming and Skipping, Lightweight Scanner Networks, Task-Oriented Input Compression, and High-Resolution Vision Transformers.
Empirical evaluation showed that uniform downsampling increased Mean Absolute Error by 43-155% and cutting into patches by 1-6% on a crowd counting dataset.
A comprehensive compilation of relevant high-resolution datasets and a detailed overview of applications in fields such as medical imaging, remote sensing, and surveillance were provided.
Takeaways: Specialized deep learning methods are essential to efficiently process high-resolution data while preserving accuracy, as simple baselines lead to significant performance degradation.

Techniques for handling high-resolution deep learning can be broadly classified based on how they manage input resolution, select regions, design lightweight architectures, compress inputs, or adapt Transformer attention mechanisms.
The choice of efficient high-resolution method depends on factors like task requirements, data saliency characteristics, and available hardware resources, each offering specific trade-offs.
