https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.01887.Title: Open-Vocabulary Multi-Label Classification via Multi-Modal Knowledge Transfer
https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.01887.Summary: Researchers from Shenzhen University, Tsinghua University, and Tencent's YouTu Lab developed the Multi-modal Knowledge Transfer (MKT) framework for open-vocabulary multi-label classification. This framework leverages pre-trained vision-language models to achieve state-of-the-art performance, demonstrated by an 11.7% absolute mAP gain over prior methods on NUS-WIDE ZSL, and accurately classifies unseen and complex multi-word labels.
Problem: Traditional multi-label classification systems are limited to predefined labels, failing to recognize new, unseen categories in dynamic environments.
Existing Multi-Label Zero-Shot Learning methods rely on single-modal textual knowledge, neglecting rich visual semantic information and struggling with complex multi-word 'text labels'.
Adapting powerful vision-language pre-training (VLP) models for open-vocabulary *multi-label* classification, especially involving unseen text labels, had remained largely unexplored.
Method: The Multi-modal Knowledge Transfer (MKT) framework is introduced, utilizing a Vision Transformer as an image encoder and leveraging a pre-trained CLIP model for multi-modal knowledge.
A two-stream module within the vision transformer extracts both global image features and discriminative local patch features for comprehensive multi-object recognition.

Knowledge distillation aligns the student model's global image features with robust multi-modal representations from the CLIP image encoder, while prompt tuning refines label embeddings generated by the CLIP text encoder for the multi-label task.
Results: The MKT framework achieved new state-of-the-art performance, consistently outperforming prior Multi-Label Zero-Shot Learning methods and a fine-tuned CLIP baseline on NUS-WIDE and Open Images datasets across ZSL and GZSL tasks.
On NUS-WIDE ZSL, MKT demonstrated an 11.7% absolute mAP gain over the BiAM method (37.6% vs. 25.9%), and a 6.5% mAP gain over ZS-SDL on GZSL (18.3% vs. 12.1%).

The framework successfully classifies complex multi-word 'text labels' and demonstrates enhanced localization of objects through Grad-CAM visualizations, all while exhibiting competitive efficiency in terms of parameters and FLOPs.
Takeaways: Multi-modal knowledge from Vision and Language Pre-training (VLP) models provides superior semantic and visual consistency for label embeddings compared to single-modal language models.
Knowledge distillation effectively transfers powerful VLP capabilities, aligning image embeddings and enhancing generalization to unseen labels while preventing overfitting.
Prompt tuning offers an efficient method to adapt VLP text embeddings, making them more discriminative for specific downstream multi-label tasks without extensive fine-tuning.
Combining global and local image feature streams within a two-stream module leads to more robust and discriminative multi-label predictions.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.07643.Title: Coarse-to-Fine Vision-Language Pre-training with Fusion in the Backbone
https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.07643.Summary: Microsoft Research, UCLA, and NYU collaborated on FIBER, a vision-language model that unifies high-level image understanding and fine-grained region-level tasks. It leverages a fusion-in-the-backbone architecture and a two-stage coarse-to-fine pre-training strategy, achieving state-of-the-art performance on various benchmarks with improved efficiency and reduced reliance on costly annotations.
Problem: Existing vision-language models specialize in either high-level image understanding or fine-grained region-level tasks, lacking a unified framework capable of handling both seamlessly.
Traditional end-to-end vision-language pre-training models struggle to extend effectively to bounding box prediction and other region-level tasks.

High computational and data annotation costs are associated with fine-grained vision-language pre-training, particularly for tasks requiring high-resolution inputs and expensive bounding box annotations.
Method: Introduces the Fusion-In-the-Backbone (FIBER) architecture, which integrates cross-attention modules deeply into vision (Swin Transformer) and language (RoBERTa) backbones with a learnable gating mechanism for efficient multimodal fusion.

Employs a two-stage coarse-to-fine pre-training strategy, starting with large-scale image-text paired data for general understanding and then specializing with a smaller amount of image-text-box data for region-level tasks.
Integrates an object detection head directly on top of the language-aware image features produced by the fused vision backbone, ensuring deep interaction for precise localization tasks.
Results: Achieves new state-of-the-art on VQAv2 (78.0%), outperforming models like BLIP (77.8%) and SimVLM (77.6%) that were trained on significantly larger datasets.
Surpasses larger models such as GLIP-L on phrase grounding (87.4% R@1 on Flickr30k Entities) and LVIS rare object detection, utilizing 25x less fine-grained pre-training data.

Attains state-of-the-art CIDEr scores for base-size models on COCO image captioning and demonstrates 1.5x faster training for object detection compared to GLIP while maintaining comparable performance.
Takeaways: Deep multimodal fusion directly within vision and language backbones, rather than in separate layers, enhances interaction efficiency and overall model performance across diverse tasks.
A phased coarse-to-fine pre-training strategy can significantly reduce reliance on expensive, fine-grained annotations while still achieving superior results on region-level tasks.

A single, unified architecture is capable of effectively bridging the gap between high-level image understanding (e.g., VQA, captioning) and fine-grained object localization tasks (e.g., object detection, phrase grounding).

https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.05836.Title: GLIPv2: Unifying Localization and Vision-Language Understanding
https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.05836.Summary: Researchers at Microsoft, University of Washington, and UCLA developed GLIPv2, a unified grounded vision-language model that achieves near state-of-the-art performance across diverse localization and VL understanding tasks. The model demonstrates superior zero-shot and few-shot capabilities on open-vocabulary benchmarks, streamlining multimodal AI pre-training.
Problem: Existing vision-language models relied on inefficient multi-stage pre-training pipelines, separating localization and high-level understanding tasks.
Prior unified approaches often failed to achieve true mutual benefits between localization and vision-language understanding, with localization remaining 'vision-only.'
Generalization to open-vocabulary object detection and novel concepts remained a challenge for traditional vision models.
Method: Introduces a unified architecture using a 'classification-to-matching trick' to reformulate diverse vision and VL tasks as grounded VL understanding problems.
Employs a multi-task pre-training strategy with phrase grounding loss, masked language modeling, and a novel inter-image region-word contrastive loss.
Leverages large-scale image-text data, including weakly supervised pseudo-boxes, for comprehensive pre-training.
Results: Achieves near state-of-the-art performance across a wide spectrum of localization and VL understanding tasks within a single, unified model.
Demonstrates superior zero-shot and few-shot transfer capabilities on open-vocabulary benchmarks like ODinW and LVIS, often outperforming prior specialized models with less data.
The novel inter-image region-word contrastive loss is shown to be critical, substantially improving performance across object detection tasks, while data scaling further enhances results.
Takeaways: Extending the 'classification-to-matching trick' to the region level enables open-vocabulary localization and a unified task formulation for fine-grained grounding.
Inter-image region-word contrastive learning, utilizing negative examples from other image-text pairs, significantly enhances discriminative region-word feature learning.
True unification of localization and VL understanding, driven by a strong grounding signal, leads to mutual performance benefits and improved generalization.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.02647.Title: Scaling Vision Transformers to Gigapixel Images via Hierarchical Self-Supervised Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.02647.Summary: Chen et al. introduce the Hierarchical Image Pyramid Transformer (HIPT), an architecture designed to process gigapixel whole slide images by learning features hierarchically across multiple magnifications. This model, employing a hierarchical self-supervised learning approach, achieved superior performance in cancer subtyping and survival prediction tasks compared to existing weakly-supervised methods.
Problem: Processing gigapixel Whole Slide Images (WSIs) for computational pathology is challenging due to their immense size (up to 10 billion pixels), leading to significant memory constraints and computational costs for traditional deep learning models.

Relevant biological features in WSIs span multiple scales, from subcellular components to tissue-level architecture, which existing Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) methods often fail to capture comprehensively.
Applying Vision Transformers (ViTs) directly to gigapixel images is computationally prohibitive due to the quadratic complexity of self-attention with respect to input size.
Method: The Hierarchical Image Pyramid Transformer (HIPT) processes WSIs in a multi-stage pipeline, featuring Cell-Level (ViT256-16), Patch-Level (ViT4K-256), and Region-Level (ViTWSI-4096) aggregation layers.

HIPT maintains a constant sequence length (M=256) in its initial two stages by dynamically adjusting patch sizes at each resolution, enabling it to scale to gigapixel images while managing computational complexity.

A hierarchical self-supervised learning strategy pretrains the lower levels (ViT256-16 and ViT4K-256) using DINO on a large dataset of 10,678 unlabeled TCGA WSIs, allowing the model to learn meaningful representations across scales.
Results: HIPT outperformed state-of-the-art weakly-supervised methods on cancer subtyping tasks for BRCA, NSCLC, and RCC.
The model demonstrated robust performance on cancer subtyping and survival prediction even with limited training data, attributing this to its hierarchical pretraining approach.

Using K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) on the pretrained HIPT features achieved competitive performance on slide-level classification tasks without fine-tuning, indicating the quality of the learned representations.
Takeaways: HIPT effectively learns visual features across multiple scales, from individual cells (16x16 pixels) to tissue organization (4096x4096 pixels), mirroring how pathologists examine slides.

A hierarchical self-supervised learning approach, leveraging DINO, enables the model to learn generalizable and robust representations from large unlabeled WSI datasets, even clustering different tissue types effectively without stain normalization.

Attention mechanisms within HIPT demonstrate specialization at different levels, with cell-level attention focusing on cellular components and patch-level attention identifying higher-level tissue structures like the tumor-stroma interface.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14949.Title: HiViT: Hierarchical Vision Transformer Meets Masked Image Modeling
https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14949.Summary: HiViT is a hierarchical Vision Transformer architecture designed for efficient Masked Image Modeling pre-training. It removes computationally intensive local operations in early stages, enabling a 1.9x speed-up over Swin Transformer during MIM while achieving 84.2% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K.
Problem: Existing hierarchical Vision Transformers (ViTs) like Swin Transformer face computational inefficiencies when applied to Masked Image Modeling (MIM) due to complex structural operations.
Their "local inter-unit operations" (e.g., shifting window attention, patch merging) prevent the efficient discarding of masked tokens, leading to higher computational costs during MIM pre-training.
The challenge is to design a hierarchical ViT that retains the benefits of multi-resolution feature maps while enabling efficient MIM pre-training by addressing these computational bottlenecks.
Method: HiViT introduces a modified hierarchical architecture that minimizes or removes "local inter-unit operations," which are inefficient for MIM pre-training.
Early stages of the network replace window attention with simple MLP blocks and use linear merging operations for downsampling.
The architecture consolidates stages, removing the fourth stage found in typical hierarchical ViTs and extending the third (main) stage to apply global attention across tokens.
Results: HiViT-B achieves 83.8% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K in supervised learning and 84.2% when pre-trained with MIM, outperforming ViT-B by 2.0% and Swin-B by 0.3%.
It demonstrates a 1.9x speed-up over Swin Transformer during Masked Image Modeling pre-training, indicating substantial computational savings without performance loss.
HiViT shows strong transfer learning capabilities, achieving 51.2% APbox and 44.2% APmask on COCO for object detection and 51.2% mIoU on ADE20K for semantic segmentation.
Takeaways: Local inter-unit operations like window attention in hierarchical Vision Transformers create a computational bottleneck for efficient Masked Image Modeling (MIM).

These computationally intensive local operations can be replaced with simpler MLP blocks and linear merging operations without sacrificing performance, while significantly improving MIM pre-training efficiency.
The hierarchical structure itself is more important for performance than the specific local inter-unit operations, and consolidating network stages can improve both efficiency and accuracy.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14756.Title: EfficientViT: Multi-Scale Linear Attention for High-Resolution Dense Prediction
https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14756.Summary: EfficientViT introduces a family of Vision Transformers for high-resolution dense prediction, utilizing a multi-scale linear attention module to achieve state-of-the-art performance with substantial hardware speedups. The architecture delivers significant latency reductions across various tasks and platforms, including enabling a 16.5x throughput increase for the Segment Anything model while improving zero-shot performance.
Problem: State-of-the-art high-resolution dense prediction models are computationally demanding, limiting their deployment on resource-constrained devices like mobile CPUs and edge GPUs.
Existing methods for global context (softmax attention) and multi-scale learning (large-kernel convolutions) incur quadratic computational complexity and are hardware-unfriendly.
Translating theoretical computational efficiency (FLOPs) into practical latency and throughput improvements on real hardware remains a challenge for current model designs.
Method: Developed EfficientViT, a novel family of Vision Transformers featuring a multi-scale linear attention module that achieves a global receptive field with linear computational complexity (O(N)).
Replaced hardware-unfriendly softmax attention with ReLU linear attention and incorporated depthwise convolutions within Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) for local feature extraction.
Implemented multi-scale token aggregation using lightweight depthwise-separable convolutions to efficiently learn features at different scales in parallel.
Results: EfficientViT-L2 achieved 86.0% Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet with a 2.6x speedup over EfficientNetV2-L on an A100 GPU.
For semantic segmentation on Cityscapes, EfficientViT delivered up to 13.9x GPU latency reduction compared to SegFormer while maintaining or exceeding mIoU.

EfficientViT-SAM-XL1, replacing SAM's image encoder, demonstrated 16.5x higher throughput on an A100 GPU and slightly outperformed SAM-ViT-H in zero-shot instance segmentation on COCO (47.8 vs 46.5 mAP).
Takeaways: Linear attention can effectively capture global context while being significantly more hardware-efficient than softmax attention, especially when augmented with local processing and multi-scale feature aggregation.
Hardware-aware design, focusing on operations friendly to specific hardware platforms, is crucial for translating theoretical efficiency gains into tangible speedups in real-world deployments.

A unified efficient architecture can achieve strong performance across diverse high-resolution dense prediction tasks, including classification, semantic segmentation, super-resolution, and as an encoder for foundation models like SAM.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.10268.Title: B-cos Networks: Alignment is All We Need for Interpretability
https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.10268.Summary: B-cos Networks introduce a method for building inherently interpretable deep neural networks by integrating a B-cos transform that promotes alignment between weights and input features. This allows models to explain their decisions through their internal structure, achieving classification accuracies comparable to conventional networks, such as 74.5% top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10 for B-cos DenseNet-121, matching the baseline.
Problem: Deep neural networks are black-box models, making their decision-making processes opaque and difficult to understand, particularly in critical applications.
Existing post-hoc explanation methods often lack faithfulness to the model's actual reasoning or produce explanations that are difficult for humans to interpret.
The complex non-linear transformations within traditional DNNs prevent tracing how specific input features contribute to model outputs.
Method: Introduce the B-cos transform, a drop-in replacement for standard linear transforms that incorporates a cosine similarity term between weights and inputs.
Utilize a hyperparameter 'B' within the transform to control the pressure for weight vectors to align with task-relevant input features.
Build B-cos networks by replacing standard linear layers with B-cos transforms, using MaxOut units to maintain non-linearity while preserving interpretability through linear transform summarization.
Results: B-cos networks achieve classification performance comparable to conventional counterparts, for instance, B-cos DenseNet-121 reached 74.5% top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10, matching the baseline.
The networks provide inherent interpretability where weights directly align with task-relevant input features, offering natural and faithful explanations for decisions.
B-cos networks quantitatively outperform various post-hoc explanation methods in localization accuracy, as demonstrated by the "grid pointing game" metric.
Takeaways: Aligning weights with input features during training can enable neural networks to inherently explain their decisions through their own structure.
The B-cos transform's exponent 'B' allows control over the degree of weight-input alignment, making weights directly interpretable as feature templates.
B-cos networks allow for summarization of sequences of transforms, enabling interpretation of both output and intermediate neurons, which often represent semantic concepts.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.09329.Title: Dataset Pruning: Reducing Training Data by Examining Generalization Influence
https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.09329.Summary: Researchers from UTS and Baidu Research introduce an optimization-based dataset pruning method that leverages influence functions to identify and remove redundant training data. This approach significantly reduces training time, for instance, halving convergence time on CIFAR-10 with a 40% data reduction and a minimal 1.3% accuracy decrease, and accelerates Neural Architecture Search by 96% while maintaining performance.
Problem: Training large deep learning models on ever-growing datasets consumes immense computational resources and energy.
A significant portion of training data might be redundant, contributing little to a model's generalization performance.
Existing sample selection methods are often heuristic, lacking theoretical guarantees, and do not adequately account for the joint influence of data subsets.
Method: Defines dataset pruning as a constrained discrete optimization problem to find the largest "redundant" data subset while maintaining a generalization guarantee.
Leverages Influence Functions to efficiently estimate the combined impact of removing a subset of training data on model parameters, avoiding costly retraining.
Employs simulated annealing to solve the combinatorial optimization problem, aiming to maximize pruned samples under a specified parameter change constraint.
Results: The proposed method consistently outperforms baseline dataset pruning techniques, particularly at higher pruning ratios, across various datasets and network architectures.
Achieved significant improvements in training efficiency, for example, halving convergence time on CIFAR-10 (40% pruned) with only a 1.3% test accuracy drop.
Substantially accelerated Neural Architecture Search, reducing search time by 96% (from 3029 to 113 minutes) while finding architectures with comparable performance (85.7% vs 85.9% full data).
Takeaways: Deep learning datasets contain substantial redundant information that can be systematically removed to improve training efficiency.
Influence functions can be effectively utilized and extended to estimate the combined impact of removing groups of data points on model parameters.
Constraining the change in model parameters by a small epsilon provides a quantifiable and empirically verifiable bound on the actual generalization gap.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.08534.Title: Vision Transformer Adapter for Dense Predictions
https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.08534.Summary: A pre-training-free adapter, the ViT-Adapter, enables plain Vision Transformers (ViTs) to perform dense prediction tasks effectively by injecting vision-specific inductive biases without altering the ViT's core architecture. This approach achieved competitive or superior performance against specialized vision transformers, reaching up to 60.9 box AP on COCO test-dev with multi-modal pre-training.
Problem: Plain Vision Transformers (ViTs) excel at general representation learning from large, multi-modal datasets due to their architectural flexibility, making them suitable for foundation models.
Plain ViTs perform suboptimally on dense prediction tasks (object detection, segmentation) due to a lack of inherent visual inductive biases, unlike specialized vision-specific transformers.
A significant gap exists in combining the benefits of multi-modal pre-training from plain ViTs with the superior dense prediction performance of vision-specific ViT variants.
Method: Developed the ViT-Adapter, a pre-training-free network that runs in parallel with a plain ViT backbone during fine-tuning, injecting vision-specific inductive biases without altering the original ViT architecture.
The ViT-Adapter comprises a Spatial Prior Module (SPM) using convolutional layers for local spatial semantics, a Spatial Feature Injector, and a Multi-Scale Feature Extractor.
Cross-attention mechanisms are employed between the ViT tokens and the adapter's spatial features to inject local information into the ViT and extract multi-scale features from its output.
Results: Consistently achieved significant performance gains across object detection (COCO) and semantic segmentation (ADE20K) tasks, outperforming plain ViT baselines.
ViT-Adapter models matched or surpassed the performance of specialized vision transformers (e.g., Swin, PVT) on dense prediction tasks using standard ImageNet pre-training.

With BEiTv2 multi-modal pre-training, ViT-Adapter-L achieved state-of-the-art results: 60.9 box AP and 53.0 mask AP on COCO test-dev and 61.5 MS mIoU on ADE20K validation, demonstrating strong synergy with advanced pre-training.
Takeaways: It is possible to effectively equip plain ViTs with necessary vision-specific inductive biases (e.g., local spatial information, multi-scale features) for dense prediction tasks through a lightweight, pre-training-free adapter.
Decoupling general representation learning (handled by the ViT backbone) from task-specific adaptation (handled by the adapter) creates an efficient and versatile paradigm for computer vision models.

The inherent flexibility of plain ViTs for multi-modal pre-training can be fully leveraged for state-of-the-art dense prediction performance when combined with an appropriate adaptation module like the ViT-Adapter.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.06230.Title: Simple Open-Vocabulary Object Detection with Vision Transformers
https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.06230.Summary: Google Research developed OWL-ViT, a simple open-vocabulary object detection method that adapts Vision Transformers, pre-trained with image-text contrastive learning, for end-to-end fine-tuning, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance in both text- and image-conditioned object detection.
Problem: Traditional object detection models operate in a 'closed-vocabulary' setting, limiting them to a fixed set of categories and making it expensive to extend to new object types.
Developing a simple yet powerful unified framework for both text-conditioned (zero-shot) and image-conditioned (one-shot/few-shot) open-vocabulary object detection has been a challenge.

Effectively transferring the rich, semantic knowledge learned by large-scale image-level vision-language models to the more granular task of object localization and classification for novel categories.
Method: Google Research developed OWL-ViT, adapting a standard Vision Transformer (ViT) and text Transformer (pre-trained with image-text contrastive learning like LiT) for end-to-end detection fine-tuning.

The model uses decoupled image and text encoders, allowing dynamic queries using either text embeddings or image-derived embeddings, enabling both text- and image-conditioned open-vocabulary detection without architectural changes.

A two-stage training recipe is employed: large-scale image-text contrastive pre-training followed by end-to-end fine-tuning on detection datasets, incorporating crucial strategies such as differential learning rates for encoders, location biases for box predictions, and robust data augmentations.
Results: Achieved 34.6% AP overall and 31.2% AP rare on the LVIS v1.0 validation set for zero-shot text-conditioned detection, competing with and often outperforming more complex existing methods.
Significantly improved one-shot image-conditioned object detection, increasing AP50 on unseen COCO categories from a prior state-of-the-art of 26.0% to 41.8%, representing a 72% improvement.
Demonstrated consistent performance gains in downstream detection by scaling both model size and the amount of image-text pre-training data, indicating the continued potential of this approach.
Takeaways: A simple adaptation of Vision Transformers (ViT) pre-trained with image-text contrastive learning can achieve state-of-the-art open-vocabulary object detection performance without complex architectural modifications or multi-stage distillation.

Effective transfer of large-scale image-level pre-training to object detection requires specific fine-tuning strategies, including differential learning rates for the text encoder, location biases for bounding box predictions, and careful data cleaning/augmentation.

Pure Vision Transformers (ViTs) demonstrate superior scaling properties and a stronger bias towards semantic generalization compared to hybrid architectures, making them particularly effective for large-scale open-vocabulary detection.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.01917.Title: CoCa: Contrastive Captioners are Image-Text Foundation Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.01917.Summary: CoCa unifies three major image-text pretraining paradigms through a novel decoupled text decoder and joint contrastive-generative training. The model from Google Research achieves state-of-the-art performance across visual recognition, crossmodal retrieval, and multimodal understanding tasks, including 91.0% top-1 ImageNet accuracy and 120.6 CIDEr on NoCaps.
Problem: Existing image-text pretraining paradigms (single-encoder, dual-encoder, encoder-decoder) specialize in certain tasks but struggle with others, leading to a fragmented approach.
The lack of a single, unified model that efficiently covers visual recognition, crossmodal retrieval, and deep multimodal understanding/generation simultaneously.
Prior unified approaches often involve multi-stage pretraining or complex, less efficient architectures, increasing development and deployment overhead.
Method: Introduces CoCa, a "Contrastive Captioner" with a novel decoupled text decoder split into unimodal (no cross-attention) and multimodal (cross-attention) parts.
Trains end-to-end and from scratch using dual objectives: a contrastive loss between image encoder and unimodal text decoder, and a generative (captioning) loss from the multimodal text decoder.
Unifies diverse data sources (e.g., JFT-3B, ALIGN) by treating all labels as text, enabling single-stage, efficient pretraining with shared computation.
Results: Achieved 91.0% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet classification (finetuned encoder), setting a new state-of-the-art among foundation models.
Improved state-of-the-art across image-text retrieval benchmarks (MSCOCO, Flickr30K) and demonstrated enhanced zero-shot robustness on ImageNet variants.
Reached state-of-the-art in multimodal understanding tasks (VQA v2 82.3%) and image captioning (NoCaps CIDEr 120.6).
Takeaways: A single, unified model architecture (CoCa's decoupled decoder) can efficiently integrate and benefit from both contrastive and generative learning objectives.
Generative captioning loss applied to annotated images can be as effective as traditional classification for learning strong visual representations.

Combining contrastive and generative losses within a single, shared forward pass yields complementary benefits, enhancing both zero-shot alignment and multimodal understanding with minimal computational overhead.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.00363.Title: Visual Spatial Reasoning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.00363.Summary: VSR, a dataset for evaluating visual spatial reasoning in natural image-text pairs, reveals a substantial gap between Vision-and-Language Model performance and human capabilities, with state-of-the-art models achieving around 70% accuracy compared to human 95.4%.
Problem: Existing generic Vision-and-Language (V&L) benchmarks often conflate various linguistic and visual challenges, making it difficult to isolate and diagnose specific VLM failures in spatial reasoning.
Prior studies indicate that state-of-the-art VLMs struggle with relational information, especially nuanced spatial relations, performing much worse than humans.

Synthetic datasets simplify real-world complexity and linguistic diversity, while natural image datasets lack the controlled focus or specific probing capabilities required for fine-grained spatial understanding.
Method: Introduces Visual Spatial Reasoning (VSR), a large-scale diagnostic dataset of 10,972 natural image-text pairs derived from MS COCO, specifically designed to evaluate VLMs' spatial reasoning abilities.

Employs a two-phase human annotation process: contrastive template-based caption generation ensures diverse and challenging spatial descriptions, followed by multi-annotator validation for quality control and consistency.
The dataset design incorporates linguistic complexities such as varying reference frames, allowing for targeted analysis of how models interpret spatial language in context.
Results: State-of-the-art VLMs (e.g., LXMERT 70.1%, ViLT 69.3%) achieve significantly lower accuracy on VSR compared to the human ceiling of 95.4%, highlighting a >25 percentage point performance gap.
Model performance drops considerably in the concept zero-shot setting (best ViLT 63.0%), indicating poor generalization of spatial reasoning to unseen visual concepts.

Models show particular weaknesses in understanding orientation-dependent relations (e.g., "facing") and struggle to infer the correct reference frame (intrinsic vs. relative), though learning latent reference frame features can improve performance.
Takeaways: Current Vision-and-Language Models (VLMs) demonstrate a substantial gap in spatial reasoning capabilities compared to humans, despite advancements in other vision-language tasks.
Explicit positional encoding and object-level features are crucial for VLM performance on spatial reasoning tasks, as models lacking these components perform significantly worse.
VLMs particularly struggle with spatial relations involving object orientation and generalize poorly on context-dependent relations like proximity when faced with unseen concepts.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.07683.Title: Safe Self-Refinement for Transformer-based Domain Adaptation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.07683.Summary: A new framework, Safe Self-Refinement for Transformer-based Domain Adaptation (SSRT), integrates Vision Transformers with a robust self-refinement and adaptive 'safe training' mechanism to improve performance in Unsupervised Domain Adaptation. This approach achieved 45.2% average accuracy on the challenging DomainNet dataset, demonstrating enhanced stability and effectiveness across large domain gaps.
Problem: Deep neural networks require extensive labeled data, which is costly, leading to the challenge of adapting models trained on a labeled source domain to an unlabeled target domain (Unsupervised Domain Adaptation).
Existing UDA methods, primarily based on CNNs, struggle to bridge large domain gaps, showing relatively low performance on complex, large-scale datasets like DomainNet.

Despite their powerful feature learning capabilities, Vision Transformers have been largely underexplored in UDA, and their high capacity can make them susceptible to model collapse when faced with noisy target domain predictions.
Method: The Safe Self-Refinement for Transformer-based Domain Adaptation (SSRT) framework utilizes pre-trained Vision Transformers (ViT) as its backbone for robust feature extraction.

SSRT employs a multi-faceted self-refinement strategy, applying random offsets to latent token sequences within transformer blocks and using a bi-directional self-refinement loss for consistency regularization, filtered by prediction confidence.

A 'Safe Training' mechanism adaptively adjusts perturbation strength and self-refinement loss weight by monitoring prediction diversity, restoring model states and resetting parameters if diversity drops to prevent model collapse.
Results: SSRT-B achieved state-of-the-art performance on Office-Home (85.43%), VisDA-2017 (88.76%), and a substantial 45.2% average accuracy on DomainNet, demonstrating significant improvements over prior methods.

A simple adversarial adaptation with a ViT-B backbone (38.5% on DomainNet) already surpassed the best CNN-based methods (33.3%), confirming the strong transferable representations of Vision Transformers.

Ablation studies showed that multi-layer perturbation, bi-directional self-refinement, and especially the 'Safe Training' mechanism, were critical for SSRT's performance and preventing model collapse, particularly on tasks with large domain gaps.
Takeaways: Vision Transformers learn highly transferable features that provide a strong foundation for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation, often outperforming CNNs even with basic adaptation techniques.

Applying perturbations to latent feature representations within transformer blocks is more effective for consistency regularization than perturbing raw input images, enhancing robustness for high-capacity models.

Adaptive monitoring of prediction diversity and dynamic adjustment of training parameters are crucial for stable training, effectively preventing model collapse in challenging UDA tasks with large domain shifts.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.01697.Title: MaxViT: Multi-Axis Vision Transformer
https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.01697.Summary: MaxViT, a hierarchical vision transformer, introduces a Multi-Axis Self-Attention module that efficiently combines blocked local and dilated global spatial interactions with linear computational complexity. It achieves 85.17% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K and demonstrates superior efficiency across classification, object detection, segmentation, and generative tasks.
Problem: Standard Vision Transformers incur quadratic computational complexity for self-attention, making them inefficient for high-resolution images and early network stages.
Current vision transformer designs struggle to effectively and efficiently integrate both fine-grained local features and long-range global dependencies throughout the network.
Many Vision Transformers lack strong inherent inductive biases for vision, often requiring extensive pre-training data to generalize well and avoid overfitting on smaller datasets.
Method: A Multi-Axis Self-Attention (Max-SA) module is proposed, which decomposes self-attention into sequential Blocked Local Attention and Dilated Global Attention for linear complexity and broad receptive fields.

Max-SA modules are integrated with efficient MBConv (MobileNetV2 Inverted Residual Block) layers within a simple, hierarchical network architecture to combine convolutional inductive biases with global reasoning.

The overall MaxViT architecture follows a hierarchical design, progressively reducing spatial resolution and increasing channel dimensions, using relative self-attention for enhanced performance on 2D vision tasks.
Results: MaxViT achieved state-of-the-art 85.17% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K (224x224 input) and 86.7% with 512x512 fine-tuning, outperforming previous models while maintaining superior efficiency.

Demonstrated enhanced parameter and computational efficiency, achieving higher accuracy with notably fewer parameters and FLOPs compared to other leading vision transformers on benchmarks like ImageNet-21K and COCO.

Exhibited broad versatility and strong performance across diverse downstream tasks including object detection (COCO), instance segmentation, image aesthetic assessment (AVA), and unconditional image generation (ImageNet-1K GANs).
Takeaways: Sequential application of blocked local and dilated global attention effectively captures both fine-grained local details and sparse global context across all network stages with linear computational cost.
Hybrid architectures that blend efficient convolutions (MBConv) with multi-axis attention provide a robust approach to combine beneficial inductive biases with global reasoning capabilities.

The optimal ordering of architectural components within a block varies for different task types, with MBConv followed by local then global attention being beneficial for discriminative tasks, and an inverse order for generative tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.00598.Title: Socratic Models: Composing Zero-Shot Multimodal Reasoning with Language
https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.00598.Summary: Socratic Models propose a modular framework that orchestrates large pretrained models to perform complex multimodal reasoning through language-based interaction, achieving new zero-shot capabilities in areas like egocentric perception and robot planning. The approach sets new zero-shot benchmarks on image captioning and video-to-text retrieval by composing distinct foundation models.
Problem: Integrating distinct large pretrained models, each specialized in a single modality, to perform complex multimodal reasoning tasks traditionally requires extensive joint training or fine-tuning.
The high computational cost, significant data demands, and potential loss of generality associated with fine-tuning large foundation models for new multimodal applications.
The scarcity of labeled multimodal datasets for emerging applications (e.g., egocentric perception, human-robot interaction) limits the applicability of traditional data-hungry approaches.
Method: Introduces Socratic Models (SMs), a modular framework that composes multiple large pretrained models (LMs, VLMs, ALMs) to perform novel multimodal reasoning tasks zero-shot.
Utilizes language as the universal intermediate representation for communication, converting information from non-language modalities into text for prompting other models.
Employs multi-model multimodal prompting and closed-loop feedback, allowing models to 'dialogue' and refine outputs without requiring task-specific training or fine-tuning.
Results: Achieved zero-shot state-of-the-art on MS COCO image captioning (CIDEr 44.5) and MSR-VTT video-to-text retrieval (R@1 44.7), outperforming prior zero-shot methods.
Demonstrated qualitative capabilities in egocentric perception, including summarizing videos into textual event logs, answering open-ended questions, and forecasting future events.
Enabled novel applications such as multimodal assistive dialogue and language-conditioned robot perception and planning by orchestrating interactions between diverse models and external APIs.
Takeaways: Different large pretrained models (LMs, VLMs, ALMs) possess complementary forms of commonsense knowledge that can be synergistically leveraged without architectural unification.
Language serves as a universal and flexible intermediate representation, enabling diverse AI modules to communicate and collaborate through prompting.

Complex multimodal reasoning tasks can be reframed as language-based reading comprehension problems, allowing LMs to apply their reasoning capabilities to non-textual data converted into linguistic form.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.17273.Title: FindIt: Generalized Localization with Natural Language Queries
https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.17273.Summary: Google Research, Brain Team developed FindIt, a unified framework that integrates referring expression comprehension (REC), text-based localization (LOC), and object detection (DET) into a single model. This framework achieves state-of-the-art results on REC and LOC, improves generalization to novel object categories and out-of-distribution data, and maintains competitive performance on traditional object detection.
Problem: Visual grounding research is fragmented into specialized models for referring expression comprehension (REC), text-based localization (LOC), and object detection (DET), preventing a holistic understanding.
Existing single-task models exhibit poor generalization to novel categories and out-of-distribution data, limiting their real-world applicability.
Developing and maintaining separate task-specific models is inefficient and often involves complex architectures or pre-computed detections.
Method: A unified, end-to-end trainable framework, FindIt, built upon a standard Faster R-CNN object detector with shared parameters across all tasks.
An efficient multi-level image-text fusion module combines Transformer-based cross-attention for high-level features and Hadamard product fusion for fine-grained localization.
Multi-task learning integrates datasets and standard detection losses from REC, LOC, and DET, allowing the model to jointly learn from diverse visual grounding signals.
Results: FindIt significantly surpasses previous state-of-the-art on all major RefCOCO benchmarks for REC, showing a 5-10 accuracy point improvement on challenging splits (e.g., RefCOCOg test-u from 80.89 to 91.72).
Establishes a new state-of-the-art on the text-based localization task, outperforming the GPV model, while also maintaining competitive performance on COCO object detection.
Demonstrates superior generalization, dramatically outperforming single-task baselines on novel categories in Objects365 and showing better understanding of super-categories across datasets.
Takeaways: A standard object detector can be surprisingly effective for unifying diverse visual grounding tasks when combined with an efficient multi-level vision-language fusion mechanism.

Joint training across referring expression comprehension, text-based localization, and object detection significantly enhances a model's ability to generalize to novel categories and out-of-distribution data.
Complex, task-specific architectures or pre-computed detections are not necessary to achieve state-of-the-art performance in visual grounding tasks, simplifying model design.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.16527.Title: Exploring Plain Vision Transformer Backbones for Object Detection
https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.16527.Summary: This research from Facebook AI Research demonstrates that plain, non-hierarchical Vision Transformer (ViT) backbones can achieve state-of-the-art results for object detection. It shows that with minimal adaptations during fine-tuning, such as a simple feature pyramid and window attention with limited cross-window propagation, and crucially, pre-training with Masked Autoencoders, these plain architectures can surpass or match performance of hierarchical ViT counterparts on COCO and LVIS datasets.
Problem: Integrating Vision Transformers (ViTs) into object detection frameworks was challenging due to their single-scale output (difficulty handling multi-scale objects) and the quadratic computational cost of global self-attention on high-resolution images.
The prevailing approach adapted ViTs into hierarchical designs (e.g., Swin Transformer) to mimic ConvNet properties, hindering the original ViT's 'plain' and 'fewer inductive biases' philosophy.

Existing object detection systems were heavily reliant on hierarchical backbones like ConvNets or hierarchically-modified ViTs, requiring complex feature pyramid networks (FPNs) for multi-scale feature fusion.
Method: Proposing a 'simple feature pyramid' that generates multi-scale feature maps from only the last single-scale feature map of a plain ViT backbone using convolutional and deconvolutional layers.

Adapting the pre-trained plain ViT backbone with window attention for computational efficiency and incorporating a few (e.g., 4) strategically placed cross-window propagation blocks (global attention or convolutional) during fine-tuning.
Leveraging Masked Autoencoders (MAE) for self-supervised pre-training of the plain ViT backbones, which proved essential for learning robust and transferable visual representations.
Results: The proposed ViTDet with a plain ViT-Huge backbone achieved 61.3 AP box on the COCO dataset, outperforming hierarchical counterparts that used larger ImageNet-21K supervised pre-training.
A simple feature pyramid built from only the last 1/16 stride feature map performed comparably to or better than FPN-mimicking variants, simplifying the detection pipeline for plain backbones.

ViTDet demonstrated competitive wall-clock performance for large models due to simpler block designs and showed consistent strong performance across different detector frameworks (Mask R-CNN, Cascade Mask R-CNN, RetinaNet) and datasets (COCO, LVIS).
Takeaways: Simple feature pyramids constructed from a single last-layer feature map are sufficient for plain Vision Transformer backbones in object detection, negating the need for complex top-down/lateral FPN connections.

Applying window attention with minimal cross-window propagation (e.g., 4 blocks) during fine-tuning is effective for handling high-resolution inputs in plain ViTs without altering the pre-training architecture.
Masked Autoencoder (MAE) self-supervised pre-training is crucial for the success of plain ViT backbones, providing substantial performance gains for object detection tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.16513.Title: PromptDet: Towards Open-vocabulary Detection using Uncurated Images
https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.16513.Summary: PromptDet presents a framework for open-vocabulary object detection, establishing an annotation-free pipeline that leverages a vision-language model (CLIP) and an iterative self-training strategy on uncurated web images. This approach achieves 21.4 AP_novel on LVIS and 26.6 AP50_box novel on MS-COCO, outperforming existing methods with lower resource requirements.
Problem: Traditional object detection models require extensive, expensive manual bounding box annotations for each new object category, limiting scalability and adaptability.
A domain gap exists between scene-level image-text pairs used for Vision-Language Pre-training (VLP) and the object-centric proposals generated by object detectors.
Lexical ambiguity in simple class names can hinder accurate classification of visual concepts in open-vocabulary settings.
Method: Integrates a pre-trained VLP model's (CLIP) frozen text encoder into a two-stage object detector to enable open-vocabulary classification via cosine similarity between visual and textual embeddings.

Implements Regional Prompt Learning (RPL) by optimizing learnable prompt vectors and incorporating detailed descriptions with the text encoder, aligning object-centric visual features with textual representations.

Develops an iterative self-training framework that sources uncurated web images, generates pseudo-labels by selecting bounding boxes with maximal classification scores, and then retrains the detector's visual backbone and RPN.
Results:
PromptDet achieved 21.4 AP
novel
on the LVIS v1.0 validation set, surpassing ViLD-ens by 4.8 AP and Detic by 3.6 AP while using fewer additional training images.

On the MS-COCO open-vocabulary benchmark, the method reached 26.6 AP50
boxnovel
and 50.6 AP50
boxall
, outperforming Detic with the same input image resolution.

Ablation studies confirmed that RPL improved novel category AP by 2.1 points over manual prompts, and iterative self-training further boosted AP
novel
from 11.1 to 19.3, demonstrating the efficacy of leveraging uncurated web images.
Takeaways: Regional Prompt Learning (RPL) effectively bridges the domain gap between scene-level VLP and object-centric detection, improving alignment of visual and textual features for novel categories.
An iterative self-training process, combined with refined prompt learning and image sourcing, can robustly extract valuable supervision from vast, noisy, and uncurated web datasets.

Selecting pseudo-labels based on the maximal classification score from RPN proposals is a critical strategy for generating high-quality annotations from noisy uncurated images, significantly outperforming other heuristics.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.16265.Title: SeqTR: A Simple yet Universal Network for Visual Grounding
https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.16265.Summary: SeqTR introduces a universal Transformer-based network that reformulates visual grounding tasks like phrase localization and referring expression segmentation into a unified auto-regressive point prediction problem. The model achieves state-of-the-art or competitive performance on benchmark datasets while utilizing a simpler architecture and a single cross-entropy loss.
Problem: Existing visual grounding methods often rely on complex, specialized network architectures and intricate multi-modal fusion mechanisms.
Previous approaches require hand-crafted, task-specific loss functions (e.g., for bounding boxes vs. segmentation) and complicated tuning of loss coefficients in multi-task settings.
Many models suffer from limited generalization, requiring significant re-engineering to adapt to different visual grounding tasks (REC vs. RES) or new datasets due to task-specific output branches.
Method: SeqTR reformulates both bounding box and binary mask outputs as sequences of discrete coordinate tokens, unifying visual grounding tasks into an auto-regressive point prediction problem.
A standard Transformer encoder-decoder architecture processes multi-modal features and auto-regressively generates the coordinate sequences.
The model is trained with a single, simple cross-entropy loss across all visual grounding tasks, eliminating the need for complex, task-specific loss functions and coefficient tuning.
Results: SeqTR achieves new state-of-the-art performance on various RefCOCO datasets for Referring Expression Comprehension (REC), reaching 85.00% Precision@0.5 on RefCOCO testA without pre-training.

For Referring Expression Segmentation (RES), SeqTR obtains results on par with state-of-the-art models, reaching 69.79% mIoU on RefCOCO testA despite using a novel contour-based segmentation approach.
The model is compact with 7.9M parameters and achieves real-time inference speed (50ms on GTX 1080 Ti), demonstrating efficiency comparable to many one-stage models.
Takeaways: Mask contour sampling, especially uniform sampling of a small number of points along the contour, effectively serializes binary masks for sequential prediction.
Randomly shuffling the order of sampled points during training for masks enhances robustness by forcing the model to learn context-independent coordinate prediction.
Surprisingly, multi-task training for REC and RES does not significantly improve performance, suggesting SeqTR's mask generation is robust independently.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.11926.Title: Focal Modulation Networks
https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.11926.Summary: Focal Modulation Networks introduce an attention-free mechanism for vision backbones that models input-dependent long-range interactions efficiently. This approach achieves new state-of-the-art results across image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation, while offering enhanced computational efficiency and inherent interpretability.
Problem: The quadratic computational complexity of Self-Attention (SA) limits Vision Transformers' efficiency, especially for high-resolution images and dense prediction tasks.
Traditional SA involves extensive and potentially inefficient query-key interactions before value aggregation, questioning its necessity for capturing long-range context.
There was a need for an alternative mechanism to model input-dependent long-range interactions without the computational burden of Self-Attention.
Method: Developed Focal Modulation, an attention-free mechanism that replaces Self-Attention by decoupling context aggregation from individual query interactions.
The mechanism first aggregates multi-level contextual features using hierarchical depth-wise convolutions around each query.
An adaptive gating mechanism is used to select and modulate the query with the aggregated context, allowing for spatial- and channel-specific adjustments.
Results: Achieved new state-of-the-art performance on COCO object detection, with FocalNet-H (integrated with DINO) reaching 64.3 mAP on minival, outperforming larger attention-based models.

Consistently outperformed state-of-the-art Vision Transformers like Swin Transformer and modernized CNNs like ConvNeXt across image classification (e.g., 83.9% top-1 on ImageNet-1K with FocalNet-B), object detection, and semantic segmentation tasks.
Exhibited inherent interpretability, as modulation maps automatically highlight task-relevant image regions, demonstrating a learned content-aware decision process.
Takeaways: Self-Attention is not indispensable for state-of-the-art vision performance; an attention-free mechanism can effectively model input-dependent long-range interactions.
Decoupling context aggregation (early aggregation) from query interactions significantly improves efficiency while retaining rich contextual understanding.
The combination of hierarchical, structure-aware depth-wise convolutions and an adaptive gating mechanism enables the network to dynamically focus on multi-granularity contexts.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.09093.Title: Semantic-aligned Fusion Transformer for One-shot Object Detection
https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.09093.Summary: Researchers from Carnegie Mellon University and Microsoft Research Asia developed the Semantic-aligned Fusion Transformer (SaFT), an attention-based one-stage detector that improves one-shot object detection by adaptively fusing features across samples and scales. SaFT established new state-of-the-art results on PASCAL-VOC and MS-COCO benchmarks, demonstrating robust detection of novel objects from a single example.
Problem: Existing one-shot object detection (OSD) methods exhibit semantic misalignment when fusing features between a query image and a single support example.
Conventional fusion techniques often compress spatial information from the support, hindering precise object localization in the query.
Current approaches frequently fail to account for scale variances and long-range cross-scale interactions, limiting detection accuracy for objects of diverse sizes.
Method: Developed the Semantic-aligned Fusion Transformer (SaFT), a one-stage, proposal-free architecture leveraging a novel semantic-aligned attention mechanism.
Introduced a Horizontal Fusion Module (HFM) for iterative cross-sample attention, enabling deformable matching and global-to-global semantic alignment between query and support features.
Implemented a Vertical Fusion Module (VFM) for cross-scale attention, allowing each support feature point to interact with the entire multi-scale query feature pyramid for enhanced semantics.
Results: Achieved state-of-the-art performance on PASCAL-VOC, boosting novel class AP50 by 1.4% and improving diverse categories like 'Person' by 13.4% over the previous best method (AIT).
Set a new state-of-the-art novel AP50 of 24.9% on the more challenging MS-COCO dataset.
SaFT is the first proposal-free, one-stage detector to reach top performance in offline one-shot object detection, demonstrating superior results with a more efficient architecture.
Takeaways: Transformer-based semantic-aligned attention effectively resolves limitations of conventional correlation methods by enabling deformable matching and preserving structural information.
The synergistic combination of cross-sample (HFM) and cross-scale (VFM) attention is vital for robustly addressing spatial and scale misalignment in one-shot object detection.
Fusing an intermediate support feature with all query feature pyramid levels proves more effective for learning generalized meta-knowledge than corresponding-scale fusion.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.07669.Title: Progressive End-to-End Object Detection in Crowded Scenes
https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.07669.Summary: Researchers from MEGVII Technology, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and the University of Hong Kong developed a progressive prediction method for end-to-end object detection in crowded scenes. This approach enhances query-based detectors by mitigating duplicate predictions and overcoming performance saturation, yielding significant improvements in detection accuracy across various crowded datasets.
Problem: Existing query-based object detectors frequently produce multiple bounding box predictions for a single object instance in crowded scenes, leading to redundant detections and false positives.
Increasing the depth of decoding stages in current query-based detectors often leads to performance saturation or degradation in crowded environments, rather than consistent improvements.
Standard object detection methods struggle with high-density scenes due to heavy object overlap, which complicates accurate instance differentiation and label assignment.
Method: A progressive prediction method integrated into the last decoding stage of query-based detectors, which divides predictions into 'accepted' (high confidence) and 'noisy' (low confidence) sets.
A relation information extractor that enables noisy queries to 'perceive' confidently detected objects by generating geometry relation features from accepted neighbors.
A Local Multi-head Self-Attention (LMSA) mechanism for noisy queries, fostering local interactions, combined with a two-step progressive label assignment that prioritizes high-confidence detections.
Results: On the heavily crowded CrowdHuman dataset, the method achieved 92.0% AP, 41.4% MR -2, and 83.2% JI with a ResNet-50 Sparse R-CNN, representing a +1.3% AP, -3.3% MR -2, and +1.8% JI gain over the baseline.

The approach is generic, demonstrating improvements when applied to Deformable DETR, achieving 92.1% AP and 84.0% JI on CrowdHuman, and consistent gains on moderately (CityPersons) and slightly crowded (COCO) datasets.

Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of the relation information extractor and local self-attention in reducing duplicate errors, improving localization accuracy, and decreasing background errors compared to the baseline Sparse R-CNN.
Takeaways: High-confidence predictions from query-based detectors are reliable true positives, even in crowded settings, which can be leveraged to guide the refinement of lower-confidence predictions.
Enabling noisy queries to understand whether their target objects have already been confidently detected by other queries can effectively reduce redundant predictions.
Local self-attention among neighboring predictions is more effective than global attention for resolving ambiguities and reducing duplicate detections in crowded scenes.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.05557.Title: Conditional Prompt Learning for Vision-Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.05557.Summary: Researchers at S-Lab, Nanyang Technological University, developed Conditional Context Optimization (CoCoOp), a method that generates instance-conditional prompts for vision-language models like CLIP. This approach significantly improves generalization to unseen classes by over 8% average accuracy compared to static prompt learning, while maintaining parameter efficiency.
Problem: Large pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs) like CLIP are computationally expensive to fully fine-tune for downstream tasks.
Previous prompt learning methods like CoOp, while parameter-efficient, suffer from poor generalizability to unseen classes within the same dataset.
Static prompt contexts in CoOp tend to overfit to the base training classes, leading to a significant performance drop on novel categories.
Method: The authors introduce Conditional Context Optimization (CoCoOp), which generates instance-conditional prompt contexts for each input image.
A lightweight Meta-Net takes the image features from a frozen CLIP image encoder as input and outputs a single 'conditional token'.

This conditional token is added to the learnable context vectors, dynamically forming the prompt for the text encoder, with both the context vectors and Meta-Net being jointly optimized while the core VLM remains frozen.
Results: CoCoOp improves accuracy on unseen classes by over 8% on average compared to CoOp (71.69% vs. 63.22%) and achieves a higher harmonic mean (75.83%) than CoOp (71.66%) and zero-shot CLIP (71.70%).
It demonstrates superior cross-dataset transferability, showing clear margins over CoOp on datasets like FGVCAircraft (+4.47%) and DTD (+3.81%).
CoCoOp exhibits stronger domain generalizability compared to CoOp across ImageNet variant datasets (ImageNet-Sketch, ImageNet-A, ImageNet-R), affirming robustness to domain shifts.
Takeaways: Dynamic, instance-conditional prompts enable better generalization compared to static, class-agnostic prompts in vision-language models.
A lightweight neural network (Meta-Net) can efficiently generate instance-specific conditional tokens for prompt learning.
Proper initialization of context vectors and longer context lengths contribute to improved generalization performance on new classes.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.12086.Title: BLIP: Bootstrapping Language-Image Pre-training for Unified Vision-Language Understanding and Generation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.12086.Summary: The BLIP model from Salesforce Research introduces a Multimodal mixture of Encoder-Decoder (MED) architecture for unified vision-language understanding and generation, alongside a Captioning and Filtering (CapFilt) method to leverage noisy web data more effectively. This approach achieves new state-of-the-art results on image-text retrieval, image captioning, VQA, and other benchmarks, improving average recall@1 on COCO retrieval by +2.7% over previous methods.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language Pre-training (VLP) models typically specialize in either understanding-based tasks (e.g., retrieval) or generation-based tasks (e.g., captioning), lacking a unified architecture.
Large-scale web-crawled image-text datasets used for VLP are often noisy and contain irrelevant or inaccurate captions, leading to suboptimal pre-training.
Method: Introduces the Multimodal mixture of Encoder-Decoder (MED) model, a unified architecture featuring a shared image encoder and a text transformer configurable as a unimodal encoder, image-grounded text encoder, or image-grounded text decoder.

Develops Captioning and Filtering (CapFilt), a data bootstrapping method that generates synthetic captions for web images and filters out noisy image-text pairs (both original and synthetic) using a finetuned captioner and filter.
Pre-trains the MED model on a new, higher-quality bootstrapped dataset created by CapFilt, combining filtered web data with human-annotated data.
Results: CapFilt yields substantial performance gains across various downstream tasks, with the combined Captioner and Filter outperforming individual components.
Achieves new state-of-the-art results on image-text retrieval (e.g., +2.7% average recall@1 on COCO over ALBEF), image captioning, Visual Question Answering (VQA), and Visual Dialog.
Demonstrates strong zero-shot transfer capabilities to video-language tasks, outperforming finetuned models on text-to-video retrieval (e.g., +12.4% recall@1 on MSRVTT).
Takeaways: The Multimodal mixture of Encoder-Decoder (MED) architecture effectively unifies vision-language understanding and generation by sharing parameters across distinct encoding and decoding functionalities.
The Captioning and Filtering (CapFilt) method significantly enhances the quality of noisy web datasets, transforming them into a more effective learning resource for pre-training.
Generating diverse synthetic captions using nucleus sampling, rather than deterministic beam search, provides richer learning signals despite increased initial "noise."
Decoupling the parameters of the captioner and filter during CapFilt fine-tuning is crucial to prevent "confirmation bias" and ensure effective noise removal.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.02609.Title: Generalized Category Discovery
https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.02609.Summary: The Visual Geometry Group (VGG) at Oxford introduces Generalized Category Discovery (GCD), a new problem setting where unlabelled data may contain instances from both known and novel categories. Their method, which combines self-supervised Vision Transformers fine-tuned with a joint contrastive loss and semi-supervised clustering, achieves substantial performance gains of up to 27% in accuracy over adapted baselines on challenging fine-grained recognition tasks.
Problem: Existing image recognition paradigms (e.g., SSL, OSR, NCD) impose restrictive assumptions on unlabelled data, assuming it's either all from known classes, entirely novel, or only requiring detection of unknowns.

Real-world scenarios often present unlabelled data that is a mix of both known and novel categories, requiring a system that can concurrently categorize known instances and discover/categorize novel ones.
Many clustering-based methods for novel category discovery assume the number of unknown classes is known a priori, which is often not the case in practical applications.
Method: Leverages a ViT-B-16 backbone pre-trained with DINO (self-supervised Vision Transformers) to generate robust feature representations from all images.
Fine-tunes the ViT model on the target dataset using a combined unsupervised and supervised contrastive loss, enabling effective learning from both labeled and unlabelled data without overfitting.

Employs a semi-supervised k-means clustering algorithm for label assignment, which guides the clustering process by fixing assignments for known labeled instances while allowing unlabelled instances to be assigned to any category.

Proposes a novel method to estimate the total number of categories by optimizing the clustering accuracy on the labeled subset using Brent's algorithm, avoiding the need for prior knowledge of the total cluster count.
Results: The proposed method substantially outperforms adapted state-of-the-art baselines, achieving an average absolute improvement of 9.3% on generic object recognition and 8.9% on challenging fine-grained datasets.

It maintains high accuracy on known ('Old') classes while drastically improving accuracy on novel ('New') classes, striking a better balance compared to baselines (e.g., 97.9% ACC on 'Old' and 88.2% on 'New' for CIFAR10).

The proposed method for estimating the total number of categories achieves good accuracy, with a maximum error of 10% on generic datasets and an average discrepancy of 18.9% on more complex fine-grained datasets.

Ablation studies confirm the critical role of the DINO pre-trained ViT backbone (nearly 20% ACC drop without it) and the combined supervised/unsupervised contrastive fine-tuning (boosting ACC by 16-19%).
Takeaways: Direct clustering in the feature space of powerful, self-supervised Vision Transformer (ViT) representations is more robust to overfitting to labeled data than traditional parametric classifiers in open-world settings.

A combined unsupervised and supervised contrastive loss during ViT fine-tuning effectively creates highly separable and semantically rich feature spaces, crucial for distinguishing both known and novel categories.

Semi-supervised k-means clustering, where known class instances are anchored to their true labels, provides essential guidance that significantly improves recognition accuracy for both known and novel categories.

Clustering accuracy on the labeled subset can serve as a reliable heuristic to estimate the total number of categories in the entire dataset, addressing a common challenge in unsupervised and semi-supervised learning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.02605.Title: Detecting Twenty-thousand Classes using Image-level Supervision
https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.02605.Summary: Detic (Detector with Image Classes) trains object detectors for 21,000 classes by effectively integrating image-level supervision, addressing the vocabulary gap between classification and detection datasets. It achieved a 2.4 mAP gain for all classes and an 8.3 mAP gain for novel classes on the open-vocabulary LVIS benchmark, and generalized to new datasets without fine-tuning.
Problem: Bridging the significant vocabulary gap between image classification (21K classes) and object detection (typically <1K classes) due to costly bounding box annotations.
Addressing the limitations of existing weakly-supervised object detection (WSOD) methods that struggle with "chicken-and-egg" prediction-based label assignments for novel or rare classes.
Improving detection performance for "long-tail" and novel categories where very few or no bounding box annotations are available.
Method: Employs a mixed supervision strategy, co-training a standard two-stage detector with both traditional bounding-box-labeled data and large-scale image-level labeled classification datasets.

Introduces a non-prediction-based classification loss for image-labeled data, which applies the loss to fixed object proposals (e.g., the largest RPN proposal) instead of error-prone, model-predicted assignments.
Integrates pre-trained CLIP embeddings as classification weights, aligning region features with language embeddings to facilitate open-vocabulary detection.
Results: Achieved a 2.4 mAP gain for all classes and an 8.3 mAP gain for novel classes on the LVIS open-vocabulary benchmark, significantly outperforming prior methods, including a 7.7-point gain on `mAP_novel` over ViLD-text.
Trained the first object detector on the full 21,000 classes of ImageNet-21K, demonstrating strong generalization to new, unseen datasets like Objects365 and OpenImages without fine-tuning.
The 21K-class detector reached 70-80% of the performance of dataset-specific oracle models trained with full bounding box annotations on those respective datasets.
Takeaways: Modern Region Proposal Networks (RPNs) already possess strong generalization capabilities for localization, allowing innovation to focus primarily on the classification sub-problem of object detection.

Simple, non-prediction-based assignment strategies for image-level labels, such as selecting the largest proposal ("max-size"), provide a more robust and effective training signal than complex prediction-based methods for weakly-supervised learning.

Large-scale image-level supervision, especially when combined with vision-language models like CLIP, can effectively bridge the performance gap for novel and rare classes, substituting for costly bounding box annotations.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.02373.Title: Mirror Learning: A Unifying Framework of Policy Optimisation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.02373.Summary: Researchers at the University of Oxford introduce Mirror Learning, a new theoretical framework that unifies diverse policy optimization algorithms, including deep reinforcement learning methods like PPO. The framework provides formal guarantees for monotonic policy improvement and convergence to optimal policies, effectively bridging the gap between theoretical understanding and the empirical success of modern RL algorithms.
Problem: A significant gap exists between the empirical success of deep reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms, particularly PPO, and the lack of robust theoretical guarantees for their practical implementations.
Existing theoretical frameworks like Generalized Policy Iteration (GPI) and Trust-Region Learning (TRL) are too restrictive or computationally intractable for scalable deep RL applications.

Widely used algorithms like PPO, despite their effectiveness, were often justified by 'approximate analogies' to TRL, with recent analyses revealing fundamental violations of trust-region constraints.
Method: Mirror Learning defines policy optimization through three core components: a flexible 'drift functional' (quantifying policy update cost), a 'neighborhood operator' (constraining update size), and a 'mirror operator' (penalizing changes based on drift).
It establishes a general update rule, formulated as maximizing a mirror operator within the defined neighborhood, which inherently guarantees monotonic policy improvement and convergence.

The framework demonstrates that existing algorithms like GPI, TRL, TRPO, PPO, and MDPO can be rigorously instantiated as specific cases of Mirror Learning by defining their respective drift functionals and neighborhood operators.
Results: The 'Fundamental Theorem of Mirror Learning' proves that any algorithm instantiated within the framework guarantees strict monotonic improvement in expected return and convergence to optimal policies.

The framework formally unifies and provides theoretical guarantees for state-of-the-art algorithms including TRPO, PPO, PPO-KL (with fixed
τ), and MDPO, for the first time in their practical formulations.

Numerical experiments on simple environments confirm that Mirror Learning instances consistently exhibit monotonic improvement in return and convergence to optimal returns, with cumulative drift remaining bounded as theoretically predicted.
Takeaways: The clipping objective in PPO is mathematically equivalent to maximizing an objective with an intrinsic 'drift functional' and a trivial neighborhood, thereby providing direct theoretical justification for its success.
Generalized Policy Iteration (GPI) and Trust-Region Learning (TRL) are revealed as pathologically restrictive corner cases within the broader Mirror Learning framework.

Policy optimization can be interpreted as a search on a directed acyclic graph (Policy DAG), where the total 'weight' (sum of drifts) along any path from an initial to an optimal policy is bounded by the optimality gap.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.11010.Title: MPViT: Multi-Path Vision Transformer for Dense Prediction
https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.11010.Summary: Researchers from ETRI and KAIST developed MPViT, a Vision Transformer architecture that enhances multi-scale feature representation for dense prediction tasks through a novel multi-scale patch embedding and multi-path processing. It achieves state-of-the-art results across image classification, object detection, and segmentation benchmarks, often with fewer parameters and FLOPs than prior ViTs.
Problem: Dense computer vision tasks require effective multi-scale feature representation to accurately process objects of widely varying sizes.
Existing Vision Transformers (ViTs) often use single-scale patches at each feature level, limiting multi-scale diversity, or incur high computational overhead for complex multi-scale interactions.
Traditional ViTs may overlook fine-grained local relationships, an area where Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) historically excel due to their local connectivity inductive bias.
Method: Introduces a multi-stage architecture with a Multi-Scale Patch Embedding (MS-PatchEmbed) module, which simultaneously tokenizes visual patches of different sizes at the same feature level using overlapping convolutional operations.
Employs Multi-Path Transformer (MP-Transformer) blocks featuring parallel independent Transformer encoders for each patch scale, combined with a Global-to-Local Feature Interaction (GLI) module.
Leverages efficient factorized self-attention and a 'deeper and thinner' model scaling strategy to manage computational costs while maximizing performance across multiple processing paths.
Results: MPViT-Small achieves 83.0% Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K with 22.8M parameters and 4.7 GFLOPs, surpassing several larger and more computationally intensive Vision Transformers.
On COCO object detection with RetinaNet, MPViT-S obtains 47.6% AP, outperforming Swin-T and Focal-T by 2.1-2.6%, and on Mask R-CNN, MPViT-S reaches 43.9% mask AP.
For ADE20K semantic segmentation using UperNet, MPViT-S achieves 48.3% mIoU, outperforming Swin-T, Focal-T, and XCiT-S12/16 by margins of 3.8%, 2.5%, and 2.4% respectively.
Takeaways: Processing truly multi-scale patches concurrently within a Transformer block, rather than relying solely on hierarchical stages, leads to richer and more diverse feature representations for dense prediction.

A hybrid Global-to-Local Feature Interaction module that concatenates and learns interactions between convolutional local features and Transformer's global features effectively combines their respective strengths.

For multi-path Transformer architectures, a 'deeper and thinner' configuration (more layers, fewer channels per path) is more effective than wider, shallower designs for improving accuracy while managing computational resources.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.09106.Title: RegionCLIP: Region-based Language-Image Pretraining
https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.09106.Summary: Researchers from the University of Wisconsin-Madison, Microsoft Research, and Microsoft Cloud + AI developed RegionCLIP, a method that extends vision-language pretraining to the region level by aligning image regions with text descriptions using a CLIP-guided pseudo-labeling approach. This enables improved object recognition and achieves state-of-the-art performance on open-vocabulary object detection benchmarks like COCO and LVIS.
Problem: Existing vision-language pretraining models, such as CLIP, primarily focus on aligning whole images with text descriptions, leading to a performance drop when applied to specific image regions.
A 'domain gap' prevents models trained on image-level understanding from effectively interpreting or classifying individual objects or regions within images.
